## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly disposed within the text itself, and with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two copious general indexes: one an index of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a single glance; the other an index of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon individual scriptural texts, and in what passages of their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if one considers: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the highly convenient form of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but for the first time gathered in our Library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Library of the Universal Clergy*, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been committed to print in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—Twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; and thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# [The Complete Works of St Bernard of Clairvaux]

[Col. 0009]

## To the Most Holy Father Alexander VIII, Supreme Pontiff

We approach the footsteps of Your Holiness, most blessed Father, with reverence but with confidence; for not less your dignity than your gracious condescension summons us. You are supreme, yet the Father of all; the same man you once were, by nature gracious and kind toward everyone—as we ourselves lately experienced before our eyes, so often in word and in deed. Therefore, since majesty yields, why should modesty not yield also? Mindful of such condescension and of the goodwill with which you have long regarded our congregation, we may celebrate the auspicious beginnings of your pontificate by a public profession of our devotion.

And behold: while we were considering this, St Bernard himself freely presented himself to our thoughts—that great Abbot of Clairvaux—who, as the presses hasten, seemed to run before your elevation and longed to emerge into new light under the auspices of Your Holiness. Indeed, he who once detested honours and dignities now seeks partnership in your supreme authority: not to diminish your authority, but to support it; to lighten the cares and anxieties of pastoral government, and to undertake in himself the ministry of sacred teaching.

Nor, most blessed Father, need Your Holiness fear to entrust its own functions to so celebrated and eminent a Doctor. For no one has deserved better of the holy Apostolic See; no one has sounder views concerning it; no one speaks more magnificently of the Supreme Pontiff. For he acknowledges and proclaims you as prince of bishops, heir of the apostles, Peter in authority, Christ in anointing. [Note: [Col. 0009] *On Consideration*, Book II, ch. 8.] Is this too little? He also professes and maintains that you are the champion of truth, defender of the faith, refuge of the oppressed, avenger of crimes, father of kings, regulator of laws, dispenser of canons, and—to include everything else in one expression—the vicar of Christ and the Christ of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0009] *Ibid.*, Book IV, ch. 7.] Finally, in you he discerns a fullness of power, but one requiring the greatest care and vigilance: so much so that he judges that anyone wishing to ascertain what matters do not pertain to your care would have to leave the world. [Note: [Col. 0009] *On Consideration*, Book II, ch. 1.]

But divine providence, most holy Father, fashioned you to bear so great a burden when it liberally bestowed upon you an apt, lofty, and wide-ranging intellect; most refined judgment; and incredible prudence and discernment. Long experience in the conduct of affairs confirmed your innate prudence. Led through every degree of honour, you did not advance from lower rank before you had prepared, by fitting merits, a path of access to higher rank. In active life you were always self-possessed; in private life never slack or idle. In the greatest and most difficult affairs, beneath whose burden others groan, you yourself calmly accomplish everything as though doing nothing. Advanced age, which commonly brings others impatience with labour and love of repose and inactive leisure, inspires in Your Holiness, on the contrary, impatience with rest and leisure, and love and diligence in labour—and increases them. Whole days do not suffice for that assiduity. You even take from your own repose the truce offered by night, being accustomed to say that at an age upon which many, indeed very great, tasks press, there is need of diligence and haste; agreeing with Bernard that there is no place for leisure where the vigilant care of all the Churches urgently presses. [Note: [Col. 0010] *Ibid.*, ch. 6.] Thus by your example you order the dismissal of laws which grant greater leisure to those above sixty years of age. [Note: [Col. 0010] Pliny, Book IV, Letter 23.]

Although, most holy Father, you are thus equipped by nature, by grace, and by experience itself, yet in administering this supreme office you place confidence not so much in your own counsels as in those of others. Hence [Col. 0011] that declaration to the cardinals—one surely worthy of a supreme pontiff—that you will never undertake or do anything concerning Christian interests which has not first been referred to their counsel. If, moreover, Your Holiness should wish to employ in that sacred senate some additional counsellor, most prudent and experienced, you will find none more suitable or more incorruptible than Bernard. His books *On Consideration* alone—entirely worthy of cedarwood—are so full of oracles that they seem almost divinely dictated for directing supreme pontiffs, indeed for governing the universal Church.

Your most holy predecessors long ago held this to be certain: not only Eugenius III, to whom the books were written, but especially Pius V and Gregory XIII, who valued those sacred books so highly that they employed their reading even at table. In those books, moreover, and in the other writings of the same holy Doctor, cardinals, bishops, and ministers of lower ranks will all find what they should avoid and what they should pursue. Kings and princes will likewise learn from them the laws of ruling; and common people themselves, no less than freeborn and noble persons, will draw instruction for Christian life suited to each one’s station. With this author as guide, through you the people will be subject to the clerics, the clerics to the priests, and the priests to God, in the humility that is fitting. [Note: [Col. 0011] *On Consideration*, Book III, ch. 5.] In monasteries and religious houses order will be maintained and discipline will keep watch. Ecclesiastical censure will flourish against depraved deeds and doctrines, and your own apostolic commands and ordinances will be observed with the diligence they deserve. [Note: [Col. 0011] *Ibid.*, ch. 1.]

Under his guidance unbelievers will be converted to the faith; the perverse will be directed to uprightness; those led astray will be recalled to truth; and those who lead others astray will be convicted by invincible arguments, so that they themselves may be corrected, if possible, or otherwise lose the power to lead others astray. Finally, under this Doctor’s instruction ambition, the lust for domination, and greed will cease; dignities will be valued not by honours, but by virtues, care, and vigilance. Thus at last the Church will flourish anew in a state worthy of the most holy Pontiff, of Alexander, of Peter, indeed of Christ her Bridegroom.

This was nearly brought to completion and perfection while Bernard lived, worked, and laboured with others; and there is no doubt that something similar will now occur if Alexander restores Bernard’s voice and authority in their full strength. The Fathers of the Council of Étampes granted that voice to Bernard when, divided among themselves over a doubtful pontiff, they collectively lodged their voices and each his vote in Bernard’s mouth and judgment. Innocent II soon found that same voice favourable to himself. At length acknowledged by all as the lawful Pontiff through the holy Father’s preaching and authority, he employed Bernard’s tongue and pen against the remnants of schism and against rising heresies and errors.

Thus Bernard became the oracle and interpreter of the Councils of Sens, Reims, and others; so that nearly everything depended upon his word, and almost nothing was done in the Church, in the courts of kings and princes, or even in private households without his counsel and judgment. Rome saw him more than once. The degree of honour it paid him may be inferred from this fact alone: after Anacletus’ death, when Bernard had brought Victor, the false pontiff stripped of the insignia he had usurped, to the feet of Innocent, Bernard was thereafter held in such reverence among the Romans that all acclaimed him Author of Peace and Father of His Country. Finally, “when he departed from Rome, the clergy accompanied and escorted him, the people honoured him, and the whole nobility attended him. For he could not be allowed to leave without common sorrow, since he was cherished with common love.” [Note: [Col. 0011] *Life*, Book II, ch. 7.]

Oh, that the books of this most holy Doctor were now treated and read with the same honour and reverence! How great a fruit, how great a benefit would flow from this into the Christian commonwealth! Certainly, so far as lay in our power, we have endeavoured to restore to his sacred writings the grace and integrity of their native form, so that they might be read with greater pleasure and profit. It is yours, most blessed Father, to restore to him the voice of power which not even death itself has yet been able wholly to take from him. His authority still flourishes among all devout persons, indeed even among heretics themselves; and it will flourish more abundantly hereafter if it is confirmed anew by the oracle of your voice.

If, with Your Holiness approving, exhorting, and commanding, Bernard is set before all as one to be read, continually studied, and followed, his voice will be like the **VOICE of the Lord breaking the cedars, cutting off the flame of fire** (Ps. XXVIII [29]). With God’s support, no vices, no adverse power or force will be able to withstand Bernard. Under Alexander the cedars—that is, the heads of the proud and tyrannical—will be broken; and [Col. 0013] the flame of discords and wars will be cut off.

God has already stirred up the spirit of a neighbouring king, who, filled with zeal and pitying the downfall of an excellent king, may bring aid, so that he may restore to his kingdom a king driven out by his own subjects and abandoned by the rest. Bernard records that such happened in his own time to that most pious king of Ireland who, expelled by his brother, yielded place to wrath in order to spare the blood of his people. [Note: [Col. 0013] *Life of St Malachy*, ch. 4.] We behold this most disastrous scene renewed before our own eyes; with minds meanwhile held in suspense, we await and desire a like conclusion through the greatest Pontiff and the greatest King. Thus James II will receive back, as one returned from exile, the same throne which Henry III formerly relinquished for the sake of honour to Cardinal and Legate Ottobono, afterwards Adrian V—by the care and assistance of another Ottobono, that is, Alexander VIII.

But the force of our wishes for the glory of your pontificate, most blessed Father, carries us too far. You need no counsellor or spur other than Alexander himself when God and the Church are at stake. May He whose vicar you are be favourable to your most holy counsels, and may He be pleased, if it may be permitted, to add years from ours to yours, so that all those things which Your Holiness considers and hopes for, to the glory of God and the benefit of the Church, may be undertaken and accomplished. We, indeed, shall consider ourselves wholly happy and fortunate if Your Holiness receives this pledge of our prayers, this monument in itself of our perpetual devotion, with the kindly eyes it is accustomed to show, and deigns to honour us all with its paternal goodwill and apostolic blessing.

Humbly presented, in the name of his congregation, by  
**Brother Jean Mabillon, M.B.**

[Col. 0013]

# General Preface

[Col. 0013]

**I.** After I had devoted the first fruits of my studies to the works of St Bernard, I did not think it right so to abandon the care of that first edition as never to consider polishing and adorning it, indeed even thoroughly reforming it if necessary. For, having undertaken it as a young man and an almost untrained beginner, I did not suppose that the work had been so completed and perfected by me in every respect that many things in Bernard could not be more finely and accurately treated, both in restoring and in elucidating them, once greater literary practice and longer experience had been acquired.

Accordingly, although in the course of time I had been led far away into studies wholly different from those of so great a Doctor, nevertheless the memory and love of that most holy man always clung to my heart. Thus, whenever, in reading and studying other authors, I came upon anything which might contribute either to correcting or elucidating his works, I did not fail to note it carefully and reserve it for a suitable time for a second edition. And so it finally happened that, although my other scholarly labours had previously left me almost no time free for this meditation, now, when the cultivation of other studies had grown lukewarm and cold amid these storms of war, Bernard alone was almost left in my hands, to occupy the leisure alike of my youth and of my advancing age.

I gladly used that leisure, by the indulgence of my superiors, to give new light to an author who has deserved supremely well of all. Nor can I conceal that, together with my colleagues and associates, I have expended no small labour and diligence upon this undertaking, so that an edition might be produced which was not so much a second edition as an entirely new and, so far as lay within our power, a carefully wrought one.

**II.** There may perhaps be those who will disapprove of the repeated issuance of so many editions and complain that they burden scholars. I do not deny that it would be far more desirable if every author could at once, in the first edition, be restored to a condition approaching perfection as nearly as possible. But those who have worked in studies of this kind know very well how laborious—indeed, not to say impossible—it is to attain this amid such a great multitude of ancient books scattered here and there, and such great disagreement among those same books.

For much and prolonged labour is required, and sometimes even an Oedipus and an interpreter, both to assemble—not so much volumes as leaves scattered in every direction—and to select variant readings; to heal corrupt passages and penetrate obscurities; and finally to establish a critical judgment concerning genuine works. To secure all these things, and very many others of the same kind, exactly to the rule on a first revision requires a more fortunate genius than I may ascribe to myself, and I do not know whether anyone can claim it for himself.

Be that as it may, I prefer to ask pardon for whatever rashness attended my first attempt rather than perhaps increase the fault by defending it, or leave the former edition imperfect. It therefore seemed worth the labour [Col. 0015] to prepare another, more corrected and polished edition. Accordingly, after a new examination of the holy Doctor’s works and their collation with old copies, I again bound myself, with my associates, to the importunate service of the typographical mill. I was encouraged by a firm confidence that this plan and our new labour would not be unwelcome to discerning men, once they had thoroughly understood the grounds of our action and the benefits, as we hope, of this new edition.

## § I.—On the various editions of St Bernard’s works; in which are explained both the grounds and principles, and the advantages and benefits, of this latest edition.

**III.** First of all, nothing demonstrates Bernard’s merit and value more clearly than the numerous and repeatedly renewed editions of his works, whether before or after the invention of printing. For this manifold publication shows how greatly Bernard is prized by many, how eagerly he is read, and, finally, how universally he is loved. Nor is this surprising. In his writings shines forth an intellect noble, generous, and lofty by nature, yet humane, cultivated, and honourable; an eloquence as though inborn, without artificial colouring, not without ornament, but naturally so; a concise style, lively expression, fitting diction, exalted thoughts, devout affections, spontaneous charms, and speech throughout breathing one God and heavenly things.

He burns, not to scorch, but to inflame. He pierces and spurs, not to irritate, but to move. He rebukes and reproves, not to disparage, but to draw. He censures, threatens, and terrifies, yet in love, not indignation. He flatters, but does not fawn; praises, but does not exalt excessively. He presses gently, strikes without offence, delights, refreshes, and pleases.

For, as Sixtus of Siena says, Bernard’s “speech is everywhere sweet and ardent; it so delights and ardently kindles that from his most sweet tongue honey and milk of words seem to flow, and from his most burning breast fires of flaming affections to burst forth.” His doctrine, moreover, is by no means ordinary, being full of the words and sap of Holy Scripture; yet it clings so closely to the judgments of the Fathers that it is nevertheless perceived to be his own. Thus he writes on divine matters, on grace and free will, and on the conduct and office of pontiffs, clerics, monks, and laypeople, as one speaking from a spring, not a stream or channel.

And are we surprised if so great a man is loved? If his writings are acquired, read, and worn by use by everyone? If editions of them are made without number? If learned and scholarly men devote their efforts to enlarging, elucidating, correcting, and restoring them to their native integrity? If Rome itself, mistress and teacher of the world—which once revered Bernard when he taught, indeed when he rebuked—if Rome itself, I say, allowed the books *On Consideration*, first presented to Eugenius III, then most elegantly transcribed by command of Nicholas V, and finally published in papal type under Clement VIII, while intending to publish all Bernard, provided Gerard Vossius had likewise devoted his labour to the whole of Bernard? It is therefore less surprising that, in the metropolis of Gaul, so great a light of France deserved to be honoured by royal printing.

**IV.** Yet there were other causes, neither blameworthy nor indeed unnecessary, why so many editions and revisions of Bernard were made. One chief cause was that the holy Doctor’s works lay dispersed here and there in many and various manuscripts. Consequently, not everything could appear at once in the first edition, but only in portions, as the works came into the hands and knowledge of learned persons.

The first edition seems to have been that produced at Mainz by Peter Schöffer in 1475. It included sermons for the liturgical seasons and for saints’ days, sermons on various subjects, the book addressed to the Knights Templar, and certain other works wrongly ascribed to Bernard.

At the same time, at Rouen, without a stated year, three little works of the blessed Father were published: namely, the books *On Consideration*, the *Apology to Abbot William*, and the book *On Precept and Dispensation*.

The Brussels edition of 1481 followed. It supplied the sermons for the liturgical seasons and saints’ days and, for the first time, the Letters, but omitted the names of both editor and printer. Then came the Paris edition of 1494, containing three hundred and ten letters together with the sermons on the *Song of Songs*, corrected and amended by Master Rouauld, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

This was followed by the Speyer edition of 1501 and, two years later, the Venetian edition, but without the letters. The latter, however, was already half filled with spurious and non-Bernardine writings. Possevino likewise mentions a Brescia edition of 1495 which contained the homilies on *Missus est* together with certain other little works.

The first edition to bring together almost all Bernard’s works in a single body was the Paris edition of 1508. It comprised, as its title declares, the writings of the seraphic, mellifluous, and devout Doctor St Bernard, most diligently reduced at last into the excellent form of a single codex through comparison with the archetypes of the library of Clairvaux, by the care and industry of Master Jean Bocard, and at the expense of Jean Petit, sworn bookseller of the University of Paris.

Six years later, in 1515, Josse Clichtove of Nieuwpoort again revised the same works and published them at Lyons through the press of Jean Cleyn, a German. He added Gilbert of Hoyland’s sermons on the *Song of Songs*. This revision was reprinted many times at Paris and Lyons.

Meanwhile, in 1520 another Lyons edition appeared, prepared by two monks of Clairvaux, Lambert Campester and Laurent Dantiscenus. It is indeed the most correct of all.

After these revisers—for I pass over the various editions—Francis Comestor of Arneduc, fellow of the Sorbonne College, undertook another revision of the holy Doctor. He prefixed a dedicatory letter to Louis de Rie, Bishop of Geneva, in which he testifies that, while examining the old copies provided by the then richly stocked library of the Sorbonne College, he had discovered an epilogue to the book *On Loving God*, omitted in the printed editions; and then a little work *On the Love of God and the Dignity of Love*. He supplied these books, together with others, to Claude Chevallon’s widow for publication in 1547.

There was more than one edition of this revision. Meanwhile Antony Marcellinus arranged another edition at Basel, published by Johann Herwagen in 1552. According to his own assertion, it was prepared by an industrious collation with older copies, together with a new critical judgment and a new arrangement of the works: sermons occupying first place, letters second, treatises third, and spurious and non-Bernardine works last.

A Venetian edition, mentioned by Jean Gillot of Campagne in the preface to the Nivellian edition published at Paris in 1572, preceded that edition. There he also mentions a revision carried out by Parisian theologians, who restored the latest editions both by their own private effort and by comparison with old codices which they were able to gather from libraries in France. Thus, he says, one who after so many and such great men attempted to renovate what had been renewed and again heal what had been cured would seem to damage it and introduce evil.

Nevertheless, Gillot adds that he introduced some corrections not to be regretted, and arguments or divisions of chapters into the five books *On Consideration, addressed to Eugenius*, and into the little book *On Precept and Dispensation*. Henry Cuyck of Culemborg had corrected these works against seven manuscript copies. Gillot then sets out his work in distinguishing Bernard’s native works from spurious ones and in arranging the genuine works in a proper and convenient order. Yet among the genuine writings he retained some spurious works already published, or added them anew, together with *Flowers Collected from the Works of St Bernard*.

But six years earlier, namely in 1566, another edition had appeared at Paris through Guillaume Merlin and Sébastien Nivelle, with the dedicatory letter of the aforementioned Francis Comestor to the Bishop of Geneva prefixed. To that edition was added the Herwagen Appendix, published at Basel by the heirs of Johann Herwagen through the labour and learning of Jacques Pamèle of Bruges. He brought to light sixteen short sermons of Bernard, then the *Parable on Christ and the Church*, likewise the book of *Soliloquies*, and several other works falsely attributed to Bernard. In the same year Louis Miraeus of Roset also arranged for another appendix to Bernard, received from Francis Comestor, to be added at Paris through Charlotte Guillard.

I pass over the almost innumerable other editions of the same century, so that scarcely a year passed without distinction from some edition of Bernard’s works. The most elegant of all was that published in 1586 under the device of a ship, with Jean Gillot’s dedicatory letter to the Reverend Father Guy Cornu, Abbot of Clairvaux, and the same editor’s preface to the reader.

Indeed, in the same century most of Bernard’s sermons and little works were translated into French: in 1575 by Hubert Lescot, a regular canon, but without the Letters. The Letters were added in the French translation of 1622 by Philippe Le Bel, Doctor of Paris, as also in the most recent translation by the Reverend Father Gabriel of St Malachy, a Feuillant.

**V.** As for the various editions produced in our own century, it would be almost endless, and by no means necessary, to list them all. It is enough to note two: one by Edmond Tiraqueau, Cistercian monk, in 1601; the other by Jean Picard in 1609, with notes and the addition of several letters, and with Tiraqueau’s dedicatory letter to the Reverend Father Edmund of the Cross, Abbot of Cîteaux, together also with Gillot’s letter and preface.

Picard’s edition was reprinted that same year at Antwerp by Jan Keerberg, and thereafter repeatedly issued until at last, in 1641, there appeared the revision of Jacob Merlo Horstius, a most devout and learned man—the best and most accurate of all editions. It eclipsed all the rest and was very frequently returned to the press thereafter.

**VI.** It is useful briefly to note what this learned man accomplished in that edition. First, he says that he wondered why, although among all the works of the holy Fathers none is more often handled than Bernard, he alone had nevertheless been so neglected that, though very frequently published, he always appeared the same, indeed sometimes more disfigured and corrupt, as though unworthy of care or in no need of it. This, he says, was why he applied a healing hand.

First, he divided all Bernard’s works into six tomes: the first containing the Letters; the second, sermons for the liturgical seasons and for saints’ days; the third, sermons on the *Song of Songs*; the fourth, various treatises; the fifth, non-Bernardine works; and the sixth, the works of the holy Doctor’s two disciples, Gilbert and Guerric—employing critical weighing and judgment wherever appropriate. Next, he divided the treatises into chapters and sections, and prefixed arguments or summaries to each letter and treatise. Further, he spared neither effort nor expense in enlarging the Bernardine edition from various libraries in various regions, although he could not obtain many things noted by certain writers, such as Possevino and others.

Besides this, he added many preliminary materials: the *Life of St Bernard* in seven books, prefaced by various encomia and a chronology. Finally, he added extensive annotations, besides shorter ones inserted here and there in the margins throughout the work, along with fuller indexes of scriptural passages, subjects, and words. Yet he acknowledged his awareness of the immense labour by which he had tried to make the edition entirely correct, though the printers’ diligence had not fully met his wishes. That learned man was preparing another edition, both enlarged and more accurate; but he died before fulfilling that purpose, on 20 April 1644.

[Col. 0019]

**VII.** Nevertheless, Horst successfully carried out that first edition as far as a learned, diligent, and deeply devoted student of Bernard, though a private individual, could do. Thus his edition was welcomed and approved by everyone, as the saying is, “with both hands,” and was very frequently reprinted in various provinces and places.

But when our Claudius Cantelou, at the command of our superiors, had compared Horst’s text of Bernard with several French codices, he nevertheless found certain blemishes in that text which required correction by the aid of those codices. He published Bernard’s sermons for the liturgical seasons and saints’ days in a second format, most carefully corrected. But while he was devoting the same diligence to publishing the rest, he surrendered this task to me by his death: to a young man new and inexperienced in scholarship, who would never have thought of matching labour and industry with the most learned Horst unless our General Superior of pious memory, the Most Reverend Bernard Audebert, had compelled me—resisting and hesitating—to continue the work of the deceased Cantelou.

I therefore obeyed, though unwillingly. With the contribution first of all of the religious man Jacques Lannoy, librarian of the Cistercian library, who collated its copies, Bernard was at last published in a larger and a smaller format. It was not indeed published in the manner it deserved, but in such a manner as my untrained age could bear, or as could be obtained from a bookseller devoted more to his own interest than to the public good.

**VIII.** But when, through continual practice in studies of this kind, I observed day after day many things that might contribute to refining and elucidating the edition of Bernard, I made it my purpose, as I have already said, carefully to record them all, so that, if time and leisure should ever be available, I might prepare another edition, more corrected, polished, and complete. Yet when I was setting myself to that work, the miserable state of the printing laws cast me upon another rock; and from it, at last, as from a kind of storm, I have been carried into this harbour, such as it is—a circumstance which there is no reason to recount now.

IX. Although it should be wholly alien to my character and to our profession to advertise my own labor, it is nevertheless important, at this threshold, to show in what respects this most recent edition differs both from Horst’s and from our earlier one. First, I have taken further pains in collating old manuscripts previously unseen by me—especially those which we were able from time to time to consult and examine in the various provinces through which we travelled, or which Stephen Baluzius, a man born to assist and advance sound learning, assembled in the Colbert Library after our edition, to the great benefit of letters. From the variant readings I took care to select and restore to the text those which seemed more suited to Bernard’s meaning. This requires an almost continual use of old books, a taste acquired through practice, and a more mature judgment than the common run of scholars suppose, who think that we are catching spiders’ webs while pursuing these, as they imagine, trifles. But let people of that sort think of us whatever they please, provided that our labor is approved not by human applause but by the public benefit of the Church and of learning.

X. Nor was critical judgment employed by me only in restoring the text, but also in separating Bernard’s genuine writings from spurious and false ones, which in Horst’s edition and in our earlier edition still lay hidden among Bernard’s works. Hence two letters, inserted by Horst among Bernard’s writings from the *Annals* of Bernard the Breton, have been struck out; four or five sermons from the sermons *On the Season* and *On the Saints* have been rejected; the book of *Declamations* has likewise been rejected; and several other pieces, which certain arguments and indications plainly show not to be Bernard’s.

XI. In making this critical discrimination, assistance came not only from the writers of Bernard’s Lives—above all Geoffrey, who provide a list of the saintly doctor’s principal works—but also from old manuscripts and citations by ancient authors. Especially useful was the old collection from Bernard’s writings called the *Book of Flowers*, *Florilegium*, and *Bernardine*, first published at Paris in 1503. It is far more trustworthy than another collection made in 1571 by Hubert Scuteputaeus, a regular canon, and thrust by John Picard into Bernard’s published works. That first collection is much older; an old Cistercian manuscript supplied us with its author, in which it occurs under the following heading:

> Here begins the prologue of Dom William, monk of Saint Martin at Tournai, to the *Bernardine*, which he himself excerpted and compiled from the books and sayings of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

The prologue begins: “When I was not greatly occupied with any task,” etc., as in the printed editions, where the author’s name is lacking. From the antiquity of the manuscripts in which this collection is found, one may readily infer that he lived in the thirteenth century.

Moreover, although this collector cites certain little works that do not have Bernard as their author—for example, the letter to the brethren of Mont-Dieu, the *Meditations*, and the book of *Declamations*—nevertheless, in other respects he is of no slight importance for distinguishing Bernard’s sermons in particular. This is why, whenever there seemed reason to doubt certain pieces, as with the sermons *On Various Subjects*, it seemed advisable to note citations from the *Bernardine*. Nor is it surprising that both the letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu and the *Declamations* and *Meditations* are cited under Bernard’s name in that collection: Saint Bonaventure commits the same error regarding the cited letter; and the books of *Declamations* and *Meditations* consist of centos from Bernard, as we shall say in their proper places.

XII. Besides the critical discrimination of works, something has also been changed in Horst’s arrangement: namely, the disposition both of the volumes and of the smaller works. Horst placed after the letters, in second place, the sermons *On the Season* and *On the Saints*; in third place the sermons on the *Song of Songs*; and in fourth place the smaller works, or treatises. It seemed more advisable to place after the letters [Col. 0021] the smaller works or treatises, most of which are either written in epistolary form or have been transferred from the class of letters into the order of treatises. This arrangement entails that the sermons *On the Season* and *On the Saints* come third; the sermons on the *Song of Songs*, fourth; and fifth, the continuation of those same sermons—that is, Gilbert’s sermons on the same *Song of Songs*. The arrangement of the two remaining volumes, namely the fifth and sixth, will be discussed more fully in the preface to the fifth volume, just as the earlier volumes will be treated in the individual prefaces prefixed to them.

XIII. And so that all Bernard’s genuine works might be contained in one volume, we moved the books concerning his Life and Deeds, which Horst had placed at the beginning of the first volume, to the end of the sixth volume, or second physical volume; lest Bernard’s genuine works be separated from one another, or the volumes be excessively unequal in size. At the end of the first volume, as also of the second, we placed very full separate indexes, so that the earlier indexes include all the genuine works, and the later ones the non-genuine works.

XIV. Finally, fuller notes and observations, formerly composed by Horst or by me on the letters and other smaller works, are placed beneath the text. A brief chronology has meanwhile been prefixed to the first volume, since it is, as it were, a lamp for the notes themselves and a kind of common foundation. In addition, we prefixed to almost every smaller work contained in the second volume preliminary notices explaining the subject of each book and other circumstances relevant to it. These, in general, are the services we have rendered in this most recent edition of Bernard.

XV. But to come down to an examination of the first volume, which contains Bernard’s letters: we have again bestowed no small labor on correcting, elucidating, arranging, and enlarging them. As regards correction, we consulted various manuscripts from various libraries: Vatican, Colbert, Belgian, Saint Peter’s at Ghent, and Orval, besides those used in the earlier edition. From a Corbie manuscript we restored several headings of considerable importance, and corrected various passages from that manuscript as well as from two notable Colbert manuscripts, one marked no. 1410 and the other no. 2476, which also contains Bernard’s smaller works and against which we collated those same works. In addition, marginal notes have been appended to almost every letter, briefly explaining chiefly historical facts.

XVI. Concerning the order of the letters, we long hesitated whether to preserve the received order or establish a new one. Various considerations presented themselves on either side. The antiquity of the order inclined us first toward preserving it; for it is clear that, while Bernard himself was still alive, it had been established for those three hundred and ten letters, the last being the letter written by Bernard at the end of his life to Arnold, abbot of Bonnevaux. The remaining letters, scattered here and there, were subsequently brought by later persons into the body of the letters in printed books—not all at once, but at different intervals, as they came to the notice either of collectors or of readers.

Secondly, the consideration of chronology favored the old order, which was in some measure maintained in that old collection of letters. Otherwise one had to fear that changing the received arrangement would produce more inconvenience than benefit, because of the established citations of the letters—not to mention the customary order of the old copies. Against this stood the intolerable confusion of certain letters, in which a reply made to some letter was sometimes placed, in a reversed order, long before it. A further resulting inconvenience was that discussions of the same subject were reported in disorder, torn apart and dispersed from one another.

In these difficulties, it seemed best to follow a middle course: to retain the familiar order in the first three hundred and ten letters, but in the others subsequently added, to restore them to chronological order, noting in the margin the position which each letter had formerly held. Whenever letters in this new order should have been joined to preceding ones, we indicated that their reading ought to be placed before or after those letters. Thus honor was preserved for the old order, while the confusion was removed by the new one.

And lest we seem to have asserted without warrant that the old order was compiled during Bernard’s lifetime, we call as witness William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry, who died before Bernard. In the first book of the Life of the holy doctor, written while Bernard was still alive, he reports, at no. 50, that Bernard’s letter to his kinsman Robert, which had not been wetted amid a downpour, “on account of so great a miracle was rightly arranged by the brethren as first in the manuscript of his letters,” namely Bernard’s. The writer of the third Life, published by us and believed by us to be Geoffrey, the saint’s secretary, further records that this arrangement was made by himself.

XVII. Yet the order of the letters is not entirely constant in all old books, although in most it agrees with the familiar order down to the three hundred and tenth letter; nor is that number found in every manuscript. From this it is understood that not one but several compilations of Bernard’s letters were made. Three Vatican manuscripts contain such letters. In the first, a very elegant manuscript marked no. 662, there are two hundred and ninety-six letters in nearly the same order as in the printed editions; the last is addressed to the Irish, on the death of Blessed Malachy. In another manuscript, no. 664, the same order likewise appears in two hundred and fifty-two letters, the last of which is to Hugh, a Knight Templar.

But in the third, [Col. 0023] marked no. 663, there are two hundred and forty letters whose order is wholly different from the printed editions. Thus the first is that which in the editions previously printed is letter 313, to Cardinal Haimeric; and the last is letter 275, to Pope Eugenius concerning the election at Auxerre. In other manuscripts substantially the same order is observed as in the printed editions, except that in the Ghent manuscript of the monastery of Saint Peter this compilation of letters is divided into three parts. The first contains one hundred letters; the second, one hundred and sixty-four letters; the third, seventy-six letters. The next-to-last of these is Bernard’s letter to Rorgon of Abbatis-Villa; the last, John of Casa-Maria’s letter to Bernard.

Perhaps in no other manuscript are so many letters of Bernard found together as in that Ghent manuscript. William, monk of Tournai, used this manuscript, or certainly one like it, in his *Bernardine* mentioned above, where he cites letters from the first, second, and third part. Further, the Clairvaux manuscript of the Cistercian Order contains three hundred and seven letters; the Orval manuscript, three hundred and six, with the letter to Abbot Arnold last in each—certainly Bernard’s final letter. John of Salisbury doubtless asked that first collection be sent to him in letter 96, to Peter of Celle; and in the following letter he thanks him “for the letters of Blessed Bernard.”

XVIII. Now, to speak of the additions to the letters made in this edition—which ought to have been treated last—it should first be stated that the first Brussels edition of Bernard’s letters, of 1481, and the Paris edition of 1494, present three hundred and ten letters. The third from the end is to Arnold, abbot of Chartres; the next-to-last to the Irish brethren, on the death of Saint Malachy, bishop; and the last to Guy, abbot of Arremar. In the edition of 1520 prepared, as we have said, by two monks of Clairvaux, there are in all three hundred and fifty-one letters, the last being to Hugh, a novice and later abbot of Bonnevaux. But the letter to Arnold is number 310, and the letter to the Irish number 311.

The reason for this difference is that the earlier edition lacks two letters: letter 84, the second to Simon, abbot of Saint-Nicholas; and letter 147, to Peter, abbot of Cluny. Jodocus Clichtoveus, in his edition of 1515 and the subsequent editions, has only three hundred and fifty letters, omitting the letter to Hugh the novice. This letter was restored by Anthony Marcellinus in the Basel edition of 1552, and in subsequent editions down to John Picard. Picard added letters to those already published, but arranged them without order. He prefixed two of them outside the sequence, taken from the Pithou manuscript; the others he published long after the familiar letters, from his own Victorine library.

After removing certain letters wrongly repeated, Horst reduced their familiar number to three hundred and sixty-six; to these he added two spurious letters from Bernard the Breton and seventeen genuine letters from English manuscripts, together with a letter of Abbot Fastred added as a finishing piece, bringing the total to three hundred and eighty-six. Finally, eleven letters were added in our earlier edition; and in this latest edition the number has grown to four hundred and eighty-two: partly from twenty-eight letters of Bernard recently discovered in Germany and appended at Cologne by Horst in the manner of an Appendix; partly from some found elsewhere; and finally from others written either to Bernard or in Bernard’s cause, which seemed necessary for elucidating Bernard’s letters.

We have arranged all these letters in three classes. The first, which comes first, presents the three hundred and ten letters and retains their ancient and familiar order. The second extends through letter 454 and contains the remaining genuine letters of Bernard. The third includes doubtful, spurious, and non-Bernardine letters. These, broadly, are what we have accomplished in revising the first volume; the diligent reader will readily observe the rest. Each of the remaining volumes has its own preface, which sufficiently explains what has been accomplished in each.

XIX. Finally, we observed long ago that the works which Horst alleged lay hidden in various libraries are not Bernard’s. The book on the *Hexaemeron* is by Arnold, abbot of Bonnevaux in the region of Chartres; the Commentary on the Penitential Psalms, by Innocent III; the exposition of the psalm *Afferte* (“Bring [unto the Lord]”), by Richard of Saint-Victor; another exposition of Psalm 50, by Urban; and the Commentary on Paul’s Epistles, according to Possevino, by Bernard of Clavaux, an Augustinian.

The Commentary on the Apocalypse was falsely attributed to Bernard by Caramuel. Since this commentary followed certain smaller works of Bernard in a manuscript under the title “of a certain person” (*cujusdam*), Caramuel read “of the same person” (*ejusdem*) and attributed it to Bernard, as also the preceding works. I certainly believe that no unpublished works of Bernard remain, at least none of any importance, apart from several letters still lacking. They are as follows:

- One letter to Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, as is evident from letter 33 to him, no. 1.
- Two letters to Innocent II against Peter of Besançon, from letter 198.
- One likewise to the same pope on behalf of Peter of Pisa, from the end of letter 213.
- Several likewise to the same pope on introducing the Premonstratensians into the monastery of Saint Paul at Verdun, from letter 253, no. 1.
- One to Ansel, subdeacon of Troyes, indicated in letter 203 to Atto.
- One apologetic letter to Suger, in letter 223 to Joscelin, no. 1.
- Two to John of Buzay, in letter 233 to him.
- One to Eugenius III on behalf of the bishop of Clermont, from the end of letter 284 to Eugenius himself.
- Another to the same Eugenius on behalf of the Church of Tournai, from Herman, monk of Tournai, no. 115. [Note: [Col. 0023] See volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 483.]
- One encyclical against judicial duels, addressed to the archbishops of Reims [Col. 0025] and Sens, to the bishops of Soissons and Auxerre, and to Counts Theobald and Ralph, from the letter formerly numbered 358, now 376.

Moreover, Peter the Venerable, in a certain letter now found among Bernard’s letters as number 388, reports at no. 4 a fragment of a certain holy doctor’s letter on behalf of an English abbot, in these words: “As though judgment had been overturned,” etc. I do not remember reading this in any of Bernard’s letters.

XX. Orderic Vitalis also mentions one letter of Bernard to Natalis, abbot of Rebais, on behalf of the monks of Ouche, who were seeking the relics of Saint Evroul. Their abbot Guarin was especially active in this matter and requested it of Abbot Natalis.

> Geoffrey declared that he wished to go to Clairvaux, and consented if he [Guarin] wished to go with him. Both therefore set out for Clairvaux with their servants. They were kindly received by the brethren of that monastery, who strive to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict wholly according to the letter. They sought out Lord Bernard, father of that monastery. They spoke with him and, asking many questions, found great wisdom in him. For he treated the holy Scriptures brilliantly and satisfied their wishes and inquiries. When he heard the case of the monks of Ouche, he kindly assisted Abbot Guarin and sent exhortatory letters to the community of Rebais. Abbot Guarin therefore produced the letter of the venerable Bernard, which the community of Rebais gladly received and, having heard it, resolved still more gladly to carry out.

Thus Orderic in book six.

XXI. Moreover, Ademar, monk of Angoulême, in his *Chronicle*, when discussing the origin of the Carthusians, says:

> “This order, Bernard testifies, holds primacy among all ecclesiastical orders—not by reason of time, but by the vigor of its holiness. Hence he himself calls it the Church’s most beautiful pillar.”

This is not found in the printed editions.

XXII. Finally, John Picard, citing John Mauburn in the treatise *On the Habit of Regular Canons*, quotes a certain letter to Fulk, from which Mauburn extracts these words:

> “You will not find black or gray [skins] hanging from their necks; rather, they borrow from little women other skins hanging from their necks, reddish mouse-skins.”

It is as though these words were cited from some letter not yet published. But in sense they occur in the second letter to Fulk, no. 11. Likewise, what the same Picard cites from the same Mauburn as though unpublished concerning the qualifications of a cardinal is found in book four of *On Consideration*, no. 12. These are the matters which it seemed worthwhile to set before the reader concerning this edition of the letters.

## § II.—On Bernard’s Holiness, Learning, and Authority in the Church

XXIII. Before proceeding further, it is useful to consider two titles commonly given to Bernard: that he is the “honey-flowing” doctor (*mellifluus*) among doctors, and the last among the Fathers, yet certainly not inferior to the first. The Church bestows the name “doctor” upon those whose teaching it has approved by its public judgment, especially when harmony with holiness is added. It calls “Fathers” those whom holiness, learning, and antiquity commend—learning, I mean, that adheres rather to Scripture and tradition than to philosophical arguments.

Therefore those distinguished for learning may be called doctors immediately after the death of a holy man; but only those whose authority, long since received, has made them venerable, and whose manner of treating matters is remote from philosophical reasoning, may be called Fathers. Bernard deserved both commendations. First, Alexander III bestowed the title on him at Bernard’s canonization, in the Mass then celebrated for him, by assigning him the Gospel passage appointed only for holy doctors, from Matthew chapter 5: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5). Innocent III expressly confirmed the same title in a Collect composed by himself, in which Bernard is called “Blessed Bernard, abbot and outstanding doctor.”

The epithet “honey-flowing,” which is more recent, was assigned to the holy doctor by Theophilus Raynaud in a separate little work entitled *The Gallic Bee*. The first editors to place this epithet on the title-page were the Lyons edition of 1508, then Jodocus Clichtoveus in 1515, and also the two monks of Clairvaux mentioned above; Horst later restored it after it had been neglected from time to time by others. Yet it is preferable to count it among the encomia, since Bernard’s bare name sufficiently commends the title of his works, and the author supplies his own praise. Indeed, if any other epithet suits Bernard, it is especially *Theodidaktos* (Θεοδιδάκτου), “taught by God,” bestowed on him by other editors, because he appears to have possessed a teaching not so much acquired by human powers as infused from heaven.

XXIV. Although he did not lack labor and diligence in reading and studying authors, not only sacred but also secular, as is clear from the words of the latter occasionally cited, he undoubtedly learned these things as a young man in the world, and they sometimes returned to his memory even in old age. But as a monk he had diligently devoted himself to theological matters. How profound and elevated his knowledge of them was is shown especially by sermons 80 and 81 on the *Song of Songs*, where he discusses the image of God in the Word and in the soul, and the simplicity of God, so loftily and appropriately that no one did so better before or after him.

The same must be said of Christ’s satisfaction for us in his suffering, which is explained in a truly remarkable way in letter 190 to Innocent. Moreover, what can be compared in knowledge of the canons to his outstanding books *On Consideration*? This confirms Leo the Great’s saying: “True love of what is right possesses in [Col. 0027] itself both apostolic authorities and canonical enactments.” Finally, how deeply the holy doctor immersed himself in reading sacred Scripture is proclaimed everywhere by his writings, which, to use the words of Sixtus of Siena, may be called “nothing but centos from the divine volumes,” since they are everywhere adorned with sayings from the Old and New Testaments as with jewelled ornaments, inserted so conveniently and aptly that they are thought to have been born there.

Although such a manner of writing should not be used indiscriminately in every subject, it ought not to be rejected in sacred matters. For one may invoke here what the apostle Peter says: “If anyone speaks, [let him speak] as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4). Yet Bernard sometimes turns certain passages of Scripture toward an improper and by no means literal sense, so that he seems to play with words rather than expound the words themselves. This may rightly be excused on the ground that the holy man believed a manifold sense useful for shaping morals could suitably be drawn from Scripture, especially where faith is not at issue, but where a devout subject is being embellished in order to arouse the hearers’ attention and delight.

XXV. No one who has carefully read Bernard’s writings will deny that the most holy man was eminently occupied, as far as his many responsibilities permitted, not only with sacred Scripture but also with the reading of the holy Fathers. For the Fathers and their opinions are sometimes cited in these writings, and their teaching is scattered throughout all his works. Thus, when he says that “oaks and beeches” were his teachers [Note: [Col. 0027] *Life*, book I, no. 23], this must be interpreted in the sense which he himself proposes to cardinals in book four of *On Consideration*, no. 12: that “in every matter prayer is to be trusted more than one’s own industry or labor.” Geoffrey in fact applied this to Bernard. [Note: [Col. 0027] *Ibid.*, book III, no. 1.]

Moreover, how much he gained from reading the Fathers, especially Saint Augustine, is demonstrated above all by the book *On Grace and Free Will*, which is a learned summary of Augustinian teaching. In letter, or little work, 11, to Hugh of Saint-Victor, he joins Ambrose to Augustine and adds that he is not easily torn away from these two pillars of the Church. He likewise praises Athanasius in little work 10, against Peter Abelard, and sometimes Gregory the Great as well. Finally, in the conclusion of the homilies *On the Praises of the Virgin*, he admits that he received much from the Fathers.

It is remarkable that a holy man subject to so many illnesses and weaknesses, distracted by so many cares, and interrupted by affairs not only domestic—certainly neither light nor few in such a numerous community of monks—but especially public affairs, could have been equal either to reading so many books or to producing writings so eloquent and learned. Thus, beyond his natural talent, which in him was most excellent and sublime, no one can doubt that a certain divine wisdom was present to him as he spoke, acted, taught, and wrote. Hence, Geoffrey says, “he once confessed that, while he was meditating or praying, the whole of sacred Scripture appeared to him as though laid open and displayed beneath him.” [Note: [Col. 0027] *Ibid.*, no. 7.]

Yet although he used to confess that he grasped the meaning of the Scriptures better “at the fountain of their first origin than in the flowing streams of expositions,” he nevertheless humbly read their holy and orthodox interpreters. He did not at all make his own meanings equal to theirs, but submitted them to be shaped by theirs; and faithfully adhering to their footsteps, he often drank himself from the fountain from which they had drawn. [Note: [Col. 0028] *Ibid.*, book I, no. 24.] This reverence of the holy doctor for the holy Fathers shines out everywhere in his writings, as in letter 98, no. 1, sermon 5 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 6, and elsewhere.

The prolonged illness which, in the early years of his leadership, compelled him to be absent from the community of brethren and to live apart in the monastery as though a private person gave him leisure to read them. At first this occurred “by the command” of William, bishop of Châlons, and of the abbots of his Order, according to the testimony of the other Abbot William; later it was due to the force of worsening illness. [Note: [Col. 0028] *Ibid.*, nos. 33, 40.] Abbot William saw him “free from every concern of the house, both inward and outward, at leisure for God and himself, and rejoicing as though amid the delights of paradise.” Then the holy man discoursed to him on the *Song of Songs*, as William relates more fully.

While Bernard was recovering, the stewardship of his brother Gerard secured for him leisure for sacred studies. Gerard supplied Bernard’s place in the monastery so effectively that Bernard, in sermon 26 on the *Song of Songs*, attributes to him the progress of his spiritual studies. These studies, according to sermon 51 on the *Song of Songs*, no. 3, consisted in praying, reading, writing, meditating, and similar activities. Thus the blessed Father lived for fifteen years: from the foundation of Clairvaux until the schism of Peter Leo. During that time, employed in great and arduous affairs, he eventually became the man whom all Europe—indeed, not to say the whole world—afterwards admired.

XXVI. Therefore that great Nicholas Faber, tutor of Louis the Just, according to Francis Balbo in his Life, rightly used to venerate all the Fathers most highly, but especially Saint Augustine, to whose reading he constantly adhered, and, among the more recent writers, Saint Bernard, whom he called the last of the Fathers. Certainly no one among the ancients after Augustine deserved this encomium better than Bernard, nor did anyone after Bernard deserve it in the same degree. For no one possessed holiness more illustrious in miracles and deeds, teaching more pure or more firmly attached to tradition, a manner of speaking and writing more divine, or, finally, greater authority.

“For to whose will,” to use William’s words, “did every height of both secular and ecclesiastical [Col. 0029] rank so yield; to whose counsel did it so humble itself? Proud kings, princes and tyrants, soldiers and plunderers feared him in such a way that what is read in the Gospel as said by the Lord to his disciples seems to have been fulfilled in them: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I have given you power to tread upon serpents’ (Luke 10), etc. But among spiritual persons . . . his authority was far different. For just as it is said through the prophet of the holy living creatures that, when a voice came from above the firmament over their heads, they stood still and lowered their wings (Ezek. 1), so today,” he says, “everywhere on earth, all spiritual persons, when he speaks or expounds, stand still, yielding to one who goes before them, and submit their own judgments or understandings to his judgments or understandings. His writings bear witness to this.” [Note: [Col. 0029] *Life*, book I, no. 70.] Etc.

Accordingly, Caesarius, monk of Heisterbach, rightly says that Bernard’s authority was so great “that scarlet-clad Fathers, kings, and princes of the earth spoke through the mouth of Bernard alone as though through a common oracle of the world.” [Note: [Col. 0029] *On Miracles*, book XIV, chapter 17.] This estimation of the holy doctor has been handed down to our own age, as the testimonies of distinguished men concerning him demonstrate; among them Bartholomew of the Martyrs, that most devout archbishop of Braga, Bernard’s devotee and admirer, ought not to hold an inferior place.

XXVII. Many things gained him this authority during his lifetime, but above all his exceptional humility even amid honors—than which, in Bernard’s own judgment, nothing is more exalted. [Note: [Col. 0029] Homily IV, *On the Praises of the Virgin*, no. 9.] Hear Ernald:

> Many admirable and praiseworthy qualities converged in him. Some marvel at his learning; others at his miracles. But I, he says, render honor to all these things; yet above all, so far as lies in me, I judge this more exalted and proclaim it more earnestly: that, though he was a chosen vessel and fearlessly bore Christ’s name before nations and kings; though the rulers of the world obeyed him and bishops in every nation stood at his command; though the Roman Church itself honored his counsels by a singular privilege and, as if granting him a general legation, subjected nations and kingdoms to him; though, what is judged still more glorious, his deeds and words were confirmed by miracles—he never exceeded himself, never walked above himself amid marvels. Rather, always thinking humbly of himself, he believed himself not the author but the minister of venerable works; and though in everyone’s judgment supreme, in his own judgment he remained lowest. [Note: [Col. 0029] *Life*, book II, no. 25.]

For “the humility of his heart overcame the loftiness of his name; nor could the whole world raise him as much as he alone cast himself down.” [Note: [Col. 0029] *Ibid.*, book III, no. 22.] Nor did so great a lowering and abasement of himself diminish his effectiveness with others; rather, it increased it. “Indeed, the humbler he was, the more useful he was always to the people of God in every saving teaching.” [Note: [Col. 0029] *Ibid.*, no. 8.]

XXVIII. The holiness of the Father was matched by the holiness of his sons, which also redounded to the Father’s glory. The Roman curia itself, which accompanied Innocent to Clairvaux, is witness:

> The bishops wept, and the supreme pontiff himself wept; and all marvelled at the gravity of that community, because amid such solemn joy everyone’s eyes were fixed on the ground and were nowhere carried about in wandering curiosity. Rather, with eyelids closed, they themselves saw no one and were seen by all. The Roman saw nothing in that church which he desired. None of their furnishings drew his gaze; in the oratory they saw nothing but bare walls. Ambition could fasten only upon their conduct; nor could such booty be harmful to the brethren, since religion could not be diminished when carried away. [Note: [Col. 0030] *Ibid.*, book II, no. 6.]

Bernard’s authority rested on these pillars and supports, so much so that “the sweetness of his character tempered his austerity, while holiness maintained his authority: as though he brought down from heaven among men a certain miracle of purity, more than human, attained before God.” [Note: [Col. 0030] *Ibid.*, book III, no. 21, and book I, no. 28.] That holiness and purity, moreover, were attested by miracles so clear and distinguished that even his adversaries acknowledged them, and so numerous and frequent that Bernard himself was astonished by them, according to Geoffrey. [Note: [Col. 0030] *Ibid.*, book III, no. 20.]

XXIX. It is therefore no wonder that his authority had such power: first, “to revive,” in William’s phrase, “the fervor of ancient religious observance in the monastic order”; [Note: [Col. 0030] William, book I, no. 42.] then, according to Geoffrey, “to correct the morals of Catholics, restrain the frenzies of schismatics, and refute the errors of heretics.” [Note: [Col. 0030] Geoffrey, book III, no. 12.] This is clear both from his Life and from his own writings, especially his letters.

## § III.—On Bernard’s Success in Reforming the Morals of Clerics, Monks, and Laypeople
XXX. The holy man everywhere lamented and deplored the corrupt morals of his age, especially among the ministers of the Church; most of them he brought to better conduct. Thus the whole face of the Church and clergy—especially of the Gallican Church—was thoroughly transformed by his counsels and sermons and restored to its ancient dignity. For he furnished the Roman See with Eugenius, a most holy man; and in him he instructed and inspired all Roman pontiffs toward the proper and lawful administration of their dignity, by publishing the plainly divine books *On Consideration*. Among bishops, he recalled Henry of Sens, Stephen of Paris, and very many others from a courtly way of life to conduct worthy of the episcopal order; and he also advanced many of his own followers as bishops, as examples to others [Note: [Col. 0030] *Life*, book II, no. 49.]. To all clerics he gave salutary counsel in the sermon *On Conversion*, addressed to clerics. Whoever wishes to examine all this closely should read the sixth book of the French *Life of Saint Bernard*, whose last three books [Col. 0031] are woven, with great piety and notable selection, from his writings. Above all should be read, concerning the morals and office of bishops, the forty-second letter to Henry of Sens, now placed among the Treatises in the second volume. Thus it is deservedly said in the book *On the Bishops of Verdun* that Bernard is the man “upon whose counsels the kingdoms and churches of Gaul today,” says the author, “rest” [Note: [Col. 0031] *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 311.].

XXXI. He possessed a marvelous grace of speech, “so that not even his own style, though outstanding, could retain all that sweetness and all that fervor.” For “God had given him a gentle, persuasive, and learned tongue, so that he knew whom and when he ought to address; to whom consolation or entreaty, exhortation or rebuke, was fitting. Those who have read his writings may perceive this to some extent, though far less than those who frequently heard his words” [Note: [Col. 0031] *Life*, book III, no. 7.]. “If, then, we are so kindled by reading his writings, how much more were those who heard him speaking? It is therefore no wonder that through him God worked so many and such great things for the salvation of the people of his time.”

XXXII. Who could set forth what and how much he accomplished in reviving anew the original fervor of the monastic institution? His outstanding letters and writings on this subject bear witness: the book *On Precept and Dispensation*, the *Apology to Abbot William*, and various sermons. In these he encouraged monks to preserve and restore the primary rule of the ancient Fathers: namely, the labors and austerities of repentance, modesty and humility, poverty, contempt for the world, love of solitude and silence, and continual progress. He understood that upon these the very hinge of monastic life turned. Hence Peter the Venerable, in the letter numbered 229 among Bernard’s letters, no. 30, rightly calls him “a strong, milky-white pillar upon which the building of the monastic order rests,” and “a glowing star,” which “by example and word bestowed remarkable light in his time not only upon monks but upon the whole Latin Church.”

XXXIII. Lawrence of Liège, in his book *On the Bishops of Verdun*, compares the Cistercian and Premonstratensian orders with the two cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat: “one of these, the Cistercian order, under the leadership of Bernard, abbot of most holy name, restored the monastic order, now almost fallen, to the first norm of apostolic life.” And “the Cistercian order, indeed, during this period of three years,” he says, “grew to about two hundred abbeys of great name, merit, and numbers; and it had already begun to spread even among the barbarous Sarmatians and the farthest Scythians” [Note: [Col. 0032] *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 325.]. So powerful was the fame and reputation for holiness of Bernard and his disciples! Consequently Bernard himself, though merely a member of the Cistercian order, came to be regarded almost as its founder; and in his own time the order was called the Order of Clairvaux from his monastery of Clairvaux—indeed, later the Order of Saint Bernard—although Innocent VIII prohibited this in the letters uniting the monastery of Clairvaux with Cîteaux.

Thus, in the letters of Albero, bishop of Verdun, cited by the recently mentioned Lawrence of Liège, the abbots of Trois-Fontaines and La Chalade are described as being “of the Order of Clairvaux” [Note: [Col. 0032] Ibid., p. 322]; and Peter of Celle calls it “the Cistercian or Clairvaux order” in book I, letter 24. Likewise, in the letter of Samson, bishop of Reims, numbered 435 among Bernard’s letters, the Order of Clairvaux is mentioned more than once. Yet it may be said that the name “Order of Clairvaux” often designates only the Clairvaux line, not the whole order.

XXXIV. What the strictness and rigor of either the Cistercians or the Clairvaux monks under Bernard were need not be explained here, since it is more than sufficiently evident both from Bernard’s letters and writings and from his *Life*, especially book I, chapter 5. There the first inhabitants of Clairvaux are said to have served God “in poverty of spirit, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils. They often prepared their dishes from beech leaves. Their bread was of barley, vetch, and millet.” Thus writes William, an eyewitness. In Bernard’s first letter, addressed to Robert, “vegetables, beans, gruel, and coarse bread with water” are called Cistercian delicacies. Nor are their provisions otherwise described by Fastred in his letter among Bernard’s correspondence. “Their economy in food is so great,” says Stephen of Tournai in letter 72, “that they use only two dishes, supplied either by the field in legumes or by the garden in vegetables. They use fish all the more rarely because it is heard of among them more often than it is seen.” More may be found in the same author and in Peter of Celle.

This vigor of the order endured not merely to the end of the twelfth century, as is evident from Peter of Blois’s eighty-second letter, but also beyond the middle of the thirteenth century, according to James of Vitry in chapter 13 of his *Eastern and Western History*: “They do not eat meat except in serious illness. They do not ordinarily consume fish, eggs, milk, or cheese.”

We French still see the same severity of life flourishing in the most devout monks of Blessed Mary of La Trappe and in certain other imitators of theirs. By purity of life, austerity, love of solitude, silence, labor, and other religious virtues, they demonstrate to be possible in practice what we read—and scarcely believed—concerning Bernard and his disciples.

XXXV. In the following chapter the same James of Vitry adds that the weaker sex of women “had not dared, from the beginning of the order, to aspire to the severity of such strictness”; but that this at last became customary later [Col. 0033]. Nevertheless, while Bernard himself was alive, women were not wholly without a share in this institution. Herman, monk of Laon, proves this in book III, chapter 17, of *The Miracles of Saint Mary*, where he treats of Montreuil, a convent for Cistercian virgins near Laon, built by Bishop Bartholomew. There the nuns, under Abbess Guiburge, “having put aside all linen garments and furs, used only woolen tunics; and they sought their living in silence, laboring continually with their own hands not only at spinning and weaving, but also at digging in the fields and, with axe and mattock, clearing felled woodland by rooting it out and pulling up thorns and brambles; and in every respect they imitated the life of the monks of Clairvaux.”

XXXVI. The discussion would extend too far if we were to bring forward all the distinguished men and women known to us whom Bernard drew to monastic life: such as Henry, son of Louis VI, king of the Franks; Ermengard, duchess of Brittany; Adelaide of Lorraine; and countless others of both sexes. But scarcely less deserving of proclamation and admiration is the fact that he persuaded those who remained in the world to adopt a most devout and upright manner of life. “Among princes Count Theobald attached himself to him above all others; he placed both himself and his possessions at the service of Clairvaux, and put his soul into the abbot’s hands. Laying aside princely loftiness, he showed himself among the servants of God as a fellow servant, not a lord, obeying in all things whatsoever the least member of that house might ask” [Note: [Col. 0033] *Life*, book II, no. 52.].

What so great a prince accomplished, at Bernard’s admonition and exhortation—in building, endowing, and assisting monasteries; relieving the poor; and finally exercising the office of an excellent ruler—is attested by Abbot Ernald, from whom we have quoted the foregoing, and also by Bernard’s letters concerning him. The devout zeal of Theobald was emulated by the noble and illustrious woman Beatrice, as we learn from letter 118. Finally, an example of the force of Bernard’s authority in reforming human conduct is the conversion of Duke William of Aquitaine, whom he made from a most obstinate schismatic into a most obedient and devout prince [Note: [Col. 0033] Ibid., no. 37 ff.]. To conclude briefly with Geoffrey: “What crimes did he not rebuke? What hatreds did he not extinguish? What scandals did he not restrain? What schisms did he not heal? What heresies did he not refute?” [Note: [Col. 0034] Ibid., book III, no. 30.] Yet these last two matters, namely schisms and heresies, require separate treatment.

§ IV.—On the schism of Anacletus, suppressed through Saint Bernard.

XXXVII. Although Baronius and other ecclesiastical writers have written much about the schism formed after the death of Honorius II in 1130 between Innocent and Anacletus, certain matters nevertheless require fuller explanation. We shall endeavor to supply this from a reading of ancient records, in order to elucidate Bernard’s letters on this subject. And, that the discussion may proceed in order, we must first inquire what sort of men Gregory of Saint Angelo, cardinal, and Peter Leonis—for these were the original names of Innocent and Anacletus—were before the schism. Next, Innocent’s election, its circumstances and conditions, and Anacletus’s opposition must be examined more closely. Finally, we must investigate what followed from these events.

XXXVIII. Peter Leonis, a Roman of the Leonine family and formerly a monk of Cluny, was first made, if we believe Onuphrius, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian by Paschal II; then, in 1120, cardinal priest of Santa Maria in Trastevere, of the title of Callistus, by Callistus II. “This Peter,” as we learn from the Chronicle of Morigny, “was the son of Peter, son of Leo. Leo, however, passing over from Judaism—that is, making a *pascha*, a passage—to Christ, deserved to be baptized by Leo and distinguished with his name.” Understand Leo IX. “This man,” namely Leo, a convert from the Jews, “because he was highly learned, became influential in the Roman curia and begot a son named Peter, destined to be a man of great fame and power. At that time the most turbulent conflict over investitures arose between the king of the Germans, who by succession from Charlemagne was patrician of the Romans, and the Roman Church. In this conflict the man proved so vigorous in arms, prudent in counsel, and faithful to the Roman Church that the pope entrusted to him, together with the other fortifications of Rome, even that fortress which seems to command the likeness of that city—I mean the Tower of Crescentius, situated on the side toward Gaul at the Tiber bridge—and held him as more familiar than the rest. Growing wonderfully through this opportunity, he improved his position daily and increased in wealth, possessions, and honors.”

These matters had to be stated beforehand, because knowledge of the events depends upon Peter’s family, Judaism, power, and the Tower of Crescentius—called the Castle of Saint Angelo—by which Anacletus defended himself. The chronicler of Morigny continues: “Among his other offspring—a very great multitude of both sexes, of which, according to some, Antichrist boasted—he begot this Peter of whom we are now speaking, who, having been committed to study, was called by some the forerunner of Antichrist.” I judge that this insult was imposed upon him from subsequent events or their outcome. “For the sake of study he visited Gaul and Paris; and on his return home he assumed the monastic habit at Cluny, a most wealthy and holy monastery. After being trained there for some time in the regular observances, he was recalled to the curia by Pope Paschal II at his father’s request; and, having become a cardinal in the time of Pope Callistus, he was sent to Gaul with that same Gregory, afterward Innocent II, and held councils at Chartres and Beauvais.”

There is here no mention of the title of cardinal deacon, which Onuphrius says was granted to Peter Leonis by Paschal. On this point the authority of the chronicler of Morigny, a contemporary, carries greater weight.

[Col. 0035] XXXIX. Gregory, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Angelo, is said to have been created by Urban II. Later he was sent as legate to Gaul by Callistus II with Peter Leonis in 1124, and with him visited Sées, a city of Neustria, according to Orderic [Note: [Col. 0035] Orderic, book XII, p. 877.]. Vincent writes of this legation in book II, chapter 49, of *The Life of Stephen of Grandmont*: “The most eminent cardinals Gregory and Peter Leonis, between whom there was afterward a schism concerning the papacy, when sent to Gaul and exercising their legation in the region of Limoges, came together to this man of God,” Stephen. Both, indeed, subscribed as legates to the constitution of Abbot Suger in 1125, in Chesne: “I, Peter, cardinal priest and legate of the Apostolic See, approve and confirm. I, Gregory of Saint Angelo, cardinal deacon and legate of the Apostolic See” [Note: [Col. 0036] Chesne, vol. IV, p. 547.], etc.
