At the same time Bernard wrote certain letters to Peter, cardinal deacon and legate—namely letter 17 and those following. With Manrique, I once thought this man to be Peter Leonis. But since it is certain that the Peter to whom Bernard writes was a cardinal deacon, not a cardinal priest, those letters cannot concern Peter Leonis, who was without doubt then a cardinal priest, as is proved not only by Onuphrius and others, but also by Peter’s foregoing subscription and by Suger's testimony, which we shall shortly cite. Therefore that Peter, cardinal deacon and legate, to whom Bernard’s earlier letters are addressed, may perhaps have been the very man who came to Gaul by command of Pope Honorius against the deposed Abbot Pons of Cluny and his supporters, then called Ponsians. We have Peter the Venerable as authority for this in book II, chapter 13, of *The Miracles*: “The aforesaid venerable Pope Callistus had already departed this life and had received as successor Pope Honorius, no inferior to himself. Hearing of such grave disturbances in so great a church,” namely Cluny, “he sent from his own side a legate, namely Lord Peter the cardinal, who, together with Hugbald, primate of Lyons, condemned Pons and all the Ponsians, as they were then called, with a terrible anathema.”

It is not easy to determine of what title that cardinal was; for besides Peter Leonis there were at that time several cardinals named Peter: Peter, bishop of Porto; Peter of Pisa, of the title of Saint Susanna; Peter Burgundus, of the title of Saint Marcellus; Peter, of the title of Saint Eusebius, promoted in Honorius’s first creation in 1125; Peter, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, in the following year; and finally, two years later, Peter, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Adrian. But Bernard’s letters appear to have been written before the creation of these last two.

XL. Meanwhile Pope Honorius died in the middle of February 1130. The chronicler of Morigny assigns the preceding year, according to the French custom by which the beginning of the new year was reckoned from Easter. Then, says the same chronicler, “the cardinals who were present there with the chancellor,” Haimeric, “and had attended the sick Honorius, set over themselves a certain Gregory”—the man just mentioned—“distinguished for learning and religion; and, as some say, they clothed him with the pontifical insignia with excessive haste. They say this was done by way of dispensation, in order to frustrate the hopes of a certain Peter who seemed to aspire to the papacy in a worldly fashion. This Peter was the son of Peter, son of Leo,” and so forth, as reported above concerning him.

Suger sets out the event more clearly in his *Life of Louis the Fat*. He says that, after the death of Honorius, “the greater and wiser men of the Roman Church,” in order “to avert disturbance from the Church,” had agreed that a celebrated election should take place “at Saint Mark’s, and nowhere else, and only jointly, according to Roman custom.” But those “who by constant attendance and familiarity had been closer to the pope, not daring to assemble there for fear of the turbulent Romans, before the death of the lord pope was made public elected as supreme pontiff the venerable person Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo; while those who favored the party of Peter Leonis, summoning others to Saint Mark’s according to the agreement, assembled there and, on learning of the lord pope’s death, elected that same Peter Leonis, cardinal priest, as they wished, with the consent of many bishops, cardinals, clerics, and Roman nobles.” Thus the destructive schism was formed.

Innocent’s election, therefore, was earlier, but precipitous and not made by the whole body of electors. “But since the party of Peter Leonis prevailed,” Suger adds, “both by the support of his relatives and by the protection of the Roman nobility,” Innocent left the city and sailed toward Gaul; sending messengers to King Louis, he sought his aid. Louis therefore summoned a council at Étampes of archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious men; and, “inquiring by their counsel more into the person than the election,” he gave his support to Innocent, at Bernard’s urging. The votes of the entire council had converged on Bernard’s judgment, as Ernald testifies in book II, chapter 1, of his *Life*.

Thereupon Suger, as he himself relates, was sent by the king to meet Innocent as far as Cluny. The abbot of that place, Peter the Venerable, and the monks preferred Innocent to Anacletus, their former monk, as we shall note later on letter 126. The king himself met the pope with his queen and sons as far as the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury; bowing his royal head “as though before Peter’s tomb, he prostrated himself at his feet.” Following his example, King Henry of England likewise “met Innocent at Chartres and, most devoutly prostrate at his feet,” promised obedience for himself and his people. Innocent then, “visiting the Gallican Church, proceeded to the regions of Lorraine. When Emperor Lothair met him in the city of Liège with a most distinguished company of archbishops, bishops, and nobles of the German realm, Lothair most humbly offered himself as his groom in the square before the episcopal church. He hurried to the pope’s feet through the middle of the holy procession, holding a staff in one hand to defend him and the bridle of his white horse in the other, and led him as his lord. When the whole procession alighted, he carried him down, supporting him, and made the greatness of his fatherhood known to those both known and unknown.” These events took place in 1130. Here Suger is silent about Bernard, whom, as we learn from Ernald, accompanied Innocent constantly on his journey through Gaul.

XLI. Before proceeding further, it will be useful to observe what was then done at Liège. The Magdeburg or Saxon manuscript Annals explain it under 1131: “On the Sunday before mid-Lent, the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, a most celebrated assembly of thirty-six bishops and princes was held at Liège, with Lord Apostolic Innocent, King Lothair, and the queen present. There many matters, both ecclesiastical and useful to the realm, were prudently ordered. There Bishop Otto of Halberstadt, whom Pope Honorius had deprived of his bishopric three years earlier, obtained restoration to his office through the intervention of the king and princes.”

Ernald relates that investitures were discussed at that assembly, which Lothair at last surrendered to the Church through Bernard’s intervention. This council had been preceded by the synod of Würzburg, as the same Annals—written by a contemporary author—record: “A council of sixteen bishops was assembled by the king at Würzburg in October, at which the archbishop of Ravenna, legate of the Apostolic See, was present. There Gregory, who is Innocent, who prevailed over Peter Leo in the election, was elected and confirmed by King Lothair and by all assembled there.”

XLII. After the assembly at Liège, Innocent, according to Suger, returned to France, spent the feast of Easter at Saint-Denis, and “after the third day following Easter” came to Paris. “Then, visiting the churches of Gaul and supplying the deficiency of his poverty from their abundance, after traveling for some time by land he chose to remain at Compiègne.” Soon afterward, after a council held at Reims, as Suger relates—and on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, according to Dodechin—Louis the Younger received the royal insignia from Innocent there on the eighth day before those Kalends, as Robert, continuator of Sigebert, noted. The Saxon manuscript Annals under 1131 state: “Pope Innocent, again gathering ecclesiastical men”—that is, after the synod of Liège—“and crowds of the faithful, presided for several days at a great synod in the city of Reims on the feast of Saint Luke.” Suger adds that the pope, “after dissolving the council,” stayed at Auxerre and finally returned to Italy with Lothair. The chronicler of Morigny likewise places his stay at Auxerre after the council of Reims.

XLIII. Ernald, in book II, chapter 1, of Bernard’s *Life*, places the Council of Reims before that of Liège and writes that Innocent went from Liège to Clairvaux and then, after a brief stay in Gaul, set out for Rome with Lothair. But it is certain that the synod of Reims followed that of Liège, both from Suger’s narrative and the Saxon Annals, and especially from the Chronicle of Morigny, which describes Innocent’s journey carefully.

The chronicler relates that after Innocent had been recognized at Chartres by Henry, king of England, “it was decided in council to direct the journey toward the patrician of the Romans and king of the Germans, and to lodge first from Chartres at Morigny,” a Benedictine monastery in the outskirts of Étampes. In that company, besides bishops and cardinals, there was “Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, who at that time was in Gaul a most renowned preacher of the divine word,” and Peter Abelard, monk and abbot, described as “a religious man and master of most excellent”—that is, theological—“schools.” After the dedication of the church of Morigny, “on the third day the lord pope departed with his company and proceeded to his conference at Liège. . . . Returning thence to Gaul, Innocent stayed a long time at Auxerre; and, when the time of the council which he was to celebrate at Reims on the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist drew near, having first reconciled Geoffrey Martel at Tours . . . he returned again through the provinces of Orléans and Étampes and honored Paris by his presence.”

Meanwhile occurred the death of Philip, king-designate. On receiving news of this death, the pope, deeply moved in his heart, sent from his side the venerable bishops Geoffrey of Châlons and Matthew of Albano to console the king. Then, proceeding to Reims, he solemnly anointed Louis king in a crowded synod. Letters, tokens of obedience and fidelity, were sent to him by Lothair, king of the Germans; Henry, king of England; and likewise by Alfonso the elder, king of nearer Spain, and Alfonso the younger, king of farther Spain. Moreover, letters of the most eminent Carthusian hermits greatly rejoiced the pope; they were brought by a certain venerable abbot of the Cistercian order and read in the council by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres. This abbot was Hugh of Pontigny, as the letters reported by the same chronicler at the end of book II attest.

At the beginning of book III he adds that Innocent returned to Rome shortly after the Council of Reims. “But because Peter, an unjust usurper, had joined the greater part of the city to himself, Innocent held alone by himself the church of Saint Peter, upon which the dignity of the divine priesthood depended; while Peter occupied the seat of the Lateran palace, to which imperial majesty pertains.” On this matter there are letters of Emperor Lothair in volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, in which Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, is given the title of chancellor, namely as acting in place of Bruno of Cologne, as is read in the Saxon Chronicle; Bruno had not gone to Italy with the emperor. But Innocent, providing for the city, withdrew to Pisa and remained there until Peter’s death, that is, until 1137.

XLIV. Meanwhile Peter, or Anacletus, left nothing undone in order to attach to his party every distinguished man he could. Among bishops, Girard of Angoulême adhered to him. Since Girard had exercised the office of legate under the preceding popes, he desired to obtain the same office from Anacletus. He also drew William, count of Poitou, to Anacletus [Col. 0039]. Moreover, in order to gain Roger, duke of Apulia, Anacletus gave him his sister in marriage and crowned him king of Sicily, as Orderic testifies in book XII [Note: [Col. 0039] Orderic, book XII, p. 498.]. Among the letters of Anacletus styling himself pope—all preserved in the Cassinese codex, some published by Baronius—there is one in which he complains bitterly of the abbot of Farfa. Because the abbot opposed him, he “struck him with the sling of the Church,” that is, “condemned him by sentence of excommunication.”

XLV. These many and great disturbances, described here perhaps more fully than the space allowed, caused Bernard much labor. He wrote various letters in every direction to reconcile schismatics to Innocent and to keep the faithful in their duty. He also undertook various journeys for the same purpose, as may be understood from the letters that follow and from book II, chapters 6 and 7, of the *Life*.

XLVI. It remains here to speak of Girard, bishop of Angoulême, whose conduct was admirably described by Arnulf—first archdeacon of Sées, then bishop of Lisieux—in a treatise published against him, printed by our Acherius in volume II of the *Spicilegium*. Arnulf says that Girard was Norman by birth and, because of the chronic poverty of his paternal household, left his homeland; that he was finally elected bishop of the Church of Angoulême “by chance,” in order that the disagreement of the electors might attain “some kind of outcome.” He then conferred the dignities of his church upon nephews born “in an obscure station,” left crimes unpunished, sought and obtained from the supreme pontiff the office of legate, preyed upon individuals, and called councils and synods for ostentation.

Arnulf adds that Girard at first favored Innocent after his election; but when he could not obtain from him the office of legate, he went over to the party of Peter Leonis. From Peter he received a new legation, such that everything lying from the Alps to the limits of the West should be subject to his jurisdiction; and it was added that “wherever his foot should tread,” there also “there should be a legation.” Having received this dignity, he made sufficient effort to draw the kings of England and Spain to Anacletus’s party, but in vain. Having expelled the bishops of the churches of Poitiers and Limoges, he installed other wicked men; he even usurped the Church of Bordeaux, being at once bishop and archbishop. Ernald also reports this in book II, chapter 5, of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

Then, listing the supporters of Anacletus, Arnulf adds: “That faithless multitude which you follow belongs to Peter Leonis, not yet wholly purged of the leaven of Jewish corruption; and that tyrant whom Sicily, the foster-mother of tyrants, supports . . . To this number is added the count of Poitou alone: a man of pleasures, an animal man, not attaining to the hidden things of the spiritual, enslaved to error because an unlawful request was refused.” These were Anacletus’s supporters. “But our party,” says Arnulf, “is professed by every emperor, every king, every prince, indeed by every person distinguished by the honor of the Christian name.” Yet “the agreement of these men is of chief importance to me in this matter; their authority moves me, draws me when moved, and holds me when drawn—the authority of those to whom it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, whose citizenship is said already in part to be in heaven: such indeed are those who inhabit the perpetual snows of the Charterhouse, and those who, flowing forth from the Cistercian or Cluniac monastery, have scattered everywhere the rays of their light.”

Thus Arnulf writes against Girard, though some others praise him. Arnulf’s authority, however, ought to prevail: “For,” he says, “I have written nothing which I did not either know myself, receive on probable authority, or which at least public report does not affirm.” More concerning him appears in the notes on letter 127. Meanwhile Girard died in 1136. Then Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, by Innocent’s command, “carefully traversing the whole region of Gaul, including Aquitaine itself, with his own hands destroyed all the altars of holy churches which either that Girard, author and maintainer of sedition, or Gilo, bishop of Tusculum, or their accomplices had consecrated during the time of schism with the blessing of chrismal anointing,” as is read in book III of the Chronicle of Morigny. But we linger too long on these matters. Whoever wishes to know more concerning the profession, life, and conduct of Innocent and Anacletus should read Arnulf’s treatise just cited. The letters of Paschal II concerning the legation entrusted to Girard are extant in volume III of the *Spicilegium*; the Synod of Laon held under him in 1109 is in volume IV.

XLVII. Through the disastrous and prolonged period of that schism, how great were Bernard’s labors and how many journeys he made may be learned, as we have said, from his *Life* and letters. For this purpose he traveled to Italy three times; and at last, through his efforts, the schism was suppressed after Anacletus died in 1138. The schismatics substituted Victor as antipope, “not so much out of obstinacy in schism as in order that they might more conveniently be reconciled to Pope Innocent after some delay.” And in fact Victor “came by night to the holy man,” that is, Bernard; “and Bernard, having stripped him of the insignia he had usurped, brought him to the feet of Lord Innocent” [Note: [Col. 0040] *Life*, book II, no. 47.]. Here was the end of that disastrous and prolonged schism.

XLVIII. Mindful of so great a benefit, received especially through Bernard, Innocent on his own authority remitted to the Cistercians tithes from all the possessions they held, without consulting those to whom such tithes belonged. This became a new cause of disputes and brought Bernard no little trouble. The Cluniacs chiefly complained, because that gratuitous liberality of Innocent caused them a great loss of property; and their indignation went so far that the monks of Gigny treated with complete contempt the neighboring Cistercian monastery called Miratorium. The whole history of this tragedy is explained principally by two letters, one of Peter the Venerable and the other of Saint Bernard, numbered [Col. 0041] 228 and 282 among Bernard’s letters, together with our notes on them. Nor was that quarrel immediately extinguished; rather, in the course of time it spread into other regions as well.

XLIX. This is clear from the eighty-second letter, which Peter of Blois wrote, in the name of Richard, Archbishop of Canterbury, “to the abbot and convent of Cîteaux.” For in that letter, after first praising the Cistercians, he adds that their reputation is tarnished in one respect: that “they take tithes away from monks and clerics. And what,” he says, “is this wrongful immunity, that you should be exempt from paying tithes, although the lands were liable for them before they became yours, and although the tithes have hitherto been paid, not on account of the persons, but by reason of the territory? If the lands have passed into your possession, why is another’s right endangered in this matter? For the lands passed to you, according to common equity, together with their burden.”

When the pope’s—that is, Innocent’s—privilege was objected to him, he replied that this could have been “tolerated for a time, since it had been introduced by necessity”: namely, while the Cistercian order “rejoiced in poverty, while it liberally poured out the resources of its slender means for the use of the needy.” But now that its possessions had been multiplied “even beyond measure, these privileges ought rather to be regarded as instruments of ambition than of religion.” Moreover, “whatever Roman Church privileges may allow, it is not expedient to usurp against conscience what belongs to another.”

Finally, if they should show themselves obstinate and inflexible in this matter, Richard threatens that he will “bind with the bond of anathema all” who have given or sold anything to the Cistercians “from which a right to tithes may accrue”; and that he will appeal to the throne of the supreme Judge, “that no one may absolve from this bond of excommunication.” Indeed, he says that he will obtain the favor of princes, “so that the civil hand may support the spiritual sword; and whatever has been sold or given” to the Cistercians “contrary to the principal decree may be confiscated.” Such was Peter of Blois’s manner.

L. Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, likewise complained of the same matter in his Chronicle. After praising the Cistercians because they gave many alms from their own labor, sang the psalms in choir in an orderly manner, and performed many honorable acts, he nevertheless notes this fault in them: that they took lands and tithes from others; and, further, that they indiscriminately abolished the commemoration of certain saints. [Note: [Col. 0041] See Labbe, *Bibliothèque*, vol. II, p. 328.] This author was writing at the end of the twelfth century, when that storm concerning the remission of tithes, granted by Innocent in favor of the Cistercians, had not yet subsided.

§ V.—On the errors of Peter Abelard and Gilbert of Poitiers, refuted by Saint Bernard.

LI. It contributes not a little to Bernard’s glory that he had no adversaries except erroneous persons or heretics; indeed, not the persons themselves, but their errors. Among the erring must above all be counted Peter Abelard and Gilbert, or Gislebert, of Poitiers; among heretics, the utterly wicked Henry and his followers, called after him Henricians. The first two are to be treated here; Henry and his adherents in the following chapter.

LII. Peter Abelard portrays himself in vivid colors in his *History of My Calamities*; and later Otto, Bishop of Freising, drew his portrait with a gentler brush. A summary of his life is found in our Notes on Bernard’s one hundred and eighty-seventh letter, where Abelard’s defenders and advocates are refuted. Here it is enough to present the substance of Bernard’s proceedings against him, and then, from the very words of his defenders, to show how unjust toward truth are those who favor Abelard over Saint Bernard.

LIII. First, it may be observed that Abelard, long before he had any dealings with Bernard, was summoned by Cono, legate of the Apostolic See, to the Council of Soissons held in 1121. There his book on Theology, containing erroneous propositions, was committed to the flames, and its author confined in the monastery of Saint-Médard. Having later left it, he continued, in various wanderings here and there, to spread his earlier doctrines. Hence he was called a heretic by many. Deeply offended by that name, he dragged Bernard—whom he supposed to be the author of the reproach—unwilling and resisting, to the Council of Sens in 1140.

There Abelard himself was again heard before bishops and other eminent men of the second rank, and was refuted by Bernard. His teaching was examined and again proscribed, while the author himself remained untouched; he appealed to the Apostolic See. But when he learned that the sentence of the synod had been approved by Innocent II, he abandoned the appeal. At the exhortation of Peter the Venerable, he withdrew to the monastery of Cluny, and finally died a praiseworthy death at Chalon, in the monastery of Saint-Marcel.

LIV. Bernard wrote several letters against Abelard, the chief being the one hundred and ninetieth letter to Innocent, listed eleventh among the shorter works. In this letter Bernard briefly sets out and vigorously refutes the principal heads of error noted in Abelard’s writings. In this edition we prefix to the same letter, or treatise, fourteen propositions extracted by Bernard from Abelard’s writings from a Vatican manuscript; these were submitted to Innocent together with the said letter. We shall treat the entire controversy at length in the prefatory notice to the same eleventh treatise. Here we touch only upon certain of Abelard’s defenders.

LV. Abelard himself is first brought forward. In his apology he complains that certain things had been imputed to him “maliciously” [Col. 0043], especially that “the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power.” He rejects these words as “not so much heretical as diabolical,” and asserts that they cannot be found in his writings. But this and the other propositions will be discussed in the observations on Bernard’s eleventh treatise.

Meanwhile, in the same apology Abelard admits that he wrote certain things “in error which ought not to have been written,” but “nothing through malice or pride.” He adds that, if through excessive talk he has gone beyond bounds in any respect, he has always been ready “to make satisfaction for his ill-spoken words,” by correcting or deleting them; and finally, that he is a son of the Church, “receiving all that she receives and rejecting what she rejects.” Very well. We do not insist that Abelard was a heretic; for Bernard’s case it is enough that he erred in certain points—something Abelard himself does not deny.

LVI. But what does Otto of Freising say against the holy doctor, or for Abelard? He says that Bernard was “zealous out of fervor for the Christian religion, and credulous out of habitual gentleness”; so much so “that he abhorred masters who clung too confidently and excessively to human reasonings and secular wisdom, and readily gave ear if anything discordant with Christian faith was reported to him concerning such men.” [Note: [Col. 0043] Otto, *On Frederick I*, ch. 47.]

But these very things redound to the holy doctor’s glory, since nothing is more incumbent upon a Catholic teacher than promptly to restrain such persons—who assign more than is right to philosophical subtleties—especially when they forge new terms capable of leading the unwary into error. “Moreover,” to speak with William, “if an excess of holy zeal is reproved in him, that excess nevertheless has its own reverence among pious minds. … Happy is he to whom alone is counted as a fault what others are accustomed to claim for themselves as glory.” [Note: [Col. 0043] *Life*, book I, no. 41.]

Yet Otto himself, however favorable to Abelard, admits that Abelard had unduly attenuated the three persons of the Holy Trinity, using unsuitable examples; and that for this reason he was judged “a Sabellian heretic” at Soissons in a provincial synod. What wonder, then, if, when he again advanced the same views, he was ill spoken of among lovers of sound faith?

LVII. We need not concern ourselves much with Berengar of Poitiers, who wrote an apology for Abelard, his teacher, against the Synod of Sens and Bernard: both because he was a man of little account and no authority, and because he himself, returning to a sounder mind, no longer wished to be “the defender of the propositions laid against Abelard, because, although they might contain sound doctrine, they nevertheless did not have a sound expression.” He says in a letter to the Bishop of Mende that he would have suppressed his book, had he been able.

Moreover, although we do not now possess all of Abelard’s works in which he scattered his errors, yet in those that remain there are many “rough places,” as the Parisian theologians noted. They placed “a safeguard against each of the more dangerous utterances” at the beginning of his works. One might wish that the apologetic preface were removed from these. But enough concerning Abelard.

LVIII. The condemnation of Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, stirred up against Bernard no less envy than did that of Abelard. “A native of Poitiers,” says Otto of Freising, Gilbert became from pupil a master, and from master finally bishop of that same city. “From youth he had subjected himself to the instruction of great men, trusting more to their weight than to his own talent; and from them he had drawn learning not light but weighty,” joining the renown of knowledge with gravity of character.

Those teachers were “first Hilary of Poitiers, then Bernard of Chartres, and finally Anselm and Ralph of Laon, brothers.” I think this Hilary to be none other than the great Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, whose authority Gilbert abused, according to Geoffrey. Bernard of Chartres is known to me only from Otto’s testimony. Ralph of Laon is very well known from Guibert, Herman the monk of Laon, and Geoffrey, notary of Saint Bernard; as is also Anselm his brother, dean of the Church of Laon.

While Gilbert composed commentaries on the Psalms, Paul’s Epistles, and Boethius, he philosophized on the Godhead and other matters of religion in certain ways not permitted. “Among other things alleged against him concerning the divine majesty,” says Otto, “were four propositions”: namely, “that the divine essence is not God; that the properties of the persons are not the persons themselves; that the theological persons are not predicated in any proposition; that the divine nature was not incarnate.” [Note: [Col. 0043] Otto, *On Frederick I*, book I, chs. 46, 50.] These will be explained more clearly below.

He also put forward other, “lesser” propositions: “that no one except Christ merits; that no one is baptized unless he is to be saved,” and other matters of that sort recorded by Geoffrey. [Note: [Col. 0044] In the tract *Against Gilbert’s Propositions*, below in the Appendix.]

LIX. When, however, the bishop had delivered a discourse before a large assembly of his clerics and had disseminated these same errors, two of his archdeacons, Arnald and Calo, brought the matter before Eugenius III, then traveling into Gaul, at Siena in Tuscany. The pope referred the examination of the case to Gaul. Meanwhile the archdeacons drew Bernard to their side.

An examination was held at Auxerre and Paris; judgment was delivered at the Council of Reims in 1148. What was done in each assembly Otto mentions briefly, Geoffrey, Bernard’s notary, at greater length. Geoffrey wrote both a treatise on the transactions in this matter at the Council of Reims and, forty years later, a letter to Henry, cardinal bishop of Albano. Both writings are given here at the end of the sixth volume.

[Col. 0045] LX. Concerning the assembly at Auxerre, mentioned by Otto alone, we have found nothing distinctive; but we have much concerning the Parisian one. Geoffrey relates that it was held “at the solemnity of Easter,” and hence in 1147, since the Council of Reims was held in mid-Lent of the following year, according to Otto, and indeed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, according to the Appendix to Sigebert.

“Thus Gilbert was brought before the pope at Paris, before cardinals, bishops, and other venerable and learned men, to answer for these propositions. The proceedings lasted for several days. Two masters were produced against him: Adam of the Little Bridge, a subtle man and recently made canon of the Church of Paris; and Hugh of the Flowery Field, the king’s chancellor. They solemnly affirmed that they had heard some of these propositions from his own mouth.

“Meanwhile, while many charges were made against him on every side, he is reported, among other things, to have said: ‘I confess that the Father is one thing as Father and another as God; yet he is not this thing and that thing.’ Joscelin, Bishop of Soissons, took offense at the saying. These things occurred on the first day. On another day he was accused of having called ‘the three persons three singular things’ in the prose hymn on the Trinity. The Archbishop of Rouen—Hugh III—aggravated the charge, saying that ‘God ought rather to be called one singular thing.’” So, approximately, Otto, Bishop of Freising, writes concerning the Parisian assembly. [Note: [Col. 0045] Otto, *On Frederick I*, book I, chs. 51–52.]

LXI. Geoffrey treats the matter somewhat differently, prefacing it with a synod at Viterbo held in the same case. He mentions one accuser of Gilbert before the pope, the archdeacon Arnald, to whom he gives the byname “Qui-non-ridet” (“He-Who-Does-Not-Laugh”).

At the Parisian assembly he sets Bernard alone against Gilbert: Bernard, “upon whom every affair of Christ, wherever he happened to be present, immediately pressed as though wholly his own.” The bishop was asked to produce his own commentary on Boethius, in which the suspect propositions were contained; he answered that he did not have it at hand.

The bishop denied that he had ever taught, believed, or committed to writing “that the divinity was not God,” and so forth. He brought forward as witnesses, especially two of his pupils: Rotold, Bishop of Évreux, later Archbishop of Rouen; and Master Ivo of Chartres, clearly another person from the famous Ivo, Bishop of Chartres. I believe this man to be Master Ivo, a regular canon of the Abbey of Saint-Victor near Paris, later created cardinal by Innocent II, to whom Bernard’s one hundred and ninety-third letter is addressed.

In these altercations the pope ordered the said book to be brought to the future council, “which he proposed to hold that same year in the city of Reims.” Yet it was postponed until mid-Lent of the following year, though still within one year of the Parisian assembly, which we have said was held at the preceding Easter festival.

LXII. “Meanwhile Gottschalk, at that time abbot of Mont-Saint-Éloi near Arras and later bishop of that same city, examined, by Eugenius’s command, the commentary on Boethius sent by its author. He extracted from it the suspect propositions and marked them as contrary to the authority of the books of the holy Fathers. Alberic, Bishop of Ostia and legate in Aquitaine, would have brought forward more concerning Gilbert’s life and doctrine, had premature death not shortly before removed him from the midst of men.

“At last, at the Council of Reims, they came to the discussion of the propositions which the aforesaid Abbot Gottschalk had marked. But because he was very inarticulate, the book, together with the testimonies of the saints contrary to it, was handed by the lord pope to Saint Bernard. The council consisted of bishops from four kingdoms: France, Germany, England, and Spain. Among them were great and notably learned men: Geoffrey of Loroux, Archbishop of Bordeaux, of whom Gilbert was a suffragan; Milo, Bishop of Thérouanne; Joscelin of Soissons; and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, to whom King Louis of the Franks, when leaving for Jerusalem, had entrusted the administration of the whole kingdom—and this,” Otto adds, “in accordance with the prerogative of that monastery.” [Note: [Col. 0046] Otto, *On Frederick I*, book I, ch. 55.] Geoffrey of Loroux, though he did not approve Gilbert’s doctrine, favored the man.

LXIII. “On the first day, when they entered the consistory, Gilbert had the bulk of great volumes brought in by his clerics, alleging that his opponents produced only truncated testimonies. Then Bernard said: ‘Why is it necessary to linger longer over words of this kind? The origin of this scandal comes from no other source than that many believe you to hold and teach that the divine essence or nature—his divinity, wisdom, goodness, and greatness—is not God, but is the form by which God is God. If you believe this, say so openly; or deny it.’

“He dared to say that this form was not God. Then Bernard said: ‘Behold, we have what we sought. Let this confession be written down.’ The supreme pontiff ordered this to be done; and Lord Henry of Pisa, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, later a monk of Clairvaux and, after being abbot of Saint Anastasius, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, went at his command and brought paper, pen, and ink.

“But while he was writing down that confession, Gilbert said to Bernard: ‘And you, write that divinity is God.’ Bernard replied: ‘Let it be written with an iron stylus and an adamantine nail.’ After much disputation back and forth, the cardinals said that they would henceforth decide the matter. The bishops, disturbed that the cardinals reserved the determination of the case to themselves alone, appealed to Bernard that propositions contrary to Gilbert’s should be composed together with a creed of faith, lest—as many among the cardinals who favored Gilbert wished—the council should dissolve without accomplishing anything.

“Bernard therefore did so. Then the bishops, through Hugh of Auxerre and Milo of Thérouanne, bishops, and Suger the abbot, offered the pope for confirmation a confession subscribed by themselves; and they readily obtained it. Finally Gilbert was summoned into the assembly, in the notable palace called Tau”—thus the residence of the Archbishop of Reims was named because of its resemblance to the Greek letter τ—“and freely renounced, one by one, the propositions he had himself put forward. The pope condemned them, together with their author’s book, strictly commanding that no one should dare to read or copy the same book until the Roman Church had first corrected it. When Gilbert said that he would correct it at the pope’s direction, the pope refused.” These details are taken piecemeal from Geoffrey.

LXIV. Otto has certain distinctive details, and certain details differing from Geoffrey. First, he reports that Gilbert’s examination began “after the synod had ended and the decrees had been promulgated”; then, after the week of mid-Lent had elapsed and the holy season of Passion Sunday was beginning, Gilbert was called into the midst for judgment.

Next, after he had read books of orthodox Fathers in his own defense, Eugenius—who had become weary, according to what Geoffrey ascribes to Bernard—simply asked Gilbert whether he believed that supreme essence to be God. Gilbert, wearied by the prolonged discussion, carelessly answered, “No.” A notary immediately recorded the utterance snatched from his lips.

After this, the assembly having been dismissed, Gilbert spent all that remained of the day and the following night courting his cardinal friends, of whom he had not a few.

LXV. On the following day his writing was read aloud and an explanation of it required by the bishops. Gilbert finally explained his opinion thus: if the name God is taken for nature itself, he granted that it is God; but not if it is taken for person. Otherwise, if he professed this “without qualification,” he would be led to assert that whatever is said of any person must equally be affirmed of the essence; and thus he would be compelled to confess “that, just as the person of the Son, so the divine essence without qualification, was incarnate and suffered.”

He supported this distinction by testimonies of the Fathers, Theodoret and Hilary, and by the authority of the Council of Toledo. “When the Abbot of Clairvaux wished to define that authority, and had put forward some words displeasing to the cardinals,” Gilbert requested that this be written down. Bernard, as Geoffrey records, replied: “Let it be written with an iron stylus and an adamantine nail.”

Finally, the holy abbot met with the bishops and set forth to them his faith against Gilbert’s propositions. The sacred senate of cardinals took this action by the Gallican Church so seriously that they complained to the pope against both the bishops and Bernard himself: because, “as though putting the finishing touch upon a judgment about to be rendered,” they had dared, without consulting the cardinals, to put their creed in writing, though this matter belonged to the Roman See.

At last Bernard, summoned at the pope’s command to appease the cardinals, answered humbly and reverently: “Neither he nor the lord bishops had determined anything concerning the aforesaid propositions. But because he had heard the Bishop of Poitiers say that his faith should be written down, and because he did not wish to do it alone, he had simply set forth what he thought under their authority and testimony.”

When this humble and modest answer had been received, the anger of the cardinals subsided, “yet in such a way that the aforesaid writing, as having been produced without consultation of the curia and as lacking the weight of authority, should not be held in the Church as a creed.” Thus “nothing could be defined concerning the three propositions because of the foregoing tumult.”

Otto says that this is not surprising. He adds that Gilbert differed from the other bishops on the fourth point: they professed that the nature was incarnate, but in the Son; Gilbert, that “the person of the Son was incarnate, not without his nature.” The Roman pontiff defined only the first point: that no reasoning in theology should divide nature and person, and that God should be said to be the divine essence not only in an ablative sense—“God by divine essence”—but also in the nominative sense—“the divine essence is God.”

Gilbert reverently accepted the pope’s judgment and, having been reconciled with his archdeacons, returned to his own diocese “with the integrity of his order and the fullness of his honor.” [Note: [Col. 0047] Otto, *On Frederick I*, book I, chs. 56–57.]

LXVI. In all this Otto plainly appears to have been greatly favorable to Gilbert. Nor therefore is it surprising that he subsequently doubts “whether the aforesaid Abbot of Clairvaux in this affair was deceived, as a man, through the frailty of human weakness; or whether the bishop, as a very learned man, escaped the Church’s judgment by shrewdly concealing his true opinion.”

But when Otto was near death, according to Radevicus, he ordered the book in which he had written these things to be brought to him and handed it to religious men, “that, if he seemed to have said anything in favor of Master Gilbert’s opinion which could offend anyone, it might be corrected at their judgment.” [Note: [Col. 0048] Radevicus, book II, ch. 11.]

On the whole dispute Geoffrey rightly refers readers to Bernard’s sermons on the Song of Songs, namely the eightieth sermon. In it the holy man does not hesitate to pronounce heretics those who persisted in defending Gilbert’s view, although he spared the author’s name because of his repentance.

§ VI.—On the Henricians and other heretics suppressed by Bernard.

LXVII. Bernard overcame Gilbert and Abelard, who distorted theology through a perverse use of philosophy, by reason and authority; but he overcame heretics also by deeds and examples. Various plagues of this kind infested various provinces of Gaul in that age: Tanchelm of Antwerp in Flanders; Peter of Bruys in Provence, from whom the Petrobrusians were named; Henry in Aquitaine; others, without a fixed leader, in Lorraine and in places neighboring Cologne, whom for that reason we shall call Cologne heretics. The Arnoldists may be added to all these.

[Col. 0049] LXVIII. Blessed Norbert attacked Tanchelm and his followers, as appears from his Life; and Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, “checked their course and assault” in the diocese of Utrecht. On this matter there survives in Tengnagel a letter of the Church of Utrecht to the same Frederick, “On Tanchelm the Seducer,” in which the origin and substance of that heresy are described.

What Peter the Venerable did against the Petrobrusians is taught by the treatise published by him against them. Bernard’s zeal for the Christian cause was exercised especially against the Henrician heresy, which he vigorously assailed in deeds and writings. On this subject one should read the two hundred and fortieth letter and the following letter, together with chapter six of book three of Geoffrey’s *Life of Bernard*; it is useful to elucidate all these from other records.

LXIX. Henry, whom the holy man calls “an apostate monk,” and whom Geoffrey after him calls a “pseudo-hermit,” is so termed in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, in the third volume of the *Analecta*, where his character and perverse actions are accurately described. The following words do not sufficiently indicate the place from which he came: “At about the same time,” namely under Bishop Hildebert, “there arose in the borders of the neighboring regions a certain hypocrite, whom his own conduct, perverse morals, and detestable doctrine declare worthy of scorpions and parricidal punishments.”

Under a pretended name of “holiness and learning,” he committed shameful offenses, claiming that from sight alone he knew the “faults of all mortals, unknown to others.” Two of his disciples, sent to Le Mans, reached “the suburbs of the city on Ash Wednesday.” “According to their master’s custom, they carried staffs and a banner of the cross, displaying by color and outward conduct the appearance of penitents.” Deceived by this appearance, the people of Le Mans “received them as angels.”

Bishop Hildebert also received them “kindly.” As he was about to undertake “the Roman journey,” he instructed his archdeacons, among other things, to permit “that pseudo-hermit Henry peaceful entry and leave to preach to the people”; a matter of which he later repented greatly. From this someone might infer that Henry came from the region near Le Mans, where he first offered the poison of his perverse teaching. For had he already been known elsewhere, the learned and discerning Bishop Hildebert would not so readily have admitted him into his city. Yet he could have come there from a distant region, perhaps even from Italy, as we shall say later.

LXX. When Henry entered the city, “the mob, according to its customary fashion, applauded the novelty.” Indeed, “many of the clerics supplied him with food and prepared a platform from which that preacher might address the crowds”; for “he was extraordinarily eloquent.” When he had been heard, “the common people turned in fury upon the clerics,” treating them “as heathens and tax collectors,” so that “they threatened their servants with tortures and would neither sell anything to them nor buy from them.” Indeed, “they had resolved not merely to demolish their houses and scatter their goods, but to stone them or hang them on the gallows, unless the prince and leading men had resisted their wicked attempts.”

LXXI. Though he learned of this late, the clergy of Le Mans forbade Henry and his associates to preach in a published document. Therefore Henry, learning of Hildebert’s return, “withdrew to the castle of Saint-Calais,” by no means abandoning his enterprises but daily breaking out into worse deeds.

Meanwhile, when Hildebert returned from the Roman journey and wished to impart his blessing to the people, he was received with indignity by a populace corrupted by the heretic’s discourses. He then approached the seducer and asked “what order’s office he exercised.” Henry answered that he was a deacon. Ordered to leave that province, he “secretly fled, intending in like manner to disturb other regions, unless rumor should outstrip him,” and to infect them with his venomous breath. Thus far the *Acts of Hildebert*.

LXXII. Meanwhile two disciples of Henry, Cyprian and Peter, recovered from his deceptions, as Hildebert’s seventy-eighth encyclical letter attests. There he portrays their master thus: “That Henry was a great snare of the devil and a renowned armor-bearer of Antichrist. Those aforementioned brethren clung for a long time to him, who counterfeited religion in dress and learning in speech, until both baseness in his life and error in his teaching became known to them. For when they learned that his ways were not right ways, they first returned to themselves; then they came over to us. He had infected our diocese so deeply that the clergy resisting him could scarcely preserve their liberty within the walls of the church.”

Thus Hildebert learned too late how great a danger follows from incautiously approving new teachers who corrupt their hearers’ minds under a show of piety.

LXXIII. From this it is clear that Henry infected Le Mans long before he entered the region of Toulouse, from which Bernard expelled him. For the Roman journey undertaken by Hildebert while still Bishop of Le Mans—at the time when that notorious deceiver sowed his tares at Le Mans—occurred before 1125, the year in which Hildebert was transferred to the metropolitan see of Tours. Bernard, however, did not travel to the Toulouse region until 1147.

Certainly, in his two hundred and forty-first letter, written while he was in the Toulouse region, the holy man sufficiently indicates this in these words: “Inquire, if you please, how he departed from the city of Lausanne, how from Le Mans, how from Poitiers, how from Bordeaux.” This appears to be the course of that apostate’s journey: from Lausanne and then from Le Mans he began his preaching. Perhaps he came to Lausanne from Italy, from which such dregs migrated into the regions of Gaul: remnants of the Manichees, as were also those heretics of Cambrai, brought from Italy, who were condemned in 1025 at the Synod of Arras; at which time similar plagues at Orléans likewise perished by fire.

Indeed, the *Cistercian Exordium*, in book seven of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 17, calls the Henricians Manichees. It relates that the papal legate and other bishops came with the holy man into the Toulouse region “to refute the heresy of the Manichees.” Now the most illustrious Bishop of Meaux, in his outstanding work *On the Variations of Heretics*, book XI, clearly shows how the name and errors of Manichees apply to such heretics and their followers.

LXXIV. These same Henrician heretics spread into Périgueux under the leadership and standard-bearer Pontius, as is taught by Heribert’s letter in the third volume of our *Analecta*, where the distinctive doctrines of those Pontians are reported. Hence Bernard went to the peoples of Périgueux, or Périgord, as is clear from the third part of book six concerning his Miracles, no. 4. It states that he found many Arians among the people of Toulouse and put them to flight, together with Henry the heretic.

Indeed, this same Henry, previously condemned at the Council of Pisa, is said to have been entrusted to Bernard in order that he might become a monk at Clairvaux. But after receiving from Bernard letters addressed to the brethren of Clairvaux, he preferred stubbornly to persist in the error once undertaken rather than to return by this short path to the way of salvation.

LXXV. Bernard portrays Henry in vivid colors in the aforesaid two hundred and forty-first letter. He writes that Henry was learned and had an appearance of piety, but was devoted to gambling and prostitutes. He records approximately these impious doctrines: no respect was due to priests and clerics; the sacraments and feast days were to be abolished; baptism was denied to little children.

A heretic of another class appears in Hildebert’s fifty-first letter: one who rejected the intercessions of saints and wrongly tried to enlist Hildebert himself as patron of his sect. It must now be investigated whether those heretics were the same as those whom Bernard attacks in the sixty-fifth sermon and the following sermons on the Song of Songs.

LXXVI. I was once persuaded that they were no others; but, having found the letter of Everwin, Abbot of Steinfeld, which gave occasion to the aforesaid sermons, the opinion must be changed. These were Cologne heretics, agreeing with the Henricians in some things, but differing from them in many.

Everwin divides the Cologne heretics into two classes. Some said that the Church existed only among themselves, as if they alone adhered to Christ’s footsteps. In food they prohibited the use of milk and everything made from it. In their sacraments they covered themselves with a veil and declared that each day they consecrated their own food and drink into Christ’s body and blood; all others, they said, were far from the truth in the sacraments.

Besides baptism in water, they admitted another baptism in fire and Spirit, conferred by the laying on of hands alone. They rejected our baptism together with marriage. Finally, they said that any one of their elect or baptized members had the power to baptize others who were worthy, and to make Christ’s body and blood upon his own table.

LXXVII. Others, however, granted to the priests of the Church—because they lived in a secular manner—the power of consecrating and administering the other sacraments, except baptism, which they administered only to adults, not to little children. They regarded every marriage as fornication except that contracted between a male and female virgin. Finally, they rejected the suffrages of the saints, fasts, and other mortifications of the body, as well as purgatory and prayers for the dead.

LXXVIII. Thus the Henricians and the Cologne heretics shared the same disposition: hatred of the ministers of the Church, of the sacraments, of infant baptism, and of marriage. Their distinctive points were few, indicating not a different kind of sect but merely a certain diversity among its heads. In a word, they were different branches growing from the same root. Nor do I doubt that those Cologne heretics came from Tanchelm’s workshop. This layman, in Flanders—especially around Antwerp, according to Abelard—spread his errors and rose to such madness that he had himself called the Son of God and, as is said, caused a temple to be built for himself by the people whom he had deceived. For this reason, at Antwerp, in the church of St. Michael, the bishop of Tournai, under whose jurisdiction that place then lay, established a body of twelve clerics to oppose these impious doctrines. That church was afterwards entrusted to St. Norbert.

What Tanchelm’s perverse doctrines were, we learn from the letter of the Church of Utrecht to Frederick, bishop of Cologne, “concerning Tanchelm the deceiver.” For he maintained “that the churches of God ought to be regarded as brothels; that nothing is effected through the ministry of priests at the Lord’s table; that these should be called pollutions, not sacraments; and that the efficacy of the sacraments derives from the merits and holiness of their ministers.” All these notions agree remarkably with the ravings of the heretics mentioned above. A certain priest named Evervacher, “apostatizing from priestly dignity, attached himself to the teaching of that nefarious man and followed him to Rome”; and later he inflicted much injury upon the Church of Utrecht. The clergy of Utrecht further thank Frederick because he “checked Tanchelm’s course and assault.” From this it is understood that his errors had penetrated as far as the diocese of Utrecht, indeed also that of Cologne (as is clear from Everwin’s letter), and that those Cologne heretics arose from the same author.

LXXIX. Hugh Metellus, then a regular canon at Toul, testifies in a letter to Henry, bishop of that city, that plagues of this sort had crept into the territory of Toul. “There lurk within your bishopric,” he says, “indeed they now openly appear, pestilent men who may more rightly be called beasts, because they live beast-like. For they detest marriage, abominate baptism, mock the sacraments of the Church, and abhor the Christian name.” This was undoubtedly the hostile and ill-fated offspring of the Cologne heretics.

[Col. 0053]

LXXX. The Henricians were succeeded—or joined—by people of the same stamp, who styled themselves Cathars, that is, “the pure alone.” Bonacursus, who had formerly been their master at Milan, exposed and refuted their errors in a book published in volume thirteen of the *Spicilegium*. From it it is evident that they, like the earlier heretics, were infected with Manichaean errors. Gilbert of Hoyland seems to attack the Cathars in the thirty-sixth sermon on the Song of Songs, no. 6:

> “In these days certain trees spring up which the heavenly Father has not planted—trees not planted from our Lebanon. They display strength in work, insensibility to injuries, endurance in frugality. They seem to be cedars, but they are not of Lebanon, because their mind and conscience are unclean.”

There are likewise extant sermons of Ekbert, abbot of Schönau, against the Cathars.

LXXXI. Bonacursus joins the Passagians and Arnoldists to the Cathars. The former said that all the rites of the Mosaic law must be observed; they denied the equality of the Son and the Holy Spirit, and rejected all the teachers of the universal Church, especially the authority of the Roman Church. The latter—that is, the Arnoldists—held that “because of the wickedness of the clergy, the sacraments of the Church ought to be avoided.”

LXXXII. I think they were so called from that Arnold, a factious man, who, under the pretext of restoring liberty and the republic in the City, wished all temporal rights to be taken from the pope, leaving him only spiritual authority together with tithes and offerings. He was a native of Brescia, an Italian city, and a cleric of that church; he had had Peter Abelard as his teacher. According to Otto of Freising, he was a lover of singularity and eager for novelty. Returning to Italy from his studies in France, he put on a religious habit, so as the more readily to deceive the unsuspecting. Yet he hated monks, and especially clerics, while flattering laymen.

“For he said that neither clerics possessing property, nor bishops possessing regalian rights, nor monks possessing estates, could by any means be saved: all these things belonged to the prince. Besides this, he is said not to have held sound views concerning the sacrament of the altar and infant baptism.” [Note: [Col. 0053] Otto, *De Friderico*, book II, chapter 20.]

And so he was tainted with the errors of the Petrobrusians and Henricians. Innocent II expelled the man from Italy and compelled him to withdraw to Zürich among the Swiss. When he learned of Innocent’s death, he entered Rome near the beginning of Eugenius’s pontificate; seeing that the city had turned against the pope, he kindled the fire of sedition. The affair finally advanced so far that the cardinals were maltreated, some even wounded, and Eugenius himself was driven from the City. Bernard undertook the defense of the pope’s cause and wrote on this matter his excellent letter to the Romans, numbered 242. It is followed by another on the same subject to Conrad, king of the Romans, whom the Romans vainly attempted to draw to their side by letters reported by Otto. [Note: [Col. 0053] Otto, *De Friderico*, book I, chapter 28.] Thus the holy man failed neither in any affair of the Church nor in any necessity, being born for the common benefit of the Christian commonwealth. At last Arnold was seized and, by the prefect of the City whom he had so extravagantly flattered, was put to death by the gallows; his corpse was reduced to ashes “lest his body should be held in veneration by the foolish populace.” For more concerning him, see Otto and, from him, the notes on Bernard’s 195th letter.

§ VII.—On the preaching of the holy expedition by St. Bernard, and its unhappy outcome.

LXXXIII. Among Bernard’s last labors must be counted his preaching of the holy expedition to the Holy Land. How much toil and distress this affair caused him may readily be understood from his *Life* and writings. The occasion of this expedition, as we learn from Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0054] Ibid., chapter 34 ff.], arose through Louis the Younger, king of the Franks. Pressed by a desire to go to the holy places, because his brother Philip, “bound by the same vow,” had been prevented by death from fulfilling it, he disclosed his plan to the princes of the realm. They resolved that Bernard should be consulted. When the holy abbot was summoned, he judged that a matter of such importance ought to be referred “to the judgment of the Roman pontiff.” Eugenius greatly praised and approved this decision, granting to the aforesaid abbot—regarded among all the peoples of Gaul and Germany as a prophet or apostle—authority to preach and to move everyone’s minds toward this undertaking. Bernard at length obeyed the apostolic letters and, “having stirred the hearts of many toward the overseas expedition,” marked King Louis with the cross at Vézelay, “together with Count Thierry of Flanders, Henry, son of Theobald of Blois, and” other barons and nobles.

LXXXIV. Meanwhile, a certain monk Ralph, while similarly preaching the cross in Germany, incited Christians to massacre the Jews. Bernard restrained the man by letters and himself undertook to preach the holy expedition in the eastern kingdom of the Franks—that is, in that region of Germany which lies on the Rhine. Consequently Emperor Conrad convened a general assembly at Speyer. Bernard went there and “persuaded the prince, together with Frederick his brother’s son and other princes and illustrious men, to take the cross, performing many miracles publicly and privately.” Bernard softened Frederick, duke of Swabia, who bitterly resented his son’s having been marked with the cross; he ordered the monk Ralph to be shut up again in his cloister; and, in his own place, gave Abbot Adam of Ebrach as a companion to Conrad, who was departing for Bavaria, to press forward the business of the journey.

There survives Bernard’s letter on this matter to the Eastern Franks, now numbered 363, followed immediately by another to Henry, archbishop of Mainz, to restrain Ralph. “Therefore,” says Otto, “not only from the Roman Empire but also from neighboring kingdoms—that is, western France, England, and Pannonia—countless peoples and nations were moved by the report of this expedition to take the cross; and suddenly almost the entire West became so quiet that it was regarded as unlawful not only to wage war, but even for anyone to carry arms publicly.” [Col. 0055]

LXXXV. This great movement of the entire West was attributed to Bernard’s preaching. Yet when the expedition did not succeed as hoped, all the odium of its ill result, according to the common habit of mortals who judge matters by their outcomes, was also thrown upon him. Scarcely anything caused Bernard greater sorrow than this—not so much on his own account as on God’s. Hence, at the beginning of the second book of *On Consideration*, he says:

> “If one of two things must happen, I prefer the murmuring of men to be against us rather than against God. It is good for me if he deigns to use me as a shield. I willingly receive upon myself the abusive tongues of detractors,”

and so forth.

Indeed, almost everyone’s minds were so disturbed by this outcome that the holy teacher calls blessed the man “who has not been offended in him.” Finally, how great Bernard’s grief was over this matter is evident both from letter 288, which he wrote concerning it while confined to bed, perhaps from distress of mind, and from the letter of John, abbot of La Maison-Dieu, to Bernard himself, now counted among Bernard’s letters as no. 386. In it he consoles the holy man, whom he had heard to be afflicted by the adverse outcome of the expedition.

LXXXVI. Yet there were those who undertook to defend Bernard’s cause. Among them, not least should be counted Otto, bishop of Freising, who was not generally very favorable to Bernard. In the *Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 60, he makes a digression to excuse the outcome of that expedition, in which he himself took part. At the end of this digression, philosophical rather than historical, he concludes in Bernard’s favor:

> “Although, if we should say that the holy abbot was inspired by the Spirit of God to stir us up, but that we, through our pride and self-indulgence, did not observe wholesome commands and thus deservedly incurred loss of goods and persons, this would not be at variance with ancient reasoning or examples.”

Yet he adds one point: namely, that “the spirits of prophets are not always subject to prophets,” thereby suggesting that it is uncertain whether Bernard had formed his judgment concerning this expedition and its outcome by a divine spirit.

LXXXVII. Nevertheless Bernard himself, at the beginning of the second book of *On Consideration* addressed to Eugenius, where he defends his action against calumny, does not deny that he was divinely moved to it. “We said,” he declares, “‘Peace,’ and there is no peace; we promised good things, and behold, trouble.” Then, in his defense, he adds: “As though we had acted in this undertaking rashly or lightly. We certainly ran in it, not as uncertainly, but at your command—indeed, through you, at God’s command.” Further on, when men’s reproaches are cast at him—“How do we know that the word has gone forth from the Lord? What signs do you perform, that we may believe you?”—he replies, addressing Eugenius: “There is no reason why I should answer these things myself; my modesty must indeed be spared. Answer for me—and for yourself too—according to what you have heard and seen.” By these words he undoubtedly and modestly alludes to the miracles he had performed to confirm his preaching.

LXXXVIII. But Geoffrey most effectively vindicates his holy father from calumny in book III of his *Life*, chapter 4. First, because the original proposal of that expedition did not come from Bernard:

> “For when the reported necessity had already moved the minds of many, and he had been asked once and again by the king of the Franks on this account, and had also been urged by apostolic letters, he did not even then consent to speak or give advice concerning it, until at last he was commanded by the general letter of the pope himself to set it forth to peoples and princes as the tongue of the Roman Church.”

Secondly, because the office of preaching, which he had undertaken in obedience, was divinely confirmed by so many and such great miracles and signs “that it would be difficult even to count them, much less to relate them.” Finally, if by that departure the Eastern Church did not deserve to be delivered, the heavenly Church at least deserved to be filled and gladdened through the death of those “who, in the fruits of repentance, rendered to Christ souls purified by various tribulations.” And this is precisely what John, the holy abbot of La Maison-Dieu, reported to Bernard that he had learned by revelation.

LXXXIX. But why delay in defending Bernard, whose authority has long since prevailed so greatly with all—even the heterodox—that his life, outstanding holiness, and teaching have been approved by the common judgment and esteem of all?

XC. These are the matters which seemed fit to preface concerning this new edition of the works of St. Bernard. If it appears accurate to learned men, they will owe thanks to my fellow laborers, Dom Michel Germain and Dom Thierry Ruinart, and also Dom Edmond Martène, who devoted their work vigorously and most affectionately to this edition. As for me, let this be my sole recompense—the only object I had—that I may, by however slight a labor of mine, have been of some service to the devotees of St. Bernard, to the Church, and to the Christian commonwealth.

[Col. 0057]

Added in the edition of 1719.

These are the matters which Dom Mabillon thought fit to preface concerning this new edition of the works of St. Bernard. If it appears accurate to learned men, they will owe thanks to that learned author, who throughout his life, though occupied with other and very weighty studies, devoted every care and all diligence to recovering and polishing Bernard’s works. They will also owe thanks to Dom Massuet, who had begun to contribute his labor to this edition and would have continued to do so, had premature death not cut short the course of his studies.

To him are due, in volume I, two newly discovered letters, namely 418 and 419; a third taken from volume IV of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, numbered 425; and also two charters, the first for the monasteries of Luxeuil and St. Aper, the second for the monastery of St. Amand. In the second volume the following new items will be found: namely, the third book of the letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, and Dom Massuet’s admonition, in which he vindicates for Guigo V, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, the complete letter attributed to William of St. Thierry. Also included is another observation of his, attributing to William of St. Thierry the *Treatise on Contemplating God* and the *Treatise on the Nature and Dignity of Love*. Finally, there is the hitherto unpublished letter of Tromundus, monk of Clairvaux, concerning the canonization of St. Bernard.

[Col. 0057]

# BERNARDINE CHRONOLOGY

[Col. 0057A] In the year of Christ 1091, the fourth of Pope Urban II, the thirty-fifth of Emperor Henry IV, and the thirty-first of Philip I, king of the Franks, Bernard was born in the castle called Fontaines, near Dijon in Burgundy. His father was Tescelin Sor, lord of Fontaines; his mother was Aleth, daughter of Bernard, lord of Montbard. His paternal house was recently granted, through the favor of Louis XIII, king of the Franks, to the Reverend Fathers of the Feuillant Congregation and converted into a monastery. On the lineage of St. Bernard, read the preliminary Admonition at the beginning of the *Life of St. Bernard*, and John the Hermit in the fourth *Life*, where the holy man’s paternal line is said to have drawn its origin from the ancient family of the dukes of Burgundy.

1098. Blessed Robert, abbot of Molesme, taking with him twenty-one monks from that same monastery, withdrew into the wilderness of Cîteaux and there built a new monastery, in the diocese of Chalon, about five leagues from Dijon. Walter, bishop of Chalon, and Hugh, bishop of Lyon, assisted and approved; Duke Odo of Burgundy granted the lands. There, with his companions, Robert observed the Rule of St. Benedict more strictly and exactly. Since Benedict’s feast fell this year on Palm Sunday, that work first began then. Among Blessed Robert’s first companions were Alberic, Odo, John, Stephen, Letaldus, and Peter.

1099. In the forty-third year of Emperor Henry IV, the thirty-ninth of Philip, king of the Franks, and the nineteenth year of Urban II’s pontificate, Urban died on the fourth day before the Kalends of August; Paschal II, formerly a monk of Cluny, succeeded him.

At the entreaties of the monks of Molesme, in a Roman council and by command of the pope, Blessed Robert returned to Molesme; Alberic, formerly prior, succeeded him at Cîteaux. The church was dedicated this year in honor of the Blessed Virgin.

1100. This year the monks John and Ilbodus were sent to Rome by Alberic, abbot of Cîteaux, bearing letters of recommendation from Cardinals John and Benedict, Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and Walter, bishop of Chalon. At their request Paschal II confirmed the Cistercian institute by a special privilege issued at Troyes on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth indiction and second year of his pontificate. It is found in Baronius and Manriquez.

1101. Alberic, abbot, established in the new monastery the strictest observance of the Rule of St. Benedict, rejecting everything contrary to the Rule.

Blessed Bruno, founder of the Carthusian Order—which began in 1086—died. He was a native of Cologne, distinguished for holiness and learning.

1102. Odo, duke of Burgundy and founder of Cîteaux, died and was buried in the church of Cîteaux. In the same year his son Henry assumed the monastic habit there.

1103. The Cistercians are believed to have changed their black habit for white and to have undertaken the daily recitation of the Office of the Blessed Virgin.

1105. Aleth, St. Bernard’s mother, is thought to have died on the Kalends of September, according to the necrology of St. Benignus at Dijon, where she was buried. Her body was transferred to Clairvaux 145 years later. William describes her death in book I, chapter 2, of the *Life of St. Bernard*.

1106. In the seventh year of Paschal II, the forty-sixth of Philip I, king of the Franks, Henry IV ended his unhappy life in the forty-ninth year of his reign. He was succeeded by his son Henry V, no less hostile than his father toward the Church. Journeying to Rome, he laid hands upon Pope Paschal and violently extorted from him the investitures of churches; he also extorted the imperial crown in 1111.

1108. In the ninth year of Paschal II and the second of Henry V, Philip, king of the Franks, died at Melun on the third day before the Kalends of August. His son Louis, surnamed the Fat, succeeded him.

1109. Blessed Alberic, second abbot of Cîteaux, died on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, after nine and a half years of rule. Blessed Stephen Harding succeeded him; he was of noble English birth, had formerly served as prior, and had himself left Molesme with others in pursuit of a stricter life.

1110. This year, on the third day before the Kalends of May, Blessed Robert, abbot of Molesme and first founder of Cîteaux, passed to heaven—not in 1098, as is commonly believed.

1113. The fourteenth year of Paschal II, eighth of Henry V, and sixth of Louis VI is famous for Blessed Bernard’s conversion. At about twenty-three years of age, he entered Stephen’s Cistercian community with thirty companions. From that time the Cistercian Order began wonderfully to expand and flourish.

[Col. 0058C] In the same year La Ferté, the first daughter-house of Cîteaux, was founded in the diocese of Chalon on the river Grosne by the lords of Vergy, Savaric and his son William, counts of Chalon. Its first abbot was Bertrand.

1114. St. Bernard divinely obtained skill and strength for reaping, since bodily weakness prevented him from other work; *Life*, book I, chapter 4.

Pontigny, Cîteaux’s second daughter-house, was founded four leagues from Auxerre, on the freehold of Herbert, canon of Auxerre, with the support of Count Hervé of Nevers, under Bishop Humbald. The basilica of this monastery, afterwards built by Theobald, count of Champagne, retained its founder’s name. Its first abbot was Hugh of Mâcon, later bishop of Auxerre, to whom several of Bernard’s letters are addressed. [Col. 0059A]

1115. Clairvaux and Morimond, the third and fourth daughters of Cîteaux, were founded this year. Clairvaux, on the river Aube in the county of Champagne and the diocese of Langres, was founded on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, not by Theobald—as some think, confusing the translation of Clairvaux monastery, discussed under the year 1035, with its foundation—but by Hugh, count of Troyes, as will be proved in the notes on letter 31. Bernard, aged twenty-four, was appointed over Clairvaux and consecrated by William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, while Joscerand, bishop of Langres, was absent; *Life*, book I, chapter 7.

Morimond, in the same diocese, was founded by Odolric of Aigremont and his wife Adeline, lords of Choiseul. Its first abbot was Arnold, to whom letter 4 is addressed. These are the four abbeys, as it were the four original daughters of Cîteaux, from which all the rest afterwards sprang.

[Col. 0059B] In the same year Ivo, bishop of Chartres, a most learned man, died. He was succeeded by Geoffrey, who had served as papal legate in Gaul and was very dear to St. Bernard; see letters 15, 47, and 55, *On Consideration*, book IV, chapter 5, and the *Life of St. Bernard*, book II, chapters 1 and 6, and book IV, chapter 4.

1116. Blessed Stephen convened the first general chapter of Cîteaux, thereafter to be held annually on the Ides of September, as Jacques de Vitry states in chapter 14 of his *Western History*.

1117. Blessed Bernard, held by a grave illness, was entrusted to the care of a rustic physician through the intervention of William, bishop of Châlons; *Life*, book I, chapter 7. In or about this year occurred, it is said, the conversion of Tescelin, St. Bernard’s father. Not long afterwards, renowned for sanctity, he died on 11 April, according to the necrology of St. Benignus at Dijon.

1118. In the twelfth year of Henry V and tenth of Louis VI, Paschal II died after eighteen years and five months of pontificate. He was succeeded by Gelasius II, likewise formerly a monk of Cluny. Emperor Henry set against him Maurice Burdinus, archbishop of Braga, under the name Gregory.

In this same year began the Order of the Knights of the Temple, whose first founders were Hugh of Payns and Geoffrey of St. Omer, as William of Tyre testifies in book XII of his *History of the Holy War*. According to the same author, the Order was confirmed at the council of Troyes in 1128, as is expressly stated by the scribe of the council at Michaelbeuern. It was later suppressed by Clement V under Philip IV, king of the Franks, in the year of Christ 1313, at the Council of Vienne.

The monastery of Trois-Fontaines, the first daughter-house of Clairvaux, was founded in the diocese of Châlons. Its first abbot was Roger; its second, Guy, to whom letters 69 and 70 are addressed. Fontenay also was founded, Clairvaux’s second daughter-house, in the diocese of Autun. Its first abbot was Godfrey, Bernard’s kinsman. Having founded and regularly organized the place, the Clairvaux book of burials reports that he returned to his own Clairvaux, where he became third prior and finally bishop of Langres. [Col. 0059D]

1119. In the thirteenth year of Henry V and eleventh of Louis VI, Gelasius II was taken from life at Cluny. He was succeeded by Callistus II, formerly bishop of Vienne and called Guy. This year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, he held a council at Reims and happily suppressed Burdinus’s schism.

In the same year the document commonly called the *Charter of Charity*, consisting of thirty articles or chapters, was drawn up under Blessed Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, with the assent of the other co-abbots, to provide for the peace and tranquility of the Cistercian Order. It was approved by Pope Callistus II. It is found in Manriquez.

1120. St. Norbert, whom Bernard calls “the flute of the Holy Spirit” in letter 56, founded the Premonstratensian Order at a place in the territory of Laon commonly called Prémontré. See letter 255 and its notes. [Col. 0060A]

1121. The synod of Soissons against Peter Abelard was held under the presidency of Conon, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See. Peter himself was compelled to commit his book on the Trinity to the flames. William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, died at the beginning of the same year; see the notes on letter 3.

Foigny was founded in the diocese of Laon; Bernard wrote letters 72, 73, and 74 to its abbot, Rainald.

1122. Peter Maurice, an Auvergnat by nationality, surnamed the Venerable and Bernard’s dearest friend, became abbot of Cluny during the octave of the Assumption. See the notes on St. Bernard’s first letter.

1123. About this year Peter, abbot of La Ferté, was elected bishop of Tarentaise, the first bishop from the Cistercian family. He was replaced by Bartholomew, Bernard’s brother.

[Col. 0060B] Likewise, after Adam, abbot of St. Denis near Paris, died, Suger was declared his successor by the unanimous votes of the electors. Several of Bernard’s letters to him survive.

1124. In the eighteenth year of Emperor Henry V and sixteenth of Louis VI, king of the Franks, Pope Callistus died in the sixth year of his pontificate. Honorius II, formerly called Lambert and bishop of Ostia, ascended the apostolic see in the same year.

1125. Emperor Henry V died at Utrecht on the Rhine after reigning nineteen years. Since he left no children, a disastrous and prolonged conflict arose between Lothair, duke of Saxony, and Conrad, nephew through the sister of the deceased Henry. Conrad, proclaimed king by his brother Frederick and others, crossed the Alps, was received by the Milanese, and was anointed king at Monza, the seat of the Italian kingdom, by their archbishop Anselm; Otto of Freising relates this in book VII, chapter 17, of the *Chronicle*. Bernard was later obliged to labor greatly for the reconciliation of the Milanese with Innocent and Lothair II, in whose favor Conrad yielded the supreme authority of the Empire by right of election.

In the same year a severe famine, raging especially in Gaul and Burgundy, exercised Bernard’s charity; *Life*, book I, chapter 10.
