In that year he was also attacked by a grave disease and came into danger of death, but was at last restored to health through the aid of the Blessed Virgin and Saints Benedict and Lawrence; ibid. Thereafter the fame of his exceptional holiness and heavenly teaching spread through city and world. [Col. 0060C]

1126. Otto, later bishop of Freising and a celebrated historian, assumed the monastic habit at Morimond. As his intimate friend Rahewin writes, he was grandson of Emperor Henry IV, nephew of Henry V, half-brother of Conrad, and uncle of Frederick, through his father Leopold, the most illustrious and pious margrave of Austria, and his mother Agnes, daughter of Henry IV.

[Col. 0060D] 1127. About this year Stephen, formerly chancellor and now bishop of Paris, was recalled from attendance at court to a better course of life by Bernard’s admonitions. He was grievously harassed by King Louis but at last, after many attacks, was restored to favor through the efforts of the Cistercians, especially Bernard. Henry, archbishop of Sens, experienced the same thing not long afterward and for the same reason, and had the same patron and defender of his cause. Consult letter 45 and its notes.

Igny, the fourth daughter-house of Clairvaux, was founded in the diocese of Reims by Rainald of Prats, archbishop of Reims. Its first abbot was Humbert, a monk of La Chaise-Dieu who became a monk of Clairvaux. Not long afterwards, out of love of quiet, he resigned his office and returned to Clairvaux. Bernard, then detained in Italy because of the schism, sharply rebuked him in letter 141; nevertheless, he continued in this holy retirement until the day of his death, when St. Bernard delivered a sermon on his eminent virtues. The second abbot was Guerric, equally renowned for piety and writings; his sermons are here in volume VI. [Col. 0061A]

1128. The Council of Troyes was held—not in 1127, as the council’s scribe at Michaelbeuern testifies—on the feast of St. Hilary, under the presidency of Matthew of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See. Stephen of Cîteaux, Bernard of Clairvaux, and other abbots of the same Order attended. There the Fathers prescribed a Rule and white garments for the Templars; Eugenius III later had a red cross sewn onto them.

Regny was founded in the diocese of Auxerre.

1129. Matthew of Albano—these are the words of Alberic in his *Chronicle*—a legate from the Cluniac Order, held a council at Châlons on the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There, on the advice of St. Bernard the abbot, Henry, bishop of Verdun, resigned his bishopric; and a certain Ursio, abbot of St. Denis at Reims, became bishop for two years.

Ourscamp was founded in the diocese of Noyon by Bishop Simon. [Col. 0061B]

1130. In the fifth year of Emperor Lothair II and twenty-second of Louis VI, king of the Franks, Pope Honorius died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of his pontificate. A most serious schism arose in the Church of God. Innocent II, formerly called Gregory, was canonically elected on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March; but Peter, son of Peter Leo, was intruded through the violence of his friends, who were very powerful in the City, and through the support of Roger of Sicily. Bernard vigorously defended Innocent’s cause for eight years. See letter 124 and those following. For among other things, in that same year, he was unanimously appointed arbiter by the Fathers of the council held at Étampes on this matter; he declared Innocent preferable to Anacletus and persuaded King Henry of England to receive him; *Life*, book II, chapter 1. See our General Preface, § 4.

In the same year Bernard, with the greatest humility of spirit, refused the bishopric of Genoa, vacant through the death in the previous year of Sigefrid. Baldwin, however, at the council held at Clermont in Gaul, was the first Cistercian enrolled in the sacred college of cardinals. Martin, that most upright man whom Bernard mentions in book IV, chapter 5, of *On Consideration*, is thought to have been associated with him. On Baldwin, see letters 144 and 244. [Col. 0061C]

1131. After Innocent, who had withdrawn to Gaul toward the end of the preceding year, was magnificently received at Liège, Bernard checked Emperor Lothair, who was demanding episcopal investitures. There the supreme pontiff crowned him king of Germany, to receive the imperial diadem at Rome two years later. When Lent of the present year had been completed at Liège, Innocent returned to Gaul and set out for the council against Anacletus, convened at Reims in October. He consecrated Louis the Younger king in place of his brother Philip, who had been unhappily killed by a fall from a horse.

When that council had ended, Suger says in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, the lord pope chose to stay at Auxerre during the remaining part of the passing year, after first visiting Cluny, whose church he dedicated, then Clairvaux and other churches, with Bernard accompanying him everywhere. Ernaldus, in book II, chapter 1, of the *Life of Bernard*, relates the assembly at Liège after the Council of Reims, contrary to Suger’s explicit authority. [Col. 0061D]

In this year also, according to the great Belgian Chronicle, Bernard was elected to the bishopric of Châlons but refused it, and through his intervention Geoffrey, abbot of St. Médard at Soissons, became bishop of Châlons. Alberic reports the same and adds that Innocent consecrated the church of St. Médard on the Ides of October, before the Council of Reims, as the chronicle of that monastery states.

In the same year Thomas, prior of St. Victor at Paris, a most upright man, was cruelly murdered by the nephews of Theobald Neoterius, archdeacon of Paris. Thomas had become hated by him for reproaching ecclesiastics with their exactions. Not long afterward Archembald, subdeacon of Orléans, suffered the same death and for the same cause, through John, likewise archdeacon of the church of the Holy Cross. Bernard wrote letters 158, 159, 160, and 162 on behalf of the prior of St. Victor, and letter 61 on behalf of the subdeacon. Both causes were undertaken and heard in the Council of Jouarre, in the diocese of Meaux. [Col. 0062A]

Moreruela was founded in Castile and the territory of Zamora; the monastery of St. John of Tarouca in Portugal, diocese of Lamego; Longpont in the diocese of Soissons; Cherlieu in the diocese of Besançon; Bonmont in Savoy, diocese of Geneva; and Rievaulx in England, diocese of York.

1132. Bernard accompanied Innocent, departing from Gaul, into Italy; he reconciled the Pisans and Genoese, and modestly and steadfastly refused the bishopric of Genoa again offered to him, whether Sirus had relinquished it or had not yet been raised to the see.

A great controversy also arose between the Cluniacs and the Cistercians, namely on account of the privilege by which Innocent exempted the latter from payment of tithes. See letters 228 and 283.

The monastery of Vaucelles was founded in the diocese of Cambrai; see letter 186. The monastery of Fountains was also founded in England, diocese of York. See letters 92, 94 ff. [Col. 0062B]

1133. When St Bernard had set out for Italy in the preceding year, and Innocent lacked sufficient forces to conquer Rome—for Lothair supplied only two thousand armed men—he wrote Letter 138 to Henry, king of Great Britain, asking him to bring assistance. At last, however, Innocent entered the city and crowned Lothair emperor in the Lateran basilica. When Lothair departed, Innocent was compelled to yield to Anacletus, who was ravaging the city, and withdrew to Pisa. From there Bernard was sent to Germany to reconcile Conrad [Col. 0062C] with Emperor Lothair. Taking advantage of this occasion, Roger, tyrant of Sicily, who had been granted the title of king by Anacletus, attempted to draw the Pisans away from obedience to Innocent. Since they remained steadfast in the faith, the holy abbot sent them a congratulatory letter that year, Letter 130. Moreover, during that journey occurred the conversion of Mascelin, concerning which see *Life*, Book 4, chapter 3, and likewise that of the duchess of Lorraine, ibid.

1134. The Council of Pisa was held. As Bernard, by Innocent’s command, was travelling through Lombardy to attend it after peace had been made between Lothair and Conrad, the Milanese—deprived of communion in the sacraments and of metropolitan rank because, having followed Archbishop Anselm, they had adhered to Conrad and Anacletus—addressed him by letter concerning their restoration to the favour of the pope and Emperor Lothair. He promised them that he would come after the council, in Letters 132 and 133. Without delay, once the council had been concluded chiefly through his prudence, he was deputed, together with Matthew of Albano and Guido, bishop of Pisa, both cardinals, and Geoffrey of Chartres [Col. 0062D], to arrange peace for the Milanese. Received by them with immense applause and the highest reverence, he scarcely escaped the archiepiscopal office, which they obstinately pressed upon him. Many there were converted, concerning whom see Letter 135; and in that same place he established the first colony of his Order, namely Chiaravalle—incorrectly called by some Clairvaux.

Then, by Innocent’s command, as Sigonius relates in *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book 11, he set out to reconcile the Lombard cities among themselves, and went to Pavia and Cremona. But when he achieved nothing among the people of Crema, he reported their obstinacy to Innocent in Letter 318.

Meanwhile, after the council Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian Order, passed to heaven. Stephen, too, abbot of Cîteaux, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of April [28 March]. After the rejection of Guy, who, elected while Stephen was still living, had carried the pastoral staff for six months, he was succeeded by Rainald, son of Milo, count of [Col. 0063A] Bar-sur-Seine, as Orderic, monk of Clairvaux, says in Book 8. He arranged at the General Chapter the distinguished ordinances, comprising eighty-seven chapters, which may be seen in the *Annals* of Manriquez.

Besides the Milanese Chiaravalle, the following were founded: Hem [lacuna]erodium, in the diocese of Trier; and Clairvallis, in the diocese of Laon. The first abbot was Henry of Murdach, to whom Letter 321 is addressed.

1135. As Bernard was returning from Italy through the city of Milan, see *Life*, Book 2, chapter 4, Clairvaux was transferred to a more convenient site, *Life*, Book 2, chapter 5. When he had scarcely settled there even briefly, he was commanded to go to Aquitaine with Geoffrey of Chartres, in order to recall Count William of Poitiers and other schismatics, seduced by Gerard, bishop of Angoulême; ibid., chapter 6. Afterwards, restored for a while to himself, he undertook that celebrated exposition of the *Song of Songs*, encouraged by the other Bernard, prior [Col. 0063B] of the Carthusian Portes. See Letters 153 and 154.

Buzay was founded in the diocese of Nantes by Ermengarde, countess of Brittany, whom during the aforesaid journey he recalled from the vanity of the world. See Letters 116 and 117. The first abbot was John, to whom Letter 232 is addressed. Hautecombe was also founded, in the diocese of Geneva; La Grâce-Dieu, in the diocese of Saintes; and Eberbach, in the diocese of Mainz.

1136. Guy, the elder among Bernard’s brothers, died outside Clairvaux, in accordance with his brother’s prophecy, *Life*, Book 2, chapter 12—namely at Pontigny.

The following were founded: Balerne, in the diocese of Besançon; its first abbot was Burchard, to whom Letter 146 is addressed; La Maison-Dieu, on the river Cher in the diocese of Bourges, whose abbot was Robert, a kinsman of Bernard, to whom Letter 1 is addressed; and L’Alba-Ripa, in the diocese of Langres. Finally, the monastery of Alp, in the diocese of Geneva, was adopted, having been handed over by Abbot Guarin, later bishop of Sion. See Letter 253.

1137. In the eighth year of Innocent II, the twelfth of Emperor Lothair II, [Col. 0063C] and the twenty-ninth of the reign of Louis VI, Louis died at Paris on the Kalends of August [1 August]. He was succeeded by his son Louis VII, called “the Younger” because he had begun to reign while his father was still alive.

In that very year Bernard, summoned by Innocent, proceeded to Italy for the third time. Innocent was oppressed by the assaults of Roger the Sicilian. Roger, defeated by Duke Rainulf through Bernard’s prayers, could not prevail by arms and so turned to words. Pretending to place Anacletus’s cause in the mouth of Peter of Pisa, a most eloquent man, he saw Peter himself convicted and reclaimed by Bernard; yet not even thus could he be softened toward better counsels.

The monastery of La Colomba was founded in Italy, in the diocese of Piacenza; and Bocchia in Hungary, in the diocese of Veszprém, although some assign it to 1153. Likewise, the monastery of Bellefont, now called Vallis Paradisi, in Spain, in the diocese of Zamora, was adopted.

[Col. 0063D] 1138. In the thirteenth year of his empire Lothair II ceased to reign on the third day before the Nones of December [3 December], and was succeeded by Conrad, duke of Franconia, once his rival. In the same year Anacletus, the pseudo-pontiff, died miserably. From Roger’s faction Cardinal Gregory was substituted for him and called Victor. Resigning the insignia of the highest office to Bernard, he at last put the desired end to the schism, which after seven years had been suppressed through the zeal and prudence of the holy Doctor. See Letter 317.

The holy abbot, however, immediately left the Roman curia, wishing to carry back to Gaul no gifts except a tooth of St Caesarius and other relics of saints; *Life*, Book 4, chapter 1. Having learned of the condition of the election at Langres, conducted by the metropolitan of Lyons contrary to the undertaking made at Rome, he wrote various Letters, 165 and following. To this grief was added another, far more severe: the death of his brother Gerard. Bernard had obtained him from God in Italy, where he had had him as his companion on his last [Col. 0064A] journey; and he mourned him with many tears in the twenty-sixth sermon on the *Song of Songs*, from which he resumed that golden work which he had interrupted.

In the same year Rainald, archbishop of Reims, died, as the *Continuation of Gembloux* relates. Two years later, namely in 1140, Samson, provost of the church of Chartres, was ordained archbishop of Reims, after Bernard himself had declined that dignity.

The monastery of La Bénisson-Dieu was founded in the diocese of Lyons and Alberic, to whom Letter 173 is addressed, was placed over it. The monastery of Dunes, in the diocese of Bruges, was also adopted. Its first abbot was Robert, to whom Letter 324 was written, and who would later succeed Bernard at Clairvaux.

1139. A Lateran council of about one thousand bishops was convened at Rome. There the supporters of Peter Leonis were again condemned; ordinations performed by him were invalidated; tournaments were prohibited; and Arnold [Col. 0064B] of Brescia was ordered to leave Italy as a heretic. Bernard nevertheless worked to protect Cardinal Peter of Pisa, formerly reconciled to Innocent by Bernard, from the severity of that sentence against Anacletus’s supporters, as is clear from Letter 213. Not long afterwards Innocent himself was deceitfully captured by Roger, duke of Sicily; this became the occasion for arranging the long-desired peace between them.

In the same year Archbishop Malachy, primate of Ireland, set out for Rome—not, however, in 1137, as Baronius maintains. For Bernard makes it clear in chapter 10 of the *Life of St Malachy* that Malachy lived only nine years after this journey; and the final chapter likewise states that he died in 1148. On this journey, when Malachy visited Clairvaux, he left six companions there. Having been instructed in the Cistercian observance, they later carried it into Ireland.

1140. The Council of Sens was held against Abelard. After the articles of error [Col. 0064C] had been condemned, Abelard appealed to the Roman See indeed; but, yielding to the persuasion of Peter the Venerable, he abandoned the appeal and remained at Cluny. Reconciled to the Church through Peter’s efforts, after he had lived there commendably for two years, he died in the monastery of St Marcellus at Chalon, to which he had gone for treatment of illness. See Letter 197 and following, and the notes there.

There were founded that year: Clairmarais, in the diocese of Saint-Omer; Blanchelande, in Wales, a province of England, in the diocese of St Davids; Oseira, in the kingdom of Galicia, in the diocese of Ourense; and Aripatorium, called Ripatorium by others, in the diocese of Troyes, over which Alan was placed—later bishop of Auxerre and compiler of the *Life of St Bernard*. Innocent also entrusted to the monks of Clairvaux the restored monastery of St Anastasius at Aquae Salviae, placing over it Bernard of Pisa, St Bernard’s disciple, who subsequently was raised to the Roman See under the name Eugenius III. Finally, the monastery of Bangor, granted to Bernard by Malachy, primate of [Col. 0064D] Ireland, was adopted; and likewise Casamari, in the Italian city of Veroli.

1141. “Pope Innocent,” says Robert of Torigni, “placed the lord king Louis’s land under interdict because he would not receive the archbishop of Bourges; but afterwards he received him and absolved him from the oath which he had made unreasonably.” See Letter 218 and following.

In the same year, as the same author relates, King Louis of France oppressed Count Theobald and devastated his land, especially in Champagne. There he burned the castle of Vitry—or Vitriacum—where a multitude of persons of both sexes and every age, namely thirteen hundred souls, were burned, according to Robert of Torigni in his supplement to Sigebert, who assigns this to 1143. Consult Letters 217, 220, 222, and 223.

At this time occurred the death of Humbeline, sister of St Bernard, concerning whom see *Life*, Book 1, chapter 6.

[Col. 0065A] The abbey of Mellifont was founded in Ireland, in the diocese of Armagh, through Malachy’s agency. Christian and his companions from Clairvaux were summoned there—the men whom the aforesaid bishop had left there to be trained. See Letters 356 and 357.

1142. Ivo, cardinal-priest, formerly a regular canon of St Victor’s at Paris, was sent into France to pronounce sentence against Ralph, count of Vermandois. Having repudiated his former wife Petronilla, sister of Count Theobald, he had taken as an additional wife the daughter of William, duke of Aquitaine, sister of the queen. Bartholomew of Laon, Simon of Noyon, and Peter, bishop of Senlis, the authors of the divorce, were likewise involved in this anathema. See Letters 216, 217, 220, and 221.

Alfonso, king of Portugal, also made himself and his kingdom tributary to Clairvaux, assigning fifty maravedís, or double-dinars, of tested gold.

In that year, according to Robert of Torigni—or in the year immediately preceding, as Ortelius reports in Anselm [Col. 0065B] of Gembloux, cited by Miraeus—that great Hugh of St Victor, St Bernard’s friend and especial admirer, another Augustine of his age, yielded his soul to heaven. See Letter 70.

The monasteries of Melón, in Galicia, in the diocese of Tui, and Sobrado, around this period in the diocese of Compostela, were founded. Likewise Alta-Crista was founded in Savoy, in the diocese of Lausanne.

1143. In the fifth year of Emperor Conrad III and the sixth of Louis VII, king of France, Pope Innocent died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], after sitting for almost fourteen years. He was succeeded by Guy of Castello, called Celestine II, to whom Letters 234 and 235 are addressed.

The following were founded: Alvastra, in Sweden, in the diocese of Linköping; New Valley—according to others, four years later—in the same place; Belleperche, in the diocese of Montauban; and Meyra, in Galicia, in the diocese of Lugo.

1144. Pope Celestine died before six months had elapsed. Gerard, chamberlain, formerly a regular canon and cardinal-priest of the title of Holy Cross [Col. 0065C] in Jerusalem, was substituted for him and was called Lucius II. At this time Bernard arranged peace between King Louis and Count Theobald. Read Letters 220 and following.

In the same year Bartholomew, abbot of La Ferté and brother of St Bernard, died. So too did Stephen of Châlons, cardinal-bishop of Palestrina, of the Cistercian Order, a man of great holiness, to whom Bernard addressed several letters.

Beaulieu was founded in the diocese of Rodez.

1145. In the seventh year of Emperor Conrad III and the eighth of Louis VII, king of France, Pope Lucius died on the fifth day before the Kalends of March [25 February]. He was succeeded by Eugenius III, formerly abbot of St Anastasius at Aquae Salviae and previously called Bernard, mentioned above under 1140. See Letter 237 and following. At this time St Bernard, consulted by King Louis concerning the holy expedition, referred the matter to the judgement of the supreme pontiff; see our General Preface, §7.

[Col. 0065D] Prée was founded in the diocese of Bourges.

1146. At the Council of Chartres, convened that year concerning the holy expedition, Peter the Venerable, though invited in Letter 364, could not come, as may be inferred from his reply, Letter 18, Book 6. St Bernard, elected chief leader of the military enterprise, by Eugenius’s command exhorted the peoples of Germany—the East Franks, Bavarians, English, and others—to take up the Cross, both in letters and by spoken word; many miracles supported him. See Letters 363 and 365, and the book *On the Miracles of St Bernard*.

In the same year the Church of Tournai, which for more than five hundred years had been entrusted to the bishops of the Church of Noyon, received from Pope Eugenius III its own bishop, named Anselm, formerly abbot of St Vincent’s at Laon. Among those who secured this was Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

Boxley was founded in England, in the diocese of Canterbury; and Villers in Brabant, in the diocese of Namur. [Col. 0066A] The *Continuation of Gembloux*, cited by Miraeus, assigns its foundation to the following year in these words: “Twelve monks with Abbot Lawrence, and five lay brothers, sent by Blessed Bernard from Clairvaux into Brabant, built the monastery of Villers.”

1147. Eugenius, who in the preceding year had fled into Gaul because the Romans, under Arnold’s faction—concerning which see Letter 242—were attacking him, was honourably received at Paris that year by King Louis. Louis, having taken the Cross at Vézelay on Palm Sunday in the preceding year, as Robert of Torigni relates in the Appendix to Sigebert, departed from Paris that year, namely on 14 June, according to the Cluniac Chronology, for Syria against the Saracens, together with his brother Robert, Geoffrey count of Mellent, and many others.

In the same year several synods were held in different places. The first was at Étampes, where, in Bernard’s presence, the affair of Jerusalem [Col. 0066B] and the disposition of the kingdom were discussed, and the administration of France was entrusted to Suger, abbot of St Denis. See the *Chronicle of St Denis*, vol. 2, the *Spicilegium*, and *The Miracles of St Bernard*, chapter 16. The second was at Auxerre, with Eugenius presiding. The third was at Paris, according to Otto of Freising, *Frederick*, Book 1, chapter 50. At these, the case of Gilbert of Poitiers was brought forward and postponed until the Council of Reims to be held in the next year. See the General Preface.

Moreover, Bernard went into Aquitaine with Alberic, cardinal-bishop of Ostia and legate, and Geoffrey of Chartres, against the heretic Henry, concerning whom see our General Preface and Letter 241. In that same year Alfonso, king of Portugal, having captured the city of Santarém through the merits of St Bernard, asked by letter for monks to establish in his kingdom a monastery of the Cistercian Order.

Alcobaça was founded in Portugal by the aforesaid king, in the diocese of Lisbon; Le Val-Richer, in the diocese [Col. 0066C] of Bayeux; Margam, in Wales; and the monastery of La Espina, in the diocese of Palencia in Castile, by Sancha, sister of King Alfonso. See Letter 301. Likewise, Grand-Selve, of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Toulouse, was adopted when Bernard, its abbot, handed over himself and his house. See Letter 242.

1148. At the opening of the Council of Reims on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April [19 March], with Eugenius presiding, the foolish heretic Eon was sentenced to prison. Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, convicted by Bernard, retracted his errors. Not long afterwards Eugenius, at the holy abbot’s urging, approved Hildegard’s writings at the Council of Trier, after first completing the dedication of the church of Toul, at which Bernard was also present. In the same year Eugenius attended the Cistercian Chapter and consecrated its new cemetery; taking leave of the brethren not without tears, he returned to Italy.

After Eugenius’s departure from Gaul, St Malachy, primate of Ireland, intending again to set out for Rome to obtain the pallium from the supreme pontiff [Col. 0066D], happily ended his days, at the desired place and on the desired day, at Clairvaux—on the very day of the solemn Commemoration of All the Departed, whose observance began to be celebrated at once from his death. See Letter 374, the letter of consolation to the Irish; likewise his *Life*, volume 2; and the two sermons delivered on his death, volume 3. Moreover, when St Malachy was almost at the point of death, the building of the new Clairvaux having been completed, the bones of the venerable Fathers who had fallen asleep in the former monastery were transferred from the old cemetery to the new on the feast of All Saints, according to the first sermon on St Malachy, no. 2. His canonization is assigned to the year 1192 in the *Chronicle of Clairvaux*, cited by Francis Chifflet.

In the same year Blessed Humbert, abbot of Igny, died—not in 1145, as Manriquez supposes. See the proofs in the annotation to Bernard’s sermon on his death, printed in volume III.

[Col. 0067A] Cambron was founded in the diocese of Cambrai. Its first abbot was Fastrad of Clairvaux, who later ruled it after Robert. Alne was also adopted, formerly Benedictine and then of regular canons, in the diocese of Liège. Likewise, at the Cistercian Chapter that year, Serlo, abbot of Savigny, subjected himself and thirty monasteries dependent on the Benedictine monastery of Savigny in the diocese of Avranches to Clairvaux; and Stephen, father and founder of the emerging congregation of Obazine in the diocese of Limoges, subjected four.

1149. In that year, when the overseas expedition had ended unsuccessfully, Louis returned to Gaul. See Letter 386, *On Consideration*, Book 2, chapter 1, and the *Life of St Bernard*, Book 3, chapter 4. When he prepared to undertake it again, he was restrained by the Cistercians, as Abbot Robert relates in the *Chronicle* under 1150.

In the same year Henry, brother of Louis, king of France—these are the words of the *Chronicle of Tours*—formerly treasurer [Col. 0067B] of Blessed Martin at Tours and later clothed in the habit of a monk at Clairvaux, was promoted to the bishopric of Beauvais. The *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens* assigns this to the following year. Read Letter 307 and its notes.

The following were founded: Fontmorigny, in the diocese of Bourges; Les Chassagnes, in the diocese of Limoges; Longuay, in the diocese of Langres; and Praise of the Blessed Virgin, in the diocese of Tournai. Boulancourt, of regular canons in the diocese of Troyes, was adopted.

1150. After Eugenius had been restored at Rome to St Peter’s following many conflicts, Bernard sent him the second book of *On Consideration*, prefacing it with an apology concerning the counsel given for the Jerusalem expedition. He received a consolatory letter from John, abbot of Casamari in the city of Veroli, which is now Letter 386 among Bernard’s letters.

1151. Rainald having died toward the end of the preceding year [Col. 0067C], namely on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January [16 December], Gosevinus, formerly abbot of Bonneval in the diocese of Vienne, was appointed in his place. See Letter 270.

Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, likewise died, a man called “of good memory” in the *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif*. Concerning the election of his successor, see Letters 261, 274, and [Col. 0068A] following. Suger, abbot of St Denis, also died, a man of the highest integrity, to whom Bernard wrote Letter 266 as he lay at the point of death. “This year,” says Robert of Torigni, “Louis and Eleanor, in Lent at Beaugency, having sworn before archbishops and bishops that they were related by blood, were separated by the authority of Christendom.”

The monastery of Esrum was founded in Denmark, in the diocese of Roskilde.

1152. In the eighth year of Eugenius III and the fifteenth of Louis VII, king of France, Conrad, in the thirteenth year of his empire, relinquished the purple through death to Frederick, surnamed Barbarossa, duke of Swabia, Conrad’s nephew through his brother. Theobald, count of Champagne, likewise a man of distinguished piety, died on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January], and was buried in the monastery of Lagny on the Marne, of which he had been advocate. Not long before his death Bernard had written to him Letter 271.

The abbey of Moroliis was adopted in the diocese of Maillezais. The abbey of Clermont was founded in the diocese [Col. 0068B] of Le Mans. Around this time Armentaria, in Galicia, in the diocese of Compostela, was adopted.

1153. In the second year of Emperor Frederick I and the sixteenth of Louis VII, king of France, Eugenius died on the sixth day before the Ides of July [10 July], after sitting eight years, four months, and thirteen days. He was succeeded by Conrad, formerly a regular canon and bishop of Sabina, called Anastasius IV.

Not long afterwards Bernard, the most holy Doctor, having completed many labours for God and the Church, was seized by grave illness amid the storms of midwinter. Yet, as he writes in Letters 288, 307, and 308, he had arranged peace among the people of Metz; finally he himself rested in peace on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], at the third hour before noon, in the sixty-third year of his age, the fortieth of his monastic profession, and the thirty-eighth of his governance. In that same week Ascalon, a most strongly fortified city in Palestine, was taken by Christians, according to the Saint’s oft-repeated promise, as Geoffrey testifies in *Life of St Bernard*, Book 3, chapter 4. Bernard was succeeded at Clairvaux by Robert [Col. 0068C], formerly abbot of Dunes.

The monasteries of La Peyrouse, in the diocese of Périgueux, and De Moris, in the diocese of Langres, were founded; and the abbey of Mont-Rami, in the diocese of Ourense in Galicia, was adopted.

# FIRST VOLUME OF THE WORKS OF ST BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, CONTAINING FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-TWO LETTERS

(Collated against three Colbert manuscripts, two Cistercian manuscripts, one Corbie manuscript, and one Compiègne manuscript; the Vatican manuscripts, the Sorbonne manuscript, those of the Royal College of Navarre, St Peter’s at Ghent, Clairvaux, Clairval, Val d’Or, etc., were also consulted.)

[Col. 0067]

## LETTERS

[Col. 0067]

## LETTERS.(G)*

# 1. FIRST LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0067C] Written about the year 1119.]

## TO ROBERT, HIS NEPHEW, WHO HAD PASSED FROM THE CISTERCIAN ORDER TO THE CLUNIAC ORDER

[Note: [Col. 0067C] Thus nearly all the manuscripts read. In one manuscript of Saint-Germain: “Here begins the letter of Blessed Bernard, abbot, to Lord Robert, monk and his kinsman, who, after profession, had abandoned the Cistercian Order and transferred himself to Cluny.”]

He recalls Robert, his kinsman, who had passed from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs, whether induced by dread of a stricter rule, the attraction of a more relaxed life, or the flatteries and subtle whisperings of others, with wonderful charity and more-than-paternal affection.

[Col. 0068C]

1. Long enough—more than long enough—have I waited, my dearest son Robert, [Col. 0069A] [Note: [Col. 0069B] This letter has no superscription, except in two Saint-Germain manuscripts: “Bernard, abbot, to Robert the young man”; whether this is genuine is uncertain. This letter, dictated by Bernard in the open air, “in the midst of rain without rain,” as William, abbot of St Thierry, says in Book 1, chapter 2 of the *Life of St Bernard*, was for this miracle placed before the other letters.

The place where this occurred, near Clairvaux, is noteworthy for its little chapel in memory of the event. The letter was written down by William, who later became the first abbot of Rievaulx in England. Some wrongly attribute to him the eulogies that Gilbert of Hoyland, in Sermon 41 on the *Song of Songs*, recalls concerning a certain abbot of Rievaulx. They undoubtedly concern William’s successor, named Aelred, who, according to Pits, died in 1166. For it cannot be that that William of Rievaulx, who passed to heaven in 1143, should be celebrated by Gilbert in that sermon with a funeral eulogy as one recently dead, since Gilbert undertook to continue the exposition of the *Song of Songs* only after the death of St Bernard, namely [Col. 0069C] after 1153, and in Sermon 30 mentions the schism raised in 1159 by Emperor Frederick against Alexander III.

Robert, to whom this letter is directed, is called Bernard’s relative by blood in the letter itself, no. 9, and in Letter 32, no. 3. John the Hermit, an author of that time, writes thus of him in *Life of St Bernard*, Book 1, chapter 2, no. 5: “He was the grandson of the same matron”—namely Aleth, St Bernard’s mother—“of whom we mean to treat; and the son of her sister, to whom Blessed Bernard also directs the first of his letters.” In the same place Robert is said, after returning to Clairvaux, to have lived sixty-seven years under the yoke of regular discipline.

Peter Francis Chifflet of the Society of Jesus, in the appendix to his *Dissertation on the Illustrious Family of St Bernard*, conjectures that Robert’s mother was Diana, wife of Otto of Châtillon, from the family of Montbard; and that he was commonly called Bernard’s [Col. 0069D] “nephew” either through an error by the collector of the letters or because of an ancient idiom in which a cousin on the paternal side, maternal side, or through an aunt could be called *nepos* if he were younger than his cousin. That Robert was younger than St Bernard is sufficiently clear both from this letter and from Book 1, chapter 2 of the *Life*.

As regards the date, this letter appears to have been written around 1119. Robert seems to have made his solemn profession among the Cistercians in 1116, as will be demonstrated below; on hearing this, the Cluniacs immediately attempted craftily to draw him to themselves. Thus the *Exordium of Cîteaux*, distinction 3, chapter 9, reports: “Meanwhile the brothers of Cluny, hearing that the same young man had committed himself to the Cistercian Order, were greatly indignant … And since they were constrained by the authority of Blessed Bernard not to presume publicly to reclaim him, they turned to more cunning devices. For a certain prior was sent,” [Col. 0070A] etc.

Meanwhile St Bernard long concealed his feelings, as is clear from the beginning of this letter. But at last, unable to bear the pain he had conceived [Col. 0070B], he wrote this letter, by which Robert could not even then be recalled, as Bernard complains in Letter 32, until he was restored by Peter the Venerable.

That Robert made his profession in 1116 can seemingly be shown as follows. Nearly all writers, both internal and external, think that Robert was one of the thirty companions whom Bernard withdrew from the world and brought with him to Cîteaux. Bernard himself seems to indicate this in the present letter: “For, if you permit it, I begot you into the religious life both by my word and by my example.” But because of his younger age he had been sent back for two years, as Bernard likewise states below, no. 8; after those had elapsed, he was finally received for conversion. Bernard entered Cîteaux in 1113. If to that number you add three years—namely two years’ postponement and one of probation—you will have Robert professed in 1116.

This argument is considerably strengthened by the authority of the already cited [Col. 0070C] *Exordium*, where Robert is said to have been admitted at Cîteaux for probation before Bernard was placed over Clairvaux, and therefore before 1115, when Clairvaux is recorded as having been founded. Thus the *Exordium of Cîteaux* says: “Lord Robert, formerly abbot of La Maison-Dieu and a relative of Blessed Bernard according to the flesh, had in his youth accepted at Cîteaux the sweet yoke of the Lord and His light burden. Afterwards, when the most reverend man of God Bernard had been appointed abbot of Clairvaux, Robert was instructed under him in heavenly disciplines in that same monastery.”

From this it plainly appears that Robert’s departure from Clairvaux, or rather his seduction, took place through the counsel and urging of Pons, abbot of Cluny, who governed Cluny from 1109 to 1122, rather than under the rule of Peter the Venerable, who succeeded Pons after Hugh II once three months had elapsed, as the *Cluniac Chronicle* attests. And surely who would suppose it consistent with Peter the Venerable—a most devoted lover of peace and sincerity [Col. 0070D]—that he sent a prior to Clairvaux to deceive the young man? Even if one grants that he did this, how could Peter then count Robert’s restoration among the benefits and charitable services he rendered to St Bernard, as though he could have earned a benefit from an injury? For in one letter to Bernard he says: “Why then, my dearest friend, is not even one man granted to me for a month, when I have granted you Robert, your close blood-relative, Garnerius, and certain others, drawn by love of you, not for one month but permanently?” (Book 6, Letter 35).

From this, incidentally, observe that Robert at last returned to Clairvaux, having been restored by Peter of Cluny at the beginning of his administration, and that Bernard subsequently made him abbot of La Maison-Dieu in the diocese of Besançon. See Manriquez’s *Annals* under 1113 and 1117, from which some of these details have been taken.], if perhaps God’s mercy might deign to visit both your soul directly and mine through you: yours, by inspiring saving compunction; mine, by granting joy over your salvation. But since I see that my expectation has hitherto been disappointed, I can no longer conceal my pain, restrain my anxiety, or disguise my sorrow. Thus, contrary to the order of justice, I am compelled—I who have been injured—to call back him who injured me; I who have been rejected, to seek my despiser; I who have suffered wrong, to make satisfaction to my wrongdoer; and finally, to entreat him by whom I ought to have been entreated.

For excessive grief does not deliberate, is not ashamed, takes no counsel from reason, does not fear loss of dignity; it obeys no law, [Col. 0070A] accepts no judgement, knows neither measure nor order. Its whole and sole concern is either to lack what it grieves to possess, or to possess what it grieves to lack.

“But,” you say, “I injured no one and despised no one. Rather, I myself was despised and wronged in many ways; I merely fled from my wrongdoer. Whom did I wrong if I fled wrongs? Is it not better to yield to a persecutor than to resist? To flee one who strikes than to strike back?” Correct: I agree. I began this not to contend, but to put an end to contention. To flee persecution is not the fault of the fugitive but of the persecutor. I do not dispute it. I pass over what occurred; I do not ask why or how it happened. I do not examine faults, [Col. 0071A] reconsider causes, or remember injuries. Such matters commonly inflame rather than soothe disputes.

I speak only of what most occupies my heart. Wretched me: I lack you; I do not see you; I live without you—for you, to die is life to me; without you, to live is death. Therefore I do not ask why you went away; I lament that you have not now returned. I do not complain of the causes of your departure, but of the delays of your return. Only come, and there will be peace; return, and satisfaction is made. Return, I say, return, and joyfully I shall sing: “He was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

2. Certainly it may have been my fault that you left. For I was harsh toward a delicate young man, and I treated you, still tender, too hard and inhumanely. For this reason, when you were present, as I remember, you were accustomed to murmur against me; [Col. 0071B] and now, as I have heard, you do not cease to speak ill even of me in my absence. Let it not be charged against you. Perhaps I could excuse myself and say that the impulses of a wayward youth had to be restrained in this way, and that those severe beginnings of stricter discipline were due to unformed years. Scripture bears witness: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will save his soul from death” (Prov. 23:13); and again, “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6); and, “The blows of a friend are more useful than the kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6).

But let it be, as I have said, my fault that you left, lest, while there is dispute about assigning blame, amendment be delayed. Yet from this point it will undoubtedly begin to be yours also, if you do not spare one who repents or show indulgence to one who confesses [Col. 0071C]. For I may once have been indiscreet toward you in some things, but certainly not ill-disposed. And if you are suspicious even for the future of this indiscretion of mine, know that I am no longer what I was, because I do not think that you will be what you were either. Changed, you will find one changed; and the master whom you formerly feared, embrace safely as a companion.

Thus, whether you withdrew through my fault, as you think—and I do not excuse myself—or through yours, as many think—although I do not accuse you—or through both mine and yours, which I think more likely: if from this point you refuse to return, you alone will certainly be without excuse. Do you wish to be free of every fault? Return. If you acknowledge your own, I forgive you; forgive me also where I acknowledge mine. Otherwise, either you indulge yourself too much, in that you both recognize and [Col. 0071D] conceal your fault; or you are too merciless toward me, judging that I am not to be forgiven even when I make satisfaction.

3. But if you refuse to return, seek some other pretext by which falsely to flatter your conscience; for there will no longer be anything for you to fear from the severity of my discipline. For one need not fear that I shall be formidable when present to him before whom, though still absent, I already lie prostrate with all my heart [or: body], my whole inmost being constrained. I offer humility; I promise charity—and are you afraid? Come fearlessly where humility calls you and charity draws you. Approach in confidence, protected by such pledges. You fled from one severe; return to one gentle. Let my mildness call you back—the severity of which drove you away. See, son, how I long for you to be led, not by a spirit of slavery again unto fear, but by the spirit of adoption as sons, in which you too need not be ashamed to cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15): thus I pursue the cause of my great grief, not with threats before you but with entreaties; with prayers, not terrors.

Another perhaps would have tried differently. Indeed, who else would not rather investigate the offense and instill fear; set before you, not a plea, but judgment; accuse you of disobedience and be indignant at your apostasy—because you have passed from tunics to furs, from vegetables to delicacies, and finally from poverty to riches? But I know your mind: it can be bent more easily by love than forced by fear. Besides, what need is there to prick one who is not kicking back, to terrify more greatly one already very fearful, to put further to shame one sufficiently ashamed of himself—one for whom his own reason is a teacher, his own conscience a rod, and innate modesty a law of discipline?

But if anyone wonders how a modest, simple, God-fearing boy dared, against the will of the brethren, the command of his master, and the decree of the rule, to abandon his own vow and place: let him also wonder that David’s holiness was ensnared (2 Kings [Samuel] 11), Solomon’s wisdom mocked (3 Kings [1 Kings] 11), and Samson’s strength overcome (Judges 16). He who by deceit captured the first-created man and expelled him from the homeland of blessedness—what wonder if he deceived a tender youth in a place of terror and vast solitude? Add to this that neither beauty deceived him, as it did those Babylonian elders (Dan. 13:8), nor love of money, as it did Gehazi (4 Kings [2 Kings] 5:20), nor ambition for honor, as it did Julian the Apostate.

> [Note: [Col. 0071D] Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 3, testifies that Julian, inflamed with desire for imperial power, travelled through Greece and sought out seers and diviners, intending to ask them whether he would obtain the object of his desire. By chance he came upon a man who promised to foretell this for him. This man led him into a temple of idols and placed him within its inner sanctuary, then invoked deceitful demons. When they appeared in their usual guise, fear compelled Julian to mark his forehead with the sign of the cross. The demons, seeing the image of the Lord’s trophy and remembering their own defeat, immediately vanished. Then the sorcerer, understanding why they had fled, rebuked Julian. Julian then disclosed the fear that had seized him and said that he greatly marvelled at the power of the cross, since the demons had fled because they could not endure its image. To this the sorcerer replied: “Do not, I beg you, suppose this. They were not afraid for that reason; rather, detesting your arrogance, they removed themselves from our sight.” Thus the wretched man, urged by him into deception, was initiated into impious mysteries; his breast was filled with wickedness; and, unhappy through desire of empire, he was utterly stripped of piety. Thus Theodoret. I have recounted his words, though somewhat lengthy, because Bernard seems to me clearly to have alluded to them.] 

Rather, holiness deceived him, religion led him astray, and the authority of elders ruined him. Do you ask how?

4. First, a certain great prior was sent by the very prince of priors—outwardly appearing in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly a ravening wolf. The guards were deceived, judging him to be a sheep; alas, alas! the wolf alone was admitted to the lone little sheep. Nor did the little sheep avoid the wolf, whom he too supposed to be a sheep. Why say more? He draws him, entices him, flatters him; and this preacher of a new gospel commends gluttony and condemns frugality. Voluntary poverty he calls misery; fasts, vigils, silence, and manual labor he calls madness. Conversely, idleness he calls contemplation; greediness, talkativeness, curiosity, and, in short, every kind of intemperance, he calls discretion.

“When,” he says, “does God delight in our torments? Where does Scripture command anyone to kill himself? What sort of religion is it to dig the earth, cut down woodland, and carry manure? Is it not the saying of Truth: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Matt. 9:13)? And: ‘I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live’ (Ezek. 33:11)? And: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’ (Matt. 5:7)? Why, moreover, did God create foods, if it is not permitted to eat them? Why did he give us bodies, if he forbids us to sustain them? Finally, ‘He who is bad to himself, to whom is he good?’ (Sir. 14:5). Who, being wise and in his right mind, has ever hated his own flesh?” (Eph. 5:29).

5. At length the boy, too ready to believe such arguments, is ensnared and deceived; he follows his deceiver and is taken to Cluny. He is shorn, shaved, and washed; stripped of rustic, old, dirty garments; clothed in costly, new, shining ones; and thus received into the community. But with what honor, do you suppose; with what triumph; with what reverence? He is preferred above all his contemporaries; and, like a victor returning from battle, “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 10:3). He is lifted high and placed in no mean rank, so that, though a youth, he is set above many elders. The entire brotherhood favors him, flatters him, and rejoices with him; all exult “as victors rejoicing when they divide the spoils” (Isa. 9:3).

O good Jesus, how much was done for the ruin of one little soul! Whose heart, however strong, would not be softened by this? Whose inward eye, however spiritual, would not be clouded? Who amid such things can be free to return to his own conscience? Finally, who in so great a pageantry can either recognize truth or retain humility?

6. Meanwhile, someone is sent to Rome on his behalf. Apostolic authority is invoked; and, so that the Pope may not withhold his consent, he is told that the boy had formerly been offered to a monastery by his parents. There was no one to refute this—for no opponent was expected. Judgment was rendered for one party; those absent were deprived of their case. Those who committed the wrong were justified; those who suffered it were shut out from their cause; the guilty party was absolved without making satisfaction. By a cruel privilege the overly merciful sentence of absolution was confirmed, so that, when it had been brought back, firmness might be confirmed in one wrongly persuaded and wavering, confidence in one doubting. This was the tenor of the letter, the sum of the judgment, the resolution of the entire case: let those who took him keep him; let those who lost him be silent. Meanwhile let the soul for which Christ died perish, simply because the Cluniacs will it.

Profession is made upon profession; a vow is made that will not be paid, and a purpose set forth that will not be kept. Since the first covenant has been made void, transgression is doubled in the second; and sin becomes exceedingly sinful (Rom. 7:13).

7. He will come—he will come—who will rejudge what was wrongly judged and overturn what was unlawfully sworn; who “executes judgment for those suffering wrong” (Ps. 145:7); who “will judge the poor in righteousness and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth” (Isa. 11:4). He will surely come, who threatens through the prophet in the Psalm, saying: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justices” (Ps. 74:3). What will he do with unjust judgments, he who will judge even acts of justice themselves? The day of judgment will come, I say, will come, when pure hearts will avail more than crafty words, and a good conscience more than full purses; for that Judge will neither be deceived by words nor swayed by gifts.

I appeal to your tribunal, Lord Jesus. I reserve myself for your judgment; I entrust my cause to you, Lord God of hosts, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts (Jer. 11:20), whose eyes, as they do not wish to deceive, so cannot be deceived. You see those who seek what is yours; you see those who seek their own (cf. 1 Cor. 13:5). You know with what affection I have always stood by him in all his temptations; with how many groans I have besieged the ears of your mercy for him; how, at each of his scandals, disturbances, and troubles, I was burned, tortured, and afflicted. And now I fear that it is in vain. For, as far as experience has taught me, I think that neither such indulgences are suitable for the body of a youth already sufficiently fervent and presumptuous in himself, nor such temptations of glory for his mind. Therefore, Lord Jesus, my judge, “let my judgment come forth from your presence; let your eyes behold equity” (Ps. 16:2).

8. Let them see and judge which ought rather to stand: a father’s vow concerning his son, or the son’s vow concerning himself—especially when the son has vowed something greater. Let your servant Benedict, our lawgiver, also see which was more regular: what was done concerning the little boy without his knowledge, or what he himself later did, prudently and knowingly, when he had reached the age to speak for himself. Yet there is no doubt that he was promised, not given.

> [Note: [Col. 0073D] “Promise” refers to the parents’ vow; “gift” to the offering of the boy made by those same parents. Its form is prescribed by Saint Benedict in chapter 59 of the Rule; in former times that offering bound boys.]

For the petition prescribed by the Rule was not made for him by his parents; nor was his hand wrapped with that petition in the altar-cloth, so that he might thus be offered before witnesses. Next, land is produced, which is said to have been given with him and for him. But if they received him with the land, why did they not keep him with the land? Or did they seek the gift more than the fruit, and esteem the land at a higher price than the soul? Otherwise, if he had been offered to a monastery, what was he doing in the world? If he was to be nurtured for God, why was he exposed to the devil? Why was Christ’s sheep found open to the wolf’s bites?

For it was from the world, not from Cluny, that you came to Cîteaux—Robert, you yourself are witness. You sought, asked, and knocked; but because of your still tender age, you were deferred for two years, though against your will. When that time had been patiently completed, and without complaint, you finally obtained, by your prayers and by many tears, if you remember, the mercy for which you had long waited; and you gained the entrance you had earnestly desired. After this, for a year, according to the Rule (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapters 58–59), you were tested in all patience, persevered, and lived without complaint. After a year you voluntarily made profession; only then, having cast off secular clothing, you received the religious habit.

> [Note: [Col. 0075D] Boys offered to God were, of course, immediately clothed in monastic garments; adults, however, only after a year’s probation, according to chapters 58 and 59 of the Rule. This custom, observed at first among the Cistercians, as this letter shows, was later changed after the example of the Cluniacs. Among the latter the novices’ habit was “entirely similar” to the professed brethren’s garment, as it is now everywhere, “except that, so long as they were without blessing”—as they called profession—“they lacked only the cowl,” according to Udalric, book II, chapter 1. For the time when the Cistercians adopted this custom, see book VII of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 15.]

9. O foolish boy! Who has bewitched you not to fulfill the vows that your lips have uttered? Shall you not be justified from your own mouth, or condemned from your own mouth? Why are you concerned about a parent’s vow while neglecting your own, when you are to be judged from your mouth, not his, and when the vows of your lips, not his, will be required of you? Why does anyone vainly flatter you with apostolic absolution when the divine sentence holds your conscience bound? “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). Will they persuade you that this too is not looking back, when they say to you, “Aha, aha!” (Ps. 39:16)? My little son, “if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). “Do not believe every spirit” (1 John 4:1). “Let many be your friends, but let one man out of a thousand be your counselor” (Sir. 6:6).

Remove occasions; reject flatteries; close your ears to adulations. Question yourself concerning yourself, because you know yourself better than another does. Attend to your heart; examine your intention; consult truth. Let your conscience answer why you departed; why you abandoned your Order,

> [Note: [Col. 0075D] Thus Bernard, in the *Life of Saint Malachy*, no. 36, calls Melrose a monastery “of our Order”; and in Letter 2, no. 9, seems to use “Order” and “discipline” as near synonyms. Compare Letter 4, no. 2, and Letter 198, no. 2. Peter the Venerable likewise calls Cluniacs and Cistercians “men of the same Order” in the following Letter 229, no. 10; and at no. 30, “the greatest congregations of one Order and name.” Finally, Bernard himself calls William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, a man “of our Order” in Letter 79; and in Letter 42, no. 33, he calls even the abbots of the so-called black monks abbots “of our Order.” Nicholas of Clairvaux speaks of a different Order in his Letter 22.]

why you abandoned the brethren, the place, and me, who am related to you in the flesh and more closely related in spirit. If it was in order to live more strictly, more rightly, and more perfectly, be confident: you have not looked back. Rather, glory with the Apostle, saying: “Forgetting the things behind and stretching forward to those before me, I press on toward the prize of glory” (Phil. 3:13). But if it was for other reasons, “do not think highly, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). For, if you will allow me to say so, whatever greater indulgence you grant yourself in food, superfluous clothing, idle speech, and unrestrained, curious wandering, beyond what you promised and maintained among us—this is, beyond doubt, to look back; this is to transgress; this is to apostatize.

> [Note: [Col. 0076D] A fearful judgment upon monks who, seeking laxer ways, count regular observances as nothing. “If shame prevents apostasy of the body, one must fear lest lukewarmness itself gradually introduce apostasy of the heart,” as Bernard says in Sermon 3 on Psalm 90. Compare Letter 382, especially Letter 313.]

10. And I say these things, son, not to shame you, but to admonish you as a most beloved son; for though you may have many pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers (1 Cor. 4:14). If you deign to acknowledge it, I begot you into religious life both by word and example. Then I nourished you with milk, which alone you could yet receive as a little child; and I would have given you bread, if you had waited to grow up. But alas, how prematurely and untimely you were weaned! I fear lest all that I had cherished with tenderness, strengthened by exhortations, and established by prayers should now vanish, fail, and perish; and lest I, unhappy man, should mourn not so much the loss of fruitless labor as the miserable fall of a condemned child.

Does it please you that another should now glory in you, though he certainly labored not at all upon you? What happened to me resembles what happened to that harlot before Solomon: her own child was secretly taken away by another woman, who had killed her own child by overlaying it (3 Kings [1 Kings] 3:20). You too have been torn from my bosom and womb. I lament the one taken away; I demand back the one violently torn off. I cannot forget my own inward parts; when no small part of them has been taken away, the part remaining cannot but be tormented.

11. Yet for what advantage to you, what necessity of yours, have our friends contrived this against us? Their hands are full of blood (Isa. 1:15; 59:3); their sword has pierced my soul (Luke 2:35); “their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). For if I had ever offended them in anything—which I am certainly not conscious of—they have indeed repaid me in full. It would be strange if I had not received more than strict retaliation, if I could have sinned against them in any way comparable to what I have now suffered from them. For, to confess the truth, they have not taken from me a bone of my bones or flesh of my flesh, but they have taken the joy of my heart, the fruit of my spirit, the crown of my hope, and—as I seem to feel it—the half of my soul.

Why this? Perhaps they took pity on you; and, indignant at a blind man leading the blind, lest you perish after me, they transferred you to their own guidance. O troublesome charity! O harsh affection! They loved your salvation so greatly that they struck at mine. Could you not be saved unless I were destroyed? And would that they might save you without me. Would that, even if I die, you may live. But what? Is salvation then more in the display of garments and abundance of foods than in sober fare and moderate dress? If soft, warm furs; fine and costly cloth; long sleeves and a broad hood; a wild-animal covering and soft woolen bedding make a man holy—why do I delay in not following you?

> [Note: [Col. 0077C] Here Bernard notes kinds of garments which the Cistercians had rejected as contrary to the Rule, though they were in use among the Cluniacs. The former had rejected “froccos, furs, woolen garments, hoods also and breeches, combs and bed-coverings,” as is read in the Cistercian *Little Exordium*. Hence, in the *Book of Institutes*, chapter 15, “cowls shaggy on the outside” are rejected. Bernard of Cluny, in the manuscript codex of the *Customs of Cluny*, chapter 30, grants the Cluniacs among other clothing “two frocks and two cowls, two woolen garments, three furs”; and for the bed, “a pillow, covering, over-covering, quilt, and bedclothes.” Frocks differed from cowls in material and shape: cowls had no sleeves, or at least narrow sleeves and a narrow hood; frocks had both broad sleeves and broad hoods, and were made of costly cloth called *froccus* or *floccus*, whence the name *froccus*. Among us the old popular name *floccus* adhered to cowls; among the Cistercians the word *cuculla*, commonly *coulle*, arose from their innate dislike of frocks. For Saint Bernard, a “wild covering” was the first bed-covering, made from the skins of wild animals. Bernard criticizes cat-skin in the *Apology to William*, no. 24. Bernard of Cluny, in the passage just cited, says: “Bed-coverings, which may not be uncovered, are either of lamb, colt, or hare, and never of any kind of greater cost.” Compare book IV of the *Life*, no. 36.]

But these are supports for the weak, not weapons for combatants. “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8). Wine and fine flour, mead and rich foods serve the body, not the spirit. The soul is not fattened by fried dishes, but the flesh. Many brethren in Egypt served God for a long time without fish.

> [Note: [Col. 0077D] From this it is evident that fish were then not in use among the Cistercians, except perhaps rarely and while travelling, as appears from book VII, chapter 20, of the *Life*. Indeed, neither eggs nor wine were in use, as follows from the next item. The point about eggs is inferred from the letter of Abbot Fastred, printed here after Bernard’s letters, where a novice, during the nausea of his final illness, “was seized by a desire for a cooked egg,” yet maintained abstinence to the end. In the same place vegetables are said to be “cooked without oil and without fat”; and Bernard himself ate, “with scruple,” porridge made from flour, with oil and honey added—not butter—to warm his stomach. Read that letter together with the following letter of Peter of Roya, in which we learn that the brethren of Clairvaux used beer and, instead of it, plain water; wine rarely, and then “mixed with a great deal of water.” Humbert, of whom Bernard speaks in Sermons on the Saints, no. 4, used such wine only under obedience because of illness; so too Bernard himself, according to book I of his *Life*, no. 46. See Sermon 30 on the Song of Songs. On the cursed vineyard of Clairvaux, see John the Hermit, book II of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 10.]

Pepper, ginger, cumin, sage, and a thousand such seasonings delight the palate indeed, but inflame lust. And will you place security for me in such things? Will you consider youth safe amid such things? For one who lives prudently and soberly, salt with hunger is sufficient for every seasoning. When hunger alone is not awaited, it becomes necessary to concoct mixture after mixture from I know not what foreign juices—mixtures which restore the palate, provoke the throat, and stir appetite.

12. “But what,” you say, “will one do who cannot do otherwise?” Very well. I know that you are delicate, and that, now accustomed to these things, you cannot endure harder ones. But what if you can act so as to become able? Do you ask how? Rise, gird yourself, set aside idleness, exert your strength, move your arms, unfold your clasped hands, busy yourself with some work; and at once you will find yourself desiring only what removes hunger, not what caresses the throat. Exercise will restore to things the flavors that idleness took away. Many things which you reject while idle, after labor you will take with desire. For idleness produces disgust, exercise hunger; and hunger in a marvelous way makes sweet what disgust renders tasteless.

Vegetables, beans, porridge, and coarse bread

> [Note: [Col. 0078D] What sort of bread the brethren of Clairvaux used at that time is taught by book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, no. 6; and the letter of Fastred just mentioned speaks of bread made “from oats.”]

with water are distasteful to one at rest, but seem great delicacies to one who has labored. Perhaps, now unaccustomed to tunics,

> [Note: [Col. 0078D] The Cistercians wore tunics clinging to the body, without an intervening undergarment of wool or woolen cloth, according to the passages cited; they did not, however, wear haircloth, according to book I of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 39. See the preface to volume II.]

you shudder excessively at them, both because of winter cold and because of the heat of youth. But have you not read: “He who fears frost, snow shall come upon him” (Job 6:16)? You fear vigils, fasts, and manual labor; but these are light to one who meditates on everlasting flames. Again, remembrance of outer darkness makes one not shrink from solitude. If you consider the future accounting for idle words (Matt. 12:36), silence will not greatly displease you. Eternal weeping and that gnashing of teeth, brought before the eyes of the heart, will make mat and mattress alike acceptable to you. Finally, if you have kept watch well through the whole of the night, as the Rule prescribes, at the psalms (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 9 ff.), no bed will be so hard that you will not sleep peacefully upon it. If in the day you labor with your hands as much as you have professed, no food will be so hard that you will not gladly eat it.

13. Rise, soldier of Christ; rise, shake off the dust; return to the battle from which you fled, that after flight you may fight more bravely and triumph more gloriously. Christ indeed has many soldiers who began most bravely, stood firm, and conquered; but few who, having turned back from flight, again exposed themselves to the danger they had avoided, and again put to flight the enemies from whom they had fled. And because everything rare is precious, I rejoice that you may be among those who, the rarer they are, will appear the more glorious.

But if you are very fearful, why do you fear where there is no fear, and not fear where there is greater cause for fear? Because you fled from the battle-line, do you suppose that you have escaped the enemy’s hands? The adversary prefers to pursue you while fleeing rather than confront you while resisting; he presses more boldly from behind than he withstands face to face. Now, having cast away your weapons, you confidently take your morning sleep, although Christ rose at that hour; and do you not know that, being unarmed, you are more fearful and less feared by the enemy? A host of armed men have surrounded the house, and you sleep? Already they climb the rampart, already break down the hedge, already rush in by the rear entrance. Is it therefore safer for you that they should find you alone rather than with others, naked in bed rather than armed in the field?

Wake up, take arms, and flee to your fellow-soldiers whom in fleeing you abandoned, so that the very fear which separated you from them may unite you with them again. Why do you shrink from the weight and roughness of arms, delicate soldier? The pressing adversary and the flying darts will make the shield no burden, the breastplate and helmet unfelt. To one suddenly going from shade into sunlight and from idleness into labor, everything at its beginning seems hard; but when he begins to become unaccustomed to these things and to accustom himself a little to those, practice removes difficulty and finds easy what he had previously thought impossible.

Even the bravest soldiers are accustomed to tremble at the sound of the trumpet before the engagement; but once they come to battle, hope of victory and fear of defeat make them fearless. Why, then, do you tremble, when the united ranks of armed brethren will surround you, angels stand at your side, and Christ, the leader of the war, goes before you, encouraging his own toward victory and saying, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33)? “If Christ is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31). You may fight confidently where you are confident of victory.

O truly safe battle with Christ and for Christ! In it, neither wounded nor struck down nor trampled underfoot, nor even killed a thousand times, if that were possible, will you be deprived of victory—provided only that you do not flee. Flight is the sole cause by which you can lose victory. By fleeing you can lose it; by dying you cannot. Blessed are you if you die fighting, for once dead you will immediately be crowned. But woe to you if, by avoiding battle, you lose both victory and crown together! May he avert this from you, most beloved son, he who at the judgment will bring upon you a greater condemnation on account of this letter of mine if he finds in you no amendment from it.

## LETTER II

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] Written about the year 1120.]

### TO FULCO, A BOY WHO LATER BECAME ARCHDEACON OF LANGRES

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] Thus the title in the manuscripts, from which it is clear that Fulco did not obey Bernard’s admonitions but remained in the world.]

He earnestly and seriously admonishes Fulco, a regular canon whom his uncle had drawn back into the world by flatteries and promises, to obey and cleave to God rather than to his uncle.

To FULCO, a youth of good disposition: Brother BERNARD, a sinner—may you rejoice in youth in that from which you will not repent in old age.

1. I do not wonder that you wonder; but I wonder if you do not wonder why I, a rustic writing to a citizen, a monk to a scholar-boy, should wish to write to you, when no necessary occasion for doing so presents itself, and no evident reason appears. But if you attend to what you read written—“I am debtor to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1:14)—and also, “Charity does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 13:5), perhaps you will understand that whatever charity commands is not presumptuous.

For charity compelled me to rebuke you: charity which grieves for you, though you do not grieve; which pities you, though you do not appear pitiable. And it grieves the more because, though you ought to grieve, you do not; and pities the more because, though you are wretched, you do not appear wretched. Nor perhaps does it compassionately suffer with you in vain, provided you patiently hear why it suffers with you. It wishes you to feel your pain, so that you may no longer have cause for pain; it wishes you to know your misery, so that you may begin not to be miserable.

O good mother Charity, who, whether she cherishes the weak, exercises the advanced, or rebukes the restless, gives different things to different persons, while loving all alike as children! When she rebukes you, she is gentle; when she flatters, she is straightforward. She is accustomed to be severe piously and to soothe without guile; she knows how to be angry patiently and indignant humbly. She is the mother of humans and angels, who has made peace not only among those on earth but also among those in heaven. She is the one who, making God favorable to humankind, reconciled humankind to God. She, my Fulco, is the one who makes those brothers with whom you once took sweet food dwell in one manner in one house (Ps. 67:7).

This mother, such and so honorable, complains that you have offended her and protests that she has been wounded. Yet wounded, she does not provoke; rather, though scorned, she calls you back, showing you that it is truly written of her in you: “Charity is patient; charity is kind” (1 Cor. 13:4). Though wounded, though offended, if you turn back to her, she will meet you like an honored mother. Forgetting her own contempt, she will rush into your embrace, rejoicing that the one she had lost is found, and that he who had been dead is alive (Luke 15:32).

2. “But,” you ask, “in what have I wounded her? In what have I despised her?” Listen. Beyond doubt, in this: that you weaned yourself before the time from the motherly bosom which had received you to nourish you with milk; that you so lightly and quickly spurned the sweetness of the milk by which you could grow unto salvation. O foolish boy! O boy more deficient in sense than in age! Who bewitched you to depart so quickly from the path you had begun well? “My uncle,” you will say. Thus Adam once put forward his wife, and his wife the serpent, “to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4); yet each received the sentence deserved by his own fault (Gen. 3:16).

I do not wish you to accuse the dean; I do not wish you to excuse yourself through him, for you are without excuse. His fault does not excuse yours. What did he do? Did he carry you off? Did he use force? He asked; he did not bind. He drew you by flattering; he did not drag you violently. Who compelled you to believe one flattering you, to agree with one drawing you? He had not yet left his own possessions. What wonder if he sought you, who belonged to him? If a lamb from the flock or a calf from the herd is lost, he seeks it, and no one complains. If he seeks you too, who are worth more to him than many sheep or calves, once you have been taken away, who can wonder at that? For he does not claim for himself that perfection of which it is said, “If anyone takes what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6:30). Therefore he was demanding back his own, since he still held his own possessions. But you, who had already despised the world—ought you to follow a worldly man?

The trembling sheep flees when the wolf comes; the trembling dove hides when it sees the hawk; the hungry mouse does not dare leave its little hole when the cat is prowling about; and you, when you saw a thief, ran with him? (Ps. 49:18). For what else should I call one who did not hesitate to steal Christ’s precious pearl—that is, your soul—than a thief?

3. I wished, if I could, to pass over his error in silence, lest I gain hatred and no fruit from truth. But I could not, I confess, pass untouched over one whom I have discovered, up to this day, to have resisted the Holy Spirit to the full extent of his power. For one who does not withhold his hand from an evil which he can do is no less blameworthy in intention, even if the result is sometimes frustrated. He certainly wished to extinguish in me the fervor of my novitiate; but, thanks be to God, he could not. He also strongly opposed his other nephew, Guirric, your kinsman. But what harm did he do? Indeed, he did much good. At last the old uncle reluctantly ceased from persecution; the boy-nephew remained unconquered, more glorious because of temptation. But alas, how did he conquer you, when he could not conquer him? Or how was he defeated by the one whom he defeated in you? Was he stronger than you? Was he wiser? Certainly, those who had previously known both preferred Fulco to Guirric. But when they came to battle, the outcome showed that human judgment had erred. There, shame upon it, the one preferred fled, while the one believed inferior conquered bravely.

4. But what shall I say of the uncle’s wickedness, when he draws his nephews back from Christ’s soldiery in order to drag them with him to hell? Is this how he customarily makes his friends blessed? Those whom Christ calls to remain with him forever, the uncle calls back to burn with him forever. I wonder whether Christ is not already angry with him and saying: “How often I wished to gather your nephews, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you would not! Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:37). Christ says, “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:14); the uncle says, “Allow my nephews to burn with me.” Christ says, “They are mine; they ought to serve me.” “But,” says the uncle, “they must perish with me.” Christ says, “They are mine; I redeemed them.” “But I,” says the uncle, “nourished them.” “You did indeed nourish them,” Christ says, “but with my bread, not yours; I redeemed them not with your blood, but with mine.”

Thus a carnal uncle contends against the Father of spirits for his nephews; while desiring to burden them with earthly goods, he disinherits them of heavenly ones. Yet Christ did not regard it as robbery if he gathered to himself those who came to him, whom he had made and redeemed with his own blood, according to what he had previously promised: “Him who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37). To Fulco, knocking for the first time, he joyfully opened; he joyfully received the joyful youth in joyful embraces. What more? The old man is put off and the new put on; and what he had been in name alone, he professes in conduct and life: a canon. The report flies—a sweet savor for Christ. The novelty of the event, spread everywhere, reaches the uncle’s ears.

5. What, then, was the carnal guardian to do, who was losing the comfort of the flesh which he had reared and loved carnally? Though to others that event was “an aroma of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:16), it was not so to him. Why? Because “the natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for they seem foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:14). For, if he had possessed the Spirit of Christ, he would not have grieved so much over the flesh as rejoiced over the spirit. But because he savoured earthly things, not those above, he was troubled and sorrowful, turning over in his mind something like this: “What do I hear? Woe is me! From [Col. 0082B] how great a hope have I fallen! But what? Must whatever he has done without my counsel, without my permission, stand? What right, what law, what justice, what reason is there that another should enjoy him grown to manhood whom I received from the womb to rear? Now, alas, with my head sprinkled with grey hairs, shall I spend the remainder of my life in mourning, because the staff of my old age has deserted me. Woe is me! If my soul is required of me this night, whose shall the things be which I have prepared?” (Luke 12:20). “My storehouses are full, overflowing from one into another; my sheep are fruitful, multiplying in their goings forth; to whom will my fat cattle remain?” (Ps. 143:13).
