My estates, meadows, houses, silver and gold vessels—to whom have I amassed them? I had acquired for myself the richer and more profitable dignities of my church; the rest, although I was not permitted to [Col. 0082C] possess them, I nevertheless held in expectation through Fulco. What, therefore, shall I do? Shall I lose so many and such great things for the sake of this one man? For whatever I possess without him, I consider myself to have lost. Rather, I shall retain these things and recall him, if I can. But how? It has been done; it has been heard. What has been done cannot be undone; what has been heard cannot be concealed. Fulco is a regular canon; if he returns to the world, he will be conspicuous and disgraced. Yet it is more tolerable to hear this of him than to live without him. Let honour, then, now give way to advantage, and shame to necessity. I prefer not to spare the young man’s reputation rather than to lie under miserable grief.”

6. Yielding therefore to the counsel of the flesh, forgetful of reason [Col. 0082D] and of the law, like “a lion ready for prey” (Ps. 16:12), and like a lioness whose cub has been seized, himself snatching and roaring, he did not fear holy things but burst into the dwelling of the saints, where Christ had hidden His young recruit from the contradiction of tongues, intending later to join him to the fellowship of angels. He demands and insists that his nephew be restored to him; he complains and cries out that he has been unjustly abandoned by him, while Christ protests and says: “What are you doing, wretch? Why do you rage? Why do you persecute Me? Is it not enough for you that you have taken from Me your own soul, and, by your example, the souls of many, unless you also seize this man sacrilegiously from My hand? Do you not fear the judgment to come? Or do you despise My terror? Against whom do you do this? Against whom do you declare war? Surely against the Terrible One, and Him ‘who takes away the spirit of princes’” (Ps. 75:13). [Col. 0083A] “Madman, return to your heart; remember your last things, and you shall not sin” (Sir. 7:40); remember what your condition is, and you will fear profitably. “And you, young man,” He says, “if you consent, if you yield, you shall die the death.”

> [Note: Bernard is accustomed to doubt the salvation of those who, called to the religious life, do not yield to God’s call; still more of those who, having entered but not professed, return to the world. Compare Letters 107 and 108. Fulco, however, had professed the religious life.]

“Remember Lot’s wife: rescued indeed from Sodom because she believed God, but changed on the way because she looked back” (Gen. 19:26). Learn from the Gospel that one who has once put his hand to the plough may not look back (Luke 9:62). Your uncle seeks your soul, though he has already lost his own. “The words of his mouth are iniquity and deceit.” Do not understand, my son, so as to do evil (Ps. 35:4); do not give heed to false vanities and madness (Ps. 39:5). Behold, in the path in which you walk he has hidden snares and spread nets. “His words are softer than oil, [Col. 0083B] yet they are darts” (Ps. 54:22). See, my son, that you are not taken by wicked lips and a deceitful tongue. Let divine fear pierce your flesh, lest carnal love deceive you. He flatters, but under his tongue are toil and pain; he weeps, but he lays snares; he lays snares “that he may seize the poor, to seize the poor while he draws him in” (Ps. 10:7, 9). Beware, I say, my son, lest you yield to flesh and blood (Gal. 1:16); for “My sword shall devour flesh” (Deut. 32:42). Spurn blandishments; despise promises. He promises great things, but I greater; he offers many things, but I very many. Will you then abandon heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for temporal? Otherwise you must pay your vows, which your lips have uttered. He is justly required to pay who was not compelled to vow; for although [Col. 0083C] I did not reject you when you knocked, neither did I compel you to enter. Therefore you may not abandon what you freely promised; it is not lawful to reclaim what you yourself renounced. Behold, I warn you both beforehand and give wholesome counsel to each. To you,” He says to the uncle, “do not bring a regular back to the world; for if you bring him back, you lead astray one whom you make apostatize. And you, regular canon, do not follow a worldly man; for if you follow him, you persecute Me, against whom you commit an injury in your own person. If you seduce a soul for whom I died, you make yourself an enemy of My cross. For ‘he who does not gather with Me scatters’” (Matt. 12:30); “how much more he who scatters those already gathered? But if you consent to him, you dissent from Me; for ‘he who is not with Me is against Me’” (ibid.). How much more is he against Me who was with Me, if he abandons Me? “If you ensnare the little one who has come to Me, you shall be judged a seducer and a sacrilegious man; but if you destroy again what you had built, you make yourself a transgressor. Both of you must appear before My judgment; both must stand before My tribunal: the one will be judged for his own transgression, [Col. 0083D] the other for seducing another; and where one shall die in his iniquity, there the blood of him who dies shall be required from the hand of the other” (Ezek. 3:18). These things and others like them, Christ, with the conscience of each bearing witness, were invisibly yet terribly thundering to both of them; by these sacred admonitions You were mercifully striking their minds with fear. Who would not at this fear, by fearing return to his senses, except one who, after the manner of a deaf asp stopping its ears, either did not hear, or pretended not to hear, “the voice of the enchanter charming wisely” (Ps. 57:5–6)?

7. But how long shall we now prolong a letter already sufficiently—or excessively—long, while we unwillingly speak of a matter worthy of silence? Why do we approach the truth by such circuitous paths, while we fear to uncover shameful things? Yet I shall speak; I shall speak with shame, what, though known to many, I cannot conceal even if I wish. But why with shame? Why should I be ashamed to write what they were not ashamed to do? If one ought to be ashamed to hear what they have shamelessly done, one ought not be ashamed to correct what they are unwilling [Col. 0084B] to hear. Alas for grief! Neither could be recalled: neither fear nor reason could turn the one from seduction, nor shame and profession the other from transgression. What more? A deceitful tongue devises words of ruin: it conceived pain and persuaded iniquity. The perverse man overthrew the convert: “the dog returns to his vomit” (2 Pet. 2:22). Your church received back its foster-child, whom it had been better off having lost. Thus Lyons once, through the like zeal and contrivance of its dean, recovered badly the dean’s nephew, its canon, whom it had rightly lost. As that man stole Fulco from blessed Augustine, so this man stole Othbert from Saint Benedict. How much more fittingly would he himself have become holy with a saint than have been perverted from holiness with a perverse man! How much more beautifully would a religious youth draw an aged worldly man [Col. 0084C] to himself, so that both might conquer, than a worldly man draw back a religious man to himself, in which both are conquered! O unhappy old man! O cruel uncle! Already decrepit and soon to die, he first killed his nephew’s soul; and, in order to have him as heir to his sins, deprived him of Christ’s inheritance! But “he who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Sir. 14:5). He preferred to have a successor in his possessions rather than an intercessor for his iniquities.

8. But what have I to do with the deans, our masters, who have attained precedence in churches? They hold the key of knowledge and occupy the chief seats in assemblies. Let them themselves see how they judge their subjects, recall fugitives, make those recalled flee again if they wish, gather the dispersed, and scatter those gathered: what is that to me? I confess that, for your sake, my Fulco, I have exceeded somewhat the measure of my smallness against them, wishing to cover your shame at their expense and mitigate your fault. I therefore leave them alone, lest they rightly be angry not so much at the rebuke as at the rebuker; and lest, instead of considering their own correction, they should accuse me of presumption. I have undertaken to scold not a prince of the Church, but a schoolboy, who does not know how to be indignant or to be angry. Unless perhaps you too, a child in understanding though not in malice, [Col. 0085A] accuse me of this very thing and say: “Indeed, what have I to do with him? What has he to do with my sin? Am I a monk?” To this, I confess, I have no answer, except that I trusted both in your inborn gentleness, which I believed to be in you, and in the charity of God, by which I remember that I excused myself even at the beginning of this letter. Moved only by zeal for God, pitying so greatly your error and sympathizing so greatly with your misery, I have involved myself beyond my measure and custom in an affair not my own. Your grievous fall and pitiable collapse have prompted me to presume this. Which of your contemporaries have you seen me rebuke? To whom have I ever directed even the briefest letter? This is not because I considered all the rest holy or found nothing in them worthy of rebuke.

9. “Why then,” you ask, “do you rebuke me alone, when you see in others what perhaps you might more justly rebuke?” My answer is: Because of the singularity of your error, because of the enormity of your sin. For although [Col. 0085B] many others live wickedly, although they are disorderly and undisciplined, they have not yet professed an order or discipline. They are indeed sinners, but not transgressors. But you, however modestly and honourably you may live—however chaste, sober, and altogether religious your conduct—your religious life is nevertheless less acceptable to God than the transgression of your vow defiles it. Therefore, dearest friend, do not compare yourself with your contemporaries, from whom your profession separates you; nor, by comparison with worldly men, flatter yourself about your perhaps somewhat stricter continence, when the Lord says to you: “Would that I had found you hot or cold.” Here it is plainly shown that you, being lukewarm, please God less than if you were cold like those men. God patiently awaits their progress from coldness at some time to warmth; but He observes you with indignation, since you have already fallen from warmth into lukewarmness. “Because I have found you lukewarm,” He says, “I will begin to vomit you out of My mouth” (Rev. 3:15–16). And deservedly, because you have returned to your own vomit, because you have vomited out His grace.

10. Alas! How quickly you have come to loathe Christ, of whom it is written: “Honey and milk are under His tongue” (Song 4:11). I marvel that you are nauseated by the taste of the sweetest food—if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet. [Col. 0085D] Or perhaps you have not yet tasted, and do not know what Christ tastes like; and therefore you do not desire what you have not experienced. Or, if you have tasted and it did not seem sweet, your palate is not sound. For He is the wisdom of God, who says: “He who eats Me shall still hunger, and he who drinks Me shall still thirst” (Sir. 24:29). But how can one hunger or thirst for Christ while daily filled with the husks of swine? “You cannot drink at once the cup of Christ and the cup of demons” (1 Cor. 10:20). The cup of demons is pride; the cup of demons is detraction and envy; the cup of demons is gluttony and drunkenness. When these have filled either your mind or your belly, Christ finds no place in you. Do not wonder that I say this. In your uncle’s house you cannot be made drunk [Col. 0086A] from “the abundance of the house of God.” Why, you ask? Because it is a house of delights. Just as fire and water cannot exist together, so spiritual and carnal delights do not tolerate one another in the same place. Where Christ perceives the belching of a glutton amid drinking bouts, He does not deem the mind worthy to receive His wines, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Where a curious variety of dishes and the many-coloured diversity of costly furnishings feed alike the eyes and the belly, the heavenly bread abandons the fasting mind. Come then, rejoice, young man, in your youth, so that, when temporal joy departs together with your age, the eternal sorrow which will engulf you may succeed it. But far be this from our young man; may God turn this from His child. Rather, may the Lord destroy every deceitful lip of those who give you such counsel, who say to you every day, “Well done, well done,” [Col. 0086B] and seek your soul. These are those among whom you dwell, whose wicked conversations [variant: “counsels”] corrupt the good morals of a young man.

11. But how long will you not leave their midst? What are you doing in the city, you who chose the cloister? What have you to do with the world, you who despised the world? “The lines have fallen for you in pleasant places,” and do you covet earthly riches? If you wish to possess both these things and those, the short answer to you will be: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your life” (Luke 16:25). He said, “You received,” not, “You seized,” lest you flatter yourself in vain even in this, that, content with what is yours, you do not seize what belongs to others. Yet what are those things that are yours? The benefices of the Church? Certainly. Because you rise for vigils, go to Masses, and attend the choir at the [Col. 0086C] canonical hours of night and day, you do well. Thus you do not receive the Church’s prebend for nothing. It is fitting that he who serves at the altar should live by the altar. It is therefore granted you, if you serve well, to live by the altar; but not to indulge in luxury by the altar, to be proud by the altar, or from it to procure golden bridles, painted saddles, silvered spurs, and variegated grey furs ornamented at neck and hands with purple decoration. In short, whatever you retain from the altar beyond necessary food and simple clothing is not yours: it is robbery, it is sacrilege. The wise man prayed that only what was necessary for his sustenance, not superfluities, might be given to him (Prov. 30:8). “Having,” says the Apostle, “food and clothing” (1 Tim. 4:8), not “food and adornment.” And another saint says: “If the Lord gives me bread to eat, and clothing with which I may be covered” (Gen. 28:20). Note: “with which I may be covered.” Therefore let us too be content with garments by which we may be covered, not garments in which we may indulge, not garments in which we may be proud, not garments by which we may seek either to imitate or please little women. “But,” you say, “those with whom I live do these things; if I do not do what the others do, I shall be marked for singularity.” For that very reason, I say, leave their midst, lest you either live conspicuously in the city or perish by the example of others.

12. What are you doing in the city, delicate soldier? Your fellow soldiers, whom you fled and deserted, fight and conquer; knock and enter; seize heaven and reign—[Col. 0087A] while you, seated upon your riding-horse, clothed in purple and fine linen, circle the squares and wander through the streets? These are ornaments of peace, not defences of war. Or do you say, “Peace,” when there is no peace? (Ezek. 13:10). Purple does not drive back lust, repel pride or avarice, or extinguish any other fiery darts of the enemy. Indeed, what you fear more, it does not prevent fever or ward off death. Where are the weapons of war? Where the shield of faith? Where the helmet of salvation? Where the breastplate of patience? Why do you tremble? “There are more with us than with them.” Take up arms, recover your strength, while the battle still lasts. The angels are present as spectators and protectors; the Lord Himself is present as helper and defender, He “who teaches your hands for battle and your fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1). Let us go forth to help [Col. 0087B] our brethren, lest perhaps they fight without us, conquer without us, and enter without us; and at last, when the door has been shut, to us who knock late there may be answered from within: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Take care, I beg you, first to make yourself known, first to make yourself seen, lest then you be unknown for glory but known for punishment. If Christ recognizes you in battle, He will recognize you in heaven; and, as He promised, He will manifest Himself to you (John 14:21), provided that you too, by repenting and coming to your senses, show yourself such that you may confidently say: “Then I shall know, even as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). For the present, let it suffice that the modest mind of the young man has been struck by these admonitions. Now divine mercy too must be entreated for him by our prayers; and if it finds his mind even somewhat softened by the blows of our rebukes, I trust that it will soon make us rejoice over him.

## LETTER III

> [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1120.]

### TO THE REGULAR CANONS OF AILDICURT

He says that their praises frighten him rather than flatter him. Then, concerning certain canons of Saint Augustine who had come to him, he says that they should not be hindered.

[Col. 0088A]

To the holy community of clergy serving God in the place called Aildicurt, to Master S. and his disciples: the little flock of brothers of Clairvaux, and Brother Bernard, their servant of whatever worth, wish them to walk in the Spirit and to examine all things spiritually.

> [Note: We have restored this address from the Corbie manuscript. Who these regular canons were is not clear.]

The exhortation in your letter, so salutary and so concise, offers us, as we marvel and rejoice, great proofs of your learning and of your wonderful charity. But the exceedingly high praises which, out of your devotion, though you had not tested them, you prefaced concerning us—even though they could, so far as you are concerned, instruct [Col. 0088B] us not a little in the practice of humility—nevertheless greatly terrified our consciences, which, so far as lies in us, are cast much lower. For which of us, considering his own manner of life, could hear such great and so undeserved things about himself without great fear or danger? It is not safe to entrust oneself to another’s—or even one’s own—judgment in such matters. For “the Lord is He who judges us” (1 Cor. 4:4).

Moreover, concerning the brethren whose salvation we have learned that your charity is undoubtedly concerned for: to set you at ease, know that at the exhortation and advice of many distinguished men, and especially of the most renowned William, bishop of Châlons, they came to us and obtained admission from us by many prayers and supplications. Their intention, namely, is that, on account of the stricter rule of life, they may, with God’s help, pass from the institutions of blessed Augustine to the observances of Saint Benedict, yet not depart from the teaching of Him who alone is Master of all in heaven and on earth (Matt. 23:8); and that they may not make void the first faith which they promised among you—or rather, which they first promised in Baptism—but keep it safe and whole.

> [Note: This was William of Champeaux, who died in 1121, a foremost friend of Bernard and repeatedly praised in his *Life*. Before becoming bishop, having abandoned teaching, he withdrew to the Parisian monastery of Saint-Victor. Hildebert, then bishop of Le Mans, congratulates him upon this action in the first letter, which is without a title in the printed editions but in the manuscript of Saint-Taurin at Évreux is inscribed “To William of Champeaux.” In 1120 Cardinal Conon, legate, came to the monastery of Mauriniac near Étampes, “having with him as a great helper William, bishop of Châlons, who had directed the higher schools,” that is, theological schools, “and who then, possessing zeal for God, shone above all the bishops of all Gaul in knowledge of the divine Scriptures”: from the *Chronicle of Mauriniac*. Hence you may refute those who place his death in 1119. Hugh of Métel, in Letter 4 to Innocent, on the occasion of Abelard—who had been William’s pupil and adversary—says: “When Anselm of Laon and William of Châlons died, the fire of God’s word failed on earth.” Concerning this William, an anonymous author cited by Chesne in notes to Abelard says: “At the same time Master William of Champeaux, formerly archdeacon of Paris, a man exceedingly learned and religious, took the habit of a regular canon and, with some disciples outside the city of Paris, in a place where there was a chapel of Saint Victor the martyr, began to build a monastery [Col. 0088C] of clergy,” which King Louis the Fat afterward magnificently completed. “But when he was made bishop of Châlons,” namely in 1113, as Alberic states in his *Chronicle*, “the venerable Gilduin, his disciple, was made the first abbot there.” This is the same William who consecrated Saint Bernard as abbot, *Life*, book 1, chapter 7; and he cherished Bernard so warmly that when the saint fell into serious illness, he undertook his care: ibid., where more is said of him. He happily ended his days not in 1119, as many maintain, dating his consecration to 1112, but in 1121, as the same Alberic mentioned above writes; he is supported by ancient records of the Church of Châlons and by the *Acts of the Bishops* of that church in Charles Rapine. Concerning him Robert of Howden, in the first part of his *Annals*, under the year 1121, writes: “William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, eight days before his death, having received the monastic habit”—that is, as he lay near death in bed, according to the custom of those times—“departed this life on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February” [18 January]. In this matter the Corbeil necrology differs; according to the testimony of Jean Picard it reads: “On the eighth day before the Kalends of February, the anniversary of William, bishop of Châlons and our canon.” He was buried at Clairvaux, according to Rapine, in a chapel which he had built. Moreover, since this letter was written while he was still alive, it must be assigned to about the year 1121. Various theological writings of William of Champeaux are mentioned in the manuscript *Panchrysis* of Cheminon; an epitome of his *Morals* is at Clairvaux.]

Accordingly, since such men have been received in this manner, far be it from us to believe that your integrity has been injured by receiving them, or ought to be injured by retaining them, provided that, should they happen within the year of probation established by rule to abandon what they have begun and wish to return to you, we do not hold them against their will. Otherwise, most holy brethren, it is not your concern to strive, by an ill-considered anathema, vainly to hinder the spirit of liberty which is in them—unless perhaps, which may God avert, you seek your own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ.

## LETTER IV

> [Note: Written about the year 1127.]

### TO ARNOLD, ABBOT OF MORIMOND

He recalls Abbot Arnold, who has rashly left his monastery and is wandering abroad, to the care of the monastery, setting forth the scandals among the brethren and the dangers to the flock.

> [Note: Arnold was a native of Cologne, noble by birth, brother of Frederick, then bishop of Cologne, and a young man of great promise. Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, first appointed him over Morimond—the fourth daughter of Cîteaux—founded in 1115 in the diocese of Langres. After governing it for ten years and founding three monasteries, namely Bellevaux in the diocese of Besançon, La Crête-Blanche in the diocese of Langres, and Altenkamp in the diocese of Cologne, he was at last troubled by the harassment of neighbouring secular persons and by the disobedience of certain of his own brethren, as Bernard testifies in Letter 141 to Humbert. He abandoned the monastery, taking several monks with him, among whom were four principal men: Adam, Everard, Henry, and Conrad. Meanwhile Stephen of Cîteaux was detained in Flanders on business of his Order. Manriquez maintains that this happened in 1125. Bernard meanwhile tried to recall the fugitives by letters separately sent to Arnold and Adam, namely Letters 4 and 5; he also wrote another letter, Letter 6, to the noble Bruno of Cologne, afterward Frederick’s successor, asking him to arrange their recall. But in vain: Arnold ended his days in Belgium in 1126, on the third day before the Nones of January [3 January]. When Bernard heard this, after a general chapter had been convened, he again pursued the other wanderers, writing to Adam—Letter 7—and threatening excommunication unless they came to their senses. He succeeded happily; writers commonly suppose that this Adam was the man first placed over the monastery of Eberbach in the diocese of Würzburg in Franconia in 1127, who preached the holy expedition to the German princes, as Otto of Freising reports in *The Deeds of the Emperor Frederick*, book 1, chapter 40, and who finally ended his days in the reputation of holiness. For more on these men see Manriquez, *Annals*, volumes 1 and 2, especially under the years 1115, 1125, and 1127.]

[Col. 0089B]

To Lord Abbot Arnold, Brother Bernard of Clairvaux: the spirit of compunction and counsel.

1. First I want you to know that the lord abbot of Cîteaux had not yet returned from Flanders, through which he had passed a little earlier by way of us, when your messenger came to us; and therefore he has received neither the letter which you ordered to be delivered to him nor any knowledge as yet of this great novelty rashly undertaken by you. Happy for the moment, that he may be permitted to be ignorant, even for a time, of such sad reports. Next, as for your forbidding us to hope for your recall, thereby driving us to despair, and to attempt by letters to dissuade you from what seems fixed in you as if unshakably: perhaps I ought not in reason to obey you in this; but truly, I confess, I could not do so for grief. Even if I knew for certain where I might conveniently find you, I would rather have come in person than sent this letter, perhaps accomplishing by myself what I cannot accomplish by any letters. Perhaps you laugh at this confidence of mine as vain, conscious as you are of your own obstinacy; and you hope that no force, prayer, or effort can prevail to bend it. But I, not distrusting the power of Him who said, “All things are possible to him who believes” (Mark 9:22), confidently claiming also for myself the saying, “I can do all things in Him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13), although I too know very well the obstinacy of your stony heart in large measure—would that now, [Col. 0090A] whether fruitfully or fruitlessly, I might cling to your side. How many things that move me against you would I cast in your face, I know not whether in vain or with profit, not with words alone but with face and eyes. Then, falling at your feet, I would hold them; I would embrace your knees; hanging wholly from your neck, I would kiss that most sweet head, worn for many years beneath the same purpose with me under the sweet yoke of Christ. I would also weep as much as I could, pray and beseech you through the Lord Jesus, that you would spare, first indeed, His cross, by which He redeemed those whom you, so far as lies in you, destroy; gathered those whom you scatter. You destroy and scatter, I say, both those whom you take with you and those whom you leave here; although we fear different, yet not unequal, danger for both alike. [Col. 0090B] Then I would beg you also to spare us, your friends, to whom, though unworthy, you have left nothing but weeping and tears. Oh, had this been permitted me! Perhaps I would have bent by affection him whom I cannot bend by reason; perhaps fraternal pity would have softened that iron breast which, at least in this matter, refuses to yield even through fear of Christ. But alas! You have deprived us of this opportunity also.

2. O great pillar of our Order! Patiently, I beseech you, hear a friend even though absent, one wholly unable to endure your departure and deeply sharing both your labour and your danger. O great pillar of our Order! Do you not fear that, when you fall, a great collapse will undoubtedly soon follow? “But I,” you say, “do not fall: I know what I am doing; I have a good conscience.” So be it: we believe you concerning yourself. But what of us, who now endure grievous scandals caused by your departure and await, with fear, graver dangers? Or do you also know these things but feign not to know? How, then, can you presume that you do not fall while causing the fall of many, since you were placed in this office in order that you should seek not what is useful to yourself but rather what is useful to others; not your own interests but those of Jesus Christ? How, I ask, do you depart without concern, you who take away forever every assurance from the flock entrusted to you? Who will meet the wolves as they rush in? Who will comfort them in tribulations? Who will provide for them in temptations? Who, finally, will withstand the roaring lion seeking someone to devour? [Col. 0091A] Undoubtedly they will be exposed to the bites of the wicked, who devour Christ’s people as though eating bread. Alas! What will become of Christ’s new plantations, planted by your hands in diverse places—places of horror and vast solitude? Who will dig about them? Who will enrich them with manure? Who will place a hedge around them? Who will be concerned to cut back their growing shoots? Either, when the wind of temptations blows, still very tender, alas, they will easily be uprooted; or, as brambles spring up with them, and there is no one to clear them away, they will be choked and bear no fruit.

3. Since this is so, judge for yourself what sort of good this good of yours will be, or whether it can even be good amid such great evils. However much you may trust that you will produce fruits worthy of repentance, must they not be choked by thorns of this kind? Finally, if you “offer rightly but divide not rightly,” do you not sin? (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint.) What is this? Would you perhaps call it right division to provide only for your own soul, while depriving of a father’s counsel your children whom you leave orphaned? O wretched and pitiable men—and the more pitiable because, while their father lives, they see themselves bereft of him! Yet you ought also to doubt whether you provide rightly even for yourself, since you undertake so novel a matter without the counsel of your brethren and fellow abbots, and without the permission of your father and master. This also especially troubles many: that you take with you weak boys and delicate youths. For if they are good and strong, they were needed by the desolate house; but if, as I said, they are delicate and weak, they will not be fit for a harsh and laborious wandering. Nor do we believe that you still wish to preside over the governance of their souls; for we have learned that your purpose is simply to cast aside the pastoral burden of your own people and henceforth live for yourself alone. It would indeed be very incongruous for you presumptuously to resume elsewhere, without being called, what you rashly abandon elsewhere though forbidden to do so. But lest I needlessly press many things upon one who knows them all: at the end, and in good faith, I promise that, if you give me an opportunity to speak with you, I will endeavour to ensure that what you have undertaken disorderly and dangerously you may carry out lawfully and therefore safely. Farewell.

## LETTER V

> [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1125.]

### TO ADAM THE MONK

He dissuades him from adhering to Arnold, abbot of Morimond, and from making himself a companion in his pilgrimage—or rather, wandering.

[Col. 0091D]

1. Your humility, sufficiently known to me, and the necessity of the danger now at hand give me confidence to address you more sharply and rebuke you more freely. O senseless man! Who has bewitched you to depart so quickly from that most salutary counsel upon which, long ago, you and I agreed together, with God alone as witness? Consider, foolish man, your ways, and turn your feet toward the testimonies of the Lord. Do you not remember that you first dedicated the beginnings of your conversion at Marmoutier; secondly, at Foigny, you entrusted yourself to our poor providence; thirdly, at Morimond you confirmed your stability; fourthly, after again taking counsel with me, you frankly renounced the pilgrimage—or rather wandering—suggested to you by Abbot Arnold, and judged fellowship with him unlawful if he himself could not lawfully depart?

> [Note: On Marmoutier near Tours, see Letter 397; on Foigny, in the diocese of Laon, Letter 72.]

What then? Will you say that it is lawful for him to depart, when he has left a lamentable scandal to those entrusted to him and did not wait for the permission of the one who entrusted them?

2. “But to what end,” you ask, “do these things tend, which you have wished to recount in this way?” That I may accuse you of evident fickleness; that I may plainly show that with you it is both “Yes” and “No”; and that thus, at last recognizing [Col. 0092B] and blushing for your error, you may learn, even late, from the Apostle not to believe every spirit (1 John 4:1); learn from Solomon to have many friends but one counsellor out of a thousand (Sir. 6:6); learn from the example of the Lord’s Forerunner not merely not to be clothed in soft garments, but also not to be carried about like a reed shaken by the wind (Matt. 11:8–9), with every wind of doctrine; learn from the Gospel to found your house upon the rock (Matt. 7:24); and learn, with the disciples of the serpent, not to forget prudence together with the simplicity of the dove (Matt. 10:16). From these and many other testimonies of Scripture, gather this conclusion: that the manifold seducer has hitherto mocked you greatly, who, since he could not prevent the beginning of good in you, begrudged your perseverance. [Col. 0092C] He judged this sufficient for his malice: if he could take from you that one thing which he knew alone among virtues to be crowned. I beseech you through the bowels of Christ’s mercy: by no means depart, or at least do not depart before you come to speak with us at a suitable place, in case some remedy may perhaps be found for the many evils which, from your departure, we already feel to have come upon us or fear are yet to come. Farewell.

## Letter VI

[Note: [Col. 0092D] Written in the year of Christ 1125.]  
To Bruno of Cologne. He desires certain wandering monks of the abbot of Morimond to be brought back to their monastery through Bruno’s efforts.

To the lord Bruno, illustrious man [Note: [Col. 0092D] He later became archbishop of Cologne; Letters 8 and 9 are addressed to him.], and his beloved, Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting, [Col. 0092D] and whatever the prayer of a sinner may avail.

1. Since long ago at Rheims we both acquired a welcome mutual acquaintance, I do not think that you have entirely forgotten our insignificance. Therefore I write to you without timidity, as not to a stranger but with the fullest confidence, whatever I wish, as to one known and familiar to us. Arnold, abbot of Morimond, has lately deserted his monastery in a sufficiently disorderly fashion, to the grave scandal of our whole Order. For in so scrupulous a matter he waited neither for the counsel of his fellow abbots nor for the permission or consent of the abbot to whom he owed principal [Col. 0093A] subjection—namely, the abbot of Cîteaux. Although he was a man under authority, having soldiers himself under him, impatient of a higher authority, he proudly cast off a foreign yoke from his own neck, while more proudly retaining his own over his subjects.

Indeed, out of the great multitude of monks whom, travelling over sea and land, he had vainly gathered—not for Christ but for himself—he left behind only very few, and those the simpler and more lax, in desolation; while he took with him as companions in his error all the better and more perfect men. Among these he dared also to seduce, and resolved to take with him, three men whose removal distressed us especially: namely, Evrard, our brother [variant: your brother], and Adam, whom you know well, and that noble boy [Col. 0093B] Conrad, whom he had earlier brought away from Cologne, not without scandal. Yet, if you are willing to exert yourself, we trust that these men may be recalled through your efforts.

2. As for recalling Arnold himself, because we have already tested the obstinacy of his inflexible mind on many occasions, we do not wish you to labour in vain. But we have heard that Evrard and Adam, along with certain other brethren of the same company, are still remaining in your region. If this is true, you should meanwhile, if you please, meet with them personally; bend them by prayers; convince them by reason; and instruct their dove-like simplicity with serpentine prudence. Let them not suppose that obedience consists in attaching themselves to one who is disobedient; let them not trust that they may lawfully follow one who is unlawfully wandering; let them not be deceived into deserting the Order which they professed [Col. 0093C] for the sake of a disorderly man. For, by apostolic authority, they ought not hesitate to call even an angel from heaven anathema—rejected—if he should preach to them another gospel (Gal. 1:8). [Note: [Col. 0093D] Thus in all manuscripts, and rightly according to the Apostle’s meaning: to call the angel himself anathema, that is, rejected.] Let them also learn from the Apostle that they must withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly (2 Thess. 3:6).

May he also teach you not to think proudly or to place hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6:17), until Christ may claim as his approved disciple one who has renounced all things. Farewell.

## Letter VII

[Note: [Col. 0093D] Written in the year of Christ 1126.]  
To Adam the monk. [Note: [Col. 0094D] In the royal manuscript it is entitled, “On the discernment of obedience.” This letter was written after the death of Abbot Arnold, which occurred in Belgium in 1126.] He urges Adam to return to the monastery, now at last that the abbot has died; he shows that in such a matter there was no bond of obedience. Finally, he replies why he receives religious from other Orders.

[Col. 0093D]

1. If charity had remained in you—as we once either knew or believed it to be—you would surely have felt the injuries done to charity, which indeed are the scandals of the little ones. For charity would not offend or despise charity when it felt the offence. It cannot deny itself, for it is not divided against itself. Rather, it knows how to unite those divided within itself; it does not know how to divide those united. Therefore, as I said, if it had remained in you, it would not have kept silence, rested, or dissembled; groaning and burning, [Col. 0094A] and undoubtedly murmuring within your pious breast: “Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

For charity is kind; it loves peace and rejoices together with unity. It alone generates, gathers, strengthens, and preserves unity wherever unity is known to be preserved in the bond of peace. Therefore, since this most honourable mother of unity and peace is hostile to you, how, I ask, do you presume that any sacrifice of yours can be acceptable to God, when the Apostle judges that even martyrdom is nothing without her? (1 Cor. 13:3.) Or why do you trust [variant: believe] that she is perhaps not hostile to you, when by acting so inhumanely you have neither spared nor do spare her chaste womb and her dear children, tearing unity apart and breaking the bond of peace?

You must therefore lay down whatever offering you are preparing to present, and first be reconciled to that which has something against you—not a brother, but a multitude of brothers. Behold, the unity of the whole brotherhood, as though wounded by the sword of your departure, complains against your small number, [Col. 0094B] as one lamenting miserably might say: “The sons of my mother have fought against me” (Song 1:5). And rightly so: for whoever is not with her is against her. Do you think that the pious mother, charity, can hear the just groaning of her daughter without groaning herself? Therefore, joining her own tears to ours, she says of you: “I have nourished and brought up sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2).

Charity is God himself. Our peace is Christ, “who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). In the Trinity, unity is especially commended. Therefore, one against whom charity, peace, and unity are known to be angry—what has he in the kingdom of Christ and of God? [Col. 0094C]

2. But perhaps you say: “Our abbot led us away and commanded us to go with him. Were we to be disobedient?” You know—unless perhaps you have forgotten—what was agreed between us on a certain day, after the plan of the conspiracy and scandal already communicated to me had been carefully examined in mutual discussion. Had you remained in that agreement, this might fittingly have been said of you: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. 1:1).

But let it be so: sons ought to obey their father; disciples ought to follow their teacher. Certainly an abbot might be permitted to lead his monks where he pleased and teach what he pleased—but only while he lived. Now that he is dead, whom are you compelled still to hear as teacher [Col. 0094D] or follow as guide, that you hesitate any longer to repair so grave a scandal? Who now prevents you from hearing—not me, I say, but our God—who graciously calls you back through the mouth of Jeremiah? For he says: “Will one who has fallen not rise again? Or will one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. 8:4.)

Did he, when dying, also forbid you, even after your fall, to attempt to rise; after turning away, to dare speak of returning? Must you obey one who is dead—and obey against charity, obey at the peril of your own salvation? Yet I suppose that you would not claim the bond between abbots and subjects to be firmer or more binding than that between spouses, whom God himself, not man, bound together by an inviolable sacrament, when the Saviour said: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. 19:6). But when the Apostle declares that a woman is released from the law of her husband upon his death (Rom. 7:2), do you consider yourself bound by the law of an abbot now dead—and that against the law which has been established, namely the law of charity? [Col. 0095A]

3. I have said this not because I think that you ought to have obeyed him even while he lived in this matter, or that compliance of this kind should even be called obedience. On the contrary, the general judgment concerning such people is: “But those who turn aside into crooked ways the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity” (Ps. 125:5). And lest any abbot perhaps maintain that obedience even in evil is free from this curse, hear elsewhere more clearly: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. 18:20).

From this it is plainly evident that commands to do evil must not be obeyed. Especially because, when you comply with wicked commands, in the very matter in which you seem obedient to a human being, you plainly show yourself disobedient to God, who has forbidden everything done wrongly. It is most perverse to profess yourself obedient in that by which you are known to dissolve the higher obedience for the lower—that is, divine obedience for human obedience. What then? A human being commands what God forbids; and shall I listen to a human being, deaf to God? The Apostles did not act thus. They cried out: “It is better to obey God than men” (Acts 5:29).

Hence the Lord, rebuking the Pharisees in the Gospel, says: [Col. 0095C] “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your traditions?” (Matt. 15:3.) And through Isaiah he says: “In vain do they worship me, holding the commandments and doctrines of men” (Isa. 29:13). And again, to the first-created man: “Because you obeyed the voice of your wife more than mine, cursed is the ground in your work” (Gen. 3:17). Therefore, to do evil at anyone’s command is manifestly not obedience but rather disobedience.

4. It should certainly be observed that some things are pure goods, while some are pure evils; and in these no obedience is owed to human beings. For the former must not be omitted even when forbidden; nor must the latter be committed even when commanded. But between these are certain intermediate matters which, according to manner, place, time, or person, can be either bad or good. In these the law of obedience is established, as in the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which stood in the midst of Paradise. In such matters it is surely not lawful for us to prescribe our own judgment in place of the decisions of our teachers; in them, the command or prohibition of superiors is in no way to be despised.

Let us see whether perhaps what we charge against you was of this kind, and for that reason perhaps ought not to have been charged. This will become clearer if I add examples of the foregoing distinction. Faith, hope, charity, and similar things are pure goods; because they cannot be commanded or held wrongly, they cannot be forbidden or not held rightly. Theft, sacrilege, adultery, and the like are pure evils; clearly, they can neither be commanded or committed rightly, nor forbidden or left undone wrongly. [Col. 0096A] “Against such things there is no law.” No one’s prohibition can oppose commands; no one’s command can override prohibitions.

There are, further, intermediate things which are by themselves known to be neither good nor bad. They may indifferently be forbidden or commanded either well or badly; but subjects can never obey badly in such matters. Of this kind, for example, are fasting, keeping vigils, reading, and similar things. Yet it should be understood that some intermediate matters frequently pass into the status of pure goods or pure evils. Marriage, for instance, may be entered into or not entered into; yet once made, it may not be dissolved. What was clearly intermediate before marriage assumes the force of a pure good in those already married. Likewise, possessing one’s own property is an intermediate matter for a secular person, since he may also possess nothing; but for a monk it is a pure evil, because he may not possess property. [Col. 0096B]

5. Do you now see, brother, to which principal category of this distinction your deed most properly belongs? If it must be assigned among pure goods, it is commendable; if among pure evils, blameworthy; but if it is to be placed among intermediate matters, perhaps the departure may be excused on account of obedience, though the delay certainly cannot be, since it is not caused by obedience. For now that the abbot is dead, if he formerly commanded something which he ought not to have commanded, it is in no way to be obeyed, as the foregoing discussion has shown.

And although the matter is already sufficiently clear in itself, nevertheless, for the sake of certain persons who seek an excuse where reason supplies none, I shall briefly make it plain—and so plain that every shadow of doubt disappears—that such obedience and such abandonment of your monastery were neither a pure nor an intermediate good, but plainly a pure evil. I say nothing, indeed, about the dead man, who now has God as his own and sole judge, and who truly now stands or falls to his own master; lest God, justly angered, perhaps say: “They have taken all judgment from me.” Yet for the correction of the living I examine, not what he did, but what he commanded—whether that command ought to have had force such that it should be followed to the scandal of many.

And first I must say that, if any followed one departing wrongly in simplicity, suspecting no evil and believing that he departed with the permission of the bishop of Langres and the abbot of Cîteaux [Col. 0096D] (for he was indebted to both)—as it is not incredible that some in that company so believed—our present rebuke does not touch them, provided that, once they learn the truth, they return without delay.

6. Therefore my discourse is directed only against those—or rather, it is for their benefit—who knowingly and deliberately put their hands into the fire; who, conscious of the presumption, followed the presumptuous man; who did not heed the Apostle forbidding and declaring that they should withdraw from every brother walking disorderly (2 Thess. 3:6); and who despised the voice of the Lord himself, saying: “He who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30).

You, brothers—you, I say—are openly and specifically marked by that reproach in Jeremiah which I recall with grief: [Col. 0097A] “This is the nation,” he says, “which has not heard the voice of the Lord its God” (Jer. 7:28). For this is properly God’s voice: he identifies his enemy by his own authority and points him out, as it were, with his finger, in order to deter simple people from following that impious man: “He who is not with me,” he says, “scatters.” It is as if he said: “Understand that you are no longer with me in this, if you follow the scatterer.”

When God cried, “He who does not gather with me scatters,” ought you to follow a scatterer? When God, I say, invited you to gather, ought you rather to obey a human being in scattering? He despised his teachers, exposed his subjects, disturbed his companions; and you, seeing a thief, ran with him! I had resolved to keep silence about the dead man; but I was compelled, I confess, to digress somewhat, because obedience could not be disproved unless the command itself were shown to be blameworthy. Since the man’s command and action were not different, it seemed impossible either to approve or reject one without the other.

Yet it is clear that this command ought not to have been obeyed, since God commanded the contrary. Again, who doubts that the ordinances of lesser persons ought not be preferred to those of greater persons, nor private commands allowed to prejudice common ones? For this is what we have from the Rule of Saint Benedict (chapter 71). [Col. 0097B]

7. I could bring forward the abbot of Cîteaux, who rightly complains that you have despised him on Arnold’s account, though he is superior to Arnold as a father to a son, a teacher to a disciple, and, finally, an abbot to a monk entrusted to him. I could also bring forward the bishop, whose contempt is likewise inexcusable because his consent was not awaited; for the Lord says to and of such men: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). But because the supposedly weightier authority of the Roman pontiff might be opposed and preferred to both of these—for they say that you set out by his permission, a permission which itself will be examined in its proper place below (§9)—let an authority be brought forward whose authority may in no way lawfully be contradicted.

Certainly that supreme High Priest who, through his own blood, entered once for all into the holy places, having found eternal redemption (Heb. 9:12), declares in the Gospel with a terrible voice that no one should dare scandalize one of his little ones (Matt. 18:6). But let the scandal of one person be granted to you, if the evil went no farther. Easy pardon will follow a fault from which no grave injury arises. But now, when many have unquestionably been scandalized, who does not plainly see how inhumanly you have preferred a human command to the divine? Who, unless insane, would dare say that this is good, or can be made good, whatever the rank of the person who commanded it? But what is neither good nor capable of being done well is undoubtedly a pure evil. Hence it follows that your journey, undertaken to the scandal of many and therefore against God’s command, was not a pure good or an intermediate matter, but altogether a pure evil. For a pure good is always good, and an intermediate matter can be done well. [Col. 0097D]

8. How, then, could either an abbot’s command or the Pope’s permission make lawful what was a pure evil—as has been irrefutably proved—when it has likewise been asserted above that things of this kind, that is, pure evils, can no more lawfully be done than justly commanded? Do you see how empty is the excuse of human obedience where transgression against God is proved? Nor do I think that I need fear your retreat to the Lord’s answer when he was told of the Pharisees’ scandal: for, just as he disregarded it, saying, “Leave them alone; they are blind, and leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15:14), you may suppose that you too need not fear our scandals.

You see, however, how completely unlike these cases are in this respect. If you compare the persons, there the proud Pharisees were scandalized; here, Christ’s poor are scandalized. If you compare the causes, here frivolity is the cause; there, truth. Again, as was also proposed above, the fact that you preferred not merely human commands to divine ones, but private commands to common ones, is sufficiently proved by this alone: not only the entire body of our Order but also the custom and institution of all monasteries seem to protest against that strange novelty and insolent presumption of yours. [Col. 0098B]

9. Fearing this not without reason, and not being sufficiently confident in your own cause, you attempted to soothe consciences that reproached and gnawed at you by an apostolic permission. What a thoroughly frivolous remedy! It is nothing else than, like the first-created humans, weaving loincloths for cauterized consciences: a covering, that is, not a cure.

“We sought and obtained apostolic permission,” they say. Would that you had sought not permission but counsel: that is, not that it might be allowed, but whether it was allowed. Yet why did you seek permission? In order that something not permitted might be permitted? You therefore wished to do what was not permitted. But what was not permitted was evil. Your intention, then, was evil, since it tended toward evil. Unless perhaps this was something which could not be done without permission but could be done if performed with permission. Yet that has already been excluded above by invincible reasoning.

For when God says, “Do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me,” he does not add, “unless with permission”; nor, when he says, “Whoever scandalizes one of my little ones” (Matt. 23:10, 6), and so forth, does he qualify it by adding, “without permission.” It is therefore established that, where truth—and necessary truth—is not at issue, no scandal whatever may lawfully be caused by anyone, justly commanded, or innocently consented to. Yet you thought permission should be sought for perpetrating this evil. But for what purpose? So that you might sin more freely, and thus more securely—and, the more securely, the more dangerously? Wonderful caution and astonishing prudence! They had already conceived evil in their hearts, but they carefully refrained from performing it until they had permission. They conceived sorrow but did not give birth to iniquity until the wicked Pope had given assent to their conception.

What advantage, or at least what mitigation, of the evil resulted? Did it cease to be evil, or was it even diminished, because the Pope permitted it? Who indeed would deny that giving assent to evil is evil? [Col. 0099A] Yet I would by no means believe that the supreme pontiff did this, unless he had either been deceived by a lie or overcome by importunity. For how else would he have granted you permission of this sort: to sow scandals, raise schisms, grieve friends, disturb the peace of brethren, confound unity, and moreover despise your own bishop? Nor need I say under what necessity you did this, since the outcome of the affair sufficiently shows it. We lament those who departed; we see no benefit from their departure.

10. Do you call consenting to such evils—such great evils—rendering service to them, giving them assistance, “obedience”? Do you name it moderation? Do you call it gentleness? Do you, I say, try to cover the worst vices with the names of virtues? Do you think that you do this without injury to the Lord of virtues when you do injury to the virtues themselves? You veil the emptiest presumption, the basest frivolity, and the cruellest dissension with the names of obedience, moderation, and gentleness; and by veiling filth you stain those sacred words.

May I never emulate such obedience; may I never desire to imitate such moderation—or rather, such vexation; may such gentleness always be far from me. For such obedience is worse than every contempt; such moderation extends beyond every measure. Shall I say “beyond,” or “short of”? Perhaps I should speak more truly—and more aptly in both senses—if I said “outside.” Finally, what kind of gentleness is it that irritates everyone’s ears at its very hearing? Yet I want you now to show me that very gentleness. [Col. 0099C] Since you are so patient that you do not resist being dragged away by anyone, even where that is unlawful, allow me, I beg you, now to deal with you a little more boldly. Otherwise you have treated me very badly indeed, if you think that you alone should be angry with me—something you are not accustomed to do with anyone else.

11. Therefore I address your conscience. Did you depart willingly or unwillingly? If willingly, then it was no longer from obedience. But if unwillingly, you appear to have regarded with suspicion the command which you found burdensome to obey. Where there is suspicion, examination is necessary. Yet, in order to give or receive a test of your patience, examining nothing, you allowed yourself to be dragged away, not merely against your will but also against your conscience. O patience worthy of every impatience! I confess, I cannot refrain from being angry at this most contentious patience. You saw one scattering and followed him; you heard one producing scandals and obeyed him.

True patience is to suffer or do what one would not wish; but not what one may not lawfully do. [Col. 0099D] It is remarkable that you listened to a man whispering secretly, but did not hear God openly protesting, as though thunder had been sent from heaven: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7.) Not only the Lord, moreover, but his own blood likewise assailed you terribly with a mighty cry—though you were deaf. Its outcry is its shedding. Poured out for the scattered children of God in order to gather them into one, it rightly raged against scatterers. He hates scatterers who knows only how to gather.

Great and mighty was that cry which raised bodies from graves and souls from hell. That trumpet summoned earth and heaven into one, reconciling the things on earth and the things in heaven. That sound went out into all the earth, and could it not break your deafness? “That voice is in power; that voice is in magnificence.” And what does it cry? “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Ps. 17:2); and again: “Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58:12).

It is Christ’s blood, Brother Adam—it is Christ’s blood which, on behalf of godly persons gathered together, raises its voice like a trumpet against ungodly scatterers. He threatens to scatter the scatterers, though he was poured out in order to gather the scattered. And if you do not hear his voice, the one from whose side it flowed hears it. For how could he fail to hear his own blood who heard the blood of Abel? (Gen. 4:10.) [Col. 0100B]

12. “But what is that to me?” you say. “Let him see to it; I was not permitted to contradict him. A disciple is not above his teacher. I clung to his side as one to be taught, not as one to teach. As a hearer, I ought to follow, not precede, my instructor.” O Paul the Simple of these times—if only that man had presented himself to you as another Antony, so that you need not examine whatever proceeded, even casually, from his lips, but might obey everything without hesitation and without doubting!

O most obedient monk, from whom not even one iota of any old man’s words slips past! He does not consider the nature of the command; this alone satisfies him, that it is commanded; this alone satisfies him, that it is commanded. [Note: [Col. 0099D] In other copies, “this alone … commanded” is absent.] And this is obedience without delay. If this is how it must be, then it is read in vain in the Church: “Test all things; hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5:21). If this is how it must be, let us erase from the book of the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents,” since what follows is enough, “and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16).

I do not say that subjects ought to judge the commands of their superiors when nothing is found commanded contrary to divine ordinances. But I do maintain that prudence is necessary, so that one may notice whether anything conflicts with them; and freedom is necessary, so that such a command may be openly rejected. But this man says: “I have nothing to examine; let him see to what he commanded.” Tell me, I beg you: if, after putting a sword in your hand, he had ordered you to arm yourself against your own throat, would you have consented? Or if he had wished, by your thrust, to be hurled headlong into fire or water, would you have obeyed? Is it not reckoned to you as the crime of homicide if, being able, you do not prevent such things? [Col. 0100D]

Consider, then, whether perhaps, under the pretext of obedience, you have served him in something still more grievous. You certainly know who said—for perhaps you would not believe me in this matter—that it is better for those who cause scandals to be drowned in the depths of the sea (Matt. 18:6). Why did he say this, except because he intended to signify that such grievous torments await them hereafter that, compared with those torments, temporal death would seem not punitive but advantageous? Why, then, did you help him to cause scandals? For you helped him by following him and obeying him. Would it not have been more useful, according to the preceding judgment of Truth, to hang a millstone around his neck and so drown him in the depths of the sea?

What then? You, that most obedient disciple, considered that father and teacher of yours—whom you would not allow to be removed from you, while he lived, by even a moment’s interval or, as they say, a foot’s breadth—so worthy of your service that, with Balaam’s eyes not blind but open, you did not hesitate to fall into the pit after him: did you, I say, think so to bless him by your obedience that you rendered him obedience more grievous than death? Now indeed I perceive how true is that saying: “The enemies of a man are those of his household” (Mic. 7:6). Knowing this and conscious of it yourself, do you not, if you are wise, groan; and, if you are not foolish, tremble? For your obedience has been found, not in my judgment but in the judgment of Truth, worse than homicide. [Col. 0101B]

13. If you do not ignore these things, how do you not tremble? And if you tremble, how do you not hasten to amend? Otherwise, what sort of conscience will you carry hence to that dreadful tribunal, where the judge needs no witness; where truth examines intentions; where the inquiry into faults reaches the hidden places of the heart; where, finally, that divine gaze searches the most secret recesses of minds; and where, at the sudden brightness of the Sun of righteousness, the opened bosoms of souls vomit forth all things, good or evil, which they concealed?

There, Brother Adam, those who act and those who consent will be punished with equal punishment. There thieves and the companions of thieves will receive like judgment. There those who entice and those sinners who are enticed will undergo equal judgment. Go on, then, and say: “What is it to me? Let him see to it.” Touch pitch and say: “I have not been defiled by it.” Hide fire in your bosom and boast that you are not burned. Finally, place your lot with adulterers and think that it makes no difference to you.

Isaiah did not act so. He reproved himself not only because he was unclean, but because he was the companion of the unclean: “For,” he says, “I am a man with polluted lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips.” Yet I say that he reproved himself not because he lived among evil people, but because he had not reproved their evil. For thus he says: “Woe is me, because I kept silence!” (Isa. 6:5.) But when would he have consented to do the evil which he reproved himself for not reproving in others?

And what of David? Did he not feel that he could be defiled by the contagion of another’s sin, when he said: “With people who work iniquity, I will not share with their chosen ones”? (Ps. 140:4.) Finally he prays: “Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13–14). Therefore he made a point of avoiding the company of evil people whose evil he did not wish to share. For he says: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter with those who do iniquity.” The following verse agrees with this: “I have hated,” he says, “the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. 25:4–5). Hear finally the counsel of the Wise Man: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). [Col. 0101D]

14. Did you then suppose that one must obey anyone against these and countless other testimonies of truth of this kind? O hateful perversity! The virtue of obedience, which always serves truth, arms itself against truth. I would call blessed the disobedience of Brother Henry, who, quickly recovering his senses from error and returning from the journey, was fortunate not to experience such obedience. How much richer and sweeter a fruit of such disobedience he now gathers and already tastes, having the good conscience that, while his fellow members shook the hearts of their brothers with grave scandal, he himself lives among the brethren without reproach in his purpose and Order.

If a choice were given me, I would prefer his slow disobedience with its own conscience to their zealous obedience with scandal. For I judge that he does better, being thus disobedient to the abbot but not to charity, preserving unity in the bond of peace, than those who obey one man in such a way as to prefer one person to unity. I would also add confidently that it is more expedient for anyone that the obedience owed to one person alone be endangered than that all the remaining goods of piety and the vows of one’s own profession be endangered. [Col. 0102B]

15. For, to pass over other matters, two principal observances are handed down to us who live in monasteries: subjection to the abbot and stability in one’s place. They must be observed in such a way that neither obstructs the other, nor does either prejudice the other. For example, you must show yourself so stable in place that you do not despise being subject to the abbot; and so obey as subject to the abbot that you do not lose stability.

But if you detest one who, although persevering in his place, perhaps scorns to submit to the commands of his abbot, are you surprised that we rebuke an obedience which became for you either the cause or the occasion of abandoning your place? Especially since, in regular profession, stability is promised in such a manner that no mention at all is made of the subjection to be rendered to the abbot. [Col. 0102C]

16. But perhaps you ask me: “What, then, do you make of your own stability, which you pledged at Cîteaux, while you now live elsewhere?” I answer: I, indeed, professed as a monk of Cîteaux and was sent by my abbot to the place where I now live; but I was sent in peace, sent without scandal, without discord, according to custom and common institution. Therefore, as long as I persevere in the same peace and concord in which I was sent; as long as I remain in unity and do not prefer private interests to common ones; as long as I remain quiet and subject in the place where I have been established—I say with a secure conscience that I firmly keep what I promised.

For how do I violate the vow of stability when I do not break the bond of unanimity or abandon the foundation of peace? Obedience has removed my body, but harmonious devotion always keeps my spirit present there, and my manner of life is in no respect different. But on the day when—may God avert it—I begin to live by different rules, adopt different customs, serve different observances, devise novelties, or appropriate foreign usages, then, as a transgressor of my profession, I shall no longer trust that I maintain the stability I promised. [Col. 0102D]

I therefore say that an abbot must be obeyed in all things, but with one’s profession preserved. But you professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; where you promised obedience, you also promised stability. If, therefore, you obey but are not stable, then, while offending in one point, you have become guilty of all—and, if guilty of all, guilty also of obedience. [Col. 0103A]

17. Do you see, then, the weight of your obedience? How, indeed, can that which is insufficient even to defend itself suffice to excuse a violation of stability? It is likewise known that each person solemnly and regularly makes profession in the presence of the abbot. Thus one’s profession is made in his presence only, not also at his command. The abbot is therefore called in as a witness, not as the dictator of the profession; as a helper, not a frustrator of its fulfilment; as an avenger, not as the author of its violation. What then? Shall I place in the abbot’s hand what, without any exception, I confirmed before God and his saints by my own hand and mouth, hearing from the Rule [Rule of St Benedict, ch. 58] that, if ever I act otherwise, I am to be condemned by God, whom I mock? If my abbot, or even an angel from heaven, commands what is contrary, I shall freely refuse such obedience, which would make me a transgressor of my own vow and cause me to forswear the name of my God. For I know, according to the truth of Scripture, that by my own mouth I shall either be condemned [Luke XI, 22] or justified; that “a lying mouth kills the soul” [Wisdom I, 11]; that it is truly sung to God, “You will destroy all who speak falsehood” [Psalm V, 7]; and that “each shall bear his own burden” [Galatians VI, 5] and “each shall give an account for himself” [Romans XIV, 12]. Otherwise, with what face could I deceitfully sing in the sight of God and the angels that Psalm verse: “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered”? [Psalm LXV, 13–14.]

[Col. 0103C] Let my abbot, finally, consider what he judges must be done by him concerning that which the Rule directs especially to him: “That he preserve the present Rule in all things”; and likewise what is universally commanded, with no one excepted: “That all follow the Rule, their mistress, in all things, and that no one rashly depart from it” [Rule of St Benedict, chs. 64, 3]. I have resolved always and everywhere to follow him as master in such a way that I do not in any respect depart from the teaching of the Rule which, with him as witness, I swore and determined to observe.

18. Let us briefly meet the question which seems able to arise incidentally, and so bring this already overlong letter to an end. For I seem to speak contrary [Col. 0103D] to what I do. One may ask me: if I condemn those who have abandoned their monastery not merely with their abbot’s consent but even by his command, how is it that I receive and retain those who come to our Order from other monasteries, after breaking their vow of stability and despising the authority of their elders?

The answer to this is brief, but dangerous. For I fear that what I am about to say may displease some. Yet I think I ought more to fear lest, by concealing the truth, I fail to sing truthfully that verse: “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” [Psalm XXXIX, 11]. We receive them for this reason: because we do not think it wrong if they render to God, who is everywhere, wherever they can, the vows of their lips which in their own places they could indeed promise but could by no means [Col. 0104A] pay; and if they make good the loss arising from broken stability alone by the unbroken observance of the remaining precepts of the Rule.

If this displeases anyone, and he murmurs against a man seeking his salvation, the Author of salvation will answer for him: “Is your eye evil because he is good?” [Matthew XX, 15.] Whoever you are who begrudges another’s salvation, spare at least your own. Do you not know that “through the envy of the devil death entered into the world”? [Wisdom II, 24.] Take heed to yourself, then. For if where envy is, there death is also, surely one cannot at once envy and live. Why do you vex your brother because he strives not to render void what has proceeded from his lips? If a man seeks where and how to pay what he promised God, what do you lose? Perhaps, if he owed you some amount of money, you would compel him to go round sea and dry land until he had paid the whole debt to the last farthing. What, then, has your God deserved from you, that you do not wish him also to receive from his debtor that which is his own? Indeed, by begrudging one person you make two hostile to yourself: while you try to deprive both the master of the service of his servant and the servant of his master’s favour. Why do you not rather imitate him, yourself also paying what you owe? Do you suppose that your debt will not be required? Or rather, is it for this very reason that you wickedly provoke God all the more, because you say in your heart, “He will not require it”?

19. “What,” you say, “then do you condemn all who do not act similarly?” No; but hear what I think concerning them also, [Col. 0104C] and do not calumniate me in vain. Why do you wish to make me hateful to many thousands of saints who, living under our profession though not according to our manner, nevertheless either live holily or have died blessedly? I do not fail to know that God has reserved for himself seven thousand men who have not bent their knees before Baal [III Kings XIX]. Hear then [another reading: listen then], rival; listen, slanderer. I have said why I judged that those coming to us from other monasteries ought to be received. Have I condemned those who do not come? I excuse them; I do not accuse these. Only the envious are those whom I neither wish nor am able to excuse.

Excepting them, if any of the rest wishes to pass over to the purity of the Rule, but does not dare because of scandal, or certainly because of a definite bodily infirmity, I think that he does not sin, provided that [Col. 0104D] in his own place he strives to live soberly, righteously, and devoutly. For if he is compelled, through the custom of his monastery, to observe something less strictly, perhaps, than the Rule appears to have prescribed, he may be excused either by that charity through which he delays to move to something better because of scandal, according to the saying, “Charity covers a multitude of sins” [I Peter IV, 8]; or by that humility through which, conscious of his own weakness, he judges himself imperfect—for of humility too it is written: “God gives grace to the humble” [James IV, 6].

20. I have indeed said much to you, dearest brother, though you have no need of much; for you have both a quick intelligence for understanding what is said and an eager will for choosing what is usefully advised. Yet, though I write particularly to you, I did not think so much should be written merely on your account. These things, then, God has provided as being necessary. But you, as one long since most familiar to me, I admonish in few words and with complete confidence: do not any longer keep in suspense, by their expectation of you, the souls that desire you, at the dreadful peril indeed of your own soul. Behold: your death and life, and that of those who are with you (unless I am mistaken), are in your hand. For we judge that whatever you do or wish, they will do. Otherwise plainly announce to them that, in accordance with the not-to-be-despised judgment of all our abbots—which has deservedly been pronounced upon you—those who return shall live; those who refuse shall die.

26. LETTER VIII. TO BRUNO, ELECT OF COLOGNE

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Written in the year of Christ 1131. Bruno II, son of Engelbert, Count of Altena, was consecrated in 1132 by William, Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina; upon Frederick’s death near the end of 1131, he succeeded to the see of Cologne. Having set out for Italy with Emperor Lothair in 1136, he died from bloodletting on the vigil of Pentecost in the following year, and was buried at Bari in Apulia, in the church of St Nicholas. Hugh the dean succeeded him, and he too died in the same manner from bloodletting in the following year. These facts are from the unpublished Saxon Chronographer. Moreover, shortly afterwards Roger, prince of Sicily, broke open Bruno’s tomb, as also that of Duke Ranulf; he dragged their bodies, once removed, through the marketplace, and at last tore them to pieces with more than barbarous cruelty. See Baronius for this year; Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, book 17, chs. 21 and 23; Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book 2; and the unpublished Saxon Chronographer.]

Bernard, consulted by Bruno concerning whether he should accept the bishopric of Cologne, replies in such a manner as to hold him in suspense—indeed, to alarm him at the burden of so great an office—advising him to seek God’s counsel through prayer.

[Col. 0105B]

1. You ask my advice, illustrious Bruno, whether you ought to consent to those wishing to advance you to the episcopate. Which mortal would presume to decide this? Perhaps God calls you: who would dare dissuade you? Perhaps he does not call you: who would advise you to approach? But who can know whether it is a calling of God or not, except the Spirit who searches even the deep things of God, or someone to whom he himself may perhaps reveal it?

That humble but alarming confession in your letter, by which you accuse your life so gravely and, as I believe, with nothing but truth, makes advice still more doubtful. For it cannot be denied that such a life is unworthy of the dignity of so sacred a ministry. Yet again, not without reason you fear the opposite possibility—for we too fear the same thing—namely, that because of the evil conscience arising from the talent of knowledge committed to you, you make no profit; unless perhaps by another manner of trading you could bear fruit, though less abundantly, yet less dangerously.

I confess that I shudder; for I ought to speak to you, as to myself, what I think. I shudder, I say, when I consider whence and whither you are called, especially since no interval of penitence has intervened through which so exceedingly dangerous a passage might somehow be made.
