And indeed right order requires that you should first strive to care for your own conscience, and then for those of others. For the first degree of piety is that of which it is written: “Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” [Ecclesiasticus XXX, 24]. From this charity then proceeds by the right path to have mercy on one’s neighbour, since each person is commanded to love his neighbour according to the measure in which he loves himself. If you are to love those entrusted to you in the manner in which you have loved yourself up to now, I would rather that they were not entrusted to you than loved in this way [Col. 0106A]. But if you had first learned to love yourself, perhaps you would also know how to love me.

2. But what if God hastens his grace for you, multiplies his mercy, and his swift clemency proves more effective for restoring innocence than prolonged penitence? Blessed indeed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin [Psalm XXXI, 2]. For who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? If God justifies, who is there that condemns? That holy thief obtained this short path to salvation: on one and the same day he both confessed his robberies and was admitted into glory, content with the brief bridge of the cross for passing [another reading: crossing] from the region of unlikeness into the land of the living, and from the mire of dregs into the paradise of delight [Luke XXIII, 40–43].

That blessed sinful woman received this sudden remedy of mercy when, suddenly, where offences had abounded, grace also began to abound. Without the great labour of penitence, many sins were forgiven her because she loved much [Luke VII, 37–50]; and in a short time she deserved to receive the breadth of charity which, as Scripture says, “covers a multitude of sins” [I Peter IV]. This too was the double and most swift benefit of almighty goodness which the paralytic in the Gospel experienced, healed first in mind and then in flesh.

3. But it is one thing swiftly to obtain forgiveness of sins, and another to be immediately advanced from those very crimes to the mitres of dignities. I see Matthew taken from the tax-office to the summit of the apostleship [Matthew IX, 2–9]; but this again troubles me: that he did not hear with his fellow apostles, “Go into all the world, preach the Gospel to every creature” [Mark XVI, 15], until he had done penance by following the Lord wherever he went for a long time and with much labour, remaining with him in his temptations.

And even if the case of Ambrose is brought forward, that he was snatched from the tribunals to the priesthood [Theodoret, *History*, book IV, ch. 6], it does not greatly strengthen me, since from childhood he led a pure life in the world, and even then tried to avoid the office by flight, concealment, and many forms of evasion. If Saul also, suddenly made Paul, suddenly a vessel of election, suddenly a Doctor of the Gentiles, is offered as an example, the likeness of the example is nullified by this: that he obtained mercy because, as he himself testifies, he sinned in ignorance, remaining in unbelief [I Timothy I, 13]. Although, if something of this kind is ever acknowledged to have been done well and profitably, so that one can truthfully say, “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” [Psalm LXXVI, 11], it ought to be adduced not so much as an example as a miracle.

4. For the present, let these hesitant answers from me suffice for what you ask. For I cannot issue a definite judgment about what I do not know with certainty. Thus it ought to happen to one who seeks an answer where there is no prophetic utterance. Counsel must be sought from a wise man. Can you draw anything clear from mud? Yet there is one thing which we can offer to a friend without danger and not without profit: namely, such assistance as our prayer to God may provide in this matter.

Leaving, therefore, to God the secret of his counsel which we do not know, we beseech him with suppliant devotion and devout supplication that he may work in you and concerning you what befits himself and is expedient for you. You have Lord Norbert [Note: [Col. 0107D] Founder of the Premonstratensian Order. See Letter 59.] present, and being present you can more fittingly ask him concerning such matters. For that man is the readier than we are in disclosing divine mysteries, inasmuch as he is known to be nearer [Col. 0107B] to God.

LETTER IX.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

TO THE SAME MAN, NOW ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE.

He induces Bruno, recently made archbishop of Cologne, to fear.

I have devoutly received your Grace’s letter and have been diligent concerning what was enjoined; whether I have been of use, you will judge. But enough of that. In the same charity, I venture upon what follows.

If all who are called to ministry are certainly also chosen for the kingdom, then the archbishop of Cologne is assuredly safe. But if it is read that no one but God himself chose both Saul for a kingdom and Judas for the priesthood, and Scripture which asserts this cannot be broken, then the archbishop of Cologne must needs fear. But if, as is true, that saying still holds good today, “God has not chosen many noble, many powerful, many wise” [I Corinthians I, 26], does not the archbishop of Cologne likewise have a threefold reason to fear?

Let us therefore, being placed on high, not think lofty things, but fear, and associate with the humble. “They have made you a leader,” it says: “be among them as one of them” [Ecclesiasticus XXXII, 1]; and again: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things the more” [Ecclesiasticus III, 20]. He is wise who gives this counsel, for he thinks no differently from Wisdom itself, which says: “He who is greater among you, let him become as the lesser” [Luke XXII, 26]. Otherwise, “a harsh judgment is for those who rule” [Wisdom VI, 6]: let authority fear. Likewise, “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do what is worthy will be beaten with many stripes” [Luke XII, 47]: let him who has acquired learning fear. Let the nobleman fear, because the Judge of all is no respecter of persons. This threefold cord of necessary fear is indeed not easily broken.

Do I seem harsh because I do not flatter, because I instil fear, because I desire for my friend the beginning of wisdom? May it always fall to my lot to make my friends blessed—that is, by healthfully frightening them, not by deceitfully flattering them. I am urged to this by him who says: “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” [Proverbs XXVIII, 14]. I am restrained from the contrary by him who says: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you into error” [Isaiah III, 12].

28. LETTER X.

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

TO THE SAME MAN.

He urges Bruno to a righteous zeal in rebuking.

To punish a heinous crime, although this duty rests upon you for two reasons—both by the obligation of your office and because apostolic authority enjoins it—I think that a friend’s admonition is not superfluous in so great a matter. This is what we wish to remind you of, as friend and father: that this very punishment which must be inflicted should be inflicted with the zeal with which it must be inflicted, so that not only may the present offence appear to have been punished, but every malignity hearing of it may also be restrained from like rashness.

LETTER XI. TO GUIGO, PRIOR,

[Note: [Col. 0107D] Written about the year 1125. Guigo, surnamed of the Castle, a Frenchman by nation, a native of Dauphiné, born in the district of Valence, was the fifth prior general of the Grande Chartreuse after Blessed Bruno, and the first writer of the Statutes. He was most dear to Bernard, as is clear both from this letter and from book III, chapter 1, of the *Life of St Bernard*. Peter the Venerable, below in Letter 388, calls him “the singular and most illustrious flower of religious life in his time.” The same Peter, in book VI, Letter 40, to Basil, Guigo’s successor in the government of the Grande Chartreuse, says: “I had resolved to renew with you those ancient and holy conversations, often held with me, of your predecessor, the lord Guigo of happy memory; by them I was kindled as by sparks proceeding from his mouth, and was compelled to forget almost all human things.”

He was a man of outstanding modesty, as he painted himself in his own colours in a certain letter to Peter of Cluny: “We ask, by that love whose affections burn toward us unworthy men, that, when your serenity deigns to write to our lowliness, you should so consider your own edification that you do not inflate our weakness by dangerous exaltation. And above all and beyond all we ask and, with knees fixed upon the ground, beseech you not to deem our vileness any longer worthy of the name of Father. It is more than enough if one who is not considered worthy even of the name of servant is called brother, friend, or son” [among the Letters of Peter the Venerable, book I, Letter 25].

Peter the Venerable himself later used this example when writing to Bernard, as may be seen here in Letter 388; perhaps both emulated Bernard in Letter 72. Guigo himself also wrote several works by which, says Trithemius, his name was endowed with immortality: namely, the *Life of St Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, dedicated to Innocent II and found in Surius, volume II, on 1 April; the *Meditations*, extant in the *Library of the Fathers*; a treatise *On Truth and Peace*, manuscript in the Library of the Carthusian monastery at Cologne; one book of *Carthusian Institutes*; likewise a book *On Contemplation*; and finally various Letters, four of which you have here in volume 6, the others having been sought by me after Horstius with fruitless diligence.

For when I wrote about this matter to the Most Reverend Father Lord John Pegon, prior of the Grande Chartreuse and General of the Order, I was honoured to receive this answer from him: namely, that after the six fires which that sacred house had suffered from its beginnings, scarcely anything remained of that most well-provided store of manuscripts which his predecessors had assembled with the greatest care and diligence. The book *The Ladder of Monks*, printed in volume 6, is also attributed to this Guigo. Nor should we omit what Trithemius reports of him: that he corrected, through diligent study, the Letters of St Jerome, excessively corrupted through the fault of scribes, bringing them into conformity with the standard of truth and collecting them into one body. You have Guigo’s letter on this matter here from volume 1 of the *Analecta*. Moreover, in his fiftieth year, says Sutor in *The Carthusian Life*, book 2, chapter 5, and in the thirtieth year of his conversion, and about the twenty-seventh of his priorate, he rendered up his spirit to the Lord in the year 1137, not without a reputation for holiness, the fifty-third year from the foundation of the Order.]

AND TO THE OTHER RELIGIOUS OF THE GRANDE CHARTREUSE.

He devoutly discusses at length the law, signs, effects, degrees, and sincerity of true charity, whose perfection is reserved for the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0108C] To Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, most reverend [another reading: most worthy of reverence] among fathers and dearest among friends, and to the other holy men who are with him: Brother Bernard of Clairvaux, eternal salvation.

1. I received the letter of your Holiness with as much joy as I had long desired it eagerly. I read it, and in the letters which I turned over in my mouth I felt sparks in my breast; by them my heart grew warm within me, as if from that fire which the Lord sent upon the earth [Luke XII, 49]. O how great is the fire that burns in those meditations from which sparks of this kind fly out! That greeting of yours, aflame and kindling flame, was and is so welcome to me, to confess the truth, that it seemed to descend not from a man but most certainly from him who commands blessings for Jacob [Col. 0108D].

[Col. 0109A] I do not think I was greeted casually on the road, in passing, or as though merely through conventional courtesy, as is usual; rather, this welcome and unexpected blessing clearly issued, as I perceive, from the very depths of charity. Blessed are you by the Lord, who have taken care to anticipate me with blessings of such sweetness, so that your servant, since you wrote first, might be given confidence to write in reply—one who had long desired to write to you, but had not dared.

For I feared to disturb by importunate letters the holy quiet which you possess in the Lord: to interrupt, even briefly, that continual and sacred silence of yours from the world, that whispering with God; and to force our own concerns upon ears wholly occupied with secret and heavenly praises. I feared altogether to become troublesome to Moses on the mountain, to Elijah in the wilderness, or to Samuel keeping watch in the temple, if I tried in any degree to call you away from your most intent converse with God. Samuel cries, “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” [I Kings III, 10]; and should I presume to be heard? I feared, I say, lest, if I pressed importunately upon David as he withdrew, fled, and remained in solitude, he might indignantly excuse himself and say: “Leave me; I do not now hear you. Rather, I will hear what I listen to more sweetly. I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me; for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints, and to those who turn to the heart” [Psalm LXXXIV, 9]. Or perhaps: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God” [Psalm CXVIII, 115].

For what? Should I be so rash as to dare to awaken the beloved as she sweetly rests in the bridegroom’s arms, until she herself wishes? At once I would expect to hear from her: “Do not be troublesome to me. I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine, who feeds among the lilies” [Song of Songs II, 16].

29. 2. But what I do not dare, charity dares. With complete confidence it knocks at the door of a friend, judging that it ought not to suffer refusal, since it knows itself to be the mother of friendships. Nor does it fear to disturb for a little while your leisure, though most welcome, for its own business. It is charity itself—when it wills—that makes you withdraw from God; and it was charity itself, when it willed, that made you available to us, so that you judged it by no means unworthy not only to endure one speaking, but even kindly to invite one who was silent [Col. 0109D].

[Col. 0110A] I embrace your kindness; I marvel at your condescension; I praise and venerate the purity with which you glory in the Lord with such exultation concerning our progress, as you suppose it to be. I too glory greatly in so weighty a testimony and delight in the gracious and wholly unearned friendship of the servants of God. This is now my glory, this my joy, these the delights of my heart: that I have not lifted my eyes in vain to the mountains, from which no small help now comes to me. The mountains have already distilled sweetness upon us; and I still hope that they will distil it until our valleys abound with grain.

For that day will be a festival day to me and an everlasting memorial, on which I was permitted to see and receive that man through whom it came about that I was received into your hearts. Indeed, you had already received me, as appears from your letter; but now more closely and familiarly, as I learned, when he reported to you certain things about me which, though he did not prove them, he nevertheless thought true. For he is faithful and devout; far be it from him to speak otherwise than he believed.

See: I truly experience in myself what the Saviour says: “He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward” [Matthew X, 41]. I call it a righteous man’s reward that I am judged righteous, for no other reason than that I received a righteous man. For if anything has been added, the righteous man spoke it not so much from the truth of the matter as from his own purity. You heard, believed, rejoiced, wrote, and greatly gladdened me—not only because I have deserved some place, and no small place, in your holiness, but also because the purity of your hearts has become known to us in no small degree [Col. 0110C]. In a few words you have certainly made known what spirit you are of.

3. Therefore I rejoice for myself, and I rejoice for you: for my benefit and for your sincerity. For that charity is to be judged true and sincere, and wholly proceeding from a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, by which we love our neighbour’s good equally with our own. He who loves his own good more—or only his own good—is convicted of not loving goodness chastely, since he loves it for his own sake, not for its own sake. Such a man cannot obey the prophet who says: “Give thanks to the Lord, because he is good” [Psalm CXVII, 1]. He gives thanks because perhaps God is good to him, but not because God is good in himself. Therefore let him recognize as directed against himself that reproach of the same prophet: “He will give you thanks when you have done him good” [Psalm XLVIII, 19].

[Col. 0111A] One person gives thanks to the Lord because he is powerful; another, because he is good to him; and another because he is simply good. The first is a servant and fears for himself; the second is a hireling and desires for himself; the third is a son and honours his father. Thus both he who fears and he who desires act for themselves; charity alone, which is in the son, “does not seek its own things.” For this reason I think it was said of charity: “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls” [Psalm XVIII, 8], because it alone can turn the mind away from love of self and of the world and direct it toward God. Neither fear nor private love converts the soul. They sometimes alter countenance or conduct, but never the disposition.

A servant too sometimes performs God’s work; but because he does not do so willingly, he is shown still to remain in his hardness [Col. 0111B]. The hireling also does it; but because he does not do it freely, he is known to be drawn by his own greed. Now where there is private possession, there is singularity; where singularity, there is a corner; and where a corner is, there surely are filth and rust. Let fear itself be the servant’s law, by which he is constrained; let greed be the hireling’s law, by which he too is bound when he is drawn away and enticed by it. But neither of these is without stain or can convert souls. Charity, however, converts souls, making them willing.

4. Moreover, I call it undefiled in that it is accustomed to retain nothing of its own for itself. For one to whom nothing belongs as private property has, surely, everything that he has belongs to God; and what belongs to God cannot be unclean. The undefiled law of the Lord, then, is charity, which does not seek what is useful to itself but what is useful to many. It is called the law of the Lord either because he lives by it or because no one possesses it except by his gift.

Nor should it seem absurd that I have said that God too lives by law, since I have meant no other law than charity. What, indeed, preserves the supreme and ineffable unity in that supreme and blessed Trinity, except charity? Charity, therefore, is law, and the law of the Lord: it in some manner holds the Trinity together in unity and binds it in the bond of peace.

Yet let no one think that I here take charity to mean a quality or some accident; otherwise I would say—far be it—that in God there is something which is not God. Rather, it is that divine substance, which is neither new nor unusual to say, since John says, “God is charity” [I John IV, 16]. Thus charity is rightly called both God and God’s gift. Charity gives charity: the former substantively, the latter accidentally.

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Elsewhere, incorrectly, “substance.”]

Where it signifies the giver, the name denotes substance; where it signifies the gift, it denotes quality. This is the eternal law, creator and governor of the universe. For all things were made through it in weight, measure, and number; and nothing is left without law, since this law of all things is itself not without law—yet has no law other than itself, by which it governs itself, though it did not create itself.

5. But the servant and the hireling have a law not from the Lord but one which they have made for themselves: the former by not loving God, the latter by loving something else more. They have, I say, a law not the Lord’s but their own, though it is subject to the law which is the Lord’s. Each could indeed make a law for himself; yet they could not remove it from the unchangeable order of the eternal law.

I say that someone has made his own law for himself when he has preferred his own will to the common and eternal law, perversely wishing to imitate his Creator: so that, just as God is law to himself and under his own jurisdiction, so he too might govern himself and make his will his own law. This is indeed a grievous and unbearable yoke upon all the children of Adam, alas, pressing down and bending our necks, so that our life has drawn near to hell. “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” [Romans VII, 24.] I am so weighed down by it that, unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell [Psalm XCIII, 17].

He groaned beneath this burden who said: “Why have you set me as one opposed to you, and I have become burdensome to myself?” [Job VII, 20.] In saying, “I have become burdensome to myself,” he showed that he was himself a law to himself, and that no one other than he himself had made this so. But when, speaking to God, he first said, “You have set me as one opposed to you,” he indicated that he had nevertheless not escaped God’s law. For it belonged to God’s eternal and righteous law that whoever refused to be sweetly ruled by God should be punitively ruled by himself, and that whoever voluntarily cast off the sweet yoke and light burden of charity should unwillingly endure the unbearable burden of his own will.

[Col. 0112C] 6. Thus, in a wonderful manner, the eternal law pursued its fugitive, set him as one opposed to itself, and retained him as subject: for he neither escaped the law of justice according to his deserts nor remained with God in God’s light, rest, and glory; he was subjected to power and removed from blessedness.

“Lord my God, why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?” [ibid., 21.] So that, having cast off the heavy burden of my own will, I may breathe beneath the light burden of charity, and may no longer be restrained by servile fear or enticed by hireling greed, but be led by your Spirit, the Spirit of freedom by whom your sons are led. May that Spirit bear witness to my spirit that I too am one of the sons, when the same law is mine as is yours, and when, as you are, so I too am in this world.

For those who do what the Apostle says, “Owe no one anything except to love one another” [Romans XIII, 8], are beyond doubt, as God is, themselves also in this world; and they are not servants or hirelings [Col. 0112D], but sons. Therefore sons are not without law either—unless perhaps someone thinks otherwise because it is written, “A law is not laid down for the righteous” [I Timothy I, 9].

But one must know that one law is promulgated by the spirit of servitude in fear; another is given by the spirit of freedom in sweetness. Sons are neither compelled to be under the former nor allowed to be without the latter. Do you wish to hear that a law is not laid down for the righteous? “You have not received,” he says, “the spirit of servitude again in fear.” Do you wish to hear that they are nevertheless not without the law of charity? “But you have received,” he says, “the Spirit of adoption as sons” [Romans VIII, 15].

Finally, hear a righteous man confessing both concerning himself: that he was not under law, yet was not without law. “I became,” he says, “to those under law as though under law, though I myself was not under law; to those without law as though without law, though I was not without God’s law, but was within Christ’s law” [I Corinthians IX, 21]. Hence it is fittingly not said, “The righteous have no law,” or, “The righteous are without law”; but, “A law is not laid down for the righteous.” That is: it is not imposed upon them as unwilling persons, but freely given to them as willing persons because it has been sweetly inspired.

Thus the Lord also beautifully says: “Take my yoke upon yourselves” [Matthew XI, 29]. It is as if he said: I do not impose it on the unwilling; rather, take it if you wish. Otherwise you will find not rest but labour [Col. 0113B] for your souls.

7. Charity, then, is a good and sweet law: not only is it itself borne lightly and sweetly, but it also makes the laws of servants and hirelings bearable and light. It does not indeed destroy those laws, but brings about their fulfilment, as the Lord says: “I have not come to destroy the law, but to fulfil it” [Matthew V, 17]. It tempers the one, orders the other, and lightens both.

Charity is never without fear, but the fear is chaste; never without desire, but desire is ordered. Charity therefore fulfils the servant’s law when it infuses devotion, and it fulfils the hireling’s law when it orders desire. Devotion mingled with fear does not abolish fear itself but makes it chaste. Only punishment is removed, without which fear could not exist while it was servile; and fear remains chaste and filial for ever and ever [Psalm XVIII, 10].

For when we read, “Perfect charity casts out fear” [I John IV, 18], punishment must be understood, which, as we have said, is never absent from servile fear. This is that form of speech in which the cause is often put for the effect. Then desire is rightly ordered by charity when it comes upon it: evil things are wholly rejected; better things are preferred to good things; and good things are desired only for the sake of better things. When this has been fully achieved by God’s grace, the body and every good of the body will be loved only for the soul’s sake; the soul for God’s sake; and God for his own sake.

8. Yet because we are carnal and are born of the concupiscence of the flesh, it is necessary that our desire or [Col. 0113D] love should begin from the flesh. If it is guided in right order, advancing by certain stages of its own under grace’s leading, it will at last be perfected in the spirit: because “that which is spiritual is not first, but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual”; and we must first bear the image of the earthly man, then that of the heavenly (I Cor. 15:46–49). Thus, at first, a person loves himself for his own sake. For he is flesh, and can taste nothing except himself. When he sees that he cannot subsist by himself, he begins through faith to seek and love God as necessary to himself.

Thus, at the second stage, he loves God, but for his own sake, not for God’s. But when, on the occasion of his own need, he has begun to worship and frequent God in thought, reading, prayer, and obedience, God gradually and little by little becomes known through a kind of familiarity of this sort, [Col. 0114A] and consequently becomes sweet. Having thus tasted how gracious the Lord is, he passes to the third stage: he loves God no longer for his own sake, but for God’s own sake.

Certainly, one remains at this stage; and I do not know whether the fourth stage is perfectly attained by any human being in this life—namely, that a person should love himself solely for God’s sake. Let those who have experienced it affirm this; to me, I confess, it seems impossible. Yet it will undoubtedly come to pass when the good and faithful servant has been brought into his Lord’s joy and has been made drunk with the abundance of God’s house. For, as though drunk, in some wonderful way forgetful of himself and wholly failing, as it were, away from himself, he will pass entirely into God; and henceforth, cleaving to him, he will be one spirit.

9. I think that the prophet perceived this when he said: [Col. 0114B] “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70:16). Certainly he knew that, when he entered into the Lord’s spiritual powers, he would be stripped of every infirmity of the flesh, so that he would have nothing further to think about the flesh, but would wholly in the spirit remember the righteousness of God alone.

Then each individual member of Christ will be able to say of itself what Paul said of the Head: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (II Cor. 5:16). No one there knows himself according to the flesh, because flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. 15:50). Not that the substance of the flesh will not be there; rather, every carnal necessity will be absent, the love of the flesh will be swallowed up in the love of the spirit, and the weak human affections which now exist [Col. 0114C] will be transformed into certain divine powers.

Then the net of charity—which, now drawn through this great and spacious sea, does not cease to gather fish of every kind—when brought to shore, will cast out the bad and retain only the good. For in this life the net of charity encloses fish of every kind within the bosom of its breadth: adapting itself for the time being to all, passing into itself the prosperity and adversity of all alike, and in some way making them its own, it is accustomed not only to rejoice with those who rejoice, but also to weep with those who weep. But when it reaches the shore, casting out, as bad fish, everything sorrowful that it suffers, it will retain only what can be pleasing and joyful [Col. 0114D].

For will Paul then, for example, be weak with the weak, or burn for those who are scandalized, where scandal and weakness will be far away? Or will he indeed mourn those who formerly did not repent, where it is certain that there will no more be anyone who repents than anyone who sins? Far be it that, in that city which “the rushing of the river makes glad” (Ps. 45:5), whose gates the Lord loves above all the tabernacles of Jacob (Ps. 86:2), he should lament and weep even those who are to be assigned to eternal fires with the devil and his angels. For although in the tabernacles there is sometimes joy over victory, there is nevertheless toil in battle and often danger to life; but in that homeland no adversity or sorrow at all is admitted, [Col. 0115A] as is sung of it: “The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 86:7); and again: “Everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isa. 61:7).

Finally, how will he remember mercy where he will remember the righteousness of God alone? Therefore, where there will no longer be a place for misery or a time for mercy, there can certainly be no disposition of compassion.

10. I am indeed still impelled to prolong my discourse by an insatiable desire to converse with you, my dearest and most beloved brothers; but three things prescribe an end. First, and above all, I fear becoming burdensome to you; second, I am ashamed of my loquacity; third, domestic concerns press upon me. In conclusion, I pray: have mercy on me. And if you have rejoiced at hearing so much good about me—things you take as certain—then, I ask, sympathize with my evils. Perhaps he who told you these things saw some small matters and judged great things from small; while your sincerity readily believed what it gladly heard. I rejoice indeed in charity, which “believes all things” (I Cor. 13:7); but I am ashamed before truth, which knows all things. I want you to believe me about myself rather than another, who sees only what is outward. For “no one knows the things of a person except the spirit of the person that is in him” (I Cor. 2:11). I, who speak of myself not from conjecture but from judgment, tell you: I am not such as I am thought or said to be. I confess this as confidently as I know it by experience, so that there is nothing I would rather obtain especially through your prayers than that I may become such as your letters proclaim me to be.

33. EPISTLE XII. TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS. He commends himself to their prayers.

[Col. 0115C]

To his most beloved lord and most reverend father GUIGO, Prior of the Carthusians, and to the holy brothers who cleave to him: Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

First, when I came into those parts, I did not go on to reach you, see your faces, and call to mind my iniquities and needs. Though perhaps I can satisfy you, I confess that I cannot satisfy myself. I am angry with my occupations, because through them it came about not that I neglected this, but that I was unable to do it. I suffer this often, and therefore I am often angry: would that I were worthy for every saint to grieve with me. Otherwise I am doubly miserable, if I am not even pitiable.

But I offer brotherly compassion a place in myself, not merit. Have mercy on me, not because I am worthy, but because I am needy and poor. Justice seeks merit; mercy beholds misery. True mercy does not judge, but is moved; it does not depend upon examination, being content with an occasion. For an account is not awaited where affection draws. Samuel mourned Saul, pitying rather than deliberating (I Sam. 15:35). David shed tears for his parricidal son—though they could do no good, yet they were devout tears (II Sam. 18:33). So also have mercy on me, not because I have deserved it, but because I need it.

Have mercy as those who have obtained mercy from the Lord, so that, [Col. 0116B] delivered without fear from the tumults of the world, you may serve him. Blessed are those whom he hides in his tabernacle, hoping under the shadow of his wings until iniquity passes away. But I am unhappy, poor and naked, a person born for toil, a fledgling bird exiled from its nest almost all the time, exposed to wind and whirlwind. I am troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all my conscience has been swallowed up. Therefore have mercy, if not on one possessing merit, at least on one so afflicted.

EPISTLE XIII. TO LORD POPE HONORIUS.  
[Note: [Col. 0115C] Written in the year of Christ 1126. The illustrious Cardinal [Col. 0115D] Baronius assigns this letter, along with the following three, to the year 1129. But, as Manriquez rightly observes in the *Annals*, it must belong to the year 1126. For from Bernard’s suppressed name—indeed, from the context itself—it is understood to be the first letter written to Honorius, to whom Bernard then considered himself unknown. Yet there are other letters addressed to Honorius, namely letters 47 and 49, which Baronius himself places in 1127 and 1128; accordingly this one must be placed in the preceding year, namely 1126, in which, as the Acts of that Church prove, occurred the death of Ebalo of Châlons, in whose place Alberic was elected.]

He requests that Alberic’s election to the bishopric of Châlons be ratified.

To the supreme pontiff HONORIUS: a certain brother, a monk by profession, a sinner in conduct, offers himself, small as he is.

They say that with you the prayer of a poor man prevails more than the countenance of a powerful man. Such a holy reputation of your singular condescension makes me not fear the height of your dignity, so as not to dare to speak to you—especially concerning what charity suggests. I speak, lord, of the Church of Châlons, whose danger, so far as lies in me, I can neither overlook nor ought to overlook. We who are near neighbors see, and already feel to be imminent, that the peace of that Church will soon be gravely disturbed unless they obtain the assent of your piety to the election of that distinguished man, Master Alberic, [Note: [Col. 0115D] Alberic, certainly, was distinguished: called “of Rheims,” if not by birth, at least by learning and virtue; formerly Abelard’s fellow student under Anselm of Laon, and later his opponent. It was chiefly through Alberic’s action at the Council of Soissons that Abelard was compelled to commit his book on the Trinity to the flames.

Alberic himself, formerly master of the schools at Rheims, was elected bishop of Châlons after the death of Ebalo, not after that of William [Col. 0116D] of Champeaux, as Picardus, Horstius, Chesnius, and others maintain. Whether William died in 1119, as they reckon, or in 1121, as has been demonstrated above in the notes on Letter 3, it is not likely that the see of Châlons remained vacant until Honorius became pope—to whom Bernard writes on Alberic’s behalf—which occurred in 1124.

Whether the election and Bernard’s recommendation took effect, another Alberic affirms in his *Chronicle* under the year 1126; almost all others deny it, and this seems most certain. For in the list of fathers who attended the Council of Troyes in 1127 or 1128, where the fathers and the bishop of Châlons himself are listed, albeit without his name, Master Alberic of Rheims is named among others of inferior rank. Finally, it is established that he succeeded Ulgrin in the see of Bourges at the latter’s death, as Chesnius correctly proves in his notes on Abelard.

Alberic, master of the schools of the Church of Rheims, “most renowned for literary learning and prudent counsel,” according to [Col. 0117B] Robert of Torigni, is called “of Rheims” by Peter Abelard in the *History of His Misfortunes*, chapter 5; and Heloise, in Letter 2, calls him a pupil of William of Champeaux and Abelard’s “fellow student.” Walter, bishop of Laon, writes to him concerning the fear of Christ in Letter 4, printed in volume 2 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 469. I am mistaken if he is not the “master in France” whom Abelard, without naming him, ridicules in the *Introduction to Theology*, p. 1066. He died in 1141. Compare Letter 58, written before this one to Ebalo, and consult Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. 2, p. 285.

There was another Alberic of Rheims, called of Porte-Vénéris, concerning whom John of Salisbury writes in Letter 182. As to the danger which Bernard in this letter says threatens the Church of Châlons unless Alberic’s election is confirmed, it does not seem that this should be interpreted as referring to the ambition of Henry of Verdun, whom Baronius and Manriquez, under the year 1129, and the author of *Gallia Purpurata* under Matthew, state to have wished to seize the see of Châlons. It should rather be understood of the disturbance which would follow if the wishes and unanimous petition of both clergy and people were disappointed, as Bernard sufficiently indicates below.

What the aforesaid authors assert as the foundation of their opinion, namely [Col. 0117D] a fragment of Letter 48 of this same saint to Haimeric, where he says: “What, good men, in me displeased your fatherhood? Was it that at Châlons a man utterly disreputable was removed from the stewardship entrusted to him—a man who, in the Church of Verdun over which he had presided, had squandered his Lord’s goods?”—this merely indicates that Henry was deposed at Châlons by the legate Matthew. Alberic reports this under the year 1129, saying that a council was “held at Châlons by the legate Matthew on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin, where, by the counsel of Saint Bernard, Henry of Verdun relinquished the bishopric.”

At Wassebourg, *Antiquities of Belgian Gaul*, book 4, there are letters of Honorius to Matthew bearing witness to this matter, in which, among other things, occurs: “You are to summon both the aforesaid bishop”—that is, the one accused of dilapidating ecclesiastical goods—“and the opposing party”—the canons of Verdun, as each is there expressly stated—[Col. 0118B] “to appear before you. Go to Châlons, and there, having called to your aid the archbishop of Trier and other bishops, as well as wise and religious men, hear the case diligently and investigate it by careful inquiry. If suitable accusers and witnesses appear, decide the cause canonically after consultation with your brethren,” etc. But enough of this.] to which indeed the entire clergy and people [Col. 0117A] had come and still come together with equal will and voice.

If our own opinion is asked or valued in this matter, we know that he has hitherto been a man of sound faith and doctrine, prudent alike in divine and human matters; and we hope that in the house of God—if indeed God himself chose him—he will be a vessel for honor and will be useful not only to that Church, but also to the whole Gallican Church. It is now for your discernment to judge whether a dispensation is rightly requested of you from which such a recompense may be hoped.

EPISTLE XIV.  
[Note: [Col. 0118C] Written about the year 1126.]

TO THE SAME POPE HONORIUS. He commends the case of the Church of Dijon to the supreme pontiff.

[Col. 0117B]

To the supreme pontiff HONORIUS: Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting, and whatever a sinner’s prayer can accomplish.

How great is the fear with which I write to you, he himself knows whom we fear in you. Yet Lady Charity makes me dare, for she commands you also. Asked to intercede for the Church of Dijon, [Note: [Col. 0118C] That is, for the monastery of the monks of Saint Benignus at Dijon, whom Bernard, because of the ancient religious character of that church, says in the following letter are especially dear to him. His father and mother were buried in their church, and later transferred thence to Clairvaux. For Bernard and other writers of his age, it was customary to use the name “church” to signify monasteries, as below in Letters 59, 60, 339, 382, 384, 395, etc.; although churches of every kind were also not infrequently called monasteries. Note here that the church of Saint Benignus is simply called “the Church of Dijon” because it is the principal church of the city.] I have undertaken to make a petition; but I almost doubt what I ought chiefly to request. For just as it is wrong to attempt anything by prayer or payment against justice, so it is superfluous to labor greatly for justice before one who loves justice.

Yet although we do not know what we ought to pray for, [Col. 0118A] we nevertheless trust that your kindness, especially in the cause of religious persons, [Note: [Col. 0118C] Bernard and others frequently use this name for monks, as in Letters 45 and 202 and in Sermon 26 on Various Subjects, no. 2; Gregory the Great also used it long before Bernard, in Book 1, Letter 59.] cannot be inactive. What the prudence and careful examination of your holiness will discover, I do not know; but this I say, because I have heard it and hear it often: the Church of Dijon is reported to have possessed, by a long and uncontested tenure, the properties concerning which the monks of Luxeuil bring suit against it. Thus those among the neighbors who appear to be older are astonished and indignant, detesting this novel calumny. [Note: [Col. 0118D] This dispute concerned two cells, Clermont and Vangion-Rive, and was finally decided in 1129 by Stephen, archbishop of Vienne, and others; see Perardus, *Burgundian Monuments*, pp. 224 and 228.]

EPISTLE XV. TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR.  
[Note: [Col. 0118D] Written in the same year. Haimeric, a Burgundian by nationality, born in the town of Châtre in Berry—which gave its name to the family of Châtre—and cousin of Peter of Châtre, archbishop of Bourges, was made cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary the New by Calixtus II in 1120, having previously been a canon of the Lateran. He was appointed chancellor of the holy Roman Church before the death of Chrysogonus of Pisa, his predecessor in that office. After discharging it splendidly for several years, he died in 1141, on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, as the calendar of Saint-Victor at Paris attests. Bernard wrote frequent and familiar letters to him, as well as the treatise *On Loving God*.]

On the matter above.

[Col. 0118B]

To the distinguished lord HAIMERIC, chancellor of the Apostolic See: BERNARD of Clairvaux, to forget what lies behind and, with the Apostle, to follow after what lies ahead.

Our friends are not unaware that you love me with a familiar affection; and they begrudge me the fruit of so great a happiness if I should wish to possess it alone. The monks of Dijon are especially dear to me because of the ancient religious character of that Church. Let them feel, if you please, that neither your love toward us nor ours toward them is inactive—justice, however, being preserved in all things, against which it is not lawful to show regard even for a friend.

35. EPISTLE XVI.  
[Note: [Col. 0119D] Written in the same year.]

TO PETER, CARDINAL PRIEST. On the matter above.

To his dear lord Peter, cardinal priest: Brother BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, greeting—and not on the way.

I have no cause of my own; nevertheless, because the monks of Dijon are religious men, I make their cause my own. Hold it in your hand as mine—yet mine in such a way that it is also justice’s. This is what both we trust and nearly the whole country testifies.

EPISTLE XVII. TO PETER, CARDINAL DEACON.  
[Note: [Col. 0119D] Written about the year 1127. This Peter is undoubtedly distinct from Peter Leonis, likewise a legate but a cardinal priest, as we proved in the Preface to this volume. He appears to be the Peter whom Honorius II, at the beginning of his pontificate, sent to France as legate from his side against Pons and the followers of Pons, according to Peter the Venerable, *On Miracles*, book 2, chapter 13. Perhaps he was Peter of Fontaines, Bernard’s countryman, cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, created by Calixtus in 1120.]

He excuses his failure to come when summoned; he replies concerning the requested writings.

[Col. 0119B]

To the venerable lord PETER, cardinal deacon and legate of the Roman Church: Brother BERNARD, himself so far as he can be.

That I did not come to you as you commanded was caused not by my laziness but by a reason not to be despised. For, saving the reverence due to you and to all good persons, I have resolved never to leave the monastery except for definite reasons. Certainly no such reason has yet occurred by which I could lawfully comply in this matter with your will—indeed, with ours as well.

But what are you doing concerning that which we have held for some time by the promise of your earlier letters—namely, your coming, for which we still wait? Moreover, what writings are those which you both formerly ordered to be made for you [variant: for us] and now request? We entirely do not know, and therefore have prepared nothing. For I do not know that I have ever written anything about morals which I would consider worthy of Your Excellency’s attention. [Note: [Col. 0119D] Saint Bernard commonly addresses cardinals as “Your Excellency,” as in Letters 306 and 311; he sometimes calls them “Your Holiness,” Letter 306. He gives the title “Excellency” also to kings, Letter 45, no. 2; likewise to the pope, Letter 349; indeed, to bishops, Letter 63.]

Some brothers have taken down in their own style certain things which they heard me say in their presence. One of them is at hand with you: namely, Gebuin, precentor and archdeacon of Troyes. [Note: [Col. 0119D] Hildebert calls Gebuin “distinguished in character and learning” [Col. 0120D] in Letter 53. Nicholas of Clairvaux praises his eloquence and wisdom in Letter 5, where he mentions his sermon on the Gospel text, “If the Son shall make you free,” etc. A volume of his sermons exists in the Library of Saint-Victor. He is the precentor of Troyes whose “flowers” John of Salisbury requests in Letter 96. Compare Peter the Venerable, Book II, Letters 34 and 35.] You can readily obtain from him, if any please you, those things which were taken down by him.

Nevertheless, if you have leisure or are at some time free from your concerns, and if you judge it worthy—namely, to show your promised presence to the little sons awaiting the presence of your dignity—then, if anything is found at hand or seems capable of being further worked out by our attention [Col. 0119D] and ability, which might perhaps please you, I shall by no means fail, according to my powers, to meet your will [Col. 0120A]. For we love your good reputation; we revere the solicitude and sincerity concerning the things of God which we have heard are in you. Therefore we should be greatly pleased if our dutiful rusticity might perhaps be of service to you in anything.

EPISTLE XVIII.  
[Note: [Col. 0120D] Written about the year 1127.]

TO THE SAME.  
[Note: [Col. 0120D] The manuscripts vary in this title. Colbertinus no. 1410 and the Compiègne manuscript have “To the same Haimeric”; three other Colbert manuscripts have “To the same,” so that it refers to Peter the deacon. The latter is preferable, owing to the books requested in the preceding letter and in this one, no. 5.]

He seeks to dispel the opinion of his holiness and promises to share the little books he has written.

1. Even if I gave my whole self to you, it would be too little for me to seem to have worthily repaid even half the goodwill which, they say, you bear toward our lowliness. I rejoice indeed in this favor; but I confess that the thought tempers my joy over such great kindness: the same favor has been gained for me not by my work, but by reputation. For I am greatly ashamed to exult when I feel that in me is revered or loved, not what I am, but what I am thought to be. For I am not loved when I am thus loved; rather, I know not what in me is loved in my stead—something that is not I. [Note: [Col. 0120D] This is nearly Augustine’s language in Letter 143, no. 3.]

Indeed, to speak more truly, I do know: for I know most certainly that it is nothing. For whatever is thought to be and is not, is undoubtedly nothing. Now when what is not, but is thought to be, is loved, neither love nor the lover is nothing, but the thing loved is nothing. It is remarkable—but more to be lamented than wondered at—that what is nothing can be loved.

Here indeed we perceive whence we have come and where we have come to; what we have lost and what we have found. By cleaving to him who always exists and exists blessedly, we too could always exist and exist blessedly. By cleaving, I say, not merely through knowledge, but through love. For some of Adam’s children, when they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their thoughts. Therefore their foolish heart was deservedly darkened: because, knowing the truth and despising it, they justly received as punishment that they should not even know it.

Alas! Thus, cleaving to truth through knowledge but flowing away from it through love—loving vanity in place of truth—a human being became like vanity. And what is more vain than to love vanity? What is more wicked than to despise truth? What, indeed, is more just than that even knowledge itself should be withdrawn from those who despise it? What, I ask, is more just than that one who did not glorify truth when known should no longer be able to boast of knowing it? Thus the desire for vanity is contempt for truth; contempt for truth is the cause of our blindness. “And because they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, he gave them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:21, 28).

2. From this blindness, therefore, comes the fact that we often love or approve, in place of what is, that which is not. For while we are in this body, we are away from him who supremely is. And what is man, O God, except what you have made known to him? Therefore, if the knowledge of God is the cause by which a human being is something, ignorance makes him nothing.

But he who calls things that are not as though they were, having in some way had pity on us who were reduced to nothing, gave us in the meantime that hidden manna—of which the Apostle says, “And your life is hidden with Christ in God” [Col. 0121B] (Col. 3:3)—because we cannot yet behold by sight or embrace fully by love. He gave us both to taste by faith and to seek by desire. Through these two means, restored a second time from non-being to being, we begin to become some beginning of his creature, destined someday to pass into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness.

This will undoubtedly occur when righteousness is converted into judgment; that is, faith into understanding—righteousness which is from faith into the judgment of full knowledge—and likewise when the desire of pilgrimage is changed into fullness of love. For if, while we are still absent, faith and desire initiate us, then understanding and love certainly bring us to perfection when present. As faith leads to full knowledge, so desire leads to perfect [Col. 0121C] love. And just as it is said, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint), so it may equally and not unreasonably be said: “Unless you desire, you shall not love perfectly.”

Understanding, therefore, is the fruit of faith; perfect charity, of desire. Meanwhile, “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4); but the blessed person lives by understanding. Meanwhile the righteous person longs for God as the deer for springs of water; but the blessed person now draws with joy from the springs of the Savior—that is, delights in the fullness of charity.

3. Thus perhaps by these two arms of the soul, namely understanding and love—that is, knowledge and love [of truth]—one embraces and comprehends, with all the saints, length, breadth, height, and depth: that is, eternity, charity, [Col. 0121D] power, and wisdom. And all these are Christ. He is eternity, because “this is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). He is charity, because he is God: “God is charity” (I John 4:16). He is also the power of God and the wisdom of God (I Cor. 1:24).

But when will these things be? When shall we see him as he is? When shall we love him as he is? For “the expectation of the creature awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For the creature was subjected to vanity unwillingly” (Rom. 8:19–20). From this universal vanity come both our desire to be praised when we are blameworthy and our unwillingness to praise those whom we know to be praiseworthy. It is also vain that, through our ignorance, what is often true is kept silent and what is not true is proclaimed [Col. 0122A].

What shall we say to these things except that “the sons of men are vain, the sons of men are deceitful in the scales, that they may deceive—together, from vanity itself” (Ps. 61:10)? We praise [variant: we are praised] falsely; we delight vainly. Thus those who are praised are vain, and those who praise are deceitful. Some flatter and are insincere; some praise what they suppose and are false; some glory in the praises of both kinds and are vain. The only wise person is the one who says with the Apostle: “I refrain, lest anyone should think of me above what he sees in me or hears anything from me” (II Cor. 12:6).

4. For the present, I have written these things to you too hastily, and therefore less elegantly: I have rather scratched them out than dictated them, and perhaps more wordily than I ought, but I could not have written them more truthfully [Col. 0122B] according to my understanding. But, so that the letter may end where it began, I do not want you to be too credulous about my uncertain reputation, which, as you know very well, often errs in its judgment in either direction, both in praise and in blame.

Examine and judge, if you please, so that your love or favor may be just and, by being measured according to merits, more pleasing to a friend; so that, when praise proceeds from the seriousness of judgment rather than the falsehood of the crowd, it may bring less honor but also less burden. There is certainly something which makes me, insignificant as I am, more yours: namely, that you labor vigorously and sincerely, as they say, on behalf of the things of God in your office. May this always be truly said of you, because it is always truly found in you.

[Col. 0122C]

5. You have the book which you asked to have copied. The little works of ours which you request are few, and there is absolutely nothing in them that I consider worthy of your attention. Yet I judge it better that my slight talent should be blamed than my willingness; and that in your eyes my lack of skill should be put to the test rather than my obedience. Therefore tell us in writing through the present messenger which of these you wish me to send, and where; so that I may ask for those which are not now in my possession from those who have them, and send them wherever you command.

And so that you may know what you ask for: I know that I have written a little book entitled *On Humility*; and four homilies *In Praise of the Virgin Mother*—for that is their title—on the passage of the Gospel according to [Col. 0122D] Luke which says, “The angel Gabriel was sent” (Luke 1:26); as well as an *Apology* addressed to a certain friend of ours, [Note: [Col. 0121D] That is, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry; this *Apology* is printed here in volume II.] in which I discussed certain observances of the Cluniacs and of ourselves, that is, the Cistercians. I have also dictated a few letters to various persons. Some brothers who heard me speaking in their presence have taken down matters in their own style and retain them with themselves. Would that—though I scarcely hope it—our dutiful rusticity might be of some service to you.

38. EPISTLE XIX.  
[Note: [Col. 0121D] Written about the year 1127.]

TO THE SAME. He commends the envoys from Rheims.

It is time for me to claim what was promised and to prove whether perhaps I have always trusted you in vain, ever since I deserved both your acquaintance and friendship. Consider as granted to me whatever help these envoys from Rheims [Note: [Col. 0123C] I read nothing concerning this embassy in Marlot. Perhaps it was sent to Honorius to obtain the pallium for Renaud of Martigné, who was transferred from the see of Angers to that of Rheims in 1124. But the following letter suggests another matter.] have found you ready to afford them. I dare to say this not because I consider myself so important, but because you promised it. Whether you promised worthily, you yourselves must judge.

EPISTLE XX.  
[Note: [Col. 0123D] Written about the same year.]

TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR. On the matter above.

To the distinguished lord HAIMERIC, chancellor of the holy Roman See: Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux, greeting and prayer.

Since I have begun once, I shall speak—and speak to you. I shall be importunate, but importunate for charity, for truth, [Col. 0123B] and for justice. For although I am not important enough to have business of my own at Rome, I count no matter established to belong to God as foreign to me. Therefore, if that favor toward me which many believe I have with you remains genuine, I beg that the envoys of the lord archbishop of Rheims may experience it in their present affair. For we suspect that they seek or bring forward nothing except what is just.

EPISTLE XXI. TO MATTHEW, LEGATE.  
[Note: [Col. 0123D] Written toward the end of 1127. Matthew was born of noble parents in the province of Rheims. He then became a canon of Rheims; but shortly afterward, rejecting all else, he professed the Cluniac Order at Paris in the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Finally he was made bishop of Albano and cardinal by Honorius II in 1125, and as legate in France presided at the Council of Troyes in 1128, called by his authority; Bernard opposed it, but was compelled to attend. John of Michelnes, secretary of the Council, speaks thus of the celebration of the Council of Troyes: “At the feast of Saint Hilary, in the year 1128 from the incarnation of the Son of God, gathering at Troyes under God’s guidance,” etc. Peter the Venerable treats Matthew’s life and virtues at length in *On Miracles*, book 3, chapter 3 and following.]

He very elegantly excuses himself for not coming when summoned to deliberate on business.

1. My heart was indeed ready to obey, but my body was not equally ready. For my weak flesh, burned by the heat and exhausted by the sweats of a raging acute fever, [Col. 0123C] could not suffice for my willing spirit. I wished, therefore, but the circumstance I have mentioned hindered my will as it hastened forward.

Whether this reason is just, let those friends themselves judge—those who, excluding every excuse and enclosing me in the nets of obedience, endeavor daily to drag me from the cloister to the cities. Let them also consider that I did not deceitfully invent this reason, but endured it severely, so that even now they may learn that there is no counsel against the counsel of the Lord. If I had answered them, “I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile [Col. 0124A] them?” (Song 5:3), they would certainly have been indignant. But now let them either be angry with or acquiesce in the divine judgment by which it has come about that, even though I wish to travel, I cannot.

2. “But,” they say, “the cause was great, and the necessity grave.” Then someone fit to decide great matters ought to have been sought. If they think me such a man, I by no means merely think that I am not; I know it. In short, whether the matters for which they press me so insistently are great or small, I have no business with them. For I ask: are the things which you are so eager to lay upon a friend, to disturb his silence, easy or difficult? If easy, they can be done without me; if difficult, they cannot be accomplished through me—unless perhaps I am judged of such value that great and impossible matters are reserved for me, as though I could do what no one else can do. But if this is so, Lord my God, how has Your judgment concerning me alone been frustrated—You who placed under a bushel the lamp that could shine upon a lampstand, and, to speak more plainly, tried to make me a monk and wished, in the day of evils, to hide in Your tabernacle a man necessary to the world, without whom bishops cannot conduct their affairs? Yet these same persons who make me necessary have achieved this also: that I now seem to speak in agitation of a man whom I am accustomed never to remember except serenely and with every delight. Yet you yourselves—yes, I mean you, Father—should know that I am ready and not troubled, to keep your commandments. It will belong to your indulgence, however, to spare me where you decide that I should be spared.

## LETTER XXII. TO HUMBALD

[Note: Written before 1128. Orderic calls him both Humbald and Humbert; elsewhere he is named Humbaud. Formerly archdeacon of Autun, he was made primate of Lyons and, at the beginning of the pontificate of Honorius II—not under Calixtus, as Severtius states in his *History of the Bishops of Lyons*—was joined in a legation to Cardinal Peter of Fontaines, chiefly to restrain the insolence of Pons, the recently former abbot of Cluny. They indeed accomplished this, Pons being struck with an anathema, as Peter the Venerable carefully records in Book II, chapter 13, of *Miracles*. This letter therefore seems to have been written not far from 1125, certainly before 1129, the year in which Severtius consistently places the death of Rainald, Humbald’s successor, who occupied the see of Lyons for only a few days.]  
**ARCHBISHOP OF LYONS AND LEGATE.** He commends to him the cause of the bishop of Meaux.

[Col. 0124C]

To his most reverend lord and father HUMBALD, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Roman See, Brother BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: whatever the prayer of a sinner may avail.

The lord bishop of Meaux [Note: Namely Burchard, not his successor Manasses II. This is required by the chronological concurrence with Humbald, who, as we have seen, died before 1129; whereas Burchard survived until 1133, certainly after the bloody murder of Thomas, Prior of Saint-Victor, beside whom he deserved to share a common epitaph, as may be seen in *Gallia Christiana* and in Severtius. Hence it is clear that an error entered the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, reported by Chesnius in his notes on Abelard, where Manasses II is said to have granted the church of Choisy to Saint-Martin in 1125; the history of that same monastery published by Father Marrier shows that 1125 was mistakenly written for 1135. This observation also readily establishes that the bishop of Meaux whom Bernard mentions at the beginning of Letter 42, addressed to Henry of Sens, is not Manasses II, as many have hitherto supposed, but Burchard himself. For this letter was written to Henry when he had recently turned away from a courtly manner of life, as Bernard clearly intimates in these and other words: “Recently,” he says, “a more favorable breeze has begun to blow upon us from your parts. For more recent reports have announced concerning you things more joyful than usual”—namely, that through the counsels of the bishop of Chartres he had ordered his life more rightly, as Bernard explains below. Yet this change in the bishop of Sens is known to have occurred in the time of Honorius II, both from Letter 49 to Honorius himself, in which Bernard strongly commends Henry against the attacks of Louis the Fat, and from the very cause of those attacks, which he there expressly says was none other than Henry’s conversion. “Those,” he says, “who formerly, in secular dress and conduct, were honored as eminent, judged faithful, and treated as intimates, have now become enemies because they have turned to a life worthy of their priesthood and in every way honor their ministry. … Hence he now attempts to shake and undermine the constancy of the lord of Sens,” etc.] received your letters, perhaps when he was then coming to visit us. And when he was already preparing to reply from our house, he took care to join our letter to his own, as from one familiar to you, hoping that it would benefit his business. Since I could not deny him what he wished, I thought it sufficient to communicate briefly and familiarly to Your Reverence only this: if you hear persons who love themselves and seek their own interests speaking against a bishop who seeks the things of Jesus Christ, this accords neither with your dignity nor with your office.

## LETTER XXIII. TO ATTO

[Note: Written about the same year. Everyone affirms that Atto, also called Hato, was a monk of Cluny; but that this was before he attained the episcopate is readily disproved by Letter 50 of Book II of Peter the Venerable: “Where,” he says, “is that devotion, where is that affection drawing near to heaven—indeed, as it then seemed, surpassing heaven itself—by which you dedicated yourself to me, not, I say, as a brother, but, to reproach you familiarly in your own words, as a son and a monk? Where is the pledge given, where the appointed time, where the specified day, on which, while still an exalted and wealthy bishop, you vowed to leave the world and follow humble and poor Jesus?” The same is found in Letter 27 of Book IV: “What youth did not grant to friendship, old age will at least confer.” But every shadow of difficulty is removed by the congratulatory letter of Peter, Prior of Saint John the Evangelist at Sens, to the same Atto, published by Severtius in his *Catalogue of the Bishops of Mâcon*, under Joceran, §4. It is pleasing to reproduce here a few passages:

“To his dearest lord and venerable father, Bishop Hato, happily crowned with the hood of blessed Benedict, little P., servant of Christ: forget your people and your father’s house.

“Your change of dwelling, venerable Father, has not dissolved the sacrament of your anointing; rather, the more you approach the Lord, the more beautifully the jewel of your merit has shone forth. For a lamp, removed from public view lest it be blown out by the winds, shines better in the house; a ship tossed by stormy waves remains safe when it has entered the hiding-places of sheltered bays; and the person who, escaping the whirlwinds of the world, enters the house of peace, looking back upon the loss of others rejoices in his own tranquility. Withdrawal from the world, as Your Paternity knows, is approach to the heavenly throne; and a chair voluntarily relinquished is a sign of greater dignity. Therefore many have left their homes and, in a greater and sufficiently happy exchange, have gained. Gregory of Nazianzus, renouncing his see, lived the life of a monk in the country. Justus of Lyons withdrew to the Egyptian desert. Wilfrann of Sens, apostle of the Frisians, finally gave himself to the monastery of Fontenelle. Since these men, because of the worthiness of their merits, are bodily presented at sacred shrines, their episcopal title is preserved even after their burial. I could bring forward many more such examples; but in every matter the testimony of three may suffice. But now, dearest Father, I turn my pen to you and wholly rejoice in your happiness: the Church of Sens had you as dean and archdeacon; the see of Troyes possessed you as a glorious bishop; Cluny makes you a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household.”

The same bishop attended the Council of Troyes in 1128 and also that of Pisa in 1134. On his return he was wounded in the head near the Italian town of Ponte Tremolo and was carried off captive with many bishops of Gaul. Peter of Cluny protested to Innocent concerning this outrage in a letter sent to him, namely Letter 27 of Book III. Nevertheless he survived for a long time, finally dying at Cluny in 1145, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September, as recorded in the calendar of the monastery of Aremar. See Camusat, *Compendium of Sacred Antiquities of the Diocese of Troyes*, and Severtius, *Catalogue of the Bishops of Troyes* and *of Mâcon*.]  
**BISHOP OF TROYES.** He consoles and praises Bishop Atto, who, while ill and expecting death, had distributed all his possessions among the poor, but had been restored to health.

From a poor abbot to a poor bishop: may you obtain the reward of poverty, which is the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0125B]

1. I would praise you—and rightly praise you—were I not recalled by that saying, “Praise no man during his life” (Ecclus. 11:30). For you have done a deed worthy of praise; but praise must be ascribed to Him from whom you received both the willing and the accomplishing of what was deservedly praised. Therefore we glorify God working through you and in you, [Col. 0126A] who so willed to be glorified in you for this purpose also: that He might make you glorious. For although He is wonderful in His majesty, He also deigns to appear glorious in His saints, lest He alone possess glory. Though He is sufficient to Himself for every magnificence, He nevertheless seeks glory also in the saints, not to increase it for Himself, but to share it with His own. He knows who are His; but they do not readily become known to us unless He deigns to reveal them Himself.

We know, certainly, of whom it is written: “They are not in the labor of men, nor are they scourged with other men” (Ps. 72:5). And we now know, no less certainly, that this saying does not apply to you. It is also written: “Whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3:12; Heb. 12:6). I see you scourged [Col. 0126B] and corrected: shall I suspect anything other than that you are one of the sons? Moreover, we have a sufficiently clear sign of your correction: your present poverty itself. Truly noble is the title of poverty, which God Himself commends through the prophetic mouth: “I am,” He says, “the man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1). [Col. 0127A] More than all royal treasures, this title ennobles you and makes you illustrious.

2. I know that above I recalled from Scripture that a man is not to be praised during his life. But how can I restrain myself from praising one who has now ceased to pursue gold and has disdained to put hope in money’s treasures? Scripture speaks thus of such a man: “Who is he? We will praise him; for he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31:8–9). Or perhaps a man is indeed not to be praised in his life, which is temptation upon earth; yet is he not therefore to be praised when, dead to sin, he lives to God? The praise by which a sinner is praised in the desires of his soul is vain and deceptive; whoever calls me blessed on that account leads me into error. But the life of one who can say, “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20), is nevertheless to be proclaimed and highly commended. When, therefore, a man in whom it is no longer he himself but Christ who lives is praised, he is praised not in his own life but in Christ’s life; and thus he is not praised contrary to the saying which forbids praise of a man in his own life.

3. Why, then, should he not be worthy of my praise whom God also deigns to honor with praise under His own name, David saying: “The poor and needy shall praise your name” (Ps. 73:21)? Job is praised because he patiently lost his possessions; and shall not a bishop be praised who both willingly relinquished them and generously distributed them? He did not wait for death, when he would no longer have power either to give or to retain what was his. Many do this, whose testament, plainly, is confirmed only when they are dead. But while still placed between hope of life and fear of death, living and willing, he scattered abroad and gave to the poor, so that his righteousness might remain for ever and ever (Ps. 111:9). Was money likewise to remain for ever and ever? Justice, then, is a good recompense for money: in exchange for that which could not be retained, there was restored what happily remains forever. For righteousness is incomparably better than money, because money enriches and fills a chest, whereas righteousness fills the soul. Thus the priests of God are clothed with righteousness—certainly far more becomingly and richly than with gold or silk.

4. But thanks be to God, who has already wrought in you the glorious contempt of these transitory glories, [Col. 0127D] by infusing a most salutary fear concerning the danger to your soul. O marvelous divine mercy toward you! He threatened death in order not to inflict it; He wished you to fear what He did not wish you to experience. In doing this, what did He accomplish except that your possessions should not be dearer to you than yourselves? A sharp fever raged through the marrow of your limbs; and, as sweat was delayed, violent torment grew worse day by day. [Col. 0128A] When at last the limbs were growing cold outwardly, while the most grievous heat gathered inwardly and consumed your organs, exhausted by prolonged fasting, the sad image of pale death meanwhile hovered before your eyes. And behold, as though a voice sent from on high had sounded divinely: “I, I am he who blots out, not you, but your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25), immediately, when the priest of God, that he might die poor, gave away all that he possessed to the poor, unexpected streams of sweat, already despaired of, suddenly burst forth from within. Thus the salvation of soul and body alike, each proceeding in its proper order, clearly showed that in you was fulfilled what God promises in Scripture: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal, and there is none who can deliver from my hand” (Deut. 32:39). He struck the flesh that the soul might be healed; [Col. 0128B] He killed avarice that you might live for righteousness.

Thus, having been made alive and healed, what is to be hoped except that there will now be none who can snatch you from God’s hand—provided, however, that you do not neglect to observe that evangelical counsel: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). The merciful Father gives this warning precisely because He does not wish it to happen; for He does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live. And rightly so. For what profit is there in the blood of the sinner? Hell will not confess God, nor will death praise Him. But you who live, bless the Lord and say: “I shall not die, but live, and declare the works of the Lord”; and: “I was thrust down, that I might fall, but the Lord upheld me” (Ps. 117:17, 13).

## LETTER XXIV. TO MASTER GILBERT THE UNIVERSAL

[Note: Written about 1130. Gilbert was so called because, as Bernard writes here, he “played,” or excelled, in all the writings of this world’s learned men. Before attaining episcopal dignity, he was a canon of Auxerre. The necrology of that church says: “On the second Ides of August died Master Gislebert, of venerable memory, an outstanding glossator of the Old and New Testament, canon of this church, afterwards made bishop of London; who, besides the other ornaments which he sent our church from England, bestowed upon the same church eighty-two pounds,” etc. He governed the church of London from 1128 to 1133.]  
**BISHOP OF LONDON.** He praises Gilbert because, having become bishop, he cultivates poverty.

[Col. 0128C]

The discourse which you have delivered has travelled very far and has given forth a great fragrance of sweetness wherever it could reach. Avarice has been extinguished: to whom would its fragrance not be sweet? Charity reigns: to whom would it not taste delightful? In this all recognize that you are truly wise, since you have crushed wisdom’s greatest enemy. This is surely worthy alike of your priesthood and of your name. It was fitting that your special [variant: spiritual] philosophy should shine by such a witness, and that those distinguished studies of yours should be consummated in this end. [Col. 0128D]

That is true and unquestionable wisdom which despises shameful gain and judges it unworthy to share the same dwelling with the service of idols. It was no great thing that Master Gilbert became a bishop; but for the bishop of London to live poor [Note: Henry of Huntingdon, in his letter *On Contempt of the World*, printed in volume 8 of the *Spicilegium*, imputed this to Gilbert as avarice—such are human judgments.], that is plainly magnificent. For the height of his office could add no glory to so great a name; but the humility of poverty greatly increased it. To endure poverty with an even mind is the virtue of wisdom; to seek it voluntarily is wisdom’s praise. In short, he who did not go after gold is praised and proclaimed admirable; shall one who actually cast it away deserve nothing more? Except that vigilant reason finds nothing astonishing in a wise man acting wisely—especially one who, playing amid all the writings and studies of this world’s sages, has also endeavored and been able, in some fashion, to recall and renew the whole of divine Scripture.

What then? You scattered abroad and gave to the poor—but money. Yet what is money compared with the righteousness for which you exchanged it? “His righteousness,” it says, “remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9). Does money remain in the same way? Certainly a profitable and honorable exchange: to give what passes away for what endures. May you always be permitted thus to trade, good master, worthy of every praise. It remains that the laudable beginning receive a fitting end, and that the tail of the victim be joined to its head [Note: A proverb familiar to Bernard, signifying perseverance, from Leviticus 3:7.
