See notes on Letter 78. Peter of Celle, Letter 8 of Book V: “Beware the tail; since all praise, as also all blame, ends in the tail—that is, in the end.”]. We gladly received your blessing, especially because it was made still more delightful by so great a fullness of this perfection of yours. I desire that the bearer of this letter, though sufficiently commendable in his own right, be nevertheless commended to your magnificence also for my sake. For his integrity and religious devotion make him very dear to me.

## LETTER XXV. TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1130. A letter of the clergy of Rouen to Pope Honorius II concerning Hugh’s election, made in 1130, survives in volume 3 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 151, containing these words: “By a common election we have chosen our son Hugh, abbot of Reading, as bishop for ourselves.” He had first been a monk at Cluny, then first abbot of Reading in England, in the diocese of Salisbury. Hence the same letter adds: “Concerning this we sought and obtained the assent of our lord Henry, king of the English; we asked that he be released and absolved for us by the bishop of Salisbury, under whose authority he performed the office of abbot, and we received him with freedom,” etc. Orderic places his election in 1130, at the end of Book XII, in these words: “In the same year Hugh of Amiens, monk of Cluny and abbot of Reading, was made archbishop of Rouen.” The same author, Book XIII, p. 900, shows how much zeal he displayed for Innocent II.]  
He urges Hugh to strive to be patient and peaceable among his people of Rouen, and likewise to moderate zeal by discretion.

[Col. 0129C]

1. If the evil of the day grows strong, let it not prevail; if it causes disturbance, let it not disturb you. “Mighty are the surges of the sea, but mightier on high is the Lord.” Illustrious Father, heavenly mercy has dealt graciously with you thus far, provided you do not disregard it. For by provident ordering you were not placed over evil persons before you had been joined to good ones, through whose fellowship and example you might become good, and thus afterward be able to live good even among the evil. To be good among the good has salvation; to be good among the evil has praise. The former is as easy as it is secure; the latter as difficult as it is virtuous. For what is it like? To touch pitch and not be defiled by it; to move amid fire without injury, [Col. 0129D] and amid darkness without gloom.

The Egyptians once felt their way through darkness; yet Scripture says of the people [Col. 0130A] of God: “Wherever Israel was, there was light” (Exod. 10:23). David was a true Israelite and therefore cautiously said that he dwelt not in Kedar, but *with those dwelling in Kedar* (Ps. 119:5): as one who always dwelt in light, though he bodily lived among the inhabitants of Kedar. Accordingly, he rebukes certain false Israelites because “they mingled among the nations and learned their works, and it became a stumbling-block to them” (Ps. 105:35–36).

2. Therefore I say: among the Cluniacs it was enough for you to preserve innocence, as it is written: “With the innocent man you will be innocent” (Ps. 17:26). But among the people of Rouen [variant: at Rouen] patience is needed, as the Apostle teaches: “The servant of God,” he says, “must not quarrel, but must be patient toward all” (2 Tim. 2:24). And not only patient, so as not to be overcome by evil, but also peaceable, so as to overcome evil with good: the one, that you may bear evil people; the other, that you may heal those whom you endure. “By your patience you possess your soul” (Luke 21:19); but be peaceable also, so that you may possess those entrusted to you. What glory is so great as to be able to say: “With those who hate peace, I was peaceable” (Ps. 119:7)? Be patient, therefore, because you are among evil persons; be peaceable, because you preside over evil persons.

Let charity have zeal, but let severity apply moderation according to the occasion. Discipline indeed, though never relaxed, often accomplishes more when it is suspended. Let the vigor of justice always be ardent, but never headlong. As not everything one wishes is lawful, so not everything lawful is immediately expedient. You know these things better than I do; therefore I refrain. I earnestly ask that prayer be made for me, because I sin without ceasing.

## LETTER XXVI. TO GUY, BISHOP OF LAUSANNE

[Note: Written about 1130.]

You have set your hand to mighty things: strength is needed. You have been made a watchman for the house of Israel: prudence is needed [Note: The same words occur in Letter 3 of Nicholas of Clairvaux, written in Bernard’s person to the bishop of Lucca; below, Letter 463.]. You are debtor to wise and foolish alike: justice is needed. Finally, temperance is especially needed, lest he who preaches to others himself—God forbid—become reprobate.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ARDUTION [variant: ARDUTIUS], ELECT OF GENEVA

[Note: Written about 1135.]  
He warns him to attribute his election to divine grace and thereafter to strive diligently to cooperate with it.

[Col. 0130D]

We believe that your election is from God, since we have learned that it was celebrated with such great agreement of clergy and people. We congratulate His grace—rather than your merits, lest we flatter you beyond what is fitting. For this was done for you “not by works of righteousness which you have done, but according to His mercy.” If you think otherwise—God forbid—your exaltation will become a downfall. But if you acknowledge grace, see that you do not receive it in vain. Henceforth make good your ways, your endeavors, and your sacred ministry. If holiness of life has not preceded, let it at least follow. Then we shall truly confess that you have been anticipated with blessings of sweetness, hoping better things for you from good things. We shall exult and rejoice that a faithful and prudent servant has been set over the household of the Lord, destined thereby to become a blessed and mighty son, to be set over all the Father’s goods. Otherwise, if you take pleasure in being higher rather than better, [Col. 0131B] we expect not a reward but a precipice. We desire and pray that this may not happen; we are ready, if necessary, to lend helping hands and, to the small extent of our power, to assist rather toward what is fitting and expedient.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE SAME, NOW BISHOP

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1135.]  
Meanwhile he urges him to adorn by subsequent merits the dignity he obtained without preceding merits.

1. Charity gives me boldness to speak to you more freely. Dearest friend, the chair which you have recently received demands a man of many merits; and we grieve that in you such merits either did not precede at all, or did not precede in sufficient measure. Indeed, neither your deeds nor your former pursuits seemed in any respect suited to the episcopal office. Yet what of it? Cannot God raise up from this stone a son of Abraham? Cannot God cause good things, which ought to have gone before a man, to follow him instead? We would indeed receive this all the more gladly if it happens. For I do not know why this sudden change wrought by the right hand of the Most High would not please us more than if merits of your former life supported you. We shall say: “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (Ps. 117:23). Thus Paul was made from persecutor into teacher of the Gentiles; thus Matthew was called from the tax-office; thus Ambrose was taken from the palace: the one to the episcopate, the other to the apostolate. Thus we know very many others to have been beneficially promoted from secular life and dress. In short, does not grace often appear to abound all the more where offenses have abounded?

2. Therefore you also, dearest friend, encouraged by these and similar examples, gird your loins like a man; henceforth make good your ways and your pursuits, so that your latter days may put your former ones to rest and evening correction may blot out the sins of your youth. Take care to imitate Paul in honoring your ministry. [Col. 0132A] You will honor it by gravity of character, maturity of counsel, and integrity of conduct. These are the things which especially ennoble and adorn the episcopal office. Do everything with counsel—but not with the counsel of everyone or of just anyone: only of good persons. Have good people as your counselors, good people in service, good people as companions dwelling with you, who may be both guardians and witnesses of your life and integrity. For in this you will prove yourself good: if you have testimony from good people. Let our poor brothers who are near you be commended to Your Piety: the Alpine brothers, those of Bonmont, and those of Hautecombe. In them we shall discover how much care you have for us.

## LETTER XXIX. TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ

[Note: Written about 1126. In 1120, after the expulsion of Adalbero, fourth bishop of that name of Metz, Stephen was substituted for him, as I read in the brief annals of the monastery of Saint-Vincent at Metz appended to the Paschal cycles; there Stephen is recorded as having died in 1163, on the third day before the Kalends of January. Bernard makes grave complaints concerning him in Letters 177 and 178. On the peace mentioned here, read the history of Lawrence of Liège, in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 318–319.]  
He congratulates Stephen on peace restored to the Church, and declares that it must be attributed solely to the benefit of God.

[Col. 0132B]

To STEPHEN, by God’s grace a vigorous minister of the Church of Metz; from his humble brothers in Christ at Clairvaux: greeting and prayer.

Since long ago, if you recall, you graciously joined yourself to our brotherhood and humbly commended yourself to our prayers, we have always been concerned, as we ought to have been, to learn something of your condition. We have diligently sought frequent news of your fortunes from those whom we could, continually desiring and praying that you might prosper in God’s work, to which you had been called, and that your steps might be directed into the path of His commandments. Blessed therefore be God, who has not removed our prayer nor His mercy from you, gladdening us through this venerable brother William, [Col. 0132C] whose words, concerning your safety and prosperity and the peace restored to the Church through you, we trust no less than our own eyes. We congratulate you, but we give glory to God, knowing that what you are and what you can do belong to Him, not to you.

We also lovingly remind you always to think this of yourselves: lest you begin to be both nothing and able to do nothing, if you think otherwise and ascribe any of these things—God forbid—to your own merits or powers. Otherwise one must fear lest your peace be turned into disturbance and your prosperity into adversity, through the just judgment of Him who, as He is accustomed to give grace to the humble, so also resists the proud; who, as is read in the Psalm, is not only holy with the holy but also perverse with the perverse (Ps. 17:26); and who is described by the prophet not only as making peace but also as creating evil (Isa. 45:7).

### Letter XXX. To Albero, Primicerius of Metz

[Note: Written about the year 1126. I observe three men of this name succeeding one another in the dignity of primicerius: first, one of the lineage of the duke of Louvain, afterwards bishop of Liège, concerning whom Giles of Aurea Vallis, a Cistercian monk, writes in *The Deeds of the Bishops of Liège*, ch. 23: “There succeeded Lord Frederick,” namely in the year 1122, “Lord Albero, primicerius from the clergy of St Stephen at Metz, brother of Godfrey duke of Louvain, a man of the highest authority and innocence, etc. He died on the Circumcision [1 January], in the year of the Lord 1128.”

I read of another Albero, who became archbishop of Trier from being primicerius of Metz. Together with Gerard, legate of the Apostolic See, he secured the promotion of St Norbert to the see of Magdeburg. Thus Robert, in his Supplement to Sigebert, under the year 1127, writes: “After the death of the archbishop of the city of Parthenopolis [Magdeburg], when the clergy and citizens of that city had assembled before Emperor Lothair at Speyer to elect an archbishop, by the direction of Lord Gerard, legate of the Roman See, who afterwards became Pope Lucius, and of Albero, [Col. 0133C] primicerius of Metz, who afterwards became archbishop of Trier”—namely in 1132—“they elect Norbert, father of the church of Prémontré, … as pastor.” The same is read in the *Life of St Norbert* in Surius, ch. 40.

Bernard wrote Letter 176 to Innocent II on his behalf. In ancient documents he is frequently found subscribing, called indifferently Albero or Adelbero, alongside another Albero, archdeacon. Thus in a charter of St Arnulf of Metz: “I, Adelbero the primicerius, subscribed and approved; I, Richer the dean, subscribed; Adelbero the archdeacon, etc.; in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126.” But in another document of St Peter of the Mount, written in 1127: “The witnesses of this donation are Albero the primicerius, Richer the dean,” etc. These may be seen in Meuricius’s *History of the Bishops of Metz*. He wrongly identifies this Albero with another Albero, likewise primicerius, son of Count Conrad of Luxembourg, who held that dignity until the year 1086, as appears from the epitaph of his father Conrad produced by that author himself, p. 386. The Albero of whom we speak, by contrast, held this dignity chiefly only from the year 1122, when he succeeded Albero of Louvain.

Besides the Luxembourger, therefore, we have a third Albero, who from primicerius became the second bishop of Liège of that name in 1135. Of him Giles, cited above, writes: “In those days, when, through the shameful deposition of Alexander, the city of Liège had become an object of mockery and derision to those around it, the clergy and people, with common wishes and equal agreement, appointed to the see of Liège Albero, the second of that name, primicerius of the Church of Metz, a young man indeed in age, etc. The pillars of the Church chose him especially in the hope that he was of the Namur lineage,” etc.

Thus, besides the Luxembourger, we have three primicerii of Metz of the same name, succeeding one another continuously. To which of them Bernard wrote this letter is not easy to determine. Yet, so far as may be inferred from the sequence of the letters, it seems to be addressed to the second: namely, the man afterwards raised to the archbishopric of Trier, who enjoyed the Saint’s very close friendship, as is evident from several letters which Bernard addressed to Innocent and to the Roman Curia on his behalf.

Indeed, the subject of this letter, which concerns the foundation of a monastery planned by Stephen, bishop of Metz, through Albero’s agency, seems to support this. It must not, however, be understood of any monastery built by Stephen himself, but either of that house of Capet, which Bernard, when the latter conveyed it, assigned to nuns of his Order, giving it the name Clairvaux, about the year 1130; or of the foundation of Belles-Prés near Lunéville, [Col. 0134C] built by Folmar, count of Metz, which Stephen himself ratified and confirmed. This is evident from a charter whose opening reads: “I, Stephen, make known to the generation now present and to that to come that Folmar, count of Metz, has built, in the district of Morasme, an abbey of monks of the Cistercian Order called Belles-Prés, etc. Given in the year 1130.” Yet in another charter of Henry, bishop of Toul, this foundation is assigned to 1135; perhaps this should be understood of the complete finishing of the buildings.

As for the title *primicerius*, very commonly used among the ancients, it was not peculiar to one office or dignity, but was customarily given to those who held first place in any order. Thus in Novel Constitution 8, “primicerius of the notaries” is repeatedly found; and “primicerius of the factory,” law 2, *Code*, on the Fabricenses, book 11; “primicerius of the household guards and cavalry,” law 2 and final law, *Code*, on the Domestici and Protectores; “primicerius of the surveyors,” [Col. 0134D] *Code* 1, on Surveyors, book 12; “primicerius in the office of the protectores.” Further, in Vegetius, book 2, ch. 21, “primicerius protector”; in Ammianus Marcellinus, book 18, “primicerius of the officials, of the Imperial Guard, of the Augustales, of the bureaux, of the deputies, of the sacred bedchamber”; in law 1, *Code Theodosianus*, “concerning the allowance of a recruit,” and in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book 11. So too, “primicerius of a legion” in William of Tyre, *The Holy War*, book 2, ch. 19; “primicerius of the defenders and cardinal primicerius” in Liutprand, book 6, *On Affairs throughout Europe*. Likewise St Augustine calls St Stephen “the primicerius of martyrs” in Sermon 21, *On the Season*.

Here, however, in Bernard, by “primicerius of Metz” is meant the chief dignity among the canons of the church of St Stephen at Metz. Among its other prerogatives was the right to wear a cross upon the breast and a purple garment, and to hold first place in choir and chapter.]

He advises that a certain matter pressed by Albero should be carried through according to God’s good pleasure, seeking not so much the gift as its fruit.

To the honourable man ALBERO, by God’s grace primicerius of the Church of Metz, the brothers who serve God at Clairvaux in whatever [Col. 0133A] service they are able: greeting and prayer.

We had long both heard and seen your faithful concern in matters concerning God; but now we have experienced and felt it in our own case. Moreover, since in the matters which the brothers lately sent by us proposed to the bishop on your advice, we possess both your goodwill and the bishop’s ready consent: nevertheless, because in all things—and especially in those which pertain to God—it is necessary for us before and above all else to seek and preserve God’s good pleasure, we have judged that the matter, as agreed between the bishop and the monks, through your diligence acting as intermediary and arranging how it ought to be done, [Col. 0133B] urging that it be done quickly and assisting that it be done honourably, [Col. 0134A] ought not to be abandoned, but must necessarily be deferred until after harvest, awaiting both your convenience and that of the season.

Then, indeed, if the bishop’s will remains unchanged in this matter and it continues to please you no less than it does now, we shall trust more securely, from such concurrence, that this too is God’s counsel; and we hope, according to what was determined, to satisfy the devotion of you both. For we think it acceptable to God if, so far as lies in us, we endeavour to burden no one: lest we appear—far be it—to seek not so much the fruit as the gift in this affair of his; and especially lest, under the pretext of this matter, we intrude too importunately upon your greater and more pressing occupations and make ourselves troublesome to you when there is no need. We know that this is not pleasing to God [Col. 0134B] and [Col. 0135A] does not accord with our own customs.

### Letter XXXI. To Hugh, Count of Champagne, Who Had Become a Knight Templar

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1125. Hugh, son of Theobald III, count of Champagne, was extremely generous towards churches, especially those of Arram and Molesme. He was first count of Bar-sur-Aube, then count of Troyes after the death of his brother Odo. Through him it came about that, after the union of the counties of Troyes and Bar, the title of those counties disappeared and his successors were called counts of Champagne, whereas previously the name had been used separately, both for Bar and for Troyes. Francis Chifflet noted this in his *Dissertation on the Illustrious Lineage of St Bernard*.

To him belongs Letter 245 of Ivo of Chartres, whose argument we take from its opening words: “We have heard and learned that, intending to go to Jerusalem, you have devoted yourself to Christ’s warfare, intending to undertake that Gospel warfare in which one fights securely with ten thousand against one who comes to fight against us with twenty thousand.” [Col. 0135C] And below: “You have taken a wife,” etc. Finally he concludes: “You must therefore make such provision in this intention that you fulfil your final vows without breaking the established natural and legal obligations.”

Horstius conjectures that Ivo there recalls Hugh from his intended joining of the Temple’s military order because of the bond of marriage. But since, according to William of Tyre, *The Holy War*, book 11, ch. 13—and all agree with him—the Order of Templars began only in 1118, while Ivo certainly died in 1115, it follows that he must be understood either to speak of the Hospitallers’ military order, which Hugh planned to enter at Jerusalem, or of a certain spiritual and evangelical, or temporary, continence which Hugh ought to observe during the interval of his second pilgrimage to the holy places.

For it is established that he undertook the journey to Jerusalem three times, as Chifflet, cited above, rightly proves: first in 1113, again about 1121, and afterwards when he bound himself to the Templars’ military order, which Alberic expressly places in 1125. “When he was leaving for the last time,” writes Chifflet, “if Peter Pithou is to be trusted, he sold his county to Theobald, son of his brother Stephen; disinherited his son Odo; left pregnant the woman whom he had taken as his second wife—Constance, daughter of Philip I, king of France, whom he had dismissed for consanguinity in 1104—and died overseas on the fourteenth day of June, although the necrology of St Claude says that he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June].” Thus, approximately, he writes.

Moreover, this Hugh is distinct from Hugh, master of the Templar Order, to whom Bernard addressed the *Exhortation to the Knights Templar*. This is inferred from William of Tyre, *The Holy War*, book 12, ch. 7, where this man is surnamed “of the Pagans,” and appears to have had Robert as his successor, so far as may be conjectured from the same author, book 17, ch. 1.]

Bernard congratulates Hugh on his embracing holy warfare and promises remembrance of his benefits.

If for God’s cause you have become from a count a knight, and from rich poor, we rightly congratulate you in this, and glorify God in you, knowing that this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Yet we do not, I confess, bear with equanimity the fact that your pleasant presence has, by some judgment of God unknown to me, been so removed from us that we cannot even occasionally see you, though we should never wish, if it were possible, to be without you.

For what? Can we forget our former love and [Col. 0135B] the benefits which you so generously bestowed upon our house? [Col. 0136A]

[Note: Hugh himself had granted Bernard and the brothers the very site of Clairvaux with its [Col. 0136B] appurtenances, and for that reason ought rightly to be reckoned by the title of Founder. Since this has hitherto become known to few, it is pleasing here to set down the charter of donation itself, which we owe to the often-mentioned Chifflet, who first published it in his *Dissertation*, taken from the Clairvaux original:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity begins the charter of Count Hugh. Let all present and future persons know that I, count of Troyes, give to God, to blessed Mary, and to the brothers of Clairvaux, the very place called Clairvaux, with its appurtenances, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, and waters, retaining absolutely nothing for myself or my heirs. The witnesses are Acard of Reims, and Peter and Robert of Orléans, my knights. Let it be known that Geoffrey Felonia gives his pastures in the territory of Juvencourt, both in wood and in open country, at all times; and if the animals of the said brothers cause any damage, only the principal loss shall be restored, without a fine. All these things I gave in the presence of the aforesaid witnesses.

“Let it also be known that Lord Josbert of La Ferté, surnamed Rufus, and Lord Rainaud of Perceris have given to the same brothers grazing-rights and rights of use throughout all their land, and especially in waters, woods, and meadows, in the territory of Perrecin. The witnesses of this matter are Acard of Reims and Robert, my knights.

“Likewise let it also be known that I, Hugh count of Troyes, approve and grant that the same brothers possess freely and peacefully the land and wood of Aretela. We, Joscerannus bishop of Langres, and I, Hugh count of Troyes, confirm these donations by seal and by my ring.”

As to the year of the foundation, which is not expressed in these records, the same author, following the Chronicler of St Marianus of Auxerre, places it in June of the year of Christ 1114. All indeed agree as to the month; but as to the year, since both external and internal documents seem to oppose it—among others, the Cistercian *Exordium*, distinction 2, ch. 1, and the tablet hung on St Bernard’s tomb, which expressly state 1115—it seems preferable to adhere to the opinion long received. Otherwise Bernard could scarcely have made profession in June 1114, and Hugh himself, who granted the place, was still in the East.

Thus Clairvaux was first founded by Hugh, count of Champagne; then, in 1135, transferred to a larger site through the aid of Theobald, his successor, and endowed with a new building. Hence some gave Theobald the name of first founder, confusing the translation with the foundation, as Manrique rightly observes in his *Annals*, under the year 1115, ch. 1.]

Would that he for whose love you acted may never forget you forever! For we, so far as lies in us, are by no means wholly ungrateful: we retain in mind the memory of your abundant kindness, and, if permitted, would show it in deed. Oh, with what willing heart we would have provided alike for your body and your soul, if it had been granted that we might be together! Since this is not so, it remains that we should always pray for him whom we cannot have present, as absent.

### Letter XXXII. To the Abbot of Saint-Nicaise at Reims

[Note: Written about the year 1120. Drogo, on whose account both Letter 33 and Letter 34 were written, appears not to have persevered in the Cistercian Order, but finally, before profession, to have been recalled by the importunate complaints of his abbot Jorannus—to whom this letter is addressed. He seems to be the same man who, after expelling the nuns from the monastery of St John at Laon, brought there a community of monks. Having been prior of St Nicaise at Reims, he was appointed their first abbot in 1128, as will be said below at Letter 48.

Afterwards he was made cardinal and bishop of Ostia by Innocent II in 1136, as our Acherius proves in his notes on Guibert; not in 1133, as Ciaconius has it, nor in 1134, as Ughellus judges in *Italia Sacra*. Hermann recounts Drogo’s deeds in *Miracles*, book 3, ch. 22; likewise the author of the Appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1128, who asserts that he died in 1138: “Drogo, bishop of Ostia, of blessed memory, a man renowned for religious devotion and wisdom, died.” The necrology of St John at Laon says: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December] died Drogo, bishop and cardinal of Ostia, first abbot of our congregation, and Matilda his sister.” He wrote a sermon on the Passion of the Lord, extant in the *Library of the Fathers*. He is also recorded in the manuscript *Belgian Library* as having published *Soliloquies*.

As for Abbot Jorannus, the distinguished men who emerged from the ascetic house of St Nicaise in order to spread regular discipline far and wide prove how greatly it flourished under his direction. Besides Drogo, there was Geoffrey, who became abbot at St Theodoric near Reims, and after him William; Simon, at St Nicholas in the Wood, in the diocese of Laon, to whom Letters 83 and 84 are addressed; and Arnulf, at Gembloux, as the Gembloux Continuation testifies. Jorannus himself, inflamed by the love of solitude, embraced the Carthusian Order in the monastery of Mont-Dieu in 1138, where he conducted himself so outstandingly that Innocent II enrolled him among the cardinals.

Moreover, since this letter was written while Robert, St Bernard’s kinsman, had not yet been restored to him, as the holy Doctor here asserts, it should be assigned to about the year 1120.]

Bernard consoles the abbot over the departure and transfer of the monk Drogo to another monastery, and exhorts him to patience.

1. He who bore in his own body all our pains knows with what affection I sympathize with you. How gladly I would advise you, if I knew how; assist you, if I could: may he who knows all things and can do all things so effectively advise and assist me in all my necessities.

If Brother Drogo had consulted me about his departure, far be it from me to have consented; if, after his departure, he had turned aside to us, far be it from me to have received him. Finally, I immediately sent, as you know, my letters concerning him to the abbot who received him.

[Note: These earlier letters have been lost, as is evident from the following letter, in which some of their words are cited.]

What further can I do for you in this matter, Father? Yet as regards yourself, your Holiness knows with me very well that perfect men are accustomed to glory not only in hope but also in tribulations. Scripture consoles them, saying: “The furnace tests a potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous people” [Col. 0137B] (Ecclus. 27:6). “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. 33:20 [Vulgate]); “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21); and “All who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12).

Nevertheless, we do not without cause sympathize with our friends when we see them placed in distress. While we do not know the outcome, we fear their failure. For just as, in saints and elect persons, tribulation produces patience, patience tested character, tested character hope, and hope does not disappoint (Rom. 5:3–5), so in those to be condemned and rejected, tribulation produces, on the contrary, faint-heartedness; faint-heartedness, disturbance; disturbance, despair; and that destroys them.

2. Therefore, lest this dreadful storm of waters engulf you—God avert it—lest the depth of this terrible abyss swallow you, and lest this insatiable pit press its mouth upon you, let your humble prudence earnestly strive not to be conquered by evil, but to conquer evil with good. You will conquer by fixing your hope firmly in God and patiently awaiting the end of the matter.

If he comes to his senses, whether through fear of you or through his own hardship, well; but if not, it is good for you to humble yourself beneath the mighty hand of God, and by no means to wish to resist the heavenly dispensation; for [no. 46] if it is from God, it cannot be overthrown. Rather, you must strive to restrain the impulses of your righteous indignation by that saying which one of the saints is reported to have uttered in a similar case. When some brothers were urging and reproaching him for not demanding back a fugitive from another church who had been received there after injuring him, he said: “Not at all. Wherever he may be, if he is good, he is mine.”

3. I advise you deceitfully and not faithfully if I do not require the same of myself. For when one of ours, bound to us not only by religious profession but also by blood,

[Note: Robert, to whom Letter 1 is addressed.]

has been received and is kept at Cluny against my will, I grieve indeed, but remain silent, praying both for them, that they may wish to restore the one taken away, and for him, that he may wish freely to return. Otherwise, I reserve vengeance for him who will render judgment for those suffering wrong [Col. 0138B] and reprove with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth.

Through your mouth and in our spirit, we warn Brother Hugh of Lausanne not to believe every spirit, nor to be quickly moved to abandon what is certain for what is uncertain. Let him know that the devil always lies in wait for perseverance alone, since he knows that it alone of the virtues is crowned. It is safer simply to persevere in the calling in which one was called than, under the appearance of some supposedly greater good, to abandon what one has already begun and perhaps fail to be equal to what one presumes to undertake.

### Letter XXXIII. To Hugh, Abbot of Pontigny

[Note: Written about the year 1120.]

Bernard explains more plainly his intention concerning Drogo’s reception and removes every adverse suspicion from himself.

To his most beloved lord HUGH, abbot, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: the same that he wishes for himself.

1. In our earlier letter,

[Note: This letter has been lost.]

either I wrote less plainly than I intended, as appears from yours, or you understood it otherwise than you ought. For I truly feared, and still fear, precisely what I announced to you would result from the reception of that monk. Yet I did not endeavour to predict these things to you in order either to persuade or to advise you, or, as you write, to judge that he ought to be [Col. 0139A] returned. I have long known the fervency of his own desire, and I ought rather to congratulate him because he has now fulfilled it.

But when my letters were urgently demanded by his abbot, who is most closely connected with us, and by the archbishop of Reims,

[Note: Ralph the Green.]

for the purpose of demanding him back, I took care, so far as I could, to dictate such letters as would both satisfy them and, by not concealing the letters from you, protect you against their impending accusations. I believed that your discernment could perceive that this was my intention from the fact that I remember having inserted at their end the following words—provided they were read by you with the intention with which I wrote them. For, after setting forth the evils which I did not without reason fear for you, I finally added: “But if you judge it better to suffer all these things than to lose him, it makes no difference to me; you must decide.” These are either my exact words or substantially so. Since, then, I said this at the end, what else did I secretly intimate to you except that what I had written above had been written by me as a matter of administration—if I may not say dissimulation?

2. As for what you wrote—that through a messenger I had privately suggested to that monk that, if he came to us, he should seek his release—I testify to the truth that this is untrue. Would I either boast or hope that I could receive a monk from so well-known a monastery, whom not even you, I think, could retain without grave scandal? But let it be so. I envied you him and, eagerly wishing to draw him to myself, I hoped—or pretended—that I could contrive something toward obtaining his release. But could it have been believed that I wished to disclose this plan of mine to the very messenger, which I had devised against his own monastery?

But now, lest you discover that what you have hitherto believed concerning our affection for you was believed falsely, I must labour on your behalf—as I see it—not merely as much as on my own, but much more; and this not as hitherto, namely that our unanimity may be more strongly established, but lest it be entirely dissolved. What shall I say to you? I certainly could not believe of you, or concerning you, anything of the kind which you have imagined of me on suspicion alone.

Henceforth let your Kindness know that Count Theobald,

[Note: Theobald, count of Champagne. See below, Letter 37 and those following.]

has already received our letters concerning Humbert, but has not yet answered me anything in his reply. Your own compassion will teach you better what you ought to do in this matter, if you do not neglect compassionately to consider the misery of a man unjustly exiled.

### Letter XXXIV. To Drogo, a Monk

[Note: Written about the year 1120.]

[Note: In Colbert MS 1410 and in the Compiègne manuscript, the address reads “To Hugh-Drogo,” although Drogo is read in the text of the letter. The name is compounded from that of Hugh, abbot of Pontigny, to whom Drogo was especially dear.]

Bernard congratulates Drogo on transferring to a stricter observance and exhorts him to perseverance.

1. How not without reason I had long been affected by no slight love for you is now evident, dearest [Col. 0140A] Drogo. Before, indeed, all that was visible in you was beautiful, all was lovable; but I perceived in you, beyond what I saw or heard from you, something else worthy of more excellent veneration. Perhaps even then you had heard the voice of the heavenly Bridegroom, to whose chaste embraces you have now more closely pressed yourself, saying to your soul, his most chaste dove: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved; wholly beautiful, except for that which lies hidden within” (Song 4:7).

What have you done? Who would have believed it? The whole city proclaimed you holy and most devout, so that it was believed that nothing could be added to you from all good things; and yet you, as though one of the worldly, abandon a monastery as though it were the world, and do not blush to submit your neck, now worn by Christ’s burden, again to the new observances of discipline. In you now, brother, we prove true that saying: “When a man has been perfected, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18:6). Therefore the sign of your perfection is that you have now begun; and in the very matter in which you thought you had not attained, you had already attained. For no one is perfect who does not desire to be more perfect; and each proves himself more perfect insofar as [or: because] he strives toward greater perfection.

2. But behold, dearest one: he through whose envy death entered into the world has bent his bow and prepared it. Since he has been driven from your heart and has lost power within, he will rage outside as far as he can. To speak more openly: do you not know that the Pharisees [Col. 0140C] have been scandalized by this act of yours? But remember that not everyone’s offence is to be given great heed, according to the Lord’s answer: “Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). “It is better that scandal arise than that truth be abandoned” (Gregory, Homily 7 on Ezekiel).

Remember him who was born for the fall and resurrection of many (Luke 2:34); and do not be surprised if you too are to some an aroma of life unto life, but to others an aroma of death unto death. If they threaten curses and hurl the darts of anathemas, hear Isaac answering for you: “He who curses you, let him be cursed; and he who blesses you, let him be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27:29).

But you also, surrounded by the impregnable wall of your conscience, answer from within and say: “Though camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope” (Ps. 26:3 [Vulgate]). For when you thus speak to your enemies in the gate, you will not be put to shame. I trust in the Lord, however, that if you stand firmly against the first blows and yield neither to their threats nor to their flatteries, you will soon crush Satan beneath your feet; and then the upright will see and rejoice, and all iniquity will shut its mouth.

### Letter XXXV. To Master Hugh Farsitus

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1128. I had conjectured that he was the same Hugh Farsitus whose opinion Bernard attacks in Letter 77, entered among the treatises, addressed to Hugh of St Victor; yet I would not assert this. I find several Hugh Farsiti in that period.

Two were monks: one at Lagny, praised in book 6 of *On Diplomatics*, p. 585; the other at St Lucian near Beauvais, of whom the necrology says on the sixth day before the Kalends of April [27 March], “Hugh Farsitus, professed monk, died.” Is he perhaps the man in Louvet’s *History*, p. 555?

A third Hugh Farsitus is found as a regular canon of St John of the Vines, mentioned in the necrology of the Church of Soissons. A fourth Farsitus is suggested by Abelard, in his sermon on St John the Baptist, p. 967, where he mentions Norbert and his fellow-apostle [Col. 0141D] Farsitus: perhaps Hugh, abbot of Prémontré and head of the Order after Norbert, his first and principal disciple, to whom Letter 253 is addressed.

What sort of man Hugh Farsitus was, we learn from the remarkable testimony of these letters, in which Bernard calls him “most beloved brother and fellow abbot,” “a former lover and beloved,” and even “holy,” according to his reputation and renown. Yet who he finally was is not clear. His name is familiar among learned persons; almost all else is unknown.

Possevino asserts in the *Apparatus* that he was a monk of St Médard at Soissons, but this is, I think, mere conjecture. From letters formerly received from our Hildefonsus Vrayet, we learned that Hugh Farsitus was a regular canon of St John of the Vines near Soissons, as the necrologies and public documents of that abbey plainly prove; in these he is frequently found subscribing. In the calendar of the cathedral church dedicated to St Gervasius this memorial of him occurs: [Col. 0142C] “On the day before the Nones of August [4 August] died Hugh Farsitus, regular canon, who gave us his books, both of sacred Scripture and of secular learning.”

Of what place he was abbot is uncertain. Some suppose that he presided at Château-Thierry, others at Valenciennes; perhaps rather at the abbey of St John at Chartres, to which I find an abbot named Hugh appointed in 1131. Letter 35 in any event indicates a place—an abbey, namely—subject to the power of Count Theobald, whom Bernard calls Hugh’s “Count.” I think that he to whom this present letter is addressed is the man to whom Hugh Metellus, at that time a regular canon at Toul, addressed a manuscript Letter 34: “To Hugh of Chartres, venerable master.” Did this Hugh succeed Stephen in the government of the abbey of St John at Chartres? Stephen was elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 1128, and Letter 82 is addressed to him.

Finally, that he possessed no slight literary learning is proved especially by the collection of books given to the cathedral church, and also by the book on the Sacraments mentioned by Bernard in Letter 35. Since that book is reproved for having admitted something insufficiently exact concerning the articles of faith, I am readily led to think that this was Hugh of St Victor, consulting Bernard about the opinion of a certain author who held an improper view of Baptism. Bernard would have identified him without naming him because the author was his own acquaintance. Finally, there is at hand a manuscript book, divided by the same man into thirty-one chapters, *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary of Soissons*, whose title reads: “Hugh Farsitus, of venerable memory.” The whole book was published in the French history of the convent of Soissons by our Michael Germanus.]

He commends to Hugh the case of a certain Humbert and advises him not to be ashamed of correcting himself in a certain erroneous opinion.

To his most beloved brother and fellow abbot HUGH, Brother BERNARD: the due affection of most sincere love.

We commend to your patronage, trusting in your charity, that Humbert who, they say, has been unjustly disinherited, and whose cause we have undertaken to defend before your Count for the love of God. Through you, as we faithfully hope, he is to be reconciled to the prince of the land, with the Lord of heaven cooperating; and restored to his country, wife, children, possessions, and friends.

By diligently pursuing this, you will both free a needy man from the hand of the sinner and likewise provide for the salvation of his oppressor. You will also show yourself by no means lacking in service to us; and, in fulfilling the office of peacemakers, you will place for yourselves an exalted seat among the children of God.

Moreover, know that I have not, as I hear you have heard, committed to the fire that letter which your Holiness once deigned to write to me, but still keep it in my possession. For what envy—indeed, what madness—would it have been to condemn by rash judgment a useful and praiseworthy work in which I found nothing except what belongs to sound faith, most wholesome teaching, and spiritual edification?

There is one exception: among friends there ought to be no fearful flattery against truth, since it is dangerous. I confess that it has moved and still moves me that, at the beginning of the aforesaid little work, you attempted to defend and establish the discussion concerning the sacraments which had already taken place between us. If, in that discussion, you remember well the substance of your opinion, see for yourself whether it accords with ecclesiastical understanding. It belongs to your candid humility not to blush at correction if you have ever thought otherwise. Farewell.

### Letter XXXVI. To the Same Man

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1128.]

He replies to Hugh’s letter and advises him to cease attacking the opinion of a bishop now dead.

To his most beloved Hugh, holy abbot by God’s grace both formerly and now, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: the unrebuffed affection of sincere love.

[Col. 0142B] To the letter of Your Dignity—though indeed shorter than I should have wished, yet longer than I deserved—I both ought and wished to reply at greater length; but the hurried messenger did not permit it. Yet, lest he depart altogether empty-handed, in return for such great letters, for which I acknowledge myself indebted to you, I most speedily sent this very little one, which he himself scarcely waited to receive. First, I briefly and truly state that, with all the inward affections of charity, I receive our old friend—both loving and beloved—as Catholic, venerate [another reading: receive] him as holy, and embrace him as most dear. For concerning the soundness of faith, I believe your confession; concerning holiness, your reputation and public esteem; concerning the affection which I profess to bear toward you, my own conscience. For your admission that you have forgotten that opinion [Col. 0142C] which, rightly, as it seemed to my simplicity, [Col. 0143A] raised a scruple in me, I accept as willingly as I read with joy, in your most recent letter, a concise affirmation of the most unalloyed truth; so that I almost believe that I had failed to understand your views, rather than that you had entertained any evil opinion.

Then, with a brother’s presumption, I advise your modesty to cease disturbing in death the holy and learned bishop whom you allowed to live in peace; lest, while you reproach one unable to answer for himself, you hear the whole Church answering on his behalf, and saying that this proceeds more from a lack of charity than from confidence in truth.

[Note: [Col. 0143B] Unless I am mistaken, this is William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, most dear to Bernard, as appears from the remarks on Letter 3. Various theological works of this William are mentioned in the manuscript of Cheminon, in the diocese of Châlons, in the book called *Panchrysis*, in which many fragments of them are reported.]

As for Humbert, as I asked you, I ask again: whenever you can, let neither your advice nor your protection be lacking to him. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO THEOBALD, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE

[Note: [Col. 0143B] Written in the year of Christ 1128.—Wonderful and great praises of Theobald occur everywhere in writers of his age. Anselm of Gembloux, under the year 1134, says: “Theobald, count of Blois or of Chartres, surpasses all the princes of Gaul in France by the great weight of his justice; he is kindly and familiar toward religious monks and clerics, a defender of the Church, a helper of the poor, a comforter of the afflicted, cautious and discerning in merchants’ transactions, an avenger and punisher of the accused and of those who depart from right.” He is celebrated with precisely the same praises by Hugh, monk of Auxerre, under the year 1136.

As regards zeal for justice, for which he is particularly commended by this Anselm, you have a striking proof in Letter 39 and others. From them we learn how sternly he was the first, or at least among the first, to punish trial by single combat—generally tolerated everywhere by princes—though the canons had long before forbidden it to clerics, as Ivo, bishop of Chartres, teaches in Letter 247.

The same Theobald is wonderfully praised for offices of charity and mercy by Ernald, abbot of Bonneval, in the *Life of Saint Bernard*, book II, chapter 8; likewise by Geoffrey, book IV, chapter 3; to these add new Letter 416. Hence it is apparent how greatly he profited from the friendship and teaching of the holy Doctor. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January], in 1152, and was buried not in the monastery of Pontigny, as Jongelinus maintains, and Manrique after him, under the year 1114, chapter 2, no. 6, following Vincent of Beauvais; nor at Clairvaux, as the Portuguese Brito says; but in the monastery of Lagny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, on the river Marne, of which he was advocate, as Bernard testifies in Letter 230. For this abbey had been restored by Herbert, count of Champagne, around the year 990, and there Theobald’s porphyry tomb may still be seen.

Helinand, the monk, clearly indicates both the place of burial and the day of death in his *Chronicle*: “In the year 1152,” he says, “Theobald, count [Col. 0144B] of Champagne, dies on the sixth day before the Ides of January and is buried at Lagny. He had six daughters. The first was Mary, duchess of Burgundy; the second, Agnes, countess of Bar-le-Duc; the third, a certain duchess in distant regions. William Goez, in the diocese of Chartres, afterwards married her. The fourth was Countess Matilda [Col. 0144C] of Perche; the fifth, a nun of Fontevraud; the sixth was Adela, queen of the Franks.”

Alberic, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1152, confirms all this and adds that Theobald had four sons, in this order: “Henry, count palatine of Troyes, famous for generosity and liberality; Theobald, count of Blois and Chartres; Stephen, count of Sancerre; and William, archbishop of Sens and afterwards of Reims.”

The epitaph of Theobald, composed at the request of Count Henry by Master Simon, surnamed Golden Goat, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, was published by François Chifflet in his *Diatribe* from a manuscript codex of the monastery of La Charité, of the Cistercian Order. It is surely worthy to be transcribed here in honor of so great a prince:

> That count Theobald has passed away, illustrious everywhere,  
> A son—indeed, a father—of Mother Church.  
> Great in honor, mighty in arms, distinguished in birth,  
> [Col. 0144D] Keen in mind, clear in speech, gracious in bearing.  
> Small before the lowly, fierce toward the proud, harsh toward the unjust;  
> Simple with the simple, he was all things to all.  
> Joyful toward the poor, monks, and sick, he supplied  
> Unceasingly help, gifts, churches, and homes.  
> His concern was to preserve the good and punish the guilty;  
> His concern was to live justly and speak what is just.  
> You would have seen every virtue shining in him,  
> And striving together to make the man wondrous.  
> Our Gaul, mourning, bereft of so great a protector,  
> As it stood while he stood, lies fallen now that he lies.  
> Therefore the tenth day of January was his final day—  
> For him one day with God is better than thousands.

He wonders that, in Humbert’s case, though requesting what is just and fair, he suffers a refusal; and he warns the count, in view of the supreme Judge, not to deny help and mercy to a wretch.

[Col. 0143B]

To the praiseworthy prince THEOBALD, BERNARD, useless servant of the servants of God who are at Clairvaux, wishes health and peace.

1. I am not moderately grateful to have heard that you were [Col. 0144A] concerned about my illness. For in this, while I recognize your condescension toward me, I do not doubt that you also love God. For why would so great a man deign even to know so small a one as I, except for God’s sake? Since, then, it is certain that you love God, and me for his sake, I wonder how, concerning one request made in trust in God—neither unjust, as I think, nor unreasonable—I have nevertheless been refused by you. Had I asked for gold, silver, or anything of that sort, truly, as I trust concerning you, I should without doubt have received it.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Thus the manuscript of Saint-Germain. Elsewhere the words “truly, as I trust concerning you, I should without doubt have received it” are omitted.]

But why do I say, “Had I asked”? For even without asking, I have already received very many benefits from your generosity. Yet why was I judged unworthy to receive this one thing, which I asked of you not in my own cause but in God’s, and not so much for myself as for you?

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Hence it is clear that this is not the first letter on Humbert’s behalf, but that Letter 39 is earlier in time; from it we learn Humbert’s native land and the kind of punishment inflicted.]

What reason was there for this? What then? Do you judge it unworthy either for me to request or for you to grant, that you should show mercy to a Christian man, however grave the crime of which he has been accused before you, after he has cleared himself? Or at least, if you do not believe that he has fully cleared himself, because he did not do so in your court, receive his satisfaction again in your presence, and thus let him obtain pardon.

[Col. 0145A]

2. Do you not know who threatens: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge justices” [Ps. 74:3]? And if he judges acts of justice, how much more acts of injustice? Do you not fear what is again written: “With the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” [Matt. 7:2]? Do you not know that as easily as you can disinherit Humbert, God can as easily—indeed, incomparably more easily—disinherit Theobald (which may it never be)?

Certainly, in such cases, where the guilt appears so open and inexcusable that no occasion for mercy remains except at peril to justice, even then you ought to make yourself an avenger trembling and grieving, compelled, that is, more by the necessity of office than by a desire for vengeance. But where the alleged crime is found either less certain or capable of excuse, you should not merely decline no opportunity for this, but embrace it most willingly—rejoicing, of course, that while justice remains unharmed, your compassion has found a place.

Behold, for the second time I entreat Your Excellency: as you wish God to have mercy upon you, so have mercy upon Humbert—whether the Lord’s promise allures you, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” [Matt. 5:7], or his threat terrifies you, “Judgment without mercy is for him who has not shown mercy” [James 2:13]. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Written in the year of Christ 1128.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. On the same matter.

[Col. 0145C]

To the gracious prince THEOBALD, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, wishes health and prayers.

1. I greatly fear that, by presumptuously intruding upon your ears, already most occupied, with my repeated appeals, I may become burdensome. But what am I to do? If I fear offending you by writing to you too often, how much more must I fear offending God—whom I certainly ought to fear more—by failing to intercede for a wretched man?

Otherwise, may Your Kindness forgive me, because I cannot but have compassion on that miserable man, for whom I have already perhaps approached as an importunate petitioner once before, namely Humbert, a beggar and poor man, and made poor out of rich—which is more unhappy. I cannot but sympathize with his widow and orphans, deprived of a living father—which is more pitiful. I thank you [Col. 0145D] for the favor which I have deserved to find in your eyes in this matter: that you graciously consented to receive Humbert’s truthful defense on his own behalf, and that you most justly rejected the false accusation against him. Yet I cannot sufficiently wonder what prevented the completion of the work of mercy which you had most graciously resolved upon: the restoration of Humbert’s inheritance to his wife and children, [Col. 0146A] so that your pious word has not yet been followed by action.

2. If at any time we discover in other princes a word marked by frivolity or even falsehood, we regard it as neither new nor strange. But in Count Theobald we by no means patiently endure “Yes and No”; for, as is said, to speak simply is for him to swear, and a slight lie is reckoned a grave perjury. Among the many distinguished virtues which greatly ennoble your rank and make your name famous and celebrated throughout the world, steadfastness in truth is especially praised in you.

Who then has attempted, by encouragement or counsel, to weaken the strength of your most steadfast heart? Who, I say, has tried by fraud to uproot in you so holy, so eminent, and so worthy of imitation by all princes a principle of truth? He loves you deceitfully, not truthfully; he advises you fraudulently, not faithfully, who strives through his own greed to obscure your so glorious reputation for truth—while by some malice, in harming a poor man, he labors to nullify the word which your mouth has spoken: a word pleasing to God, worthy of you, mercifully just and justly merciful.

I beseech you, by the mercy of God, that you may obtain that same mercy: beware lest “the wicked be exalted, whereby the poor are set aflame”; rather, bring it about that the truth of your promise may be fulfilled. You promised first to Lord Norbert, and afterwards to us also, that you would restore Humbert’s inheritance [Col. 0146C] to him, his wife, and his children.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Elsewhere, *domno*, “lord.” See Letter 56.]

Farewell.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Written in the year of Christ 1127.—Among other matters concerning which Saint Bernard urges Theobald in this letter, he intercedes for a certain unfortunate man named Humbert. This first letter on Humbert’s behalf was written before Letter 37. Having been defeated in a duel, Humbert was deprived, by the prince’s order, both of his property and of his eyes, so that nothing was left by which he might sustain his wretched life, however meagerly. The punishment was indeed severe, and it most justly stirred Bernard’s spirit, softened by charity; but such a remedy was due to so great and obstinate a disease. On the utterly dreadful practice and ritual of judicial combat, see, if you wish, Sirmond’s notes on Geoffrey of Vendôme, book III, Letter 38; Chesnier’s notes on the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*; and others. Compare Bernard’s present Letter 376.]

He commends various causes to Theobald. Finally, he exhorts him to conduct himself honorably and reverently toward the bishops assembled in his city for a council.

1. Though you afford me many proofs of your condescension toward me, this above all binds me to you with the whole affection of love: although I know that I have already dared to appeal to Your Dignity on many persons’ behalf, I do not remember ever having been refused in anything. Thus made more confident, and not without reason, I now again approach as an unhesitating petitioner on behalf of the canons of Largicourt.

[Note: [Col. 0146D] The canons of Largicourt were Regular Canons of the Order of Saint Augustine, in the diocese of Châlons, in the deanery of Perthes, where the Fathers of the Society of Jesus once possessed a priory.]

I do not now plead for their legal right. I have such confidence in your justice and observance of law that I judge that not even your enemy, pleading in your court, need fear for his right. But this is what I beg for them and with them, with every entreaty I can make while absent; and I have learned that it is altogether necessary for them: namely, that you permit them access to the countenance of Your Serenity, more gracious and ready than usual, [Col. 0147A] so that their neighbors may learn to show due reverence to their religious life when they know that you are well disposed toward them. And if any of your soldiers or officials should attempt unjustly to seize their property, or in any respect to disturb the peace which they ought to possess in God, let him know for certain that on this account he will incur your most grievous displeasure.

2. There is another matter likewise for which I humbly entreat you. Recently, as I happened to be passing through Bar, I met a woman greatly to be pitied. Her soul was in bitterness; her sorrows stirred my heart, and by her prayers and tears she sufficiently prevailed upon me to intercede for her with you. She is [Col. 0147B] the wife of that man of yours, Belin, upon whom you long ago inflicted many and severe penalties, corresponding to the evil which he himself had committed. Show mercy to her, so that you too may find mercy with God.

3. And since I have begun, I shall speak yet with my lord. In the hand-to-hand combat formerly held before the provost of Bar, the defeated man immediately lost his eyes by your order. Moreover, as though it were a small evil that he had been defeated and deprived of sight, all his goods, as he complains, were taken away by your officials. It is just, if it pleases you, that through your mercy he should be restored something by which his wretched life may somehow be sustained. Nor should the father’s wrongdoing be imputed to his innocent children, so as to prevent them from inheriting whatever paternal holdings there may be.

[Col. 0147C]

4. Finally, we wish you to hold the holy bishops, who have assembled in your city for matters pertaining to God, worthy of every welcome. And toward the legate himself, who wished to honor you and your city with so great a celebration of a council, be in every respect devout and obedient, so far as lies in your power; take care to strengthen and confirm every good thing which he has ordered and established.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] The Council of Troyes, held at the beginning of 1128; see the notes on Letter 21. The legate mentioned here is Matthew.]

Receive also our bishop and yours alike—the bishop of Langres—with the greater honor that is fitting; and for the *casamentum* [fief] which you hold, reverently and humbly offer him the homage [another reading: *homagium*, “homage”] which you owe. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] *Casamentum*: a fief dependent upon the lord’s demesne.]

## LETTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Written about the year 1127.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. He commends to Theobald a poor religious man.

[Col. 0147D]

We commend to you two things in this man whom you see: poverty and religious devotion. If you do not pity the one, revere the other in him, so that you may by no means deny him that for which he has taken such pains to seek you from afar. Therefore, even if not for his own sake, help him at least for your own; for as much as his poverty makes you necessary to him, so much—indeed more—does his religious devotion make him necessary to you. Finally, of the many whom we have already sent to you for the same reason, we recall none through whom we know that you would please God more than if you do good to this man. Farewell.

## LETTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Written about the same year.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. He commends an aged religious man.

I fear that you are burdened by our so frequent letters; but the charity of Christ [Col. 0148B] and the need of friends press me into this importunity. We therefore beg that this man, both aged, as you see, and sent to you from a religious house, as we know, may not be sent away empty-handed. Moreover, we ask that you deign to furnish him with letters for his journey to your uncle the king.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] That is, Henry I, king of the English, who was Theobald’s uncle, as Ernald testifies near the end of book II of the *Life of Bernard*, and Robert of Mont under the year 1151. Theobald’s mother was Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror and sister of Henry.]

I wish that all servants of God, if it were possible, might become your debtors, so that they might one day receive you into eternal dwellings through the mammon of iniquity. Farewell.

## LETTER XLII. TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

This letter deserved rather the title and place of a regular treatise. It was therefore removed from its position and transferred to the second volume among the Treatises, under this title: “Letter 42, or Treatise, to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, on the Character and Office of Bishops.”

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Written about the year 1128.]

TO THE SAME HENRY. He writes for the liberty of the church of Molesme.

The gracious reception of our earlier request gives greater confidence for hope. Therefore, after first offering most devout thanks for the goodwill which I have experienced, I dare once more to ask that which may make me indebted a second time for renewed thanks: namely, that you allow the Church of Molesme to hold that church, on whose account it regretted that it had in some way clouded Your Serenity, with the same liberty which it is certain that it held in the times of your predecessors.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] A monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Langres. Its founder was Abbot Robert, who was also the first abbot of Cîteaux. Bernard therefore often pleads the cause of the monks of Molesme in Letters 44 and 60. See Letter 80. Peter of Celle, in book VII, Letter 14, to the monks of Molesme: “That hen of Molesme, full of feathers and well-winged—how many offspring, and what offspring, did she bring forth from her womb, when the community of Cîteaux sprang forth from her in its original shoot?” The matter here concerns the church of Senois, as in the following letter. It was formerly a priory in the diocese of Sens, in the deanery of Courtenay.]

Farewell.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Written about the year 1128.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. On the same matter.

[Col. 0148D]

You certainly see how much I presume upon your goodwill: [Col. 0149A] frequent petitions do not put an end to my prayers, and though heard so many times, I do not fear again to approach as an importunate petitioner. It is indeed great presumption, but it does not deserve indignation, since it proceeds from charity, not rashness.

Your Fatherhood remembers, unless I am mistaken, that at Troyes you long ago wholly relinquished, for the love of God and of us, all the complaints which you had previously entertained against the monks of Molesme concerning the church of Senois. And now those same monks complain that you are claiming in that church certain new customs, and, as they say, unlawful ones. I therefore beseech you to remit these also, trusting that I shall not suffer a refusal even this time: so that, having deserved not to be rejected in greater matters, I may not be put to shame in obtaining lesser ones. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0149B] Here the manuscript codices repeat Letter 15.]

## LETTER XLV

[Note: [Col. 0149B] Written in the year of Christ 1127.]

TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS

[Note: [Col. 0149B] Surnamed the Fat.]

The Cistercians sharply and frankly rebuke King Louis, hostile and injurious toward the bishop of Paris; they declare that they will plead his cause before the Roman pontiff if the king does not cease from what he has wickedly begun.

To the excellent king of the Franks, LOUIS, STEPHEN, abbot of Cîteaux, and the whole assembly of Cistercian abbots and brethren, wish health, well-being, and peace in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0150A]

1. The King of heaven and earth has granted you a kingdom on earth, and will grant you one in heaven also, if you endeavor to administer justly and wisely that which you have received. This is what we wish for you, and pray for you: that you may reign faithfully here and happily there. But by what counsel do you now so fiercely oppose those same prayers of ours for you—which, if you remember, you once requested so humbly? With what confidence can we now presume to raise our hands for you to the Bridegroom of the Church, whom you so grievously afflict, and without cause, as we think, by heedless boldness? For the Church lays a grave complaint against you before that same Bridegroom and her Lord, since she endures as her assailant the one whom she had received as her defender.

Do you now perceive against whom you thereby make yourself hostile? Certainly not against the bishop of Paris,

[Note: [Col. 0149C] Stephen, who governed the Church of Paris from 1124 to 1144, and was a different person from Stephen of Garland, the seneschal. The cause of this persecution was Stephen’s withdrawal from court and the liberty of the Church. The same fortune, for almost the same reasons, befell Henry of Sens, as appears from Letter 49. The king’s mind was not moved by this letter; for this reason, they say, God punished with death his son Philip, then king-designate. It is remarkable that, after Philip’s death, the nobles and bishops considered preventing the succession of Louis the Younger, as Orderic relates in book XIII, p. 895 and following.

Wonderful is the freedom of speech in holy men, and their fearless zeal for justice, by which humble monks did not fear to rise against a king in defense of a bishop. But it is not easy to discover from ancient records what method Louis employed in persecuting Stephen, bishop of Paris. Bernard gives some indication of the matter in a similar case involving Henry, archbishop of Sens, in Letter 49 to Pope Honorius: “The king,” he says, “does not so much persecute bishops as, in the bishops, he persecutes zeal for justice.” Explaining this further, he says: “Those who formerly, in secular dress and conduct, were honored as eminent, judged faithful, and regarded as intimate friends, have now become enemies because they conduct themselves worthily of their priesthood and in every way honor their ministry.”

Baronius, under the year 1127, explains this more fully in these words: “The bishops of the province of Sens had made progress by the example of the Cistercian monks and by the words and letters of Saint Bernard—especially the aforementioned bishop of Paris, and Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris, who had tightly bound that monastery, entirely loosened from monastic discipline, with the clasp of regular observance. Saint Bernard rejoiced with them on this account and sent him a letter of congratulations” [namely Letter 78]. “Moreover, Henry himself, the metropolitan archbishop of Sens, likewise admonished by the letters of Saint Bernard” [Letter 42], “and indeed by a rather long one, had turned to better fruit and diligently performed the duties of an excellent shepherd; for the same reason he incurred the indignation of the same prince, etc. But what,” he says, “was this reform that could so displease the most Christian king? It was this: bishops who had formerly been accustomed, leaving the church, to attend the king’s court and pursue military service, had now withdrawn themselves from court and military service to the church, and had at the same time recalled to it the clerics subject to them. There was no small number of these serving as soldiers in the king’s palace, and serving not merely in the palace’s military retinue but also in the army in the field. Saint Bernard laments this in many places, but especially, as concerns the matter, in his letter to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris,” etc. Thus far Baronius.

But, to cast some light from old documents also upon a history buried in deep silence among the writers of that age, it is fitting to bring forward a letter of a certain intimate friend addressed to Stephen himself, published by our Achéry in the third volume of the *Spicilegium*. Its words are these:

“Although I have so far perceived that your steadfastness has not been changed or weakened in any respect, nevertheless, concerned for you in the manner of a friend, I urge and urge again Your Fatherhood not to depart from your purpose and rigor of justice, nor to permit the liberty of your Church, which flourished in the time of your predecessors, to be annihilated. Retain in memory that saying of the Lord: ‘Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake.’ Know, moreover, that I shall persevere with you in all things and in every respect, and shall not withdraw a step from my purpose because of the losses that have befallen me and my guests on your account. The king and queen imposed twelve pounds upon my guests, and took it all as ransom for their goods. And my relatives and friends gave ten pounds to the king and queen when they ordered my vineyards to be uprooted; and all this was done at the instigation of the dean and archdeacons—or rather through the nocturnal whisperings of G., the precentor. But, God assisting you and me, I do not fear that I shall recover everything which I have lost, nor do I think that you will accept peace without me and without the recovery of my goods.

“Furthermore, unless I perceived that you have an ample supply of counsel, my insignificance would advise Your Fatherhood to win over, by your prayers and those of your friends, the lord archbishop of Sens and your fellow bishops. To reinforce your claim of justice, do not delay to obtain by every means that, in their dioceses, they cease from divine offices, so that as partners in the same justice they may assist you against all men and, if necessary, come with us to Rome.”

From this letter we gather three noteworthy points: first, that not only the bishop, but also his intimates and those connected with them, were stripped of all their goods by the king; second, that this storm of persecution was stirred up at the prompting of certain clerics; third, that ecclesiastical liberty was violated by the king. All this readily persuades me that the whole hydra of this evil must be traced back to certain clerics. When, in accordance with the king’s will, they imposed exactions upon ecclesiastical persons and found Stephen opposing them, they most wickedly inflamed the king’s mind against him and brought him into jeopardy of all his goods—indeed, even conspired for his death, as appears from another letter written to Stephen [*Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 162, Letter 37].

It came about that, even after he himself had been restored to the king’s favor and to all his goods, Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, later died in defense of this cause, as may be seen in Letter 158 and following. But whatever seedbed this tragedy may finally have had, Stephen, using spiritual weapons, placed the king’s land under interdict. Avoiding the king’s wrath, he fled to Henry of Sens; then both, taking refuge in the chapter of Cîteaux, secured letters from the Fathers by the right of fellowship, to which both they and the king had then associated themselves with Cîteaux, in order to bend the king’s mind. Bernard, together with Hugh of Pontigny and many other prelates, humbly presented these letters to Louis and suffered an undeserved refusal.

“Louis,” says Aemilius in his *Life of Louis*, “drove away from his knees the bishops who were pleading with him. Bernard the abbot is reported to have announced to him that heaven’s avenging wrath stood over such impenitence.” Geoffrey, in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, and after him Gaguin in book VI of his *History of France*, record that Bernard added: “This obstinacy of yours, king, shall be punished by the death of your son.” The truth of this prophecy was proved by Philip’s unhappy death.

Though the prince was somewhat moved from his purpose by such freedom of speech, he took courage from the letters of Pope Honorius, by which the interdict was lifted, and pursued his wicked undertaking more fiercely. Bernard, unable to bear this, sent to Honorius letters full of just complaint in his own name and that of Geoffrey of Chartres [Letters 46 and 47]. At last, this stubborn and inflamed dissension appears to have ended at the Council of Troyes in 1128, or certainly not long afterwards, through the authority of Honorius himself. Bernard gave him thanks in writing once again, in Letter 49: “For by this means,” he says, “the steadfastness of the bishop of Paris was assailed with grievous insults and injuries, but not shaken, because the Lord put forth his hand when he opposed yours.”

Moreover, Chesnier expressly proves in his notes on Abelard, and it is not obscurely apparent from a letter of Geoffrey of Chartres in the third volume of the *Spicilegium*, p. 260, that this Stephen of Paris, formerly chancellor, is distinct from Stephen of Garland, the seneschal mentioned in the *Annals of Teulfi*. In that letter Geoffrey writes that Saint Bernard was chosen to establish peace between Stephen of Paris and Stephen of Garland.

As for Louis, whom Saint Bernard, writing to Honorius in Letter 49, calls another Herod, it is surely worthy of remembrance with what religious devotion and penitence he ended his last day, namely in 1137. “Since he was prudent in counsel,” says Suger in his *Life*, “taking counsel for himself and having compassion on his own soul so as to please God, he provided for himself through frequent devotion to confession and prayer. With all the affection of his heart he desired this one thing: somehow to be carried to the holy martyrs, his protectors, Dionysius and his companions, and before their most sacred bodies, laying aside kingdom and crown, to exchange crown for crown, and royal insignia and imperial ornaments for the humble habit of blessed Benedict, and to profess the monastic order.”

“Let those who disparage monastic poverty see,” Cardinal Baronius aptly says under the year 1136, “how not only archbishops but kings themselves, preferring eternal life to transient life, flee to the most secure protection of the monastic order.”

Suger further adds that, after making confession of his sins, the king “unexpectedly raised himself, went out to meet the body of the Lord, and stood by most devoutly. There,” he says, “in the sight of all, both clerics and laypeople, the king, going out, lays aside his kingdom; he confesses that he administered the kingdom sinfully; he invests his son with the ring; he binds him by faith to protect the Church of God, the poor, and orphans. There too, distributing gold and silver to churches, poor people, and needy persons for the love of God, he spared neither cloaks nor royal garments, down to his shirt.” A marvelous example indeed in so great a king! For his most precious gifts to the Church of Saint-Denis, see the same author.

—but against the Lord of paradise, terrible indeed, and the one “who takes away the spirit of princes” [Ps. 75:12–13]. For he himself says to bishops: “He who despises you despises me” [Luke 10:16].

2. We have taken care to make these representations to you, and on your behalf, boldly indeed, yet affectionately: warning and beseeching you through that mutual friendship and brotherhood of ours, to which you condescended generously to admit us, but which you have now grievously wounded, that you desist promptly from so great an evil.
