Otherwise, if we do not deserve to be heard, but are despised—we who are your brothers and friends, and [Col. 0151A] who daily pray for you, your sons, and your kingdom—then know henceforth that our lowliness, wherever it has any power, cannot fail the Church of God and its minister, namely our venerable father and friend, the bishop of Paris. He, appealing to our humility against you, has requested, by right of brotherhood, our letters on his behalf to the lord Pope. [Note: [Col. 0152C] For those admitted into a fellowship of suffrages were reckoned brethren. Thus the monks of La Chaise-Dieu call Louis the Younger their brother in Letter 308 among the Chesnian letters, vol. IV.]

But judging it right first to address your Excellency by this letter—especially since the bishop himself offers, through the hand of all Religious, to submit to justice, provided only that, first, as justice itself seems to require, the things unjustly taken from him are restored—we have for the present deferred his request. [Note: [Col. 0152C] Those who have first been despoiled must be restored before they are summoned to trial. See the Canons collected by Gratian, Cause 3, question 1, where Pope Caius says: “All things taken from bishops despoiled of their goods or driven from their own sees must be restored to them by law; for before this has been done, no crime can be alleged against them.” [Col. 0152D] There also Pope John says: “All things must be restored to those who have been despoiled . . . and they must be fully recalled to the place from which they had departed . . . before their accusation or their regular summons to a synod,” etc. See there further material; likewise the chapters in Gregory’s Decretals, title *On the Restitution of the Despoiled*. Hence Geoffrey of Vendôme writes thus to Ivo: “When, according to the sacred canons, we have been reinstated in our property, long and lawfully possessed by us and unjustly taken away, then, if afterward they complain of us, we do not refuse to do what the just judge and the divine law shall judge ought to be done.” See the same author’s letter to Ranulf, bishop of Saintes, where, with Bernard, he also testifies that the laws of the Apostolic Church prohibit “any despoiled person from being summoned to judgment.”]

And if, by God’s inspiration, you should be pleased to incline your ear to our prayers and, by our counsel and assistance, restore peace with the bishop—or rather with God—we are ready, for this purpose, to take the trouble of coming to you wherever you please. But if not, we must listen to our friend and obey the priest of God. Farewell.

## 54. LETTER XLVI

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Written in the year of Christ 1127.]

TO LORD POPE HONORIUS II.

As above.—They complain to the Pontiff that, by a surreptitiously obtained relaxation of the interdict, the King of France, formerly inclined toward peace, has become more obstinate.

[Col. 0153A]

To the supreme Pontiff HONORIUS, HUGH of Pontigny and BERNARD of Clairvaux, abbots of Christ’s poor, whatever the prayer of sinners can accomplish.

We too, as sons of the Church—if indeed we are worthy—cannot ignore the lamentable complaint of the bishops, or rather of the whole Church. What we have seen, we speak. Great necessity has drawn us from the cloisters into public affairs; there we have seen what we speak of. We have seen sorrowful things, and sorrowfully we speak: the honour of the Church, not slightly injured in the time of Honorius.

The humility—or rather the steadfastness—of the bishops had already bent the King’s anger, [Col. 0153B] when behold, supreme authority arriving from the supreme Pontiff—alas!—cast down steadfastness and established pride. [Note: [Col. 0153D] Namely, by relaxing the interdict which the bishops of the province had imposed upon the King’s territory because of his harassment of the bishop of Paris; see the following letter.] We know indeed that this was obtained from you through falsehood—as is plainly evident from your letters—so that you ordered so just and necessary an interdict to be overturned. But when falsehood has at last been discovered, will not iniquity perceive that it has lied to itself, and lied to so great a majesty?

Yet we wonder on what grounds judgment was rendered for one party and an award made against one who was absent. We do not criticize this with rash presumption; rather, with filial affection, we lay before a father’s heart how greatly thereby the wicked man is emboldened and the poor man inflamed. But [Col. 0153C] how long you ought to endure the former, and how greatly to sympathize with the latter, is not for us to prescribe to you. Rather, sweetest Father, consult your own compassionate heart in this matter. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Written in the year of Christ 1127.]

TO THE SAME, IN THE PERSON OF GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF CHARTRES.

He sets before the Pontiff the case of the bishop of Paris, unjustly oppressed by King Louis. Compelled by an interdict from the Gallican bishops, the King had promised restitution; but, having obtained absolution from Honorius, he became more contumacious and did not perform it.

It is superfluous to repeat to you the sequence and cause of this most sorrowful affair, for I do not doubt that the heart of your Paternity has already been moved by the letter of the devout bishop of Paris. Yet, lest our testimony too should be lacking to a brother and fellow bishop, [Col. 0153D] I judged it necessary briefly to report what I have seen and heard.

Upon receiving the very moderate complaint of the aforesaid bishop, all the bishops of the diocese of Sens, together with our venerable metropolitan and certain other religious persons whom we associated with ourselves, [Col. 0154A] humbly approached the King in person, as was our duty, concerning this grave wrong. We asked that he restore to the bishop what he had taken, though the bishop had in no way deserved such treatment; but we did not obtain it. At length, perceiving that we intended to resort to the Church’s weapons for the Church’s sake, he feared and consented that he would restore everything.

But, perhaps in that very hour, your letters arrived, ordering that his land be absolved from the interdict. Thus, strengthened in evil by evil, he did not at all perform what he had rightly promised. Nevertheless, on the appointed day on which he again promised that he would perform it, we presented ourselves before him—not, however, to his sight; we waited for peace, and he did not come. We sought good things, and behold, trouble.

In short, your letters have brought this about: things wickedly taken are held still more wickedly, and the rest is everywhere plundered day by day, [Col. 0154B] all the more securely because those things are retained with impunity. For when, at your command, the bishop’s just interdict—as we judge it—was lifted, and ours, which we were preparing and by which we hoped to attain peace, was likewise suspended out of fear of you, we have meanwhile become a reproach to our neighbours. How long this is to continue, the compassion of your mercy will see.

## LETTER XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Written about the year 1130.]

TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR, AS ABOVE, AND AGAINST DETRACTORS.

Bernard clears himself of charges made against him and asks for the possibility of solitude and silence.

To the illustrious HAIMERIC, chancellor of the holy Roman see, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting, and not on the road.

1. Does truth then bring hatred even upon the poor and needy, [Col. 0154C] and can not even misery escape envy? Shall I complain, or rejoice, that I too have become an enemy by speaking truth? By speaking true things—or by doing right things? But let your brethren consider this, they who, contrary to the law, curse the deaf man (Lev. 19:14), and, fearing not the prophetic curse, call good evil and evil good (Isa. 5:20).

What, good men, has displeased your brotherhood in me? [Note: [Col. 0153D] Thus all, or almost all, manuscripts read—and rightly. For cardinals were formerly called simply “Brethren”; in Book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 42; and in the Chronicle of Andres, *Spicilegium*, vol. IX, p. 481, Abbot Peter is said to have visited, according to custom, both the lord Pope and the Brethren. At the beginning of this letter, “your Brethren” is falsely given as “our Brethren” in some copies; and in William of Tyre, Book XIII, chapter 15: “The Brethren, whether bishops, priests, or cardinal deacons,” etc. Compare *On Conversion to Clerics*, below, vol. IV.]

Was it because at Châlons a man wholly discredited was removed from the stewardship entrusted to him, because in the church of Verdun, over which he had presided, he had squandered his lord’s property? Or because, in the city of Cambrai, Fulbert, the manifest destroyer of his monastery, was compelled to yield to Parvin, whom everyone testifies to be a faithful and prudent servant? [Col. 0154D] Or indeed because at Laon God’s sanctuary was restored from being Venus’s brothel? [Note: [Col. 0154D] In this letter Bernard clears himself before Haimeric on three matters. First, concerning the deposition of Henry, bishop of Verdun. This is discussed by Laurence of Liège in the *History of Verdun*, [Col. 0155C] *Spicilegium*, vol. XII, p. 311, where his case is said to have been entrusted by Honorius to Matthew, bishop of Albano and legate in Gaul, who summoned a synod at Châlons on this matter. “Henry first takes counsel from Bernard of holy memory, abbot of Clairvaux, on whose counsels the kingdoms and churches of Gaul still rest today,” says Laurence. “He advised that it was most grievous to rule forcibly over unwilling people. Therefore, before a dishonouring accusation against him should come before the public hearing of so many great men, he should yield alone to all, renounce the bishopric. He trusted Bernard’s counsel; he gave back the staff, renounced the bishopric, and withdrew in the thirteenth year after receiving it [Col. 0155D] from the hand of the Emperor”—namely, in 1129, according to the notes on Letter 13. Letters 62 and 63 are addressed to him.

“Secondly, Bernard clears himself concerning the appointment of Parvin as abbot of St Sepulchre at Cambrai. Parvin had been a monk of St Vincent at Laon, according to the monk Herman, *On Miracles*, Book III, chapter 20; he replaced Fulbert, expelled by Renaud de Pratis, archbishop of Reims, for bad administration, as Bernard here relates. The monastery of St Sepulchre, of the Order of St Benedict, outside the walls of Cambrai, was founded in 1064 by Bishop Lietbert, whose Life appears in vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*. See Meyer and Miraeus.

“Thirdly, Bernard clears himself concerning the reform of the monastery of St John at Laon, where the girls were expelled because of the licence of their lives and monks put in their place. The aforesaid Herman describes the history of this event as follows in *On the Miracles of Blessed Mary*, Book III, chapter 22: ‘In the days of the aforesaid lord Bartholomew, namely bishop of Laon, the ancient religious observance had grown greatly cold in that monastery; its external possessions also had gradually diminished, and certain reports of ill repute were made concerning the same virgins. Greatly distressed by this—for he saw them often promise amendment in words when admonished by him, but fail to fulfil it in deed—the same pontiff, by the counsel and authority of Lord Pope Innocent, Lord Renaud, archbishop of Reims, and also Louis, king of the Franks, to whom that church was said properly to belong, expelled all those nuns together. Taking also the religious man Lord Drogo, prior of the monastery of St Nicaise at Reims, he ordained him there as its first [Col. 0156D] abbot and placed there a sufficient number of monks from various monasteries.’ Thus he.

“But when he asserts that this was done by Innocent’s authority, this must be understood of the confirmation, not of the reform itself. The reform was undertaken two years before Innocent’s elevation and decided at an assembly of bishops, held at Arras in the presence of King Louis on the sixth day before the Ides of May, 1128. Present were Renaud of Reims, Joscelin of Soissons, Bartholomew of Laon, Simon of Noyon, John of Thérouanne, Garin of Amiens, Robert of Arras, Clarembald of Senlis, and Peter of Beauvais. All this is established both by the royal diploma and by the decree of Matthew of Albano, and by other monuments of this history, which our Acherius published together with Innocent’s letters in his notes on Guibert, p. 828 ff.”]

For this, do you not, I say, stone me—but tear me to pieces—so that I may receive something less from my Lord? (John 10:32.) And I should rightly answer this, with every glory, if I recognized anything of mine in these matters. But why [Col. 0155A] am I judged for other people’s acts? Or, if for my own, why as though they were evil? For no folly can doubt, nor any impudence deny, that all these things were done justly and excellently.

Choose whichever you wish: either deny these things outright, or admit that I was their author. If I did them, it is worthy of praise to have accomplished praiseworthy things, and I am unjustly rebuked for that for which I deserved praise. If I did not do them, then, as I did not deserve praise, certainly neither did I deserve blame. A new kind of detraction, and truly something like Balaam’s work: brought and hired to curse the people, he instead heaped blessings upon them (Num. 22–24). What could be fairer or more delightful than that the person whom you intend to reproach, you should commend all the more; that, unknowingly, you should use praises instead of insults; and that, wishing to detract, you should praise against your will? [Col. 0155B] As if they can find no evils of my own, so that they may cast, or rather add, other people’s good deeds against me as evils.

2. But I am moved neither by undeserved reproaches nor do I accept unearned praises. These things do not concern me, since I was not their author. Let them praise, if they will, or blame, if they dare: in the first case, the lord bishop of Albano; in the second, the lord archbishop of Reims; and in the third, that same archbishop together with the bishop of Laon, the King, and [56] many other reverend persons, who certainly do not deny that they were the authors and leaders in these matters.

If they did well, what is that to me? If otherwise, what likewise is it to me? Is my whole and only fault that I was present—a man worthy only of hiding places—appointed my own sole judge, [Col. 0155C] sole accuser, and arbiter, so that my conduct may show what my profession contains, and a solitary manner of life may interpret for me the name of monk? For I was present, I cannot deny it; but I was summoned, I was drawn. If this displeased my friends, I confess that it displeased me too. Would that I had not gone to those events; would that I did not go to similar ones.

Would that I had not recently gone where I saw tyranny, armed violently against the Church by apostolic authority—alas!—as though it had not raged enough on its own. Then at last I felt, with the prophet, my tongue cleaving to my palate (Ps. 136:6), when suddenly a burden was laid upon our necks by the unanswerable authority of letters. Alas! I became mute; I was humbled; I kept silence even from good things, and my sorrow was renewed (Ps. 38:3), when I saw that suddenly, by those letters, the faces of the innocent were filled with disgrace, that the wicked rejoiced still more because they had done evil, and exulted in the worst of deeds. Mercy was shown to the wicked man so that, according to the prophet’s saying, he might not learn to do justice; [Col. 0156B] and he who committed wickedness in the land of the saints (Isa. 26:10) had the very land which he held most unjustly absolved from interdict. [Note: [Col. 0156D] See above, Letters 46 and 47.]

3. For reasons of this kind, even if there were no other, I am burdened by involvement in cases—especially cases in which I know that I ought not to be involved. I am burdened, yet drawn. But from this necessity through whom could I better hope to be withdrawn than through you, excellent man? For in this matter, as I have learned, you lack neither power nor will.

I rejoice, indeed, that I have learned that my involvement in such occupations displeases your prudence also. And rightly and kindly so. Therefore, if this is your wish—or rather, because this is what you see and determine to be expedient for a friend and fitting for a monk—please take care that [Col. 0156C] the shared will of both of us may swiftly be fulfilled: so that justice may be satisfied in your case, and provision made for my soul’s salvation in mine.

Let those noisy and importunate frogs, if you please, be ordered not to come out of their caverns, but to be content with their [Col. 0157A] marshes. Let them not be heard in councils, nor found in palaces. Let no necessity and no authority draw them into lawsuits or business. Thus perhaps your friend might escape the charge of presumption.

For I do not know how I could incur blame, since I know that it is my counsel and purpose never to leave the monastery—unless the cause is specifically that of our Order—except when summoned either by a legate of the Apostolic See or indeed by my own bishop. As you very well know, it is wholly unlawful for our humility to oppose these, unless by some privilege of higher authority. If such a privilege should ever, as I hope, come into my hands through yours, then without doubt I shall have peace, and there will be peace concerning me.

Yet I do not think that, even if I remain unaware and silent, the murmur of the churches will cease if the Roman curia does not cease, at the wish of those present, to prejudice those who are absent. Farewell.

## 57. LETTER XLIX

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Written in the year of Christ 1128.]

TO LORD POPE HONORIUS, ON BEHALF OF HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS.

To the supreme Pontiff HONORIUS, his servants and, if judged worthy, sons—STEPHEN of Cîteaux, HUGH of Pontigny, and BERNARD of Clairvaux—whatever is fitting for the most reverend lord and most gracious father.

Living in the monasteries to which our sins have driven us, we do not cease to pray for you and for the Church of God committed to you. We rejoice with the Bride of the Lord at so faithful a guardian, and with the Bridegroom’s [Col. 0157C] friend at so fruitful a labour. Therefore, confidently and faithfully, we lay before your Paternity what we sorrowfully see opposed to that same mother in our kingdom.

So far as we can perceive, being neighbours, King Louis persecutes in bishops not so much bishops as the zeal of justice, the practice of mercy, and religion’s very habit. Your prudent Holiness can easily discern this also from the fact that those who were formerly honoured, raised high, judged faithful, and held familiar while living and dressing in a secular manner have now become enemies, because they live worthily of their priesthood and honour their ministry in every respect.

Thus the innocence of the bishop of Paris has been assailed with grave insults and injuries, but not shaken, because the Lord put forth his hand when he set yours in opposition. Thus he now tries to shake and overthrow the constancy of this lord of Sens, so that, once the metropolitan has been cast down—God forbid!—he may readily rage against the suffragans as he pleases. Finally, who doubts that he attacks nothing but religion, which he plainly declares to be the destruction of his kingdom and the enemy of his crown? Like another Herod, he no longer suspects Christ in the cradle, but envies him exalted in the churches. [Col. 0158A]

Nor do we believe that he has anything against the archbishop except that he labours to extinguish in him, as in the others, the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0157D] This was not said absolutely against the King, who is otherwise known to have been by no means evil; rather, because he seemed in these matters to persecute zeal for justice, wishing to extinguish the first impulses toward conversion in the bishops of Sens and Paris, as though in the very cradles of a new life. Moreover, how piously Louis spent the final days of his life is shown by the notes on Letter 45, notwithstanding the charge of gluttony made against him by Henry of Huntingdon, *Spicilegium*, vol. VIII.]

But if we are thought either to deceive or to be deceived in what we attest, the investigation of your examination will quickly discover it—if only, as we strongly desire and humbly pray, judgment may proceed from your countenance, most holy Father. For we trust that you will preserve innocence and see equity. Otherwise, to have the case brought back into the King’s presence and power is plainly nothing other than to deliver, alas, the man into the hands of his enemies.

## LETTER L

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Written in the year of Christ 1128.]

TO THE SAME.

As above.—He asks that the archbishop be allowed to appeal to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0158B]

It would indeed have been proper, if such had seemed good to your authority, that the case of the lord of Sens be heard in your presence, lest a man hostile to the King, obliged to answer before the King and the power of his adversaries acting for him, should seem to be delivered into the hands of his enemies.

But since, just as we must hold without question whatever you command, so we must hope without doubt for good from everything you decide, the humility of all the Religious who are thought to be among us asks only this of your mercy, Father: that if he should find himself, as often happens, weighed down before the face of the powerful, he may be allowed to flee to the heart of his Father. We have heard that this has hitherto been denied to no oppressed person.

Otherwise let Joseph, the just man, consider what he must even now do concerning the child and his mother, because [Col. 0158C] behold, even now in the province of Sens Christ is sought in order to be destroyed. For, to state more openly what is true, the King is plainly seen to persecute new religious life in the archbishop because, when he was in his former secular manner of life and dress, the King desired by every means [variant: conveniently] to promote him and left him entirely secure from molestation.

## LETTER LI

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Written in the year of Christ 1128.]

TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR.

As above.

To the illustrious HAIMERIC, chancellor of the holy Roman See, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting, and whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

[Col. 0158D]

How long does that sentence endure: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12)? How long is the rod of sinners left over the lot of the righteous? Who will grant that the righteous begin to stand [Note: [Col. 0158D] Elsewhere is added, “in great constancy,” but it is absent from the manuscripts.] against those who have afflicted them? Who can now bear so great a discord between heaven and earth, that while the Angels rejoice at the amendment of the wicked, the children of Adam rage and waste away?

As though Jesus had not suffered, reconciling in [Col. 0159A] his blood the things on earth and the things in heaven; or as though in him God had not reconciled the world to himself. The archbishop was once praised in the desires of his soul and blessed in secular life and dress. But now simony is sought beneath the swaddling clothes of the infant Jesus, and malicious curiosity searches among nascent virtues for the dead bodies—or rather, the corpses—of vices.

You see Jesus still set as a sign that is opposed. By him I beseech you; for his sake I implore you. For you have reason both to revere him and to pity him. Stand now for him in defending the archbishop, beside whom you will one day have to stand at your own examination. Farewell.

## LETTER LII

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Written about the year 1128.]

TO THE SAME.

The bishop of Chartres had not sought to undertake the Jerusalem journey. Bernard asks to be released from public causes and business.

[Col. 0159B]

Your friend and ours, the lord bishop of Chartres [Note: [Col. 0159D] Geoffrey: below, Letter 55.] wished you also to be assured through me that the proposal which, we have learned, certain persons pressed upon the lord Pope concerning him—namely, that he should permit him to depart for Jerusalem—was neither his own initiative nor his wish. Even if he had greatly desired it, he could not have departed without grave scandal to all the good people among us, who feared that his absence would do more harm to his own people than his presence could do good to strangers.

This is on behalf of the bishop. But, that I may also say something on my own behalf, according to Scripture’s admonition, “Have mercy,” it says, “on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30:24): does it please you that I should be burdened with lawsuits and occupied with business, and that it should avail me nothing to be released from my own affairs while I am wholly entangled in other people’s? If I have found favour in your eyes, take care that I may be completely removed from such matters, so that I may be free to pray for my own sins and yours.

Indeed, I judge nothing safer for myself than obedience to the will of the lord Pope; but may he deign to consider what I am able to do. Would that he knew how unable—or how scarcely able—I am to do these things. Enough has been said about this to a wise man.

The aforesaid bishop asked me for some of my little works to send you; but nothing was at hand which I judged worthy of your attention. I have, however, recently published a small book *On Grace and Free Choice*. I shall gladly send it to you when I know that you desire it. Farewell.

## 59. LETTER LIII

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Written about the year 1128.]

TO THE SAME.

He presents two Religious persons—and himself among them—to Haimeric.

I remember having written to you for many people and through many people; but now, behold, I myself who spoke am present. You behold three in two, since they cannot be without me, in whose breasts I rest continually, and indeed more safely and sweetly than in my own. I seem to lie—but only to one who has never felt the power of friendship, who does not know the strength of charity, who does not believe that the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32).

Therefore whoever sees them sees me too, though not in my own body; and what they say, I too say, but through their tongues. In body, I confess, I am absent; but this is a small portion of myself. Moreover, whoever saw only my face can, without fault and without the charge of falsehood, assert that he saw not a part of me but me—although he saw only a part, and a small part. How much more truly, therefore, may I say that I am present, even without the presence of my body, where I perceive my will, my spirit, and my love, which are certainly [Col. 0160B] the better and worthier part of me?

Know, therefore, that in three bodies we are one—not by equal holiness, for I am inferior to both, but by the same will and the fullest concord of minds. For why should the bond of charity not produce this unity among different persons in one spirit, if carnal union makes two one flesh? I should like you to be added as a fourth, if you judge it worthy, and to enter into the same unity of love. You will readily obtain this, if you do not despise it: only make known to them that you do not at all despise it. Farewell.

## LETTER LIV

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Written about the year 1136.]

TO THE SAME.

He commends Abbot Vivian and exhorts Haimeric to take the care of his soul seriously.

I wish and pray that the bearer of this letter, Vivian, the venerable abbot of Hautecombe, [Col. 0160C] a close friend of mine because of his religious devotion, may experience you as his friend, for God’s sake and for mine, in his affair. This is for him; the rest is for you.

“What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul? Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Matt. 16:26.) Not even the whole world would suffice. The soul is a great thing, redeemed by Christ’s blood. Great is the soul’s fall, which could be repaired only by Christ’s cross. If it should fall again through sin unto death, by what means will it then be repaired? Is there to be another Christ, or must the same Christ be crucified again for it?

On this subject I would have you never forget the counsel of the Wise Man: “Son, remember [Col. 0160D] your last things, and you will never sin” (Sir. 7:40).

## LETTER LV

TO GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF CHARTRES.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Written about the year 1128. Bernard was a great admirer, herald, and eyewitness of this great prelate’s virtues, having often been called with him by pontifical authority to conduct various affairs of the Church. See the *Life of Saint Bernard*, Book II, chapters 1, 2, 6, and elsewhere. That Geoffrey was a truly apostolic man, wholly comparable in conduct, affection, and intellect to Bernard, is evident also from Bernard’s confession that his memory was most sweet to him. These are the words in which he shows it: “But, oh, a sweet place for me,” he says, “when an occasion occurs to remember and name a man of sweetest fragrance—I mean Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres—who conducted a legation in Aquitaine at his own expense, and did so for several years. I speak of a thing which I myself saw,” etc., *On Consideration*, Book IV, chapter 5. There one may read how steadfastly and generously he refused gifts offered to him, and with what praises Bernard celebrates him on that account. See also Peter, abbot of Cluny, Book IV, Letter 43, where one may see how highly he regarded him; John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, Book V, chapter 15; Henriquez, *Menologium*, 1 February; likewise *Fasciculus*, Book II, distinction 10, chapter 12, who testifies that he was taken from the Cistercian community to the see of Chartres. See also Baronius, vol. XII, under 1135 and elsewhere, where he records many entirely illustrious facts concerning him. Certainly, in the *Life of William, Duke of Aquitaine*, he is called “a man full of the spirit of counsel and fortitude.” But Bernard’s praise alone is for us equivalent to all. See the places cited above. Geoffrey died in 1138, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.]

He asks Geoffrey to receive and help a certain recluse monk, who had deserted his observance but was now coming to repentance.

To God’s most faithful and prudent servant, GEOFFREY, bishop of Chartres, BERNARD, servant of Christ’s poor [Col. 0161A] at Clairvaux: may you be flooded with the brightness of the everlasting mountains.

As much honour as your praiseworthy life brings you, so much burden does your praising reputation bring with it. For behold, the man through whom and for whom you receive this letter, stirred—like many others of the same kind whom you often experience—by your good fragrance, which he perceived from afar, seeks with confidence the compassion so common to you, in hope of finding not only counsel on what he ought to do but also assistance by which he may accomplish it.

This is his case. Of his own purpose he had enclosed himself in a certain cell for the love of God. He himself will explain to you the causes of his departure and transgression. [Note: [Col. 0161C] By established custom, recluses were not permitted to leave their cells; see Grimlaicus, *Rule of Solitaries*.] He wishes indeed to return to his purpose, but has resolved to fulfil it through you, if [Col. 0161B] he can obtain this by our prayers, with which he has taken care to fortify himself.

Do then what is customary with you: bring help to the unhappy man; or rather, since you acknowledge yourself debtor to wise and foolish alike, hasten to rescue Christ’s wandering little sheep from the wolf’s jaws. And, restoring him to his former pasture, order him to be enclosed in some cell near any [Col. 0162A] one of your sheepfolds—unless perhaps you discern something else more expedient for him, judge it permissible, and can persuade him of it.

## LETTER LVI

[Note: [Col. 0161C] Written about the year 1128.]

TO THE SAME.

He is uncertain concerning Norbert’s journey to Jerusalem. He does not agree with Norbert’s opinion about Antichrist. He also commends Humbert’s case.

What you ask me about Lord Norbert—namely, whether he is going to Jerusalem—I do not know. For although a few days ago I was granted to see his face and to draw in much from the heavenly pipe, that is, from his own mouth, I did not hear this from him.

> Note: [Col. 0161C] A distinguished eulogy of Norbert from so great a man; but no less notable is Bernard’s discernment in divine matters, for he did not readily place faith in every pious illumination, as appears from Letter 174, no. 4. Norbert, already praised above in Letter 38 as founder of the Premonstratensian Order, grew in twenty years into nearly seventy abbeys, according to Lawrence of Liège, in vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 325. See Letter 253.

But when I asked what he thought about Antichrist, he solemnly declared that he knew with absolute certainty that Antichrist would be revealed during the generation now still living.

> Note: [Col. 0161D] Not Norbert alone, but many of the ancient Fathers—without mentioning more recent writers—were at times persuaded that Antichrist and the world’s last day stood at the doors: as may be seen in Jerome, Pope Leo, Gregory the Great, and Saint Augustine himself. From the wickedness of the times and from the signs foretold by Christ as preceding the end of the world—many of which already then appeared—they did not, in their view, draw this conclusion without reason.
>
> To go a little further back, from the very times of the apostles there have always been various judgments, conjectures, opinions, and prophecies of many people concerning Antichrist and the end of the world. Most philosophers and astronomers, many impostors, jesters, and peddlers of trifles, as well as heretics and certain fanatics, have wished to appear prophets in this matter and wiser than other mortals. Yet events have already brought most of their predictions to a close and convicted these prophets of vanity and falsehood. No doubt the succeeding age will similarly mock the remaining predictions which still concern future times, so that it may be clear how truly it was said in Acts 1:7: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons”; and in Matthew 24:36: “But of that day and hour no one knows.”
>
> The reader may not find it unpleasant if, out of the many, we give examples of a few. First, the Thessalonians themselves, misunderstanding the Apostle’s words in 1 Thessalonians 4:16—“Then we who are alive, who are left behind, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with God”—soon supposed that the last day of the world was at hand. Therefore, as Jerome testifies in his letter to Minerius and Alexander, he had to write the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians in order to call them back from this opinion.
>
> Lactantius thought that the destruction of the world would occur in the year 500 after Christ (*Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. 25). Others fixed a duration of a thousand years for the world after Christ; these were called Chiliasts. They derived this from Saint John’s words, Revelation 20:7: “And when the thousand years have been completed, Satan shall be released from his prison.” A certain bishop of Florence asserted that Antichrist was born in 1105. See Platina, under Paschal II. Peter John, leader of the Beguines and Beghards, affirmed that Antichrist’s reign would end in 1335; see José de Acosta, *On the Last Times*. A Spaniard named Arnold, according to Florimond, assigned Antichrist’s time to the year 1345, the very day of Pentecost in which year Antichrist’s disciples, that is, were to reveal themselves. Abbot Joachim believed that Antichrist would appear within sixty years of his own time; he lived about the year 1200.
>
> Pierre d’Ailly, cardinal and bishop of Cambrai, predicted from astronomical signs and observations that Antichrist would arise in the year of the Lord 1789. Nicholas of Cusa did not hesitate to assert that Antichrist’s coming would occur in the year of Christ 1700 or 1734. Giovanni Pico, prince of Mirandola, in the *Assertions*, conclusion 9, conjectures that Antichrist would come in the year 1994 from the redemption of the world. Jerome Cardan, *On Variety*, book II, ch. 2, and Jacob Naclantus, in the *Prelude to the Marrow*, ch. 4, believed that Antichrist would come in 1800.
>
> In the preceding century, under some itch for prophecy, many astrologers and heterodox writers, predicting the time of the world’s destruction, supplied a tale and laughter to a world which still stood. Johannes Regiomontanus, otherwise a great mathematician, published in the year from the Virgin’s childbirth a *Prognostication concerning the Year 1588*, as though it were the world’s fated year. Johannes Stöffler, himself an eminent astrologer, produced similar work, as did the noble Dane Henry Rantzau in his book *On Climacteric Years and the Periods of Empires*. Thus many astronomers, wishing to foretell from the movement, conjunctions, and various aspects of the stars things subject wholly to God’s will and governance, made themselves ridiculous to the entire world. What Saint Thomas writes in IV, distinction 44, happened to them: “All who have wished to foretell the designated time by calculation have been found to speak falsely; their falsity is now evident, and likewise the falsity of those who still do not cease calculating will become evident.”
>
> If anyone takes greater pleasure in reading the more witty and absurd predictions—or rather dreams and ravings—of fanatical people about the end of the world, let him consult Tilmann Bredenbach’s *Sacred Collations*, book VII, chapters 32–33. Bredenbach was a most pious man and formerly a canon here of the illustrious church of Saint Gereon. Let him consult Cochlaeus, *Acts of Luther*, under the year 1533; Frederick Nausea, bishop of Vienna, *On the Consummation of the Age*; or, above all, Florimond, *On the Progress of Heresies*, book II, ch. 4, and *On Antichrist*, ch. 7; finally, the divine Harpocrates, Remaclus de Vaulx.
>
> I have thought it appropriate, on the occasion of the prophecy about Antichrist just mentioned, to recall these matters—yet not to disparage Norbert, a most holy man, whom Bernard above calls a “heavenly pipe.” For not he alone, but many holy Fathers also, thought or predicted that the end of the world was not far off in their own time: among them Tertullian, *On Flight in Persecution*, ch. 12; Cyprian, Letters 56, 58, and 63; Jerome, letter to Ageruchia or Gerontius; Leo, sermon 8, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*; Basil, Letter 71; Chrysostom, Homily 33 on John; Ambrose, funeral oration for his brother Satyrus; Gregory, book IV, letter 72, and Homilies 1 and 15 on the Gospels; Bernard, Sermon 6 on Psalm 90; Vincent Ferrer of the Order of Preachers, letter to Pope Benedict; and many others.
>
> But observe that holy men spoke of the end of the world on grounds very different from those mentioned above. Those others circulated fabrications of this kind either by observing stars and planets—which is almost always extremely deceptive in other predictions, but especially in this one—or by twisting certain sayings of Scripture into a false sense, or merely from a desire to lie and deceive, or from pursuit of popular favor and veneration. Holy men, however, appalled by the crimes and evils flooding everywhere throughout the world, thought that the world could scarcely endure much longer, and that nothing remained but for it soon to collapse under the mass of crimes and iniquities, as God’s wrath anticipated the limit fixed for the world.
>
> Hence a certain later author gives this pious and prudent warning:
>
> > “If many Fathers, whom we admire for the excellence of their holiness and learning, observing either the depravity and malice of their own times, the magnitude and atrocity of persecutions pressing upon Christians, the dreadful ravages of heretics, the burning of cities, the storms of wars, vast earthquakes, the gloomy and deadly changes of heaven, air, and the elements, the downfall of empires, and inhuman outpourings of human blood—if fear and dread at so many and such great evils led them to think that Antichrist and the end of the age were now close at hand, so that they either feared or perhaps believed it—they are not to be charged with frivolity or falsehood, nor polluted in any way by a venomous tongue. For they thought or spoke thus because present evils always seem more terrible. At the sight of them they were almost struck down by fear; and they strove both in mind and in preaching to instill fear into others, so that they might rise up and, as the saying goes, return to a good course. They also judged that all this passing time was only the briefest delay when compared with eternity. Finally, without prejudice to truth, they could say and proclaim that God’s judgment was drawing nearer day by day. That this is familiar and characteristic of Scripture cannot escape anyone who has read it.”
>
> Thus writes the author of the divine *Harpocrates*. Nor were the various oracular prophecies unlike this, which foretold that the end of the world was, as it were, already imminent because of impending evils. Such is that passage in Ezekiel 4:2: “The end has come; the end has come upon the four quarters of the earth,” and similar passages. To this may be referred the vision of Redemptus, bishop of the city of Florence, concerning which Blessed Gregory writes in *Dialogues*, book III, ch. 38.
>
> Wonderful are the things Baronius relates: namely, that about the year of the Lord 419, so many visions and such dreadful portents appeared over the Mount of Olives that many neighboring peoples, terrified both by sight and by report, hurried to Christian worship, and on the tunics of all who were baptized the cross of Christ the Savior was imprinted by divine will. On the occasion of this remarkable event, discussions concerning the time of the Lord’s coming began to be mixed everywhere with divine predictions. This seems to be why Hesychius wrote to Saint Augustine to inquire about the world’s last day. Augustine replies in Letters 78 and 88; the latter especially should be read on this subject, since it explains at length and learnedly many scriptural passages that speak in various ways of the end of the age. But let us now move on to other matters.

But when, upon my asking, he wished to explain to me the source of this same certainty, I heard his answer and did not think that I ought to believe it as certain. In short, however, he maintained this: that he would not see death unless he first saw a general persecution in the Church.

Furthermore, I wish to remind your piety of that poor exile named Humbert, who formerly, when you were at Troyes, begged you to intercede with Count Theobald, who had disinherited him. I now make the same request of your piety, both for him and with him. For I have already sent letters of intercession on this matter to the aforesaid prince; but, finding no favor, I accomplished nothing.

> Note: [Col. 0164D] Letters 37–39.

Now I ought gladly to tell you what you gladly hear. Your Stephen runs in such a way as not uncertainly; he fights in such a way as not beating the air. Pray that he may so run as to attain the prize, and so fight as to conquer.

## LETTER LVII

> Note: [Col. 0164D] Written about the year 1128.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** Lesser vows ought not to obstruct greater goods. This seems, unless I am mistaken, to have been written concerning the monk discussed above in Letter 55.

[Col. 0164B]

As he reported to me on your behalf, you have delayed until now to satisfy his desire and request because his first vow—namely, to go to Jerusalem—seems to you to have been made void by him. If you ask our judgment on this matter, I do not think that lesser vows ought to impede greater ones; nor that God demands every good thing promised to Him, if something better has been rendered in its place.

Indeed, suppose that someone owed you twelve coins: if, on the appointed day, he paid you a mark of silver instead, would you rightly be angry? And if you are also apprehensive of anything from this man’s bishop, I reassure you: not only will he not dislike any assistance you give him, but he will consider it very welcome. Farewell.

## LETTER LVIII

**TO EBALUS, BISHOP OF CHÂLONS**

> Note: [Col. 0165C] Written about the year 112—[uncertain OCR]. Ebalus was nephew of Count Hilduin of Bassigny and son of Andrew, count of Ramerupt, according to Herman, monk of Laon, in book I of *The Miracles of Blessed Mary*, ch. 2. He was made bishop of Châlons in 1122 after William of Champeaux; see Letter 3. He had Elbert, or Robert, as successor in 1126, and after him Geoffrey, formerly abbot of Saint-Médard, to whom Letter 66 is addressed. Thus this letter was written about 1126, and before Letter 13, written in favor of Alberic, who was elected after Ebalus but did not obtain his see.

He urges Ebalus to see that a suitable man is put in charge of the monastery or church of All Saints.

[Col. 0165A]

To Lord EBALUS, venerable bishop by God’s grace of the holy Church of Châlons, Brother BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

1. It is not good for you to neglect or overlook the danger facing that little vessel—I mean the church of All Saints—which, bereft of a helmsman, is tossing in the waves under your eyes.

> Note: [Col. 0165D] An abbey of canons regular of the Order of Saint Augustine at Châlons. Its abbot Peter—perhaps the first after the reform—received an unpublished letter from Hugh Metellus, likewise a canon regular of Saint-Léon at Toul.

It is a matter entrusted to your care. I therefore wonder by what reasoning or with what confidence you cease to seek the cleric who was elected to that church by religious persons as a man, as they say, “religious,” even if the negligence or sloth of certain persons in the church itself does not deserve this. For, as we have heard, those who do not want the man who was elected—offering no reason except that he is religious [alternatively, “asserting that he is religious”]—have even dared to urge your gravity to elect another: one who seems more sociable and approachable, who is not a stranger but is as welcome as he is known to the citizens, acquainted with the customs of the country, and fit to manage the church’s affairs. In truth—to turn now to these most prudent advisers—one who will not rebuke your vices, but who either agrees with your wretched way of life or dares not oppose it.

They are not to be heard. Rather, whether they wish it or not, you must take every possible care that the man of good testimony be sought out as quickly as possible for the desolate church. For if he is such as he is said to be, God will undoubtedly be with him and will grant him His grace: grace pleasing to all and effective in all things.

2. But if, perhaps because these people do not deserve him, it should prove wholly impossible to obtain this man, let another suitable man be provided from whatever other religious house. Let him not be the sort these people want, who want only what flatters their fleshly desires; but one who knows how to order the business of outward possessions in such a way that he knows to place the care of souls above everything.

Certainly, when the two monasteries of Saint Peter and Saint Urban were likewise at one time deprived of pastoral help, your predecessor of good memory, Lord William, did not count the labor of a long journey or the harshness of winter. Twice, unless I am mistaken, he went in person to Cluny, and once to Dijon. From the former place he brought away, only with many entreaties, the good man Lord Hugh, who afterward died; from the latter, the venerable Lord Ralph, who still survives. He placed one man over each monastery, judging it unsafe to entrust such care to any monk of the household.

> Note: [Col. 0165D–0166C] These monasteries belonged to the Order of Saint Benedict and afterwards to the congregation of Saint-Vanne: the first in the city itself, the other in the diocese of Châlons. William of Champeaux had restored them to better order.

I have offered this to you as an example in order to remind your charity how, in the matter now at hand, it ought to be no less careful than solicitous.

## LETTER LIX

> Note: [Col. 0166D] Written in the year of Christ 1129.

**TO GUILENCUS, BISHOP OF LANGRES.** He urges him to cede to the church of Saint Stephen at Dijon certain properties left vacant by the death of Garnerius, in order to remove grounds for scandal and litigation.

[Col. 0166B]

To his lord and father GUILENCUS, bishop of Langres by God’s grace, Brother BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, gives himself.

> Note: [Col. 0166D] Wilencus, called by others William, formerly archdeacon of Langres; see Pérard, *Burgundian Monuments*, p. 87.

Having heard of the death of Lord Garnerius, the archdeacon, we judged it necessary to anticipate your Fatherhood with prayers—indeed, to fortify you with counsel, if you deem it worthy to comply with the admonitions of our littleness—that with respect to the possessions of Saint Stephen’s, Dijon, which he held, it may please your generosity to let mercy triumph over judgment.

> Note: [Col. 0166D] He had also been abbot of the church of Saint Stephen at Dijon before canons regular were introduced there. This began in 1113, when four canons withdrew from that church to the village of Quintigny in order to profess the regular life there. In 1116, when they numbered twelve, they returned to their church. In the meantime the church was governed by the priors Arnulf and then Galo until 1125, when Lord Erbert or Harbert was installed as abbot, in the presence of Hubaud, archbishop of Lyon, Stephen, bishop of Autun, Goceran or Joceran of Langres, and other persons. For a fuller account see Pérard, pp. 86–87, where the Life of Garnerius is printed.

For we do not deny that they ought to return into your hand, as was settled in the chapter of Langres and, as we ourselves remember, confirmed in writing when your son Harbert was made the first regular abbot in that church. But we have learned that it will give the canons an occasion of grave scandal and the abbot an occasion of great reproach if, under whatever pretext, you extend your hand to possessions which that church held for so long. They will complain about him as one who came and gave an evil beginning, since because of him and at his entrance the church incurred so great a loss.

We beseech your piety and, in beseeching, advise you to spare so many little ones of Christ from so great a scandal, and at the same time to take care to free this vicar of Christ from so great a reproach, by granting to the church what is known to have belonged to it in right until now.

> Note: [Col. 0167D] That Guilencus did this is shown by his charter printed in Pérard, p. 97; among its subscribers are the abbots of Cîteaux and Clairvaux at Langres, in 1129. In that same year the dispute between this church and the monks of Saint-Seine was settled by this same Joceran, with the judgment and counsel of Walter of Chalon and the abbots of Cîteaux, Bèze, and Clairvaux; ibid., p. 102. The matter was later referred to Innocent, who entrusted it to Stephen of Cîteaux and Bernard of Clairvaux; p. 103. Thus Bernard alone did everything; Bernard alone ended every suit and controversy.

## LETTER LX

> Note: [Col. 0167D] Written about the year 1128.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** He intercedes for the church of Molesme.

I approach as a supplicant on behalf of the church of Molesme, not, I think, as an importunate intercessor. Many considerations encourage me so that this request need not fear refusal. First, because we are not pleading with you for some alien church, but for your own church. Second, because we believe that the church seeks from your equity not to usurp what belongs to another, but only its own right. Third, because this same request is made with us by one who by himself could obtain from you even something greater: namely, Count Theobald. If I add a fourth consideration, I shall not think myself rash in presuming it. For neither do I myself so distrust our humility that, if need be, we would not confidently approach the benevolence of your highness, already sufficiently proved to us, in person to request what seems reasonable. Farewell.

## LETTER LXI

> Note: [Col. 0168D] Written about the year 1125.

**TO RICUINUS, BISHOP OF TOUL.** He sends back to his care a man who, under the bishop of Toul’s command, had come to undergo penance.

To the reverend father, Lord RICUINUS, bishop of Toul by God’s grace, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and prayers.

> Note: [Col. 0168D] Ricuinus died in 1126, as the Sainte-Marthe brothers prove from Alberic. Therefore this letter cannot be dated after that year. It could scarcely have been written before 1124, when Bernard’s reputation and teaching had already become celebrated. Letter 396 is also addressed to Ricuinus.

[Col. 0167C] Concerning this sinner, whom your condescension took care to direct to us sinners for counsel about his soul, as he himself reports, we had no sounder present advice ready than that he should return to the bosom of paternal mercy and seek the law from the mouth of the priest. For, considering the measure of our lowliness and office, and not stretching ourselves beyond ourselves, we are wholly accustomed never to presume to impose penance upon any person, especially in criminal matters, except only those whom we have accepted into our own care.

For with what rashness should we sinners and inexperienced men take upon ourselves the affairs of bishops—and affairs of this kind—when we too, like other human beings, whenever some weightier matter arises among us which we do not know how, cannot, or do not dare to decide ourselves, reserve it, as is fitting, for episcopal judgment? And unless we have first been assured by the judgment or counsel of the supreme Priest, are we not without security?

Let, therefore, a suitable medicine of penance be provided for the sick sheep by its own shepherd—and such a shepherd, one who knows the canons—lest, God forbid, the soul for which Christ died should die in sin and the supreme Shepherd require its blood at your hand. Yet we have persuaded him, God inspiring it, to leave the world, provided that, old and poor as he is, he can by your intervention obtain admission to some community of saints within your diocese.

May that one day, better in the courts of the Lord than thousands, receive you full of days, holy and venerable Father.

## LETTER LXII

> Note: [Col. 0168D] Written before the year 1129.

**TO HENRY, BISHOP OF VERDUN.** He commends to the bishop a woman burdened with many sins but now repentant.

[Col. 0168B]

To LORD HENRY, bishop of Verdun by God’s grace, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and prayer.

This poor woman, whom Satan has now bound for many years in many tangled knots of sin, sought counsel from our lowliness concerning the state of her salvation. She received this counsel: that, after much and long wandering, the fugitive little sheep should confidently return to the bosom of her own shepherd. He ought all the more promptly and carefully to bring help to the needy woman, since he knows with greater certainty and strictness that he must render an account of what has been entrusted to him to the Lamb who died for her.

It was our part to correct one who had strayed; let it be yours not to despise a sinful woman, but rather to receive one who repents. And if the account of her misfortune which she related to us is true, either reconcile her with her former husband, if he is still alive; or, if he refuses, compel him, as she is unmarried, likewise to remain without a wife. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIII

> Note: [Col. 0168D] Written about the year 1128.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** He clears himself of a rash act of which he had been accused; seeks the bishop’s acquaintance; and commends Guy to him.

Regarding the matters about which it pleased your Excellency to inquire of us, either we are mistaken or the person who reported them to you is deceiving you. Yet if there was anything—since I regard my own memory, which I know to be unstable, with suspicion—rather than suspect so great a falsehood in the brother who says these things, I trust that I know this most certainly, and I wish you to believe it without doubt: I have never spoken or instructed anyone to speak words of censure or accusation concerning your name.

Far be such rashness from our lowliness as to dare to say, against bishops and in their absence, things which do not concern us—especially things we have not proved.

Further, we gladly receive your gracious desire for acquaintance with us, wishing more abundantly both to become known to you and to know you. With this confidence, then, we beseech your Eminence—or rather, confidently remind your benevolence—concerning that place which, under your protection and, as they say, at your encouragement, our reverend brother and fellow abbot, Lord Guy of Trois-Fontaines, has undertaken to build.

> Note: [Col. 0169D–0170D] That is, Chalade, in the diocese of Verdun, whose foundation was begun in 1128 under Henry and whose church was consecrated by his successor Adalbero. “There now,” says Lawrence of Liège, “nearly three hundred servants of God fight for the kingdom of heaven under Abbot Gunter, of holy memory.” It began under Bishop Henry when Robert, “a monk of our venerable monastery,” that is, Saint-Vanne of Verdun, “first lived there as a hermit with two companions, after building a little church and certain small dwellings.” But when he was summoned to the church of Bellelocus and the site remained empty, it was given by its noble owner, Walter the nephew, to the venerable Guy, abbot of Trois-Fontaines, with Bishop Henry’s consent and encouragement, and chiefly through the persistent efforts and urging of the nobleman Hervé. Hervé joined their community in a remarkable example: having left his wife and bound a rope around his neck. From vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 337.

In this matter show us how greatly you care for us; and regard whatever you do for him as done for us. Farewell.

## LETTER LXIV

> Note: [Col. 0170D] Written about the year 1129.

**TO ALEXANDER, BISHOP OF LINCOLN**

> Note: [Col. 0170D] Alexander governed the church of Lincoln, or Lincoliensis, among the English from 1123 to 1147.

Philip, intending to set out for Jerusalem, perhaps turned aside to Clairvaux and decided to remain there. Bernard seeks Alexander’s consent and commends to him Philip’s business with his creditors. Finally, he exhorts him not to put too much confidence in worldly glory.

[Col. 0169B]

To the honorable man Lord ALEXANDER, bishop of Lincoln by God’s grace, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: wishing to be honored rather in Christ than in the world.

1. Your Philip, wishing to go to Jerusalem, found a shortcut and quickly reached the place he desired. He crossed in a short time this great and wide sea, and, sailing prosperously, has already touched the desired shore and at last reached the harbor of salvation. His feet now stand in the courts of Jerusalem; and the One of whom he had heard in Ephrathah, whom he found in the fields of the forest, he gladly worships in the place where His feet stood.

He has entered the holy city. He has received an inheritance with those to whom it is deservedly said: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). Going in and out with them as one of the saints, he too glories with the rest, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). Thus he has become not merely an inquisitive observer but also a devout inhabitant and enrolled citizen of Jerusalem—not this earthly Jerusalem, to which Mount Sinai in Arabia is joined, which is in bondage with her children, but that free Jerusalem which is above and is our mother (Galatians 4:25–26).

2. And if you wish to know, it is Clairvaux. It is Jerusalem itself, joined to the Jerusalem in heaven by the whole devotion of its mind, by imitation in its manner of life, and by a certain kinship of spirit. This is His resting place, as He promises, for ever and ever; He chose it as His dwelling. And although the vision of true peace is not yet there, the expectation of it certainly is: namely, that peace of which it is said, “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7).

Yet this good, although he received it from above, he desires to do—and indeed trusts that he has done—with your approval, knowing that you do not ignore the saying of the Wise Man, that a wise son is the glory of his father (Proverbs 10:1).

> Note: [Col. 0170D] Bernard cites this passage in this form repeatedly; the Vulgate has: “A wise son makes his father glad.”

He asks your fatherhood, and we ask with him and for him, that you make stand unalterably what he has assigned from his prebend to his creditors, lest he be found, God forbid, in any respect a defrauder of a debt or a violator of an agreement, and thus the gift of a contrite heart which he offers daily be not accepted while some brother has anything against him.

> Note: [Col. 0170D] A letter of Philip, abbot, to Alexander III is of the same subject: he asks that the possessions of an archdeacon of Orléans who had entered religion be granted to his creditors; in vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, p. 246.

He further asks that the house which he built for his mother on land of the Church, together with the land assigned there, be granted to the same mother for as long as she lives. This is for Philip.

3. The following few words we thought should be added for you. Philip indeed prompted them; but truly God inspired them. We venture, in charity, to exhort you: do not look upon the glory of the world, which is about to fall, as though it stood firm, and so lose the glory which truly stands; do not love your own possessions more than yourself, or for your own sake, and thereby lose both yourself and your possessions; do not let flattering present prosperity conceal from you its end, while adversity without end follows; do not let temporal joy both conceal the eternal sorrow it produces and produce the sorrow it conceals; do not think death far away, lest it overtake one unprepared; and do not let life, while expected to be long, quickly abandon one conscious of evil. As it is written: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them, as travail upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Farewell.

## LETTER LXV

**TO ALVISUS, ABBOT OF ANCHIN**

> Note: [Col. 0170D–0172D] Written about the year 1129. Anchin was a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict on the River Scarpe, two miles from Douai. This monastery, called Saint-Sauveur, was begun in 1029 on the island called Anchin by the distinguished men Sicherius and Walter, under Gerard II, bishop of Cambrai, to whose diocese the place then belonged. See Aubertus Miraeus, *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, ch. 68.
>
> The monks of Anchin joined themselves to the Cluniac congregation and underwent its reform in 1110, as Iperius reports in his *Chronicle of Saint-Bertin*:
>
> > “In the year of the Lord 1110 the monastery of Anchin was repaired and restored to religious observance through Lord Lambert, our abbot. He had obtained an opportunity from the monks’ dissensions, since the monks of Anchin were in such turmoil among themselves that they expelled and deposed their own abbot. Observing this, Lord Lambert induced them through secret messengers to take as abbot a venerable man, distinguished in character and endowed with prudence and eloquence, so that their fallen church might be restored. He had Lord Alvisus named to them, a reformed monk of ours who was then administering the church of Saint-Vaast. Thus the monks of Anchin, at the prompting of our Abbot Lambert, chose Alvisus as their abbot. By the counsel and assistance of the same Lambert he reformed that church and raised it so greatly in spiritual and temporal matters that his name became famous everywhere; and Alvisus himself was finally chosen bishop of Arras.”
>
> Thus far Iperius. Moreover, this monastery’s fame and glory greatly increased throughout the world through the college of Anchin which John Lentailler, a most worthy abbot of the place, established in the University of Douai and, by a rare yet splendid example, entrusted to the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. See Jacques Bonfrère, theologian of the Society of Jesus and distinguished interpreter of Scripture, dedication to the *Pentateuch*. Alvisus—also mentioned below in Letter 66—governed as bishop the church of Arras, to which Anchin is subject. Letter 395 was written to him under that title.

He praises Alvisus’s fatherly gentleness toward Godwin, excuses himself concerning his admission, and asks pardon.

To ALVISUS, abbot of the monastery of Anchin, BERNARD: heartfelt greetings.

[Col. 0170D] 1. May God repay you for the mercy which you showed to your holy son Godwin. For we have heard that, on learning of his death, you at once—forgetful, as it were, of the former accusation, though not of friendship—presented yourselves as a comforter rather than an avenger. You recognized yourselves to be a father, as the situation required, not a judge. And so you endeavoured to bestow upon a true son what belongs to piety and charity. What better, more praiseworthy, or more worthy of you could you have done? Yet who would have believed it? Truly, “no one knows what is in a human being except the human spirit within him” (1 Cor. 2:11). Where now are that austerity, that severity, that indignation, which formerly tongue, countenance, and eyes were accustomed terribly to display and threaten against him? At the single report of the son’s death, the fatherly heart was moved; and suddenly all these things, which [Col. 0171B] were feigned indeed, yet administratively assumed and therefore transitory, vanished; while the things that were true but hidden—charity, piety, kindness—appeared.

For in your religious soul mercy and truth met one another; and because mercy indeed abounded over judgment, justice and peace kissed one another. For, so far as I seem able to perceive by conjecture what was then in your mind, when truth, inflamed with zeal for justice, was preparing itself to avenge the injury which appeared to have been done to you, that mercy which had previously been prudently concealed after the example of Joseph, no longer able to remain hidden—nor in this unlike Joseph (Gen. 45:1)—burst forth from the secret place of concealed affection; joining itself to truth, it restrained the impulse, moderated the zeal, and made peace [Col. 0171C] with justice.

2. Then, I believe, from the most pure fountain of your gentle heart there welled up such most limpid streams of thought:

“What need is there for anger? One ought rather to show mercy, and not forget what is written: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Hos. 6:6); and fulfil what is commanded: ‘Be eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace’ (Eph. 4:3); and await what is promised: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’ (Matt. 5:7). Besides, was this man my son? And who can be angry with a son? Unless perhaps he was a son only while he was with me, and ceased to be so when he left me. But could he withdraw in spirit because he departed for a time in body? Or can death itself perhaps take him from me? Does a necessity of place or body thus confine the freedom of souls that love one another? I am certain that neither distance of places, nor death nor absence of bodies, can separate those whom one spirit gives life and one charity binds. Finally, if ‘the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God’ (Wis. 3:1), surely those who now rest in him, having laid aside the flesh, and those of us who are still in the flesh yet do not wage war according to the flesh, are undoubtedly together. He was mine while living; he will be mine when dead; I shall recognize what is mine in the homeland. If there is anyone who can snatch him from the hand of God, he will be able to separate him from me.”

3. Thus your affection for your son has indeed made satisfaction to you; but what, Father, shall become of us? What satisfaction worthy of you, I ask, will please you from us, upon whom you lay, as a grave injury, the fact that, after leaving you, he was received by us? What shall I say? If I say, “We did not receive him” (would that I could say this without sin), I plainly lie. If I say, “We did indeed receive him, but justly,” I appear to wish to excuse myself. But I shall answer more safely: “We have sinned.” Yet how greatly? I do not say this in self-defence: for by whom would he not have been received? Who, I ask, would have repelled that holy man while knocking, or expelled him after receiving him? Who knows whether God wished to supply our poverty from your abundance, by sending to us one out of the many who perhaps were then religious among you—comfort to us indeed, but no less glory to you? For “a wise son is the glory [Col. 0172C] of his father” (Prov. 10:1).

In short, we did not forestall him by soliciting him, nor ensnare him by drawing him away, so that he might leave you or come to us. Rather, when he asked, knocked, and pleaded, we did not consent to receive him—God knows—until we had first tried to send him back to you. But when he would not agree to this, we scarcely at last yielded to his insistence. Therefore, if it is a fault that we received, and received in this way, a religious man, a stranger, and one alone, it will not be unworthy of you to forgive a fault committed only once, and such a fault—a fault for which it is not even lawful to refuse pardon to those who sin against you seventy times seven (Matt. 18:22).

4. Yet, so that you may know how far we are from taking lightly or negligently—indeed, how far from bearing with impunity—the fact that we have ever offended your Reverence in any way, I often call God to witness that, though I cannot come bodily, I approach you in mind as a suppliant; often, bending my knees and humbly making satisfaction, I see myself standing before you. May he who perhaps inspires this in me cause you also, by his Spirit, to perceive how mournfully, how miserably, as though present, I descend even to your knees! How often, with shoulders bared and rods in my hands, and as though prepared to be beaten at your command, I beg pardon and tremblingly await grace! We urgently ask that you inform us quickly by your reply, Father, how acceptable these things are to you, if it does not burden you; so that, if they suffice, we may now be assured and take comfort in pardon; but if not, we may be more deeply humbled, as is fitting, [Col. 0173B] and require something further of ourselves, if we can, by which we ought to make a worthier satisfaction. Farewell.

67. LETTER LXVI. TO GEOFFREY, ABBOT OF SAINT-MÉDARD

[Note: Written about the year 1129. All the printed and manuscript copies which we have seen, except one, read “Saint-Theodoric”; but “Saint-Médard” must be read, as in the Corbie manuscript, from which we restore the following superscription (which is absent from the others, except in volume 3 of the *Spicilegium*): “To the lord,” etc. Although Geoffrey successively presided over both monasteries—Saint-Médard at Soissons and Saint-Theodoric near Reims—he was abbot of Saint-Médard when this letter was written.

The letter was written, as is understood from the sequence of the letters, before 1131, when Geoffrey was raised from the abbacy of Saint-Médard to the bishopric of Châlons; he had presided over Saint-Médard from 1119, after eight years’ governance at Saint-Theodoric. Through the intervention of Saint Bernard, Geoffrey, though unwilling to accept the election, was appointed in 1131 to the see of Châlons in place of Herbert—not after the dedication of the church of Saint-Médard, which Alberic in his *Chronicle* states was performed by Innocent on the Ides of October that year, but before it. For the Chronicle of Saint-Médard reports that “the aforesaid Pope, before the dedication of the aforesaid church, is said to have blessed at Orléans, on the day before the Kalends of October, Odo, abbot of the church of Blessed Médard, despite the unwillingness and opposition of the bishop of Soissons.”

He died, according to Alberic, in 1143, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, as the necrology of Saint-Theodoric attests in these words: “On the sixth day before the Kalends of June died our abbot Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons.” In the register of anniversaries it is also noted that “he bequeathed three prebends in the refectory as alms for himself and for Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, who restored the monks there.”

A letter of Geoffrey to Peter the Venerable is extant in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, together with Peter’s reply to him. In it Peter calls him “the first disseminator, throughout all France, the author and promoter of the Cluniac—indeed, the divine—Order; the expeller of the ancient dragon from the lairs of so many monasteries; one of the two awakeners from prolonged sleep and monastic torpor” (Bernard was the other, indeed the first); and he declares that he not only believed but publicly proclaimed that these two should be placed above all the friends of Belgian Gaul for the summit of their unfeigned charity. These are certainly splendid encomia, which he finally concludes with these words: “Lastly, I commend to you so earnestly the brother of my dearest lord Garnier, our subprior, that, when through your labour he has become upright, wise, and learned, you may return him to us, as you did the other.” From this it may be inferred that Geoffrey, eminent for learning and wisdom, undertook the education of youth alongside his episcopal office.

Under him at Soissons a general chapter of the monks of our Order was held, concerning which see Letter 91. He attended the Council of Sens in 1140; and in the synodical letter addressed to Innocent, numbered 191 among Bernard’s letters, he is named third.]

He asks Geoffrey’s assistance in reconciling Abbot Alvisus to him; he consoles him in his troubles.

To LORD GEOFFREY, abbot of Saint-Médard, Brother BERNARD, unpolished founder of the church of Clairvaux, greeting—and not merely on the way.

First, I ask that you not consider it burdensome to send this letter to the lord abbot of the monastery of Anchin. Then, when opportunity arises, I ask you to work in person for your absent friend toward the purpose it bears. For I ought not to disregard any just or unjust offence against me on the part of any person, much less so great a father; and perhaps I could have explained to him, by speaking rather than writing, how far I do not disregard it. For in such matters the living voice is usually more welcome than writing, and speech more effective than a letter. The eyes of one speaking give credibility to his words; nor can the finger express feeling as the face can.

But now, because being absent I cannot make satisfaction in person, I do so through you as far as I can. Therefore I ask you—and ask you again—to remove, while you can do so profitably, this offence from the kingdom of God, which is within us; lest, if resentment should endure even to the angels, who at the end of the age are certainly appointed for this ministry (Mark 13:27)—which God forbid!—it become necessary that either both of us, or one of us, be removed irrevocably from our midst.

As for what you wrote to me some time ago, complaining of your troubles: you know that the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart. Trust in him, for he has overcome the world. He knows among whom you dwell, and all who trouble you are before his eyes. He who now tests you at the waters of contradiction will hear you in the hidden place of the storm. Farewell.

LETTER LXVII. TO THE MONKS OF FLAVY

[Note: This reading, *Flaviacenses*, must be followed with the better manuscripts, rather than *Flaviniacenses*, as Horstius and certain others wrongly maintain. The context of the letter itself plainly disproves their view by three arguments.

First, Saint Bernard says that he had had “not even a slight acquaintance, up to that time, with either the dwelling-place, the religious life, or the way of life” of those to whom he writes, and that he does not remember ever having heard any mention of them. Next he says: “We are separated from one another by many stretches of land, by different provinces, and by dissimilar languages.” Finally: “Not only are we apart in our respective bishoprics, but we do not even live in the same archbishopric.” It is clearer than proof could make it that none of this can apply to Flavigny.

For Flavigny is a town in the duchy of Burgundy, near Fontaines, from which Bernard sprang, and not far from Clairvaux. It formerly had a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Autun under the metropolitan see of Lyons, as was Clairvaux also, and was renowned for the precious relics of Saint Reine. The reading must therefore be restored as *Flaviacenses*, deriving its name from Flavy, a village in the diocese of Beauvais on the River Epte. There a distinguished Benedictine monastery was founded by Blessed Geremar about the year 650; it was sometimes called Flavy, but more commonly Saint-Geremar of Flavy.

As for the name of the abbot of Flavy, abbreviated in this superscription, “To Lord H., Father of the church of Flavy,” etc., I think it should be identified as Hildegarius I, who is recorded in Acherius’s published index to Guibert as having presided at Flavy from 1106 to 1123. Yet I infer from the sequence of these letters that he lived at least until 1126. Some identify him here as Hugh, but wrongly. Two abbots of that place named Hugh are indeed recorded; yet the first ceased to hold office in 1100, while the second succeeded Hildegarius II only in 1172. Both therefore lie far outside Saint Bernard’s chronological range.

Moreover, men distinguished for learning and piety came from this same monastery, including Radulfus, commentator on Leviticus, about the year 912, and many others thereafter, especially in the time of the aforesaid Hildegarius. Among them Guibert, later chosen abbot of Nogent near Coucy, shone like a star. Thus the monks of Flavy could not without reason boast in their letter to Bernard—as Bernard himself here reports—that the fame of their monastery had spread as far as Rome.]

He defends his reception of Brother B., who had departed for just reasons from a monastery previously unknown to him.

[Col. 0175A] To Lord H., Father of the church of Flavy, and to the brothers with him, the brothers at Clairvaux send greeting.

[Note: The reading must be *Flaviacensis*, not *Flaviniacensis*, as is evident from the arguments set forth in the immediately preceding note.]

1. Having read your letter, we have learned that your Reverence is distressed on account of a certain monk who is with us.
