We too have been distressed by your distress, fearing that it may not be that sorrow of which the Apostle said to some: “You were made sorrowful according to God” (2 Cor. 7:9). For if it were according to God, it would not have moved you so far as to rebuke us—though unknown to you, still your brothers, and, if you please, your friends—so suddenly and sharply on this first occasion, when neither in person had you addressed us by word, nor in absence had you forewarned us by writing.

You marvel, as you write, that we received Brother Benedict.

[Note: The printed editions read “G.”; but in not a few manuscripts, “B.” The Corbie manuscript, of the best authority, gives the full name, “Benedict,” and from it we also restore the superscription of the following letter in preference to the other readings.]

You threaten us unless we quickly restore him to you. You cite to us the Rule: that a monk is not to be received from a known monastery (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 61), taking it for granted, of course, that yours is not unknown. But what if it is known to others, provided that it is unknown to us? For although, to use your own words, “the fame of your religious life has spread so widely that your church is known even at Rome,” nevertheless we, who are certainly situated far short of Rome, have somehow been passed by in such a way that we have had up to this time not even a slight acquaintance with any one of you—whether abbot or monks—nor with your dwelling-place itself, nor with your religious life and manner of living; nor do we remember that any mention of you was ever made to us.

Nor is this surprising, since we are separated from one another by many stretches of land, different provinces, and dissimilar languages; nor are we merely in distinct bishoprics, but do not even live in the same archbishopric. We suppose that we are forbidden to receive monks not from monasteries known to anyone whatever, but only from monasteries known to us. Otherwise, since there is no monastery which is not known to someone, no monastery remains from which anyone can be regularly received.

How then shall that be fulfilled which Blessed Benedict either commands or permits: namely, that a foreign monk is not only to be received to dwell as a guest for as long as he wishes, but, if found useful, is even to be urged to remain permanently? (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 61.)

2. Yet we acted otherwise with respect to the aforesaid brother. When he came and humbly asked to be received by us, he was first refused; then he was admonished to return to his monastery. But as he did not consent, he withdrew to a hermitage near us and lived there quietly for about seven months, suffering no accusation in the meantime. But since he did not consider it safe to live alone, after his first refusal he was not ashamed to request again from us the very thing he had formerly sought.

When once more we urged him to return, and asked the reason for his departure, he said: “My abbot employed me not as a monk but as a physician.”

[Note: In former times both clerics and monks practised medicine. Christianus Lupus proves this concerning clerics in his notes on various letters of the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, p. 100 ff. Various examples of monks are likewise available, one notable instance being found in Lupus of Ferrières, Letter 72, concerning Dido, abbot of Sens. In more recent law medicine is forbidden to both.]

“He compelled me to serve; indeed, he himself, through me, served not God but the world, when, so as not to incur the ill will of secular princes, he forced me to treat even tyrants, robbers, and excommunicated persons. When I had pointed out, now privately and now publicly, the danger to my soul, and had made no progress, I finally, relying on the counsel of certain wise men, flee my condemnation, not my community; destruction, not religious life. Advise one seeking salvation; open to one who knocks.”

Seeing his constancy, hearing his reason, and finding no accusation against him, we allowed him entrance, approved him when received, bound him when approved, and retain him now professed. We did not compel him to enter, nor shall we compel him to leave. Indeed, if we expelled him, he would not return to you, as he himself declares, but would withdraw even farther from you. Therefore cease, brothers, cease to assail the innocent with such undeserved disputes, and to disturb us with futile letter-writing. For not even accumulated insults will provoke us to reply to you otherwise than with what reverence requires; nor will threats frighten us from retaining the monk whom we believe ourselves to have received according to the Rule.

69. LETTER LXVIII. TO THE SAME PERSONS. On the matter above.

To the reverend brothers of Flavy—to Abbot H. and [Col. 0177A] all the other brothers—Brother BERNARD sends greeting.

1. It belonged to your moderation, good brothers, to be content with our earlier satisfaction concerning your earlier complaint and now to cease troubling those who have not deserved it. But since you have joined worse evils to the former ones and have again sent us seeds of quarrels—which may they not germinate, just as the earlier ones did not germinate in us—still, lest by not answering we seem to acknowledge a fault which does not exist, we make this second truthful answer also to your insolent accusations.

This is our entire fault, as we judge it; this is the great injury we did you: that we received a monk—alone, a stranger, poor, pitiable, fleeing danger to his soul, diligently seeking his salvation, knocking, pleading—or that, having received such a man in such a manner, we do not then expel him without cause, lest by destroying again what we built we make ourselves transgressors. For this we are judged violators of the Rule, of the canons, and of natural law itself.

For you object indignantly: why have we presumed to associate with ourselves one who was yours and excommunicated by you, something which we ourselves would not wish another to do to us? But what shall we answer concerning the excommunication, when you satisfy yourselves on that point on our behalf, since you undoubtedly know that he was received by us before he was excommunicated by you? But if he had previously been received, provided that it was regularly done, you certainly directed the sentence of your curse no longer against one who was yours but against one who was ours. Whether that was rightly done, see to it yourselves.

2. It remains, therefore, to be known—and this alone is at issue between us—whether he was received reasonably. Since you cannot deny that a monk may regularly be received from an unknown monastery, you maintain that yours was known to us. We deny it, and you do not believe us. But if you do not believe us when we simply deny it, believe us even when we swear it. In the Truth which is God, we tell you: we neither knew you nor know you; we received the letters of persons unknown and wrote back to persons unknown. We indeed felt your goads and disturbances, but had not yet recognized the goaders and disturbers themselves.

Yet you bring forward, to convict us of feigned ignorance, an argument which you deem invincible: namely, that those whose abbot’s name and monastery’s name we put in our letter cannot be unknown to us. As though, as soon as we know the names of things, we therefore know the things themselves! Thus it greatly benefits me to know the names Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael, if from merely hearing the names I am already blessed through knowledge of those blessed spirits themselves. I have made no small progress, I say, because I learned from the Apostle how to name paradise and the third heaven, if, without being caught up with the Apostle, I already know from names alone the heavenly mysteries and have heard the ineffable words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter.

Fool that I am: though I know my God’s name, I still groan daily, uselessly, and sigh in vain, saying with the Prophet, “I shall seek your face, O Lord” (Ps. 26:8); and, “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3); and, “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4).

3. But what do we do to you which we would not wish done to ourselves? You think that we do not wish a monk leaving our monastery to be received in another. Would that you could save all who have been entrusted to us without us! If one of ours should flee to you out of a desire for greater perfection and a stricter life, not only would we not complain if you assisted him in such a pursuit, but we earnestly ask you to do so. We would not complain of being offended, but would confess that in this matter we had received great help.

Next, you deny what we had heard concerning you: that by your command or consent Brother B., while he was with you, served secular persons in the medical art; and you accuse the very man who said this of falsehood. Whether he lied, we do not know; let him see to that. But this we know: whether he did these things through himself, as you admit, or through you, as he testifies, he was meanwhile in great danger. Who could be so inhuman as not to aid such a man in peril if able, or not to give him counsel if he knew?

Still, if, as you assert, he was not compelled by obedience but ran about here and there, selling his skill for the desire of private gain and the curiosity of wandering, what reason was there for his departure from you? Was it because at last, through the strictness of pastoral discipline, what had formerly been permitted him was no longer permitted? Why then, when he was already with us, did you promise him quiet in the cloister in order to persuade him to return, unless you knew that this was what the man wanted and remembered that he had sought it? But having obtained among strangers what he could not obtain among his own, lest he abandon certainties for uncertainties, he retained what he was already enjoying, despising what was offered him too late.

4. Therefore cease, brothers; cease troubling a brother about whom you have no great need to be anxious, unless perhaps—God forbid!—you seek your own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and love your own comfort from him more than his salvation. For since he had always been a wanderer among you and, as you write, contrary to his profession and his abbot’s command, spent for his own uses what he earned by his skill, let whoever loves him rejoice that, by God’s mercy, he has been healed among us.

For we bear witness concerning him that he now wanders nowhere upon any pretext, but perseveres quietly in the monastery; poor among the poor, he lives without reproach, not rendering void, as you say, but keeping firm and whole the first pledge which he promised among you but did not keep—namely, through conversion of conduct and most obedient way of life, without which one deceives oneself who trusts in stability of place.

We ask you, brothers, that your indignation may now rest and our disturbance cease. But if not, do what you wish, write what you wish, persecute as much as you wish: charity bears all things, endures all things. For our part, it is now resolved that we shall love you sincerely, regard you reverently, and treat you with brotherly familiarity.

LETTER LXIX. TO GUIDO, ABBOT OF TROIS-FONTAINES

[Note: He was the second abbot of Trois-Fontaines, already mentioned in Letter 63. In 1129 he succeeded Roger, the first abbot, whose death is mentioned in Letter 71. We read in Book I, chapter 13 of the *Life of Saint Bernard* that Roger was the first abbot and that Guido, when Roger’s office ended in 1127, gave him his hand; in the following year Guido attended the Council of Troyes with Bernard and Hugh of Pontigny. Later he considerably advanced and enlarged his Order by founding four monasteries: La Chalade; Châtillon in the diocese of Verdun; Orval in the diocese of Trier; and Hautefontaine in the diocese of Châlons.

The monastery of Trois-Fontaines, the first daughter-house of Clairvaux, was built in 1118 in the diocese of William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, through his agency, as William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric, testifies in Book I, chapter 13 of the *Life of Saint Bernard*. Its beginnings, still somewhat obscure, it is worthwhile briefly to elucidate.

In the *Acts of the Bishops of Châlons* is recited the charter of Bozo, seventh bishop after William, by which he attests that a part of the forest called Luis, transferred by Alard and the other regular canons of Saint-Saviour, was bestowed for the foundation of a monastery. It reads thus:

“Nothing provides lasting security so much as when things given to pious and faithful churches are committed to writing with diligent care. Therefore I, Bozo, by the grace of God bishop of Châlons, make known to all present and future that Hugh, count of Troyes, left in the hands of William, bishop of the church of Châlons, that division of the forest called Luis which he had ordered to be made by Peter, provost of Vitry, and by the chief men of the same forest, namely Milo of Sera, Walter, Vierd, and others, for the priest Alard and the other brethren in the Oratory of Saint-Saviour, situated in that same district, who wished to live canonically and according to rule. He instructed Alard to receive from the brethren of the church of Compiègne what he asked from him, and to have the bishop confirm for him what they granted. All these things the inhabitants of that place gave, through the hands of William, bishop of Châlons, to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, with Count Hugh’s consent, for the building of an abbey; and this was done.”

From this you see that Hugh the count, rather than William, ought to be reckoned founder of Trois-Fontaines; Hugh has been discussed above in the notes to Letter 31. What became of the further clause concerning the grant of the brethren of Compiègne we learn from the following document, first brought forth from the archive of the monastery of Compiègne:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Geoffrey, dean of the holy church of Compiègne; John, cantor; and we, the whole community of that place together, wish all persons, future as well as present, to know that at the request of our lord King Louis, his consort Queen Adelaide, Count Theobald, the venerable men Goslin, bishop of Soissons, Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Guarin, bishop of Amiens, and the lord abbot of Clairvaux, we granted for habitation to Brother Guido, abbot, and the monks serving God with him there, a certain place called Trois-Fontaines in the forest of Luis, which wholly belongs by right to our church. And lest this should be removed from memory through the long lapse of time, we caused it to be committed to writing.

“It therefore pleased us that the said monks should possess that land, the wood, and whatever, from land belonging to our church wherever it lies, might thereafter accrue to them in the same forest, without prejudice to the boundaries of others; … and that they should hold freely and peacefully in perpetuity whatever right of ours was in it. This was therefore confirmed by the present chirograph, confirmed also by a seal, and strengthened for the knowledge of posterity by the marks of the persons present: Goslin, bishop of Soissons; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Guarin, bishop of Amiens; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; Geoffrey, dean; John, cantor; Odo and Haimo, provosts; Rainard, abbot of Saint-Bartholomew; and Theodoric, abbot of Saint-Eligius of Noyon. Done at Compiègne in public chapter, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130.”

From these matters the reliability of those times may be seen: the grant made by Hugh, without written documentation, remained in force until 1154, when Bishop Bozo began to govern the church of Châlons; and the grant of the men of Compiègne came twelve years after the monastery’s foundation.

The abbey of Hautefontaine, situated in the same diocese of Châlons, is said, as we have already stated, to have proceeded from Trois-Fontaines. Concerning its endowment we have received the following from the most illustrious abbot of that place, de Noailles:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. B. [Bozo], bishop of Châlons. We wish present and future persons to know that Theobald, the worthily reverend abbot of Der, with the common assent of his whole chapter, through the intervention of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man of the highest religious devotion, granted to the church of Hautefontaine, where Guarin was then abbot, the whole part belonging to the church of Der of the tithes from what they shall cultivate with their own ploughs in the parish of Hauteville. This was done in the presence of the abbot of Clairvaux, Theobald abbot of Der, Arald abbot of Saint-Urban, Guarin abbot of Hautefontaine, Amalucus the monk, and John, lay brother of the same place. In order that this gift may remain ratified and inviolate, we have ordered this present document to be confirmed with the impression of our seal by the hand of Manno, our chancellor.”

There is another abbey of Trois-Fontaines, or of Saints Vincent and Anastasius at Trois-Fontaines near Rome. The election of Abbot Turold, discussed in Letter 306, belongs to that abbey.]

He instructs Guido, who had erred in the consecration of the chalice through a lack of wine caused by the negligence of the ministers.

1. We have learned why you are distressed. We commend you for being distressed, but only if not excessively so. For, unless I am mistaken, you are sorrowful, as the Apostle says, “according to God” (2 Cor. 7:9); and there is no doubt that sorrow of this kind will one day be turned into joy. Therefore, dearest brother, be angry, but do not sin. Yet you will sin no less by being angry too much than by not being angry at all. For not to be angry where anger is called for is to be unwilling to correct sin; and to be more angry than is called for is to add sin [Col. 0180A] to sin. If it is evil not to correct sin, how will it not be evil to increase it?

If judgment concerning guilt depended upon the outcome of events, even your great sorrow would not be blameworthy, where it were established that the fault also had been great. For the holier the thing concerned, the graver the fault appears. But since the cause of actions, not their material, and the purpose of intention, not their outcome, distinguishes faults and merits—as the Lord says: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness” (Matt. 6:22–23)—in examining also the act you committed, one must attend, I think, not so much to the majesty of sacred things as to investigate one’s own intention.

Now our Prior and I, weighing the matter carefully both within ourselves and in discussion with one another, have found in it your ignorance and the negligence of those ministering, but plainly no one’s malice. And certainly you know very well that nothing is good unless it is voluntary. Can that, then, be a great evil which is evidently not voluntary? Otherwise, if what is done unwillingly earns no grace when it is good, but much punishment when it is evil—that is, if, in one and the same matter, evil is imputed while good is not accepted—then whoever thinks this may maintain, if he wishes, that malice conquers wisdom, not wisdom malice.

2. Yet, to satisfy your rather troubled conscience, and lest this mishap perhaps be a warning of some graver evil still hidden in the monastery, we impose upon you, by way of penance, that until Easter you daily chant the seven penitential psalms, prostrating yourself seven times, and receive seven disciplines. [Note: That is, recite; for in this sense *decantare* is commonly used among the ancients. “Saint Ambrose,” says Bede in his letter to Egbert, in Waraeus, “while speaking of the Faith, admonishes believers always to chant the words of the Creed in the morning hours.”] Let him who ministered to you at that Mass make satisfaction in the same manner. But concerning the man who had noticed it beforehand [Note: Some manuscripts read *apparaverat* (“had prepared”). Yet, with most witnesses, I think *apparuerat* is preferable; that is, “had observed it”: in French, *qui s’en était aperçu*.] and forgot to put wine into the chalice—whose fault in this we judge the greater—we leave the matter to your discretion, if you too think so. Certainly, if word has gone out among the brethren, let them all, each individually, receive a discipline, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6:2).

Then, because, though late, once the negligence was discovered you poured wine into the chalice over the particle of the consecrated Host, we commend this; nor do we think anything better could have been done in so serious a crisis. For we judge that the liquid, although not changed into Christ’s Blood by its own proper and solemn consecration, was nevertheless sacred through contact with the sacred Body. [Note: Besides the scholastics, James of Vitry holds the same opinion in his *Western History*, p. 427; this author sets out the present case on p. 444. See our commentary on the *Roman Order*; see also our Edmond Martène, *On Monastic Rites*, book II, chap. 7.] Yet they say that some other writer held a different opinion: namely, that this sacrifice cannot exist without the three elements—bread, wine, and water—so that, if any one of these should be lacking, the others are not consecrated. But on matters of this kind, let each person abound in his own judgment.

3. But I, in my foolish judgment, if what happened to you had happened to me, would have wished, as a remedy for the evil, to do one of two things: either what you did, or at least to repeat the holy words from the place where it is said, “Likewise, after supper had been taken,” and thus complete what remained of the sacrifice. [Note: See the general rubrics of the Missal, chapter “On Defects of the Matter,” article “On Defect of Wine.”] For I should not have doubted concerning the Body already consecrated. For, according to the Church’s rite, I learned from the Church herself what she too received from the Lord: namely, that bread and wine are placed upon the altar together, though the sacred mysteries are not made from them simultaneously. Therefore, since by ecclesiastical custom the Body is made from the bread before the Blood is made from the wine, if through forgetfulness that which is to be consecrated later is placed there later, I do not see how this delay of the subsequent element can take anything away from the sacred things that precede it.

For I think that, if after making His Body from the bread the Lord had chosen to suspend for a while, or even wholly omit, the consecration of the wine, the Body which He had made (*fecerat*; another reading, *fuerat*, “had been”) would nevertheless have remained; nor would things yet to be done prescribe terms to things already done. Nor do I deny that bread and wine mixed with water ought to be placed together; indeed, I affirm that it ought not to be done otherwise. But it is one thing to blame negligence, another to deny efficacy; one thing, I say, to complain that something has not been done well, another falsely to assert that it has not been done at all. This, for the present, is what I have said and thought on this matter, without prejudice either to your judgment, if you know something better, or to that of anyone who judges more soundly.

## 72. LETTER LXX. TO THE SAME PERSON

He teaches what sort of mercy ought to be in a shepherd, and urges him to reconsider the sentence pronounced upon a transgressing monk.

[Col. 0182B]

To Lord Abbot GUY, Brother BERNARD: the spirit of knowledge and piety. [Note: This heading too has been restored from the Corbie manuscript, no. 553.]

Considering this miserable man’s wretched condition, I do indeed pity him; but I fear that I do so in vain. Yet I do not think that I pity in vain merely because, though he remains in his misery, my mercy may nevertheless not be fruitless for me. It was not private advantage that inclined me to this mercy; rather, the misery of my neighbour and fraternal sorrow pressed it upon me from the depths of my heart. For mercy is an affection that is neither restrained by the will nor subjected to reason; since a person does not draw it into himself by a voluntary impulse (*motu*; another reading, *nutu*, “nod”), but it itself necessarily compels devout minds, by its feeling, to compassionate those in distress. Thus, even if it were a sin to pity, however much I wished otherwise, I could not help pitying.

Reason or will can indeed withhold an effect from affection; but can either uproot the affection itself? Let those who comfort me depart from me, saying that “my prayer shall return into my own bosom,” while he for whom it was sent forth is not yet converted. Nor do I listen to those who flatter me by bringing forward, “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him” (Ezek. 18:20), while the wicked man still lingers in his wickedness. No, I say: I do not accept consolation where I see a brother’s desolation.

Therefore, sweetest son, if your devout mind is similarly moved—or rather, because it is not moved otherwise—although this unhappy man seems to you to have unhappily undergone every regular stage of his departure from the monastery and his return to it, nevertheless, because he himself thinks otherwise, the complaint which he humbly brings must be heard not only patiently but willingly. Perhaps some reasonable occasion may be found for restoring so desperate a salvation—something which, as your experience rightly understands with me, can indeed be obtained with difficulty within the community, but much more difficultly outside it.

Therefore, after taking the counsel of all the brethren, do not disdain carefully to reconsider all the judgments you have made against him, so that by your humility his obstinacy may be healed, if in this way it may perhaps be discovered how he may yet once more be received regularly. Nor need one fear in this reconsideration that the just and merciful God will be displeased, if mercy triumphs over judgment. [Note: Of the eight manuscript copies of this letter which we have seen, five contain the following addition—namely, two Cistercian copies, one from Val-des-Lucs, one from Corbie, and a fifth from Mont-Fulcard; it is lacking in three Colbert manuscripts. After the final words, “mercy triumphs over judgment,” the addition is as follows:

“I recount to you, by way of example, a similar matter which I remember happened to me. Once, while a certain brother (another version: Bartholomew) was still alive, because he had angered me on a certain day, I was moved by fury and, with threatening face and voice, ordered him to leave the cloister. He departed at once and went to one of our granges, where he stayed. When this became known and we wished to recall him, he replied that he would return only if we received him in his former rank and not in the last place, and not as a fugitive, but as one expelled without deliberation and without judgment. For he said that he ought not to undergo regular judgment upon returning, since it had not been observed in expelling him. Because of his response and my action, since I suspected my own judgment on account of carnal affection, I referred the matter to all the brethren for decision. Accordingly, in my absence, it was decided that his reception was not subject to a regular sentence, since it was clear that his expulsion had not been carried out regularly. If, then, in the case of one who had departed only once, such consideration of mercy was shown, how great ought we to think it should be in this man at so critical a point of necessity?”

This entire addition seems wholly alien to Bernard’s genius, character, and other deeds. That outburst of fury, that precipitate expulsion of a monk from the monastery, could never have occurred in so great a man; zeal was indeed in him, but tempered by gentleness and clemency, as is evident even from this letter, where he urges that so much mildness be shown to a deserter. Indeed, even if the holy man had fallen into this fault, he would rather have laboured to wash it away by penance and cover it in silence; nor would he have descended to such imprudence as to bring before Abbot Guy as an example something both contrary to Bernard’s purpose and likely to become an occasion of scandal for Guy. It seems altogether likely that this was first written in the margin of some manuscript, perhaps a Cistercian one, by an abbot, and then transferred from the margin into the text. Some others may have received it from that manuscript, but certainly not the Clairvaux manuscripts, which carry greater weight in this matter.] Farewell.

## LETTER LXXI. TO THE MONKS OF THE SAME PLACE

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1227.] He explains that he has delayed his visitation until now not through negligence but while awaiting a suitable opportunity; he consoles them over the death of Abbot Roger.

[Col. 0183B]

Let it not be thought negligence that I have not yet come to you. We care for you as for our own inward parts. If a mother can neglect the care of the child of her womb, then perhaps I too may be suspected and accused of negligence. We have therefore awaited, and still await, an opportunity, so that when we come our visitation may not be without fruit.

Meanwhile, let not your heart be troubled over the departure of your father. God will provide you, as we hope, another worthy man in his place; yet you will not lose this one either. For though he has been transferred, he has not been taken away. Only, he who had been especially yours will be shared also with us. Therefore, until I come, act manfully; let your heart be strengthened; and let all that you do be done in charity. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXII. TO RAINALD, ABBOT OF FOIGNY

[Note: Foigny, in the diocese of Laon, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, was begun as a foundation in 1121 by Bishop Bartholomew, according to a charter cited in the notes on Guibert, p. 659. There Elbert, or Eilbert, one of ours and abbot of Saint-Michael in Thiérache, is said to have ceded the site for the establishment of a monastery. The first abbot of Foigny was Rainald, to whom this letter is addressed. On Foigny, see Letter 5 and book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 25.] He shows how far he is from a desire for praise; that Christ’s yoke is light; and that he rejects the title of father, being content to be called brother.

To his most beloved RAINALD, BERNARD his own—not father or lord, but brother and fellow-servant—what is due to a most dear brother and faithful fellow-servant.

1. First, do not be surprised if I am alarmed by titles of dignity, [Note: Namely, “Lord” (*Domnus*, for that is how it should be read) and “Father.” Certainly a remarkable example of modesty in Bernard: that he should be alarmed by titles of dignity in which others revel, indeed even more than in the dignities themselves. A similar example, besides those mentioned above in the notes to Letter 11, occurs in the *Life of Blessed Mechthild*, chap. 10: “Sister Mechthild,” says the author, “insisted on being called without the addition ‘Lady’; she despised every lofty designation; but the custom of the house and the Rule of the monastery required that she be called lady and abbess.”

As to the first title, Augustus, according to Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, chap. 53, always recoiled from the designation “lord” as from a curse and reproach; and Tiberius, once called “lord,” regarded it as an insult. Thus later writers, using a humbler word and dropping a letter by syncope, are found to have called holy men, bishops, and other persons *domni* down to Bernard’s own time. Thus Sulpicius Severus, Letter 2: “They announce,” he says, “that Lord Martin has died.” Thus Gregory the Great, book I, letter 6, and book VII, letter 127; likewise throughout the letters of Desiderius of Cahors and in Gregory of Tours, *History*, book IX, chap. 42. From these sources the practice spread and took root among Spaniards and Italians. Indeed, among the later Greeks, in a similar case, κυρός (*kyros*, “lord”) is customarily used in place of τὸ κύριος (*to kyrios*, “the lord”), as our Hugo Menard most learnedly observed in his notes on the *Concordance of Rules*, chap. 70.

Saint Father Benedict mentions this title in the Rule, chap. 63: “But since the abbot is seen to act in Christ’s place, let him be called lord and abbot, not by his own assumption, but for the honour and love of Christ.” Although, by the authority of the Rule, this name is granted to the abbot alone, by the practice of later times it was extended also to monks initiated into the priesthood, as was the title “father.” On this subject see Menard at the cited place; Haeften, book III, *Disquisitions*, treatise 4, discussions 4 and 5; Julius Nigronus, commentary on Rule 22 of the Society of Jesus.] since I feel myself unworthy of the things themselves. It is fitting for you to act as you do, but it is not expedient for me to agree with you. For if you think that you must observe, “Outdoing one another in showing honour” (Rom. 12:10), and “being subject to one another in the fear of Christ” (Eph. 5:21), and if you understand that the word “one another” is not placed in vain in both passages, then you understand that both injunctions fit me equally.

But if you think that you must observe that saying of the Rule, “Let the younger honour their elders” (*Rule of St Benedict*, chap. 63), then the opposite teaching comes to my mind from the rule of Truth: “The first shall be last, and the last first” (Matt. 20:16); “Let him who is greatest among you become as the younger” (Luke 22:26); “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20); “Have they appointed you ruler? Be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1); “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy” (2 Cor. 1:23); “Do not be called rabbi by men”; and “Call no one your father upon earth” (Matt. 23:8–9).

Therefore, as much as I am raised by your favours, so much am I weighed down by these burdens. Hence I rightly do not sing but lament in the Psalm: “Though exalted, I have been humbled and troubled” (Ps. 87:16); and, “Because, lifting me up, you dashed me down” (Ps. 102:11). Yet perhaps I would express what I feel more truly thus: he who exalts me humbles me, and he who humbles me exalts me. You, therefore, by exalting me cast me down, and by lifting me up press me down.

But lest you press me down so as to crush me, I am consoled by these and similar testimonies of Truth, which in a wonderful way raise me up while checking me, and instruct me while casting me down; so that, being cast down from that very source from which I also advance, I chant with complete gladness: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me, that I may learn your ordinances. The law of your mouth is good for me beyond thousands of gold and silver” (Ps. 119:71–72). This is the miracle wrought by the word of God, living and effective; this is what that Word through whom all things were made works most graciously and most powerfully; this, finally, is what makes Christ’s yoke sweet and his burden light (Matt. 11:30).

2. I delight to wonder how light the burden of Truth is. Is that truly light which does not weigh down its bearer but lifts him up? What burden is lighter than one which not only does not burden, but itself bears everyone upon whom it is imposed to be borne? This burden could make a virgin womb pregnant, but could not weigh it down. This burden was itself supporting the arms of the aged Simeon, whose support it had offered itself to be. This burden also caught up Paul, though set in a heavy and corruptible body, even to the third heaven.

I seek among things whether perhaps I may find something like this unburdening burden, and I think of birds’ wings, which I may in some fashion compare with it. For in a singular manner they make their substance both more massive and more agile. A wondrous work of nature! From what makes the material bulkier, the load becomes lighter; and as it increases in mass, so much does it decrease in weight. This characteristic of wings clearly expresses a likeness to Christ’s burden: they themselves carry those by whom they are carried.

And what shall I say of a four-horse chariot? Attached to a beast of burden, it increases the load which the animal could not move by itself, yet makes it easier to carry. A burden is added to a burden, and it burdens less. Thus, when the chariot of the Gospel was added to the most grievous burden of the Law, it increased perfection and lessened difficulty. “His word runs swiftly,” it says (Ps. 147:15). That word, known formerly only in Judaea, and unable to extend itself farther because of its own weight—for it weighed down even Moses’ hands so that they drooped—was lightened by grace and set upon Gospel wheels; it went swiftly into all the earth and flew most rapidly to the ends of the world. But I have strayed far too far.

3. Therefore, beloved friend, cease now to overwhelm me rather than raise me with undeserved honours; otherwise, though with friendly intention, you join yourself to the company of those who are hostile to me. They are those concerning whom I am accustomed to complain to God alone in prayer: “Those who praised me swore against me” (Ps. 102:9). To this complaint of mine I hear God immediately answer and attest that it is true: “Indeed,” he says, “those who call you blessed lead you into error” (Isa. 3:12). And I say: “Let them therefore at once be turned back in shame, who say to me, ‘Well done, well done!’” (Ps. 70:4).

Yet, lest this be thought a curse or imprecation sometimes hurled by me against any adversaries whatsoever, I must explain how I understand it. I pray that all who think of me beyond what they see in me, or hear something from me, may be turned back—that is, may recoil from my praises, toward which they are unknowingly carried too far, and draw back their foot. How? Namely, when they come to know more fully the person whom they praise too extravagantly, and consequently blush either at their own error or at their friend’s discovered worthlessness.

In this manner, both classes of those who harm me—those, namely, who wish me evil and commend me flatteringly, and those who, though innocently, nevertheless harm me by praising me kindly but excessively—may be turned back and ashamed. That is, may I appear so lowly and contemptible to them that they are ashamed to have praised such a person so highly, and thus cease to praise indiscreetly. Therefore, against both kinds of praisers I am accustomed to arm myself with those two verses: against the ill-disposed, with the former, “Let them be turned back and put to shame who desire evil for me”; but against the well-disposed, with the latter: “Let them be turned back at once, ashamed, who say to me, ‘Well done, well done!’”

4. Therefore, to return to you: since, following the Apostle’s example, I ought not to lord it over your religious life but only to rejoice with you; and since, according to the Lord’s word, our one Father is in heaven while all of us are brothers, I rightly repelled from myself with the shield of truth the lofty titles of lord and father by which you thought to honour but not burden me. In their place I call myself more fittingly brother and fellow-servant, both because of the same inheritance and because of our equal condition, and lest, if perhaps I usurp for myself what belongs to God, I hear from him: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my honour?” (Mal. 1:6).

I do not deny that I have toward you the affection of a father, but I refuse the authority. For I embrace you, I think, with no less affection than a father’s. So much for the title.

5. Now, to answer the rest of your letter: I too could with good reason make the same complaint about your absence that you make about mine, were it not that God’s will must be preferred to our feelings and our advancement—as you yourself do not deny. Otherwise, when would I allow you, my most dear and very necessary companion—so obedient in action, so zealous in inquiry, so useful in deliberation, so ready in recalling matters—to be far from me, if Christ were not the reason? Blessed are we if we remain thus to the end, always and everywhere seeking not what is our own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ.

## 75. LETTER LXXIII. TO THE SAME PERSON

He instructs Rainald, who is excessively anxious and complaining about the office of prelate entrusted to him; he urges that aid and consolation should rather be given to his monks than sought from them.

[Col. 0187B]

To his most beloved son, the abbot of Foigny: the spirit of fortitude. [Note: Thus from the Corbie manuscript. Elsewhere the heading is omitted.]

1. Beloved son Rainald, you lament over your many tribulations, and by your devout complaints stir me too to lament. For I cannot but grieve when you grieve, nor hear of your troubles and anxieties without myself being troubled and anxious. But since I had foreseen these very evils which you complain that you have encountered, and foretold them to you, if you remember, I think that you ought to bear foreknown things more lightly and not trouble me where you can spare me.

For I am sufficiently, indeed more than sufficiently, afflicted by being without you, not seeing you, not enjoying you, my sweetest consolation; so that I almost regret having sent you far from me. And although charity compelled this, nevertheless, sent away by whatever necessity so that I might not see you, I mourn you as lost. Therefore, when on top of this you strike me, as it were, with the staff of your faint-heartedness—you who ought to have been for me a staff of support—you heap sorrow upon sorrow and add torment to torments. If it is devout in me not to conceal any of your distresses, it is nevertheless hard in you to disclose them all to one so afflicted. What need is there to make one already sufficiently anxious more anxious, or to torment a father’s heart, wounded by his son’s absence, with still heavier pains?

I shared my burden with you as with a son, as with one necessary to me, as with my faithful helper. See how you ought to bear your father’s load. For if you bear it in such a way that you do not lighten me but rather weigh me down more, you are burdened indeed, but I am not relieved.

2. This burden is the burden of souls—and of weak souls. Those that are healthy do not need to be carried and, for that reason, are not burdens. Therefore, whenever you find among your own people anyone sad, faint-hearted, or murmuring, know that you are his father and his abbot. By consoling, exhorting, and rebuking, you perform your work; you bear your burden, and by bearing them you heal those whom you bear by healing them.

But if anyone is so sound that he helps you more than he is helped by you, recognize that you are not his father but his equal, not his abbot but his companion. Why then do you complain that the company of certain persons with you burdens you more than their consolation benefits you, when you alone have been given to all as consolation? You are, as it were, healthier than all and stronger than all, so that by God’s grace you may suffice to console all and need no one’s consolation. Finally, insofar as you are burdened, you gain; and insofar as you are helped, you diminish your rewards for yourself. Choose, therefore, whichever you prefer: those who help you by burdening you, or those who burden you by helping you. The former earn merit for you; the latter rob you of merits. For those who are companions in labour will without doubt also share in its reward. Therefore, knowing that you have been sent to help, not to be helped, recognize yourself as the vicar of him who came to minister, not to be ministered to.

I wished to write more for your consolation, but it was unnecessary. For what need is there to fill dead parchment with superfluous words when a living person speaks in person? When you have seen the Prior, I think this will suffice you and your spirit will revive at his presence, so that you will no longer seek the consolation of writing. Meanwhile, you may be refreshed by the consolation of his words; and in him and through him, do not doubt that my own spirit also has been sent—the spirit which in your letter you asked might be sent to you—if indeed I could send it in any way. For, as you well know, he customarily shares with me the same counsel and the same will.

## 76. LETTER LXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

Bernard had wished Rainald to abstain from troublesome complaints; now he directs that he be kept informed about Rainald’s affairs.

[Col. 0188C]

I hoped, dearest friend, that I would receive some relief from my concern for you if, unless you informed me, I did not know of your troubles. Hence I remember writing to you in another letter, among other things: “And if it is devout in me not to conceal any of your distresses, it is nevertheless hard in you to disclose them all to one so afflicted” (Letter 73, no. 1). But behold: from what I thought my cares would be lightened, I confess that I feel myself more heavily burdened. For before, I either grieved or feared only those things which I learned from you when you informed me; now, what evil can ever occur that I do not fear? Indeed, in the words of your Ovid (*Heroides*, Letter I, verse 11):

> When have I not feared dangers worse than the real ones?

For insofar as I am uncertain about everything, I suspect everything, and am often compelled to contract real sorrow over false things. A mind once touched by love is not allowed to remain its own master. It fears what it does not know, grieves over what it ought not, is troubled more than it wishes, and, from causes it would not choose, unwillingly suffers with another and reluctantly pities.

And since you see, son, that neither my anxious diligence nor your kindly prudence helps me in this matter, I beg you now: do not conceal what occurs around you, lest, where you think to spare me, you afflict me more. Make every effort, when you suitably can, to see that I have the little works of mine which you possess.

## LETTER LXXV. TO ARTALD, ABBOT OF PREUILLY

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1127. This Artald, or Artaud, was abbot of Preuilly. It should be read thus, not “of Pultaria”; see the notes to Letter 80. Preuilly was a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Sens, founded in 1118 by Count Theobald of Champagne and his mother Adela, as William of Nangis reports in his *Chronicle*, cited by Manrique in the *Annals* for that year. Nevertheless, Theobald did not yet possess the county of Champagne in that year, as you will gather from the notes to Letter 31. That this letter is addressed to the abbot of Preuilly, a Cistercian, and not to the abbot of Pultaria, is manifestly inferred from its context: Bernard says that Artald is most dear to him, not only because of their common purpose and profession, but also by reason of their former mutual companionship.] He dissuades him from founding a monastery in Spain.

[Col. 0189A]

To his sweetest friend and fellow-brother ARTALD, abbot, Brother BERNARD: greeting. [Note: This heading, like many others, was restored by the Corbie manuscript.]

Whatever grace and affection absent friends can confer upon one another, I think that I owe it to you and that you owe it to me, not only because of our common purpose and profession, but also by reason of our former mutual companionship. How warmly this devotion, so welcome to both and so much our duty, burns in each of us, we can recognize or make known more clearly in no way than by not concealing from each other anything we hear about the other which is perhaps unbecoming.

Now I have heard of you that you wish to establish an abbey in Spain from your holy community. This naturally fills me with great wonder: what reason, what plan, what benefit is there in your wishing your sons to go into exile, to a place so distant, to be sought out and built at such expense and labour, when near you there is a place where you can settle them, already built and well prepared? Nor, I think, can you excuse yourself on the ground that the place is not yours, since I know with certainty that it could very easily be yours if you wish. Would Lord Abbot of Pontigny, [Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript. In others, “Abbot P.” The place in question is Val-des-Lucs, where Artald, following Bernard’s counsel, built a monastery in 1127—the date of this letter—sending twelve monks there under Abbot Norpald.] who holds it, deny it if you asked? Indeed, if you wished to receive it, he would be very glad; not because it is not good, but because, as you know, he does not need it.

You and I alike must greatly fear that, if we do not carefully observe in our works what the Apostle says, “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:11), we shall soon be criticized for frivolity because we are young. Yet I trust that you will act more wisely and choose the place which is nearer and already built. You know that it is a burden to the friend who holds it, while it will be necessary for you. Farewell.

## 77. LETTER LXXVI. TO THE ABBOT OF THE CANONS OF SAINT PETER-OF-THE-MOUNT

[Note: In printed editions this letter has until now been headed “To the same person.” But we restore the true heading, and therefore the title, from the frequently cited Corbie manuscript. The abbey of Saint Peter-of-the-Mount was in the diocese of Toul, of the Order of Saint Augustine, not far from the stream Mortana, which flows into the Meurthe.] What should be done with a man who, after long residence in a religious house and habit, had returned to secular life and contracted a second marriage.

[Col. 0190A]

To the most reverend father, the abbot of the canons of Saint Peter-of-the-Mount, Brother BERNARD: the service of due affection.

Since it pleased your graciousness to consult our littleness about this brother, know that we have offered such counsel as seemed right to us, without prejudice to any sounder judgment. Therefore, not to burden you with a superfluous recounting of matters which you know, this is the sum of our counsel.

It is indeed dangerous, and perhaps unlawful, for a man, after long residence in the house and habit of religion, to have returned to the secular world; and for one who previously—and indeed while his wife was still alive and consenting—had maintained continence most firmly and for a very long time, to have entangled himself again most foolishly and dishonourably in second embraces. Yet because that marriage, whatever its character, was publicly and solemnly celebrated according to the custom of other people, and without complaint or legal challenge, it does not seem safe to us that he should leave her against her will, unless he is first supported by the counsel or command of episcopal authority, or else by ecclesiastical and canonical judgment. [Note: A certain man, having returned to the secular world after long residence in the house and habit of religion, married a wife. When Bernard was consulted, he does not make sufficiently clear what he thought about such a marriage. He calls it “dangerous” and “perhaps unlawful”; and because “the marriage, whatever its character, had been solemnly celebrated,” he did not think it safe for the unwilling wife to be left. Moreover, it is not sufficiently clear what sort of vow bound the man. Compare Bernard’s treatise *On Precept and Dispensation*, chap. 17, and the notes on that place.]

But because we believe that this very great danger to the man concerns you in no small measure—since, when he wished and earnestly requested you to confirm his purpose, you delayed too long in receiving him, and the devil, seizing the opportunity, cast him headlong into these evils—we wholly urge and counsel you in charity to strive by every means, expense, and labour within your power to free the unhappy man. That is, either approach the woman, so that she may leave him voluntarily and promise continence; or approach the bishop, so that he may order both to be summoned and, by what we believe can rightly be done through judgment, separate them.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO MASTER HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR

This letter too has been removed from this place and assigned a place among the Treatises in the second volume.

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Note: Written in the year 1127. The abbey of Saint Denis the Areopagite, apostle of France, stands two miles from the city of Paris, in the village of Catulliacum; it was among the most celebrated abbeys of Gaul, of the Order of Saint Benedict, and was founded by Dagobert, first French king of that name. Suger succeeded Adam, whom Abelard falsely accuses of infamous vices in the *History of My Calamities*, p. 19; see Duchesne’s notes there. He succeeded, I say, being elected in his absence in 1123. He was then with Pope Callixtus II, sent by King Louis the Fat on certain affairs of the kingdom of France. He died in 1152, at the age of seventy, and was buried in the church which he himself rebuilt, still seen in its exceedingly splendid cruciform plan: 390 feet long, 100 broad, and 80 high from pavement to vault, supported by sixty columns or piers; adorned with incomparable stained-glass windows, a choir paved with variegated marble and decorated with sixty upper seats, and with many tombs of kings and other nobles.

There, according to the annals of the said monastery, “by his diligence he restored the order of holy religion. For formerly, through the negligence of the abbots before him and of certain monks of that monastery, regular observance had been cast aside so completely from that place that the monks scarcely retained even the appearance of religion”—as Bernard himself also says here. See the notes to Letter 266.] He praises Suger, unexpectedly converted from vanity and outward splendour to concern for modesty and religious discipline; he sharply censures a cleric more devoted to courtly life than to the service of God.

[Col. 0191A]

1. A good report [Note: [Col. 0192D] Namely, of his conversion, no doubt brought about through Bernard’s admonitions about the year 1127, although the reform of the monastery of Saint-Denis by Suger, perhaps prematurely dated to 1123, is reported in the Chronicle of Nangis, in which Suger’s election is thus described: “Suger, a monk of Saint-Denis in France, renowned for his knowledge of the Scriptures, when he had been promoted only to the order of deacon, was returning from Rome, whither he had been sent by Louis, king of France, when, upon the death of his abbot Adam, he was chosen abbot. On his return he was first ordained priest, and afterwards, in the presence of the king, was blessed as abbot in his church of Saint-Denis by the archbishop of Bourges.”] has gone out into our land, doubtless to work together for good with the good wherever it may reach. For all who fear God, hearing what great things he has done for your soul, rejoice and marvel at so great and so sudden a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. Everywhere your soul is praised in the Lord; the meek hear and are glad. Even those who have not known [another reading: seen] you wonder, hearing only what you have become from what you were, and they glorify God in you. [Col. 0191B]

Moreover, joy and wonder alike are increased because you have immediately endeavoured to pour back upon your own people the counsel of salvation infused into you from heaven, and thus to fulfil what is written: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22:17); and: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, proclaim from the housetops” (Matt. 10:27).

Thus a vigorous soldier in battle—indeed, thus a devout and courageous commander of soldiers—when he sees his men perhaps turned to flight and everywhere being cut down by the enemy’s sword, though he sees that he alone might escape, yet chooses rather to die with them, without whom he would be ashamed to live. Therefore he stands in battle, fights bravely, and, running this way and that through the midst of the ranks amid bloody swords, terrifies the adversaries by voice and sword as far as [Col. 0191C] he can, and heartens his own men. Where he finds that the enemy presses more fiercely and danger more heavily threatens his companions, there he is present. He confronts the striker and aids the perishing, ready indeed to die for each one precisely because he despairs of all together. But while he strives for a little while to restrain and delay those who pursue, raising up such of his fallen men as he can and calling back the fugitives, it often happens that by a strong hand he obtains for his own men a deliverance as welcome as it is unexpected, and confusion for the enemy. At last they put to flight those before whom they fled; they overcome those whom they had scarcely withstood as victors; and those who had previously been in danger of their lives afterwards exult in victory.

2. But why do we compare so religious and courageous a deed [Col. 0192A] with secular examples, as though religion itself lacked examples for us? Was not Moses plainly certain, on God’s promise, that if the people whom he led perished, he himself would not only fail to perish with them but would moreover be sent into a great nation? Yet with what affection, what zeal, what stirrings of compassion did he come to their aid and oppose the wrathful One? Finally, offering himself for the sinners, he says: “If you forgive, forgive; but if not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. 32:31–32). A faithful advocate, who, because he does not seek what is his own, easily obtains all that he asks. Truly kind, who, as a head united to its members and cleaving to his people in steadfast love, will either save them with himself or cannot but undergo the same danger with them.

Jeremiah too, bound [another reading: joined] inseparably to his own people, though by compassionate affection rather than by consenting to their contention, in the face of their common exile and servitude despised his native soil and his own liberty [another reading: will]. For although, when the rest emigrated, he was free to remain freely in his country, he preferred to be led away captive with the people to whom he knew himself to be necessary even in captivity [another reading: perhaps]. Paul, doubtless in the same spirit, wishing himself to be accursed even from Christ for his brethren (Rom. 9:3), experienced in his own affection how true is that saying: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is harsh as hell” (Song 8:6). You see whose imitators you have shown yourselves to be. But I add also—him whom I had almost omitted—[Col. 0192C] holy David, who, seeing and grieving at the slaughter of the people, hurried to meet the smiting angel and begged that divine vengeance be transferred rather upon himself and his father’s house (2 Sam. 24:17).

3. Who set before you this perfection? I confess that I desired to hear such great things of you, but did not hope for them. Who indeed would have believed that, by a sudden leap, so to speak, you would occupy the heights of the virtues and reach sublime merits? But far be it that the immeasurable mercy of God should be measured by the narrowness of our faith or hope—he who works what he wills in whom he wills, hastening the work and lightening the burden!

For surely holy zeal censured your errors, not those of your people; it was provoked by your excesses, not theirs; brotherly murmuring grumbled against your person alone, not also against the abbey. [Col. 0193A] In short, they had called you alone to account. If you corrected yourself, nothing would remain exposed to accusation. Once you, I say, had changed, all the disturbance would at once subside and the uproar be quieted. The sole and entire matter which moved us was that manner and equipment of yours when you went abroad, which appeared somewhat too ostentatious. [Note: [Col. 0193D] Perhaps this is to be understood of the matter concerning which Bernard says in chapter 10 of the *Apology*: “I am lying if I have not seen an abbot lead sixty horses, and more, in his retinue,” etc.]

In short, if you laid aside your pomp and changed your manner, everyone’s indignation could easily be calmed. But you not only satisfied those who complained; you added what we may rightly praise. What work among human affairs could now justly be praised if this is not considered supremely worthy of wonder and praise? [Col. 0193B] Yet it is certainly not a human work, but a divine one: so great and so sudden a transformation of so many people at once. The conversion of one sinner raises great joy in heaven; what then of a whole congregation? And what of this one?

4. For from ancient times the place had been noble and of royal dignity; it was accustomed to serve the business of the palace and the armies of kings. Without hesitation or deceit, what was Caesar’s was rendered to Caesar; but what was God’s was not paid to God with equal faithfulness. [Note: [Col. 0193D] William of Nangis confirms this under the year [Col. 0194D] 1123, as has already been reported more fully above: “For through the negligence of the abbots who had preceded him, and of certain monks of that monastery, regular observances had been so cast aside from that place that the monks scarcely displayed even the appearance of religion.”]

We speak what we have heard, not what we have seen: the very cloister of the monastery, they say, was frequently crowded with soldiers, beset by business, resounding with quarrels, and at times open even to women. What heavenly, divine, or spiritual thing could be thought amid these circumstances? But now [Col. 0193C] God is given leisure there; continence is cultivated, discipline diligently observed, and attention is given to holy readings. For unbroken silence and perpetual rest from every secular clamour compel meditation upon heavenly things. Further, the labour of continence and the rigour of discipline are sweetened by the melody of psalms and hymns. Shame at the past moderates the austerity of the new way of life. The fruit of a good conscience, which is gathered in the present through patience, also produces a desire for future goods—a desire that shall not be frustrated—and hope that does not put to shame. Fear of the coming judgment yields to the devout exercise of brotherly love; for love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). The variety of holy observances drives far away weariness and sloth. [Col. 0193D]

We recount these things for the praise and glory of God, as author of all; yet not without yours, as his fellow-worker in all things. He could indeed have done them without you; but he preferred to have you as a partner in his works, that he might also have you as a partner in his glory. The Saviour rebuked certain persons because they made the house of prayer a den of thieves (Matt. 21:13). Therefore he will doubtless hold in favour the man who, in contrast, has laboured to rescue the holy thing from dogs and the pearl from swine; through whose zeal and diligence the workshop of Vulcan [Col. 0194A] seems to have been devoted to heavenly pursuits—indeed, God’s own dwelling restored to him—and restored to what it had formerly been, from a synagogue of Satan.

5. Certainly, we recount past evils not to bring confusion or reproach upon anyone, but so that, by comparison with former things, the splendour of what is new may appear more weighty and beautiful. Recent goods shine forth more pleasantly when compared with preceding evils. Like things become known from like things; but contraries, through contraries, either please more or displease more. Set black beside white, and by their mutual comparison they shine more distinctly even in their own colour. Thus ugly things placed beside beautiful make the beautiful more beautiful, while themselves becoming more ugly.

Yet lest any occasion of offence or shame intrude, we repeat to you also [Col. 0194B] that saying of the Apostle: “And such indeed you were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified” (1 Cor. 6:11). Now no entrance into God’s house lies open to secular persons, no access to holy things to the curious. No conversation with idlers is now mingled in; the customary noise of boys or girls is not heard. The holy place is open and accessible only to Christ’s children, of whom it is said, “Behold, I and my children are with me” (Isa. 8:18); it is kept with due care and reverence solely for divine praises and the discharge of sacred vows.

With what joyful ear the martyrs—whose very great multitude ennobles the place itself—hear these cries and noises of the children! And in return they answer them with no less cry of their own affection: “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” [Col. 0194C] (Ps. 152:1); and again: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises” (Ps. 46:7).

6. While hands strike breasts and knees the pavements, while altars are heaped with vows and devout prayers, cheeks are stained with tears, chambers resound with groans and sighs, and instead of legal disputes the sacred roofs echo with spiritual songs: nothing is more pleasing for the citizens of heaven to behold; nothing more delightful is offered to the highest King. For what else does he mean when he says, “A sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. 49:23)?

Oh, if someone had opened eyes such as the prophet, praying, revealed to his servant! (2 Kgs. 6:17). He would doubtless see how “the princes go before, joined with those who sing psalms, amid maidens playing timbrels” [Col. 0194D] (Ps. 67:26). He would see, I say, with what care and what rejoicing they attend those singing, are present with those praying, enter into those meditating, watch over those resting, and preside over those ordering and administering. The heavenly powers surely recognize their fellow citizens; and for those who receive the inheritance of salvation they diligently rejoice together, strengthen, instruct, protect, and all of them provide all things for all.

I should call myself happy if, while still alive, I could at least hear these things, though I cannot see them because I am absent. But [Col. 0195A] you, brethren, are far happier, since it is granted you also to practise them. Yet blessed above all is he whom the author of all good has deigned to make worthy of the primacy of so great a good. We rightly rejoice with you especially, dearest brother, in this prerogative; for through you indeed exists all that we admire.

7. Perhaps you are burdened by our praises; but you ought not to be. For what we say has nothing in common with the flatteries of those who call good evil and evil good (Isa. 5:20), and thus lead into error whomever they declare blessed. It is flattering but dangerous praise when “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unrighteous man is blessed” (Ps. 9:3). Whatever favour we show proceeds from love and, so far as we understand, does not exceed the bounds of truth. [Col. 0195B] He who glories in the Lord—that is, in truth—glories securely. We did not call evil good, but called evil what was evil.

But if we barked boldly at evils when we saw them, [Note: [Col. 0195D] From this it appears that Bernard had previously written against the lax conduct of the monks of that monastery, perhaps in the *Apology*, as is noted shortly.] ought we now, when good has come, to be silent rather than bear testimony to good? Otherwise we shall be convicted of having been destroyers rather than reformers, and of preferring to bite rather than amend, if we fall mute over good things after protesting so loudly against evil things. The righteous man rebukes in mercy; the sinner flatters in impiety: the former in order to heal, the latter in order to conceal what needed healing.

You need suspect nothing, among those who glorify the Lord by fearing him, of that oil of the sinner with which they formerly used to make your head fat. We praise you because you are doing that for which we plainly do not flatter you; [Col. 0195C] rather, in you God’s gift fulfils what you sing: “Those who fear you shall see me and be glad, because I have hoped exceedingly in your word” (Ps. 118:74); and likewise: “Many shall praise his wisdom” (Sir. 29:12). Behold, very many proclaim your wisdom—but they are those who detested your former folly.

8. I want you to take delight in the praises of such persons, who fear to stroke faults as much as to disparage virtues. These are true praisers: they are accustomed to praise good things in such a way that they do not know how to flatter in evil things. For there are false praisers, but true detractors, whom Scripture mentions in saying: “The sons of men are vain, the sons of men are liars in the balances; that they may deceive, they themselves are altogether vanity” (Ps. 61:10). These plainly are [Col. 0195D] to be avoided, in accordance with the counsel of the Wise Man: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10).

Sinners therefore have both milk and oil—pleasant indeed, but poisonous and deadly. “His words,” that is, the flatterer’s, “are softer than oil, yet they are darts” (Ps. 54:22). The righteous man too has oil, but oil of mercy, sanctification, and spiritual joy. He also has wine, which he pours into the wounds of the arrogant soul. For when he sees one grieving and contrite in heart, he is accustomed to soothe sorrow with the oil of mercy. When he rebukes, he pours in wine; [Col. 0196A] oil, when he comforts—wine indeed without hatred, oil without deceit. Therefore not every praise is flattery, just as not every rebuke springs from rancour of heart.

Blessed is he who can say: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). When you have put this far from yourself, you have shown yourself worthy of the oil and milk of the saints.

9. Let the sweet but cruel mothers now seek for themselves babes in Babylon, whom they may nurse with the milk of death, caress with flattering favours, and nourish for everlasting flames. But the foster-child of the Church, having experienced from the breasts of wisdom the sweetness of better milk, has now begun to grow by it unto salvation; now, filled with it, he pours forth, saying: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the choicest ointments” [Col. 0196B] (Song 1:1–2). And this he says to his mother.

But having likewise tasted and proved how sweet the Lord is, he says to him, as to a truly most sweet Father: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have stored up for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30:20). Our desire has surely been fulfilled. For formerly, when I grieved to see you sucking with such avidity from the lips of flatterers the food of death and the tinder of sin, [Note: [Col. 0196D] Bernard here alludes to Suger's name.] I desired this for you and groaned, saying within myself: “Who will give you to me as a brother, sucking the breasts of my mother?” (Song 8:1).

Let those smooth and deceitful nurses now be far from you, who, while blessing you to your face, exposed you to the insults and mockery of all; and their present “Well done!” (Ps. 34:21) made you a public spectacle for the world—indeed, made you a spectacle for the world. [Col. 0196C] If they still mutter, say to them: “If I still pleased you, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). Those whom we pleased in evil things, we cannot likewise please in good things, unless perhaps, changed themselves, they first begin to hate what we were and then at last to love what we are.

10. In our times two new and detestable presumptions have arisen in the Church. One of them—to mention it with your leave—is that former ostentation of your way of life. But this, through God as its author, has been corrected: to his glory, to your crown, to our joy, and as an example to all. God can also bring it about that we may soon be consoled concerning the other.

I am both very reluctant [Col. 0196D] to bring so hateful a novelty forward and burdened by the thought of passing it over. Sorrow urges my tongue to speak, but fear binds it—fear only lest I offend someone by publicly revealing what troubles me, because truth sometimes produces hatred. Yet concerning hatred of this sort, I hear Truth herself, which produces it, comforting me thus: “It is necessary,” she says, “that scandals come.” And I think that what follows does not touch me at all: “But woe to that man through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). For when faults are censured and scandal arises from it, he who has done what deserves rebuke is himself the cause of the scandal, not he who rebukes.

Finally, I am neither more cautious in speech [Col. 0197A] nor more circumspect in judgment than the man who says: “It is better that scandal arise than that truth be abandoned” (St Gregory the Great, *Homily 7 on Ezekiel*, shortly after the beginning; and St Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will* and *On the Predestination of the Saints*). Though I do not know what use it is if I keep silent about what the world cries aloud, and, when the stench has been thrust into everyone’s nostrils, I alone conceal the pestilence and do not dare to protect my own nose with my hand against the foulest odour.

11. For whose heart does not burn with indignation, whose tongue does not at least murmur secretly, at a deacon serving, contrary to the Gospel, both God and mammon—raised so high in ecclesiastical honours that he seems inferior not even to bishops, yet so entangled in military [Col. 0197B] offices that he is preferred even to dukes? I ask: what kind of monster is this, that, while wishing to appear both cleric and soldier at once, he is neither? [Note: [Col. 0197C] That deacon was Stephen of Garlande, seneschal or steward of the king of France, whom some wrongly confuse with Stephen the chancellor, who later became bishop of Paris, as Duchesne rightly proves in his notes on Abelard. Concerning him Teulfus writes as follows in book II of the *Annals of the Monastery of Morigny*: “When William, brother of the steward Anselm, had died, Stephen, brother of both, became chief of the royal household. In preceding generations it had been unheard of for a man performing the office of deacon also to hold, after the king, the chief place in military affairs. This industrious man, endowed with secular wisdom, flourishing above other mortals of our time in temporal prosperity through both the revenues of many ecclesiastical benefices and his familiarity with the king—such that some said he commanded rather than served him—gave his niece in [Col. 0197D] marriage to Amaury of Montfort, together with the honour of Rochefort which had come to the girl through the marriage. Then, puffed up and forgetful of himself, he rendered Queen Adela hostile to himself by very frequent vexations; and as their enmities increased and the king was disturbed, he was deprived of his office and expelled from court. But he, as though seized with a kind of madness, strove with all his strength to disturb the kingdom; and, relying on the assistance of the valiant man in arms, Amaury, I mean, he set this country ablaze with wars,” etc.

Unless I am mistaken, this same Stephen—for he is also called of Guarlande—receives a bad report in Ivo, bishop of Chartres, letter 87, where, before the cardinals, he accuses the people of Beauvais of choosing him as their bishop: “For, setting aside all canonical obedience, they chose as bishop, at the king’s will and that of his female companion, a certain unlettered cleric, a gambler, occupied with other such debaucheries, found far removed from holy orders, and once expelled from the Church for public adultery by the legate of the Roman Church, the archbishop of Lyons. This aforesaid intruder is called Stephen of Guarlande; if at any time the way to episcopal ministry should be opened to him by apostolic authority, it is manifest that in our times a ruinous silence has been imposed upon the canonical laws. For how shall we reach the fountain of knowledge if we are not permitted to enter by those who hold the key?” Thus Ivo. Bernard also won this Stephen for God.]

It is an equal abuse in either direction: whether a deacon is assigned to the service of the royal table, or the king’s steward serves at the mysteries of the altar. Who indeed would not wonder—nay, detest—that one person should both lead an armed army, being himself armed, and, clothed in alb and stole, proclaim the Gospel in the midst of the church; that he should sound the trumpet to summon soldiers to war and announce the bishop’s commands to the people?

Unless perhaps—what is more intolerable—he is ashamed of the Gospel, in which the chosen vessel so greatly glories (Rom. 1:16; 2 Tim. 1:8, etc.); ashamed to be seen as a cleric and judging it more honourable to be thought a soldier; preferring the court to the Church, the king’s table to the altar [Col. 0197C] of Christ, and the cup of demons to the cup of the Lord. [Col. 0198A] This seems all the more credible because, though he holds in the Church not a few honours, but as many as even the canons endure only unwillingly, he nevertheless, as they say, boasts more in the name of the one office that he has gained in the palace than in being called by any of the others. Though he is archdeacon, dean, and provost in different churches, none of these titles pleases him so much as to be called the king’s steward.

O new and hateful perversity! Is it therefore more fitting to be called the servant of a man than of God? Is being called an official of an earthly rather than a heavenly King judged a higher dignity? Whoever prefers military service to clerical service, and the court to the Church, is plainly convicted of preferring human things to divine and earthly things to heavenly. Is it then more splendid to be called a steward than a dean or archdeacon? Certainly—but for a layman, not a cleric; for a soldier, not a deacon.

12. A remarkable but blind ambition: to delight more in lower things than in higher, and, though the lines had fallen to him in pleasant places, to embrace dung with insatiable desire and esteem the desirable land as nothing! He utterly confounds the orders and makes an equally refined misuse of both offices, since on the one side the pomp, not the military service, of secular life delights him; and on the other, profit, not religious observance.

Who does not readily perceive in this how great is the dishonour, no less to the kingdom than to the priesthood? For just as it is manifestly not consonant with clerical dignity to serve under the pay of kings, so it is not consonant with royal majesty to administer the affairs of warriors through clerics. [Note: [Col. 0198C] Here Bernard alike reproves the cleric who serves the king in military matters and censures the king who commits military duties to a cleric. Indeed, both are blameworthy: the former because he does not recognize the dignity of his own state; the latter because he bestows offices of court and military service without selection or distinction of persons, employing clerics where laymen ought to be employed.

Something similar occurred also under another king of France, Louis [Col. 0198D] XI.
