When Cardinal Balue, bishop of Évreux, was sent by him to Paris to inspect the soldiers, and carried out that task, unworthy of a bishop, dressed in linen garments and riding a mule, Chabannes, master of the horse, took it most ill. He approached the king and asked that the province of visiting the collegiate body of canons at Évreux, or of examining those to be ordained clerics there, be entrusted to him. “It is remarkable,” said the king, “with what face you dare to ask for this. Do you not know that such a duty is far too alien to your person and condition?” Then Chabannes said: “Why,” he asked, “is it less fitting for me to compel clerics into order than for a bishop to inspect soldiers?” These words caused astonishment in the king and laughter in the rest. Guaguin, *History*, book X; Claude d’Espence, a man celebrated in France for learning and holiness, book II, chapter 6, *Digression on the First Epistle to Timothy*; Bosquier, *Christian Plutarch*; Dorozet, *Gallic Apophthegms*.]

For what king ever set over his army an unwarlike cleric [Col. 0198C] rather than some very brave soldier? And what cleric has ever judged it not equally unworthy of himself to be made subject to the services of any lay person whatsoever? The very emblem which he bears upon his head is more suited to royal pomp than to service; likewise, royal preeminence rests more upon arms than upon psalms.

Certainly, if what is taken from one had perhaps, as often happens, accrued to the other—if, for example, the king’s humiliation had raised the cleric higher, or the cleric’s degradation had contributed to royal honour (as when a noblewoman marries a common man: she is lowered by him, but he is raised by her)—if, I say, either king gained from cleric or cleric from king, then perhaps an evil which existed on one side might somehow have had to be tolerated. But now, when the diminution of either benefits neither, but each rather greatly detracts from the other’s dignity—since, as was said, it neither becomes a cleric to be or to be called the king’s steward, nor a king, except by the hand of warriors, to hold the reins of the kingdom—it is very remarkable how each authority permits this: how either the Church does not reject a military deacon [another reading: soldier], or the court does not disdain a clerical commander. [Col. 0199B]

13. I wished, and perhaps ought, to press these points more sharply and at greater length, had the brevity of a letter not indicated that I should refrain, especially because, fearing to offend you, I spared the man, since they say he has long been bound to you in intimate friendship. But I should not want you to have a friend against truth. If nevertheless you persist, prove yourself a true friend, [Col. 0199C] and take pains that he too may be a friend of truth. Only then will friendships be true if they are joined in the fellowship of truth.

But if he will not heed you, hold fast what you have, and join the tail of the victim to its head; [Note: [Col. 0199D] That is, join the end to the beginning. He exhorts him to perseverance, alluding to the rite of the Law which commanded the victim’s tail to be offered together with it. Exodus 29; Leviticus 3. Radulf gives the tropological explanation: “The tail,” he says, “which is the end of the body, is a symbol of completion and perseverance in holy works.” Hence also St Gregory, *Morals*, book I, chapter 40: “The tail,” he says, “is commanded to be burned for God, so that every good thing which we begin may also be fulfilled by the end of perseverance.” The same, *Homily 25 on the Gospels*: “By the precept of the Law,” he says, “the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in sacrifice. For the tail is the end of the body, and he sacrifices well who carries the sacrifice of a good work through the due action to the end.”] and take care to make the tunic, now variegated by God’s grace, reach to the ankles; for beginning will avail nothing if, God forbid, perseverance should fail. Let this be the end of the letter, where you have been admonished concerning the end of good.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO ABBOT LUKE

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Not at all of Mont-Cornillon near Liège [Col. 0200D] (now called Beaurepart), as Picard and Horstius wrongly thought; rather, of the monastery of Cuissy, of the Premonstratensian Order in the diocese of Laon, as the Premonstratensian library states and Bernard himself sufficiently indicates, when he professes surprise that Luke consulted him rather than William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, as nearer at hand, or someone from nearby Prémontré. Concerning Luke and the monastery of Cuissy, Hermann the monk writes: “He”—Bartholomew, bishop of Laon—“also built another monastery of clerics in the place called Cuissy, and appointed as abbot there Lord Luke, a religious man.” So he says in *The Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon*, book III, chapter 16.]

He warns that cohabitation with women must be avoided. And what should be done concerning a brother fallen into sin.

1. You have shown us something good in yourself, dearest brother, and very rare: you have not only not despised the warnings of one your inferior, [Col. 0199D] but have even thanked your admonisher, wisely attending not to the person from whom, but to the matter concerning which, you were warned. I too give thanks to God that my presumption has gained favour rather than deserved indignation. Therefore, holding fast the mark of such great humility in you, we now warn you with greater confidence of what we warned before.

We beseech you, by that blood which was shed for souls, that the danger to those bought at so great a price be not lightly regarded—a danger especially to be feared, and not without reason, from the cohabitation of men and women, by those who, long struggling in God’s school against the devil’s temptations, can say from their own experience with the Apostle: “We are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:11). Finally, how diligently you ought to heed not my counsel but that of the Apostle himself on this matter—indeed, his command, crying openly, “Flee fornication” [Col. 0200B] (1 Cor. 6:18)—let the experience of that brother who has now fallen so shamefully teach you. You have deigned to consult even our insignificance concerning him.

I wonder, however, why you thought fit to seek me, so remote, as your counsellor, when you have close at hand a wise man of our Order and one especially devoted to your house: namely, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry. Nor do I doubt that at Prémontré there are men of counsel, prudent and faithful in resolving doubtful matters.

2. Nevertheless, since this pleased you, see to it yourself why it pleased you; I shall not restrain my lips. If the brother himself had first confessed his fall, however grave and shameful it might have been, he ought both to have been treated and not driven away. But now, because the stench of so great an evil has emerged from another source, it is still necessary to work, if possible, for his cure, though in another way. For perhaps it is not expedient that he be permitted to remain any longer among you, lest—as you wrote, and not without reason you fear—the little and newly formed flock be contaminated by such an infection. Yet a father’s heart must not be altogether closed against his son, however sinful he may be.

I judge it a devout counsel for the father and a safe one for the son if you seek a way for him to be received in one of the more remote houses of Lord Norbert, where, under stricter discipline and with a change of place but not of purpose, he may do penance until at some time, when it seems good to you, he is recalled to his proper place. For it may perhaps not be expedient for him to transfer to our Order, given your own.

And indeed, concerning what you wrote—that he had often said he held us bound by our promise, because we would receive him if he came with permission—he himself denied this in our presence. Certainly, if it does not please you to send him anywhere to dwell in one of the places I have mentioned, or if perhaps he does not consent although you desire it, or if, though both of you are agreeable, no one can be found willing to receive him, then he must either, under the pressure of necessity, be dismissed with letters to go wherever he wishes for the salvation of his soul; or, by the dispensation of merciful grace, be retained in his own place—provided it can be ensured how every opportunity for repeating or spreading this shameful conduct may there be wholly removed from him. And enough concerning him.

3. There is another matter among you about which, with the same frankness I ordinarily use, I shall not hesitate to say what I think. I mean that mill which the lay brothers [Note: [Col. 0201D] Concerning lay brothers, see below, Letter 143. A similar Letter 404 concerns avoiding the company of women.] are obliged to guard, [Col. 0201B] and where they must endure the frequent presence of women. If you take my advice, one of three things will be done: either women’s access to the mill will be prohibited altogether; or the mill will be entrusted for guarding to some outsider and not to lay brothers; or the mill itself will be entirely abandoned.

## LETTER LXXX

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Written about the year 1130.]

### TO GUY, ABBOT OF MOLÈSME

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Guy, the second abbot of the monastery of Molesme after St Robert, concerning whom see Letters 43, 44, and 60.]

He consoles one afflicted by a grave injury; but teaches that vengeance must be moderated by mercy.

How deeply I sympathize with you in this adversity of yours, of which I have heard, God, the knower and inspirer of all good affections, knows. But when I consider again not through whom, but from whom, this tribulation has been sent, I hope to rejoice with you as much over the prosperity soon to come as I sympathize with you over the present distress—provided that you too do not lose counsel amid disturbance, but think the same with me and receive evil from the hand of the Lord as equably as good, with holy Job (Job 2:10). Or rather, following the example of holy David, know that you ought not so much to be angry over these great evils, even though done by your servants, as to humble yourself under the mighty hand of God, who beyond doubt sent them to do evil to you (2 Sam. 16:10).

But because their correction plainly belongs to you, as they are servants of the church entrusted to you, it is fitting that these wicked servants be corrected for so nefarious a presumption, and that the monastery’s loss be compensated in some measure from their goods. Yet lest you appear to avenge your own injury rather than to punish their fault, I ask you—and in asking, advise you—not so to weigh [Col. 0201D] what they deserve that you fail to consider what is worthy of you: namely, that mercy may triumph over judgment and God may be glorified in your gentleness. [Col. 0202A]

Moreover, we admonish that son of yours—dear enough to me also for your sake and for his own—with your voice and our spirit, not to become so intoxicated by his own indignation, even if it is just, that he forgets the Lord’s command by which we are bidden, to one who strikes us on one cheek, to offer the other also (Matt. 5:39).

## LETTER LXXXI. TO GERARD, ABBOT OF PULTARIUM

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Written about the year 1130. Horstius thinks the reading should be *Prulliaciensis*; but wrongly, as the manuscripts, indeed the very words of the letter, protest. From them it is sufficiently clear that Bernard is not speaking to any abbot of the Cistercian Order, such as the abbot of Prully; otherwise he would by no means have appealed to the Count of Nevers to reform the abuses of that monastery. From this observation Gerard appears to be added to the succession of abbots of Pultarium, from which he has hitherto been omitted. The monastery of Pultarium was of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Langres, [Col. 0202D] founded by Count Gerard not far from his own castle, where he was afterwards buried with his wife Bertha. See the notes of our Acherius on the Works of Guibert of Nogent, p. 953 ff.]. He clears himself of an unjust accusation.

I neither remember having written anything to the Count of Nevers accusing you personally, nor is it true. Yet if I sent letters to that same prince on behalf of your church, [Col. 0202B] I believe that I acted not against you but for you. For I had heard that, with your consent and advice, he had proposed to come and visit you, in order to ascertain whether the many evils reported concerning your house were true, and whose fault they were; so that whatever wrong he might find there might be corrected on the spot through his effort and diligence. [Note: [Col. 0202D] Namely, he had succeeded to the legal rights of Count Gerard, founder of the monastery of Pultarium.] If I endeavoured by my encouragement to strengthen so just and pious a purpose, I do not see how you can rightly complain that you have thereby been injured. For I think that I acted properly if, having zeal for the house of God, I urged the care of the man who was to correct it.

But whereas you argue, on Scriptural authority, that I have sinned, as one who did not first rebuke you: [Col. 0202C] know that I have no complaint concerning your person. I seek only, in charity, that peace may be made in your church. Finally, you will learn the truth of the matter more fully if, as you say, you bring the case itself to us. You may find me here on any day of the coming week that you please.

## LETTER LXXXII. TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT JOHN OF CHARTRES

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Written about the year 1128. It undoubtedly refers to Stephen, who, from being abbot of Saint John at Chartres, of the Order of St. Augustine, became Patriarch of Jerusalem at the beginning of 1128 after Gormond, according to Orderic Vitalis at the end of Book XII. In the third volume of the *Analecta*, p. 335, he is likewise said to have sent letters to Fulk, Count of Anjou, through William of Bures. Compare Letters 35 and 82, and Papebroch’s Preface on the Patriarchs of Jerusalem in vol. III for May.]. He dissuades him from relinquishing pastoral care and from a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

1. Concerning the matters on which you have been pleased to consult my insignificance, I had at first determined to make no reply: not because I doubted what I ought to answer, but because I judged it either presumptuous or superfluous to offer counsel to a man of counsel. Yet, [Col. 0202D] reflecting that what commonly happens to many—indeed, almost all—wise men occurs especially in doubtful matters, [Col. 0203A] namely, that they trust another’s judgment more than their own; and that those who readily clear up every ambiguity in the affairs of others are accustomed to hesitate more scrupulously in their own: I abandon my resolution, not, I think, unreasonably, and simply set forth what has seemed good to me, without prejudging one wiser than myself.

You informed me, unless I am mistaken, through the religious man Ursus, abbot of Saint Denis, [Note: [Col. 0203C] Ursus, or Ursio, fifth abbot of Saint Denis near Rheims, of Canons Regular of the Order of St. Augustine, later bishop of Verdun; concerning him see vol. XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 312. [Col. 0203D] When he was raised to the see of Verdun in 1129, Gilbert succeeded him at Saint Denis; but, having laid aside that dignity, he eventually returned to his own brethren and again assumed the government of the abbey: see Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 152. In the necrology of his abbey “Ursio, abbot of pious memory,” is commemorated on the fourth day before the Kalends of March.] that your thoughts suggest to you that you should leave your country and the house over which, by God’s appointment, you preside; go to Jerusalem; henceforth devote yourself to God and live for yourself.

Now for one advancing toward perfection, it may perhaps be expedient to leave one’s country, as God says: “Go forth from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. 12:1). But I do not at all see by what reasoning you ought to expose to danger the care of souls entrusted to you. What then? Does the freedom gained by laying down the burden entice you? But charity “does not seek its own.” Perhaps the sweeter taste of rest and leisure beckons you? But it is nullified by the loss of peace. I would gladly forgo any gain, even a spiritual one, that cannot be acquired except by scandal. For where there is scandal, there is undoubtedly injury to charity; and where charity is diminished, I wonder what profit, or what kind of profit, can be hoped for from spiritual exercise.

Finally, if each person prefers his own repose to the common good, who will now be able truly to say, “To me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21)? Where will be what the Apostle likewise says: “No one lives to himself, and no one dies to himself” (Rom. 14:7); and, “Not what is useful to me, but what is useful to many” (1 Cor. 10:33); and, “That he who lives may no longer live for himself, but for him who died for all”? [Col. 0203C] (2 Cor. 5:15).

2. But you say: “Then whence comes so great a desire in me, if it is not from God?” With your leave, I shall say what I think. “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. 9:17); and anyone not ignorant of Satan’s devices does not doubt that an angel of Satan, under the guise of an angel of light, pours into your thirsty heart a sweetness of this sort, more bitter, if I may so speak, than every kind of wormwood. And truly, who else could be the instigator of scandals, the author of division, the disturber of unity and peace, except the enemy of truth, the rival of charity, the ancient enemy of our race, and [Col. 0204A] the enemy of Christ’s cross—the devil?

For he through whose envy death entered the world still envies the good works which he sees you doing. And since he has been a liar from the beginning, he lies now also, promising better things that he does not see. For when would truth contradict that most faithful saying, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:27)? Or when would charity counsel scandal, charity which declares itself to burn at the scandals of all? (2 Cor. 11:29). Therefore he—that most wicked one, I say—opposed to charity through envy and to truth through falsehood, mingling false honey with true gall, while promising uncertain things in exchange for certain, introduces even true things in place of false ones: not in order to confer what you vainly hope for, but to take away what you fruitfully possess.

He goes about seeking how he may rob the sheep of a shepherd’s care, [Col. 0204B] so that they will certainly perish when there is no one to rescue them; and nonetheless subject the shepherd to that dreadful curse: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18:7). But I trust in the wisdom given you by God, that no wiles of the evil one will be able to draw or deceive you into entering, in hope of an uncertain good, upon a certain evil, and abandoning an equally certain good.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO SIMON, ABBOT OF SAINT NICHOLAS

[Note: [Col. 0203D] Written about the year 1129. Simon, originally a monk of Saint Nicaise near Rheims, became abbot of Saint Nicholas in the forest of Vedogium, in the diocese of Laon; see Herman, monk of Laon, Book III of the *Miracles of Blessed Mary*, ch. 18. He was the brother of William, abbot of Saint Thierry, mentioned above in Letters 85 and 86. See below, in vol. V, the Notice on the letter or book to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu.]. He consoles him in persecution. Pious undertakings do not always have their desired success. What a superior zealous for stricter discipline should do with his subjects.

1. Having learned from your letter, not without compassion, of the persecution [Note: [Col. 0203D] This also concerns the persecution suffered by Simon at the hands of his monks because [Col. 0204C] he had surrendered to the bishop of Arras certain altars—thus they called parish cures—on account of simony. On this matter we read letters of Samson of Rheims and Joscelin of Soissons to Innocent II, who had appointed them arbitrators in this cause; and also other letters of Eugenius III to Bartholomew of Laon, in which he states that he wishes to investigate the case of litigation between Alvisus, bishop of Arras, and G., abbot of Saint Nicholas. In Samson’s letter to Innocent it is said that Abbot Simon, “because his monks did not agree with him that those altars should be restored, left the abbey for some time and went into a distant region”; but that at last, recalled by his own brethren, they “preferred to be without those altars rather than without their abbot.” Hence may be inferred both Simon’s integrity and uprightness—under whom the monastery is said by Herman to have flourished “in religion and manifold possessions”—and the date of this letter, undoubtedly before Innocent’s pontificate, that is, before 1130. On Gilbert, Simon’s successor, see the note to Letter 399.] which you endure for righteousness’ sake, although Christ’s consolation in the promise of the kingdom may suffice you, we nevertheless faithfully offer what lies within our power: such consolation as we can give, and such counsel as we understand to be sound.

For who can without anguish see Peter stretching out his arms amid the waves? Who can without sorrow hear Christ’s dove, not singing but groaning, as though saying, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4). Who, I say, can without tears behold the tears of Christ himself, who even now raises his eyes from the deep mire to the mountains, from which help may come to him? Yet we, to whom you say that you look because of your humility, [Col. 0205A] are not mountains. We too, from the valley of tears, strive with laborious efforts against the snares of the resistant enemy and the violence of worldly wickedness; and with you we cry: “Our help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:2).

2. For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12); so that, although the will to live devoutly [variant: “to live”] never fails them, the ability to accomplish according to their good will is not always present. Just as it belongs to the impious constantly to oppose the good purposes of the devout, so it is not contrary to godliness that, because of the multitude of opponents, the just and holy desires of a few often remain unfulfilled.

Thus Aaron yielded against his will to the clamorous demands of a wickedly tumultuous people [Col. 0205B] (Exod. 32). Thus Samuel, unwillingly, anointed Saul for the same people when they disorderly demanded a king (1 Sam. 10). Thus David, though he wished to build the temple, was forbidden to do what he had piously intended because of the wars of hostile enemies, since he was a man of war (2 Sam. 7).

In like manner, venerable father, while not prejudging the counsel of wiser men, we advise you to temper for a time the severity of your purpose and of those who agree with you, so that you do not neglect the salvation of the weak. They who once consented to live under your rule in that Cluniac Order must be invited to a stricter life, not compelled. Those who desire to live more strictly should either be urged, out of charity, to accommodate themselves to the weaker as far as they can without sin; or be allowed there to maintain [Col. 0205C] what they desire, if this can be done without scandal to either party; or else be released from the community and joined to other brethren living according to their own purpose.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO THE SAME PERSON

He sends back a wandering monk [Note: [Col. 0205C] But such acts are not alike. For, according to the philosophers, final and impelling causes establish distinctions among actions. Thus things are alike only in the category of being, so that we may speak of them as the same; they are not alike in the category of morals. But let us hear Augustine expounding this axiom elegantly. “When good and evil persons do the same things and suffer the same things,” he says, “they are to be distinguished not by their deeds and punishments, but certainly by their causes. Pharaoh oppressed God’s people with harsh labours; Moses afflicted the same people, when they acted impiously, with stern punishments. They did similar things, but they did not intend to benefit in a similar way: the one was puffed up by domination, the other was inflamed by love. Jezebel killed prophets; Elijah killed false prophets. I think the merits of those acting, and those suffering, are different.

“Look also at the times of the New Testament, when the gentleness of charity had to be preserved not only in the heart but also displayed openly; when Peter’s sword was called back into its sheath by Christ, and it was shown that it ought not to have been drawn from its sheath, even for Christ. Yet we read not only that the Jews struck down the Apostle Paul, but also that Greeks struck down Sosthenes the Jew for the Apostle Paul. Does not the similarity of the deed seem to join both parties, while [Col. 0206C] the dissimilarity of their causes distinguishes them? Certainly God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all; certainly it is said of the Son himself, ‘Who loved me and delivered himself up for me’; certainly it is said also of Judas that Satan entered into him, [Col. 0206D] so that he might betray Christ. Therefore, since both the Father delivered up his Son, and Christ himself his body, and Judas his Lord, why in this delivering-up is God devout and man guilty, except because, in the one thing they did, the cause for which they did it was not one?”

And, after adducing many examples, he finally adds: “Let us learn, amid the similarity of deeds, to distinguish the minds of those acting.” Thus St Augustine, Letter 93, §§6–7.], but advises that the returned monk be treated more gently and mildly.

See to it: as you see, and not without reason, your wandering little sheep, contrary to our custom, has been held by us not for ourselves, [Col. 0206A] but for himself and for you; and this through such a stratagem—or rather, such a helpful intervention—that both the brother’s desire for a stricter life and your own eventual desire for the brother’s return have nonetheless been satisfied. I say this not because I wish to commend to you our goodwill in this matter—a goodwill which I could scarcely sufficiently demonstrate, as it is, by anything I might do—but that you may now be certain of what I remember having told you before: that restless minds, for whom the life in which they are does not suffice, are often restrained when they have experienced a stricter one.

You wrote that you wished to hear our counsel concerning the brother now reconciled. But I did not think it would be necessary, since he comes prepared not, as he is accustomed, to extort his own will from you, but, as is fitting, to submit to yours in all things. We beseech you that the severity which he greatly fears on entering again [Col. 0206B] may be mercifully moderated for his sake and with him in mind, and that he may be treated somewhat more gently than other fugitives are usually treated. For in similar acts [Note: [Col. 0206D] Bernard himself calls him Nicholas in the *Apology to William*, §4.] an unlike cause rejects a like judgment. For there is a great difference between one who flees the monastery through fear or hatred of religious life and one who passes to another through love and desire for that same life.

## TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF SAINT THIERRY

Here some insert the Letter to William, abbot of Saint Thierry, which was written as a Preface to the *Apology* addressed to the same man; see it prefixed there in vol. II.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO THE SAME WILLIAM

[Note: [Col. 0206D] Written about the year 1125. The Venerable William, once the delight of St Bernard, was born into a noble family in the city of Liège. He was sent to Rheims for his studies with another noble youth named Simon—whom a manuscript codex of Marmoutier containing several letters of Bernard testifies to have been [Col. 0207B] William’s brother. Spurning worldly delights, he entered with Simon the ascetic community of Saint Nicaise at Rheims, then famous for its regular observance. After happily completing his novitiate there, when both excelled in the renown of virtues, Simon was appointed to the abbey of Saint Nicholas of the Wood in the diocese of Laon, and William, in place of Geoffrey, who had been transferred to Saint Médard of Soissons, was set over the monastery of Saint Thierry near Rheims in 1120.

When the fame of Bernard’s holiness was spreading everywhere and drawing many to look upon and admire him, our William, then a private monk at Saint Nicaise, heard of the illness [Col. 0207C] which afflicted the holy man not long after his ordination and visited him with a certain abbot. After spending some time with him, he fastened the bond of that most intimate friendship in which they afterwards embraced one another mutually. “For William was affected by such sweetness toward Bernard, and by so great a longing to live with him in that poverty and simplicity, that if the choice had been offered him that day, he would have desired nothing so much as always to remain there with him in order to serve him.” *Life of St Bernard*, Book I, ch. 7.

From this arose the feeling of sorrow through which, taking too grievously the calumnies directed against Bernard, he induced Bernard to clear himself of the Cluniacs’ complaints in the elegant *Apology* written to him; see vol. II and the notes there. But William’s love for Bernard did not endure even these separations. Wearied indeed of the pastoral burden and most eager for Bernard’s companionship, after he had often been refused entrance to Clairvaux [Col. 0207D]—as is clear also from this letter—he finally renounced his office and transferred himself about 1135 to the Cistercian monastery of Signy, in the diocese of Rheims. For the manuscript catalogue of the abbots of that monastery testifies that he had been abbot at Saint Thierry for fourteen years and five months. This is supported by a charter of the monastery of Saint Nicaise at Rheims, in which Rainald, archbishop of Rheims, confirms possessions acquired by Abbot Jorann in 1135, Helinus, abbot of Saint Thierry, being witness; Helinus had succeeded William from the priorate of Saint Amand.

William professed stability at Signy about 1135 and, after spending several years in the utmost humility and modesty and in unremitting contemplation of heavenly things—which the manuscript Chronicle of Signy calls “his daily exercise”—passed to the world above about 1150; certainly after 1144, since the letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, of which he was the author, is dedicated to Haimon, prior, who [Col. 0208B] succeeded Geoffrey, the first prior, in that year; but before St Bernard’s death, for immediately after William’s death Ernald began Book II of Bernard’s *Life*, as you will understand from the notes to Letter 310.

The Chronicle of Signy writes thus concerning William’s death: “Having completed the course of his life with a holy end, he fell asleep in the Lord. His body was committed to burial in the cloister beside the entrance to the chapter-house.” Later, namely in the eightieth year after his death, Aegidius, ninth abbot of Signy, “raised,” continues the same Chronicle, “the bones of Lord William, abbot of Saint Thierry; of Arnulf, abbot of Saint Nicaise”—in the catalogue of the Abbots of Saint Nicaise he is called simply a monk—“and [Col. 0208C] of Gerard, abbot of Florennes,” whom William had as companions in conversion at Signy, “from the tombs in which they had lain until that time, and placed them with due honour in a certain shrine within the wall of the oratory and near the entrance of the church, on the cloister side.”

This is perhaps an extended account of William, but not an idle one. How highly Bernard valued him and how warmly he returned his affection is evident from Bernard’s own letters, especially Letter 85. There Bernard offers an elegant and wholly Christian reply to William, who had lovingly complained that, though he loved deeply, he was less loved by Bernard. It appears also from Letter 88 to Ogerius, where, unexpectedly mentioning William, he breaks out in these words: “But alas! Into what narrow confines of speech has the mention of such a man thrust itself, so that we are not permitted, as was fitting, to linger for a while upon a memory so sweet to us, because the letter is already demanding its end?”

Bernard also so fully approved William’s learning [Col. 0208D] and doctrine that he submitted to William’s judgment his book *On Grace and Free Choice*, which he dedicated to him. And to Luke of Cuisy, who consulted him on certain difficulties, he replied (Letter 79) that he wondered why, passing William over, Luke had sought Bernard’s own assistance. Certainly the man’s learning and piety breathe and speak through his outstanding writings, especially through that eloquent and truly golden letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, William’s last offspring, unless perhaps Book I of the *Life of St Bernard* be excepted. Since, in the preface—which we print in full here in vol. V—he provides a catalogue of his writings, there is no reason to dwell upon them further. More concerning him is found in the Notice to the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu in vol. V, and in vol. III of the *Library of Cistercian Fathers*.]. He gently reproves William, who complains that Bernard does not return equal offices of love.

[Col. 0206C]

To Lord Abbot WILLIAM, brother BERNARD: charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. [Note: [Col. 0206D] The superscription from the Corbie codex.]

1. If “no one knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man which is in him” (1 Cor. 2:11); if man sees only what is outward, because God alone looks upon the heart (1 Sam. 16:7), I wonder—and cannot sufficiently wonder—how and on what grounds you have been able thus to weigh and distinguish your love and mine toward one another, so as to pronounce judgment not only concerning your own heart but also [Col. 0207A] concerning another’s.

For it is an error of the human mind not only to think good evil and evil good, or truth falsehood and the reverse; but also to accept certainties as doubtful and doubts as certain. Perhaps what you say is true, namely, that you are loved by me less than you love me. But I am certainly sure that it is not certain to you. How then do you affirm as certain something of which it is certain that you are by no means certain? Strange! Paul does not trust his own judgment: “I do not,” he says, “even judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3). Peter mourns the presumption by which he deceived himself when he spoke about his own heart: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26:35). The disciples, not trusting their own consciences concerning the Lord’s betrayal, each replied: “Is it I, Lord?” (ibid.). David confesses [Col. 0207B] his ignorance concerning himself, praying and crying: “Do not remember my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7). But you, with I do not know what confidence, pronounce so openly not only on your own heart but on mine: “Though loving more,” you say, “I am loved less.”

2. These are indeed your words, which I wish were not yours, because I do not know whether they are true. But you too—if you know—how do you know? How, I ask, have you proved that we are more loved by you than you are by us? Is it from what you added in your letter: namely, that those of ours who come and go through your place bring you no token from us of favour or love? But what token, what proof of love do you demand from us? Does it perhaps trouble you that, although you have now written to us several times, I have not yet replied even once? [Note: [Col. 0208D] This, then, is Bernard’s first letter to William, and was accordingly written about 1125.] But when did I suppose that the maturity of your wisdom could take pleasure in the frequent scribblings of my ignorance?

For I knew him who said: “Little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18). When did you ever have need of my service, and lack it? [Col. 0208B] O God, who searches hearts and reins! You, the one sun of righteousness, illuminate the diverse hearts of your servants by diverse graces as by rays. You know, and I feel, that I love him by your gift and by his own merit; but how greatly I love him, you know and I do not. You, Lord, [Col. 0209A] who gave, know how much you gave—whether you gave him to love me, or me to love him. And how can either of us, to whom you have not said it, dare to say, “Though loving more, I am loved less,” unless perhaps he already sees his own light in your light—that is, recognizes in the light of your truth how intensely he burns with the fire of charity?

3. But I, Lord, am meanwhile content to see my darkness in your light, until you visit one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death; until, through you, the thoughts of hearts are revealed and the hidden things of darkness made manifest; and, when darkness has been driven away, nothing is seen in your light but light. I indeed feel, through your gift, that I love him; but I do not yet see in your light whether I love him sufficiently. For I do not know whether I have yet attained that love than which no one has greater: that one lay down his life for his friends. [Col. 0209B] For who shall boast that he has a chaste heart, much less a perfect one?

O Lord, who illumine my lamp, by which I now see and shudder at my darkness—my God, illumine also that darkness of mine, that I may see and rejoice in charity ordered within me, knowing and loving the things that ought to be loved, and how greatly and for what end they ought to be loved; unwilling that I too be loved except in you, and only as much as I ought to be loved. For woe to me if—as I greatly fear—either I am loved by him more than I deserve, or he is loved by me less than he deserves. Yet if the better ought to be loved more—and those are better who love more—what else can I say except that he loves me more, whom I do not doubt to be better; while I love [Col. 0209C] him less than I ought because I am less able?

4. But the greater your charity is—I speak to you, father—the less you ought to despise our capacity. For although you love more because you are more able, you nevertheless do not love more than you are able. We, however, although we love less than we ought, nevertheless love as much as we are able; and we are able only as much as we have received. Draw us after you, that we may lay hold of you and receive more with you, and so love more abundantly.

Why then do you strive to lay hold of us and complain that you cannot? You have laid hold of us, if you have paid attention; and you may still make us, whenever you wish, what we are—not what you hoped. For I do not know what else you perceive in us that we do not possess; and you pursue [Col. 0209D] for our sake what we are not. Therefore you do not catch us, because we are insufficient. Thus, as you rightly complain in your letter, it is God—not we—who fails you in us.

But now, if things such as those with which I have just trifled please you, command me, and I shall add more, so that, in obeying, I may not fear the charge of presumption. The little preface [Note: [Col. 0209D] Namely, the letter prefixed to the *Apology* addressed to the same William, which in most manuscripts is placed before this letter. Compare Letter 88, §3, and the other letters to William.] which you ordered sent to you I did not at present have at hand; for I had not yet dictated it, [Col. 0210A] because I did not think it necessary. Whatever you rightly desire for yourself or for your friends, may he who gave you the will also grant fulfilment according to your good will—father to be piously and most reverently honoured by every right of friendship.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO THE SAME PERSON

[Note: [Col. 0209D] Written about the year 1130.] He sends back a fugitive monk who has been harshly rebuked and should be rebuked. He advises William himself, who contemplates a change or private life, to persevere.

Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux, to his own, who is his.

1. You gave me this formula of greeting when you wrote, “His own, who is his.” Receive what is yours, and recognize that the appropriation of mutual belonging is a sign of unity of mind; and that one with whom I share a word is not distant from me in spirit.

Now I must answer your letter briefly, as time permits. When it came into my hands, the feast-day of the Nativity of our Lady [Note: [Col. 0209D] I suppose by the example of the Cistercians, whose monasteries are all dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, she began to be called “our Lady.” Hence Peter of Celle says of Bernard, in Book VI, Letter 23: “For he was the most intimate foster-child of our Lady, to whom he dedicated not one basilica only, but the basilicas of the whole Cistercian Order.”] had dawned; and the devotion rightly claiming me entirely for her allowed me to think of nothing else. Moreover, the messenger was hastening to return and scarcely waited until the next day, so that, now free from the feast, I might write this poor reply.

Therefore, having severely rebuked the fugitive brother, as one hard of heart, I could meanwhile do nothing better than send him back to the place from which he had fled [variant: “gone forth”]; since, according to our customs, I ought not to retain him in my house without his abbot’s consent. You too must rebuke him similarly and sharply, and summon him to humble satisfaction; [Col. 0210C] afterwards you should strengthen him by letters sent to his abbot on his behalf.

2. Since you ask particularly about our illness, I can tell you nothing more certain at present than that I have been ill and am ill: neither less than usual nor much more. The reason why I did not send the person whom I intended to send is that I feared the scandal of many souls more than danger to one body.

Now, lest I omit altogether any of the matters concerning which you gave directions, I turn also to you. You wrote that you wished to hear what I—supposing I knew all that concerned you—would have you do. But, unless I am mistaken, if I were to say that now, neither could you do it nor could I advise it. For I too desire what you desire concerning yourself, as has long not escaped me. [Note: [Col. 0210D] William desired, namely, after renouncing the dignity of abbot, to retire to Clairvaux; but since Bernard did not permit it, he withdrew to Signy, as was stated above in the note to Letter 85.]

Yet, setting aside equally, as is right, both your will and mine, I judge it safer to urge upon you what I think God wills concerning you, and not disadvantageous to you if I persuade you. Therefore, on my advice, retain what you retain; remain where you are, and strive to benefit those over whom you preside. Do not refuse to preside while you can benefit them. For woe indeed to you if you preside and do not benefit them; but a graver woe if, because you fear to preside, you refuse to benefit them.

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO OGERIUS, A CANON REGULAR

[Note: [Col. 0211C] Many criticize or ridicule this sort of title because it uselessly doubles words that are synonymous or have the same meaning, though in different idioms—as though there were canons who were not regular, or as though among regulars some were regular and others irregular. But see John Baptist of Signa, Book *On the Order of Canons*, ch. 2; and Navarrus, Commentary I *On Regulars*, on ch. 12, *Cui portio Deus*, question 1, where he teaches that not every repetition of words ought to be judged tautology. For even among jurists the repetition of the same clause or word has considerable force. See J. B. [John Baptist], § *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*. Add that the doubling of the same word among the Hebrews has a special force and increases or intensifies what is said: Ps. 86:5, “Man and man was born in her,” that is, many men; [Col. 0211D] Ps. 67:13, “King of powers of the beloved, of the beloved,” that is, of the most beloved; and often elsewhere. See Genebrard at the passages cited.

Moreover, we learn of which place Ogerius was abbot from the *History of the Restoration of the Monastery of Saint Martin of Tournai*, by Herman, monk of Tournai. There Oggerus, a religious canon of Mont-Saint-Éloi near Arras, is said to have been called to Tournai by Simon, bishop of Tournai, to preside over the church of Saint Médard; and there “upon the plain of the river Scheldt he built a stone church, with suitable offices, in honour of St Nicholas, gathered there many persons—clerics, laypeople, and women—and caused that abbey to be called Saint Nicholas of the Meadow.” This is found in vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 469. The dedication of the new church took place in 1125. Picard, from the notes of Denis Villery, canon and chancellor of Tournai, likewise testifies that Ogerius was the first superior of Saint Nicholas of the Meadow at Tournai of the Nervii.]. He disapproves the renunciation of pastoral care, even if undertaken from love of pious repose. Nevertheless, he instructs him how he ought thereafter to live as a private member in a monastery.

[Col. 0211A]

To brother OGERIUS, canon, to be embraced with all the affections of charity, brother BERNARD, a monk but a sinner: may you walk worthily before God unto the end.

1. If I seem to have replied rather slowly to your letter, know that it was rather the opportunity of a messenger that was lacking. What you are now reading for the first time, believe to have been dictated long ago; but, as I said, I delayed sending what I had not delayed writing because no bearer was available. Thus I read in your letter that you had laid down the burden of pastoral care, which you found grievous to bear, having scarcely obtained—indeed, wrung out—permission from the bishop by your importunity; and this only on condition that, remaining anywhere else within his bishopric, you should not withdraw from his jurisdiction. But since this did not please you, you approached the archbishop and, receiving from him assurance as from a superior authority, returned to your former place and to your abbot. There you ask to be taught by me how you ought thereafter to live: by an eminent teacher indeed, an incomparable master, who, when I begin to teach what I do not know, will then make known how little I know. Does a sheep seek wool from a goat, a mill seek water from an oven, a wise word from a fool?

Moreover, throughout the course of your letter you exalt me above myself and intersperse many commendatory things about me. Since I myself am not conscious of these, I attribute them both to your goodwill and to your ignorance, and forgive the latter.

[Col. 0211C] You see the outward appearance, but God sees the heart; and if I examine myself carefully beneath his dreadful gaze, it is certain that I know myself better than you do, insofar as I am nearer to myself. Therefore I trust more my own sight of myself than your opinion of what you do not see in me. If, however, you have perhaps heard something from me that could profit you, give thanks to God, in whose hand are we and our words.

2. You also make satisfaction to me because you did not follow my counsel, which had encouraged and warned you not to be broken in spirit, not to be overcome by faint-heartedness, but patiently to carry the burden laid upon you—a burden which, once undertaken, you were not permitted to lay aside. Concerning this, as you request, I myself make satisfaction for you. For, recognizing the dryness of my wisdom—or rather, always suspecting the rashness of my folly—when what I commend is not done, I neither dare nor ought to be angry, since I desire everyone to act more wisely than he has learned from me. Yet whenever my judgment is chosen and followed, I confess that I feel myself weighed down by a heavy burden, always awaiting the outcome with fear and never with security.

Consider, however, whether you altered my counsel in this matter prudently.

> [Note: Col. 0212C] Bernard had advised him not to renounce pastoral care, even out of love for personal quiet. Hence he now disapproves Ogerius’s action in not obeying that counsel; and, although Ogerius obtained permission from the bishop, he nevertheless judges him not secure, since the permission was extorted and ought rather to be called compulsion. He adds that Ogerius resists the divine ordering, since, having been promoted by God, he demotes himself; and he says much else to the same effect.
>
> Hence arises a grave question: is it not lawful to resign pastoral care and withdraw from crowds and affairs in order to devote oneself more peacefully to God and to one’s own salvation? The difficulty is increased by the many examples of holy men whom we know to have done this. Among lesser prelates there were very many, but there were also no few bishops, cardinals, and even some popes.
>
> Bruno III, Count of Altena, Archbishop of Cologne, having resigned his episcopal office, withdrew in 1119 to the Cistercian monastery of Altenberg. Eskil, Archbishop of Lund in Denmark, gave himself to private life at Clairvaux. Peter Damian, formerly a Benedictine monk and later cardinal and bishop of Ostia, after for several years vigorously and remarkably steadfastly conducting the cause of the Church in accordance with the demands of his office and dignity, returned through love of solitude and quiet to his cell and thereafter lived peacefully with the brethren. Yet the supreme pontiff rebuked him for preferring his private salvation to public care, though he was a useful and suitable man.
>
> It is memorably related of him that he completed in one year, whole and entire, the hundred years’ penance imposed by the pope for abandoning the bishopric. By this penance he was commanded to perform a discipline daily during the recitation of Psalm 50, and to do so for a hundred years, if he lived that long. I remember reading this elsewhere. See volume I of his works, letter 10; or, according to the new edition, volume III, Opuscule 20, addressed to Pope Alexander and Cardinal Hildebrand, afterward Pope Gregory VII. There he defends himself for having relinquished the bishopric and supports his action—condemned by the pope and cardinal—by adducing many examples.
>
> But if judgment should be made by laws rather than examples, as the jurist says, see Augustine, Letter 84, to Eudoxius; Pope Liberius, letter to all bishops; Leo I, Letter 32, to Rusticus of Narbonne; Innocent III, to the bishop of Arles, and *De Regularibus*, chapter *Licet*; Bellarmine, to Henry of Lorraine, bishop of Verdun; St Gregory, *On Pastoral Care*, book I, chapter 5 and following; Peter of Blois, letters 44 and 101; St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 85; Gilbert of Hoyland, in his very elegant letter to Ogerius—perhaps indeed the same man to whom the present letter of Bernard is addressed, since the inscription and subject of both letters agree—which you have here in volume V. See also our *Trumpets of Ecclesiastical Discipline*, p. 521; Claude d’Espence, book III of the *Digressions on the First Epistle to Timothy*.

Let those see—those whose sounder counsel, if indeed any such counsel exists, you have relied on in this matter—whether you have acted reasonably. Let them see, I say, whether it is lawful for a Christian to abandon before death an obedience enjoined upon him, when Christ became obedient to the Father unto death.

“But,” you say, “I did so by permission, for I asked it of the bishop and received it.” Very well: you asked permission—but in a manner in which you were not permitted to ask it; and therefore you did not receive it, but extorted it.

[Col. 0213A] Permission extorted or compelled is not permission but violence. Therefore what the bishop, conquered by your importunity, did unwillingly was not an absolution but a breaking-off.

3. I do indeed rejoice with you that you have been relieved of the burden; but I fear that God has been dishonoured by you, so far as lies in you. Without doubt you resist his ordering when, having been promoted by him, you demote yourself. If, in excuse, you allege the necessity of poverty, necessity produces a crown; if difficulty or impossibility, all things are possible to one who believes. But give the truer answer: namely, that your own quiet pleased you more than the benefit of others. Nor is this surprising. I confess that it pleases me too that this quiet pleases you—provided only that it does not please you too much.

Whatever good pleases one in such a way that, if it cannot be done rightly, one nevertheless wishes it done even in a manner not lawful, is excessive; and for that reason, because it is not done rightly, it is no longer good. For it is written: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4:7, LXX). Either, then, you ought not to have accepted the Lord’s flock without being willing to tend it, or, having accepted it, you ought by no means to leave it, according to the saying: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:27).

4. But why do I exert myself in these arguments? Do I advise you to return to the burden of governance, now that no opportunity of recovering it remains? Or do I mean to drive you to despair, as though you had bound yourself by a fault which you could no longer undo? Far from it. I merely do not want you to disregard it as no evil or a slight one. Rather, always fear, always repent, never be secure, as it is written: “Blessed is the man who is always afraid” (Prov. 28:14).

You see what kind of fear I seek to instil in you: not a fear that may become a snare of despair, but one that gains the hope of blessedness. There is a useless, sorrowful, cruel fear, which, because it does not seek pardon, does not obtain it. There is also a devout, humble, fruitful fear, which readily merits mercy for anyone, however great a sinner. Such fear generates, nourishes, and preserves humility, gentleness, patience, and long-suffering. Who would not delight in such illustrious offspring? But the wretched progeny of the other fear are obstinacy, immoderate sorrow, rancour, horror, contempt, and despair. Therefore I thought your fault should be recalled to your mind in this way, fearing not with the fear that produces despair, but with that which generates hope: lest you should not fear, or fear too little.

5. There is another matter concerning you which I fear even more: perhaps, as it is written of some, that “they rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14), you too may be deceived into thinking not only that this is no fault, but even—God forbid—may glory in your heart that you have done something great, something which few are accustomed to do: namely, that though emancipated and set over others, you despised pre-eminence and chose again to be subject to a superior.

This is false humility, introducing real pride into the heart of one who thinks such things. For what is more proud than to ascribe to spontaneous and supposedly free will that which either the force of necessity compels or the weakness of faint-heartedness produces? But if you did this neither conquered by labour nor compelled by necessity, but willingly, there is nothing more proud than this either. For you preferred your own counsel to God’s, choosing rather to rest for yourself than to serve in the work to which he himself had appointed you.

[Col. 0214B] If, therefore, you glory in a greater contempt of God precisely in that whereby you despised God, your glorying is not good. But beware of glorying; put away security also, so that you may always be usefully anxious and humbly afraid—not with that fear which, as I have already said, provokes wrath, but with that which mitigates it.

6. If at any time that dreadful fear should strike your heart by terrifying it, secretly suggesting that your service cannot be accepted by God and that your repentance is fruitless because the offence by which God has been offended through you cannot be amended by you, do not receive it even for a moment. Rather answer confidently and say: “I have indeed acted badly, but it has been done, and it cannot now be undone. Who knows whether God may have foreseen that this was expedient for me, and whether he himself, who is good, may have wished to work good for me from my evil? Therefore let him punish the evil that I did, but let the good remain which he himself provided.”

For the goodness of God knows how to use our disordered wills and actions: always rightly, for the beauty of his own order; often also mercifully, for our benefit. O most merciful remembrance of divine compassion toward the children of Adam, which does not cease to bestow its benefits, not only where it finds no merit, but very often where it sees everything contrary to merit!

But let us return to you. According, then, to the two fears distinguished above, I wish you both to fear and not to fear; to presume and not to presume. Fear, that you may repent; do not fear, that you may hope. Further, presume, lest you despair; do not presume, lest you become slothful.

7. Recognize, brother, how much confidence I have placed in you: I have not hesitated to rebuke you so sharply and to judge so boldly an action of yours that is not sufficiently approved by me, though perhaps you acted more reasonably than has thus far become known to me. For perhaps you did not wish in your letter to set out all the grounds upon which this action might be excused, whether through humility or through the brevity of the letter.

Therefore, leaving my judgment suspended concerning a matter which I do not fully know, I unreservedly praise one thing you did: when you laid down the yoke of government, you nevertheless did not wish to be without a yoke. Returning to beloved discipline, you were not ashamed to become once more a disciple instead of a master. For, released from the pastoral bond, you could have remained your own master; since the promotion of an abbot is the emancipation of a son.

> [Note: Col. 0215D] Certainly, one who becomes abbot from being a monk is exempted from the authority and subjection of his own abbot.

Yet you did not use this power over yourself. As you had refused to rule others, so you feared also to rule yourself. Judging yourself less fit to be the master of others, you did not despise to become your own disciple, not entrusting even yourself to yourself. And rightly so: for he who appoints himself his own master subjects himself as disciple to a fool.

> [Note: Col. 0215D] A witty and wise saying of St Bernard. For *philautia* (φιλαυτία), or self-love, a great artificer of errors, ordinarily steals from a person’s mind and eyes the power of judgment in his own affairs. It makes him so foolish and causes him to lose true judgment concerning matters that those who can often advise others rightly are shamefully blind—or rather senseless—in their own affairs, and miserably deceive themselves.
>
> Moreover, in the path of spiritual or religious life, to wish to proceed without a guide is a matter full of danger, as the holy Fathers and ascetical writers commonly show. See Augustine, Prologue to *On Christian Doctrine*; Basil, *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 23, and *Shorter Questions*, II.301; Gregory of Nyssa, *On Virginity*; Jerome, Letter 4, to Rusticus; Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 1, and book II, on 1 Kings; Cassian, *Conferences*, Conference 2, chapters 11 and 15; St Dorotheus, Discourse 5; Vincent Ferrer, *Treatise on the Spiritual Life*, chapter 4; Torquemada, Treatise 9 on the Rule of St Benedict; St Bonaventure, *On the Six Wings*; Alphonsus Rodriguez, part III, *Exercises*, treatise 7, chapters 2–4; Louis of Ponte, part II, *Spiritual Guide*, treatise 4, chapter 2, and part I, *On Christian Perfection*, treatise 2, chapter 9; Rossignol, *On the Discipline of Perfection*, book I, chapter 1; Jerome Platus, *On the Good of the Religious State*, book I, chapter 24; James Alvarez de Paz, *On the Spiritual Life*, volume I, book V, chapters 12–13; and finally Julius Nigronus, *Ascetical Treatise*, treatise 1.

What others think of themselves, I do not know; but I have experienced [or: “I think”] in myself what I say: I can command, and can more safely preside over, many others more easily than I can over myself alone. It was therefore prudent humility and humble prudence that, not believing you could suffice for your own salvation, you chose henceforth to live under another’s judgment.

8. I also praise you because you sought neither a new master nor a new place, but returned affectionately to the cloister from which you had gone out and to the father under whom you had made progress. It was indeed more fitting that the house which had nourished you, though it had released you for brotherly love, should receive you back when unoccupied, than that another should rejoice in its desolation.

Yet I do not want you to regard lightly the fact that you did not obtain the bishop’s permission in this matter. Rather, either personally or through an intermediary, do not delay, so far as lies in you, to make satisfaction. Thereafter live simply among the brethren: devoted to God, subject to your master, obedient to your elders, accommodating [variant: obedient] to your juniors; pleasing to the angels, useful in speech, humble in heart, gentle toward all.

But beware lest, because you were formerly established in honour, you should think yourself even now to deserve honour above the rest. Instead, show yourself humble before all, as one among the rest. For it is not fitting that you demand honour from the very source from which you flee labour.

9. From this may arise another danger, against which I wish you to be forewarned and fortified. For we are all so changeable that we often reject today what we wished yesterday and desire tomorrow what we do not want today. So perhaps, at the devil’s suggestion, longing may at some time strike your mind from the memory of the honour you left behind, so that you begin childishly to desire everything which you had manfully despised.

The things formerly bitter will become sweet to your mind: the eminence of office, the management of a household, the administration of property, the services of attendants, independence, authority over others. You may even nearly repent of having left what formerly wearied you to retain. If you give assent to this most evil temptation even for an hour—God forbid—you will incur no slight injury to your manner of life.

10. Behold the whole wisdom of that most elegant and eloquent doctor from whom you asked, at so great a distance, to be taught. Behold the awaited and desired *eulogy*—the blessing—which you were so eager to hear. This is the sum of our learning. Do you still expect something great? You have heard it all. What more do you seek? The spring is exhausted, and do you look for water in dry ground?

Following the example of the widow in the Gospel, from my poverty I have sent all that I had (Luke 21:2–4). Why are you ashamed? Why do you cast down your face? You compelled me. You asked for a discourse; you have a discourse. You have, I say, a discourse long enough now, but mute: full of words, empty of meanings; not one by which, as you had asked, your charity may be ordered in your heart, but one by which my ignorance may be made public.

For how can it now be excused? Perhaps I might say that I dictated these things while suffering from a tertian fever or while burdened with the concerns of my office, since it is written: “Write wisdom in leisure” (Ecclus. 38:25). But I might rightly plead these excuses if I had undertaken some great and laborious work. As it is, in so small a composition, I can offer no more certain excuse than—what I have already often said—the poverty of my knowledge.

11. Yet I have some consolation for my embarrassment. For even if I have not done what you asked, even if I have not sent what you hoped for, you at least recognize that I wished to do so. Willingness is sufficient where you see the power to perform is lacking. Finally, even if it brings you no benefit, it will contribute to my humility.

For “a fool, when he keeps silence, is considered wise” (Prov. 17:28): his silence is believed to arise not from poverty of understanding but from the restraint of humility. Therefore, if I had remained silent until now, I should be called wise, though I should not be wise. But now some will laugh at me as foolish, others will mock me as ignorant, others will be indignant with me as presumptuous.

Do you think this brings me little spiritual profit, when humility—to which humiliation surely leads—is the foundation of the entire spiritual structure? Humiliation is the way to humility, as patience is the way to peace and reading to knowledge. If you seek the virtue of humility, do not flee the way of humiliation. For if you do not endure being humbled, you cannot advance to humility.

Thus it benefits me that my folly is known and that I am justly put to shame by the knowledgeable [variant: wise], since it has often happened that I have been unjustly praised by the ignorant. The Apostle terrifies me; he himself, being terrified, says: “But I refrain, lest anyone think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me” (2 Cor. 12:6). How beautifully he said, “I refrain.” The arrogant man does not spare himself; neither does the proud man, nor one eager for empty glory and vaunting his deeds—whether he arrogates to himself what he is, or lies about himself in what he is not.

Only the truly humble person spares his own soul: lest he be thought to be what he is not, he always wishes, so far as he can, that what he is should remain unknown.

12. It is indeed a great danger for anyone to hear about himself what exceeds what he recognizes in himself. Who will grant me to be worthily humbled before people as much for true things as I have undeservedly been exalted for false ones? I might rightly take up that prophetic utterance: “But I was exalted, humbled, and troubled” (Ps. 87:16); and that other: “I will play, and I will become still more contemptible” (2 Sam. 6:22).

I will play, that I may be mocked. It is a good sport at which Michal is angry and God delights. It is a good sport which presents to men a ridiculous sight indeed, but to angels a most beautiful spectacle. It is a good sport, I say, by which we become “a reproach to the prosperous and a contempt to the proud.” For what else do we seem to worldly people but to play, when we flee, on the contrary, what they seek in this world, and seek what they flee?

We do so after the fashion of jesters and acrobats, who, with their heads lowered and their feet raised upward, stand upon their hands or walk in a manner contrary to ordinary human practice, and thus draw all eyes upon themselves. This is no childish sport, no theatrical spectacle that provokes lust by effeminate and shameful contortions or represents filthy acts. Rather, it is a joyful, honourable, serious, and splendid sport, capable of delighting the gaze of heavenly spectators.

He played this chaste and religious sport who said: “We have become a spectacle to angels and to men” (1 Cor. 4:9). Let us too play this sport meanwhile, that we may be mocked, put to shame, and humbled, until he comes who casts down the mighty and exalts the humble; who may gladden us, glorify us, and exalt us for ever.

## LETTER LXXXVIII

> [Note: Col. 0217D] Written about the year 1127.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** He says that, impeded by many occupations, he has hitherto been unable to satisfy Ogerius’s wishes, and is even now compelled to write more sparingly. He forbids a certain work of his to be published unless it has been reviewed.

1. I now pass over my lack of skill; I am silent about the lowliness of my profession—or my profession of humility. I no longer urge either the abjection, or rather the modest station, of my place and name. For whatever such things I might say, you would call them not a necessary excuse but a delaying pretext, since you interpret my modesty—which seemed to me just—as now indiscretion, now false humility, now even genuine pride, according to your own inclination. Therefore I assert none of these things, because they can be doubtful to you.

But I tell your love simply this, and I want you to believe it without doubt: throughout all this time since your messenger—not that one, but another—departed from me, I have had absolutely no leisure suitable for doing what you request, both because the days are evil and because the nights are short. Even now your latest letter found me so occupied that it would take a long time to write you even the causes of those occupations in my defence. I could scarcely read through your letter while dining, for it was first handed to me at that hour. I have scarcely written this little reply, whatever it is worth, furtively, hurriedly, at hours stolen beforehand, briefly and compactly. Whether you bear its brevity patiently, you must decide.

2. For, to tell the truth, because of you, my Ogerius, I am compelled to be angry with my very occupations, although my conscience bears witness that in them I desire to serve charity alone. And indeed it was the command of charity—since I am debtor to wise and unwise alike—which alone could bring it about that I have not yet been able to satisfy you.

What then? Does charity deny you what you ask from charity? You asked, sought, and knocked; and charity has disappointed you. Why are you angry with me? If you wish, if you dare, be angry with charity. The very charity from which you expect to obtain what you ask prevents you from obtaining it. And behold: he who makes a long speech now complains, and is angry with you who compel him.

Not that the zeal with which you do this displeases charity; indeed, charity herself gave it to you. But she wants you to possess it according to knowledge, so that you may take care not to hinder greater matters by lesser ones. You see how unwillingly I am torn away from a longer letter: carried along by the pleasure of conversing with you and the desire to satisfy you, I become troublesome to Lady Charity, though she has long commanded me to end and I have not yet fallen silent.

How broad a subject for reply lies open in your letter! If I had been permitted as worthily as I wished, perhaps you would have had enough, and I too. But she who commands otherwise is mistress—indeed, lord. For God is charity (1 John 4:16), and he acts sufficiently by his command to require me to obey him rather than either myself or you.

And because one must obey charity—God—rather than human beings, unwillingly and sorrowfully I do not refuse what you request, but postpone it for the present, lest, while I desire humbly to comply with your will, I should seem, under the pretext of false humility and by real pride, as an earthly little worm to attack on earth the citadel of so great a power which, as you truly testify, commands even angels in heaven.

3. The little work you seek I had myself requested, before your messenger came to us, from the person to whom I had entrusted it; but I have not yet received it. I shall take care that when you come—if indeed you ever come at all—you may find it, see it, and read it; but not copy it.

For the other work which you say you copied, I sent to you to be read, not to be copied. You must see for what benefit, or for whose benefit, you copied it. That the abbot of Saint-Theodoric now has it because you sent it, I did not command; yet it does not displease me.

> [Note: Col. 0219C] This little work is undoubtedly none other than the *Apology to Abbot William*, which Ogerius was expecting and urging for at Clairvaux while Bernard was completing it, as is apparent from the final words of that *Apology*. But because Ogerius had been unable to obtain it accurately copied before his departure, Bernard later sent it to him for examination. Without consulting Bernard, Ogerius shared it with Abbot William, to whom it is addressed, although Bernard himself intended to send it after correction.

For why should my little work fear the eyes of one to whom my own mind would lay itself wholly open to be seen, if it could? But alas, in what narrow confines of discourse has the mention of such a man entered, so that I cannot linger for a while, as was fitting, upon a memory so sweet to us, when the letter is already demanding its end!

I beg you not to find it burdensome to seek an opportunity to visit him. Do not allow the aforesaid work to be copied or shown for reading to anyone before you have examined it all with him, compared it together, and corrected what requires correction, so that every word may stand upon the testimony of two witnesses. Only then let it be decided whether it is expedient for it to be shown generally to everyone, or only to a few, or to anyone at all, or perhaps even to no one; and whether that little preface which you fitted to it from our other letters is suitably placed, or whether a more suitable one should be sought. I leave this to the judgment of you both.

> [Note: Col. 0219D] This little preface is the letter to the same William, usually reckoned among Bernard’s letters as number 85, printed at the beginning of the *Apology*.

4. But I had almost forgotten the complaint you made at the beginning of your letter: that I had accused you of lying. I do not sufficiently remember ever having said this. Yet if there was anything of the kind—for I would sooner believe that I have forgotten than that your messenger lied—do not doubt that it was said in jest rather than seriously.

Would I think you guilty of frivolity, or that with you there is “Yes and No”? Far be it from me to think this of you, who, blessed under the yoke of truth which you have borne from youth, surpass the frivolous years by the gravity of your character. Nor am I so simple as to call a simple utterance of the mouth, without duplicity of heart, a lie; nor am I so inattentive to you as to have forgotten either what you conceived long ago in affection or what prevented it from being carried into effect.

## LETTER LXXXIX

> [Note: Col. 0219D] Written about the year 1127.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** He excuses the brevity of his writing on the ground of the sacred season, to which silence is more appropriate; likewise on the ground of his religious profession and lack of learning, so that he does not dare to usurp the office of teaching.

1. Perhaps you are indignant—or, to speak more moderately, surprised—that instead of the longer letter you had expected from us, you received so brief a sheet. But remember, according to the Wise Man, that everything under heaven has its season: a time to speak, and a time to be silent (Eccl. 3:1, 7). When, however, will silence have its own time if even during these sacred days of Lent our correspondence claims them for itself?

And that correspondence is more engrossing the more laborious it is. For we cannot lightly say to each other in person what we wish; being absent, we must carefully dictate to one another what we ask of each other or what is asked of us. But while absent I think, dictate, write, and send what you may read when present, I ask: where is leisure, where is the repose of silence?

> [Note: Col. 0219D] In this letter the holy man declares in serious terms how alien he is from writing letters to friends that are less useful and necessary, because this is done at the cost of time and leisure, which should be given to graver and holier matters; also at the cost of the silence incumbent upon religious persons; and finally at the cost of inward quiet and tranquillity, which is diminished by the concern and occupation of writing.
>
> Bernard speaks of the office and vocation of a monk considered as such. A monk, insofar as he is a monk, is not called to preach and teach, but to devote himself in solitude to God and his own salvation through meditations and the exercises of virtues. Thus in Letter 42—found in volume II among the treatises—St Bernard says: “Labour, concealment, and voluntary poverty: these are the marks of monks; these are accustomed to ennoble the monastic life.”
>
> Therefore, lest perhaps idle monks, if any such lurk somewhere, should rashly and imprudently abuse the authority of the holy Father as a pretext for their idleness, as though he condemned literary studies and learning among monks, let them hear him elsewhere plainly rebuking such persons. “Perhaps,” he says, “I may appear excessive in disparaging learning, as though I censured learned men and prohibited literary studies. Far from it! I do not fail to know how much their learned men have benefited and benefit the Church, whether in refuting those who oppose it or in instructing the simple,” etc. See the remainder of the same passage in Sermon 36 on the Song of Songs, no. 2.

“But,” you say, “you can do all this in silence.” It would be strange if you said this seriously. For what great tumult is there in the mind of those who dictate, where a multitude of words resounds, where various forms of expression and diverse meanings meet; where what occurs is often rejected and what has escaped is sought; where the writer attends most intently to what is more beautiful in wording, more coherent in meaning, clearer for understanding, more useful for conscience, and finally to what should be placed for whom, either before or after, together with many other matters which the learned observe more carefully in such writing? And will you tell me that there is quiet in this? Will you call this silence, even if the tongue is silent?

2. Yet it is not only not the business of this season, but not even of my profession, to devote myself to the task you request; nor is it in my power to fulfil what you desire. For the office of one who appears to be a monk, or of one who truly is a sinner, is not to teach but to mourn. Furthermore, an unlearned man—as I truly confess myself to be—if he presumes to teach what he does not know, does nothing more unlearned.

Therefore teaching is not ready to hand for the unlearned, not something a monk dares undertake, nor something a penitent desires. It is for this reason that “I fled far away and remained in solitude”; and with the prophet I resolved to guard my ways, that I might not sin with my tongue (Ps. 38:2), because, according to the same prophet, “a man given to speech shall not be established on the earth” (Ps. 140:12), and according to another scripture, “Death and life are in the hands” (Prov. 18:21).

But silence, Isaiah says, is “the cultivation of righteousness” (Isa. 32:17); and, as Jeremiah teaches, “It is good to wait in silence for the saving help of God” (Lam. 3:26). Therefore, toward this cultivation of righteousness—the mother, nurse, and guardian of all virtues—lest I seem altogether to deny what you asked, I invite and urge both you and all who, like you, desire to advance in virtues: if not by a word of instruction, then at least by the example of my silence, so that by being silent I may teach you to be silent, you who by speaking compel me to teach what I do not know.

3. But what am I doing? It would be strange if you did not laugh that I, who seem to condemn verbosity so strongly, am now proceeding so talkatively into so many words; and while I wish to commend silence to you, am fighting against silence through verbosity.
