As for our Guerric, concerning whose way of life and repentance you desire consolation, know from the fruits we discern in him that he lives worthily before God and produces fruits worthy of repentance.

> [Note: Col. 0221D] This Guerric became abbot of Igny in 1138; his sermons are in volume VI. Bernard refers to him again in the following letter.

The little work you demand from me I do not presently have with me. For a certain friend of ours, moved by the same zeal with which you urge me, has kept it with him for a long time. But lest I allow the request of your piety [variant: kindness] to go away entirely disappointed, I send you another work recently composed by me, *In Praise of the Virgin Mother*.

> [Note: Col. 0221D] This is the title Bernard gives to the homilies on *Missus est* (“The angel was sent”).

Since I do not retain a copy of it, I ask you to return it to me as soon as possible; or, if you come sooner, bring it yourself with you.

## LETTER XC

> [Note: Col. 0221D] Written about the year 1127.

**TO THE SAME PERSON.** Sincere love has no need of lengthy letters or many words; Bernard is recovering from an illness from which there had been almost no hope of recovery.

[Col. 0221D] 1. I have returned a short letter for a short one, gladly taking from the brevity of yours the occasion of replying briefly. And indeed, what advantage is there in displaying true—and, as you truly say, eternal—friendships with empty and fleeting little words? However great the variety of your lines, the abundance of your words, the diversity of your writings with which you may try to show or commend your affection for me, I certainly perceive that you express less than you love [Col. 0222A]; and you are not mistaken in feeling the same about me. When your letter came into our hands, it found in our heart you who had sent it. Likewise, I am sure that I do not write this letter without you, nor do I suppose that you will read it without me. We both labor by writing to one another; messengers too are wearied by carrying writings from one to the other. But are spirits burdened by loving? Let those things therefore cease which cannot be done without labor; and let that be frequent which, the more diligently it is pursued, is found to involve the less labor. Let minds rest, I say, from dictation; lips from conversation; fingers from writing; messengers from travelling about. [Note: [Col. 0221D] In the prefixed letter to the *Apology to Abbot William* [Col. 0222D], and above in Letter 89, he says that such continual letter-writing hinders devotion and prayer.] But let hearts not rest, day and night, from meditating upon the law of the Lord, which is charity. The more free we are from that occupation, the less we rest; and the more occupied we are in it, the more rest we experience from it. Let us love and be loved, caring in the one case for ourselves, in the other for those who are ours. For in those whom we love we certainly rest; while by those who love us, we prepare rest for them within ourselves. To love in God is to possess charity; but to seek to be loved for God’s sake is to serve charity.

2. But what am I doing? I, who promised brevity, am now caught proving myself prolix. If you wish—or rather, since you wish—to know about Brother Guerric: he runs not as one uncertain; he fights not as one beating the air. But because he knows that it belongs neither to the fighter nor to the runner, but to God who shows mercy, he asks you to pray for him, that he who has already granted him both to fight and to run may also grant him to conquer and to arrive. I greet your abbot, most dear to me not only on your account but also because of his own good reputation, with my heart through your mouth; I shall most gladly see him at the time and place you promised. I also inform you that, as the Lord’s hand has again been somewhat heavy upon me, I was thrust down and overthrown so as to fall; the axe having been laid to the root of the fruitless tree of my body, I feared that I was on the point of being cut down. But behold: through your prayers and those of our other friends, the merciful Lord spared me on this occasion also, though under hope of the fruit promised hereafter.

## LETTER XCI

[Note: [Col. 0221D] Written about the year 1130.—This is one of the earliest general chapters of the “black,” as they are called, monks of the province of Rheims. Its cause and occasion appear to have been Bernard’s *Apology to William*, which prompted, by the example of the Cluniacs and Cistercians [Col. 0223C], the convening of this assembly, so that aid might be given to declining regular observance [Col. 0223D]. It was undoubtedly held at Saint-Médard, under Abbot Geoffrey, to whom Letter 66 is addressed. Peter the Venerable, in Letter 43 of Book II, praises this man, already bishop of Châlons, as “a Cluniac, the first disseminator, author, and promoter throughout all France of the divine Order,” indeed “the expeller of the ancient dragon from the lairs of so many monasteries, and the reviver of the monastic body.” These words perhaps belong here with reverence. Innocent II desired that such general chapters should thereafter be held annually by the black monks, as is clear from Letter 480 below, in the appendix to the letters.]

### To the Abbots Gathered at Soissons

He urges the abbots vigorously to pursue the business for which they assembled. He earnestly commends zeal for progress: nothing must be delayed if some lukewarm and lax persons should perhaps object and murmur.

[Col. 0222D]

To the reverend abbots gathered at Soissons in the name of the Lord, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, servant of their holiness [Col. 0223A]: to discern, establish, and hold fast what is right.

1. I am angry with my occupations, by which I am prevented from attending your assembly—only in body, however. For neither distances of land nor the throng of cares can make my spirit absent: it is praying for you, rejoicing with you, and resting in you. The assembly of saints, I say, cannot lack me; nor does distance of place or body wholly deprive me of the counsel of the righteous and the congregation—especially of that counsel in which human traditions [Note: [Col. 0223D] Here “human traditions” means dispensations and relaxations of regular life, discussed below and in Letter 154, no. 1.] are not defended with excessive obstinacy or observed with excessive superstition, but in which men diligently and humbly inquire what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God. Toward that gathering I am carried with all desire; I remain there in devotion; I delight in it [Col. 0223B] through love; I cling to it by consent; I persist in it through emulation.

2. Therefore, lest those who say to you, “Well done! well done!” should mockingly claim that you have assembled in vain—which may it never be—strive, I beseech you, to make your ways and pursuits good; for they certainly cannot be too good. Granted that perhaps one may be excessively righteous and excessively wise; but one plainly cannot be good beyond measure. For I read: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. 7:17); I read: “Do not be wiser than is necessary to be wise” (Rom. 12:3). But do I read, “Do not be too good,” or, “Do not be better than is necessary”? No one can be good beyond what is necessary. Paul was already good; yet, far from content, he gladly stretched himself toward the things before him, forgetting those behind [Col. 0223C] (Phil. 3:13), and always endeavoring to become better than himself. God alone does not will to be better than himself, because he cannot be.

3. Let those withdraw from me and from you who say, “We do not wish to be better than our fathers,” thereby professing themselves children of the lukewarm and lax. Their memory is accursed, because they ate sour grapes, at which their children’s teeth were set on edge. Or, if they glory in holy fathers of blessed memory, let them certainly imitate the holiness of those whose indulgences and dispensations they defend as law. Yet holy Elijah said, “I am not better than [Col. 0224A] my fathers” (3 Kings 19:4); he did not say that he did not wish to be better than his fathers. Jacob saw angels ascending and descending upon the ladder (Gen. 28:12): did he see anyone standing still or sitting? There is no standing at all upon the precarious ladder of frailty; nor does anything remain in the same state amid the uncertainty of this mortal life. We do not have here an abiding city, nor do we yet possess the city to come; rather, we seek it. You must either ascend or descend: if you try to stand still, you must fall. Certainly he is not good who does not wish to become better; and where you begin not to wish to become better, there you also cease to be good.

4. Let those also withdraw from me and from you who call good evil and evil good. If they call the cultivation of righteousness evil, what good will they then regard as good [Col. 0224B]? The Lord once spoke one word, and the Pharisees were offended (Matt. 15:12). Yet now the new Pharisees are offended, not by a word but by silence. In this one matter you may certainly perceive that they seek an occasion against you. But leave them alone: they are blind guides of the blind. Attend to the salvation of the little ones, not to the murmur of the ill-disposed. You need not be greatly concerned about the offense of those who cannot be healed unless you become sick. Nor should you wait until everything you establish pleases even your own people in every respect. Otherwise, you will establish either no good thing or only a rare one. You provide better for their progress than for their wishes; and you draw them more faithfully to God against their will than you leave them to the desires of their hearts. I commend myself to your holy prayers.

## LETTER XCII

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

### To Henry, King of the English

He asks the king’s favor for monks sent by him to establish a monastery.

[Col. 0224C]

To HENRY, illustrious king of the English, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: faithfully to serve the King of heaven from an earthly kingdom, and humbly to obey him.

In your land there is held captive the prey of my Lord and yours [Note: [Col. 0223D] What Bernard indicates by this mode of speaking is revealed by the history of the origin of Rievaulx monastery in these words: “Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, having sent the soldiers of his expedition, had already occupied neighboring regions, winning splendid triumphs over the ancient enemy, rescuing prey and restoring it to his King. By divine prompting, from his noble vineyard of Clairvaux he had directed a certain planting of good hope toward the English regions, seeking fruit among that people, as everywhere in the world. The very letter which he had written for them to the king still survives, asserting that the prey of his Lord was being held in the king’s land, and that he had sent valiant men of his own soldiery to seek it, recover it, and bring it back. He urges the king to assist the messengers and not abandon his fief in this matter; and this was done. Received with honor by king and kingdom, they laid new foundations in the province of York, establishing the abbey called Rievaulx. This was the first planting of the Cistercian Order in the territory of York.” From *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. 1, p. 733. For more on Henry I, see, if desired, the notes to Letter 138.]; and it is that prey for which he preferred to die rather than be without it. I have resolved to pursue it and to send men from our soldiery who, with a strong hand—if it is not displeasing to you—may seek, recover, and bring it back. For this purpose I have now sent ahead these scouts whom you see before you [Col. 0225A], that they may skilfully investigate the state of the matter and faithfully report it. [Note: [Col. 0225B] “To be” (*esse*) is a familiar word with Bernard for signifying the condition of a thing or person; see Letters 118 and 304.] Assist them as messengers of your Lord, and in them render the service due from your fief. [Note: [Col. 0225B] For kings and princes are, as it were, God’s vassals.] May he himself bring you, for his own honor, for your salvation, and for the welfare and peace of your country, joyful and renowned to a good and peaceful end.

## LETTER XCIII

[Note: [Col. 0225B] Written about the year 1132.—Henry, nephew through his sister of Henry I, king of the English; brother of Stephen, likewise king of England; and son of Stephen, count of Blois, was later bishop of Winchester in England. Formerly abbot of Glastonbury, he succeeded William Giffard at Winchester in 1128. English historians praise him, except Henry of Huntingdon [Col. 0225C], who in vol. VIII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 190, calls him, as nephew of King Henry, “a certain new monster—namely, monk and knight.” “His mother,” Adela, says William of Newburgh in *History of England*, Book I, ch. 4, “had him tonsured at Cluny, lest she should seem to have borne children only for the world”: namely, in 1126, as the *History of Glastonbury* expressly reports (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. II, p. 18), counting him among its abbots and describing him as “a man whom abundant literary learning made illustrious, and exceptional uprightness of character greatly adorned; whose industry conferred such benefits upon the church of Glastonbury that his memory will flourish there eternally through the ages,” etc. After Henry was raised to the see of Winchester, St Bernard complained of him in Letter 237 to Eugenius: “What shall I say of the lord of Winchester? ‘The works which he does bear witness concerning him’”—meaning, among other matters, that he extorted castles from princes invited to a banquet, as Harpsfield relates [Col. 0225D] in the twelfth century in his account of Henry; and that he consecrated the intruded William of York, according to Roger in the *Annals* for the year 1140, where he calls him legate of the Roman See. He is therefore wrongly numbered among the Cistercians by Brito and Henriquez; nor perhaps more correctly by the latter among men distinguished for holiness (*Cistercian Menology*, 11 October), on the basis of Wion’s testimony in the *Tree of Life*, which declares him renowned for the spirit of prophecy because, when his nephew Henry visited him, he foretold while dying that Henry would be chastised by God for the murder of St Thomas of Canterbury, whom Henry himself had consecrated. As Manrique rightly says in the *Annals*, that utterance might rather have been that of a man afraid than of a prophet. Many letters of Peter the Venerable to him survive. In particular, Letters 24 and 25 of Book IV urge him to return to his Cluniac monastery to lay down his body there. Invited also by the letters of Adrian IV, by the requests of Louis, king of the French, and of the primates of Burgundy [Col. 0226B], he secretly came from England to Cluny in 1155 without the king’s permission, having sent his treasure beforehand through Peter the Venerable, as Chesnius relates in notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*. He relieved the monastery, burdened by a heavy weight of debt, by expenditures amounting to seven thousand marks of silver, or forty thousand pounds; fed more than four hundred monks living at Cluny; gave the church forty chalices for celebrating Mass and costly silk cloth; and with his own hands buried Peter the Venerable, who died on the Kalends of January 1157 [Col. 0226C]. Finally, having returned to his see, he ended his days amid great mourning by the Cluniacs, on the fifth day before the Ides of August, 1171.]

### To Henry, Bishop of Winchester

He courteously greets him.

To the illustrious lord HENRY, by God’s grace bishop of Winchester, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting in the Lord.

I have joyfully learned from the report of many that our lowliness holds no small place of favor with Your Highness [Col. 0225B]. I have not deserved it, but neither am I ungrateful for it. Therefore I return favor for favor: not an equal return, indeed, but at least what I can. Nor do I fear that, however small it may be, my offering—or rather my repayment—will be despised by you, since you have taken care both lovingly to earn it and graciously to anticipate it [Col. 0226A]. For the present, however, I have refrained from writing more, until I learn from your reply, if you judge it worthy, how you receive these few words. Whatever you may please to write in reply or to enjoin verbally, you can safely entrust to Abbot Ogerius [Note: [Col. 0226C] To him Letters 87 and following are addressed.], through whom you received this letter of ours also. We also commend him to Your Excellency, that you may thereby know and recommend him, as a man commendable for integrity, learning, and religious devotion.

## LETTER XCIV

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

### To the Abbot of a Certain Monastery of York, from Which a Prior Had Departed with Certain Brothers

[Note: [Col. 0226C] That is, Geoffrey, abbot of the monastery of St Mary in the diocese of York, of the Order of St Benedict. Twelve monks with their prior departed from this place, and, since they were not allowed to go over to the Cistercians, took refuge with Thurstan, archbishop of York. Bernard praises him in the following letter for the protection he gave them. Compare Letter 313, to the same Geoffrey.]

[Note: [Col. 0226C] Letter 313 indicates distinctly that they passed from the Benedictine monastery of St Mary at York to the Cistercians; this is confirmed by the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, both in its history of the York monastery itself and especially in the history of Fountains. From the latter we here summarize the subject of this and the two preceding letters [Col. 0226D]. The abbey of St Mary at York was founded in 1088 by Count Alan, son of Guy, count of Brittany, in a church dedicated to St Olaf near York; King William, surnamed Rufus, later gave it the name of St Mary. Abbot Stephen and Benedictine monks were summoned there from Whitby, and under them regular discipline spread with no small increase. Around 1132, under Geoffrey, its third abbot, it began for a time to languish. At that time Cistercian religious life was spreading its fame everywhere; it had first been introduced into England in 1128, its first foundation being Waverley in Surrey. Moved by holy emulation of it, twelve monks of that monastery, not being permitted by their abbot to go over to the Cistercians, implored Thurstan, archbishop of York, to become patron of their purpose. Under his leadership, therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, on the day before the Nones of October, twelve priests and one deacon departed from that monastery despite their abbot’s protest: namely, Richard the prior; another Richard, the sacrist; and others listed in the aforesaid history. They took nothing of the monastery’s goods except their clothing. Disturbed by this desertion, Abbot Geoffrey complained in letters to the king, neighboring bishops and abbots, and especially to St Bernard, of the common injury done to violated religious observance. Bishop Thurstan wrote an apologetic letter to William, metropolitan of Canterbury—printed above, p. 793. Bernard himself sent a congratulatory letter to Thurstan and to those thirteen monks, but an apologetic one to Abbot Geoffrey (Letters 94, 96, and 313). Meanwhile the monks were kept within Thurstan’s episcopal household. Since their abbot’s censures could not recall them, they received from the bishop a place to dwell near Ripon [Col. 0228D], uncultivated through all preceding ages, overgrown with thorns, and lying amid rounded hills and rocks projecting here and there. On Christmas Day, Thurstan ordained Richard the prior as abbot. After passing the winter under an elm in unbelievable austerity of life, Richard and his community, together with their place—called Fountains by themselves—gave themselves to St Bernard. Bernard sent them a religious man, Geoffrey of Amiens; see Book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, ch. 2. Under him they embraced the Cistercian institution with incredible devotion and eagerness.]

1. You seek counsel from me by a letter sent across the sea [Col. 0226B]; would that you had rather sought it from someone else. For I am constrained in two ways. If I do not answer, silence will seem in some manner to signify contempt. But I do not see how I can answer without danger, since whatever I answer must either create scandal for someone, or make someone more secure than he ought to be, or secure in a matter in which he ought not to be. So far as I know, the fact that your brothers departed from you did not occur through the counsel or urging of myself or ours. Yet we believe it was from God, since it could not be undone by such great efforts. We believe that the brothers themselves feel this too: they so earnestly seek our counsel about themselves, I think because their conscience reproaches them for having gone back. Otherwise, according to the Apostle, they are blessed if they do not judge themselves in what they approve (Rom. 14:22). But what am I to do, so that, being questioned, I may trouble no one either by silence or by answer? Perhaps I shall extricate myself in this way: by sending those who question me to one more learned, whose authority is more venerable and holy. St Gregory the Pope says in the *Pastoral Rule*: “Whoever has proposed to undertake a greater good has made unlawful for himself the lesser good which he could have done.” To prove this he adds the Gospel testimony: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62); and he concludes: “Therefore, one who had directed himself toward a stronger pursuit is convicted of looking back if, after leaving greater goods, he turns again to lesser ones” (Part III, ch. 28). Again, in his third homily on Ezekiel, he says: “There are some who do indeed perform the good things they know, and while doing them deliberate upon better things; but, reconsidering, they change the better things they had deliberated. They certainly perform the good things they began, but fall away from the better things they had deliberated [Col. 0227C]. Such persons seem to stand in their work before human judgments; but in their deliberation they have fallen dead before the eyes of almighty God.”

2. Behold the mirror. Let them consider in it not the face of their birth, but the deed of their return; let them examine themselves here and judge themselves here, while their own thoughts accuse or defend them, and indeed before the spiritual person who judges all things and is himself judged by no one. What is greater or lesser, higher or lower, stricter or more relaxed—what they left, or that to which they returned—I would not rashly determine; let them see for themselves. And this is Gregory’s word to them. But to you, reverend father, I will say with as much safe certainty as bare truth: it is altogether unfitting to wish to extinguish the Spirit [Col. 0227D]. “Do not,” he says, [Col. 0228A] “prevent one who is able to do good; but if you can, do good yourself also” (Prov. 3:27). Rather, one ought to glory in the progress of one’s sons, for “a wise son is the glory of his father” (Prov. 10:1). Henceforth let no one trouble me because I have not hidden the righteousness of God in my heart—except that, perhaps in order to avoid scandal, I have said less than I ought.

## LETTER XCV

[Note: [Col. 0228D] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

### To Thurstan, Archbishop of York

He praises his charity and beneficence toward religious persons.

To the most dear father and reverend lord THURSTAN, by God’s grace archbishop of York, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, sends fullest greeting.

The splendor of the deed and the fragrance of reputation have, as I learn, fittingly come together [Col. 0228B] in your glory. The deed proves that the reputation was neither false nor empty, since the reality itself makes manifest what flying fame had previously spread everywhere. How brilliantly the zeal of righteousness has now shone forth; how priestly vigor has stood out and prevailed, namely in defending the poor—and poor persons who had no helper! [Note: [Col. 0228D] What Thurstan did in defense of the aforementioned monks, who fled to him in pursuit of greater perfection, is taught by his own letter, to be reproduced after Bernard’s letters from the *Monasticon Anglicanum*.] Formerly the whole Church of the saints proclaimed your works of mercy and almsgiving; but this you share with many, since it is required of all who possess this world’s goods. Yet this is an episcopal work; this is so distinguished an example of fatherly compassion; this is truly divine fervor, by which he who makes his angels spirits [Col. 0228C] and his ministers a burning fire undoubtedly kindled and armed your zeal to protect his own poor. All this, I say, is a special addition: the glory of your rank, the distinction of your office, the ornament of your crown. It is one thing to restore the hungry belly, another to be zealous for holy poverty. There nature is served; here grace. “You shall inspect your estate, and you shall not sin” (Job 5:24). Thus, one who nourishes another’s flesh acts so that he himself may not sin; but one who honors another’s holiness bears fruit for himself. Therefore it says: “Let alms sweat in your hand until you find [variant: see] a righteous man to whom you may give.” With what fruit? “For he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matt. 10:41). Let us therefore pay nature’s debt, lest we sin; let us be fellow-workers with grace, that we may deserve also to become sharers in it. Truly, we so admire both in you that [Col. 0228D] we confess both to have been given you from above, so that whatever is bestowed by you upon our temporal needs may be eternally joined to divine praises: father deservedly reverend, and to be honored and embraced with every sincerity of love.

## LETTER XCVI

[Note: [Col. 0229C] Written in 1132. Richard had been prior [Col. 0229D] in the monastery of St Mary at York and departed from it with the twelve monks mentioned above; he died at Rome, according to vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 744. He was succeeded by another Richard, formerly sacrist in the aforesaid York monastery, who died at Clairvaux, as is recorded on p. 745 of the same volume; see Letter 320 concerning him. The monastery of Fountains in the diocese of York transferred to the Cistercian institution in 1132. Remarkable matters concerning the fervor of these monks are found in vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, pp. 733 ff. Compare present Letter 313 and Letter 320, which concerns the death of Richard, the second abbot of that name and order.]

### To Richard, Abbot of Fountains, and His Companions, Who Had Transferred from Another Order to the Cistercian

He praises them for renewing religious discipline.

What great things we have heard and come to know, both our brothers named Geoffrey have reported to us: how you have lately been rekindled by the fire of God, strengthened from weakness, and flowered again in holy newness. This is the finger of God: working subtly, renewing gently, changing healthfully [Col. 0229B]—not making good men out of bad, but better men out of good. Who will grant me that I may pass over and see this great vision? For this advance is no less wonderful or delightful than that conversion—except that it is far easier to find many secular persons converted to good than even one religious person passing to what is better. A very rare bird on earth is one who rises even a little from the rank which he may once have attained in religious life. Therefore your deed, beloved brothers, so conspicuous as it is salutary, rightly rejoices not only us, who greatly desire to be servants of your holiness, but the whole city of God: the rarer it is, the more brilliant it is. Moreover, it was necessary as a precaution to pass beyond the mediocrity nearest to failure and to avoid the lukewarmness which provokes God to vomit; and it was also necessary for conscience’ sake. For you who professed the holy Rule have yourselves perceived whether it is safe to stop short of its purity. I deeply regret that, because of the pressure of the day’s trouble and the messenger’s haste, I am compelled to express full affection with a scanty pen and to contain broad charity in a short sheet [Col. 0229C]. Whatever is lacking, Brother Geoffrey will supply by word of mouth. [Note: [Col. 0229D] This is Geoffrey, called of Amiens, “a holy and religious man, organizer and founder of many monasteries,” whom St Bernard sent to the monks of Fountains to teach them the form of the Cistercian Order; from vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 741. On the same Geoffrey, see *Life of St Bernard*, Book IV, ch. 2, no. 10 [Col. 0230C].]

## LETTER XCVII

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Written about the same year.—Conrad, duke of Zähringen, is said by Samuel Guichenon, in his *French History of the Dukes of Savoy*, to have contemplated war at this time against Amadeus I, count of Geneva. Zähringen, Münster says in Book III of the *Cosmography*, was a certain castle, now ruined, from which the dukes of Zähringen took their title, half a mile below Freiburg im Breisgau. According to Gebizo, these dukes descended from the counts of Habsburg and arose around the time of Emperor Henry III; in the sixth heir, named Egon, they finally ended in 1357.]

### To Duke Conrad

He dissuades him from making war on the count of Geneva, lest he provoke God as his avenger.

1. All power is from him to whom the prophet says: “Yours is power, yours the kingdom, O Lord; you are above all nations” (1 Chron. 29:11). Therefore I have thought it fitting, illustrious prince, to remind Your Excellency how greatly you ought to defer to the Terrible One, to him who takes away the spirit of princes. The count of Geneva, as we have learned from his own mouth, has submitted himself to justice and offers satisfaction for all the claims which you say you have against him. If in this matter you continue to invade another’s land, destroy churches, burn houses, drive the poor into exile, commit murders, and shed human blood, there is no doubt that you will grievously provoke against yourself the Father of orphans and Judge of widows. With him angered, it is not to your advantage to fight, however great your multitude or strength. For to the almighty Lord of hosts it makes no difference whether he gives victory through many or [Col. 0230B] through few, to whom he wills. When he willed, he made one chase a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight (Deut. 32:30).

2. I, a poor man moved by the cries of the poor, wished to write these things to Your Magnificence, knowing that it is more honorable for you to agree with the humble than to yield to enemies: not because I think your enemy stronger than you, but because I know almighty God to be stronger, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. For this purpose, noble sir, I would have come into your presence if I had been able. But now I have taken care to send these of our brothers in my place, that perhaps through their prayers and ours they may obtain from Your Dignity either a complete reconciliation, if possible, or at least a truce, until we may be allowed to seek a firm peace [Col. 0230C], according to God’s will, for your honor and the country’s safety. Otherwise, if you neither accept justice when it is offered nor regard us who entreat you—indeed, if you do not heed God, who in us warns you concerning your salvation—may he himself see and judge. We know, moreover, what we rightly fear: that such great armies can scarcely meet without a most grievous slaughter on one side.

## LETTER XCVIII

[Note: [Col. 0230D] On the Maccabees, but to whom it was written is unknown. Nearly all manuscripts have this title. Yet in one Cistercian manuscript the letter is entitled: “To Bruno of Cologne, as is thought, on the martyrdom of the Maccabees.” The old edition reads: “Thought to have been written to Hugh of St Victor.” The conjecture concerning Bruno, bishop of Cologne, seems to have arisen because the relics of the holy Maccabees are preserved in that city. But they were brought there from Milan after Bernard’s death by Archbishop Rainald, who obtained them from Emperor Frederick I. In some manuscripts Letter 77 to Hugh of St Victor immediately precedes this letter.]

### On the Maccabees

He answers the question why, among the righteous of the old law, the Church decreed a feast day for the Maccabees alone.

1. What your Charity asked of my lowliness through Brother Hescelin [Note: [Col. 0230D] Hescelin, mentioned here, seems to be the canon of Lille discussed in vol. I of the *Analecta*, p. 289.], Abbot Fulk of Épernay had already written to me about. [Note: [Col. 0231D] Fulk, abbot of St Martin of Épernay on the Marne in the diocese of Rheims, is the man to whom Hugh Metellus’s Letter 13 is addressed: “To Fulk, the reverend and blessed in Christ abbot of Épernay,” concerning the restoration of a certain canon of Épernay by Abbot William. Fulk was the first abbot of that place after the Order of Regular Canons had been introduced in 1128 through the counsel of Bernard and his brother Guy; he had been brought there from the abbey of St Leo at Toul. The letters concerning the affair appear in vol. XIII of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 305 ff. On the foundation of the basilica of St Martin by Count Odo, see p. 281.] I wrote him nothing in reply, wishing, if I happened to find any opinion of the Fathers on this subject, to send him that rather than answer something new or of our own. Since such an opinion did not readily present itself, I now give you both, for the moment, what I myself think—on the condition that if either of you should at any time read, hear, or himself devise anything more reasonable on this same small question, he will not neglect to share it in return with me. You ask, then, what seemed good to the Fathers, that among all the righteous men of old, the Maccabees alone should by a certain singular privilege be granted an annual feast, solemnly celebrated in the Church with equal reverence to that given our martyrs. If I say that they were rightly judged worthy of the glory of martyrs, since their courage in martyrdom was not inferior, perhaps I shall have resolved why they were honored, but not yet fully why they alone were honored. For it is established that some others among the ancients also died with equal zeal for godliness, yet did not deserve to be commemorated with an equal celebration and rejoicing. But if such solemn celebration is rightly read to have been granted to those others because what courage supplied, time forestalled—since, according to their time, they descended not immediately to the joys of heaven, but to the darkness of hell—why should the same consideration not apply to the Maccabees also? For the Firstborn from the dead had not then appeared, to open the kingdoms of heaven to believers; that is, the Lamb from the tribe of Judah, who opens and no one shuts, at whose entrance the words were spoken with all authority to the heavenly powers: “Lift up your gates, O princes [Col. 0231C]; and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7). Therefore, if it seems unsuitable to commemorate joyfully a passing which was not joyful, let this be guarded against in their case as well. Or, if it pleases us to pursue these men with festive favor because of the merit of their courage, why should not equal honor likewise be shown to those others?

2. Must we say that both groups indeed had, in death, a cause of piety in common with the martyrs, but that both did not equally attain the same form of martyrdom as they did? For to all martyrs alike, whether of the Old or of the New Testament, it belongs to have died for righteousness; but there is this difference: these suffered because they upheld it; those because, though not upholding it, they reproved it. These suffered so as not to abandon it; those because they declared that those abandoning it would perish. And, to state briefly the whole point of difference: worship made the former martyrs, zeal for righteousness the latter. The Maccabees alone among the ancients, because they possessed not only the cause but also, as I have said, the form of the new martyrdom, perhaps rightly obtained in the Church, together with the new martyrs of the Church, the same glory of customary celebration. For, in the manner of our martyrs, they too were compelled to pour libations to foreign gods, to abandon the law of their homeland—indeed, to transgress God’s commandments; they refused, and died.

3. Isaiah did not die thus, nor Zechariah, nor finally even that great man John the Baptist: the first of whom is said to have been sawn asunder; the second is read to have been slain between the temple and the altar (Matt. 23:35); the third beheaded in prison. If one asks by whom: by the unjust and impious. If for what cause: for righteousness and piety. If in what manner: not so much by confessing them as by setting them forth. They set forth the truth to those who hated [variant: heard] it; the truth gave birth to hatred in them, and hatred to death. Although unjust and impious, these men nevertheless persecuted not so much piety in the saints as they repelled it from themselves; nor were they so much directed against the others’ righteousness as they defended their own unrighteousness. It is one thing to attack what belongs to another; another to defend one’s own. It is not the same thing not to wish to follow the truth and to persecute it; to envy believers and to be angered by reprovers; to stop the mouths of confessors and not patiently bear the goads of rebuke.

Thus Herod sent and arrested John. For what reason? Because he preached Christ? Because he was a good and righteous man? On the contrary, for this very reason he reverenced him and, having heard him, did many things. But because John rebuked Herod concerning Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, he was therefore bound and therefore beheaded (Mark 6:17–28): he too suffered indeed for the truth, but for truth as one who appeared to zeal for it, not as one compelled to deny it. Hence the passion of so great a martyr itself is commemorated less festively than the feasts of many martyrs, even far lesser ones.

4. Certainly, had the Maccabees suffered according to such a rationale and order, no commemoration of them at all would be observed. But because a confession of truth not unlike that of Christian martyrs made them like those martyrs, similar veneration rightly attends them as well. Nor should it trouble us that, just as the martyrs, they too did not suffer expressly for Christ by name: for it makes no difference whether one suffers under the Law for legal observances or under Grace for evangelical commandments. Each alike is known to suffer for truth, and thereby for Christ, who said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6).

Thus, in this respect, the kind of martyrdom contributed more to the Maccabees than did their virtue; since the present Church, at least, does not celebrate with equal honour even those Fathers who, as is agreed, strove with equal virtue for righteousness in that age. I think it judges it unfitting to devote a feast day, however praiseworthy the death, to one preceding Christ’s death—especially since, before that saving Passion, not festive joys but gloomy confinements received all who died. Yet the Church judged that the Maccabees were to be received, as has been said, because the kind of their martyrdom bestowed upon them what their time denied them.

5. And not only them, but also those who anticipated by their own death the death of Life already manifested in the flesh: whether dying in that Life itself, as Simeon and John the Baptist; or even for it, as the Innocents. These too, though they likewise descended to the underworld, we nevertheless venerate with solemn rite for another reason. The Innocents, indeed, because it would plainly have been unjust for innocence dying for righteousness to be deprived of any present glory. John also, knowing that from his days the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and therefore crying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2), and at the same time seeing that Life would immediately follow him, gladly welcomed death.

Indeed, he had anxiously inquired of the Lord himself, being about to die, and deserved to be assured. For when, through his disciples, he asked him, saying, “Are you he who is to come, or are we to await another?” after many miracles had been recounted, he heard: “And blessed is he who shall not be offended in me” (Matt. 11:3–6). By this saying the Lord plainly indicated that he would die, and by such a death as might be a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles. At this word of the bridegroom, the rejoicing friend of the bridegroom went before with eager spirit, no longer able to doubt that he too would come shortly.

Moreover, that man who could die gladly—and so gladly—could also deserve a joyful remembrance. And that old man, as full of virtues as of days, bearing Life in his hands while death was near, said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30); as though saying: “I descend securely into prison, for I feel my redemption so close at hand.” Therefore he too, who dies with such secure joy and joyful security, is rightly remembered with celebration in the Church.

6. But by what reasoning can that death be accounted festive which no festivity of joys accompanies? Or whence could one about to die draw joy, who was certain that he too would descend to the infernal darkness and bore with him no certain assurance by which to be consoled concerning his Deliverer’s imminent coming? Hence it is that one of the saints, on hearing, “Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live,” turned himself to the wall and wept with a great weeping, and thus obtained some delay of the death he hated. Indeed, he lamented this miserably, saying: “In the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of the underworld”; and shortly afterward: “I shall not see,” he says, “the Lord God in the land of the living; I shall behold man no more, nor the inhabitant of rest” (Isa. 38:1–11).

Likewise another said: “Who will grant me this—that you would protect me in the underworld and hide me until your wrath has passed, and appoint me a time when you will remember me?” (Job 14:13). Israel also said to his sons: “You will bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the underworld” (Gen. 42:38). What of solemn joy or festive celebration appears in these words?

7. But our martyrs desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, certain that wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered without delay. Immediately, I say, the righteous rejoice there in God’s presence and delight in gladness. There—there, most gracious Jesus—there, as soon as any saint is snatched from this wicked world, joy is fulfilled with your countenance. There one voice resounds with everlasting jubilation, one voice of exultation and salvation in the tents of the righteous: “Our soul has escaped like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters; the snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 124:7).

Would those sitting in the underworld, in darkness and the shadow of death, have wished to sing this while there was none to redeem or save, when the Dayspring from on high had not yet visited us—Christ, namely, the firstfruits of those who sleep? The Church therefore, which knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep, judges them equal in virtue, yet distinguishes them by time; nor does it think that passage into life and descent into the underworld should be attended with equal observance.

8. Thus the cause makes martyrdom; time and kind distinguish it. Time separates the Maccabees from the new martyrs and joins them to the ancient ones. Their kind, however, joins them to the new martyrs and separates them from the ancient. Such differences are observed in the Church for the reasons stated above. But before God, this is common to the entire company of saints, as the holy Prophet says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 116:15). Let him explain to us why he calls it precious: “When he gives sleep to his beloved,” he says, “behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord, the fruit of the womb a reward” (Ps. 127:2–3).

Nor should we suppose that martyrs alone are beloved, when we recall what was said of Lazarus: “Lazarus our friend sleeps” (John 11:11); and again: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13). Not only those who die for the Lord, like martyrs, but also those who die in the Lord, like confessors, are certainly blessed. Two things therefore seem to me to make death precious: life and cause; but cause more than life. That death, then, will be most precious which both cause and life commend.

## LETTER XCIX. TO A CERTAIN MONK

> **Note:** [Col. 0233D] In quite a few writings the following four letters have no title other than this: “On the same matter,” that is, the Maccabees—which is false. William, [Col. 0234D] mentioned at the beginning of the letter, was that monk of Clairvaux concerning whom Letter 103 following speaks.

Troubled by the departure of a certain monk from his monastery, he writes that the latter’s letter has freed him from an unfavourable suspicion.

The message by which you say you were disturbed Brother William thought should be sent to you, not because of his own need but because of yours. For he himself, in his customary manner, acts strongly by God’s grace, meanwhile keeping far from himself that saying: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James 1:8). Since he walks simply, and therefore confidently, in the Lord’s ways, he does not experience that woe of which it is said: “Woe to the man who enters the land by two ways!” (Ecclus. 2:14).

But we had heard that you were involved in discord, had left your house amid no slight scandal to the abbot and brethren, and were living alone in some place altogether unsuitable. Moved by this report, and anxiously asking whether we could in any way provide for you, nothing more ready occurred to us than to summon you to us, so that we might first become better informed about you from yourself; and thus, being present, might give present counsel concerning what was at hand. But now, by your letter and our reply, since the fear of false suspicion on both sides has been removed, let us both rest.

Yet this false report has proved how genuine is our love for one another. I should judge that love now fruitfully renewed through this mutual concern for each other; and we should hope then to receive its abundant fruit if an opportunity for your presence with us were afforded. Otherwise, we judge it more fitting to be content with our lack than to abound in an importunate abundance.

## LETTER C. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP

He praises the bishop’s favour and generosity toward poor religious persons.

If we had found you less ardent in undertaking so great a work, we would have had to exhort and entreat you in this matter. But now, since your zeal, going before, first invited us, it remains for us both to render thanks to him from whom all good things proceed, for giving you the will for good; and to pour out prayers that he may add the power to accomplish what accords with that good will.

Still, I shall not conceal my joy from you. What delights do you think such an intention on your part brings to my heart? “My soul shall delight in abundance,” if I know you to be untiring in salutary and honourable pursuits. For I rejoice, not because I seek a gift, but because I seek the fruit. I gladly receive a benefit that profits its giver; otherwise I do not walk in that love which “does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). And indeed in this you do good to us, but better to yourselves—unless perhaps you have forgotten that saying: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

This truly befits a bishop; this commends your priesthood, adorns your crown, ennobles your dignity: if ministry prevents someone from being poor, let administration prove him a lover of the poor. For poverty is not reckoned a virtue, but love of poverty is. Thus: “Blessed are the poor,” not in possessions, but “in spirit” (Matt. 5:3).

## LETTER CI. TO RELIGIOUS PERSONS

He asks that a monk who had departed without permission be kindly received on his return.

Brother Lambert, whom we received while perhaps wavering in certain matters, we have sent back at your request, now steadfast, and, as we think, no longer troubled by any scruple from the past. For, carefully investigating the cause of his coming, as well as the manner and intention of his departure, we found his intention indeed blameless, but his cause plainly insufficient for departing in such a manner—that is, without permission.

Accordingly, having taken occasion for a just reproof of him, rebuking him as was fitting and strengthening him in those matters in which he wavered, we persuaded him to return. And for this returning brother we ask you, most beloved brethren, to show yourselves indulgent toward his presumption—but a presumption, as you see, sufficiently simple and not malicious. For he turned neither to right nor left, but came straight to us, whom he certainly knew to be servants of your holiness, most sincere lovers of your religious life, and most faithful emulators of it.

Receive him therefore, you who are spiritual, in a spirit of gentleness; let love be strengthened in him, and let a good intention excuse the wrongful deed. Rather, receive back with joy him whose loss grieved you; and let the swift joy at his return put to flight the sorrow contracted through the brother’s departure and transgression. I trust, moreover, in the mercy of the Almighty, that whatever his disorderly departure embittered, his reformed conduct will afterward soften.

## LETTER CII. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT

The reformation of a troublesome monk must be attempted by every means; but one who is incorrigible must be expelled, lest many be corrupted by his company.

1. Concerning a disturbed brother, who disturbs the brethren and despises his master, we give you brief but faithful counsel. It is the devil’s aim to go about in God’s house and seek whom he may devour; on the contrary, it belongs to your vigilance, so far as you can, never to give the devil an opportunity. Therefore, the more keenly he presses to separate a weak little sheep from the flock, that he may seize it more freely when there is no longer anyone to rescue it, the more earnestly must you resist, as far as lies in you, lest he be able to snatch it from your hand, lest the enemy should ever say: “I have prevailed against him.”

Therefore approach the brother with every service of charity: with benefits, salutary admonitions, private rebukes, public exhortations, even stern corrections both of words and of blows; and, what is usually more effective, with your own devout prayers to God for him and those of the brethren.

2. But if you have now done all these things and have made no progress, one must have recourse to the Apostle’s counsel: “Remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13). Let the wicked man then be removed, lest he produce wicked men. For an evil tree can bear none but evil fruit. But, I say, let him be removed—not in the way he himself wishes: namely, that, as though by your permission, with a conscience wickedly at ease outside the community, contrary to his profession, evading submission, he be allowed to be his own master and live by his own law.

> **Note:** [Col. 0237D] Discipline concerning incorrigible monks varied according to times and places. The Rule of Saint Benedict commands their expulsion in chapters 28 and 29. The Council of Clovesho of 747 provides in canon 24 that this be done only by decree of a synod. The case of nuns is different: when one had been expelled from the monastery of Saint Peter at Metz after her veil had been removed, she was ordered to be received and “placed within the monastery in a prison,” by decree of the Synod of Metz in 888, canon 9. In the twelfth century regular canons were expelled, according to Letter 38 of Stephen of Tournai.

But let him be cut off as a diseased sheep from the flock, as a rotten limb from the body; so that from then on he may know certainly that you regard him as a heathen and a publican. And do not fear that you act against charity if, by the peace of many, you compensate for the scandal of one—

> **Note:** [Col. 0237D] The printed editions add “by expulsion,” but it is absent from the manuscripts.

—for perhaps by his own malice he could easily disturb the unanimity of the brethren living together. Let that saying of Solomon console you: “Whom God neglects, no one can correct” (Eccles. 7:14); and that of the Saviour: “Every plant which my Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13); and that of the blessed evangelist John concerning schismatics: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19); and again in the Apostle: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Cor. 7:15). Otherwise the rod of sinners must not be left over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity. For it is better that one should perish than unity.

> **Note:** [Col. 0237D] On this question—whether monasteries have the right to expel an incorrigible religious—consult Haeftenus, *Monastic Investigations*, and our Menard and Edmund Martene in their commentaries on the Rule.

## LETTER CIII. TO THE BROTHER OF WILLIAM, MONK OF CLAIRVAUX

> **Note:** [Col. 0238D] This is the title in two Vatican manuscripts and in some of ours. In Cistercian manuscripts it is entitled, “Exhortation to a Friend.” From the end of Letter 106, however, we conjecture that he is Ivo, who signs together with William.

After an outstanding commendation of religious poverty, he censures in him an excessive attachment to earthly things, joined with harm to the poor—indeed, to himself—since he would rather yield his possessions to death than to the love of Christ.

1. Though unknown to us in face and though remote from us in body, you are nevertheless our friend; and friendship makes you already known and present to us. Flesh and blood did not procure this friendship for you, though you did not know it, but the Spirit of God, who bound your brother William to us in eternal fellowship and spiritual love, and through him bound you also, if you judge it worthy.

But if you are wise, you will not despise the friendship of those whom Truth calls blessed and pronounces kings of heaven (Matt. 5:3). We do not begrudge you that blessedness: for when it is shared with you, it is not diminished in us; nor are our own boundaries narrowed if you too reign. What cause for envy can there be where the multitude of those sharing in it takes nothing from the greatness of the inheritances?

I want you to be a friend of the poor, but still more an imitator of them. The former is the stage of those making progress; the latter, of the perfect. Friendship with the poor makes one a friend of kings; love of poverty makes kings. For the kingdom of heaven belongs to the poor; and it is a royal power to bless one’s friends as one wills. “Make for yourselves friends,” he says, “from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). You see how great is the dignity of holy poverty: not only does it seek no patronage for itself, but it affords protection to the needy. What a thing it is, without the intervention of any angels or men, in confidence in divine grace alone, to approach by yourself the face of glory, take possession of the highest things, and attain the summit of all magnificence!

2. But would that you considered without dissembling the things by which you hinder yourself from these blessings. Alas, alas! What is this vapour, appearing for a little while, that closes the entrance to eternal blessedness, hides the unbounded charity of everlasting light, defrauds one of knowledge of the universe, and deprives one of the honour of highest dignity? How long will you prefer to so great a glory the grass that is today and tomorrow cast into the furnace—I mean the flesh and its glory? “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

If you are wise, if you have a heart, if the light of your eyes is with you, cease now to pursue things which it is wretched even to attain. Blessed is he who has not gone after things that, when possessed, burden; when loved, defile; when lost, torment. Is it not better to despise them with honour than lose them with grief? Is it not wiser to surrender them to Christ’s love than to death? A robber lies in ambush, from whose hands you cannot withdraw either yourself or your possessions. His coming cannot be foreseen, for he will come like a thief in the night. “You brought nothing into this world; undoubtedly you can carry nothing out” (1 Tim. 6:7). You shall sleep your sleep and find nothing in your hands. But you know these things; there is no need to labour superfluously in teaching you. Rather, we should pray that you may be granted to fulfil as you ought what you have already been granted to know.

## LETTER CIV. TO MASTER WALTER OF CALVO-MONTE

> **Note:** [Col. 0238D] By this name he is accustomed to call teachers and instructors in letters, as in Letters 77 and 106, etc. Thus Thomas of Étampes sometimes calls himself master, sometimes teacher of Caen, in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 137, 140. In one Vatican manuscript it reads: “To Master Walcher.”

He exhorts him to flee the world, warning that the cause of Christ and of the soul is more important than that of one’s parents.

1. When the sweetest remembrance of you often comes into my mind, I grieve for you, dearest Walter. I think of that distinction of your youth, the keenness of your intellect, the adornment of knowledge and learning, and—what is more excellent than all these in a Christian—your noble character; and I grieve that you wear these out in empty pursuits while, with such great gifts, you serve not their author Christ but transitory things. Oh, if—may God avert it!—sudden death should snatch you and shake these things, alas, suddenly all would wither, as grass swiftly dries at the blast of a scorching, raging wind, and as green herbs quickly fall.

What then will you take with you from all your labour which you have performed upon the earth? What will you render to the Lord for all that he has given you? What profit, I ask, will you return to the creditor for all the talents entrusted to you? Oh, if he finds your hand empty—he who is indeed a ready giver of gifts, but an exacting collector! For he will come, he will come and will not delay, to demand his own with interest. He claims as his own all that seems to make you distinguished in your native land by splendid but perilous favour: illustrious lineage, a well-proportioned body, elegant appearance, quick intelligence, the usefulness of learning, and uprightness of character. These are indeed glorious things—but to him from whom they come. If you claim them for yourself, there is one who will require an account and judge.

2. But let it be so: suppose you may meanwhile ascribe these things to your own name, glory in your praise, be called *rabbi* by men, and make yourself a great name only upon earth. What will remain to you after death from all these things, except perhaps memory alone—and that only upon earth? For it is written: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 76:6). If this is the end of all your labours, then, with your leave, what do you have beyond a beast of burden? For even of your palfrey, when it has died, it will be said that it was good.

> **Note:** [Col. 0239D] A *palefridus* is a large and distinguished horse led by a bridle.

At the same time consider what answer you must give before that dreadful tribunal for having received your soul in vain—and such a soul—if you are found to have done no more with your immortal and rational spirit than any beast does with its own. For the brute spirit lives only so long as it gives life, and at one and the same instant ceases both to give life and to live. What, I ask, will you judge yourself worthy of, if, made in the image of your Maker, you do not defend the dignity of such majesty in yourself, and you—a man who, though you were—

> **Note:** [Col. 0239D] The printed editions add “in honour,” from Psalm 48 [Col. 0240D]; but this is absent from the manuscripts and is certainly redundant here.

—did not understand your honour, have been compared to senseless beasts and made like them? For you will have laboured for nothing spiritual or eternal, but, like the animal spirit which is dissolved from the body and with the body, you will have been content with bodily and temporal goods alone, a deaf hearer of that evangelical counsel: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6:27).

It is written that none ascends the mountain of the Lord except he who has not received his soul in vain. But neither does even he ascend unless he is also innocent in hands and pure in heart (Ps. 24:4). See whether you dare presume this of your works and thoughts alike; but if not, consider what iniquity deserves, if uselessness alone suffices for condemnation. And indeed no thorn or thistle will be safe when the axe is seen laid to the unfruitful tree; nor will he spare what pricks who threatens the barren. Woe, therefore, and woe again to him of whom it shall be said: “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes!” (Isa. 5:4).

3. But I know how clearly and copiously you are able to reflect on these things even if I say nothing. Bound, however, by maternal love, you cannot yet cast aside what you already know how to despise. What shall I answer you in this matter? That you should leave your mother? It seems inhuman. That you should remain with her? But it is not good for her either that she should be the cause of her son’s destruction. Perhaps that you should serve the world and Christ at the same time? But no one can serve two masters.

Your mother wills what is contrary to your salvation and therefore to her own. Choose then which of two things you wish: to satisfy the will of one, or to secure the salvation of both. Yet if you love her greatly, leave her rather for her own sake, lest, if you leave Christ so as to remain with her, she too perish because of you. Otherwise she who bore you has earned ill from you if she perishes because of you. For how does she not perish who destroys the very one she bore? I say this to accommodate and to give counsel, in some degree, to your fleshly affection. But this saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: although it is impious to despise one’s mother, to despise her for Christ is most pious. For he who said, “Honour your father and mother” (Matt. 15:4), also said: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

## LETTER CV. TO ROMANUS, SUBDEACON OF THE ROMAN CURIA

He presses upon him the purpose of religious life, impressing on him the remembrance of death.

BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, to his Romanus—his own—what is due to his own.

You have done well, dearest friend, both in renewing by letter your sweet remembrance among us and in excusing your most unwelcome delay. No forgetfulness of your affection could ever steal into hearts desiring you; but, I confess, before seeing that letter, we thought you had almost forgotten yourself. Therefore now break off delays; quickly do what you wrote. And if your pen truthfully expressed your affection, let the deed effectively bear witness to the pen.

Why do you delay to bring forth that spirit of salvation which you conceived long ago? To mortals nothing is more certain than death, or more uncertain than the hour of death: for it will come like a thief in the night. Woe to those with child on that day! If it comes upon and overtakes this most salutary birth, alas, it will break into the house and extinguish the holy offspring. “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, as labour pains upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3).

I want you, if not to escape death, at least not to fear it. For the righteous man, though he does not avoid death, does not dread it. Indeed, if he is overtaken by death, he shall be in refreshment (Wis. 4:7). The righteous man does die, but securely; for his death is an exit from the present life and likewise an entrance into a better one. Death is good if you die to sin in order to live to righteousness. This death must come first, so that the secure death may follow.

In this life, while it lasts, acquire for yourself that life which lasts forever. While you live in the flesh, die to the world, so that after the flesh’s death you may begin to live to God. For what if death should strike down the sack of your body while joy surrounds you on every side? Oh, how blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, hearing from the Spirit that they may now rest from their labours! (Rev. 14:13.) And not only this: delight follows from newness, and security from eternity. Therefore the death of the righteous is good because of rest, better because of newness, best because of security. On the other hand, “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. 34:22).

And hear why it is most evil. It is evil in the loss of the world, worse in separation from the flesh, and most evil in the twofold torment of worm and fire. Come then, hasten, go out, depart. Let your soul die the death of the righteous, so that your last things may become like theirs. “Oh, how precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints!” (Ps. 116:15.) Flee, I beg you; do not stand in the path of sinners. How can you live where you do not dare to die? Be assured that we stand ready to meet you in your flight with loaves.

> **Note:** [Col. 0241D] A mode of expression familiar to Bernard, as in Letter 107, no. 13, and Letter 124, no. 2, etc.

## LETTER CVI. TO MASTER HENRY MURDACH

> **Note:** [Col. 0241D] This Henry, an Englishman by nation, was head of the schools among the English. That William and Ivo were his pupils is apparent from the end of the letter. At last Henry yielded to Bernard’s counsels, became a monk of Clairvaux, then abbot of Vallis-Clara; afterward the third abbot of Fountains in England, as Letters 320 and 321 below, now in their proper order, show; and finally, after William the treasurer had been deposed by Eugenius III, archbishop of York. On this matter there are various letters below. Read William of Newburgh, Book I, chapter 7; Roger of Hoveden, under the year 1140; and Robert of Torigni’s appendix to Sigebert.

He urges him to embrace the religious life, briefly indicating its delights.

To his beloved HENRY MURDACH, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting—and not on the road.

1. What wonder if you are tossed amid prosperity and adversity, when you have not yet set your feet upon the rock? But if you swear and determine to keep the judgments of the Lord’s righteousness, what of these things can separate you from Christ’s love? Oh, if you knew—and what shall I say?—“Eye, O God, has not seen apart from you the things which you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64:4).

But you, brother, who, as I hear, read the Prophets—do you think you understand what you read? For if you understand, you surely perceive that Christ is the meaning of prophetic reading. If you wish to apprehend him, you can attain him more quickly by following than by reading. Why do you seek the Word in the Word, when he who was made flesh is already before your eyes? He has now come out from the prophets’ hiding-place into the sight of fishermen; from the shadowy and dense mountain, like a bridegroom coming from his chamber, he has leapt forth into the field of the Gospel.

Let him who has ears to hear now hear him crying in the temple: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37); and: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28). Do you then fear to fail where Truth promises to refresh you? Surely, if the dark water from the clouds of the air delights you so much, how much more pleasantly will you drink from the Saviour’s most clear springs?

2. Oh, if you once tasted ever so little of the rich fat of the wheat with which Jerusalem is satisfied, how willingly you would leave their crusts to be gnawed by the learned Jews! Oh, if I might someday have you as a companion in the school of piety under Jesus as master! Oh, if I might be permitted first to set the purified little vessel of your breast beneath the anointing that teaches concerning all things! How gladly I would offer you warm loaves as well, still steaming and—as they say—freshly taken from the oven, which Christ frequently breaks for his poor from heavenly bounty!

Would that, if God should ever deign to let some drop of the voluntary rain which he has set apart for his inheritance fall upon me, his poor man, in his sweetness, I might immediately pour it out for you and receive back from you in turn what you have experienced! Believe one who has tried it: you will find something more in forests than in books. Woods and stones will teach you what you cannot hear from masters. Do you not think you can suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone? Do not the mountains drip sweetness, the hills flow with milk and honey, and the valleys abound with grain?

Though many things occur to me to say to you, I scarcely restrain myself. But because you ask not for a reading, but for prayer, may the Lord open your heart in his law and in his commandments. Farewell.

3. William and Ivo say the same. What shall we say further to you on this subject? You know what we desire—to see you—and for what purpose; but how greatly we desire it, neither can we say nor can you know. Therefore we pray God to grant you to follow, at least, where you ought to have gone before us; so that even in this we may acknowledge you as a master of such great humility, since you have not disdained to follow your pupils, though you are their master.

## LETTER CVII. TO THOMAS, PROVOST OF BEVERLEY

> **Note:** [Col. 0242D] Elsewhere “of Beverlac.” See Letter 411.

This Thomas had devoted himself to the Cistercian Order at Clairvaux. Bernard urges him, while he delays, to fulfil his vows. The following letter will show that he sang to a deaf man, when it recounts Thomas’s unhappy end. In this letter, however, the whole economy of salvation is described with the greatest depth.

To THOMAS, beloved son, BERNARD, what is due to a son.

[Col. 0242D] **1.** What need is there of words? A fervent spirit and vehement desire cannot be disclosed by the tongue alone. Let your other members speak to us of your affection as well. In person you will both become better known to us and come to know us. For a long time now we have been mutually bound to one another: I by faithful care, you by humble obedience. Let action, not pen, prove both, if you please. I wish both to claim you for myself and for you, and to prove in myself that saying of the Only-begotten Son: [Col. 0243A] “The works which the Father has given me to accomplish, these bear witness concerning me” (John 5:36). Thus indeed, thus does the Spirit of the only Son bear witness to our spirit that we too are children of God, when, raising us from dead works, he grants us works of life. A good or bad tree is recognized not from its leaves or flowers, but from its fruit. “By their fruits,” he says, “you will know them” (Matt. 7:16). Works, therefore, and not words, distinguish the children of God from the children of unbelief. Accordingly, disclose your desire through works, and test ours.

**2.** We desire your presence; we seek for what is longed for—indeed, we demand what was promised. Why so greatly? Certainly we seek from it nothing of flesh and blood. We wish either to profit through you or to benefit you. Nobility of [Col. 0243B] blood, height of body, graceful appearance, youthful beauty, estates, palaces, immense furnishings, the insignia of high office—and add worldly wisdom as well: these things are of the world, and the world loves what belongs to it. But for how long? Not merely not forever, since the world itself will not endure forever; indeed, not even for long. For the world will not be able to retain these things in you for long, since before long it will not retain you yourself: human days are brief. The world passes away with its desires; but it sends you forth before it itself has passed away. Why does a love soon to end delight you without end? But we love you, not your possessions; let your possessions belong to him from whom they come. Remembering your promise, do not any longer deny us the gift of yourself—us who love you sincerely [Col. 0243C] and will love you forever. For if we love you purely in this life, we shall not be separated from you even in death. What we desire in you—or rather, for you—is not of this body, nor merely of this time; consequently it does not fail with the body or pass away with time. Rather, when the body has been laid aside it gives greater delight, and it endures beyond times. It has nothing in common with the things listed above, or with things like them—things that are indeed present in you, but are not from the Father, rather from the world. For which of them either does not anticipate death or does not encounter it?

**3.** But this is that best portion which shall never be taken away. What is it? “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.” Whoever is merely human and walks according to man—that is, to say it more plainly, whoever still yields to flesh [Col. 0243D] and blood—has no knowledge whatever of what it is, because flesh and blood do not reveal what God alone reveals through his Spirit. The natural person, therefore, is by no means admitted to this secret, for “he does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Blessed are those who hear: “I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). O wicked age, which is accustomed thus to make only your own friends blessed, by making them enemies of God and consequently unworthy of the counsel of the blessed! [Col. 0244A] For whoever wishes to be your friend is made an enemy of God. And if a servant does not know what his master does, how much less does an enemy? But the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice; hence he also says, “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5:6). Thus the friend of the world is excluded from the counsel of God’s friends, who have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that they may know the things granted to them by God. “I confess to thee, Father, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing before thee” (Matt. 11:25–26)—not because it was thus deserved by them. For all have sinned and need your glory, so that you may freely send the Spirit of your Son, crying [Col. 0244B] in the hearts of the children of adoption, “Abba, Father.” For those who are led by this Spirit are sons, and are in no way to be shut out from the Father’s counsel. They have within themselves the abiding Spirit, who searches even the deep things of God. Indeed, what can those fail to know whom the anointing teaches concerning all things?

**4.** Woe to you, children of this age, because of your foolish wisdom: you do not know the saving Spirit and do not share in that counsel which the Father alone discloses to the Son alone, except to one to whom the Son wills to reveal it! “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11:34). Certainly not no one, but few: only those, indeed, who can truly say, “The Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared [him] to us” (John [Col. 0244C] 1:18). Woe to the world because of its noise! The same Only-begotten cries out among the peoples, as the Angel of Great Counsel: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” And because he finds no minds worthy to receive the Father’s secret, he veils it in parables for the crowds, “so that hearing they may not hear and seeing they may not understand.” But his friends hear apart: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Luke 8:8, 10); and to them he says, “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Who are these? Surely those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. A great and secret counsel has become known. “The Lord knows those who are his”; but what was known to God has been made manifest to human beings. Nor does he deem any others worthy of sharing so great a mystery except those very persons whom he foreknew and predestined as his own. For those whom he predestined, them he also called. Who, indeed, unless called, approaches God’s counsel? And those whom he called, them he also justified. For the Sun rises—not that sun which is daily seen to rise upon good and evil alike, since by prophetic proclamation the Sun is promised to those called to the counsel, [Col. 0244D] “To you who fear God the Sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. 4:2).

> **[Note: Col. 0243D]** Thus all the manuscripts, except that some read: “For that Sun [*is*] promised to those called to the counsel,” etc. In the first editions and most later ones: “For the Sun rises—not that sun which is daily seen to rise upon [Col. 0244D] good and evil alike, but that which, by prophetic proclamation, is promised to those who fear God, called to the counsel: ‘To you,’ he says, ‘who fear the Lord, the Sun of righteousness shall arise.’”

Thus, while the children of unbelief remain in darkness, the child of light escapes from the power of [Col. 0245A] darkness into this new light, provided that he can now confidently say to God: “I am a companion of all who fear thee” (Ps. 118:63). You see that fear comes first, so that justification may follow? Perhaps, then, we are called by fear and justified by love. For “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), namely, that faith which works through love.

**5.** Therefore let the sinner hear, in his calling, what he may fear; and thus, approaching the Sun of righteousness, let him see, once illumined, what he may love. What is that? “The mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him” (Ps. 102:17). From eternity, because of predestination; unto eternity, because of glorification. The one lacks a beginning; the other knows no end. For those whom he predestines from eternity, he [Col. 0245B] glorifies unto eternity, with the single intervening calling together with justification—at least in adults.
