Thus, at the rising of the Sun of righteousness, the mystery hidden from the ages concerning those predestined and to be glorified begins, as it were, to emerge from the abyss 113 of eternity, when one who has been called through fear and justified through love presumes that he too belongs to the number of the blessed, knowing that “those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–30). For what is this? He hears himself called when he is shaken by fear; he also feels himself justified when he is suffused with love: and does he distrust glorification? He is initiated and advances—will he despair only of consummation? Indeed, if the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, in which our [Col. 0245C] calling was said to consist, what is progress in wisdom except the love of God—at least that love which meanwhile comes from faith, and by which our justification occurs? And what is consummation in wisdom except that glorification, hoped for at the end, through the divine and deifying vision? Thus “deep calls to deep at the voice of thy waterfalls,” when, in the terror of his judgments, that immeasurable eternity and eternal immensity, whose wisdom is without number, by its wondrous goodness and power draws the perverse and unsearchable human heart into his marvelous light.

**6.** For example, let us suppose a person in the world, still held by love of the world and of his own flesh; bearing the image of the earthly man, bent upon earthly things, thinking nothing of heavenly things. [Col. 0245D] Who would not see him surrounded by dreadful darkness, except one who sits in the same shadow of death? For no sign of his salvation has yet shone forth; nor has any inner inspiration yet testified to him whether eternal predestination holds any good thing in store for him. But if heavenly mercy should at some time graciously look upon him and send into him the spirit of compunction, so that he groans and comes to his senses, changes his life, subdues the flesh, loves his neighbor, cries out to God, and resolves henceforth to live for God rather than the world—then, from that gratuitous visitation of heavenly light and sudden change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, he comes to know that he is deservedly now a child not of wrath but of grace, since he experiences the paternal affection of divine goodness toward himself. Yet this had hitherto been so hidden from [Col. 0246A] him that not only did he not know whether he was worthy of love or hatred, but his own conduct bore witness rather to hatred than to love. For darkness was still upon the face of the deep. Does he not seem to you to be drawn, as it were, from the deepest and darkest abyss of dreadful ignorance into another abyss, opposite to it—pleasant and radiant with eternal brightness?

**7.** And then at last God, as it were, divides light from darkness, when the sinner, as the Sun of righteousness begins to shine, casts off the works of darkness and puts on the armor of light. He whom his former life and his own conscience had assigned, as truly a child of Gehenna, to everlasting fires, recovering breath at the great condescension of the Dayspring from on high which visits him, begins even [Col. 0246B] beyond hope to glory in hope of the glory of the children of God. This glory he now beholds rejoicingly in a new light, with unveiled face, and says: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; thou hast given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). “O Lord, what is man, that thou makest thyself known to him? Or the son of man, that thou accountest him worthy?” (Ps. 143:3). Now, O good Father, the most worthless little worm, most worthy of eternal hatred, nevertheless trusts that he is loved, because he feels himself loving; indeed, because he senses beforehand that he is loved, he is not ashamed to return love. Now it appears in your light, O inaccessible Light, what good was with you for the wretched little human being even while he remained evil. Therefore he loves, not without reason, because he was loved without merit; he loves without end because he knows himself to have been loved without beginning. There comes to light, for the consolation of the wretched, [Col. 0246C] the great counsel which lay hidden from eternity in the bosom of eternity: namely, that God does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live. You have, O man, as the indicator of this secret, the justifying Spirit, who thereby bears witness to your spirit that you too are a child of God. Recognize God’s counsel in your justification; confess it and say, “Thy justifications are my counsel” (Ps. 118:24). For your present justification is both a revelation of the divine counsel and a certain preparation for future 114 glory. Or rather, predestination itself is preparation, while justification is more nearly an approach. Thus he says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). Hear also concerning predestination that it is preparation: “Receive,” he says, “the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

**8.** Therefore let no one who now loves distrust that he is loved. God’s love, which precedes our love, gladly follows it. For how could he be reluctant to love again those whom he loved even when they did not yet love? He loved, I say, he loved. For you have the Spirit as the pledge of love; you also have Jesus as a faithful witness—and him crucified. O twofold and most certain proof of God’s love for us! Christ dies and merits being loved. The Spirit moves the affections and causes love. The former provides the reason why he is loved; the latter causes him to be loved. The former commends to us his great love; the latter gives it. In the former we see what we ought to love; from the latter we receive the means by which we love. Thus [Col. 0247A] the occasion for charity is from the former, its affection from the latter. What great confusion it is to behold the Son of God dying with ungrateful eyes! This readily happens if the Spirit is absent. But now, because “the charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5), being loved we love, and loving we deserve to be loved more. For if, while we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved by his life. For what? “He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, will he not also give us all things with him?” (Rom. 8:32).

**9.** Since, therefore, we hold the twofold proof of our salvation, the twofold outpouring of blood and Spirit, neither is of benefit without the other. [Col. 0247B] For the Spirit is given only to those who believe in the Crucified One; nor is faith effectual unless it works through love. Love, moreover, is the gift of the Spirit. If the second man—I mean Christ—was made not only into a living soul but also into a life-giving spirit, dying through the one and raising the dead through the other, what benefit can that which dies in him bring me without that which gives life? For he himself says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life” (John 6:64). And what does “gives life” mean except “justifies”? Since sin is the death of the soul—for “the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:4)—its life without doubt is righteousness, since “the righteous lives by faith.” But who is righteous except one who returns love to the God who loves him? This cannot occur unless the Spirit, through faith, reveals to the person [Col. 0247C] God’s eternal purpose concerning his future salvation. That revelation is nothing other than the infusion of spiritual grace, through which, while the deeds of the flesh are put to death, the person is prepared for the kingdom which flesh and blood do not possess; receiving in one Spirit both the ground for presuming himself loved and the means by which to return love, lest he should be loved gratuitously.

**10.** This, therefore, is that sacred and secret counsel which the Son receives from the Father in the Holy Spirit and communicates, through that same Spirit, to those whom he knows, by justifying them; and by communicating it he justifies them. Each person receives it in his justification so as to begin himself also to know as he is known, when he is granted to sense beforehand [Col. 0247D] something of his own future blessedness, as it lay hidden from eternity in the One who predestines and will appear more fully in the One who glorifies. Yet because of this knowledge of himself already received in part, let him meanwhile glory in hope, though not yet in security. How pitiable are those who have as yet no testimony of their calling to this most joyful counsel of the righteous! “Lord, who has believed our report?” O that they might be wise and understand! But unless they believe, they will not understand.

**11.** But you too, O unhappy lovers of the age, falsely 115 [Col. 0248A] secure, have your own counsel apart from the righteous. “Scale is joined to scale, and there is no breath in you.” You too, I say, O impious ones, have a counsel shared among yourselves, but plainly against the Lord and against his Christ. For if, as Scripture says, “Piety is the worship of God,” then whoever loves the world more than God is proved to be impious and an idolater, worshipping and serving the creature rather than the Creator.

> **[Note: Col. 0247D]** The passage is Job 28:28. The Septuagint translators: *Idou theosebeia esti sophia*—“Behold, the worship of God is wisdom.” The Vulgate: “Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom.”

Since, as has been said, the holy and the impious each have their own counsel among themselves, there is undoubtedly a great fixed chasm between the two. For just as the righteous person keeps far from the counsel and assembly of evildoers, so “the impious shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel [Col. 0248B] of the righteous.”

> **[Note: Col. 0248D]** This is how it should be written, not “assembly,” as in Psalm 2. For the sense requires “counsel,” and this is how the manuscripts read.

For the counsel of the righteous is a voluntary rain which God has set apart for his inheritance; it is a truly secret counsel, descending like rain upon the fleece; it is a sealed fountain in which no stranger shares; it is the Sun of righteousness, which rises only for those who fear God.

**12.** But the prophet, observing the rest remaining in their dryness and blindness—deprived of the rain and light of the righteous, barren and dark, confounded and turned away—mocks and marks them: “This,” he says, “is the nation that did not hear the voice of the Lord its God” (Jer. 7:28). You do not wish, O wretched people, to say with David, “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me” (Ps. 84:9). Dispersed abroad in vanities and false madnesses, you do not seek the inward and most excellent hearing of truth. “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). [Col. 0248C] Deaf to the voice of truth, you do not know the counsel of him who thinks thoughts of peace, and who speaks peace to his people, to his saints, and to those who turn to their hearts. “Now,” he says, “you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). Therefore those who do not hear this word are unclean.

**13.** But you, dearest one, if you prepare the inward ear for this voice of your God, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, flee outward concern, so that, with the inner sense unencumbered and at leisure, you too may say with Samuel: “Speak, Lord, for thy servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:10). This voice does not sound in the marketplace, nor is it heard in [Col. 0248D] public. A secret counsel seeks and hears a secret hearing. It will surely give joy and gladness to your hearing, if you receive it with a sober ear. Abraham is commanded to leave his land and his kindred, so that he may deserve to see and possess the land of the living (Gen. 12:1). Jacob, leaving brother and homeland, crosses the Jordan with his staff (Gen. 32:10), and is received in Rachel’s embraces (Gen. 29:11). Joseph rules Egypt (Gen. 41), having been stolen away from his father and homeland by a furtive sale (Gen. 37). The Church is commanded, if the King is to desire her beauty, to forget her people and the house [Col. 0249A] of her father (Ps. 44:11–12). The boy Jesus is sought by his parents among kinsfolk and acquaintances, yet is not found (Luke 2:44–45). Flee your brothers too, if you wish to find your salvation. Flee, I say, from the midst of Babylon; flee from the face of the sword of the north. We are ready to meet the fugitive with loaves. You call me your abbot; for the present I do not refuse, for the sake of service. I say service, not something that I demand but something that I render: just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his soul as a ransom for many. Yet if you judge it fitting, receive as a fellow-disciple the one whom you choose as master. Let Christ alone be master to us both; and let him be the end of this letter, who is “the end unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

## LETTER CVIII. TO THOMAS OF SAINT-OMER

> **[Note: Col. 0249D]** See Letter 382.

**After he broke his promise to come for conversion.** He urges him, leaving his studies, to enter religious life, proposing the unhappy end of Thomas of Beverley.

[Col. 0249B]

To his dearest son THOMAS, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: to walk in the spirit of fear.

**1.** You do well in acknowledging the debt of your promise and not denying the fault of delaying its fulfillment. But I wish 116 you to consider not only what you promised, but also to whom you promised it. For I claim nothing for myself from the fact that you recall privately that it was promised before me, though not to me. [Col. 0249C] Therefore you are wrong to fear that I shall reproach you for a futile delay, since I was called as a witness, not as lord of the vow.

> **[Note: Col. 0249D]** Bernard calls a promise of this kind a “vow,” when a person had resolved before him to enter religious life. Compare Letter 395 and Sermon 63 on the Song of Songs, no. 6, where he laments the lapse and fall of novices.

I saw it and rejoiced; and I pray that my joy may be full. It will not be so unless the promise is fulfilled. You set a deadline which you ought not to have overstepped. You have overstepped it: what is that to me? Before your own lord you stand or fall. For my part, because of the impending danger, I have resolved to deal with you not by reproaches or threats but by admonitions—and this only insofar as you receive them with an even mind. If you listen to me, well; if not, I judge no one. There is one who seeks and judges, for “the Lord is he who judges us” (1 Cor. 4:4). And I judge that you ought on this account to fear and grieve more: because you have lied not to a human being but to God. Even if, as you wish, I spare your shame before people, is that shamelessness which is before God left unpunished? What reason, I ask, is there to be ashamed before the day of man and not to fear the face of God? For “the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17). Thus you fear reproaches more than torments; trembling before the tongue of flesh, do you despise the sword that devours flesh? Is this that most beautiful ordering of morals by which, you write, you are being formed through acquisition of that knowledge for whose study and love you burn so ardently that you do not fear to harm a holy purpose?

**2.** [Col. 0250A] But I ask you: what memorial of virtue, what praise of discipline, what progress in knowledge, or what fruit of art is it, to tremble with fear where there is no fear, and to abandon the fear of the Lord? How much more healthfully would you learn Jesus, and him crucified! That knowledge is not easily attained except by one crucified to the world. You are deceived, my son, deceived, if you think you can find among the masters of the world what only Christ’s disciples—that is, the despisers of the world—attain through God’s gift. For reading does not teach this, but anointing; not the letter, but the Spirit; not instruction, but exercise in the commandments of the Lord. “Sow righteousness for yourselves, reap the hope of life, make the light of knowledge shine for yourselves” (Hos. 10:12). You see that one does not rightly advance to the light of knowledge unless the seed of righteousness first proceeds [alternative: “precedes”] into the soul, from which the grain of life may be formed, and not the chaff [Col. 0250B] of glory. What then? You have not yet sown for yourself unto righteousness, you have not yet reaped sheaves of hope, and yet you presume that you pursue true knowledge! Unless perhaps that knowledge which puffs up is put forward as the true kind. You err still more foolishly, spending your money not on bread and your labors not on satisfaction. I beg you, return to your heart and consider that this year [edition: “annual period”], the term which you allowed yourself in contempt of God, is not a year acceptable to the Lord, but a seedbed of discord, fuel for wrath, nourishment for apostasy; it extinguishes the Spirit, bars grace, and brings on that lukewarmness which is accustomed to provoke God to vomit.

**3.** Alas, alas! You seem to me to walk in one spirit, just as you bear one name, with that other Thomas—formerly provost of Beverley—who, having [Col. 0250C] similarly devoted himself with all desire to our Order and our house, began to seek delays and gradually grew cold, until he was snatched away by a sudden and dreadful death, taken away as a worldly man, a transgressor, and a twofold child of Gehenna. May the merciful and compassionate Lord avert this from you, if it may be so! A letter which I wrote to him in vain still survives (the preceding letter), except that I delivered my own soul by declaring, as far as lay in me, what ought quickly to be done. He would have been blessed if he had listened to me. He ignored it; I am clean of his blood. Yet this does not suffice for me, because, though in this matter I am secure concerning myself, charity—which “does not seek its own”—presses me to mourn for him who did not depart secure, because he lived in evil security. [Col. 0250D] O abyss of God’s many judgments! O God, terrible 117 in thy counsels over the children of men! He gave a spirit which he was afterward to take away, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful; grace entered in so that the offense might abound. Yet this was not the fault of the Giver, but of the one who added transgression. It lay, indeed, within his own choice, by which he, free in an evil way, freely chose to grieve the Spirit, despise grace, and not subject God’s prompting to effect, so that he might have been able to say: “The grace of God in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10).

**4.** If you are wise, his folly will benefit you. [Col. 0251A] You will wash your hands in the blood of the sinner, hasten to free yourself from the snare of destruction, and free me from dreadful fear. For I confess that I endure your turning away no otherwise than as my own disembowelment, because you have become very dear to me and I embrace you with paternal affection. Therefore, at every remembrance of you this sword of fear pierces my soul, and the more painfully because I see you fear less. For I know where I have read concerning such persons: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, as upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3). I foresee many fearful things threatening you while you delay to come to your senses, as one who has experienced much—things which, oh, if you too had known them! Therefore trust one who has experience; trust one who loves you. [Col. 0251B] You know that in the one respect he cannot be deceived, and in the other cannot deceive.

## LETTER CIX. TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS YOUNG MAN GEOFFREY OF PÉRONNE

> **[Note: Col. 0251C]** In the older edition, “of Parrona,” a very strongly fortified town on the Somme. Geoffrey therefore derived both his name and origin from it. He was one of those whom St Bernard is said to have converted to religious life in Belgium [Col. 0251D] in Book Four of his *Life*, chapter 3. Another Geoffrey, later prior of Clairvaux, was his companion in conversion. Hermann, monk of Tournai, is to be understood as speaking of these men in volume 12 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 479, where, concerning St Bernard, he says that “many renowned clerics, both from the church of Saint Mary of Tournai and from the diocese itself, followed Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, for the sake of conversion.” Hermann relates this event on p. 476, after the twenty-fourth year of the pontificate of Simon of Noyon, who began to hold office in 1122. This letter therefore cannot, as Manriquez thinks, be assigned to the year 1131. Peter of Roya, a novice of Clairvaux, praises Geoffrey of Péronne above, in Letter 479, no. 9.—Thus far Mabillon. Horst, however, does not agree with him in identifying this Geoffrey with the prior of Clairvaux, concerning whom he writes as follows: “Saint Bernard converted him, with twenty-nine other noble and learned young men, to religious life in Flanders; and when he wavered or delayed, he stirred him by this letter. He afterward became fifth prior in succession at Clairvaux; finally, when elected bishop of Tournai—others read Nantes—he refused to consent.” Peter of Blois relates this as follows: “We read that Geoffrey of Péronne, prior of Clairvaux, when elected bishop of Tournai, in no way consented to the election. After he had died, he appeared to a certain brother, who asked how matters stood with him; he replied: ‘The Holy Trinity revealed to me that, if I had accepted the bishopric, I would have been among the number of the reprobate.’ By his example he struck the minds of certain other prelates, saying: ‘What then will unhappy men do, who voluntarily and gladly plunge themselves into the waves of temporal anxieties? Who, by feasting splendidly, sleeping, drinking, sitting at the tax office, administering the fiscal accounts, seeking what is their own—or rather what belongs to Caesar and not to God—spend their lives in vanities?’” Thus Peter of Blois, Letter 102. Caesarius relates the same in Book 2, chapter 29. See Henriquez on him in the *Menologium* for 15 February.

**And to his companions.** He praises noble young men for their resolution to adopt religious life and exhorts them to perseverance.

To his beloved sons GEOFFREY and his companions, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

**1.** The report that has resounded builds up many—indeed, it gladdens the whole city of God—so that the heavens rejoice, the earth exults, and every tongue glorifies God for your conversion. The earth was moved because the heavens dropped [rain] before the face of God of Sinai, pouring in these days more abundantly than usual the voluntary rain which [Col. 0251C] God has set apart for his inheritance. The cross of Christ will no longer appear empty in you, as it does in many children of unbelief, who delay from day to day to turn to the Lord and, snatched away by unforeseen death, go down to hell in an instant. The tree upon which the Lord of glory hung has altogether flowered again, as though anew: he who died not only for the nation, but also “that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.” He, he gathers you, who loves you as his own inward parts, as the most precious fruit of his cross, [Col. 0252A] as the worthiest recompense for his blood poured out. If angels rejoice over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15:10), what joy must there be over so many, and sinners who, the more distinguished they seemed in the world by learning, birth, and youth, were examples of perdition to the greater number? I had read: “God has not chosen many noble, many wise, many powerful” (1 Cor. 1:26–27); but now, beyond the rule, a multitude of such persons is converted by the wondrous power of God. Present glory is made cheap; the flower of youth is trampled underfoot; nobility is not regarded; the wisdom of the world is judged folly; flesh and blood are not yielded to; the affections of parents and loved ones are renounced; favor, honors, and offices are reckoned as dung, that Christ may be gained. I would praise you if I knew that these things had happened to you from yourselves. [Col. 0252B] But this is the finger of God, plainly a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. It is a good gift and a perfect gift 118, and doubtless comes down from the Father of lights. Accordingly, we rightly refer all praise to him who alone does wonders, who has made the abundant redemption that is with him no longer idle in you.

**2.** What remains to be done, then, beloved ones, except to strive that a worthy result may follow your praiseworthy resolution? Strive, therefore, for perseverance, which alone is crowned among the virtues. Let there not be found in you “Yes and No,” so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning. You also, brothers, be transformed into the same image from brightness [Col. 0252C] to brightness, as by the Spirit of the Lord, taking every care that you too are not found frivolous, unstable, and wavering. For it is written: “A double-minded man is inconstant in all his ways” (Jas. 1:8); and again: “Woe to the one who enters the land by two ways!” (Ecclus. 2:14). And I, beloved ones, as much as I rejoice with you, so much do I rejoice for myself, because, as I have heard, I have been deemed worthy to be chosen as a minister of this counsel. I give counsel and promise assistance. If I seem necessary, or at least if I am judged worthy, I do not refuse the labor; [Col. 0253A] I shall not fail according to my strength. Devotedly I set my shoulders, though already weary,

> **[Note: Col. 0253D]** From this it is clear that Bernard was then already approaching old age.

under this burden, if it is imposed upon me from heaven. Gladly, and with open hands, as the saying is, I receive fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. How willingly, in accordance with the prophetic command, do I meet those fleeing the sword with loaves and bring water to the thirsty! (Isa. 21:14). I have placed the rest in the mouth of our—indeed, of your—Geoffrey. Whatever he says to you in our stead, do not doubt that it is our counsel.

## LETTER CX. A CONSOLATION TO THE PARENTS OF THE SAME GEOFFREY

There is no reason why they should mourn their son as lost because he has become religious, nor why they should fear for one so delicately nurtured.

**1.** If God makes your son his own as well, what do you lose, or what does he lose? From rich he becomes richer; from noble, more noble; [Col. 0253B] from illustrious, more illustrious; and, greater than all these, from a sinner, holy. But he must be prepared for the kingdom prepared for him from the foundation of the world; and for this purpose he must remain with us for the little time he has to live, until the filth of worldly life has been scraped away and earthly dust washed off, and he is made fit for the heavenly dwelling. If you love him, you will surely rejoice because he goes to the Father—and to such a Father. He indeed goes to God, but you do not lose him; rather, through him you acquire many sons for yourselves. All of us who are in Clairvaux or belong to Clairvaux receive him as a brother and you as parents.

2. But perhaps you fear the harshness of his way of life for his body, knowing it to be tender and delicate. [Col. 0253C] Yet of such fear it is said: “There they trembled with fear, where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII, 5). Trust and be comforted: I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son, until the Father of mercies and God of all consolation receives him from my hands. Therefore do not mourn and do not weep; for your Geoffrey hastens toward joy, not grief. I shall be to him father, mother, brother, and sister. I shall make crooked things straight for him, and rough places into level paths; I shall so moderate and order everything for him that his spirit may advance and his body not fail. In short, he shall serve the Lord in gladness and exultation, and shall sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.

119  
## LETTER CXI. WRITTEN IN THE PERSON OF THE MONK ELIAS TO HIS PARENTS

He urges them not to try to hinder or draw back one who wishes to serve God; this would be both unworthy and futile.

[Col. 0253D]

To his dear parents, INGORRAN and IVETTA, ELIAS, [Col. 0254A] a monk, but a sinner, offers daily prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] This superscription is now restored for the first time from the often-cited Corbie manuscript. Is this letter one of those which the holy man sometimes prescribed for writers to compose, as appears from the letter now numbered 389? In any case Horstius says of these letters: “Bernard wrote this letter in the name of his novice Elias to Elias’s parents, in order to restrain them as they tried to recall their son from his purpose.” “These words indeed,” says Lessius, [Col. 0254D] “might seem too severe, were they not the utterance of such great wisdom and holiness. For who would dare censure that chosen instrument of the Holy Spirit? He knew the importance of the matter. Yet his meaning is not that parents should everywhere be addressed so sharply, unless a person sees that their importunity will cast him into grave dangers to salvation, or unless they do not cease their solicitations.” Thus he writes in his most useful treatise *On Choosing a State of Life*, question 1, §36. Compare the notes to Letter 104.]

1. God is the sole cause for which it is not lawful to obey parents. For he himself says: “He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.” If you truly love me as good and devout parents; if you have a true and faithful parental affection toward your son: why do you trouble me as I strive to please God, the Father of all, and attempt to draw me back from his service—to serve whom is to reign? Truly I now know that “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Micah VII, 6). In this I ought not to obey you; in this I acknowledge you not as parents but as enemies. If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I am going to my Father and yours—indeed, the Father of all. Otherwise, what have I to do with you, and you with me? What have I from you but [Col. 0254B] sin and misery? This alone I confess and acknowledge: that this corruptible body which I bear I have from you. Is it not enough that you, miserable yourselves, brought me miserable into this misery of the world; that in your sin you begot me, a sinner, as sinners; that, born in sin, I was nourished out of sin? Must you also, by begrudging me the mercy I have obtained from him who does not will the death of a sinner, make me besides a son of Gehenna?

2. O hard father! O cruel mother! O cruel and impious parents—or rather, not parents but destroyers: whose sorrow is the safety of their child, whose consolation is the death of their son; who would rather that I perish with them than reign without them; who try to call me back again to the shipwreck [Col. 0254C] from which at last I escaped naked, back again to the fire from which I came out scarcely half-burned, back again to the robbers by whom I was left half-dead, though through the mercy of the Samaritan I have now recovered somewhat. And they endeavor to bring back to the world the soldier of Christ, almost already triumphing, heaven being seized—as I glory not in myself, but in him who conquered the world—from the very threshold of glory, like a dog to its vomit or a sow to the mire!

What a monstrous perversity! The house is burning, fire presses from behind, and the fugitive is forbidden to leave; one escaping is urged to return. And this comes from persons caught in the blaze, who, in most stubborn madness and most mad obstinacy, refuse to flee the danger. Alas for this madness! If you despise your own death, why do you seek mine as well? If, I say, you neglect your own salvation, [Col. 0254D] what is gained by persecuting mine also? Why do you not rather follow me as I flee, so that you may not burn? Or is this the relief of your torment—that you should destroy me too, fearing only that you may not perish alone? What consolation can one burning give to those who burn? What consolation, I ask, is it to the condemned [Col. 0255A] to have companions in their condemnation? Or what remedy is it to the dying to see others dying? That rich man does not persuade me of this: in his torments, despairing of his own deliverance, he begged that word should be sent to his brothers, lest they too come into the same place of torments (Luke XVI, 28), no doubt fearing that his own anguish would be increased by the suffering of his kin.

3. What then? Shall I go and comfort my mother, mourning for me, by a temporary visit, so that eternally I may mourn both myself and her without consolation? Shall I go, I say, and satisfy my father, angry at my temporary absence—he to be comforted for a time by my presence—so that afterward each for himself, and each for the other, may be desolated by inconsolable sorrow? Or rather, not consenting with the Apostle [Col. 0255B] “to flesh and blood” (Gal. I, 16), 120 shall I hear the voice of the Lord commanding: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22); and shall I sing with David, “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. LXXVI, 3); and with Jeremiah, “I have not desired the day of man, O Lord, you know” (Jer. XVII, 16)?

For what is it? “The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places,” and the heavenly inheritance is splendid for me (Ps. XV, 6); and yet an earthly promise flatters me, the consolation of the flesh allures me! Once the spirit has been tasted, the flesh must lose its savor; for one who seeks heavenly things, earthly things have no taste; transient things are wearisome to one who longs for eternal things. Therefore cease, my parents: cease both to afflict yourselves uselessly with weeping and to trouble me vainly by recalling me. Otherwise, if you continue to send messengers after me, you will compel me [Col. 0255C] to go farther away. But if you let me be, I shall never leave Clairvaux. “This is my rest for ever and ever; here shall I dwell, for I have chosen it.” There I shall pray continually for my sins and yours; there, by unceasing prayers—as you also desire—I shall obtain, if I can, that we who for this short time are separated from one another by love of him may in the other world live together, in his love, in a happy and inseparable fellowship through all ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER CXII. TO GEOFFREY OF LISIEUX

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Others read “of Luxeuil.” Orderic also commonly uses this word to denote the people of Lisieux in Neustria; thus, among writers of that period, there is commonly no distinction in the name [Col. 0256D] between the people of Lisieux and those of Luxeuil in the county of Burgundy.]

He grieves that Geoffrey has abandoned his religious purpose and returned to the world, and urges him to repentance.

1. I grieve for you, my son Geoffrey; I grieve for you. And rightly so. For who would not grieve that the flower of your youth, which, amid the rejoicing of angels, you had offered to God unstained as an odor of sweetness, should now be trampled by demons and defiled by the filth of vices and the stains of the world? How is it that you, called by God, follow the devil as he calls you back, and that you, whom Christ had begun to draw after himself, suddenly withdrew your foot from the very entrance to glory? In you I now experience the truth of the Lord’s saying: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X, 36). Your friends and neighbors came near and stood against you. They called you back into the lion’s jaws and set you again at the gates of death. They placed you in darkness, like [Col. 0256A] those dead from of old; and it is now but a little before you descend into the belly of hell. It hastens to swallow you and give you over, as prey, to roaring creatures prepared to devour you.

2. Return, I beg you, return, before the deep swallows you and the pit closes its mouth over you; before you sink where you can rise no more; before, with hands and feet bound, you are cast into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth; before you are thrust down into a dark place covered with death’s gloom. Perhaps you are ashamed to return because you yielded for an hour. Be ashamed of flight, not of returning after flight to battle and fighting again. The battle is not yet ended; the opposing ranks have not yet departed from one another. Victory is still at hand. If you will, we do not wish to conquer without you, nor do we begrudge you your portion [Col. 0256B] of glory. We shall gladly run to meet you, gladly receive you in our embrace, and say: “It is fitting to feast and rejoice, because this son of ours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 32).

## LETTER CXIII. TO THE VIRGIN SOPHIA

He praises her for despising worldly glory; and, setting out the praises, privileges, rewards, and adornments of religious virgins, urges her to perseverance.

BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, to SOPHIA, a virgin: may you preserve the title of virginity and attain its fruit.

1. “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; a woman who fears God shall be praised” (Prov. XXXI, 30). I rejoice, daughter, in the glory of your virtue, by which you are said to have rejected the deceitful glory of the world. It is indeed rightly rejected; but because many 121, wise in another fashion, become foolish in their esteem for it, you are justly praised because you are not deceived. It is a flower of grass, a vapor appearing for a little while. Does not its condition, whatever it may be, contain more anxiety than delight? While you claim, defend, envy, suspect, always seek what you do not have, and—even after gaining some things—the ardor of acquisition does not cool, what rest is there in your glory? Whatever rest there may be passes away, never to return; anxiety remains and never departs.

Moreover, you see that very many fail to attain it, while very few despise it. Why is this? Certainly because it is a necessity for many, but a virtue for few—few, I say, especially among the noble. For God chose not many noble, but the lowly things of the world (1 Cor. I, 26–28). Therefore blessed are you among noblewomen: while all the rest contend for glory, you are more gloriously exalted and more sublimely glorify yourself by contempt for glory. You are plainly more distinguished and illustrious because you have become one of the few than because you were born of the great. The former is yours by God’s gift; the latter belongs to your family. And what is yours is dearer in proportion as it is rarer. For if virtue in men is “a rare bird upon the earth” [Juvenal, *Satires* VI], how much more so in a frail and noble woman? “Who shall find a strong woman?” [Col. 0257A] (Prov. XXXI, 10). How much more one both strong and noble? Certainly God is no respecter of persons; yet I do not know how it is that virtue pleases more in a noble person. Is it perhaps because it shines more clearly? For when a low-born person lacks glory, it is not easily evident whether this is because she does not wish to have it or because she cannot. I praise virtue made from necessity; but I praise more that virtue which freedom chooses rather than necessity imposes.

2. Let the others, then, who have no hope contend for the cheap and brief little glory of fleeting and deceptive things; but do you rest upon the hope that does not put to shame. Reserve yourself, I say, for that weight of glory which this brief and momentary tribulation of yours works beyond measure unto sublimity. And if the daughters of Belial reproach you—those who walk with outstretched necks and mincing steps, dressed and adorned like the likeness of a temple [Col. 0257B]—answer: “My kingdom is not of this world”; answer: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready”; answer: “My glory is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, my life, appears, then I too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 4).

And yet, if one must glory, you too may do so frankly and safely—provided it is in the Lord. I pass over the crown which the Lord has prepared for you for eternity. I say nothing of the promises awaiting you hereafter: that, as a blessed bride, you shall be admitted with unveiled face to behold the glory of your bridegroom; that he will present you to himself glorious, having neither spot nor [Col. 0257C] wrinkle nor anything of the sort; that, receiving you in eternal embraces, he will place his left hand beneath your head and his right hand will embrace you. I pass over the distinguished place which, by the prerogative of virginity, you will without doubt receive as a special lot apart from sons and daughters in the kingdom. I also pass over that new song which you, a virgin among virgins, shall sing with a distinctive and sweet melody; [Note: [Col. 0257] Thus the manuscripts and the older editions. Elsewhere, *cantatura*, “about to sing.”] in it you shall rejoice and make glad the city of God, singing and running and following the Lamb wherever he goes. For “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” is what has been prepared for you, and that for which you must prepare yourself.

3. I pass over, then, these things laid up for you in the future. I speak only of present things: of what you already possess from the firstfruits of the Spirit—the bridegroom’s gifts, the betrothal pledges, [Col. 0257D] the blessings of sweetness—by which he has gone before you, whom you await to follow and complete what is lacking. Let him, let him come into the midst, beautiful in supreme splendor, adorned so as to be admired even by angels; and let the daughters of Babylon produce, if they possess it, anything comparable—for their glory is truly in confusion. They are clothed in purple and fine linen, while their conscience lies in filthy rags; they glitter with necklaces, but are foul in character. You, on the contrary, shine outwardly in rags, inwardly in beauty—but before divine eyes, not human ones. Within is what delights, because within is he whom it delights—unless perhaps you doubt 122 that Christ dwells by faith in your heart. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” [Col. 0258A] (Ps. XLIV, 14). Rejoice, daughter Zion, and exult exceedingly, daughter Jerusalem, because the King has desired your beauty—provided you put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment. For confession and beauty are in his presence. In whose presence? In the presence of him “beautiful in form above the sons of men,” he into whom angels desire to look.

4. You hear whom you please; love that by which you please; love confession, for which you are loved. Love confession if you seek beauty. Beauty and comeliness are joined to confession. You have both: “You have put on confession and beauty” (Ps. CIII, 1); and, “Confession and beauty are in his presence” (Ps. XCV, 6). Truly where there is confession, there is beauty; there is comeliness. If there are sins, they are washed in confession; if there are good works, they are commended through confession. When you confess your evils, “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God”; when you confess God’s benefits, you offer to God a sacrifice of praise. Confession is a good adornment of the soul: it cleanses the sinner and makes the righteous purer. Without confession the righteous is judged ungrateful, and the sinner is reckoned dead. For from a dead man, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes (Ecclus. XVII, 26). Confession, then, is the life of the sinner and the glory of the righteous: it is necessary for the sinner, and nevertheless befitting to the righteous. For “praise befits the upright” [Col. 0258B] (Ps. XXXII, 1).

Silks, purple, and the cosmetic coloring of dyes possess beauty but do not confer it. Whatever of this kind you put upon the body displays its own appearance; it does not impart it. Indeed, it takes its appearance away with itself when it is itself removed. But the beauty that is put on with a garment and laid aside with a garment is plainly the beauty of the garment, not of the wearer.

5. Therefore do not emulate evildoers, who beg for another’s beauty after losing their own. They reveal themselves naked of their native, inward beauty, when with so much zeal and expense they labor outwardly to fashion for themselves, out of the diverse and varied appearances of that passing fashion of the world, an appearance by which they may seem beautiful to foolish eyes. Judge it unworthy of yourself to borrow beauty from the skins of mice and the work of worms. Let your own beauty suffice you. The true and proper beauty of anything is that which belongs to it in itself, without the intervention of any material. O with what becoming blush does the native jewel of modesty suffuse maidenly cheeks! What earrings of queens [Col. 0258D] could compare with it? Nor does discipline offer an ornament of lesser beauty. O how discipline gives composure to the entire bearing of a maiden’s body, and indeed also to the disposition of her mind! It lowers the neck, settles the brows, composes the face, restrains the eyes, checks laughter, moderates the tongue, curbs gluttony, calms anger, and forms the gait. Such pearls ought to adorn the garment of chastity. Virginity surrounded by such variety—to what glory is it not deservedly preferred? To angelic glory? An angel has virginity, but not flesh; in this respect he is indeed happier, but not stronger. This is an excellent and most desirable adornment, one which may even be the envy of angels.

[Col. 0259A] 6. But consider another point concerning the same matter. Certainly your adornment remains secure for you in proportion as it is your own. You see women burdened rather than adorned with gold, silver, precious stones, and every royal decoration. You see them dragging long, exceedingly costly trains after them, raising thick clouds of dust into the air. Let these things not move you. They will lay them aside even in death; your holiness will not leave you. What they wear is not their own. “When they die, they shall not take all things with them, nor shall this glory descend with them.” The world, to which those things belong, will retain them when they depart naked, and will likewise deceive other vain women by the same vanities.

But your adornment is not so. As I said, it remains most securely yours, and therefore is safe because it is yours. It scarcely yields to anyone’s injury or lies open to anyone’s snares. Against such an adornment [Col. 0259B] the cunning of a thief can do nothing, nor the cruelty of one who rages. It is neither eaten by moths, corrupted by age, nor consumed by use. It lives in death. It belongs to the soul, not the body; and therefore it departs from the body together with the soul, but does not perish with the body. Those who kill the body have nothing they can do to the soul.

123  
## LETTER CXIV. TO ANOTHER RELIGIOUS WOMAN

She had retained a mind devoted to the world beneath a religious habit; now that she is repenting, he praises her and urges her not to neglect grace.

1. It gives me great joy to learn that you wish to strive toward true and perfect joy—joy [Col. 0259C] not from earth but from heaven; that is, not from this valley of tears, but from that city of God which the rush of the river makes glad. And truly that alone is true joy, because it is conceived not from the creature but from the Creator; and when you possess it, no one shall take it from you. Compared with it, every pleasure from elsewhere is sorrow; every sweetness is pain; everything sweet is bitter; everything fair is foul; and, finally, whatever else can delight is burdensome.

You yourself are my witness in this matter. Ask yourself, for you will trust yourself more intimately. Does not the Holy Spirit himself cry this very thing in your heart? Has not the truth of it already been persuaded you by him before it was by me? For how could you—a woman and a young woman, beautiful and noble-born—so overcome both the frailty of your sex [Col. 0259D] and your age, so despise beauty and high birth, unless all things subject to the bodily senses had already become cheap to you in comparison with those things which inwardly strengthen you to conquer and delight you to prefer them?

2. And not without reason. The things you despise are small, transient, and earthly; those you seek are greatest, eternal, and heavenly. I shall say more, and say what is true: you leave darkness and enter light; you rise from the depths of the waves into harbor; you breathe again from wretched slavery into blessed freedom; finally, you pass from death to life. For until now, living by your own will rather than God’s and by your own law rather than God’s law, you were dead while alive: alive to the world and dead to God—or, more truly, alive neither to the world nor to God. For though under the habit and name of religion you wished to conduct yourself as one in the world, you had rejected God from yourself by your will alone; but, being unable to do the foolish thing you wished, it was not you who rejected the world, but the world that rejected you. Thus, rejecting God and rejected by the world, you had fallen between two stools, as the saying is.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Aptly applicable here is Book I, chapter 25, of *The Imitation of Christ*: “The negligent and lukewarm religious suffers tribulation upon tribulation and endures distress on every side, because he lacks inward consolation and is forbidden to seek outward consolation.” See Sermons 3 and 5 on the Ascension.]

You did not live for God, then, because you did not wish to; nor for the world, because you could not. You were devoted to one willingly, to the other unwillingly, yet dead to both. So it must happen to those who vow and do not fulfil [variant: “and do not render”] their vow, who make one display outwardly and desire another thing inwardly. But now, through God’s mercy, you begin to live again: not for sin but for righteousness, not for the world but for Christ. You know that even to live for the world is death, and to die in Christ is life. For “blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.”

3. Henceforth we shall not call your vow void or your profession empty; henceforth [Col. 0260C] the integrity of your body shall not be invalidated by corruption of mind, nor the title of virginity obscured by depravity of character; henceforth you shall bear neither a false name nor an empty veil. For why until now were you called a *nonna* [nun] and a religious woman, when under the name of holiness you did not live holily?

[Note: [Col. 0259D] A word formed from the Rule of St Benedict, in which juniors are commanded in chapter 63 to call their elders *nonni*.]

Why did the veil upon your head falsely profess reverence, while beneath the veil a wanton eye displayed impudence? You wore a veiled head, but a proud one; beneath the sign of modesty, your speech resounded immodestly. Excessive laughter, overly free gait, overly ornamented dress—*wimpled* rather than veiled would have suited you.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] All the manuscripts I have seen—namely those of the Royal Library, the Colbert Library, the Sorbonne, the Royal College of Navarre, St Victor of Paris, Compiègne, and others in other libraries—read *wimplatae*, whereas all editions except two (the Paris edition of 1494 and the Lyons edition of 1530) read *uni inflatae* [meaning uncertain]. “What,” they ask, “are *wimplatae*?” Certainly the word is formed from *wimpla* or *guimpla*, with the readily made change of the letter *g* into *v*: French *guimpe* or *guimple*, a woman’s head-dress, formerly customary for noblewomen, as we learn from old images of noble matrons, but rejected by simpler women for modesty’s sake. Hence the French poet quoted by Borel in his *French Glossary*:

> *Moult fut humiliant et simple,*  
> *Elle eut un voile en lieu de guimpte.*

This may be rendered:

> She wore a humble, simple veil in place of a wimple.

Now the name *guimpe* is almost unknown outside the cloister of nuns.]

But behold: through Christ’s working, old things have passed away and all things begin to become new, as you exchange outward adornment for inward and seek to have your life rather than your dress adorned. You do 124 [Col. 0260D] what you ought—indeed what you ought long ago to have done, since long ago you had vowed it. But the Spirit, who blows where he wills and when he wills, had not yet blown. And perhaps therefore what you have done until now has an excuse. But if you allow the flaming Spirit—by whom your heart has now undoubtedly been warmed within you, and the divine fire kindles in your meditations—to be extinguished, what remains except that you must know yourself reserved for that fire which cannot be extinguished? May that same Spirit instead extinguish in you fleshly desires, lest perhaps, if the holy desire newly conceived is choked by them—which God forbid—you should fall into the flames of Gehenna.

## LETTER CXV. TO ANOTHER RELIGIOUS WOMAN, OF THE MONASTERY OF ST MARY AT TROYES

[Note: [Col. 0261D] This monastery still survives at Troyes under the Rule of St Benedict; there religious observance had then been renewed, as Bernard testifies.]

He dissuades her from the desert life which she was rashly and imprudently seeking.

[Col. 0261B]

1. I have been told that, as though from a desire for a more austere life, you wish to leave your monastery. When your spiritual mother or your sisters dissuaded you from this and prohibited it in every way, and you would not agree, you finally chose to seek our counsel on the matter, thinking that whatever I should approve you ought to regard as expedient. You should indeed have chosen someone more learned for such counsel; yet, since this seemed good to you, I will not conceal what seems more correct to me on the matter.

Since I learned of this desire of yours, I have considered and reconsidered in what spirit you conceived it, and I do not readily dare decide. In this matter you may have zeal for God, so that your intention is excusable; but I do not at all see how such a will of yours may be fulfilled according to knowledge. Why, you ask? Is it not wisdom to flee wealth, the crowds of a city, abundance, and pleasures? Will not my chastity be safer for me in the desert, where, living in peace among a few or alone, I may please him alone to whom I have devoted myself?

Not at all. For the person who wishes to act perversely finds abundance even in the desert, shade in the grove, and silence in solitude. Evil which no one sees, no one rebukes. Where no reprover is feared, the tempter approaches more boldly and wickedness is committed more freely. But in a community, whatever good you do, no one prevents; if you wish to do evil, you are not permitted. It is at once [Col. 0261D] discovered by many, reproved, and corrected; while conversely, when they see good, all admire, venerate, and imitate it. [Col. 0262A] You see, then, daughter, that in a community greater glory follows your merits and swifter correction your faults, since there are there both persons to whom you may offer an example of good and persons whom you may offend by evil.

2. Finally, to remove from you every excuse for your error by that Gospel division, you are either one of the foolish virgins, if indeed you are a virgin, or one of the wise (Matt. XXV, 1–12). If you are among the foolish, you need the community; if among the wise, the community needs you. For if you are wise and proved, the religious observance which was newly renewed in that place and is now everywhere praised will, we fear, be greatly discredited and weakened by your departure. For it will be said that, being good, [Col. 0262B] you would by no means abandon a good order.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] Commonly, *le bon ordre*; that is, the exact discipline of monastic life.]

But if you are known to be foolish and depart, people will say that, because it is not permitted to live badly among the good, you, evil and unable to bear good women, seek a place where you may live as you please. And justly so. For before the reform of the Order, as they say, you never spoke of leaving there; but when religious observance increased, suddenly made holier and with sudden fervor, you began to think of the desert. I recognize, daughter—I recognize, so that you too may recognize with me—the serpent’s venom, the deceiver’s trick, the cunning of the shape-shifter. The wolf lives in the grove. 125 If you, a lone little sheep, enter the shadows of the grove, you wish to be the wolf’s prey.

But hear me, daughter; hear faithful counsel. Whether you are a sinner or holy, do not separate yourself from the flock, lest he seize you and there be none to rescue you. Are you holy? Strive by your example to bring your companions [Col. 0262C] to your holiness. Are you a sinner? Do not add sins to sins, but repent where you are, lest, by departing at peril to yourself, as has been shown, you leave scandal to your sisters and provoke many tongues to speak ill of you.

## LETTER CXVI. TO ERMENGARD, FORMER COUNTESS OF BRITTANY

[Note: [Col. 0261D] She was the wife of Count Alan and especially beneficent to the monks of Clairvaux, for whom she founded a monastery near the city of Nantes, as Ernald testifies in Book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, no. 34; this was in the year 1135, according to our chronology. The monastery is called Buzay, and its most illustrious abbot Caumartin is now its head; from him we received the principal charters concerning the foundation of the monastery. In these charters Duke Conan, son of Alan and Ermengard, declares that he and his mother had determined to build the abbey of Buzay, but had abandoned the undertaking because they had been misled by the unfavorable advice of certain persons. When Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, came into those parts—the monastery of Buzay being subject to his abbey—and saw the place almost deserted, he was deeply grieved. “And me,” says Conan, “rebuking as faithless and deceitful in the sternest reprimands, he commanded the abbot and brothers dwelling there to leave the place and return to Clairvaux.” Conan intervened and, after restoring the monastery’s possessions which he had taken away, saw that its buildings were completed. The charter is subscribed by the bishops Rotaud of Vannes, Alan of Rennes, John of Saint-Malo, and Iterius of Nantes, together with Peter, abbot of the same monastery, and Andrew, a monk. To return to Ermengard: Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, urges her in Letter 23 of Book V to resume the religious purpose from which she seemed to have turned aside. In the following letter the same Geoffrey calls her of royal offspring.]

He gently and intimately communicates the affection of his heart and the force of religious love.

To his beloved daughter in Christ, ERMENGARD, formerly an eminent countess, now a humble handmaid of Christ: BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, offers the devoted affection of holy love.

[Col. 0263A] Would that I could unfold my mind to you as I now unfold this letter! O if you could read in my heart what God has deigned to write there concerning love for you with his own finger! You would surely recognize that no tongue or pen is sufficient to express what the Spirit of God has been able to imprint in the innermost marrow of my being. Even now I am present in spirit, though absent in body; yet there is no means for either me or you to make this apparent. You do, however, possess something by which you may in some measure conjecture, if not yet know, what I say concerning me. Enter, therefore, into your own heart and look into mine; and grant me at least as much love toward you as you perceive in yourself toward me. Otherwise, should you presume that we love you less while you love us more, you might think yourself superior to us insofar as you judged yourself to surpass us in charity.

But it accords with your modesty rather to think this of us: that he who has moved you to love me so and to choose me as adviser for your salvation has equally moved me to the service of your affection. See, therefore, how you have kept me with you; for I, to confess the truth, never withdraw from you without you. I wished for the present to write these few words to you briefly, as in passing upon my journey, hoping, if God grants it, to send greater things when I have greater leisure.

## LETTER CXVII. TO THE SAME WOMAN

He praises her cheerfulness in divine service and indicates his desire to see her.

I have received [variant: “I have accepted”] the delight of my heart: your peace. I rejoice because you are reported to be joyful, and your known cheerfulness restores my spirit exceedingly [Col. 0263C] to health. This joy indeed has nothing of flesh and blood in it, since you live as one made humble from exalted, lowly from noble-born, poor from rich, deprived of the consolation of brother, son, and homeland. Therefore the cheerfulness born in you is undoubtedly from the Holy Spirit. For, having long ago conceived from the fear of God, you have at last brought forth the spirit of salvation, since charity casts fear out.

O how much more gladly I would say these things in your presence than write them in your absence! Believe me, I am angry with the occupations by which I seem often to be hindered from seeing you; and I delight in the opportunities by which I sometimes seem to be freed to see you. Such an opportunity is indeed rarely given, but I confess that even its rarity is dear to me. For it is certainly better to see you, even occasionally, [Col. 0263D] than never at all. I hope soon to come to you, already tasting beforehand the joy that will shortly be complete.

## LETTER CXVIII. TO BEATRICE, A NOBLE AND RELIGIOUS LADY

He commends her obliging charity and solicitude.

I marvel at the zeal of your devotion and the affection of your love toward us. O good lady, what have you to do with [Col. 0264A] us, or we with you? Whence comes such concern for us? If we were joined to you as sons, grandchildren, or even by some remote degree of kinship, your frequent kindnesses, repeated greetings, and indeed the innumerable signs of your love which we experience daily would seem to us not so much astonishing as received by right. But now, since we know you only as our lady by rank, not our mother by family, it is no wonder that we marvel; rather, it is astonishing if we can marvel enough. For which of our acquaintances or relatives cares for us? Who ever asks about our welfare? Who, I say, is in the world not merely solicitous for us but even mindful of us? To friends, relatives, and neighbors we have become like a lost vessel; you alone cannot forget us.

You inquire about our condition and health, [Col. 0264B] about the journey we recently made, and about the monks whom we transferred to another place. In brief I reply concerning them that they have been brought from a deserted land, a place of horror and vast solitude, into an abundance of possessions, buildings, and friends: in short, into a fertile land and a place of pleasant habitation. Thus we left them joyful and at peace, and ourselves returned joyful and at peace—except that for a few days, though severely, I was afflicted by a returning fever, so that I feared I might die. But through God’s mercy I soon recovered, so that now, after completing the journey, I feel stronger and healthier than before I began it.

## Letter CXIX. To the Duke and Duchess of Lorraine

[Note: [Col. 0263D] Namely Simon and Adelaide, not Gertrude, as most writers state. On the conversion of this duchess brought about by Bernard, see Book I of the *Life*, ch. 14. For she received the veil of a religious woman at the convent of Tart, formerly near Dijon, as is clear from the autograph letters of Duke Matthew, her son, who calls his mother Atheleide. Peter Francis Chifflet prints these letters [Col. 0264D] after the four *Opuscula* published at Paris in 1679. Away, then, with letters of Gertrude to Bernard and of Bernard to Gertrude, translated by Bernard the Breton from French into Portuguese and then into Latin.]

He gives thanks for the tolls remitted thus far, but asks that the goodwill of the rulers not be undermined by their officials.

[Col. 0264C]

To the DUKE and DUCHESS of Lorraine, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: may you take delight in embraces mutually dear and chaste, such that the love of Christ alone surpasses them both.

Ever since we began to send into your territory for our needs, we have always found much friendliness and favour in the eyes of your Highnesses. Whenever necessary, you have generously extended the blessing of your liberality to our people. You have willingly remitted the passage-toll [Note: [Col. 0264D] A payment customarily made by persons passing through; commonly, *droit de passage*.] for travellers, and whatever other due belonged to your jurisdiction, for merchants. Of all these things your reward is undoubtedly great in heaven—if, that is, we believe true what the Lord promises in the Gospel: “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40).

But why do you permit your officials to demand again what you yourselves have bestowed? It is fitting and honourable for you that no one belonging to you should dare reclaim what you were pleased to give for the salvation of your souls. Therefore, if—far be it from you!—you do not repent of your benefactions, and if it is still the pleasure of you both that we should retain on equal terms the gift which we have often received from you through your gracious will [Col. 0265A], command that it be maintained firmly and without disturbance, so that henceforth none of our brethren may fear being troubled in this matter by any one of your 127 officials.

Otherwise, we do not refuse to follow the example of our Lord, who did not disdain to pay the tax for himself (Matt. 17:26). We too are ready gladly to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and toll to whom toll is due, and tribute to whom tribute is due (Rom. 13:7); especially since, according to the Apostle, we ought to seek not so much our own gift as your gain (Phil. 4:17).

## Letter CXX. To the Duchess of Lorraine

He gives thanks for the benefits offered and dissuades her from an unjust war.

[Col. 0265B]

We give thanks to God for the devotion of will which we have learned that you bear toward him and his servants. Whenever, in a fleshly heart elevated by earthly dignities, even the smallest spark of heavenly love appears to have been kindled, it is undoubtedly a divine gift, not a human virtue.

We gladly accept the benefits offered us in your letter from your generosity. Yet, having learned of the sudden and considerable business by which you must now be occupied, we judge it fitting to wait for your convenience, so far as it shall please you. For, as far as lies in us, we would wish to be a burden to no one, especially in matters relating to God, where we ought to seek not the gain of what is given, but rather the fruit of the giver [Col. 0265C].

Therefore, if it please you, name to us by return through this messenger a day and place at which, God helping, once your present urgent business has been settled, you may come near to our region. Then, after Brother Guy [Note: [Col. 0265C] We think this is Guy, abbot of Trois-Fontaines [Col. 0265D], who travelled to Lorraine more than once; see notes on Letters 63 and 69.] has met you and found anything in your territory suitable for our Order, you may fulfil your promises more readily and cheerfully. For “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Or, if delay does not please you, let us know this as well; for in this matter we are prepared, insofar as reason permits, to comply with your will.

We greet the Duke through your mouth; and we admonish both him and you that, if you know that the castle for which you intend to make war is not yours by right, you should relinquish it for the love of God. For it is written [Col. 0266A]: “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world, but lose himself and suffer the loss of his own soul?” (Matt. 16:26).

## Letter CXX. To the Duchess of Burgundy

[Note: [Col. 0265D] To Matilda, wife of Hugh I, Duke of Burgundy, who was nursing anger against Hugh of Bèze—a place situated four leagues from Dijon and noted for the Benedictine monastery of Bèze. On this Hugh see Perard, pp. 221–222.]

He seeks to appease her resentment toward Hugh and requests her consent to a certain marriage.

The special kindness of Your Highness, which you seem [variant: deign] to extend toward us poor men, has advanced so far that whoever feels that Your Highness is hostile to him trusts that he can return to favour through no one more easily than through us. Hence it was that, when I was at Dijon some time ago, Hugh of Bèze earnestly begged me to intervene to appease the indignation which he had incurred from you. He also asked that, for the love of God and of us, you should give your consent to the marriage of his son—a marriage which was indeed displeasing to you, but which he had irrevocably resolved to arrange as advantageous to himself, or so he thinks.

For this reason, behold, he has now again taken care to assail our ears with the entreaties both of himself and of his friends [Col. 0266B]. We do not greatly concern ourselves with his earthly advantage. Yet because, as he says, the matter seems to be so narrowly placed that the marriage cannot possibly be prevented except by his perjury, we judged it fitting to tell you that the advantage which you ought to prefer to the good faith [Note: [Col. 0265D] *Legalitati*: that is, good faith, consisting in fulfilling promises.] of a Christian and your own subject ought to be very great indeed. For he cannot at once be perjured and remain faithful to his pledged word.

Moreover, we see that not only will no gain accrue to you, but that great danger will threaten [Col. 0266C], should those whom perhaps God has intended to join be separated through your action. May the Lord add his grace upon you and upon your children, most noble lady and most beloved to me in Christ. “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation”: distribute your grain among Christ’s poor, that you may receive it back eternally with increase.

## Letter CXXII. Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, to Abbot Bernard

[Note: [Col. 0265D] Written about the year 1130. In many writings this letter, together with the following reply, is placed after Letter 127; in some, after Letter 252. Hildebert, author of this letter, governed the Church of Le Mans from 1098 to 1125, when, after the death of Giselbert, he was appointed to the metropolitan see of Tours. This is established both from Orderic Vitalis, Book X, under the year 1098, and from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, published in vol. III of the *Analecta*, where Guy, his successor in the see of Le Mans, is said to have been consecrated after long disputes in 1126 [Col. 0266C–D].

He ruled Tours for only six years and the same number of months. So state the aforementioned *Acts*, with which the Chesnian copy agrees, as does John Maan in his *Metropolis of Tours*, and even Orderic under the year 1125, p. 882, where he assigns Hildebert almost seven years as archbishop. Hildebert therefore did not live until 1136, as is stated in *Gallia Christiana*, but died in 1132, the year in which John Maan likewise places his death.

In his notes on this letter, Horstius cited another letter of Hildebert, twenty-fourth in order, which he likewise thought addressed to Bernard. But this letter, found in printed editions without the name of its addressee, is addressed in two manuscripts to H., abbot of Cluny; we restore it to him. From that letter we learn that Hildebert intended to retire to Cluny, if the supreme pontiff had permitted him. Peter of Blois praises his letters in Letter 101.]

Moved by the renown of Bernard’s name and holiness, he seeks his friendship.

1. Few, we think, are ignorant that balm is known by its fragrance and a tree by its fruit [Col. 0267A]. Thus from the report concerning you, dearest brother, we have learned how fitted you are for holiness and how sound for teaching. Although we are separated from you by a great interval of places, news has nevertheless reached us of how pleasant are the nights you spend with your Rachel, what offspring in abundance springs for you from Leah, and how wholly you show yourself both a cultivator of virtue and an enemy of the flesh.

All who speak to us of you speak of no other than this. Such is the fragrance of your name, like ointment poured out; such already are the rewards of your merits. You gather these ears of grain from your field before the final harvest. For in this life there is a certain reward of virtue: conspicuous and imperishable testimony. Virtue itself gains this testimony and preserves it for itself. Its brightness is not diminished by envy [Col. 0267B], nor aided by external efforts. For the esteem accorded to good people can no more be taken away by false accusations than it can be gained by flattering favour. It rests with themselves either to increase it by the abundance of their virtues or lessen it by their deficiency.

Indeed, hope has been laid up in the bosom of the Church concerning your most celebrated reputation: that it will by no means fall, since it is believed to be founded upon a firm rock.

2. Having learned from it of your devotion, we have longed with longing to be received into the sanctuary of your friendship; and there to be with you in remembrance, where, having stolen yourself away from conversations with mortals, you speak with the King of Angels on behalf of mortals.

Moreover N., archdeacon of Troyes [Note: [Col. 0267D] Gebuinus. See notes on Letter 17.], a man distinguished in character and learning, has greatly increased this desire of ours. We would think him worthy of recommendation to you, unless it were clear that those whom you deem worthy of your favour need no other recommendation. If you do not know it already, we have learned also from his testimony that you are such a man in the Church as to suffice for the instruction of virtue both by example and by word [Col. 0267C].

But lest you be burdened by a more lengthy letter, we put an end to our writing—though we shall by no means put an end to the petition mentioned above until we deserve to be heard. We beg to be informed, by the return of your letter, what disposition you bear toward this request.

## Letter CXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0267D] Written about the year 1130.]

Reply of Abbot Bernard to Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours. He repays praises with praise.

“A good man brings forth good things out of the good treasure of his heart” [Col. 0267D]. I received the writings of your glory—indeed, of my own—with great pleasure, man worthy of every reverence; for in them I have what enables me deservedly to glorify you, and myself deservedly to glory. For this is our glory: the condescension of your Sublimity, your esteem for our littleness.

Indeed, not to be high-minded when one is in a high position, but to associate with the lowly—nothing is dearer to God, nothing rarer among human beings. Who is wise except the one who submits to Wisdom’s counsels? And Wisdom says: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Sir. 3:20). This you have shown me: a greater person to a lesser, an elder to a younger.

I too, then, might extol your proven wisdom with praises not undeserved [Col. 0268A], perhaps with praise more just than that with which it has deigned to honour me. For, in establishing certainty about matters, there is a difference between what uncertain report asserts and what manifest action makes unquestionable. What we prove more certainly, we proclaim more confidently.

As for what you were pleased to write to me about me, you must see how you have proved it. I possess a wholly unquestionable proof of your praises: your own letters praising me. In them perhaps another might delight in the distinction of learning, the sweet and pure style, the lucid discourse, the agreeable and praiseworthy concision. But for me, beyond these, there is that humility to be wondered at: that, though so great, you took care to anticipate one so small by the courtesy of greeting, the proclamation of praise, and the reverence of prayer.

Certainly, as far as I am concerned, I read in your letter about myself not what I am, but what I should wish to be—and what I am ashamed not to be [Col. 0268B]. Yet what I am is yours; and whatever better thing I may ever become by God’s gift, be assured, most reverend and beloved Father, that it will be yours.

## Letter CXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Written about the year 1131.]

To the Same Hildebert, Who Had Not Yet Received Pope Innocent. He urges him to acknowledge Innocent, exiled in France because of the schism of Peter Leo, as the lawful pontiff.

To HILDEBERT, great priest and lofty in the word of glory, by God’s grace Archbishop of Tours, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: may you walk in the Spirit and examine all things spiritually.

[Col. 0268C]

1. To address you in the words of the prophet: “Consolation is hidden from my eyes, because death divides between brothers” (Hos. 13:14). For some, according to Isaiah, seem to have “made a covenant with death and an agreement with hell” (Isa. 28:15). Behold, this anointed one of the Lord, Innocent, is set for the fall and rising again of many. Those who belong to God willingly unite themselves to him; but whoever stands opposed is either of Antichrist or is Antichrist.

The abomination is seen standing in the holy place; in order to obtain it, a fire has burned the sanctuary of God. He persecutes Innocent and, with him, all innocence. Innocent indeed flees from the face of Leo, as the prophet says: “The lion has roared; who will not fear?” (Amos 3:8). He flees in accordance with the Lord’s command: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” [Col. 0268D] (Matt. 10:23). He flees; and in this he truly proves himself an apostolic man, because he has marked himself with the apostolic pattern. For Paul was not ashamed to be lowered in a basket through the wall and thus escape the hands of those seeking his life (Acts 9:25).

He withdrew, moreover, not sparing his own life but giving place to wrath; not in order to escape death, but in order to gain life. Rightly does the Church grant Innocent the place of Paul, whom she sees walking in the same footsteps.

2. Nor indeed is Innocent’s flight idle. He labours, but is honoured in his labours. Driven from the City [Rome], he is received by the world [Col. 0269A]. From the ends of the earth people come out with bread to meet the fugitive, although the rage of Shimei—Gerard of Angoulême—has not yet wholly ceased to curse David. Whether he wishes it or not, the sinner who sees and is enraged, he is magnified in the sight of kings, bearing the crown of glory.
