Have not all princes recognized that he is truly God’s chosen one? The kings of the French, English, Spaniards, and finally Romans receive Innocent as pope and acknowledge him as the unique bishop of their souls. Achitophel alone still fails to perceive that his scheme has now been disclosed and destroyed (2 Sam. 17). In vain the wretch strives to devise malign counsel against God’s people and to scheme against the saints who cling most firmly to the Holy One and disdain to bend the knee before Baal [Col. 0269B].

By no trickery will that parricide prevail in gaining for himself rule over Israel and over the holy city, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar of faith and foundation of truth. “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccl. 4:12). The choice of the better party, the approval of the larger number, and—more effective than these—the testimony of his character commend Innocent to all and establish him as supreme pontiff.

3. For this, Father, your own judgment is awaited, like rain upon the fleece or a tardy verdict. We do not disapprove of delay that savours of gravity and removes the taint of fickleness. For Mary did not immediately answer the angel’s greeting, but first considered what manner of greeting it was (Luke 1:29); and Timothy is commanded, “Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Tim. 5:22).

Yet I say, as one known to the pontiff: “Nothing in excess”; I say, as an intimate and acquaintance: “Do not think more highly than you ought to think” [Col. 0269C] (Rom. 12:3). I confess I am ashamed that the most ancient serpent, with new audacity, having left foolish women behind, has seemed even to attack the strength of your breast and has dared to shake so great a pillar of the Church. Yet we trust that, although it shakes you, it does not cast you down: for “the friend of the bridegroom stands and rejoices at the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29)—the voice of exultation and salvation, the voice of unity and peace.

## Letter CXXV. To Master Geoffrey of Lorratoire

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Written in the year of Christ 1131. Geoffrey of Lorratoire, a most celebrated teacher and later Archbishop of Bordeaux, was so called from Lorratoire, a place in the diocese of Tours adjoining Poitou, once notable for its priory and subject to Marmoutier. Hence Gerard of Angoulême is called Geoffrey’s “neighbouring beast” in this letter. The Oratory, a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Angers, is another place.]

He seeks his assistance in defending Innocent’s pontificate against the schism of Peter Leo.

[Col. 0269D]

1. Fragrance is sought in the flower, taste in the fruit. Drawn by the fragrance of your name, like ointment poured out, dearest brother, we desire to know you also from the fruit of your work. For not only we, but God himself, who needs nothing, nevertheless needs your work in this present time—if you do not hold back.

It is glorious for you to be able to be God’s fellow-worker; to be able and not to be one is harmful. You have favour with God and with human beings; you have knowledge; you have the spirit of freedom; you have a living and effective word, seasoned with salt. With such great powers you ought not fail Christ’s bride in so great a crisis, since you are the friend of the bridegroom. For a friend is proved in need.

What then? Are you at rest for yourself while your mother, the Church, is grievously troubled? Rest has had its time, and holy leisure has until now freely and gladly pursued its own affairs. Now is the time to act, because they have scattered the law. That beast of the Apocalypse, to which “was given a mouth speaking blasphemies” and power “to make war with the saints” (Rev. 13:5–7), occupies Peter’s chair like a lion ready for prey [Col. 0270A]. Another beast also hisses near you, like a cub dwelling in hiding. The former is fiercer; the latter more cunning. Together they have assembled against the Lord and against his anointed. Let us hasten to break their bonds and cast their yoke from us.

2. In our regions, together with other servants of God kindled by divine fire, we have laboured, God cooperating, to bring peoples together and kings to break up [variant: plunder] the agreement of the wicked and destroy every height raised against the knowledge of God. And not without fruit. The kings of Germany, France, England, Scotland, the Spains, and Jerusalem, with all their clergy and peoples, favour and adhere to Lord Innocent as children to their father and members to their head, being eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace [Col. 0270C].

The Church rightly receives him whose reputation has proved brighter and whose election sounder—clearly surpassing in both the number and worth of those electing him. But you, brother, why are you still negligent? How long will your otherwise ill-secure diligence sleep while the neighbouring serpent is at hand? We know, indeed, that no consideration can induce you, a son of peace, to desert unity. But certainly that is not enough unless you also endeavour to defend it and to wage war with all your strength against those who disturb it.

Nor should you fear the loss of your repose; it will be repaid by no small increase in your glory if, through your effort, that beast neighbouring you is tamed or silenced, and if God’s mercy in your hand rescues from Leo’s mouth so great a prey of the Church—I mean the Count of Poitou [Note: [Col. 0269D] William.].

## Letter CXXVI. To the Bishops of Aquitaine against Gerard of Angoulême

[Variant: Egolismensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0270D] Written about the year 1132. Gerard II of that name, a Norman by birth and of the diocese of Bayeux, is called by Orderic, Book XIII under the year 1136, “a most learned man, and of great name and influence in the Roman senate.” Evidence for this is that under Paschal II and the other lawful pontiffs down to Innocent he acted almost continuously as the representative of the Apostolic See in Aquitaine.

He was not lacking in zeal, for on another occasion he forcefully and courageously rebuked William, prince of Aquitaine, as another Herod, for violating the laws of marriage—if we accept the testimony of William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of England*, Book V. John Besly, *History of the Counts of Poitou*, ch. 32, contends that this was maliciously said against Count William.

But after Gerard disgracefully deserted Innocent, who had refused him the legation, and, intending to attach himself to Anacletus at the price of that title, performed the office not of a legate but of a disrupter, he drew as many as he could to the schismatic side. Bernard therefore warns the neighbouring bishops of Aquitaine to scorn the seducer’s voice, follow Innocent, their lawful shepherd, and consider the prerogatives of his title: “the integrity of the person elected, the priority of the election, and the solemnity of the consecration.”

There were nevertheless people who defended Anacletus’s claim and advanced contrary arguments, as is evident from the letter of Peter, Bishop of Porto, author and supporter of that ordination, sent to William of Palestrina, Matthew of Albano, Conrad of Sabina, and John of Ostia, who adhered to Innocent. William of Malmesbury reports it in Book I of his *Modern History* [Col. 0271D].

Innocent’s side, however, prevailed. All ecclesiastical rulers—except Gerard of Angoulême and a few others—and all secular rulers favoured him, except Count William of Poitiers and Roger, Duke of Sicily. Gerard, hardened in the defence of the schism, departed this life in 1136, as Orderic records, by the unhappy sort of death described by Ernald in Book II, ch. 7, of the *Life of St Bernard*.

Some nevertheless think that this author, from excessive religious zeal, invented much against Gerard of Angoulême: for example, that he died suddenly, unrepentant, without confession and Viaticum; that his body was found lifeless and monstrously swollen in his bed; and other such details, which they say are unworthy of a prudent man. They cite the authority of the *Acts of the Bishops of Angoulême* in these words:

> “On the day before his death we learned that in his confession he had told the priests that, in ignorance and against God’s will, he had upheld the party of Peter Leo; that he confessed and repented; and that nearly everything he had possessed in his life he gave either to the Church or distributed to the poor. On Saturday, while celebrating Mass with the greatest devotion and an outpouring of tears, he departed from the world on the following Sunday, in the year 1136 from the incarnation of the Lord. He sat in the episcopate for thirty-three years, … months, … days; and because he had harassed some chaplains with burdens or lodging, at his end he gave each chaplain of his bishopric one mina and one obol. And that splendid star which had illuminated the western regions by its brightness—alas!—lies hidden beneath a humble stone outside the church which he built.”

John Besly, *History of the Counts of Poitou*. Yet since the preceding account rests only upon an uncertain report, there is no reason to deny credence to Ernald—especially since Alan of Auxerre, who reviewed the books written on the life of St Bernard, does not depart from Ernald in this respect by even a finger’s breadth [Col. 0272D].

As for Anacletus, he too died miserably in 1138, on the seventh day of January, according to Falco of Benevento: “having sat,” he says, “seven years, eleven months, and twenty-two days.” William of Malmesbury likewise confirms this in Book I of his *Modern History*: “After Anacletus had died in the eighth year of his assumed”—as it was called—“episcopate, Lord Innocent enjoyed the apostolic dignity, with peace unshaken to this time.” On this matter see St Bernard, Letters 144, 146, and 147, and the beginning of Sermon 24 on the *Song of Songs*. See also, if you wish, the notes on Letter 147. From these facts you may conclude that Besly erred when he said that Gerard died in 1131 and that the schism had been extinguished before that year.]

He vigorously defends Innocent’s cause as lawful pontiff against Gerard of Angoulême, who supports the schismatic party; he portrays Gerard’s character and exposes his evasions.

[Col. 0270D]

To his honourable lords and fathers, the holy bishops of Limoges, Poitiers [Col. 0271A], Périgueux, and Saintes, by the grace of God: Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, steadfastness in adversity.

1. Virtue is acquired in peace, tested in pressure, and approved in victory. The time has come, reverend and deservedly esteemed fathers, when whatever virtue is yours must no longer be permitted either to lie hidden or to remain idle. For the hostile sword, which at this time seems to threaten death afresh to Christ’s whole body, hangs especially over your necks and rages against you all the more fiercely because it is close at hand. Thus, by its daily assaults, you are compelled either to resist bravely or—God forbid!—to yield shamefully.

For Diotrephes, who loves to hold first place among you, does not receive you [Note: [Col. 0272D] Gerard, who aspired to the primacy, that is, the office of legate. An allusion to 3 John 9.]; for he does not acknowledge him whom the whole Church, together with you, receives as coming in the name of the Lord [Col. 0271B]. Not him, I say, but the one who comes in his own name, he receives. Nor is this surprising. He himself, even at his age, pants tirelessly after a great name.

I do not, indeed, accuse the man of this sort of vanity on false or uncertain report; I judge him by his own mouth. For in a familiar letter which he recently wrote to the chancellor, does he not petition—so much the more unworthily as he does so more humbly—that he be honoured both with the burden and the title of the legation? [Note: [Col. 0272D] The printed editions read: “that he be burdened with its burden and honoured with its title”; but *be burdened* is absent from the manuscripts.] Would that he had obtained it! Ambition perhaps would have done less harm had it attained its desires than it does disappointed. Then it would have harmed only, or almost only, himself [Col. 0272A]; now it rages through the world. Do you see what love of glory does? A legation is a heavy burden, especially on aged shoulders—who does not know this? Yet to this very old man it seems a heavier punishment to live out the remaining brief days of his life without this punishment.

2. But perhaps he will allege that he is judged on suspicion and will accuse us of rashness for condemning hidden matters which we have not proved. I confess that I am suspicious in this respect; and I do not know whether even the simplest person could think otherwise, given such manifest evidence. To state the plain course of events briefly: he was the first, or among the first, to write to Pope Innocent; he sought the legation and did not obtain it. He became angry, recoiled from Innocent, went over to another, and boasts that he is that other’s legate [Col. 0272B].

If he had not asked the former for it before, or had not later received it from the latter, one might believe that he had had some other aim in his defection, even if it were not a right one. But now he has no excuse for his ambition. Let him now, at least, lay aside even the empty title of legate—for he has lost its work—and I shall, if I can, be free of this suspicion. If not, I shall suspect unwillingly and shall blame myself for intemperance. But I know that he will scarcely be persuaded to do this. For a man long regarded as great among his own people is ashamed to appear inferior to himself.

He is recognized as the man of whom Scripture speaks: “shame bringing sin” [Col. 0273A] (Sir. 4:25). Is not that proud shame a great sin and a very great offence—by which earth and ashes is ashamed, not merely to be subject, but even not to rule?

3. For this reason the man left that holy father of his, Innocent—as he used to call him—and his holy mother, the Catholic Church; he clings to his schismatic leader, and the two are one in vanity. They have struck a pact with each other and devised malicious counsel against God’s people. “Scale is joined to scale, and there is no breath between them” (Job 41:7). This man writes of the other as pope, and the other in turn writes of this man as legate, so that together they may deceive themselves by vanity. They console, protect, and commend one another; yet each acts for himself, not for the other [Col. 0273B]. Truly, they are people who love themselves.

With equal zeal they have assembled against the Lord and against his anointed; but their intentions plainly do not cohere. Each certainly seeks from the other what is his own—and this, which it is wicked even to dare, in Christ’s inheritance. What are they trying to do before your eyes, if you permit it, except proscribe Christ? Already the legate is coining new bishops among you for his pope [Note: [Col. 0273] Thus he intruded Ramnulf, abbot of Dorat, into the see of Limoges; see the *Life of Bernard*, Book III, no. 33.], lest his pope be left alone. Supported by tyrannical power, he forces in, not successors for the dead, but invaders upon the living, having found an opportunity in the malice of princes who persecute the bishops of their cities with unjust hatred. Thus “he sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent.” Through such a door he enters the sheepfold.

[Col. 0273C]

4. Does the legate, then, perform such deeds for his pope without payment? Behold, that pope has added, as Gerard boasts, all France and Burgundy to the territory of his former legation. If he wishes, he can also add the Medes and Persians, and the regions in the middle of Decapolis. Why not even beyond the Sarmatians, so that wherever his foot has trodden may be his—places in which he may glory, if only in empty titles?

O man no less shameless than senseless, mindful neither of the fear of God nor of his own honour! He thinks himself unseen, though he is an object of mockery and derision to all around him. And deservedly so. For he uses the sanctuary as a market-place; like a trader seeking his own profit, now canvassing this seller and now that one in order finally to buy what he desires from the person from whom he can obtain it more cheaply [Col. 0273D], so he carefully searches here and there for ecclesiastical dignity and at last chooses, according to his own will, to have as pope the man who consents to make him legate.

Therefore Rome cannot have a pope unless you are legate? Whence comes this privilege of yours in the Church of God? Who granted you this prerogative in Christ’s inheritance? Do you possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance? For as long as you had any hope of gaining Lord Innocent’s favour by obtaining your shameful and shameless petition, that holy man was, in your own writing, also pope. How then do you now accuse him of being a schismatic? Did both his holiness and his papacy vanish together [Col. 0274A] with that same vain hope of yours?

It is astonishing that sweet and bitter could thus proceed so quickly from the same fountain. Yesterday he was Catholic, holy, and supreme pontiff; today he is wicked, a schismatic, and a disturber. Yesterday, Father Innocent; today, Gregory, deacon of Saint Angelo. Thus opposite statements came from one mouth indeed, but from a divided heart. “They have spoken with deceitful lips, with a heart and a heart.” But do you suppose that a man whose double heart rends his conscience and whose tongue divides “Yes” from “No” has fear in his mind or shame on his brow? He provides badly, according to the Apostle, “things honest in the sight of God and of men” (2 Cor. 8:21), who, in the manner of that unjust judge, neither fears God nor respects man (Luke 18:2).

[Col. 0274B]

5. Certainly, when ambition breaks out into shamelessness, it loses its effectiveness; and when an evil desire discloses itself, its result perishes. Ambition, the mother of hypocrisy, loves hiding places and darkness; it cannot endure the light. Ambition, a foul vice, lies low; yet it sees every high place while shunning being seen itself. Nor is this surprising: it must lose what it seeks unless it avoids observers. For the more glory is desired, the less it is gained when the desire for it is detected.

What, finally, is so inglorious as to be caught craving glory—especially among bishops? Indeed, not even an ordinary Christian ought to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. An ambitious person will be illustrious only while he moves in the night; and while he conducts the business of shameful gain in darkness, the hypocrite may appear just and holy to the eye that sees the face. But when shamelessness or imprudence [variant, corruptly: “by shameless or imprudent …”] casts outside what lies hidden in the conscience [Col. 0274C], does not the uncontrolled desire appear more brazen in disgrace than ready for glory?

Thus indeed is proved what we read: “Their glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things” (Phil. 3:19); and again: “If I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54). And in such a person is fulfilled what the holy prophet, unless I am mistaken, imprecates upon hypocrites: “Let them be,” he says, “as the grass upon the housetops, which withers before it is plucked” (Ps. 128:5).

Shame has not so entirely vanished from mortals that naked and shameless ambition should be honoured even by them—especially in an old man and priest. This childish vanity is certainly the more unbecoming in him because greater gravity and greater holiness are fitting for him. Though he is blessed to his face by the flatterer, he is mocked behind his back by everyone.

There is a certain sober and, in some sense, clear-sighted [variant: hidden] ambition, which at least acts cautiously, though not chastely. If it can make progress, it attends to its affairs secretly. If it cannot, it remains within itself and does not abandon even the appearance of shame. Such a person, although he does not yet fear God unto salvation, nevertheless retains for a time a measure of decency through innate modesty, because he respects human beings and is ashamed before the public.

6. But what is this headlong, brazen [Col. 0275A] lust for dominion, that, for the prospect of an embassy scarcely lasting a year (as is certainly plain), he first spares neither his own old age nor shows reverence for the priesthood; and then does not spare even the Saviour’s side, which, in water and blood, brought forth the redemption of the people to be gathered into the unity of faith—so that whoever should attempt to divide those whom He gathers and thereby redeems would prove himself not a Christian but an antichrist, guilty of Christ’s death and crucifixion? O impatient and unbridled desire for shameful gain! O intemperate passion! O blind and disgraceful ambition! First, openly and brazenly, as I have said, he himself—shame upon it!—does not deny it; he even adds the attempt to solicit a Catholic with a request altogether unworthy. Grieved by the refusal, he immediately has recourse to a schismatic; and, having received from a sacrilegious hand the authority he wickedly coveted, he does not hesitate once more cruelly to pierce the side of the Lord of glory [Col. 0275B].

For he divides the Church, for which that side was divided upon the cross; and without doubt he too shall look upon Him whom he has pierced. The Lord shall certainly be known when He executes judgments—He who is now unknown while enduring injury. For when He begins to render judgment for all who suffer injury and to rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth, do you suppose He will be able to turn His ear away from His dearest bride when she cries out against those who have afflicted her? No; He certainly cannot fail to hear her lamenting: “My friends and my neighbours drew near and stood against me; and those who were near me stood far off, and those who sought my life used violence” (Ps. 37:12–13).

For how will He not recognize bone of His bones and flesh of [Col. 0275C] His flesh—indeed, now in some sense spirit of His Spirit? As though she were not that beloved one whose beauty He desired, whose form He assumed, to whom in marvellous condescension He bound Himself in chaste and indivisible embraces, so that the two might be one flesh, and might one day become one in one Spirit! For though she once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet then she shall know Him so no longer, because “the spirit before His face is Christ the Lord”; and, cleaving to Him, she shall be one spirit, when death has been swallowed up in victory and what is infirm in the flesh has become strong in the power of the Spirit; when the Bridegroom of glory presents her to Himself as His glorious dove, His perfect one, His beautiful one, having neither the stain of sin nor the wrinkle of corruption nor anything of the kind.

[Col. 0275D] 7. While I willingly linger over these matters, I have almost forgotten my purpose, so eager am I to redeem the time, because the days are evil. Devotion carries me beyond bounds, but zeal calls me back; and where I am carried away, there also I am compelled to cut short and lament my grief. The enemy of Christ’s cross dares—what I say weeping—to drive holy men from their sees because they refuse to worship the beast that opened its mouth in blasphemies, to blaspheme the name of God and His tabernacle (Rev. 13:6). He attempts to set altar against altar, and is not ashamed to confound right and wrong [Col. 0276A]. He strives to thrust abbots upon abbots and bishops upon bishops; to remove Catholics and advance schismatics.

> [Note: [Col. 0275D] Orderic, book XIII, p. 895: “In very many monasteries two abbots arose, and in bishoprics two prelates contended for the pontificate; one of whom adhered to Peter Anacletus, while the other favoured Gregory Innocent.” The same is found in the Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 338, concerning Philip intruded into the Church of Tours; see Letters 150 and 151.] 

Wretched and pitiable are those who consent to be promoted in this way, and by such a man. For he goes round sea and land to make one bishop; and when he has made him, he makes him twice as much a son of Gehenna as himself. What, do you suppose, is the cause of such great madness? Surely none other than this: mortals dislike that angelic division by which glory is proclaimed to God and peace to humankind; and while they usurp glory, they disturb peace. He alone deserves glory who alone does wondrous things, as the Apostle says: “To God alone be honour and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17). But our race fares well if it is granted to enjoy the peace of God and peace with God—and that happily and mercifully. In what way, then, can the peace of human beings stand before God or with God, if His own glory cannot be secure among human beings? O foolish children of Adam, who, despising peace and seeking glory, lose both peace and glory! Therefore even now the God of vengeances has moved the earth and shaken it; He has shown His people hard things and given us the wine of compunction to drink.

8. Whether we wish it or not, the truth of the Holy Spirit must at some time be fulfilled, and that apostasy must occur which Scripture declares was foretold by the prophetic Spirit (2 Thess. 2:3). But woe to the man through whom it comes! It would have been better for that man had he not been born. And who is that man, if not the man of sin who has seized the holy place over a Catholic who had been elected canonically by Catholics? He seized it, I say—seized it by arms, fire, and money, not by merit of life or virtues; he has attained the position in which he stands, and stands in the position he has attained. For that which he boasts of as the election of his sworn supporters was not an election but a faction: only a shadow, an occasion, and a veil for wickedness. It may be called an election—but shamelessly, falsely. For the ecclesiastical and authoritative ruling stands: after a first election, there is to be no second. Therefore, once the first election has been held, that which was presumptuously undertaken as a second is not a second election, but no election at all. For even if something perhaps proceeded with less solemnity or less orderly arrangement in the earlier election, as the enemies of unity contend, should another election nevertheless have been presumed upon before the first had first been examined on its merits and annulled by judgment? [Col. 0276D] Therefore those who hasten to intrude themselves, and who likewise hastened rashly to lay hands upon a rash man, though the Apostle forbids it—“Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Tim. 5:22)—undoubtedly bear the greater sin. They are the authors of the schism; they have become the leaders of this great host.

9. But now they demand a judgment which they ought previously to have awaited [variant: “sought”]; and, having rejected justice when it was offered in its proper place, they at last offer it [Col. 0277A], so that, if it is refused, you may appear just [Note: [Col. 0277B] The old books and most printed editions read “unjust” instead of “just,” by antiphrasis or irony. [Col. 0277C] Yet one Colbert manuscript, no. 1410, has both words: “that you may appear unjust, just”—an excellent sense, namely, that you who are just may appear unjust. One Beauvais manuscript simply reads “unjust.”]; if it is accepted, the delay caused by the parties’ disputing among themselves may buy time, and meanwhile something may happen. Do you despair of your justice, and no longer fear that the loss will grow, whatever outcome the case may have?

“Whatsoever has been done up to now,” they say, “we now seek a hearing; we are ready to undergo judgment.” It is evasion. What else remains to you in all your impious undertaking that you can offer, to deceive the simple, arm ill-disposed persons, and cloak your own wickedness? If you did not say this, what would you say? Yet God has already judged what man now belatedly demands. He has judged by the evident fact of the deed, not by a sentence of decree. Does human rashness dare to reopen God’s judgment? What if God complains and cries out through the prophet: “Men have taken judgment away from me”?

> [Note: [Col. 0277C] This is found in no prophet; but it occurs in the teaching of the Holy Fathers, book II, chapter 7, *Against Rash Judgments*.]

There is no counsel against the Lord’s counsel. His word runs swiftly, in gathering peoples and kings together into one, that they may serve and obey Pope Innocent as lord. Who will revoke this? Walter of Ravenna, Hildegarius of Tarragona, Norbert of Magdeburg, and Conrad of Salzburg, archbishops, recognized and accepted that it was God’s judgment.

> [Note: [Col. 0277C] Hildegarius had succeeded Odelric, whom Orderic calls a most learned old man in book XIII, pp. 891–892.]

The bishops Equipertus of Münster, Hildebrand of Pistoia, Bernard of Pavia, Landulf of Asti, Hugh of Grenoble, and Bernard of Parma recognized God’s judgment and acquiesced.

> [Note: [Col. 0277C] In certain manuscripts Bernard of Parma is placed after Bernard of Pavia; in some he is omitted, as in two Colbert manuscripts. Ughelli says that he died near the end of the pontificate of Paschal II.]

Their special glory, their eminent holiness [Col. 0278A], and their authority, worthy of reverence even from enemies, readily persuaded us, who hold a lesser place both in merit and office, either to err with them or to be wise with them. I pass over the multitude of others in Tuscany, Campania, Lombardy, Germany, Aquitaine, indeed in all the Gauls and Spains, and also throughout the whole Eastern Church, both archbishops and bishops, whose names are in the book of life but whom the brevity of a letter does not permit me to name.

> [Note: [Col. 0277C] The words “but whom the brevity of a letter does not permit me to name” are absent from two Colbert manuscripts; they are present in a third.]

10. All these, unanimous—not bought with money, not deceived by fraud, not enticed by private affection for flesh or kinship, not compelled by fear of secular power, but undoubtedly recognizing and not disguising God’s will—frankly rejected Peter [Col. 0278B] Leonis and securely received Gregory, Pope Innocent. Certainly none of our own people is named expressly in this letter, because it does not allow a complete enumeration and because the invidious naming of some cannot escape the charge of flattery.

Yet I ought not to pass over the saints who, dead to the world, live more fully to God, whose life is hidden with Christ in glory. There, assuredly, they diligently seek and undoubtedly find the good pleasure of God, since they are concerned with how to please Him. Accordingly the Camaldolese, the Vallombrosans, the Carthusians, the Cluniacs, those of Marmoutier, my own Cistercians, the Caen monks, [Col. 0279A] the Tironensians, and the Savigniacs—indeed, the whole united body of brethren, both clerics and monks of regular life and approved conduct—following bishops as flocks follow their shepherds, steadfastly cling to Innocent, sincerely support him, humbly obey him, and faithfully recognize him as the true successor of the apostles.

> [Note: [Col. 0277C] This is the reading of nearly all old manuscripts; some read “Camaudillienses.” The Camaldolese and Vallombrosan congregations, two Italian congregations of the Benedictine Order, are too well known to require explanation here.]

> [Note: [Col. 0277D] It should not be passed over in silence what Orderic relates of the Cluniacs on this occasion in book XIII, under the year 1134. “When the Cluniacs,” he says, “learned of Innocent’s arrival, they sent sixty horses or mules, with all fitting equipment, for the pope and cardinal-clerics, and honourably escorted them as far as their basilica. There they kept the pope and his party for eleven days, and had their new church, in honour of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, dedicated by him with great rejoicing and a multitude of people. Hence he gained great authority among Westerners, because he was preferred to Peter by the Cluniacs. For Peter Leonis had been reared among them in childhood and became a monk in their habit and profession.” Thus he. To the same effect belongs what Peter the Venerable, who originated this exception, declares in praise of Cluny: “From its beginning,” he says, “it became not merely lodging for strangers, not merely a refuge for fugitives, but, so to speak, the public treasury of the Christian commonwealth,” book IV, letter 27.]

> [Note: [Col. 0278C] Marmoutier was a distinguished monastery near Tours, founded by Saint Martin. Its abbot at that time was Odo, to whom Letter 397 is addressed. Very many priories depended upon this monastery and formed, as it were, a congregation. Bernard mentions here only the more distinguished monasteries.]

> [Note: [Col. 0278C] Two Colbert manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript read “Cistellenses,” from which nearly all printed editions fabricated “Cistemblenses”; through a second error they added these after “Cistercians,” as though they were different groups. In certain manuscripts the Cistercians are called *Cistercienses*, in others *Cistellenses*, then a common popular name. The Cistercians are called *Cistellenses* by the monk Hermann, book III of *The Miracles of the Blessed Mary of Laon*, chapter 7, in Pérard, p. 103; and by Robert of Torigni under the year 1140, “Monks of Cistelth.” They are also called *Cistell* in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 703, col. 1.]

> [Note: [Col. 0278D] Caen is a city on the River Orne in Neustria, not far from the Ocean, distinguished by its famous academy from the year 1433. In its suburb stands the notable Benedictine abbey, founded by William the Conqueror, duke of that province and king of the English, under the title of Saint Stephen. Its first abbot was Lanfranc, formerly prior of Bec and later archbishop of Canterbury. For more about him and about Saint Stephen’s Abbey at Caen, see the notes to Lanfranc’s works and *Neustria Pia*. Among the Cadomenses was the notable monastery of Savigny in the diocese of Avranches. “From it,” says Peregrine in the *History of Fontaines*, vol. X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 372, “many monasteries have already sprung forth, whose abbots gather for chapter; the Order flourishes there, and their sweet reputation is fragrant everywhere.”

> This abbey, with thirty others subject to it, was joined by Abbot Serlo to the Cistercians in 1148; ibid., p. 374.]

> [Note: [Col. 0279D] The monastery of Tiron, in the diocese of Chartres, was then also among the more distinguished monasteries. It was named from the stream flowing by it, situated in the region of Perche, founded by its first and most devout abbot Bernard, whose Life survives with Souchet’s notes. It became the head, as it were, of a congregation; see Bishop Ivo of Chartres, letter 229. James of Vitry praises the religious life of the Tironensian monks in chapter 20 of his *Western History*. This abbey, like Marmoutier, flourished under the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur and was distinguished as a seminary for young scholars.]

> [Note: [Col. 0279D] There are two monasteries in Gaul named Savigny: one in the diocese of Lyons, the other in that of Avranches. Bernard here means the latter, situated on the borders of Normandy, Armorica, and the region of Le Mans. It was founded in 1112 by the most devout Abbot Vitalis. His successor Geoffrey subjected himself and his monasteries—nineteen in number, for he is said to have founded that many—to the Cistercians. For the history of this monastery see Arthur du Monstier, *Neustria Pia*. For the other Savigny see Letter 173. In *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 704, the Savigniacs are said, before their union with the Cistercians, to have belonged to the Tironensian Order, from whose monastery many abbeys then depended. To all these religious who recognized Innocent, Ernald adds the Grandmontines, book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, II.45.]

11. What of the kings and princes of the earth? Do they not, in the same spirit, together with the peoples subject to them, alike embrace Innocent, themselves confessing him to be pope and bishop of their souls? Finally, what man illustrious and of good reputation, in whatever rank of life, does not think the same? Yet these men still object, through some contentious importunity and untimely contention. They summon the world to judgment [Col. 0279B], and demand that the whole body be judged along with their small number. Having prejudged the matter in the election, they strive to reconsider it at confirmation: acting too hastily then, reconsidering perversely now.

Who, I ask, can gather into one such vast hosts of princes of both orders, not to mention the peoples, and bring them to examination? Who can persuade so many thousands of saints to destroy again what they previously built and to lead themselves into transgression? What place, moreover, could be large enough and safe enough for all? For this is the business of the whole Church, not the case of one person. You see that you construct an accusation against your mother out of the impossible; indeed, you dig a pit for yourselves into which you may fall headlong, and weave a snare by which you may be held fast, lest you return to your mother’s bosom [Col. 0279C]. There will never be lacking an occasion to one who wishes to leave his friend.

12. But let it be so. Let God change His counsel—I speak in human terms—revoke His sentence, summon a council from the ends of the earth, and allow the same matter to be judged twice, though He Himself does not do so. Whom, I ask, will they appoint as judges? For all are on one side, and the parties will hardly agree about judgment; thus such a great assembly will be wearied for litigation rather than peace. Then I should like to know to whom he would meanwhile entrust Rome, which for so long he coveted with such great love, acquired with such labour and expense, possesses with such pride, and fears to lose with such shame—lest the entire world be seen to have gathered in vain if, [Col. 0279D] when he loses the case, he nevertheless does not lose Rome. Otherwise, who enters into litigation after being stripped of the disputed possession? Neither laws [Col. 0280A] nor canons compel it.

And we say these things not because we distrust our justice, but because we are wary of your cunning. For God has already brought forth His justice as light and His judgment as the noonday, even though to a blind man neither light appears nor noon shines; for as His darkness is, so also is His light.

137. 13. Therefore there are two men concerning whom the dispute is: which of them more rightly appears to be pope. First, if you compare the persons, so that I may seem neither to disparage one nor flatter the other, I shall say what you will find said everywhere and what, I think, no one denies: namely, that the life and reputation of our Innocent fear no rival, whereas the other’s are safe not even from a friend. Next, if you examine the elections, that of our man likewise at once appears [Col. 0280B] both purer in its promotion, more probable in its rationale, and earlier in time. The matter of time is established; the other two points are proven by the merits and standing of the electors. For you will find, unless I am mistaken, that side to be the sounder one: both bishops and cardinal-deacons or cardinal-priests, including those most directly concerned in the election of the supreme pontiff and those who, according to the decrees of the Fathers, are sufficient for electing him. What also of the consecration? Do we not have the Bishop of Ostia, to whom it especially belongs? Therefore, since the person elected is worthier, the election sounder, and the procedure more orderly, by what reasoning—or rather, by what contentiousness—do these men attempt, against law, right, and the wishes of all good people, to place another over God’s Church against her will and resistance, and to depose him?

14. You see, most reverend and illustrious Fathers, that this undertaking, so malicious, so unworthy [Col. 0280C], so rash, must certainly be resisted with all strength. This befits the whole household of God, but above all you and yours, if indeed zeal for God’s house consumes your souls. You and yours, I say, must especially watch and pray that you do not enter into temptation. In that region especially there is need for courage and vigilance, whence the adversary attacks more fiercely and the greater force of war presses on. You know by your own experience how savage and crafty an enemy has risen against you. Alas! How far his wickedness in those regions has already advanced through the authority he has received, raging in both kinds of malice, force and deceit! Yet will malice finally conquer wisdom? This, however, is his hour [Col. 0280D] and the power of darkness. But it is the last hour, and this power soon passes away. Do not be frightened; do not be deceived.

[Col. 0281A] Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, is with you, and He is also engaged in the cause. Take courage: He has conquered the world. He is faithful and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able. Do you see the fool firmly rooted? Without doubt his beauty shall immediately be cursed. For the Lord will not leave the sceptre of sinners long over the lot of the righteous. Yet it belongs to your vigilance, and you diligently provide for it according to your office, as you do provide, that the righteous may not stretch out their hands to iniquity.

Prayer for Catholics: “Do good, O Lord, to the good and upright in heart” (Ps. 124:4).

For schismatics: “Fill, O Lord, their faces with shame, that they may seek Your name” (Ps. 82:17).

## LETTER 127. TO WILLIAM, COUNT OF POITIERS

> [Note: [Col. 0281C] Written about the year 1132. William, the ninth of that name [Col. 0281D]—though some wish him to be counted the tenth—at the urging of Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, supported Anacletus’s party and grievously persecuted those who adhered to Innocent. See *The Life of Saint Bernard*, book II, chapter 6. What William of Malmesbury relates in book V of *The Kings of the English* concerning incest and other crimes of William, Count of Poitiers, should rightly be understood of William VIII, this man’s father, as Jean Besly observed. For Peter, bishop of Poitiers, whom the Count is there said to have sent into exile, died in that exile in 1117. William IX, by contrast, succeeded his father only in 1126, as the same author proves in his *Gallic History of the Counts of Poitiers*. Consult him if you wish to investigate more carefully William’s other deeds, especially his death; see also Baronius under the year 1135. He is discussed at length in book II, chapter 6 of the *Life of Bernard*, where his conversion through Bernard is recorded. Many fables are told about him. It is certain, on the testimony of Orderic, his contemporary, corroborated by comparable authors, that William, moved by penitence, made pilgrimage to Saint James, “and on Friday, Parasceve, the fifth day before the Ides of April, fortified by holy communion, died before the altar of the blessed Apostle,” about the year 1137, under which year Orderic records these facts.]

TO WILLIAM, ILLUSTRIOUS COUNT OF POITIERS AND DUKE OF AQUITAINE, WRITTEN IN THE PERSON OF HUGH, DUKE OF BURGUNDY. He exhorts William, a supporter of the antipope Anacletus, to receive Innocent as the true pontiff.

[Col. 0281B]

HUGH, by the same grace Duke of Burgundy, to WILLIAM, by God’s grace illustrious Count of Poitiers and Duke of the Aquitanians: fear Him who is terrible and who takes away the spirit of princes.

1. I cannot bear any longer to conceal your error, since I am your kinsman by flesh and friend at heart. If someone among the people goes astray, he perishes alone; but a ruler’s error entangles many and harms as many as he governs. We do not preside, as you know, in order to destroy, but in order to care for those subject to us. He through whom kings reign has placed us over His peoples to protect, not overthrow, them—plainly, as ministers of His holy Church, not its lords. Since you are known to have served that ministry worthily elsewhere, in a manner befitting the greatness of your power and commendably, [Col. 0281C] I wonder by what trick your prudence has now been deceived, so that you should desert that same mother and mistress of yours in an evil time—unless perhaps those advisers of yours are trying to persuade you of this also: that the universal Church has been reduced to the house of Peter Leonis alone. Lying men, whom Truth destroys by the breath of His mouth, as He destroys their head the antichrist, declaring through David that the Church is extended to all the ends of the earth and to all families of the nations (Ps. 21:28).

[Col. 0282A] 2. They do indeed have [variant: “he has”] the duke of Apulia,

> [Note: [Col. 0282D] The pseudo-pope Anacletus, in order to bind Roger, duke of Apulia, more firmly to himself as the chief supporter of his faction, granted him the title of king of Sicily, as may be seen in Baronius under the year 1130, no. 6. Innocent afterward confirmed that title to him when he had unfortunately marched against him in battle and had been captured, being unable otherwise to escape his hands. How much better it would have been for the Pontiff to pursue his claim through another’s hand, if arms were necessary at all, than himself to go to war, yield to his enemy, and be driven to unjust terms! See Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1139.]

—but he alone among the princes, and himself obtained at the ridiculous price of an usurped crown. Finally, what goodness, virtue, or honourable quality do they put forward concerning their supreme pontiff to induce us also to support him? If the reports everywhere spread by public opinion are true, he is unworthy to govern even a single village; if they are not true, nonetheless the head of the Church ought to possess not only soundness of life but also honourable reputation. It is therefore safer for you, my dearest kinsman, not to depart, in receiving the universal pope, from the consensus and counsel of the universal Church. Since every religious body and the whole body of kings have received him, it is both honourable and saving for you also to receive him. Pope Innocent’s life is proclaimed innocent, his reputation unimpaired [Col. 0282B], and his election canonical. The first two points even his enemies do not deny; the third was assailed by slander, but recently the false slanderers have been caught in their lie by the most Christian Lothair.

> [Note: [Col. 0282D] The Roman emperor. See Letter 139.]

## LETTER 128. TO THE SAME

> [Note: [Col. 0282D] Written in the year of Christ 1132.]

He earnestly exhorts him to restore to the Church the clerics whom he had expelled.

I remember that when I left you some time ago, most excellent prince, my purpose and desire were to wish good to you and yours with all my heart, and to assist your salvation and honour with every effort wherever I could. For I did not return from my visit to you deprived of its fruit, but, beyond the expectation of many, joyfully brought back with me [Col. 0282C] the peace of the Church, amid the exultation of the whole land. Yet I wonder by what counsel, or whose, that marvellous change of the right hand of the Most High has so suddenly changed for the worse: so that you should once more, to the injury of the Church, expel from the city the clerics of Saint Hilary and as swiftly as possible more grievously stir up God’s anger against yourself. Who has bewitched you to depart so quickly from the way of truth and salvation? Assuredly, whoever he is shall bear judgment. Would that those who trouble you might also be cut off! Return, I beg you, return, lest you too—God forbid!—be cut off. Return, I say; call your friends back to peace and the clerics back to the church, before you make terrible and irretrievably turned away from you Him [Col. 0283A] who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth.

## LETTER 129. TO THE GENOESE

> [Note: [Col. 0283C] Written in the year of Christ 1133.]

He exhorts them steadfastly to maintain and defend the peace which he had formerly established among them.

BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, to his Genoese—consuls, counsellors, and all citizens: peace, salvation, and eternal life.

1. That our visit to you last year was not fruitless was proved shortly afterward by the Church in her need, on whose mission we had come. You received and entertained us honourably during the short time we were with you, indeed with a generosity worthy of you but exceeding the measure of our humility. Certainly, as we have not forgotten, so we are not ungrateful [Col. 0283B]. May He who can, and who was the cause of it, God, repay you in return. For how can we recompense that reverence, service, and affection full of love and grace? Not that we delight in favour shown to ourselves, but that we rejoice together in your devotion. O those festal days for me—few though they were! I shall never forget you: devoted people, honourable nation, illustrious city.

> [Note: [Col. 0283D] Here must not be passed over what Manrique relates in his *Annals*, under the year 1132, chapter 6. Bernard’s promise, he says, remained so ratified and firm that almost five hundred years later, in 1625, when the most excellent prince Charles Emmanuel, duke of Savoy—whom the Genoese endured as a most hostile enemy—was ravaging the towns of their dominion and was already seen scarcely five miles from the city, and when they were wholly deprived of human aid, they invoked Saint Bernard’s pledge by a formal vow, which I shall not hesitate to transcribe word for word.

> “After this, we promise and vow to enrol and number among the holy guardians of our republic Saint Bernard, who, while living among humankind, pledged by his letters never to forget us; to celebrate his day and to ensure that it is celebrated by our people and clergy, with the consent of the most illustrious archbishop and most reverend bishops; to build in this principal church or another at our discretion a chapel dedicated to him; on Saint Bernard’s day every year forever to hold a solemn procession and have solemn Mass celebrated at his altar, with our devout attendance; and finally, through the hand of the Doge, to pay every year forever the observances of the appointed rite, and for this year dowries for twelve girls, as they are called, namely one hundred livres to each. In testimony of this matter, etc. Given in the cathedral church, Sunday, 25 April 1625.”

> Thus spoke the Genoese when the ruin of their republic was imminent. How their vow succeeded was proved by the event: for, on the very eve of Bernard’s feast, a Spanish fleet arrived and quickly put the hostile forces to flight. Thus, in substance, Manrique.]

Morning, evening, and noon, in the prophet’s manner, I was recounting and announcing (Ps. 54:18), and there was as much eagerness to hear as love in those who heard. We brought the word of peace; and when we found children of peace, our peace rested upon them. I had indeed gone out to sow seed—not my own but God’s; and the good seed, falling into good ground, bore fruit [Col. 0283C] a hundredfold and in due season. Wonderful speed, because the need was great. I suffered neither delay nor difficulty: almost in a single day I sowed, reaped, and returned bearing sheaves of peace with rejoicing. This was the harvest I reaped: to exiles, captives, those in fetters and prisoners, we brought back a joyful hope of escape and return home; to enemies, fear; to schismatics, confusion; to the Church, glory; to the world, joy.

2. And now what remains, dearest friends, except that you be reminded of perseverance? It alone earns glory for men and crowns for virtues. Indeed, without perseverance neither one who fights obtains victory nor the victor gains the palm. It is the strength of powers and the completion of virtues [Col. 0284A], the nurse of merit and mediator of reward. It is patience’s sister, constancy’s daughter, peace’s friend, the knot of friendships, the bond of unanimity, and the bulwark of holiness. Take away perseverance, and service has no recompense, kindness no gratitude, courage no praise. Finally, “not he who begins, but he who perseveres to the end, shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). When Saul was little in his own eyes, he was made king over Israel; not persevering in humility, he lost both kingdom and life. If Samson’s prudence and Solomon’s devotion had retained perseverance, neither would the latter have been deprived of wisdom nor the former of strength. I urge and beg you firmly [Col. 0284B] to preserve this supreme mark of honour, this sole and faithful guardian of every uprightness. Carefully preserve what you gladly heard. Remember what is written: Herod feared John and gladly heard him (Mark 6:20). But he would have been blessed had he preserved what he gladly heard just as readily. For it is not those who hear, but, He says, “Blessed are those who hear and keep the word of God” (Luke 11:28).

3. Therefore preserve peace with your Pisan brothers, faith toward the lord pope, loyalty toward the king, and honour for yourselves. For this is expedient, fitting, and required by justice. We have heard that envoys of Duke Roger came to you.

> [Note: [Col. 0284D] Concerning him, see Letter 127, no. 2.]

What they brought or took back, we do not know. But I, following the poet’s saying, to speak truthfully, have always feared the Greeks, even bearing gifts (*Virgil, Aeneid* II.49). If anyone among you—may God avert it!—should be found to commit so foul a deed [Col. 0284C] as to stretch out his hand toward shameful gain, mark and judge him at once as an enemy of your name, a betrayer of your fellow citizens, and a seller of the common honour and integrity. If likewise someone is found whispering among the people, taking upon himself the devil’s role, desiring to sow quarrels and disturb peace—as that one is ever the lover and author of discord—let him be promptly opposed by the remedy of strict discipline: for the pest is worse because it is more inward. A hostile army lays waste fields and plunders houses; but corrupt counsels corrupt good morals, and a little leaven corrupts the whole lump (1 Cor. 5:6).

Sow, plant, trade, so that you may not only fail to repeat your former evils, but may also expiate and erase them through your just labours [Col. 0285A]. For it is written: “A man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. 13:8); and again: “Give alms, and all things are clean to you” (Luke 11:41). But if you wish to make war, and to test again the strength of your courage and vigour, if you delight in trying arms, this must assuredly not be undertaken against neighbours and friends. Rather, it would be fitting both to attack the enemies of the Church and to defend your kingdom’s crown, invaded by the Sicilians. Against them you will acquire more honourably and possess more justly what you acquire. May the God of peace and love remain always with you all. Amen.

## LETTER 130. TO THE PISANS

> [Note: [Col. 0285D] Written in the year of Christ 1133.]

He praises the Pisans for their zeal and support for Pope Innocent, who, when Rome had been occupied by the antipope Anacletus, came as an exile to Pisa.

[Col. 0285B]

BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, to his Pisans—consuls, counsellors, and citizens: salvation, peace, and eternal life to all.

May God do you good and remember the faithful service, the devout compassion, consolation, and honor which you have shown and continue to show to the bride of his Son in the evil time and in the days of her affliction. Indeed, this is already being fulfilled in part, and some fruit of this prayer is being received. A worthy recompense is already being rendered with swift effect. God is now dealing with you according to your merits, O people whom he chose as his inheritance, altogether an acceptable people, zealous for good works. Pisa is being taken in Rome’s place, and from all the cities of the earth it is chosen for the height of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0285C] This has happened neither by chance nor by human counsel, but comes about through heavenly providence and God’s gracious favor: he loves those who love him, he who said to his Christ, Innocent: “Dwell in Pisa, and I, blessing, will bless it. Here will I dwell, because I have chosen it.” With me as author, Pisan constancy does not yield to the malice of the Sicilian tyrant [Note: [Col. 0285D] Roger, concerning whom see Letter 127, no. 2.]; it is not shaken by threats, corrupted by gifts, or ensnared by deceits. O Pisans, Pisans, the Lord has magnified his dealings with you; we have become joyful. What city does not envy you? Keep the deposit, faithful city; acknowledge grace; strive not to be found ungrateful for your prerogative. Honor your Father and the Father of the whole community; honor the princes of the world who are within you, and the judges of the earth, whose presence makes you illustrious, glorious, [Col. 0285D] renowned. Otherwise, if you do not know yourself, O fair one among cities, [Col. 0286A] you will go out after the flocks of your companions to pasture your kids. Enough has been said for the wise.

I commend to you Margrave Engelbert [Note: [Col. 0285D] Who is this Margrave Engelbert? We suppose that he is the man called, in Book of the Life of St. Norbert, ch. 32, the brother of the bishop of Regensburg; one of Engelbert’s daughters was betrothed to Count Theobald. Here is the passage: “Accordingly, having taken with him the envoys of Count Theobald, Norbert brought them as far as Regensburg. The bishop of that city was of most noble lineage and had a brother, Engelbert, a most powerful margrave, who had daughters of marriageable age. One of these, free to marry, was betrothed to Count Theobald. The envoys returned thither, announcing this,” etc. She was named Matilda, according to Orderic Vitalis near the end of Book XIII: “He took as wife Matilda, daughter of Duke Engelbert.” Engelbert, moreover, or Ingelbert, was Duke of Carinthia and Margrave of Friuli. Compare the note to Letter 299, [Col. 0286D].], who has been sent to aid the lord Pope and his friends: a young man strong and energetic and, if I am not mistaken, faithful. Hold him especially commended by our prayers, since I have also taken care to commend you to him still more earnestly, and have advised him to rely chiefly on your counsels.

## LETTER CXXXI

[Note: [Col. 0286D] Written in the year of Christ 1135.]

### TO THE MILANESE

Since the Milanese, reconciled to Innocent, nevertheless seemed to waver in duty and obedience, he urges them to maintain constancy, recalling the recent benefits of the Roman Church toward them.

To his MILANESE, namely the entire clergy and [Col. 0286B] people, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: greeting in the Lord.

1. God deals well with you; the Roman Church deals well with you. He does what a father does; she does what a mother does. And truly, what ought she to have done for you that she has not done? If you asked that honorable [141] persons from the curia be sent to you for the honor of God and of yourselves, it was done. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Guido of Pisa, Matthew of Albano, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, were sent with Bernard, according to Book II, no. 9 of the Life—namely, to reconcile to the Roman Church the Milanese, who had produced a schism because Anselm, the archbishop whom they had elected, had been deposed.] If you asked that what your unanimity had established concerning the election of your venerable father [Note: [Col. 0286D] Namely Ribaldi, whom they elected in the place of the rejected Anselm.] be confirmed, it was done. If you wished to be permitted what the sacred canons judge unlawful except in a grave necessity—namely, the transfer of a bishopric into an archbishopric—it was granted. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Understand the restoration of archiepiscopal rank, which the pontiff had withdrawn from this church because of the schism.] If you asked that your citizens be released from the chains of the Piacentines [Note: [Col. 0286D] For, while both sides were contending against each other in war, many Milanese had been carried off captive by the Piacentines.], a matter which I neither wish nor am able to pass over, [Col. 0286C] this too was done. In this last matter, what reasonable request of a daughter has suffered—not to say refusal—but even delay from a compassionate mother? Behold, to complete the matter, the pallium is ready: the fullness of honor.

Now hear me, illustrious people, noble nation, glorious city. Hear me, I say—I speak the truth, I do not lie—as one who loves you and is zealous for your salvation. The Roman Church is very merciful, but no less powerful. This is faithful counsel, worthy of every acceptance: do not abuse mercy, lest you be crushed by power.

2. But someone says: “I shall render it the reverence due to it, and nothing more.” Very well: do what you say; for if you render what is due, you render it wholly. For the fullness [Col. 0286D] of power over all the churches of the world has been granted, by a singular prerogative, to the Apostolic See. Therefore whoever resists this power resists God’s ordinance. It can establish new bishoprics where none have hitherto existed. It can lower some of those which do exist and raise others, as reason may direct it, so that it may make archbishops from bishops, and the reverse, if necessity seems to require it. It can summon eminent ecclesiastical persons from the ends of the earth and compel them to appear before it—not once or twice, but as often as it sees fit. Moreover, it stands ready to avenge every disobedience, should anyone perhaps attempt resistance.

Finally, you too have experienced this. What, after all, did your former rebellion and defiance, ill-advised by your false prophets [Note: [Col. 0287C] He speaks of the rebellion in which the Milanese, following their archbishop Anselm [Col. 0287D] of Pusterla, supported Conrad’s party against Lothair, the legitimate emperor. Sigonius recounts the matter in Book XI of *The Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 1128: “Conrad,” he says, “with certain princes supporting him against Lothair, declared himself king. Elated by the submissive service of a proud good fortune that smiled upon him, he hastened into Italy with an army; having gained Anselm the archbishop and the people of Milan as friends, he received at Monza the crown of the kingdom, and then, after traversing Lombardy, brought almost all the cities over to his side. For this reason the archbishops of Mainz, Magdeburg, and Trier, by Lothair’s command, cast him out from the communion of the faithful. Honorius, moreover, struck not only him, but also Anselm, who had placed the crown upon him, and the people who had received him.” Otto of Freising reports the same in Book VII, ch. 17 of his *Chronicle*.] profit you—those things of which you are now ashamed? [Col. 0287B] Rather recognize what power, glory, and honor over your suffragans you were so long deprived of. [Note: [Col. 0287D] That is, because the Milanese, following Archbishop Anselm, [Col. 0288C] had adhered to Anacletus and Conrad, [Col. 0288D] as stated above and as will be explained more fully below. When they repented, Innocent restored that dignity to them. Bernard must be understood to refer to this restoration in the preceding passages, when he says that, in favor of the Milanese, the transfer of a bishopric into an archbishopric had been made. Otherwise the see had held metropolitan rank from the beginning. Nevertheless, it should not be omitted that Sigonius reports in Book XI of *The Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 1133: “Innocent, having already twice been courteously and honorably received by the Genoese, returned them this favor: he exempted their bishop from obedience to the Archbishop of Milan, made him an archbishop, and subjected to him one half of the bishops of Corsica.”]

Who was able, on your behalf, to withstand the most just severity of Apostolic authority when, provoked by your excesses, it decreed that you should be stripped of those ancient and splendid ornaments of yours, mutilated in your members? Even today you would lie humbled and shorn, had you not been treated more graciously than powerfully. Who will be able to restrain it from even harsher measures if you again—God forbid—add provocation? See to it that you do not suffer a relapse; for certainly, unless I am mistaken, a remedy cannot so readily be found again. Therefore, if anyone says to you, “In part one must obey, in part one need not,” when you have experienced in yourselves the fullness of Apostolic power and the integrity of its authority, is such a person not either deceived [Col. 0287C] or wishing to deceive? But do what I say, for I do not deceive you. Turn rather to humility and gentleness; for God gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5), and the meek shall inherit the earth (Ps. 36:11). Take care to preserve the recovered favor of your lady and mother; and henceforth strive to please her, so that she may be pleased not only to keep for you what she has restored, but also to add what she has not yet given.

[142]

## LETTER CXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Written in the year of Christ 1134.]

### TO THE CLERGY OF MILAN

He congratulates the clergy of Milan, through whose efforts the city, having renounced Anacletus’s schism, had returned to the unity of the Church.

Blessed are you by the Lord, through whose zeal and diligence [Col. 0288A] your city has been freed from error and, abandoning schism, has returned to Catholic unity. This report went forth among Catholics; Zion heard and rejoiced, and you have glory before God and all people. With what joyful embraces Mother Church gathers so great a multitude of such important children, whom she had grieved to have lost! With what glad and serene countenance God the Father receives this sacrifice from your hands! And in also directing your efforts to the peace of the land, you do what sons of peace do.

And I, brothers, wishing to become a participant and companion in your joy, was coming to you, as you requested, with our beloved brothers, your messengers, concerning whom you wrote to me, in order to satisfy you more fully, according to reason, in what pleases God. But because the time is short in which we are hastening to the council [Note: [Col. 0288D] The council mentioned here and in the following letters is the Council of Pisa of 1134. See the *Life of Bernard*, Book II, no. 8.], do not [Col. 0288B] be troubled to wait until our return.

## LETTER CXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Written in the year of Christ 1134.]

### TO ALL THE CITIZENS OF MILAN

Invited to make peace, he rejoices that his service is sought for this work.

As I gather from your letters, I have some place in your favor; and since I find no merit of my own, I believe this has been given by God. I do not refuse the favor of so great and distinguished a people. I embrace the grace offered me, and with eager hands, myself devoted, receive the devotion of a glorious city—especially at this time, when, casting away the error of the schismatics, it has returned with the joy of the whole world to the bosom [Col. 0288C] of Mother Church.

Yet I judge that not only I should glory because I am invited to seek peace, and because I, a poor and obscure person, am chosen as mediator and servant of so great a good by a most renowned city; but that it is likewise an honor to you to be bent toward peace and concord with your neighbors—neighbors whom, as the world well knows, even the hostile attack of many cities has never compelled to yield. Therefore, as I hasten to the council, I hope to return by way of you and to find proof of the favor you promise. May he who gave the favor ensure that it is not empty in me.

## LETTER CXXXIV

### TO NOVICES CONVERTED AT MILAN

[Note: [Col. 0289C] Written in 1134.—From this title Baronius infers that, before Bernard’s arrival in Milan—that is, before 1134—a Cistercian community had already been sent there and a monastery founded to which these novices had committed themselves. Ughelli, however, in vol. IV of *Italia Sacra*, judges that the first Cistercian monastery in that city was Chara-Vallis, which he proves was founded only in 1135, two miles from the city. He accordingly holds that “novices” in this letter means those who, recently converted through Bernard’s work while he was travelling to the Council of Pisa, had already sincerely devoted themselves to his instruction. Ughelli’s date for the monastery’s foundation rests on an ancient inscription and the earliest documents of the site, which consistently call it *Chara-Vallis*, not *Clara-Vallis*. [Col. 0289D] “That it should be read *Chara-Vallis*,” says Mabillon himself in *Italian Journey*, p. 18, “is shown by all the principal documents of the site, and likewise by an ancient inscription carved on the cloister wall in this form: ‘In the year of grace 1135, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, this monastery was founded by Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux. In 1221 this church was consecrated by Lord Henry, Archbishop of Milan, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in honor of Saint Mary of Chara-Vallis.’” See Letter 281.] He congratulates the Milanese novices on their conversion and promises to visit them when the council is over.

[Col. 0289A]

To the dearest brothers of Milan, recently converted to God, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: may you bring what has been well begun to a worthy completion in the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Blessed be God, who has made the glory of the world seem cheap to you, intending to bestow his own. O how vain are the sons of men; how deceitful are the sons of men in the scales, who, in accordance with that saying of the Gospel, seek glory from one another and refuse the glory that comes from God alone (John 5:44)—indeed, thereby deceiving themselves [143] in vanity together! (Ps. 61:10). But you are not so. [Col. 0289B] Divine mercy has now freed you from this reproach, so that you may be Christ’s sweet fragrance to God in every place: for yourselves, unto glory; for angels, unto joy; for human beings, unto example. For there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance; how much more over so many and such men, converted from so great a city?

And I, brothers, stirred by so great a joy and also invited by you through the dearest brothers Otto and Ambrose, whom you sent for this very purpose, had resolved to come to you with them. But judging it better not to see you at a moment of crisis or merely in passing, I postponed this until our return. For we are hastening to the council and, God helping, will return by way of you, to offer to your holy purpose such counsel and help as [Col. 0289C] we can reasonably provide.

## LETTER CXXXV

### TO PETER, BISHOP OF PAVIA

[Note: [Col. 0290C] Written about the year 1135.—Ughelli lists two bishops of Pavia of this name: one elected in 1130 or 1131; the other, after the intervening Alfonso and Conrad, in 1148, to whom he assigns this letter. It fits the former better, since this letter immediately follows Letter 134, written in 1134.] He redirects to God the praises brought to him. He commends the bishop for works of mercy.

If good seed cast upon good soil seems to have borne fruit, the glory belongs to him who gave seed to the sower, fertility to the ground, and growth to the seed. What share do we have in these things? Certainly, I will not give Christ’s glory to another; much less will I usurp it for myself. Assuredly, the law of the Lord converts souls, not I; the Lord’s testimony is faithful and gives wisdom to little ones (Ps. 18:8), not I. [Col. 0290A] The hand is praised for the fine shape of the letter, not the pen. I confess—so that I may attribute much to myself—that my tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe (Ps. 44:2).

“What good, then,” you ask, “do the beautiful feet of those who proclaim good news bring to themselves?” Much in every respect. First, because they are children of their Father who is in heaven, and the glory which they bring to their Father is by no means alien to themselves. For if children, then heirs. Next, because they count their neighbors’ salvation as their own, since they love them as themselves. Thirdly, because the labor of their lips cannot wholly perish for them. For each shall receive a reward according to his own labor (1 Cor. 3:8).

I did not keep my lips closed; you opened your heart in compassion. Therefore, without doubt, you will receive more, [Col. 0290B] because you labored more. For I am certain that it is not without effect that you gave water to the thirsty and met fugitives with loaves. No, I say: acts of humanity are not fruitless, nor are the encouragements to salvation by which you truly refreshed Christ’s own heart in those poor persons. Yet we are both fellow laborers and fellow helpers of God; together we both hope for fruit at the visitation of holy souls. Who will grant that I may never cease to remember you, nor ever be abandoned by that remembrance?

## LETTER CXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0290D] Written in the year of Christ 1134.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT

[Note: [Col. 0290D] Earlier editions read “To the Same,” referring it to Peter, bishop of Pavia, to whom the preceding letter was addressed. But in two Cistercian manuscripts and two Colbert manuscripts, Letter 178, to Pope Innocent, is inserted here. This letter was written because of robbers who plundered bishops returning from the Council of Pisa in 1134. See the notes to Letter 23.] He asks that Dalfinus, prepared to make satisfaction for the injuries inflicted, be treated more leniently.

If sad events always occurred, who could endure them? If prosperous events always occurred, who would not grow contemptuous? But Wisdom, the prudent governor of affairs, alternates these things in a most necessary succession along the course of temporal life for her elect, with such moderation that adversities do not break them and joys do not dissolve them; rather, the latter are made more welcome by the former, and the former more bearable by the latter.

Blessed be God in [144] all things. Our sorrow has been turned into joy; after wine, our wounds have received oil. The ravagers and robbers, struck with compunction, humble themselves. They send back with honor the priest of the Lord upon whom they dared to lay hands; the spoils they had seized they gather again without delay and restore without fraud. If any of these things [Col. 0291A] cannot be found, Dalfinus will make satisfaction for it according to your good pleasure; for he affirmed this to us in his own hand.

If, in order to fulfill this promise, he comes to the feet of your Majesty [Note: [Col. 0291B] From this it is inferred that this letter is addressed to the supreme pontiff, who is not infrequently addressed by others as “Majesty,” as by Bernard in Letters 46, 150, no. 3, and 166, and also by Odo of Deuil and others. Although this title is sometimes also accorded to lower prelates; see the notes to Letter 370.], as he has resolved to do, we ask that the young man be treated more leniently than he deserves. We do not wish so great a crime to go unpunished, but rather that, if possible, the Church may be honored by due satisfaction; that the man making satisfaction may not be exasperated beyond the strength of his patience, and may not repent [Note: [Col. 0291C] Supply “not” from the preceding clause: “may not be exasperated and may not repent”; compare the end of the following letter.] of having accepted our counsels.

## LETTER CXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0291C] Written in the year of Christ 1134.]

### TO THE EMPRESS OF THE ROMANS

[Note: [Col. 0291C] Richenza. Elsewhere, incorrectly, “to the emperor.”] The Milanese were not received into the Pope’s favor until they had received Emperor Lothair. Therefore he commends them to the Empress’s mercy.

[Col. 0291B] In the reconciliation of the Milanese [Note: [Col. 0291C] On this matter Sigonius writes as follows in Book II of *The Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 1134: “When the Milanese saw that they had been deprived of communion in the sacred rites and stripped of metropolitan rank because, following Anselm, they had adhered to Conrad and Anacletus, they were led by repentance for their actions, under the leadership of Bishop Ribaldi, whom they had chosen after rejecting Anselm, to seek the recovered favor of Innocent and Lothair. On this matter they also wrote to Bernard, whose authority they knew to be very great. Bernard, summoned by Innocent to the Council of Pisa, as he hastened there through Lombardy, congratulated them by letter for having abandoned their error, promised to comply with their wishes and to visit them on his return.

“Having gone to Pisa, he convened the council, and it was chiefly completed by his wisdom and counsel. The council held many sessions, but its principal business concerned condemning Anacletus and his supporters. Many marks of honor were granted to the Milanese, who had returned to Innocent’s authority under Ribaldi: Ribaldi, whom they had chosen, was to retain his rank; that see was to retain its former metropolitan dignity and be honored with the pallium; and a most honorable embassy was sent to expiate their offence. Guido, bishop of Pisa, and Matthew, bishop of Albano, were sent as legates *a latere*; and Bernard himself, whom they especially requested, was associated with them, to extinguish the discord stirred up by Archbishop Anselm [Col. 0292B] and free the people, tainted by a crime against religion.

“When the Milanese learned that Bernard was approaching with the legates, they immediately poured from the city in immense joy and came out to meet him seven thousand paces away, with so great a multitude of every rank, age, and sex that you would have thought they wished to abandon the city and move elsewhere. Receiving him in ranks interspersed and divided into groups, they eagerly competed to look at him, speak to him, and even kiss his feet. They also preserved hairs pulled from his clothes as appropriate remedies for ailments that arose, judging holy everything he had touched and believing that they would become holy through contact with those things. Thus they escorted him amid joyful cries into the city and to his lodging.

“On the appointed day the council was held. There, first rejecting Anacletus, they acknowledged Innocent as the true and Catholic pontiff. Then, repudiating Conrad, they publicly received Lothair as king and lord and confessed him, together with the whole world, to be Augustus, Emperor of the Romans. Touching the most holy Gospel, they promised to make satisfaction, by the counsel and command of Innocent, for their defiance; and immediately submitting to Bernard’s judgment, they accepted the penance he imposed. While Bernard was in Milan, he healed with divine power and to everyone’s amazement very many afflicted people who were brought to him: he restored walking to the lame, sight to the blind, and the former movement of limbs to the disabled; above all, many whom the devil had possessed through the schism were delivered.

“Then, by Innocent’s command, he set out to make peace among the Lombard cities themselves and proceeded to Pavia and Cremona.
