Since he achieved nothing among the Cremonese, he reported their obstinacy to Innocent in these words: ‘The Cremonese have hardened themselves, and their prosperity destroys them. The Milanese despise them, and their confidence deceives them. These people, putting their hope in chariots and horses, have frustrated me and made my labor vain.’” Thus he.] we have not forgotten what your Excellence had previously impressed upon us. Even if you had not reminded us, we would nevertheless have given attention to your honor and the interests of the realm, as we faithfully do everywhere and always, insofar as we can.

Certainly, the Milanese were not received into the favor of the lord Pope and the unity of the Church until, openly rejecting and renouncing Conrad, they received our lord Lothair as their king and lord and confessed him, together with the whole world, to be Augustus, Emperor of the Romans. Touching the most holy Gospel, they promised that they would make worthy satisfaction to you, according to the counsel and command of the lord Pope, [Col. 0292A] for the injury previously done. Therefore, giving great thanks to divine goodness, which has thus humbled your enemies without dangers of war or the shedding of human blood, we ask your mercy, which we have sufficiently experienced, that, at the appropriate time, when the aforesaid Milanese seek your favor through the lord Pope—the mediator, of course, of their reconciliation—you may be found gracious and placable. Thus they may not regret having obeyed sound counsel, and you may have from them the service and honor due to you. For it is not fitting that your faithful subjects, who labor for your honor, should be put to shame before you. But they will be put to shame if those who promised them hope of pardon from your kindness, when they intervene on their behalf, [Col. 0292B] find you—God forbid—inexorable.

## LETTER CXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0292D] Written in the year of Christ 1133.]

### TO HENRY, KING OF ENGLAND

He asks the king for assistance for Pope Innocent.

To HENRY, most illustrious King of the English, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: honor, well-being, and peace.

To wish to instruct you, especially in matters that concern honorable conduct, is either foolishness or a sign of complete ignorance of you. Therefore it is enough simply to state the matter, and to do so briefly, since superfluous material is offered in abundance to one who readily grasps everything. We are at the entrance of the city; salvation is at the gates; justice is with us; but this food does not please the Roman soldiers. Therefore by justice we appease God; by military force we terrify our enemies. We do not have the necessities necessary even for necessities [145] alone. What needs to be done in order that the work you performed in the lord Pope Innocent’s magnificent and honorable reception may be completed, you know better. [Note: [Col. 0293B] For what Henry, first of that name, King of England, did, see Book II, ch. 1, no. 4 of the *Life of St. Bernard*. William of Malmesbury, an English writer of the same age, likewise describes the reception in Book I of his *Historia Novella*, in these exact words: “Innocent, expelled from Rome, crossed the Alps and made for Gaul. There he was received by the whole Church on this side of the mountains. Indeed King Henry—who did not know how to be lightly dislodged from an opinion once formed—freely gave him his hand at Chartres and at Rouen honored him not only with his own gifts but also with those of his nobles and even of the Jews.” Roger of Hoveden likewise records the same reception in his *Annals* under the year 1131. Moreover, in 1132, according to Fulk, author of the *Beneventan Chronicle*, when Emperor Lothair was besieging Rome in order to restore Innocent and lacked sufficient strength to take it, being provided with a garrison of only two thousand men, Bernard, who was himself present, sought aid from the King of England in this letter; the king, however, could not provide it. Finally, how religiously and Christianly he met his last day in 1135 we learn from the letter of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, written to Pope Innocent—a letter certainly most worthy to be read in William of Malmesbury, *Historia Novella*, Book I, and in Baronius under the year 1135.]

## LETTER CXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0293D] Written about the year 1135.]

### TO EMPEROR LOTHAIR

He urges the Emperor to suppress the schismatics. He commends to him the cause of a certain church situated at Toul.

To LOTHAIR, by the grace of God Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: whatever a sinner’s prayer may avail.

[Col. 0293B]

1. Blessed be God, who chose you [Note: [Col. 0293D] That is, Lothair, Duke of Saxony, a man commendable in every respect, according to William of Tyre, Book XII, ch. 16; Otto of Freising, Book VII, ch. 17; Sigonius, who says that he has been commended to human memory no less for piety than for valor; Abbot of Ursperg, who celebrates him as an energetic commander in war, prudent in counsel, terrible to the enemies of God and of Holy Church, etc.; and Peter the Deacon, who proclaims him with remarkable and magnificent praises: “Who would not admire the spirit of so great an emperor? He sat in chapter from the first hour of the day until Vespers, without food or drink, in order to settle the disagreements of the brethren, while he consulted for peace and unity. Under the imperial cloak, indeed, he served the heavenly King as a soldier. For, as I myself bear witness, when on campaign, very early at dawn he heard a Mass for the dead, then one for the army, and finally a third Mass of the day—perhaps for himself.” See the remainder, altogether worthy of reading and destined to be examples for good rulers; so that Bernard rightly praises God for providing such a prince for the Empire.], and raised up for us a horn of salvation, for the praise and glory of his name, for restoring the Empire’s honor, for helping his Church in an evil time, and finally for working salvation even now in the midst of the earth. For it is his work that the crown of your glory is enlarged and exalted day by day, growing and advancing wonderfully in every splendor and magnificence before God and human beings.

It was surely his work and power also recently [Col. 0294A] that you accomplished, in such prosperity, the journey undertaken for the peace of the realm and the liberation of the Church, though it was arduous enough and fraught with danger. [Note: [Col. 0294B] Namely, at Bernard’s urging, he came from Germany into Italy and as far as Rome, though accompanied by scanty forces, in order to restore Innocent to his see and receive from him in return the solemn imperial crown. This occurred in the City itself, at the Lateran, while the antipope Anacletus held the Vatican basilica and the most fortified places of the City, secured both by his men and by fortifications and garrisons. See Baronius under 1132; Sigonius, Book XI, under the same year; and the *Life of St. Bernard*, Book II, ch. 2. Yet Orderic, in Book XIII, p. 896, where he describes Lothair’s Roman expedition undertaken in 1133, says that he directed Peter “either to yield to the other or submit to judgment concerning his ordination”; and that he directed the same to Innocent. Peter indeed complied, but Innocent did not. Hence Lothair became angry with him, left Peter in possession of what he held, “and withdrew with the matter unfinished.”]

For in Rome you most gloriously attained the fullness of the imperial summit—and this, what was greater, with no large host, so that the greatness of your courage and faith might shine more clearly. If before so small an army the earth trembled and was still, how great, we think, will be the terror invading the hearts of enemies when the king begins to go forth in the greatness of his strength? The justice of the cause will also encourage you; indeed, a twofold necessity will impel you. It is not mine to urge you to battle; but it is, I say confidently, the duty of the Church’s advocate to ward off from the Church the raging assault of schismatics; it is Caesar’s duty to vindicate his own crown against the Sicilian usurper. [Col. 0294B] [Note: [Col. 0294C] There was formerly much dispute concerning the right to the Sicilian kingdom. That matter does not concern us now. Whoever wishes may consult Baronius’s writing on it, if it still exists today, and those who wrote against him. Bernard not without reason calls him a Sicilian usurper: he usurped the duchies of Apulia and Calabria, entrusted by feudal right to his kinsman William, and held them from the pontificate of Calixtus until 1136, when Lothair entered Italy for the second time, according to Ursperg, invaded Apulia, and defeated Roger. He especially inflamed his soldiers for battle by saying that they were taking arms against an enemy of the Church, expelled from its sacred communion. See Otto of Freising, Book VII, chs. 16 and 20; Fazellus, Book VII, latter decade. Yet he later came to his senses, through the efforts of Bernard and Peter of Cluny, who admonished him of reconciliation by letter.] For as it is established that a Jewish offspring has occupied Peter’s See to Christ’s injury [Note: [Col. 0294D] This is the same point that we noted from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* in the preface to this volume: namely, that Anacletus, or Peter Leonis, was of Jewish origin.], so without doubt everyone who makes himself king in Sicily opposes Caesar.

2. But if both tasks lie upon Caesar—to render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s—why are God’s affairs diminished at Toul, when Caesar gains nothing there? There is reason to fear that neglect of very small matters may hinder the greatest. This [Col. 0295A] is what I mean. The Church of Saint Gengulf [Note: [Col. 0295D] Concerning St. Gengulf—called Gangulf or Jangulf by others—Sigebert writes under the year 759: “St. Gengulf flourishes in Burgundy, and he also shone with the glory of martyrdom.” In his honor, around 1065, St. Gerard, bishop of that city, built a notable basilica at Toul in Lorraine, as the most illustrious and reverend Lord André Saussay, bishop and count of Toul, no less distinguished for learning and writings than for rank, informed me by letter. Thus, in an old codex in his possession: “St. Gerard first built the abbey of Saint Gengulf at the southern entrance of that same city, and brought the arm of the aforesaid saint into this city. Udo, likewise bishop of Toul, restored the same church.” Here you see that the Church of Saint Gengulf is designated by the name “abbey,” a word formerly also given to some collegiate churches, as may still be observed at Saint-Exupéry of Corbeil, where the provost, or first dignity of the chapter, is called abbot. [Col. 0296D]] is said to be grievously and unjustly oppressed in that city; and they say that, by some deception, your Prudence was induced to intervene by your petition against the lord Pope, who was preparing to provide justice. I beg and advise that the matter be handled more wisely: withdraw the harmful request and give place to justice, before that church is utterly destroyed. I am poor, yet I am your faithful servant; and if I seem importunate, perhaps that is why. We most earnestly greet the Lady Empress in the charity of Christ.

## Letter 140  
*[Written about the year 1135.]*  
**To the Same Recipient.** He commends to Lothair the Pisans, who zealously support the pope.

[Col. 0295B] I wonder by whose prompting or counsel it could have been surreptitiously brought about that your vigilance should make men—certainly worthy of double honour and favour—hear the opposite from you. I mean the Pisans, who first, and alone until now, raised their banner 146 against the invader of the empire. *[That is, Roger.]* How much more justly should royal indignation have flamed against those who dared, on any pretext, to injure a people valiant and devoted—especially at the very time when, equipped in many thousands, they had gone out to attack the tyrant, avenge the injury done to their lord, and defend the imperial crown!

For, to apply most fittingly to this people what was once said of Saint David: what city, I ask, is so faithful as Pisa—going out, coming in, and proceeding in the service of the king’s rule? (1 Sam. 22:14). Are not [Col. 0295C] these the men who recently drove that sole and most powerful enemy of the realm away from the siege of Naples? Are not these the men who also—what is almost incredible to relate—carried Amalfi, Rebello [variant: Rivello], Scala, and Atturnia in a single assault: cities indeed most wealthy and strongly fortified, and, as they say, until this time impregnable to all who had previously attempted them?

How worthy, just, and full of reason and justice it would have been for the land of the faithful, at least while these things were being accomplished, to remain secure from every enemy: both because of the presence of the supreme pontiff, whom the Pisans had long sheltered, and still shelter, among themselves in the highest honour, although exiled; and because of their service to the emperor, [Col. 0295D] for whose sake they too were then in exile. [Col. 0296A] Yet the opposite occurred: those who gave offence received favour, while those who served incurred anger.

But perhaps you did not yet know these things. Now, therefore, when the matter is known to you, it is necessary—and indeed fitting and expedient—for you to alter both your words and your attitude, so that men more deserving of royal favour and gifts may henceforth hear and receive from your side what they have deserved. Oh, how much the Pisans have deserved, and how much they can yet deserve! Enough has been said for the wise.

## Letter 141  
**To Humbert, Abbot of Igny.**  
*[Written in 1138. Humbert, a monk of La Chaise-Dieu, became a monk of Clairvaux; then Bernard appointed him first abbot of Igny, in the diocese of Rheims, in 1127. Seeking private life, he resigned the governance in 1138, the year in which this letter was written from Italy. Humbert nevertheless persisted in his resignation; Guerric was appointed in his place. He died at Clairvaux in 1148, as we shall say in volume II when reporting Bernard’s excellent sermon at his death.]*

He sharply reproves him for rashly abandoning, without consultation, the office of prelate.

1. May almighty God spare you: what did you intend to do? Who would have believed that a man endowed with such great goods could rush into so great [Col. 0296B] an evil? How could a good tree produce this most evil fruit from itself? Oh, how terrible is God in his judgments upon the children of men! I do not wonder that the devil could do this; I wonder that God permitted it—God whom, as we believe, you have served purely and devoutly for so many years.

What will he do to me, certainly a slothful and negligent servant, when he has thus, even temporarily, delivered his faithful servant into the power of his enemies? What reason, I ask—or rather, what impiety—is there in this flight of yours, at which your sons mourn and your adversaries laugh? I am astonished that the example of Abbot Arnold *[namely, of Morimond, to whom Letter 4 is addressed]* did not frighten you. As you well remember, his like presumption was punished within a short time by an end deserved, but dreadful. And he indeed had some sort of cause, as I know well; you have none.

[Col. 0296C] For were your monks disobedient to your commands? Were the lay brothers sluggish in their work? Were your neighbours perhaps hostile to you or your property? Or was your worldly substance so slight and insufficient that you were compelled to leave those whom you could not sufficiently govern or feed?

2. Beware lest that saying of God touch you too: “They hated me without cause” (John 15:25). For what ought he to have done for you that he did not do? He planted for you a choice and most beautiful vineyard. He surrounded it with the hedge of vowed continence; he dug in it the winepress 147 of most exacting discipline; and he built the tower of holy poverty, reaching even to heaven. He appointed you its cultivator and guardian; he honoured you in your labours, [Col. 0296D] and he will bring them to completion, if you allow him.

But you—shame upon it!—[Col. 0297A] are tearing down its wall and exposing it, full of the finest clusters, to all who pass along the road. Alas! Who will restrain the boar from the forest, lest it lay it waste, and the solitary wild beast, lest it graze upon it? It is strange indeed if you think that you are well preparing yourself for death by this action—as you wrote to me—so that you are not afraid to wish to die amid so great a scandal and under the anathema of the lord pope.

Moreover, if this was so necessary, could no other time have been considered than when I am detained by the necessities of the universal Church, so that I cannot come to the aid of that unhappy community which you expose? I beg you, by him who was crucified for you, spare those already sufficiently afflicted from further torment, and cease adding sorrow to sorrow. For, to tell the truth, I am so affected by this grave and general division of the Church that my soul is weary [Col. 0297B] of my life, even though you and yours are living in peace.

## Letter 142  
**To the Monks of Alp.**  
*[Written in the year of Christ 1138. The monastery of Alp, in the diocese of Geneva in Savoy, is now in the diocese of Annecy. It was founded by Count Humbert II of Savoy, under its first abbot, Guarin, who afterwards became bishop of Sion. This gave occasion for the present letter, in which Bernard consoles the monks of Alp, deprived of their abbot. Gaspar Jongelinus, in his Notice of Cistercian Abbeys, assigns this monastery’s foundation to 1136. But that it was founded before that year, and that the monks did not from the beginning embrace the habit and institutions of the Cistercians, but finally submitted themselves to them, is easily inferred from this letter, especially from the words: “With what joyful bosom did the Cistercian multitude receive you!” That they joined themselves particularly to Clairvaux is clear from Bernard’s following words. See also Letter 253, to the said Guarin, and Manrique’s Annals under 1136, when he records their incorporation. Concerning this monastery, read further the Life of St Bernard, book 1, no. 67.]*

He commends and consoles the Alpine monks, who had joined themselves under the Cistercian order to the community of Clairvaux, because of the absence of their father, raised to a higher rank. He then counsels them concerning the election of a new abbot.

1. Your good Father and ours has, by God’s ordering, been raised to a higher rank. Let us therefore, beloved, do what the prophet says: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in her order” (Hab. 3:11). He is the sun through whom the congregation of Alp is made illustrious everywhere, as the moon is by the sun. Since, therefore, he has been lifted up, [Col. 0297C] let us stand in our own order, all of us who have chosen rather to be lowly in the house of our God than to dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83:11).

Our order is lowliness; it is humility; it is voluntary poverty, obedience, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Our order is to be under a master, under an abbot, under a rule, under discipline. Our order is to give ourselves to silence, to be exercised in fasts, vigils, prayers, and manual labour; and above all, to follow the more excellent way, which is charity; and furthermore, in all these things, to advance from day to day and persevere in them until the last day. We trust that you are continually doing these things.

2. Yet you have performed one deed, and everyone marvels: [Col. 0297D] although you were holy, you did not reckon your own holiness sufficient, but took care to participate in another’s, so that you might be holier. What is written in the Gospel has been fulfilled: “When you have done all that is commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10). [Col. 0298A] You count yourselves unprofitable, and have been found humble.

To do what is right and count oneself unprofitable is found in few people; therefore many marvel. This, I say—this precisely—makes you more illustrious though already illustrious, holier though holy. Wherever this report has spread, it has filled everything with the fragrance of sweetness. In my judgment this virtue surpasses even prolonged fasts, early vigils, and every bodily exercise, as truly being the godliness “which is profitable for all things” (1 Tim. 4:8).

With what joyful embrace the multitude of Cîteaux received you! With what eager countenance the angelic height looked upon this! For those spirits know that brotherly fellowship and confederation please almighty God above all things, since he says through the prophet, “It is good to fasten together” (Isa. 41:7), and through another: [Col. 0298B] “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1); likewise: “A brother helping a brother, both shall be comforted” (Prov. 18:19).

3. This deed is also seen to breathe humility. How acceptable humility is to the divine majesty, he teaches who says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6); and the Master of humility himself shows it by saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

What can I say of our little flock of Clairvaux, to which you have attached yourselves more particularly—how greatly and with what special affection it embraces you? No words can express what the spiritual outpouring of mutual charity wonderfully accomplishes between us and you. It remains, brothers, that, having invoked the Holy Spirit, you hasten to choose a father for yourselves. For if you were waiting for me, I fear that our coming would be delayed long, and that delay would be dangerous.

But summon to yourselves our dearest brother Godfrey, prior of Clairvaux, that he may in this, as in other matters, fulfill our role: so that by his counsel—or perhaps by the counsel of those whom he may send in his place if he cannot come—and also by that of your Father Guarin, you may choose such a person that God may receive honour and you salvation. Remember me, brothers.

## Letter 143  
*[Written about the year 1135.]*  
**To His Own Community at Clairvaux.** He excuses his prolonged absence, which is no less—indeed more—burdensome to himself than to his own brethren. Meanwhile, he briefly reminds them of their duty.

[Col. 0298D]

To the dearest brothers, the monks, [Col. 0299A] lay brothers, *[“Conversi” were formerly those converted to religious life as adults, distinguished by this designation from boys offered to the monastery. Here “conversi” means the lay or bearded brothers, mentioned above in Letter 141, §1. They were present at elections of abbots, according to Letter 36, §2, just as the people were formerly present with the clergy in episcopal elections. Here they are named before novices; but in Sermon 22 on Various Subjects, §2, they are not admitted to choir. Bernard distinguishes them from monks. At that time, among Cistercians, they were not properly counted monks, as chapter 15 of the Cistercian Exordium proves, although they made a certain profession. Hence Innocent II, in a privilege—or in Letter 352 here—says: “No archbishop, bishop, or abbot shall presume, without your willing permission, to receive or retain a lay brother of yours who is not a monk after he has made profession in your monasteries.” At the Council of Rheims under Eugenius III, professed lay brothers are mentioned in canon 7; if they return to worldly vows, they are declared incapable of marriage, as are monks, from whom they are nevertheless distinguished. For the beginnings of Clairvaux, see the notes on Letter 31.]* and novices: Brother Bernard, may you always rejoice in the Lord.

1. Judge from yourselves what I suffer. If my absence is burdensome to you, let no one doubt that it is more burdensome to me. It is not a loss or burden of equal measure for you to be without me alone and for me to be deprived of your whole community. I must be affected by as many anxieties as there are of you; I grieve at being absent from each of you and fear dangers for each.

This double anguish will not leave me until I am restored to my own heart’s inward parts. I do not doubt that you feel this for me also; but I am only one. Thus one reason for grief presses upon you, while many press upon me, since I grieve for all of you. Nor am I tormented merely because I am compelled, even temporarily, to live without you—without whom I count even reigning [Col. 0299B] a wretched slavery—but also because I am forced to be occupied in matters that wholly disturb beloved quiet and perhaps suit my purpose less well.

2. Knowing this, you ought not to be indignant at my delay, which is not of my will but required by the Church’s necessity; rather, you should sympathize. I hope, however, it will not be long. Pray that it may not be fruitless. Any losses that perhaps occur meanwhile should be counted gains, because God is concerned in the matter; and since he is gracious and can do all things, he will easily repair the damage—not only fully, but abundantly.

Therefore let us be of good courage, having God with us; and in him we are present with you, however great the stretches of land that seem to divide us. Whoever among you shows himself well disposed in service, humble, God-fearing, devoted to reading, watchful in prayer, and solicitous for brotherly charity, should not think that I am absent from him. How could I not be present in spirit to one with whom I have one heart and one soul?

But if anyone among you is, God forbid, whispering, double-tongued, grumbling, stubborn, impatient of discipline, restless and wandering, or not ashamed to eat bread in idleness, 149 then even if I were physically present, my soul would be far from him, because he himself has made God far from himself by distance of conduct, not of place.

3. Meanwhile, brothers, until I come, serve the Lord in fear, so that, someday delivered without fear from the hand of your enemies, [Col. 0299D] you may serve him. Serve in hope, for he is faithful in his promises. Serve from merit, for he is rich in rewards. For, even if I say nothing of the rest, he surely claims our life as his by no undeserved right on this ground alone: he gave his own life for it.

Let no one, [Col. 0300A] therefore, live for himself, but for him who died for him (2 Cor. 5:15). For whom should I live more justly than for him without whose death I would not live? For whom more advantageously than for him who promises eternal life? For whom more necessarily than for him who threatens perpetual flames? Yet I serve willingly, because charity gives freedom. To this I summon my own inward affections.

Serve in that charity which drives out fear, does not feel labours, does not regard merit, does not seek reward—and yet urges more strongly than all else. No terror so impels; no rewards so invite; no justice so demands. May charity itself bind you to me inseparably, and continually make me present to you, especially in the hours when you pray, dearest and most longed-for brothers.

## Letter 144  
*[Written in the year of Christ 1137.]*  
**To the Same Brethren.** He expresses the burden of his prolonged absence from beloved Clairvaux, and his tender affection and longing for his sons. Yet he states what consolation he has amid such labours for the Church.

[Col. 0300B]

1. My soul is sorrowful until I return, and refuses consolation until it reaches you. For what consolation is there for me in an evil time and in the place of my pilgrimage? Are you not my consolation in the Lord? Your sweet remembrance never leaves me wherever I go; but the sweeter the remembrance, the more burdensome the absence. Woe is me, for my exile has not only been prolonged but increased! Indeed, according to the Prophet, “they added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 68:27)—those who sometimes separate me from you, even [Col. 0300C] physically.

There is the common exile itself, grievous enough: as long as we are in this body, we are pilgrims away from the Lord. To it has been added a special exile, which makes me almost impatient: I am compelled to live without you. It is a long affliction and wearisome waiting: to remain for so long subject to this vanity that occupies everything; to be enclosed in the horrible prison of a foul body; not yet to be released from the bonds of death and the cords of sins; and for so long not to be with Christ.

Yet against all these things I had one remedy of a sort, truly given from above: in place of the face of glory, still hidden, to see for the present the holy temple of God—which you are. From this temple, passage seemed easy to me [Col. 0300D] toward that glorious one for which the Prophet longs, saying: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit his temple” (Ps. 26:4).

[Col. 0301A] 2. What shall I say? How often has that consolation been interrupted for me? Behold, this is the third time, unless I am mistaken, that my inward parts have been torn away from me. *[This shows that Bernard travelled to Italy three times. See the Bernardine Chronology below.]* My little children have been weaned before their time; those whom I begot through the Gospel I am not permitted to rear. I am compelled to abandon my own and care for others; and I scarcely know which I bear more painfully: being taken away from them or entangled among these others.

Is it so, good Jesus, that my whole life will fail in sorrow and my years in groanings? It is better for me, Lord, to die than to live—but only among my brothers, my household, my dearest ones. For that, surely, is known to be sweeter, more humane, and safer. Indeed, grant me this mercy: let me be refreshed before I go away and am no more. If it pleases my Lord that the eyes of a father, such as I am—though I am not [Col. 0301B] worthy to be called father—should be closed by the hands of his sons; that they should see his last moments, comfort his departure, raise his spirit by their loving desires toward the fellowship of the blessed, if you judge him worthy; and bury the poor man’s body with the bodies of the poor: this, if I have found grace in your eyes, I desire with all my affection to obtain through the prayers and merits of these same brothers of mine. Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done. I do not wish either to live or to die for myself.

3. But it is fitting that you who have heard my sorrow should also know my consolation, if I have any. First, in every labour and affliction I endure, I judge that he alone is concerned to whom all things live. Whether I wish it or not, I must live for him who acquired me for himself by laying down [Col. 0301C] his own life; and he is able, if we suffer anything for him, to repay us on that day as merciful and just Judge.

If I serve him unwillingly, a stewardship alone has been entrusted to me, and I shall be an evil servant; but if willingly, it is glory for me. In this consideration, then, I take some breath. Further, heavenly grace has often honoured me in my labours, not by my merits, and that grace has not been empty in me, as I have experienced in many cases and as you yourselves have not wholly failed to see.

And on this occasion too, I might say, for your consolation, how necessary the presence of my littleness is or has been to the Church of God, if it did not savour of self-glory. It is better now for you to learn this from others.

4. Yielding to the emperor’s most urgent request, the apostolic command, and the prayers of the Church and princes, grieving and unwilling, weak and infirm—and, to confess the truth, bearing about the pale image of timorous death—we are drawn into Apulia. [Col. 0302A] Pray for what serves the Church’s peace; pray for what serves our salvation; so that we may see you again, live and die with you. And live in such a way that you may obtain this.

Weak amid the pressure of time, I dictated these words with tears and sobs, as our dearest brother Baldwin testifies, [who took them down in writing. Baldwin, the first cardinal from the Cistercian family, was created by Innocent II in 1130 at the Council of Clermont, and later became archbishop of Pisa. Concerning him, see book 2 of the Life of St Bernard, no. 49: “In Tuscany, at Pisa alone, Baldwin shone forth in the glory of his birth and as a great light of the Church.” So great a man did not consider it beneath him to serve Bernard as a scribe; he is praised in Letter 245. Compare Letter 201.] The Church has called him to another office and another dignity. Pray for him too, as my sole consolation and the one in whom my spirit finds the greatest rest.

Pray for the lord pope, who cherishes both me and your whole community with fatherly affection. Pray also for the lord chancellor, [Col. 0302D] namely Haimeric, who is a mother to me; and for those with him, Lord Luke, Lord Chrysogonus, and Master Ivo. *[All are cardinals: Luke, cardinal-priest of Saints John and Paul, created in 1132; Chrysogonus, created in 1134, cardinal-priest of Santa Maria in Portico; and Ivo, formerly a regular canon of St Victor at Paris, created in 1130, cardinal-priest of St Lawrence in Damaso, to whom Letter 193 is addressed.]* They show themselves to us as brothers born of the same womb.

The brothers with me, Bruno and Girard, [Col. 0302B] greet you and likewise beg your prayers for themselves. *[Bruno is called the father of many disciples in Sicily in Letter 209. Girard appears to be Bernard’s brother. See again Letter 165, §4, concerning Bruno.]*

## Letter 145  
*[Written about the year 1137.]*  
**To the Abbots Assembled at Cîteaux.** He wishes them to be aware of his labours and sorrows, perhaps thereby excusing his absence. He earnestly wishes to die not abroad, but among his own.

In great weakness of body and anxiety of heart, God knows, I dictated these words to you: a miserable man, a man born for labour, yet your brother. Would that I might now have the Spirit himself, in whom you are assembled, as an advocate with your unanimity: that he might impress upon your hearts the calamity I suffer; that he might set before your brotherly affections my sad and suppliant image, [Col. 0302C] as it is.

I do not ask this in order that he may create a new compassion in you, for I know how familiar that virtue is to your whole community. Rather, I ask that you may feel inwardly why and how greatly you ought to have compassion. For I am certain that, if this is granted, tears will immediately burst forth from the treasury of piety; sobs, groans, and sighs will strike heaven on every side; and God will hear, be appeased toward me, and say: “I have restored you to your brothers. You shall not die among strangers, but among your own.”

For I am afflicted by such great labours and pains that I am often weary even of living. Yet I speak humanly, because of our weakness: I desire to have my end deferred until I return to you, so that I may [Col. 0302D] die only among you. For the rest, brothers, make your ways and pursuits good, establishing and maintaining what is right, honourable, and wholesome; above all, being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit [Col. 0303A] in the bond of peace. And the God of peace will be with you.

## Letter 146  
**To Burchard, Abbot of Balerne.**  
*[Balerne, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Besançon, was founded in 1136. Its first abbot was Burchard, whose rebuke is found at the end of book 1 of the Life of St Bernard.]*

He rejoices that his labours in forming Burchard have not been fruitless, but attributes the happy outcome to God alone.

1. Your speech is fiery—fiery with that fire which the Lord sent upon the earth. I read it, and my heart grew warm within me. I blessed the furnace from which sparks of this kind had flown out. Was not your heart burning within you while you dictated these things? A good man brings forth good things from his good treasure.

If I laboured over you, as you humbly recall, I do not regret it. I ploughed in hope of receiving [Col. 0303B] fruit, and hope does not disappoint. Behold, my inward parts are satisfied in a foreign land by the fruit of my labours; and by my own experience I perceive that my seed has fallen neither beside the road, nor upon stones, nor among thorns, but into good and excellent soil.

If, when I gave birth, I had sorrow, I now remember the distress no longer because of joy that a child has been born into the world. I call him a child in malice, not in understanding: one whom the Saviour could set before elders as an example to imitate, saying, “Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). A child who can say, “I have understood above the aged, because I have sought your commandments”; who can say, “I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes” (Ps. 118:100, 141).

[Col. 0303C] 2. “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, for so it has pleased you” (Matt. 11:25–26). By your good pleasure they are what they are, not by their own merit. For you do not find merits; you go before them. We have all sinned and need to be anticipated by grace.

Therefore, brother, recognize that you have been anticipated—anticipated by blessings of sweetness—not by me, who am nothing, but by him who, by inspiring me, went before me so that I might admonish you concerning your salvation. For, to attribute much to myself, I am a planter and a waterer; yet without him who gives the increase, what am I?

Submit yourself to him in all humility and cling to him in wholehearted devotion. As for me, use me as his servant, your fellow servant, your companion on the way, and your future co-heir in the homeland—provided that I most diligently fulfill the ministry for which I was sent to you, and accomplish, insofar as lies in me, that you may receive the inheritance of salvation. To the matters of which you complained, I answer thus: when I come, I shall bear your necessities as my own.

## Letter 147  
**To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.**  
*[Written in the year of Christ 1138. Bernard’s present reply is lacking in many manuscripts; in the first editions it was placed after Letter 307. This Letter 147 answers two letters of Peter, one in book 2, Letter 29, and the other Letter 37, which we print here so that you may see how closely those holy souls were joined in a bond of friendship. For this friendship, see again the notes to Letter 228. Peter’s letter reads: “To the venerable and most beloved lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes continual health in the Lord. He knows whom I venerate and embrace in you, and how much reverence and love my soul keeps for you in its inmost chambers. I did so even when your absence, begrudging me the sight of your bodily countenance, concealed it; for fame, swifter than the body, brought the face of your blessed soul, as far as it could, before the eyes of my mind. But when at last I attained what had long been denied, and the phantoms of dreams vanished as truth succeeded them, my soul clung to yours and could no longer be torn from your love. Thus your charity thereafter claimed me wholly for itself; thus your virtues and known character seized me, that they left me nothing of myself which was not yours, and permitted nothing of you not to be mine. From that time mutual charity has remained steadfast in me—and may the cause of Christ, thus begun, remain in you! Since it alone knows never to fail, it has, so far as depends upon me, kept its character in me most perfectly. Since I have stored this charity, dearer than all gold and brighter than every jewel, in my bosom and hidden it among my treasures, I wonder that for so long I have received from you no such tokens as I would wish of this charity which you keep for me. I do indeed give thanks that, often sending greetings through various persons, you have shown that you have not wholly forgotten your friend. But I complain that you have not hitherto given more certain signs through letters. I said ‘more certain,’ because writing does not know how to alter the words impressed upon it, whereas the tongue of messengers often changes the truth entrusted to it by adding or subtracting. Therefore, since, as a chosen warrior prepared for the day of battle, you employ right hand and left for the perils of God’s Church, and contend with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, I confidently entrust my messengers, whom I send to the lord pope, to your friendship. For you who assist the causes of others cannot fail in the concerns of your own. By them, so that my complaint may be silenced, communicate to my envoys—and in your own letters—your welfare, return, and the position of the lord pope. Would that, you freed from the laborious court and I from perilous care, one unchanging place might retain us, one charity unite us, and one Christ receive us, as I have always wished!”]*

Peter had consoled Bernard, labouring abroad amid varied and difficult tasks for the Church, by sending Gebuin, archdeacon of Troyes. Bernard therefore recalls Peter’s goodwill most sweetly and proclaims the Church’s happier condition now that the schism has been extinguished.

[Col. 0304B]

To the most reverend lord and Father Peter, abbot of Cluny, Bernard, his own, because he is his own.

1. May the Dayspring from on high visit you, good man, because you visited me in a foreign land and consoled me in the place of my pilgrimage. You did well, showing understanding toward the needy and poor. I was absent—and absent for a long time—and you remembered my name, a great man occupied with great matters.

Blessed be your holy angel, who suggested this to your devout heart; blessed be our God, who persuaded you. [Col. 0304C] Behold, I have in your letters something in which to glory among strangers—those letters in which you poured out your soul to me. I glory that you hold me not only in memory but also in favour. I glory in the privilege of your love; I have been refreshed by the abundance of sweetness in your heart.

Nor only this: I also glory in tribulations, if I have been counted worthy to suffer any for the Church. This indeed [Col. 0305A] is my glory and what lifts up my head: the triumph of the Church. For if we have been companions in labour, we shall also be companions in consolation. We had to labour and suffer with our mother, lest she complain also of us, saying: “Those near me stood at a distance, and those who sought my life used violence” (Ps. 37:12–13).

2. But thanks be to God, who gave her victory, honoured her in her labours, and completed her labours. Our sorrow has been turned into joy and our mourning into a harp. Winter has passed; the rain has gone away and departed; flowers have appeared in our land; the time for pruning has come; the useless branch, the rotten limb, has been cut off.

That wicked man—he who caused Israel to sin—has been swallowed up by death *[the antipope Anacletus, who died in 1138. Ernald describes the manner of his death in book 2, chapter 7, of the Life of St Bernard; Orderic, p. 915, relates that Anacletus died suddenly. According to the Life of Bernard, Victor was set up by Innocent’s rivals]* and carried into the belly of hell. For, according to [Col. 0305B] the prophet, he had “made a covenant with death and entered into an agreement with hell” (Isa. 28:15); therefore, according to Ezekiel, he became destruction and shall not endure forever.

Another enemy, as he was the greatest of all, so also the worst, has likewise been cut off. *[He seems to be Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, who died in 1136; see the notes to Letter 126. Concerning his death, Orderic, p. 908, calls him most learned and a man “of great name and power in the Roman senate in the time of Popes Paschal and Gelasius, Calixtus and Honorius.”]* He was one of the Church’s friends, but one of those of whom she is accustomed to complain and say: “My friends and neighbours drew near and stood against me” (Ps. 37:12).

If any remain, we hope soon that the same judgment will fall upon their like. I am near to returning to my brothers, if life accompanies me, intending to pass by way of you. Meanwhile I commend myself to your holy prayers. We greet Brother Hugh the Chamberlain and all those around you, together with the rest of the holy community.

## Letter 148  
*[Written about the year 1138.]*  
**To the Same Recipient.** He replies briefly to Peter, reserving more for another occasion.

[Col. 0305C]

To Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny: Bernard offers humble service of love.

Having read your letter, I rejoiced in it because so great a man, rich in blessings of sweetness, took care to anticipate one so small. But since you judge it fitting that we see one another and speak together, when will that opportunity present itself? When will there be a suitable place and a fitting occasion?

Meanwhile, in response to your few words, we have sent a few of our own, gladly prepared to give more when we know that they will not be [Col. 0305D] burdensome to you. Otherwise, when [Col. 0306A] would our littleness dare even this, unless the humility of your condescension gave access to your dignity?

## Letter 149  
*[Written in the year of Christ 1138.]*  
**To the Same Recipient.** He urges Peter to desist from laboriously asserting his claim over the monastery of Saint-Bertin.

What I would least wish to occur—because I think it would run counter to your Reverence—I trust is not hidden from your sincerity. With this confidence I do not hesitate to lay before you what seems ought to be laid before you. Concerning the monastery of Saint-Bertin [Note: [Col. 0305D] The monastery of Saint-Bertin near Saint-Omer, also called Sithiu, having fallen into extreme poverty, was entrusted in 1101 by Abbot Lambert to Hugh, abbot of Cluny. It then flourished again in resources, religious observance, and number of monks, so that whereas scarcely twelve monks had formerly been able to live there, their number grew to one hundred and fifty; from these many monasteries of Belgium and France received regular discipline, as Hermann the monk testifies in volume 12 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 443, with whom Iperius agrees. After Hugh, abbot of Cluny, died, the monks of Sithiu cast off the yoke: without consulting the Cluniacs, they brought their own abbot into litigation. The dispute went so far that Innocent II had already deposed two abbots, John and Simon, at the urging of Peter the Venerable; Peter at last, under Bernard’s pressure, yielded his claim and allowed the monks of Saint-Bertin to be independent. See the notes to the *Apology*, vol. II.] I should like you to proceed more moderately than you have begun to do. For even if you could subject it to yourselves peacefully and without any contradiction [Col. 0306B], I do not see what benefit this would bring you even then. For I would not suppose that you take pleasure in an honour attended by so great a burden. But now, since you can neither reclaim the aforesaid monastery for yourselves without great labour nor possess it peacefully, as the saying goes, an honourable occasion for resting is offered you, together with a fear of causing disturbance.

## LETTER 150

[Note: [Col. 0306D] Written in the year of Christ 1133.]

**TO POPE INNOCENT.** He praises the pontiff for various good actions and stirs up his zeal against the ambition of Philip, who was attempting by illegitimate means to seize the see of Tours.

1. May the health of the head flow over into the members. May the ointment which descends from the head upon the beard reach also the lowest fringe [Col. 0306C] of the garment. If, when the shepherd was struck, the sheep were scattered, then, now that he is strong and safe, may they return securely to pasture. This is what we mean: frequent reports of the repeated successes of your glory make the city of God rejoice. It is right, therefore, that your prosperity should be the strengthening of the Church; and when God exalts one chosen from his people, she too should feel herself exalted and recognize herself as stronger through the increase of strength. For if she has suffered with him, she must also reign with him. Thus it is fitting for you and necessary for us. What then? If, amid fear and distress, the vigour of justice did not grow weak and zeal did not grow cold, shall we yield now when we are approaching the palm? Shall the power which stood forth in weakness collapse in exaltation?

2. Was it not with a strong hand that your Apostolic Highness set in order [Col. 0307A] that noble monastery of Vézelay [Note: [Col. 0307A] Elsewhere called Vézelay, in the diocese of Autun, built about the year 821 by Gerard, count of Nevers, and his wife Bertha, for nuns; monks were substituted for them, and finally secular canons in 1537. The reform of this monastery was first instituted, through the action of Henry, duke of Burgundy, by William, disciple of Saint Mayeul, abbot of Cluny; afterward Saint Hugh, likewise abbot of Cluny, restored its discipline when it had again declined. By Paschal II’s authority it was therefore made wholly subject to the abbot of Cluny in 1103. See Duchesne’s notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*. But the monks of Vézelay, gradually rejecting the Cluniac yoke, were again compelled by Innocent II to be subject to the Cluniacs. On this matter the historian of Vézelay speaks as follows: “Although the Church of Vézelay had peacefully and without challenge possessed this liberty for almost three hundred years, from the beginning of its foundation, and had indiscriminately set over itself superiors from among both its own brethren and those of other monasteries, the Cluniacs, arising much later, tried by surreptitious means to claim it for themselves, first demanding assent and then arrogating to themselves the right of election, falsely alleging that Paschal had entrusted to them the care of the order of the Church of Vézelay. For this very reason the same Church suffered a grave scandal under Pope Innocent II, claiming its native liberty, when, through the violence of Innocent himself and the count of Nevers, a certain Alberic was forced upon it by the Cluniacs, and almost all the brethren of the aforesaid monastery were bound in chains,” etc. Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. III.]? He did not think that he ought to yield even a little either to the mad tumults of an armed populace, or to the unbridled frenzy of enraged and clamorous monks, or—more powerful than these—to the forces of Mammon. What of Saint-Benedict [Note: [Col. 0307C] Understand Saint Benedict on the Po, called Polirone. The same provision had been made concerning it by Gregory VII and Calixtus II as concerning Vézelay: namely, that no abbot might in any way be elected there without the counsel, direction, and command of the abbot of Cluny, nor might an elected abbot be blessed by any bishop without letters of recommendation from him. When the contrary began to be done, Innocent, at Peter the Venerable’s request, ordered by letter—as may be inferred from a bull of Clement III issued in 1187 [Col. 0307D], *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 2452—that Abbot William, elected and ordained without consultation with the Cluniacs, should present himself to them and show obedience and reverence.]? Could royal indignation prevent the spirit of liberty, kindled and armed against flesh and blood? Thus the churches of Saint-Memmie [Note: [Col. 0307D] Saint Memmie, descended from the once-famous Roman family of the Memmii, was sent into Gaul by the blessed Apostle Peter and became the first bishop of Châlons. In his honour an important church of canons was founded in that city; by Innocent II’s authority it adopted the institution of regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine.] and Saint-Satyrus [Note: [Col. 0307D] Matilda, wife of Godfrey of Boulogne—or Boulogne-sur-Mer, “the city of Boulogne which lies beside the English sea,” as William of Tyre says, book 9, chapter 5—and of the first king of recovered Jerusalem, obtained from Pope Paschal the body of the blessed martyr Satyrus, whose feast is celebrated on the Nones of March. She established for him, in the diocese of Bourges, a college of secular canons; within a few [Col. 0308A] years—so readily and prone are we toward worse things!—they had degenerated into so worldly and immoderate a life that Innocent ordered them to be removed and canons of Saint Augustine installed in their place. The *Memoriale historiarum* relates this as follows: “In the year 1138 the canonical order of Saint-Victor at Paris was flourishing and enjoyed renown throughout the world because of eminent persons, distinguished in morals and learning, whom it scattered among churches in various parts of the world, like a fruitful vine sending forth shoots for transplantation. At that time there had been received there professed canons who became prelates in the Roman Church: two cardinals, Lord Hugh, bishop of Tusculum, and Master Ivo; and likewise nine abbots. At the church of Saint-Satyrus at Bourges, Abbot Ralph,” and so forth. The necrology of Saint-Victor at Paris agrees, where under the fifth day before the Ides of February one reads: “Lord Andrew, abbot of Saint-Satyrus and our canon, died.” Stephen, formerly abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris and bishop of Tournai, in his letter to Pope Lucius III—which begins, *Movetur usque*, etc.—commends the grave and constant discipline of the same monastery. Add that in the little book of assessments of the bishoprics and benefices of France this abbey is listed [Col. 0308C] under the Order of Saint Augustine.] were changed in a remarkable manner [Col. 0308A], and, from being the synagogue of Satan, restored to the sanctuary of God—whether all those who acted wickedly wished it or not, and to no purpose. Nor did the barbarian sword hanging over the necks of Liège compel acquiescence in the importunate and wicked demands of the angry and wrathful king [Note: [Col. 0308C] This seems especially to be understood of the investitures of churches demanded again by Emperor Lothair and refused by Innocent. “At that same time,” says Abbot of Ursperg, “the Pope himself went to Emperor Lothair, asking his support against Peter Leonis and his supporters.” The Emperor, having taken counsel concerning this answer, began to demand from the pope the investitures of bishoprics which emperors before him had possessed for a long time. The Apostolic See was therefore greatly troubled, grieved at his coming and anxious about his return. For he could not grant the prince’s request on a point for which the Church had endured so many evils. Yet, through the intervention of Saint Bernard’s counsel and prayers, he withdrew safely from the Emperor. Otto of Freising, book 7, chapter 18, narrates the same event, but more mildly.]. And who could adequately celebrate with worthy praises what has lately, in these days, been sent forth, even from afar, from the hand of the mighty one against the disturbers of the Church of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0308C] Who these persons were we learn from several letters which Acherius inserted in *Spicilegium*, vol. III, pp. 153 ff. First, from the letter of Archembald, subdean of the Church of Orléans, to Henry, archbishop of Sens, we learn that the instigator of this disturbance was a certain John of Orléans—who later ordered Archembald himself to be killed; see Letter 161—intruded into the rank of archdeacon. When Archembald and certain other clerics opposed him, they suffered grave injuries and the loss of nearly all their goods, both from John himself and from his supporters: Bartholomew Capicerius, Zachary “the Pagan,” archdeacon, James, subdeacon of Saint-Aignan, and others. At the end he therefore asks Henry, archbishop—to whom they had fled while the see of Orléans was vacant—“to render him full justice upon his evildoers; to order the Church, polluted by the shedding of blood and by many sacrileges, to cease its services or be placed under interdict; and not to delay avenging this injury, which redounded upon the lord pope” [Col. 0309C]. There is extant in the same place another letter on the same subject, sent by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, to the aforesaid Henry. Perhaps that intruded John maintained his dignity by royal authority. But Pope Innocent at last took up the protection of the oppressed, entrusted the care and advocacy of this cause to the aforesaid Geoffrey of Chartres, legate of the Apostolic See, and compelled the guilty parties to make satisfaction.]? Truly now Jonathan’s arrow has not turned backward (2 Kings [Col. 0309A] 1:22), nor has his spear been turned aside. At this word, indeed, the king was troubled—but not all Jerusalem with him. Indeed, he himself at last moderated all his anger. For he was ashamed and afraid to arm himself in vain against the Lord and against his Christ. Hence your magnificence has indeed been raised above the heavens—provided only that this praiseworthy beginning is adorned by an outcome worthy of it [Note: [Col. 0309D] Here some printed editions insert two verses, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.]. All who love you await this most eagerly and demand that it be brought promptly to completion.

3. Certainly, with similar zeal and an equally powerful hand, it is now necessary to come to the aid of the Church of Tours, which is on the very point of ruin unless you quickly bring help. The spirit of Gilbert has revived, they say, in Philip—clearly both his nephew [Col. 0309B] in the flesh and his heir in ambition. How fiercely this young man too burns with desire to rule is shown by the long and wretched torment of his mother Church, whom the miserable man almost disembowels so that she may bear him forth into honour. Yet, by God’s action, an end has at last been imposed upon his evasions—if only what has been done against him at the prompting of justice, under the compulsion of wickedness, and at peace’s urging, may please Apostolic authority to hold ratified. Far be it that gracious Majesty should confound his faithful servants, to whom he judged this very business worthy to entrust for completion! Far be it—far be it—that cruel ambition should find refuge with the defender of innocence! How great is the audacity of what he attempts, and how great the madness of what he hopes for! Already once and twice a despiser of the Apostolic command [Col. 0309C], he has evaded justice; and now, with still more shameless recklessness, he dares nevertheless again to present himself before the face of so great an equity! Who fails to see how impiously he intends, relying on the powers of Mammon, to attack the tower of strength—a man who places no confidence whatever in justice? But we are secure: for the one being assailed is Innocent [Col. 0310A], and the son of iniquity shall not continue to harm him.

4. Moreover, sweetest Father, while we sigh for your presence, we sweetly pour forth to one another the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness; because, deprived of that presence, we find consolation in this remembrance. This remembrance, constant in our hearts and frequent on our lips, is salt in every discourse: it soothes ears, sweetens mouths, refreshes and inflames hearts; it is most celebrated in the gatherings of the saints, seasons conversations, enriches prayers, and incites to prayer. We pray now also, earnestly, for you and yours: may eternity itself deem you worthy of eternal remembrance—you who labour temporally in and for it. Amen.

## LETTER 151

**TO PHILIP, USURPER OF THE CHURCH OF TOURS**

[Note: [Col. 0309D] This letter was written in the year 1133. Elsewhere it is entitled, “To Philip, elect of the Church of Tours.” “In the year 1137, after Hildebert, bishop of the Church of Tours, had died, its canons were expelled from their own seats by the violence of Count Geoffrey. When they ought canonically to have elected a bishop, they were divided into parties. Some of them, contrary to the decrees of the sacred canons and despite the objections of the others, elected a certain Philip, nephew of Gilbert, an ambitious bishop in the same see before Hildebert [Col. 0310C]. Philip immediately went to Anacletus the pseudo-pontiff, that he might be confirmed and ordained by him, and soon returned to Tours. Meanwhile Hugh, a prudent and noble man, was canonically elected by the sounder party of the same clerics and consecrated in the Church of Le Mans by Guy and the bishops of the province. When Philip learned this, he secretly fled, taking with him the ornaments of the Church” [Col. 0310D]. These details are from the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans*, published in vol. III of the *Analecta*. While these things were occurring Bernard, who was then staying at Viterbo, wrote this letter to Philip. Philip became somewhat more restrained; but after Anacletus’s death he thereafter harassed the Church of Tours by his intrigues. Against him the holy man wrote the preceding letter to Innocent in the following year, 1138. Under Archbishop Hugh, however, who at last overcame Philip, there occurred what Innocent III recalls in Letter 79 of book III: “The party of Dol further alleged that, in the course of time, Pope Eugenius of good memory, our predecessor, sent Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux of blessed memory, to settle the controversy between those same churches; the Church of Tours refused to observe his ruling.” These words were written much later, near the beginning of Innocent III’s letter in the cause of the Church of Tours against the metropolitan see of Dol.]

He expresses the grievous sorrow of his soul over Philip, who was seeking the prelacy of the Church of Tours by unlawful means.

[Col. 0310B]

I grieve for you, dearest Philip; but I beg you not to laugh at my grief. For if perhaps you do not think yourself an object of grief at all, you are for that very reason all the more to be grieved over. You may see what you think of yourself; I judge that you should be mourned with every fountain of tears. My sorrow is not worthy of mockery but of compassion, because my sorrow concerns neither flesh nor blood, nor the loss of perishable things, but you, Philip! I could not have shown more clearly the greatness of the cause of sorrow: Philip is the cause. When I say this, I pronounce a grievous mourning upon the Church which once cherished you in her bosom, putting forth growth [Col. 0310C] like a lily and flourishing in heavenly gifts [variant: “flourishing in innumerable gifts”]. Who at that time did not call you a youth of good hope, a young man of good natural disposition? But alas, the finest colour has changed (Lam. 4:1). From what great hope has France, which bore and nourished you, fallen! Oh, if only you too had known! (Luke [Col. 0311A] 19:42.) You, I say: if you added knowledge, you would add sorrow also (Eccl. 1:18), and your sorrow would ensure that ours, the sorrow of us all, was not fruitless.

I would proceed if I followed my own spirit; but I do not wish to utter too much into uncertainty and be like one beating the air (1 Cor. 9:26). Yet I have written this so that you might know, at least in some measure, our disposition toward you, and so that you might know we are nearby, should God perhaps inspire you to seek a conversation with us and should you be willing to grant us your presence, which we desire. We are at Viterbo [Note: [Col. 0311D] Thus Bernard was then at Viterbo in Etruria, in the year 1133, when Innocent sent him to Lothair in Germany. The preceding letter to Innocent seems to have been written from that place. For another stay of his at Viterbo, see Sermon 2 on the Song of Songs, no. 14.], and we have heard that you are staying in the City. Deign to write back to us whatever you have conceived in your heart regarding this letter of ours, so that we may know what we should do: namely, whether we should grieve more or less. But if you despise everything and heed us in nothing [Col. 0311B], I indeed shall not lose the fruit of a letter that proceeds from charity; but you will answer for your contempt before the dreadful judgment-seat.

## LETTER 152

[Note: [Col. 0311D] Written about the year 1135.]

**TO POPE INNOCENT, ON BEHALF OF THE BISHOP OF TROYES.** The insolence of clerics is nourished by the negligence of bishops; but the bishop of Troyes is burdened because he rebuked clerics.

The insolence of clerics, whose mother is the negligence of bishops, everywhere disturbs and troubles the Church. Bishops give what is holy to dogs and a pearl to swine; and the latter turn and trample them. Rightly do they endure the sort of men whom they foster. Those whom they enrich with the Church’s goods, they do not correct for their evils; and burdened, they carry evil men [Col. 0311C]. Clerics, to be sure, grow rich through the labours of others; they eat the fruit of the earth without payment, and their iniquity comes forth as though from fatness. The ancient Scripture still properly looks upon such men today: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). A mind accustomed to luxuries and not cultivated by the hoe of discipline contracts many stains. If you try to scrape away its inveterate rust, they will not endure even to be touched with the tips of the fingers; rather, as it is written, “The beloved grew fat and kicked” (Deut. 32:15). Unjust witnesses have risen up—men who delight always in gnawing at another’s life while neglecting their own.

Your servant pleads for the man whose entire fault in this dispute, if I am not mistaken [Col. 0311D], is that he reproved the faults of the clerics. This is on behalf of the bishop [Note: [Col. 0311D] Namely, Atton, bishop of Troyes.]. For the rest, I make satisfaction concerning myself. Let your Fatherhood know that letters of your graciousness—in which, though you could have commanded me to come to you, you most graciously preferred to request it—did not reach me before the Nativity of the Blessed Mary. Therefore I do not say, “I have bought five yoke of oxen,” or, “I have bought a farm,” or, “I have taken a wife” (Luke 14:18–20); but I frankly confess—as you too know—that I am nursing little children, and therefore I do not see how I can come without grave scandal and danger to them.

## LETTER 153

**TO BERNARD OF PORTES**

[Note: [Col. 0311D] Written in the year of Christ 1135. This observation is found in the Cistercian codex: “It should be known that there were two Bernards in the house of Portes: one Prior, the other under-prior, who afterward became cardinal.” The first, formerly a monk of Ambronay, founded the Carthusian house of Portes in 1115. The necrology says: “On the day before the Ides of February Bernard, first prior of Portes, died, 1152.” Long before [Col. 0312D] that time he had resigned his office and had as successor the other Bernard, likewise prior of Portes, after he had resigned the bishopric of Belley, as Pierre-François Chifflet judges in the preface to the *Manuale solitariorum*. Chifflet thinks this letter and the following one were addressed to this second Bernard; he also adds a third Bernard, prior of the same place after Blessed Nantelmus, and later bishop of Die. Certainly the Bernard to whom this letter and the following one are addressed was not prior in 1135, when this letter was written, as is clear from section 2, where Bernard salutes “your lord and father, the prior”—that is, the first Bernard, inhabitant and prior of Portes. The place is in Bugey, in the diocese of Lyon, near the Rhône, three leagues from Belley, the episcopal city. Compare Letter 250.]

**ON THE CARTHUSIAN ORDER.** In response to a request for an exposition of the Song of Solomon, he pleads his own insufficiency for so great a work and for the expectations of others.

[Col. 0312B]

1. You ask insistently, and I constantly refuse—not in contempt of you, but in sparing myself. Oh, that I could produce something worthy of your zeal and ability! My very eyes and my very soul, if it were possible, I would give to you together, dearest friend and brother, whom I most especially embrace spiritually in the fullness of love, in the inward parts of Christ [variant: “specially”]. But where is the ability—or when is there leisure sufficient for me—for what you ask? For you do not seem to ask for anything light or trivial, such as we can manage. Certainly you would not press so urgently for very small things. Your frequent letters, and the more vehement spirit that animates them, sufficiently reveal your desire and concern in this matter. Therefore, the more eagerly I perceive you to desire it, believe me, the more scrupulously I assent.

[Col. 0312C] Why is this? Lest, to one expecting great things, I should produce a ridiculous mouse. This I fear, and this is the cause of my delay. And what wonder if I fear to give what I am ashamed to publish? I confess that I reluctantly offer what I think will not so much benefit me to publish as expose me to contempt. Who, after all, wishes to give what would disgrace him to have given and not benefit the recipient to have received? Gladly I give; reluctantly I waste. We know that modest gifts are usually less welcome to one who hopes for great things. What does not come welcome is lost, not given.

2. Your concern, being a man at leisure and free from occupations, is to seek everywhere fuel for the fire with which you burn, so that you may burn more greatly and fulfil the will of your Lord, who says: “What do I will but that it burn?” (Luke 12:49.) [Col. 0312D] I praise this—provided that you seek it where you will not later complain that you have been disappointed. You are mistaken if you seek it from me. [Col. 0313A] I ought rather to beg it from you. I know indeed that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35 [printed: 22:39]); but this is so only if what is given is honourable to the giver and useful to the receiver—and I know absolutely nothing of this kind to be in my possession. What I do have, I fear that, if it comes before the public, you too will be ashamed to have desired it and will regret having requested it.

But why? Would you not better excuse us before yourself? Certainly let your own eyes establish your confidence in you. I yield to your importunity, so that the very production may remove suspicion. It is a matter between friends. I no longer spare my modesty: indeed, so long as what you wish is done, I shall not remember my foolishness. Behold: I am having a few discourses, recently composed, transcribed on the beginning of the Song of Solomon, and I send them to you as soon as possible, although I have not yet published them. When, in this work, I receive time—Christ commanding my concerns—I shall try to proceed, if only you strengthen me in it. Through you I devoutly greet your lord and our father, your prior, together with the other brethren; and with a humble heart I beg that they may have me in God’s favour.

## LETTER 154

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Written about the year 1136.]

**TO THE SAME MAN.** He was unable, because of business, to fulfil his promise to visit the Carthusians. He sends the requested sermons on the Song of Songs.

I cannot conceal the sadness of my heart, nor can I endure any longer that the anguish I suffer should remain hidden from you, dearest Bernard. Remembering my former promise, I had formed the purpose and great desire [Col. 0313C] to pass by you, to see again those whom my soul loves, and to seek comfort for my journey, relief for my labours, and a remedy for my sins. But, as my sins deserved, it came about not that I was unwilling, but that I was unable. For I recognize this as a punishment for sins, not as a sin. Be assured, man of God, that it was not at all through disregard of a friend, nor through sloth, nor through negligence; rather, a cause plainly not to be neglected stood in the way—and it was God’s cause.

Yet this worm continually gnaws at me, and my grief is ever before me. I am troubled enough in other matters, indeed; but, to confess the truth, in none equally. It surpasses the labours of travel, the discomfort of heat, and the anxieties of cares. Behold, I have opened my wound to a friend. It is your part, brother, to have compassion on me—that is, to bear with me what I suffer, so that I may be relieved. I humbly beg your prayers [Col. 0313D], and through you those of the saints with whom you dwell. I send you the sermons on the beginnings of the Song of Songs which you requested and I had promised. When you have read them, I ask that, as soon as you conveniently can, you advise me by your reply whether I should proceed or refrain.

## LETTER 155

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Written about the year 1135.]

**TO POPE INNOCENT, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME MAN WHEN HE WAS ELECTED.** Bernard of Portes, appointed bishop in Lombardy, is indeed worthy of that honour, but less suitable for such a place; he should therefore be reserved for another, more fitting position.

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Perhaps this was in the Church of Pavia, vacant at that time after Peter’s death. This election did not prevail; Saint Bernard’s counsel prevailed, and Bernard of Portes, mentioned above, was elected bishop of Belley. From the matters already stated, he had relinquished that dignity by 1147 and was then prior of Portes, according to an authentic charter cited by Chifflet.]

[Col. 0314A]

We have heard, venerable Father, that Bernard of Portes, beloved by God and men, is being compelled by your summons to undertake the work and burden of the episcopate. This is a commendable matter, wholly worthy of your apostolate: to set a hidden light in the open, lest one who can draw others to life should live for himself alone. For how long shall one who can also shine remain hidden and merely burn? Let him, if you please, be raised upon the lampstand, so that he may be a lamp burning and shining—but assuredly where the force of winds does not prevail [Col. 0314B], lest perhaps—God forbid!—he be extinguished. For who does not know the insolence and turbulence of the Lombards? Or who knows it better than you? You know better than we how disordered that bishopric is and how exasperating its household. What do we think a young man, weakened in bodily strength and accustomed to the quiet of the wilderness, will do among a barbarous, turbulent, stormy people? How can such holiness agree with such perversity, such simplicity with such deceitfulness? Let him, if you please, be reserved for a more suitable place and another people, that he may govern in such a way as to benefit them, and that the fruit which he can yield in its season may not perish through haste.

## LETTER 156

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Written in the year of Christ 1135 or the following year.]

**TO THE SAME MAN, ON BEHALF OF THE CLERICS OF ORLÉANS.**

[Col. 0314C]

How long shall that wretched Church of Orléans vainly beat upon the heart of the father of orphans and judge of widows? For Israel’s noble virgin has long lain in the dust, not only widowed of her husband [Note: [Col. 0314D] That is, after the death of Bishop John, which occurred in 1133. The see was vacant for four years, according to Charles Saussay in the *Annals of Orléans*. Hugh, the dean, who had been elected, was struck on the road by reckless men while returning from the royal court, as Orderic Vitalis testifies under the year 1134. This letter, like the following one, was written by Bernard before his third journey to Rome in 1137.], but also bereft of her dear pledges. Alas! There is no one to raise her up. How long do you also leave her children, together with their wretched mother, crying after you? I mean those who, having lost their property and homes, found in flight their only refuge for their lives. What delays that fearless hand, which has hitherto neither refused the oppressed nor spared the presumptuous? What delays it, I say, from rescuing the afflicted from the hand of the mighty and rendering repayment to the proud? And if it delays [Col. 0314D], let it not abandon them utterly. The more delayed help must finally come with greater strength and provide more perfect aid. Let this, if you please, be the recompense for troublesome delay: that those who have proudly abused apostolic patience may gain nothing from it in the end, and that those who have patiently suffered in reliance upon your word may never have cause to regret their patience.

## LETTER 157

[Note: [Col. 0315B] Written in the year of Christ 1135.]

**TO HAIMERIC, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME PERSONS.**

[Col. 0315A]

To his special friend HAIMERIC, by God’s grace cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Apostolic See: Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux wishes that he may shine in the light of wisdom and virtue.

If I did not know your compassion toward the afflicted and your indignation against the insolent, I would press you, in season and out of season, on behalf of Master William of Meung [Note: [Col. 0315B] Meung, or Magdunum, is a town below Orléans on the Loire, where there is the collegiate church of Saint-Liphard [Col. 0315C] and a residence of the bishop of Orléans.] and his companions; I would appeal to you against their oppressors and false accusers. But now it is enough to have mentioned them: it is yours to prove promptly by action that this is truly enough.

## Letter CLVIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133.] To Pope Innocent, concerning the murder of Master Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor at Paris.

[Note: Because of the wicked murder of Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, Bernard urgently appeals to the Pope in this letter, that he may exercise the justice and vengeance due against the sacrilegious offenders. Bernard here indicates the occasion of the murder. Thomas, in zeal for ecclesiastical discipline, opposed the greed and unjust exactions by which the archdeacon of Paris oppressed the clergy. Inflamed by hatred, the archdeacon nursed vengeance in his mind, until at last his nephews—whether sharing his anger and hatred because they regarded his kinsman’s cause as their own, or hired and incited by him for the crime—attacked Thomas on the road, indeed while he was in the bishop’s company. Stephen, bishop of Paris, promptly struck the author of the murder and his accomplices or supporters with an anathema. Profoundly shaken by the enormity of so great a crime, he sought Clairvaux for a brief retreat, as if to lighten his grief; and from there sent the following letter to Geoffrey, legate of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Chartres.]

[Col. 0315D] Geoffrey, by God’s grace venerable bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See: Stephen, by that same grace unworthy minister of the Church of Paris, but now unhappy herald of misery and affliction, wishes you well in the Lord.

1. I do not know whether the burden of this unprecedented calamity, which I am about to bring before your ears—indeed, before your heart—can adequately be expressed in words. It is news harsh and grievous to hear for all to whom the reproaches suffered by Christ Jesus and holy mother Church are harsh and grievous; especially for us, placed beneath the habit and sign of religion.
