For these events must prove all the more grievous to us, since the downfall of one among us threatens, in a particular way, our injury—indeed, the oppression and ruin of us all.

Know that Master Thomas, prior of the monastery of Saint-Victor—a man tested and approved, beloved and dear to all good people, and a most devoted and vigorous helper and champion in the defense of holy Church—has been slain by the hands of the wicked: dead indeed in the flesh, but, as we unquestionably believe, living with Christ. For he for whom Christ was truly the cause of dying cannot possibly lack glory. When he breathed his last breath in our hands, he declared freely that he was dying for justice, leaving the surest testimony to his past and present righteousness, by which he had fought in Christ’s Church against the wicked: namely, that he was being brought to completion in that same righteousness. This was both the first and the last cause of his labor.

For the sake of that justice he was then present with me. At his particular admonition—as he had always been concerned about such matters—and with the King’s request and consent, I had, through him, also persuaded Thomas himself to proceed to reform and order the abbey of nuns at Chelles. I had taken with me religious men: namely, the abbot of Saint-Victor and of Saint-Magloire, the subprior of Saint-Martin, and several other monks, canons, and clerics. When, according to our ability, the business was completed and I was returning, I was suddenly attacked near the castle of Lord Stephen called Gournay, by his men—that is, the nephews of Theobald the archdeacon—who had laid an ambush for me on the road.

Though we were unarmed, since it was the Lord’s Day, and were proceeding in peace, they suddenly rushed upon us with drawn swords. Showing respect neither for God nor for the holy day, neither for me nor for the religious men with me, they butchered an innocent man in our very hands; and they threatened me with death unless I quickly withdrew from their sight. But we acted more boldly, throwing ourselves into the midst of the swords. We pulled him away from their hands, already half-dead and horribly mangled; and, surrounding him on every side, we spoke to him of his confession and of forgiving the wickedness of the enemies by whom he had suffered.

Then he willingly forgave all who had sinned against him, earnestly sought forgiveness for his own sins, and at last received communion of Christ’s body and blood. Before all he freely declared that he was dying for justice, and so gave up his spirit.

2. Therefore, although the assured confidence of our hope does not doubt that, as regards his salvation and glory, we ought altogether to rejoice, and although we know that the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord, still the grave sorrow and mourning arising from the loss of our friend and the common humiliation of us all is tempered in our hearts by no consolation at all. For I see myself slain in him, and myself slain far more than he; for in his death I see myself exposed to dangers, while I see him freed from dangers.

It remains, therefore, that, since you see me now so grievously bereft and sorrowful, you should not delay to come to console me and to take counsel with me. Since I can hardly bear the detestable sight of the place itself, I have fled to Clairvaux in retreat, where I shall await you, that together we may decide what must be done concerning so intolerable an injury to holy Church. For this attack threatens ruin to us all, and it will come unless the Lord prevents it.

Therefore I direct and most earnestly entreat you, setting aside every delay, to hasten to Clairvaux; for dangers press upon me from every side, and counsel concerning them cannot be deferred.

Having received this letter, Geoffrey hastened to Clairvaux and, by apostolic command, ordered the bishops of the dioceses of Rheims, Rouen, Tours, and Sens to assemble in large numbers for the synod proclaimed at Jouarre. When they had assembled, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and the Carthusian community wrote back, “asking and beseeching that the sword of ecclesiastical severity be drawn against the sacrilegious murderers.” Innocent too, instructed by Saint Bernard’s writings, wrote to the Fathers concerning their decree, confirming it and adding a more severe sentence.

As to the date when this murder was committed, J. Picard, in his notes on Innocent’s letter, and others following him, commonly assign it to 1130, although Baronius postpones it to 1135. [Col. 0317D] But that opinion cannot be established. For Letter 159 makes clear that Thomas was killed on a Sunday, specifically on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, as is read in the Victorine necrology in these words:

> The anniversary of Master Thomas, prior of this church, who, cruelly killed by the enemies of justice for defending justice, left his followers, in life and death, a worthy and imitable pattern of uprightness and patience.

The calendar of Saint-Guinal of Corbeil also agrees, according to Picard. Therefore, the day consecrated by Thomas’s blood ought to bear the dominical letter of the year 1130; but the contrary is the case. For the dominical letter of that year is E, while the letter corresponding to the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September is A.

Picard adds two arguments to confirm his opinion. The first is that the death of Prior Thomas preceded that of Saint Hugh of Grenoble, since Hugh wrote, together with the Carthusians, to the Fathers assembled at the Council of Jouarre for Thomas’s vindication. But, he says, since Guigo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, records in the *Life of Saint Hugh* that Hugh died in 1132, Thomas’s death must be placed, not in 1131—when Innocent was present in Gaul and Bernard accompanied him everywhere, so that he would not have needed to be urgently addressed in so many letters—but in 1130, when Innocent was created pope.

The second argument is that, at the beginning of 1131, Innocent entered Paris and, while visiting the church of Saint-Victor, ordered the body of blessed Thomas to be transferred from the cloister into the church on the seventh day before the Ides of March. Thus Thomas must have been removed from the world in August of the preceding year.

But neither argument settles the matter. Not the first, certainly. What prevents us from saying that the above-mentioned letter of Hugh of Grenoble was written, not by Saint Hugh, but by his successor of the same name? Nor is the latter argument any more compelling. Even if Innocent ordered the blessed man’s body to be moved to a more fitting place, one must not claim that he did this in person. Rather, it was done at his command sent from Italy, as is clear from a letter included in volume five of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, page 567, in which he reproves the archbishops of Rheims and Sens for delaying the sentence of excommunication to be pronounced against those who had killed Thomas. He concludes thus:

> Furthermore, we command that the body of the aforesaid good man, who now before the heavenly Judge bears witness to his justice and innocence, and who, while living under obedience, was killed in the service of his own bishop, be honorably buried in his church. Given at Pisa, 21 December.

It must therefore be said that Thomas’s death occurred not in 1130 but in 1133: the year in which the dominical letter E corresponded to the letter of the aforesaid day, namely the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September; in which the second Hugh occupied the see of Grenoble after Saint Hugh; in which Innocent, at Pisa, awaited the time of the council he had summoned; and in which Bernard, sent from Italy into Germany to make peace between Lothair and Conrad, had returned to Gaul and remained there for a time, intending to be present at the Cistercian chapter customarily celebrated on the Ides of September that year. This appears from the heading of a letter sent by Peter of Cluny that year to the said chapter (*Peter the Venerable*, Letter 36, book I), in which Bernard is listed as present.

Finally, Orderic supports our opinion. In book XIII, under the year 1134, after briefly collecting several events belonging to earlier years, he recounts the death of John, bishop of Orléans, and of Hugh, dean designated after him—events which, according to the Annals of Orléans, befell John in 1133—and says: “Then also Thomas, canon of Saint-Victor, a man of great authority, was killed,” etc. Let this suffice on these matters.]

[Col. 0315B]

To his most loving father and lord Innocent, supreme pontiff: Bernard, unworthy abbot of Clairvaux, offers the least that he is and that he can offer in the Lord.

1. The most savage beast that devoured Joseph, unable to endure the importunity of our dogs, is said to have fled for aid to the protection of Your Holiness. Into what wretched madness has he fallen, that, wandering, fugitive, and trembling upon the earth, he has chosen especially to flee where he ought to have feared most? Most wicked man, do you think the seat of supreme justice a den of robbers or a lions’ lair? You, still foaming and chewing with rabid, savage mouth the fresh blood of your son, flee to your mother’s bosom and dare to appear before your father’s eyes?

Yet if he seeks repentance, it must not be denied him. But if he seeks a hearing, let him receive, if you please, the hearing that Moses granted the people bowing before the molten calf (Exod. 32:25); or Phinehas granted the fornicating Israelite (Num. 25:8); or Mattathias granted one sacrificing to demons (1 Macc. 2:24); or indeed, to offer you an example from among your own, the hearing which Ananias and Sapphira deserved from blessed Peter (Acts 5:1–10); finally, the hearing which the Savior gave to the merchants in the temple (Matt. 21:12).

Do we not know that the sins of some go beforehand to judgment? (1 Tim. 5:24.) Does not the voice of your brother’s blood cry against you from the ground? We believe that the spirit of our martyr, whom your cruelty lately put to death in these days, cries with the other souls of the slain beneath the altar in a loud voice and demands vengeance—more urgently because his blood has been shed so recently upon the earth.

2. “But,” he says, “did I kill him?” Certainly not you, but your men—and on your account. Whether also through you, let God see and judge. If you are excusable—whose teeth are weapons and arrows, whose tongue is a sharp sword—then the Jews too are not to be blamed for Christ’s death, since they also prudently held back their hands.

Because, under pretext of his archdeaconry, he was no longer allowed to exact unlawfully from priests what he had formerly claimed as his right, and because blessed Thomas, a lover and defender of justice, opposed him with zeal and vigor, he hated Thomas and, himself a murderer through hatred, habitually threatened him with death. Many now testify that they heard him; they are not to be disbelieved. Finally, let him say, if he can, what else his nephews ever had against Thomas that led them to lay impious hands upon the Lord’s holy one.

If, therefore, this man—the cause, the instigator, and, as almost everyone suspects, even the planner of the crime—if he, I say, goes unpunished, as he confidently presumes from your apostolic authority with astonishing shamelessness, how many things requiring punishment do we think this impunity will bring forth in the Church? One of two things must follow: either no noble or powerful persons according to this world are henceforth to be admitted to ecclesiastical offices; or clerics everywhere must freely be allowed to abuse sacred functions for every unlawful purpose, lest perhaps anyone inflamed with zeal for God should attempt to prohibit them and be immediately cut down by the military sword as a criminal for justice’s sake.

And so what remains for the spiritual sword, for ecclesiastical censure, for Christian law and discipline, for priestly reverence, or finally for the fear of God, if, through fear of secular power, no one now dares utter a word against the insolence of clerics? For what can be more insolent or more unworthy in the Church than for each man to claim ecclesiastical dignities by the violence of arms rather than by integrity of character?

Therefore, lord Father, as you see, something must certainly be decreed against this man which benefits the Church, so that the salvation accomplished in this time through you may pass into posterity and a later generation may know not only what was dared, but also how it was avenged. Otherwise, if the poison spreads and no antidote follows with it, it has the power to destroy many—God forbid.

## Letter CLIX

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133.] To the same, in the person of Stephen, bishop of Paris. On the same matter.

To the most merciful father Innocent, supreme pontiff: Stephen, pitiable bishop of the Church of Paris, mercy and judgment.

1. The religious man Master Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor, while performing a service of charity, on a journey appointed by piety, in a holy work, in the company of holy men, on the Lord’s Day—indeed in my bosom and between my own hands—had his brains cruelly dashed out by wicked men for justice’s sake, becoming obedient unto death.

There is no need for entreaty where tears better summon compassion in silence, and the sob that interrupts prayer expresses feeling. These things truly deserve, though they do not ask for, genuine compassion, since they reveal and betray real sorrow and remove all doubt of pretense. I think it sufficient, therefore, simply to have made known, as it is, the calamity I suffer, in order to impress it upon paternal compassion. The sad and tearful story speaks sufficiently for itself, especially before you; it does not need to be embellished by persuasion.

Let my eyes pour forth streams of water, for my strength has abandoned me, and the light of my eyes—he too is no longer with me. For I do not mourn him, but myself. How indeed should he be mourned who, by the short path of a precious death, has passed to life?

2. Who would not rather follow him with praises than with tears, he for whom to live was Christ and to die gain? I bore the name of bishop; he performed the work. Disdaining honor, he bore the burden with all his strength. Therefore he is truly dead unto life, while I am alive in death. He did not cut the bonds of death but escaped them; and behold, the pains of death surround me, and torrents of iniquity trouble me.

I, then—I, wretched and to be pitied in your death, my sweetest brother Thomas—am, alas, weaned from gentle comfort, deprived of prudent counsel, and certainly left without safe protection. It would have been better for me to die for you than to live after you. Therefore my life has failed in sorrow and my years in groaning. The Church grieves with me, but also grieves for herself. The loss is common; the desolation is common. All religious life weeps with me and together implores paternal consolation.

If Theobald Noterius [Note: Here the manuscripts vary. Some have simply “Noterius”; others, “Theobald Noterius,” who was archdeacon of Paris, according to the letter of Stephen, bishop of Paris, reproduced in the notes, which I do not know whether Bernard himself wrote in Stephen’s name to Geoffrey of Chartres, then legate.] comes before you, let him experience in himself that the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. His nephews were the authors [variant: actors] of the crime; he was its cause. Whether he was also its planner is in question. Do not heed his words until the man who is to be sent arrives, who will explain the truth to you more fully and make you wary of wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

## Letter CLX

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133.] To Chancellor Haimeric, in the person of the same bishop. On the same matter.

To Lord Haimeric, most dear and venerable cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church: his own Stephen of Paris, what is due to a lord and friend.

A friend is proved in necessity. I say this not because I doubt the holiness of your affection, but lest it should happen that I do doubt it. And it certainly will happen if I discover that you are now concealing that zeal of yours—God forbid. You should know that I shall take it as an inexcusable proof of such concealment if, on any pretext, Theobald Noterius is not received as his deserts require: he who, by the cruel ambition of his nephews’ hands, has cut off half my soul, leaving its remaining part for torment alone.

## Letter CLXI

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133.] To Pope Innocent, against those responsible for the murder of Archembald, subdean of Orléans.

[Col. 0320C]

The voice of the blood of Archembald, subdean of Orléans, [Note: Concerning his murderers, see the notes to Letter 150. Peter the Venerable likewise complains of Archembald’s murder in Letter 17 of book I, suggesting that Archembald was killed before Thomas of Saint-Victor, in these words: “Their impunity for crime supplies weapons for fury, so that, after the subdean of Orléans, the persecutors’ sword turned against Lord Thomas of Paris because the former had remained unavenged.” Yet the contrary seems to follow not obscurely from this letter of Bernard. Moreover, John, the author of Archembald’s death, may perhaps have been the same John, dean of Orléans, who met a like fate; concerning his murder, the *Lament of the Same Church* is found in Stephen of Tournai.] has prevailed. For behold, alas, in the prophet’s words, blood touches blood (Hos. 4:2), and the two joined together cry more loudly to you from France. Each blood, I say, cries aloud and clamors with a cry so powerful that it could shake even the heavenly palace itself, and so piteous that it ought to soften hearts of stone.

What are you doing, friend of the Bridegroom, guardian of Christ’s bride, shepherd of Christ’s sheep? Do you think you will suffice to devise a remedy able to oppose this pestilence so wicked and unheard-of? A remedy must indeed be found which both presently brings healing to the Church’s fresh wound and serves as a warning to posterity.

Therefore gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one. Unless Phinehas stands now also and makes atonement, the shaking will not cease. If, I say, ecclesiastical vigor spares these men—John and Theobald Noterius—by whose consent, if not by whose hand, perhaps even by whose instigation, innocent blood has been shed upon the earth, who does not see what will follow? How many in the clergy will their impunity cause to be promoted against right and justice, through fear of their own people rather than by the merit of their own holiness?

New diseases must be met by new medicines. It would be most beneficial, as it seems to many, and most just, if you cut them off with the apostolic sickle from every ecclesiastical dignity, so that they may lose those already held and never rise thereafter to others.

## Letter CLXII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133. In the Colbert manuscript marked 1038, and in an older edition, this letter is attributed to John of Crema and the following one to Haimeric. But what is said in the latter concerning the conversion of the man to whom it is addressed fits John better.] To Chancellor Haimeric concerning the same matter.

I have subsequently often testified to the bishop of Paris himself concerning the frequent and friendly remembrance by which you are accustomed to commend him. Now you are required to prove, not in word or tongue but in deed and truth, that neither I was deceptive nor you false. This concerns you, not only for the bishop’s sake, but also for the sake of your other friends, who would certainly be greatly troubled for your sake if the case should proceed in any way contrary to expectation.

## Letter CLXIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1133.] To John of Crema, cardinal-priest [Note: Of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. According to Laurence of Liège, in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 307, this John absolved Henry of Verdun, to whom Letter 62 is addressed, from excommunication.] concerning the same matter.

I shall never forget the affection and condescension by which I, a little man of no rank, perceived that you embraced me. I continually desire and frequently pray that your repentance and conversion, over which I have already rejoiced with the angels and rejoiced myself, may produce worthy fruits. And now especially, I believe, the Gallican Church expects those fruits with me—not inappropriately.

It concerns both your reputation and mine that I should not be put to shame in you. Therefore let it be manifest to all that zeal for truth and justice burns within you against the murderers of clerics and their instigators, so that I need not regret having gloried in you.

## Letter CLXIV

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1138.] Pleading the cause of the Church of Langres before Pope Innocent.

[Note: This is the title of the letter in the manuscripts. This action occurred not after the death of Guilenc or Wilenc, bishop of Langres, to whom Letters 59 and 60 are addressed, but after the death of his successor William of Sabrano. Guilenc died on the Kalends of August, 1135; William in 1138. Hence arose disputes concerning the future successor. Peter, archbishop of Lyons, and Hugh, prince of Burgundy and later duke, supported the election of a certain Cluniac monk. Robert, dean of Langres, Pontius the archdeacon, Odolric, and other canons opposed it. Bernard was chosen arbiter of the dispute; finally, after the exclusion of the Cluniac monk, Geoffrey, prior of Clairvaux and Bernard’s kinsman, was elected.

I read three letters of Peter, abbot of Cluny, concerning this controversy in the Church of Langres over the election of a bishop: one, Letter 29 of book I, written to Bernard, in which he attempts to clear a certain monk of his from the disgrace cast upon him after his election as bishop of Langres; another, Letter 28 of book II, to Pope Innocent, in which he demands that confirmation be denied to the election of the abbot of Vézelay as bishop of that same Church; and the last, Letter 36 of the same book, to the same Innocent, in which he insists that the Church of Langres be left its full canonical right concerning the election of its future bishop.

It is evident from comparison of them that the first and third letters concern the election discussed here by Bernard. Whether the second concerns it also, I would find harder to say. I am persuaded that it concerns a different person. In the first, Peter the Venerable calls the elect simply “a Cluniac monk and my son”; in the second, “the abbot of Vézelay.” In the former he says that the canons of Langres, meeting him as he returned from the territory of Poitou, announced the election of his monk; in the latter he says that “a report had reached him” that the abbot of Vézelay was being sought as bishop of Langres through the importunate petitions of certain persons before Innocent. Finally, in the former he endeavors to advance confirmation of his monk; in the latter he strives to prevent confirmation of the abbot of Vézelay.

Accordingly, I consider not to be disregarded the opinion of those who, following the Catalogues of Saint-Étienne and Thou, place after Wilenc, bishop of Langres, William of Sabrano—perhaps transferred from the abbacy of Vézelay to the see of Langres—and after him Geoffrey, as will shortly be said. Geoffrey, after the rejection of the Cluniac monk discussed here, was finally elected and confirmed in 1138, when Bernard had returned to Gaul after the schism was extinguished.

Moreover, reader, please observe in this history what Baronius had previously noted under the year 1138: Peter of Cluny so vigorously supported his son’s cause that he could not, even when defeated, be torn in spirit from Saint Bernard and his monks. Peter himself testified to this in a letter:

> For when can the sincere and ardent affection of my heart toward you be extinguished or overwhelmed by any streams of unfavorable rumor, when neither the many waters of tithes could extinguish it nor the force of the rivers of Langres overwhelm it?]

Bernard complains that the election of a bishop for the Church of Langres was attempted deceitfully and contrary to a pledged promise.

1. While we were still at Rome, it happened that the lord archbishop of Lyons came there. Robert, dean of the Church of Langres, and Olric, a canon, also came with him, seeking permission for themselves and the chapter of Langres to elect a bishop. They had received an instruction from the Pope not to presume to do this except by the counsel of religious men.

When they wished and asked to obtain this through me, I said: “Far be it from me, unless I know and am certain that you intend to elect a good and suitable person.” They replied that their plan and intention depended upon my judgment, and that they would do nothing other than what I advised. And they promised it. But because I did not give sufficient credit to them, the archbishop came forward to persuade me, firmly promising the same thing. He added that, if the clerics should attempt to act otherwise, whatever else they might do, he would by no means confirm it or consider it valid. The lord chancellor was also brought in as witness.

Not content with this, we also approached the Pope himself, that what had been agreed among us might be confirmed by his favor and authority. Before this, however, we had held a mutual and prolonged discussion concerning the election to be made. Of many persons then mentioned, two were eventually named, from neither of whom any of us dissented at all; it was agreed that either might be elected. Accordingly, the Pope commanded that what had pleased us should be observed without alteration, and both the archbishop and the clerics made a firm promise.

After they departed, I remained a few days in the City; then, when I had obtained from my lord permission to return, I set out for the brethren.

2. After crossing the Alps, we learned that the day was near on which a man was to be consecrated bishop of Langres—concerning whom I wish we had heard better and more honorable things. But I do not wish to state what I heard unwillingly. Why say more? Several religious men who had come to meet us in greeting persuaded us to turn aside through Lyons, in order that, if possible, we might prevent the wicked act from being done.

For I had decided to go by another route to shorten the journey and spare the health and weariness of my body, especially since, I confess, I did not wholly believe the reports. Who would have believed that so great a man could act with such levity that, setting aside his very recent promise and even his lord’s command, he would not fear to lay hands upon a prominent person?

Yielding therefore to the counsel of religious men, we directed our journey to Lyons. On arriving, we saw everything exactly as we had heard. Those preparations were being made—not festive solemnities, but ill-omened ones. Yet the dean and, unless I am mistaken, the greater part of the canons of Lyons openly and steadfastly objected. A shameful and lamentable rumor, spreading and gaining strength everywhere, had filled the city.

3. What was I to do? I approached the archbishop respectfully concerning the agreement he had made and the instruction he had received; and he denied neither. But he assigned the cause of his breach of faith to the duke’s son [Note: namely Hugh, son of Odo, duke of Burgundy, by Mary, daughter of Theobald, count of Champagne.], who had withdrawn from the settlement. To prevent that man from being disturbed, he said, he had fallen into this changeableness for the sake of peace. He added that henceforth he would do whatever was determined by our judgment.

Then I gave thanks and said: “Far be it! Yet let not our will but rather God’s will be done. Perhaps it will be recognized thus: let the matter be placed before the counsel of the bishops and other religious persons who have assembled here at your own summons, or who are yet to come. If, after the Holy Spirit has been invoked, the agreement of all encourages you to proceed with the work begun, proceed as you began. But if not, we must yield to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Do not lay hands hastily upon anyone’” (1 Tim. 5:22).

The proposal seemed to have pleased the council. Meanwhile, it was reported that the man had arrived, but at an inn rather than at the palace. He arrived on the evening of Friday and departed on Saturday morning. It is not for me to say why he did not wish even to appear at the court which he had taken pains to reach by a long journey—unless perhaps it could have been thought to be monastic modesty and contempt for honor, had not the subsequent events indicated otherwise. Indeed, what else could we then have suspected, when the archbishop, returning from him, testified before all that the man was unwilling in any way to consent and wholly rejected whatever had been done concerning him?

4. Finally, the archbishop immediately ordered an election to be held. This he did through certain canons of Langres then present, and also by letters that still survive. When those letters had been produced and read in the chapter of Langres, alas for shame, others were immediately read wholly contrary to them. They asserted that the consecration had been postponed, not abandoned, and appointed a day and place for deciding a case which the earlier letters had announced as decided.

You would have thought that the letters spoke not merely from distinct but from opposing persons, disputing with one another—had not one and the same image impressed in wax [Note: namely the image of Archbishop Peter impressed upon a wax seal, according to the custom of those times. For the death of this Peter, see below in Letter 172; Letter 394 is addressed to him.] and the same name written at the head of the documents made manifest to all present, who wondered, that this sweet and bitter matter flowed from one source.

Contradictory letters are held in the hands. Whichever you decide to obey, you must be considered disobedient. For if you receive the earlier letter, the later will condemn you; or if you choose to follow the later, the earlier will murmur against you. And would that the second letter, as it was able to overturn the first, might itself defend itself against the third. But behold: letters against letters, command against command; so that now, not as in the prophet, “Command, command again” (Isa. 28:10, 13), but rather “Command, revoke the command,” is repeatedly impressed.

5. Meanwhile, the man who had both fled the consecration and rejected the election hurried to the King. He obtained investiture of the *regalia* [Note: Investiture of the *regalia* is the grant by the king to a new bishop, after he has rendered an oath of fealty, of temporal lordship and the Church’s estates. On the *regalia*, see also Letter 170, especially Letters 19 and 20 of Suger, and Du Cange’s *Glossarium*.]; by what merits, let him judge for himself.

Soon letters were dispatched, the assigned place was changed, and the day advanced, so that by removing the advantage of place and time, the opportunity to act might likewise be removed from objectors and the day of consecration stolen from appellants. Yet there is no counsel against the counsel of the Lord, whose providence ensured that neither objectors nor appellants were lacking.

An appeal was made by Falcon, dean of the Church of Lyons; an appeal by Pontius, archdeacon of Langres; an appeal by Bon-Amicus, priest and likewise canon of Langres; and an appeal by our brothers Bruno and Geoffrey [Note: Bruno was discussed above in the note to Letter 144. Geoffrey appears to be the one who later became Bernard’s secretary.]. All were unaware of the inward preparation of their hearts, but arrived by chance—without doubt through God’s provident will.

The interval was so brief that, from the time we learned of the day, our messenger could scarcely arrive with letters within four days in order to forestall what was being prepared: not a sacrament, but a sacrilege. He nevertheless objected, and appealed both the man to be consecrated and those who were to consecrate him to the Apostolic See. He too was a canon of Langres.

I speak the truth; I do not lie. Nothing here has been said by me from hatred of any person; everything has been set forth truthfully from love of truth alone, with Truth itself as witness.

## Letter 165

*[Written in the year of Christ 1138. Falco was afterwards elected archbishop of Lyons; concerning his election, see Letters 171 and 172, to Pope Innocent. Letter 173 is addressed to Falco himself.]*

**To Falco, Dean, and Guy, Treasurer, of the Church of Lyons.** On the matter mentioned above.

[Col. 0325B]

The wound of our Church, as you see, dearest friends, is great and needs much care; indeed, not merely much care, but swift care. Thus we must continually, with tears, press the heavenly physician, saying: “Lord, come down before he dies” (John 4:49). One thing aggravates the pain still more and almost makes the cure hopeless: namely, that the trouble has arisen from the very quarter from which consolation should have been hoped for. For who, miserable Church, has brought upon you this evil which you lament? Surely not an enemy, nor one who hated you, but a man at one with you, your leader and your metropolitan.

How is it that “from the south,” [Col. 0325C] and no longer from the north, “every evil is opened”? Rightly, then, “there is no sorrow like my sorrow,” since we have suffered from those in whom we chiefly trusted, and not from others. O pious mother Church of Lyons! What manner of husband—rather, monster—have you now procured for your daughter! In this matter we have experienced you not as a mother but as a stepmother. How far this son-in-law of yours has degenerated from your noble ancient honour, dignity, and integrity! What then? Shall I call an honourable marriage, and an undefiled bed, what has been done in such a case and in such a manner?

Without law, without order, without reason, everything has been thrown into confusion. Indeed, it is evident that all has been commanded and presumed upon with such fraud and recklessness that not merely a bishop, but not even a steward or a tax-collector [Col. 0325D] ought to have been appointed in this fashion.

With what praises shall I extol you, beloved friends, who alone grieved with her in her affliction, who stood by her, oppressed as she was, both in her first and in her second defence, “coming up against the enemy and standing in the breach for the house of Israel”? No one like you was found in that assembly: no one to preserve the law of the Most High, to obey the sacred canons, or finally to take upon himself the zeal of Phinehas and pierce the fornicators with the sword-point of his tongue (Num. 25:8). Since these things shine abroad everywhere to the glory of God and to your own glory, it remains for you to strive to give an end worthy of so praiseworthy a beginning, and to join the tail to the head of the sacrifice.

## Letter 166

*[Written in the year of Christ 1138.]*

**To Pope Innocent.** On the matter mentioned above.

1. Again I cry out; again I knock. If not with loud voices, then certainly with tearful groans. The repeated injury done to us by those who are lost, and who prolong their wickedness, compels me to repeat my cries. “They have grown strong, adding transgression to transgression.” They heap iniquity upon iniquity, and their pride continually rises. Fury has prevailed; shame has vanished, and the fear of God.

The man whom they did not fear to choose contrary to your prudent [variant: “chaste”] and just disposition, Father, they dared, even after appeal had been made in your name, to execrate. And this the men of Lyons, Autun, Mâcon, and our Cluniac friends presumed to do. In the fraud and rashness of these men—alas!—how vast a multitude of saints will be troubled, if they are compelled to bear such a yoke, so imposed! What wickedness! They will receive this as though forced to bend their knees before Baal, or, as the prophet says, to “make a covenant with death” and “make an agreement with hell” (Isa. 28:15).

I ask: where is justice? Where is law? Where the authority of the sacred canons? Where, finally, reverence for majesty? That appeal—which is denied to no oppressed person—has availed me alone nothing. For there gold commanded, silver judged; laws and canons were silent; reason and equity had no place. And, what is more intolerable, with the same weapons they threaten to assail even the citadel of the apostolic height. Yet this is ridiculous: for it is founded upon the firm rock.

2. But what am I doing? I have gone too far, I confess. It is not for me to accuse or rebuke anyone; it is enough that I lament my own grief. After a long delay and many labours which I endured in the service of the Roman Church, when at length it pleased Your Serenity to grant my return to my brethren, though broken in bodily strength, and treated as an evildoer, yet rejoicing in the sheaves of peace which I brought back, I arrived safely at the monastery. I believed that I had escaped labour for rest; that I might in some measure repair the losses to spiritual study and holy quiet which I had suffered abroad. But behold, tribulation and distress found me.

Here I lie upon my bed, tormented more by anguish of heart than of body. For I do not lament any temporal inconvenience. “My soul is in my hands”: its salvation is at stake. Do you wish me to entrust my soul to that man who has lost his own? I know that you do not. Therefore I said to my soul that it would be better to flee, than both to consume the remainder of my days in grief and nevertheless fall into danger concerning salvation.

[Col. 0327A] But may God rather inspire you with what is better: namely, if you judge it worthy, to recall how I have acted with you; to set the eyes of your compassion upon your little servant; and to free the afflicted man from distress. Or rather, do not forget how much God Himself has done for you; and, in however slight a return of recompense, for His glory revoke what has been so wrongly done.

## Letter 167

*[Written in the year of Christ 1138.]*

**To the same.** On the same matter.

Most merciful Father, did you not expressly command that, in the Church of Langres, a religious and suitable person should be elected, and that this should be done according to the counsel of your little servant? Did not the lord of Lyons, being present, receive this very command from your apostolic lips, undertaking to execute it as faithfully as it had been firmly enjoined and repeatedly impressed upon him? Did he not, finally, promise it?

Why then did he think fit to change what had been established most usefully and wisely, and by his own presumption undertake something else which was improper, to the contempt of Your Majesty itself and to the scandal of our weakness? How was that good man not ashamed to be found within himself both “Yes” and “No,” attempting to impose such an unworthy yoke upon the necks of so great a multitude of religious men, your servants, against your decree and his own promise?

Inquire, Father—carefully inquire—what testimony that man upon whom he hastens to lay hands has, both from those near at hand and those far away. Shame forbids me to say what public report says of him—indeed, what a most widespread ill repute has proclaimed. And what shall I say? “My soul is sorrowful even unto flight.” I would perhaps already have fled, had not the hope of consolation, which I await from your compassion, held me back.

I wished to write in order the deeply lamentable history of our misery; but grief weakens my hand, dulls my mind, and makes my tongue shrink from uttering this malicious fraud—this stealthy deception, this circumvention, this recklessness, this faithlessness. What then? Your son Pontius, archdeacon, who has behaved steadfastly and faithfully in this matter also, will tell you everything, Father: both what has been done that we lament, and what we urgently ask to be done. Believe him as you would me.

As for me, I say only this, like a woman in labour: unless these men desist from so criminal and reckless an undertaking, as I now feel myself failing, so my life will fail in grief and my years in groanings.

## Letter 168

*[Written in the same year.]*

**To the Bishops and Cardinals of the Roman Curia.** On the matter mentioned above.

1. You know—if you deem it worthy to remember—how I lived among you in an evil time: going out and returning, journeying at the king’s command, standing firm and remaining with you in your trials, so that, with my bodily strength nearly exhausted, I could scarcely return home after peace had been restored to the Church from heaven.

I recall this not in boastfulness or reproach, but to urge and entreat you, to remind you and demand the affection of compassion which is due from you. Necessity now presses all to call in their debts. If I did what I ought to have done, I count myself nothing more than an unprofitable servant, according to the Lord’s saying (Luke 17:10). Yet if I did what was required or ought to have been done, have I deserved to be beaten? And behold, returning from you, I found tribulation and grief. I called upon the name of the Lord, but it did not help; I called also upon yours, but it did not prevail. For “the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted”: namely, the archbishop of Lyons and the abbot of Cluny. Trusting in their own strength and glorying in their abundance of riches, they have drawn near and taken their stand against me—and not against me alone, but against a great multitude of God’s servants, against you also, against themselves, against God, against all equity and uprightness.

2. Finally, they have set a man over our heads whom—shameful to say—the good abhor and the wicked mock. By what order, or rather by what disorder, let God see and judge; let the Roman Curia see, grieve, show pity, and arm itself for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good.

What then? Does it please you, mistress of the world, established for all as an avenger in wrath and a judge in mercy—does it please you, I say, that while the wicked exults, the poor man is set ablaze: that poor man who, in your service, when he had no revenue to expend, did not spare his blood? Do you think it worthy of you to enjoy your own peace and to care nothing for ours, not admitting into the share of consolation those whom you had as partners in labour?

If I have found favour in your eyes, rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the helpless and poor from those who plunder him. Otherwise, as I can, I shall labour in my groaning, and my tears will be my bread day and night. But to you I shall read that verse: “He who removes mercy from his friend abandons the fear of the Lord”; and that other: “All those near to me have withdrawn from me” (Job 6:14, 13); and also: “Those who were near me stood afar off, and those who sought my life used violence” (Ps. 37:12–13).

## Letter 169

*[Written in the year of Christ 1138.]*

**To Pope Innocent.** On why he detained the summoned clerics of the Church of Langres, and to whom the task of election should be entrusted.

[Col. 0328D]

Your condescension made me familiar with you; familiarity made me presumptuous. May the customary kindness of your heart be present, lest perhaps presumption give birth to indignation. Yet hear patiently not only what I did, but also why I did it, in case the reason may at least somewhat excuse the deed.

I dared to retain the clerics of Langres who had been summoned, having nevertheless made peace among them and persuaded them henceforth to abide, concerning the election to be made, by your good pleasure and the counsel of worthy men, as is contained in their letter. It was, moreover, most necessary that on this occasion they should remain, because the lands and possessions of the Church have been handed over to plunder and devastation, while there is no one to guard or defend them.

Therefore let the care of choosing a man pleasing to God, who may finally put an end to the Church’s long and pitiable harassment, be entrusted, if it please you, to persons who are not suspect, who do not seek what is their own but what belongs to Jesus Christ. We entrusted the remaining matters to Lord Herbert, abbot of Saint Stephen’s at Dijon [Note: Concerning him, see Letter 59.], and to the archdeacon of Langres and their companions.

We add also this request: receive into your protection the archdeacon of Langres and Bon-Amicus, priest of the same church, together with their goods, because they have proved faithful in the cause of God. [Col. 0329B] “The labourer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10:7).

## Letter 170

**To Louis the Younger, King of the Franks.**

*[Written in the year of Christ 1138. Orderic, in Book XI, p. 813, calls him simply Florus; and more than once in Book XIII, pp. 901, 911, Louis Florus. In the earlier passage, under the year 1135, Louis the Fat is said to have reconciled Theobald of Blois and Ralph of Péronne, “because they were at variance,” and to have entrusted the kingdom of France to his son Louis Florus, whom three years before he had established king at Rheims. In the later passage, under the year 1137, the same Louis, near death, is said to have committed “his son Louis Florus to the guardianship of Count Palatine Theobald and of his cousin Ralph of Péronne.”]*

He seeks to vindicate the election of Geoffrey, his prior, as bishop of Langres, to which the king seemed opposed.

1. If the whole world conspired against me to make me undertake anything against royal majesty, I should nevertheless fear God and would not dare rashly to offend the king ordained by Him. For I do not fail to know where I have read: “He who resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:2). Nor is it hidden from me how opposed falsehood is to every Christian, and especially to my own profession.

I speak the truth; I do not lie: what was done at Langres concerning our prior [Note: Understand Geoffrey, Bernard’s kinsman, who, after many disputes, was at length unanimously elected bishop of Langres in 1138 from being the third prior of Clairvaux, once the schism had been suppressed. While Geoffrey was still prior, Bernard wrote to him from Italy in Letter 317, during the octave of Pentecost in that year. When Bernard returned from Italy, this history of the election at Langres occurred, after peace had been restored to the Church, as Letter 166 expressly states. How highly Bernard esteemed Geoffrey appears from this letter, in which he calls him “the staff of my old age, the light of my eyes, my right arm.” See Book II of the Life of St Bernard, ch. 5; also several other passages, and the Preface to Book III of the same Life. Geoffrey’s election was finally confirmed in 1139, as may be inferred from an instrument in Perard, p. 134, where he is said to have consecrated the church of Saint Stephen at Dijon in 1141, “in the second year of his episcopate.”] happened contrary to the expectation and intention of the bishops and of myself.

But there is One who in a certain way wrings assent even from the unwilling, and who compels even opposing human wills to serve His purpose as He wills. For why should I not fear for him the danger which I feared for myself, when I love him as myself? Why should I not dread the company of those who “bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon men’s shoulders, while they themselves refuse to move them with a finger”? Yet what has been done has been done: nothing against you, much against me. The staff of my weakness has been taken from me; the light of my eyes has been snatched away; my right arm has been cut off. All those towering things and these waves have passed over me. Wrath has passed over me; no way of escape opens to me from any quarter. From the burdens I flee, I am forced, unwilling and reluctant, to take them up. I find it hard to kick against the goad. Perhaps it would have been more tolerable for one willing than for one unwilling and refusing. For if I possess any strength, would I not more readily exercise it on my own shoulders than on those of another?

2. Yet I submit to Him who disposes otherwise, with whom it is neither safe nor at all possible for me—or even for a king—to contend either in judgment or in power. For He is “terrible even to the kings of the earth” (Ps. 75:13). “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31), even for you, O King.

Oh, with what troubled ears do we hear things contrary to the beginnings so good in you! Oh, how much bitterer will be the Church’s grief after joys so great already tasted, if—God forbid!—she should be disappointed of the delightful hope which she has found in your character, the singular shield of her defence! Alas, the virgin Church of Rheims has fallen [Note: After the death of Archbishop Reginald, which occurred on the Ides of January 1139, the Church of Rheims remained without a pastor for nearly two years, not so much owing to division among the electing clerics as to the tumult of the citizens over the establishment of what they call a commune, and to Louis VII’s inborn hatred of Count Theobald of Champagne, which likewise spread over the counts and neighbouring churches; see Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 328. Bernard complains again of this in Letter 318. Finally, when Bernard declined the dignity, Samson was elected in 1140; his election was disturbed for some time, according to Letter 222. Compare Letters 210 and 224.], and there is none to raise her up; the Church of Langres also has fallen, and there is none to stretch out a hand.

May divine mercy prevent you from adding to our pain and heaping sorrow upon sorrow in your heart and counsel. Who will grant me to die, lest I see a king of good repute—and of still better hope—attempting to oppose God’s counsel, stir up against himself the wrath of the supreme Judge, wet the feet of the Father of orphans with the tears of the afflicted, and strike heaven with the cries of the poor, the prayers of the saints, and the just complaints of the most beloved Bride of Christ, which is the Church of the living God?

Far be it, far be it! We hope for better things; we await more joyful things. God will not forget to show mercy, nor will He restrain His mercies in His wrath. Through him and concerning him He will not afflict His Church, whom He has already so greatly gladdened through and concerning him. Him whom God granted by His gift, He will preserve by His long-suffering; and if you think otherwise, He will reveal even this to you and instruct your heart in wisdom. This we desire; this we pray day and night. Think this of us; think this of our people. This fidelity will not be broken in us; through us neither the honour of the king nor the welfare of the kingdom will be diminished.

3. We give thanks to Your Clemency for the kindly answer which we have received from your condescension. Yet delay alarms us, seeing that the land has been handed over to plunder and devastation. It is your land; and in this we plainly recognize and lament an indignity to your kingdom, which you have rightly commanded us to abhor, if there is no one to defend it. For in what other respect could royal majesty rightly be said to have been impaired by what has occurred?

The election has been duly conducted; the man elected is faithful. Nor would he be faithful if he wished to possess what is yours without possessing it through you. He has not yet stretched out his hand to what is yours; he has not yet entered your city; he has in no way yet involved himself in anything, although the invitation of clergy and people, the oppression of the afflicted, and the desires of the good have most urgently demanded it from him.

Since this is so, there is need, as you see, for speedy counsel, no less for your honour than for our necessity. Unless Your Serenity, through the present messengers, gives the answer desired by the awaiting people, who are yours, you will disturb hearts now devoted to you—the hearts of many religious persons—against you, which is not expedient; and you will, as we fear, bring no small injury upon your own royal interests which pertain to the Church.

## Letter 171

*[Written in the year of Christ 1139. See Letter 165.]*

**To Pope Innocent.** On behalf of Falco, archbishop-elect of Lyons.

Having so often been heard in the affairs of others, I think I shall not be put to shame in my own. My lord, I regard my archbishop’s cause as my own, being a member which considers nothing foreign to itself that belongs to the head. Yet I would not say this if the man had assumed the honour for himself, rather than having been called by God as Aaron was.

For I judge that what happened could have come from no other source: the votes of so many men converged upon him so readily that there was not merely no opposition, but not even hesitation. And rightly so. He is distinguished no less by nobility of mind than by blood; he possesses learning and uprightness of life. In short, the integrity of his reputation fears not even the tooth of an enemy.

Therefore what has been done in the case of such a man and in such a manner is surely worthy to be followed by the favour of apostolic grace; and, by the fullness of honour—the one thing lacking—the joys of his people should be increased through your customary kindness, indeed through your due generosity. The entire Church seeks this with most urgent supplication; your little servant demands it with his customary boldness.

## Letter 172

*[Written in the same year.]*

**To the same, in the name of Geoffrey, bishop of Langres.** On the same subject as the preceding letter.

Among the frequent evils which in these days are seen to happen in the churches on the occasion of elections, the Lord looked down from heaven upon our mother Church of Lyons. When Peter, the archbishop of pious memory, died, He replaced him in complete peace with that excellent man Falco, the dean.

I ask, my lord, that he who has been unanimously elected by his own people, beneficially advanced, and duly consecrated, may receive from you the fullness of his honour and office. What emboldens me to make this request is not consciousness of merit, but of duty. I call it a duty not only because that Church justly demands it of me by metropolitan right, but because I have been placed here to bear witness to the truth.

## Letter 173

*[Written in the same year.]*

**To Falco himself.** He commends the cause of certain religious persons.

The lord bishop [Note: Namely, Geoffrey, bishop of Langres.] and I have written to the lord Pope on your behalf, as we judged fitting; and you have a copy of the letter. We intend never to fail you, according to our ability, because of the good which we hope for from you. It is your concern, however, to ensure that we are not put to shame in holding such hope.

Moreover, if I have found favour in your eyes, attend to those needy and poor persons at Benediction of God [Note: Benediction-of-God, a Cistercian daughter-house of Clairvaux in the diocese of Lyons, was founded in 1138; its first abbot was Alberic. Not far from it stood the monastery of Savigny, of the Order of St Benedict and in the same diocese; its abbot at that time was Iterius, of whom Bernard complains elsewhere.]. Whatever you do for one of them, you will do for me—indeed, for Christ. For they are poor, and they live among the poor.

We especially beseech you to restrain the monks of Savigny from harassing them, because, as we believe, they unjustly bring accusations against them. Or, if they are confident that they have justice on their side, judge between them. We beseech you that our son Abbot Alberic, though more commendable by his own merits, may be more commended to you by our prayers. I love him tenderly, as a mother loves an only son; and he who loves me loves him. In short, in him I shall discover whether you care for me. For the farther he is from me, the more he needs your fatherly consolation.

## Letter 174

*[Written about the year of Christ 1140.]*

**To the Canons of Lyons, concerning the Conception of St Mary.** The feast of the Conception is new and rests upon no lawful foundation; moreover, it ought not to have been instituted without consulting the Apostolic See, to whose judgment he submits his own opinion.

1. Among the churches of Gaul, it is surely agreed that the Church of Lyons has hitherto held preeminence, as much in the dignity of its see as in honourable pursuits and praiseworthy institutions. Where else have the strictness of discipline, gravity of manners, maturity of counsel, weight of authority, and distinction of antiquity flourished equally? Especially in ecclesiastical offices, that Church—full of judgment—has scarcely ever appeared readily to yield to sudden novelties, nor has it ever allowed itself to be disfigured by youthful frivolity.

We therefore greatly wonder what induced some among you at this time to wish to change this excellent colour by introducing a new celebration which the Church’s rite does not know, reason does not approve, and ancient tradition does not commend. Are we wiser or more devout than the Fathers? We dangerously presume whatever their prudence in such matters passed over. Nor is this a matter such that, unless it should have been passed over, it could at all have escaped the Fathers’ diligence.

2. “But,” you say, “the Mother of the Lord is to be greatly honoured.” You give a good reminder; but honour for the Queen loves judgment. The royal Virgin has no need of false honour, being filled with the true titles of honour and the ornaments of dignity. Honour, indeed, the integrity of her flesh and the holiness of her life. Marvel at her fruitfulness in virginity; venerate her divine Offspring. Extol her who knew neither concupiscence in conceiving nor pain in giving birth. Proclaim her revered by angels, desired by nations, foreknown by patriarchs and prophets, chosen from all, preferred above all. Magnify her as finder of grace, mediator of salvation, renewer of the ages; finally, exalt her as exalted above the choirs of angels to the heavenly kingdoms.

These things the Church sings to me concerning her, and has taught me to sing. What I have received from the Church, I securely hold and pass on; what I have not received, I confess, I admit with greater hesitation.

3. I have certainly received from the Church that day as one to be commemorated with the highest reverence, on which, taken from this wicked world, she brought to heaven also a feast of most celebrated joys. I have likewise learned in the Church, and received without hesitation from the Church, that the Virgin’s birth is festive and holy; and I most firmly hold with the Church that she received sanctification in the womb, so that she came forth holy.

For I read concerning Jeremiah that, before he came forth from the womb [variant: “from the vulva”], he was sanctified. I think no differently concerning John the Baptist, who in the womb perceived the Lord in the womb (Luke 1:41). Consider also whether the same may be thought concerning holy David, because he said to God: “Upon you I was upheld from the womb; from my mother’s belly you are my protector” (Ps. 70:6); and likewise: “From my mother’s belly you are my God; do not depart from me” (Ps. 21:11).

To Jeremiah, indeed, it was said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1:5). How beautifully the divine oracle distinguished between formation in the womb and birth from the womb, showing the former only as foreknown, but the latter as endowed beforehand with the gift of holiness, lest anyone should think that the prophet’s prerogative was to be judged from foreknowledge or predestination alone.

4. Let us, however, grant this concerning Jeremiah. [Col. 0334A] What shall be answered concerning John the Baptist, whom the angel foretold would be filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb? I certainly do not think this can be referred to predestination or foreknowledge. The angel’s words, as he himself foretold, were undoubtedly fulfilled in their time; and it is not permissible to believe that the one whom he declared would be filled with the Holy Spirit was not filled—and this in the place and at the time which he foretold.

Most certainly, the Holy Spirit, whom He filled, sanctified. Yet how far this sanctification prevailed against original sin—whether for this prophet or that, or if anyone else was visited by similar prevenient grace—I would not rashly say. Nevertheless, I would not hesitate to call those sanctified whom God sanctified, and to say that they came forth from the womb with the same sanctification which they received in the womb; nor could the guilt which they contracted in conception in any way prevent or take away, at their birth, the blessing already bestowed.

Yet who would say that one filled with the Holy Spirit nevertheless remained a child of wrath, and that, if he had happened to die in the womb with this fullness of the Spirit, he would suffer the punishments of damnation? It is harsh. Still, I would not venture to define anything on this point according to my own judgment.

But whatever may be the case concerning this, the Church—who judges and proclaims precious not the birth but the death of other saints—rightly, by a certain singular exception, prefers John’s birth with festal joys and venerates it, since she reads that the angel uniquely declared concerning him: “Many shall rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1:14–15). For why should not the departure of him who could exult even in the womb be holy, and therefore festive and joyful?

5. Therefore, what is known to have been granted even to a few mortals cannot lawfully be suspected to have been denied to so great a Virgin, through whom all mortality emerged into life. Without doubt, the Mother of the Lord too was holy before she was born. Nor is holy Church at all mistaken in considering the very day of her Nativity holy and receiving it yearly with the vowed celebration and exultation of the whole earth.

I think that a more abundant blessing of sanctification descended upon her: one which not only sanctified her birth but also preserved her life thereafter free from every sin. This is believed to have been granted to no other among those born of women. It was fitting that the Queen of virgins, by the privilege of singular holiness, should live without any sin, so that, while she brought forth the destroyer of sin and death, she might obtain for all the gift of life and righteousness. Her birth, therefore, was holy, because the immense holiness with which she came forth from the womb made it holy.

6. What more, then, do they think should be added to these honours? “Let her conception also,” they say, “be honoured, since it preceded the birth which is honoured; for unless it had preceded, the birth which is honoured would not have existed.” What if someone, for the same reason, should assert that festal honours ought also to be paid to both her parents? For the same reason, anyone might demand this of grandparents and great-grandparents; thus it would extend to infinity, and there would be no number to the feasts.

This abundance of joys belongs to one’s homeland, not to exile; a multitude of feasts befits citizens, not exiles. But a writing of heavenly revelation, as they call it, is put forward [Note: A writing of this sort is attributed to Elsinus, an English abbot, in Anselm, pp. 505 and 507 of the new edition.], as if anyone could not equally produce a writing in which the Virgin herself appears to command the same concerning her parents, according to the Lord’s command: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12).

I readily persuade myself not to be moved by writings of this kind, for which reason supplies no support and no certain authority is found to favour them. For what consequence is there in this: that because conception preceded the holy birth, it must therefore itself be considered holy? Did it make the birth holy merely because it preceded it? Though it preceded so that the birth might exist, it did not precede so that it might be holy. From where, indeed, had conception itself that holiness which it might transmit to what followed? Was it not rather because conception preceded without holiness that the one conceived had to be sanctified, so that a holy birth might afterwards follow? Or did the earlier receive holiness by borrowing it from the later?

Certainly the sanctification which took place in one already conceived could pass on to the birth which followed; but it could by no means go back again to the conception which had preceded.

7. From where, then, comes the holiness of conception? Is she said to have been forestalled by sanctification, so that she was conceived already holy, and thereby the conception too was holy—as she is said to have been sanctified already in the womb so that a holy birth might follow? But she could not be holy before she existed, for she did not exist before she was conceived.

Or perhaps amid the marital embraces holiness mingled itself with conception, so that she was sanctified and conceived simultaneously? Reason does not admit this either. For how could there be holiness without the sanctifying Spirit? Or how could there be fellowship between the Holy Spirit and sin? Or, certainly, how could there not be sin where lust was present? Unless perhaps someone says that she was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and not by a man—but this has until now been unheard of.

Finally, I read that the Holy Spirit came upon her, not with her, as the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” (Luke 1:35). And if it is permitted to say what the Church thinks—and what she thinks is true—I say that the glorious Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, but was not herself conceived by the Holy Spirit; I say that she gave birth as a virgin, but was not herself born of a virgin. Otherwise, where will be the prerogative of the Mother of the Lord, in which she is uniquely believed to rejoice both in the gift of offspring and in integrity of flesh, if you grant just as much to her mother?

This is not to honour the Virgin but to diminish her honour. Therefore, if she could not possibly have been sanctified before her own conception, because she did not yet exist, nor even in conception itself because of the sin present there, it remains that she must be believed to have received sanctification after conception, while already existing in the womb. This sanctification excluded sin and made her birth holy, but not her conception.

8. Therefore, although it was granted to some few children of men to be born with holiness, it was not granted to them to be conceived with holiness. Thus the prerogative of holy conception was reserved to One alone: He who sanctified all, and who, alone coming without sin, made purification for sins. The Lord Jesus alone, therefore, was conceived of the Holy Spirit, because He alone was holy before conception.

With Him excepted, this applies to all who are born from Adam, as one man humbly and truthfully confesses concerning himself: “I was conceived in iniquities,” he says, “and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7).

9. Since these things are so, what basis can there now be for celebrating the Conception? How, I ask, can a conception be declared holy which is not of the Holy Spirit—not to say, is of sin? Or how can that be regarded as a feast which is not holy at all? The glorious Virgin would gladly lack an honour by which either sin seems to be honoured or a false holiness introduced. Otherwise, a novelty rashly presumed upon against the rite of the Church—a mother of rashness, sister of superstition, daughter of frivolity—could in no way please her. For, if this seemed right, the authority of the Apostolic See should first have been consulted, rather than the unlearned simplicity of a few persons followed so precipitately and without deliberation [Col. 0336C].

I had indeed previously discovered this error among some people; but I passed it over, sparing their devotion, which proceeded from a simple heart and love for the Virgin. But when superstition has been found among the wise, and in a famous and noble Church—and one of which I am especially a son—I do not know whether I could have passed it over without grave offence even to all of you.

[Note: That is, the Church of Lyons, Bernard’s mother “by metropolitan right,” as he himself says in Letter 172; for Fontaines, his birthplace near Dijon, and the seat of the monastery of Clairvaux, lay under the metropolitan jurisdiction of Lyons, in the diocese of Langres.]

But let what I have said be said without prejudice to the judgment of one wiser than I. I reserve this whole matter, especially, as also all other matters of this kind, for the authority and examination of the Roman Church; if I think otherwise than I should, I am ready to correct myself by its judgment.

## LETTER CLXXV. TO THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM

[Note: Written about the year 1135.—This is William, a Gallo-Belgian, formerly a hermit of Tours, Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1130 to 1145. Concerning him, see the *History of Blessed Mary of Fontaines*, in vol. X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 369, where mention is made of relics sent by him to Fontaines through Lambert, hermit of that place. Orderic also writes thus near the end of Book XIII: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1128, in the sixth indiction, Germund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, died. Stephen of Chartres then governed holy Sion for two years after him; when he departed, William of Flanders succeeded.” The same author, under the year 1137, p. 912, mentions Ralph, prelate of Jerusalem, whom Papebroch omitted in the preliminary treatise to vol. III for May. And indeed, according to William of Tyre, William buried King Baldwin in 1142, and in 1145 had Fulcher as his successor. Was William perhaps a man with two names? Or is this an error of Orderic? A further letter to William appears below, Letter 393.]

In friendly reply to his letter, he commends the Knights Templar.

[Col. 0336D]

Having often been visited by your patriarchal letters, I shall now seem ungrateful if I do not reply. Yet if I greet one who has greeted me, what more have I done? For you have anticipated me with blessings of sweetness; you first deigned to visit me with your letters from beyond the sea [Col. 0337A]; you have taken for yourself the first part in humility and charity. What worthy return can I now make? You have left me nothing by which I can repay you in equal measure, since you have even taken care to share with me from the treasure of the ages—that is, from the wood of the Lord.

What then? Should I omit what I can do because I cannot do what I ought? At least I disclose my feeling and intention by writing in reply and returning your greeting, which alone is meanwhile possible over such expanses of land and sea. If I ever receive the opportunity, however, I shall show that I love not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.

I beg you, set your eyes upon the Knights of the Temple, and open the bowels of so great compassion to these valiant defenders of the Church. For it will be acceptable to God and pleasing to men if you foster those who have laid down their souls for their brethren. As for the place to which you invite us, Brother Andrew will tell you our intention.

[Note: Is this Andrew Bernard’s uncle, a Knight Templar, to whom Letter 288 is addressed? Or rather Bernard’s brother Andrew, monk of Clairvaux, perhaps the same as in Letter 184? Or Andrew of Baldement, in Letter 226, no. 2? I do not know whether the place indicated here is that which Bernard granted to the Premonstratensians, according to Letter 252.]

## LETTER CLXXVI

[Note: Written in the same year. See the note to Letter 30.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT, IN THE PERSON OF ALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

[Note: This man, formerly primicerius of Metz, to whom Letter 30 is addressed, was Archbishop of Trier. Hugh Metellus addresses Letter 6 to him: “To Albero, venerable bishop of the Treveri. The legation of blessed Peter has been entrusted to you, and adds something of dignity and power to you.” In Letter 30 he calls him the archangel of the Treveri.]

He declares his zeal and obedience toward Innocent and toward the Church north of the Alps.

1. The desire of my heart, very restless in its longing to approach and behold the wished-for presence of Your Blessedness, and also more certainly to learn how matters stand with you, and in turn more diligently to report to you how our own affairs stand, has long urged me to travel and incessantly presses me to do so. Yet the evil of the land and of the day, and my being hindered not only by my daily engagements but also by certain needs of yours, have until now prevented me from fulfilling my desire; and I still cannot do so.

But what then? Was a sound and just purpose to be wholly abandoned because it could not be wholly fulfilled? I therefore resolved, through this venerable Hugh, archdeacon of the Church of Toul, at least in some measure meanwhile to console the desire long conceived and to relieve the anxiety I suffer.

[Note: Concerning him, see Book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, ch. 3, no. 31.]

For no one could be more trustworthy, diligent, or cautious at hand than he—whether in conveying to you what we entrust to him, or in bringing back to us whatever Your Dignity may wish to send in reply. We therefore desire, and humbly ask, to be more fully informed concerning your good pleasure, the condition of the curia, the safety of your person, and whether some gentler, more favourable breeze has perhaps lately blown upon the Church from divine mercy as she toils against the insolent but ineffectual rage of the schismatics [Col. 0337D–0338A].

2. Furthermore, know that our Church north of the Alps, both in our own realm and in the kingdom of the Franks, is strong in faith, peaceful in unity, devoted in obedience to you, and ready for service. The loss of Benevento, of Capua—

[Note: These remarks concern Apulia, seized by Roger, whom Bernard here and elsewhere calls the Sicilian tyrant.]

—and even of Rome herself does not frighten us, since God so judges; for we know that the condition of the Church is not measured by arms but by merits. We acknowledge as her own, and not another’s, those words in the Psalm: “Though camps should stand against me, my heart shall not fear; though battle should rise against me, in this I shall hope” (Ps. 26:3).

Therefore, because we belong to the Church, neither shall we fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are carried into the heart of the sea [Col. 0338B]. Let the Sicilian tyrant boast as much as he wishes; let him boast in wickedness, since he is powerful in iniquity. But our strength is made perfect in weakness. When the Church is weakened, she has learned from Paul’s teaching to be stronger (2 Cor. 12:10). Conversely, she has learned also from Solomon that “the prosperity of fools destroys them” (Prov. 1:32); and she has learned that, when one sees a fool firmly rooted, one immediately curses his beauty (Job 5:3).

Therefore, with holy David she consoles herself in both respects: in the fall of her enemies and in her own deliverance. For he says: “These are in chariots and those in horses; but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God. They have been bound and have fallen; but we have risen and stand upright” (Ps. 19:8–9).

I thought that these few things, of which I was certain, should be communicated to you in faithful testimony for your consolation, in order to relieve at least in some measure the anxiety which unceasingly afflicts your heart: the care of all the Churches. I add also that the lord King—

[Note: Emperor Lothair.]

—strengthened by God, burns with zeal and arms himself for the liberation of the Church; he is preparing for himself a very great army. We too are faithfully working, exhorting, and urging all whom we can to this same end; and when the time comes, he will spare neither expense nor his own person.

## LETTER CLXXVII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

### TO THE SAME, IN THE PERSON OF THE SAME

He complains of the pastoral office imposed upon him; in carrying out the duties of that office he is obstructed by the rivalry of others, not without fault on the Pope’s own part.

[Col. 0338D]

1. Did I ask my Lord for a bishopric? And even if I happened to desire a see, it was not Trier. For I knew it to be a provoking house and a stiff-necked people. I hated them, because they had always lain in the dregs of discord, resisting the Church. I do not regret whatever labours I may at times have borne for her sake; but I neither expected nor desired this as their fruit. I laboured in endurance, willingly indeed, but not in hope of this reward.

By the demands of my sins I have received a harsh province. Among the other things by which I am distressed, I have received as suffragans young and noble men.

[Note: Namely Stephen of Metz, nephew through a sister of Pope Calixtus II, from the year 1120; Albero of Verdun, son of Arnulf, Count of Chiny, from the year 1126; and Henry of Toul, son of Duke Theodoric of Lorraine, from the year 1124. Much praiseworthy matter is nevertheless reported of them. On Stephen see the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz*, in vol. VI of the *Spicilegium*; on Albero, vol. XII, where both are nevertheless said to have been too devoted to waging wars. Albero’s complaints are explained in the following letter.]

They ought to be helpers—and would that they were not adversaries. But I refrain from saying more; I would rather that you learn from another, if you do not know them, their character and pursuits. Yet I say this: law, right, honour, and religion have perished in our bishoprics. I have briefly and simply reported an evil which I do not dare to conceal as a matter of official duty, so that what your providence is unwilling to correct through me may at least be made known through me to you, who are able to correct it, lest I seem altogether to bear the name of archbishop in vain. And it would certainly have been better for me not to have ascended than to descend thus in shame.

2. But what concern is there about me? I shall suffer what I deserve, as one who has acted wickedly. Indeed, I shall become a reproach even to my own people, whose hope will plainly have been disappointed—the hope they conceived concerning me when they wished me to preside over them—when they discover that through me the dignity of their Church is diminished rather than that her former losses might be restored through me, as they had hoped.

I endure all these things, if not gladly, at least patiently, lest I ever seem to kick against obedience, for which I confess that I ought, if necessary, even to give my life. But I would have your concern attend to this: let the injury done to the one created be referred to the Creator; the strength which you withdraw from me, you lessen in yourselves; and my contempt and humiliation recoil upon you.

I have much to complain to you concerning yourselves; but I reserve it for disclosure to a messenger whom I know to be sufficiently capable and trustworthy for this purpose.
