I also inform you that we suffer danger from false brethren. For envoys of the schismatics enter and leave more freely than formerly among certain of our people, and the words of the Sicilian tyrant are received familiarly.

## LETTER CLXXVIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1139, according to Brouwer.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT ON BEHALF OF ALBERO, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER

He complains that certain perverse and Church-destroying men are supported by papal authority in carrying out their evil designs, while other prelates, who have zeal for God, are meanwhile abandoned and despised.

[Col. 0340A]

To the most beloved Father and lord INNOCENT, supreme Pontiff, his own BERNARD, because he is his own.

1. I speak confidently because I love faithfully. For love is not sincere where the scruple of doubt retains the dregs of suspicion. The complaint of the lord of Trier is not his alone, but that of many in common, especially of those who love you with a more sincere affection. One is the voice of all those who faithfully preside among us over peoples entrusted to their care: justice is perishing in the Church; the keys of the Church are nullified; episcopal authority is altogether cheapened, while no bishop readily has the power to avenge the wrongs done to God, and no one is permitted to punish any unlawful acts, even within his own diocese.

[Note: By the term *parochia*, as everyone knows, the ancients understood a bishop’s diocese.]

They lay the blame upon you and the Roman curia.

[Note: Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, wrote Letter 82 to Honorius II also concerning the frequent practice—or abuse—of appeals. See Book III of *On Consideration*, ch. 2.]

You overturn, they say, what they have rightly done, and establish what has justly been overthrown. Wicked and contentious persons, driven out from the people, the clergy, or even monasteries, run to you; on returning they boast and exult that they have obtained protectors, when they ought rather to have found avengers.

Was not the sword of Phinehas most promptly and justly drawn to condemn the incestuous union of Drogo and Milis? Yet it departed backward confused and blunted, since the shield of apostolic protection had been set against it. Shame! What laughter this matter has caused, and causes, among the enemies of the Church—and even among those very persons by whose fear or favour we may perhaps have been drawn away from the straight path! Friends are put to shame, the faithful are insulted, bishops everywhere are brought into reproach and contempt; and when their right judgments are despised, your own authority too is greatly diminished [Col. 0340C].

2. For these are the very men who are zealous for your honour, who labour faithfully for your peace and exaltation—yet, I fear, ineffectually. Why do you diminish your own strength? Why do you weaken your own power? How long will you blunt the faithful weapons fighting for you, the horns of humility raised up for your strength and salvation?

The Church of St Gangulf at Toul weeps bitterly over her desolation, and there is no one to comfort her.

[Note: See Letter 139.]

For who would set himself against the lifted arm, the force of a torrent, the decision of supreme power? St Paul’s at Verdun complains that it endures the same violence, since the archbishop can no longer defend it from the madness of the monks, who have been strengthened still further by apostolic support, as though they were not mad enough by themselves.

[Note: The monastery of St Paul near Verdun, of the Order of St Benedict, had relaxed the reins of regular discipline and fallen into a certain licentiousness of conduct. On this occasion Albero II, bishop of Verdun, successor of Ursio in 1131, arranged for its transfer to the Premonstratensians, with Pope Innocent’s approval and a threefold confirmation. The resident monks of the place protested and resisted for a long time; indeed Peter the Venerable himself, otherwise a most moderate man, complained vehemently about the matter to Matthew of Albano. Moved somewhat by these complaints, Innocent was preparing to call the case back into judicial examination and discussion. But finally overcome by Bernard’s recommendation, he settled the entire matter, again confirming by his letters what Albero had done.]

What new principle, I ask, has finally been devised, by which that which your provident and necessary dispensation had once granted to canons of good reputation and life, confirmed a second time and, as they say, strengthened a third time, should again come into litigation and be recalled for discussion? For those two matters mentioned above, likewise established by you, are said to have been overthrown by you as well.

By such offerings God is not won over; alas, wrath is not appeased, grace is not reconciled, mercy is not called forth. Because of these and similar things the anger of the Lord has not yet turned away; rather, his arm is still stretched out, and that rod in Jeremiah is still watching over our sins.

3. God is indeed angry with the schismatics; but he is by no means favourable to the Catholics. The Church of Metz also is endangered by a serious dispute—as is well known to you [variant: to us]—between the bishop and the clergy. What you may decide concerning this, you know; but peace has not yet come, nor is it hoped for soon.

For my part, lest I conceal what seems good to my smallness concerning these matters, I think that this affair, together with those other two—that is, Toul and Verdun—could more safely and suitably be entrusted for settlement to the metropolitan, who knows everything and, having been tested in many matters, has been found trustworthy by the testimony of the Church. Otherwise, consider what you are doing to those bishoprics, namely Metz and Toul; for, to speak the truth, they seem to be without bishops—and would that they were without tyrants.

[Note: What Bernard here hurls against the bishops of Metz and Toul must be understood of Stephen of Metz and Henry of Toul, since this letter was written while the schism of Anacletus still raged, as has been said above, indeed about the year 1135, as will be said below. The first appendix to the *History of the Bishops of Metz* says of Stephen: “The lord Stephen, illustrious in birth through his lord Poppo, eminent among both Burgundians and Lotharingians, but more illustrious in virtue and nobility of spirit, succeeded in the year of the Lord 1120, namely the second year of Pope Calixtus II. This nephew of Calixtus through a sister, since he had not yet received the regalian rights from Henry V, who at that time held the citadel of the Empire, while the schism between kingdom and priesthood still endured, was consecrated at Rome by the same supreme pontiff and honoured both with the dignity of the pallium and with the title of cardinal.” (*Spicilegium*, vol. VI, p. 661.) Why Bernard complains of him so sharply is not easy to conjecture. For, apart from the foregoing, the said History reads of him: “If I wished to enumerate his illustrious deeds, worthy of annals, and set them forth in writing, parchment would fail before the material.” Indeed Bernard himself congratulates him in Letter 29 upon peace restored to the Church of Metz, and commends him to Chancellor Guy in Letter 367. It is likely that Stephen displeased Bernard because of the various armed conflicts he stirred up in recovering Church estates seized by nobles: sieges undertaken, castles demolished, and many other things of that kind, described in the same History, which expressed more “some little lion,” to use Bernard’s words in Letter 230, than a shepherd of sheep. Moreover, when Albero the primicerius was raised to the bishopric of Liège in 1135—as may be inferred from the established sequence of dates; see the notes to Letter 30—and the canons by their electoral votes appointed another primicerius, Stephen wished by his own authority to impose another. A great dispute arose from this, which Innocent undertook to settle while passing over the judgment of the metropolitan, namely the Archbishop of Trier. Bernard here complains to Innocent on that account. As for Henry, bishop of Toul, perhaps he was ill spoken of by the holy man for the same reason: namely, because of military business long conducted with Frederick, count of Toul, and finally settled in 1136, as may be understood from Innocent’s letters published by Chesnius from the charter archive of the Church of Toul.]

When such men are defended, supported, honoured, and cherished, many are naturally astonished and scandalized who know with complete certainty such things about their conduct and life as ought to be wholly condemned and detested—not merely in bishops, I do not say, but even in any secular persons. I was ashamed to write these things, and it would not have been fitting for you to hear them. Grant that they cannot be deposed when no one accuses them: nevertheless, ought those whom public report accuses everywhere to be granted special familiarity with the Apostolic See, or exalted still further?

4. For by what merit of his priestly holiness or episcopal honourableness did the bishop of Metz obtain both that an election made by the canons should, at his nod, be annulled together with the Church’s liberty, and that a primicerius should be chosen at his counsel against the privileges of that Church? How much more just and honourable it would have been, had it pleased your discernment, that a man worthy of greater honour should not be deprived of what was due and proper to him! I mean the man of Trier, whom you have excluded from settling both this and the other affairs of his diocese, as though he were suspect or insufficiently experienced, not without the murmuring of many who fear God. Believe one faithful to you: as far as I have learned, this is wholly harmful to that province.

5. In writing this, I would fear the charge of presumption, if I did not know both to whom and as what person I write. But I know your innate gentleness; and I know that I am known to you, and the affection in which I dare to write these things to you, sweetest and most beloved Father.

Again, concerning the man of Trier, so that you may know how his messenger and the words he carries should be received: I tell you that he holds a great place in that kingdom, a man faithful and steadfast to you and to the Church of God, who in no way gives assent to the ill-disposed and subversive persons by whom he is frequently and rather importunately tempted; nor will mockery be lacking if it happens that he is less than heard by you.

I wished at the end to commend the messenger; but the merits of his own honourableness sufficiently commend him, and especially the special love and faithful devotion by which he clings firmly to you. If I did not believe this, I would never write to you so familiarly through him.

## LETTER CLXXIX

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

### TO THE SAME ON BEHALF OF THE SAME

He pleads the cause of Albero, Archbishop of Trier, against the abbot of St Maximin and rebellious, contumacious monks.

How does malice conquer wisdom? Do you know, pious lord, do you know the Archbishop of Trier? I know that you know him. Do you also know that unholy abbot of Saint Maximin? I think you do not know him. Who is more worthy of honour than the former? So no one is more worthy of disgrace than the latter; and yet this man has been honoured, while that one has been laden with reproach.

What sin has the archbishop committed? He recovered the prey of his Church; he freed a captive Church from a lay hand.

[Note: Archbishop Albero of Trier claimed for himself the monastery of St Maximin near Trier, against the resistance of its abbot and monks. Conversely, Count Henry of Luxembourg attempted, by right of advocacy, to claim its temporal subjection for himself. This matter divided both parties in mind and committed them to arms, not without great slaughter on each side. This is what Bernard means when he says that the archbishop recovered the prey of his Church and freed the captive Church from a lay hand.]

Is evil repaid for good, and hatred for love? Here, I beg you, let the eye of compassion awaken; setting aside occupations for a little while, let it consider how greatly it has been deceived, so that such a man—such as I am ashamed to describe, such as you yourself know him—should be made a reproach to his neighbours, who are your enemies.

Most pious Father, filial affection speaks. Until now we have grieved with the wretched and pitiable archbishop [Col. 0343B]. But if this is not now corrected, the pain of our heart and compassion from our inmost marrow will wholly pass to him through whom it could have been corrected. There are other injuries suffered by the said man; when you relieve them, you will undoubtedly be labouring for yourselves. Whatever stains the name of my sweetest lord flays my heart.

## LETTER CLXXX

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1136.]

### TO THE SAME ON BEHALF OF THE SAME

Again he commends to the Pope the affair of the Archbishop of Trier, asking him, after a better preliminary examination of the case, to revoke a judgment obtained by deception.

Again a petition; again prayers; and though repeated ten times, they will not cease. We do not desist because we do not despair. We have a good cause and a just judge [Col. 0343C], who will not hesitate to annul what has been obtained by deception when what is true becomes clear. Nor will he who wished to mock be able to laugh thereafter; rather, as it is written, “iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. 26:12).

This is an especial quality of the Apostolic See: it does not begrudge revoking what it may discover was drawn forth from it by fraud rather than deserved by truth. It is a matter full of justice and worthy of praise that no one should profit from a lie, especially before the holy and supreme See.

Knowing this, your child confidently petitions for the man of Trier, and presses the case not as one uncertain. For I, yes I, know that man’s merits, cause, and intention. Why do the monks wish to stone him on these grounds? Because he deserved ill? Rather, he stood faithfully by them and served them much. Because of the injustice of his cause? But no one except an unjust man will plead an unjust cause. Because he claimed it from a lay hand? Rather, he recovered for the episcopal see a monastery, tearing the club from Hercules’ hand into the hand of one stronger. Because of depravity of intention? But it is pious to reform religious observance in a monastery, and that is his purpose. May the Lord be present to the heart of my lord, so that he may not again be deceived by monks who seek not so much, as they pretend, liberty as they flee discipline.

## LETTER CLXXXI

[Note: Written about the same year.]

### TO AIMERY, CHANCELLOR

He declares that he is unequal to his benefactions and can be grateful only in the affection of his will.

If I wished to contend in words against the benefits with which you overwhelm me, it would be the same as if, attacked with arrows, I fought with straws—except that the one would seem a joke, the other a deceit. Deeds must be repaid with deeds. But that is far beyond me. For how could I, poor and insignificant, suffice? Yet I am poor in resources and strength, not in will [Col. 0344B].

Therefore I shall equal benefits with wishes, since I cannot do so with deeds. I am rich in desires; I abound in affections. And certainly a truly beneficent man asks for nothing more. For how can one be beneficent who is not also benevolent? Moreover, the benevolent person judges nothing dearer to himself than benevolence itself, by which he is both called benevolent and is beneficent. In short, benevolence is the fruit of a benefit—unless perhaps someone considers that to be a benefit which he has sown in hope or relinquished through fear. But who does not see that the latter is abandoned, the former sold, and neither given?

A benefit, if it is truly such, must be gratuitous. Therefore nothing more pleasing can be rendered by the recipient to the giver than that he should be grateful for what he received freely. This benevolence is created in the recipient’s mind from the giver’s benevolence, the benefit itself intervening. I confess that I am rich in this; from a full heart I offer it as a worthy recompense to my benefactor; devotedly I sacrifice it as a sacrifice of praise to the Maker of all things for the salvation of my benefactor.

## LETTER CLXXXII. TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1139. This is a sharp letter to a bishop to whom, in Letter 42, Bernard had given such wholesome admonitions concerning the morals and office of bishops. It was written about the year 1140, certainly before 1144, in which year Henry died and was succeeded by Hugh, according to the *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif*, in vol. II of the *Spicilegium*. On his death, see Letter 102.]

He sharply censures him, as a harsh man who had improperly deposed an archdeacon and was resistant to fair requests and counsels of peace.

I seem to have written many times, I confess, for many people on your account; and because of your hateful harshness I had decided not to do so. But charity will prevail. I wish you to retain your friends, and you refuse; I wish to reconcile your enemies, and you do not allow it. You do not wish to have peace. With hands and feet you summon your own disturbance—indeed, confusion and deposition.

[Note: That he was suspended in 1136 is evident from the fact that Hugh, formerly abbot of Pontigny and bishop of Auxerre, was consecrated at Ferrières by Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, “because of the suspension of Lord Henry the metropolitan,” according to the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, ch. 55, in Labbe.]

You multiply your accusers and remove your defenders. You rouse again against yourself dangers formerly laid to rest; you provoke adversaries and offend patrons. With you, will is everywhere in place of reason; everything proceeds from arbitrary power, nothing from fear of God. Which of your enemies does not laugh at you? Which of your friends does not complain?

How have you stripped a man of office—not merely one not convicted by a judgment, but one not even summoned by a word? How many will this report scandalize? How many mouths will it move to mockery, how many hearts to indignation? Do you suppose that justice has perished from the entire world just as it has from your heart, so that a man thus removed should lose his archdeaconry? But perhaps you prefer to restore favour and lose it rather than retain it through a benefit.

Do not, I beg you, do this thing. All who hear of it will marvel; no one will praise it. I have written this more sharply and boldly than you would wish to hear; but not for your folly, if you are willing to correct yourself.

## LETTER CLXXXIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

### TO CONRAD, KING OF THE ROMANS

He commends to him reverence for the Apostolic See.

I receive your letters and greetings with as much devotion as I am small in relation to them. I call myself small in dignity, but not in devotion. The King’s complaints are ours—

[Note: That is, Conrad complained that Bernard had supported Lothair against him.]

—and especially the complaint which you graciously express concerning the invasion of the Empire. I have never wished for the King’s dishonour or the diminution of the kingdom; my soul hates those who wish these things. For I have read: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers,” and, “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1–2).

Yet I desire and urge you by every means to observe this teaching in rendering reverence to the supreme and Apostolic See [Col. 0345C] and to the Vicar of blessed Peter—

[Note: Thus the supreme pontiff is called the Vicar of Peter in Letter 346; the Vicar of Peter and Paul in Letter 243. Compare Guigo’s letter in vol. VI here, and our notes on this matter in Part I of the Second Century, p. 362. Bernard nevertheless calls the Pope the Vicar of Christ in Letter 42, no. 31; Letter 251, no. 1; and at the end of Book IV of *On Consideration*. Compare Book II of *On Consideration*, no. 16. James the cardinal calls him the Vicar of Jesus Christ in Letter 246, to Louis the Younger among the Chesnian letters.]

—as you wish it to be rendered to yourselves by the whole Empire. There are matters which I did not think should be written; perhaps I would communicate them more suitably in person.

## LETTER CLXXXIV

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT

That the monks whom the Pope had requested cannot be sent.

We welcomed [variant: received] Brother Andrew, joyful and safe, bringing happy news of your safety and glory, of the peace and prosperity of the Church, of the flourishing and vigorous condition of the curia, and finally of the grace and goodwill which continue for us with you.

[Note: Is this Andrew Bernard’s brother, a Cistercian monk, according to Book I of his *Life*, no. 10? Or the same man mentioned in Letter 176? Or Andrew of Baldement, in Letter 226?]

God has graciously deigned in his mercy to deal well with us; we have become joyful. But your wish concerning brothers to be sent to you will be difficult to fulfil, especially since there is not the abundance of persons that formerly existed. Besides those who have been sent two or three at a time to various places, three new monasteries have been completely established since we left you, and other foundations still remain to be established shortly.

[Note: Namely Bénisson-Dieu in the diocese of Lyons, mentioned above in Letter 173; Dun, and Clairmarais in Belgium.]

Nevertheless, we endeavour to summon from wherever we can those whom we may send to you, desiring in all things to obey your commands.

[Note: The Pontiff wished to establish Cistercians at Rome in the church of St Anastasius at Aquae Salviae. A second colony, led by another Bernard, later Pope Eugenius III, had occupied the place after being sent to the abbot of Farfa, and was settled at Aquae Salviae in 1140, according to Book III of the *Life*, no. 23. See here Letters 343 and 345.]

## LETTER CLXXXV

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1138.]

### TO EUSTACE, OCCUPIER OF THE SEE OF VALENCE

[Note: In Narbonensian Gaul; there is another Valence in Spain.]

He exhorts him, mindful of his age, approaching death, and divine judgment, to come to his senses and not obey the evil counsels of flatterers.

To the illustrious man EUSTACE, Brother BERNARD.

1. I wish you well, most illustrious sir, although I do not write to you, [Col. 0346B] I nevertheless desire it. Who can forbid one to desire? Neither laws rule over affection, nor princes hold dominion over it. It is free—especially when it is led by the Spirit; for “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). Hence indeed this present boldness of mine, by which I presume to write to your Magnificence—as though I were some great person, I confess—although neither commanded, requested, nor invited by you. But what if charity commands?

Perhaps another will take it differently. For my part, so far as lies in me, I have resolved by this letter to remind a noble man of his own true salvation, to rouse him from sleep, recall him to himself, and summon him to grace. Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him? Indeed, who does not know what great and abundant treasures of his goodness and forbearance the merciful and compassionate Lord has already stored up for him? [Col. 0346C] For he has mercy, spares, waits, and still bears with him, having become like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth—slow to strike, ready to forgive. But you, my lord—how long? You, I say, good sir, how long will you dissemble? How long will you despise? “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5). Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? Yet how long, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, will you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath? (Rom. 2:4–5).

2. Or is it not from hardness, but from shame? What difference does it make through what cause you perish? O shame devoid of reason, enemy of salvation, ignorant of all honour and uprightness! This is plainly [Col. 0346D] that shame of which the Wise Man speaks: “shame that brings sin” [Col. 0347A] (Ecclus. 4:25). Is it then shameful for a man to be overcome by God? Is it accounted disgrace to be humbled beneath the mighty hand of the Most High?

Not so that glorious king David: “Against you alone,” he says, “have I sinned, and done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6). The highest kind of victory is to yield to the divine majesty; and not to resist the authority of mother Church is the highest honour and glory. O perversity! One is not ashamed to be defiled, yet is ashamed to be washed! There is, according to the Wise Man, a shame that brings glory (Ecclus. 4:25): namely, if one is ashamed to sin, but not ashamed even to have sinned. Thus you will not lack even a late glory, when shame restores what guilt had driven away. They hold the second place in blessedness whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered (Ps. 31:1).

[Col. 0347B] An honourable covering, of which it is written: “Confession and beauty are before him” (Ps. 95:6). Who will grant me to see you in golden raiment, so that we too may say to you: “You have put on confession and splendour, clothed in light as in a garment” (Ps. 103:1–2). “Return, return, Shunammite, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12). Arise, arise; put on strength; put on the garment of salvation (Isa. 52:1). “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light” (Eph. 5:14). “From one who is dead, as though he were not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26).

3. How long will you forget yourself utterly? How long do you sleep in death, glory of nobles, grief of the faithful? How long, stubborn against your own character, estranged from your own honour, rebellious against your own salvation? [Col. 0347C] Why do you persist in bringing those excellent morals and deeds of yours to so unlike an end? How is it that this old age, which ought to rest in abundant mercy, pays the penalty for all your former days, yet does not wash away its faults? Why, alas, is venerable grey hair alone deprived of its customary veneration, alone withering without honour, though it was especially fitting that it be honoured?

“Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). For those who please men are put to shame, because God has despised them (Ps. 52:6). The days of man are brief (Job 14:5); for an old man death stands at the door. You have little time—indeed, very little—with those who say to you, “Well done, well done.” Let it also be a small thing to you to be judged by them or by a human day, since you are shortly to be brought before the judgment of angels, and are now, through nature’s very failure, pitiably pressed toward [Col. 0347D] the dreadful tribunal of Christ. You must prepare yourself for that judgment, conform yourself to that world, seek the favour of that court, and fear its rejection. Why are you disturbed by the verdict of those by whose praise you are not approved, nor by whose blame found reprobate? For “the sons of men are vain; the sons of men are liars in the balances, that they may deceive together through vanity” (Ps. 61:10).

4. Therefore those who call you blessed lead you into error: they give words and carry away gifts. These things are vain, as are those; but words are worth more. “And you deceive together through vanity”; yet you are more deceived, they less so. For you give what is in some measure more valuable; and you give to the ungrateful, you give to the undeserving. They love what is yours, not you. Indeed, they seek neither you nor what is yours, but what is their own. So far as they can, they will hunt after your possessions by vain and false flatteries. “Their words are softened above oil, and yet they are darts” (Ps. 54:22). Therefore David said: “Let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). By such men the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked is blessed (Ps. 9:24).

[Col. 0348A] Let not me, therefore, but the Wise Man teach you to beware of them: “My son,” he says, “if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). Attend rather to him who judges with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth, whom not your pastoral care feeds, but secular power oppresses—a power which you would possess over them only because it has been given you from above. But this is your hour and the power of darkness. Yet consider: “A severe judgment is for those who rule, and the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:6–7). If you fear this, you will beware; if you neglect it, you will fall into it. And “it is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). May the one true God avert this, he who does not will the death of the sinner but rather that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18:23, 32).

My mind urges me to say more, but perhaps your hearing cannot bear it. Harsh things are not pleasing, however right they may be; and wholesome things, because bitter, do not taste sweet. I shall therefore put my finger upon my mouth until I learn how these things are received. [Col. 0348C] Yet, if I can, I shall be pleasing—not by pen or tongue, but by deed and truth.

## Letter 186

**To Simon, son of the Castellan of Cambrai**  
[Note: Written about the year 1140.—In all the manuscripts, *of Cambrai* is absent; some have *of Oisy*. Both are correct, for this letter mentions the monks of Vaucelles, of the Cistercian Order, whose monastery was founded in 1132 near Cambrai. [Col. 0348D] Simon of Oisy is praised by the author of the *Life of St Goswin, Abbot of Anchin*, book II, chapter 19. Simon’s father was Hugh of Mercœur, mentioned in the body of the letter.]

He commends the monks of Vaucelles to Simon’s protection, asking him to ratify his father’s donation.

Dearest friend, I was greatly delighted to learn from the report of Abbot Radulf [Note: [Col. 0348D] In ancient books the name is abbreviated as “R.”], of Vaucelles, that you desire my presence and conversation; nor am I certainly ungrateful for your goodwill toward me. Know that it is also my wish to satisfy your desire; but bodily infirmity prevents me from carrying out this wish, as it does also many other and very necessary affairs.

Yet although absent in body, I am present in spirit, [Col. 0348D] until, God willing, I may one day be present both in body and spirit—provided that we love not merely in word or speech, but in deed and truth. Therefore the truth of love will be made evident in the rendering of practical assistance. This, then, is what I ask: that, for my sake, you love, cherish, and, wherever necessary, uphold with your hand what is mine with you—that is, the brethren of Vaucelles and their church. In this you will both provide a conspicuous proof of your generosity and make clear the evidence of that charity which you promise me.

I now especially desire to test this charity in one matter: that you too grant Ligecourt, which your father gave me in my presence for the use of that monastery, [Col. 0349A] and do not render your father’s gift void. For our part, giving thanks for what has gone before, and hoping for similar things hereafter, we pour out prayers for you and yours to him who fulfils the desire of those who fear him and hears their petition (Ps. 144:19). We pray that you, your wife, and all who belong to you may be well.

## Letter 187

**To the Bishops to Be Summoned to Sens, against Peter Abelard**  
[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1140.—Abelard was born in the diocese of Nantes, of Berengar his father and Lucia his mother. He first studied philosophy at Paris under William of Champeaux; then mathematics under Roscelin; and finally theology under Anselm of Laon, not without envy and admiration. Afterwards, having begun at Paris to interpret the sacred books, he attracted many pupils, among them a certain Heloise, niece of Fulbert, canon of Paris. While instructing her mind, he violated her body.

Fulbert, bearing this injury impatiently, shamefully castrated Abelard, who had wished to make restitution by the honour of marriage, while he was spending the night at his lodging. Then both lovers, unable to endure their disgrace, sought hiding places: she became a nun at Argenteuil near Paris, [Col. 0349C] he a monk at Saint-Denis. But, everywhere either harassed or unhappy, he withdrew to a cell near the monastery, namely at Dégueil, and there publicly professed theology.

Yet, indulging too much in his own talent and reason, and advancing many matters insufficiently consonant with faith, he was brought before the council of Soissons, held by the legate Cono about the year 1121, as will be said below. There he was compelled to commit his book on the Trinity, or *Introduction to Theology*, containing suspect chapters, to the flames; he himself was confined in the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons. The *Life of St Goswin, Abbot*, book I, chapter 18, wrongly reports that this happened by order of Pope Innocent II, whereas Calixtus II was then pope.

At length, when Abelard was permitted to seek the desert, he retired to a wilderness in the diocese of Troyes and there built an oratory, first dedicated to the Holy Trinity and later distinguished by the name of the Paraclete. But he was not permitted to remain quiet even there. [Col. 0349D] Accordingly, summoned as abbot by the monks of Saint-Gildas in Lesser Brittany, in the diocese of Vannes, he found, as he himself relates in his *History of My Calamities*, “Christians and monks far more cruel and worse than pagans.”

He therefore returned again to his Paraclete oratory, and there installed Heloise with the sisters expelled from the monastery of Argenteuil, which Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, recovered in 1127. While living there, writing and teaching perversely, he was again called a heretic. Meanwhile several persons examined his writings, above all William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, who collected and refuted the chapters containing errors and sent the refutations to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in order to move them to avenge the injury done to faith. See Letters 326 and 327.

Abelard, unwilling to bear the name of heretic, challenged St Bernard, as though he were author of so great a calumny, to the council of Sens convened in 1140. Bernard accordingly attended the synod, though reluctantly. Impious doctrines from Abelard’s writings were produced, which he must either deny as not his own, or, if his own, abjure. But he, disturbed and unable to speak, as Geoffrey of Auxerre relates in his commentary on the Apocalypse; or fearing a popular uprising, as Otto of Freising has it in the passage cited below; or considering it safer to plead his case at Rome, as St Bernard says in Letter 193, because he had cardinal and clerical disciples there, appealed to the Roman curia.

Nonetheless the Fathers of the council condemned the errors and sent their list to Innocent, the supreme pontiff, together with several letters which Bernard wrote, both in his own name and in that of the Fathers, to Innocent and the cardinals. Especially worth seeing is Letter 190, in which he forcefully refutes the chief articles of error. Among Abelard’s own works there survive seventeen articles of error which a Paraclete manuscript there cited attests were sent by the synod to Innocent. But since we have nearly all of them in Bernard’s Letter 190 itself and in William’s Letter 390 here, it did not seem necessary to insert them at this point. The chapters which we report below from the Vatican manuscript are to be preferred—namely, in volume II, before the treatise *On the Errors of Abelard*.

When Innocent received the synodal letters, he immediately replied by the letter here numbered 194, to the Fathers of the council, condemning the errors. He also added another letter pronouncing sentence against Abelard himself, in these terms:

“Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren Samson, archbishop of Reims, Henry, archbishop of Sens, and his dearest son in Christ Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and apostolic blessing. [Col. 0350D] By these present writings we command your Fraternity to cause Peter Abelard and Arnold of Brescia, fabricators of perverse doctrine and attackers of the Catholic faith, to be separately confined in religious places, wherever shall seem best to you; and to have their books of error burned by fire wherever they may be found. Given at the Lateran, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of August.”

These letters bore the superscription: “Do not show these copies to anyone until these letters have been presented to the archbishops themselves at the Parisian conference which is near at hand.”

Abelard, therefore, understanding that he had been condemned at Rome, abandoned his appeal at the persuasion of Peter, abbot of Cluny. Received kindly by him, through his agency he was afterwards reconciled with St Bernard, and then with Innocent together with the Church. After spending two years at Cluny in great humility of mind, he died in the monastery of Saint-Marcel at Chalon, to which he had been sent by Abbot Peter for the treatment of illness, in the year of Christ 1142, in the sixty-third year of his age. Peter the Venerable greatly extolled the remarkable virtues displayed in that final course of Abelard’s life in book IV, letter 21, addressed to Heloise.

There are some who favour Abelard beyond measure and have gone so far as to declare him free from every error; first alleging that Bernard fought against phantoms and shadows, then undermining the authority of the council of Sens, and finally diminishing the judgment pronounced against Abelard by the Roman curia. Something brief must be said about these persons.

[Col. 0351B] I. Against Bernard, first, the authority of Otto of Freising is advanced. Although, as they say, he held “his abbot”—that is, the abbot of his own Order—in great veneration, he nevertheless writes that Bernard was “jealous from fervour for the Christian religion, and credulous from habitual gentleness, so that he abhorred masters who relied excessively and confidently upon human reasoning and secular wisdom, and readily lent his ear when someone reported something unfavourable about such men.” Otto indeed says this in book I of the *Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 47, on the occasion of Gilbert of Poitiers; yet it is also turned to Abelard’s advantage.

But since, according to Radevic, book II of the *Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 11, Otto was too devoted to Gilbert and, when death approached, requested that anything he had said in support of Gilbert’s view which could offend anyone should be corrected, this must be counted among his retractions. Indeed, Otto himself sufficiently expressed afterwards what he thought of Abelard. Thus he writes of him: “From his earliest age he devoted himself to the study of letters and other accomplishments; [Col. 0351C] but he was so arrogant, and so trusting in his own talent alone, that he scarcely condescended from the height of his mind to listen to teachers.” And below: “Taking the meaning of words or names in a natural sense, he rashly mixed it with theology. Therefore, teaching and writing about the Holy Trinity, he excessively attenuated the three persons … employing unsound examples,” and so forth. Add that, by Otto’s own admission, Abelard was judged a Sabellian heretic at the council of Soissons. Such is the authority of Otto against Bernard.

In the second place is advanced the testimony of Peter the Venerable on behalf of Abelard. Writing the letter already cited to Heloise, he affirms of Abelard that “no German appeared more abject than he, nor Martin himself poorer.” This is what Peter of Cluny truly says in describing the final period of Abelard’s life, spent at Cluny. But was Bernard contending over his future merits, so that he may be said to have fought against phantoms? Very aptly does the Chronicle of Cluny say, under Peter the Venerable: “Peter Abelard, recalled from errors of faith by Peter the Venerable, our abbot, and St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, abjuring what he had previously impiously taught concerning the faith, became a monk of Cluny. Then his mind, his tongue, and his work were always devoted to divine things … And, as is read of Gregory the Great, he allowed scarcely a moment to pass without either praying, reading, writing, or dictating … Therefore Peter the Venerable commended him earnestly,” and so forth.

Finally, many arguments of this kind are amassed, extolling either the man’s talent, his learning, or the excellent manner of his death, as though Bernard had denied any of these things.

II. Against the council of Sens, lack of power or jurisdiction is alleged, on the ground that neither the archbishop of Sens nor that of Reims, who were present at the council, had jurisdiction over Abelard, abbot of Saint-Gildas in the diocese of Vannes, [Col. 0352A] but rather the metropolitan of Tours, who was absent. Yet twelve years earlier Abelard had returned to the Paraclete oratory in the diocese of Troyes and was subject to the archbishop of Sens. Moreover, he had as judges those whom he himself sought, as Bernard testifies in Letter 191, written in the name of the council to Innocent: “From the place and the judge whom he had chosen, he appealed to the Apostolic See.”

For it was not Saint Bernard the abbot, as some mistakenly suppose, who stirred up this synod against Abelard. On the contrary, Abelard compelled St Bernard, reluctant and unwilling, to attend; this the holy Doctor plainly affirms in Letters 187 and 189, as does Geoffrey of Auxerre, formerly Abelard’s pupil, who speaks thus in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*: “Finally, Abelard approached the metropolitan of Sens, since a great council was shortly to be held in his church, and accused the abbot of Clairvaux of secretly disparaging his books. He further declared that he was prepared publicly to defend his writings, asking that the aforesaid abbot, if he had anything to say, be summoned to the council.” Abelard was therefore rightly condemned, since, as jurists say, anyone has jurisdiction over consenting parties: Law II, *On Judgments*.

The second device employed to undermine the authority of the synod is the testimony of Peter Berengar of Poitiers. In the *Apology* which he wrote for Abelard, his teacher, against the Fathers of the council and Bernard himself, he emitted such stale falsehoods and such monstrous, unworthy calumnies that it is astonishing that a man of sense could tolerate or bring forward so shameless and faithless a person. This man laughs at venerable bishops assailed as “drunkards, dogs, swine,” and by other insults, exposing himself not merely to mockery, but to the readers’ just indignation.

But let us see what he afterwards wrote, when more sound in mind, to the bishop of Mende: “But why, they ask, after finishing the first volume, do you not compose the second, as you had promised? Because in the course of time my good sense increased, and I went over, as the saying is, with both feet to the opinion of Abbot Bernard. I did not wish to be the defender of the chapters objected against Abelard, because, even if they contained sound doctrine, they did not sound sound. Then why, they ask, after your hand grew numb for the second book, did you not erase the first? I would have done so, I reply, had the effort not been futile; for copies would remain,” and so forth.

III. In the third place against the judgment of the Roman pontiff, the alleged undue haste of the sentence is urged: that, without examining the case, he condemned Abelard unheard. But did not the proceedings of the council of Sens suffice to inform the case, at which Abelard himself was present? Which cardinal or cleric of the Roman curia was ignorant of his doctrines, or—if it had been lawful—would not have attempted to shield from censure an author whom many of them had had as teacher?

Let Innocent’s sentence, therefore, stand; let the authority of the council of Sens and of St Bernard stand uninjured; and let there remain to Abelard no other means of defending error than the correction of his life and error. How much more soundly did that Heloise, after the death of her Abelard, request from Peter the Venerable an absolution for him to be placed upon Abelard’s tomb—this survives in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* and among Abelard’s works—than certain persons who labour to weave apologies excusing the errors which he himself did not cease to wash away to the end by tears and repentance. But enough of this.]

It urges the bishops energetically to undertake the cause of religion against Abelard.

[Col. 0349B] A report has gone out among many, and we believe it has reached you: namely, that we are summoned and challenged at Sens in the octave of [Col. 0350A] Pentecost to a contest for the defence of the faith—although “the servant of God ought not to strive, but rather to be patient toward all” (2 Tim. 2:24). If it were my own private cause, perhaps the child of your Holiness might not without reason glory in your patronage. But now, because the cause is yours as well—indeed, more yours—I exhort you with greater confidence and beg you more earnestly to prove yourselves friends in time of need.

I call you friends not of us, but of Christ, whose Bride cries to you amid the forest of heresies and the field of errors. These, springing up under your guardianship and protection, now almost choke her. The friend of the Bridegroom will not abandon her in times of need, in tribulation. Nor should you wonder that we summon you so suddenly and with such brief notice. For the opposing party in its craftiness [Col. 0350B] and cunning made this provision also: to attack us unprepared and compel us, unarmed, to fight.

## Letter 188

**To the Bishops and Cardinals of the Curia, on the Same Matter**  
[Note: [Col. 0352D] Written in the same year.]

He warns them to be vigilant against the errors of Peter Abelard.

[Col. 0351A]

To his lords and reverend fathers, the bishops and cardinals who are of the curia, the child of their holiness.

[Col. 0352A]

1. No one doubts that it belongs especially to you to remove scandals from the kingdom of God, cut down the thorns that arise, and quiet disputes. Thus Moses commanded when he went up the mountain: “You have Aaron and Hur with you,” he said; “if any question arises, you shall refer it to them” (Exod. 24:14). I mean that Moses who came through water, and not in water only, but in water and blood. Therefore he is greater than Moses, because he came also in blood.

And since zeal and the authority of the Roman Church stand for Hur and Aaron over the people of God, we rightly refer to it not questions but injuries to faith and wrongs against Christ; the reproaches and contempt directed against the Fathers; the scandals of the present and dangers to posterity. The faith of the simple is mocked; the mysteries of God are laid bare; questions concerning the highest matters are rashly debated; the Fathers are insulted because they judged these questions rather to be silenced than resolved.

Hence it happens that the Paschal Lamb, contrary to God’s ordinance (Exod. 12:9), is either boiled in water or torn apart raw, after the manner and in the speech of beasts. What remains is not burned with fire, but trampled underfoot. Thus human ingenuity claims everything for itself, reserving nothing for faith. It attempts things higher than itself, searches out stronger things, rushes into divine matters, profanes holy things rather than discloses them; what is closed and sealed it does not open, but plunders; and whatever it does not find accessible to itself, it judges to be nothing and disdains to believe.

2. Read, if you please, Peter Abelard’s book which he calls *Theology*; for it is readily available, since, as he boasts, it is much read in the curia. See what is there said concerning the Holy Trinity, the generation of the Son, the procession of the Holy Spirit, and countless other matters wholly unfamiliar to Catholic ears and minds. Read also another book called his *Sentences* [Note: Abelard denies in his *Apology* that he wrote any book under this title, and consequently charges that this attribution against him is made “through malice or ignorance”; Chesnius also maintains this in his notes. “St Bernard,” he says, “through ignorance attributes to Abelard himself a book of *Sentences* in Letter 188,” as though Bernard had attributed to Abelard the books of *Sentences* written by Peter the Master. But Peter was not so unknown to Bernard—who praises him in Letter 410—that he could have fallen into this error. Nor, at the time this letter was written, had Peter the Master issued his books of *Sentences*. We possess a book undoubtedly composed by Abelard himself, commonly called *Sic et Non* (“Yes and No”), whose title a former manuscript gives thus: “Here begin Sentences collected from the divine Scriptures which appear contradictory; because of this apparent contradiction, this compilation of Sentences is called *Yes and No*.” Whether St Bernard had this book in view when he wrote this is unknown to me. Besides the works of Abelard listed by the aforesaid Chesnius, we further possess his book on the Hexaemeron, dedicated to his Heloise.]; likewise the book entitled *Know Thyself*; and observe how great a crop of sacrileges and errors grows wild in them [Note: This is the reading of the better manuscripts; the printed editions read: “how great crops grow wild there also.”]: what he thinks concerning the soul of Christ, the person of Christ, Christ’s descent into hell, the sacrament of the altar; the power of binding and loosing; original sin, concupiscence, the sin of delight, the sin of weakness, the sin of ignorance, the act of sin, and the will to sin.

If you judge that I am rightly moved, then be moved yourselves. And lest you be moved in vain, act in accordance with the office you hold, the dignity in which you stand, and the power you have received: so that he who ascended to heaven may descend as far as hell; and that works of darkness which have dared to come into light may be exposed from light into light, so that, while one who sins publicly is publicly rebuked, others also may restrain themselves—those who make darkness light, disputing at crossroads [Col. 0353D] concerning divine things, speaking evil in their hearts and writing it in their books. Thus let the mouth of those who speak iniquity be stopped.

## Letter 189

**To Pope Innocent, on the Same Matter**  
[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

He expresses his distress over Abelard’s errors, which arose immediately after the schism, and urges the Pope to oppose them.

[Col. 0354A]

To his most loving father and lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

1. Scandals must come: they must, but they are not pleasant. Therefore the prophet says: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7). And the Apostle desires to be dissolved and to rest with Christ. Another of the saints says: “It is enough for me, Lord; take away my soul, for I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings 19:4).

I too now have something in common with the saints—in will only, not in merit. For I too would now wish to be removed from the midst, overcome, I confess, by faintness of spirit and the tempest. Yet I fear that I shall not be found as ready as I am affected. I am weary of life, and do not know whether it is expedient to die. Perhaps I differ even from the saints in my desires: they are drawn out by desire for better things, whereas I am compelled to depart by scandals and afflictions. For he says: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is far better” (Phil. 1:23). Thus in the saint desire prevails, and in me feeling prevails. But in this most miserable life neither he can obtain the good which he desires, nor can I be without what I suffer as grievous. Therefore we both desire to depart with equal willingness, but not with equal intention.

2. Foolishly, I had long promised myself rest if only the Leonine rage should cease [Note: That is, the schism of Peter Leo.] and peace be restored to the Church. For behold, it has ceased, but I have not. I did not know that I was in the valley of tears, or I had forgotten that I dwell in the land of forgetfulness. I did not consider that the land in which I live brings forth thorns and thistles for me: when these are cut down, new ones succeed them, and then others again grow up after them without end and without interruption.

I had heard this; but, as I now experience, affliction itself gives understanding to what is heard. The sorrow has been renewed, not eradicated; tears have overflowed because evils have prevailed; and upon those who have experienced frost, snow has rushed. Who can stand before this cold? By this cold charity grows cold, so that iniquity may abound. [Col. 0354D] We escaped the lion, but fell into the dragon [Note: Peter Abelard.], who perhaps harms no less by lying in wait than the former did by roaring from on high.

Indeed, he no longer lies in wait. Would that his poisonous leaves still lay hidden in chests and were not read in public places! Books fly abroad; and those who hated light because they are evil have rushed into the light, imagining light to be darkness. Darkness is forced upon cities and castles in place of light; instead of honey—or rather, poison in honey—is everywhere offered for people to drink. They have passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people. A new Gospel is coined for peoples and nations; a new faith is set forth; another foundation is laid besides that which has been laid. Virtues and vices are discussed not morally, the sacraments of the Church not faithfully, and the mystery of the Holy Trinity not simply or soberly; but all things are offered to us perversely, all contrary to custom and contrary to what we have received.

3. Goliath advances, towering in body, surrounded by his famous martial equipment; and his armour-bearer Arnold of Brescia goes before him. Scale is joined to scale, and no breath passes between them. For the bee that was in France whistled to the bee from Italy [Note: This is the genuine reading, alluding to Isaiah 7:18: “The Lord shall whistle for the fly which is at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee which is in the land of Assyria.” The bee from France is Abelard; the bee from Italy is Arnold of Brescia, a city in Italy; see the notes on Letter 195.], and they came together against the Lord and against his Christ. They bent the bow; they prepared [Col. 0355C] their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. Yet in food and clothing they possess the appearance of godliness, while denying its power. They deceive many all the more because they transform themselves into angels of light when they are servants of Satan.

Thus Goliath, together with his armour-bearer, standing between the two battle lines, cries out against the ranks of Israel and reproaches the companies of the saints—boldly, of course, because he perceives that David is absent. Finally, in disparagement of the doctors of the Church, he exalts philosophers with great praises; he prefers their inventions and his own novelties to the doctrine and faith of the Catholic Fathers. And while all flee from his face, he seeks me, the least of all, for single combat.

4. Finally, the archbishop of Sens wrote to me—at his own instigation—appointing a day for a meeting, on which that man was to establish, if he could, in the presence of the archbishop and his fellow bishops, his perverse doctrines, against which I had dared to utter a protest. I refused: first, because I am a child, while he is a warrior from his youth; secondly, because I judged it unworthy that the rationale of the faith [Col. 0355D] should be handed over to petty human arguments for debate, when it is known to rest upon truth so certain and stable. I said that his writings sufficed to accuse him, and that the matter was not mine, but the bishops’, whose ministry it was to judge doctrines. Nevertheless, he raised his voice no less—indeed, all the more; he summoned many people and gathered accomplices. What he may have written about me to his disciples, I do not care to say. Everywhere he spread the report that, on the appointed day, he would answer me at Sens. The report went out to everyone and could not remain hidden from me. At first I disregarded it, for I was not greatly moved by popular rumor. Yet, yielding—though reluctantly, so much so that I wept—[Col. 0356A] to the advice of friends, who saw how everyone was preparing themselves as though for a spectacle, they feared both that our absence would cause scandal among the people and that it would give the adversary greater boldness; and that the error would be more strongly confirmed when there was no one to answer or oppose it. Therefore I came to the place on the appointed day, unprepared and unarmed, except that I turned over in my mind: “Do not prepare beforehand how you are to answer; for in that hour you will be given what to say” (Matt. 10:19); and: “The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me” (Ps. 117:6).

Besides the bishops and abbots, there assembled very many religious men, masters of schools from the cities, many learned clerics, and the king himself was present. Thus, before them all, with my opponent standing opposite, [Col. 0356B] certain chapters extracted from his books were produced. When they began to be read, he went out, unwilling to hear them, appealing from the judges whom he himself had chosen—an appeal which we do not think permissible. The chapters, however, having been examined by the judgment of all, were found hostile to the faith and contrary to truth. I say this in my own defense, lest I be thought to have acted in so grave a matter out of frivolity or rashness.

5. But you, O successor of Peter, will judge whether one who attacks Peter’s faith ought to find refuge in Peter’s See. You, I say, friend of the Bridegroom, will see how to free the Bride from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue. Yet, that I may speak a little more boldly with my lord, attend also to yourself, most loving Father, and to the grace of God which is in you. Was it not when you were little in your own eyes that he himself set you over nations and kingdoms? [Col. 0356C] For what purpose, except that you might uproot and destroy, and build and plant? Therefore, he who took you from your father’s house and anointed you with the anointing of his mercy—consider, I beg you, from that time onward, how great things he has done for your soul; how great things through you for his Church; how much in the Lord’s field, with heaven and earth as witnesses, has been uprooted and destroyed as powerfully as it was beneficially; and how much, in turn, has been well built, planted, and propagated.

God stirred up the fury of schismatics in your time so that they might be crushed through your work. “I saw a fool firmly rooted, and immediately his beauty was cursed. I saw, yes, I saw the wicked man exalted exceedingly and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. 36:35–36). “There must,” he says, “be heresies and schisms, [Col. 0356D] so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19). And in the schism, as has been said, the Lord has already tested you and known you. But lest anything be wanting to your crown, behold, heresies have arisen.

Therefore, for the completion of your virtues, and lest you be found to have done less than your great episcopal predecessors, seize for us, most loving Father, the foxes that devastate the Lord’s vineyard while they are still small, lest, if they grow and multiply, whatever creatures of this kind are not exterminated by you should be despaired of by posterity. Although they are no longer small, nor few, but certainly rather large and numerous, and will not be exterminated except by a strong hand—by yours. [Col. 0357A] Jacinctus has shown us many evils; for he did not do, or could not do, all that he wished. Yet it seemed to me that he ought to be borne with patiently in his treatment of me, since in that court he spared neither your person nor the Curia. This my Nicholas—indeed yours as well—will report better by living voice.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] The same words occur at the end of Letter 338, to Haimeric. Who this Jacinctus or Hyacinthus was is uncertain. Was he the man later made cardinal by Lucius II, surnamed Bobo, of the title of Santa Maria in Cosmedin? He appears to be mentioned in Letter 508, in Chesnius, vol. II. Nicholas was a monk of Clairvaux and later St Bernard’s notary; see the note to Letter 298.]

## LETTER 190

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

**TO POPE INNOCENT, CONCERNING CERTAIN ERRORS OF PETER ABELARD.**

Because of its length, this letter is included among the Treatises in volume two.

## LETTER 191

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Written in the same year.]

**TO INNOCENT, ON BEHALF OF THE LORD ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS, ETC.** Abelard, swollen with a vain opinion of learning and boasting of the favor of the Roman Curia, should promptly be restrained by pontifical authority.

[Col. 0357B]

To the most reverend lord and dearest Father, INNOCENT, by the grace of God supreme pontiff: SAMSON, archbishop of Rheims; JOSCELIN of Soissons; GEOFFREY of Châlons; and ALVISUS of Arras, the willing service of due submission.

1. Since your ears are occupied with many matters, we make our account brief concerning a lengthy affair, especially because the same matter is set forth more fully and at greater length in the letters of the archbishop of Sens. Peter Abelard strives to empty the Christian faith of its merit, since he imagines that he can comprehend by human reason all that God is. He has ascended to the heavens and descended to the depths. Nothing is hidden from him, whether in the depth of hell or in the heights above. [Col. 0357C] He is a great man in his own eyes, disputing about faith against faith, walking in things great and too wonderful for himself, a searcher of majesty, a maker of heresies.

Long ago he composed a book on his Trinity; but it was examined by fire under the legate of the Roman Church, because iniquity was found in it.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Namely, under Cono, at the Synod of Soissons in 1121; see the notes to Letter 187 and the Preface to volume I, on the schism of Anacletus.]

“Cursed be he who rebuilds the ruins of Jericho.” That book rose from the dead, and with it the heresies of many that had slept; they rose and appeared to many. Already it has stretched its branches to the sea and its shoots to Rome. This is that man’s boast: that his book has a place in the Roman Curia where it may lay its head. From this his madness has been confirmed and strengthened.

[Col. 0357D]

2. Therefore, when the abbot of Clairvaux, armed with zeal for faith and justice, accused him in the presence of bishops on these matters, he neither confessed nor denied; but, from the place and judge which he himself had chosen, without injury or burden, in order to prolong his iniquity, [Col. 0358A] he appealed to the Apostolic See. The bishops, however, who had assembled for this purpose, deferring to Your Reverence, took no action against his person. They merely condemned, as a medicinal necessity lest the disease spread, the chapters of his books which had been condemned by the holy Fathers. Since, therefore, that man draws a multitude after himself and has people who believe him, it is necessary for you to meet this contagion with a swift remedy.

> Medicine is prepared too late  
> When evils have gained strength through long delay.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, V. 91–92.)

[Note: [Col. 0358D] The editions of Ovid which I have examined read *convaluere* (“have grown strong”), as Bernard himself does below, Letter 342, §3.]

We have proceeded in this affair as far as we dared. It remains for you, most blessed Father, to take care lest in your days some stain of heretical perversity [Col. 0358B] should blemish the beauty of the Church. The Bride of Christ has been entrusted to you, friend of the Bridegroom; it is yours at last to present the chaste virgin to Christ as to one husband.

## LETTER 192. TO MASTER GUIDO OF CASTELLO

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Written in the year of Christ 1140.—In three Colbert manuscripts: “To Master Guido of Castello, who had been Peter’s disciple and in whom he especially placed his confidence, and who later became Pope Celestine, namely the second of that name, in 1143.” To the same person, Letter 169; after it this letter is placed in certain manuscripts, as is the following one.]

He urges him to love and support Abelard in such a way that he does not support his errors.

To the venerable lord and dearest Father, Master GUIGO, by the grace of God priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church: BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, not to turn aside to the right hand or to the left.

I wrong you if I believe that you love anyone so much that you love his errors along with him. [Col. 0358C] For whoever loves someone in that fashion does not yet know how he ought to love him. Such love is earthly, animal, devilish, harmful alike to the lover and the beloved. Let others think of others as they please; I still cannot judge otherwise of you than reason and the rule of equity require. Some judge first and prove afterward; but I shall not decide, before tasting, whether a drink is sweet or bitter.

Master Peter introduces into his books profane novelties of words and meanings. Disputing concerning faith against faith, he attacks the law with the words of the law. He sees nothing through a mirror or in an enigma; rather, he beholds all things face to face, walking in things great and marvelous beyond himself. It would have been better for him, according to the title of his book—

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Which he entitled *Know Yourself*.]

—to know himself [Col. 0358D] and not exceed his measure, but to think with sobriety. I do not accuse him before the Father; his own book accuses him, the book in which he took evil pleasure. When he speaks of the Trinity, he savors of Arius; when of grace, of Pelagius; when of [Col. 0359A] the person of Christ, of Nestorius. I presume too little upon your fairness if I ask you long and earnestly to place no one before Christ in the cause of Christ. But know this: it is expedient for you, to whom authority has been given by the Lord; expedient for the Church of Christ; expedient also for that man himself, that silence be imposed upon him whose mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit.

## LETTER 193. TO MASTER IVO, CARDINAL

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Written in the year of Christ 1140.—Ivo, formerly a canon of Saint-Victor at Paris, was created cardinal-priest of Saint Lawrence in Damaso in 1130; see Letter 144. Sent as legate into France, he excommunicated Count Ralph of Vermandois; see the note to Letter 216. On his will, read Letter 218.]

**ON THE SAME MATTER.** It is unworthy that Abelard should find supporters in the Roman Curia.

To his beloved IVO, by the grace of God priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church: BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, to love justice and hate iniquity.

[Col. 0359B] Master Peter Abelard, a monk without rule and a prelate without solicitude, neither keeps order nor is held by order. He is unlike himself: Herod within, John without; altogether ambiguous, possessing nothing of a monk except name and habit. But what is that to me? “Each shall bear his own burden.” There is another matter which I cannot conceal, one belonging to all who love Christ’s name. He speaks iniquity on high; he corrupts the integrity of faith and the chastity of the Church. He transgresses the boundaries set by our fathers: [p. 186] in disputing and writing concerning faith, the sacraments, and the holy Trinity, he changes, adds to, and diminishes every individual thing according to his own will.

In his books and works he shows himself to be a fabricator of falsehood and a devotee of perverse doctrines, proving himself a heretic [Col. 0359C] not so much by error as by obstinacy and defense of error. He is a man exceeding his measure, who by the wisdom of speech empties the cross of Christ of its power. He knows nothing of all that is in heaven and on earth except himself. He was condemned at Soissons with his work before the legate of the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] Namely, about the year 1121.]

But as though that condemnation did not suffice him, he acts again so as to be condemned again; and now his latest error is worse than the former. Yet he is secure because he boasts that he has had cardinals and clerics of the Curia as disciples, and he enlists them in defense of his former and present error—those by whom he ought to fear being judged and condemned. Whoever has the Spirit of God should remember that verse: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies?” [Col. 0359D] (Ps. 138:21). May God through you and through his other sons deliver his Church from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

## LETTER 194

[Note: [Col. 0360D] Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

**RESPONSE OF POPE INNOCENT AGAINST THE HERESIES OF PETER ABELARD.**

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers HENRY of Sens and SAMSON of Rheims, archbishops, and their suffragans; and [Col. 0360A] to his dearest son in Christ BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

1. As the Apostle testifies, just as there is one Lord, so there is known to be one faith (Eph. 4:5). Upon it, as upon an immovable foundation—beside which no one can lay another—the inviolable firmness of the Catholic Church stands established. Therefore blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles, because of his outstanding confession of this faith, deserved to hear from our Lord and Savior: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18), the rock plainly signifying the firmness of faith and the solidity of Catholic unity. This indeed is the seamless garment of our Redeemer, for which the soldiers cast lots but which they could not divide (John [Col. 0360B] 19:23, 34). Against it, in the beginning, the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things; the kings of the earth stood forth and princes gathered together as one (Ps. 2:1–2). But the Apostles, leaders of the Lord’s flock, and their successors, apostolic men, inflamed by the ardor of love and zeal for rectitude, did not hesitate to defend the faith and to plant it in others’ hearts by the shedding of their own blood. Finally, when the rage of persecutors had ceased, the Lord commanded the winds, and there was a great calm in the Church.

2. But because the enemy of the human race always prowls about seeking whom he may devour, he brought in the deceitful deception of heretics to assail the purity of the faith. Against them the pastors of the Churches rose manfully and condemned their perverse doctrines together with their authors. At the great Synod of Nicaea the heretic Arius was condemned. The Synod of Constantinople condemned the heretic Manichaeus by due sentence. At the Synod of Ephesus Nestorius received the deserved condemnation of his error. Likewise, the Synod of Chalcedon refuted by a most just sentence the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his accomplices.

Moreover Marcian, though a layman, was nevertheless a most Christian emperor. Inflamed by love for the Catholic faith, he wrote to our most holy predecessor Pope John against those who endeavor to profane the sacred mysteries, and among other things said:

> “Let no cleric, soldier, or person of any other condition henceforth attempt publicly to treat of the Christian faith. For whoever seeks to reopen and dispute anew matters once judged and rightly determined injures the judgment of the most reverend synod. Nor shall punishment be lacking for those who despise this law, as for sacrilegious persons. Therefore, if the person who has dared publicly to treat of religion is a cleric, he shall be removed from the fellowship of clerics.” [p. 187]

[Note: [Col. 0360D] A double error seems to have crept into this passage: one concerning the heading and another concerning the name of the pope then reigning. This letter or decree of Emperor Marcian is indeed found among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, celebrated under Pope Leo the Great in 451; but it is addressed to the citizens of Constantinople, not to Pope Leo, much less to John, who occupied the Roman see more than eighty years after the death of Emperor Marcian. The passage may therefore be restored by expressing the pope’s name in the ablative absolute, thus: “Writing to our most holy predecessor Pope Leo,” etc.]

3. We grieve, however, because, as we have learned from inspection of your letters and from the chapters of errors sent by your Fraternity [Col. 0361A] to us,

[Note: [Col. 0361C] These may be found in volume II, with Opusculum 11.]

in these last days, when perilous times are at hand, both the heresies previously mentioned and other perverse doctrines opposed to the Catholic faith have begun to spring up in the ruinous teaching of Peter Abelard. Yet in this we find special consolation and give thanks to almighty God, who in your regions has raised up such sons in place of fathers and has willed, in the time of our apostolate, that his Church should have such distinguished pastors, who strive to withstand the calumnies of the new heretic and to present the spotless Bride as a chaste virgin to Christ, one husband.

We therefore, who, though unworthy, are seen to sit in the chair of blessed Peter, to whom the Lord said, “And you, when once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32), having taken counsel with our brother [Col. 0361B] bishops and cardinals, have condemned by the authority of the holy canons the chapters sent to us by your discretion and all the perverse doctrines of Peter himself together with their author, and have imposed perpetual silence upon him as upon a heretic. We also decree that all followers and defenders of his error are to be separated from communion with the faithful and bound by the bond of excommunication. Given at the Lateran, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [16 July].

## LETTER 195. TO THE BISHOP OF CONSTANCE

[Note: [Col. 0361C] Written in the year of Christ 1140.—It is uncertain whether this letter is to be understood as addressed to the bishop of Constance in Gaul or to the bishop of Constance on the Rhine. The latter seems more likely, because Arnold, expelled from the kingdom of the Franks, is said to have been hiding with the recipient of this letter. Hermann of Arbon then presided over this see. From Book VI, chapter 1, of *The Miracles of Bernard*, he visited Bernard at Frankfurt and brought Bernard himself to Constance. Geoffrey likewise dedicated the miracles of the same saint to him, beginning with Book VI, chapter 10.]

He urges him to expel Arnold of Brescia, driven from Italy and Gaul and now hiding with him, or rather to keep him in chains in order to avert greater harm.

[Col. 0361C]

1. “If the master of the house knew at what hour the thief would come, he would surely watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” [Col. 0362A] (Matt. 24:43). Do you know that a thief has broken into a house by night—not yours, but the Lord’s, though entrusted to you? Yet it cannot be doubtful that you know what is happening with you, when it could reach even us, so far away. Nor is it surprising if you could not foresee the hour or watch the thief’s nocturnal entrance. But it is surprising if, now that he has been caught, you do not recognize him, do not hold him, and do not prevent him from carrying away your spoils—or rather, Christ’s most precious possessions: namely, souls, whom he marked beforehand with his image and redeemed with his blood.

Perhaps you still hesitate and wonder whom I mean. I speak of Arnold of Brescia.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Otto of Freising portrays the man as follows, in *The Deeds of Frederick*, Book II, chapter 20: “This Arnold, native of Brescia, a city of Italy, and a cleric of that church, ordained only as a reader, had once had Peter Abelard as his teacher. He was a man not dull by nature, yet more abundant in a flood of words than in weight of thought; a lover of singularity and eager for novelty—the sort of character whose talents incline toward the fabrication of heresies and disturbances of schisms. Returning from study in Gaul to Italy, he assumed a religious habit in order to deceive more effectively, attacking everything, gnawing at everything, sparing no one, detracting from clerics and bishops, persecuting monks, and flattering only laymen. [Col. 0362C] For he said that neither clerics possessing property, nor bishops possessing regalian rights, nor monks possessing possessions could in any way be saved; that all such things belonged to the prince and ought to be granted from his beneficence for the use of laymen alone. Besides this, he is said not to have held sound views concerning the sacrament of the altar and infant baptism.”

The same author adds that “he was punished with silence at a Roman council, namely in 1138, expelled from Italy, and withdrew to the German town of Zürich, where he poured forth perverse doctrines. At length, when the death of Innocent became known, at the beginning of Eugenius’s pontificate he entered the city and stirred it more strongly into sedition, proposing the examples of the ancient Romans, who, by the mature counsel of the senate [Col. 0362D] … had made the whole world their own. Therefore he taught that the Capitol must be rebuilt, senatorial dignity renewed, and the equestrian order reformed; that nothing in the administration of the city belonged to the Roman Pontiff, who ought to be content with ecclesiastical jurisdiction. The evil of this poisonous teaching began to grow so strong that not only were the houses and splendid palaces of Roman nobles and cardinals destroyed, but the venerable persons of cardinals also were dragged about by the furious mob, some having been shamefully wounded.”

The same author attests, in Book VII, chapter 20 of his *Chronicle*, that Jordan, son of Peter Leo, was elected Patrician. “At last,” he says, “falling into the hands of certain men, he was captured on the borders of Tuscany, reserved for the judgment of the Emperor, and finally hanged by the prefect of the city. His body was reduced to ashes on a pyre and scattered into the Tiber, lest the foolish populace should hold his corpse in veneration.” These details have been given at length, but suitably to the occasion.]

Would that his teaching were as sound as his manner of life is austere. And if you wish to know, he is a man who neither eats nor drinks, hungering and thirsting with the devil alone for the blood of souls.
