He is one of those whom apostolic vigilance identifies as “having the appearance of piety but utterly denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5); and the Lord himself says: “They will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves” (Matt. 7:15).

Up to this time, wherever he has lived, he has left behind such foul and savage traces that, once he has set foot somewhere, he does not dare at all to return there. Indeed, he violently agitated and disturbed the very land in which he was born. Therefore, accused before the lord pope of a most evil schism, he was driven from his native soil and compelled also to swear that he would not return except by permission of the Apostolic See. Later, for a similar reason, this notable schismatic was expelled from the kingdom of the Franks. Cursed by the Apostle Peter, [Col. 0363A] he had attached himself to Peter Abelard, and with him—and even before him—he tried fiercely and obstinately to defend all Abelard’s errors already exposed and condemned by the Church. [p. 188]

2. Yet in all this his fury has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Even as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, unable now to remain among his own people, he does not cease among strangers to go about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. And now with you, as we have heard, he works iniquity and devours your people like bread for food. His mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; his feet are swift to shed blood; ruin and misery are in his ways, and he has not known the way of peace. He is an enemy of Christ’s cross, a sower of discord, a maker [Col. 0363B] of schisms, a disturber of peace, a divider of unity; his teeth are weapons and arrows, and his tongue a sharp sword. His words are smoother than oil, yet they are darts. Thus, by flattering speech and an imitation of virtue, he is accustomed to entice the rich and powerful, according to the saying: “He sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, to kill the innocent” (Ps. 9:29).

Finally, once he has secured their goodwill and friendship, you will see the man openly rise against the clergy, relying on military tyranny; rise against the bishops themselves; and rage indiscriminately against every ecclesiastical order. Knowing this, I do not know whether in so grave a crisis you can act better or more beneficially than, according to the Apostle’s admonition, to “remove the evil one from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13). Yet the friend of the Bridegroom will take care rather to bind than to drive him away, lest he now be able to roam about and do still more harm. For while the lord pope was still among us, because of the evil reports he heard about him, he commanded this to be done in writing; but there was no one to do what was good. Finally, if Scripture beneficially commands the capture of the little foxes that devastate the vineyard (Song 2:15), how much more should the great and savage wolf be bound, lest he burst into Christ’s sheepfolds and slaughter and destroy the sheep?

## LETTER 196. TO GUIDO, LEGATE, ON THE SAME MATTER

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

He warns him to avoid familiarity with Arnold of Brescia, lest under Guido’s authority Arnold disseminate his errors more securely.

1. Arnold of Brescia, whose manner of life is honey and whose teaching poison; whose head is that of a dove and whose tail that of a scorpion; whom Brescia vomited out, Rome recoiled from, France rejected, Germany abhors, and Italy refuses to receive, is said to be with you. See, I beg you, that he does not do greater harm under your authority. For since he possesses both skill and will to harm, if your favor is added, [Col. 0364A] it will be a threefold cord, difficult to break and, I fear, exceedingly harmful.

I think one of two things, if indeed it is true that you have the man with you: either he is insufficiently known to you, or—what is more credible—you are confident of his correction. Would that this confidence not be vain. Who will grant that a son of Abraham may be raised from this stone? What a welcome gift would Mother Church receive from your hands: a vessel for honor which she has endured so long as an instrument of dishonor! It is permissible to make the attempt; but a prudent man will be cautious not to go beyond the limit fixed by the Apostle, who says: “Avoid a heretical man after a first and second admonition, knowing that one of this sort is perverted and sins, condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10–11).

Otherwise, [Col. 0364B] to keep him as a familiar companion and frequently admit him to conversation—not to mention dining—is evidence of favor and armor for a strong enemy. A member of the household and table-companion of the legate of the Apostolic See will safely proclaim and easily persuade whatever he wishes. For who would suspect anything evil of a man at the lord pope’s side? And even if he speaks perversely in public, who would readily dare oppose one who stands at your side?

2. Moreover, you see what traces he has left behind wherever he has lived. Not without cause did apostolic authority compel a man born in Italy to cross the Alps, and does not permit him to return home. Who among the foreigners to whom he has been expelled would not desire by every means to return him to his own people? And surely, his relation to all is such that [Col. 0364C] he is hated by all: this confirms the justice of the judgment he bears, so that no one may say that the lord pope was deceived.

What, then, is it to disparage the sentence of the supreme pontiff—and a sentence whose rectitude the life of the very man against whom it was given proclaims, even if his tongue conceals it? Therefore, to favor this man is to oppose the lord pope, and even the Lord God. For by whomever a just sentence is justly given, it is certain that it has proceeded from him who speaks in the prophet: “I am he who speaks righteousness” (Isa. 63:1). Yet I trust in your prudence and integrity that, once you have seen this letter and are certain of the truth, you will henceforth not be led to consent to anything in this matter except what befits you and benefits the Church of God, for whose sake you discharge this legation. We love [Col. 0364D] you and are ready for your service.

## LETTER 197. TO PETER, DEAN OF BESANÇON

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Written in the year of Christ 1141.—In two Colbert manuscripts this letter is titled “To Peter of Besançon,” without an added office; in a third, “of Besançon”; in a fourth, “of Bisupinum.” In the earliest editions, “To Peter at Besançon”; later editions added “dean,” and some “archdeacon.” We once conjectured that he had been a monk of La Chaise-Dieu—an eminent Benedictine monastery among the Auvergnats—from the two following letters, which seemed to have been written about the same person. [Col. 0364D] But from a charter of Anseric, archbishop of Besançon, concerning Faverney, we infer that they were different persons. To this charter, in 1132, Peter de Treva, dean of Saint Stephen’s, subscribed together with Hugh, archdeacon of Faverney. The church of Saint Stephen was the cathedral at Besançon, as was also that of Saint John the Evangelist, which alone now remains; the other was recently demolished.]

He rebukes him for injuries inflicted upon the abbot of Chari-Locus.

We take the journey of the abbot of Chari-Locus [Col. 0365A] as though we already saw him dead. Whatever danger threatens him, whatever labor presses upon him, is attributed chiefly to you—and this I grieve deeply. We did not expect this from you, for neither did we deserve it. We thought you one sort of man and find you another. Those who were present at the proceeding bear witness concerning you that you conducted yourself in it neither sincerely nor according to justice. And I believe this in part. For the venerable abbot of Bellevaux [Col. 0366D] also is not very pleased with you.

[Note: [Col. 0364D] Chari-Locus—“Dear Place”—in the diocese of Besançon, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, was founded in 1131. Its first abbot [Col. 0365D] was Guido, who is the subject of this letter and the next. A monk named Peter harassed and unjustly oppressed him, and he appealed to Pope Innocent with Bernard’s letters of recommendation (Letter 198). But when that crafty man obtained that his case be remitted to Gallican judges, judgment was entrusted to John, formerly abbot of Bonnevaux of the Cistercians and then bishop of Valence, who was to settle the dispute together with the bishop of Grenoble. On that occasion it was first established that Cistercians should be entrusted with judging disputes concerning their Order, because of their proven integrity of faith. Subsequent practice introduced the famous and honorable legal exception: “Although no one may be a judge not only in his own case but not even in that of his associates” (Digest, “On the Jurisdiction of All Judges,” law I, *Qui de jurisdictione*, *Judicium*), “nevertheless, if the judge’s character is such that every reasonable suspicion disappears—as if he is a Cistercian monk—this rule does not apply, nor may such a person be challenged,” as Tiraquellus, *On Penalties for Temporary Remission*, 15, no. 60, and many others state. After judgment was pronounced in favor of the abbot of Chari-Locus, the aforesaid Peter again appealed to Innocent, to whom Bernard wrote Letter 199, asking that the just sentence of the bishops be confirmed.]

[Col. 0365B] Do not, I beg you, do not persecute the servants of God, of whom you read that God himself has said: “Whoever touches you touches the apple of my eye” (Zech. 2:8). Do not uproot from our hearts, once and for all, whatever good opinion we may formerly have held of you. And we say this to you not because we do not love you, but so that that may be removed from between us which could lead us not to love you. I speak as a friend: it is not advantageous to you, nor to your Church, that the lord pope should learn what was done, exactly as it was done.

## LETTER 198

[Note: [Col. 0366D] Written in the year of Christ 1141.]

**TO LORD POPE INNOCENT.** He asks that Guido be vindicated against the force and wrongs of his oppressor. Nothing is more fitting for the supreme prelate of the Church than zeal for justice.

1. In the prosecution of the case which is being laid before your presence by our dearest brother Guy, abbot of Charieu, I think the wrong done by the aggressor, the innocence of the sufferer, and the negligence of the judge are sufficiently evident. In short, driven by the violence of his calumniator and by the lack of justice, the poor man has been compelled to flee to your presence [Col. 0365C], reckoning neither the labor of the journey, nor the expense, nor the danger of the time. A lover of peace, he has given himself into the hands of death lest he live amid disturbance. Graciously, I beg you, look upon the needy and poor man, lest so great labor and suffering on the part of one so slight in strength have been made known to your fatherly ears in vain. Long ago, in letters once and twice, I testified to you concerning that man who now calumniates him, that he was both a betrayer of his own profession and a destroyer of a monastery. [Note: [Col. 0366D] This monastery appears to be none other than the abbey of Blessed Mary of Faverney, whose government Anseric, archbishop of Besançon, entrusted in 1133 to Stephen of Mercœur, then abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. Bernard rightly calls this Stephen a religious man, since he is said to have shone with miracles; he died on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in 1146. On the abbey of Faverney, see below in Letter 391.] But now I say, even weeping, that he is an enemy of Christ’s cross, a most violent oppressor of the saints who dwell around him, and a calumniator of the poor: having now scarcely anything of his own left to devour, he rages tyrannically everywhere against what belongs to his neighbors. [Col. 0366A] He lies in claiming the habit of a monk, but in deed proves himself one of the robbers: altogether forgetful of monastic observances, a despiser of laws and canons. Brazen against shame, senseless against fear, inflexible against compassion, rash in anger, bold in crime, prone to wrongs. And I wonder how the religious man, the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, can either fail to know or dissemble so many and such great vices in his monk.

2. But what is that to us? Let him see to it himself: he stands or falls before his own lord. It is enough for us to be delivered from his hands. We urgently demand from you what has been tried elsewhere in vain. We looked around, and there was no helper. We have come to the common refuge; to that refuge we flee, and there we trust that we shall be delivered. Let compassion only be present; for power is not lacking. Indeed, from the privilege of the Apostolic See it is evident that the highest authority and full power in these matters belong preeminently to your supreme authority. Yet among the other distinctions of your singular primacy, this more especially and more nobly ennobles your apostolate and makes it illustrious: that you rescue the poor man from the hand of those stronger than he. In my judgment, there is no gem more precious in your crown than that zeal by which you are accustomed to champion the oppressed and do not allow the rod of sinners to rest upon the lot of the righteous—namely, because of what follows: “That the righteous may not stretch out their hands to iniquity” (Ps. 124:3); or because of what is said elsewhere: “For while the wicked exalts himself, the poor man is consumed” (Ps. 9:23). Thus, from the very thing by which one man is tortured in body, another perishes more grievously in soul. [Col. 0366C]

3. There is likewise a monastery of our Order near this one, harassed in the same way by the grievous attacks of evil men; and there is none to ransom it or make it safe. On its behalf also your servant does not fear to stir your fatherly compassion with tearful prayers. Who these men are, and what pretext they have for calumniating, the bearer of this letter, the abbot, will relate to you truthfully and in person. May Almighty God preserve you for us through long years, for the protection of us all who, in the habit and profession of penitence, lead a poor life, so that, delivered from the hand of our enemies, we may serve him without fear (Luke 1:74).

## LETTER CXCIX

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Written in the same year.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. On the matter above.—He asks that the judgment given for religious persons unjustly oppressed be confirmed, and that no further hearing be granted to calumnies.

[Col. 0367A]

How long shall the wicked still be proud, and the poor be consumed? How long shall such great innocence be harassed by such great shamelessness—and this while Innocent lives? Without doubt our sins are the cause that my lord so late detects those who deceive him, and so slowly hears those crying to him—at least in this case. For in other matters we know that it is customary for my lord both to understand quickly and to show mercy readily. For the sake of him who chose you and set you as a refuge for the oppressed, put an end at last both to the malice of the oppressor and to the labors of the afflicted; for both matters have sufficiently come to light and been made manifest. [Col. 0367B] Indeed, at the command of my lord’s good pleasure, the case has been examined and decided. It remains for the sentence rendered to be confirmed by his authority. Shall a lying man then, coming against the testimony of such great men—I mean the bishop of Valence and the bishop of Grenoble—be heard? [Note: [Col. 0367D] See the notes to Letter 197.] Again I entreat you, and with all the anxiety I can muster I cast myself at my lord’s feet, that he not allow a religious monastery to be destroyed by an unjust and deceitful man. For he will not spare ours, who has almost destroyed his own. Therefore I add, with my accustomed boldness: if you believed your servant, you would send this man, who abuses the favor of your mercy, back to his cloister; and you would command the lord abbot of La Chaise-Dieu to promote a religious man in the monastery which [Col. 0367C] he uselessly occupies, and to establish a regular community there. This would surely be worthy of your apostolate, pleasing to God, and an honor to the lord abbot of La Chaise-Dieu and to his monastery. Thus you would deliver both the soul of the aforesaid man and the monastery upon which he presses.

## LETTER CC

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Written about the year 1140.]

TO MASTER ULGER, BISHOP OF ANGERS, CONCERNING THE SERIOUS DISPUTE BETWEEN HIM AND THE ABBESS OF FONTEVRAULT.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Namely Petronilla, the first abbess, who was succeeded in 1150 by Matilda. Petronilla’s death is entered in the Necrology on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, where she is said to have been appointed abbess by Master Robert, founder of the Order of Fontevrault. This famous convent of virgins lies in the diocese of Poitiers, not far from the borders of Tours and Anjou. A serious controversy was brought against the nuns of that place by Ulger, bishop of Angers. Orderic, in Book XII, p. 882, under the year 1124, praises his religious devotion and learning; in that year he succeeded Rainald, transferred to the see of Reims. He surpassed the other bishops of his age in wisdom, morals, and holiness, according to the Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans, *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 335. For the sake of this lawsuit he went more than once to Rome, to Innocent and Lucius, who took up the nuns’ defense, as appears from their published bulls, both in the *History of Fontevrault* and in the second dissertation on Blessed Robert of Arbrissel. See Letter 340.]

1. I would rather send tears than letters. But since charity is not lacking for either task, it must give the one and not omit the other: these to you, those to me and to many little ones like myself, who are scandalized. Perhaps you say that the scandal does not arise through you. Will you deny that it arises because of you? I could easily bear everything else, provided only that you were not the cause. For I do not dare say that you are at fault. It is not mine to investigate this; there is one who will inquire and judge. “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes!” Whoever he or she may be, that person will surely bear judgment. [Col. 0368A] But now my address is to you: bear with a little of my foolishness. Since I have once begun, I will speak to my lord; I shall satisfy, at least in part, the zeal and affection that speak. I shall not fear age, nor be intimidated by rank, nor hesitate before the great name of Master Ulger. For the greater the name, the greater the scandal. Therefore I shall go beyond myself and become foolish. I shall rebuke an elder, accuse a bishop, endeavor to teach a master, and offer counsel to a wise man. Let charity and the zeal which I once conceived for the holiness and glory of your name pass over no kind of presumption. That the spiritual fragrance of this glory, diffused everywhere, should be even slightly tainted by the devil’s envy is no slight thing to me; nor is it slight to the Church of God, [Col. 0368B] which everywhere used to rejoice in this noonday light with such celebrated joy.

2. Yet how greatly you despise your own glory is sufficiently plain. I praise this—but only if it does not extend to an injury against God. I praise also the firmness with which you yield to no highest powers concerning what you consider your right—but only if your action did not appear more stubborn than steadfast. How much more gloriously, and certainly more holily, would you bear courageously an injury done to you, and preserve your reputation for God’s glory! Yet I do not know how you can be confident that your conscience is secure beneath this scandal. For you are not excused, even if you rightly lay the blame upon someone else. Grant that another has caused the scandal: you can certainly restrain it. Will refusal to restrain it be without fault? Or will restraining it be without glory? If you suppress an evil that is your own, it will be reckoned to you for righteousness; if an evil that is another’s, for glory. Whoever may be the author of the scandal, it is required of you by every means that it be removed; and in that case we call you excused if you cannot remove it. Is it not, after all, the ministry of angels to remove scandals from the kingdom of God? (Matt. 13:41.) If you say, “What is that to us?” that saying will rebuke you: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the Lord” (Mal. 2:7). If, therefore, when you can remove this scandal, you do not remove it, you plainly do not fulfill your ministry. Whether that is no fault, you will judge. But I would say that even this is insufficient [Col. 0368D] unless you also honor your ministry.

3. There is something further that I might add, were I not, I confess, more timid than I promised. But more safely I bring forward a master who does not fear to speak naked truth to a bishop. “This very thing,” he says, “is already altogether a fault among you: that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer wrong?” (1 Cor. 6:7.) He set up a mirror; the sun of righteousness shone back, truth flashed forth, and the blemish appeared. What value, then, has that accursed little possession, whatever it may be, that it can any longer either overshadow so manifest a truth or hinder so desired a correction? May God inspire you to acquiesce in the counsel—not, I say, ours, but that of all who are zealous for you with God’s zeal—reverend father, who deserves every honor.

## LETTER CCI

TO BALDWIN, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF RIETI.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] This Baldwin was different from Baldwin the cardinal, likewise Bernard’s disciple, concerning whom see Letters 144 and 245. The latter was already a cardinal when this other Baldwin governed the Cistercian monastery of Rieti, which was twofold: one of Saint Matthew and the other of Saint Pastor, over which Baldwin was set. Read Ughelli’s additions to Ciaconius under Innocent II, and the other letter to the abbot of Rieti after Bernard’s letters.]

He urges him to apply himself vigorously to his office; this requires the word of preaching, the example of works, and especially devotion to prayer.

1. The letter you sent breathes your affection and moves mine. And I grieve that I cannot reply according to the degree in which I am moved. Nor do I linger over excuses for excuses, knowing that I speak to one who knows. You know, I say, under what burden I groan; and my groaning is not hidden from you. But do not estimate my affection by the brevity of this little letter, an affection which no length of discourse could adequately unfold. The malignity of occupations can indeed make me write little, but not love little. Action may indeed exclude or impede action—but can it impede affection? As a mother loves her only son, so I loved you when you clung to my side and pleased my heart. I shall love you absent too, lest I seem to have loved my consolation from you rather than you yourself. You were most necessary to me. And from this it is especially evident how sincerely I love you. For today [Col. 0369C] I would not have lacked you, had I sought what was my own. But now you see that, despising my own advantages, I did not begrudge yours, placing you there from where you may someday be set over all your Lord’s goods.

2. Take care, then, to be found a faithful and prudent servant, sharing the heavenly wheat with your fellow servants without envy and distributing it without negligence. Do not take up in vain the excuse of your newness or inexperience, which perhaps you think—or pretend. For neither barren shamefacedness is pleasing, nor humility apart from truth praiseworthy. Attend therefore to your office. Drive away modesty by considering your office; act as a master. You are new, but you are a debtor; and know yourself a debtor from the moment when you bound yourself. Will newness excuse, before the creditor [alternative reading: Creator], losses of profit? Does the moneylender allow the first periods to pass empty? But, you will say, “I am not sufficient for these things.” As though your devotion were not accepted according to what you have, not according to what you do not have. Prepare to render an account of the single talent entrusted to you, secure concerning the rest. If you have received much, give much. [Col. 0370A] But if it is little, give that also. For one who is not faithful in little is not faithful in much. Give all, because you will be called to account for all, even to the last farthing—but certainly for what you have, not for what you do not have.

3. Remember also to give your voice the voice of power. “What is that?” you ask. It is that your works may accord with your words—or rather, your words with your works—that you take care first to do and then to teach. It is a most beautiful and salutary order: that you first bear the burden which you impose for others to bear, and learn from yourself how you ought to regulate others. Otherwise the wise man will mock you, like that sluggard for whom it is labor to stretch out his hand to his mouth (Prov. 26:15); and the Apostle will rebuke you, saying, “You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?” (Rom. 2:21). You will also be marked with the vice of the Pharisees, who “bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on men’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23:4). The living and effective word is the example of action; it readily makes persuasive what is said by showing that what is urged is practicable. Therefore understand that the chief part of your office, for the security of your conscience, rests upon these two commands: word and example. Yet, if you are wise, you will join a third: devotion to prayer, for the completion of that threefold repetition in the Gospel concerning the feeding of the sheep (John 21:15–17). Know that in this the sacrament of that Trinity is in no respect unfulfilled by you, if you feed them by word, feed them by example, and feed them also by the fruit of holy prayers. These three, therefore, remain: word, example, prayer; but prayer is greater than these. For although, as has been said, the power of the voice is action, prayer nevertheless obtains grace and efficacy both for action and for speech. Alas, I am torn away, snatched away! I may not continue. Yet be briefly advised to relieve me as soon as you can of a serious anxiety, and do not neglect to explain more clearly what you meant when, among other complaints, you said that you had received a wound from one from whom you had not expected it. That matter disturbs me anxiously.

## LETTER CCII

[Note: [Col. 0370D] Written in the year of Christ 1144.]

TO THE CLERGY OF SENS. The election of a new bishop is not to be undertaken rashly or without deliberation.

Deprived of your blessed shepherd [Note: [Col. 0370D] Namely Henry, whom Hugh, formerly abbot of Pontigny, succeeded in 1114, as the Chronicle of Hugh, monk of Saint-Marien, and another of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif testify. Compare Letter 182.], it is necessary, dearest friends, that you diligently concern yourselves with appointing another. But certainly this must not be done precipitately, tumultuously, or without deliberation, lest what is presumptuously undertaken contrary to reason and order come to nothing, and lest you begin to enter the circuit of certain people who are around you. Take, if you please, instruction from the neighboring Churches [Note: [Col. 0370D] He means the Churches of Orléans, concerning which see Letter 156; Châlons, from Letter 224; and Langres, concerning which see above, Letters 164 ff.]; let their affliction give understanding to your hearing in the present matter. For it is a great matter [Col. 0371A] now in your hands: to restore a shepherd to the noble Church of Sens. It is indeed a great matter, and not one to be undertaken without great counsel. Therefore the counsel of the suffragan bishops must be awaited, the assent of the religious persons within the diocese must be awaited, and a common business must be discussed in common. Otherwise, dearest friends, believe me, we shall grieve to see the tribulation of your Church, and grieve at your own confusion. Both will easily happen if that is brought about which ought to be revoked. Therefore let a fast be proclaimed, let the bishops be summoned, let religious persons be called in; and let the election of so great a bishop, which should be duly celebrated, not be deprived—God forbid—of its proper solemnity. The Holy Spirit will be present, as we trust, at your prayers; and there will be honor for you in honoring [Col. 0371B] your ministry, when with equal vote and counsel you apply yourselves to what is God’s glory and the people’s salvation.

## LETTER CCIII

[Note: [Col. 0371C] Written about the year 1140.]

TO ATTO, BISHOP, AND THE CLERGY OF TROYES. He urges them to call back Ansel, a cleric of Troyes, from arms and marriage.

We read: “If anyone among you has wandered from the truth, and someone converts him, he ought to know that he who causes a sinner to turn from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (Jas. 5:19–20). Our Ansel is wandering, he is wandering: who can doubt it? If we leave him so, he will not wander alone. How many will that most illustrious young man draw after him by his example? And we judge that not only his followers but also all who can call him back and do not call him back are involved in the same error. I am free from his blood. I foretold it to him in a letter, and I now tell you: he is undertaking an unlawful thing. It is not for a cleric to fight with military weapons, nor for a subdeacon to take a wife. [Note: [Col. 0371C] On the celibacy of subdeacons, read Gregory the Great, Letter 42, Book I, etc.] Announce to the sinner his deed, lest he die in his sin and he who redeemed him with his precious blood require his blood from your hand. Behold, heaven cries out: “The virgin Israel has fallen, and there is none to raise her up” (Amos 5:2). How long does gold lie in the mud? Lift up the pearl, lift it up; raise [Col. 0372A] the most splendid and precious jewel from the dung-heap; raise it before it is trampled under the feet of swine—that is, of unclean spirits—and is no longer a vessel for honor but for dishonor.

## LETTER CCIV

[Note: [Col. 0371C] Written about the year 1140.]

TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT-ALBIN.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] In some sources, Saint Alban; this was a famous monastery among the English Mercians, built by King Offa. But our reading is preferable: the monastery of Saint-Albin among the Angevins, from which William, when passing through, “was received by Abbot Bernard; such grace of virtues shone from him that he appeared wonderful in every holiness even to all who were perfect,” *Exordium Cisterciense*, Book III, ch. 14.]

He reveals his affection for him; if this present life does not permit their mutual meeting, it is reserved for the future.

Though you are unknown to me in face, you are not unknown in reputation; nor do I count it a small or worthless gift that I possess some part of you through the latter. For through it, I confess, you have been so presented to my heart that, though I am occupied with many things, the serene recollection of you, my dearest brother [alternative reading: my sweetest brother], often easily claims me for itself out of all [Col. 0372B] things, so that I gladly dwell and sweetly rest in it. Moreover, the more welcome your memory is to me, the more eagerly I sigh for your presence. But when will this be, or whether will it ever be? Certainly, if not before, then surely in the city of our God—provided that we do not have here an abiding city, but seek that city. There, there we shall see one another, and our hearts shall rejoice. Meanwhile I shall nonetheless delight and rejoice in the things said to me, hoping and awaiting what remains of bodily sight on the day of the Lord, so that my joy may be full. Add, I beg you, to those good things which continually come to us from you and concerning you, the prayers of yourself and your people for us, dearest and most longed-for father.

## LETTER CCV

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Written about the year 1140.]

TO THE BISHOP OF ROCHESTER.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] In some sources, Roverensem or Rovrensem; but more correctly Roffensem, that is, Rochester, whose see in England was then governed by Ascelin or Anselm, who succeeded John in 1137 and held office for ten years.]

He says that the bishop’s letter censured him rather harshly, though without cause.

[Col. 0372C]

You write harshly to one who does not deserve it. What have I done wrong? If I advised Master Robert Pullen [Note: [Col. 0371D] He was English by birth. He first taught letters at Paris, then, returning to his country, restored the academy of Oxford, which had almost collapsed. Later, because of his singular gifts of mind and outstanding learning, he was summoned to Rome by Innocent II and created cardinal of the title of Saint Eusebius—the first of his nation, unless one prefers to place a certain Ultrinus before him. But in what year? In 1134, if we believe Onuphrius and Ciaconius. Yet it is wholly evident that he had not obtained this dignity when this letter was written, which from the sequence of Bernard’s letters seems to have been composed about 1140. Moreover, Godwin affirms that this same letter was sent to Ascelin—called Anselm by some—who entered the see of Rochester in 1137. Furthermore, at the end of the letter Bernard thanks the bishop of Rochester for having “cherished his own bowels,” namely, sons sent by him into Ireland. But no Cistercian monks are known to have lived in Ireland before 1139, when Saint Malachy first visited Clairvaux. Bernard writes in chapter 16 of his Life that certain companions left at Clairvaux by the holy bishop, after being instructed in the Cistercian way, brought it to Ireland in 1141 and built the monastery of Mellifont, the first Cistercian monastery in that province—unless one excepts the monastery of Blessed Mary at Dublin, which some authors state accepted the Cistercian yoke about 1139. Therefore the opinion of that Anglo-Benedictine writer seems preferable—reported among the encomia prefixed to Pullen’s works—who believes that Robert Pullen was summoned to Rome by Innocent, made cardinal by his successor Lucius, and afterward held the office of chancellor and died under Pope Eugenius III. The most ancient among theologians, as they call him, and most learned, he is attested by so many distinguished monuments of genius, the catalogue of which Pits has compiled. All would even now lie hidden in darkness had not Father Dom Hugh Mathoud, of our Congregation of Saint Columba and superior of the monastery of Sens, brought out the eight books of *Sentences*, illustrated with most learned notes and observations. For more about him, if you wish, see the notes to Letter 334.] to remain for some time at Paris, because of the sound doctrine known to be found in him, I thought it necessary, and still think so. If I asked Your Highness to allow it, I would ask the same even now, had I not perceived that you were angered by the former request. If I said that the man was supported by the favor of friends whose authority in the curia [Col. 0373A] [Note: [Col. 0373D] By *curia* Bernard usually means the Roman Curia, as in the title of Letter 219 and elsewhere.] is not slight, I said so because I feared for you, and still fear for you. For that after an appeal had been made you stretched out your hand, as we have heard, against the property of the appellant, I neither praised nor praise. Yet I neither advised nor advise opposing your will in any respect. Henceforth we are yours, prepared always to receive your crown [Note: [Col. 0373D] By the encomium “crown,” the holy man, after the manner of the ancients, not infrequently addresses bishops, as also kings; see below, Letter 221, nos. 2–3.] and honor it with worthy and due reverence. Bearing this witness of conscience, we still venture to ask you, only by entreaty and counsel, that Master Robert may be able to remain at Paris for some time without loss of your favor. May the Lord repay you in eternal life for having cherished our own bowels: I mean our sons whom we sent into Ireland.

## LETTER CCVI

TO THE QUEEN OF JERUSALEM.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] She was called Melisende; Letters 289, 354, and 355 are addressed to her.]

He commends a kinsman to her and briefly exhorts the queen to live in such a way that she may reign forever.

[Col. 0373B]

People have heard that I enjoy favor with you, and many who are about to go to Jerusalem ask to be commended through me to Your Excellency. Among them is this young kinsman of mine, a young man, as they say, brave in arms and gracious in manners. I rejoice that for a time he has chosen to serve as a soldier of God rather than of the world. Therefore act according to your custom, and let him fare well for my sake, as it has fared with all my other relatives who could become known to you through me. For the rest, beware lest pleasure of the flesh and temporal glory hinder your journey toward the heavenly kingdom. For what profit is there in reigning over earth for a few days [Col. 0373C] and being deprived of the eternal kingdom of heaven? But I trust in the Lord that you will do better; and if the testimony which my dearest uncle Andrew gives concerning you is true—Andrew, to whom we give much credence—then, by God’s mercy, you will reign both here and in eternity. Bestow care upon pilgrims, the needy, and especially recluses, for God is won by such sacrifices. Write to us more frequently, for it will not harm you and will benefit us if we know more fully and surely your condition [Note: [Col. 0373D] That is, her circumstances or state.] and your good endeavors.

## LETTER CCVII

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

TO ROGER, KING OF SICILY. He urges him to show himself kindly and beneficent toward poor religious persons.

[Col. 0374A]

Your magnificence has spread itself far and wide over the earth. [Note: [Col. 0373D] Bernard now addresses Roger far differently than he addressed him above: just as he did not spare sinners, so he was kind and gracious to those who repented; and, as he indicates at the end of Letter 224, when manners changed he knew how to change his style. Thus it appears that Roger at last repented: he who had once been a grave enemy of the Church, disturber of peace, supporter of schism, persecutor of Pope Innocent, and rival of the emperor. His ferocity was so great that he spared neither sacred things nor persons, nor even enemies when dead, as may be seen in Otto of Freising, Book VII, ch. 23, and Baronius, vol. XII, under the year 1136. Hence Bernard’s descriptions of him: “the Sicilian tyrant,” Letters 130 and 136; “invader of the royal crown, Sicilian usurper,” Letter 139; and “duke of Apulia, whom Pope Anacletus gained for himself at the ridiculous price of an usurped crown,” Letter 127. Peter, abbot of Cluny, praises him greatly in Book IV, Letter 37. Indeed, after he humbled himself before Pope Innocent—even though he held him captive—and obtained confirmation of his royal crown (see Baronius, under 1139), he invited religious men, Cluniacs and Cistercians, into his dominions. He also desired to see Bernard himself, as appears from the following letter.] For what lands has the glory of your name not reached? But hear the counsel of one who loves you. Strive, as far as lies in you, to refer this very glory back to him from whom it comes, if you do not wish either to lose it or indeed be lost through it. This will happen if, among those whom the celebrated report of royal magnificence summons from afar, you open the eye of discernment and extend your hand not so much to the greedy as to the needy. And truly blessed is one who gives heed, not to the greedy, [Col. 0374B] but to the needy and poor man (Ps. 40:1). I mean that poor man who asks unwillingly, receives shamefacedly, and in receiving glorifies his Father who is in heaven. When, however, God’s glory is thus faithfully rendered back from the mouths of the needy because of your gift, that fountain of glory—which loves those who love it and glorifies those who glorify it—must without doubt flow to you in a richer stream, so that “he who sows in blessings shall also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9:6). For people of this kind I ask you to set your eyes upon the bearer of this letter, whom certainly not greed but necessity has drawn to your royal presence. I mean a necessity not his own, but that of his people—many faithful servants of God by whom he has been sent. Patiently hear what they suffer [Col. 0374C], hear and have compassion; for if you have compassion, you will also reign with them. Nor is it beneath a king to reign with such people, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who have despised worldly life. Make them friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you depart from your earthly kingdom they may receive you into their eternal kingdom (Luke 16:9).

## LETTER CCVIII

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Written in the same year.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. Desired by the king, he sends some of his own people, asking that they be kindly received and supported as his own bowels.

[Col. 0375A]

If you seek me, behold me—and my children whom God has given me. For it is said that my humility has found favor with the royal majesty, so that the king desires to see me. And who am I, that I should conceal the king’s good pleasure? I run to you, and behold, I whom you sought am present: not in the presence of my weak body, in which Herod despised the Lord (Luke 23:11), but nevertheless in my own bowels. For who shall separate me from them? I shall follow them wherever they go; and if they dwell at the ends of the sea, they will not be without me. You have, O king, the light of my eyes; you have my heart and my soul. What if a small part of me is absent? I mean this little body, this worthless slave, which necessity retains even if my will would offer it. [Col. 0375B] It cannot follow the soaring mind, because it is weak, and scarcely anything remains to it but the grave. But what concern is that? “My soul shall dwell in prosperity, and my seed shall inherit the earth.” My seed—good seed. It will spring up, provided it falls into good ground. My soul will rejoice and delight in abundance, for, as I trust, it will be given the fruit of its hands. This hope is laid up in my bosom, so that I may patiently endure even bodily separation from them. Do not wonder, O king. I would sooner have chosen to be absent from the body than to send them away, if God alone were not wanting to the cause. Receive them as strangers and pilgrims, [Col. 0375C] yet as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. I have said too little in calling them fellow citizens: they are kings. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them by the right and merit of poverty. It is not fitting that they should be summoned in vain from afar and wander as exiles from their own homes in a useless pilgrimage. Do you think they can sing the Lord’s song in a strange land? Yet perhaps I have wrongly called that land strange which opens its willing bosom to good seed and has lovingly undertaken to nurture the precious deposit in its now joyful lap. The good grain has fallen, as I see, into good and excellent soil. I hope in the Lord that it will take root, spring up, multiply, and bear fruit with patience (Luke 8:15). Moreover, I shall share this fruit with the king, and each shall receive according to his own work (cf. 1 Cor. 3:8; the printed reference reads “I Cor. VIII, 8”).

## LETTER CCIX

TO THE SAME PERSON. He praises the king’s royal generosity in receiving and supporting the religious persons sent by him.

[Col. 0375D]

You have what you asked for; you have done what you promised. Those whom, trusting your word, we exposed and sent to travel as pilgrims have been received with royal generosity. You met them with bread, led them out into refreshment, and set them upon a high land, that they might eat the fruit of the fields and suck honey from the rock, [Col. 0376A] and oil from the hardest stone; butter from the herd and milk from the sheep, and figs with the marrow of wheat, and drink the purest blood of the grape. These are indeed earthly things, but they purchase heavenly things. “Thus is the way to the stars” (Virgil, *Aeneid* IX.640): God is propitiated by such sacrifices. For the kingdom of heaven belongs to these people, who will be able to repay the earthly king, in the land of the living, for these earthly gifts with everlasting life and glory. We have sent you Master Bruno, once for many days my inseparable companion, but now the father of many souls who rejoice indeed in Christ but are needy in the world. Let him too experience the king’s generous hand, so that the number of friends who will receive the king into eternal dwellings may be increased. What you do for him, you do for me, because what he lacks is demanded from me. [Col. 0376B] But because our purse is too inadequate, I have rightly taken care to send Christ’s poor man to yours, which is evidently at times somewhat fuller.

## LETTER CCX

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Written about the year 1139.]

TO LORD POPE INNOCENT. He commends the bishop of Reims to the pope.

We commend to Your Glory the lord of Reims—namely Samson—not as one among the rest, but truly as one before the rest; and this as confidently as we are certain of his faithful devotion, sincere love, submissive will, and most obedient disposition toward you. Let him be honored, because he is a vessel for honor. Let him feel that, so far as lies in you, he does not honor his ministry in vain, nor in vain possesses those qualities by which God is honored, the Church adorned, and which, finally, befit a priest of the Lord.

## LETTER CCXI

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Written about the year 1139.]

TO THE SAME PERSON. He commends the cause of the archbishop of Canterbury and likewise that of the bishop of London.

The Lord of Canterbury [Note: [Col. 0375D] Theobald, formerly abbot of Bec.], a good man and one who has a good testimony from good people, is unjustly being summoned to court and forcibly prevented from proceeding with his case. He was preparing for the journey, for it was to be concluded in your presence; but behold, he is cut off by the storm and tempest of wars. Let him be excused before you, for whom the necessity of making an excuse is burdensome: both because he trusts in justice and because he greatly desired to see your face. Your servant adds [Col. 0376D] this also: if the venerable priest has any other petition [Note: [Col. 0376D] Bernard frequently retains ancient terms, being knowledgeable and fond of antiquity, as here *Sacerdos* (“priest”), a title by which even priests of the first Order were formerly accustomed to be called; above, in Letters 61, 202, etc.], let it be granted all the more promptly in proportion as the petitioner is more worthy.

I dare further; and since I have begun, I shall speak to my lord. That—yes, that—old friend, faithful servant, devoted son (I mean Robert, bishop of London) cries out to you that the usurper who preceded him into the see which he himself, under God’s authorship, received by lot, has alienated the pledges [Note: [Col. 0376D] That is, securities or mortgages.] and lands of that Church, and refuses to restore what he alienated. How wrongful this is, [Col. 0377A] and how it ought to be corrected, it does not belong to the wisdom of one as humble as I am to prescribe.

## LETTER CCXII

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

TO THE SAME. He pleads movingly with the Pontiff the cause of the bishop of Salamanca, commending that man’s remarkable humility.

An illustrious man, formerly bishop of Salamanca, returning from the City, did not hesitate to turn aside to your servant, nor did he disdain to seek help from a poor little man. [Note: [Col. 0377D] This was Peter. When the Church of Salamanca had long been troubled by schism under three heads, he, though enjoying the right of possession, was summoned to Rome by Innocent, who removed Peter and the other claimants from the office. Peter then went to the Cluniacs, and afterwards to Bernard; perhaps he would have obtained restoration, had not the prelates of Toledo, Zamora, and Segovia, sent by King Alfonso, intervened and promoted the election of Berengarius, Alfonso’s own chancellor. This is from Manriquez, under the year 1139.] When I heard this, I remembered the prophecy which says: “Mountains and hills shall be humbled before God; crooked things shall become straight, and rough places level ways” (Isa. 40:4). Thus you know how to play: to press down what is lofty, calm what is swollen, and reduce monstrous excesses to measure.

Yet when the man had set forth, point by point, the history of his tragedy [Col. 0377B] in my hearing, I praised the judge and approved the judgment; but, I tell you, I felt compassion for the one judged. For he concluded all that tearful speech of his as though, at its end, he were saying with the Prophet: “But I have been exalted, humbled, and distressed” (Ps. 87:16); and, “Because, lifting me up, you dashed me down” (Ps. 101:11). And while I recalled your justice and the manly spirit which I knew you possessed, I began at the same time to consider the riches of your mercies, which I have experienced in very many instances, and I said: “Who knows whether the Lord may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” Certainly, I said, in all things and through all things he is equipped alike to contend fiercely, to forgive, to subdue [Col. 0377C] the proud, and nevertheless to spare the submissive (Vergil, *Aeneid* IV.852), except that, following his Master, he is also accustomed to make mercy triumph over judgment.

And I yielded to my customary presumption in speaking to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. What supplied matter for hope, confidence for prayer, and a rationale for pity was my observation that the man had not, as is customary, departed in a fury of indignation, returned to his native land, plotted scandals, or attempted seditions. Rather, he gave place to wrath, put on the spirit of gentleness, turned aside to your Cluniacs, humbled himself at the knees of the humble, and armed himself with the prayers of the humble, weapons mighty through God. With these weapons he has resolved to contend against you, and he will attempt, as he boasts, to shake the wall of severity raised against him by such engines of mercy. [Col. 0377D] He trusts that you will look upon the prayer of the humble and will not despise their petition; and mercy will prevail over him before whom powers tremble. I too, secure in such allies, stretch out my hands, bend my knees, and plead for one who pleads—boldly declaring that his humility ought to benefit the wretched man whose arrogance so greatly harmed him, and that virtue ought not, in recompense, to be conquered by vice.

## LETTER CCXIII

[Note: [Col. 0378D] Written in the same year.]

TO THE SAME. He remonstrates with the Pontiff because the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa, effected through Bernard’s agency and by the Pope’s authority, has been nullified.

[Col. 0378A]

Who will secure justice for me against you? If I had a judge before whom I could summon you, I would already show you—as one in labour speaks—what you deserve. Christ’s tribunal indeed exists; but far be it from me to appeal you to it, for there—if it were necessary for you and possible for me—I would rather stand with all my strength and answer on your behalf! Therefore I return to him to whom, in the present, judgment over all things has been given: that is, to you. I appeal you to yourself; judge between me and yourself.

In what respect, I ask, has your servant [Col. 0378B] so ill deserved of your Paternity that it pleased you to brand and mark him with the stigma and name of traitor? Did not your graciousness appoint me your vicar in the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa [Note: [Col. 0378D] See the *Life of St Bernard*, book II, chapter 7.], in case God might deign through me to recall him from the dregs of schism? If you deny it, I shall prove it by as many witnesses as were then in the curia. Did not the man, finally, after this, in accordance with my lord’s word, receive back his rank and honour? Who then, by his counsel—or rather by his deceit—induced your constancy to retract what it had granted and render void what had proceeded from your lips?

And I say this not in order to rebuke apostolic severity and zeal, kindled by the fire of God against schismatics, which [Col. 0378C] “in a mighty wind shatters the ships of Tarshish,” and which, like Phinehas, pierces the fornicators, according to the saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies?” (Ps. 138:21). But where guilt is unequal, punishment plainly ought not to be equal; nor is it fitting that one who has abandoned sin should be involved in the same sentence with those whom sin has more thoroughly abandoned. For the sake of him who, in order to spare sinners, did not spare himself, remove my reproach; and, by restoring the man whom you have established, provide also for your own so sound and unblemished reputation. I wrote to you once before on this matter; but because I received no answer, I think that what I wrote did not reach you.

## LETTER CCXIV

[Note: [Col. 0378D] Written about the year 1140.]

TO THE SAME. He commends the bishop of Cambrai and Abbot Godescalc.

[Col. 0378D]

If any care or however slight remembrance of me still remains in my lord’s heart, and if even now any small portion of former favour is found in his eyes toward his servant, let a noble and humble man, [Col. 0379A] Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai, test it. [Note: [Col. 0379C] In most manuscripts Nicholas’s name is absent, not even indicated, as usual, by its first letter. Of four Colbert manuscripts, only one codex has in the margin “Nicholas,” to whom these words certainly fit; but [Col. 0379D] the reader should be warned of this. Nicholas governed the Church of Cambrai from 1140 to 1167.] I acknowledge myself indebted to him and bound to do everything I can for him—not only because, wherever he can, he honours us and ours, but also because of his truth, gentleness, and justice, which can make him commendable even to you. And, unless I am mistaken, those who trouble him are false, and truth is not in their mouths. You will in due course prove this; I need not labour over it in words.

There is also with him a religious and holy man, Abbot Godescalc. [Note: [Col. 0379D] The printed editions add “of Mont-Saint-Martin,” but these words are absent from all manuscripts; indeed, in some the name Godescalc is absent, while in others only the initial G. is given. Yet he was abbot of Mont-Saint-Martin near Arras, of the Premonstratensian Order; he is praised in Letter 253, no. 4, and later became bishop of Arras, in Letter 284.] Likewise, if our intervention can add anything to his merits, I earnestly ask that he be heard in his petitions. For I judge that he makes none which is not worthy to be granted.

## LETTER CCXV

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Written about the same year.]

TO THE SAME. On behalf of the bishop and dean of Auxerre.

[Col. 0379B]

I, a worthless little worm, write to you very frequently, and am driven to this boldness by the prayers of friends. I admit that I am bold, but not deceitful. Let not my lord suspect that a lie will be found in his servant’s mouth in anything he writes to him. I wish to comply with my friends’ wishes, but not at the cost of my death. For I do not fail to know where I read: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). Therefore I deny falsehood; I do not excuse importunity. Let importunity itself find pardon; for the rest, we have no fear.

The lord bishop of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0379D] That is, Hugh.] is a friend—and a special friend; who does not know it? He has anxiety, not falsehood, to share with a friend. We offer a trustworthy excuse on behalf of his dean [Col. 0379C] and demand absolution. We are sons of one father—which I say in my usual presumption—namely, you. We trust that a father will not reject his sons, but will fulfil the desire of those who fear him, hear their prayer, and make them glad (Ps. 144:19).

## LETTER CCXVI

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE SAME. He complains that Count Ralph, having repudiated his wife and taken another, finds patrons in the curia.

It is written: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). Bold men have arisen who did not fear [Col. 0380A] to divide, against God, those united by God. [Note: [Col. 0379D] Here Bernard marks the bishops who approved the divorce of Ralph, count of Vermandois: namely Simon of Tournai, his brother; Bartholomew of Laon; and Peter of Senlis. Herman, monk of Tournai, or his continuator, recounts the event in detail in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 480; from him receive the matter briefly. Count Ralph, wishing to marry Petronilla, sister of Eleanor, queen of the French, repudiated his lawful wife—who was a niece of Count Theobald of Champagne—on a pretext of consanguinity, with the approval of the three bishops named above. The complaint was brought to the Pope’s attention through Count Theobald, prince of Burgundy. The Pope bound the count with the bond of anathema and suspended the bishops from office for a time. Compare Sigebert’s Appendix and the following letters.] Nor did they stop at this: they added the joining together of those who ought not to be joined, adding transgression to transgression.

The sacred things of the Church are torn; alas, the garments of Christ are rent—and, to increase the grief, by those by whom they ought to have been mended. “Your friends, O God, and your neighbours have drawn near and stood against you” (Ps. 37:12). For those who transgress your commandment are not strangers, not foreigners to your sanctuary; rather, today they occupy the place of those to whom you said: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15). God joined Count Ralph and his wife through the ministers of the Church, and the Church through God, who gave such power to men. How can those whom the Church joined together have been separated by the chamber? [Col. 0380B] In this deed only one provision was suitably observed: deeds of darkness were done in darkness. For whoever does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds be rebuked by the light.

What did Count Theobald deserve? What sin did that man commit? If it is a sin that he loves justice and hates iniquity, he cannot be excused. If it is a sin that he rendered to the King what belongs to the King, and to God what belongs to God, he cannot be excused. If he received the archbishop of Bourges at your command, this is his greatest and first sin. [Note: [Col. 0380D] This was also a great cause of hostility against Theobald. Thus Herman, just cited, says: “The Pope consecrated as archbishop of Bourges a certain cleric, a kinsman of his chancellor, named Peter. Because the king refused to allow this, he was deprived of communion.” This occurred in 1144, after the death of Archbishop Alberic. The remainder will be found in the notes on Letter 219, where you will read that Theobald was badly treated by the king because he admitted Peter as archbishop. Compare Letter 219 and book IV of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 12.] Behold, this blood is demanded from his hand! Those who return evil for good slander him because he follows goodness. Many cry to you with all their heart that you may avenge, with fitting [Col. 0380C] punishment, the injury done to your son and the oppression of the Church; that with apostolic vigour you may restrain the authors of this crime together with their chief, for whom whatever he pleased was permitted, so that his iniquity may descend upon his own head.

## LETTER CCXVII

[Note: [Col. 0380D] Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE SAME. He complains that Theobald is being oppressed for the cause of justice and fidelity toward the Apostolic See, but asks that, with the Pontiff’s help, he be released from unjust promises to which he has been compelled.

Tribulation and distress have found us. The earth has been shaken and trembled at the deaths of men, the [Col. 0381A] exile of the poor, and the chains and prisons of the rich as well. Religion itself has fallen into reproach and contempt. Among us, even mentioning peace is regarded as shameful. Nowhere are faith and innocence safe (Vergil, *Aeneid* IV.672). Count Theobald, a lover of innocence and cultivator of piety, has almost been delivered over to the will of his enemies. He was thrust so as to fall, but the Lord sustained him; and he rejoices that justice and obedience to you are at stake, agreeing with the Apostle, who says: “If you suffer anything for justice, blessed are you” (1 Pet. 3:14), and in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice’s sake” (Matt. 5:10).

Alas, we could foresee all these things but could in no way prevent them. What more need I say? So that the land might not be utterly laid waste and every kingdom divided against itself fall, [Col. 0381B] that most devoted son of yours, lover and defender of ecclesiastical liberty, was compelled under oath to promise that he would procure the removal of the sentence of excommunication pronounced by your legate of blessed memory, Master Ivo, against the territory and person of the adulterous tyrant [Note: [Col. 0381D] Ralph, mentioned in the preceding letter.], who was the head and author of all these evils and sorrows, and against the adulteress herself. The aforesaid prince did indeed do this at the request and counsel of certain faithful and wise men. They said that this could easily be obtained from you without injury to the Church, since it lay in your power immediately to reimpose and irrevocably confirm the same sentence that had been justly pronounced. Thus craft would be outwitted by craft, peace would consequently be secured, and one who glories in malice and [Col. 0381C] is mighty in iniquity would gain nothing from it.

I have much to say to you, but there is no need to write everything, since one is present who knows all things and can explain them more clearly and fully by word of mouth.

## LETTER CCXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO THE SAME: AN APOLOGY, AND THE LAST LETTER. Observing that he has lost Innocent’s customary favour, Bernard modestly clears himself of the causes of offence that arose over the will of Cardinal Ivo.

To his most reverend lord and father INNOCENT, BERNARD, the nothing that he is.

1. I once thought that I was something, however small; but now, as I perceive, I have been reduced altogether to nothing, though I did not know it. For I would not say [Col. 0381D] that I was wholly nothing at the time when my lord’s eyes were upon his servant and his ears open to my prayers; when he received with open hands everything I wrote and read it with a cheerful countenance, answering with the greatest kindness and fullness every request. But now I call myself deservedly not something small, but nothing, since yesterday and the day before he turned his face away from me. Why is this? What sin have I committed?

Much, [Col. 0382A] I confess, if the money of Cardinal Ivo of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0381D] See Letters 144 and 193.] was distributed at my discretion and not at his own direction. I have been told that this, certainly, has been reported to my lord. But I trust that you will now learn the truth of the matter, and the truth will set me free. I am not so dull as not to know that whatever he did not dispose of among his possessions belongs to the Church.

2. But now hear the truth plainly. If a lie is found in my mouth, my own mouth shall condemn me. When the man put off the man, I was absent—indeed, very far away. But I heard from those who were present that he made his will; that what he did, he also had written down; and that he himself divided his goods as he wished and among whom he wished. What remained, he entrusted to be divided among two abbots then attending him [Col. 0382B] and myself, though I was absent, because the poorer houses of the saints were known to us. When those abbots returned home and did not find me—for at that time I was detained by your command on affairs concerning the pursuit of peace—they nevertheless divided the money as seemed right to them, without my not merely consenting but even knowing what they had done.

Let indignation now, if you please, yield to manifest truth; let no brow henceforth be furrowed against me, nor let any brow be lowered. Rather, let your customary serenity return to your gracious and kindly face, and let that joyful countenance again put on its own sun.

3. [Col. 0382C] For as to what I also learned—that you were displeased with me because of my many letters—I need no longer fear this, since I shall easily correct it. I know, I know: I presumed beyond what was fitting, paying too little attention to who I was to presume to write so often. Yet your kindness had armed me for this boldness; you will not deny it. Then the affection of friends pressed upon me; indeed, I wrote very little on my own behalf, if I remember rightly. But nothing in excess. If I can, I shall henceforth give my zeal moderation, together with knowledge, and place my finger upon my mouth. For it is more tolerable to offend some friends than to weary the Lord’s Christ with many petitions.

Even now I have not dared to write to you of the dangers threatening the Church, the grave schism that we fear, and the many hardships we endure. But I have written to the holy bishops who adhere to your side; from them, if you wish to know, you will be able to hear what [Col. 0382D] I have written.

## LETTER CCXIX

[Note: [Col. 0381D] Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO THREE [Note: [Col. 0381D] In some manuscripts, “four”; but the received reading is better. For Gerard the chancellor, mentioned here in fourth place and later made Pope under the name Lucius II, was not a bishop.] BISHOPS OF THE CURIA: ALBERIC OF OSTIA, STEPHEN OF PRAENESTE [Note: [Col. 0382D] Alberic died at Verdun in France. Bernard is said in book IV of the *Life*, no. 21, to have offered the Sacrifice of Praise at his tomb. He is also mentioned in Letter 241. On Stephen, see Letter 224.], IGMAR OF TUSCULUM [Note: [Col. 0382D] Igmar, or Ymar, was formerly a Cluniac monk, prior of La Charité-sur-Loire of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, then abbot of Nouaillé near Poitiers [Col. 0383C]—under which title he is party to the agreement between Louis the Younger and Argrimus, archdeacon of Orléans, printed by Chesne, vol. IV, p. 764—and finally a cardinal created by Innocent. According to the Cluniac Chronicle, he was a man of great integrity under Abbot Pons. Letters 230 and the two following are likewise addressed to these cardinals.], AND GERARD THE CHANCELLOR. On the interdict imposed upon the King’s territory because of the archbishop of Bourges.

1. How great an evil schism is in the Church, and [Col. 0383A] how detestable and to be avoided by every means, was once clearly shown by the famous and dreadful death of those men whom, because of such a plague, the earth swallowed up and sent alive to hell. The Guibertine persecution [Note: [Col. 0383C] So called from Guibert, bishop of Ravenna, whom Emperor Henry IV set up as antipope against Gregory VII and the three succeeding legitimate pontiffs. Likewise Maurice Burdinus, archbishop of Braga, was intruded by Henry V into the Roman see; he was eventually confined by Calixtus II in the monastery of Cava. Stephen Baluze elegantly wrote his life in volume III of the *Miscellanea*.], or the audacity of Burdinus, has also shown it: our own times have experienced these things, dividing kingdom and priesthood by a wound almost incurable and a cruel chastisement. The recent Leonine fury [Note: [Col. 0383D] The schism of Peter Leonis.] showed it too, after manifold and prolonged harassment and devastation of the Church, finally brought to an end by God’s mercy.

Therefore the Saviour rightly says in the Gospel: “Woe to that man through whom scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7). Woe to us who live to lament what we have endured, grieve over what we feel, and tremble at what we expect! And, what is [Col. 0383B] worse, human affairs have reached such a habit of evil that neither the guilty are willing to humble themselves nor the judges to show mercy. We say to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly,” and to offenders: “Do not lift up the horn” (Ps. 74:5); and they do not listen to us, because they are a rebellious house (Ezek. 2:5). We entreat those whose task it is to rebuke sins and save sinners not to break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax; yet they rather shatter the ships of Tarshish in a mighty wind.

2. If, with the Apostle, we charge children to obey their parents in all things, we seem to beat the air. If we speak to parents, bidding them not provoke their children to anger (Eph. 6:1, 4), we provoke their anger against ourselves instead. Neither do offenders consent in any way to make satisfaction, [Col. 0383C] nor rulers or correctors to yield. All follow their own temper; pulling the rope in opposite directions with all their strength, they break it. Alas! The scar from the Church’s still recent wound [Note: [Col. 0383D] Namely, the schism of Anacletus.] has not yet hardened, and they prepare again to rend it; again to fasten Christ’s body to the cross, again to pierce [Col. 0384A] the innocent side, again to divide the garments, and—even though vainly—to strive to tear apart the seamless tunic itself, as far as they are concerned.

If you have any bowels of compassion, set yourselves against such evils, lest a division arise especially in that land in which, as you know very well, other divisions are customarily repaired. For if the author of scandal is singled out by the Judge’s mouth for a dreadful curse, what blessings, we think, do those who drive off and fight against this wickedness deserve? [Note: [Col. 0383D] In one Colbert manuscript, *pugnatores* (“fighters”), which fits the sense; *expugnatores* (“assailants” or “overthrowers”) is better.]

3. We do not excuse the King on two counts. For he both swore unlawfully and persists unjustly. [Note: [Col. 0383D] William of Nangis recounts the matter thus in his *Chronicle*: “In the year 1142, a dispute arose between Pope Innocent and Louis, king of the French, and the Gallican Church was troubled. For when Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, had died, Peter was sent and consecrated by the Pope as pastor of that Church. But King Louis rejected him and would not receive him into the city, because he had been appointed without the King’s assent. King Louis had, however, granted the Church of Bourges the liberty to elect whom it wished as bishop, except the said Peter; and he had publicly sworn that during his lifetime there would not [Col. 0384C] be an archbishop. Yet the man was elected, went to Rome, and was consecrated by Pope Innocent, who said that the boy-king must be instructed and restrained lest he grow accustomed to such conduct. He added that liberty is not true where someone is excepted by the prince, unless the prince proves before an ecclesiastical judge that the person ought not to be elected; for then another is heard. But, as stated above, King Louis excluded the archbishop upon his return. Count Theobald of Champagne received him into his territory, and all the churches obeyed him. Angered by this, King Louis summoned nearly all his magnates to wage war with him against Count Theobald.” Thus William; Matthew Paris, who assigns this to the year 1146, seems to require correction. This conflict went so far that King Louis not only devastated Count Theobald’s lands in war, but also burned the castle of Vitry, with a great mixed multitude of both sexes, and even forbade episcopal elections and ordinations in the churches of Theobald’s domain, entrusting them to his brother Robert to be occupied. Bernard bitterly complained of this concerning the churches of Rheims, Paris, and Châlons—both in Letter 222 to Josselin of Soissons and especially in Letter 224 to Stephen of Palestrina. At last, when Eugenius III began his Roman pontificate, this disastrous divorce was extinguished through the work of the holy Doctor.]

But this is not from intention but from shame; for, as you know very well, among the French it is regarded as more disgraceful to break an oath publicly sworn, however wickedly, [Col. 0384B] than to keep it—although no wise person doubts that unlawful oaths ought not to be kept. Yet we admit that he cannot be excused even on this account. For we have undertaken not to excuse him, but to ask pardon. Consider whether anger, youth, and majesty can in any degree excuse him. Without doubt they can, if you decree that mercy is to triumph over judgment: so that some such consideration may be given to the King and the boy, sparing him this once on such terms that he may not presume anything similar hereafter.

Let him indeed be spared, if it can be done while preserving in all respects the Church’s liberty and also the due reverence owed to the archbishop whom the apostolic hand consecrated. This the King himself humbly requests; this our whole Church on this side of the mountains, now so grievously afflicted, suppliantly begs. [Col. 0384C] Otherwise we give ourselves over to death, wasting away and withering in fear, in expectation of the things that have come upon the whole world. For I have been pleading on this matter since the preceding year; and, because my sins require it, my plea was followed not by being heard but by indignation, and indignation in turn by the devastation of nearly [Col. 0385A] the whole land. If zeal has driven me to say anything improper, or otherwise than it ought to have been said, let it, I pray, be treated by you as unsaid; but where I have said what was necessary, and where it was necessary to say it, let it not have been said in vain.

## LETTER CCXX

[Note: [Col. 0385D] Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRENCH. He rejects the King’s unjust request in Ralph’s case, warning him not to oppress the innocent or provoke against himself the supreme King.

1. Gladly indeed, as you yourself deign to acknowledge, with your own conscience also testifying, we seek—and, insofar as our small ability permits, shall seek—those things which concern your honour and the benefit of your kingdom. [Col. 0385B] But as for your complaint to our humility concerning the anathema about to be renewed against Count Ralph [Note: [Col. 0385D] The King was angered by the anathema inflicted upon Ralph for two reasons: because Ralph was his kinsman, as Herman, monk of Tournai, testifies, and because he had married the Queen’s sister, as stated above.], and your wish that I exert every effort to prevent it because you suppose many evils will follow, I do not see at all how I could comply without opposing the apostolic command; and even if I could, I do not see how I could reasonably do so. I grieve indeed if evils result from it; but we ought not therefore to do evil so that good may come. It is better and safer, certainly, to leave the whole matter to the judgment and disposition of almighty God, who can ensure both that the good things he wills to be done are done and endure, and that the evils wicked people devise do not come to pass—or, at least, come instead upon those who will and seek them.

2. One point in the letter of [Col. 0385C] Your Highness greatly grieves me: namely, that this matter ought to stand in the way of the peace made between you and Count Theobald. Do you not know that you gravely offended when Count Theobald, through the violence of your war, was compelled against God and justice to swear not only that he would seek, but that he would accomplish, the release of the aforesaid Count Ralph and his land from a sentence so undeserved—indeed, so unlawful? Why do you wish again to add sin to sin and heap God’s wrath upon yourselves—God forbid? What offence has Count Theobald committed, that he should deserve once more to incur your anger? He obtained the release of Count Ralph, though unjust, as you know, with such great labour and difficulty; and he neither sought nor seeks the revived excommunication, though it is returning with the fullest justice, since [Col. 0385D] out of fear of you he even swore to renounce it.

Do not, I beg you, do not, my lord King, dare so manifestly in your King’s kingdom and possession to resist your King—indeed, the Creator of all—and by such frequent and reckless presumption stretch out your hand against the Terrible One, who takes away the breath of princes and is terrible among the kings of the earth. I speak sharply because I fear sharper things for you; and I would not fear them so intensely unless I loved you intensely.

## LETTER CCXXI

[Note: [Col. 0386D] Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE SAME. On the foregoing matter. He strongly reproves King Louis because, clinging to perverse counsels, he rejects counsels of peace. Bernard declares that, although hitherto devoted to the royal name, henceforth he will be a defender solely of truth and a witness against the King’s wrongdoing.

[Col. 0386A]

1. God knows how much I have loved you since I came to know you, and how earnestly I have desired your honour. You know with what labour and what anxiety, throughout the whole preceding year, I devoted myself with your other faithful men to seeking your peace. But I fear that we have laboured over you in vain. For you, as is evident, withdraw far too quickly and lightly from the good and sound counsel which you had received; and, while those wounds are still fresh, you hasten again, as I hear, by some diabolical counsel I know not what, toward the former evils which you had not without reason long ago mourned having committed. For from whom but the devil can I say that this counsel proceeds, by which fires are added to fires and murders to murders, [Col. 0386B] and once more the cries of the poor, the groans of prisoners in chains, and the blood of the slain resound in the ears of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows? (Ps. 67:6). Certainly, that ancient enemy of our race delights in these sacrifices, because he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8:44).

And do not vainly take occasion from Count Theobald “to make excuses for sins” (Ps. 140:4), since that man declares himself ready—and earnestly requests—to come to the conferences agreed between you [Col. 0386C] when peace was made, and, in accordance with the judgment of those who love your name, namely those who acted as mediators between you, he wishes to make satisfaction in every respect. Thus, if he can perhaps be convicted by them of breaking the agreement—which he does not expect—he will not delay immediately to make amends for your honour.

2. But you neither receive words of peace, nor keep your agreements, nor accept sound counsel.
