Instead, by some judgment of God unknown to me, you turn everything so perversely that you regard dishonour as honour and honour as dishonour, fear what is safe, and despise what ought to be feared. And, as Joab is read to have reproached the holy and glorious King David long ago, you love those who hate you and hate those who wish to love you (2 Sam. 19:6). For those who urge you to repeat your former wickedness against one who does not deserve it [Col. 0386D] do not seek your honour in this, but their own advantage—or rather, not even their own advantage, but the devil’s will: so that, God forbid, they may make the King’s power the executor of a wrath they have conceived, which enemies of your crown and most evident disturbers of the kingdom do not trust themselves able to accomplish by their own strength.

3. But whatever you please to do regarding your kingdom, your soul, and your crown, we, the Church’s children, cannot at all conceal the injuries, contempt, and trampling suffered by our mother. Beyond the things which, already inflicted upon her, we mourn with sorrow, we perceive further injuries partly being inflicted anew and partly threatening her. [Col. 0387A] Certainly we shall stand and fight, even unto death if necessary, for our mother—with such weapons as are permitted us: not shields and swords, but prayers and tears before God.

And I, who remember that, besides the daily prayers which I myself, with God as witness, humbly poured out before the Lord for your peace, welfare, and kingdom, I also pleaded your cause before the Apostolic See by letters and messengers—indeed, almost to the injury of my own conscience and to the just indignation against me of the supreme Pontiff himself, as I cannot deny—I, I say, provoked by your continual offences, which you do not cease to renew daily, [Col. 0387B] tell you that I begin to repent of my former folly, by which I have hitherto indulged your youth more than was right; and henceforth, according to my small measure, I shall not fail the truth.

4. I shall not be silent that you are zealously seeking once again to enter into league and alliance with excommunicated persons; that you are attaching yourselves, as is said, to plunderers and robbers intent upon the killing of men, the burning of houses, the destruction of churches, and the scattering of the poor, according to the Prophet’s words: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Ps. 49:18)—as though you were not able to do enough evil by yourselves. I shall not keep silent that you do not at last so correct that unlawful and accursed oath, most recklessly employed by you against the Church of Bourges—an oath from which, alas, so many and such great evils have already deservedly arisen [Col. 0387C]—as to permit a pastor to be set over Christ’s sheep at Châlons. Moreover, you most rashly make available to your brother [Note: [Col. 0387D] Robert, namely, concerning whom see the following letters, no. 224, note 2, and no. 304. In Letter 293 among the Chesnian letters, which is from the Cistercian Chapter to Louis the Younger, the Fathers complain that Count Robert, his full brother, ate meat in their own granges contrary to the order’s prohibition. On the church of Châlons, see below at Letter 224.], and to his knights, archers, and crossbowmen, episcopal residences to occupy against law and right, and you boldly lavish the Church’s property upon such wicked uses. I tell you: it will not remain unavenged for long if you persist in doing these things. Therefore, my lord king, I admonish you as a friend and faithfully advise you to desist quickly from this wickedness, if perhaps by repentance and humility, after the example of the king of Nineveh, you may forestall the hand already preparing to strike. I speak harshly because I fear harsher things for you; but remember the saying of the Wise Man: “The blows of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6).

## LETTER 222

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO JOSCELIN [Note: [Col. 0387D] Orderic calls him Rufus, “the Red,” p. 889. Letter 342 is addressed to him, besides the following three.] BISHOP OF SOISSONS, AND SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS. He complains to them, as counsellors of the King, concerning the King’s unjust schemes against Theobald, contrary to the agreement and peace concluded.

[Col. 0387D]

1. I had written to the King, reproving him for the evils [Col. 0388A] done in his kingdom, as is said, with his consent; and I judged what he wrote back worthy to be communicated to you, who are of his council. For I wonder whether he really believes what he says; and, if he does not believe it, how he can try to persuade me—who am surely aware of all that was done for the restoration of peace, as you know—of such things. For he says, as you can see in his letter, while trying to show that the agreements had been badly observed on the Count’s side: “Our bishops still remain suspended; our land is still under interdict.” As if the absolution of any ecclesiastic from an interdict concerned Count Theobald, or as if he had in any way promised that he would accomplish this. “Count Ralph,” he says, “has been deceived and exiled again.” What has this to do with Count Theobald? Did he not faithfully labour to do, and effectively fulfil, whatever he had promised regarding [Col. 0388B] this affair? But Ralph was caught in his own cunning and fell into the pit he had made. Is this, then, the whole reason why the King should render void his agreements, which your lips had set forth? Was it fitting on that account for the King’s wrath to blaze against God and His Church, against himself and his kingdom? For this was he to forget his own honour, so that, in order to wage war against his own man—whom, I do not say he had defied, but whom he had not even summoned or called to account—he should send his brother, and that through Châlons [206], the very city concerning which you know what the King had agreed with Count Theobald?

2. But the King adds another charge: that, by marriages, the Count is trying to unite to himself, contrary to his allegiance, the Count of Flanders [Col. 0388C] and the Count of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0388D] Bernard calls them the king’s barons in Letter 224, no. 3. Herman of Tournai explains this passage, p. 394, when speaking of Count Thierry of Flanders, who “had promised his daughter to Henry, son of Count Theobald, although the king of the Franks strove to dissolve the marriage, saying that they were related to one another in the third degree of consanguinity.” Theobald was also contemplating another marriage, namely that of his daughter to the Count of Soissons; below, Letter 224, no. 4.]. Yet concerning this alleged disloyalty there is suspicion, not certainty. You may consider what it means for empty suspicions to override firm agreements. Besides, such a thing ought not at all to be believed of such a man. Are those to whom the Count is joined enemies of the King, rather than his own men and friends? Is not the Count of Flanders a kinsman of the King and, as the King admits, a pillar of the realm? What, then, does the King’s own man and faithful subject do against his loyalty if he is joined in marriage to the King’s other friends? Indeed, if anyone regarded the matter simply as it is, might it not rather be thought to promise great peace for the realm, great strength, and great security?

[Col. 0388D] 3. Yet I wonder how the King was not afraid to say that he knew that I knew Count Theobald had attempted to draw Count Ralph to his side against the King. For in an oral message he said more than he wrote: namely, that I had repeatedly instructed the said Ralph that I would take upon myself the greater part of his sins if he would attach himself to Count Theobald [Col. 0389A]. If the man through whom I sent such instructions has been born, let him come and accuse me publicly; if I wrote letters, let them be produced openly. The King may see whom he has believed; I am certain that I never knew what he lays to my charge. I judge the same concerning Count Theobald, since he too wholly denies it. Let God therefore see and judge that Count Theobald is now accused on suspicion by one who, plainly contrary to his own agreements, drew Count Ralph to himself, in defiance of God’s commandments and of the judgment of the supreme Pontiff, associating with an adulterer and an excommunicate.

4. The King also says: “We have almost had two most grievous assailants.” And the Prophet answers mockingly: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). “Behold,” he says, “we are attacked [Col. 0389B] though we have not attacked; we suffer persecution though we have not persecuted.” Who attacks, I ask? Who attacks, or who persecutes? Does not the Count entreat and humble himself, ready to honour the King as king, to serve and obey him as his lord, earnestly beseeching peace and striving, so far as lies in him, to win for himself the King’s good will? Suppose this is not so, but that the Count is rather plotting every evil against the King: should recourse not have been had to that which, as you know, had been settled? For they agreed between themselves that, should any dispute or disagreement arise concerning those arrangements, they would do or seek no harm against one another until the matter had been aired and examined before us three together and before the lord of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0389D] Hugh, whose Letter 226 follows.], who had been mediators on that occasion; and if any [Col. 0389C] controversy arose, we were to be reconcilers. The Count now urgently demands precisely this; but the King refuses.

5. Finally, suppose the Count has wholly deserved ill: but what has the Church of God deserved? What, I say, has deserved it—not only the Church of Bourges, but also that of Châlons, of Rheims, and of Paris? [Note: [Col. 0389D] As to Bourges, this is clear from the note to Letter 216; as to the others, it is understood from Letter 224.] Let the King have a claim against the Count; but by what right, I ask, by what right does he presume to ravage the possessions and lands of churches, to prevent pastors being set over Christ’s sheep? For to some he forbids the advancement of those elected, while to others—something hitherto unheard of—he orders an election to be delayed, until he has consumed everything, until he has plundered the resources of the poor, until the land has been utterly laid waste. Do you advise him to do such things? It is very strange if these things are done [207] [Col. 0389D] against your counsel; stranger and worse if they are done by your counsel. For to advise such things is openly to fashion schism, resist God, enslave the Church, and reduce ecclesiastical liberty to a new slavery. If anyone is faithful to God, if anyone is a son of the Church, he will surely stand and set himself, so far as he can, as a wall for the house of God. And you yourselves, if you desire peace for the Church as sons of peace ought, how can I say not that you promote [Col. 0390A] such malignant counsels, but that you even take part in them? For whatever evil he does is rightly imputed, not to the young King, but to his aged counsellors.

## LETTER 223

[Note: [Col. 0389D] Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS. He satisfies the bishop, whose letter had borne the following salutation: “Health in the Lord, but not the spirit of blasphemy.” Nevertheless, he demands in him a greater zeal for avenging the injuries done to Christ and the Church.

1. I certainly do not think that I possess a spirit of blasphemy; nor do I know that I have cursed anyone, or wish to curse anyone—especially the ruler of my people. Yet whatever it may be by which Your Dignity considers itself offended, I ask pardon. For I know Him who said: “We are reviled, and we entreat” (1 Cor. 4:13). [Col. 0390B] Therefore I say with blessed Job: “What I have spoken, would that I had not said; and I will add no more” (Job 39:35). I had already replied to both of you when writing to the lord Abbot of Saint-Denis concerning the common complaint, and I thought I had done enough. Since, however, as I see, your indignation has not yet subsided—though perhaps it might more justly have blazed against those who trample down the Church—I also say to you: I neither said nor wrote nor believed that you are schismatics or a source of scandal; and I say this with confidence, nor do I fear that my own page will convict me of lying. Examine it, if you please; and if you find it so, I will confess myself guilty of great sacrilege and that I truly wrote those things, as you observe, moved by a spirit of blasphemy.

2. Yet lest humble satisfaction seem [Col. 0390C] to exclude freedom of spirit, I confess that I have grieved, and still grieve, that we have not yet found you avenging Christ’s injuries and defending the Church’s liberty with the freedom fitting to you. This grief compelled me to write harsh things, though not those with which you charge me. For I had thought—and would still think, unless I feared that in this respect I might be troublesome to you—that it did not at all suffice that you were not authors of schism, unless you also restrained, with complete freedom and according to your ability, those who are schismatics, of whatever rank they may be, and detested their counsel and fellowship. I would think it a glory to you if you too could say: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. 25:5). Was that zeal fitting only for the prophet, and is it not also required today of the Lord’s priest, of whom he said: [Col. 0390D] “Did I not hate those who hate Thee, O Lord, and did I not waste away because of Thine enemies?” (Ps. 138:21). I should indeed have wished—if, with your Serenity preserved [Note: [Col. 0389D] The title “Serenity,” which above he gives to the king of the Franks in Letter 170, no. 3, he here gives to a bishop, [Col. 0390D] but to one who was a counsellor in the royal court; by the same title he also greets Innocent in Letter 337, no. 1.] I may say this also—that you had exercised this zeal toward the boy-king [Note: [Col. 0390D] Following the usage of Scripture, he calls Louis the Younger a “boy,” though he was then married and more than twenty-two years old. The same word is used in the same sense in Letter 170 and frequently elsewhere.], who, not so much childishly as cruelly, without cause rendered void both your counsels and his own agreements. Without cause he throws his kingdom into turmoil; everywhere he raises wars in heaven and on earth; he ravages churches, profanes sacred things, exalts the wicked, persecutes the good, [Col. 0391A] and kills the innocent. These are the things, I say, that I should have wished you to grieve over, oppose, and resist, as far as lies in you. But it is not mine to teach Master Joscelin, still less to rebuke a bishop, who ought rather to reprove me and other sinners and correct those who err. See [208] how greatly I fear you: you have received a sealed letter, you who formed a bad suspicion about the earlier open one. For I had thought of nothing else in this matter than that, when writing to different persons, it is necessary, according to custom, not to seal a letter with wax [Note: [Col. 0391B] Hence in Letter 304: “The seal was not at hand.” The same occurs in Letter 402. Bernard’s name and likeness were impressed on his seal, according to Letter 284.]. I now ask pardon for this also.

## LETTER 224

TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF PRAENESTE [Note: [Col. 0391B] Written in the year 1143.—Stephen of Palestrina, also the recipient of Letter 219, was a cardinal of the Cistercian Order from 1140 and died in 1144. Ernald calls him “Stephen, a man of every moderation” in Book II of the Life of Bernard, no. 49. [Col. 0391C] Besides others, John of Salisbury praises him in *Polycraticus*, Book VI, ch. 24. We infer from no. 2 of this letter that he was from Châlons.]. He sets forth the misdeeds of King Louis and his injuries against the Church, bishops, and others.

[Col. 0391B]

1. Jeremiah speaks to God concerning his adversaries in these words: “Remember, O Lord, that I stood in Thy presence to speak good for them and to turn away Thy wrath from them”; and he adds: “Therefore,” he says, “give their sons to famine and deliver them into the hands of the sword” (Jer. 18:20–21). He goes on to utter against them other imprecations equally severe in this manner. I have thought it necessary [Col. 0392A] now to recall this to Your Reverence, because I see something similar has happened to me with the Prophet. For you know how I too stood before my Lord on behalf of the King, absent indeed in body but present in spirit, to speak good on his behalf. For he promised good things. But now, as he repays good with evil, I am compelled to write the contrary. I am ashamed of my error and of the false hope I had conceived concerning him; and I give thanks that, while praying simply for him, I was not heard. I thought I was showing deference to a peaceable king, and behold I find that I had assented to a most grievous enemy of the Church [Note: [Col. 0391C] What the condition of Church and state in Gaul was at that time under this King Louis the Younger, he sufficiently shows in the preceding Letters 216–222; but especially in the present letter he depicts the harsh and mournful condition of the Gallican Church. Otto of Freising likewise testifies to this in *Chronicle*, Book VII, ch. 21, where he says: “Western Francia, having lost its king, under his son Louis, who is still living, endured, because of the war between him and Count Theobald of Blois, such disasters of pillage and fire that, unless it had recently been pacified by the merits, prayers, and counsel of the religious persons dwelling there, it would have been thought destroyed to the point of mutual extermination.” Thus Otto. Behold, the safety of Gaul is ascribed to the prayers and counsel of religious persons. For who doubts that, as that man said, the world stands by the merits of the saints? And who can doubt that among these Bernard led the host, as a kind of common counsellor and peacemaker not merely of Gaul [Col. 0391D] but of all Europe—indeed, not to say, of the whole world—as may be gathered from his letters written in every direction? Yet, to note this in passing, one may wonder why that Louis the Younger has been so highly praised by historians, as Gordon asserts under the year 1180. Certainly, if you consult Bernard, an unquestionably uncorrupt judge, especially in the cited letters and most of all in this present one, you will say that he was not particularly praiseworthy. But such are human dispositions: men praise and blame according to their inclination. There is no need to seek examples far away. For even today, how divergent are the appraisers and judges of the counsels, expeditions, alliances, and other deeds of certain kings and princes! Some indeed turn into matter for praise and glory what others most severely attack and condemn. Some judge that wars of this kind are carried on to the detriment of religion and the Church: that heresies are fostered, places dedicated to God profaned, sacred things trampled down, the wretched oppressed, the state of the commonwealth ruined, and the Church’s [Col. 0392B] strength and dignity undermined. Yet you will find others who know how to conceal or gloss over these evils and raise to the skies with the highest praises those through whose actions and auspices such things are done. Nevertheless, by this we do not intend to take away from Louis whatever praise he later deserved at a more mature age. For perhaps, when older, he washed away the stains of his earlier years by illustrious deeds. He survived Bernard by many years, dying, namely, in 1180. Although I read that he gave Bernard himself indications of repentance. For Aemilius says of him in *Louis VII*: “The King (Louis), carried away by great anger and force”—namely, against Count Theobald of Blois—“captured and plundered Vitry, a town under the power of Blois. He burned secular and sacred places without distinction; in the chief church about fifteen hundred persons, adults and children indiscriminately, were burned, having fled in supplication to the protection of the altars, hoping to find safety under the holiness of the church. Soon recovering himself, the King, seized by immense grief and then sorrow, afflicted himself and could not be relieved by any consolations. Saint Bernard was then summoned to him, because much divine power shone in him; and earlier, under King Louis the Fat, he had been, as was said, a disciple of oaks and retreats, most learned without any other teacher, bringing holiness and learning out of solitude into public life, out of shadow into the sun. He was admitted and received most reverently [Col. 0392D] by the King; and when he saw his tears and learned their cause, he said: ‘Unless these tears quickly dry up, they can extinguish the memory of the fire at Vitry. Only add constancy and strength to them, and let there be no womanish lamentation; bear a manly and truly royal spirit.’” Moreover, what is said here concerning the election of bishops frustrated by Louis is clear from the notes to Letter 219.]. Among us holy Church is trampled down and shamefully enslaved. Elections of bishops are forbidden to take place; and if clerics anywhere presume to hold one, the person elected is not allowed [Col. 0392B] to be consecrated bishop. Thus the Church of Paris sits in sorrow, deprived of its own pastor; and no one dares even to speak of appointing another.

2. It does not suffice that episcopal residences are despoiled of their present goods: a sacrilegious hand also rages everywhere over their lands and people, appropriating for itself from them the revenues of an entire year. Your church of Châlons did indeed hold an election; but the man elected [Note: [Col. 0392D] Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, mentioned in Letter 66, died in 1142; Guy, mentioned here, was elected in his place. Royal agents had expelled Samson, Archbishop of Rheims, because he favoured Theobald; they were plundering the churches of Saint Mary, Saint Remigius, and Saint Nicasius in the city, and the suburban monastery of Saint Theodoric. Here there is no mention—as in Letter 222, no. 4—of the bishopric of Paris, where Theobald had already been installed after Stephen’s death.], [Col. 0393A] behold, has now for many days been deprived of his due honour, and you know how not without grave loss to the Lord’s flock. The King entrusted his brother Robert with the bishop’s functions [Note: [Col. 0393D] See Letter 222, no. 1.]; and he, wielding arbitrary power over all the lands and possessions of the Church and acting everywhere with no little activity in his office, daily offers to heaven sacrifices that are by no means peace offerings: the cries of the poor, the tears of widows, the lamentations of orphans, the groans of prisoners in chains, the blood of the slain. Yet that bishopric is too narrow for his wickedness. He attacks Rheims and acts wickedly in the land of the saints, sparing neither clerics, monks, nor nuns. Finally, he has so ravaged with the sword the fruitful lands and populous villages of Saint Mary, Saint Remigius, Saint Nicasius, and Saint Theodoric that [Col. 0393B] he has reduced almost all of them to a wilderness. The cry is common in every ear: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as our inheritance” (Ps. 82:13). Thus the King makes amends for what he committed against the Church of Bourges by a Herodian oath.

3. Moreover, the King had made peace with Count Theobald, though not without considerable labour on our part; he had entered into a pact, as we thought, of firm friendship; and behold, he seeks occasions to withdraw from his friend. The great crime laid to the Count’s charge is that he contracts marriages for his children with the King’s barons [Note: [Col. 0393D] See Letter 222.]. [209] The extension of affection is suspect to him, and he does not think himself king if the princes love one another. Let Your Prudence infer what spirit he bears toward his subjects, who thinks himself stronger when hatred and discord exist among [Col. 0393C] his own. Let him see and consider whether this man is from God, who places confidence more in the mutual enmity of his subjects than in their affection, although “God is love” (1 John 4:8). He would certainly not do this if he possessed the wisdom of him who said: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell” (Song 8:6). For this reason, then, he openly violates the conventions and settlements of peace, and does not keep his agreements, which his lips had declared. Finally, he recalled to his household and council the adulterous and excommunicated man [Note: [Col. 0393D] Namely Ralph. See Letter 216 and those following.], whom he had expelled by agreement; and, in order to practise greater wickedness, the King and advocate of the Church again associates himself with many other equally wicked excommunicates, perjurers, incendiaries, and murderers, against a lover and defender of the Church—as is beyond doubt—according to the Prophet’s words: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Ps. 69:18).

4. In addition, according to his custom, he compels bishops to curse those who ought to be blessed and again to bless those who ought to be cursed; and, because they do not obey [Col. 0394A] his will and pleasure, he traverses sea and dry land to find oath-takers by whose perjuries those whom perhaps God joins together may be separated by men. With what face, I ask, does a man who remains—as is publicly known—with his own cousin in almost the third degree of consanguinity labour so intensely to prescribe rules of consanguinity for others? [Note: [Col. 0393D] John Besly, in his *French History of the Counts of Poitou*, p. 145, explains this degree of consanguinity between Louis VII and his wife Eleanor, daughter of William, Count of Aquitaine, as follows: Aldeardis, Eleanor’s great-grandmother, was sister to the wife of Humbert II, Count of Maurienne, and therefore aunt on the mother’s side to Adela, mother of King Louis. [Col. 0394D]] Whether there is consanguinity between the son of Count Theobald and the daughter of the Count of Flanders, and likewise between the Count of Soissons and the daughter of Count Theobald, I do not know; for I have never knowingly praised, nor do I praise, unlawful marriages. But you should know, and my lord should know, that to prevent these marriages, if they may lawfully be contracted, is to disarm the Church and to take much strength from her. Nor do I think that those opposing the marriages have any other intention [Col. 0394B] than that, in the lands of the aforesaid princes, those who dare oppose the schism they threaten may be unable to find refuge. Thus far my zeal. For I cannot correct what I was able to reprove; I was also able to warn him who can correct it. My lord’s zeal will accomplish this. I judged it necessary that he be appealed to amid the great distress and peril of the Church; and through no one more fittingly than through you, who adhere to his side and his spirit. I beg you, excuse me to him because, when the King changed, I changed my manner of writing; for you know that the prophet of God said to God Himself: “With the innocent man Thou wilt be innocent, and with the perverse Thou wilt be perverse” (Ps. 17:26).

## LETTER 225

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO THE LORD BISHOP OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 0394D] Joscelin.]. He exhorts him to seek peace.

[Col. 0394C]

We have laboured, but the outcome is still in question. We have sown much, but brought in little. We confess that we have needed your aid and presence. Yet why we did not request it in so great a necessity you will learn from our mutual friend, the Abbot of Saint-Denis. Therefore we now urge your holy concern that henceforth you do not disregard this matter, but, according to the wisdom given you by God, strive for the things that make for peace. For you are not to be entreated concerning such a matter, in which it is plainly evident that your ministry is not only greatly honoured when you act, but also greatly disgraced if you neglect it. We hope to see you at the appointed celebration at Saint-Denis [Col. 0394D] [Note: [Col. 0394D] Was it an appointed assembly of the magnates of the realm? Or the feast called the Indict, celebrated at Saint-Denis in February on the feast of the dedication, the very day of Saint Matthias?].

[210]

## LETTER 226

[Note: [Col. 0394D] Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS. Bernard and Hugh complain of the King’s obstinacy in his wrongful undertakings; they grieve that their labours to establish peace are fruitless, not without ruin to his kingdom.

TO LOUIS, by God’s grace illustrious King of the Franks and [Col. 0395A] Duke of Aquitaine: HUGH, unworthy minister of Auxerre; and BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux—may you love justice and judge the earth wisely.

1. For a long time now we have left our homes and put aside our own interests, labouring faithfully for peace for you and your kingdom, as God is our witness. But we grieve that we have as yet obtained either no fruit or very little from our labour. The poor still cry out after us; the land still daily falls into desolation. You ask: what land? Yours, and no other. For all these evils are perpetrated within your realm and against your realm. Whether those impoverished, captured, and crushed by this war are your friends or your enemies, they are from no place [Col. 0395B] but your kingdom. In it the saying of the Saviour already seems plainly to threaten and nearly to be fulfilled: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” (Luke 11:17). Added to this is that the very dividers and desolators have made you their head and prince in this wickedness—you whom they ought especially to have feared as their defender and felt as their avenger. Yet we believed that, touched and enlightened by God, you had perceived the greatness of their wickedness and recognized your error, and that you wholly desired, by sounder counsels, to draw your foot back from this snare.

2. But that conference held recently between us at Corbeil has almost cast us down from this hope. For you know how, and how unreasonably—[Col. 0395C] if we may say so without offence to you—you then departed from us. As a result, we were not permitted, because of your agitation, to give a full explanation of that statement in our address which displeased you; if you had deigned to await it with a willing heart, perhaps you too would have recognized that nothing unseemly or intolerable had been said to you, in light of the course your affairs have now taken. But now, disturbed without cause, you keep us disturbed and confused, doubtful and anxious as to what we should do—men who desire and seek your good. This can arise only because the deception of the wicked and the rumours of ill-informed persons, who call evil good and good evil, trouble you. Yet we, though troubled, are not wholly without hope in the help of the Spirit, who, as we have perceived, has [Col. 0395D] beneficially shaken your mind concerning past evils. We still stand and wait for you to return to your senses and effectively complete what you wisely began. For this purpose we have sent our most beloved brother Andrew of Baudement [Note: [Col. 0395D] This Andrew was distinguished and employed in various affairs. He subscribes to the principal charters of the Abbey of Caricamp in *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 329; and together with Bernard he appears as witness to the agreement concluded between Louis the Younger and Algrin, Archdeacon of Orléans, in Chesne, vol. IV, p. 764. In the grant of the church of Vieux-Crecey, made through Burchard, Bishop of Meaux, in 1122 to the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, a donation of other property is also made by Stephen, son of Roric, “Count Theobald being present, and Lord Andrew of Baudement approving those matters which pertained to him.” The same Andrew attended [Col. 0396D] the Council of Troyes in 1128, according to the prologue of the Rule of the Templars. Compare Letter 284.], [Col. 0396A] that he may explain these matters to you more fully in person and faithfully report to us whatever answer you may wish to give. But if—God forbid—you persist in refusing to heed sound counsel, we are clean of your blood: God will not permit His Church to be trampled down much longer, whether by you or by yours.

## LETTER 227

[Note: [Col. 0396D] Written in the same year.]

TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS [Note: [Col. 0396D] Joscelin, mentioned above.]. He most earnestly and urgently implores the bishop’s help.

I have always needed the services of friends, being indeed a man always pitiable both in mind and body; but now [211] there is especially need and time for compassion, since, under the pressure of conscience and the heavy hand of the Lord upon me, I have consigned myself to a harsh prison [Note: [Col. 0396D] That is, to monastic enclosure and solitude, concerning which see the following letter, no. 2.]—a stern judge against myself. If you are still a father—for I acknowledge [Col. 0396B] that you have been—let the son feel it: that son in whom filial affection toward you has not cooled to this day. I know, I know that it is difficult to wrench Hercules’ club from his hand; and therefore I press hard, because I ask a difficult thing. The more difficult it is, the more forceful must be the effort to win deliverance. I shall confess myself deeply indebted for a great favour—indeed, a very great one—if I obtain it. Nor am I ignorant that “it is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35); but I yield to necessity, meet dangers, provide for distress, and now plainly either disregard or forget what is honourable. Therefore, yielding to you the more honourable part, as is fitting, I take for myself the more shamefaced one: not only the more shameless in receiving, but also the more importunate in asking. I ask, then, humbly; I ask urgently; I ask in season and out of season. [Col. 0396C] For I do not ask what would be unfitting for you to give or what I should later regret having received, though at present it is less fitting for me to ask in this way. For if you free the poor man from the powerful, in this you will do much for us, and very much for yourselves. Come then: we have shown our feeling; you know the matter; the afflicted await the result.

## LETTER 228

TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY, COMPLAINING THAT HE HAD NOT RECEIVED A REPLY [Note: [Col. 0396D] Manrique, in the *Annals* under the year 1135, ch. 3, thinks this letter was written in 1135; but the sequence of the letters, such as it is, seems to oppose this. And certainly, if it is compared with the following letter, written in reply by Peter the Venerable on this occasion, it will become clear that this one was written after the disturbances attending the election of Langres [Col. 0397C], which occurred in 1138, as was said above at Letter 164. For Peter the Venerable replies: “When can the sincere and fervent affection of my breast toward you be extinguished or overwhelmed by any little streams of hostile rumour, when neither many waters of tithes could extinguish it nor the torrent of the Langres rivers overwhelm it?” [Col. 0397D] Indeed, in the final part—which we have omitted—of the aforesaid letter, Peter also mentions the translation of the Qur’an, later dedicated to Saint Bernard by him, which, according to the Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, was made in 1143; for that reason this letter has seemed best referred to that year.].

To the reverend father and lord PETER, by God’s grace Abbot of the Cluniacs: brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, his own self, such as he is.

1. Is it then your pleasure to jest? Graciously, indeed, and in a friendly way—but only if you jest so as not to make me your sport. Do not be surprised at this. For your very sudden and unexpected condescension [Col. 0396D] makes it suspect to me. It is not long since, writing to you with due reverence, I greeted your Greatness, and you did not answer me a word. Nor much before that had I again written to you from the city of Rome, and even then I received not so much as one [Col. 0397A] iota. And now you wonder that, when you had lately returned from Spain, I did not presume once more to thrust my trifles upon you? But if it is blameworthy, for whatever reason, not to have written, surely it will not be blameless to have been unwilling—or, not to say, to have scorned—to reply. See how justice would favor me here (for this is what you demand of me), unless I preferred to meet your returning favor rather than delay it for myself while I either sought uselessly to excuse myself or to accuse another. Yet I have said this lest I keep concealed in my mind anything that I do not utter with my mouth; for true friendship refuses that. Henceforth, because charity believes all things (1 Cor. 13:7), let every suspicion be put away. I rejoice that you have warmed again to the remembrance of our former friendship, and that you call back even a friend who has been wronged. Gladly I return when called back. Happy am I to be recalled. I remember no wrongs [Col. 0397B] any longer.

> [Note: [Col. 0397D] There is no need to labor greatly to discover the wrongs mentioned here. For the context of both letters—this one, namely, and the following—declares more than sufficiently that this is said with a certain urbane and familiar wit and pleasantry. I know, indeed, that certain causes of controversy arose between the two saints: namely, the election at Langres, discussed in the note to Letter 164, and the exemption from tithes. Yet I would never concede that they proceeded as far as the name of injury. As for tithes, when Innocent was staying in Gaul in 1132, having learned of the poverty of the Cistercians, he ordered that all tithes be remitted to them. The Cluniacs, among others, took this privilege very ill. Hence arose grounds for complaints, [Col. 0398C] which Abbot Peter set forth moderately before Innocent first, then before Haimeric, and even before the Cistercian Fathers gathered in general chapter. When he found them somewhat disturbed on this account, in the following year he sent them a letter of apology, so that charity might be kept whole and uninjured. What, however, was subsequently perpetrated against the Cistercians [Col. 0398D] by the monks of Gigny will be stated in the notes to Letter 283. Moreover, since that letter of Peter of Cluny which gave occasion for the writing of this one seems to be lacking, it will not be out of place to append, in the series of St. Bernard’s letters, another letter written in reply by Peter himself, so that the most complete model may be set before all cultivators of true and Christian friendship, especially religious persons: that noble pair of friends, namely St. Bernard and the Venerable Peter, so highly commended by Cardinal Baronius that he declared Peter “not unequal to Bernard in that holiness which works through love.” For other letters on the same subject, see, if you wish, Peter himself, Letter 28 of Book I and Letter 46 of Book IV.]

Behold, I who truly was the servant of your Holiness, both now and before, give thanks: I am excellently placed, having again become close to you, as you graciously write. If perhaps I had grown cold, as you charge me, there is no doubt that I shall quickly grow warm again, cherished in the inmost tenderness of your charity.

2. And now I have received with open hands what you were pleased to write. I read it eagerly, gladly read it again, and like it the more often it is repeated. I confess: I like the jest. For it is agreeable in its pleasantness and serious in its gravity. I do not know how, in jesting, you so arrange your words with judgment that neither does the jest savor of frivolity nor does the authority retained lessen the charm of the cheerfulness. Indeed, authority is so preserved that the saying of the holy man may fittingly be applied to you: “When I smiled, they did not believe it” (Job 29:24). Come then: we have replied to you, and I think we may now rightly demand more ample things than you promised. It is fitting that you should know what concerns us. It has been decreed for me that I am no longer to leave the monastery, except once a year for the gathering of the Cistercian abbots. Here, upheld by your prayers and comforted by your blessings, I await, during the few days in which I now serve, until my change comes. May God be gracious to me, that He remove not [Col. 0398A] your prayer and His mercy from me. I am broken in strength, and have a lawful excuse that I can no longer run about as I used to do. I shall sit and keep silence, if perhaps I may experience what the holy prophet pours forth from the abundance of inward sweetness: “It is good,” he says, “to wait for the Lord in silence” (Lam. 3:26). And lest you seem to me to have jested alone, I think you will now not dare to reproach me for this silence of mine and, in your customary manner, call it slumber—what, I think, the holy Isaiah calls, more fittingly and more properly, “the cultivation of righteousness” (Isa. 32:17), and of which you read in this same prophet, the Lord saying: “In silence and hope shall be our strength” (Isa. 30:15). Commend me to the prayers of the holy Cluniac congregation, having first greeted them on my behalf—as servant of all—if you judge me worthy.

## LETTER CCXXI OF PETER THE VENERABLE TO ABBOT BERNARD

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] This letter, written in the year of Christ 1143, is Letter 17 of Book IV. Another on the same subject appears in Book I, namely Letter 28.]

He responds most graciously to Bernard’s letter, and at the same time sets forth the causes of the dissensions between the Cluniacs and the Cistercians.

To him who is to be honored with singular reverence, embraced with all the arms of charity, the inseparable guest of my heart, Lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, eternal salvation, for which he longs.

1. Since I, though I ought myself to have promptly and gladly met the letters of so sweet and pleasant a friend, come as a tardy respondent, your discerning Holiness will perhaps wonder and, I fear, attribute it to sloth or contempt [Col. 0398C]. But far be both! Nor merely far be they: both are altogether absent. For, so far as letters are concerned, I have almost never received anything more gladly or read anything more attentively. One cause of delay was in part their bearer, who, coming to Cluny and not finding me there—while I myself was not very far away, that is, at Marcigny—

> [Note: [Col. 0398D] Marcigny, a convent of virgins on the Loire, founded by St. Hugh, abbot of Cluny.]

—neither delivered nor sent me the letters he carried, but left them at Cluny. And lest I seem to accuse a good man [Col. 0399A], I believe that he was either detained by some business or deterred from attempting to visit me by the severity of the very harsh winter then prevailing. I too remained there, held both by snow and by business, for a month; and only at the beginning of Lent did I return home. At last I received from the subprior, to whom they had been entrusted, those letters of yours. My heart was immediately drawn; and, since it had long before been very warm in affection for you, kindled far more by those very letters through the breath of your breast, it allowed nothing further cold or lukewarm to remain within it. It was drawn, I say, and so drawn that—I do not remember ever having done this except out of reverence for the sacred Books—I kissed the letter as soon as I had read it through. And, in my customary manner, in order to stir up toward the affection of your [Col. 0399B] charity those whom I could—for at that time I could not stir up all—I reread, with everyone around me, what I had read by myself, and, so far as I could, moved them toward a greater affection of love for you. I immediately stored the letter away and placed it among the silver or gold coins which, according to a custom handed down to me by the fathers, I usually carry with me for almsgiving. Nor was this unfitting. For, above all gold and silver, your favor—your good charity—is precious to me.

2. I wished immediately to write back what had settled in my mind on the following day; but I kept silence, prevented by a daily—indeed almost continual—exactor demanding other things. A most harsh commander, whom I could not resist, plainly imposed silence upon me; and the manifold care of countless affairs compelled me to be silent not for one day only but [Col. 0399C] for many days. Sometimes fifteen days passed, sometimes a whole month, sometimes successive months, during which I continually strove to write, but was not permitted by the commander just mentioned. At last I broke the troublesome bond and, though with difficulty, by writing in stolen moments overcame the yoke of the burden and the scepter of the taskmaster. And lest I seem excessive in so earnestly excusing the delay in replying, you yourselves compelled me to excuse it when you said: “It is not long since, writing to you, I greeted your crown—

> [Note: [Col. 0399] The preceding letter reads, “your greatness.”]

—with due veneration, and you did not answer me a word; nor much earlier had I again written to you from the city of Rome, and even then I received not one iota. And now you wonder that, when you had lately returned from [Col. 0399D] Spain, I did not presume to thrust my trifles upon you anew? But if it is blameworthy, for whatever reason, not to have written, surely it will not be blameless to have been unwilling—or, not to say, to have scorned—to reply.” Thus indeed you.

3. But what of me? Precisely this. I could by no means deny the fault which you lay upon me, if I had scorned to reply to so great a friend when he first wrote. For I confess that I truly ought to have replied to one writing first. But, as far as I can remember, while you were staying in Rome, I wrote first and you wrote in reply afterward. Therefore it did not belong to me to reply, since I had written first; rather, it belonged to you [Col. 0400A] to reply, because I had written first. And I could indeed have written even to one replying; but your answer, full and satisfying my written letter to the last detail, imposed upon me the silence of not replying. If this is so, the fault laid upon me leaves me and begins to look toward you, since you wished to blame one who was without fault and to burden the shoulders of an innocent brother with another’s burden—not to say your own. As for what you say was done by me on another occasion, since the memory of the matter is not present to my mind, an answer is lacking. If one should perhaps become available, either a probable excuse or a humble satisfaction will not be lacking. But you added: “See how justice would favor me here.” And I say: meanwhile, according to the causes stated above, justice favors me, since no fault is found in me. Now, if I did not spare you, I could call myself the injured friend whom you spoke of [Col. 0400B] concerning yourself, and could rightly demand punishment for the injury or wrongs. But I spare you according to my custom; I remit everything, even unasked. “I remember no wrongs,” as you said. For this too belongs to the matter that follows: since I endeavor, not in jest but in earnest, to exclude notorious hostilities from the hearts of many and intend to urge you to exclude them, I myself first pardon all things and do beforehand what I labor to have others do.

4. But perhaps you will again say: “Is it then your pleasure to jest?” It is indeed, but with you. Certainly with you—but not so with others. For with certain others I would fear to exceed gravity and fall into frivolity; but with you I do not fear frivolity: I pursue charity, lest it slip. Hence it is always sweet to me [Col. 0400C] to speak with you and to preserve between us, through pleasant words, the honeyed sweetness of charity. For, as far as I can, I take care not to be among those brothers who “hated Joseph in their hearts and could not speak peaceably to him” (Gen. 37:4). Would that all our brethren and yours likewise did so—this I say not boastfully—and did not degenerate from the line of charity by which alone, after faith and the sacrament of Baptism, they are called brothers and by which they are joined to one another in a special kinship; and would that they feared what the Apostle says: “Perils among false brethren” (2 Cor. 11:26). Would that all plainly did this, and guarded their heart from deceitful thought and their tongue, according to the Psalm they often recite, from harsh speech. These things [Col. 0400D] which I have prefaced seem to promise great matters and, as it were, to prepare themselves for the accomplishment of the greatest things. But lest that familiar saying be applied to them:

> What worthy thing will this promiser produce with so great a gaping mouth?  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, v. 138)

I confess that I have no very great, nor even great, nor moderate reason for writing to you—of those matters, however, which the secular judge great or greatest and through which the sons of this age hope that they may become great or greatest. Yet it is great, and so surpasses every cause that the Apostle calls it greater than all; and, if its name is asked, he names it charity [Col. 0401A] (1 Cor. 12:31; 13:13).

5. This was my whole and only reason for writing: that charity which I trust I preserve whole toward your person, and which, especially through your zeal, I do not despair that ours and yours will preserve toward one another better than usual. For as regards the charity which from long ago I have reserved for you in the hidden place of my heart, it seems to me that, as is written, many waters cannot quench it, nor rivers overwhelm it. In certain circumstances I seem often to have experienced that many waters cannot quench it, nor rivers overwhelm it (Song 8:7). For when can the sincere and ardent affection of my breast toward you be quenched or overwhelmed [Col. 0401B] by any streams of unfavorable report, when neither the many waters of tithes could quench it nor the torrent of the rivers of Langres overwhelm it?

> [Note: [Col. 0401] These are the principal injuries to which Bernard referred in the preceding letter.]

You know what I mean; and I say it for no other reason than that, recalling the marks of my heart’s steadfast purpose of love toward you, your prudence may be assured that I can henceforth remain firm. I presume the same of you and trust that no impulse whatsoever can exclude me from the inner chambers of your heart. But since each of us is called a shepherd, since our folds are filled with no small multitude of Christ, and since each of us is commanded, “Know diligently the condition of your flock” (Prov. 27:23), we must see whether our flock is known to us, whether it is well or sick, weak [Col. 0401C] or strong, and indeed whether dead or living. For since that beloved disciple says, “He who does not love remains in death” (John 3:14), why should I concern myself with the sickness of my sheep when I know it already to be dead? For if he who does not love remains in death, in what death does he remain who hates? If he who does not love remains in death, in what death does he remain who slanders? Why do I say this?

6. I see some, from both our folds and yours, engaged in sworn wars against one another, and those who ought to dwell in the house of the Lord with one mind fallen away from mutual charity. I see them to belong to the household of the same Lord and to serve in the army of the same King; to be called Christians by the same name and monks as well. I behold them cultivating the Lord’s field, under the yoke not [Col. 0401D] only of the common bond of faith but also of the same monastic Rule, with many yet diverse labors; and though, as I have said, the Christian name joins them and monastic profession unites them, some hidden and unspeakable diversity of minds alone separates them and disperses them from that sincere unity of hearts into which they seem gathered. And—O thing full of lamentation, not adequately to be lamented by any fountains of tears!—the proud archangel, cast down from heaven, has again occupied heavenly places; and he who could not establish his seat in the north has established it in the southern—that is, in the brighter—part of heaven. Truly, yes, precisely so [Col. 0402A] he boasts that he has done when, having expelled Him who dwells in heaven and whose place is made not in mutual rancor but in brotherly peace, he rules by tyrannical right over the minds of men who shine by profession of heavenly things and by example. And when one stronger than that strong man, who guarded his court in long-standing peace, came upon him and conquered him; when He cast out the prince of this world; when He overthrew the throne of him who is king over the children of pride even among Christian laypeople—under what planets, do you think, should lamentation be made if Satan erects in monks’ hearts the throne of his wickedness that has been overthrown elsewhere? Far be it, far be it that he who is said to have been so weakened by the Savior that he is even bound by His maidservants, and is mocked like a bird by His servants, should so utterly mock His servants and maidservants [Col. 0402B] and rule over them as worthless slaves!

7. But why do they oppose one another? Why do they slander one another? Why are they consumed by one another? Let, I pray, let the matter of dispute be brought forth; and if they can offer any just complaint against one another, let it be settled by impartial judges. What, I ask, does brother demand of brother? And that the diversity of all who disagree may be comprehended in two named persons: what do you demand, I say, Cluniac brother, from Cistercian brother, or conversely? If there are cities, fortresses, villages, an estate, or any earthly possession, small or great; finally, if there is gold, silver, or any quantity or kind of money: speak, tell us, set it forth. Judges are present, not judges of iniquity [Col. 0402C] but of equity, prepared immediately to settle all disputes of this kind. Peace will easily be restored and wounded charity healed, once it is known that so great a division of hearts arose from such things or similar ones. But I see that each of you has cast all these things aside, leaving nothing remaining to you on earth; that you have resolved to follow poor Christ, enriched by blessed poverty. This, then, is not the matter I sought. Yet I shall not desist, grow weary, or rest until I reach the bottom of the truth I seek.

8. Perhaps the cause of this quarrel among you is a diversity of customs, a varied observance of the monastic order. But if this, dearest brothers, is the cause of so great an evil, it is very unreasonable and, speaking without offense to either of you [Col. 0402D], very childish and foolish. Does not that appear to you unreasonable, childish, and foolish which all reason abandons and which everyone of sound judgment contradicts? For if variety of custom—if the manifold diversity of countless things—ought to tear Christ’s servants from mutual charity, what peace, concord, unity, or, in the end, what remains of Christ’s law, not only for monks but for all Christians, concerning which the great Apostle said: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2)? If, I say, the law of Christ—that is, charity—must be abandoned by all who follow different usages, then it must nowhere further be sought. For it could nowhere be found after it had been excluded from all who follow a different custom. Is not the whole world, dearest brothers, filled from ancient times with Christ’s Churches? And while the multitude of Churches serving God under one faith and the same charity exceeds almost every number, among them there is found nearly as great a variety of usages as there is an infinity of places. This occurs in chants, in readings, in all ecclesiastical offices, in varied clothing; this occurs, apart from the established fasts which cannot be changed, in diverse fasts; this occurs in all similar matters which, according to the diversities of times, places, peoples, and regions, have been established by the prelates of the Churches—who, in such matters, according to the Apostle, [Col. 0403B] may abound in their own judgment (Rom. 14:5). Shall all these Churches then abandon charity because they have changed custom? Shall they cease to be Christians because they seem varied in different usages? Shall the supreme good of peace perish from them all because each works good in a different manner? Ambrose, teacher of the Church in life and word, did not think so. Speaking of the Saturday fast, which he had seen observed at Rome but, after becoming bishop at Milan, had not found observed there, he said: “When I am at Rome, I keep the fast observed by the Roman Church; when at Milan, following the custom of that Church, I do not fast” (AUGUSTINE, Letter 54). Accordingly, Father Augustine, describing the devotion of his good mother, relates that she wished at Milan, according to the custom she had seen observed in the African Churches, to offer her offerings contrary to the observance of the Churches of Italy, but was forbidden by Ambrose (Confessions, Book VI, ch. 2).

9. But why do I labor over these things? It would be useless to surround an evident matter with many testimonies or examples, especially since neither among the ancients the disagreement over the very time of Easter, nor among the moderns the well-known difference in the Christian sacrifice between Greeks and Latins, has been able to injure charity or produce any schism of unity. The holy Fathers of the former matter and the approved books which the Churches have left us as theirs bear witness that the East celebrated the Lord’s Easter at one time, the West at another, and on the same island of Britain [Col. 0403D] the English at one time and the Christian Scots—that is, the more ancient Scots—at another. We too, people of our own time, are witnesses: we see the Roman Church and the whole Latin-speaking world offer to God the saving sacrifice of unleavened bread, while the Greek Church, the greater part of the East, and barbarian yet Christian peoples are said to sacrifice with leavened bread. Since this is so, neither ancients nor moderns have fallen away from mutual charity because of such notable and famous differences of usage, because they found in all these matters nothing that injured faith or charity. Why say this? So that, if your minds, O brothers, have become divided because of varied usages; if they have become diversified because of diversity of customs; if, because of one custom and another handed down to you by founders of Churches, they have grown sick in charity toward peace [Col. 0404A] or unity, they may return to unity through the most venerable examples of so great Fathers and, in the manner of the saints who “were made strong from weakness and became mighty in battle,” recover from the fearful sickness that is opposed to charity above every disease.

10. But you will say: “Variety of usages must be regarded differently in different Churches and differently among men of the same Order. If the usages of many Churches differ without harm to faith and charity, that is no wonder; but if persons of the same purpose and profession do not keep the same custom of institutions, that is remarkable.” Is this, I ask, the whole thing which divides you, dearest brothers, from one another? Is this the whole thing which wounds charity in you? Is this the whole thing which does not permit the children of peace to be at peace with one another? If a layman was “at peace with those who hated peace” [Col. 0404B] (Ps. 119:7), shall a monk wage an impious duel with a monk? The son of light loves the sons of darkness lest the good of peace be disturbed; shall the son of light attack the son of light—referring this to the purpose, not to the monk? If this is indeed the entire indignation of your minds, if this is the whole injury to charity, it will easily be healed, provided obstinacy is absent. Take heed, then, lest love of your own opinion darken the light of your understanding; for whoever defends not unity itself but what he himself wishes does not deserve to attain unity. Therefore I ask you, without party spirit or eagerness to defend your own opinion, to examine whether this is a just cause for division; and, when you have learned that it is unjust, to unite your divided minds. For behold, each of you serves under the same Rule [Col. 0404C] by which each hopes, in a distinctive warfare, to attain eternal salvation. But if neither of you is disappointed in his hope, I do not know what room can now remain for discord, division, or hostile criticism.

11. For you said that it is remarkable if persons of the same purpose and profession do not keep the same custom of institutions. To this I answer: if persons of the same purpose and profession do not keep the same custom of institutions, yet arrive through diverse observances at the same salvation and eternal life, what does it matter? What indeed does it matter, what harm is there, if by a varied path to the same country, by many ways to the same life, by many journeys [Col. 0404D] to the same Jerusalem which is above—that Jerusalem which is our mother—one arrives? For if you, O Cluniac, knew the Cistercian—or you, Cistercian, the Cluniac—to be erring in his adopted purpose and foresaw him, according to Scripture, tending to destruction by a way that appears right to men, then, I confess, you would have a just cause to correct, recall, or, if he refused to hear you, rebuke and condemn your brother. Then certainly, if you spoke against him, opposed him, and even hated him, I would acknowledge that you judged justly and acted rightly, especially since I hear the great prophet say to God concerning such persons: “Do I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and waste away because of Your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me” (Ps. 138:21–22). Moreover, I would rejoice that you were not [Col. 0405A] a deaf hearer of Scripture saying: “Run, hasten, rouse your friend; give no sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Prov. 6:3–4); and: “Cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). Then I would plainly acknowledge that you had just causes of hatred, and, girded with the sword of zeal, I too would accompany you as an inseparable companion to wage war against God’s enemies and those who, according to the Apostle, “speak lies in hypocrisy” (1 Tim. 4:2). But now, when under the same [supply: Rule] I see each of you tending from earth to heaven by varied yet sacred institutions, and running along different paths toward the same prize in such a way as to obtain it, there remains for you, as it seems to me, no cause for indignation, hatred, or hostile speech.

12. But you still demand that I prove what I have said and show how, under the same Rule or profession of the same Rule, a monk can walk safely by diverse paths. To this my answer is very easy and authority joined to reason is not lacking: both you, Cluniac, in your usage, and you, Cistercian, in your custom, can run happily in the way of God’s commandments and arrive still more happily at the goal due to your course. And because I have introduced the authority which must always be placed first in such matters, let it be placed first in this sequence also, and let reason not be separated from it by even a slight interval.

13. But what do you object, brother? “I say that those professing the same Rule do not observe the commands of the same Rule in the same manner.” What you say is true: the commands of the same Rule are observed differently in certain chapters by those professing the same Rule. But lest you judge monks of this kind guilty on that account, lest you dare accuse them of transgression for this reason, hear the authority of heaven—indeed, of the King of heaven: “If your eye be single, your whole body shall be full of light” (Luke 11:34). Hear also the Apostle: “Let all your things be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16:14). Hear Father Augustine: “Have charity, and do whatever you will.” Hear also the writer of the Rule itself—rather, the Holy Spirit, the dictator of the Rule itself: “Thus,” he says, “let the abbot temper and order all things, so that souls may be saved; and let the brethren do what they do [Col. 0405D] without murmuring” (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 41). And what is clearer? What more open? What brighter? Does not the very serenity of these words display itself wholly without any cloud and reveal to mortals the clearest light of truth, with the veil of all clouds removed? Behold, the heavenly Master teaches you, O brother, that your whole body—that is, all your works—are to be bright through singleness of eye, that is, purity of intention. Behold, after Him the supreme doctor of the Church commands that all your things be done in charity. Behold, the greatest instructor of the Churches after the Apostles grants you, so long as charity remains, full power to do whatever you wish. Behold, Benedict the father upon whom you rely commands the abbot so to temper all things that souls may be saved and murmuring absent. And do you fear for the salvation of those who follow diverse practices under the same Rule [Col. 0406A]? Do you not see how wholly secure from every danger are those whose intention of saving souls, according to the Rule itself, excuses their precepts from every fault or instability arising from diversity—and this is the greater point?

14. But now, that reason itself may be understood in every respect to serve the authorities set forth above and adhere to them indivisibly, let some chapters of the present question be added, in which certain alterations are shown to have been made with a single eye, sincere charity, and an intention to save souls. Once these have been demonstrated, I think I shall leave you nothing further to seek concerning the present question. For you use a single eye when you do not open the entrance of the cloister to a novice until after a year [Col. 0406B], because, according to the Apostle (1 John 4:1) and the words of the Rule (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 58), you examine throughout an entire year whether the spirit of the newcomer is from God. And you use a single eye when you receive one who arrives before the end of that same year, because you fear that, delayed for so long, he may return to his former dregs and the detestable evils of his previous life. You use a single eye when you are content with two tunics and two cowls, or with a few added garments of the same kind, because, though this is not a command (ibid., ch. 55), you preferred to follow the counsel or judgment of the writer of the Rule rather than add or adopt garments of another kind. And you use a single eye when you have admitted the use of 218 moderate furs, because you have provided for the weak, the infirm, the delicate—indeed, for all, as concerns colder regions of the earth—lest they murmur, grow ill, or, with a reasonable necessity withdrawn, some withdraw from their purpose [Col. 0406C]. You use a single eye when you receive returned fugitives only up to the third time, because you seek both to preserve the very words of the Rule (ibid., ch. 29) and, by finally denying them an entrance for return, to deter foolish or unstable monks from frequent flight. And you use a single eye when you receive a monk returning more than three times, because you fear that, if pardon is denied, he may perish exposed to enemies, and that the wolf—who is accustomed even to seize and scatter enclosed sheep—may destroy the wandering sheep.

15. You use a single eye when, without any exception, you observe the regular fasts of both summer and winter, because you wish both to preserve them as they were handed down and to receive the more abundant fruit of longer abstinence. But, speaking with a pure heart of charity, I do not sufficiently approve that fasts should be observed by anyone during the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord, at Epiphany, and at Purification—days which are truly in every respect days of the Lord. And you use a single eye when you exempt both the days I have mentioned and every established solemnity of twelve lessons from this custom of regular fasts, because you endeavor thus to honor the Lord Himself, the Apostles, and certain other saints, and propose to imitate the custom of almost all religious persons who fast in this way. You use a single [Col. 0407A] eye when you observe manual labor according to the command of the Rule, because you wish both to obey the Rule (Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 48), to avoid idleness—the enemy of the soul—by such exercises, according to the sayings of the same Rule, exercises holy not only by monastic but also by apostolic institutions, and, insofar as ability permits, according to the ancient fathers, to provide the necessities of life. And you use a single eye when you have partly set aside this manual labor, because, situated not in forests or deserts but in the midst of cities and strongholds and surrounded on every side by peoples, you cannot go and return again and again for the sake of these labors through a mixed multitude of both sexes without some—or considerable—danger; nor, moreover, do you generally possess suitable places where you can engage in such work [Col. 0407B]. But lest idleness, hostile to religious persons, find opportunity to harm you when you are unoccupied, either you work with your hands where and when you can, or, where you cannot, you make up for this manual work by alternating in turns the divine offices. Thus, lest an evil spirit claim for itself the vacant house of your breast, you occupy the whole time of your life with such sacred studies as you can undertake.

16. You use a single eye when, before all guests arriving or departing, you bow your head or prostrate your entire body upon the ground, worshiping Christ, and wash the feet of them all; because, according to the ordinances of the Gospel and the Rule (ibid., ch. 53), you strive, as is fitting, with the utmost zeal to cultivate the chief good of hospitality and seek to obtain for yourself the worthy reward of so holy an exercise of kindness. And you use a single eye when you do not prostrate yourself before all guests and do not wash everyone’s feet, because it would be altogether impossible for you continually to prostrate yourself upon the ground before so great a multitude of guests constantly arriving and to wash everyone’s feet—so impossible that, if you wished to devote yourself continuously to these things, abandoning all the other exercises of your Order, you could not accomplish even this alone [Col. 0407C]. And because you omit what you clearly see to be impossible for you, while you provide according to your ability what is necessary for receiving guests and honor them in whatever way you can, you are excused by singleness of eye from the things already mentioned which you cannot fulfill. You use a single eye when you wish the abbot’s table always to be shared with guests and pilgrims, because you seem both to obey the Rule (ibid., ch. 56) and to serve guests more humanely. And you use a single eye when you decree that the abbot’s table is not always to be shared with guests, but always with the brethren, because you remedy the extravagance—to speak mildly—of many abbots, who under the pretext of guests were accustomed to be indulgent toward themselves and harsh toward their own brethren, by recalling the abbot to the common table.

17. You too use the single eye, you who, as Ezra did with the Law and the Maccabees with the ruins of God’s Temple, labour to repair the many injuries of the monastic Order and the widespread ruin of many monasteries and their customs; and who, having expelled concessions made for indulgence rather than necessity, strive to call back the lukewarmness of our times to the practice of the ancient and original fervour. You too use the single eye, who so regulate both the commands of the Rule and of the Order that, in the words of that same Rule (ibid., ch. 64), “there may be something for which the strong may long, and from which the weak need not flee”: so that one unable to subsist on bread may at least be nourished with milk, lest he lose his life; and one unable, at a breathless pace, to seize the prize set before him may be taught at least to attain it with a slow step. For he who returns to his homeland after a year is called no less an inhabitant of it than he who returns after a month. Yet I say this while preserving the difference in the labour of travellers; for, according to the apostolic saying, “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labour” (1 Cor. 3:8).

You have Benedict as the author of this purpose of yours. Although, where charity commands, you may be compelled—on his own testimony—not to follow his writings strictly, nevertheless you take praiseworthy delight in following them out of devotion, because they seemed fitting to so great a man. You also have that same Benedict as the author of your institutions, who commands that all his writings be directed to the end of charity and serve the salvation of souls in whatever way, by this order or that. You have also Maurus, the chief disciple among his disciples, who, sent by him into Gaul, is reported to have altered some or many things in his Rule, with the eye of which I wrote above. You have, after him, very many fathers of monasteries, whom both their eminent life and the innumerable miracles wrought by God through them, both during life and after death, make clearer than light to have been moved by God’s Spirit, according to times, places, and persons, often to regulate the writings of the aforesaid Rule.

18. And what more shall I say? If the same principle runs through all the remaining chapters that appear different, everywhere you will find the single eye, which one calls charity and another the intention of saving souls. In this way you will find nothing different, nothing discordant—for all things done through charity are one—in practices that appear to be observed variously.

To these I add what is plain to all: almost nothing of this kind is laid down in the Rule as an absolute command; rather, it is expressed with a qualifying condition and left to the abbot’s discretion. Even if it had been stated imperatively, it could in no way prejudice the single eye—that is, evangelical charity. Such matters, as you know, belong among mutable precepts; and when charity commands, they must be changed without any fear of transgression. Nor should a departure from the Rule be suspect on this account to those professing the Rule, because the rule of that holy father depends upon that sublime and universal rule of charity, from which and in which, according to the words of Truth, “the whole Law and the Prophets hang” (Matt. 22:40). And if the whole Law hangs from it, then so does the law of that Rule. Therefore the monk who professes the Rule of Father Benedict truly observes it when, whether he preserves or changes any of its chapters, he preserves everywhere the law of charity.

19. What then? If this, brothers, was certainly the whole cause of your mutual division, does it not now appear altogether removed? Should not the hearts of monks now be united in fraternal peace, when simple charity has made one those varied practices on account of which they had been torn apart? Does not it make many things one—things diverse under the purpose of one monastic Order or one Rule, yet pursuing what is good—and lead them to the one appointed end of the supreme good or everlasting life?

“Let peace be in your strength, O Jerusalem,” so that abundance may follow in your towers. But lest perhaps we be found among those who say, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jer. 6:14), let us search whether any cause of separation still remains, lest, while we sleep in security, the serpent suddenly leap from its cave and bite some member of ours or yours who rests too carelessly.

20. Perhaps these garments of different colour furnish an incentive to discord, and the manifold variety of clothing produces variety also of minds. For, as I see almost continually—and as it is very easy for anyone even casually looking on to notice—a black monk, so to speak, looks askance upon a white monk whom he happens to meet; a white monk scarcely looks upon a black one with half an eye, and only when he forces himself into view. I have seen very many—how often I do not remember—from among the black-clad, laughing at a white-clad man whom they met as if he were a monster, and showing by voice or bodily gesture that they were astonished, as though a chimera, a centaur, or some strange portent had appeared before their eyes.

Conversely, I have seen white-clad men, formerly talkative and exchanging many observations with one another as they met, suddenly fall silent whenever any black-clad man approached, and, as though enemies were probing secrets hostile to them, guard themselves by the remedy of silence. I have watched the silent tongues of both sorts of men, and their speaking eyes, hands, and feet; what they refused to indicate by voice lest they betray themselves, they proclaimed more clearly with the aid of gestures. Mute speech and eloquent limbs: by a perverse order of nature, men noisier than stones and more silent than men.

Often, seeing such things, I recalled that saying of Solomon, in which he describes a similar kind of person: “He winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger; with a perverse heart he devises evil, and at every time stirs up quarrels” (Prov. 6:13–14).

And, O evil counsel of the wicked and stubborn angel cast down from God! Unwilling to perish alone from eternal peace, he gathers for himself companions in his destruction from every quarter; and, that he may rejoice in a more glorious triumph, he strives by the violent impulse of his wickedness to overthrow the cedars or firs of God’s paradise, of which he himself was once an inhabitant. He grieves that he has lost the palm of heresies, by which in former times he used to divide the Church of God. Seeing that he can now injure the faith by no means, since the Spirit of God fills the whole world with that same faith, he turns all his effort toward injuring mutual charity. Since he can no longer persuade Christian people to become unbelievers, he labours with all his strength to prevent them from loving one another.

The sects of Arius, Sabellius, Novatus, Donatus, Pelagius, and the still more ancient and accursed Manichaeus have now perished. The clouds of innumerable heretics which darkened the light of faith have vanished at the breath of God’s Spirit and have left us clear daylight, every mist removed. But the south-west wind that succeeds them strives suddenly to throw all things into confusion; and, because it recognizes that faith has prevailed, it seeks to compensate for its former losses by wounding charity.
