21. But, leaving lamentation aside, let me bring my pen back to what I began. Why does the blackness of your brother—not of his mind but of his garment—seem detestable to you, white monk? Why is the whiteness of your brother—not of his mind but of his garment—regarded by you, black monk, as something astonishing? Are you not both among the sheep of that Shepherd who says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I the Lord know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:27–28)?

What shepherd ever—not God, I do not say, but even a human being—disputed about the differing fleeces of his sheep? Who ever complained? Who ever judged white sheep more his own than black, or black more his own than white? Who ever attended not to whether they were black or white, but to whether black or white sheep belonged to his same flock?

O human malice—and the innocence of beasts! O stable substance, created in brute animals according to its own origin; O perverted nature in the rational creature! What white ram ever despised a black one? What black sheep ever detested a white one? Do they not fill the shepherds’ folds together, peacefully, altogether quietly, without any dispute concerning their varied colours and without any disturbance? Indeed, sometimes ram attacks ram with horns, and sheep batters sheep with repeated blows; yet variety of colour does not excite these or those to fight. Rather, anger innate in all animals, aroused in whatever way, provokes them.

But now, as I see, man—more foolish than a beast—though placed in honour does not understand; and, what is more lamentable, the monk, varied by a varied colour, separates himself from the unity of charity. Do not, do not, I beseech you, brother, if you desire to be Christ’s sheep, complain over the diversity of fleece. For that Shepherd casts no one out of his fold except one whom not variety of colour but injury to faith or charity separates from the flock of his sheep. He does not, I say, separate anyone from his fold because of colour—he who gathered together in the one fold of Christian faith both Jew and Gentile, from regions so remote and religions so diverse.

22. Perhaps the patience of the holy patriarch Jacob taught this as well: he bore with an even mind the wages which Laban changed ten times, and by tending his multicoloured flock with the same disposition and care of a good shepherd showed that white, black, and spotted cattle made no difference (Gen. 30). And since the Apostle says, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 6:15), and elsewhere, “Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. 3:11), what childish mind could be so foolish as to think that, if the new creation in Christ is preserved, either the colour of different garments or the differing custom of practices makes any difference for salvation?

But if it makes no difference for salvation, why does differing colour of clothing separate monks? Why does it produce schism? Why divide minds? Why injure charity? There is no cause, no rationale—not, I say, for listening, not for division, but not even for grunting—over these matters.

You have a suitable defender of your whiteness: the single eye, as I said above, of your conscience. So that a black garment, introduced by long use, might not lead people to suppose that a monk could exist only beneath its dark colour, you put on a white cowl and tunic; and because beneath the black habit you saw countless members of this Order grown lukewarm in their purpose, you commendably wished by this previously unheard-of whiteness of clothing to arouse them to a greater and fresh fervour of monastic religion. Likewise, you have a plausible author for your blackness: the very ancient custom handed down from the fathers. By this you seem safer in following the old ways than in devising new ones.

You both have an unassailable advocate for each of your colours in the voice of the common Rule itself (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 55), which commands monks not to dispute about the colour or coarseness of clothing, but to use garments of that colour or quality which can be found more easily or acquired more cheaply in the province where they live. Thus the reason already stated, or perhaps some greater reason still unknown to me, protects your whiteness; paternal authority, equal in force to every reason and not rightly judged inferior by anyone of sound mind, protects your blackness.

23. Whose example among the fathers can I bring forward to establish this? Whom can I find greater than great Martin? That great Martin—monk and bishop, I say—consecrated to his own use the colour of black garments. For this is read in his Life: “When the neighbouring beasts of burden saw him wrapped in a black, hanging cloak, they moved somewhat frightened to the other side.” That he was a monk is attested by the monastery not far from the town of Poitiers, the monastery at Milan, and the monastery which he built for himself at Tours. Behold Martin the monk; behold Martin clothed in black garments.

But what does Jerome write concerning such garments in his letter to Nepotian? “Avoid,” he says, “dark garments no less than white ones.” He warns, of course, that one should avoid pride or ostentation not only in white garments, then more commonly used by secular people, but also in dark garments, which professed religious of that age were accustomed to wear.

Concerning these garments, that admirable bishop of Nola, Paulinus—the contemporary and friend of the aforementioned Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, often praised by them and also by Pope Gregory the Great—describing the journey of a certain most noble woman recently converted to the monastic religious purpose, speaks thus in a letter addressed to Sulpicius Severus:

> “We saw the glory of the Lord in that journey of mother and sons: one journey indeed, but with very different attire. She rode on the lean and rather shabby back of a little ass, while senators, resplendent with all the pomp of this world which could belong to honoured and wealthy men, attended her: with swaying carriages, caparisoned horses, gilded litters, and many carts, so that the Appian Way groaned and gleamed. But the grace of Christian humility outshone the splendours of vanity. The rich marvelled at holy poverty, while our poverty laughed at them. We saw a confusion of this world worthy of God: purple, silk, and gilded finery serving old and black rags. We blessed the Lord, who makes the humble exalted, fills the hungry with good things, and sends the rich away empty.”

Behold: not only men of ancient religious profession, but also women embracing the purpose of holiness, are recorded as having worn black clothing.

24. For, to confess what I think, it seemed to those great fathers, as it seems to me, that this black colour under discussion suited humility, repentance, and mourning more closely. Since the whole life of a monk ought chiefly to be devoted to these pursuits, they decided that colour should be joined in whatever kinship it could have with character, and garments with virtues.

For white garments in antiquity signified glory rather than lowliness, joy rather than grief; as is commonly interpreted in the Church, the angel of the Resurrection, the angels heralding the ascending Lord, and the Saviour himself, appearing splendid in snow-white garments in the glory of his Transfiguration, all indicated this. Hence Sidonius of Auvergne, a good and learned bishop, ridiculing the faults of certain persons with biting rebuke, says among other attacks upon them: “They go forth white-clad to funerals, dark-clad to weddings,” showing that they were so confused in character and conduct that they perversely exchanged funeral attire for bridal and bridal attire for funeral dress. Those who followed the common custom of that age did not go white-clad to funerals and dark-clad to weddings; rather, they went white-clad to weddings and dark-clad to funerals, so that white clothing matched bridal joy and dark clothing funeral mourning.

I myself, while recently staying in Spain, saw and marvelled that this ancient custom is still observed by all Spaniards. When a wife dies, the husband; when a husband dies, the wife; when children die, their parents; when parents die, their children; when any relatives die, their relatives; when friends perish by whatever chance, their friends—immediately lay aside their arms and cast away silken garments and coverings of foreign skins. Renouncing altogether every multicoloured and costly dress, they cover themselves only with black and humble clothing. They cut short their own hair and the tails of their beasts of burden, and make themselves and the animals wholly black. With such marks of mourning and grief they lament their beloved ones taken away, and by public law remain wholly in this mourning for at least a year.

25. With so great an authority and rationale I satisfy you, black monk, and your colour; yet I do not thereby condemn the whiteness of the white-clad. You are praised because you do not wish to depart from the holy custom of your fathers; he too is praised because, by the unusual whiteness of his clothing, he thus stirs his own spirit more and more to fervour in the holy purpose. By such colour he distinguishes himself in some fashion, not from common charity—which would be wicked—but from the notorious lukewarmness of many in this Order.

Therefore, since you are under one shepherd, Jesus Christ; since you dwell in the one fold of the Church; since you live from one faith and hope of eternal things—you white monk and you black monk—why, to speak somewhat sternly, do you make complaint like most foolish sheep about diverse fleeces? Why do you stir yourselves against one another for so utterly groundless—indeed, so foolish—a cause? Why do you tear the first robe of charity on so childish a pretext? Why do you separate the very dwellings? Why do you bite one another, now not with sheep’s teeth but wolves’ teeth? Why do you speak evil? Why do you tear each other to pieces?

See to it; beware lest this name of innocence, by which you are called sheep, make you not among those whom the supreme Shepherd will place at his right hand and of whom he himself says, “My sheep hear my voice, and I the Lord know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish” (John 10:27–28), but—God forbid—place you among those of whom it is read and sung: “Like sheep they are set in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48:15 [Vulgate]).

Do you still see that it is foolish to dispute about colour; damnable to hate a brother over colour; utterly wicked to slander a brother over colour? If this was the entire cause of your mutual division, if this alone the material of so great a separation, if, I say, this alone and entire was the occasion of monastic schism—will not the old rift of your hearts now be healed when this cause has been rejected for so many reasons? Will not injured charity be cured? Will not evangelical peace return to the children of peace?

Therefore make satisfaction to peace, children of peace, and make with it an everlasting covenant within yourselves, lest otherwise that most terrible sentence of the prophet should at some time be brought even against you: “There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked” (Isa. 48:22). And now, thanks be to God, I think that I have penetrated the ancient causes and hiding-places of hatred among certain men of our Order, and that nothing remains even for anxious thought to seek. If the matter stands thus, neither you, white monk, will assail the black-clad, nor you, black monk, the white-clad, if you wish to observe what has been prescribed; nor will you depart from the state of highest charity against a brother because of a differing custom or the often-mentioned variety of colour.

26. But what have I said? How have I lost my mind? Where is the understanding of my soul? Whence comes this darkened power of sight? I thought I had found every source of scandal; I imagined I had exposed every hiding-place of hatred. I supposed, as I said, that diversity of customs alone, variety of colours alone, the quality or quantity of garments or foods, had wounded charity among monks, and that this alone was the cause of so great an evil. I saw the speck in my brother’s eye, but I could not see the enormous beam and mighty oak in my own eye or in his.

But now that the eye has been clarified, the day made serene, and the midday sun permits nothing to remain hidden, I see—I see, I say—what I may say with the goodwill of all, though I am certain that I may say it with the goodwill of all good people. For whoever is angered will confess, as Jerome says, that it was said of himself. The sound part of a body does not shrink from the hand of its healer; but a part that trembles and draws itself away from the probing fingers shows beyond doubt that a disease lies hidden within. What, then, was it that I had missed?

27. Speak, speak, I say—you, that I may first address the man of my original purpose—speak, black monk; give glory to God, and disclose what still lies hidden in the depths of your heart against your brother. “Who,” you say, “can endure new men being preferred to old; their efforts set above the deeds of our men; our people appearing inferior and theirs dearer? Who can view with an even eye that the greater part of the world turns away from our ancient Order and converts to their new purpose; that paths worn smooth through ages are abandoned and crowds flock to hitherto unknown tracks? Who can endure new monks being preferred to old, younger to senior, white-clad to black-clad?” This, black monk, is what you say.

But what do you, white monk, put forward? “How blessed are we,” you say, “whom a far more worthy institution commends; whom the world proclaims happier than other monks; whose reputation darkens the esteem of others, whose day darkens their lamp, whose sun their star. We are restorers of religion that has perished; we are revivers of an Order that has died; we are the most righteous condemners of monks who are languishing, lukewarm, and foul. We, separated from others in character, deeds, practices, and garments, have exposed the lukewarmness of the old and proved the superiority of our own fresh fervour.”

Behold, behold the true cause: more hidden, but far more hostile to charity than the others. It was this that split the unity of your minds, separated your very houses from one another, and, as the prophet says, often sharpened your tongues like a sword for slanderous or abusive speech (Ps. 139:4).

28. But let the deadly sword be blunted by the sword of God’s word; and lest fruits gathered with such great sweat be scattered by the light wind of vain glory, if you are wise, take care. And O unhappy and deeply lamentable loss! If a single wicked hiss of the serpent should scatter the spotless continence of your very long life, your invincible obedience, your unbroken fasts, your continual vigils, the so heavy yoke of discipline, and so many crowns of patience—if, in short, I gather many things into few words, it should scatter the great and countless labours, no longer of earthly but of heavenly life, which by God’s grace you have amassed over so long a time for the reward of eternity; and if the ancient dragon, emptying you by one breath, should make you empty in the sight of the supreme Judge—where is what the Saviour said to disciples still suffering from this disease: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18)?

Where is what he says elsewhere, when a similar dispute arose among them as to which of them seemed to be greatest: “But you are not so; rather, let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the servant” (Luke 22:26)? Where lies hidden from the eyes of memory the saying that the exalted and great one, of whose greatness, according to the Psalm, “there is no end” (Ps. 144:3 [Vulgate]), and who, according to the Apostle, “is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9:5), does not set himself above or compare himself with his servants, but lowers himself and goes on to say: “But I am among you as one who serves” (Luke 22:27)?

An apostle is rebuked lest he prefer himself to an apostle—and shall a monk not be rebuked lest he prefer himself to a monk? By Christ the master, the greater disciple is set beneath the lesser, the superior beneath the inferior—and shall I, a Cluniac, strive to be raised above a Cistercian? Christ himself submits to his disciples—and shall a Christian and monk raise a neck swollen with pride above a brother perhaps far better than himself? Majesty lowers itself, and weakness boasts? Loftiness humbles itself, and corruption exalts itself? God serves, and clay strives to rule?

And how, brother, have you fallen from that step of your Rule which you gloried to have ascended: “that the monk should pronounce himself lower and more worthless than all, not merely with his tongue but believe it with the inmost affection of his heart” (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 7)? Why should I labour further? There is no need to press the point harder for religious, wise, learned men, or—as people say—to teach Minerva, or carry wood to the forest, or water to rivers or the sea. The wisdom of both of you understands and acknowledges that, as without faith, so without charity it is impossible to please God; nor can anyone, once humility has been cast aside, retain that same charity by any effort whatever.

For where humility departs, pride necessarily succeeds; where pride succeeds, envy immediately arrives; where envy arises, charity at once dies. The envious person cannot love the one whom he envies, and charity can in no way remain in one who does not love.

29. For this reason, where charity is absent, humility is absent; and where humility is absent, charity too is absent. The Apostle clearly teaches this when he says: “Charity is not envious, does not act perversely, is not ambitious.” And because it does not even covet things belonging to others, he adds: “It does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 13:4–5). Charity therefore excludes every swelling of pride, every ambition, every covetousness, every avarice; indeed, through charity, according to the Apostle’s subsequent words, all iniquity together is cast out.

Now if you wish, brother Cluniac and brother Cistercian, to preserve whole this charity which the same Apostle calls the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2); if through it you wish to store up for yourselves the greatest treasures in heaven and preserve them once stored up: make every effort you can, and drive from yourselves causes not merely of its flight, not merely of its death, but even of the slightest injury to it. If they seek to return once expelled, shut the door of a firm heart against their return, and retain your everlasting fellow-dweller, charity, in the full embrace of your holy soul.

Charity itself, firmly retained, will lift you to the kingdom of heaven—charity which by its immense and sweet power bent the King of Heaven down to earth. The Apostle is a faithful witness, saying that because of his immense charity God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3). You will rejoice for ever before God in charity, and, as he himself promised, no one shall take your joy from you (John 16:22), when God shall be all in all; when you shall be satisfied from your long hunger, when his glory is revealed; when, at his appearing, you shall be like him; and, united to him for ever through this charity, you shall see him as he is.

30. At last let my pen return to you, my dearest friend, to whom this present letter is sent, so that where it took its beginning it may perhaps end its importunate length. As I professed above, conscience being witness, the sole and true cause of my writing was charity: that, insofar as concerns each of us, I might cause it to grow warm again by the breath of conversation and break forth into its customary—or greater—flames of mutual affection.

It remains for you—whom supreme Providence has prepared as a strong, milk-white pillar on which the structure of the monastic Order rests, and who, like a shining star, have in our time conspicuously given light by example and word not only to monks but to the whole Latin Church—it remains, I say, for you to devote all the effort you can to this divine work and not permit the great congregations of one name and Order any longer to disagree.

I have always striven to commend those holy monks of your congregation to our brothers, and, if possible, to graft them into those brothers by a perfect union of charity. I have not neglected to do this publicly, privately, and in the great assemblies of our people; and I have laboured by every means I could to scrape away that rust of envy and hostile zeal which is accustomed secretly to gnaw at the inward parts.

31. You too, by the great grace bestowed on you by God, work earnestly in the common field, so that, just as no one in our age is shown to have planted more useful things in it after you, so by praiseworthy zeal and industry everything contrary to what is useful may be uprooted. By that lofty eloquence aflame with the Spirit of God, drive from their hearts, to speak mildly, that childish rivalry, and from their tongue whispering; and in their place, whether they wish it or not, instil brotherly love.

Let diversity of practices and variety of colours no longer separate your flocks from ours. Rather, let charity, derived from the highest unity, repairing what is corrupt, restoring what is torn, giving life to what is divided, unite all things. This indeed is fitting: that those who have one Lord, one faith, one Baptism, who are held in one Church, and whom one eternal and blessed life awaits, should also, according to Scripture, have “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

I have sent to my jewel-like friend a jewel of salt, whose bodily use I formerly heard to be beneficial to you, and whose special meaning I judged necessary to the matters written above. For however many and precious displays of their virtues they may bring to the table of the eternal King, if they bring them without the salt of brotherly love, they will be rejected as tasteless; if they season them with this salt, their dishes, now pleasing, will be accepted along with those who offer them. For he who accepts no sacrifice in his Law without salt shows that no offering of virtue is pleasing to him without such seasoning, etc.

## LETTER CCXXX. TO THE THREE BISHOPS OF OSTIA, TUSCULUM, AND PRAENESTE

[Note: The title gives the names Alberic, Stephen, and Igmar. This letter is found in few manuscripts, as in the Compendiensis manuscript.]

He exhorts them to their duty: that they should keep wolves away from Christ’s flock in the bishopric of Metz.

God has set you on high for this purpose: that you may live for the greater benefit of his Church, in proportion as you preside over it with more eminent authority. Otherwise that Master of the Household will cast down the mighty from their seat who are found, despite the authority entrusted to them, to have failed their duties. Though we perhaps shudder more at the losses suffered by Christ’s bride in the bishopric of Metz because we are nearer, I nevertheless think that they are not unknown to you either.

See how great a wolf daily seeks, both by plots and by open assaults, to break into that fold of Christ and scatter the sheep gathered by Christ’s blood. And he has not ceased from harassing that Lord’s flock with all the strength he can command, and ravaging it with plunder, arson, and murder, not merely since yesterday or the day before, but from the time when he was still a little wolf. I therefore, so far as lies in me, point out the wolf and urge on the dogs. You must see to what belongs to you; it is not for me to teach teachers.

## LETTER CCXXXI. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE ABBOT OF LAGNY

[Note: Lagny, in the diocese of Paris on the Marne, where a monastery was founded by Saint Fursa, with the assistance of Erchinoald, and restored by Herbert II, count of Champagne; on this matter a diploma of King Robert survives in *De re diplomatica*, book 6, no. 151. The church of Lagny, famous and renowned, is described in letters of the general chapter of our monks, of which we shall speak shortly, as formerly flourishing in holiness and religious life.]

He asserts and defends the abbot’s innocence, refutes the charges brought against him, and finally demands from the bishops zeal for religious discipline.

1. I dare to say to you whatever comes to my lips. For, even if you must put up with a little of my foolishness, your goodwill—which is debtor to the wise and the foolish alike—will undoubtedly indulge me. I say this not because I intend to rush into speech irrelevant to the matter, to proceed frivolously, or to take pleasure in trifling—especially before you, who seem to be pillars of the Church. Rather, “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,” and truth, pressed by inward grief and unable to endure silence, bursts forth into the open.

For I tell you that my feet have almost slipped and my steps have almost been poured out, because wickedness, by a detestable reversal as it seems, so often conquers wisdom. Everywhere horns are added to the wicked, and zeal for justice is disarmed; and there is no one who can do good—not merely who is willing, but who is able. The proud act wickedly everywhere, and no one dares utter a word against them. Would that innocence were at least safe, and justice itself sufficient for its own defence.

What has the abbot of Lagny done wrong?

[Note: In the archive of Saint-Martin-des-Champs we find Geoffrey, abbot of Lagny in 1122, successor to Abbot Arnulf, who died in 1106. In 1224, as we read in the Roman manuscript of the Vallicellian Library, Ralph was made abbot of Lagny. Hermann, monk of Laon, speaks of him in book 3, chapter 18, of *On the Miracles of the Blessed Mary*, where “Theobald, count of Champagne, on the advice of Lord Norbert, appointed as abbot over the very wealthy monastery of Lagny a monk named Ralph from the monastery of Saint Nicholas in the forest of Vosago” (perhaps Voago; more correctly Vedogio, in the diocese of Laon). We do not doubt that these statements apply to him. He died in 1148, according to the Vallicellian manuscript, and was succeeded by Godfrey, called Galfridus in the archive of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, who died in 1162. Against him you have two letters of the general chapter of the black monks: one to Adrian III, the other likewise to Alexander III, printed in the Appendix of this volume.]

Is it because he is a good monk and a better abbot; because he enjoys a good reputation and has a still better life? Or because he has adorned the monastery over which he presides with religious discipline, enlarged it with temporal goods, and increased it in the number of good brothers? See: this blood is required from his hand. If it is a crime to be acceptable to God and human beings, let him be removed and crucified. For it cannot be denied that he is the man in question, with heaven and earth as witnesses. If it is a crime to be hospitable, kind, sober, chaste, and humble, let him deservedly fall empty before his enemies. In truth, he cannot excuse himself even in these matters, convicted by the holiness of his own life and the glory of his reputation.

2. But the charge is made against him that he was unwilling to receive my lord’s messenger. A very serious offence indeed—if it is so. The abbot does not deny that the man being sent to England, having been honourably received as a guest, sought to speak with him; but as he was preparing to leave, Humbert the provost intervened, saying that he himself would go out instead and satisfy the man on the abbot’s behalf. If, then, what ought to have been done for the man was not done, we leave it to you to judge whose fault that was. He is likewise accused of violently taking from the aforesaid Humbert letters of the lord Pope and tearing them up. But the letters remain intact and sealed with bulls; nor did he lose them by force, as he falsely claims, but surrendered them voluntarily, certainly on the advice of Count Theobald and of ourselves. [Note: Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, advocate of Lagny, was buried there. At his tomb his son Count Henry established a lamp, according to *De re diplomatica*, book VI, no. 206. Henry was sometimes resident there, as appears from Suger’s Letter 120. On Theobald see the notes to Letter 37, and Baldwin of Avesnes in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 584, where he is said to lie at Lagny.] It is also said that he put certain monks into custody. This indeed is false. But if he separated certain disturbers and conspirators among different cloisters, lest, being kept together, they should do greater harm, who, judging rightly, would blame him for this? As for the lands and goods of the church, allegedly dissipated and alienated, and given by him to his relatives: before the venerable bishops of Soissons and Auxerre, and Count Theobald, unquestionably the monastery’s advocate, a sufficient answer has been given and is still given—that he bestowed them upon his own people in the same way as upon outsiders, namely at the same rent or customary due.

3. Moreover, it has not been heard since the beginning of the world that a rebellious, proud, ambitious monk obtained, by apostolic authority, the privilege of his own freedom. Since the time of Judas Iscariot no one like him has been found, who should so rise against his master and betray innocent blood. Happy the master to whom, together with the Master of all, that prophetic saying is common: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up his heel against me” (Ps. 40:10). And formerly you were, against the apostle Peter, “lords over the clergy” (1 Pet. 5:3); indeed, against his fellow apostle Paul, you ruled over the faith of the whole world (2 Cor. 1:23). But now you have added something new, claiming authority even over religious life itself. What remains except that you should add dominion over the holy angels themselves?

Except that in this Judas seems to have surpassed the former in cunning and fraud: whereas all the former’s fellow disciples shuddered at his deed, this more crafty man was able to deceive into connivance—or rather into favouring—his wickedness, not just any persons, but the very chiefs of the Apostles. I do not blame my lord [Note: Pope Innocent.], who, being human, could have been deceived; and I pray that God may not impute it to him. Yet, once he has recognized the truth, far be it that this execrable, sacrilegious attempt of this wicked man should prevail! I too would have written to him about this matter with my customary boldness, had I not perceived that he receives less favourably than usual whatever we write. [Note: See Letter 218.] I beg you—you who are monks [Note: Alberic of Ostia and Ymarus of Tusculum were Cluniacs; Stephen of Palestrina was of Clairvaux.]—to grieve for the lot of your master, blessed Benedict. For now, as you see, it is nearly the case that he is everywhere contradicted and that all the strength of monastic discipline perishes, while monks take horns against their abbots from a strong hand.

## LETTER CCXXXII. TO THE SAME PERSONS. Against the Abbot of Saint-Theofred.

If the things you have heard concerning the abbot of Saint-Theofred [Note: Of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Le Puy.] are true, you cannot conceal them without danger to yourselves, both because of your office and because of conscience. I mean not only your conscience, but that of others as well. They are plausible things—and I believe them true. For the bearer of these letters, who bears witness concerning these matters, is truthful. You ask how I know this too? I hold a bundle of letters sent by holy men, whom I know to be holy and truthful; and all alike contain both praises and commendations of this man and the dreadful blasphemies of the other whom he accuses.

## LETTER CCXXXIII. TO ABBOT JOHN OF BUZAY, WHO HAD LEFT HIS ABBEY AND GONE INTO SOLITUDE.

[Note: A Cistercian abbey in Lesser Brittany, in the diocese of Nantes, a daughter-house of Clairvaux, founded in 1135. See Letter 116.]

He gently recalls him from the solitude to which he had withdrawn after abandoning the government of his monastery.

To his most beloved son JOHN, Brother BERNARD: may you walk in the Spirit and not forsake the fear of the Lord.

1. I cannot say with how great bitterness of soul and sorrow of heart I write to you, dearest John, because I see that in all my repeated writings I make no progress at all, since my word finds no place in you. I wrote once and again, unless I am mistaken [Note: These letters are not extant.]; and, because my sins demand it, my labour has as yet answered me in nothing. Behold, for the third time I cast the seed, beseeching almighty God that it may not return to me empty, but prosper and accomplish that for which I send it, gladdening us at last with the fruit of your obedience and salvation. If you hear me—or rather, if God hears me—I have regained my son. If not, I shall turn again to my customary weapons: prayers, namely, and tears, not against you indeed, but for you. I have mourned, and I shall mourn; and I shall draw anxious sighs from my inmost depths for one who is of my own flesh. Who will grant that you may be to me a brother sucking at my mother’s breasts? Who will call you back to that tranquillity of mind, harmony of conduct, fellowship of spirit, serenity of conscience, in which I once held and possessed you?

2. And lest you think that you have suffered from me any injury or hindrance, do not doubt that the report which, we have heard, certain false speakers—whom I know not—persuaded you of is untrue: namely, that I intended, without reason or judgment, to remove you from the governance of the souls of the brethren which I had entrusted to you. This is not true. Rather, hear briefly from me what is true in this matter. Even if I had wished it, it would not have been lawful; and even if it had been lawful—to speak from my own conscience—I would by no means have wished it. This is the truth. If, then, this was the whole cause that turned your heart away, now that you know the truth what remains except that you come to your senses, return to yourself, return to us, and moreover accuse yourself of fickleness and rash credulity? For if one cursed suspicion had such power to estrange and cast you down, how much more should certain assurance, now fully established, avail to raise and recall you! It is shameful for you to be capable of being led astray by falsehood and incapable of being brought back by truth. Let there indeed be pardon for having assented for a time to falsehood in disguise; but, once it has been discovered and stripped bare, how shameful is it still to assent—or even not to be greatly angered! Therefore “be angry, and do not sin,” if you wish us—or rather God—not to be angry. For what was secretly imposed upon you deserves compassion rather than indignation.

You are, undoubtedly, a man sailing—as is the whole human race—on this great and wide sea, where there are creeping things beyond number. Who can boast that there he is not continually driven by winds and tossed by waves? Know that you have suffered shipwreck among them; you have fallen into danger from false brethren. Again I say: this is the truth. You were deceived, and a lying spirit in the mouths of false prophets tripped you up.

3. But behold, falsehood has vanished, now that the light of truth has arisen. If still—far be it!—you persist in remaining in your obstinacy, I shall not for the present judge you; there is One who investigates and judges. But I spare you, for the time being overlooking the matter and delaying to come to you with the rod. Rather, in mercy and a spirit of gentleness I shall endeavour to draw you back to us, if I can; for I find this more natural to myself, and I do not doubt it will be more persuasive to you.

Yet I shall not hesitate to draw against you the sword that lies sheathed in my motherly breast: namely, continual grief in my heart and most frequent groans to God for you, until you return. But if, in accordance with your hardness and impenitent heart, you render futile every blow of these darts that strike so lovingly, and your soul can never say, “I am wounded by love,” then you must look to yourself. For now not truth only, but love too will set us free. But what have I said? How, wretched man, how shall I be freed while my heart is poured out and my son is perishing? Affection will not rest, even if effect does not follow; sorrow will not be soothed, nor will tears cease. So long as I live, I shall show myself to you another Samuel. Would that you might not be another Saul to me! I shall beg you; I shall beg for you, that you may come. Come, come, before we die, so that we who loved one another in life may not be separated in death.

## LETTER CCXXXIV. TO HERBERT, ABBOT OF SAINT STEPHEN AT DIJON.

He asks that John be forgiven the fault of his rash writing.

If Brother John said or wrote against us what was unfitting, or in an unfitting manner [Note: This John was a regular canon in the church of Saint Stephen at Dijon, where Herbert was abbot; see Letter 59. What it was that he wrote against Bernard is unclear. Nor do we think that he was John of Cornwall, Abelard’s pupil, concerning whom Chesnius writes in his notes on Abelard, p. 1159. Did this man write on the Conception?], he injured not us so much as himself. For by writing so he revealed his own frivolity more than he detected any error in us. Even if he had injured us in some respect, it would not have been for us to repay evil. Accordingly, considering not what he deserves but what befits me, I ask and entreat that you too forgive the young man this fault, which seems to savour more of a desire for petty glory than of malice—provided, however, that henceforth he restrain his hand from writing or treating of matters shown to be beyond him. For, as appears quite clearly, in this small matter which he ventured to undertake, a more mature pen and mind were needed. Let it be certain to you that, even in a short page, the man either did not write as he thought, or did not think as he ought.

## LETTER CCXXXV. TO LORD POPE CELESTINE, CONCERNING THE INTRUDER AT YORK.

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

He implores the authority of the Apostolic See against the notorious simoniacal usurper of the Church of York.

1. According to the justice that comes from the Law, you ought to raise up seed to your deceased brother. This will be worthily fulfilled if, in the inheritance of the Lord, you uphold the good acts of Pope Innocent, whose successor you are, and complete those which were less fully carried out. The matter in which this may be tested is at hand. Who does not know that the case of the Church of York was decided by him? [Note: The state of the case is related by William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, book I, ch. 17; Francis Godwin, *On the Bishops of England*, or among the Archbishops of York, no. 29; and Roger of Howden, in the latter part of the *Annals*. Briefly: in 1140 Thurstan (others call him Thurstan; William of Newburgh, Trustin—see Ivo of Chartres, Letter 274, and Juret’s notes there) died, Archbishop of York. The election of a successor was contested: some chose William, nephew of King Stephen and treasurer of York Church; others Henry Murdac, abbot of Fountains, formerly Bernard’s disciple at Clairvaux. William was consecrated by Henry, bishop of Winchester, but when he sought the pallium at Rome, the Pope rejected him. The king was offended by this rejection and refused to receive Henry, confirmed by the Pope and granted the pallium. Indeed, citizens and subjects, following the king’s example, would not admit their pastor. At length, after the king was reconciled, Henry was received by his people and presided for ten years, dying at Sherborne in 1153. Meanwhile William lived with Henry of Winchester. But upon learning of the deaths of Pope Eugenius, Bernard, and Archbishop Henry, he hastened to Rome and at last easily obtained, from Anastasius, Eugenius’s successor, confirmation and the pallium through the aid of Cardinal Gregory. He survived only a short time, dying in 1154, not without suspicion of administered poison. Godwin records that he was enrolled among the saints and that frequent miracles were performed at his tomb. Yet he adds: “Whoever wishes to believe this should remember that this saint, such as he was, was certainly deprived of office and driven from his archbishopric by Saint Bernard—or at least through Bernard’s agency.” On the affairs of York Church compare Letters 238–240, 252, and 346 ff.]

But would that it were unknown how what issued from the lips of so great a man has been put into execution. Would that it were not proclaimed in Gath or published in the streets of Ashkelon! (2 Sam. 1:20.) Yet, to make a short statement for busy ears, let my lord hear briefly what was said and what was done. Since the man who wickedly desired to claim for himself the election in the aforesaid Church was accused on many counts, the whole controversy was finally ordered to rest upon the testimony of the distinguished William [Note: He was called William of Saint Barbara, dean of York Church at that time, later bishop of Durham.], then dean of that Church: unless he removed by an oath on his own hand the charge of intrusion laid against this man among the other accusations, that great ambition was to be wholly frustrated in all its endeavours. This was granted not as a matter of judgment but of mercy, for he himself had requested it. A remarkably lenient sentence, since he was accused of very many and very grave charges which he was utterly unable to repel. Yet would that even this sentence stood! For if it does not suffice for justice, let it at least suffice for the Church’s liberation. We do not complain of the remission in the sentence, which harmed no one. For the more generous indulgence did not benefit the adversary, since he could not perform even what he had voluntarily promised. The very person in whom he appeared to place confidence failed him, lest he should fail himself by perjury. For when would a good man bear witness for one whom both the report of public opinion and the reality of his deeds condemn? What then? That man did not swear, and this man is bishop.

2. O matter worthy of the ignorance of all and, if possible, of perpetual suppression in silence! Yet that is too late. Alas! the devil’s triumph is known to the world. Everywhere the applause of the uncircumcised resounds, and the lament of good people, because wickedness seems to have overcome wisdom. The shame of Mother Church is pointed out with the finger; the venerable acts of Father Innocent are mocked, stripped bare by a wicked servant because he thinks him dead—but he lives in you.

If this outcome was impending, why was this most foul cause drawn from afar to Rome, when it was more fit for a shadow and a corner? Why did so many undertake such toil by sea and land? Why were religious men summoned from the ends of the earth to accuse him, and the purses of Christ’s poor exhausted by the expenses of a long journey? Could that shameful and notorious person not become bishop—though I say it unwillingly and sorrowfully—unless England, which recoiled from him, France, which abominated him, and Rome too should know him? How much better if his case had never been agitated in the Roman court and its universal, horrible stench had not touched even the sacred thresholds! How much more tolerable if the Apostolic See had remained ignorant of so intolerable an evil than that it should endure it openly known!

What rashness was this? Publicly defamed, accused before a judge, not cleared—indeed, convicted—and then consecrated. Let him who laid hands upon him after these things consider whether I ought rather to have said “execrated.” [Note: In the same sense, the word *exsecrare*, as opposed to legitimate consecration, occurs in Letter 166, no. 1; Letter 223, no. 2; and Letter 300 among Chesnius’s letters, vol. IV, which is a letter of Drogo, archbishop-elect of Lyons, to Louis the Younger.] For he will not deny that the matter stands thus; he will not deny that he learned these very facts from apostolic letters sent to him concerning this very case. Perhaps someone will say that, because no judgment was given, he was not convicted. I say he confessed as well. For the man who, in order to evade judgment, voluntarily chose to take refuge in the testimony of Dean William—when that testimony failed him, by what but his own judgment did he fall from his cause, condemned by his own mouth?

3. Since these things are so, see to it, lord Father, that your heart does not turn aside to the work of wickedness, because, according to the prophet, “the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity those who turn aside into crooked ways” (Ps. 125:5). Otherwise, what counsel do you give to those poor abbots whom an apostolic summons drew to Rome in order to accuse him, and likewise to very many religious men from that diocese? Are they to obey him and receive sacraments from a man twice intruded—first through the King, then through the Legate? For he broke into the sanctuary of God, against law and right, against the command of the supreme Pontiff, to the injury of the supreme See and the whole Roman court; when he could not enter by the door, he dug in, as they say, with a silver hoe, and shamelessly intruded himself. Unless your forceful authority intervenes, they will, I think, go into exile from their own seats before consenting to lay hands upon this idol. Besides, with how much holier a zeal, and one more worthy of your apostolate, would you draw the sword of Phinehas to confound two persons so shamefully fornicating, rather than allow so many holy men either to flee their places or compel them to remain against their consciences?

## LETTER CCXXXVI. TO THE WHOLE ROMAN CURIA. On the Same Subject.

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

To the reverend lords and fathers, the bishops and cardinals of the Curia, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and such prayers as are mine.

1. It was necessary to write to all concerning that which concerns all. Nor do I fear perhaps being accused of presumption, since, though least of all, I do not judge an injury to the Roman Curia foreign to myself. We are continually burned, I tell you—burned grievously—so that we are weary even of living. In the house of God we see horrors; and because we cannot correct them, at least we bring them to the notice of those to whom the matter belongs. If they correct them, well; but if not, we have delivered our souls, while you will have no excuse for sin.

You know that a sentence was pronounced by the late lord Pope Innocent, with the general agreement of yourselves and of the Roman Curia: that the election—or rather intrusion—of William of York was void unless the other William, then dean, repelled by an oath sworn on his own hand the accusation brought against him. Nor were you unaware that this sentence was full of mercy, not judgment, since William himself had sought this. But would that even it stood, and that what was done against it could not stand! For what is the situation? He did not swear, and this man sits in the seat of pestilence. Who will grant that Phinehas may come forth with a dagger against this fornication, or that Peter may live in his see and slay the wicked with the breath of his lips? Many cry to you with all their heart that you should endeavour to punish this sacrilege with due severity. Otherwise, I tell you, there will be an exceedingly great scandal in the Church of God; and I fear that the authority of the Roman See will suffer a very serious loss and great harm unless vengeance proceeds against him who overturned its general sentence, and proceeds in such a manner that others may fear.

2. What shall I say of the fact that this William boasts of possessing secret letters—letters truly of darkness? Would that they came from the princes of darkness, not from the princes of the Apostles. And behold, the children of the uncircumcised have heard it: they mock the Roman Curia, saying that, after so manifest a sentence had been given, contrary letters were furtively issued by it. What am I to say to you? If the grave scandal that scandalizes not little ones but great and perfect men does not burn you; if you do not sympathize with the poor abbots whom an apostolic summons drew from the ends of the earth to Rome; if you do not pity great and religious monasteries, upon which utter destruction threatens under that incubus; if—what I ought to have said first—the zeal of God’s house does not consume you: will the cunning of the enemy of mankind prevail so far that the leaders of the Church calmly endure their own contempt and this most shameful disgrace?

For what if that man received a sacrilegious consecration? Certainly it will now be far more glorious to cast down Simon after he has been elevated than to prevent him while he attempts it. Otherwise, what will you do with religious men who absolutely cannot, with a safe conscience, receive even the common sacraments from a leprous hand? They will, I think, choose flight rather than to give their hands to death; they will go into exile rather than eat things sacrificed to idols. But if the Roman Curia compels them, against their consciences, to bend the knee before Baal, let God see and judge; let that heavenly court see, in which judgment cannot be overthrown by any ambition. Finally, your child entreats you through the tender mercies of our God: if any zeal for God is in you, have mercy on the holy Church—at least you who are her friends—and, as far as you can, take care that assent is not given to so detestable an act.

## LETTER CCXXXVII. TO THE WHOLE ROMAN CURIA, WHEN THEY ELECTED THE ABBOT OF SAINT ANASTASIUS AS POPE EUGENIUS.

[Note: In 1145, after the death of Pope Lucius II, successor of Celestine, Bernard, abbot in Rome of Saint Anastasius and disciple of Saint Bernard, was elected and called Eugenius III. The books *On Consideration* are addressed to him. Here, at no. 344, is his letter as abbot to Bernard; likewise, another letter of his as pope precedes Letter 273; finally, the letter concerning his death appears in the Appendix, no. 475.]

Bernard marvels that Bernard, abbot of Saint Anastasius, has been taken from leisure and solitude and carried off to the care of the whole Church. He fears that a man accustomed to quiet and less practised in public affairs will not prove equal to so great a burden; therefore he asks that the faithful assistance of the cardinals support him.

To the reverend lords and fathers, the cardinals and all the bishops of the Curia: the child of their Holiness.

1. May God pardon you: what have you done? You have called a buried man back to mankind; one fleeing cares and crowds you have again entangled in cares and thrust among crowds. You have made the last first, and behold, his latter things are more perilous than the former. Through you, one crucified to the world has come alive again to the world; and one who had chosen to be lowly in the house of his God, you have chosen as lord over all. Why have you frustrated the counsel of the poor? Why have you disturbed the judgment of a poor and needy man, contrite in heart? He was running well: why did you think it fit to fence in his paths, turn aside his tracks, and entangle his steps? As though he were descending from Jerusalem rather than ascending from Jericho, he fell among robbers. Though he had powerfully shaken himself free, as from certain violent hands of the devil, from carnal allurements and worldly glory, he could not escape your hands.

Did he leave Pisa in order to receive Rome? [Note: Eugenius was formerly *vicedominus*—vice-lord—of the Church of Pisa; a manuscript of Dunes cited by Henriquez calls him suffragan. Then he was Bernard’s disciple at Clairvaux, and soon abbot of the monastery of Saint Anastasius, or Three Fountains, at Aquae Salviae near Rome. Contrary to custom, he was elected by the cardinals supreme Pontiff of the Church in 1145, not from the cardinalate but from the abbacy, in place of Lucius, who, as already stated, departed this life in the same year, on 25 February. Bernard therefore marvels that one who did not endure the vice-lordship of a single particular church was called to rule the whole universal Church. Let us briefly explain what office or dignity is meant by the title *vicedominus*, for there are still churches or bishoprics that retain it. Formerly every bishop was required to have a *vicedominus* and an *oeconomus* (Distinction 89, chapter “Volumus”). On this Gregory the Great writes to the subdeacon Anthelmus, book IX, Letter 66: “We wish that our brother Paschasius appoint for himself both a vice-lord and the chief officer of the household, so that he may be fit and ready both for guests who arrive and for matters that arise, etc.” There the Gloss on the cited chapter “Volumus” explains “vice-lord” as “the manager of episcopal property, who provides for episcopal affairs and for arriving guests,” because “the bishop cannot conduct such business in his own person.” See Question 3, “Quia Episcopus,” and apply what is said about guests to the vice-lord. Thus the Gloss. But Filesac, doctor of theology at Paris, in his treatment of title *De Officio Judicis Ordinarii*, book I of the *Decretals*, or *On the Sacred Authority of Bishops*, ch. 4, §5, considers that the two should rather be distinguished: the *oeconomus* is responsible for guests, while the vice-lord presides in the bishop’s name over causes and litigation.] Did one who could not endure vice-lordship in one Church seek lordship in every Church?

2. What reason or deliberation, then, was there in rushing suddenly, when the supreme Pontiff had died, upon a rustic man, laying hands on one in hiding, snatching axe, adze, or mattock from his hands, dragging him to the palace, raising him onto the throne, clothing him in purple and fine linen [Note: By this time pontiffs wore the red cloak, concerning which Peter Damian writes in Book I, Letter 20.], girding him with a sword “to execute vengeance among the nations, punishments among the peoples, to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron shackles”? Was there no wise and experienced man among you to whom these things would be more suited? It seems ridiculous indeed that a shabby little fellow should be taken up to preside over princes, command bishops, and dispose of kingdoms and empires. Ridiculous—or miraculous? Certainly one of the two.

I do not deny, nor do I despair, that this too could have been God’s work—he who alone performs great wonders—especially since I hear people everywhere saying that this has been done by the Lord. Yet neither have I forgotten the ancient judgments of God, and Scripture records many who in earlier times were taken from private or even rustic life, by the Lord’s will, to govern his people. For example, did he not choose David his servant in such a manner, and take him from the sheepfolds, taking him from following the nursing ewes? (Ps. 77:70–71.) Thus, I say, thus it could also have happened concerning our Eugenius, by the good pleasure of the Lord.

3. Yet I am not at ease, because he is a delicate son, and his modesty is tender, accustomed rather to leisure and quiet than to handling matters outside; and one must fear that he will not discharge the duties of his apostolate with the authority required. What do you think that man now feels, who, disturbed suddenly as an infant from his mother’s lap and bosom, sees himself drawn from the secrecy of inward contemplation and the friendly solitude of the heart into the public midst, and led, as it were, like a sheep to slaughter, to things so unfamiliar and disagreeable? Unless the Lord puts his hand beneath him, alas, he must needs be overwhelmed and crushed by an unfamiliar and excessive burden, terrible—as they say—even to gigantic or angelic shoulders.

Nevertheless, since it has been done, and, as many say, has been done by the Lord, it concerns you, dearest friends, diligently to foster by your fervent efforts and faithful services what you know has been brought about by your hands. Therefore, if there is in you any encouragement, any power of love in the Lord, any compassion of mercy, any bowels of pity, stand by him and cooperate with him in the work to which the Lord has called him through you. Whatever things are true, whatever chaste, whatever just, whatever holy, whatever lovely, whatever of good report—place these before him, urge these upon him, do these; and the God of peace will be with you.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS: THE FIRST.

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1145.]

Bernard both congratulates and sympathizes with Eugenius, newly raised to the pontificate. He encourages him courageously to discharge the apostolic office, so that he may answer the high expectations many have formed of him.

To the most beloved Father and lord, EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme Pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

1. The report has been heard in our land, and this word concerning what the Lord has done with you has been widely spread. Until now I held back my pen and silently considered the matter. For I awaited your letters and hoped to be anticipated by you with blessings of sweetness. I awaited a faithful man coming from your side, who would recount everything in order—what was done, how, and in what manner. I awaited perhaps one of my sons returning, who would soothe his father’s grief and say, “Joseph your son is alive, and he rules over all the land of Egypt” (Gen. 45:26).

Hence this letter arises not from choice but necessity, wrung from me by the prayers of friends, to whom I cannot deny the little, whatever it may be, that remains of my life. For henceforth my days will be short, and only the grave remains for me. [Note: We find the sentence, “For henceforth my days will be short, and only the grave remains for me,” in only two manuscripts, those of Compiègne and Saint-Theodoric.] Yet since I have begun, I shall speak to my lord. I no longer dare call you son, because the son has become father and the father has been changed into son. [Note: Below, no. 3: “For although I have laid aside the name of father, I have not laid aside fear,” etc. The same occurs in the prologue to the books *On Consideration*.] “He who comes after me has been made before me”; yet I do not envy it, because I trust that I possess in him what I lacked, since he came not only after me but also through me. For if you deign to allow it, in a certain sense I begot you through the Gospel. What, then, is our hope, joy, and crown of glory? Is it not you before God? For “a wise son is his father’s glory” (Prov. 10:1).

Henceforth, however, you will not be called son, but a new name will be called for you, which the mouth of the Lord has named (Isa. 62:2). This is a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, and many will rejoice in this change. For as Abram was changed into Abraham (Gen. 17:5), Jacob into Israel (Gen. 32:28), and—as I may set before you examples more especially from among your predecessors—Simon into Cephas (John 1:42), Saul into Paul (Acts 13:9), so my son Bernard has been advanced into my father Eugenius by a change altogether joyful and, we hope, beneficial. This is the finger of God, raising the needy from the dust and lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.

2. It remains that, now this change in you has occurred, the bride of your Lord entrusted to you should likewise be changed for the better, and no longer be called Sarai but henceforth Sarah (Gen. 17:15). Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding. If you are the bridegroom’s friend, do not call his beloved “my princess,” but “the Princess”; claiming nothing in her as your own, except that, for her, if need be, you must even give your life. If Christ has sent you, you will reckon that you came not to be served but to serve—and to serve not only with your resources but with your very life, as I said before.

The true successor of Paul will say with Paul: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy” (2 Cor. 1:23). The heir of Peter will hear Peter saying: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but being made an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3). Thus, through you, she will no longer be a slave woman, but free and beautiful, received into the desired embraces of her most beautiful Bridegroom. Otherwise, through whom else may this liberty, so rightly due, be hoped for, if even you—far be it!—seek your own interests in Christ’s inheritance, you who had already learned not merely not to retain what is yours, but not even to belong to yourself?

[Col. 0429A] 3. Therefore, since it has such confidence in you as it has not appeared to have had in any of your predecessors for many generations past, the whole Church of the saints everywhere rightly exults and glories in the Lord; but especially that one whose womb bore you and whose breasts you sucked. [Note: [Col. 0429D] Namely Clairvaux or the Cistercian Order, but rather Clairvaux, which is again called his mother in §6.] What then? Am I not also permitted to rejoice with those who rejoice? Shall I not be one among the number of the joyful? I exulted, I confess—but with trembling. I exulted, yet at the very moment of my exultation fear and trembling came upon me. For although I have laid aside the name of father, I have not laid aside a father’s fear, anxiety, affection, or, in short, a father’s heart. I consider the rank, and fear the fall; I consider the summit of dignity, and behold the face of the abyss lying below. [Col. 0429B] I attend to the height of the honour and dread, close at hand, the danger, because it is written: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand” (Ps. 48:13, 21). This, I think, refers rather to the cause than to the time, so that “when he was in honour, he did not understand” means: Honour swallowed up understanding.

4. Indeed, you had chosen to be lowly in the house of your God and to recline in the lowest place at his banquet; but it pleased him who invited you to say: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10). You have therefore ascended on high. Do not be high-minded, but fear, lest perhaps at last you utter that pitiable cry: “Because of the face of your wrath and indignation, lifting me up, you dashed me down” [Col. 0429C] (Ps. 101:11). For you have obtained a higher place, but not a safer one; a more exalted, not a more secure one. This place is truly terrible—terrible indeed. The place, I say, where you stand is holy ground: it is Peter’s place, the place of the Prince of the Apostles, where his feet stood. It is the place of him whom the Lord appointed lord of his household and ruler over all his possession. If perhaps you turn aside from the way of the Lord, he was buried in that same place, that he may be a witness against you.

Rightly was the Church, while she was still tender, while still in the cradle, entrusted to such a shepherd, such a nursling, while still in the cradle: taught by his doctrine and reared by his example, she would trample all earthly things beneath her feet. For he had shaken his hands free of every gift, and could say from a pure heart and good conscience: “Silver and gold I have none” [Col. 0429D] (Acts 3:6). So much on this point.

5. Moreover, this is why I have written to you before the time. The Bishop of Winchester and the Archbishop of York do not walk in one spirit with the Archbishop of Canterbury [Note: The Bishop of Winchester was Henry of Blois, formerly Abbot of Glastonbury, nephew of King Henry and thus a supporter of his kinsman William. The Archbishop of Canterbury was Theobald, formerly Abbot of Bec, to whom Letter 361 is addressed.]; rather, they proceed against him, and this is an old complaint concerning the legation.

[Col. 0430A] Yet who is he, and who are they? Is not the Archbishop of York [Note: The case of William of York, discussed in Letter [Col. 0430D] 235, had not yet been settled in this year. For, according to Serlo in vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 747, “he presided over the see, employing royal power against those who resisted.” Henry, Abbot of Fountains, with others, brought him before Eugenius, by whom William was removed. His supporters plundered Fountains Abbey. On Henry’s election, see below at Letter 252.] the very man whom, in your presence, when you were still almost one of us, your brethren opposed to his face because he was blameworthy? But he trusted in the abundance of his riches and prevailed in his vanity. It is nevertheless certain that he did not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbed up another way. If he had been a shepherd, he should have been loved; if a hired servant, tolerated. But now he must be avoided and repelled, being a thief and [p. 235] robber. What shall I say of the Lord of Winchester? “The works which he does bear witness concerning him.” But the Archbishop of Canterbury, whom they oppose, is a religious man and of fragrant reputation. We pray for him, that his righteousness may answer for him. But may their iniquity be upon [Col. 0430B] them, as it is written: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. 18:20). When you have received the appointed time, you will repay them according to the works of their hands, so that they may know that there is a prophet in Israel.

6. Who will grant me, before I die, to see the Church of God as in ancient days, when the apostles cast their nets for a catch—not a catch of silver or gold, but a catch of souls? How I desire that you should inherit the voice of him whose seat you have obtained: “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20). O voice of thunder! O voice of majesty and power! At its terror may all who hate Zion be confounded and turned backward [Col. 0430C]!

This is what your mother earnestly awaits and wholly demands of you; this is what the children of your mother, the little ones with the great, desire and sigh for: that every plant which the heavenly Father did not plant may be uprooted by your hands. For you have been appointed over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and destroy, and to build and plant. Many, hearing this word, have said to themselves: “Now the axe has been laid to the root of the trees.” Many say in their heart: “Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come,” when barren branches will be cut away, so that those which thrive may bear more abundant fruit.

7. Therefore be strengthened and be valiant: let your hands be upon the necks of your enemies. Claim for yourself, by steadfastness of soul and vigour of spirit, that portion which [Col. 0430D] the almighty Father gave you beyond your brothers, and which he took from the hand of the Amorite with his sword and bow. Yet in all your works remember that you are a human being, and let the fear of him who takes away the spirit of princes always be before your eyes. How many deaths of Roman pontiffs have your own eyes seen in a short time [Col. 0431A]?

[Note: It may rightly seem remarkable that there is reason why Roman pontiffs should be so short-lived that Peter alone is thought to have reached his twenty-fifth year, while premature death has carried off very many after only a few years or months, indeed after not many days, although we see that many emperors and kings lived much longer. The matter is altogether worthy of inquiry. But who knows the mind of the Lord?

I see, however, that the same question was put to Blessed Peter Damian by Pope Alexander. Damian treats and explains it carefully; what he writes is entirely worth reading. See Letter 17 of Book I among his letters; elsewhere, *Opuscule* 23. “At one time,” he says, “you earnestly asked me what cause I thought there was for the bishop of the Apostolic See never to live longer, but to close his final day within a short space of time; so much so that after Saint Peter the Apostle, who presided for about five periods of five years, no subsequent Roman pontiff equalled this duration of pontificate. Indeed, in modern times scarcely anyone is raised to the summit of that See who passes the limit of four or, at most, five years. As we consider this, a prodigious amazement, so to speak, arises, because this necessity of living briefly is found in no other church in the whole world. But insofar as the secret of divine dispensation is revealed to mortals, it seems to us that the order of heavenly judgment has arranged this in order to instil fear of death into the human race and to show clearly, in the very primacy of glory, how contemptible the glory of temporal life is. Thus, while the foremost of human beings dies within so brief a span of time, every person, shaken with fear, may be summoned to watchfulness for his own coming death; and the tree of the human race, seeing its crown and summit so readily fall, may tremble in all its branches, shaken by the breath of fear.”]

Damian, I confess, confined the lives of pontiffs within narrow limits when he extended them no further than four or five years. Yet they seem to me to have been restricted to even shorter spans, if the histories of the pontiffs are consulted. Therefore Saint Bernard most rightly exhorts Eugenius in this letter to learn, from the exceedingly brief rule of his predecessors, to regard his own as uncertain.]

Let your predecessors themselves remind you of your most certain and very swift departure; and let the brief duration of their rule announce to you the fewness of your days. Amid the allurements of this passing glory, therefore, remember your last things in continual meditation: for those whose seat you have succeeded to, you will without doubt follow in death.

## LETTER CCXXXIX

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1145.]

### TO THE SAME PERSON

He presses the deposition of William of York before the Pope, to whom alone this authority belongs.

[Col. 0432B]

I am importunate, but I have an excuse: the apostolic office of Eugenius excuses me. They say that you are not the Pope, but I am; and people with [Col. 0431B] business come flocking to me from every side. Nor, amid so great a multitude of friends, are there lacking those to whom I cannot refuse service—not merely without causing offence, but even without sin. And now there is another excuse, no less suitable, because the cause [variant: *cura*, “concern”] is most honourable.

Once more my pen is directed against that idol of York: for this reason, namely, that although we have often attacked him with this weapon, he has not yet been pierced through. Why is this? Perhaps because nothing of the kind has been directed by us that was like Jonathan’s sword, which never returned backward. Nor indeed was the fault in the missile, but in the one who aimed it. It is evident that it was not sent with the strength it should have had. Nor is this surprising. For who can shoot arrows with a strong hand except the son of the Mighty One?

He who holds [Col. 0431C] Peter’s place can, with one blow, strike down Ananias, and with one strike Simon Magus. And, to state more plainly what I mean: the issuing of a definitive sentence for the deposition of bishops is known to belong to the Roman Pontiff alone [p. 236], because, although many others are called to share in the burden of pastoral concern, he alone possesses the fullness of authority. Therefore, if I may dare say it, he alone is at fault if an offence which ought to be struck is not struck—and struck with the force with which it ought to be struck. But with what force the fault of the aforesaid Archbishop of York ought not merely to be struck, but thunderbolted [Col. 0432A], I leave to your conscience.

Moreover, we believe that what has not been done has been reserved for you, so that in it the Church of God, over which by its author you preside, may experience the ardour of your zeal, the power of your arm, and the wisdom of your mind; and so that all the people may fear the priest of the Lord, hearing that the wisdom of God is in him to execute judgment.

## LETTER CCXL

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE SAME PERSON, CONCERNING THE INTRUDER AT YORK

He praises Eugenius’ zeal, and now wishes it displayed in deposing the man fraudulently occupying the see of York.

1. How I desire always to hear such things about you, by which God is glorified, your ministry honoured, and my soul made glad! Thus, when we heard your answer concerning certain persons who appeared to aspire too eagerly and ambitiously to the office of legate, and to hope for it shamelessly beyond what can be said, we were made glad beyond words. Not we alone, but all who love your name rejoiced with great joy.

Then, when we saw your letters sent concerning the cause of the Church of Rodez [Rutinensis] [Note: That is, in rejecting the unworthy man elected or promoted to that see; see Letters 328 and 329.], then indeed, then our mouth was filled with joy and our tongue with exultation. Such acts are worthy of your apostolic office; they ennoble the supreme See and truly befit the Bishop of the world. Therefore I bend my knees to the very author of this your unique primacy, that he may grant you always to think [Col. 0432C] and act thus: in plucking up and planting, in destroying and building. For you have ascended this throne for the fall and resurrection of many. Let those who stand harmfully fall—let them fall; let the worthy be raised up. Let the axe be laid to the root of barren plantings; let the fruitful be pruned, that they may bear more fruit. While humble Eugenius presides, I say, let the proud be cast down from their seat and the humble exalted; let the hungry be filled with good things and the rich sent away empty.

[Col. 0433A] For recently, to the exultation of the whole earth, this was done in the case of a certain poor bishop. [Note: This unnamed bishop is discussed in Book III of *On Consideration*, ch. 3, where Eugenius is praised for giving the poor bishop something to give, lest he be thought ungenerous. There also is noted a bishop from overseas regions who wished to purchase a bishopric at Rome—perhaps William is meant.]

2. Come then: let this holy zeal of compassion now pass also to that wretched transmarine Church, for the time has come to have mercy upon it. It is the vineyard of the Lord of hosts: a chosen vineyard, a most beautiful vineyard; but alas, almost reduced to a wilderness, because a solitary beast feeds upon it. Why do the nations say: “Where is her God? Where is he whom they appointed keeper in the vineyards? Where is the pruning hand? Where the cultivator’s hoe?” How long shall the ground be occupied by a useless branch and the fruit be choked? The time for pruning has indeed come.

For the man of his peace [Note: Namely William, Dean of York, by whose oath the intruder William had wished to clear himself; see above, Letters 235 and 236.], in whom he trusted and by whom he should have been cleared, testifies that he needs not clearing but cutting off. There are, moreover, that man’s letters concerning him to the legate of [Col. 0433B] the Apostolic See, in which he openly affirms a manifest intrusion and denies that there was an election. Thus the man whom he had prepared for himself as a defender he finds to be an accuser. Besides, the public report everywhere proclaimed concerning him could with every right deprive even a military man of his military belt.

3. How can he now stand when you have many grounds for casting him down, and the will is not lacking? I have read of your zeal for that Church in your letters, and now I demand its exercise from your hands. It is not for me to prescribe to one who is wise by what path his removal should proceed—for more than one path seems open to me [p. 237]. Nor does it greatly matter to us on which side the unfruitful tree falls, provided it falls.

Yet I say this: is not one who claims possession for himself by trafficking in stolen letters a thief and a robber? Finally, where he asserts that he had secret letters of his consecration, what he says is either true or false. If true, he is guilty of theft and an accuser of the supreme pontiff; if false, he must hear: “You have killed and taken possession.” For “a lying mouth kills the soul” [Col. 0433C] (Wis. 1:11). But far be it that such duplicity should be believed of so great a man as this fellow imputes to him. For this was Innocent; and, if he were allowed to answer for himself, he would undoubtedly say to him: “I gave sentence against you openly, and in secret I said nothing.”

## LETTER CCXLI

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1147.]

### TO ALPHONSE, COUNT OF SAINT-GILLES

[Note: Add: also of Toulouse. Born in the East to his father Raymond, Count of Toulouse, and his mother Elvira—as William of Tyre relates, *History of the Holy War*, Book 10, ch. 27, calling him Anfossus—he was immersed in the waters of the Jordan itself at his baptism. The same author writes of him as follows in Book 16, ch. 28, while recounting his journey to the East: “In those same days there arrived at the port of Acre a magnificent and illustrious man, the Count of Toulouse, named Anfossus, son of the elder Lord Count Raymond. His father had been so great a prince and of such merit in the first expedition, a man distinguished by his own notable titles but more illustrious through the pious memory of his father. From there he went to Jerusalem in order to give thanks to the Lord for the happily completed pilgrimage; but at the maritime city of Caesarea, a few days after he arrived, poison was administered to him, as is said, and the author of so great a crime being unknown, he ended his life,” etc.

Moreover, the county of Saint-Gilles is a part of Narbonese Gaul, so named after Saint Giles, once its inhabitant, though it had formerly been included in Septimania. In a certain agreement concluded in 1125 between himself and Raymond, Count of Barcelona, the Count of Saint-Gilles calls himself Hildefonsus; there his wife is called Fardida.]

### CONCERNING HENRY THE HERETIC

He describes Henry, successor of the heretic Peter of Bruys, together with his impious doctrines and impure deeds, reproaching the Count for allowing such a man to range unpunished within his jurisdiction.

[Col. 0434A]

1. What great evils have we heard and learned that Henry the heretic has done, and daily continues to do, in the Churches of God? [Note: We have treated Henry and the Henrician heretics at length in the Preface to this volume, §6.] A ravening wolf moves about in your land under sheep’s clothing; but, according to the Lord’s designation, we know him by his fruits (Matt. 7:15–16). Churches are without congregations, congregations without priests, priests without due reverence, and finally Christians without Christ.
