Churches are reckoned synagogues [Col. 0434B]; the sanctuary of God is denied to be holy; the sacraments are not judged sacred; feast days are deprived of their solemn observances. People die in their sins; souls are snatched everywhere to the fearful tribunal—alas, neither reconciled by repentance nor fortified by holy [variant: sacramental] communion.

The life of Christ is shut off from the little children of Christians when baptismal grace is denied them. They are not permitted even to approach salvation, although the Saviour mercifully cries out for them: “Let the little children come to me” (Matt. 19:14). Does he, then, who saved humans and beasts, and who has multiplied his mercy—God—nevertheless not allow that same great mercy to reach the innocent alone? What, I ask, what does he begrudge little children in the infant Saviour, who was born for them? [Col. 0434C] This is diabolical envy; through this envy death entered the world. Does he think that little children do not need the Saviour because they are little? If so, then the great Lord became little for no purpose—to say nothing of his being scourged, smeared with spittle, fastened to the cross, and finally dying.

2. This man is not from God, who both acts and speaks so contrary to God. Alas! Yet he is heard by many and has a people who believe him. O most unhappy people! At the voice of one heretic, all prophetic and apostolic voices have fallen silent among them—voices which proclaimed that the Church was to be gathered from every nation into the one faith of Christ by the one Spirit of truth. Therefore the divine oracles have deceived us, and [Col. 0435A] the eyes and minds of all are mistaken—those who see fulfilled what they read was foretold.

This man alone, with astounding and altogether Jewish blindness, either not seeing or begrudging the fulfillment of a truth so manifest to all, has by some diabolical art persuaded a stupid and senseless people, concerning an evident matter, not to believe even their own eyes: that former generations were deceived, later ones are in error, that the whole world even after Christ’s blood was shed will be lost, and that all the riches of God’s mercies and the grace intended for all have come to those alone whom he deceives.

For this reason I have now, though suffering great bodily weakness, undertaken a journey to these regions [Note: See Book III of the *Life*, ch. 6.], which that solitary beast especially devours, since there is no one to resist or to save. For, driven from all France [Col. 0435B] because of like wickedness, he found these lands alone exposed to him; there, under your lordship, he rages with all fury against Christ’s flock. Whether this accords with your honour, illustrious prince, judge for yourself. Yet it is not surprising if that crafty serpent deceived you, since he has the appearance of piety but utterly denies its power.

3. But now hear who he is. He is an apostate: having abandoned the religious habit—for he had been a monk [Note: Geoffrey likewise calls Henry a monk in Book III of the *Life of Bernard*, §16; and the Cistercian *Exordium*, cited in Book III of the same *Life*, ch. 17. The *Acts of Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans*, in vol. III of the *Analecta*, p. 314, where more is said about Henry, call him a hermit.]—he returned to the filth of flesh and world, like a dog to its vomit. Ashamed to live among relatives and acquaintances, or rather forbidden to do so because of the enormity of his offence, he girded his loins and rushed off he knew not where, becoming a wanderer and fugitive over [Col. 0435C] the earth.

When he began to beg, he made the Gospel a source of income—for he was educated—and, peddling the word of God for sale, preached in order to eat. Whatever he could extract beyond subsistence from the simpler people, or from some woman, he shamefully squandered in gambling with dice or in still more shameful uses. After the people’s applause by day, this distinguished preacher was frequently found at night with prostitutes, and sometimes even with married women. Inquire, if you please, noble sir, how he left the city of Lausanne; how Le Mans; how Poitiers; how Bordeaux. No way back is open to him anywhere, since everywhere he has left foul traces behind him.

Did you, at last, expect good fruit from such a tree? He has indeed made the very land in which he is stink throughout the whole world, because, according to the Lord’s saying, a bad tree cannot produce good fruit [Col. 0435D] (Matt. 7:18).

4. This, then, as I said, is the reason for my coming. I do not now come of my own accord; I am drawn equally by the summons and compassion [Col. 0436A] of the Church, in hope that that thorn and its perversities, while their shoots are still small, may be uprooted from the Lord’s field—not by the hand of me, who am nothing, but by that of the holy bishops among whom I am, with your powerful right hand cooperating.

Chief among them is the venerable Bishop of Ostia [Note: Alberic, on whom see Book III of the *Life of Bernard*, §17. Born at Beauvais, a monk of Cluny, created cardinal by Innocent in 1138, legate [Col. 0436D] to England, then Syria, and finally France; Letter 219 is addressed to him.], sent by the Apostolic See for this very purpose. He is a man who has done great things in Israel, and through him the almighty Lord has given victory to his Church in many matters.

It concerns you, illustrious man, to receive him and those with him honourably; and, lest the great labour of so many great men, undertaken above all for the salvation of you and yours, should prove ineffective, to give assistance according to the authority granted you from above.

## LETTER CCXLII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1147.]

### TO THE PEOPLE OF TOULOUSE, AFTER HIS RETURN

Heretics must be diligently avoided—indeed, driven away. Hospitality must be practised. Not every preacher is to be admitted.

[Col. 0436B]

1. At the arrival of our dearest brother and fellow-abbot Bernard of Grand-Selve, we rejoiced and were delighted by what he told us of the steadfastness and sincerity of your faith in God, of the perseverance of your love and devotion toward us, and of your zeal and hatred against heretics. Thus each of you may rightly say: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Ps. 138:21–22).

We give thanks to God because our visit to you was not fruitless. Our stay among you was indeed brief [Col. 0436C], but not unproductive. For the truth was made manifest through us—not only in word, but also in power [p. 239] [Note: That is, by the remarkable miracles performed by Bernard himself; see Book III of the *Life*, ch. 6. Berengar also acknowledges them in his apology for Abelard: “Long ago swift-flying fame spread the fragrance of your holiness through the world, proclaimed your merits, and celebrated your miracles,” etc.]—and the wolves were exposed. Coming to you in sheep’s clothing, they had been devouring your people like bread for food, like sheep for slaughter. The foxes which were destroying the Lord’s most precious vineyard, your city, were exposed—but not captured.

Therefore, beloved, pursue and seize them; do not desist until they perish utterly and flee from all your borders, for it is not safe to sleep near serpents. They sit in ambush with the rich in secret places in order to kill the innocent. They are thieves and robbers, of the sort the Lord marks out in the Gospel [Col. 0436D] (John 10:8). They have been subverted and are ready to subvert others; plainly they stain your reputation and corrupt your faith. “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33), especially since the speech of such men, as the blessed Apostle says, spreads like a cancer (2 Tim. 2:17).

[Col. 0437A] 2. Who will grant me an opportunity to come to you once more? For I desire, if somehow I can do so in the Lord’s will, to see you a second time. For your exhortation and salvation I shall not count the labour, though weak and frail in body. Meanwhile, beloved, stand firm in the Lord as you began and as you received from us. Obey your bishop and your other superiors, the teachers of the Church.

Be diligent in hospitality, because through it many have pleased God. Your father Abraham, because of the holy care he customarily devoted to receiving pilgrims, deserved to receive angels as guests (Gen. 18). Likewise Lot, his nephew, rejoiced in their reception through a like devotion and pious custom [Col. 0437B] (Gen. 19). You likewise, in the same fashion, receive not angels but the Lord of angels in strangers; feed him in the needy, clothe him in the naked, visit him in the sick, ransom him in captives. God is won by such sacrifices, and at the judgment he will say: “What you did to one of these least ones of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40).

3. I also warn you, beloved, as I said when I was present with you: receive no foreign or unknown preacher unless he preaches as one sent by the supreme pontiff or authorized by your own bishop. “How,” he says, “will they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15). These are the people who clothe themselves in an appearance of piety while utterly denying its power; like poison in honey, they mix profane innovations of words and meanings into heavenly words. Therefore beware of them as poisoners, and recognize ravening wolves in sheep’s clothing.

Let the bearer of this letter, the venerable Abbot of Grand-Selve, be commended to you [Col. 0437C] [Note: This is Bernard mentioned above, designated in the manuscripts only by the initial letter B; he joined the abbey of Grand-Selve, of the Order of Saint Benedict in the district of Toulouse, to the Cistercians.], and also his house, which is ours as well: recently entrusted to us and our Order by himself, and especially associated with the church of Clairvaux. Show us in him and in the holy men with him how much you have profited from our admonition in works of mercy; and give, in them, proof of your love and devotion toward us. Whatever you do for them, consider it done for me. May the grace and peace of God be with you. Amen.

## LETTER CCXLIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE ROMANS, WHEN THEY WITHDREW FROM LORD POPE EUGENIUS

[Note: Compare Book IV of *On Consideration*, ch. 2; Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, Book 7, ch. 31; and Book II of *The Deeds of Frederick*, ch. 20. The Arnoldists are called heretics by Bonacursus and are joined with the Cathars and Passagians; they are accused of saying that sacraments administered by evil ministers are invalid: *Spicilegium*, vol. XIII, p. 85.]

The Romans, with the heretic Arnold inflaming their faction, sought to restore the form of the ancient republic and liberty, leaving the Pope only the care of sacred things. They therefore claimed the papal revenues for themselves, ordering the Pope to live, as formerly, content only with tithes and offerings. Hence arose the rebellion, violently directed against Eugenius. On this occasion Bernard sternly but justly reproves the Romans for their injustice toward the Pope: an injury which rebounds upon the saints and all Catholics and will not escape God’s vengeance unless they speedily repent.

[Col. 0437D]

To the nobles, leading men, and entire Roman people [Col. 0438A], Brother Bernard, called Abbot of Clairvaux: turn away from evil and do what is good.

1. My speech is addressed to you, exalted and illustrious people, though I am a lowly and insignificant person, a little man of almost no consequence. This seems shameful and burdensome to me as I consider who I am writing to, and to whom, and also how another might judge this action differently. Yet I think it less grievous to risk shame before human beings than to be condemned before God for silence—for withholding the truth and concealing righteousness. For he himself says: “Declare to my people their crimes” (Isa. 58:1). It will also be a testimony for me before the Lord if I can say: “I have not hidden your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” [Col. 0438B] (Ps. 39:11).

For such reasons, then, I do not fear, although shame resists, because of my low estate to write from afar to a glorious people and, in this letter sent across the mountains, to remind the Romans of their own peril and sin—if perhaps they may hear and be quieted. Who knows whether those who do not yield to the threats of the powerful or to all the armour of the strong may be converted by a poor man’s plea? Did not, once in Babylon, that whole people, misled by the wicked judgments of judges, return to judgment at the voice of a single younger boy, and thus innocent blood was saved on that day (Dan. 13)? So now also: though I am a youth and despised—a youth, I mean, not through fewness of years but of merits—God is nevertheless able to give even my voice a voice of power [Col. 0438C], through which that people, who are likewise plainly deceived, may return to judgment. Let this, therefore, be my defence against those who perhaps think that I ought to incur anger or indignation for this.

2. If even this is insufficient, I add this also. The cause is common, and there is no distinction between small and great. For the pain is in the head, and therefore it is not foreign even to the smallest or most remote parts of the body. Nor, then, is it foreign to me. This very great pain reaches even me, though least of all, because it is great; and because, being the pain of the head, it cannot but be also that of the body, of which I am a member.

Does not the tongue, when the head suffers, cry out on behalf of all the body’s members that it suffers in its head, and do not all, through the tongue, acknowledge the affliction of their own [Col. 0438D] head to be their own? Permit me, therefore, I beg—permit me to lament a little among you for my pain: not mine alone, but that of the whole Church. Is not her voice today throughout the world: “My head aches; my head aches”? For what Christian, even the least in the whole world, does not glory in this head, which those two glorious princes of the earth, one losing his head and the other bowing his head on the cross, exalted by their triumph and adorned with their blood?

[Col. 0439A] Therefore the injury done to the Apostles concerns every Christian [p. 241]; and as “their sound went forth into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5), so their injury is felt, lamented, and grieved everywhere by all.

3. What has seemed good to you, O Romans: to offend the princes of the world, who are your own special protectors? Why do you provoke against yourselves, with fury as intolerable as it is irrational, the King of earth and the Lord of heaven alike, by striving with sacrilegious audacity to assail and diminish in honour the holy and apostolic See, singularly exalted by divine and royal privileges—a See which you ought, if necessary, even alone against all others, to have defended?

Thus foolish Romans, neither judging nor distinguishing what is honourable [Col. 0439B], you disfigure, so far as lies in you, your head and the head of all—the very head for which you ought not to have spared even your own necks, had necessity required it. Your fathers subjected the world to the City; you hasten to make the City a mockery to the world. Behold: Peter’s heir has been expelled by you from Peter’s see and city. Behold: cardinals and bishops, the ministers of the Lord, have been stripped by your hands of their goods and houses.

O foolish and senseless people, O deceived dove without understanding! Was he not your head, and were they not your eyes? What, then, is Rome now but a trunk without a head, a brow hollowed out without eyes, a face in darkness? Open your eyes, wretched nation—open them, and see the desolation now hanging over you. How quickly “the finest colour has changed” (Lam. 4:1); she who was mistress of nations and princess of provinces has become like a widow [Col. 0439C] (Lam. 1:1).

4. But these are the beginnings of evils: we fear worse. Are you not near destruction, if you persist? Return, return, O Shunammite; return to your heart. Recognize at last, even if late, what things, how great they are, and from whom you are suffering, or have suffered. Remember for what cause, to what end, by whose agency, and for whose benefit, not many days ago all the ornaments and revenues of all the churches within you were plundered and scattered.

[Note: [Col. 0439D] By the antipope Anacletus—a matter described by Abbot Ernald in Book II of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 1, and by Baronius under the year 1130.]

Whatever gold and silver could then be found on the altars, in the vessels of the altars, and in the sacred images themselves, was seized and carried away by impious hands. What of all this do you now find [Col. 0439D] in your own purses? Moreover, the beauty of the Lord’s house has perished beyond recovery. And now, why have you resolved to repeat wickedness and renew evil days upon yourself? What prospect of greater gain or surer hope now smiles upon you? Unless it be this: that your latter end is seen to be more heedless than the former. For then not only many among the people, but also among the clergy and some among the rulers throughout the world, favored you in that schism; but now, as your hands are against all, so the hands of all are against you. The whole world is clean from your blood—everyone except you alone and your children who are within you.

Therefore woe to you now, pitiable people; woe doubly more than before—not from foreign nations, not from the savagery of barbarians, not from thousands of armed men. Woe to you solely from the face of your own people; woe from your household and friends, from internal ruin, from anguish of heart, from the tortures of your inmost parts.

5. Do you now recognize that not all members of one household are peaceful, nor all who appear to be friends are friends? And although we knew it at other times, yet now through you we are taught more manifestly the entire truth of that saying of the Lord: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7:6; Matt. 10:36). Woe to brother from brother in your midst, and to children from their parents! Woe—not from swords, but from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue! How long will you strengthen one another in evil for evil, and [Col. 0440B] strike one another down with the swords of your lips, destroy one another, until you are consumed by one another?

Gather together, scattered sheep; return to the pastures; return to the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls. Return to your heart, you transgressors. What I say is not the reviling of an enemy, but the rebuke of a friend. True friendship sometimes has rebuke, but never flattery.

6. We add entreaty also. We beseech you for Christ’s sake: be reconciled to God; be reconciled to your princes—I mean Peter and Paul—whom indeed, in their vicar and successor Eugene, you have driven from their seats and homes. Be reconciled, I say, to the princes of the world, lest perhaps the world begin to fight on their behalf against the senseless. Do you not know [Col. 0440C] that, while they are offended, you have no strength whatever, but while they are favorable, you fear nothing whatever? No, I say, under their protection you, illustrious city, city of the mighty, will not fear thousands of people surrounding you.

Be reconciled, therefore, to them, and likewise to the thousands of martyrs who are indeed with you, but against you, because of the great sin which you have committed and in which you persist. Be reconciled also to the whole Church of the saints, who everywhere on earth have been scandalized on hearing this report. Otherwise this page shall stand as testimony against you; and your Apostles and martyrs themselves shall stand with great steadfastness against those who afflicted them and took away their labors.

But now let us all alike hear the conclusion of the matter. I have declared righteousness; I have foretold danger; [Col. 0440D] I have not concealed the truth; I have exhorted you to better things. It remains either that we may soon rejoice in your correction, or, certain of the just condemnation that threatens, mourn inconsolably, withering and wasting away through fear and expectation of the things that shall come upon the whole city.

## LETTER CCXLIV

[Note: [Col. 0440D] Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO CONRAD, KING OF THE ROMANS

He exhorts the King to defend pontifical authority against the rebellious Romans.

1. Neither more sweetly, nor more amicably, nor indeed more closely could kingship and priesthood be joined or planted together [Col. 0441A] in one another than by both meeting together in the person of the Lord; since he was made for us, according to the flesh, from both tribes, both supreme Priest and King. Nor only so: he also united and bound them together in his body, which is the Christian people, he himself being its head.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Suger rightly says on this point in Letter 74: “Since the glory of Christ’s body—that is, of the Church [Col. 0441D] of God—consists in the indissoluble unity of kingship and priesthood, it is surely clear that whoever provides for one assists the other; since all discerning persons plainly recognize that the temporal kingdom stands through the Church of God, and the Church of God flourishes through the temporal kingdom.” See John of Salisbury, Letter 44.]

Thus this kind of people is called by the apostolic voice “a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). In another Scripture, are not all who are predestined to life called kings and priests? (Rev. 1:6; 5:10). Therefore, what God has joined, let no human being separate. Rather, what divine authority has ordained, let human will strive to fulfill; and let those who are joined in institution join themselves in spirit. Let them cherish one another, [Col. 0441B] defend one another, and bear one another’s burdens. The Wise Man says: “A brother helping a brother—both shall be comforted” (Prov. 18:19). But if, which God forbid, they gnaw at and bite one another, will not both be laid waste? May my soul not enter into the counsel of those who say that either peace and liberty for the churches would harm imperial authority, or the prosperity and exaltation of the empire would harm the churches. For God, founder of both, joined them not for destruction but for edification.

2. If you know this, how long will you disregard the common insult, the common injury done to you? Is not Rome the head of the empire as the Apostolic See is the head of the Church? Thus, to say nothing of the Church, is it an honor to the King to hold in his hands an empire whose trunk has been cut off? And indeed [Col. 0441C] I do not know what your wise men and the princes of the realm advise you on this matter; but I, speaking in my folly, shall not conceal what I think.

The Church of God, from its beginning until these times, has often been troubled and often delivered. Hear, then, what she herself says in the Psalm. For it is her voice: “Many times have they assailed me from my youth; yet they have not prevailed against me. Sinners have built upon my back; they have prolonged their iniquity” (Ps. 128:2–3). Be certain, O King, that the Lord will not now leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous. The Lord’s hand has not been shortened [Col. 0442A] or rendered powerless to save. Without doubt, at this time too he will deliver his bride—he who redeemed her at his own cost, endowed her with his Spirit, adorned her with heavenly gifts, and enriched her also with earthly goods. He will deliver her, I say, he will deliver her. But if she is delivered by another’s hand, let the princes of the realm consider whether that will be the King’s honor or the kingdom’s advantage. It certainly will not.

3. Therefore gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty one; and let Caesar render to himself the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s. It is plainly Caesar’s concern both to protect his own crown and to defend the Church. The one befits the king, the other the advocate of the Church. Victory, as we trust in the Lord, is close at hand. The pride and arrogance of the Romans exceed their strength.

For what is this? Does any great or powerful person—for example, an emperor or king—venture upon this shameful enterprise against both empire and priesthood? But this accursed and tumultuous people, which knows neither how to measure its strength, consider its end, nor contemplate the outcome, has dared in its folly and fury to attempt this great sacrilege. Far be it that a popular mob, the rashness of the rabble, should be able even for a moment to stand before the face of the King.

I have become foolish, inserting myself—though I am an insignificant and obscure person—as though I were someone great, into counsels of such magnitude and wisdom, and concerning so great a matter. Yet the more obscure and lowly I am, the freer I am to say what charity suggests. Therefore I add further in the same folly: if anyone should try to persuade you [Col. 0442C] otherwise than I have spoken—which we do not believe—then assuredly he either does not love the King, or understands too little what befits royal majesty; or certainly he seeks his own interests and is proved not greatly to care for the interests either of God or of the King.

## LETTER CCXLV

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO LORD POPE EUGENE, ON BEHALF OF THE BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Namely, Elias. After the death of John, bishop of Orléans, in 1133, Orderic states in Book 13, under the year 1134, that Hugh the dean was elected to succeed the deceased—though I see that historians of the Church of Orléans have passed this over. For he writes: “After John, the aged bishop of Orléans, relinquished his bishopric, Hugh the dean, who had been elected to the pontificate, returned from the King’s court and was struck by rash men on the road and died; and the bishopric, like a ship without a helmsman at sea, long tossed about without a bishop.” That is, until the year 1136, when our Elias [Col. 0442C] was elected, after a long discord between clergy and people, by the unanimous consent of all, from being a monk and abbot of Saint-Sulpice [Col. 0442D] at Bourges. Peter of Cluny, in Book I, Letter 11, calls him “a religious, prudent, and learned man,” writing to Pope Innocent for his confirmation; Innocent consecrated him in April 1137.

After some years, namely in 1144, he was accused before Lucius II by the clergy of Orléans of serious crimes. Since he could not clear himself, and neither Peter the Venerable (Book V, Letters 19, 21, 27) nor even King Louis himself could bend the supreme Pontiff in his favor, he resigned the bishopric voluntarily in 1146, on the advice of St Bernard, while Eugene III sat as pope. It is therefore strange that Alberic says in his chronicle, under the year 1149, that “Atto, bishop of Troyes, and the bishop of Orléans were deposed at the Council of Rheims,” since both relinquished their office by their own motion. This is clear concerning the bishop of Orléans from this letter; and it has also been demonstrated concerning Atto in the notes to Letter 23.]

He rejoices in the pope’s zeal in the matter of the bishop of Orléans, etc.

Yes, I beseech you, act thus. Let consideration always be given, not to who asks, but to what is asked. The King was not heard on behalf of the bishop of Orléans [Col. 0443A], yet he was not offended in the least, because his heart is in God’s hand. Even if that had happened, it should have been borne rather than that God should be offended. For God will assuredly be more propitious on this account, and will more swiftly grant relief from the tribulation and grief of evils, if justice is maintained and truth is not abandoned.

How great a sweetness these and similar reports about you, which are daily spread throughout the world with renowned joy, fill my heart with is not easy to say. So much for these matters. Henceforth, if anyone has suggested to you that I should be burdened still further, know that my strength is not sufficient for the burdens I carry. In sparing me, you will spare yourselves equally. I believe it does not escape you that my purpose is not to leave the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] See Letter 227 and Letter 228, no. 2.]

Concerning Brother Baldicius, though beloved and necessary, the command has been obeyed without delay. [Col. 0443B] Concerning the sending of an abbot to Saint-Anastasius—

[Note: [Col. 0443D] Rualenus was sent; see Letters 258 and 258, and the two following.]

—if it has not been done, it shall be done as soon as we learn that it has not been done. But concerning the other person to be sent, because you wrote nothing in your latest letters, we presumed nothing. Yet this too shall be done as swiftly as you are pleased to hasten it. Lord Hugh of Auxerre and Brother Baldicius will answer you more fully and clearly about all these matters.

We ask that what Baldwin, archbishop of Pisa of holy memory, did in Sardinia regarding the excommunication of the judge of Arborea—because we believe that this good man did it only justly—may, by your authority, remain ratified and unshaken.

[Note: [Col. 0443D] See Letters 144 and 261.]

But let the Judge of Torres—

[Note: [Col. 0443D] He seems to be Gunnarius, formerly Judge and lord of the fourfold Sardinian jurisdiction. Having approached the tomb of St Martin, he returned by Clairvaux, where he was received by Bernard and afterward became a monk there, according to Heribert, Book II of the *Miracles of St Bernard*, chapter 13.]

—because he is said to be a good prince, be commended to you [Col. 0443C] and supported by you.

## LETTER CCXLVI

[Note: [Col. 0444D] Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE SAME, ON THE SAME MATTER, WHEN THE AFOREMENTIONED BISHOP OF ORLÉANS HAD BEEN DEPOSED

He commends to the pope the bishop of Orléans, who voluntarily resigns his bishopric, asking him to safeguard the man’s honor; this befits the bishop’s humility and the pope’s clemency.

1. It is time for me too to write, no longer on behalf of a bishop, but on behalf of a poor and humble monk—

[Note: [Col. 0444D] From abbot of Saint-Sulpice at Bourges he became bishop, and from bishop once again a monk.]

—and, what is more pitiable, one made such from being rich and exalted. Here flattery has no place; pity has its place. Many wrote for him that he might remain bishop; but this was too much, and I could not bring myself to dare it. Now, however, if the matter is judged more humanely, his present condition itself demands what I formerly avoided.

The man still had hope [Col. 0443D], for there was such ground for hoping. He said: “The state of affairs has greatly changed since the sentence requiring my purgation was imposed on me. I indeed received it as sufficiently burdensome, such that even the most innocent person could scarcely fulfill it. What now, when almost everything has become impossible? There is no bishop at Nevers—

[Note: [Col. 0444D] See Letter 275.]

—nor indeed at Troyes; the bishop of Auxerre has crossed the Alps. A large part of my fellow-provincial [Col. 0444A] bishops, by whom I ought to clear myself, is thus absent. Certainly I do not lack persons to conduct the purgation; but bishops are either lacking or absent. What then? Can that which cannot be found rightly be demanded from me? If the judge finds the matter so established, it would be strange if he pronounced sentence regarding an impossibility; or if it is not wholly impossible, then surely what is perhaps merely very difficult [variant: *minimum*, ‘very small’] will easily escape the notice of one who investigates it less carefully—since he desires mercy, not sacrifice. For what profit is there in my blood, that he should seek out my iniquity and scrutinize my sin? Rather, because he is gracious and merciful, he will forget something, overlook something, and add something of his own. He is lord. Is he not permitted to do what he wishes? Even if not, once he has noticed that sufficient reason is supplied to me, why should he nevertheless not exercise full freedom and promptly exalt mercy over judgment, a man of apostolic gentleness and authority?”

2. Therefore, although he could so hope while fearing—and not without reason, as it seemed to himself and his friends—he nevertheless resigned and entrusted himself wholly to our judgment. And lest the Church should be troubled longer on his account, he anticipated, on my advice, the appointed end and the stroke of the axe, and voluntarily put off the episcopate.

There is one thing, most clement Father, from which considerable consolation might be brought to a generous and modest man in so miserable a fortune. Do you ask what? Certainly he does not walk in great things or in things too wonderful for him. It is enough if your [Col. 0444C] indulgence can preserve the priesthood of one who was a bishop; if only he may be sheltered from the brand of infamy and the cautery of perpetual disgrace beneath the shield of your good will. O request worthy of every hearing! He does not ask to be glorious, but that he who has been glorious may not be dishonored. Whatever lies between those two conditions, he is content with it. Let one falling from glory be allowed to sustain himself at whatever honorable degree of mediocrity he can, and not to descend into the very extremity of disgrace.

He is young; he is noble by birth; he stood in an exalted position. Yet he does not shrink from a humble station, but from disgrace. Shall not even such humility earn anything? Wicked Ahab humbled himself, and it benefited him (3 Kings 21:27–29); and shall humility have no value in a faithful and noble man? Far be it from the supreme [Col. 0444D] See, far be it from your holy mind, to despise a contrite and humbled heart.

3. If we were to say, “He has humbled himself; let him be exalted,” we should not be presuming rashly in this. Perhaps we could excuse it from the rule you know so well (Matt. 23:12). But now we do not say, “Let him be exalted,” but, “Let him not be trampled down,” lest we be put to shame in our expectation. Indeed, if we have received evil [Col. 0445A] from the Lord’s hand, why should we not receive good? Do you have authority to cast down the mighty from their seat, but not authority to exalt the humble? Moreover, to prefer using received power for evil rather than for good is to abuse it.

Furthermore, he is distressed by many debts, although he is poor and needy. Let your authority command that these be paid from episcopal property. For it is hard both to be deprived of honor and pressed down by the burden of debts.

## LETTER CCXLVII

[Note: [Col. 0445B] Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE SAME, CONCERNING THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS

He disapproves the hasty and overly severe sentence against Samson, archbishop of Rheims, whereby use of the pallium was withdrawn.

To his most beloved father and lord EUGENE, by God’s grace supreme Pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux [Col. 0445B], sends the little that he is.

1. May God spare you: what have you done? You have put to shame the face of a most modest man; and him whose praise is [Col. 0446A] in the Church, you have humbled before the face of the Church. You have made all his enemies glad; but how many do you think you have grieved? There is no limit to the mourning, because there is no number of friends. Beloved by God and men, he pays the penalties of a great crime, though convicted by none and having confessed to none.

We acknowledge Phinehas; we perceive zeal. An Israelite is pierced through, but not together with a Midianite woman. It is laid to his charge that he crowned the King—

[Note: [Col. 0445B] I read that Louis the Younger was crowned more than once. First, while his father still lived, he received the inaugural crown at Rheims from Pope Innocent in 1131. Then Orderic Vitalis, Book XIII, under the year 1138, states that he was crowned at Bourges in these words: “In the year 1138, indiction 1, Louis, king of the French, was crowned at Bourges on the Nativity of the Lord; and there a great court of noble and lesser men from all Gaul and Aquitaine and the surrounding nations was assembled. Metropolitan bishops and their suffragans came there; counts and other dignitaries flocked thither and rendered their service to the new king.” Thus Orderic, who calls him “new king” because he was then, after his father’s death, crowned king of Aquitaine.

Here we see him again crowned by Samson, archbishop of Rheims, before the Jerusalem expedition, perhaps so that, as he was about to depart, he might receive in a solemn assembly an oath of fidelity from his subjects. Horstius conjectures that the place of this final ceremony was Chartres, where the Jerusalem expedition was discussed. But that this coronation took place at Bourges is clear from the context of the letter and from letters of Eugene III reported in the *Patriarchium Bituricense*. From these we understand that Eugene considered the Church of Bourges, in which Samson performed sacred rites, to have been placed under interdict. You will find the *Patriarchium Bituricense* published by Labbe in volume two of the *Bibliotheca nova*.

Moreover, this letter and another letter of Ivo, shortly to be cited, show that the archbishop of Rheims claimed that the right of crowning kings, wherever that coronation might take place, belonged to him. Peter of Bourges and, before him, Ivo of Chartres denied this. Yet in this letter St Bernard does not wholly deny this prerogative of the archbishop of Rheims; indeed, he seems to admit it.

Pope Sylvester II mentions it in a bull addressed to Arnulf, prelate of Rheims, whom, having suspended him on a charge of treachery, he restored in 999 to his former dignity and all his rights: “We grant you,” he says, “by the provisions of this privilege, that, your staff and ring having been restored, you may discharge the archiepiscopal office and enjoy in the customary manner all the insignia belonging to the holy metropolitan Church of Rheims; that you may use the pallium on the accustomed solemnities, and perform the blessing of kings and of subject bishops.”

Certainly it was most fitting that, since the most Christian kings received from blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, the dignity of royal priesthood and the pledge of the heavenly crown through baptism and profession of the Christian faith, the prerogative of consecrating and crowning kings should also pass to his successors. Emperors granted this to the archbishop of Mainz because of St Boniface; the kings of Spain, to Toledo because of St Eleutherius; and the kings of England, to Canterbury because of St Augustine—although, as required by circumstances of place and time, this privilege of the archbishop of Rheims remained subject to lawful dispensation.

Nor do I think Ivo of Chartres intended otherwise in his celebrated Letter 189, in which he defended the solemn inauguration of Louis VI performed at Orléans by Daimbert, archbishop of Sens. Elsewhere, in Letter 48, writing to Pope Urban, he acknowledges this prerogative of the Church of Rheims, saying that that see “possesses the diadem of the kingdom.” Indeed, in the other letter he declares that he does “not envy the Church of Rheims, oppose it, or regret it,” [Col. 0446C] “if the kings of France have such devotion toward it that they prefer to be consecrated by its metropolitan rather than by another”; yet he defends the lawful dispensation in Daimbert’s act. “What we did,” he says in Letter 189, “we did with salutary deliberation and provident dispensation. For there were certain disturbers of the kingdom who watched for these things with every effort, so that either the kingdom might be transferred to another person or grievously diminished.”

Therefore, when he asserts that this privilege is supported neither by reason, custom, nor law, he should not be understood absolutely; the force of his argument, which he sets against custom, tends only to show that “not all kings of the Franks were consecrated in the Church of Rheims or by archbishops of Rheims”—which we readily admit. His whole effort seems directed to denying that, apart from every dispensation, kings must always be consecrated in the Church of Rheims and by the archbishop of Rheims, under penalty of anathema incurred by anyone who attempted otherwise in any manner; this was apparently the point urged in the case by the delegates of Rheims, according to Aimoin’s continuator in Book 5 of the *Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 50. Compare Hugh in the Chronicle of Auxerre under the year 1154.

Finally, lest any dispute on this matter arise in future, Louis VII confirmed this prerogative of the archbishop of Rheims by a solemn judgment in 1179; this was afterward approved by letters of Alexander III and Innocent III. Whoever wishes for more may read the book of William Marlot, archpriest of Saint-Nicaise at Rheims, *On the Inauguration of the Kings of France*, published in French in 1654, in which he treats this subject very learnedly and fully.

As to the use of the pallium, which the Pontiff had forbidden Samson, it is remarkable how highly it was valued especially in that century: St Bernard judged it more tolerable for himself to be prohibited from celebrating Mass than for the archbishop of Rheims to be prohibited from using the pallium; for the sake of obtaining it St Malachy did not hesitate to travel twice from Ireland to Rome.]

—but in this matter he does not think that he exceeded the limits of his privileges. It is objected that he knowingly presumed to celebrate divine rites in an interdicted church; he denies it. The former charge will be proved in its time; the latter will be cleared. Yet let it be so: let us suppose every allegation established which his adversaries were permitted or pleased to make against one absent. Ought he, for this single offense—when all else in him has been praiseworthy [Col. 0446B]—to be struck so harshly and punished so severely? Even having transgressed once might have been reckoned a virtue, had the judgment issued from your own countenance rather than from the face of his enemies [Col. 0447A].

Further, what ought to have been done in that pressing situation? It was a festal day, a solemn assembly, a young king; and, greater than these, the business of God—namely, the Jerusalem expedition—for which all had gathered. All these things absolutely did not permit the frustration of the Mass, the royal crown, and the solemn and due honor. Nor was it wholly expedient for the archbishop of Bourges himself that the King’s honor should be hindered through him.

2. Since matters stood thus, we judge that there is room for mercy where such necessity excuses the pride—

[Note: [Col. 0447D] The printed text has *typum*. The ancients indeed wrote thus for *typho*, that is, “pride.”]

—of contumacy. Do you have authority only to strike, and none whatever to heal? You know who said: “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32:39). Far be it that you should not employ the voice, especially the voice of compassion, of him whose place you hold [Col. 0447B]. Therefore let Jonathan’s arrow on this occasion alone return backward; and, if necessary, let it rather be aimed at me.

I confess that I should have borne more tolerably the prohibition of my own celebration of Mass than the prohibition of an archbishop’s use of the pallium. There is also a matter which considerably opposes your pious severity in this case: this may give your son King Louis no small occasion for offense and resentment, since he seems to himself to be the entire cause of this evil. This is plainly inexpedient at the present time, lest the good undertaking which he has begun, with good and great spirit at your exhortation, should, God forbid, fail to have a worthy outcome if he pursues it amid scandal and disturbance of mind.

For the rest, you commanded and I obeyed; and the authority of the one commanding made obedience fruitful [Col. 0447C]. For I proclaimed and spoke, and they have multiplied beyond number. Cities and castles are emptied; and already the seven women can scarcely find one man to seize, so greatly do women everywhere remain widows while their husbands live.

## LETTER CCXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0447D] Written about the year 1146.]

### TO THE SAME

He warns the Pontiff not to give a ready hearing to the bishop of Sées, however supplicating, as he seeks to return to the bishopric.

1. It is not my way, like many others, to use preambles or circumlocution with you; I begin with the matter itself. A deceitful man comes to you, I believe in order to deceive; but God forbid that he should deceive you. For this could happen only to the very great danger of many people. As it is always evil to deceive, so being deceived by an evil person is generally evil. But it matters who is deceived and in what matter. The greater your power and dignity, the more any deception which perhaps steals upon you is not only more dangerous but also more shameful, especially in ecclesiastical causes.

If, for example, this fraudulent little fox of Sées, weaving deceits for you, should be able, as he craftily intends to mock you, to return by your authority to the vineyard of the Lord of hosts, which in a short time he has in no small part demolished, [Col. 0448A] with how much malice do you think he will rage thereafter? Alas! What remains, he will devour. He comes as a little fox; he will return as a lioness. And against clergy and people alike he will use no longer cunning but cruelty. We must therefore be watchful against his craft, lest he be able again to burst forth into such savagery.

2. Therefore, do not let the man’s pitiable appearance, mean clothing, suppliant face, lowered brow, [Col. 0448B] or humble words move you; nor even his little tears, which, as they say, run at his bidding and have learned to lie. All these things are outward; and you know who said, “Do not judge according to appearance” (John 7:24). In these and similar things there is a form of piety, but not always its power. These are sheep’s garments, often, as the Lord showed, assumed by wolves for the greatest slaughter of sheep; they do not hide themselves because the wolves come secretly (Matt. 7:15).

For this reason some of our own people have written on his behalf, deceived by such lies and giving little heed to what the Wise Man wisely and truly says: “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit” (Ecclus. 19:23). Therefore pay no attention to his words or bodily gestures; [Col. 0448C] question his deeds. By his fruits you will know him.

Many grave things are said about him; and they will be said against him, if there is someone to investigate and judge. I do not wish to state everything I have heard. For neither should everyone be believed, nor should everyone be disbelieved. I set forth briefly one conjecture of my own; you will judge whether it has anything certain. Why did he avoid the judges assigned to him? If he alleges their persons, they were not suspect. If the inconvenience of the place, it was in his own country and among his own kin, where, with little expense and no long journey, he could easily and without labor have settled the entire matter. Nothing else therefore remains to be suspected except that this deceitful man fled the multitude of accusers, who could not follow him outside their homeland because of poverty.

[Col. 0448D] We give thanks to the lord of Lisieux, who, touched by zeal for the Lord’s house, spared neither purse nor body. He is a good brother, whose endeavor is to raise up the seed of his dead brother.

[Note: [Col. 0447D] With ingenuity and aptness he applies to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, the ancient and now obsolete commandment of God, by which he commanded that the surviving brother should raise up offspring for a brother who died childless. Arnulf upheld the discipline of St Augustine, handed down to his secular canons by his own brother John, bishop of Sées, and grievously weakened by the successor; he did so both by writings addressed to the supreme Pontiffs and by particular effort. Thus St Bernard splendidly says here that he raised up his brother’s seed—a seed that foreign rashness and license had almost smothered.

That Arnulf labored in this business for about twenty years may be inferred from his letter to Pope Alexander III beginning, “There is a certain matter in which,” etc. See volume twelve of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. His brother John died in 1143; Girard II, formerly a secular canon, succeeded him. As Arnulf says in the cited letter, the Roman Church did not permit him to be ordained bishop until he had professed the same Order in his own person. But, as Arnulf adds there, this bishop was reported to have conceived the detestable intention of utterly uprooting this plantation, namely, the regular canons. For this reason Bernard censures him here.]

Give thanks to him also, because [Col. 0449A] this care of his appears to contribute considerably to your own renown: by it the wicked man is convicted and so cast down; and this is your glory.

## LETTER CCXLIX

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Written in the year of Christ 1145.]

### TO THE SAME

He commends, as worthy, the prior of Chaise-Dieu, elected bishop of Valence.

If rarity gives things their value, nothing in the Church is more precious or more desirable than a good and useful shepherd. For such a bird is rare. Therefore, wherever one is at times found and an opportunity arises, hands must immediately be laid upon him, and every effort exerted lest a fruitful promotion be impeded by any force or artifice of malice.

We have heard that the Prior of Chaise-Dieu has been elected in the Church of Valence by the united vote of clergy and people.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Upon the death of holy John, bishop of Valence in Dauphiné, in 1145, the Prior of Chaise-Dieu, named Orilbert, was elected. This letter, together with Letter 270, was written in his favor.]

[Col. 0449B] It would be surprising if he were not good for the work to which he is being called. Do you wish to know why I hope this? Good people desire it, and one whom good people please cannot fail to be good. It seems to me an argument of no less force that he is good if, conversely, he displeases the wicked. It befits Your Holiness to assent to the wishes of good people, lest, if this man should perhaps be rejected, another whom you would not wish might be accepted through the exertions and agreement of the perverse.

## LETTER CCL

### TO BERNARD

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The second of this name. Having left the see of Belley in 1142, he returned to the Charterhouse of Portes. There, before 1147, he succeeded Bernard the first as prior when that man resigned, according to the note to Letter 153. I would not venture to affirm that Natalis, the subject here, was requested for the government of the Church of Belley after him. William certainly succeeded Bernard; Pons succeeded William; and after Pons came Anthelmus, or Nantelmus, likewise formerly Prior of Portes. He appears to be the author of the letter to Louis [Col. 0450D] the Younger concerning his promotion, which is Letter 234 among the Chesnian letters.]

### PRIOR OF PORTES

The refusal of Brother Natalis, elected bishop, ought not to have been taken so grievously by religious persons. It was not effected by his own efforts. Perhaps the Pope feared that faults of youthful age would only now be exposed to accusation.

To the most reverend fathers and most beloved lords, [Col. 0449C] BERNARD, Prior of Portes, and the holy brothers who are with him: BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting in the Lord.

1. From a certain reply of Your Blessedness I learned that I had written something which showed me to be disturbed, and that you feared this not a little. Yet you did so in vain. There is nothing that you, most reverend fathers, ought to fear from your little son, who loves you truly as friends and reveres you as saints. Unless perhaps you feared not me, but for me with fatherly affection, because I seemed to you disturbed without reason; or, if with reason, perhaps more than was proper. I admit that I was disturbed, but for you, not against you—and only rather mildly. If even this was rash, I do not rashly confess my injustice against myself; and you will forgive [Col. 0449D] the rashness of my sin. Forgive me: this is what I am; zeal for your house has consumed me. So far as lies in me, I cannot endure that so great an exemplar of holiness should be disfigured; [Col. 0450A] for may it be far from me to fear that it can be corrupted. In a most beautiful body, indeed, not only disease but even a mole is displeasing. The complexion is surely not altogether sound if any saint appears anxiously to bear his rejection—a rejection in which both not to rejoice and not to glory falls short of perfection. But for imperfection to appear in one whose purpose is perfection is a blemish. Thus this complexion in Brother Natalis displeased me. For what if it was pure before God? One must, indeed, provide what is good also before human beings.

2. But you say: “It was not he who took it grievously, but we.” It comes back to the same thing. Again I say what I think. I do not see why it should have been grievous to you unless you perceived that it was grievous to him. Judge yourselves whether this became him, especially in the newness of his life. For before this—as I say, [Col. 0450B] without offense to him—he was not without this mark; whether he was also without fault must be left to his own conscience. And what if perhaps the lord Pope thought [alternative reading: judged] this when, as you say, he refused to assent to his election? For, as I suppose, fearing the tongues of detractors, he forbade the hasty promotion of a new hermit, lest, as I have said, the malicious tongue should be able to say that this was the fruit of the wilderness which he had always desired. Nevertheless, whatever the lord Pope intended, whether this or something else, know that I was ignorant of his decision, lest anyone say that he acted at my instigation. For as far as I am concerned, I had resolved, whenever I could fittingly do so, not merely not to impede him, but even with all my strength and, as the saying goes, with both hands to draw him forward, wherever he might be able to make fruitful for God the grace that is in him. Who will grant me learned and holy men to preside as shepherds in the churches of God—if not in all, at least in most, or at least in some? For what if a young man is remembered to have acted youthfully on some occasion? The old things have passed away; all things have become new. He has been buried with Christ anew through the baptism of the wilderness. [Note: [Col. 0450D] Bernard, along with other Fathers, regarded the profession of religious life as a kind of second baptism, as he states expressly in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 17.] Shall I revisit vices long ago buried?

3. Now as to the report that the abbot of Caziac [Note: [Col. 0450D] In three Colbert manuscripts, “Cazicensis.” Is this Simon, abbot of Caziac, to whom Letter 263 was written? His successor, Tes. (thus we read it abbreviated), whom Peter, abbot of Celle at Troyes, identifies in Letter 14 of Book Two, seems to be intended here; although no letters of his against the Carthusians, but many on their behalf, are found.] or of Troyes wrote harshly to you: when I heard it, I took it very harshly; and when opportunity comes, I shall not pass it over, so far as charity and the familiarity which I have with them because of their religious profession may require. But thanks be to God, who granted you not [Col. 0450D] to be overcome by evil, but to overcome evil with good, because you did not answer them evil for evil or curse for curse. Further, know that the letters which you had previously written to me against the aforesaid abbots did not come to their knowledge either through my effort or through my wish. And enough about this.

4. It is time that I should not forget myself. [Col. 0451A] My monstrous life, my wretched conscience, cries out to you. For I am a kind of chimera of my age: I bear neither the character of cleric nor that of layman. Long ago I stripped off the manner of life of a monk, though not the habit. I do not wish to write about myself what I think you have heard through others: what I do, what I pursue, amid what dangers I move in the world—or rather, over what precipices I am tossed. If you have not heard, I beg you to inquire; and according to what you hear, provide both counsel and the aid of prayers.

## LETTER CCLI

[Note: [Col. 0451D] Written in the year of Christ 1147.]

TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS. He desires that the monks of Balma, duly punished, should be received again into favor and reconciled with the Aedui.

[Col. 0451B]

To his most beloved father and lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme Pontiff, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

The monks of Balma committed a grave offense, but not without punishment. [Note: [Col. 0451D] We understand this crime of the monks of Balma, in the diocese of Besançon, from two rescripts of Pope Eugenius—one to Humbert, archbishop of Besançon, the other to William or Guy, count of Mâcon—by which rescripts he reduced the abbey of Balma to a priory “because of an execrable and horrible crime, and an unheard-of contempt of the holy Roman Church, committed against his beloved Master Osbert”; and also from the letter of Count William of Mâcon consenting to this. Eugenius’s letters were given at Paris on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, that is, in 1147. They survive in the Cluniac archive. Later, however, the title of abbey was restored to Balma.] For this very reason praise and thanksgiving are owed to you by the whole Church: because you were not silent, did not overlook it, did not rest. You burned with zeal as you ought: you struck, but in order to heal. But if the Lord should forget to show mercy and restrain his mercies in his anger, whence would healing come? Therefore, after judgment we confidently await mercy, [Col. 0451C] so that we may sing to the Lord of mercy and judgment. We know, we know, that the Vicar [Note: [Col. 0451D] Here the Pope is not obscurely called Christ’s Vicar, whereas among those ancient writers he was otherwise usually called St. Peter’s Vicar, as we have shown elsewhere.] will not depart from the footsteps of him whose vicar he is; for he says: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12:26). And the prophet says of him: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” (Joel 2:14). We confidently demand the same from your successors. Otherwise, it is not fitting that you should destroy the innocent with the wicked. For those who did evil have been removed from the midst. What remains except that the remnant be saved? Why should not those be saved who obeyed you, who obeyed your predecessor? I speak with Paul, who said: “Remove evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:13). Therefore have mercy upon them, and let not [Col. 0452A] the iniquity of criminals prejudice the justice of the innocent. I say this because they have a case against the Aedui before Your Majesty at present, and they fear that the wrongdoing of others may harm them. Indeed, we especially entreat you to labor for their concord and peace. For we wish well to both parties, and believe such an outcome advantageous to both.

## LETTER CCLII

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Written in the same year.]

TO THE SAME, CONCERNING YORK. He asks that the judgment long ago pronounced by Innocent against the man of York finally be executed, lest the Pope who overlooks his evil deeds be held accountable for them.

Frustrated ambition rages—indeed, despair drives it mad. The man of perdition runs [Col. 0452B] toward the noose and hastens the sentence of condemnation long ago due upon himself. Even now his sins are manifest, going before him to judgment. The accursed and thorny tree anticipates the hand of the cutter and provokes the hesitating axe against itself. Alas! how much more justly it would long ago have fallen—or, in another reading, been cut down—than those holy men whom, by unlawfully standing, it wickedly cast down. For if it had not stood, it could never have cast down those who stood. They, indeed, fell in their innocence and for innocence’s sake—much better while standing. [Note: [Col. 0452D] Bernard here means the slaughter at Fontenay, a monastery of his Order in England, carried out by supporters of the intruded William. Serlo the monk recounts it explicitly in his history of that monastery, *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 747. There, after Eugenius had removed William, his supporters are said to have rushed into the monastery, whose abbot Henry opposed them; then to have plundered, burned, and devastated everything, although the monks and abbot survived. Bernard nevertheless implies here that some of them were killed. Serlo adds that Abbot Henry, elected to the archbishopric, immediately went to Clairvaux to St. Bernard; from there he proceeded to Trier to meet Pope Eugenius, by whom he was consecrated and given the pallium, and was finally admitted by his own people only after much opposition.] But innocent blood will without doubt be required from the hands of those who supplied stolen strength to that most harmful tree so that it should not immediately fall. The blood of the saints cries from the earth against their heads—[Col. 0452C] saints whose souls are in the hand of God, and whom the torment of malice shall not touch. Yet they were my own entrails: they have been poured out; I accept no consolation from words. Even if words could furnish some consolation or remedy, they fail before my grief; they are cut off by sorrow and broken by sobs. Yet hear—or rather read—one final thing, the very last thing, which I can more readily write than utter. If he still remains standing, alas, it is to be feared that his standing will be your fall, since whatever he adds—as an evil tree that can bear only evil fruits (Matt. 7:18)—will deservedly be imputed no longer to him but to you.

## LETTER CCLIII

[Note: [Col. 0453B] Written in the year 1150.—He means Hugh, Norbert’s first disciple, formerly chaplain to the bishop of Cambrai and Norbert’s successor in governing Prémontré. This Hugh is wonderfully praised not only in the *Life of St. Norbert*, but also by his namesake Hugh, the chronicler of St. Marianus at Auxerre, and by Herman, monk of Laon, in Book Three of *The Miracles of St. Mary*, chapters 6, 8, and 10. Norbert too is frequently praised by the same author, especially in chapter 7, where he is placed before Bernard, both because he was the first founder of his Order and because he instituted nuns of the same Order, who already then exceeded ten thousand in number. For more on Norbert, see the notes to Letters 35 and 56. In not a few manuscripts—and this also deserves notice—Letter 123 with Bernard’s reply is put in the place of this letter; this one, however, is placed after Letter 296. Thus the position of the next two letters also varies in the manuscripts.]

TO THE ABBOT OF PRÉMONTRÉ. He replies calmly to the rather harsh letter of the Premonstratensians, recounting his benefits toward them. He also refutes each article of complaint and declares that he will remain their steadfast friend.

[Col. 0453A]

1. I have heard your report and was afraid. For you write bitter things against me—though far be it from me to think them as reasonable as they are alarming. What sin have I committed? Is it that I have always loved your person, cherished your Order, and promoted it, insofar as lay in me? If faith is not placed in words, deeds supply it. As my conscience answers me, I ought to have received commendation from you. But since you prefer to speak and write the contrary, I shall give my voice strength from the testimony of deeds. This is surely serious: I may seem to reproach you [Col. 0453B] with benefits, something which certainly did not become me. You compel me to act as one less wise. Whichever one of you, or of your people, has had need of our assistance and [Col. 0454A] lacked it?

First, the very place of Prémontré in which you dwell was ours, and you had it by our gift. [Note: [Col. 0453C] Authors differ concerning the origin of Prémontré. What is read in Francis Aluteus, *History of the Cistercian Family*, Book 2, chapter 19, seems fabulous. Gordonius of the Society of Jesus, in his *Chronology* for the year 1116, says that this Order received its name from the divinely prefigured character of its institution. But that the place was so called before St. Norbert is evident both from his *Life*, chapter 17, where he is said to have chosen “a very deserted and solitary place, which was called Prémontré by the ancients,” and from Herman the monk in passages cited below. Yet what Bernard says here about the place of Prémontré having been granted by him appears to conflict with the foundation letters of Prémontré, drawn up in the name of Bartholomew, bishop of Laon, which survive in the Premonstratensian library and in the notes to Guibert. These state that the aforesaid place belonged to the monks of St. Vincent, and was delivered to St. Norbert by Bartholomew himself, to whom it had first been granted by Adalbero, abbot of St. Vincent, and afterward confirmed by his successor Seifrid. Herman the monk also noted this in Book Three of *The Miracles of Blessed Mary of Laon*, chapter 4: “Coming therefore to the aforesaid place Prémontré, they entered for prayer a certain church built there in honor of St. John the Baptist. This was under the jurisdiction of the monastery of St. Vincent at Laon,” etc. From these facts a recent writer in his notes to the *Life of St. Norbert*, chapter 19, declares himself perplexed in explaining Bernard’s grant, which he reads as made by the Vincentian monks through the hand of Bishop Bartholomew. But even if six hundred arguments of this sort stood to the contrary, Bernard’s word must retain irresistible authority. And indeed, if you consider the matter a little more carefully, you will easily reconcile the apparent contradictions. For it is certain that the monastery of Prémontré, in its original state, was not situated where it had first been founded by St. Norbert, but on the other side of the mountain, to which Hugh, Norbert’s successor and the recipient of this letter, had transferred it. Herman mentions this both in the passage cited, where he reports St. Norbert’s foreknowledge of the monastery’s transfer, and there, chapter 10, where he describes the change at Prémontré as follows: “But when Hugh saw that that church”—namely, St. John the Baptist’s, which the Vincentian monks had granted, as he had stated in chapter 4—“could no longer suffice for the great multitude which had assembled and was daily increasing through God’s grace, and also knew that Lord Norbert, as was said above, had foreseen in the spirit that a larger church would be built on the other side of the mountain, he took counsel with his brethren and asked Lord Bishop Bartholomew, as founder and father of the place, to come, so that, after all the workshops had been arranged, he might lay the first stone in the foundation of the church.” Therefore that first seat or church was granted by our Vincentian brethren; but what prevents this second one from having been granted to the Premonstratensians by St. Bernard, who had previously received it from the hermit Wido? Let the two letters of Philip, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, to which this seems to reply, be read.]

For Brother Wido [Note: [Col. 0454C] We read of Wido in the *History of the Monastery of Vicogne near Valenciennes*, printed in vol. 12 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 534. There Wido or Guido, “a Breton by birth and a priest by office,” is said to have lived there when Norbert came to Prémontré, and to have yielded the place to one greater than himself, withdrawing to Vicogne, [Col. 0454D] where he laid the foundations of a monastery which he made subject to Walter, abbot of St. Martin at Laon.]—this being the name of the first inhabitant of the place—had previously given it to us through the bishop’s hand. Next, it was chiefly through our effort that those of Beau Lieu [Note: [Col. 0454D] Beau Lieu, of the Premonstratensian Order, in the diocese of Troyes, where the Premonstratensians succeeded the regular canons in 1140. Letter 407 is addressed to Odo, abbot of this Beau Lieu.] joined themselves to you. At Jerusalem King Baldwin, while still alive, gave us the place of St. Samuel [Note: [Col. 0454D] On this place Geoffrey writes in Book Three of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 22: “Finally, like a most fruitful vine, he spread his branches in every direction, except that he did not consent to send his brethren into the land of Jerusalem, although a place had been prepared by the king, because of pagan attacks and the unhealthiness of the climate.” Compare Letter 175, to the Patriarch of Jerusalem who offered the place, and Letter 355, in which he commends the Premonstratensians to the queen of Jerusalem. On the monastery of St. Paul, see the notes to Letter 178.] and at the same time a thousand gold pieces for its construction: by our gift you have both the place and the gold. At Verdun, for the church of St. Paul to be yours, many know how much I labored—and you yourselves know how much I accomplished. If you do not recognize this, our letters to Pope Innocent of blessed memory remain, true judges [Col. 0454B] and, as it were, living witnesses of the matter. To those of Sept-Fons [Note: [Col. 0454D] Sept-Fons, in the diocese of Langres, near Montclair.] we granted the place which they first inhabited; its name is Francevals.

[Col. 0455A]

2. Is it because of these things that you wish to withdraw from your friends? Is evil returned for good, because you threaten to violate the agreement, [Note: [Col. 0455D] Manriquez describes this agreement, concluded in 1142 for concord between Cistercians and Premonstratensians: between monasteries of the two Orders there were to be two leagues, and between granges or villages one league. Hence Bernard says that the house of Basse-Fontaine had been established outside the stipulated boundaries. It was situated in the diocese of Troyes and founded in 1143.] bid farewell to peace, abandon fellowship, and rend unity? But let it be so. You do not stone me for a good work but for an injury: because I received Brother Robert, although he was of your profession, giving him the monastic habit. I do not deny it: he is with us. But I thought I had satisfied you on this point when I explained, more than once, in a living and truthful voice, the reason, procedure, and necessity of his reception. Since you are not yet at rest, it will not weary me to write again what I answered, since it does not weary you to repeat what I had excused.

3. I never, therefore, urged the aforesaid Brother Robert to leave you. Rather, when for many years he had desired this, I restrained him not once but often. How, finally, can I be suspected of having taken Brother Robert away from you, when you have Master Otho by his advice and urging? If you do not know this, ask him; if I know the man well, he will not deny it. Perhaps I could name quite a few others as well, whether converted to you or returned to you, whom you would not have today unless they had been persuaded or compelled by us. But I spare you: not because I lack material, but because I possess an abundance of modesty sufficient for the matter. In your cloisters I found men who, pierced by the word of our preaching, had determined to be converted and to come to us. Yet at your solicitations they drew back their foot and were received and retained in your Order and habit. Later, however, conscience reproached them, and they wished to leave; and, unless I am mistaken, they would have left had they not been confirmed by not merely our assent but also our urging.

4. But now hear—for you wish to hear again—how I finally received Brother Robert. The lord Pope commanded it, having been asked, of course, by him and his friends. He said that he had obtained by his request the assent of you and your abbot, so that no one might say that he had extorted it by command. You deny this: what is that to us? Let him see to it. If it pleases you to accuse the supreme and holy Pontiff of falsehood, forgive us: for we deem it wicked neither to believe such holiness nor to obey such majesty. Moreover, the venerable abbot Godescalc [Note: [Col. 0456D] See Letter 14 concerning him.], who is one of your own—for he had been sent to you by the lord [Col. 0455D] Pope concerning this business—did not altogether deny that he had brought back from you both the brother’s free release and your own voluntary concession; another reading, incorrectly, has “assembly” (*consessionem*).

5. As for Brother Fromund, there is no reason why you should attack us, since I by no means received him without the voluntary concession of his own abbot. Indeed, your bitter letter itself shows that this was not unknown to you, for in it you bring an accusation against us only because the chapter’s consent had not been awaited. [Col. 0456A] As though this had been prohibited in our mutual agreement, or as though the emancipation of a son pertained to the chapter rather than solely to the abbot.

6. You also add the matter of a certain house of your brethren at Basse-Fontaine, saying that we removed it, although it had been established outside the fixed boundaries. Would that, before accusing us, you had asked those brethren themselves not only who had removed it, but also for what reason. For, as we are confident, they would not have concealed the truth of the matter from you. But hear it now from us, and afterward, if you please, ask them. They had begun to build a place in which to station some of their sisters, far indeed from their own abbey, but on the boundary of two granges of our house and near the pasture of [Col. 0456B] our sheep. We asked them as friends—and as people to whom perhaps we had not been useless—not to prepare for their own people and ours a seedbed of scandal and fuel for dissensions, to be left to posterity. Yet they nonetheless continued building. This was the whole of our violence: thus we “removed” that house. We are inexcusable if asking is to inflict force.

7. In truth, the bishop—as cannot be denied—was indignant that they had presumed, without consulting him, to build not only an oratory in his bishopric but a house on the estate of the church and land held in fief from him. He intervened in the work they had begun, though in vain; for they did not desist even when forbidden by him. Thereafter, as I was passing through that land, the abbot who was then at Basse-Fontaine [Col. 0456C] met me and told me that they had ceased from building. Yet, as I learned from his report, this was not so much because of us as because of that knight who had appeared to have given them the land and was burdening them in many ways, so that they made numerous complaints about him. Although, even if they had voluntarily abandoned it solely out of love for us, it would neither have disgraced their religious profession nor, perhaps, have appeared an undeserved favor to us. I am truly astonished whence this complaint has at last arisen, since that abbot, unless I am mistaken, ended his life with a good and devout will toward us; and the man substituted for him, frequently and familiarly meeting us in his needs, never once mentioned this grievance to us. Finally, when I was later most humanely received as a guest in that same house, I heard nothing of this from the abbot himself or from anyone else. Moreover, the abbot was afterward present with you at Clairvaux, and very recently at Barri, when your chapter was now imminent, from which those complaining—lest I say slanderous—letters came; and neither there nor here do I remember having been challenged on this matter, even slightly, either by him or by you.

8. Further, you complain that a convert of Igny burned down a little hut of your brethren at Brana. [Note: [Col. 0456D] Bréna or Brana, a town on the Aisne, four leagues above Soissons, possessed a notable Premonstratensian abbey dedicated to St. Evodius. Not far from it lies Igny, a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Reims. Humbert, abbot of Igny, is the recipient of Letter 141.] [Col. 0457A] A little hut indeed! It was a kind of shelter of branches, where the brother who guarded standing grain still in the field might sit. Nor was it burned through malice, as we learned from trustworthy report, but because, being placed in a field belonging to the brethren of Igny, it occupied land which had to be cultivated. Finally, this little hut was valued at scarcely one small coin; and, unless we are mistaken, satisfaction has already been made to the abbot of Brana such that he neither complains at all nor has grounds for complaint. If not, once you make this known to us, we are ready to make every satisfaction. Likewise, concerning the abbot of Longpont, [Note: [Col. 0457D] Longpont Abbey, two leagues near Soissons, was also of the Cistercian Order, as was Villers in Brabant in the diocese of Namur, where Fastred was then abbot; his letter is printed in the Appendix.] when we first received your complaint that he wished to build a house within your boundaries, we forbade him; and we believe he has already desisted. But if not, that too shall be done once [Col. 0457B] we know it has not been done.

9. Above all, you lament that our abbot of Villers had the church of St. Foillan [Note: [Col. 0457D] The abbey of St. Foillan the Irishman, situated near the town of Le Rœulx in Hainaut, on the site of his martyrdom, [Col. 0458D] belonged to the Premonstratensian Order. To all these benefits of Bernard toward the Premonstratensians add the gift of a place in the forest of Orta, made by Louis the Younger “through the intervention of Lord Bernard of pious memory, abbot of Clairvaux,” as the abbot of St. Marianus at Auxerre acknowledges in Letter 282 among the Chesnian letters.] placed under ban [that is, interdicted]. But perhaps the incredible obstinacy of your brother and fellow abbot of the aforesaid house of St. Foillan ought more justly to displease you than the entirely just—or, in another reading, blameworthy—punishment of the supreme Pontiff. For I know that the high-handedness of that abbot greatly displeases many of your people; it would be very strange if it did not displease you too. Therefore I say to you: be indignant with him, for he is the one whose greed or obstinacy caused the divine offices to be forbidden to your brethren. This affair is indeed prolonged, and it would be difficult [Col. 0457C] to set out all its evasions within the brevity of a letter; nevertheless I shall briefly state the cause of the interdict.

After two or more conferences for peace, after a definitive judicial sentence pronounced in accordance with the command of your chapter by your abbots and ours, the bishop of Cambrai was finally summoned, since the place of St. Foillan was known to belong to his diocese. When he saw that the abbot, with obstinate mind, was violating everything, he wished, as he said, to compel him even by an ecclesiastical sentence.
