But the abbot, to gain time, appealed to a hearing before the supreme Pontiff. They came before him; and after he had learned beyond doubt, from the testimony both of your abbots and of other religious men, that the abbot of St. Foillan not only had withdrawn from the settlements but was also opposing the judgment, [Col. 0457D] he ordered his church interdicted until he should make satisfaction. Finally, both you and he asked the lord of Cîteaux, and us; and by many requests from you and yours, with the bishop himself present—who had received the order to promulgate the sentence of interdict—you obtained that some further form of peace should be provided. In the absence of the abbot of Villers, a settlement was negotiated, and the bishop was told that, if the abbot of St. Foillan observed even that settlement, he should refrain from the interdict.

But when he departed, [Col. 0458A] he did not keep even this. Instead, he kept—and still keeps—the house which both the judicial sentence and all the settlements had determined must be demolished, and which had even once already been demolished, but meanwhile had been rebuilt contrary to agreement and judgment. This house, I say, he retained and retains, and built another upon it as well. Why should the bishop not execute the apostolic command he had received to promulgate the sentence of interdict, especially now that breach of faith had been added? Yet I, hoping at last somehow to overcome evil with good, caused the same sentence to be deferred [Col. 0458B] until the octave of Epiphany, in case that man might meanwhile reconsider and either carry out the terms of the judgment or observe some settlement. And would that it might so happen, and that the God of peace might grant that our peace rest upon him!

10. Since these things are so, there is no reason why you should complain of us, when, as is clear, we might more justly complain of you. It remains for you to love those who love you, especially being careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace—that bond, I mean, which has been ratified between us and you for the sake of peace and charity, to the advantage indeed of both, and perhaps no less of you than of us. If you determine that it must be broken, it is certainly not expedient; indeed, I do not think it can be lawful in any way. For where the cause is common, an individual’s guilt ought not to prejudice it, even if what you say against us were true. But I, brothers, whatever you do, have resolved always [Col. 0458C] to love you, even if I am not loved. Let him seek occasions who wishes to withdraw from a friend. It is and shall be my endeavor neither to give any friend a just cause for withdrawing from me, nor to search for one in another; for the former belongs to feigned friendship, the latter to neglected friendship. And because, according to the prophet, it is good to be joined together with glue (Isa. 41:7), you may loose—or rather break—this bond, but not I. I shall cling to you even if you do not wish it; I shall cling even if I myself do not wish it. Long ago I bound myself with a strong bond, with unfeigned charity, that charity which never fails. With those who are troubled I shall be peaceful; to those who trouble me I shall also give place to wrath, lest I give place to the devil. I shall be overcome in disputes; I shall overcome by service. I shall confer benefits on the unwilling, add benefits for the ungrateful, and honor even those who despise me. And now my soul [Col. 0458D] is sad because I have offended you on any occasion whatsoever; and it shall remain sad until it is relieved by your forgiveness. If you delay, I shall come and keep watch at your doors; I shall persevere in knocking, I shall press seasonably and unseasonably, until I either deserve or compel a blessing. More than half the winter has already passed, and until now I wait in vain for our tunic [that is, charity].

## LETTER CCLIV

[Note: [Col. 0459D] This letter was written in 1136, when the Alpine monastery mentioned in Letter 152 was united to Cîteaux.]

TO GUARINUS, ABBOT OF THE ALPS. He praises the aged abbot’s zeal in reforming the Order. The brevity of time is no obstacle to the pursuit of perfection. In the spiritual life one must always advance and never stand still.

[Col. 0459A]

To the reverend father, worthy of every veneration, Lord GUARINUS, abbot of the Alps, and to all the brethren of the same place: Brother BERNARD, servant of your holiness, wishes always to advance from good to better.

1. Truly, Father, I now experience in you what I remember having read in the sacred Scriptures: “When a man is finished, then he begins” (Sirach 18:6). Rest was already due to you as an old man; a crown was already due to you as one who had completed his service. And behold, [Col. 0459B] like a new soldier in Christ, you raise new wars again, challenge the adversary, and, an exhausted old man, undertake the work of the strong, compelling the ancient enemy to renew the contest, even though he is in some sense unwilling. For when, contrary to your own custom and to the traditions of your predecessors—[Note: [Col. 0459D] That is, relaxations of regular discipline introduced by forebears, as in Letter 91.]—divinely inspired, you relinquish churches and ecclesiastical benefices; when you destroy synagogues of Satan, that is, cells outside the monastery [Note: [Col. 0459D] Such cells, of course, are generally fatal to regular observance, which can scarcely be maintained among so small a number. Letter 400 calls them obediences. Bernard used the same words above in Letter 150, §2.], in which three or four brethren commonly live without order and discipline; when you exclude women from the monastery; [Note: [Col. 0460D] That is, from the church. This too was formerly received in our Order, as among the Cistercians, who, according to Orderic Vitalis, Book VIII, p. 714, did not admit even foreign monks to their churches. The Carthusians admitted “only religious guests into the choir,” according to Guigo, chapter 10 of the *Statutes*. On the former prohibition of women from entering our churches, see the Preface to the First Century, no. 112, and to the Second Century, no. 53.] and when you more diligently than usual attend to the other goods of piety and discipline—what else will that first and greatest sinner do but see and be angry, gnash [Col. 0459C] his teeth, and waste away? But what concern is that? On the contrary, in his confusion and in your consolation, you shall sing to your God: “Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words” (Ps. 118:74). Nor need one fear that he will yield to the enemy who does not yield even to age. The spirit conquers the years; though the body is now growing cold, holy desire burns in the heart. Though the limbs fail, the vigor of his purpose nevertheless remains sound; the willing spirit does not feel the weakness of wrinkled flesh. Nor is this surprising. For why should he fear the collapse of his old dwelling, when he sees the spiritual structure rising day by day on high and advancing into eternity? For he is certain that, if this earthly house is dissolved, he has a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens (2 Cor. 5:1).

[Col. 0459D] 2. But someone will say: What if a man is forestalled by death before the spiritual edifice has yet been completed? For the perfect man has nothing in which to advance; and he who advances is thereby proved not to be perfect. We have an answer to give concerning him with full confidence: “Being made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long ages” (Wisdom 4:13). Rightly “long,” since he embraces all things. For how has he not fulfilled all times, when he has passed into eternity? Whatever extent of time he was able to traverse—not by length of life, but by long-suffering; that is, not by a succession of years or number of days, but by devotion of mind and by an ever-inextinguishable desire for advancement—he rightly claimed for himself in merits. For by virtue he retains what he lost in time. True virtue, moreover, knows no end and is not confined by time. Hence: “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8); likewise: “The patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. 9:19); and: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18:10). The righteous person never considers that he has attained [Col. 0460B] it (Phil. 3:13); he never says, “It is enough,” but always hungers and thirsts for righteousness. Thus, if he were always to live, then, as far as lay within him, he would always strive to become more righteous, always endeavoring with all his strength to advance from good to better. For he gives himself to divine service not for a year or for a time, like a hired laborer, but forever. Hear, finally, the voice of the righteous: “I will never forget your statutes, for by them you have given me life”; and again: “I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever” (Ps. 118:93, 112). Thus, not for a time. Accordingly, his righteousness endures, not for some period, but “for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:3). The everlasting hunger of the righteous therefore deserves everlasting refreshment; and although he is made perfect in a short time [Col. 0460C] as regards time, he is nevertheless judged to have fulfilled long ages because of the permanence of his virtue.

3. How, finally, could brevity of time prejudice a perpetual devotion to good, when it is insufficient to excuse the persistent malice of the reprobate? For this reason, without doubt, an evil of an inflexible and obstinate mind is punished eternally, though committed in time: because what was brief in time or act is known to be long in a stubborn will. Thus, if such a person never died, he would never cease willing to sin; indeed, he would wish to live forever, that he might always be able to sin. Accordingly, the converse may likewise be said of him: “Being made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled long ages”; because he has deservedly received the recompense of many—indeed, of all—times, since at no time [Col. 0460D] would he have been willing to change his evil intention [variant: will]. Thus unwearied zeal for advancement and continual striving toward perfection are reckoned as perfection.

4. If striving for perfection is to be perfect, then surely unwillingness to advance is failure. Where, then, are those accustomed to say: “It is enough for us; we do not wish to be better [Col. 0461A] than our fathers”? O monk, do you not wish to advance? “No.” Then do you wish to fail? “Not at all.” What then? “I wish,” you say, “to live thus and remain where I have arrived; I allow myself neither to become worse nor desire to become better.” You therefore will what cannot be. For what stands still in this world? And certainly it was said especially of man: “He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14:2). Finally, the very Author of man and of the world, so long as he was seen on earth and conversed with men, never stood still [variant: “ever”]. Indeed, Scripture testifies that “he went about doing good and healing all” (Acts 10:38). He went about not unfruitfully, but neither sluggishly nor lazily nor with slow step; rather, as is likewise written of him: “He rejoiced [Col. 0461B] as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6).

Moreover, one does not overtake a runner unless one also runs alongside him. And what profit is there in following Christ, if one does not succeed in attaining him? Therefore Paul said: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24). There, Christian, fix the goal of your course and progress where Christ placed his own. “He became,” it says, “obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8). Therefore, however far you may have run, if you do not reach death, you do not obtain the prize. Christ is the prize. If, while he runs, you halt your step, you do not draw nearer to Christ but rather remove yourself farther from him; and you must fear what David says: “Behold, those who remove themselves far from you, O Lord, shall perish” (Ps. 72:27). Therefore, if advancing is running, [Col. 0461C] where you cease to advance, there you also cease to run; but where [variant: “therefore where”] you do not run, there you begin to fail. From this it is plainly inferred that unwillingness to advance is nothing other than failure.

5. Jacob saw a ladder, and angels upon the ladder; none appeared seated or standing still, but all seemed either to be ascending or descending (Gen. 28:12). Thus it was openly made clear that, in this state of mortal life, no middle condition is found between advancement and decline. Rather, just as our body is continually known either to grow or to diminish, so the spirit too must either always advance or fail. Yet there is this difference: the spirit does not receive its increases or suffer its [Col. 0461D] losses according to the order of bodily changes. For in a body that is always vigorous and flourishing, the soul lies softer and more lukewarm; while again, in a weak and infirm body, the spirit thrives stronger and more ready. The Apostle testifies that he experienced this in himself: “When I am weak,” he says, “then I am stronger”; and he gladly glories in his weaknesses: “That the power of Christ,” he says, “may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9–10).

256. 6. We establish this by examples, so that [Col. 0462A] we may prove it even to the eyes, since in you, Father, what is said becomes manifest to us: although “the outward man” in you “is decaying,” nevertheless “the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). For whence comes such zeal for renewing the Order, unless from renewal of mind? Thus “a good man brings forth good things from his good treasure” (Matt. 12:35); thus “a good tree bears good fruit” (ibid. 7:17). These are your first and purest fruits. But what tree produced them, if not purity of heart? Otherwise, when would an impure mind seek and choose, with such zeal, the purity of the Rule? A clear stream does not flow from a turbid spring, nor does a clean thought arise from a filthy mind. Without doubt, what delights is within; within is the source. From that inward fullness bursts forth all that overflows outwardly; and [Col. 0462B] what thus pleases in the work shines in the mind.

7. Follow your father, children; be imitators of him, as he is of Christ. Say: “We will run in the fragrance [Note: [Col. 0461D] Thus Bernard, as do the ancients generally, reads “in the fragrance,” not “into the fragrance.” For the bride does not run into the fragrance, but runs in the fragrance toward the bridegroom. Peter the Venerable says below, in Letter 264: “drawn after you by the fragrance of your ointments.”] of your ointments” (Song 1:3), since “the good fragrance of Christ” is in every place (2 Cor. 2:14). For, not to speak of you, who are present and perceive the fragrance close at hand: such an abundance of this most delightful sprinkling reaches even us who are far away through his good endeavors, that it most certainly becomes for us “a fragrance of life unto life.” I think that those in heaven have already perceived the fragrance of sweetness and, with an exultation more festive than usual, sing: “Who is this that comes up through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense, and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3:6); and this: “Your shoots [Col. 0462C] are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apples” (Song 4:13). Whoever among you does not hear this jubilation in heaven is envious; whoever does not perceive this fragrance—if I may say so with peace toward all—let him suspect himself.

## LETTER 255

[Note: [Col. 0461D] Written in the year of Christ 1134.]

### TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS

[Note: [Col. 0461D] That is, Louis the Fat. This is clear both from the manuscripts [Col. 0462D] in which this letter is placed after Letter 126 to the bishops of Aquitaine, and from the context itself, since he is said to have chosen a pope as a Samuel for his son. This must be understood of Innocent II, who anointed Louis the Younger at Rheims in 1131.]

He urges the king not to hinder a council, necessary at this time both for the Church and the kingdom and destined to redound to the king’s honor.

To LOUIS, by God’s grace most excellent king of the Franks, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, his faithful servant: greeting from the King of kings and Lord of lords to him, to his beloved wife, and to his sons.

1. The kingdoms of the earth and the rights of kingdoms then indeed remain sound and unimpaired for their lords when they do not resist divine ordinances and appointments. Why, lord, does your anger rage against God’s chosen one, whom your own highness has also received and preferred—indeed, as a father for yourself, and as a Samuel also for your son? Royal indignation arms itself, not plainly against strangers, but against itself and its own. It is no wonder if, according to Scripture, “the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (James 1:20); for it often causes you neither to perceive a danger evident to all nor to feel the harm done to your own advantage, dignity, and safety.

A council is being assembled. [Note: [Col. 0463D] Understand the Council of Pisa, held in 1134, which the king was preventing French prelates from attending on the pretext of excessive heat.] What is thereby taken from royal glory or from the interests of the kingdom? There before the whole Church your Highness’s ready and particular devotion will be commended and recalled: that, first among kings, or at least among the foremost, you most vigorously and most Christianly opposed the rage of those persecuting that same mother of yours by defending her. There, glorious king, due thanks will be rendered to you by that vast multitude; there thousands of saints will pray for you and yours.

2. Moreover, no one is ignorant how necessary at this time a gathering of bishops is, except one hard of heart who does not heed the distresses of Mother Church. [Col. 0463B] “But,” they say, “the heat is excessive.” As though we had bodies of ice. Or are our hearts more frozen, and is there no one who, according to the prophet, grieves over the ruin of Joseph? (Amos 6:6). But enough of this elsewhere. Now I, the least in your kingdom—though least in dignity, not in loyalty—say to you: It is not expedient to wish to hinder so great and necessary a good. Nor do evident reasons fail by which I could make this clear; and I have them ready at hand to bring forward now, except that I judge enough has been said to a wise man. Nevertheless, if anything has proceeded from the rigor of apostolic authority by which your serene Highness may reasonably consider itself offended, your faithful servants who will be present [variant: [Col. 0463C] wrongly, “who adhere”] will strive with all their strength to have that very matter recalled or moderated, as is fitting for your honor. Among them, we also will not hold back if we can do anything.

## LETTER 256

[Note: [Col. 0463D] Written in the year of Christ.]

### TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

He urges Eugenius to bring aid to the Eastern Church and not to lose heart over the defeat suffered in the loss of the city of Edessa. He is astonished that he himself was chosen at Chartres as leader of the expedition.

1. The report that has sounded forth is no light matter: it is grievous indeed and heavy. And grievous to whom? Rather, to whom is it not grievous? Only the children of wrath do not feel wrath; they are not saddened by sorrowful things, but rejoice and exult in evils. Otherwise, the sorrow is common because the cause is common. You did well to praise the most just zeal of our Gallican Church and to strengthen it with the authority of your letters. I tell you: in so general and so grave a cause, action must not be lukewarm, nor even timid. I read in a certain wise man: “He is no strong man whose courage does not rise in the very difficulty of circumstances” (SENECA, Letter 22 to Lucilius). But I say that a faithful person should trust all the more even amid scourges. Waters have entered up to the soul of Christ; the apple of his eye has been touched. Both swords must now be drawn [Note: [Col. 0464D] On this twofold sword, see *On Consideration*, chapter 3, and *To the Knights Templar*, chapter 2.] in [Col. 0464A] the Lord’s passion, while Christ suffers anew where he suffered a second time. But through whom if not through you? Both belong to Peter: one to be drawn at his command, the other by his hand, whenever necessary. And indeed, concerning the one which seemed less so, it was said to Peter: “Put your sword into its sheath” (John 18:11). Therefore that sword too was his, though certainly not to be drawn by his own hand.

2. I judge that both ought now to be drawn and put to work in defense of the Eastern Church. You hold its place; you must not neglect zeal for it. What is this: to hold primacy and decline ministry? A voice cries: “I come to Jerusalem to be crucified again” (HEGESIPPUS, *On the Destruction* 3.2). Though some may be lukewarm at this voice and others deaf, Peter’s successor may not dissemble. He too will say: “Even if [Col. 0464B] all are scandalized, yet not I” (Matt. 26:33); nor will he be frightened by the losses of the former army, to repairing which he will apply himself all the more. Must a man therefore not do what he ought because God does what he wills? For my part, amid such great evils, as a Christian and believer, I shall hope for better things and “count it all joy when we fall into diverse trials” (James 1:2). Truly, we eat the bread of sorrow and have been given the wine of compunction to drink. Why do you despair, friend of the Bridegroom, as though the kind and wise Bridegroom had not, as is his custom, kept the good wine until now? “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” (Joel 2:14). And certainly it is the custom of the divine power above to work and judge thus—I speak as one who knows. When have great goods come to mortals that great evils did not precede? For, to omit other instances, did not the death of the Savior precede that unique and singular benefit of our salvation?

3. Therefore, friend of the Bridegroom, prove yourself his friend in necessity. If, with the threefold love about which your predecessor was questioned (John 21:15–17), you too love Christ with all your heart, all your soul, and [Col. 0464C] all your strength, as you ought, you will reserve nothing and conceal nothing in so great a danger to his Bride; but you will expend whatever strength, zeal, care, authority, and power you possess. A singular danger requires singular effort. The foundation is shaken, and every effort must be made to meet the impending ruin. These things have been said on your account, confidently indeed, but faithfully.

4. As for that report which, unless I am mistaken, you have already heard—namely, how at the gathering at Chartres [Note: [Col. 0464D] On this gathering, convened in 1146, the letters of Peter the Venerable and Suger should be read.] they elected me, to my great astonishment, as though commander and leader of the army—be assured that this neither was nor is of my counsel or will, nor is it within my power, so far as I measure my own strength, to proceed so far. Who am I to arrange battle lines or go forth before the faces of armed men? [Col. 0465A] What could be more remote from my profession, even if strength were available and skill not lacking? Yet it is not for me to instruct your wisdom in these matters: you know them all. I only beseech you, by that love through which you are especially indebted to me, do not expose me to human wills; but, since this charge rests especially upon you, seek divine counsel and labor so that, as the will has been in heaven, so it may be done.

## LETTER 257

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF BROTHER PHILIP

1. There is a matter which we do not mingle with the others [Note: [Col. 0465D] From this it is inferred that this letter was sent at the same time as the preceding one, on Philip’s behalf. Concerning him the following is found in the *Catalogue of the Priors of Clairvaux*: “Philip, who had been bishop of Tarentum and was deposed during the schism”—namely, because he had adhered to Anacletus—“came to Clairvaux, and by mercy was granted the office of deacon.” This is the occasion of the present letter. He was prior when blessed Bernard died.], because it touches and pains us more than the others, and requires the singular urgency of a special prayer. Our Philip, when he exalted himself, was humbled; but when he humbled himself, [Col. 0465B] he was not exalted—as though the Lord had not said both things alike (Matt. 23:12). There is rigor, but without dispensation; judgment, but without mercy. Many, it cannot be denied, have measured in this way; but no one has wished such measure to be applied to himself. Yet “with what measure we have measured, it shall be measured to us again” (Matt. 7:2); and surely there will be judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy. Your apostolic office is capable of both matters: namely, zeal and compassion. The honor of majesty indeed loves judgment; but far be it from prejudicing gentleness. Indeed, that steward whose praise is found in the Gospel chose rather to defraud his master than not to pity his neighbor. Finally, he had one render eighty instead of one hundred, another fifty instead of one hundred. He was rightly praised because he preferred to cause his master a loss of goods rather than a loss of persons. And because one who acts thus is worthy of his reward, by that one act he made his own friends of those whom his master had retained as servants (Luke 16:1–8).

2. What are we doing? We seem to have entered upon pleading a case, rather than offering a petition. This is not expedient. If we continue to say these things, we provoke judgment, not mercy. I have no confidence in these arguments, any more than in spider’s webs. “The net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17). I know how much stronger the replies that may be made to me are, especially from such an intellect. Therefore the weapons I have are the prayers of the poor, and we abound in this kind. Before these engines, the tower of strength must yield, though otherwise impregnable. The Father of the poor, the lover of poverty, will not repel the prayers of the poor. Who are they? I am not alone; and if I were alone, perhaps I might presume. All your sons who are with me, and those not with me, are nevertheless with me in this supplication. Who can number them? Brother Philip alone is excepted: [Col. 0466A] he neither asks nor requests that others ask, and whether he even wishes it I do not know. Rather, so far as lies in him, he has chosen “to be lowly in the house of his God.” Yet we ask not for the man, but for the Order, which we trust will benefit greatly from a dispensation granted in his case.

## LETTER 258

### TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF BROTHER RUALENUS

[Note: [Col. 0466D] Written in 1145. Rualenus, formerly prior of Clairvaux, was made abbot at Rome of Saint Anastasius after Eugenius was elected pope, as in Letter 245; Bernard laments his absence in Letter 43. Nicholas of Clairvaux, admitted to Clairvaux chiefly through Rualenus’s support, later wrote several letters in Rualenus’s name, among them 23 and 25, which wrongly bear the heading “of Rievaulx” instead of Rualenus.]

He asks that Rualenus, appointed abbot of Saint Anastasius by the Pope’s order, though very unwilling and resistant, be sent back to him.

In truth, we have learned that our Rualenus not only does not rest in the position in which he has been placed, but will never rest there. Therefore prompt remedy is necessary, not only for him but also for me. [Col. 0466B] I burn, I tell you, so long as he remains in distress. Do not be surprised at this: we are one soul, except that I am the mother and he the son; for in his case I yielded to you both the name and authority of father. Affection alone, which could not be transferred, has remained to me, and it tortures me. “Can a mother forget the child of her womb?” (Isa. 49:15). Who could say that I once was that mother? I feel that I still am. My sorrowing breast cries out “mother,” and continual pain of heart cries out for him. Do you ask of whom I complain? Of myself. I do not complain about you, but to you. I, I—a cruel yet loving mother—spared not my own entrails, in order to make my heart chaste in the obedience of love. From my bosom I offered the sacrifice of a dear pledge; and I obeyed the will—not under compulsion, I confess, but willingly—the will which compels whom it wishes. But he was not so. He resisted, though in vain, plainly compelled both by me and by you. Could I have feared that he would forever resist with such obstinacy? It belongs to a compassionate heart to yield to importunity, which does not allow itself to be brought to what is right. Otherwise, to retain unwillingly a man who has been unwillingly drawn to something is hard upon him and fruitful for no one. Moreover, to occupy a place and produce no fruit benefits neither the place, nor befits you, nor us. “No one,” as blessed Ambrose says, “does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good; for the spirit of fear profits nothing where there is no spirit of love” (St. AMBROSE, on Psalm 1). Therefore we beseech you through the bowels of the mercy of our God: show a father’s bowels, and send the child, while he still lives, back to his mother’s breasts, whose [Col. 0466D] entire languor perhaps lies in his being weaned too early. For he is better allowed to live than divided. What profit is there in his blood? One thing I know: that will not be the voice of a father or mother, “Let him be neither mine nor yours, but let him be divided” (3 Kings 3:26). Perhaps you do not fear this, because you do not believe it will happen. But writings and whispered reports very frequently coming into [Col. 0467A] our hands are full of this fear, threatening the man’s flight and separation—or rather, rupture—not only from you but also from us.

## LETTER 259

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Written in the year of Christ 1145.]

### TO THE SAME

On the preceding matter.—He declares that he wills and does not will the same things as the Pope; and therefore that he willingly presents his Rualenus, as the Pope commands, for the abbacy of Saint Anastasius.

Even if I have ever wished something which you did not wish me to wish, the gracious condescension of your gentleness moves me so that what you wish I not only wish, but eagerly wish. Does it please you that Brother Rualenus should be abbot at Saint Anastasius? It pleased me before as well; but because he was so greatly unwilling, what pleased became displeasing. Yet, since your good pleasure does not permit otherwise, [Col. 0467B] what displeased returns, as is just, to being pleasing. You may test it. What you commanded has been done, not because you commanded it, but because you wished it. It has therefore been done willingly, not as from sorrow or necessity. The prompt carrying out of the command proves obedience; let this letter be questioned concerning willingness. If I were content merely to carry out the command, would I not, according to the Lord’s saying, be an unprofitable servant, discharging a debt? (Luke 17:10). But now, because I have added willing it, I am no longer a servant but a son.

## LETTER 260

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Written in the same year.]

### TO RUALENUS, ABBOT

He sympathizes with Rualenus in the charge entrusted to him, which he urges him finally to accept.

[Col. 0467C] Your absence, dearest Rualenus, afflicted us more than enough; but we were troubled much more deeply on learning of your sadness. For we think it more just that we should lament your distress or deprivation of us than our own desolation or loss of you. This deprivation is indeed not a little harmful and not a little burdensome—the loss of so sweet a son, so useful a brother, so necessary a helper. Yet the more truly we acknowledge these things about your lovableness, the more affectionately we sympathize with your sorrow, esteeming your hardship far more and bearing it far more painfully than our own loss. Finally, we neither concealed the matter, nor rested, nor kept silent, testing God in this matter almost to the point of provoking the supreme and holy Pontiff to anger, so that somehow we might call you back even at our own risk. But because we have so far been frustrated in all our plans and efforts, we finally yield, wearied, to heavenly judgments and surrender to power: since we cannot achieve what we wish, we are compelled to will what we can.

[Col. 0467D] Therefore, dearest and most longed-for brother, be strengthened in the Lord and do not now kick against the goad, lest, when you are pricked, the many who love you exceedingly in the Lord may likewise be pierced. Spare yourself and us, who in love for you did not spare even ourselves. Rather, clothe yourself with strength, trusting and knowing that the joy of the Lord is your strength. Put on the joy of salvation, so that we too, rejoicing in your gladness, may give praises and thanks to God, who loves a cheerful giver, both for your peace and for our consolation.

## LETTER 261

### TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

He asks that the abbot of Saint Urban, placed under censures for receiving a Knight Templar, be absolved.

One of the Knights Templar wished to become a monk in our Order, and some of our men did not refuse to support him in [Col. 0468B] this intention. But, because they did not dare receive him in their own cloisters—for it was not permitted—they secretly brought him to a certain abbey called Vallis [Note: [Col. 0467D] It is uncertain which abbey this was. It belonged to the Cistercian Order and was situated either in, or not far from, the diocese of Châlons, where the monastery of Saint Urban was located, mentioned below. Herchenraus, bishop of the people of Châlons, built it in 865, according to the monk Heric, *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, ch. 14.]. They instructed and urged the abbot to have a black habit of another monastic Order given to him; then to receive him in that habit and give him ours. And so it was done. The matter became known to us, and through us was referred to the chapter. By decree of the chapter, that brother was expelled. Yet the brothers of the Temple were by no means satisfied with this; rather, they brought letters from your Majesty to the bishop of Châlons, directing him to suspend the abbot of Saint Urban—for he was the one who had given the habit to the knight—from entering the church until he presented himself before you. Consequently, the abbot of Vallis, at whose request the other had done this [Col. 0468C] without suspecting anything evil, has been compelled in great anguish of mind to send the brother bearing this letter to the feet of your mercy, so that he who became entangled through him may be released through him—if both he and we, your other sons, can obtain this from your holy Fatherhood.

## LETTER 262

### TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE MONKS OF MOUZON

[Note: [Col. 0468D] In the Cistercian manuscript: “On behalf of Samson, archbishop of Rheims.” But this is equivalent, since the letter was written at Samson’s request on behalf of the monks of Mouzon. Their monastery was the notable monastery of Blessed Mary on the Meuse, in the diocese of Rheims, under the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Vitonus. Moreover, nothing concerning this affair is found in the *Chronicle of Mouzon*, *Spicilegium*, vol. 7.]

I cannot fail the lord of Rheims in his petition, especially since it deserves to be heard. Therefore we ask and entreat with every urgency on behalf of the poor monks of Mouzon, that they may swiftly be delivered from the oppression they endure, as you will be able to learn through the bearer of this letter; [Col. 0468D] and that the injuries or malicious accusations brought against them may be repelled by your strong hand. For this is why the poor men have sent to you from afar, crying out. What answer ought to be brought back from you, let the justice and poverty of those who love you teach you; and let the reverence due to the aforementioned man, who intercedes for them and loves you greatly, teach you.

## LETTER 263

### TO THE BISHOP OF SOISSONS, ON BEHALF OF THE ABBOT OF CUISY

[Note: [Col. 0469D] Namely Simon, concerning whom see Letter 293. In earlier editions and some manuscripts this letter is addressed “To the Same,” that is, Eugenius. But the Cistercian and Clairvaux manuscripts, besides others, favor our reading; and in my judgment it is more rightly addressed to Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, in whose diocese Cuisy stood, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict on the Marne. Perhaps Peter of Celle, book 2, Letter 14, should be understood to refer to the deposition of this Simon.]

[Col. 0469A]

I had offered prayers when perhaps I could have commanded, and I thought I had been heard. But since I have learned that it is not so, it seems to me that I must now ask not simply and ordinarily, but cry aloud: for I do not bear with composure or equanimity a refusal such as I have not hitherto experienced. Do therefore what you ought; do what you are accustomed to do, for custom has made you a debtor. Do it, I say, if not because you are asked, then at least because you are commanded. Return, therefore, to judgment. For it does not seem to accord with justice that a religious man, our friend and your son, the abbot of Cuisy, should lose what belongs by right to his monastery because of a word rashly and imprudently [Col. 0469B] uttered by him, and without his church’s consent. Even if his adversary stubbornly clings wholly to that word, as one not confident in justice, this ought not, we think, to prejudice the aforesaid abbot in a just judgment, since the men at whose discretion [that is, arbitration] the matter rests are known not to have agreed but rather to have disagreed. From this we believe that you will neither grieve nor trouble us. May God gladden your soul and preserve you from every disturbance, beloved and honored Father—beloved by all servants of Christ, but especially by us.

## LETTER 264

[Note: [Col. 0470D] Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### FROM PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO BERNARD, ABBOT

He declares his longing for Bernard and earnestly asks that Nicholas, beloved to him, be sent as a consolation in Bernard’s absence.

[Col. 0469C]

To the strong and splendid pillar of the monastic Order—indeed, of the whole Church of God—Lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: the greeting which God has promised to those who love him.

If it were permitted, if God’s dispensation did not stand in the way, if a man’s path were in his own power, I would rather cling to your most dear Blessedness in an indissoluble bond than rule anywhere among mortals or reign. For what? Should not your companionship, pleasing not only to men but even to angels themselves, be preferred by me to all earthly kingdoms? If I call you a fellow citizen of those angels, I shall not be false—even though hope has not yet passed into reality—through the grace of the merciful God. If it had indeed [Col. 0469D] been granted to me to be here with you until my last breath, perhaps it would afterwards have been granted to me to be forever where you were also. For where would I run, if not after you, drawn after you by the fragrance of your ointments? Since this cannot always be granted, would that it were granted at least often! And because even that is not possible, would that I might at least frequently see those sent by you! Since this too occurs rarely, I wish that at least soon your Holiness might visit one who loves you through your Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0470D] See Letter 298 and Peter the Venerable, book 3, Letters 33–35.], who is to remain with me until the Octaves of the Lord, and in whom, as it seems to me, your spirit rests in part and mine wholly. In him I shall see you, holy brother; through him I shall hear you; and through him I shall entrust certain matters, which I wish to make known secretly to your wisdom. I commend myself and my people, with whatever prayers and devotion I can, to your holy soul and to those who, under your rule, serve Almighty God.

## LETTER 265

[Note: [Col. 0470D] Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### BERNARD THE ABBOT’S REPLY TO THE SAME

He refuses praise as unworthy of it, yet in return offers praises to his encomiast.

What are you doing, good man? You praise a sinner; you pronounce a wretch [Col. 0470B] blessed! It remains for you to pray that I may not be led into error. I am led into error if, delighted by such great praises, I begin not to know myself. This almost happened to me when I read the letter of your Blessedness and of my blessedness. How blessed I would now be, if I could be made blessed by words! Yet I shall call myself blessed—but by your favor, not by my own merits: blessed because I am loved by you and because I love you. Though I judge that even this sweet morsel must be melted, and not, as they say, taken in with cheeks completely full.

Do you wonder why? Certainly, I see nothing in myself by which I could have deserved to be so greatly loved, especially by so great a man. But I know that to wish to be loved beyond what is right is unworthy of a righteous person. Who will grant me to imitate, as much as admire, this distinction of such great humility? Who will grant me to enjoy your holy and longed-for [Col. 0470C] presence—not always, not often, but even once a year? I think that I would never return empty on any occasion. I would not, I say, behold in vain an exemplar of virtue, the height of discipline, a mirror of holiness; and what I confess that I have learned too little from Christ until now, I would not fruitlessly perceive with seeing faith: namely, how gentle and humble of heart you too are. But if I go on doing to you what I complain that you have done to me, then, even if I speak the truth, I shall not agree with the law of truth in which it is written: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16).

Let us therefore now reply to your little request, with which you closed your letter. The man whom you command to be sent to you is not with me at present, but with the lord of Auxerre; and he is so ill that it is said he cannot yet come even to us without serious inconvenience.

## LETTER CCLXVI. TO SUGER, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Note: Written in 1151.—Bernard urges Suger to meet death with a cheerful spirit; it came upon him in 1152, as the Chronicle of Saint-Denis attests in these words: “This is the last year of Abbot Suger of blessed memory. But since no one is exempt from the condition of dying, when he began to be afflicted by the illness of which he died, he was supported by the hands of the brethren and asked to be led into the chapter-house. There, after words of edification, he cast himself at the feet of all the brethren amid their tears and groans, submitted himself to their judgment, and tearfully begged that, out of regard for mercy, they would forgive whatever offense he had committed against them or whatever he had done too negligently. All the brethren most willingly did so, with the greatest devotion and an abundant outpouring of tears. This venerable father passed away between the words of the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, on the Ides of January, in the seventieth year of his age, nearly the sixtieth since assuming the monastic habit, and the twenty-ninth of his prelacy. Six bishops, with many abbots and Louis, the Most Christian king of the Franks, attended his burial and funeral rites; mindful there of his devotion and forgetful of royal majesty, he wept most bitterly while Suger was buried.” Thus far the Chronicle. This epitaph was inscribed upon his tomb: HERE LIES SUGER, ABBOT—brief indeed, yet expressing the whole of Suger in Suger’s name alone. Robert of Hereford praises him admirably in Letter 216 among the Sugerian letters. Francis Chifflet published a most elegant poem, composed by Simon Capra-Aurea, canon of Saint-Victor at Paris:

> The Church’s flower has fallen—its gem, crown, pillar,  
> Its banner, shield, helmet, light, and summit:  
> Abbot Suger, a pattern of virtue and justice,  
> Weighty in piety, pious in gravity.  
> Great-souled, wise, eloquent, generous, honorable,  
> Present in judgment in body, self-possessed in mind.  
>   
> Through him the king prudently guided the reins of the realm;  
> He ruled the king, and the king was almost the king of a king.  
> While the king prolonged his stay beyond the sea for many years,  
> This man governed the kingdom, acting in the king’s place.  
> What scarcely any other man could unite in himself, he united:  
> Upright toward men and good toward God.  
>   
> He adorned the see of the noble church with glory, repelled its losses with vigor, and enlarged its choir with men.  
> The seventh day of Theophany took his light away;  
> True Theophany gave true light to the man.

A lengthy and elegant eulogy of him was inscribed in golden letters upon a bronze plaque by the Fathers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur. More concerning him appears in the notes to Letters 78 and 369.]

He encourages him to face death fearlessly, and expresses his wish to see him before his death.

To his dearest and most intimate friend SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, glory which is within and grace which comes from above.

1. Man of God, do not tremble to put off that man who is of the earth, who presses you down to the earth and strives to press you down to hell. He is the one who troubles, burdens, and attacks you. What have you to do with earthly wrappings, when you are about to go to heaven and must soon be clothed in the robe of glory? It is ready, but it will not be given to one who is clothed already: it knows how to clothe, not to clothe over another garment. Endure, then, patiently—indeed, gladly accept—to be found naked and not clothed. For God himself also wishes to be clothed, but when he is naked, not when he is clothed. The man of God will not return to God unless he who is of earth and is earth goes into the earth. For these two men oppose one another, and there will be no peace until they are separated from one another; and if there is peace, it will not be the peace of the Lord, nor peace with the Lord. You are not among those who say, “Peace,” when there is no peace (Ezek. 13:10). That peace which surpasses all understanding awaits you; the righteous await you until recompense is made to you; the joy of your Lord awaits you.

2. And I, dearest friend, am indeed intensely moved by the desire to see you beforehand, that the blessing of one dying may come upon me. And since a man’s way is not in his own power, I do not dare promise as certain that of which I am not certain; but, as for what I do not yet see, I do enough that I may be able to do it. Perhaps I shall come; perhaps I shall not. But whichever occurs, I loved you from the beginning and shall love you without end. I say confidently: I cannot lose one so loved unto the end. He is not lost to me, but goes before me—he to whose soul mine has clung with a bond that will not be scattered and a tie that will not be broken. Only remember us when you arrive where you go before us, so that it may soon be granted to us also to come after you and arrive at you. Meanwhile, however, do not in any way suppose that your sweet memory will depart from ours, even if your presence is withdrawn from those who grieve. Yet God is able still to give you to us who ask and preserve you for us who need you; of this certainly we must not despair.

## LETTER CCLXVII. TO THE ABBOT OF CLUNY

Your son, Brother Galcher, has become ours also, according to that rule: “All that is mine is yours, and yours mine” (John 17:10). Let him not be less familiar because he belongs to us both; but, if some further grace can make this so, let him be more familiar and more welcome—to me because he is yours, and to you because he is ours.

## LETTER CCLXVIII. TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

He warns that the promotion of an unworthy man was obtained by deception and that the decision must therefore be revoked.

Others may stand in awe of your majesty and, with trembling lips and fingers, scarcely arrive at the point after long circumlocutions and windings. But I, attending only to your advantage and your honor, immediately lay the matter open, naked and plain, as it is; and, without delay or concealment, I do not hesitate to disclose to the apostolic lord, as to one of ourselves, what must be said. Something has been fraudulently obtained from you—and gravely so; this I would affirm without hesitation. Who suggested to you that a man marked, convicted, and condemned for ambition should be forced into ecclesiastical rank? As though he had not sufficiently wished to thrust himself forward on his own.

Is this not the man whom Bishop Lambert of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0472D] He was bishop of Angoulême after Gerard; in that diocese lies the monastery of La Couronne, of the Order of Saint Benedict. Lambert is praised in Book IV of the *Life of Bernard*, no. 29.]—having caught him in detestable crimes which he had committed at ambition’s prompting—solemnly degraded, as he ought, not only from the rank which he held but from all hope of promotion? The only course is to revoke the decision, both because of the distress of the holy brothers of La Couronne, who cry out to you about this, and out of reverence for the holy and learned bishop who was responsible in this matter; but also because of conscience—I mean your conscience, not another’s. One thing remains: that I should add this for the sake of my own conscience: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). For you sin if you are not angry with the proposer of so great a falsehood, the fraudulent procurer of so unworthy a decision.

## LETTER CCLXIX. TO THE SAME

He deprives letters extorted from him by deceit of force and authority.

The serpent deceived me. A shifty and crafty man, devoid of justice, avoiding a hearing, hostile to his own conscience, intent upon injury to his brother, obtained from me, while I was unaware, letters on his own behalf through the lord of Beauvais. [Note: [Col. 0473C] Arnulf of Mailly, I suppose; concerning whom see Letter 278.] What, indeed, would he not have obtained from me? If you do not wish to burden my conscience beyond measure, let the deceitful man gain nothing by fraud, nor oppress the innocent by means of our letters. Yet even this would not satisfy me unless that most malicious fraudster and most grasping extortioner also bears the punishment he deserves.

## LETTER CCLXX. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0473C] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]

He writes in the case of the Carthusian Prior against certain transgressors; he announces the death of the Abbot of Cîteaux and commends his successor.

1. Those who tempt us neither slumber nor sleep. How they have lately persecuted us again in the mountains and laid snares in the wilderness! The Carthusians have been troubled [Note: [Col. 0473C] The author of the French *Life of Saint Bernard*, Book VI, chapter 10, explains the matter, drawing upon the *Life of Saint Anthelm, or Nanthelm*, first Prior of the Great Charterhouse and later bishop of Belley. “For,” as it says there, “when the new Prior Anthelm exerted himself to reform according to the Constitutions formerly written down whatever harm the ancient religion and observance of the holy Order had sustained, he strove to bring back to better conduct anyone whom he saw to be negligent or disobedient, by gentle admonitions, words and threats, commands and rebukes. But if anyone refused to come to his senses and remained plainly obstinate, he did not hesitate to expel him from the fellowship of the brethren. For there were some who could not bear his sound institutions; great in their own eyes, men of malicious mind and inclined to disputes, they did not fear to oppose him. But he, unable to tolerate their arrogance lest they disturb the peace and quiet of the others, expelled them from the monastery.”

Some of these men, as is likely, fled to Eugenius and were sent back absolved and subject to no penance. Bernard here complains of this, because “from the very foundation of the place it had been unheard of for anyone who departed to be received back without satisfaction.” Manrique gives another explanation in his *Annals* for the year 1151, chapter 2, from the letters of Peter the Venerable (Book VI, Letter 12): namely, the dispute which arose in 1151, when Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, was promoted to the archbishopric of Vienne, concerning a new election among several Carthusian houses—Chartreuse, Les Écouges, Durbon, Portes, Meyriat, Sylve-Bénite, and Arvières. Some maintained that “the elected man ought not to become a bishop” and pursued the case in courts; others, on the contrary, asserted that “it was not their business to litigate, but simply to state what they thought, not to enter palaces for legal proceedings.” But since the latter case concerns a quarrel among monasteries, not the rebellion of monks which Bernard indicates in this letter, these matters should rather be referred to the former case. We assign them to 1151 because they occurred shortly after the death of Rainald, Abbot of Cîteaux—as this letter shows—who died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, 1150, as Manrique proves from the Cistercian Martyrology in his *Annals* for 1151, chapter 1.]—they have been troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and almost all their wisdom has been swallowed up. Know, my lord: an enemy has done this. What do I say, “has done”? He is still doing it. He still has the confidence for that holiness even to flow into his mouth. His food is choice—you know this very well. He has already made some men transgressors; others, whom he could not overcome by himself, he attacks through them in domestic and civil war.

From the very foundation of the place and Order, it has not been heard that one who departed could be received back without satisfaction. Those who had gone out badly re-entered worse, adding transgression to transgression. What do you think, holy Father, will those men do whose departure is in transgression and whose return is in pride? “And now their pride rises continually” (Ps. 73:23). They exult in the very evil they have done and insult those suffering injury. They have prevailed; they triumph: the Prior is no longer Prior. “While the wicked is proud, the poor is set on fire.” He wishes even to leave; he cannot look upon the destruction of his Order. And he would already have departed, if he could have departed alone. The man who is Prior must necessarily be good; for we have heard from good men that those on whose counsel he relies are good.

2. Do you see, most merciful Father, how greatly you have been deceived? Shall the author of this deception receive nothing worthy of his fraud? If I know you well, whoever he is will bear judgment. They came to you in sheep’s clothing, in a holy habit; appearance deceived you. What wonder? You too are a man. But now that the fraud has been brought to light, let zeal arise and manfully carry out its task against evildoers. “Let not your soul enter into their counsel”; let Ahithophel’s counsel be scattered. Guard yourself. It is not equally perilous to be deceived through ignorance and for zeal to sleep. Ignorance excuses the former; negligence makes the latter inexcusable. Perhaps he will come up in opposition and try to persuade you otherwise. Let iniquity lie to itself, not to my lord. For this is the truth, and the matter stands thus.

Nothing, indeed, is more pleasing or more just in your judgments than this: whenever such an occasion presents itself, let one who wished to harm another fall into the pit he made, and let his grief return upon his own head, and his iniquity descend upon his own crown (Ps. 7:16–17). My lord’s zeal will do this. And he who was Prior will, I trust, be made Prior again, so that all iniquity may not boast. Otherwise—as we do not fear without reason—unless the Prior is restored to his rank, the Order will not long remain in its own state. May God inspire you to receive these things as a father and to answer with good news, for the consolation of us all, who are greatly desolate and afflicted beyond measure.

3. The lord of Cîteaux [Note: [Col. 0475C] Rainald, whose death occurred in 1151, had as successor Goswin, formerly abbot of Bonneval.] has left us: a great wound in the Order. But I have a twofold cause of sorrow, since in one man I have lost both father and son. And now we have in his place Lord Goswin, abbot of Bonneval. May it please you to strengthen him by apostolic letters and confirm by your favor what has been done concerning him. You know him, and he needs no recommender with you, for his life and the wisdom given him by God sufficiently commend him.

The lord of Valence [Note: [Col. 0475C] Oribert, formerly Prior of La Chaise-Dieu; concerning his election, Letter 249.] is recovering; and where he is strong, he does good. Therefore lovers of goodness love him, and he loves good men. In this it appears that he is good. It belongs to you to love and foster such men. Your little son is more infirm than usual: he is wasting away drop by drop, perhaps utterly unworthy to be killed once and to enter life swiftly.

## LETTER CCLXXI. TO THEOBALD, COUNT OF CHAMPAGNE

[Note: [Col. 0475C] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]

[Note: [Col. 0475D] See Letter 37 and the following letter.]

He warns him that, because of his son’s tender age, he ought not to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities.

You know that I love you; but how greatly, God knows better than you do. I do not doubt that I too am loved by you, but for God’s sake; and if I offend him, there will be no reason why you should love me, since God will no longer be the cause. For who am I, that so great a prince should concern himself with so insignificant a person as I, except while you believe that God is in me? Therefore, perhaps it is not even to your advantage that I should offend him. Yet I undoubtedly offend him if I do what you request.

For I know that ecclesiastical honors and dignities are owed to those who both wish and are able to administer them worthily according to God. But know that it is neither just for you nor safe for me for ecclesiastical dignities to be acquired for your little son by my prayers or yours. [Note: [Col. 0475D] In this letter, reader, observe and admire the outstanding virtue, zeal, and constancy of the holy man: in a matter which he judged contrary to the Church of God and to his own conscience, he would not comply with the wishes and desire of the great prince Theobald, to whom, as a great benefactor of Clairvaux, he owed much. Bernard grievously complains in Letter 42, no. 25, that boys are promoted to ecclesiastical dignities because of the splendor of their birth and that several benefices are given to one person. It is found among the treatises, second in order, Volume II.] For no one, not even an adult, may hold several offices in several churches except by dispensation, and then only because of a great necessity of the Church or benefit to persons.

Therefore, if this saying seems hard to you, and you are pleased to fulfill what you have conceived, spare me in this matter. For you can, I think, obtain this through yourselves and through your other friends. Thus you will nevertheless accomplish what you wish, and I shall not have sinned. Certainly, I wish every good for our William [Note: [Col. 0475D] This was Theobald’s fourth son, called of the White Hands. He was first raised to the see of Chartres, then to that of Sens, afterward to Reims, and finally was created cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate in Gaul. He consecrated his nephew Philip Augustus; and, in his favor, Alexander III confirmed to the Archbishop of Reims the right of crowning the kings of France. Peter of Celle, Book I, Letter 5; Peter of Blois, Letters 28 and 122; and many others write concerning him.]—but before all else, God. This is why I do not wish him to possess anything contrary to God, lest he not possess God. If another wishes otherwise, I do not wish him to possess it through me, lest I too lose God. But when an opportunity arises for him to possess something according to God, I shall show myself a friend and shall not withhold my assistance, if it is needed. Before one who loves justice, I need not labor much in excusing what is done for justice.

But before the countess [Note: [Col. 0476C] Matilda, daughter of Engelbert, margrave and brother of the bishop of Regensburg, as appears from the *Life of Saint Norbert*, chapter 32. Here is the passage: “Therefore Norbert, having taken up the envoys of Count Theobald, brought them as far as Regensburg. For there was a bishop of that city, of most noble lineage, who had a brother, Engelbert, a most powerful margrave, with daughters of marriageable age. One of these—named Matilda, according to Orderic near the end of Book XIII—was betrothed to Count Theobald.” On Engelbert, see the note to Letter 130.] regard me as excused by what I have written back to you. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXXII. TO THE BISHOP OF LAON

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Written in 1152.—He was Walter of Saint-Maurice, formerly abbot of Saint-Martin near Laon, appointed in 1151 in place of the most pious Bishop Bartholomew, who, after thirty-eight years of government, retired to the Cistercian monastery of Foigny, which he himself had founded. His excellent letter to Samson, Archbishop of Reims, survives, in which—then a monk of Foigny—he refutes the false charge that he had squandered the goods of the church of Laon; it is printed in the Appendix to this volume.]

He reminds him of pious liberality.

[Col. 0476B]

We are yours. If you know this—indeed, since you do not deny it—let the bearer of this letter be effectively and firmly reconciled through us to you, and through you to all others whom he seems to have offended. Otherwise you offend one whom you do not deny is yours, which you certainly do not dare to do. Since you began to be a bishop, we have as yet received no blessing from you: neither purse, nor bag, nor shoes for our feet—

## LETTER OF POPE EUGENIUS TO THE CHAPTER OF CÎTEAUX, PREFIXED TO LETTER CCLXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Previously Letter 384. Written in the year of Christ 1150.]

He says that he wishes to be present at the Chapter of Cîteaux if pontifical occupations permit, and exhorts it to promote in the Chapter zeal and devotion to discipline and religious perfection.

[Col. 0476C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G. [Note: [Col. 0476D] Namely, Goswin, the fifth abbot of Cîteaux.] of Cîteaux, and to all the abbots assembled at Cîteaux in the name of the Lord: greeting and apostolic blessing.

1. Most beloved sons, we would wish to be present in body at your sacred assembly, so that, just as we walk with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, so we might treat, personally and jointly, of the life-giving work of the Holy Spirit and the soul’s progress. But because, by the determination of divine providence, we have been placed amid the sea to steer the ship of the Church, and are battered by the flooding onset of raging storms, so that we do not do what we wish but what we do not wish; and because we are bound by the office of administration we have undertaken, so that we cannot turn our steps to the desired place: we offer you our presence in spirit and letter. So far as we are permitted, we present ourselves to your assembly in love and desire, both wishing and earnestly asking, with all the affection we can, that you too may keep your spirit united with us and more earnestly implore together upon us the grace of almighty God.

For, set upon a mountain peak, where we are assailed on every side by gusts of wind, we hope that by God’s gift we may in some measure stand firm amid so great a tempest, if we are granted to obtain with God the intervention of your prayers. And that we may always find ready confidence before him through your prayers, and attain through your intercessions what we cannot attain by our merits, we desire that your charity may always be so solicitous concerning the things that belong to God—concerning observance of the Order and preservation of discipline—and that, despising what lies behind, each of you may so stretch himself toward what lies ahead that no cloud may appear in your works which could ever hinder your prayers from penetrating to God.

2. Therefore, whenever you assemble together, most beloved sons, to correct what needs correcting in any among you and to establish what should be established for the salvation of souls and the advancement of the Order, exercise common care. For “he who despises small things falls little by little” (Ecclus. 19:1); do not leave uncorrected among you those things which seem smaller. For one uselessly bars [variant: guards] the gates of a city if he leaves open even one hole through which enemies may enter, as Scripture says: “A neglected bilge does the same as an invading wind”; and: “You have avoided great dangers; take care lest you be buried by sand.”

Look, I beseech you, to the ancient fathers who established our sacred Order; and consider how, leaving the world and despising all things, abandoning the dead to bury their own dead, they flew to the wilderness. There, while others were busy with frequent ministry, they themselves sat with Mary at Jesus’ feet (Luke 10:39–40), so that they might receive heavenly manna more abundantly the farther they had withdrawn from Egypt. They went forth from their land and their kindred; they forgot their people and their father’s house. And because their King desired their beauty, he made them grow into a great nation and extended their branches to the ends of the earth, so that the brightness of their splendor illuminated the whole body of the Church; and the woman of Zarephath, at their word, filled innumerable vessels from the little oil which she had in her flask (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17:10, 16). They indeed received the firstfruits of the Spirit, and the oil of their sweetness has flowed down even to us.

3. Therefore you must consider and act more attentively, so that you may not degenerate from their virtues, but may be in the branch what you were in the shoot; and, having received from them the seeds of life, may bring forth with them the same shoot and fruit. Consider how those whose lamps are going out long to receive from your oil; and how many who have rotted like beasts in their own dung desire, through the regard of heavenly grace, to be entrusted to your governance and commended to your prayers.

And because the children of this age strive even against your will to draw you into governing them, and sometimes wish to call you back from the quiet of contemplation and the silence of the desert to occupations and affairs, bring your fathers’ institutions before the eye of your mind. Keeping before you the prophetic example, choose rather to be lowly in the house of God than to dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83:11). And because you have nothing that you did not receive, think of the Lord in goodness and of yourselves in humility, so that you may seem to follow the footsteps of him who said: “When you have done all things well, say, ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10). For if you have received kinds of tongues, the grace of healing, or knowledge of prophecy; if your words are better—indeed, more fragrant—than the choicest ointments; if the world reveres you and delights to run after the fragrance of your ointments: it is certainly the work of him who says, “My Father works even until now” (John 5:17).

## LETTER CCLXXIII. TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Written in the year of Christ 1150.]

He rejoices at the Pope’s letters to the Chapter, full of zeal and affection. He urges him to continue fostering all with that solicitude, but especially the religious of his own Order. He laments that the Abbot of Trois-Fontaines has been withdrawn from his office.

To his most loving father and lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme Pontiff, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

1. The voice of the turtledove was heard in our chapter: we rejoiced and were delighted. Truly, the utterance was chaste, fervent with zeal, prudent in knowledge. The spirit of life breathed in the letter: a mighty spirit, thundering, rebuking, and making us jealous with God’s jealousy. I confess that I could not easily say what pleased me more in it: your kindness or our benefit; majesty stooping down or humility raised up; severity that bites or fatherhood that soothes. Those among us who hungered for righteousness, however little, were refreshed; those who did so less were pierced with compunction; those who did so least were put to shame. [Note: [Col. 0477D] Thus in every order, however holy, these three classes of people are found; and chaff will never be absent from the Lord’s threshing floor. See Sermon 3 on the Ascension, no. 6; likewise the sermon on the Dedication of a Church, no. 3, and Sermon 30 on diverse subjects, no. 1; also Sermon 46 on the Song of Songs, no. 6.] Thus, I pray, thus may you act continually.

The solicitude owed to all must by no means be withheld from those to whom it is owed more particularly, but must be bestowed upon them more generously. Kindly love knows how to expand itself, not to diminish itself. Let it gather others indeed, but together with us; nor is it alien to your apostolic office to foster such men as can say with the apostles: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Those who have left themselves are not to be abandoned. They are the Lord’s little ones, believing in him; the faithful and prudent servant—especially he to whom the whole household has been entrusted—will not forsake them.

For they are a portion of the whole household: indeed a little flock, but one which, unless I am mistaken, has deserved to have God as Father and will receive a crown of glory from the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem from the hand of their God. For they do not count it robbery to be heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. In short, they have heard: “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). Enough of these matters for the present.

2. The Abbot of Trois-Fontaines [Note: [Col. 0479C] That is, Hugh, to whom the following letter is addressed—abbot of Trois-Fontaines in Champagne, not of Saint Anastasius at Tre Fontane near Rome, whatever Wion, Ciaconius, and others may think to the contrary. First, during precisely these times, the designation *Trois-Fontaines* without qualification was assigned only to the monastery in Champagne, as appears from the *Life of Saint Bernard* and the heading of Letter 69, “To the Abbot of Trois-Fontaines”; whereas the Roman house is usually called Saint Anastasius, as is shown especially by the heading of present Letter 345, directed “To the Brothers of Saint Anastasius.” Secondly, Rualen, formerly Prior of Clairvaux, was then abbot of Saint Anastasius, as appears from Letters 245, 258, and the following two letters; compare Nicholas of Clairvaux, Letter 43, “To Rualen, Abbot of Saint Anastasius.” Moreover, the following Bernardine Letter 274 bears in manuscripts the title, “To Hugh, Abbot of Trois-Fontaines, when he was at Rome,” words which sufficiently indicate that this monastery was situated at a greater distance from Rome. Further, Bernard tells Eugenius in this Letter 273 that he takes it ill that Hugh has been summoned to Rome, apparently to be made cardinal, and adds that he will be grievously wounded unless Hugh is sent back to him. Thus Hugh was abbot in Gaul. Finally, Bernard himself, then in Gaul, was present at the election held to appoint a successor in Hugh’s place, as Letter 274 shows. Hugh became Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1150, in the third creation made by Eugenius; and with him two other monks of Clairvaux, Henry and Roland, were made cardinals, according to Ciaconius. At that time the church of Velletri was joined to that of Ostia because of the scarcity of its inhabitants. On Hugh again, see Letters 274, 287, 290, 296, 306, and 307.] was well planted, like one beside streams of water. I fear that a good tree bearing good fruit, if uprooted, will bear none. We have sometimes seen a vine fruitful in its first planting and barren in its second. We have seen a well-planted tree flourish, then wither when transplanted.

You have therefore grievously wounded my heart if you do not send him back, because we are one heart and one soul. So long as it is divided, each part must necessarily be stained by its own blood. Alas! How shall I bear alone the burden which we two could scarcely bear, now that the staff of my old age has been taken away? If concern for me is too little, let the considerable wound of the whole Order move you; and do not, in hope of an uncertain good, choose to bring about such certain evils in the meantime. But if he has so entirely pleased you that you intend to retain him, then please, I beg you, keep him in your care and henceforth lift your hands to God, that he may deign to provide a suitable man for that house in his place.

As for the matters which, for the common benefit of the entire Order and for other business, we judged it proper—indeed necessary—to entrust to this same abbot for presentation to you, we urgently request a prompt reply from your Kindness: a reply in deed, not in word.

## LETTER CCLXXIV. TO HUGH, ABBOT OF TROIS-FONTAINES, WHEN HE WAS AT ROME

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Elsewhere: “Against the nephew of the bishop of Auxerre.” Elsewhere: “For the nephew of the bishop of Auxerre.” See Letter 276.—Letter 274, which in printed editions bears this title, “To Abbot Hugh,” etc., is headed in the Liège manuscript and another manuscript of Val-Saint-Lambert: “To Bishop Hugh, concerning the provost of Auxerre.” MARTÈNE.]

He repents of having recommended the nephew of the bishop of Auxerre, disapproving the provostship conferred upon him.

I repent of having written on behalf of that young man, and I wish, if possible, that the request might be recalled by which I seem to have approved my friend’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0480D] Hugh, bishop of Auxerre.] concerning the provostship bestowed and badly bestowed by him. This I certainly do not do, and have never done. But I confess that love overcame me, so that I wrote thus, being bound very closely to the young man’s uncle by an affection great indeed but in this respect insufficiently spiritual. The fresh wound caused by his death pressed me strongly. I may seem to have acted lightly; but I prefer to incur risk before my lord through haste in writing rather than before God through suspicion of falsehood.

Yet I wrote concerning the provostship carefully and prudently, saying nothing regarding him personally, because I knew without doubt that, as I remember, two of his predecessors had arranged that office otherwise and had confirmed it with their own privilege. But if you can prevail upon him to restore to the Church both its privilege and the privilege’s effectiveness, you will have performed a good work. Would that he might cleanse the holy bishop from this stain of blood and provide otherwise for the young man.

## LETTER CCLXXV. TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS, CONCERNING THE ELECTION AT AUXERRE

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]

He informs the Pope of the state of the election at Auxerre and of fraud committed in it.

[Col. 0480C]

When I first wrote to you concerning the Church of Auxerre, I had heard of the first election, but nothing of the second. And behold, as though I had prophesied, the disgrace I suspected has followed, and the fear I feared has occurred. Remember how matters were conducted at Nevers [Note: [Col. 0480D] He repeats the same point at the end of the following letter. He means the disturbances that occurred in the election of Raymond, bishop of Nevers. Compare Letter 246.], and see whether, by a similar device—indeed, by fraud not unlike it, and by the same author, as they say—the second election has not now also been attempted: namely, so that, one man having been nominated, [Col. 0481A] they may cast out two and then at last bring in a third, whom they want.

These men too sent to me, asking me to write on their side; and it seemed [269] fitting to me to send a brother from my side, who could ascertain the facts of both proceedings more certainly and inform us. Entering the church and investigating everything carefully, he found, on the testimony of all who had assembled, that no priest, except one—namely Hugh, brother of that same brother Geoffrey [Note: [Col. 0481D] This man seems to have been elected by the faction causing the disturbance; but in the end the election of Alan prevailed, formerly abbot of Ripailles, of the Cistercian Order, in the diocese of Troyes, who abridged the Life of St Bernard. In the Acts of the Bishops of Auxerre the bishopric is said to have been vacant for a year. See Letters 280 and 282, etc., and Book III of *On Consideration*, no. 11.]—nor any deacon except Stephen alone, belonged to that party, apart from those ecclesiastical persons who had been its instigators: the chanter, the archdeacon, and, it was said, the treasurer; for the latter himself was not then present. On the other side, however, besides others of lower rank, nine deacons and eleven priests concurred. The twelfth, [Col. 0481B] who is also archpriest, testified that he wished to subscribe to neither party and had written for neither, although he preferred the former more. The aforesaid Hugh held the seal of the Church [Note: [Col. 0481D] From this it is understood that from this time the Church of Auxerre possessed its own seal in addition to the episcopal seal.], a man not of peace but of the opposite faction; and, in surrendering it, he considered not what he ought, but what he wished.

This is how the matter stands. And I, with my customary boldness, draw one conclusion: malice ought not to boast, wisdom ought not to be deceived, and the Church ought not to be kept in suspense any longer.

## LETTER CCLXXVI  
[Note: [Col. 0481D] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]  
TO THE SAME PERSON, AFTER THE DEATH OF THE BISHOP OF AUXERRE

He warns the Pope of the irreligious will of the bishop of Auxerre, drawn up not without Stephen the deacon’s fraud; and that it ought to be annulled as a cause of scandal.

1. I still lay before you something which I would not previously have kept silent, had it been known to me before, as it now [Col. 0481C] is. The man is present who caused Israel to sin—I mean the holy bishop [Note: [Col. 0481D] That is, Hugh, formerly the first abbot of Pontigny and then bishop of Auxerre. He died in 1151 [Col. 0482D] on the tenth day of October. On this man’s miraculous conversion, virtues, and holiness, read Henriquez, *Fasciculus*, Book II, distinction 10, chapter 28, and the *Menology* for the twenty-first day of January.
