Read also Book I, chapter 3, of the *Life of St Bernard.*]—who, since at his death he was somewhat stupefied and confused, was made by this man to die almost intestate. For when he gave either nothing or little to the poor and to churches, he left to his young fleshly nephew, a secular and useless youth, almost everything that he had acquired for the episcopal table, Stephen suggesting and urging it.

They say that he left seven churches, tithes, and meadows in the bishop’s own woodland; moreover—what is disgraceful to all religion—his gold among the movable goods and his own riding-horses; and, since these were insufficient for making the journey to you to have these grants confirmed, he ordered even the monastery’s horses to be handed over. Yet some think that the bishop [Col. 0481D] knew nothing of these gifts, but that Stephen did and sealed whatever he wished; and this is credible. Indeed, last year, when he was thought to be at the point of death, they had him grant a certain church to the same nephew; but when he later recovered, as we learned with complete certainty, he by no means acknowledged that he had made the gift. Who, in short, would believe that a holy and spiritual man, if he was in his right mind and master of himself, made such a will? What man, however worldly, would call this the will of a priest? Is this the disposition of a sober and spiritual man, of one who judges all things and is himself judged by no one? For by whom, if this remains so, will this man not be judged, whether in heaven or on earth?

2. Therefore you, servant of God, who hold Peter’s sword, cut away from religion the shame of this reproach; from the Church its scandal; from the man his crime; and from the heart of all spiritual persons who loved him spiritually rather than carnally—and from your own heart—bitterness and grief. [Col. 0482B] Rise up, Phinehas; stand and make atonement, so that the shaking may be healed. Stand, I say, unyielding against flesh and blood: [270] with this battering-ram the children of this age will undoubtedly try to shake the wall of your constancy. True piety toward the uncle consists in being merciless toward the nephew in such a matter.

3. And know this: religious men—the dean of St Peter’s at Auxerre and the prior of St Eusebius—ready to come to you, both on their own behalf and on behalf of the abbot of St Lawrence, concerning the first election of the Church of Auxerre, were detained and intimidated by the opposing party through the count of Nevers [Note: [Col. 0482D] William IV, who succeeded his father William III when the latter withdrew into the Carthusian Order, from the year 1147. Compare Letter 280 below and its note.], lest they should come. For the count himself summoned them and warned them not to involve themselves, forbidding them by very grave and open threats; as the prior himself, sent to us for this very reason by his aforesaid [Col. 0482C] abbot and his fleshly brother, and by the dean, confessed and complained to us, asking also that we make this known to you.

I have said it, and say it again: remember what was done at Nevers. It is most orderly that something sometimes be done less than orderly. Those who are of sound mind place one of your keys in discernment, the other in power.

## LETTER CCLXXVII  
TO THE SAME PERSON, ON BEHALF OF THE ABBOT OF CLUNY  
[Note: [Col. 0482D] Written in the year 1146.—Bernard commended by this letter Peter the Venerable, who was proceeding to Eugenius in a matter of honour. Peter recalls this journey both in Book II, chapter 25, of *On Miracles*: “In the first,” he says, “year of the pontificate of Pope Eugenius [Col. 0483B] I went to Rome to visit both him and the common mother, the Roman Church”; and also in writing to Bernard, Book VI, Letter 46: “I had seen him,” he says (that is, Eugenius), [Col. 0483C] “in Rome in the first year of his pontificate.” On this journey he experienced what he later wrote to Eugenius about in Book VI, Letter 44: he was plundered in Italy by Marquess Opizo, but recovered everything with the aid of the people of Piacenza. He visited Eugenius again about the year 1151; and in a certain letter to St Bernard he testifies how kindly he was received, acknowledging in this respect the service of Bernard’s friendship.]

He asks that the abbot of Cluny be received kindly and treated honourably.

It seems foolish to write to you on behalf of the lord of Cluny, and as though to wish to offer patronage to one whom everyone desires to have as patron. Yet I write, [Col. 0482D] though not necessarily for his sake, satisfying nevertheless an affection—my own affection, I say, not another’s. Since I cannot accompany in body my friend who is travelling abroad, I accompany him in spirit. Who shall separate us? Neither the height of the Alps, nor the cold of the snows, nor the length of the journey. Even now I am present, standing beside him in this letter. Nowhere will he be able to be without me.

I am indebted to his graciousness, through which I was deemed worthy to be admitted to such favour. But grace itself discharges the debt, because necessity has passed into willingness. Honour the man as a truly honourable member in Christ’s body. He is, unless I am mistaken, a vessel for honour, full of grace and truth, filled with very many good things. Send him back with joy, for on his return he will bring joy to very many. Deign to receive him with ampler favour, as is fitting, so that, when he returns, we may all receive from his fullness.

Certainly, if he asks anything in the name of the Lord Jesus, he ought not to encounter difficulty with you. For, if you do not know, this is the man who stretches out his hands to the poor of our Order; this [Col. 0483B] is the man who, from the possessions of his church, so far as he can do so without disturbance among his own people, gladly and frequently gives for sustenance. Hear why I have said “in the name of Jesus.” For if he should ask—as I suspect and fear—to be released from the governance of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0483C] Perhaps Peter was considering, after relinquishing the government, withdrawing to St Bernard, as he himself avows above in Letter 264.], who that knows him would suppose that he was asking in the name of Jesus? I am mistaken if he has not become more fearful than usual, if he has not become better than himself, since you saw him.

Although from almost the beginning of his tenure he is known to have improved that Order in many respects: for example, in the observance of fasts, silence, and costly and elaborate clothing [Note: [Col. 0483C] All these things are attested by his distinguished Statutes in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*. Compare Orderic, Book XIII, for the year 1132.].

## LETTER CCLXXVIII  
[Note: [Col. 0483C] Written in the year of Christ 1150.]  
TO THE SAME PERSON, ON BEHALF OF THE BISHOP OF BEAUVAIS  
[Note: [Col. 0483C] Henry, brother of Louis the Younger, later archbishop of Rheims. Compare Letters 269, 305, and 307. Honorius II took him under his protection after he had been devoted to divine service by his father Louis, as his letter in Volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 150, attests; there another letter follows, from King Louis to the apostolic legate, regarding the granting to Henry of a prebend in the Church of Pontoise. He was abbot of St Mary of Étampes and archdeacon of Orléans, according to the cartulary of St Martin of the Fields.]

[Col. 0484A]

There is no need for us to teach you how worthy the petitions of your son, the bishop of Beauvais, are of being heard: they themselves will readily persuade your fatherly heart of what is worthy [271] and just. Yet we plead for him. This devout young man should be supported with paternal favour; and the good zeal which he bears for his Church should not only be approved but assisted. Thus he will daily become more devout, more fervent, and stronger in himself, when he feels himself raised up by the hand of your unfailing aid against the vexations and tribulations which never fail that Church [Note: [Col. 0483D] This is evident from two letters of Anselm to Urban II, Book II, Letters 33 and 34. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, writes something similar concerning the condition of the Church of Beauvais in Letter 87: “That aforesaid Church of Beauvais has for so long been unaccustomed to having good shepherds that to have bad ones seems almost lawful to it, while to elect good ones seems almost criminal,” etc.] from evil men.

We ask that the petition of Brother Arnulf of Maiole be heard. Master G. (I give the messenger this name) will state it to you. [Col. 0484B] You can also learn from him, if you please, what the abbess of the Paraclete asks [Note: [Col. 0483D] Heloise, formerly the wife of Peter Abelard, afterwards a nun, and finally abbess of the women’s monastery of Argenteuil, on the River Seine, in the diocese of Paris. To this place, in the year 1127, the monks of St Denis [Col. 0484B] returned after a long exile, having proved from very ancient charters that it belonged to them by the gift of Hermenric and his wife Numma. Theodrada, daughter of Charlemagne, had gathered veiled women there, [Col. 0484C] who, after monastic discipline was cast out, were themselves expelled. Shortly before, as we have said above, Peter Abelard, having obtained leave from the abbot of St Denis, had departed into the wilderness of the region of Troyes. There he dedicated first to the most holy Trinity an oratory made of patched coverings of marsh reeds, straw, and rushes; then he gave it the name Paraclete, because after many calamities he thought that there at last he had breathed again with some consolation. He later yielded the place to Heloise. Some call Heloise Helwida. Hugh Metellus wrote two letters to her under that name: “To Helwida, venerable abbess of the Paraclete. Report has made known to us that you have surpassed the female sex. How, by dictating, composing verse, and—what excels all these things—by overcoming feminine softness,” etc. Bernard once visited her and honoured her with his exhortation, as Abelard testifies in Letter 5.]; and you may act, if you judge it fitting.

## LETTER CCLXXIX  
[Note: [Col. 0484C] Written in the year of Christ 1152.]  
TO COUNT HENRY  
[Note: [Col. 0484C] He was the son of Theobald the Great, count of Champagne, [Col. 0484D] and succeeded to his dignities in 1151.]

He urges the count to restore fully what had been wrongfully taken by his subjects.

The abbot of Châtillon [Note: [Col. 0484D] Baldwin, to whom Letter 401 is addressed, later bishop of Noyon, according to Letter 402. The abbey of Châtillon discussed here is undoubtedly that of the regular canons of the Order of St Augustine on the Seine in the diocese of Langres, where Bernard learned the first elements of letters and which, as Book I, chapter 1, no. 3, of his Life states, he converted from secular to regular; not Châtillon in Neustria, as some wrongly maintain. For Châtillon, whose abbot was this Baldwin, was not far from Clairvaux, since, when setting out for Rome, the abbot entrusted his affairs to Bernard. Moreover, from the context of the letter, the place called Beaufort, not far from Châtillon, lay on the River Vingeanne, which flows into the Aube below Clairvaux and the town of Bar. Finally, in the ancient charters of Châtillon in the diocese of Langres, as also in the published list of abbots, Baldwin is counted as the second abbot after Aldo, the first abbot.], a religious man, set out for Rome and left all his goods in the care of God and of ourselves; and behold, the officials of Simon, men of Belfort, carried off their pigs. I would have preferred, [Col. 0485A] I tell you, that they had seized our own. We demand them back from you.

For this purpose the Prince of the kings of the earth appointed you prince over the earth: that under Him and for Him you might cherish the good, restrain the wicked, defend the poor, and render judgment for those suffering injustice. If you do these things, you perform a prince’s work; and there is hope that God ought to enlarge and strengthen your principality. If not, you must fear lest that very honour and power which you appear to possess be taken from you—may it not be so!

## LETTER CCLXXX  
[Note: [Col. 0485C] Written about the year 1152. See Letters 275 and 282.]  
TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS, ON THE AFFAIR OF AUXERRE

He complains that the apostolic decision in the case of the election of Auxerre, which by the Pope’s command he had announced, is being disregarded.

[Col. 0485B]

1. You do well, by frequent and gracious hearings, to comfort the wearied man during the short time I am here and to raise up the faint-hearted. You do what becomes you, if not what I deserve. Not that I delight in abusing so great a kindness for the use of my own will; my conscience bears witness that I am ready to receive with an equally calm mind whatever you choose to deny as whatever you choose to grant. Like every man, I desire to have my wishes followed, but not where this opposes justice, prejudices truth, or finally displeases your will. I say this lest you suppose that I either fail to perceive the kindness or am ungrateful for it.

Now let your Holiness hear what the matter requires. When action is taken against me, the loss is slight and can easily be repaired. I judge no remedy more suitable to the wounds of [Col. 0485C] my conscience than reproaches and insults. Therefore there is no reason for me to be moved on my own account—a little man worthy of every reproach and contempt. But if malice perhaps reaches even to the Christ of the Lord, patience, I confess, wavers, and almost all gentleness gives way [272]. Did I ask my lord that Churches should be ordered through me, bishoprics arranged, bishops created? Truly a fitting instrument: an ant drawing a cart. You chose to advance a man, and rightly so, unless I am mistaken—a man against whom even those who oppose him cannot find what to say.

[Col. 0486A]

2. The mystery of your good will was made known to those to whom it ought to have been made known. The mystery, indeed, was published, but hitherto we have been cheated of its fruit and benefit. Do you ask who did this? The man of your peace, in whom you trusted: a man to whom religion is hateful, wisdom burdensome, justice terrifying; who did not fear to betray his lord’s secret and nullify his decree. Nor is it surprising that a man who was not ashamed to reveal himself as such should do this; while yielding to his own envy, he spared not even your reverence.

I am ashamed; but what concern is that? I do not refuse the shame which zeal for obedience has brought upon me. The cup indeed did not pass away from me; but through me it plainly passed even to you. When the judgment pronounced is slighted—indeed, I might say, perverted—who does not see that the author is touched rather than its announcer? [Col. 0486B] Should the promotion be weakened of one whose person could not be defamed [Note: [Col. 0485C] After Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, died in 1151, “when the clerics wished, as is customary, to elect another bishop,” Bernard says in Book III, chapter 2, of *On Consideration*, “a certain youth intervened, appealing and forbidding it to be done until he had gone to and returned from Rome; but the appeal was not respected even by himself. For, when he saw that he was disregarded, as one who had appealed irrationally, having gathered to himself whom he could, on the third day after the election had been made by the others he held his own.” See Letter 275. When Eugenius learned this, he entrusted the election to three men, one of whom was Bernard, as is said here. Bernard’s vote and that of another agreed, while the third objected; hence Bernard asks Eugenius here to supply what is lacking. The man elected seems to have been Alan, who eventually succeeded Hugh. The Book of the Burials of Clairvaux says of him: “At the right hand of Lord Geoffrey, sometime bishop of Langres, toward the choir, lies Lord Alan, bishop of Auxerre. Educated from childhood in a certain church of the famous Flemish town called Lille [*Insula*], he received the religious habit under Blessed Bernard at Clairvaux. Afterwards he became the first abbot [Col. 0486D] of the monastery called Ripailles. Presiding over it for twelve years, with the Lord’s help he laboured to enrich it with useful persons and necessary possessions . . . In the last year of Blessed Bernard’s life he was unanimously elected bishop by the Church of Auxerre. He displayed great hospitality to all religious persons who frequented his houses . . . At length, after completing thirteen years in the episcopate, he resigned the bishopric with permission of the Apostolic See and returned to his Clairvaux. He died on the day before the Ides of October, about the year of the Lord 1181.” Where he is said to have been elected unanimously, it must be understood that the votes of the electors eventually concurred in him, as Bernard also expressly testifies in Letter 282 to King Louis.]?

There are two alternatives: either the word which we testified had gone forth from you will stand, or we shall be deemed liars, as we already are deemed. But the better and more worthy course for your apostolate is that he who has been powerful in iniquity shall not boast in malice.

3. Yet the command was obeyed in part—and in the greater part. It was entrusted to three; one dissenting and two consenting, what remains except that your voice should supply what is lacking? And do it yourself. You need not fear the scandal of those of whom the Lord says: “Let them alone; they are blind, and leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). For the rest, the people will rejoice; the sounder part of the clergy will rejoice; the king himself [Col. 0486C] will rejoice; finally, the whole Church of the saints will rejoice.

By the grace given you, you have shown many good works to our age; but, in my judgment, none will do more for your glory than this, if you act thus. I bear them witness that they have named many religious men, not because they delight in religion but because they are powerless: they cannot restrain their malice nor suffice to repel force by force, so that, though they do not love their holiness, they may have no reason to fear their power.

The count of Nevers does not walk in his father’s ways [Note: [Col. 0486D] Count William IV of Nevers, mentioned in Letter 276; nevertheless we read that he conferred many benefits on many churches. He restored to the monastery of Vézelay the goods which his father had taken away; [Col. 0487C] gave broad estates to Pontigny; and, to omit other things, also bestowed favours on the abbey of St Germanus at Auxerre, where he has a tomb [Col. 0487D] in the chapter house, although he had chosen burial in the cemetery. His father, whose ways he is said not to follow, was William III, a man indeed very pious and religious. Hugh, monk of Auxerre, says of him: “In the year 1147, William, count of Nevers, abandoning secular rule and trampling down every honour, entered the Carthusian Order; and there, living for God in the humblest poverty, he happily completed the course of his life within a year of his conversion.”—Letter 280 bears this title in an old codex of the monastery of Cambron: “To Lord Pope Eugenius, concerning the election of Nevers.” Conversely, printed editions read “on the affair of Auxerre.” MARTÈNE.]: he opposes this man and every good thing. He hangs over the lands and goods of churches like a lion [Col. 0487A] ready for prey. He is ready to accept even a Saracen or some Jew rather than have this man, because he alone seems to him to know how, and to be able, to resist his malice and cunning. This is why, as some clerics themselves confessed to us, he imposed silence upon them by threats and open oppression, lest the opposing party should boast of its numbers.

4. And, to state briefly what I think: if it is judged worthwhile that monasteries be impoverished in that bishopric, churches trampled down, religion mocked, and the episcopal see itself—whose resources and possessions he especially covets—reduced to servitude, then by no means let the man of Regnié reign [Note: [Col. 0487D] This is said ironically, if we understand it of Alan, as seems likely; St Bernard may have designated him by this name because perhaps he came from the district of Regnié among the Belgians, not far from Ypres. For when he is commonly called “of Lille,” this should be understood of the place of his education, as the Book of the Burials of Clairvaux cited above indicates: “He was educated from childhood in a certain church of the famous town in Flanders called Lille,” not born there. Nor can he be called “of Regnié” from the monastery of Regnié, mentioned under the year 1128 in our Chronology, since he was taken from Clairvaux to be abbot of Ripailles and then bishop of Auxerre. Unless perhaps someone should say that in the second election at Auxerre a monk of Regnié was elected, for whom St Bernard wrote here, but that after much disagreement Alan was at last elected.].

Where now is that spirit which you showed in the affair of York? [273] Will he not feel it who attempts a similar deed [Col. 0487B]? Behold, as we have heard, he has come in the spirit of the man who stirred up the curia against you, and, if permitted, intends to carry out the same thing. We recall to your mind the affair of the lord of Lund [Note: [Col. 0488D] Eskil. See Letter 390.]. Since the cause of delay has been removed, nothing remains but that what ought to have been done be done.

And I will add this: to have a good, just, and well-reputed chancellor [Note: [Col. 0488D] Perhaps after the death of Guy the chancellor, to whom Letter 367 is addressed.] is no small part of apostolic dignity, no slight assistance to apostolic administration, and no moderate safeguard for apostolic conscience. A harmful appointment is always notable; but after long deliberation, it is also shameful.

## LETTER CCLXXXI  
TO ABBOT BRUNO OF CHIARAVALLE  
[Note: [Col. 0488D] Earlier editions read “Clairvaux”; but manuscripts of better quality prefer “Chiaravalle,” supported by the local records of Chiaravalle itself. Chiaravalle is a distinguished Cistercian abbey near Milan, discussed at length above in connection with Letter 134.]

He rebukes Bruno for writing in agitation and imprudence.

[Col. 0487C]

Are you right to be angry now? No, I think not. Your own words convict you: they were not composed in judgment but rushed out in agitation. For the judgment is this: “The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6). But, you say, “I am beaten without cause.” Be it so; nevertheless, the blows of our words sound with friendly concern. I have said too little: they speak a fatherly solicitude.

Accordingly, if you are not at fault, we have done you no injury: your own conscience acquits you. If you are at fault, you should rather be angry with yourself [Col. 0488A] than with me. You complain that I did not believe you, as though you had said anything to me about it. Be it so: I believed one who complained of you. How could I either believe or disbelieve you, when you had said nothing?

Do what you said. Pay what you owe as soon as you can [variant: “as quickly as you can”], lest perhaps scandal arise not only between us but also concerning us. Think well of us, who think well of you and do not disbelieve you, as in your agitation you say, not knowing what you are saying. They are my words; they express my affection.

## LETTER CCLXXXII  
[Note: [Col. 0488D] Written in the year of Christ 1152.]  
TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRENCH, THE YOUNGER, ON THE ELECTION OF AUXERRE

He urges the king not to oppose the bishop-elect of Auxerre.

[Col. 0488B]

1. Have I ever wished in any matter to diminish the king’s honour or the kingdom’s dignity? God knows, and, as I trust, neither does your conscience answer this concerning you. See rather lest those act more against you who disturb elections, so that there may not be in the Churches men who serve the king, but instead that they themselves may be served from the revenues of the Churches.

I, I was present at the election of Auxerre. It was unanimous, because the clerics who previously had split into factions finally came together, by God’s mercy, without contradiction. We know the elect well; we bear witness to him that he is good. I think that no one at all was present at that assembly who doubted your consent, since that very consent was already held in your letters. For who could even imagine that another consent had to be sought [Col. 0488C] and that one was not enough, especially where no further election had intervened since then? Must the king’s favour be sought anew as often as the clerics disagree? Neither reason nor custom allows this.

Finally, recently, if you remember, how often did the clerics of the Church of Soissons gather to elect, how often did they disagree and depart with the matter unfinished; yet I do not think that they sought your consent as often as this, though they had obtained it once.

[274]

2. It is so, my lord king: you ought not to disapprove elections already made, to the making of which it is established that you once consented. But there are certain persons who disturb you and strive to disturb the Churches, pursuing their own profits; and, what is more grievous, seeking with diabolical zeal to rupture the mutual favour and affection of the supreme Pontiff and the most serene King. Far be this from you. Whoever those men are will bear their judgment, and the King will always do what a good king does, as he has done until now.

Therefore let more joyful orders be issued swiftly, lest the Church, so long vexed and afflicted, sit longer in sorrow. Let no suspicion arise concerning the person: either I am greatly mistaken, or he will be faithful and acceptable to the King. I trust in the Lord that you will not grieve the multitude of saints in that bishopric, nor me your servant, who, to confess the truth, have never endured anything from you equally grievous [Col. 0489B] as I would if you persist in this counsel—which may it not happen.

## LETTER CCLXXXIII  
[Note: [Col. 0489C] Written in the year of Christ 1150.]  
TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS, ON BEHALF OF THE BROTHERS OF MIRATORY

Efforts to settle a dispute by agreement have been in vain; apostolic authority is therefore necessary.

At Cluny we met with the men of Gigny [Note: [Col. 0489C] In some writings this letter is entitled simply “On Behalf of the Brothers”; in printed editions, “On Behalf of the Men of Gigny,” that is, against the monks of Gigny. Cistercian manuscripts have “On Behalf of the Brothers of Miratory.” But the sense is the same. This letter was written against the men of Gigny in the cause of the brothers of Miratory. For when the exemption from tithes granted to the Cistercians by Innocent [Col. 0489D] had greatly embittered the Cluniacs—as was said in the notes to Letter 228—the men of Gigny in particular, Cluniacs in the county of Burgundy, so burned with resentment against their neighbouring Cistercians of Miratory, both communities belonging to the province of Lyons, that some of the men of Gigny did not hesitate to turn the monastery of Miratory upside down. When Eugenius learned of this, he issued very severe letters to Peter the Venerable, declaring that satisfaction must be made to the Cistercians by immediate compensation for the damage, otherwise stern punishment would be imposed on the offenders. He gave the archbishop of Lyons authority to employ ecclesiastical censures unless they reached an agreement over the injuries within twenty days. Maurice published these letters from the monastery of Lucelle, as may be seen in the Appendix to Volume II of the *Annals*. The most holy men Bernard and Peter the Venerable met at Cluny concerning this affair; for four days [Col. 0490C] the matter was discussed, and the damages were assessed at more than thirty thousand solidi. But when the men of Gigny delayed in accepting the settlement, Bernard informed Eugenius in this letter of the delay. After Bernard’s death, the monks of both places reached an agreement concerning the tithes in 1155, as Guichenon reports in the *History of Savoy*, p. 113. Although we do not know the compensation made by the men of Gigny, we do know, as Manrique observed, of Peter the Venerable’s generosity toward the Cistercians out of the deposit of the Roman subdeacon Baro. This deposit had been left at Cluny; after Baro’s death Peter generously handed it over to the Cistercians, as is clear from Letters 388 and 389.], in hope of peace; much labour was expended for it, but nothing achieved. For after all our four days’ labour, the only result was the collapse of hope.

In accordance with the tenor of your letters, restoration of losses and restitution of what had been taken were demanded, but in vain. Much was demanded from men who had done much harm: for the assessment of losses amounted to more than thirty thousand solidi [Col. 0489C], since one abbey alone—to avoid wandering through every item—was wholly destroyed. Yet we were ready to remit much of these great losses, whereas they offered so little that the venerable abbot of Cluny, who worked more earnestly than effectively for the restoration of peace, did not judge it worthy even of mention. Thus no settlement resulted, because so ridiculous a reparation was offered.

They said: “Certain wicked men of ours did all the evil. What is that to us? Let them answer for themselves.” This too was ridiculous. It was clear throughout the whole region that this great crime had been committed by men of the Church; that some monks had also been present; and that all had consented. For up to this time we have heard that not one person opposed the evildoers. Finally, the lord abbot himself openly refuted and convicted such evasive men, affirming that the Church justly demanded back what it was clear had been lost through the Church. Your final hand is awaited in a matter which has been proved more than sufficiently capable of correction only by a strong hand.

## LETTER CCLXXXIV  
[Note: [Col. 0490D] Written about the year 1151.]  
TO LORD POPE EUGENIUS, ON BEHALF OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF RHEIMS AND OTHER PERSONS

[Col. 0490B]

The lord Archbishop of Rheims [Note: [Col. 0490D] That is, Samson.] serves in the house of the great Householder as a vessel unto honour. If you know this, preserve his honour—the honour of his Church. If I know the man well, the more you honour him, the more God will be honoured through him and in him. The lord of Arras [Note: [Col. 0490D] Godescalcus, mentioned in Letters 214 and 253; he succeeded Alvisus, mentioned in Letters 65 and 395, in 1150. The case discussed here appears to concern Guerric, Abbot of Saint-Vaast, to whom Eugenius wrote that he should “promise obedience by hand to Godescalcus regarding those things which he possessed from the Church of Arras,” as we read in manuscript letters.] is a simple and upright man, still abiding in his humility. There is no need for him to be humbled further by another, lest he lose authority and consequently usefulness. If you judge it fitting, grant him this, because by his own efforts he will never possess it: for, so far as he is concerned, he is more content with moderation. There is one who opposes and exalts himself: he plainly needs to be humbled by the bishop, and no less by that bishop himself. To resist the proud and give grace to the humble [Col. 0490C] is customary with your Lord; and you have heard Him say: “He who serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). The Abbot of Aucourt [Note: [Col. 0490D] Undoubtedly Aucourt, an abbey of Regular Canons of Saint Augustine near Bapaume, called Aviulficurtis and Aiulficurtis in ancient records, and now Aquae Curtum.] is a good man; let him be answered according to his goodness. Let him be heard concerning his needs, and let no apostate be heard against him. The dean of Béthune, by the will of the bishop and with the advocate’s consent, has established a good arrangement for his church within that same church; [Col. 0491A] it is good that it should be confirmed by your authority. Likewise, we ask on behalf of the deans of Soissons and Cambrai that their worthy petitions be heard.

We have been endangered among false brethren, and many forged letters, under our forged seal, have passed into many hands; and, what I fear more, falsehood is said to have flown even as far as you. [Note: [Col. 0491D] See Letter 298.] Because of this necessity, having discarded that seal, we now use this new one which you see, bearing both our likeness and our name. [Note: [Col. 0491D] From this it is clear that William, Abbot of Cîteaux, was not correct in what he says in the letter printed here to Theobald, Count of Champagne: namely, that the seal of the Abbot of Buzay, in which the abbot’s name was impressed, was false, asserting that no seal of the Order had ever borne the proper name of an abbot. Certainly, on Bernard’s own charter concerning the settlement of the dispute between the monasteries of Sainte-Geneviève and Saint-Victor, Bernard’s seal is appended with his name and likeness, holding a book in his right hand and a crosier in his left. See the account of Saint Bernard’s seal below, in the final volume of his Works, after the *Life* and *Acts*. EDITORS.] Henceforth do not accept, as coming from us, any other likeness, except perhaps in the case of the Bishop of Clermont, to whom I gave letters under another seal, when I did not yet possess this one.

## LETTER CCLXXXV. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF ODO, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Written about the year 1153. Odo, formerly a monk of Saint-Denis near Paris, became Abbot of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne, and then succeeded Suger as Abbot of Saint-Denis in 1151. For his appointment and praises, see Suger’s Letters 156 and following, especially Letter 162, by Baldwin, Bishop of Noyon, who, writing to Eugenius, calls Odo “a religious and energetic man,” canonically elected and blessed by himself.]

He commends Odo, Abbot of Saint-Denis, and defends him against the suspect accusations of others, born of envy and ambition.

[Col. 0491B]

1. On behalf of the Church of Saint-Denis and of the person of Abbot Odo, even if no one else wrote, I should not hesitate to write. The cause is good and does not waver on either side; the church is noble, and the abbot has a good reputation. The former is most widely known to the world, the latter to us who are neighbours. Moreover, both he and it are especially your concern. For all these reasons, even alone, as I have said, if necessary, I am not ashamed to write. But now such persons write with me that they will be least of all disbelieved, even if I do not write. They are the very men whose hands have dealt more than sufficiently with this affair. Behold, they know [Col. 0491C] what the abbot has done; and what they know, they say. The petitions which we put forward for him come forth confidently, supported by testimonies beyond doubt.

With confidence I stir and urge your concern on behalf of your own possession, wickedly invaded and cruelly harassed. I ask, I beseech you: raise your hand, extend your arm, oppose the shield. Let Peter’s sword defend Peter’s patrimony.

2. Certain persons have risen against a man whom public report sufficiently acquits—indeed, whom celebrated opinion commends. These are fine sons indeed, who have searched so curiously into their father’s shame, dreaming up certain crimes unknown to everyone. [Note: [Col. 0492D] See the following letters.] Those who hear of this sudden and unexpected accusation are astonished. They blush, because nothing of this sort had ever been said about Odo. The Abbot of Saint-Denis [Col. 0491D] is by no means hidden under a bushel. He stands upon a lampstand, so that, even if he wished it, he could not conceal what he is. Both his light and his smoke must necessarily be seen by all. Have these men fixed lynx-like eyes upon him, [Col. 0492A] seeing what no one else has yet been able to see?

I confess that their accusation is suspect to me. One of them, named Raymond, whom they say is the leader of this attempted malice, makes it still more incredible: a man, as I have learned, 276 openly talkative, secretly a whisperer; anxiously ambitious, flatteringly ingratiating; wholly fashioned for deceiving, no less for disturbing. I have recognized the wolf beneath the sheep’s skin, and have marked him with sure signs, so that he now either does not dare to bite or is unable to harm.

## LETTER CCLXXXVI. TO THE SAME, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME MAN

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Written in the year of Christ 1153.]

If whisperings and secret insinuations prevail against the Abbot of Saint-Denis, I am innocent of his blood, since on another occasion I wrote against those who malign him. [Col. 0492B] Yet what accusation do they bring against that man? Is it that they find nothing with which to accuse him? And how, if these men rightly accuse him, is he excused by all his neighbours who are upright in heart?

He is accused of having incurred many debts, mortgaged lands, and squandered property—as if these things could not have happened for necessary or just reasons. The convent of that church informed us concerning all these matters, and through a trustworthy person testified that its circumstances are otherwise than has been reported to you. Yet let an inquiry be made; for sight will establish the truth about these things more surely than an oath. If they are found to be as these men maliciously allege, however they happened, let the abbot not be excused. If they are not so, let the informers gain nothing from their falsehood. [Col. 0492C]

They charge him with the death of a man: if he cannot clear himself, let him die. Yet who does not see that it is not even plausible that he should have handed over to death the very man whom a little before he had rescued from death? With what face do they dare whisper these things to you, when they saw and knew the abbot’s zeal in securing the release of those who had previously committed murder, and in punishing those who had avenged their neighbour’s blood? Finally, if you knew these men well, it could surely suffice to disbelieve whatever you receive only through them. May God be present to your holy mind, lest a deceitful tongue be able to insinuate anything against innocence.

## LETTER CCLXXXVII. TO THE LORD OF OSTIA, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0492D] Written in the same year.]  
[Note: [Col. 0492D] That is, Hugh. See Letters 273, 274, 290, 296, 306.]

[Col. 0492D]

The lord Abbot of Saint-Denis is accused by wicked men, but is acquitted by good men in the church and its vicinity. We therefore ask your Charity for him all the more earnestly because we have held, and continue to hold, [Col. 0493A] a better opinion of him. Let your kindness stand for him, if not because he is our friend, then because the things alleged against him are neither true nor plausible. If he has been burdened with debts, the circumstances of the time supplied an evident cause, although there are almost no debts. The charge of alienating lands is proved to be manifest falsehood. For concerning the death of G., I do not think that he could have been suspected even by his opponents, since he rescued that same G. and all his people, shut in by enemies, from the very point of death, and did so with great labour. For all these reasons, and especially because Raymond’s cunning is not unknown to us, we ask more attentively that your concern protect the abbot’s innocence.

## LETTER CCLXXXVIII. TO ANDREW, HIS UNCLE, A KNIGHT TEMPLAR

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Written in the year of Christ 1153.]

He laments the unhappy outcome of the holy expedition and desires his uncle’s arrival.

[Col. 0493B]

1. Your letter, which you most recently sent, found me lying sick in bed. I received it with open hands; I read it gladly and read it again gladly, but I would have seen you more gladly. In it I read your desire to see me, and also your fear for the danger threatening the land which the Lord honoured with His presence, and the city which He consecrated with His blood. Woe to our princes! [Note: [Col. 0493D] Understand this of the unhappy expedition to the East. Ambition, rivalry, and jealousy among the Christian princes broke the strength and efforts of that holy expedition. Bernard indicates this in Book II of *On Consideration*, chapter 1. Otto of Freising, an eyewitness, indicates it also in *The Deeds of Frederick*, Book I, chapter 78, where, after recounting the immense defeats of the Christian armies, he adds: “Yet from so many and such great disasters the royal arrogance among them had not been diminished or brought to rest.” See Aemilius on Louis VII, where he treats the siege of Damascus, already nearly captured, had not all hope been frustrated by the ambition of the princes. See also Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book XI. For more on the causes of the failure of the overseas expedition, see the notes on Book II of *On Consideration*, chapter 1.] In the Lord’s land they have done nothing good; in their own lands, to which they swiftly returned, they practise incredible wickedness and do not grieve over Joseph’s ruin. They are mighty in doing evil, but are unable [variant: do not know how] to do good. [Col. 0493C]

Yet we trust that the Lord will not reject His people nor forsake His inheritance. Rather, the Lord’s right hand will act mightily, and His arm will help it, so that all may know that it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes. You do well in comparing yourself to an ant. For what else are all of us earthborn and children of men but ants, labouring over useless and empty things? And what profit has a man from all his labour which he performs under the sun? Let us therefore rise above the sun, and let our citizenship be in heaven, already preceding in mind to the place which we are to follow also in body. There, my Andrew, there is the fruit of your labour; there is your reward. You serve as a soldier beneath the sun, but for Him who sits above the sun. Serving here, let us expect our donatives from there. The reward of our service is not from the earth, nor from below; its price is far away, beyond the utmost bounds. Beneath the sun [Col. 0494A] there is scarcity; above the sun there is abundance. “They will give into our bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6:38).

2. You desire to see me; and, as you write, the fulfilment of your desire depends upon my decision. For you say that you await my command concerning this. And what shall I say to you? I both desire you to come and fear that you may come. Thus, placed between willing and unwilling, I am constrained by two alternatives and do not know which to choose: whether to satisfy your desire and mine together, or rather to believe the widespread opinion concerning you, by which you are proclaimed so necessary to that land that no small desolation is thought likely to follow from your absence.

Therefore, though I do not dare command it, I nevertheless desire to see you before I die. You can see and know better whether you can come in some way without harm and without scandal to that people. It could happen that your arrival would not be entirely without use. Perhaps, by God’s favour, there would be no lack of persons to follow you back in order to aid the Church of God, since you are known and loved by all. God can bring it about that you too may say with the holy patriarch Jacob: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and behold, I return with three companies” (Gen. 32:10).

One thing I say: if you are coming, do not delay, lest perhaps you come and do not find me. For I am already being poured out, and I do not think that I shall remain long upon the earth. Who will grant me, in the Lord’s will, to be refreshed even a little by your beloved and sweet presence before I depart? I have written to the queen, [Note: [Col. 0494D] See the following letter.] as you wished, and I rejoice in the good testimony [Col. 0494C] which you bear concerning her. Through you we greet in the Lord your Master and all your brethren of the Temple, as well as those of the Hospital. Through you, greeting in the Lord also the enclosed religious and all holy persons to whom you may fittingly speak, we commend ourselves to their prayers. Be our representative before them. We also most devotedly greet with great affection our Gerard, [Note: [Col. 0494D] Is this Gerard, Bishop of Bethlehem, mentioned by William of Tyre at the beginning of Book XVII under the year 1146 and near the end under 1152? Or the Bishop of Sidon, mentioned there?] who at one time lived in our house and is now, as we have heard, made a bishop.

## LETTER CCLXXXIX. TO THE QUEEN OF JERUSALEM

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Written in the year of Christ 1153.]

He instructs her how to conduct herself, so as to fulfil the part of a worthy widow before God and of a queen before men.

To his beloved daughter in Christ, M. [Note: [Col. 0494D] Melisende, called Melusina by others, daughter of Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem of the Latins; Fulk, her husband and Baldwin’s son-in-law, succeeded him. While pursuing a hare on horseback, Fulk was thrown headlong and died three days later in 1142. Letters 206, 354, and 355 are addressed to her. Ivera, her sister, was a nun, according to William of Tyre near the end of Book XV.] Queen of Jerusalem, [Col. 0494D] Bernard, called Abbot of Clairvaux, mercy from God her Saviour.

1. I wonder that for so long a time we have not seen [Col. 0495A] your letters or received your customary greetings, as though we had forgotten your former devotion toward us, which we have experienced in many ways. I confess that we heard certain unfavourable reports. Although we did not believe them as certain, we nonetheless grieved that your reputation should be somewhat tarnished, whether by truth or falsehood.

But my most dear uncle Andrew has intervened, a man whom we cannot disbelieve in anything; in his letter he has signified better news to us: namely, that you conduct yourself peaceably and gently; that you govern yourself and your affairs wisely and by the counsel of wise persons; that you love and treat as intimate friends the brethren of the Temple; and that you prudently and wisely [variant: vigilantly], according to the wisdom given you by God, meet the dangers threatening the land with salutary counsels and assistance. Such deeds indeed, such deeds, befit a strong woman, [Col. 0495B] a humble widow, an exalted queen.

For, because you are a queen, it is not unworthy of you to be a widow—something which, had you wished, you would not be. I think it is a glory to you, especially among Christians, to live as a widow no less than as a queen. The one is from succession; the other, from virtue. The one is yours by birth; the other, by God’s gift. To the one you were happily born; the other you acquired with courage. It is a double honour: one according to the world, the other according to God; both from God. Nor should the honour of widowhood seem slight to you, concerning which the Apostle says: “Honour widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3).

2. You certainly have within yourself a familiar reminder of the Apostle’s further salutary saying, by which you are taught to provide good things not only before God but also before men (2 Cor. 8:21): before [Col. 0495C] God as a widow, before men as a queen. Consider the queen, whose worthiness or unworthiness cannot be hidden beneath a bushel: both are upon a lampstand, so as to appear to all. Remember the widow, who no longer has anything by which she might wish to please a husband, so that she may please God alone.

Blessed are you if you set the Saviour as a wall to protect your conscience and as an outer rampart to repel disgrace. Blessed, I say, if, like one bereft and a widow, you entrust your whole self to God’s governance. Otherwise you do not govern well unless you are governed well. The Queen of the South came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, in order that she might learn to rule from a king and thus rule herself. And behold, here is more than Solomon (Matt. 12:42): I speak of Jesus, and Him crucified. Entrust yourself to Him to be governed; entrust yourself to Him to be taught how you ought to govern.

Learn as a widow that He is meek and [Col. 0495D] humble of heart (Matt. 11:29); learn as a queen that He judges the poor in righteousness and reproves with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth (Isa. 11:4). Therefore, when you think of your dignity, consider also your widowhood. For, to state plainly what I think, you cannot be [Col. 0496A] a good queen if you are not a good widow. Do you ask by what a good widow is judged? Surely by the things the Apostle says: “If she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has relieved those suffering tribulation, if she has pursued every good work” (1 Tim. 5:10). If you do these things, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.

May the Lord bless you from Zion, exceptional daughter in the Lord and worthy of every reverence. The admonition has been given beforehand; its continuation is now awaited from your graciousness. An opportunity has been afforded; excuse will no longer be admitted if renewed familiarity from our side is not henceforth fostered by familiar words and frequent letters from you.

## LETTER CCXC. TO THE LORD OF OSTIA, CONCERNING CARDINAL JORDAN

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Written in 1152. In certain manuscripts this letter to the Lord of Ostia, namely Hugh, is placed after the letter to the Premonstratensians, which in the same manuscripts follows Letter 296. The legate discussed here was Jordan of the Orsini family, sent as legate to Emperor Conrad in Germany in 1151.]

He describes the apostolic legate and the foul traces he left everywhere.

[Col. 0496B]

Your legate has passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people, leaving everywhere among us foul and horrible traces. From the foot of the Alps and the German kingdom, through almost all the churches of France and Normandy, wandering about in every direction as far as Rouen, this apostolic man has filled the land not with the Gospel but with sacrilege. He is said everywhere to have committed shameful acts and carried off the spoils of churches; wherever he could, he promoted handsome boys to ecclesiastical dignities; where he could not, he wished to do so. Many ransomed themselves to keep him from coming to them; from those whom he could not reach, he demanded and extorted money through messengers. In the schools, the courts, and the crossroads, he made himself a public tale. [Col. 0496C] Seculars and religious alike, all speak ill of him; the poor, monks, and clerics complain of him. Men of his own profession are those who most abhor both his reputation and his life. He has this testimony from those within and those without.

Not so Lord John Paparo, [Note: [Col. 0495D] John Paparo, or Papyrio, in 1152, according to John of Hexham, “set out for Ireland, distributed four pallia among designated sees, and greatly reformed a people not accustomed to the law of marriage.” Until that time bishops had consecrated one another, according to Gerald, *Topography of Ireland*, chapter 17.] not so: his praise is in the Church, since everywhere he honours his ministry. Read these letters to my lord. Let him see what ought to be done about such a man; I have delivered my soul. Yet I say, with my customary impetuosity: it is good for him to cleanse his own court, and thus free his own conscience. I had resolved to keep these things silent, but the venerable Prior of Mont-Dieu [Note: [Col. 0496D] Gervase was then Prior of Mont-Dieu, a Carthusian house in the diocese of Rheims, founded by Odo, Abbot of Saint-Remi, in 1136. This passage shows that Gervase, as well as the place, was dear to Bernard. Yet do not suppose him to be the author of the Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu, mentioned in chapter 5.] urged and encouraged me to write. And know that I have said less [Col. 0496D] than is publicly proclaimed.

## LETTER CCXCI. TO POPE EUGENIUS, ON BEHALF OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT-EUGENDUS OF THE JURA

[Note: [Col. 0496D] The ancients called him Augendus; he was the holy abbot of the notable monastery of Condat, built by Saint Romanus in the Jura mountains. The monastery took the name of Saint Eugendus from him, later changed to Saint-Claude, in the diocese of Lyons.]

The noble monastery of Saint Eugendus, formerly famous [Col. 0497A] for riches and religious observance, is, if what is said is true, near destruction. Nor should everything be disbelieved. We see houses belonging to it near us and known to you, some already destroyed and others being destroyed day by day, and we grieve. What we see in the members, rumour has reported to us also of the head, and in still graver form.

But should I now rehearse for you an account of evils beyond number? The bearer of this letter, a monk of the aforesaid monastery, and Archegaud, its prior—a man long dear to us because of his integrity and religious life—will be able to inform you more fully of what they know, though not of everything; for who could do that? These things are certainly so numerous and so grave that it is astonishing if they do not compel the apostolic axe, even if it dissimulates, even if it slumbers, to rise and strike. [Col. 0497B] I have delivered my soul, but that is insufficient unless the monastery too is delivered. Its death and life are in your hands.

## LETTER CCXCII. TO A CERTAIN LAYMAN

[Note: [Col. 0497D] And indeed to a married man, as is clear from the end of the letter. Vatican manuscript no. 663 is mistaken in assigning it to Peter, Abbot of La Celle, to whom the following letter is addressed.]

He reproves him because he tried to draw his kinsman Peter away from his purpose of religious life.

1. Though unknown to us by face, you are not unknown by reputation. By that reputation we have learned that you are a wise man and honoured according to the world. My beloved son Peter, to whom you appear to be more known and more closely connected by blood relationship, wished me to write to you—or rather, to reply to you. For you had written to him; and would that you had written as became you [Col. 0497C] and was expedient for him. You did not do so. You dared to dissuade a new soldier of Christ from the service of his Lord. I tell you: there is One who will seek this out and judge it.

Were your own sins not enough for you, unless you also entangled yourself in those of another and, so far as lay in you, recalled to sin a repentant young man, and thus, according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, stored up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath? As though the devil did not sufficiently tempt him by himself, unless you, a Christian man, his leader and acquaintance, should assist him! You presented him with another serpent, but he did not present you with another Eve. He was urged by your hands, but not overthrown, for he is founded upon firm rock.

2. Yet we do not repay you in kind, but overcome evil with good, praying for you, wishing you better things, [Col. 0497D] and writing better things to you. First, because you are called wise, in order that you may more truly be what you are called, I send you to a wise man who says: “Do not hinder one who is able to do good; if you too are able, do good” (Prov. 3:27). You have time to act. But [Col. 0498A] how long will you have it? How little of life remains for you, especially now that you are growing old? It is a vapour appearing for a little while and afterward vanishing.

If you are wise, that curse will not come upon you: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job 5:3). The true Wise One aptly called the falsely wise man a fool, knowing that “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3:19). Oh, if only you were wise and understood and foresaw your latter end! (Deut. 32:29). You would be wise concerning the things of God, understand the things of the world, and foresee the things of hell. You would surely dread the things below, seek the things above, and despise what is at hand [variant: what is for evil].

My mind—indeed, the Spirit—suggests much to say to you concerning the salvation of your soul. But until I know by your reply how you have received these things, [Col. 0498B] I shall add no more, lest I become burdensome to one whom henceforth I wish to be a friend and helper, if you are willing, toward salvation. Through you, we greet in Christ your wife, dear to us though undeserving of it.

## LETTER CCXCIII. TO PETER, ABBOT OF LA CELLE, ON BEHALF OF A CAZIAC MONK WHO HAD TRANSFERRED TO CLAIRVAUX

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Written about the year 1150. Peter of La Celle is better known from the monastery of La Celle in the outskirts of Troyes than from the abbey of Saint-Remi or the church of Chartres, over which he also presided. He wrote two letters to the Caziacenses, namely Book II, Letters 14 and 15; none concerning this monk, whose name is understood to have been Adam from two letters written in his name by Nicholas of Clairvaux to our Peter—that is, Peter of La Celle—who, in Letter 25, praises Peter concerning the reformed monastery. This is the Peter who defended Bernard’s memory and his opinion concerning the Conception of Blessed Mary against the attacks of another Nicholas, according to the notes on Letter 174. In Book IX, Letter 8, to the Cistercian chapter, he calls himself Bernard’s pupil. On Caziac, see above on Letter 263.]

I reply to you concerning the matter about which you have written to me. I think no one is more troubled by the distress of the lord of Caziac than I am. But I suppose it has not escaped you that, by his own will and command, that monk has long since become ours; that he promised obedience to me, and that I undertook his care. It is not easy to remember how often since then I have repelled him when he wished to come and sent him back when he had come. At last, when he came recently, he remained against my will, and I could in no way persuade him to return. [Col. 0498C] He said that, if we cast him out, he would go farther away and would by no means return. Yet he did not have my consent even so; indeed, he entered against my counsel.

From this entrance I could neither forbid him with a clear conscience nor cast him out, since, as I have said, he had long ago been received into my care, and I must render an account of him. I confess that I had long overlooked this danger to my conscience because of the distress of that good man, and I would still have overlooked it if this man had been willing in any way to comply with my counsel. Since this is so, it is your part to console the man, to soothe his grief, and to regard me [Col. 0498D] as excused for so reasonable a cause.

Finally, as you know, he too is unsettled and has often thought of leaving his house. [Note: [Col. 0498D] This relates to Peter of La Celle’s Book II, Letter 15 to the Caziacenses: “So long as you can retain your father—indeed, our father—with you, think of no other.” This must be understood of Simon, who at last, after Bernard’s death, entered Clairvaux; see above on Letter 263.] If he wished now to put this into effect, I would not hinder him, because he remains there in no small distress.

## LETTER CCXCIV. TO POPE EUGENIUS, ON BEHALF OF THE BISHOP OF LE MANS

[Note: [Col. 0499C] Written about the same year.]

He commends the Bishop of Le Mans and others to the Pope.

[Col. 0499A]

The Bishop of Le Mans is present: [Note: [Col. 0499C] William de Passavant, formerly Archdeacon of Rheims and Bishop of Le Mans; his acts, in volume III of the *Veterum Analectorum*, from page 357, show the character of his religious life.] he is, if you do not know it, a man whose truthfulness and integrity no one doubts except one who does not know him well. He has been known and dear to me from his early youth, both for the virtues already mentioned and for his other good habits. If anything else has been whispered to your Paternity concerning him, either I am mistaken or that man has lied at the peril of his own head. Hear him, and send him away with the fullness of your favour. For I am deceived if your favour will not have been well bestowed.

We ask that the Abbot of Vendôme, [Col. 0499B] who is especially yours, [Note: [Col. 0499C] Thus above concerning Odo, Abbot of Saint-Denis: “Moreover, both he and that church are especially your concern”; namely, because the abbeys of Saint-Denis and Vendôme, then ruled by Robert, were directly under the power and jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff.] may likewise find special favour, and that his reasonable request may deserve to attain an outcome not difficult to obtain. The lord of Anjou sends his messenger, requesting something both on his own behalf and through us. Let him too be heard according to his justice, and let no lying whisperer be heard against him. For it is fitting that, since you live for all, you should avail all according to their merits.

## LETTER CCXCV. TO LORD CARDINAL HENRY, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME BISHOP

[Note: [Col. 0499C] Written about the year 1150. Elsewhere: To Lord Cardinal Elias. Concerning him Ernald writes in Book I of the *Life of Bernard*: Henry, formerly a monk at Clairvaux, was then cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. His letter concerning the lawful election of Alexander III is extant in volume III of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, p. 239.]

I write to you as though to myself, and I do so whenever I write to you. For where you are, I trust that I am also, since I love you as myself. If you love me equally—or rather, because you love me—see that the lord Bishop of Le Mans [Col. 0499C] does not leave you, so far as lies in your power, grieved in any respect. Otherwise I should be grieved for a man whom I love greatly for his integrity and whom I wish to be loved by you.

## LETTER CCXCVI. TO THE LORD OF OSTIA, ON BEHALF OF THE SAME MAN

[Note: [Col. 0499D] That is, Hugh. See Letters 287 and 290.]

[Col. 0500A]

A certain cleric is said to have deceived my lord’s ears, scheming something against his bishop and our friend out of his own greed. If you care for me, 282 indeed for the justice of God, take care that the malicious whisperer gains nothing from his lying insinuation, and that an innocent bishop and faithful friend suffers no harm. [Note: [Col. 0499D] After this letter, in quite a number of manuscripts, are placed Letter 259 to the Premonstratensians, Letter 290 to the Bishop of Ostia, and Letter 311—now 374—to the Irish monks, with which Bernard’s letters formerly ended.]

## LETTER CCXCVII. TO THE ABBOT OF ARREMAR

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Guy, to whom Letter 398 is addressed.]

He requests the readmission of a repentant apostate monk.

The bearer of this letter, formerly received into your community at our request, foolishly and lightly cast off the holy habit and departed from you. But because, led by repentance as it appears, he desires to return and humbly asks to be received again, we too ask that he be received again, and that entrance and the habit be not denied to the penitent man for the love of God and of us.

## LETTER CCXCVIII. TO POPE EUGENIUS

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Written in the year of Christ 1151.]

He exposes the frauds and impostures of Nicholas the notary.

Nicolaus [Note: [Col. 0499D] This is that Nicolaus whom Peter, abbot of Cluny, valued so highly, as may be seen in his letters: originally a monk of Arremar, he became a Cistercian and Bernard’s secretary. He was effective with the pen and reproduced Bernard’s manner almost exactly. His letters survive in the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, edited by Jean Picard, a Victorine of Paris. But this man was deceitful, and for some time concealed a wolfish mind beneath a sheepskin; at last he exposed his hypocrisy. For he repeatedly misused Bernard’s seal and, discovered as a forger, took flight. Not without reason, therefore, Bernard elsewhere wrote to Eugenius that he had been endangered by false brethren, Letter 284. It is commonly reported that he fled to England, prompted by the case of a certain Nicolaus, a monk of St Albans in England, who attacked the opinion of St Bernard—now removed from the living—on the Conception of the Blessed Virgin. But Peter of Celle, who undertook to defend the holy Doctor’s cause, calls this man an Englishman in Letter 23 of Book VI and Letter 9 of Book IX, and indicates that he knew him and regarded him as a friend only through these literary skirmishes; whereas the other Nicolaus was a Frenchman and, as letters exchanged in both directions establish, was intimately known and very dear to Peter of Celle. They must therefore be different men. I pass over the fact that the latter’s style is not so biting but more polished than one would expect from someone who behaved so insolently toward Peter of Celle—as Peter himself repeatedly complains concerning Nicolaus the Englishman in Letter 9 of Book IX, and as becomes evident to a reader from the Englishman’s own letter immediately preceding it. Nicolaus, moreover, passed from the monastery of Arremar to Clairvaux during Bernard’s absence, about the year 1146, certainly after Eugenius had been raised to the papacy, as is clear from Letter 7, which he wrote before being admitted to Clairvaux. He fled about 1151, namely after the election at Grenoble, discussed above in the notes to Letter 270; for he is found to have subscribed Bernard’s Letter 389, where that election is discussed. More concerning him is found in the Preface to Volume III.] left us, because he was not of us; but he departed leaving foul traces behind him. And I had known the man long beforehand, but waited either for God to convert him or for him, like Judas, to betray himself; and this has happened.

Besides books, money, and many gold coins, three seals were found on him when he left: one his own, [Col. 0500C] another the Prior’s, and a third ours—not the old seal, but a new one, which I had recently been compelled to change because of his deceits and stealthy frauds. This is what I remember writing to you without naming him [Note: [Col. 0501C] Letter 284.]: namely, that we have been endangered by false brethren. Who could say to how many persons, under my name and without my knowledge, he wrote whatever he pleased? Who will grant me that your very curia may be thoroughly cleansed of the dregs of his lies? Who will grant me that the innocence of those who are with me may be sufficient to excuse them before people deceived and forestalled by his shameless lies? He has been partly convicted and partly confessed that he wrote to you also, more than once, in the same fraudulent manner. I forbear to pollute my lips and your ears with his shameful acts, by which the earth is defiled and which have become a byword to all. If he comes to you—for he boasts of this and trusts that he has friends in the [Col. 0501B] curia—remember Arnold of Brescia: for behold, here is one worse than Arnold. No one deserves perpetual confinement more; nothing is more just for him than perpetual silence.

## LETTER CCXCIX. TO THE COUNT OF ANGOULÊME, ON BEHALF OF THE BRETHREN OF BUXIA

[Note: [Col. 0501C] Written about the year 1150.—In the first Lyons edition of 1494 the reading is: “To Count Angelbert (is he the person of Letter 123?), on behalf of the brethren of Bruxia.” In another edition of 1530: “To Count Engelbert, on behalf of the brethren of Bruxia.” In the Lyons edition of 1520, and in subsequent editions except one: “To the Count of Angoulême, on behalf of the brethren of Buxia.” Authors of our century prefer this reading, maintaining that William, surnamed Iron-Cutter, Count of Angoulême, granted the Cistercians a site in 1143 in the village of Buxia, where stood the Benedictine monastery of St Amantius, built by Count Arnold in the tenth century. But when they objected to the grant of the place to the Cistercians, Bernard, seeking peace, yielded the place in 1153, on the condition, Picard says, that the monks of St Amantius should repay the monks of Clairvaux sixty marks of silver for the buildings and other things acquired there by them. Bernard accordingly wrote as follows: “In the name of the Lord. I, Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, wish it to be known that we have granted to the church of Saint-Amantius the place of Buxia and all that we possess in it, received as a gift from the Count of Angoulême and Peter of Austent. Witnesses were Lord Hugh, bishop of Angoulême; Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Langres; Junius, abbot of La Couronne; likewise Brother Philip, our Prior; and Brothers Gerard and Geoffrey, monks of our house. Done at Clairvaux in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1153.” Thus Picard, from the records of the monastery of Saint-Amantius.] He complains of a heavy exaction imposed upon his monks by the count.

Do not be surprised if so large a payment, demanded from our brethren from that land of Buxia, seems burdensome to us, since we are not accustomed to anything of the kind. For we have founded many abbeys, and none of them is subject to such an exaction. But because this is your will, and God accepts a voluntary good more readily than one compelled, we endure it according to the agreement which our brethren [Col. 0501C] made with you, until God inspires you with a better will—which we do not doubt He will do. Henceforth love them, cherish them, defend them, support them. For you will stand more securely before Christ’s tribunal if you have His poor as those who love you and intercede for you.

## LETTER CCC. TO THE COUNTESS OF BLOIS

[Note: [Col. 0502C] Written about the year 1152.—Bernard seems to have consoled the Countess not with vain hope, but rather with prophecy. For I find that she bore Count Theobald the Great of Champagne four sons: Henry, Count of Blois, who succeeded his father in 1151; Theobald, seneschal of Kings Louis the Younger and later Philip Augustus, in which office he succeeded Ralph, Count of Vermandois; Stephen, the “Holy Caesar,” later a Carthusian; and William, mentioned above in Letter 271, for whose promotion, while still a boy, to ecclesiastical dignities Bernard was already declining to exert himself. In this letter Bernard seems to address the eldest son, Henry, to whom Letter 279 is directed. Returning from Syria and puffed up by succeeding to his father’s power, he was carried into certain excesses by the ardour of youth. Among these, the Saint mentions in Letter 376 that “he had arranged accursed games with Robert, the king’s brother, after the Easter feast,” so that they might meet one another in single combat. Yet, through Bernard’s admonitions and his pious mother’s tears, he soon recovered his senses so thoroughly that writers of that age judged him worthy to be counted among illustrious men.] He consoles the countess, excusing her son’s offences on account of his age and holding out hope of better fruit; he therefore advises that he be handled gently and mildly rather than harshly.

[Col. 0502A]

Whenever your son has seemed to offend against you, we have grieved; and we grieve no less at the son’s offence than at the injury done to his mother. Yet this too is excusable in a youthful son. Indeed, the very age more prone to such things excuses the sins of youth that it has committed. Do you not know that human inclinations and thoughts are prone to evil from youth? (Gen. VIII, 21.) We must trust that he will be changed for the better through his father’s merits and almsgiving [Note: [Col. 0502D] Namely, those of Theobald the Great, mentioned above in the notes to Letter 37. Not only Bernard’s Life, but also the lives of Norbert and others, praise his alms and benefactions; see also the new Letter 416.]. Therefore one must persist more and more in vows and prayers to God for him. For although he has sometimes shown himself less filial than he ought, nevertheless a mother, because of her own flesh, ought not—and indeed cannot—abandon her maternal affection. Can a mother forget the child of her womb? “Even if she should forget,” He says, “yet I will not forget you” (Isa. XLIX, 15). Let us pray and weep before the Lord, that God in His mercy may make this young man of such great promise an imitator of his father’s uprightness—as we do not doubt He will. He must be dealt with in a spirit of gentleness and with kindly attentions; for in this way he will be more effectively encouraged toward good works than if he is embittered by provocations and rebukes. Thus we trust that your heart and ours alike may be gladdened by his swift and happy change. Why should I not desire with all my heart that each day he become [Col. 0502C] better than himself? Would that I might always find him toward all men as I have found him toward me. For what, so far as I am concerned, have I ever wished that he did not do? May the Lord reward him. As for you, however, as you have often requested, I have often admonished you as was fitting, and shall continue to do so.

## LETTER CCCI. TO THE HOLY SISTER OF THE EMPEROR OF SPAIN

[Note: [Col. 0503C] That is, of Alfonso, surnamed the Good, king or emperor of Castile and León; for the kings of that time liked to be honoured with this title. This Sancha, remarkably devoted to St Bernard, founded in 1147 a Cistercian house called St Peter of Spina in the diocese of Palencia, with a colony sent by Bernard and led by his brother Nivard. Not long afterward, the black monks of the monastery of Toldanos in the kingdom of León, recently founded by the infanta Elvira, cast off the yoke of the monastery of Carracedo, to which they were subject, and submitted themselves to the Cistercians. The monks of Carracedo immediately objected, invoking Sancha’s authority with Bernard. What followed may be learned from an old document produced by Manrique in the *Annals*, under the year 1148, chapter 8, where among other things the following is read: “After the death of Lord Florentius, this Ferdinand, abbot of Toldanos, conceived an unmerited hatred for the church of Carracedo; rebellious toward it, he transferred himself through obstinacy to the church of Clairvaux. Queen Lady Sancha, who loved the monastery of Carracedo warmly, took this badly and sent letters to the abbot and convent of Clairvaux, asking them not to receive the aforesaid abbot unlawfully. The abbot of Clairvaux heard the Queen’s request and refused to receive Abbot Ferdinand unless he obtained leave to be received from the church of Carracedo. Since he could not obtain it, for some time he obeyed neither the church of Clairvaux nor that of Carracedo.” So it says there. Nevertheless, after many years this monastery came under the Cistercian yoke.] He desires that, through her intervention, a controversy arising between his monks and certain other religious from the reception of a monastery may be quieted.

[Col. 0503A]

1. You should know that what was done concerning the reception of the monastery of Toldanos was not done by me, since I was absent and unaware of what was taking place. I do not deny that it was done by our brethren, however, on the counsel of many religious persons, with the bishop’s knowledge and consent, and at the request and by the will of the noble lady who founded that place on her own estate; it was done publicly, as we have learned, and nothing was done in secret. They believed themselves free to receive a place which she who had founded it declared had been established in the freedom of God and without subjection to another church; and, they say, the privileges [Col. 0503B] were at hand. But since the brethren of Carracedo [variant: Carracenses] complain, as you write, that an injury has been done them in this matter, and—without heeding Solomon, who says, “Do not prevent one who wishes to do good; if you can, do good yourself” (Prov. III, 27)—oppose us in so holy a work; and since servants of God ought not to quarrel (II Tim. II, 24), we have resolved especially to refer the case to your counsel, so that by your authority and effort every foolish and unjust accusation, as they call it, may be laid to rest, and that the Order received in God’s house may henceforth remain in peace, for His glory and for your own salvation.

[Col. 0504A]

2. For Brother Nivard [Note: [Col. 0503D] From this passage Cistercian writers rightly infer that Nivard, Bernard’s youngest full brother, was sent by his holy brother into Spain to lead a colony to the aforesaid monastery of Spina. See Letters 372 and 373. Earlier he had likewise been sent by Bernard into Neustria to organize a new monastery in the diocese of Bayeux at a place called Solopera or Soleuvria, situated not far from the town of Vire. Robert, son of Heirnesius, granted his dwelling near the Hanging Beech to “Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and the church of Blessed Mary of Solenvria,” about the year 1146. Algar, bishop of Coutances, confirmed a gift made by a certain William Silvanus “to God, to Blessed Mary of Soleuvria, and to the brethren serving God there,” into the hand of Nivard, brother of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. From this they infer that Nivard was then abbot of that monastery. A little later, that is, in 1150, the same monastery was transferred because of the narrowness and inconveniences of the site to Val-Richer; Solopera, which belonged to the fief of the church and parish of Bayeux, was restored to the lordship of the bishop of Bayeux, as it had formerly been, with Abbot Bernard’s consent. In Neustria survive the pious letters of Philip, bishop of Bayeux, concerning the agreement made between him “and Abbot Thomas of Val-Richer concerning the place called Solopera, where his abbey had formerly been,” exchanged for Val-Richer, a place granted him by Bishop Philip, just as the abbot of Mortemer had formerly received it from him. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, confirmed this exchange at Bayeux in 1150. Roger succeeded Thomas as abbot of Val-Richer and is called in his epitaph the second abbot of that place.], who rejoices greatly concerning you, advised us to have considerable confidence in you in this matter, both because of your special devotion toward us and because of the favourable promise concerning this very matter which he heard from you. But if those opponents refuse—as we do not believe they will—to acquiesce in your salutary admonitions or counsels, then let every controversy between them be decided by the judgment of the two bishops to whom those two places are known to belong by parochial right. Whatever they judge or establish jointly, it will be yours to ratify and thereafter firmly uphold. If you fear God, you will not permit so great a good to be impeded; you will not allow that good woman to be frustrated in her desire, those brethren to be deprived of the fruit of their devotion, or finally God to be deprived of so acceptable a sacrifice of a reformed Order [Note: [Col. 0504D] Lambertus Campester, editor of the edition of 1520, notes here in the margin that reformation is mentioned in Bernard’s time.]. We beseech you also on behalf of your new plantation—I mean those at Spina—that you show them bowels of mercy, so that, sustained by your benefaction, they may persevere in God’s service and in their Order.

## LETTER CCCII. TO THE APOSTOLIC LEGATES, ON BEHALF OF THE ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ
