[Note: [Col. 0504D] Written in the year of Christ 1153.—Baronius writes concerning this legation under the year 1153: “In the same year,” he says, “Pope Eugenius decreed a legation to Germany to judge the bishop of Mainz. Bernard the priest and Gregory the deacon were chosen for this duty,” etc. Bernard, formerly prior of the Lateran monastery and a regular canon, was created by Eugenius in 1145 cardinal-priest of the title of St Clement. Gregory is believed to be the man whom Innocent made cardinal of the title of St Angelo in 1137. Conrad, bishop, who wrote the *Chronicle of Mainz* a hundred years later, says that Henry was deposed and lays the whole blame on a certain Arnold, a traitor to the bishop; Dodechin, in his Appendix to Marianus, blames the canons; both blame the legates, corrupted by money, Arnold the Chancellor having been appointed in his place. Nevertheless Otto of Freising, in Book II, chapter 9 of the *Life of Frederick*, who was present, states that he was justly deposed: “The king, keeping the next Pentecost feast at Worms, deposed through those same cardinals Henry, archbishop of the see of Mainz, a man often rebuked for defending the Church yet not corrected,” etc. Let the reader see to whom he should assent: a writer of equal rank, or an eyewitness who was learned and sincere. Certainly Conrad’s added statement that both cardinals shortly afterward died a shameful death is shown to be false, since Otto there asserts that they survived for a long time, and it is known that Bernard discharged another legation in Germany under Adrian IV. Be that as it may, Henry, after his deposition, withdrew into Saxony and not long afterward piously and happily ended his final day in a Cistercian monastery. See Serarius, *On the Affairs of Mainz*, Book V, and Baronius under the year 1153. Letter 365 is addressed to this same Henry.] He commends the cause of the archbishop, burdened by his opponents.

To his reverend lords and fathers, the LEGATES of the Apostolic See, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, the little child of their Holiness: may they please God in all things and carry home welcome sheaves from their fruitful legation.

Although distant in body, we have drawn near to you in affection and good will, desiring and praying that your actions and endeavors may be directed toward everything proper and expedient. Therefore, hearing that the pitiable archbishop of Mainz has been summoned before you to answer his opponents there, we have ventured to appeal to your goodness on his behalf. For we believe that your ministry is honoured in this: if, so far as justice permits, you place the shoulders of your authority beneath a leaning wall and a shattered fence, and do not allow the bruised reed to be broken or the smoking flax—as far as lies with you—to be extinguished. We beseech you, let him perceive that both our prayer and [Col. 0505B] his own simplicity have benefited him—a simplicity through which he is said to have been ensnared by false brethren rather than found guilty of anything deserving deposition.

## LETTER CCCIII. TO LOUIS THE YOUNGER, KING OF THE FRENCH

What the king should do in the case of a certain adulterer from Brittany who has been excommunicated.

If that man from Brittany were willing to dismiss the adulteress, so that he might be released from the bond of anathema by which he is held, and if she were to claim from you her paternal inheritance in accordance with the division which she made with her brother, then, although she is thereby unworthy, it perhaps should not be refused, [Col. 0505C] so that you might have the service and help of a powerful man. Otherwise, it is not the counsel of your humble faithful servant that either land be granted to a foreigner or the favour of your lordship to an excommunicated and incestuous man, lest—God forbid—you too should one day hear: “If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you cast your lot with adulterers” (Ps. XLIX, 18). Yet I would not advise that you break off negotiation precipitately and, as it were, abruptly. Rather, let the matter be managed through a faithful and prudent messenger, so that, if possible, he may be persuaded and time may be gained. But if he also refuses this and prefers to act wickedly, trust in the Lord that he will not prevail; for the justice that is with the king will be [Col. 0506A] for the king. I do not know whether the bishop [Note: [Col. 0506D] Perhaps John, bishop of Alet or Saint-Malo, formerly a monk of the Cistercian Order, to whom several letters of Peter of Celle are addressed, Book I, Letters 15 and following.] is suitable and competent enough for this—not because he is not faithful, indeed most faithful, but because he hates the man, and I fear he will not trust him with his counsel. Yet he himself is prepared, at your will, for everything that he can do in accordance with God’s will. If there is anything that he may suggest to you privately, as though on my behalf, know that he received that very thing from me and accept it as from my own mouth. For he is a man whom I love greatly and trust sufficiently; and you too, unless I am mistaken, may safely trust him in whatever you wish.

## LETTER CCCIV. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Written in the same year.] He rejoices that the king is concerned for his health; he commends Robert, the king’s brother.

[Col. 0506B]

By the letter that Your Dignity sent, you gladdened my soul. May God Himself, who is its cause, gladden you. Who am I, or what is my father’s house, that royal Majesty should concern itself with my death or life? And now, since I have been so highly esteemed that you take care to learn how I am, know that I have recovered somewhat [Note: [Col. 0506D] See Letter 307, no. 2.], and that, as I feel it, I have for the present been rescued from the danger of death, though I remain pitiable and very weak. Moreover, I wish you to know that Lord Robert [Note: [Col. 0506D] See Letters 222, 224, 376.], your brother, has visited us graciously and most devoutly in our illness, and has spoken in our hearing in such a way as to leave us joy and better hope concerning himself. Love him; for if he matches deeds to words, he will please you in him. And, if you think it fitting, let him know that it pleases you that henceforth he has promised to submit himself to our counsel and that of good men. No seal was at hand; but let the reader recognize the style, for I dictated it myself [Note: [Col. 0506D] That is, “I wrote it,” as the words themselves make clear. In this sense the verb is used also in other letters: Letter 85, no. 4, and Letters 307 and 310. Nevertheless, *dicto* differs from *scribo* in Letters 89 and 90, no. 1.].

## LETTER CCCV. TO POPE EUGENIUS

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Written in the year of Christ 1153.] The bishop of Beauvais is kept from a journey to Rome for just causes. Bernard therefore entrusts his entire case to the pope’s judgment.

That son of yours, the bishop of Beauvais [Note: [Col. 0506D] Henry, brother of Louis the Younger, mentioned in Letter 278. Compare Letter 307. Bernard calls him “ours” here and “your brother” in the following letter, because Henry had been a monk of Clairvaux; see Book IV, no. 15 of the *Life*. See the notes to Letter 307.]—whom I would call ours also, were it not redolent of presumption—was coming, willingly, when summoned to your presence, since he was secure in [Col. 0507A] his justice and did not doubt your fatherly favour. But I opposed him and could scarcely keep him back, so eager was he to see your face. Of the many reasons which occurred to me for wishing to restrain him, the chief was that we were uncertain of your will. Then, apart from not a few other inconveniences which seemed likely to arise, he and his brother the King are not walking in one spirit, and it was not sufficiently safe for him to be absent from his own people for long. Do not ask me whose fault this is; it is not mine to accuse anyone. It is enough for me to excuse the bishop. We have seen him show every humility and service which he could offer in his own person, [Col. 0507B] and accomplish nothing. Yet know that, whatever he fears and whatever may happen, he will come without delay as soon as he knows that his person will be acceptable to you and that his case is in your hands. For in what has been entrusted to him he neither acts nor conducts himself as one who regards himself unworthy of such a prerogative. Accordingly, he has sent this man in his stead, knowing that he is sending him to a father. Do you wish to know what charge he has given him? To do nothing by command, but to commit everything to your counsel, upon which he wholly depends. For he is confident not only that his case will be judged by you, but assisted, supported, and upheld. If you please to entrust it to the Lord Archbishop of Reims, we trust that it may attain a swift conclusion with the Lord’s help, provided that the refuge of appeal is removed from both parties.

## LETTER CCCVI. TO THE LORD OF OSTIA, ON THE ELECTION OF ABBOT TUROLD OF THREE FOUNTAINS

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Written in the year of Christ 1151. To Hugh, formerly abbot of Trois-Fontaines in the province of Champagne in France, as appears from Letters 273 and 274. Thus even as cardinal he retained special care of that place.] Bernard clears himself against the accusation of Hugh, bishop of Ostia, who took ill the promotion of Turold to abbot of Trois-Fontaines, since he himself had designated another man, Nicolaus. He excuses the election of Robert as abbot of a new monastery.

[Col. 0507C]

1. “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matt. XVIII, 7). Do I scandalize you? Am I a scandal to you? Who could believe this possible, unless he did not know our unanimity, our mutual charity, and how we walked together in the house of God? What a sudden and grievous change for me! He who sustained me now prepares to crush me; he who defended me now terrifies me with threats, attacks me with abusive accusations, and charges me with treachery. The first-created human beings were asked for a confession concerning an exceedingly grave and singular sin (Gen. III); the Ninevites were allowed time for repentance (Jon. III); the Sodomites were punished not on hearsay but rather after direct observation (Gen. XIX). With me, the proceeding has been the more irregular because it has been the more contemptuous. I was not deemed worthy to be called to account, invited to make satisfaction, asked for the case against me, or given the opportunity [Col. 0508A] to answer for myself. I was not summoned, yet judged; not convicted, yet condemned.

2. And now hear, if you deign, our defence: perhaps not sufficient for you, but true nonetheless. You wished Brother Nicolaus to be appointed in your place; and I remember it, I do not deny it. You and I agreed upon this together; I believed it would occur, and therefore I said so. That it was not done resulted from necessity, not duplicity. The matter turned into disagreement. What do I say, disagreement? It was rather agreement. All were found so unanimously opposed to this understanding of ours that not one monk or lay brother, apart from two or three who belonged to you, consented to agree. [Col. 0508B] Nevertheless we tried, by many arguments, now coaxing and now threatening, to bring the matter to completion; but they opposed us as unanimously as they did stubbornly. We could have used force; but may God spare me as we spared him, lest a man who is modest and faint-hearted—as you know—and shrinking from the burden should remain in so great a storm. For, besides the external matters which you too have tested, everything seemed beyond his strength. Therefore, taking him together with his own brethren, we laid upon them a burden which he would bear more lightly because it was borne with him by our own. For it is a place newly established from our brethren and nearer to us, so that it can be more easily visited by us. Concerning abbots belonging to that place, because we did not have your assent, we dared nothing. We wished to give Brother Robert, [Col. 0508C] than whom no one then seemed more suitable at hand, when your discretion informed us that he had been forbidden. What more? They received a man who, as we have learned, displeases Your Holiness.

3. Nor is the reason hidden. You publicly proclaim him dishonourable, as they say, and say that he was driven from his former monastery because of the stigma of immorality [Note: [Col. 0507D] That is, from Fountains Abbey in England, over which Turold or Turoldus presided after Maurice “for two years, doing many things by his authority and even rashly undertaking some things against the counsel and will of the venerable archbishop. Thus, a quarrel having arisen between them, by command of the holy father Bernard he resigned his office and returned to Rievaulx, from which he had been taken,” according to Serlo in the *History of Fountains*, *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 748.], which he had formerly governed. Perhaps this was so. But God and His angels are my witnesses that, so far as I remember, up to this time I had never heard such a report concerning him. Nor did the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0508D] Of York, named Henry Murdac, also an Englishman and formerly a monk of Clairvaux, to whom Letter 106 is addressed; he too had been abbot of Fountains, as appears both from this letter and from the notes to what is now Letter 321.], while striving by every means to remove him, ever made anything of the kind known to us either in writing or by messenger. Would I be an approver [variant: supporter] of immorality or dishonour? If this is your opinion of me, see lest this cloud envelop Your Excellency also, since, after once beginning so notorious a familiarity and friendship with such a man, you have fostered it until now with such zeal. And what do you say of the archbishop? What do you think? Would he too [Col. 0509A] have first promoted to a position—and in the very place which he himself had governed—a man he knew to be such? For he could not have been ignorant, since the man had long been known to him. I would not so much as faintly suspect this of such a man and such a lover of honour. He both promoted and removed him: I do not deny it. Let him see by what reasoning he did this. For the deed is known to have displeased many, since they discerned neither reason, order, nor custom in his removal. The archbishop simply so wished; and, so that we should not grieve him, at our urging this man yielded peacefully and gave place to wrath.

4. This one thing I say: from the time he entered among us [Note: [Col. 0509C] Therefore, having left Rievaulx, he had come to Clairvaux. What follows concerning his learning is confirmed by Serlo in these words: “A man not moderately learned in the Sacred Scriptures, and sufficiently instructed in the liberal arts.”]—as he has testimony from all—nothing has been discovered in him which would obstruct this promotion. He has conducted himself without complaint. Nor does the man yet lack [Col. 0509B] suitable learning, teaching, graciousness, or charm in face and speech. But the short time he has been with us makes him suspect to you; I confess, it does to me as well. Perhaps he will act well; perhaps badly. I fear all my works, and I do not understand what I am doing. Therefore I am not certain, and I cannot make you certain. It has been done, and what has been done cannot be undone. Had I been a prophet, I certainly would not have done that by which I should offend a friend, trouble a saint, and scandalize a bishop. What do you wish me to do? It was done under such necessity and in such a manner.

5. This is my defence. If it suffices, let the scandal be removed from our midst; if not, let me bear whatever judgment, and of whatever kind, you decree. For if I should so soon destroy again what I have built, it would be grievous—unless perhaps a fitting reason should arise, which perhaps may occur in the course of time. If you wish to remove him, you have the power. I do not resist; I do not set myself against the torrent. I have not acted unjustly. If I seem foolish, it is within your power to correct [Col. 0510A] my foolishness; or, if you judge this more fitting, even to punish it. Yet I say that, if I am treated piously and as a Christian, “the just man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me”; he will not defame me among others in anger. Here you have my account, unless you take offence also at this present letter. Since I learned of your indignation from others, and not from you, I took care not to return like for like, but immediately to complain to you of you through this letter. Henceforth, blessed be God, who before my departure has taken away that consolation which He had given and in which I perhaps took excessive pleasure: namely, the favour of you and of my lord [Note: [Col. 0509C] Namely, Eugenius. Bernard likewise incurred the displeasure of Innocent II by speaking the truth, as appears from Letter 218; so difficult it is to retain the favour of great men, however much they have been benefited, without injury to truth!], so that I may learn even by my own experience not to place my hope in man.

## LETTER CCCVII. TO THE SAME

[Note: [Col. 0509C] Written in the year of Christ 1153.] He defends the bishop of Beauvais against hostile rumours. He states that his health is extremely afflicted, and relates what has happened to the archbishop of Lyons.

[Col. 0510B]

1. I dictated these words in haste, and for that reason with less polish; for the traveller is pressing on, eager to pass through. A remarkable thing, but a happier one still: Brother G. Fulcher arrived almost at the same moment with the letters of my lord and yours, and likewise the pilgrim who bears this present letter, undoubtedly by God’s providence, so that I might have someone through whom to reply speedily—a speed that could not be swift enough for my desire. This is why I myself dictated these words in my illness, since there was then no one else at hand.

Concerning the lord of Beauvais [Note: Henry, son of Louis the Fat and brother of Louis the Younger, king of France, bishop of Beauvais, apparently fell into ill repute with the Pope. Bernard therefore replies that he can grieve at his errors, if there are any, but cannot correct them as he would wish. Bernard would rather that the Pope himself had undertaken the task of correcting him and had fraternally warned him concerning what he had heard about him.

For his sudden conversion to the religious life—a conversion foreseen by Bernard—see *Life of St Bernard*, book IV, chapter 3. Following Baronius, we assigned it in the *Chronology* to the year 1149, since the more certain chronological indication seems to prove that he was made bishop of Beauvais in that year, as Jacques Sirmond notes on the *Letters of Peter of Celle*, from the Supplement of Sigebert, book I, letter 24. But Henriquez, in the *Menologium*, citing Jean Chenu, is further from the truth in assigning the beginning of Henry’s episcopate at Beauvais to 1161. Finally, he was elevated to the see of Reims in 1163.

Moreover, how unwillingly he first accepted the episcopate is shown by letters written to various persons; indeed, even Bernard regarded his premature promotion as not free from scruple, and therefore thought that Peter, abbot of Cluny, should be consulted, as may be seen in the latter’s book V, letter 8. See also Henry’s own letter, written to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, in *Gallia Christiana*, under the bishops of Beauvais.

We have thought fit to present here another letter of his to the said abbot of Cluny, either because we suspect it was dictated by Bernard himself, or at least composed in imitation of Bernard. The former is not improbable, since it was not unusual for Bernard to issue letters in the name of others, even bishops; we possess several such among the published letters. If that is less certain, the matter itself establishes the latter. Compare its opening with letter 236, to the cardinals concerning the election of Pope Eugenius; compare what follows with letter 16, where the wording is identical.

“To the most reverend father among fathers and dearest lord among friends, PETER, abbot of Cluny, brother HENRY, elected bishop of Beauvais, whether by God’s command or permission, offers himself and whatever more he can offer.

“May almighty God pardon you: what have you done? You have recalled a buried man to men; by your counsel, in which too much trust was placed, I have been exposed and plunged again into the dreadful sea of cares, so that the height of honour may swallow me up anew. I knew not; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab, which I have undertaken to govern—being one who needs to be governed, not to govern. They have put my hands to mighty works; strength was needed. I have been made a watchman for the house of Israel; prudence was needed. I have become debtor to wise and foolish alike; justice was needed. I have been given as preacher to God’s people; temperance was needed, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I should be found reprobate—God forbid. But what are these things, and who am I? Or where are these things, and where am I? Lord, Father, and God of my life, your eyes have seen my imperfection. Lord, I have suffered violence; answer for me, because obedience alone compelled me—without which, according to the holy man, whoever is proved disobedient is unfaithful, even though he may appear faithful.

“And because no one acts with greater confidence than one who loves from affection, I now address you as a portion of my soul, depositing with you this intimate and grieving complaint. What seemed good to you, that by your letters sent to the lord abbot you should set my folly upon a lampstand? You believed, lord, and therefore spoke; you wished neither to deceive nor be deceived, but you did not escape the latter. Yet, however this came about, and whatever outcome the Lord our God may turn the matter toward, I am yours and, if you deem me worthy, prepared for your service. Receive me as servant, friend, and son; and bind me in an everlasting fellowship with that holy multitude over which, by God’s authorship, you preside, as a monk especially close to you and of your own womb, not to say as a bishop.”

I judge that the foregoing letter was not written by Bernard, but rather by Nicholas of Clairvaux, his secretary, who wrote other letters in Henry’s name: namely, the thirteenth, to Peter the Venerable himself, and the twenty-sixth, to Hugh of Compiègne. There is also another letter of the same Nicholas to Henry himself, namely the thirty-ninth, from which it appears with what affection he cherished him.]

—I answer first to the first matter you set forth. He is his own master; his life and conduct are now no longer in my power but in the city. If he sometimes acts otherwise than he ought or than is fitting, I can grieve; but I cannot correct him as I wish. Yet, as to the report made to you about his wandering—that he has indulged in it excessively—we have so far learned nothing; nor have we ever heard him reproached for it among us. Since Brother Robert, who is with him, came to him, nothing disgraceful or serious has yet come at all to our ears as having been done by him, or as having been urged by him upon the bishop. It would be strange if something could reach you which could remain hidden from us. Nevertheless, I shall endeavour to do what you wish concerning his recall, whenever I can do so honourably and opportunely. I would already have done it, had I been able to do so with the bishop’s consent and had I not feared that someone less useful would be put in his place.

During Lent the bishop himself came to us, ready to go to the curia because of a certain appeal; and he would have gone, had we not dissuaded him. The purpose of our dissuasion was that he did not seem adequately prepared, either in counsel or in retinue, as befitted the position of a young bishop. Yet he intends to set out at a suitable time. He is your brother: show him mercy, lest his adversaries prevail against him. I wish that you had written to him rather than to us, and had fraternally warned him about what you heard concerning him.

2. Next, I learned that you are concerned about the condition of my body. What you have heard is true: I have been ill unto death, but for the present recalled from death; and, as I feel it, not for long. For I am far weaker than can be believed. Yet I say this without prejudice to divine providence, which can also raise the dead. Let this be an answer not only to you, but also to my lord, to whom I wish and ask that, with whatever devotion you can, and with the lord of Tusculum summoned together with you, you return fullest thanks for such great condescension and such devout concern. [Note: Ymarus or Igmarus, bishop of Tusculum, formerly a monk of Cluny, to whom letter 219 is addressed. Ymarus, then a monk, subscribed to the letters of Gilbert, bishop of Paris, concerning peace between Drogo of Clacy and the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, namely in 1122.]

3. Now hear the truth about the lord of Lyons, and what may be certain to you. [Note: Namely Heraclius.] This man undertook a journey with much money and an honourable retinue, as befitted so great an archbishop; and behold, enemies’ ambushes surrounded him on every side, almost at the very outset. What was this man of desire to do? He was not allowed to proceed, and he judged abandoning his purpose more grievous than any captivity. He sent some of his companions back and dispersed others. He rid himself of his mass of money, retaining a little with which he might complete the journey with a few companions. Why say more? He came with three or four attendants, himself nevertheless in an attendant’s dress; and so, travelling the public road amid a mixed crowd of pilgrims, as though one of them, he arrived at Saint-Gilles. [Note: See the notes to letter 241.] When he fell ill, he continued as far as Montpellier. There, staying for some time, he spent with physicians both what he had and what he did not have. [Note: In the old editions, letters 147 and 230 are wrongly repeated here.]

## LETTER CCCVIII

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 1153. See letter 419.]

### TO ALFONSO, KING OF PORTUGAL

He replies that he has laboured at the king’s request, and predicts that the king’s brother will soon pass from earthly warfare to heavenly.

To ALFONSO, illustrious king of the Portuguese, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

We received the letters and greetings of Your Highness with joy in him who commands greetings for Jacob. What we have done in this matter, both the outcome for us and you yourselves will demonstrate by the result; from the promptness of our spirit in the care imposed upon us, or at least from the obligation mentioned, you will infer it. Peter, brother of Your Highness and worthy of every glory, has conveyed what you enjoined; and, having travelled through Gaul in arms, he serves in Lorraine, soon to serve the Lord of hosts. [Note: This Peter, brother of Alfonso, king of Portugal, was one of those young men devoted to tournaments whom St Bernard, by a draught of blessed beer, moved to conversion; see book I of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 11, no. 55. What he brought to Bernard from his brother Alfonso is known from the king’s own letter to the saint, reported by Henriquez in the *Menologium* for 9 May: after defeating the Moors, he had accepted the royal title bestowed on him by his subjects, but the king of Castile opposed this unless he paid him a fixed tribute. He therefore asks that Bernard secure papal confirmation of his royal title, preferring to be liable to pay tribute to St Peter, that is, to the Apostolic See, rather than to a neighbouring and rival king. See letter 419.] Brother Roland, our son, bears letters of apostolic generosity. Hold him, our brothers living among you, and myself in your good favour.

## LETTER CCCIX

[Note: This letter, numbered 361 in the royal edition, is listed first among the Sugerian letters in Chesne, where Eugenius’s reply is appended. Compare the seventh letter there.]

### TO POPE EUGENIUS

He praises Abbot Suger and commends Suger’s envoys to the Pope.

To his most loving father and lord EUGENIUS, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

If any vessel of the great house of the great King is held in honour in our Gallican Church, if there is anyone who, like David, faithfully goes in and comes out at the command of the Lord (1 Sam. 22:14), then, in my judgment, it is the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis. For I know the man: in temporal matters faithful and prudent, in spiritual matters fervent and humble; and in both—what is most difficult—he conducts himself irreproachably. Before Caesar he is as one of the Roman court; before God, as one of the court of heaven. We ask and entreat that you graciously receive the envoys of so great a man and, as befits you and as he is altogether worthy, write back to him good and friendly words, full of intimacy and affection, full of favour and grace. For to love and honour his person especially is to honour your ministry.

## LETTER CCCX

### TO ARNOLD, ABBOT OF BONNEVAL AT CHARTRES

[Note: Written in 1153. More recent writers—namely Horstius, Charles de Visch, and the author of the French *Life of St Bernard*—against the opinion of Trithemius, Bellarmine, and others, maintain that this Arnold was distinct from the author of the second book of the *Life of St Bernard*. They call that author Bernard and make him abbot of Bonneval, not in Poitou or Rouergue, but in Vienne, of the Cistercian Order. They identify another Arnold as abbot of Bonneval at Chartres, a Benedictine monastery, to whom this letter was written.

But, with due respect to such great men, I would say that they are one and the same. As to the difference of names, the author of the second book of the *Life of St Bernard* is called Ernaldus in a very ancient manuscript from Corbie; and by this name our Arnold, abbot at Chartres, is designated by Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, in the letters he wrote to him. But leaving the controversy about the name aside, it is certain that book II of the *Life of St Bernard* was written while Geoffrey was still bishop of Langres. Thus we read in chapter 5, no. 29: “Geoffrey, prior of the same place, his kinsman in flesh and spirit . . . who afterward became bishop in the church of Langres . . . and to this day continues commendably in going in and coming out.” It was therefore written before 1161, when Geoffrey, having resigned the episcopate, “returned to Clairvaux to the embrace of his Rachel,” as the *Chronicle of Clairvaux* relates; there he is reported to have died in 1164, on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

But from the foundation of Bonneval in Vienne in 1117 to 1180, no abbot there bore the name Bernard. St John was first over it, from 1118 to 1138; when he was made bishop of Valence, he yielded the place to Gozevin, the second abbot. In 1151 Gozevin succeeded Rainald as abbot of Cîteaux and had Peter as his successor at Bonneval. Peter in turn was succeeded in 1171 by blessed Hugh, formerly abbot of Léoncel; he ruled Bonneval in Vienne until 1180, when the Cistercian *Menologium* reports that he died. Where, then, is this Bernard, abbot of Bonneval in Vienne, who supposedly wrote the second book of the *Life of St Bernard* before 1164, when Geoffrey of Langres died? All these points are established from Manrique’s *Annals*.

Add that the second book of Bernard’s Life was composed by a man of a congregation other than the Cistercian, as will be clear to anyone who carefully considers its preface. Therefore the author of that book and the friend of St Bernard to whom, near death, he wrote this final letter are one and the same: our Arnold, or Ernald, abbot of Bonneval at Chartres. The most learned R. P. Bertrand Tissier, who, with his customary candour and judgment, possessed the works of our Arnold and knew that they could not be included in the *Library of the Cistercian Fathers*, most kindly sent them to our Acherius. He made the following observations about our Arnold:

“This author wrote the second book of the *Life of St Bernard*, likewise the *Hexaemeron*, or treatise on the Work of the Six Days; a book on the Principal Works of Christ; and a treatise on the Words of the Lord on the Cross. The Library of Clairvaux supplied us with these three little works. Later I found the third in the *Library of the Fathers*, with another brief work on the Blessed Virgin appended to it. Now, in the aforesaid Library of Clairvaux, the book on the Principal Works of Christ is attributed to him in two manuscript copies under this title: ‘Prologue of Lord Ernald, abbot of Bonneval, to the book on the Principal Works of Christ, which he wrote to Pope Adrian, namely Adrian III.’”

So he writes. Two other treatises are attributed to him in the Cistercian Library: the first, *On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, beginning, “No one, when he has seen these chapters,” etc.; the second, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, as R. P. Dom Jacques Lannoy informed me by letter, having sent us a copy of the former transcribed in his own hand. Yet whether that first book truly belongs to him I would not readily say; concerning the latter, since I have not seen it, it is not clear what judgment should be made.

For the present, these remarks suffice about our Arnold, who seems to have died about 1154, when Geoffrey undertook after him the continuation of Bernard’s Life. For Geoffrey himself, in book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, or the second written by himself, chapter 4, no. 25, says that three years had elapsed from Archbishop Eskil of Denmark’s first journey to Clairvaux to visit Bernard. That journey occurred shortly before or after St Bernard’s death, namely in 1152, as may be inferred from these words of the *Cistercian Exordium*, distinction 3, chapter 25: “Not very long after this time had elapsed”—that is, after Eskil’s return to Denmark—“the most sorrowful report struck his ears concerning the falling asleep of the blessed Man, his special friend,” namely Bernard. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, praises Ernald’s letters, all of which we deeply regret have perished.]

Bernard, close to death, wrote this last letter to his friend.

We received your affection with affection, but not with pleasure. For what pleasure can there be where bitterness claims everything for itself? Except that it is in some way pleasant to eat nothing at all. Sleep has departed from me, lest pain should ever depart, even through the benefit of senses lulled to rest. Weakness of the stomach is almost the whole of what I suffer. Frequently, by day and night, it demands to be strengthened with a very small amount of some liquid or other; for it stubbornly refuses every solid food. Even the little which it deigns to admit it receives only with severe distress; yet it fears a greater distress if it leaves itself entirely empty. If at times it agrees to receive a little more, that is most grievous. My feet and legs have swollen, as commonly happens to dropsical persons.

And amid all this, lest anything concerning the state of a friend should be hidden from an anxious friend, according to the inward person—to speak foolishly—the spirit is willing, though the flesh is weak. Pray to the Saviour, who does not will the death of a sinner, that he may not delay the timely departure now at hand, but guard it. Take care to fortify with prayers a heel bare of merits, so that he who lies in wait may not find where to fasten his tooth and inflict a wound. I dictated these words myself, being as I am, so that by the familiar hand you may recognize the affection. Yet I would rather have written back than written.

## NOTICE

Thus far extends the first collection of the letters of St Bernard, made in his own lifetime by his disciples, as we said in the Preface. We judged it a matter of conscience to alter the order of these letters, so ancient and so established. But the following letters, which in earlier editions were added confusedly and rashly, with no regard for chronology, seemed worth arranging in order; at the margin we have placed the customary number that each letter previously held. Those, however, which now for the first time have been added to this edition, we have individually marked at the foot of the page with the name **NEW**. After all these will follow an **APPENDIX**, containing doubtful letters of Bernard, charters and instruments drawn up in his name, together with letters written to him or on his behalf, and certain other items which seemed useful for elucidating his letters.

## LETTER CCCXI

[Note: Formerly letter 313; the letter formerly numbered 311 is now 374. Written about 1125.]

### TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR

He sharply rebukes certain rivals who oppose the pious undertakings of others, and urges Haimeric, when the opportunity is offered, to diligent concern for the common good.

To the illustrious man, Lord HAIMERIC, chancellor of the holy Roman See, HUGH, abbot of Pontigny, and BERNARD of Clairvaux: how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God.

1. What the bishops seek, Christ, as we believe, obtains; and their cause is God’s cause. Whoever belongs to God, then, let him join them. If anyone refuses, let him hear from the Lord: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12:30). Indeed, let him either assent to the Apostle who says, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19), or certainly hear with the Jews: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51); and from the prophet: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good” (Isa. 5:20), “who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2:14). They cannot both exult in prosperity; nor can the righteous man for his righteousness and the sinner in the desires of his soul both be praised from one and the same mouth at the same time.

Yet what wonder if the good which is to the good an odour of life produces the opposite effect in those who are opposed, when the very fountain and source of good was born for the fall and resurrection of many, and as a sign still contradicted today? (Luke 2:34). Even now the Saviour is found by very many to be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence (Isa. 8:14), though there are not lacking those who say with joyful heart: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. 2:14). But he to whom peace gives rise to offence—in what shall he find peace? He to whom salvation itself is condemnation—in what shall he be saved?

It is written: “Glory and riches are in his house”—undoubtedly the house of the righteous man. But what glory and what riches are meant, he immediately shows: “His righteousness,” he says, “remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:3). And truly there is no glory like it, no riches so great, as righteousness in the house of the righteous person’s conscience. But what does the unrighteous man lose? If Paul glories in the riches of his heart—“This,” he says, “is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12)—who is thereby burdened? Yet the Prophet adds: “The sinner shall see and be angry” (Ps. 111:10). What great malice! Are these riches like earthly possessions, so that, as with those, one person’s abundance diminishes another’s? Why then are you angry where you lose nothing? Indeed, why do you envy good people their goods—goods which you do not care to claim for yourself? Thus, as people say, a dog guards hay which it does not eat. But though you gnash your teeth and waste away, what is from God cannot be utterly dissolved. Whether you will or not, the righteous shall see and rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop its mouth.

2. But these words are for those who may be suspected. To you, however, we say this: behold, gain lies ready; prepare the talent. What is it doing in a napkin when it will one day be demanded with interest? While we have time, why do we neglect to work? Certainly, even though by virtue of your office you are always ready to devote yourselves to the gains of charity, at present an especially great profit of holy avarice lies open. Only do not shrink from bringing forth into the open the Lord’s money which you received for this very purpose. Otherwise, “What use is there in hidden wisdom and unseen treasure?” (Sir. 20:32).

Finally, if it truly belongs to you not merely by office, but also, as they say, by earnest endeavour, to do good to all, you ought especially to do so to those of the household of faith. Although this was proclaimed by the Apostle as a general command for everyone (Gal. 6:10), we confidently demand it from you in a special manner by the privilege of your very position and ministry. Unless perhaps—which we least suppose—you occupy the office more than you honour the ministry. For scarcely any good is done in the world which does not in some way have to pass through the hands of the Roman chancellor, so that scarcely anything is judged good unless it has first been examined by his judgment, moderated by his counsel, strengthened by his zeal, and confirmed by his help. To whom, then, more justly than to him should be assigned whatever in righteous affairs is found unfinished or less than perfect, just as likewise everything found usefully and commendably completed?

Accordingly, we must call most fortunate the man who holds that office—or, indeed, most miserable, since he will invariably prove himself either a participant in all good or its enemy. With justice all praise or blame will fall upon him according to the outcomes of affairs and the merits of his own efforts. Blessed, moreover, is the man who can say to the Lord: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:63).

3. But what are we doing? While we strive to make known to you a necessary matter, we have almost forgotten into what busy ears we are pressing these words. Yet if confidence is also needed for the task, perhaps we shall by no means seem importunate—provided you remember not our merits but your gifts, by which you have graciously taken care to open beforehand, toward our lowliness, so great a door of friendship. [Note: From this it is evident that this letter was either the first or one of the first written by Bernard to Haimeric, and indeed before letter 15, which we noted above was dictated in 1126. Haimeric was already chancellor from 1125 onward, as is proved by a bull of Honorius II in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 1379.]

This indeed, this is the very conspicuous mark of your condescension and devotion that we retain: that you, so great and occupied with such great matters, judged that persons so small ought not merely to be rewarded, but even greeted by Your Excellency. May he who has already granted us not so much to enjoy your gift as to delight in your gain, repay you with spiritual gold—namely wisdom—in return for material gold. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXII

[Note: A new letter; the letter formerly numbered 312 is now 398. Written about 1130.]

### TO RAYNALD, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Note: Raynald or Reginald, the second of that name, presided over the Church of Reims from 1124 to the beginning of 1139, according to our reckoning; he died on the Ides of January, as we noted on letter 170.]

He gives thanks for the letter sent to him.

To the most reverend father and lord R., by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: greeting, and whatever the prayer of a sinner can accomplish.

Blessed be God, who has deigned to comfort us by the visitation of your letter. We could indeed somehow repay letter with letter; but when can we sufficiently return the favour of that grace by which we rightly glory that we have been anticipated by you with blessings of such sweetness, stirred by exhortations, and honoured by greetings? We are people as unworthy of such names as we are unknown to you; yet certainly all the less ungrateful because all the less worthy.

Nevertheless, in doing these things you do what you ought, because you recognize yourself as debtor to wise and foolish alike. That reputation, whose good fragrance, you say, moved the excellence of your dignity to such condescension toward our littleness, is certainly dangerous; but in this respect it is not moderately serviceable, because from this preceding wind there has resulted for us that most excellent and welcome fruit—which has nothing wind-like about it—that we have deserved to be received into favour before we came to be known by so great a priest of the Most High God.

Concerning our arrival—why we have not now come, when we intend to come, and anything else which Your Holiness may meanwhile wish to learn concerning us—the monk who bears this letter, whom we have taken care to send ahead for this very purpose, will be able faithfully to satisfy you fully about everything.

## LETTER CCCXIII

[Note: Formerly letter 371; the letter formerly numbered 313 is now 311. Written in the year of Christ 1132. The subject of this letter depends upon letter 94.]

### TO GEOFFREY, ABBOT OF SAINT MARY’S, YORK

Those religious who wish to move from a looser to a stricter way of life are not to be hindered; and those who, after making the transition, fall back into their former life are to be regarded as apostates.

To the venerable man Lord GEOFFREY, abbot of the church of Saint Mary’s at York, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting in the Lord.

1. It pleased Your Reverence to direct letters to my littleness, in which you wished to consult me concerning doubtful matters. But concerning these and similar matters, we fear to give any certain answer in proportion as, being men who do not see the good pleasure of the divine will clearly, we doubt whether, if we declare anything other than what our neighbours themselves wish, we may offend their minds. This happens especially to those whose conscience, confused by the anguish of a disgusted mind, tries to pursue difficult and tortuous reasonings of its impurity. Yet that conscience itself is the avenger of its blindness: while it strives, as it were, to flatter itself about what it has done, immediately it is pricked and bitten by the returning sting of truth in the very thing it remembers.

Lamenting the misery of this difficulty, the Psalmist prays and says: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141:8). Therefore, good sir, do not accuse me of feigned cunning if I cannot adequately answer your questions as fully as you wish, or if, whatever I can do, I still do not dare to explain everything. For the first appearance of your letter took its beginning from complaints: namely, that it is a grievous misfortune to your old age that some of your monks have ventured to pass to a stricter and safer manner of life. In this matter you have rather to fear that “the sorrow of this world works death.”

2. Surely, if reason has force in human judgments, one ought not to grieve when a person ventures at some point to adhere more rightly to the laws of his Creator. Nor do we keep watch over paternal concerns in a holy or sufficiently devout manner if we envy the progress of our children. Therefore, if you wish to have one counsellor among a thousand—or rather, as I think, especially wish it—it is necessary to take counsel so that you attend to your sons who remain with you in the middle course, lest they fail; but meet with bread, according to the prophet, those others who fear to remain short of the purity of their profession because of conscience, and who strive to rise, by the purpose of religious life, from the good they once undertook to a higher degree (Isa. 21:14).

Bestow the greatest care on the former, lest they become insolent to their ruin; offer goodwill to the latter, that they may advance to the crown. Those who “set ascents in their hearts,” who go “from strength to strength,” deserve to see the God of gods in Zion more happily in recompense, in proportion as they have endeavoured by a purer rule of life to cling more intimately to the highest good.

3. Finally, concerning the two monks, Gervase and Ralph, [Note: On their defection see volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 738, col. 2, and the following column. There it is recorded that Gervase, recovering strength, returned to the camp and wiped away the stain of apostasy by reformation of life; Ralph, however, wholly returned to a relaxed manner of life.] who, together with others, left while Lord Thurstan the archbishop was working in a fatherly and episcopal manner, and who, as you testify, were at some time dismissed with your absolution: I am certain that, if they had remained within the degree of purity to which they had ascended, they would have acted not wrongly but commendably. I am likewise certain that, if they wish to resume the degree of purity from which they rashly fell, they will be more praiseworthy through that grace of courage by which soldiers, after the cowardice of flight, are usually made more glorious in victory, in proportion as, after disgrace, they return more eagerly to battle in hope of victory.

And I believe, unless I am mistaken, that the absolution which has been given may meanwhile be impeded, but cannot be nullified before the judgment of almighty God. Lastly, you admit that this life is holier; but you say that they cannot endure the difficulty of this narrow way because of bodily weakness or affection for relatives. To this you add that their presence will be necessary to you; and therefore you ask very urgently whether they can remain without fault in the place from which they departed not without scandal.

4. The Gospel thunders loudly concerning the discernment of the character of scandals, the complete cutting away of fleshly affection for Christ’s sake, and the fleeing of temporal advantages for the salvation of the soul; the whole sequence of Scripture cries it everywhere. To be ignorant of this is not so much evil as almost heretical. Yet I am not certain whether such a return of theirs ought to be judged free from blame deserving punishment. For it is exceedingly dangerous and near to grievous ruin to presume upon God’s mercy against God’s justice, and to wish to defend the one against the other. Scripture says: “Do not add sin to sin and say, ‘God’s mercy is great’” (Sir. 5:5–6). For it is also an evil mode of judgment when lesser things outweigh greater, or inferior things are compared with better ones.

5. And then after this you vehemently complain why they ought deservedly to be called apostates if, on returning to their cenobium, they endeavor to fulfill their profession together with good observances. I, for my part, say that I ought not to condemn them. “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19), and “each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). For he whom darkness does not overtake—“the Lord shall be known when he executes judgment; every sinner shall be caught in the works of his own hands” (Ps. 9:17). Let each person think for himself what is good for him; I shall say of myself what I think. I, Bernard, if I had freely passed, in vow and deed, from good things to better, or from dangerous things to safer, and had presumptuously returned, by an unlawful desire, to what I had changed, I should fear that I had become not merely an apostate but even unfit for the kingdom of God. Blessed Gregory says this also: “Whoever,” he says, “has purposed to undertake a greater good has made unlawful the lesser good which was permitted. For it is written: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God’ (Luke 9:62). Therefore one who had applied himself to a more strenuous pursuit is proved to look back if, after abandoning greater goods, he turns back to lesser ones” (*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 28). But as to the matter of a certain excommunication which you wished to insert, it seems to me that it was neither your concern to investigate nor mine to judge. For the law judges no one unless he is first heard; and judgment is rashly pronounced against one who is absent.

## LETTER CCCXIV

[Note: [Col. 0520D] Elsewhere Letter 318; that which was formerly 314 is now 390. Written in the year of Christ 1134. This letter is connected with Letters 131, 132, and 133.]

### TO LORD POPE INNOCENT

After reconciling the Milanese to the Church, Bernard, by Innocent’s command, set out to make peace among the Lombard cities themselves, and went to Pavia and Cremona. But, making no progress among the Cremonese, he reports their obstinacy to the Pontiff and urges him to suspend for a little while the more severe sentence which he was preparing against the Archbishop of Milan.

[Col. 0520D]

To his most loving father and lord INNOCENT, supreme Pontiff, Brother BERNARD, the little that he is.

The Cremonese have hardened themselves, and their prosperity destroys them; they despise the Milanese, and their self-confidence deceives them. Placing their hope in chariots and horses, they have frustrated me and made my labor vain. I was departing sadly when, behold, no slight consolation came from your side: so that, although tribulations for Christ abound, consolations through him may also abound. I received the letters I desired, bearing the delights of my heart: certainty of your safety, the misfortunes of enemies, and the successes of friends. Yet, as I read further, a sadder ending tempered my joy. Whom would not your indignation frighten? I confess it is just, and for that very reason I fear it more. Yet I say this: what has not yet been done ought to be done, but at the time God foresees. Otherwise, whatever you intend to inflict will be equally ready to your hand, and perhaps not equally dangerous. For otherwise, what has newly been built up among this people by so many mercies of God and by so many labors of yours and your servants—[Note: [Col. 0521D] namely Guy of Pisa and Matthew of Albano, sent by Innocent as legates to the Milanese together with Bernard, as appears from Letters 131, 132, and 133.]—alas, how easily it may be destroyed! It would be surprising if this could please him who is said to exalt mercy over judgment (James 2:13).

But O unhappy bishop—[Note: [Col. 0521D] I suppose Ribald, elected and confirmed by Innocent in place of the rejected Anselm, as in the same Letters 131, 132, and 133.]—who, transferred from Ur of the Chaldeans, as from a kind of paradise, has become brother to dragons and companion to ostriches! What will he do? He wishes to obey, and behold the beasts of Ephesus gnash their teeth against him. He wishes prudently to dissemble for a time, and he incurs your indignation, more dreadful than every wild beast. He is hemmed in on every side, except that he judges it more tolerable to be without a people than without a lord: rightly valuing apostolic favor more highly than the Milanese see. Do you doubt his fidelity? If anyone has tried maliciously to persuade you otherwise concerning him, he has rather exposed himself as faithless, pursuing with a treacherous tongue, in his envy, a man of such good testimony. Spare him, gracious Father; spare your faithful servant; spare a structure still newly built; spare a new plantation; spare, finally, the people of your acquisition, and these very benefits of yours which you most truthfully remember having bestowed upon it. Remember, merciful lord, the word of your Lord, who said: “Behold, for three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree and have found none” (Luke 13:7). But you have scarcely waited three months, and already you prepare the axe. If you had endured for three years, we should rightly demand even a fourth from the faithful servant, following the Lord’s example. Therefore we too say: “Leave it also this year”; perhaps, if in some way the soil has been dug around with the spade of repentance and the manure of their tears applied, he to whom you entrusted it may be able to remedy the barrenness of the Milanese and draw forth fruit.

## LETTER CCCXV

[Note: [Col. 0521D] Elsewhere Letter 344; that which was formerly 315 is now 341. Written about the year 1134.]

### TO MATILDA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

[Note: [Col. 0521D] Matilda, daughter of Malcolm III, king of Scotland, wife first of Emperor Henry V and then of Henry I, king of the English. By the latter she bore Henry II, of whom Bernard speaks at the end of the letter. The letter was written before the death of Henry I, before the year 1135. There was another Matilda, daughter of Fulk V, Count of Anjou, betrothed to William, son of that same Henry I; after he was swallowed by the waters of the Ocean, she became a religious and abbess of Fontevraud. Peter of Celle addresses her in Letter 10 of the first book.]

He asks her to grant a request previously made on behalf of the monks of La Chapelle.

[Col. 0522A]

To the most illustrious lady and most beloved daughter in Christ—this I say not from presumption but from affection—MATILDA, by God’s grace Queen of the English, BERNARD.

If I presume upon your high station, it is no wonder. For now not I alone know, but nearly everyone knows, how kindly you receive us and with what affection you love us. Therefore I have been asked by a friend of yours, the venerable abbot of La Chapelle, to ask you concerning a certain tithe—a matter about which, if you remember, I asked you at Bologna, and you in your usual kindness heard me. [Note: [Col. 0522D] Matilda showed such zeal and affection toward Bernard that, when he came to Bologna, she went out beyond the city to meet him and fell at his feet; see Book IV of the *Life*, no. 6.] But because what we ask has not yet been done, it is time that this petition should now be put into effect. Moreover, keep safe for me the son you have now borne; for I too, if it does not displease the king, claim a share in him for myself. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXVI

[Note: [Col. 0522D] Elsewhere Letter 375; that which was formerly 316 is now 356. Written about the year 1135.]

### TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF SENS, AND TO HAIMERIC, CHANCELLOR

He urges them not to oppose a certain nobleman who possesses ecclesiastical goods but now wishes to surrender them to certain religious persons.

When laymen wish to relinquish churches or ecclesiastical benefices which they hold unlawfully, there is one good; but when they wish them to pass into the use of God’s servants, the good is doubled. But since this cannot occur except through the bishop’s hands, the bishop will show himself either guilty of a twofold evil or the author of a twofold good, according as he withholds or gives his assent. What a certain knight asks of you is something that you yourselves ought to have asked of him. What then? Do you judge it better that the sanctuary of God should be possessed as an inheritance by a military man than by God’s holy people? It would be surprising if all who hear this are not astonished. Do not, I beg you, do not act thus, lest perhaps the sons of the uncircumcised hear of it and rejoice. Let it be that you can rescue the captive church from the hand of a powerful man and claim it for your own right—which we by no means suppose: whom, I ask, would you more willingly choose from it as your heir and successor: one who serves from it in the king’s armies, or one who intercedes for your sins? Do, therefore, what is just, what is worthy of you, what is pleasing to God and to all good people; what, finally, even if there were no other reason, I should confidently ask to be done out of love for me.

## LETTER CCCXVII

[Note: [Col. 0523C] Elsewhere Letter 320; that which was formerly 317 is now 357. Written in the year of Christ 1138.]

### TO HIS PRIOR GODFREY

[Note: [Col. 0523D] Bernard calls him “most dear” in Letter 142. He was later Bishop of Langres, as stated in the notes to Letter 164. His letters are found in Pérard, p. 122. In the year 1141 the second year of his episcopate is reckoned, p. 134.]

With the schism extinguished and peace established, he promises that he will return to his own people as soon as possible.

[Col. 0523A]

To Brother GODFREY, Brother BERNARD, greeting.

On the very day of the Octave of Pentecost God fulfilled our desire by giving unity to the Church and peace to the City. For on that day all the sons of Peter Leonis together humbled themselves at the feet of the lord Pope, became his liegemen, and swore liege fidelity to him. [Note: [Col. 0523D] A liegeman is one who, by reason of fief or subjection, owes his lord complete fidelity against every person.] Likewise the clerics who were in schism, together with the idol whom they had set up—[Note: [Col. 0523D] Victor, the antipope, elected by the schismatics after the death of Anacletus.]—humbled themselves at the feet of the lord Pope, promised him obedience according to custom, and there was great rejoicing among the people. Unless we had awaited this peace with a certain security, though it was long concealed from us, we should have come long ago. Henceforth there is nothing here to detain us. I do what you commanded: we turn “I shall come” into “I am coming.” For behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me: Christ’s victory and the Church’s peace. On the Friday after that day our party departed from the city. Thus, coming, we shall come with exultation, bearing sheaves of peace. These words are indeed beautiful, but the deeds are more beautiful. For they are so beautiful that whoever does not rejoice in them is either foolish or wicked. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0523D] Elsewhere Letter 329; that which was formerly 318 is now 314. Written about the year 1138.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT

He reports the perils of the Church of Rheims and seeks swift help from the Pontiff.

[Col. 0523C]

To his most loving father and lord INNOCENT, supreme Pontiff, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

The Church of Rheims is falling into ruin; the glorious city has been given over to reproach. She cries out to those passing along the way that no grief is like her grief. For without are conflicts, within are fears. Indeed, within also are conflicts, because her children fight against her, and she has no begetter to deliver her. Her sole hope is Innocent, to wipe tears from her cheeks. But how long, lord, will the shield of your protection not be set before her? How long will she be trampled down and find none to raise her up? Behold, the king has humbled himself and his indignation has now ceased. What then remains, except that the apostolic hand be placed beneath the afflicted woman, applying care and soothing remedies to her wounds? We believe, therefore, that the first thing is for the election to be hastened, lest the insolence of the people of Rheims destroy whatever remains, unless their fury is resisted by a mighty arm. If this is duly accomplished, we trust that the Lord will grant grace and success in the remaining matters as well.

## LETTER CCCXIX

[Note: [Col. 0523D] Elsewhere Letter 372; that which was formerly 319 is now 399. Written about the year 1138.]

### TO THURSTAN, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

He urges him not to abandon pastoral care; yet, if there is a just cause or the consent of the Pontiff, to seek a place where religious discipline is more strictly observed.

To the reverend father and lord THURSTAN, by God’s grace Archbishop of York, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting—not so much on the way as in the homeland.

1. We commend your desire for rest and your longing to fall asleep in the Lord in peace. Nevertheless, the grounds you put forward do not seem able to override pastoral responsibility—unless perhaps, which God forbid and we do not believe, some mortal sin has been committed, or permission has been granted for retirement by the authority of the supreme Pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0523D] Here Bernard approves two grounds for a bishop’s withdrawal: repentance for a crime and permission from the supreme Pontiff. Formerly bishops were reduced to the ranks on account of capital crimes, such as a lapse of the flesh, theft, perjury, and homicide. Here another mortal sin seems intended, for the expiation of which monastic seclusion is necessary. This letter appears to have been written shortly before Thurstan’s death, which Orderic states occurred in 1139, in Book 13, p. 919, where he is called brother of Andin, Bishop of Évreux. Letters 195 and 235 were written to the same Thurstan.] For we do not believe that you are unaware of the Apostle’s saying: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7:27). A bishop is not bound by a vow of the kind you say you have made so as to prevent him from persevering in the ministry to which he has been called.

2. Therefore, without presuming to prescribe to one wiser than ourselves, it seems healthier to us that you should retain what you hold and, in humility of habit and holiness of life, display the monk in the bishop. [Note: [Col. 0524D] Monks who became bishops were not allowed to lay aside their habit and former manner of life. Read Preface 2 to Century 4, nos. 178 ff. and 189. But how changed today is that excellent appearance! Read Abelard in his sermon on Saint John the Baptist, fol. 966. Since some were persuaded that episcopal life, as it was then conducted, could not cohere with monastic institutes, men elected to the episcopate utterly refused to acquiesce. A notable example is Guy, Abbot of Clairvaux, who, after the death of Archbishop William, was chosen for the see of Rheims but steadfastly refused the election for that very reason; see Baluze, *Miscellanea*, vol. 2, p. 247.] But if either a hidden cause compels you to withdraw, or the lord Pope grants you rest, then, according to our small measure of understanding, we advise that no harshness of food or clothing, no poverty whatsoever, should deter you from going where you hope to find greater purity. Yet in houses of this kind provision is so made for souls that appropriate care for bodies is not denied on account of age and weakness. We are yours; we pray earnestly to God for you, that what is better may breathe upon you and that he may grant you to bear the burden of the day and the heat in such a way that at evening you may receive the denarius stamped with the royal image.

## LETTER CCCXX

[Note: [Col. 0525C] Elsewhere Letter 381; that which was formerly 320 is now 317. Written in the year of Christ 1138.]

### TO ALEXANDER, PRIOR OF FOUNTAINS

[Note: [Col. 0525D] This was the uterine brother of Richard, the second Abbot of Fountains in England, who rested in peace at Clairvaux, according to Serlo, in vol. 1 of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 854, in the section on the monastery of Kirkstall, or Mount Saint Mary, in the territory of York. Alexander was appointed first abbot of that place in 1147, when Henry of Murdac—recipient of the following letter—was archbishop. There was another Alexander, likewise an Englishman and indeed Abbot of Fountains, but in the Diocese of Tours; see vol. 10 of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 374 and 377. On Fountains Abbey in England, compare Letters 235 and 252.]

### AND TO THE BRETHREN OF THE SAME PLACE

He exhorts them unanimously to elect a new abbot.

To the beloved brethren in Christ, ALEXANDER, Prior, and the whole convent of Fountains, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and such prayers as are ours.

1. Your venerable father—[Note: [Col. 0525D] namely Richard II, not Richard I, to whom Letter 96 is addressed; he died at Clairvaux on 15 May 1138.]—finished his course with a blessed end and fell asleep in the Lord. Although at all times I have been solicitous for you with a fatherly love, as for our own very entrails, I now bear so much greater concern for you as a greater necessity presses upon you. I would therefore have sent to you before now, had I not waited until I could act more opportunely and beneficially, because the venerable Abbot Henry—[Note: [Col. 0525D] Henry of Murdac, then Abbot of Vauclair, to whom the following letter is addressed, was occupied with the dispute then raging between the monasteries of Vauclair and Cuissy; see Herman, monk of Laon, Book 3, ch. 16. Luke, Abbot of Cuissy, was opposing Henry; Letter 79 is addressed to him.]—could not arrive sooner because he was occupied with certain affairs. From the beginning I had especially intended to send him, because he seemed more useful and more suited to this business. Receive him, therefore, most beloved brethren, with the honor and affection which he deserves, and obey him in all things as you would myself—indeed, even more, as he surpasses me both in prudence and in merits. For I have entirely entrusted to him my place, both in making the election and in arranging or correcting whatever must be arranged or corrected in this monastery or in the others which proceeded from it. [Note: [Col. 0526D] Namely Fountains itself and the three other houses sprung from it: Newminster, in the Diocese of Carlisle; Kirkstall; and Louth Park, in Lincolnshire.] I have sent with him Brother William, our beloved son.

2. And now I beseech you as dearest sons that in your election you may all be of one mind and that there be no schisms among you, but that, unanimous, you may glorify God with one voice. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace; hence “his place has been made in peace,” and he says: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23). Far be it from those who dwell in Christ’s school under the instruction of the Holy Spirit that the enemy should rejoice over them and glory in their dissension: that their own souls should be endangered, that all their labor of repentance should perish in vain, that they should make the good odor of our Order stink, and that Christ’s name should be blasphemed through those by whom it ought especially to be glorified! Rather, as we trust concerning you, as becomes saints, and as befits Christ’s servants, choose unanimously, I beseech you, a suitable shepherd for your souls, together with the venerable abbots of Rievaulx and Vauclair. I wish you in all things to acquiesce in their counsel as in ours.

## LETTER CCCXXI

[Note: [Col. 0526D] Elsewhere Letter 382; that which was formerly 321 is now 345. Written in the year of Christ 1138.]

### TO HENRY OF MURDAC

[Note: [Col. 0526D] This Henry, an Englishman to whom Letter 106 is addressed, was first a monk at Clairvaux. Toward the end of 1135 he was sent with twelve companions to establish the monastery of Vauclair in the Diocese of Laon. He governed it until the end of 1138, when, as these letters show, Bernard ordered and arranged his transfer to the government of Fountains Abbey. He was made Archbishop of York in 1147 and died in 1153, according to the necrology of Vauclair, on the day before the Ides of October.]

### FIRST ABBOT OF VAUCLAIR, LATER OF FOUNTAINS, AND FINALLY ARCHBISHOP OF YORK

He orders him not to refuse his election as Abbot of Fountains.

[Col. 0526B]

To his beloved brother and fellow abbot HENRY, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and prayers.

I command you, Brother Henry, that if the election of our brethren at Fountains falls upon you, you are not to refuse but to obey in charity, with the counsel of the venerable Abbot of Rievaulx. I do this unwillingly, knowing how great a consolation I lose by your absence; but I fear to oppose them when they agree, believing that this word in which the wishes of so many religious persons concur has gone forth from the Lord, since I have read in the Gospel: “Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20). Proceed, therefore, beloved brother: receive their professions and henceforth care for them as shepherd of their souls. Do not fear for the house whose governance you had undertaken. For I shall, God willing, provide it with a useful steward; it is nearer to me. Nor need you hesitate because of the bishop—[Note: [Col. 0526D] namely Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, in whose diocese Vauclair was situated.]—leave that matter to me.

## LETTER CCCXXII

[Note: [Col. 0527C] Elsewhere Letter 351; that which was formerly 322 is now 363. Written about the year 1138.]

### TO HUGH, A NOVICE, LATER ABBOT OF BONNEVAL

[Note: [Col. 0527C] That is, Bonneval in the Diocese of Besançon, of which this most devout Hugh, nephew of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, was later abbot; see Book IV of the *Life*, no. 40.]

He praises Hugh’s resolve to enter religious life, forewarns him against temptations, and urges him to constancy and perseverance.

[Col. 0527A]

To his dearest son in Christ HUGH, a new creature in Christ, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: be strengthened in the Lord.

1. On hearing of your conversion, we rejoiced and were delighted. Why should people not rejoice in that over which angels also rejoice? Already a festival day is celebrated; already thanksgiving and a voice of praise resound in the heights. A noble and delicately reared young man has conquered the evil one, despised the world, exposed his body to hardship, renounced the affections of his kindred, and leaped over the snares of wealth prepared for him, because he was a winged creature. Whence came this wisdom to you, my son? For we do not find so great a wisdom among the elders of Babylon. They are those who, according to the Apostle—indeed, contrary to him—wish to become rich in this world, that they may fall into temptation and the devil’s snare (1 Tim. 6:9). The wisdom of our Hugh is not from earth but from heaven. “I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to a little one.” You too, son, do not be ungrateful for the Redeemer’s benefit; lay aside childishness—or rather, be a little child in malice, but not in understanding (1 Cor. 14:20). Let not the severity of the Order frighten your tender age. Remember that the harsher thistle makes cloth softer; religious life makes the conscience gentler. [Variant: *cardo*, “hinge,” wrongly.] Christ’s sweetness will be present, and the prophet’s little meal will season the inedible stew (4 Kings 4:39–41). If you feel the stings of temptations, look upon the bronze serpent lifted up on the wood; and draw not so much upon the wounds as upon the breasts of the Crucified One. He will be a mother to you, and you will be a son to him; nor can the nails in any way wound the Crucified One without at the same time reaching even to your own hands and feet through his.

2. But “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Micah 7:6). They are those who do not love you, but love their own pleasure in you. Otherwise let them hear from our little child: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father” (John 14:28). Blessed Jerome says: “If your father lies prostrate on the threshold; if your mother, with breast bared, displays the breasts by which she nursed you; if a little nephew hangs from your neck: pass over your father though he be trampled underfoot; go on over your mother though she be trampled underfoot; and fly with dry eyes to the banner of the cross. It is the highest kind of piety, in this matter, to be cruel for Christ” (Jerome, Letter 1, to Heliodorus). Do not be moved by the tears of madmen who lament that from a son of Gehenna you have become a son of God. Alas! what cruel desire possesses the wretched? What love is so cruel, what affection so unjust? (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.720). “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). Therefore, son, so far as you can, avoid conversations with visitors, which, while they fill the ear, empty the mind. Learn to pray to God; learn to lift up your heart with your hands; learn to raise suppliant eyes to heaven and, in every necessity, present your pitiable face to the Father of mercies. It is impious to think of God that he can restrain his compassion from you and turn his ear away from your sobbing or cry. Moreover, remember that you must obey in all things the counsels of spiritual fathers no less than the commands of divine majesty. Do this and you shall live; do this and blessing shall come upon you, so that for every single thing you have left you may receive a hundredfold, even in the present life. Nor should you believe the spirit that suggests that this was undertaken too hastily and should have been deferred to a more mature age; believe rather him who said: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone, for he has raised himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27–28). Fare well, and strive for perseverance, which alone is crowned.

## LETTER CCCXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0528C] A new letter; that which was formerly 323 is now 365. Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT

On behalf of the Archbishop of Trier against the Abbot of Saint-Maximin.

[Note: [Col. 0528C] See Letters 179 and 180.]

1. How great, lord, is the abundance of your sweetness and love toward us, as we have often experienced! And it remains for us to experience it still at a fitting time. But far be it from us to dare request anything which we perceive to be contrary to God’s will and your honor. Therefore, since our heart does not reproach us for a request lacking reason or propriety, we have confidence that our prayers will not return to us empty, especially because we plead with a father for a son, and with Innocent for an innocent man. How faithfully the Archbishop of Trier has loved, from his youth, the honor of the Apostolic See and the peace of the Roman Church; how immovably and diligently he adhered to it in time of tribulation; how, while others sat in the shade, he bore with it the burden of the day and the heat; how steadfastly and fearlessly he spoke the word of truth for its testimonies before kings on behalf of his companions—you need not have this written to you by us, for you yourselves know it most certainly. Moreover, we speak what we know and testify to what we have seen, if indeed you receive our testimony: how prudently and carefully he rescued the Church’s affairs and possessions from the hand of strangers; how liberally and kindly he always brought his goods into common use, especially for those of the household of faith; and how diligently and circumspectly he guarded the integrity of his reputation from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.

2. What, then, displeased Your Paternity in him? Was it that he withdrew that church of Saint Maximin from royal power in order to subject it to priestly authority? Was it that he did not receive that man who, they say, wished to be a duke before being a knight and an abbot before being a monk? If this, then, or something else displeased you in him, nevertheless his long-established love ought not easily to have perished with a merciful Father; grace ought to have covered fault, and recollection of many benefits ought to have excused one blameworthy in a few respects but praiseworthy in many. But now, lord, you have exalted the right hand of those who oppress him; you have made all his enemies glad. For it is remarkable in the eyes of many by what merit of life, by what reputation for goodness, a man who has taken up his soul in vain has been placed in the governance of souls. How can he govern who could not be governed? How dare he preside who has not learned to be subject?
