Or how can he command obedience from subjects which he does not know how to render to prelates? “If a man does not know how to govern his own house,” says the Teacher of the Gentiles, “how shall he take care of the Church of God?” (1 Tim. 3:5). Finally, such as the father is, such are the sons: they cruelly disemboweled their mother in order to have means by which to foster schisms and dissensions. Yet concerning their morals and manner of life it is more honorable to be silent than to say anything. Nor did we say even this in order to judge servants belonging to another; they stand or fall to their own lord. But we know that if the unhappy will of these men prevails, undisciplined young men will shake the yoke of discipline from their necks, so that they may roam about and walk through the earth in the likeness of these men; and even if their desire does not attain its effect, it will itself be their glory that they have been able to resist their prelates. Alas! How many persons, and what persons, who trust in their own merits before your mercy, will have their hope and confidence shaken from its place if a son once so beloved is suddenly cast out from your bosom and from the breasts of your consolation!

3. If therefore our prayers have any place with Your Excellency, blessed Father, we who love you rather than what belongs to you humbly ask that, on a day of prosperity, you do not reject one who remained with you in your temptations, so that something may perish before you from the right of one who expected to increase rather than diminish in your favor. Otherwise, if, against everyone’s hope and against the man’s merits, it should happen that strangers plunder his labors, that evils be set against him for goods and hatred for love: he himself will receive alone the wound from one whom he does not fear, but many will grieve at his persecution. May the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, teach you in every work to divide light from darkness, so that you may know how to reject evil and choose good.

## LETTER CCCXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Elsewhere Letter 336; that which was formerly 324 is now 382. Written in the year of Christ 1139.]

### TO ROBERT, ABBOT OF THE DUNES

[Note: [Col. 0529D] This is that Robert who succeeded Blessed Bernard at Clairvaux—indeed, whom Bernard himself, when already dying, named as his successor. See the book *On the Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 2, ch. 23; Meyer, *Annals of Flanders*; and Manriquez, *Annals*. The people of coastal Flanders call *dunas* the mounds or hills of white sand, accumulated either naturally or by the surging sea. In these there was formerly the most flourishing Abbey of the Dunes, but it is now buried under growing sands because the wooden barriers were neglected during the calamities of war.]

He offers consolation for their mutual absence: namely, the union of their souls, and indeed, one day, of their bodies.

To Brother and dearest friend ROBERT, abbot, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: that which is due to a dearest friend.

Though I knew you late, you have been taken from me quickly, dearest Robert. Yet I am consoled because I suffer this only in body; for in spirit you are always with me. But when would I bear even this with equanimity, if God alone were not the cause? The time will come—yes, it will come—when we shall be restored to one another, when each will rejoice fully in himself and both in each other, present to ourselves in both portions of our being, never afterwards to be divided from one another in either. The bond of so great a union will be he who is now the cause of so slight a separation: ever to be present to us, ever to preserve us present to ourselves. We greet all your sons and ours, and ask that they pray for us.

## LETTER CCCXXV

[Note: [Col. 0530D] Elsewhere Letter 337; that which was formerly 325 is now 395. Written about the year 1139.]

### TO THE SAME, CONCERNING THE NOVICE IDERIUS

Asked what should be done with an unruly novice, he gives his advice.

[Col. 0530C]

To his most beloved brother and fellow abbot ROBERT of the Dunes, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting.

Regarding this brother, whom you report to be not merely useless but burdensome, apart from what lies hidden within, we give Your Love the same counsel that we would give ourselves. For, in view of what you have related about him, it seems to us that during his probation he has shown himself neither commendable nor fit to be received; and therefore you may, reasonably and with a sound conscience, remove evil from among yourselves. Nevertheless, if your compassion pleases to exalt mercy over judgment, you may still retain him without profession for as long as seems good to you. But we strongly advise against receiving him to profession in this state. Rather, let him be tested again, in case he may be able to show himself such as he ought to be. But if not, the knife of excision must be used, lest one diseased sheep infect the whole flock.

## LETTER CCCXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Elsewhere Letter 391; that which was formerly 326 is now 400. Written about the year 1139.]

### OF ABBOT WILLIAM, TO GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, AND BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Note: [Col. 0531D] This letter was prefixed by way of preface to the disputation of the same William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry near Rheims, against Abelard, published in vol. 4 of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. It was written before all Bernard’s letters against Abelard, as is evident from the beginning of the letter, and thus before the year 1140.]

That they may defend the cause of God and the Church against the errors of Peter Abelard, of which he sets forth several articles.

[Col. 0531A]

To the reverend lords and fathers in Christ, GEOFFREY, Bishop of Chartres, and BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: life and good days.

1. I am ashamed before you, God knows, that concerning a matter of common and grave necessity, while you and 302 others whose duty it was to speak remain silent, I, a person of no standing, am compelled to address you, my lords and fathers. For when I see the faith of our common hope—[Col. 0531B] which Christ consecrated for us by his own blood, for which apostles and martyrs fought unto death, and which holy teachers, having defended it through harsh labours and great exertions, handed down whole and uncorrupted to the very dregs of our times—being grievously and dangerously corrupted, with no one resisting and no one speaking against it, I waste away within myself; and the burning of my heart and the pain of my spirit compel me to speak for that faith, for which, if necessary and fitting, I would even wish to die. Nor is this a matter of trifles, but of faith in the holy Trinity, the person of the Mediator, the Holy Spirit, the grace of God, and the sacrament of our common redemption. For Peter Abelard again teaches novelties and writes novelties; his books cross the seas and leap over the Alps; and his new opinions concerning faith and new doctrines are carried through provinces and kingdoms, publicly preached and [Col. 0531C] freely defended—to such an extent that they are said to possess authority in the Roman curia. I tell you: you are dangerously silent, both for yourselves and for the Church of God. We count it as nothing that the faith for which we have denied ourselves should be corrupted; we do not fear offending God, lest we cause offence. I tell you: this evil, still in labour, is bringing forth; but unless it is forestalled, it will break out into a basilisk, for which scarcely an enchanter may be found. Consider why I say this.

2. By chance I recently came upon the reading of a little book by that man, entitled *The Theology of Peter Abelard*. I confess that the title made me curious to read it. There were, moreover, two little books containing nearly the same matter, except that one contained somewhat more and the other somewhat less. [Col. 0531D] When I found in them certain things which greatly disturbed me, I noted them, and noted beneath them why they disturbed me; and I sent them to you together with the books themselves. Whether they disturbed me rightly is for your judgment. For when I was deeply troubled by unprecedented novelties of language in matters of faith, and by new inventions of unheard-of meanings, and had no one upon whom to lay the matter, I chose you above all others, to whom I might turn and whom I might summon in the cause of God and of the whole Latin Church. This man also [Col. 0532A] fears and dreads you. Close your eyes—whom will he fear? And he who already says what he says, what will he not say when he fears no one? For when almost all teachers of ecclesiastical doctrine had died out from the Church, [Note: [Col. 0532D] Hugo Metellus writes almost the same in his fourth letter to Innocent against the same Abelard: “When Anselm of Laon and William of Châlons had died, the fire of the word of God failed upon the earth,” etc.] the enemy within, rushing as it were into an empty commonwealth of the Church, seized for himself a singular mastery within it. In divine Scripture he does what he used to do in dialectic: he produces inventions of his own, yearly novelties; a censor of faith, not its pupil; a corrector, not an imitator.

3. These, therefore, are the propositions collected from his little works which I thought should be laid before you:

1. That he defines faith as an estimation of things not seen.
2. That he calls the names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit improper when applied to God, and says that this is a description [Col. 0532B] of the fullness of the highest good.
3. That the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power.
4. Concerning the Holy Spirit, that he is not from the substance of the Father and Son as the Son is from the substance of the Father.
5. That the Holy Spirit is the soul of the world.
6. That by free choice, without assisting grace, we are able both to will and to act rightly.
7. That Christ did not assume flesh and suffer in order to free us from the devil’s right.
8. That Christ, God and man, is not the third person in the Trinity.
9. That in the sacrament of the altar the form of the former substance remains in the air.
10. That he says demonic suggestions occur in human beings through natural causes (*per physicam*).
11. That from Adam we inherit not the guilt of original sin but its punishment.
12. That there is no sin except in consent to sin [Col. 0532C] and contempt of God.
13. That he says no sin is committed through concupiscence, pleasure, or ignorance, and that such things are not sin but nature.

4. For the moment, I judged that these few propositions, gathered together from his works, ought first to be offered to you, in order to stir you up and excuse us, so that we may not seem to have been disturbed without cause. With other relevant matters, however, I shall undertake to set these out more fully, with the aid of him in whose hand are both we and our words; making little of it if I displease you in speech, provided that I do not displease in faith. Thus, if I can in any way persuade you that I have been rightly disturbed, you too may be moved; and in a matter concerning the head, whether he be [Col. 0532D] foot, hand, or even eye, do not be afraid. I too loved him, and would wish to love him—God is witness—but in this matter no one shall ever be my neighbour or friend. Nor should this evil be approached by secret admonition or correction, since, by betraying himself, he has made it so public. There are, I hear, other works of his still, whose titles are *Yes and No* and *Know Yourself*, and some others of which I fear that, just as they are monstrous in title, [Col. 0533A] so they may be monstrous in doctrine. But, as they say, they hate the light, and are not found even when sought. But now let us come to the matter itself, etc.

## LETTER CCCXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0533D] Letter 392 in other editions; what was formerly 327 is now 339. Written about the year 1139.]

### BERNARD’S REPLY TO ABBOT WILLIAM

He commends the treatise written against Peter Abelard and promises a mutual conference after Easter.

To his most beloved William, brother Bernard.

I judge your agitation both just and necessary. That it is not idle, moreover, is shown by the little book which strikes at and stops the mouths of those speaking iniquity. Not that I have yet examined it as carefully as you direct; but from what I was able to see in a rapid reading, I confess that it pleases me, and I judge it powerful to overwhelm false doctrine. Yet because, as you know very well, I am not accustomed to place sufficient trust in my own judgment, especially in matters so great, I think it worthwhile—particularly considering the opportunity—that you and I should meet somewhere and discuss everything together. I do not, however, think this can take place before Easter, lest the devotion to prayer which the present season requires should be hindered. As for my silence and patience in these matters, be patient with me: for until now I have known little, indeed almost nothing, of these things. [Note: [Col. 0533D] Hence it is clear that William was among the first instigators against Abelard, as William himself expressly affirms in the preceding letter by complaining of Geoffrey’s and Bernard’s silence.] Yet God is able, through your prayers, to give me a good spirit for the course to which you exhort me. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0533D] A new letter; what was formerly 328 is now 414. Written about the year 1140.]

### TO THE ROMAN PONTIFF

[Note: [Col. 0533D] This letter followed another by a certain A., addressed to the abbot of the monastery of Rieti, and was entitled “To the Same Person.” That it was sent to Innocent or Eugenius, and indeed by Bernard, is evident from the following letter, which concerns the same matter: namely, the elected bishop of Rodez, successor to Adhemar, whose name is unknown. In Letter 240, no. 1, Bernard congratulates Eugenius upon the conclusion [Col. 0534D] of the affair of the Church of Rodez—namely, upon the deposition, it seems, of the unworthy bishop of Rodez, of whom this and the following letter speak.]

Against the elected bishop of Rodez.

[Col. 0533C] Until now, yielding to the prayers of friends, we have written in season and out of season; but now, even if we wished to remain silent, Christian religion forbids it. “Cursed,” says the prophet, “is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48:10). Wickedness prospers daily; the desires of evil men succeed; and there is no one who comes up against them or sets himself as a wall for the house of Israel. Behold, even in your days, utterly corrupt men, who have made a covenant with death and a compact with hell, are striving with hands and feet to enter the Holy of Holies. Why this patience? The clergy of Rodez [Note: [Col. 0534D] One should read *Rutinenses*, as is gathered from the following letter. Rutila is a monastery in the diocese of Trier, mentioned in Book IV of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 47; it is irrelevant to this passage.] chose a person congenial to their vices; nor were they ashamed, even before your eyes, to cover truth with falsehood, as is said, both concerning the person elected and concerning the business of the election. [Col. 0534A] This man, elected not by God but by men, has many witnesses to his disgrace and none to his exoneration; and, to speak elliptically with you, it is more honourable to be silent about him than to speak. Far be it that in your days such monsters should be promoted: that he should be appointed guardian of souls who counts for nothing the shedding of Christ’s blood and the price of his own soul’s redemption! Why did they cunningly insert into their case some mention of wrong and oppression in relation to an appeal, so that by these means they might incline the curia toward themselves? Do not accept a lying word. For, as is learned from the testimony of truthful men, no oppression of an appeal followed where no appeal had preceded. Therefore what was done, on the counsel of religious persons, through the bishop must receive confirmation through you, with mighty hand [Col. 0534B] and uplifted arm. We also wish that the archbishop himself [Note: [Col. 0534D] Namely, the archbishop of Bourges, whose suffragan is the bishop of Rodez.] be commended to you more and more—a person for whom we would neither ask nor wish to be heard, unless he honoured his ministry.

## LETTER CCCXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0534D] A new letter; what was formerly 329 is now 318. Written about the year 1140.]

### TO THE BISHOP OF LIMOGES

Against the same elected bishop of Rodez.

The words which I speak to you I do not speak for my own sake, nor do I seek in them what is mine. I speak to you for your own sake. The days of man are brief. So long as you are bishop of Limoges, honour your ministry, so that we may see your good works. Hearing that the case of the elected bishop of Cahors [Note: [Col. 0534D] Perhaps one should read *Caturcensis* [of Cahors], for this letter can scarcely be referred to another city. If this seems correct, this passage appears to concern the election of Raymond, whom William of the Cross therefore wrongly removes from the list of bishops of Cahors.] has been entrusted to you by the lord Pope and must be concluded by you according to canonical procedure, all appeal being set aside, we [Col. 0534C] became as those comforted. For behold, the time and the business are at hand in which the Church of God will see whether there is sound judgment in the breast of a bishop. The fear of God, the force of the canons, and the love of justice will no longer be idle—if indeed they are in you. In the Church of Rodez the question concerns a shepherd, a bishop of souls, and a successor of Christ: that man, I mean, who is to raise up seed for his deceased brother. And who is so suited to this? Is it he whom life has stained, conscience accused, and public report exposed? Is it he who has descended from abbey to abbey—or rather, from abyss to abyss—so that the same man is both violator of virgins and consecrator? And where now will be that saying of the Apostle: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1:7)? [Col. 0535A] Do not, therefore, stand against yourself by saying one thing and doing another. Let your works answer your words in agreement upon the same matter, lest that saying concerning certain persons be applied to you: “Their tongues have failed against them” (Ps. 63:9). Behold, the matter is in your hand. Nevertheless guard your soul, and do not share in the sins of others. Through you he will stand, or through you he will fall; but if through you he falls, you will consecrate your hands to the Lord.

## LETTER CCCXXX

[Note: [Col. 0535D] A new letter; what was formerly 330 is now 349. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT, AGAINST PETER ABELARD

To his most beloved father and lord Innocent, Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

[Col. 0535B] The bride of Christ has wept bitterly in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks; among all her beloved there is none to comfort her. While the Bridegroom delays, the Shunammite has been entrusted to you, lord, in the place of her pilgrimage. To no one does she confess her injuries more familiarly, to no one does she disclose more secretly her ardours and groans, than to the friend of the Bridegroom. For because you love the Bridegroom, you do not despise the bride when she cries to you in need and tribulation. Among all the kinds of enemies by whom the Church of God is surrounded, like a lily among thorns, nothing is more dangerous or troublesome than when she is torn inwardly by those whom she holds in her bosom and nourishes at her breasts. Of and concerning such persons is that voice [Col. 0535C] of one grieving and groaning: “My friends and my neighbours drew near against me and stood” (Ps. 37:12). No plague is more effective in doing harm than an intimate enemy. The familiarity of Absalom and the kiss of Judas are proofs for us. Another foundation is being laid for us besides that which has been laid. A new faith is being forged in France: virtue and vice are discussed not morally; sacraments, not faithfully; and the mystery of the holy Trinity, not simply and soberly, but contrary to what we have received. [Note: [Col. 0535D] Here *praeter ut* has the force of *praeterquam*, “contrary to”; it is used with precisely the same intent and formula concerning Abelard in Letter CCCXXXVI: “declaring concerning the Holy Spirit contrary to what we have received.” EDIT.]

Master Peter and Arnold, from whose pestilence you cleansed Italy, have stood and gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. Scale is joined to scale, and not even a breath passes between them. They have become corrupt and abominable in their pursuits; and by the leaven of their corruption they corrupt the faith of the simple, disturb the order of morals, and stain the chastity of the Church. In the image and likeness of him who transforms himself into an angel of light, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power, they are adorned like the likeness of a temple, that they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. [Col. 0535D] We escaped the roar of Peter Leo, who occupied the seat of Simon Peter; but we have encountered Peter the Dragon, who attacks the faith of Simon Peter. The former persecuted the Church of God openly, like a ravening lion; this man, however, like [Col. 0536A] a dragon, sits in ambush in secret places, to kill the innocent. But you, Lord God, will humble the eyes of the proud; you will tread upon the Lion and the Dragon. That man harmed while he lived, and the end of his life was also the end of his malice; but this one, writing new doctrines, has already provided means of pouring his poison into posterity, of harming every generation yet to come.

Finally, to say a few things out of many: our theologian, with Arius, establishes degrees and ladders in the Trinity; with Pelagius, sets free will before grace; with Nestorius, divides Christ and excludes the assumed man from fellowship in the Trinity. Yet in all this he boasts that he has opened the fountains of knowledge to the cardinals and clerics of the curia; that he has enclosed his books and opinions in the hands and bosoms of Romans; and he takes into the protection of his error those by whom he ought to be judged and condemned. [Col. 0536B] With what mind, with what conscience, do you have recourse to the defender of faith, you persecutor of faith? With what eyes, with what face, will you look upon the friend of the Bridegroom, you violator of the bride? Oh, if the care of the brethren did not detain me! Oh, if bodily weakness did not hinder me! How greatly would I desire to see the friend of the Bridegroom zealously defending the bride in the Bridegroom’s absence! Shall I, who could not be silent concerning injuries done to my Lord, endure the wounds of the suffering Church? But you, most beloved Father, do not withdraw your help far from her. Look to her defence; gird yourself with your sword. For because iniquity abounds, the love of many is growing cold; and unless you [Col. 0536C] apply your hand, the bride of Christ will presently go out and depart after the tracks of the flocks, and feed flocks beside the shepherds’ tents.

## LETTER CCCXXXI

[Note: [Col. 0536D] A new letter; what was formerly 331 is now 350. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO STEPHEN, CARDINAL AND BISHOP OF PALESTRINA

On the same subject.

To the venerable lord and most beloved Father S., by God’s grace bishop of Palestrina, brother Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord.

I report to you the distress and groans of Christ’s bride all the more familiarly because I have known you to be the friend of the Bridegroom, rejoicing with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice. For I am confident concerning you in the Lord, if I know your inward man well, that you seek not your own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Peter [Col. 0536D] Abelard, persecutor of the Catholic faith and enemy of Christ’s cross, is shown by his life, conduct, and books now emerging from darkness into light to be such. Outwardly he shows himself a monk, inwardly a heretic, possessing nothing of the monk except name and habit. He opens the old cisterns and broken reservoirs of heretics, so that ox and ass may fall into them. He had been silent for many days; but when he was silent in Brittany, he conceived pain, and now in France he has conceived iniquity. The twisting serpent came forth from his cave, and, in the likeness of the hydra, after one head had first been cut off, produced seven [Col. 0537A] heads in place of one. When one was cut off, one of his heresies was cut off at Soissons; but now in its place seven and more heresies have arisen, a copy of which we have had and sent to you.

He introduces crude and inexperienced hearers, newly separated from the breasts of dialectic, and those who, so to speak, can scarcely bear the first elements of faith, into the mystery of the holy Trinity, into the Holy of Holies, into the King’s chamber, and to him who made darkness his hiding-place. Finally, our theologian, with Arius, establishes degrees and ladders in the Trinity; with Pelagius, sets free will before grace; with Nestorius, divides Christ and excludes the assumed man from fellowship in the Trinity. Thus, yes, thus, ranging through almost all the sacraments, he reaches mightily from end to end [Col. 0537B] and orders all things damnably. Moreover, he boasts that he has infected the Roman curia with the poison of his novelty, that he has enclosed his books and opinions in Roman hands and bosoms, and he takes into the protection of his error those by whom he ought to be judged and condemned. May God provide for his Church, for which he died, so as to present her to himself without spot or wrinkle, so that perpetual silence may be imposed upon the man whose mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit.

## LETTER CCCXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0537D] A new letter; what was formerly 332 is now 367. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO CARDINAL G.

Again against Peter Abelard.

To his venerable lord and beloved father, G., cardinal of the holy [Col. 0537C] Roman Church, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

I cannot be silent concerning the injuries of Christ; the anguish and sorrows of the Church, the misery of the needy, and the groaning of the poor. We have fallen upon perilous times. We have teachers with itching ears; disciples turn their hearing from truth and are converted to fables. In France we have Peter Abelard, a monk without rule, a prelate without care, an abbot without discipline, disputing with boys and associating with women. He sets before his household stolen waters and hidden bread in his books; and in his sermons he introduces profane novelties of words and meanings. He does not approach the darkness in which God was, as Moses did, alone, but with a great crowd and [Col. 0537D] his disciples. In lanes and streets there is disputation concerning the Catholic faith, the Virgin’s childbirth, the sacrament of the altar, and the incomprehensible mystery of the holy Trinity. We escaped the roar of Peter Leo; we have encountered the hissing of Peter the Dragon. But you, Lord Jesus, will humble the eyes of the proud; you will tread upon the Lion and the Dragon. That man harmed while he lived, and the end of his life was also the end of his malice; but this one has already provided how he may pour his poison into posterity and harm every generation yet to come. [Col. 0538A] He has marked the leprosy of his inventions with ink and pen. We have had his books and have sent them to you. Know the author of the work from the work itself. See that our theologian, with Arius, establishes degrees and ladders in the Trinity; with Pelagius, sets free will before grace; and with Nestorius, dividing Christ, excludes the assumed man from fellowship in the Trinity. And these are but a few things out of many. Will there be no one among you to feel Christ’s injury, to love justice, to hate iniquity? If the mouth speaking iniquity is not stopped, let him see and judge who alone considers labour and pain.

## LETTER CCCXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0537D] A new letter; what was formerly 333 is now 386. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO CARDINAL G.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] This is Gregory of Tarquinia, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, created by Callistus II [Col. 0538D].]

Again on the same subject.

[Col. 0538B] To the venerable man and his friend G., cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and affection.

According to your custom, whenever I enter the curia, you must always rise for me. The words seem as though spoken in jest, but the matter is serious. Behold, I enter the curia, I say, according to the cause, not according to the person. You who used to rise for my person, rise now for my cause—or rather, for Christ’s cause: for Christ is in the cause and truth is in danger. Rise—indeed, arise—against him who disputes concerning faith against faith, who attacks the law with the words of the law, whose hand is against all and the hands of all against him. This is Peter Abelard, who writes, teaches, and disputes concerning morals, sacraments, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, dividing them as he wishes. [Col. 0538C] Now he enters the curia after he has agitated and disturbed the Church, not to heal her wounds, but to make excuses excusing sins. If you are her son, defend the womb that bore you and the breasts that you sucked.

## LETTER CCCXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0538D] A new letter; what was formerly 334 is now 362. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO GUIDO OF PISA

[Note: [Col. 0538D] Guido Moricotus of Vico, a Pisan, cardinal of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, created by Innocent.]

Against the same Abelard.

To Guido of Pisa, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: a sound mind in a sound body (JUVENAL).

I could confidently entrust my own cause to you because of the duty of our mutual affection; but I entrust this cause with so much greater confidence as the one whose cause it is deserves greater love. [Col. 0538D] It is Christ’s cause—indeed, Christ is in the cause and truth is in danger. Christ’s garments are divided and the Church’s sacraments are torn apart; but the seamless tunic, woven from above throughout, remains whole. This tunic is the unity of the Church, which knows no tearing and accepts no division. For what is woven from above, what has been joined together by the Holy Spirit, will not be dissolved by men. Although heretics have sharpened their tongues like serpents and discharged every sting of their ingenuity in order to disturb the Church’s peace, [Col. 0539A] yet the gates of hell shall not prevail against her. If you are her son, if you acknowledge your mother’s breasts, do not abandon your mother in danger; do not withdraw your shoulders in the time of tribulation. Master Peter enters the curia so that the authority of the Apostolic See may be made a wall and bulwark for him, to confirm the errors which he has written, taught, and used to assail the Catholic faith.

## LETTER CCCXXXV

[Note: [Col. 0539D] A new letter; what was formerly 335 is now 368. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO A CERTAIN CARDINAL PRIEST

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The manuscript of Saint-Vaast names him explicitly: to Cardinal Peter. MARTÈNE.]

Again against Peter Abelard.

To the cardinal priest, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and affection in the Lord.

Let no one despise your youth. For the Lord requires not grey hair [Col. 0539B] of the head, but of the mind; and the age of old age is an unstained life. Jeremiah did not fear, nor Daniel shrink back, though both were boys, before shameless elders grown old in evil days. I too would rightly call shameless the man who stains the beauty of the Church and the chastity of faith. This is Peter Abelard, who disputes concerning faith, sacraments, and the mystery of the holy Trinity contrary to what he has received, dividing the matters severally as he wills. Now he enters the curia after he has agitated and disturbed the Church, not to heal her wounds, but because he has turned to words of malice, to make excuses excusing sins. Those who know themselves to be sons of the Church will stand confidently for the Church.

## LETTER CCCXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0539D] A new letter; what was formerly 336 is now 324. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO A CERTAIN ABBOT

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Perhaps to Bernard, an Italian abbot, who had then been sent to Rome by Bernard; see below, Letters 343 and 344.]

On the same subject.

[Col. 0539C]

To his most beloved brother and fellow abbot, brother Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: may you have zeal for God according to knowledge.

“There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest.” If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join himself to him. For God is in the cause. Truth is in danger; Christ’s garments are divided, the Church’s sacraments are torn apart. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head soundness is corrupted; the simplicity of the faithful is mocked. The lion is near to rising from his lair, the plunderer of nations to lift himself against the Church. Peter Abelard already goes before [Col. 0539D] the face of Antichrist to prepare his ways, declaring concerning faith, sacraments, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit contrary to what we have received. He writes, [Col. 0540A] teaches, and contends in words for the overthrow of his hearers. With Arius he establishes degrees and ladders in the Trinity; with Pelagius he sets free will before grace; he excludes the assumed man from fellowship in the Trinity; with Nestorius he divides Christ. Yet in all this he boasts that he has reconciled the Roman Church to himself, that he has enclosed his books and opinions in Roman hands and bosoms; and in defence of his error he takes those by whom he ought to be judged and condemned. May God see and judge, if the mouth speaking iniquity is not speedily stopped. The bearer of this letter will explain the rest more fully.

## LETTER CCCXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Letter 370 in other editions; what was formerly 337 is now 325. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT, IN THE PERSON OF THE BISHOPS OF FRANCE

[Note: [Col. 0539D] In Vatican manuscript 662 it appears in its proper order after Letter 189, with this heading: “The bishops of France to Lord Pope Innocent.” Here “France” means the metropolitan province of Sens. Hence, in Letter 161, the blood of Archembald, subdeacon of Aurillac, is said to cry to Innocent from France; and Letter 126, no. 4, distinguishes France from Burgundy. Yet under the name France at that time a great part of Second Belgica was also included.]

The bishops of Gaul report to the pontiff what was done in the case of Peter Abelard, who challenged Bernard to a disputation in synod, but refused to answer the articles of heresy brought against him and appealed to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0540B]

To the most reverend father and lord Innocent, by God’s grace supreme pontiff: Henry, archbishop of Sens; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, servant of the holy Apostolic See; [Note: [Col. 0540D] That is, legate. Geoffrey customarily used this title from modesty, as is read in the cartulary of the church of Saint Stephen at Dreux. Others were commonly called vicars of the Holy See.] Elias of Orléans; Hugh of Auxerre; Hatto of Troyes; and Manasses, bishop of Meaux: devoted prayers and due obedience.

1. No one doubts that things confirmed by apostolic authority are always held ratified and can thereafter be impaired by no one’s cavilling or corrupted by envy. Therefore, most blessed Father, we judged it fitting to refer to your Apostolic See certain matters which recently occurred to be dealt with in our presence. Since they appeared to us and to many religious and learned men to have been reasonably conducted, they await the confirmation of your Serenity’s judgment and, together with it, strengthening by your authority in perpetuity. Accordingly, since throughout almost all Gaul, in cities, villages, and castles, scholars were disputing about the holy Trinity—which is God—not only within the schools but even at street corners; and not only the learned or mature, but boys and simple people, or indeed fools; and since they were also propounding many other things wholly discordant, absurd, and plainly opposed to the Catholic faith [Col. 0540D] and the authorities of the holy Fathers; and since those who held sound views and judged that these follies ought to be rejected [Col. 0541A] [Note: [Col. 0541D] The ancients called even the gravest heresies “follies,” as has elsewhere been observed in Preface 2 to the Fourth Century, Benedictines, no. 133. Jerome, writing to Alypius and Augustine concerning the Celestian heresy, says: “Nor is it a great matter to answer most foolish nonsense”; and Bernard himself again does so in Sermon 65 on the Song of Songs, no. 8.] repeatedly admonished and rebuked them, they grew stronger all the more vehemently. Relying on the authority of their master Peter Abelard and on a certain book of his which he had entitled *Theology*, as well as on other little works by the same author, they armed themselves more and more to establish those profane inventions, not without the loss of many souls. Yet those who held sound views were afraid to raise a formal question concerning matters which had deeply disturbed and harmed both us and many others.

2. But the lord abbot of Clairvaux, having heard these things from various persons repeatedly, indeed having carefully examined them in the aforesaid *Theology* of Master Peter and in other books of his upon whose reading he had perhaps happened, first privately and then, with two or three witnesses brought in, according to the Gospel precept, [Col. 0541B] approached the man. He admonished him quite amicably and familiarly to restrain his hearers from such things and correct his books. He also urged many scholars to repudiate and reject the books full of poisons, and to beware of and abstain from teaching that harmed the Catholic faith.

Master Peter bore this rather impatiently and with excessive bitterness. He began repeatedly to press us, and would not cease until, writing to the lord abbot of Clairvaux upon the matter, we summoned him to appear before us at Sens on an appointed day, namely the octave of Pentecost. Master Peter declared and offered himself ready to prove and defend the opinions for which the lord abbot of Clairvaux had rebuked him, [Col. 0541C] as stated above. The lord abbot, however, replied to us neither that he would come on the appointed day nor that he would dispute against Peter. But because Master Peter nevertheless meanwhile began to summon his disciples from every side and to entreat them to come to the forthcoming disputation between himself and the lord abbot of Clairvaux, there to defend with him both his opinion and learning; and because this was by no means unknown to the lord abbot of Clairvaux, he feared that, because of the occasion provided by his absence, so many profane—not opinions, but insanities—might seem worthy of greater authority both to those less able to understand and to their defenders. Therefore, on the day we had appointed for him, although he had by no means accepted it, touched by the zeal of pious fervour—indeed, inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit—he voluntarily presented himself before us at Sens. On that day, namely the octave of Pentecost, our brother bishops and suffragans had assembled with us at Sens, on account of the honour and reverence due to the holy relics which we had announced that we would reveal to the people in our church.

[Col. 0542A] 3. Accordingly, in the presence of the glorious king of the French, Louis, together with William, the religious count of Nevers, and the lord archbishop of Reims with certain of his suffragan bishops; with ourselves also and our suffragans present, excepting the bishops of Paris and Nevers; with many religious abbots and wise, highly learned clerics—there were present the lord abbot of Clairvaux and Master Peter with his supporters. [Note: [Col. 0541D] Besides others, Hugh the Chronographer of Saint-Marian reports that this occurred in the year 1140, though neither he nor the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif mentions the discovery of relics. In his treatment of this synod, Otto, bishop of Freising, writes in Book I, chapter 48, of the *Deeds of Frederick* that Count Palatine Theobald, with other nobles, was present.]

Why say more? When the lord abbot brought forward Master Peter’s book of *Theology*, and presented from that same book the 310 passages he had marked as absurd—indeed plainly heretical—so that Master Peter might either deny having written them, or, if he acknowledged them as his own, prove or correct them, Master Peter Abelard seemed distrustful [Col. 0542B] and evasive, and refused to answer. Although he was granted a free hearing, a safe venue, and impartial judges, he nevertheless appealed to your presence, most holy Father, and left the assembly with his followers.

4. Yet, although this appeal appeared less than canonical, out of deference to the Apostolic See we were unwilling to pronounce any sentence upon the man himself. But the propositions of his perverse doctrine, since they had infected many people and by their contagion had penetrated to the innermost recesses of hearts—having often been read and reread in public hearing, and having been proved most plainly, both by the truest arguments and by the authorities of blessed Augustine and other holy Fathers adduced by the lord of Clairvaux, to be not merely false but heretical—we condemned on the day before the appeal was made to you. And because they draw many into a most pernicious and plainly damnable error, we unanimously and with many urgent prayers request, beloved lord, that by your authority they be marked with perpetual condemnation, and that all who stubbornly and contentious­ly defend them be punished by you, most just Father, with a fitting penalty. If moreover your Reverence were to impose silence upon the oft-mentioned Peter, wholly take away his freedom both to read and to write, and condemn his books, undoubtedly stained with perverse doctrine, then, once thorns and briars had been torn away from the Church of God, the glad harvest of Christ might still grow, flourish, and bear fruit. We have sent you in writing, reverend Father, certain of the [Col. 0542D] chapters condemned by us, so that, having heard these, you may more readily judge the remaining body of the work.

## LETTER CCCXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0542D] Elsewhere Letter 369; what was formerly 338 is now 401. Written in the year of Christ 1140. See Letter 187 and following, and the Notes.]

### TO HAIMERIC, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR

Since Peter Abelard has been convicted of heresy, he ought not to find refuge among the cardinals and the Roman curia.

To the illustrious man and intimate friend HAIMERIC, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy [Col. 0543A] Roman Church, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: to provide what is good before God and men.

1. As we have heard, so we have seen the books and propositions of Master Peter Abelard. We marked the words, we examined the mysteries—and mysteries of iniquity were found. Our theologian attacks the Law with the words of the Law. He casts what is holy to dogs and pearls before swine; he corrupts the faith of the simple and stains the Church’s chastity.

> The jar will long retain the scent  
> With which, when new, it was once steeped.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.69

His book had passed through fire and been brought into refreshment. And now, within the Church, an enemy of the Church, [Col. 0543B] a persecutor of the faith, rests in the bosom of the faith. He has been poured out like water. Let not him who went up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch increase. That man has defiled the Church; he has rubbed his rust upon the minds of the simple. He strives by reasoning to investigate what a devout mind apprehends by the living power of faith. The faith of the devout believes; it does not dispute. But this man, holding God in suspicion, refuses to believe except what he has first examined by reason. And whereas the prophet says, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint), he rebukes voluntary faith under the name of light-mindedness, abusing that testimony of Solomon: “He who readily believes is light of heart” (Ecclus. 19:4). Let him then rebuke the blessed Virgin Mary, because she readily believed the angel who announced [Col. 0543C] and said, “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1:31). Let him likewise reproach the man who, at life’s final extremity, believed the word of the dying one who said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Conversely, let him praise the hardness of heart of those to whom it was said: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the Prophets have spoken!” (Luke 24:25). Let him also commend the slowness of the one to whom it was said: “Because you did not believe my words, you shall be silent and unable to speak” (Luke 1:20).

2. Finally, to say a little of much for the brevity of a letter: this outstanding teacher, with Arius, arranges ranks and ladders within the Trinity; with Pelagius, he sets free choice above grace; with Nestorius, by dividing Christ, he excludes the assumed man from fellowship with the Trinity [Col. 0543D]. Yet in all this he boasts that he has opened the springs of knowledge to the cardinals and clerics of the curia, that he has lodged his books and opinions in the hands and bosoms of the Romans; and he enlists in protection of his error those by whom he ought to have been judged and condemned. Hyacinth showed us many evils. [Note: [Col. 0543D] See Letter 189.] He did not commit them—not because he was unwilling, but because he was unable. Yet we bear it calmly, since in that curia he spared neither the person of the lord Pope nor the curia itself. My Nicholas—indeed yours as well—will report more fully in person the other matters [Col. 0544A] that he saw and heard.

## LETTER CCCXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0543D] Elsewhere Letter 327; what was formerly 339 is now 402. Written about the year 1140.]

### TO POPE INNOCENT

He affirms the innocence of Alvis, bishop of Arras, against his slanderers.

To his most beloved father and lord, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

It is neither new nor surprising that the human mind can be deceived or can deceive. One must guard against both, because danger lies on either side. The Angel of great counsel provided you a safeguard against both when he said: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16), so that neither prudence might be deceived [Col. 0544B] nor simplicity deceive. The monks of Marchiennes [Note: [Col. 0543D] Marchiennes was a noble Benedictine monastery on the Scarpe, in the diocese of Tournai, founded by Saint Rictrude in the seventh century.] came to you in a spirit of lying and a spirit of error, against the Lord and against his anointed. They framed an iniquitous charge against the bishop of Arras, whose manner of life and conduct have hitherto been of good repute everywhere. Who are these men who bite like dogs, who call good evil and make light darkness? Who are they who, contrary to the Law, curse the deaf and put a stumbling block before the blind? (Lev. 19:14). Why, lord, are you angry with your son? Why have you made his enemies rejoice? Where is that saying of the Apostle: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1)? I trust in the Lord that their counsel shall be scattered; and when what is true appears, what rests upon falsehood shall be brought to nothing, so that iniquity may have lied to itself. We have heard with our own ears how faithfully and steadfastly he spoke before the king and princes in defense of fidelity to the Roman Church. He will come to you in his innocence on the day of his summons. He has sent ahead his son, the archdeacon who bears this letter, whose person and character we commend to your gentleness. Moreover, the abbot of Saint-Vaast is coming to you [Col. 0544C]—a man plainly hostile to himself, to his own people, and to his church; a man who has taken the title of abbot in vain, for he seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. And such a father, such also is the son who is with him: one who has spared neither his conscience nor his reputation. Mockery and derision are the lot of those around [Col. 0544D] him—I mean G., his monk. May the Spirit of truth grant you to divide light from darkness, to reject evil and choose good.

## LETTER CCCXL

[Note: [Col. 0544D] A new letter; what was formerly 340 is now 403. Written about the year 1140.]

### TO THE SAME POPE INNOCENT

On behalf of the bishop of Angers.

To his most beloved lord and father, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

[Col. 0545A] The bishop of Angers [Note: [Col. 0545D] Ulgerius, to whom Letter 200 is addressed.] is now worn down by age, labors, and dangers. Whose heart would not be moved, unless it were that of one who has stripped himself of all feelings of compassion and humanity? These things move me on behalf of this man, whose old age is made venerable by both his life and learning, if one act alone be excepted. Since we do not yet know what was done between him and the abbey, we presume to write nothing concerning an unknown matter. But if it is established that he has done what he promised, we believe that nothing remains except that he be restored to the fullness of his favor and office.

## LETTER CCCXLI

[Note: [Col. 0545D] Elsewhere Letter 315; what was formerly 341 is now 385. Written about the year 1140.]

### TO MALACHY, ARCHBISHOP OF IRELAND

He receives gratefully the brothers, letter, and staff sent by him. He directs that a suitable place be prepared for religious men, and commends himself to Malachy’s prayers.

[Col. 0545B]

To the venerable lord and most blessed father MALACHY, by God’s grace archbishop of the Irish [Note: [Col. 0545D] Ussher includes this letter among the Irish letters, where, against John Picard, he observes that the primates of Armagh, before receiving the pallium—which was granted to them only in 1150—were called archbishops and exercised metropolitan authority. Ussher is especially influenced by the title “archbishop” applied to Malachy, who some years before had relinquished his archbishopric and assumed administration of the bishopric of Down, *Life*, chapter 14. Yet Bernard could have given him the title archbishop by reason of his former rank, though in what follows he calls him only bishop.], legate of the Apostolic See, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: may you find grace with the Lord.

1. Amid the many storms and cares of my heart, amid whose multitude my soul has been greatly troubled, the brothers coming from a distant land to serve the Lord, your letter, and your staff have themselves consoled me: the letter by displaying good will; the staff by supporting the body in its weakness; the brothers by serving God in a spirit of humility. We have received all; all please us; all together work for good. But as for your wish that two of the brothers [Col. 0545C] should be sent to you to inspect a site [Note: [Col. 0546D] That is, the site of Mellifont monastery, founded in 1141 in the diocese of Armagh, with Christian as abbot of Mellifont; see Letter now numbered 357, no. 3. On this monastery, see the Acts of St Malachy and St Bernard, and Letter 254, in Chesne, vol. 4.], after taking counsel with the brothers we judged that they should not be separated from one another until Christ is more fully formed in them, until they are thoroughly taught the battles of the Lord. When, therefore, they have been trained in the school of the Holy Spirit and clothed with power from on high, then at last the sons will return to their father, that they may sing the song of the Lord no longer in a foreign land but in their own.

2. Meanwhile, according to the wisdom given you by the Lord, and following the character of the places you saw among us, provide and prepare for them a site set apart from the tumults of the world. For the time is near when, through God’s grace working in you, we shall produce for you new men out of old. Blessed be the name of the Lord [Col. 0545D] for ever, by whose gift it comes about that I have sons in common with you: your preaching planted them, our exhortation watered them, but God [Col. 0546A] gave the increase. We ask your Holiness to preach the word of the Lord, to give the knowledge of salvation to his people. For a twofold obligation rests upon you, both from the office of legate and from episcopal business. Moreover, since we all offend in many things (James 3:2), and, being often among worldly people, gather much of the world’s dust, I commend myself to your prayers and those of your people, that Jesus Christ himself, the fountain of mercy and source of loving-kindness, may deign to wash and cleanse us in the fountain of his mercy. He said to Peter: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (John 13:8). Yet I ask this not only through prayers but almost as a debt, since I cry to the Lord for you, if the prayer of a sinner can avail. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CCCXLII

[Note: [Col. 0546D] A new letter; what was formerly 342 is now 383. Written in the year of Christ 1140. See Letter 223.]

### TO JOSCELIN, BISHOP OF SOISSONS

He requests that the archbishop of Bordeaux be vindicated before the king.

[Col. 0546B]

To the venerable lord and most beloved father JOSCELIN, by God’s grace bishop of Soissons, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: may you find grace with the Lord.

1. It is an injury to the kingdom and its princes if the king’s affairs burst from his own bosom into public view, and are conducted with counsel not so much deliberate as rash. It pleases me—and pleases me greatly—that the king believes you and trusts you. For I know that you zealously seek the king’s good and the honor of his kingdom, and I know likewise that the spirit of counsel [Col. 0546C] is with you. So it ought to be. This order, this principle, this measure should be seen in a man of counsel: that he should love and be wise. Upon the mouth of these two—that is, love and wisdom—every word of counsel shall stand. If these two come together as one, he will be able to utter a good word and discern the deeds to be done for the king. But if, in administering counsel, love abandons prudence, or prudence abandons love, “woe to the land whose king is a child!” Let my soul not enter the counsel of those who either love me but are not prudent, or are prudent but do not love me. For thus unhappy Adam fell from the degrees of eternity when he followed the counsel of the ungodly: Eve, who loved but was not prudent; and the serpent, who was prudent but did not love.

[Col. 0546D] 2. Why does my lord king seek to bring the archbishop of Bordeaux [Note: [Col. 0546D] This was then Geoffrey of Loratorium, to whom, before he became archbishop, Letter 125 was written. In printed editions this is wrongly addressed to John.] into a suit without cause? Is this done on your advice? Far be such counsel [Col. 0547A] from you; far be this suspicion from me. What evil, after all, has that man done? That he consecrated, in canonical liberty, the person elected by the equal peace, desire, and voice of the people of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0547D] Grimoard, formerly abbot of Blessed Mary of Allodiis; his election, made in 1140, was for some time suspended by Louis VII.]? That he gave to the poor and to churches the money of the people of Poitiers, which the deceased had distributed, rather than taking it from the mouths of the hungry or from the bosom of the Church? Behold, this blood is demanded from his hand. If it is a fault that he appointed a shepherd to wandering sheep, that he did not despoil the orphan and widow, that he preserved inviolate the privileges of the Apostolic See, then he cannot be excused. O counsel without counsel, in which justice is reckoned a crime and innocence an offense! Take heed to yourselves, bishops: for this is your own concern—“when your neighbor’s wall is burning” (Horace, *Epistles* I.2.84).

[Col. 0547B] 3. But upon you, lord, since you are more closely attached to the king’s side and his affairs depend upon your nod, lies the duty of acting with the king for your fellow bishops, so that he may not kindle the full force of his anger. I tell you: that man is undaunted, a man powerful in deed and word; he can scarcely be torn from his right. For he holds a great place in that land. If the matter is stirred up, many will stand with him in his trials. Therefore see that no one adds oil to the flame. Let the fire be extinguished before the conflagration gathers strength:

> Too late is medicine prepared  
> When evils have gained strength through long delay.  
> —Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, 91–92

## LETTER CCCXLIII

[Note: [Col. 0547D] A new letter; what was formerly 343 is now 384. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### FROM BERNARD, ABBOT IN ITALY, TO INNOCENT

He complains that not everything at the monastery of the Savior has occurred according to the pontiff’s promises.

[Col. 0547C]

To his desired lord and most delightful father, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, his servant BERNARD: the prayers of the poor.

I am constrained by two things: shame commands silence, and necessity commands speech. I shall therefore speak to the lord, though I am dust and ashes; but I shall speak in the bitterness of my soul. We complain of you, lord, but before you. The complaint indeed is in shadow, but the cause of complaint has now pitched its tent in the sun. What you commanded has been done: we came to the monastery of Saint Savior [Note: [Col. 0547D] This monastery still exists, eight miles from Farfa and subject to it; the monks of Farfa migrate there in summer. Compare Letter 184 and the Notes there.] as you instructed your servant, our father, in your letter. Where, then, [Col. 0547D] are now my expectation and your promise? We passed through fire and water, and, unless the Lord had been in us, perhaps the water would have swallowed us up. We have been exhausted by dangers of robbers and rivers, dangers in cities and in the wilderness, dangers on land and at sea; and there was none to help. All these things have come [Col. 0548A] upon us, yet the end has not at once come. By your letters, lord, we were drawn from the bosom of our father; at the word of a single command, leaving brothers and father, we ran in the fragrance of your commandments. By your letters we were shaken from our mother’s lap and from the breasts of her consolation; we were cast out from the place of delight, and you set, lord, a flaming sword to prevent our return—would that it were a turning sword. The crown has fallen from our head; our dance has become mourning. How shall we sing, lord, the song of the Lord in a foreign land? O how much sweeter and safer it would have been for us to rejoice in our mother’s bosom and in the chamber of our mother! Thus we ran as though toward an uncertain goal; thus we fought as though beating the air. Yet your promise [Col. 0548B] was the cause, a promise we believed full of grace and truth. But now—since winter has gone and departed—if it so pleases my lord, let us go forth to see where we may find rest for our feet; for until now hail, snow, ice, and storm winds have prevented us. For it seems most cruel, and far removed from every duty of humanity, to defraud of his desire that man [Note: [Col. 0547D] Namely Atenulf, abbot of Farfa, concerning whom see below.] who began to love us before he knew us, who adopted us as sons with a father’s affection, so that, if it had been possible, he would have plucked out his own eyes and given them to us. My King and my God had nowhere to lay his head, he whose kingdom was not of this world. Would that the world too might reject us and cast us out, wandering in wildernesses, mountains, caves, and caverns [Col. 0548C] of the earth!

## LETTER CCCXLIV

[Note: [Col. 0548D] A new letter; what was formerly 344 is now 315. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### FROM THE SAME BERNARD TO SAINT BERNARD

He complains of the office of superior imposed upon him.

To the venerable lord and most beloved Father P. [Note: [Col. 0548D] That is, Father Bernard. For it is established that this letter was written to St Bernard, and by that Bernard who afterwards became abbot of Saint Anastasius at Aquae Salviae near Rome and finally pope under the name Eugenius III. The preceding letter is also his, as is Letter 428. All these were first published under the name of Bernard.], abbot of Clairvaux, his son B.: that anointing which teaches concerning all things.

Whenever the memory of that day of misery and calamity comes before me, when I was torn from the breasts of your consolation, I feel more inclined to weep than to write anything. If my abundance of prayer equaled that of my tears, it would be easy for you to understand the poor and needy man. My mind turned to meditation, my hand [315] to the pen, and my sorrow was renewed. That most bitter bitterness [Col. 0548D] met me as I wrote, and that sad image of the day on which folly was lifted up upon the lampstand and I was made distraught. I do not reproach, lord, either the work or the intention of your work, which is believed to be in the finger of God; but I lament my own pain a little. For behold, after I was cast [Col. 0549A] away from before your eyes, my life has failed in sorrow and my days in groaning. Alas for me! For I have lost the form by which I was shaped, the mirror of my formation, the light of my eyes. No longer does that sweet voice sound in my ears, nor does that beautiful face appear before my sight, at which my errors used to blush. Why, lord, have I been frustrated of my hope? Why deprived of my desire? My life has been cut off like a weaver’s; while I was still setting up the warp, I was cut down. That wretched sentence has been fulfilled in me; and, as you said in the *Song of Songs*, lord, today I read in the book of experience: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand” (Ps. 48:13). For when I was at Clairvaux I did not sufficiently understand that I was in a place of delight, among the trees of paradise; [Col. 0549B] therefore I treated the desirable land as nothing. What, lord, what did your discernment find pleasing in me, that you made me leader and teacher of nations, that you appointed me prince over your people? Was it my conduct in the world? But that was foul. Was it my conduct in the monastery? But that was sluggish and lukewarm. Why, when I was small in my own eyes, was I made head in the tribe of Israel? Why, when I was not clean from my hidden faults, did you not spare your servant from the faults of others? What shall a man do whom sorrow for the past presses, present labor burdens, and fear of the future terrifies? To the height of my sorrow and the sum of my misery, I presume only to say this to you, desired lord: “I received an unlooked-for wound from the enemy” (Ovid). Moreover, lord, as to the place to which you sent me, “I ran as though toward an uncertain goal; I fought as though beating the air.” For the lord pope, by whose letters we were summoned, has not fulfilled in deed the promise he made concerning the confirmation of that place, as the present time itself proves. The lord of Farfa [Note: [Col. 0549D] Read: “the abbot of Farfa,” whose name was Atenulf; he had requested monks from Bernard. See Book III of the *Life of St Bernard*, chapter 7, no. 23.] rejoiced greatly at our arrival and received your children with all his heart, so that, if possible, he would have plucked out his eyes and given them to us. In this alone he is blameworthy and should be corrected by you: he does everything too vehemently, beyond both his own promise and our wish. Since my discourse has already run long, I can say nothing briefer or truer about my inner person than this: I am washing a brick.

## LETTER CCCXLV

[Note: [Col. 0549D] Elsewhere Letter 321; what was formerly 345 is now 321. Written in the year of Christ 1140.]

### TO THE BROTHERS OF SAINT ANASTASIUS

[Note: [Col. 0549D] Namely at Tre Fontane in Rome, whence Eugenius III—previously called Bernard, above—was taken.]

He commends their zeal and observance in religious discipline, but disapproves excessive concern for preserving health by medicines.

[Col. 0550A]

To our most beloved sons in Christ at Saint Anastasius, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and devout prayers.

1. I have a witness in heaven how greatly I long for all of you in the bowels of Jesus Christ, how earnestly, if it were possible, I desire to see you—not for your sake alone but for mine, for it would surely be great consolation and surpassing joy for me to embrace my own bowels, my joy, and my crown, which you are. But since this is not yet granted—it shall be granted, as I confidently hope in God’s mercy, and the time will come when we shall see you, our heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take [Col. 0550B] our joy from us—in the meantime, certainly, I have great consolation and much joy in what I have heard of you through our most beloved brother and fellow abbot, your venerable Bernard. For I am deeply grateful to you because he finds such pleasure in you for your discipline and zeal for the Order, for obedience and voluntary poverty, for which your reward is undoubtedly great in heaven. Therefore, brothers, I ask and earnestly beseech you: act thus and stand thus in the Lord, beloved ones. Always be diligent in guarding the Order, so that the Order may guard you; be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3), maintaining among yourselves—and especially toward your superiors—humble mutual charity, which is the bond of perfection (Col. 3:14). Above all [Col. 0550C] pursue humility, and beyond all things peace, on account of the Spirit of God dwelling in you, who rests only upon the quiet and humble person (Isa. 66:2).

2. Yet your venerable abbot asks one thing of me which seems to me by no means good. But I believe that I too have the Spirit of God and God’s counsel in this matter. I know indeed that you live in an unhealthy region, and that some of you suffer from many illnesses; but remember him who said: “I will gladly glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me”; and, “When I am weak,” he says, “then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12:9–10). I do sympathize, and I sympathize deeply, with bodily infirmity; but infirmity of souls is much more to be feared and guarded against. Therefore it is by no means fitting for [Col. 0550D] your religious profession to seek bodily medicines, nor is it beneficial to salvation. [Note: [Col. 0549D] A paradox astonishing in our own time. Yet this passage, compared with another from Sermon 50 on the *Song of Songs*, should at least call monks, who profess hatred of their flesh, away from excessive concern for health, following the example of the ancient monks. These sometimes admitted physicians in order to regulate their diet—as in the *Life of Pachomius*, concerning Palaemon, chapter 1—and more rarely remedies obtained by art. Indeed, Cistercians allowed medicines to their own members, as is clear from Letter now numbered 405 and from Herbert, Book 3, chapter 15. Nor does Bernard deny such remedies in this letter; rather, he permits those supplied by the garden and by naturally occurring kinds of herbs, not those supplied by physicians’ dispensaries. Meanwhile, if you wish, you may profitably read the following authors on this question: St Basil, *Longer Rules*, disputed question, chapter 55; Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 31; Estius, Cornelius, and Oliv. Bonart. on Ecclesiasticus chapter 38; Rossignol, *On the Religious Life*, Book II, chapter 12; Nigronius on Rule, commentary 17; Francis Arias, *On Mortification*; Blosius, final edition, p. 654; Molanus, *On Holy Physicians*; Rodriguez, Part III, treatise 5, chapter 17; Platus, *On the Good State*, Book III, chapter 28; Barradas, on the Gospels, vol. II, Book V, chapter 20.]

To take something at times from cheap herbs [Col. 0551A] suitable for the poor is tolerable, and is sometimes done. But to buy medicinal preparations, seek physicians, or take potions is unbecoming to religious life and contrary to purity; above all, it accords neither with the dignity nor with the purity of our Order. For all these things the Gentiles seek. Yet we know that those who live according to the flesh cannot please God (Rom. 8:8). Spiritual things, therefore, must be compared with spiritual things (1 Cor. 2:13); seek the draught of humility, and cry with your whole heart: “Heal my soul, Lord, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). Beloved brothers, devote yourselves to this health; seek it and preserve it, for human salvation is vain.

## LETTER CCCXLVI

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Elsewhere Letter 377; what was formerly 346 is now 405. Written about the year 1141. See Letter 235.]

### TO THE LORD POPE INNOCENT

He urges the pontiff not to favor the case of the archbishop of York, since it is unjust.

[Col. 0551B]

To his most beloved father and lord, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

Since many are called but few are chosen (Matt. 20:16 and 22:14), it is no great argument for establishing a doubtful case that a thing is praiseworthy because it is praised by many. The archbishop of York has come to you [variant: *to us*], that man of whom we have already written very often to your Holiness: a man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the abundance of his riches. His cause is weak and sickly; and, as we have learned from the testimony [Col. 0551C] of truthful men, from sole of foot to crown of head there is no soundness in it. What then? What does a man without justice seek from the examiner of justice, the guardian of equity? Does he suppose that he can swallow up justice in the curia as he swallowed it up in England? “He swallows a river and is not astonished; he is confident that the Jordan may flow into his mouth.” Behold, he comes with many whom he has enlisted by entreaties and money. This man alone escaped to report it to you; this man alone exposed himself to mortal peril and stood in the breach for the house of Israel, who, with the others, did not worship the statue at the king’s command. He is alone—except that justice has not left him alone. She met her son as an honored mother (Ecclus. 15:2). What then will Peter’s Vicar do in this affair, except [Col. 0551D] what Peter did to the man who thought God’s house could be possessed for money? (Acts 8:20). If the Church is founded upon the rock, the gates of hell shall not prevail against it (Matt. 16:18). I do not say [Col. 0552A] this from myself, but on the testimony of those led by the Spirit of God.

## LETTER CCCXLVII

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Elsewhere Letter 378; what was formerly 347 is now 391. Written about the year 1141.]

### TO THE SAME LORD POPE INNOCENT

He commends envoys travelling to Rome concerning the archbishopric of York.

To his most beloved father and lord INNOCENT, supreme pontiff, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

These men whom you see are simple and upright men who fear God. They have now ascended in spirit before the presence of your glory, solely for the sake and defense of justice. I beg you, set your eyes upon these weary poor men [Note: [Col. 0551D] These are undoubtedly the abbot and monks of Fountains, who were especially hostile to the intruder, as were the monks of Rievaulx, concerning whom see the following two letters—namely Letters 353 and 360.], for it is not without reason that they come to you from afar, reckoning neither the long distances of the lands, [Col. 0552B] nor the danger of the sea, nor the snows of the Alps, nor the great expense of the journey, though they are poor. Let my lord therefore take care that no one’s deceit or ambition is able to render so many labors futile, especially since they seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. Nor do I think that even an enemy could suspect that private love or hatred stirred them to this undertaking, but only fear of God. Therefore, if anyone belongs to God, let him join them. If henceforth an unfruitful tree occupies the ground, whom shall I call responsible except the one holding the axe?

## LETTER CCCXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Elsewhere Letter 388; what was formerly 348 is now 407. Written in the year of Christ 1141.]

### TO THE SAME INNOCENT

On behalf of Arnulf, bishop-elect of Lisieux. [Note: [Col. 0551D] Arnulf, raised from archdeacon of Sées to the see of Lisieux in 1141; Orderic frequently calls it “Luxovium,” in Neustria. He was a learned man, renowned for his letters. Peter the Venerable also wrote to Innocent concerning his election: this is Book IV, Letter 7. Bernard’s present letter was first published by John Picard as the last letter, no. 367; later omitted by Horst, and reprinted in volume III of the *Spicilegium*. Letter 248 also concerns this same Arnulf.]

[Col. 0552C] To his most beloved father and lord, INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the little that he is.

1. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in our days has kept his Church—the spotless bride of his beloved Son—free and delivered from the tribulations of the wicked and from sorrow. The schisms have collapsed; the heresies have fallen silent. [Note: He means the schisms of Anacletus and Victor, and the heresies of Peter Abelard.] The necks of the proud and exalted are trodden underfoot. In the schism I saw the ungodly exalted and raised high like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more. In the heresy the revived errors of many were springing up, but the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped. The tyrant of Sicily [Note: That is, Roger.] had lifted his heart on high, but now he is humbled beneath the mighty hand of God. There is no rank [Col. 0552D] from which the Church of God has not, through you, won victory by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.

2. Yet at the third rank there remains the Count of Anjou [Note: Geoffrey, surnamed Plantagenet, son of Fulk, king of Jerusalem, and father of Henry II, king of England.], [Col. 0553A] the hammer of good men, the oppressor of the peace and liberty of the Church. He persecutes the church of Lisieux, so that the shepherd of that church may have no entrance into the sheepfold except by another way. But what has been done cannot be undone. Indeed, if the matter itself has a careful examiner and is prudently weighed, everything contributes to the good of the cause and to confirmation of what has been done: the person, the affair, the author of the act, and its assailant.

For, if you look to the person, this is your beloved son, in whom you are well pleased. 318 If to the affair, it has been accomplished with due order and canonical liberty intact. If to the author of the act, he is a religious man and fears God. If to the assailant of the act, behold a man who has not set God as his helper: an enemy of the Church, an enemy [Col. 0553B] of Christ’s cross. For in every matter the strongest argument for establishing a doubtful case is always that what pleases the good and displeases the wicked is the better course.

But the Count of Anjou has appealed to the Apostolic See. Why, I ask? What injury has he suffered? What burden compels him? Not because he was oppressed, but because he oppressed; not to relieve an injury done to himself through the remedy of appeal, but to obstruct, through the impediment of appeal, the blessing of this man.

3. Since, therefore, the religious character of the promoter, the belovedness of the promoted man, and the justice of the cause all converge in one point, it seems superfluous and vain to ask on his behalf where his humility itself has made petition. Yet I shall speak to my lord, though I am dust and ashes. I shall speak, a servant of the Bride, to the Bridegroom’s friend: may my speech be pleasing [Col. 0553C] to you.

To you, lord, the Church has been entrusted from the rising of the sun to its setting. You ought to be for her a wall and an outer defense against the enemy and persecutor; you ought to cherish her children beneath the shadow of your wings. Receive the bishop of Lisieux, a son of the same womb as the Roman Church, and send him back with blessings of sweetness, lest his enemy should ever say: “I have prevailed against him.” Gird on your sword, Father, for the exaltation of your son, the humbling of the enemy, and the preservation of the Church’s liberty. For we are not children of a slave woman, but of the free woman—the freedom by which Christ has made us free.

## LETTER CCCXLIX

[Note: Also Letter 330; what was formerly 349 is now 408. Written about the year of Christ 1141.]

TO THE SAME [INNOCENT]. He commends a friend to the Pope.

[Col. 0553D]

To his most loving father and lord INNOCENT, by God’s grace supreme pontiff, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

The favor which I have found in your eyes I do not wish to possess alone; I wish to share it with my friends. For I do not fear that it may perhaps be insufficient for both them and me. It is great. I can make many participants in it, yet I shall not thereby be impoverished. What therefore I have received freely, I shall freely give; and your generosity makes me generous [Col. 0554A]—but with what is yours.

We commend to you the bearer of this letter, a man worthy of recommendation. He is, lord, a friend of Christ’s poor and a servant of your servants. I ask, lord, that, if he has any business before Your Excellency, you may graciously hear him for our sake with your customary kindness—or rather for his own sake, since he is such a man that he ought by his own merits alone to be heard.

## LETTER CCCL

[Note: Also Letter 331; what was formerly 350 is now 409. Written about the year of Christ 1141.]

TO THE SAME [INNOCENT]. He asks that a kinsman of his be strengthened by the Pope’s blessing.

This young man, high-spirited, as they say, and vigorous in military service, is setting out for Jerusalem in order to fight the better warfare. Your servant, at his own request, asks that in the good work he has begun he may deserve to receive [Col. 0554B] your consolation—indeed, your favor, your prayer, and your blessing. He is our kinsman, and, according to the prophet, I ought not to have despised my own flesh (Isa. 58:7).

## LETTER CCCLI

[Note: A new letter; what was formerly 351 is now 322.]

TO THE SAME INNOCENT. He commends certain poor persons.

I write to you often. You have my prayers and letters every day. I am constrained between two things: lest I prove ungrateful to my friends, or burdensome to you.
