Affection urges me on, but embarrassment calls me back, and almost shame excludes the duty of charity. Christ’s Bride has nowhere to lay her head, nowhere to flee, except to the Bridegroom’s friend in a time of tribulation.

These persons whom you see as poor, sent by poor people through many dangers [Col. 0554C] of land and sea, flee beneath the shadow of your wings; they have recourse to the rock of Catholic faith and to the bosom of apostolic mercy. For, vexed in many ways, they are granted some relief from the tribulation and affliction of evildoers. If you maintain the office of your apostolate and the ancient custom, you can neither reject the causes of the poor nor show favor to the face of the powerful. We pray you for them, because they are our brothers and belong to our Order, from whose members they have been sent, that for the sake of their prayers you may incline the ear of mercy, for love of him who does not despise the prayers of the poor.

## LETTER CCCLII

[Note: A new letter; what was formerly 352 is now 389. Written in the year of Christ 1131.]

OR THE PRIVILEGE GRANTED BY POPE INNOCENT II TO SAINT BERNARD

[Note: It seemed proper to print this privilege after Bernard’s letters to Innocent, from volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 383, where the history of the monastery of Fontaines in the diocese of Tours is found.]

Innocent grants Bernard and the Cistercian Order very extensive privileges in view of his outstanding merits toward the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0554D]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity, etc.

Moreover, with what firm and persevering constancy, beloved son in the Lord Bernard, abbot, when the schism of Peter Leo was inflamed, the fervor of your religious zeal and discernment undertook to defend the cause of blessed Peter and of your holy mother, the Roman [Col. 0555A] Church; and how, setting yourself as an impregnable wall before God’s house, you labored by frequent arguments fortified with reason to lead the minds of kings and princes and other persons, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to the unity of the Catholic Church and to obedience to blessed Peter and to us—the great benefit that has thereby come to God’s Church and to us makes clear. [Note: These words are quoted by Geoffrey in the *Life of St Bernard*, book III, no. 13.]

Therefore, assenting to your just desires, we have strengthened with the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, over which, by God’s authorship, you preside, together with all that belongs to it. We decree that whatever possessions [Col. 0555B] or goods are known at present to belong justly and canonically to that same place, or may in the future, with the Lord’s help, come to be granted to it through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We forbid any archbishop or bishop to compel you, your successors, or any abbot of the Cistercian Order to come to a council or synod, except on a matter of faith. Since the monastery of Cîteaux is the origin and beginning of this religious observance, it shall deservedly enjoy, by our grant, this prerogative: that, whenever it is deprived of its proper pastor, it may freely elect and, without any opposition, obtain as its head any abbot from among all the abbots of your Order, or any monk.

But to the other abbeys of your Order which have one or more abbeys subject to them and derived from the fruitful abundance of their own body, we grant free authority, when their abbot has been removed from human affairs, to elect whomsoever they prefer from among the abbots subject to them, or any monk from all Cistercian congregations. 320 But any abbey having no dependent house may freely elect and possess as abbot any monk from all congregations of the aforesaid observance.

Furthermore, no archbishop, bishop, or abbot shall presume, without your welcome permission, to receive or retain one of your lay brothers who is not a monk after he has made profession in your monasteries. We decree that no one may presume to demand or receive tithes from you from the produce which you and the brothers of your whole congregation cultivate by your own hands and at your own expense, or from your animals. Therefore let no one, etc. But may those who preserve for that place what belongs to it have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

[Col. 0556A]

I, Innocent, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Matthew, bishop of Albano.  
I, Romanus, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico.  
I, John, cardinal priest of the title of St Chrysogonus.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus.

Given at Lyons, through the hand of Haimeric, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the tenth indiction, in the year 1131 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## LETTER CCCLIII

[Note: Also Letter 379; what was formerly 353 is now 387. Written about the year of Christ 1141.]

TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX

[Note: This is William, Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx in the diocese of York. Bernard employed him as an intermediary in writing Letter 1 to Robert. On Rievaulx, see *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 727.]

He urges him to bear with equanimity the illegitimate ordination of the Archbishop of York.

[Col. 0556B]

To his beloved brother and fellow abbot WILLIAM of Rievaulx, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

I have heard what has happened concerning that archbishop, and I grieve deeply. Therefore, knowing your zeal, lest perhaps it should burn more than is right, without the moderation of knowledge—which neither befits our Order nor is necessary for your house—I have thought it fitting to write you words of consolation. For all other things ought to be borne with sufficient equanimity, since our own conscience does not accuse us.

I say with assurance: neither is it your iniquity nor your sin. You resisted as far as you could. Now, according to Augustine’s judgment, another’s evil does not [Col. 0556C] defile you, since you did not consent in heart and rebuked it in speech. For he says: “In two ways another’s evil does not defile you [otherwise: an evil man does not defile you]: if you do not consent and if you rebuke it.” (*Sermon* 88, ch. 18, no. 19.)

Henceforth, then, be of good courage and do not be troubled. But concerning orders and the other sacraments, know that Christ the Lord himself—the bishop of our souls—is he who baptizes and he who consecrates. If anyone is contentious about the ordination, no one compels you to be ordained. Nevertheless, I say altogether confidently that, if he is received together with the Church, there is no danger. Otherwise, we should have to leave this world if we wished to avoid all the evil persons whom the Church tolerates.

In short, the matter will not be long in becoming known to the supreme pontiff; and whatever he shall ordain or command, follow and observe it with a wholly good conscience. Meanwhile wait with equanimity.

## LETTER CCCLIV

[Note: A new letter; what was formerly 354 is now 388. Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO MELISENDE, QUEEN OF JERUSALEM, DAUGHTER OF KING BALDWIN AND WIFE OF FULK. How she ought to conduct herself after the death of her husband Fulk.

To the most illustrious queen of Jerusalem, M., BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: may you find grace before the Lord.

[Col. 0557A]

Among the many cares and affairs of a royal court, it would seem quite unsuitable for me to write to you if I regarded in you only the glory of your kingdom, your power, and your noble lineage. All these things appear in the eyes of men; those who do not possess them envy those who do and call blessed the person who has them. But what blessedness is there in possessing things which all wither swiftly as hay and fall quickly like the green plants of the field? These are good things, but unstable, mutable, passing, and perishable, because they are goods of the flesh. Moreover, it has been said of the flesh and its goods: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6).

Therefore one writing to you ought not to pay much reverence to these things, in which favor is deceitful and beauty vain. Receive [Col. 0557B] in few words what I say. For though I have much to say to you, I shall make my speech brief because of your many cares and mine. Receive brief but useful counsel from a distant land, counsel from which, as from a small seed, a great harvest may hereafter arise. Receive, I say, counsel from the hand of a friend, one who seeks not his own advantage but your honor. For no one can be more faithful to you in counsel than one who loves not what is yours, but you yourself.

Now that your husband the king has died, and the young king is still too unfit to bear the affairs of the kingdom and discharge the kingly office, the eyes of all look toward you, and the whole weight of the kingdom leans and rests upon you alone. You must put your hand to strong things and show a man in a woman, doing what must be done in the spirit [Col. 0557C] of counsel and fortitude. You ought so prudently and moderately to order all things that all who see you may judge from your deeds that you are rather a king than a queen, lest the nations perhaps say: “Where is the king of Jerusalem?”

“But,” you will say, “I am unequal to these tasks. They are great, beyond my strength and beyond my knowledge. These are a man’s works; but I am a woman—weak in body, changeable in heart, neither prudent in counsel nor accustomed to affairs.” I know, daughter, I know that these things are great; but I also know that, though the waves of the sea are wonderful, the Lord on high is more wonderful. These things are great, but our Lord is great, and great is his power.

## LETTER CCCLV

[Note: Also Letter 376; what was formerly 355 is now 364. Written about the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE SAME QUEEN OF JERUSALEM. He commends Premonstratensians journeying to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0557D]

You see how much I presume upon you, since I dare to commend others to you as well. Yet perhaps in commending these Premonstratensian brothers I have done so more superfluously than rashly. They are so worthy of recommendation in their own right that they need no one else’s. They will be found, I think, to be men of counsel, fervent in spirit, patient in tribulation, mighty in deed and word. They have clothed themselves in the armor [Col. 0558A] of God and girded themselves with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Receive them as warriors of peace: gentle toward human beings, violent toward demons. Indeed, receive Christ in them, for he is the cause of their pilgrimage.

## LETTER CCCLVI

[Note: Also Letter 316; what was formerly 356 is now 369. Written in the year of Christ 1141.]

TO MALACHY, ARCHBISHOP OF IRELAND

[Note: Usher also places this letter forty-third among the Irish letters, where he notes much concerning Mellifont and other Cistercian monasteries of the same province.]

He sends back religious men, though—not sufficiently cultivated and instructed, as he attributes to circumstances.

To MALACHY, bishop by the grace of God and legate of the Apostolic See, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: whatever the prayer of a sinner may avail, and whatever the devotion of a poor man may profit.

[Col. 0558B]

We have done what Your Holiness commanded, if not as worthily as we ought, then at least as was possible at the time. Such great wickedness is rampant everywhere among us that scarcely even this little which has been done could have been accomplished. We have sent such [otherwise: nevertheless, such] a small quantity of seed as you see, to sow even a modest part of that field into which the true Isaac once went out to meditate, when Rebecca was first brought to him by Abraham’s servant, happily to be joined to him in a lasting marriage (Gen. 24).

Nor is this seed to be despised, for in your fathers we experience at this time the fulfillment of that saying: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we should have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9). Therefore I have planted; do you water; and God will give the increase. Through you we greet all the saints who are with [Col. 0558C] you, humbly commending ourselves to their and to your holy prayers. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLVII

[Note: Also Letter 317; what was formerly 357 is now 370. Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE SAME [MALACHY]. He asks for the love which Malachy has shown, continuing and even increasing, and desires that it be displayed in care and support for the brothers sent by him.

To his most loving father and most reverend lord MALACHY, bishop by God’s grace and legate of the holy and Apostolic See, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, the servant of his holiness: greeting and whatever prayers of ours may be.

1. How sweet to my palate are your words, lord father! How delightful the memory of your Holiness! Whatever affection, devotion, or spirit is in us is, beyond doubt, wholly claimed by the love of Your Belovedness. There is no need of a multitude of words where affection is strong. For I trust that the Spirit whom you have from God bears witness to your spirit that the little that we are is yours.

You also, most loving and deeply desired father, do not consign to oblivion the soul of a poor man bound to you by the ties of charity; and do not forget forever the soul of your poor servant. We do not, as if for the first time, [Col. 0559A] commend ourselves to you, since for a long time we have gloried in the Lord that our littleness has deserved to find favor in the eyes of your Holiness. Rather, we pray that this love, no longer new, may daily advance through new increases.

We commend to you our sons—indeed yours—with all the greater earnestness because they are farther removed from us. You know that, after God, our whole confidence in sending them lay in this: that it seemed unlawful not to comply with Your Holiness’s prayers. Do what becomes you: embrace and cherish them with all the depths of charity. Let not care and diligence for them grow lukewarm through any circumstance, lest what your right hand has planted perish.

2. We have now learned, both from your letters and from the report of our brothers, that the house is prospering well and is increasing in temporal as well as spiritual things. We therefore rejoice greatly and give thanks with all our heart to God and to your fatherly care. And because much watchfulness is still needed, as in a new place and in a land so unaccustomed—indeed, untried—in monastic observance, we beseech you in the Lord not to withdraw your hand, but to bring to the best completion what you have well 323 begun.

Concerning our brothers who returned from that place, it would have pleased us had they remained. Perhaps the less disciplined customs of the brothers native to that land gave them some occasion to leave, especially because those brothers seem less readily willing to accept their counsel in matters which they had formerly not experienced.

3. We have sent back to you our most beloved son—and yours—Christian, instructed as fully as we could in matters belonging to the Order, and, as we hope, henceforth to be more attentive to its observances. Do not wonder that we did not send more brothers with him, since we found neither suitable brothers who would readily consent nor thought it right to compel unwilling men.

Our most beloved brother Robert [Note: Who is this Robert? Is he that holy Robert praised by Serlo in the *History of Fontaines*, in vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, pp. 743 and 749—a former monk of Whitby, associated with the monks who left the monastery of York, concerning whom see above, Letter 95 and those following? Or is he Robert, Bernard’s kinsman, to whom Letter 1 is addressed?] consented to our requests on this occasion also, as a son of obedience. It will be for you to assist him, so that your house may now make progress in buildings and in its other necessities. We also suggest to Your Fatherhood that you persuade religious men, whom you expect will be useful to the monastery, to enter their Order; for this will be of the greatest benefit to the house, and they will more readily comply with you. May Your Holiness prosper, always mindful of us in Christ.

## LETTER CCCLVIII

[Note: Also Letter 374; what was formerly 358 is now 376. Written in the year of Christ 1142.]

TO THE LORD POPE, NAMELY CELESTINE. He seeks the Pope’s assistance and authority in securing peace for Theobald, Count of Champagne.

[Col. 0560A]

What Count Theobald asks, I ask also; for he is a son of peace. He has zeal for peace, but from you we demand its accomplishment. Your apostolate is indebted to peace, as is the place which you occupy. All love peace; few deserve it. Your servant, moreover, confesses himself to be among its lovers; whether he is also among those who deserve it, you will judge.

There is one thing: although we do not deserve it, the necessity of Christ’s Bride, which is the Church, requires it. The Bridegroom’s friend will not grieve her. [Note: After the words “The Bridegroom’s friend will not grieve her,” the manuscript of Saint-Vaast adds: “We have both commended and commend Brother N. to Your Majesty, because he deserves recommendation.” What follows in the same letter in that manuscript begins a new line under the title “To the Same,” as though it were another letter. MARTÈNE.] For upon that one Apostolic See rests the care of all churches, so that all may be united under it and in it, [Col. 0560B] and that it, solicitous for all, may preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace for all.

Give us peace, therefore; send us peace. If not because you owe it, at least because you ought to obey. Enough for a command.

## LETTER CCCLIX

[Note: A new letter; what was formerly 359 is now 377. Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

FROM THE MEN OF CLAIRVAUX TO THE SAME CELESTINE. They wish to keep the abbot of Morimond, who intends to make pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

To the supreme pontiff C., the little flock of Clairvaux: the most devoted obedience of due submission, and whatever the prayer of sinners may avail.

Since we rejoice that you bear the office of him who said that his daily concern was the care of all the churches (2 Cor. 11:28), our littleness does not fear rejection at the ears [Col. 0560C] of Your Holiness, though they are occupied by greater affairs; rather, great necessity compels us. For you cannot regard as insignificant those concerning whom you will hear: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

This matter is not only ours, but that of our whole Order. For this reason too, your son—our father, that is, the father of us all—if he had been at home when this letter was written, [Note: A gloss had crept in here: “Perhaps it happened that he was absent at that time and still unaware of this matter.”] would either have approached Your Majesty in person or at least have entrusted this pitiable and tearful complaint to be written in his name.

But not to keep your anxious charity in suspense too long: one of our brother abbots, called the abbot of Morimond [Col. 0560D] [Note: Namely Raynald, the fourth abbot of Morimond after Arnold, its first abbot, who likewise abandoned the abbey, according to Letter 4. Raynald also resigned his office after fifteen years of governance.], rashly enough abandoning the monastery over which he presided, resolved, driven by a spirit of fickleness, to go to Jerusalem. First, as they say, he intended to test the prudence of your discernment, to see whether he might somehow wring from you permission for his error.

[Col. 0561A]

If in this matter you grant him any assent—which God forbid!—consider yourselves how great an occasion of ruin this may be for our Order. By this example, any abbot who feels himself burdened by the pastoral load will at once lay it aside, judging that he may lawfully do so—especially among us, where great honor is not sought and the office seems a great burden.

Then, for the greater desolation of the house entrusted to him, he took with him as companions in his wandering the best and most perfect men who lived under him. Among these he even presumed to lead away with him, to a greater scandal, that noble young man whom he had earlier brought from Cologne—not without scandal, as we believe was not unknown to you.

If, as has been reported to you, he says that he wishes in that land to preserve the observances of our Order, and therefore says that he is taking with him a multitude of brothers, who does not see that soldiers fighting are more necessary there than monks singing or weeping? Moreover, our observance will suffer great harm from this: for it will be easy for anyone who longs to wander to presume, as though without any danger, to undertake pilgrimage to a place where he will find the same rule of life that he professed to be observed.

What pleases you in this matter, therefore, and what your authority ought to decide, it is not for our presumption to pronounce, but for your discernment to examine.

## LETTER CCCLX

[Note: Also Letter 380; what was formerly 360 is now 378. Written in the year of Christ 1143.]

TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX. Again he exhorts William to patience and equanimity.

[Col. 0561C]

To his dearest brother and fellow abbot WILLIAM of Rievaulx, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and the spirit of counsel.

We have labored as far as we could against the common plague; and, if we have not obtained what we desired, the fruit of our labor nevertheless remains for us with him before whom no good thing goes unrewarded. This, then, is the true consolation of us and of all who contend for truth: that there is laid up for us a crown of righteousness, which the righteous Judge will render to us on that day.

Henceforth we wish you to remember that if we suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, we are blessed; and that another’s evil does not defile [Col. 0561D] us when we have not consented to it—indeed, when we have rebuked it. This, then, is also our consolation: that in patience we may now possess our souls, and that what we could not obtain from men we may hope for from the Lord [Col. 0562A], who will not despise those hoping in him.

For I trust in the mercy of our Father who is in heaven that every planting which he has not planted will be uprooted, and that the barren fig tree will wither under his curse and will no longer occupy the ground. Therefore I ask and beseech your Brotherhood not to be disturbed, nor to disturb God’s flock entrusted to you; rather, console yourselves and act manfully, so that we may serve the Lord in holiness and he may deliver us from our enemies.

Nevertheless, we have represented, so far as we could, the matter to the bishop of Tusculum [Note: Ymar, who was legate in England in 1143, the year in which this letter was written. Letters 219 and 230 to this same Ymar survive.], who has been charged to act as legate in those regions. He absolutely promised us that, unless he could do something better for us, he would at least by every means observe this: that he would not hand over to him [Col. 0562B] the pallium which he bears unless that dean, now bishop [Note: William of St Barbara, formerly dean of York and bishop of Durham; see Letter 235.], in whose oath the case depended, should swear; but that he should refer the case to the lord pope.

## LETTER CCCLXI

[Note: Also Letter 383; what was formerly 361 is now 379. Written about the year of Christ 1144.]

TO ARCHBISHOP THEOBALD, ON BEHALF OF JOHN OF SALISBURY

[Note: Concerning Theobald, who was made Archbishop of Canterbury from being a monk of Bec, mention has already been made above in Letter 238. Orderic records his promotion in 1138, p. 919.]

Trusting in Theobald’s friendship, he commends John to him.

You increase my favor and multiply my glory if, for my sake, my friends find favor in your eyes. Yet I do not seek glory from man, but the kingdom of God and his righteousness. Accordingly, I shall send to Your Sublimity the bearer of this letter, John [Note: This is John of Salisbury, so called from the English city of that name, the principal friend of Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury. He used to acknowledge that he had obtained the bishopric of Chartres through Thomas’s merits, beginning his letters: “John, by God’s grace and the merits of blessed Thomas the martyr, humble minister of the Church of Chartres,” as in vol. X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 391, where the word “merits” is omitted.], my friend [Col. 0562C] and the friend of my friends, to the familiarity which I presume to enjoy in you and from you.

For he has a good report from good people, which he has earned no less by his life than by his learning. Nor did I learn this from those who know how to cast about words merely as words, but from my sons who are with me, whose words I trust as I would my own eyes. While present, I had commended him to you; but now that he is absent I commend him much more, and indeed with all the greater confidence because I have learned both the man’s life and character more sincerely from most trustworthy informants.

If, therefore, I have any influence—or rather, since I have very great influence before you—provide for him the means to live respectably—indeed, honorably; and do so quickly, because he has nowhere to turn. Meanwhile provide for him in his necessities, and permit me to experience [Col. 0562D] all that hidden treasury of affection which you preserve for me in your heart, most loving father.

## LETTER CCCLXII

[Note: Also Letter 334; what was formerly 362 is now 380. Written in the year of Christ 1145.]

TO ROBERT PULLUS, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR

[Note: Elsewhere, “To Roland the Chancellor.” But a Cistercian manuscript reads “To Robert Pullus,” and indeed more correctly, so far as I can reach by conjecture. First, that Robert was most dear and especially intimate to Saint Bernard is clear from Letter 205, to the Bishop of Rochester; and Bernard plainly suggests the same of the person to whom he writes here. Next, he asserts here, with heaven and earth as witnesses, that this man faithfully and profitably devoted himself to the instruction of many—a statement better understood of no one than Robert Pullus, who lectured at Paris and restored the University of Oxford in England. Finally, the chancellor in question here is said to have been sent beforehand by God to aid Eugene before Eugene’s pontificate. Robert Pullus, according to Onuphrius, acted as chancellor under Pope Lucius II until the third year of Eugene—indeed, if Ciaconius is believed, until the fifth. Roland, surnamed Blandinellus or Paparo, a native of Siena and later Alexander III, was created by Eugene cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and obtained the dignity of chancellor only in the eighth year of Eugene’s pontificate. For more concerning Robert Pullus, see, if you wish, the notes on Letter 205. Meanwhile, however, regarding the time when Robert held the chancellorship, I note that Onuphrius’s opinion is to be preferred. For I read that Guido signed apostolic letters with the title of chancellor in 1146 in vol. I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 108, and in 1147 in the notes on Guibert of Nogent, p. 620.]

He exhorts him to offer himself as a vigorous helper, in accordance with his office, to Eugene, recently elected pope, in the affairs of the Church.

[Col. 0563A]

To his lord and dearest friend ROBERT, by God’s grace cardinal priest and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and devoted prayers.

1. We received the letter of Your Affection with the feeling with which your memory is always held among us in blessing. Nor indeed do we think that you need words of human favor, or letters of recommendation to us; since, I think, the Spirit of truth bears to each of us an unquestionable testimony [Col. 0563B] of how sincerely we love you and are loved by you—namely, that Spirit through whom this charity is also poured out into our hearts. Blessed be God, who according to his mercy has forestalled our Eugenius—indeed, his own—in blessings of sweetness: that is, by preparing a lamp for his Christ, and by sending beforehand a faithful man to assist him, and to be a very great consolation to us as well. For when the calling away and absence of a friend was painful to his friend, whose presence he delights to enjoy in the Lord, then already, as I clearly see, he was devising thoughts of peace and not of affliction, and saying: “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will know afterwards” (John 13:7). Therefore be diligent, dearest one, on behalf of him for whom God has appointed you counsellor and adviser [Col. 0563C]; and watch carefully, according to the wisdom given you, lest amid the turmoil of so many affairs he may perhaps be ensnared by the deceit of malicious persons, so that some word unworthy of Eugenius’ apostolic office may be slipped in upon him.

[Col. 0564A]

2. Come then, dearest one, for the sake of the position you hold and the dignity you have attained: manfully and wisely exercise the zeal for God which is in you, for his glory, your salvation, and the great benefit of the holy Church, so that you too may say, “The grace of God in me was not empty” (1 Cor. 15:10). Until now, as heaven and earth bear witness, you have labored faithfully and usefully for the instruction of many; but now it is time to act for the Lord, lest you allow, so far as you are able, his law to be scattered by the ungodly. Take care, therefore, dearest and most desired father, to be found also in this stewardship a faithful and prudent servant of the Lord: so that dove-like simplicity may serve you, and serpent-like prudence may fight on behalf of the bride of your Lord, entrusted to your very great faithfulness and care, against [Col. 0564B] the poisonous wiles of the wicked and ancient serpent; and that God may be glorified in both. I have indeed many things to say to you; but a long letter is unnecessary where the living voice is present. Therefore, sparing both your occupations and ours, I have put my words into the mouths of the brethren who are present: hear them as though you were hearing me. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXIII

[Note: [Col. 0564C] Formerly Letter 322; what was previously 363 is now 371. Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF EASTERN FRANCE

He exhorts them to take up arms against the unbelievers for the defense of the Eastern Church. He further teaches, against a certain turbulent preacher, that Jews are not to be persecuted, much less killed.

To the most beloved lords and fathers, the archbishops, bishops, and all the clergy and people of eastern France and Bavaria: BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, [Col. 0564C] may abound in the spirit of strength.

[Note: [Col. 0564C] The inscription of this letter in the editions published hitherto seemed to me too narrow—for it mentioned only the bishop of Speyer and his clergy and people—for the scope of the letter allowed. Therefore we prefixed another, broader one [Col. 0564D], which Otto of Freising gives in *The Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 41. But afterwards I discovered that the same letter was sent, not only on the same theme but in almost exactly the same words, with merely its address changed, to different peoples, provinces, and cities. For in a manuscript sent to me from England, likewise in another from Koblenz, I found it addressed “To the People of England” (it appears in a manuscript of Saint-Victor at Paris under the same address) [[Col. 0563] In the Liège codex of St. James it bears this title: “This letter Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, dictated when already near death, to the English nation.” MARTÈNE.]. Indeed Baronius gives the same letter, with only a few words changed, under this address: “To Mainfred, bishop of the church of Brescia, and likewise to the consuls, knights, and all the peoples subject to him, Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, abundance in the spirit of strength.” See Baronius, under the year 1146, no. 15. This is, as it were, a trumpet-call to the holy expedition. Speaking of it, William of Tyre says: “The lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux—a man of immortal memory and a mirror of honorable conduct, of devout and in every way worthy remembrance in the Lord—was chosen above all for carrying out the aforesaid gift of God. A diligent executor of the charge laid upon him, drawing with him fellow-workers beloved by God in the same work, tireless and unwearied, though weak in body because of fasting and an excessively spare diet, he traversed kingdoms and went through regions, everywhere preaching the kingdom of God,” etc. Add what is read on this subject in his *Life and Miracles*, and compare Letter 355. A large assembly of princes was held at Speyer for the purpose of the holy expedition, where who can doubt that these letters of Bernard were read publicly? Hence the address to the people of Speyer: “To the most beloved lord and father, the bishop of Speyer, [Col. 0566D] and all the clergy and people, Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, abundance in the spirit of strength.” Likewise, a little later in Bavaria, at an assembly of nobles, Sigonius testifies that these letters were read by the abbot of Ebrach together with letters of Pope Eugenius; see *On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 1147, and Otto, *The Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 41. Moreover, among the letters of Nicholas of Clairvaux in volume XII of the Cologne edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, there is another letter in Bernard’s name, of the same subject, to the count and nobles of Brittany; it is printed here at the end of St. Bernard’s letters.]

1. I speak to you concerning the cause of Christ, in which our salvation surely lies. I say this so that the Lord’s authority may excuse the unworthiness of the speaker’s person; and so also may consideration of your own benefit excuse it. I am small indeed, [Col. 0565A] but I desire you all with no small desire in the inward affections of Jesus Christ. This is my reason for writing to you; this is my ground for daring to address your whole body by letter. I would act more gladly by living voice, if, as willingness is not lacking, ability were also at hand. Behold now, brothers, the acceptable time; behold now, the day of abundant salvation. For the earth has been shaken and has trembled, because the God of heaven has begun to destroy his own land—his own, I say, in which the Word of his Father was seen to teach [Note: [Col. 0566D] In Horstius: “his own, in which he was seen.”], and for more than thirty years, as a man, to dwell among men; his own, indeed, which he illumined with miracles, which he consecrated with his own blood, in which the first flowers of resurrection appeared. And now, because our sins demand it, the adversaries of the cross have raised their sacrilegious head, laying waste [Col. 0565B] the land of promise by the edge of the sword. For it is near at hand—unless someone resists—that they will rush upon the city of the living God itself, overthrow the workshops of our redemption, and defile the holy places purpled with the blood of the spotless Lamb. Alas, with sacrilegious mouth they gape after the very sanctuary of the Christian religion, and they attempt to invade and trample the very bed in which our Life, for our sakes, slept in death.

2. What are you doing, brave men? What are you doing, servants of the cross? Will you thus give what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine? How many sinners there obtained pardon, confessing their sins with tears, after the filth of the pagans had been removed by the swords of their fathers! The wicked man sees and envies; he gnashes [Col. 0565C] his teeth and wastes away. He stirs up the instruments of his iniquity, and would leave behind no traces or signs of so great a mercy if ever—as God forbid!—he were able to gain possession of that holy of holies. Yet this would be an inconsolable sorrow for all succeeding ages, because an irrecoverable loss; but especially for this most wicked generation, an infinite disgrace and everlasting reproach.

3. Yet what do we suppose, brothers? Has the hand of the Lord been shortened, or has it become powerless to save, that he calls poor little worms to defend and restore to himself his inheritance? Cannot he send more than twelve legions of angels, or at least speak a word and the land will be delivered? Certainly the power to do so lies at his command whenever he wills; [Col. 0566A] but, I tell you, the Lord your God is testing you. He looks upon the children of men to see whether there may be anyone who understands, seeks him, and grieves at his plight. For the Lord has compassion on his people, and provides a saving remedy for those who have grievously fallen.

4. Consider with what skill he acts to save you, and be astonished; behold the abyss of his mercy and take confidence, sinners. He does not desire your death, but that you turn and live; for thus he seeks an occasion, not against you but for you. For what is this except an occasion of salvation most ingeniously devised, and discoverable by God alone: that the Almighty deigns to summon murderers, robbers, adulterers, perjurers, and persons bound by other crimes into his service as though they were a people that had practiced righteousness? Do not [Col. 0566B] despair, sinners: the Lord is gracious. If he wished to punish you, he would not merely fail to seek your service; he would not even accept it if offered. Again I say: weigh the riches of the goodness of the most high God; attend to his merciful design. He makes it appear, or pretends, that he has a need, while wishing to relieve your needs. He wishes to be held as debtor, in order to give those who serve as his soldiers their wages: forgiveness of sins and eternal glory. Blessed, then, I would call the generation overtaken by so fruitful a season of pardon, which this year pleasing to the Lord, and truly jubilee, has found still surviving. For this blessing is poured out over the whole world, and all hasten in rivalry to the sign of life.

[Note: [Col. 0566D] The sign of the cross, in the following paragraph; there also concerning the indulgence granted to those marked with the cross for all sins of which confession has been made with contrite heart. Compare Letter 423.]

5. Therefore, because your land is fruitful in brave men [Col. 0566C] and is known to be filled with vigorous youth, just as your praise is throughout the whole world and the fame of your valor has filled the entire earth: gird yourselves manfully and take up the fortunate arms of zeal for the Christian name. Let that former pursuit cease—not warfare, but sheer wickedness—by which you are accustomed to strike one another down and destroy one another, so as to be consumed by one another. What dreadful lust stirs miserable men to pierce with the sword the body of a neighbor, whose soul perhaps also perishes? Nor does the man who boasts escape: a sword will pass through his own soul too, when he rejoices merely that an enemy has fallen. To expose oneself to such danger is madness, not valor; it should be attributed not to courage but rather to insanity. Now, brave soldier, now, man of war, you have a place where you may fight without peril, where victory is glory and [Col. 0567A] death is gain. If you are a prudent merchant, if you are a trader in this world, I point out to you a great fair; see that you do not miss it. Receive the sign of the cross, and you shall obtain forgiveness alike for all sins of which you have made confession with contrite heart. If the material itself is purchased, it costs little; if it is taken upon a devout shoulder, it is unquestionably worth the kingdom of God. Those, therefore, who have already received the heavenly seal have acted well; the rest act well too, nor is it folly for them if they hasten likewise to seize what will prove their salvation.

6. For the rest, brothers, I warn you—not I, but God’s apostle together with me—not to believe every spirit (1 John 4:1). We have heard, and rejoice, that zeal for God burns in you; but it is absolutely necessary that the restraint of knowledge not be lacking. The Jews are not to be persecuted, slaughtered, or even driven out.

[Note: [Col. 0567C] Bernard rightly and religiously teaches this, and on a far weightier ground than in the case of Gentiles: because living Jews are letters representing the Lord’s passion [Col. 0567D] and witnesses to the divine pages; Gentiles are not so. Compare the following letter, Sermon 64 on the Song of Songs, and the book *To the Knights Templar*, chapter 10.]

Question them concerning the divine pages. I know what is prophetically written in the Psalm concerning the Jews: “God has shown me,” says the Church, “over my enemies: do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget” [Ps. 58:12]. They are, as it were, living letters to us, representing the Lord’s passion. For this reason they have been dispersed into all regions: so that, while they pay the just penalty for so great a crime, they may be witnesses to our redemption. Hence the Church, speaking in the same Psalm, adds: “Scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Ps. 58:12). Thus it has happened: they have been scattered; they have been cast down; they endure harsh captivity under Christian rulers. Yet they shall return at evening, and in due time there shall be regard for them. Finally, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved, says the Apostle (Rom. 11:25–26). Meanwhile, certainly, whoever dies remains in death.

7. I pass over the fact that, wherever Jews are absent, we grieve that Christian moneylenders Judaize more grievously—if indeed they ought to be called Christians and not rather baptized Jews.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] Here Bernard condemns usury universally among Christians, much more among clerics.]

Certainly, if the Jews were utterly crushed, from where would their promised salvation or conversion at the end henceforth arise? Clearly, if Gentiles were likewise to be awaited, they should be endured rather than sought with swords. But now, since they have begun to use violence against us, it is necessary to repel force by force against those who do not bear swords without cause. Yet it belongs to Christian piety both to subdue the proud and to spare the subject, especially those to whom belong the promised lawgiving, the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh—he who is blessed for ever. Nevertheless, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic command, it must be required of them [Col. 0568A] that they entirely release from the exaction of interest all who have received the sign of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] The letters of Eugenius III concerning the expedition to the Holy Land are quoted by Otto of Freising, *The Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 38. There the pope frees those pledged to the holy military undertaking not only from debts of the soul but also from interest payable. “Whoever,” he says, “is burdened by debt and begins so holy a journey with a pure heart shall not pay interest accrued in the past; and if they themselves or others on their behalf are bound by oath or pledge on account of interest, we absolve them by apostolic authority.”]

8. It is also necessary, most beloved brothers, that you be warned of this: if anyone, perhaps desiring to exercise primacy among you, should wish by his own expedition to precede the army of the kingdom, he must by no means dare to do so. If he pretends that he was sent by us, it is not true; or if [Col. 0568B] he displays letters as though issued by us, you must say that they are entirely false—indeed, not to say stolen. Choose as leaders men skilled in war and experienced in such matters, and let the army of the Lord set out together, so that it may have strength everywhere and may not suffer violence from anyone. For in the earlier expedition, before Jerusalem was taken, there was a certain man named Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0567D] This famous Peter, surnamed the Hermit, is frequently discussed by William of Tyre in book I of *The Holy War*, and by James of Vitry in chapter 17 of the *Western History*. In the Corbie necrology we find a Peter the Hermit of this name, prior of Mont-Saint-Quentin near Péronne [Col. 0568C]. Whether he is the same as this man, who was also called “of Acheris,” we do not yet know for certain.]

You too, unless I am mistaken, have often heard mention of him. Going forward alone with his own followers, he exposed the people who had trusted him to such great dangers that either none or very few of them escaped falling by hunger or sword. Therefore it is wholly to be feared that, if you act similarly, the same may happen to you. May God avert this from you—he who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## LETTER CCCLXIV

[Note: [Col. 0568D] Formerly Letter 355; what was previously 364 is now 381. Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY

He invites Peter to the council at Chartres, where consultation is to be held concerning aid to be given to the Eastern Church.

[Col. 0568C]

To the most loving father PETER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Cluny, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: greeting, and such prayers as he can offer.

1. I believe that the grievous and most pitiable groaning of the Eastern Church [Note: [Col. 0568D] Namely, when in the year 1144 the noble city of Edessa in Mesopotamia, beyond the Euphrates, which from the time of Constantine the Great had been devoted to the worship of the Christian religion and was illustrious for relics of the blessed apostle Thomas brought from India, was at last brought into the power of the unbelievers, with a very great slaughter of the Christian people. “For when, many years earlier,” as William of Newburgh says in *The Affairs of England*, “the Saracens, by God’s hidden judgment permitted beyond measure to ravage the Christians, had taken very famous cities—Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Damascus—and had occupied Egypt, Syria, and other eastern provinces in which Christ was worshiped, this city alone, a defender not only of its walls but also of its territories, remained unconquered amid countless and most fierce enemies until the time of the earlier Jerusalem expedition, in which the Christians, having conquered the Saracens, obtained Jerusalem and Antioch.” He then proceeds to recount the occasion upon which Edessa yielded to the unbelievers. “A certain Armenian, a citizen of Edessa, living in a tower adjoining the wall, brooding on revenge because his daughter had been violated by the prince of the city, admitted Turks, invited by secret arrangements, into the city on the very night of the Lord’s Nativity. Rushing upon the people, who were keeping vigil securely in church, they slaughtered the archbishop as he stood at the altar; and they butchered with swords the people, offering no resistance but frozen in shock at the sudden disaster. Thus Edessa, for so many ages unconquered and an ancient foster-child of the Christian faith, was captured and reduced to the power of a most filthy people. Its broad territories also were overrun by the persistent fury of the enemy and passed into their possession; and the worship of the Christian religion beyond the Euphrates was utterly destroyed. Christians, stirred by the report of so great an evil,” etc. Thus William of Newburgh, *The Affairs of England*, book I, chapter 18. This is the grievous and pitiable groaning of the Eastern Church of which Bernard speaks.] has reached your ears, indeed, I think, the very inner chambers of your heart. [Col. 0569A] For it is fitting that, in accordance with your greatness, you display a great feeling of compassion for that mother of yours and of all the faithful, especially while she is so violently afflicted and so gravely endangered. It is fitting, I say, that zeal for the house of God should consume you all the more because, through its author, you hold a more extensive place in it. Otherwise, if we harden our feelings, if we harden our hearts, if we regard this wound lightly and do not grieve at its crushing, where is our love for God, where our love of neighbor? Indeed, if we do not strive with all the care we can to devise some counsel and remedy for such great evils and dangers, how are we not proved ungrateful to him who hid us in the day of evils in his tabernacle, and therefore more justly and more severely to be punished, as neglectful both of divine glory and of our brothers’ salvation? We have thought it right to suggest this to you as confidently as familiarly, because of the favor with which your excellence deigns to honor our unworthiness.

2. For our fathers, the bishops of France, together with the lord King and the princes, are to come on the third Sunday after Easter to the city of Chartres and deliberate about this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0569D] At this council Bernard, chosen as leader of the military expedition, refused to take up that office as contrary to his character and monastic profession; see Letter 256 to Eugenius, II.4. Compare the present Letter 363 and the letters of Suger, the 133rd of which is by Peter the Venerable excusing himself from this council because a general chapter at Cluny had been appointed for the same day.]

Would that we might be worthy to have your presence there. For this matter plainly requires the great counsels of great men; you will surely render a pleasing service to God if you do not regard his cause as foreign to you, but demonstrate the zeal of your charity in times of need and distress. For you know, most loving father, [Col. 0569C] you know that a friend is proved in necessity. We trust, moreover, that your presence will contribute greatly to this cause: both because of the authority of the holy church of Cluny, over which by God’s appointment you preside, and especially because of the wisdom and grace which he himself has given you, surely for the benefit of your neighbors and for his own honor. May he now also deign to inspire you not to be burdened by coming, [Col. 0570A] and to grant your most desired presence to his servants gathering in his name and for zeal for that name.

## LETTER CCCLXV

[Note: [Col. 0570C] Formerly Letter 323; what was previously 365 is now 396. Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

[Note: [Col. 0570C] Concerning him, see above, Letter 302. In the Aquicinctum codex this title is prefixed to the letter: “To Henry, [Col. 0570D] archbishop of Mainz, against Brother Rudolf, who had consented to the killing of Jews.” MARTÈNE.]

He rebukes the monk Radulf, who was arming the faithful to kill Jews.

To the venerable lord and most beloved father HENRY, archbishop of Mainz, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: may he find favor with God.

1. I received the letters of Your Affection with due reverence; but because of the multitude of affairs, my reply is brief. Your entrusting to us the matter of your complaint is a sign and pledge of affection and a particular indication of humility. [Col. 0570B] For who am I, or what is my father’s house, that the contempt shown to an archbishop and the injury done to a metropolitan see should be referred to me? Am I not a little child, ignorant of my coming in and going out? Yet I do not fail to know the word of truth, proceeding everywhere from the mouth of the Most High: “It is necessary that scandals come, but woe to the one through whom they come!” (Matt. 18:7). That man of whom your letter speaks [Note: [Col. 0570D] He is named Radulf or Rudolf and is described by Otto of Freising, *The Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 37, as the author of a bloody persecution of the Jews. Bernard opposed his seditious teaching and warned Radulf himself—whom he found at Mainz enjoying immense popular favor—not to wander through the world contrary to the monastic rule and presume, on his own authority, to assume the office of preaching. At length Bernard induced him to return to his monastery under promised obedience, although the people were greatly angered and, had they not been restrained by regard for Bernard’s holiness, were even ready to raise a rebellion. Thus Otto, *The Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 39.] came neither from man nor through man, nor indeed was he sent by God. If he boasts that he is a monk or hermit and on that basis arrogates to himself liberty or the office of preaching, he can and ought to know [that a monk’s office is not to teach but to mourn].

[Note: [Col. 0570D] See Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, chapter 6, and the notes to Letter 89.]

For a town ought to be his prison, and solitude his paradise. [Col. 0570C] But this man has the opposite: he treats solitude as a prison and a town as paradise. O man without heart! O shameless man! His folly has been raised on a lampstand, that it may appear to all who are in the house.

2. There are, indeed, three things in him most worthy of blame: usurpation of preaching, contempt for bishops, and the license of approved murder. A new kind of power! [Col. 0571A] Are you greater than our father Abraham, who laid down the sword at the command of him at whose command he had raised it? (Gen. 22.) Are you greater than the prince of the Apostles, who asked the Lord, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” (Luke 22:49.) But you have been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians—that is, the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19). You solve Peter’s question differently from him who says: “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). Does not the Church triumph more abundantly over the Jews by daily either refuting or converting them than if she consumed them all at once by the edge of the sword? Was that universal prayer of the Church established in vain, offered for the faithless Jews from the rising to the setting of the sun, that God and Lord might remove the veil from their hearts and draw them out of their darkness into the light of truth?

[Note: [Col. 0571D] This prayer is offered annually on Friday of Holy Week, in precisely the words Bernard uses here.]

For unless she hoped that those who disbelieve would believe, it would seem superfluous and vain to pray for them. But she sees with the eye of compassion that the Lord looks graciously upon the one who returns good for evil and love for hatred. Where then is what was said: “See that you do not kill them”? (Ps. 58:12.) Where is: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved”? (Rom. 11:25–26.) Where is: “The Lord, building Jerusalem, will gather together the dispersions of Israel”? (Ps. 146:2.) Are you the one who will make the Prophets false and empty all the treasures of the mercy and compassion of Jesus Christ? Your teaching is not yours, [Col. 0571C] but that of the father who sent you. Yet I suppose it is enough for you if you are like your master. For he was a murderer from the beginning; he was a liar and father of falsehood (John 8:44). O monstrous knowledge! O infernal wisdom, contrary to the Prophets, hostile to the Apostles, overthrowing mercy and grace! O most unclean heresy! O sacrilegious harlot, which, pregnant by the spirit of falsehood, conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity! (Ps. 7:15.) I would like to proceed further, but may not. Finally, to sum up briefly everything I think about these matters: he is a man great in his own eyes, filled with a spirit of arrogance. His words and deeds make it appear that he is trying to make for himself a name alongside the names of the great men of the earth; but he does not have the resources to complete it. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXVI

[Note: [Col. 0571D] Formerly Letter 386; what was previously 366 is now 410. Written in the year of Christ 1146.]

### TO HILDEGARD, ABBESS

[Note: [Col. 0571D] The abbess famous for revelations, namely of the monastery of St. Rupert the Confessor, opposite the town of Bingen in the diocese of Mainz, of the Order of St. Benedict, says Trithemius in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. The Monk of Auxerre seems to mean Hildegard under the year 1146 in these words: “At the same time in parts of Germany there was an admirable virgin of advanced age, upon whom divine power had bestowed such grace that, though she was a laywoman and unlearned, she was nevertheless most wonderfully often carried away from this world and in the highest regions learned not only what she afterwards spoke in lower ones, but rather—what is very marvelous and unheard of—even dictated in Latin by writing and composed, by dictating, books of Catholic doctrine.” See our Chronology under the year 1148. Hildegard’s letters are found in the *Library of the Fathers*, including one to Bernard in which she praises his zeal in preaching the holy expedition and says that she saw him “two years earlier as a man in the sun.” John of Salisbury asks Master Gerard about her visions and says that she was most pleasing to Pope Eugenius.]

Having modestly rejected the praises addressed to her, he warns her to acknowledge God’s grace within her, and asks her prayers for himself and his brethren.

[Col. 0572A]

To HILDEGARD, beloved daughter in Christ, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: whatever a sinner’s prayer can accomplish.

Some appear to judge our insignificance quite differently from what our own conscience judges of it; this must be attributed not to our merits but to human foolishness. Yet I hastened to write to the sweetness of your devout charity, although the multitude of affairs compels me to do so much more briefly than I would wish. We rejoice in the grace of God which is in you, and we warn you to regard it [Col. 0572B] as grace, and to strive to respond to it with every affection of humility and devotion, knowing that “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). So far as lies in us, we exhort and beseech you. But where there is inward instruction and the anointing which teaches concerning all things, what can we teach or admonish? For you are said to search out heavenly secrets and, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, to discern things beyond human capacity. Therefore we ask—and earnestly beg—that you remember before God both us and those joined with us in spiritual fellowship. For when a spirit is united to God, we trust that you can greatly assist and help us. “For the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James 5:16). We pray constantly [Col. 0572C] for you: that you may be strengthened for good, instructed in inward things, and guided toward things enduring; so that those who have placed their hope in God may not falter in despair concerning you, but may, strengthened in the progress of the blessing which you are known to have received from God, advance better and better.

## LETTER CCCLXVII

[Note: [Col. 0572D] Formerly Letter 332; what was previously 367 is now 419. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO G., CHANCELLOR

[Note: [Col. 0572D] To Guido Moricato de Vico, a Pisan, who was chancellor after Robert Pullen from the year 1146; from the notes to Letter 334.]

He recommends the bishop of Metz.

Your predecessor, Haimeric, of good memory, the chancellor, embraced the lord bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 0572D] Namely Stephen.] with special affection; and whenever his envoys came to Rome, he received them most graciously and gave them diligent assistance. I therefore ask you also to follow in the same [Col. 0573A] footsteps and to aid, with the weapons of the Church, this noble bishop, who has been placed in great need.

## LETTER CCCLXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Formerly Letter 335; what was previously 368 is now 420. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO G., CARDINAL DEACON

He gratefully embraces the affection expressed in the latter’s letter and gift, and calls him away from love of earthly riches and possessions.

To the lord and most beloved friend G., by God’s grace cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and devout prayers.

1. Blessed are you by the Lord, who have so abundantly forestalled us with blessings of sweetness, so that, if any bowels of mercy, any affection, or any charity are found in us, the deeply devoted humility [Col. 0573B] and humble devotion of your noble spirit may rightly claim it all for itself. For previously I rejoiced altogether and gave thanks for the good zeal which, through the report of our brethren, I had learned was in you. But now, to the degree that I have any power in the Lord, I feel myself all the more indebted to your affection, because you have been more devoutly and humbly eager to commend yourself to our lowliness. Therefore I was careful to have our brethren read the letters revealing your heart, full of devout affection, full of mercy and grace; and to display the blessing [Note: [Col. 0573D] That is, the gift or sacred vessels which Guido had designated for the altar-service of Clairvaux; below, undoubtedly vessels of gold or silver.] which you had sent; and, as you requested, to direct that the solemnities of Mass be celebrated in those very vessels in remembrance of you and yours. May God make you a vessel unto honor in his great house, so that we, who hold you most dear, may deserve from the witness of your deeds—which we greatly desire—to hear also concerning you: “This man is for me a chosen vessel” [Col. 0573C] (Acts 9:15). For the Spirit of truth, through whom this charity is poured out in our hearts (Rom. 5:5), is witness to us how we long for you in the inward affections of Jesus Christ.

2. Since, therefore, we are zealous for you with the zeal of God, our prayer is made not only to Him on your behalf, but also to yourself: that you may carefully consider how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God and in the portion of this ministry. I say this not presumptuously—God knows—but out of charity: for judgment is severe upon those who preside, if they do not also labour to be of benefit; and conversely, “he who has ministered well will acquire a good standing” (1 Tim. 3:13). Therefore, most beloved and most dearly desired lord, turn aside, I beseech you,

[Col. 0574A]

more and more from evil, and do good. Do not be found in Christ’s inheritance seeking what is your own; but always remember that apostolic saying: “We brought nothing into this world; without doubt neither can we carry anything out” (1 Tim. 6:7).

Therefore guard your soul, which is immortal, dearest friend, lest on any occasion that which the Lord says in the Gospel be torn away or uprooted from your heart’s affection: “What does it profit a man if he gain the whole world, but lose himself and suffer the loss of himself?” (Matt. 16:26). Utterly wretched, wretched are those “who spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment go down to hell” (Job 21:13). For when they perish, they will not take all things with them, nor will their glory descend with them (Ps. 48:18), since

[Col. 0574B]

it is “a vapour appearing for a little while” (Jas. 4:15).

Think upon these things, dearest friend; meditate upon them continually; inscribe them upon your heart; and let them never depart from your memory. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXIX

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Otherwise Letter 356; what was formerly 369 is now 338. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO SUGER, ABBOT

He congratulates Suger on the happily instituted reform of the church of St Geneviève, and exhorts him to persevere in what he has well begun.

To his most loving father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] Bernard customarily uses this formula of prayer when writing to Suger.]

Blessed be God, who has wrought salvation through your hand in the church of Saint Geneviève.

[Note: [Col. 0573D] What this salvation was may be gathered from Stephen of Tournai, bishop and formerly abbot of Saint Geneviève, in his sermon on the reform of discipline made there. “In the year,” he says, “from the Lord’s Incarnation, a word was spoken in the King’s palace; it was solemnly discussed, faithfully pursued, and happily brought to completion. Messengers came to say that the church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, situated on Mount Leucotitius, where the glorious virgin Geneviève rests in the body, was exposed to many dangers and, by the disorderly condition of the conduct of its members rather than of its walls, threatened ruin: that its sons, living in a singular and secular manner, sought what was their own and wandered after the flocks of their companions; that they consumed church revenues, which are the tributes of needy souls, according to their own pleasure; made private portions from what was common and did not live in common; and celebrated the divine offices with insufficient devotion and insufficient religious seriousness. For these and other matters which need not be mentioned, the condition of the persons had to be changed, the holy place cleansed, and it put in better order. This proposal and its beginning pleased the eyes of the Lord of hosts, and all marvelled, not without joy.”

In that church Suger had established the regular canons of St Augustine in place of monks, whom Eugenius had ordered to be introduced there in place of secular canons. The matter is likewise mentioned in the following letter, where the church is called that “of the Mount,” namely Leucotitius, as it was formerly called. See Suger’s letters, in which these and the following letters are included.]

[Col. 0574C]

Thus the house of God was restored to order and discipline. Apostolic authority itself gives you thanks because you have faithfully and effectively begun a magnificent work; we too give such thanks as we can, as do all who love God in truth. We therefore earnestly ask and entreat you, in accordance with the tenor of the apostolic letters, to lend your hand to the work of your hands, so that what has been magnificently begun may daily advance through the work of Your Greatness and be happily brought to completion.

We judge it superfluous to urge your charity concerning the church of Saint-Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0574D] See Letter 410.]

For the guardianship of all churches is known to have been entrusted to you. Yet greater assistance is due to those whose religious life is known to be in greater need.

## 333. LETTER CCCLXX

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Otherwise Letter 357; what was formerly 370 is now 337. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO THE SAME

He commends to him the church of the Mount.

[Col. 0575A]

To his dearest father and lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux, called abbot: greeting and affection.

You ought to do the works of him who left you in his place—indeed, the works of the Lord your God, who chose you for such a ministry.

[Note: [Col. 0575D] This is to be understood of Louis the Younger, who, having departed for the East, entrusted his responsibilities to Suger. Hence Bernard says in the preceding letter that the care of all churches had been entrusted to him; and in Letter 376, now numbered thus, to the same man: “You are the greatest prince in the kingdom.” Ulger, bishop of Angers, therefore addresses him by the title “Majesty” in Letter 3 among Suger’s letters.]

Among his works is this: that the church of the Mount has put on religious observance and beauty, where that new planting has found in you a great counsellor and helper. We beg you to bring to a better completion what you have well begun, and to set yourself as a wall for the house of Israel, lest man prevail. Deign also to console the abbot of that place—

[Col. 0575B]

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Namely Odo.]

—for he is faint-hearted. This befits the honour of your person and the salvation of your soul, especially at this time.

## LETTER CCCLXXI

[Note: [Col. 0575D] Otherwise Letter 363; what was formerly 371 is now 323. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO THE SAME

He dissuades him from a marriage between the son of the Count of Anjou and the daughter of the King of France, on account of the impediment of consanguinity.

To the lord abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

Thus I wrote to the lord King: “You have undertaken a great work and an inestimable burden, which none but divine power can bear. Your undertaking is beyond human strength—

[Note: [Col. 0575D] That is, the holy expedition. Therefore this letter must without doubt be referred to Louis the Younger, who wished to unite his firstborn daughter Maria to the son of Fulk, Count of Anjou, who had likewise departed for the East. The plan came to nothing; Maria was given to Henry, Count of Champagne.]

—but what is impossible for men is easy for God” (Luke 18:27).

[Col. 0575C]

“If you know this, you must take the greatest care lest on any occasion you reject such necessary aid, lest by any suggestion you offend God and render his grace hostile to you. You must take care, I say, especially now, lest God, provoked by you, become angry, turn his face from you, and withdraw his helping hand. For this danger concerns not the King alone but the whole Church of God, since from this point your cause and that of the whole world are one.

“Listen to the point of these remarks. I hasten to you, as this letter does, intending to be at Laon on the vigil of blessed Mary Magdalene; but I have taken care to forewarn and fortify you by another letter. For I have heard that the Count of Anjou is hastening to bind you by faith and oath concerning a marriage to be contracted between—

[Col. 0575D]

—his son and your daughter. This is not merely inexpedient but unlawful, not only for other reasons, but because the impediment of consanguinity forbids it.

[Col. 0576A]

For, as we have learned by truthful testimony, the queen’s mother and this boy, the son of the Count of Anjou, are found to be related in the third degree of consanguinity. For this reason we warn you in every way not to do this thing, but to fear God and turn aside from evil. You promised that on no account would you do it without our counsel; and if I kept silence, I myself would sin. This, therefore, is our counsel: that you do not do it in any way.

“If you do it, know that you have acted against our counsel, against the counsel of many who cherish your name, and even against God. And do not suppose that your sacrifice will be acceptable to God when, though you are concerned for another’s realm, you do not spare your own kingdom, disposing of it against God, against law and right, and against what is useful and honourable.

[Col. 0576B]

“I have delivered my soul; may God also deliver yours from wicked lips and a deceitful tongue.”

## 334. LETTER CCCLXXII

[Note: [Col. 0576D] A new letter; what was formerly 372 is now 319. Written about the year 1147.]

### TO P., BISHOP OF PALENCIA IN SPAIN

He praises him for humility, but especially for devotion to reading.

To the venerable lord and dearest father P., by God’s grace bishop of Palencia, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: may you be anticipated by the Lord with blessings of sweetness.

Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and rest amid the fragrance of your ointments? Your venerable conduct and integrity of character have filled my nostrils with a sweet fragrance; and behold, that fragrance has become to me like the scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed. Truly my soul has been filled, as with fat and richness,

[Col. 0576C]

by this fragrance, and in such things is the life of my spirit. For how can my soul hear and not delight in its abundance when it hears of a man who is exalted and humble, active and tranquil, and who trembles at the words of the Lord? O rare bird upon earth: humility together with eminence, and a peaceful mind amid business! You have gladdened the soul of your servant, O Lord; may the merciful Lord also gladden yours in the joy of his people.

I rejoiced with very great joy that such things concerning you were reported by such persons, whom I could not possibly have thought mistaken. For the brothers who bear this letter told us of the discipline by which you bring your flesh into subjection; of the lifting up of the spirit; of love of reading; of gentleness of conduct; and of the working of good toward all,

[Col. 0576D]

but especially toward the household of faith.

Therefore, dearest friend, do not suppose that in these words I am intent upon praising you. That prophetic rebuke has not yet departed from my mind:

[Col. 0577A]

“My people, those who call you blessed deceive you” (Isa. 9:16). For I do not wish your head to be fattened with the oil of the sinner, because I am a sinner; but rather with the oil of gladness, which proceeds from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. I am not a seller of oil, for I have only a little oil with which to anoint myself in the arena of this world; nevertheless I cannot keep silent about Christ’s praises.

Let not the creature therefore be praised, but the Creator; not he who has received, but he from whom he received; not he who plants nor he who waters, since they are nothing, but God who gives the increase. I will therefore praise not the hand receiving but the hand extending; my mouth shall speak not praise of the servant, but praise of the Lord.

Therefore, dearest friend, if you are wise—indeed, because you are wise—

[Col. 0577B]

recognize grace in yourself, but not as from yourself. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.” I know that some people wish, as it were knowingly, not to know what they have received from the Lord, lest, lifted up in pride, they fall into the devil’s snare. But it seems to me that I ought to know what I have received, so that I may know what I lack. It seems to me, in accordance with the Apostle, that we should know the things given us by God, lest we fail to know what we ought to long for in asking.

For one who has received and does not know what he has received places himself near a twofold danger: he is ungrateful for what has been received and careless in preserving the benefit. How, indeed, does he give thanks to the one from whom he received, if he does not know that he has received what he received? Or how will he be diligent in guarding it if he does not remember that he has received anything?

[Col. 0577C]

Take from me, Lord, the reproach of that ungrateful people of whom it is said: “They forgot his benefactions and his wonders which he showed them” (Ps. 77:11). A benefit received, therefore, even according to the wise men of this world, should be fixed in everlasting memory. We must consequently know how to preserve what we have received, and the grace of God must not be empty in us; rather, so that it may always remain in us, let us always give thanks to the Lord our God.

I do not think it irrelevant to add this also: that, in order to obtain salvation and grace, you should ascend by three steps—humility, faith, and fear. For humility is that to which grace is given; faith is that in which it is received; fear is that by which it is preserved. For if without these three we ascend toward grace, I fear it may be said to us: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep” (John 4:11).

[Col. 0577D]

Let the cord of inheritance, then, serve for drawing the water of wisdom; and let this humility be in the mouth, in the heart, and in deed, because “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” Let faith be the water-jar, and let it be large, so that much grace may be drawn from it. Let fear be its covering, lest the water of wisdom be polluted by the defilements of vain glory. For it is written: “A vessel that has no cover shall be unclean” (Num. 19:15).

[Col. 0578A]

That devotion of yours to reading has moved my hand to write, by which you embrace not only the works of great men but even our trifles; so that through those by whom your goodness was reported, it might also be reported to you how great a joy you have given my heart.

## LETTER CCCLXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0577D] A new letter; what was formerly 373 is now 411. Written about the year 1147.]

### FROM THE ABBOT SP. TO SAINT BERNARD

[Note: [Col. 0577D] Doubtless the abbot of La Espina, in the diocese of Palencia, whose foundress Sancia, sister of Emperor Alfonso, to whom Letter 301 was written, gave the place to St Bernard. Bernard’s brother Nivard was sent there with companions. Manriquez does not know the name of the first abbot, under the year 1147, [Col. 0578D] chapter 18, no. 3.]

He laments the office of superior imposed upon him.

To his desirable lord and dearest father BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, his son SP., unprofitable servant of the brethren of the church: the blessing of all nations.

I have earnestly desired, if it could be done, that this letter might find you free and released from other business. For I fear—and feared when I wrote it—

[Col. 0578B]

remembering him who sought to see Jesus but could not because of the crowd, since he was small in stature (Luke 19:3). But what if I find leisure and do not find favour in your eyes? Will leisure alone be a consolation to me? May God forgive you. What have you done? Where have you placed me, and as what sort of man? Would that my strength and the burden I bear were weighed in a balance! This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea.

For who am I, or what is my father’s house? Am I not a little child, ignorant of my going out and coming in? Who am I, or what am I, that I should be able alone to meet—rather, to succour—the church in which I have been placed, like a leaning wall and a tottering fence? This business is beyond my strength;

[Col. 0578C]

I am worn out by foolish labour. “I labour in my groaning”; but what profit is there in my labours and groanings? The diseases have grown old, the wound is cruel, and the pain incurable except by a strong hand. For vices have become customs, customs habit, habit nature, and nature necessity. O how necessary it would be to uproot this necessity! Yet—what ought to be said with tears—it has been strengthened, and I shall not prevail against it.

For behold, there is no help in me. Moreover this brother who bears the present letter, and who was greatly necessary to us, is leaving us. He taught the novices; they made progress, while I rejoiced and hoped through God’s mercy that at some time “what is mortal might be swallowed up by life.” I bear him witness, so far as one man may judge another, that his conduct

[Col. 0578D]

among us was pleasing to God and sweet to men. Therefore his departure could not be without sorrow. You are able, Lord, to turn my mourning into joy for me, if I have found favour in your eyes. Thus far. The bearer of this letter will explain the rest more fully.

## 336. LETTER CCCLXXIV
