[Note: [Col. 0578D] Otherwise Letter 311; what was formerly 374 is now 358. Written in the year of Christ 1148.]

### TO THE BRETHREN IN IRELAND, ON THE PASSING OF BLESSED BISHOP MALACHY

[Note: [Col. 0578D] In the year 1148, on the second day of November, the death of Saint Malachy occurred. Bernard wrote of him in his Life, in volume II. Add the two sermons on the same subject in volume III.]

The deaths of saints are to be marked with joy rather than mourning. By a singular benefit of God, Clairvaux was likewise honoured by the death and burial of so great a man.

[Col. 0579A]

To the religious brethren who are in Ireland, and especially to those communities which Malachy, bishop of blessed memory, founded, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the consolation of the Paraclete.

1. If we had here an abiding city, we should rightly bewail with most abundant tears that we had lost such a fellow-citizen. But if, as we ought, we seek rather the city to come, then although being deprived of so necessary a guide is no small cause of sorrow, knowledge should moderate zeal and confidence in hope should soften grief. No one should marvel if affection wrings forth groaning and desolation draws out tears; nevertheless a measure must be kept, indeed we ought also to find no small consolation, looking not at the things which are seen but at those which are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

[Col. 0579B]

First, then, we should congratulate the holy soul, lest he accuse us of a lack of charity, saying what the Lord himself said to the Apostles: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father” (John 14:28). The spirit of our father has gone before us to the Father of spirits. We shall be convicted not only of lacking charity but also of ingratitude for all the benefits that came to us through him, unless we congratulate him who has passed from labour to rest, from danger to security, from the world to the Father. It is therefore pious to weep for Malachy dead, but more pious to rejoice with Malachy living. Does he not live?

[Col. 0579C]

Certainly—and blessedly. “He seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die,” but he is in peace.

2. Then the consideration of our own advantage also suggests that we should exult and rejoice because so powerful a patron has preceded his own people to the heavenly court, so faithful an advocate; one whose most fervent charity cannot forget his children, and whose proven holiness obtains favour with God. For who would now dare to suspect that holy Malachy is either less able to help or less loving toward his own? Since he was formerly loved, he now receives from God more certain proofs of his love; and since he loved his own, “he loved them unto the end.”

Far be it that your prayer, O holy soul, should now be judged less efficacious, when you can plead more vividly before the present Majesty and no longer walk by faith, but reign in sight!

[Col. 0579D]

Far be it that your charity, so laborious, should be thought diminished, much less emptied, now that you fall before the very fountain of eternal charity, drinking with a full mouth from that for whose drops you yourself formerly thirsted! Charity, strong as death—indeed stronger than death—could not yield to death. For even in departing he did not forget you: he commended you to God with deepest affection, and in his habitual gentleness and humility asked even our own small community not to forget you to the end.

We have therefore considered it fitting to write to you, so that you may know that, in spiritual matters—if ever our smallness can accomplish anything through the merits of this blessed father of ours—and in bodily matters, should opportunity at any time be offered, we are ready with entire devotion to bestow every consolation upon you.

[Col. 0580A]

3. Even now, beloved, we grieve with all our heart for this grievous bereavement of the Irish Church; and we sympathize with you all the more because we recognize ourselves as all the more indebted on this account. For the Lord has magnified his dealings with us, in that he deigned to honour our place by the presence of Malachy’s blessed death and enrich it with the most precious treasure of his body.

Do not be troubled that he has his burial among us, for God has so ordained according to the multitude of his mercies that you might have him while living, while we might be permitted to have him even when dead.

[Col. 0580B]

That great father was, and is, our father in common with you; for even in his death this testament was confirmed to us. Therefore, as we embrace all of you, by the grace of so great a father, as brothers of one blood, with all the inward affection of charity, so spiritual kinship itself persuades us that you feel the same toward us.

4. We exhort you, brethren, always to take care to follow the footsteps of this blessed father of ours, with all the more zeal because his holy conduct has become known to you with greater certainty through long experience. For in this you will prove yourselves to be his true sons: if you keep his fatherly ordinances with courage; and if, as you saw in him and heard from him how you ought to walk, so you walk—

[Col. 0580C]

—that you may abound more and more. For “the glory of a father is the wisdom of his children” (Prov. 10:1).

The example of such great perfection, present among us, has begun both to shake our sloth considerably and to inspire reverence. May it draw us after itself in such a way that it draws us all the way through, as, in the fresh fragrance of his virtues, we run more eagerly and more gladly. May Christ preserve your whole community, which prays for us.

## LETTER CCCLXXV

[Note: [Col. 0579D] Otherwise Letter 390; what was formerly 375 is now 316. Written in the year of Christ 1148.]

### TO IDA, COUNTESS OF NEVERS

He complains that the monks of Vézelay are being harassed by the Countess’s retainers.

To his beloved daughter in Christ, the Countess of Nevers, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux:

[Col. 0580D]

greeting and prayers.

The venerable abbot of Vézelay complains—

[Note: [Col. 0579D] Namely Pons.]

—that you and your retainers prevent merchants and others wishing to go to Vézelay from doing so. Since Count William of good memory, and his son in the presence of the lord bishop of Auxerre and ourselves, entirely repudiated this as impious and unjust—

[Note: [Col. 0580D] This William, retiring, as has already been noted, into the Charterhouse, had as his successor from the year 1147 another William, his son.]

—we warn and beg you not henceforth to do this in any way. For we fear that if you begin to do such things, they may perhaps do very great harm both to you here and to your husband where he is, which we would not wish at all. Trust us, therefore, and wholly desist from this wickedness.

## LETTER CCCLXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0581C] Otherwise Letter 358; what was formerly 376 is now 355. Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### TO SUGER, ABBOT

He exhorts and asks him to oppose the tournaments of certain princes.

[Col. 0581A]

To the venerable father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

Now is the time and the task for you to take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, against the devilish devices that are attempting to sprout again. For those men who have returned have set and arranged, after the Easter feasts, those accursed fairs—

[Note: [Col. 0581D] What are these fairs? This may be stated from William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, *Life of St Bernard*, book I, chapter 11, where he says: “A company of noble soldiers once turned aside to Clairvaux . . . The holy season of Lent was near, and nearly all those young men, devoted to secular warfare, went about seeking those execrable fairs which are commonly called *Tornetae*.” Others call them a “tournament”; Matthew Paris, *History of England*, p. 258. They were not that jousting display which is commonly called a “tournament,” but rather that military game called the “Round Table.” “It was indeed an amusement, appearing to be a probation—or rather an exercise—in military service, and customarily instituted in order to acquire agility and skill in handling weapons. Richard, king of England, therefore wished his men, in imitation of the French, to be trained in tournaments, so that from the customary prelude to wars they might learn the art of real warfare,” says William of Newburgh, book V, chapter 4. But sports often turned serious, and games ended in slaughter. Hence, according to the testimony of the same Newburgh, such exercises of arms were prohibited at three different general councils under three Roman pontiffs. At the Lateran Council Pope Alexander said: “Following in the footsteps of our predecessors, Popes Innocent and Eugenius of blessed memory, we prohibit the detestable fairs which are commonly called tournaments, in which knights customarily assemble by agreement and engage one another with rash boldness, whence deaths of men and dangers to souls often arise. And if anyone should die there, although penance is not denied him if he seeks it, he shall nevertheless lack Christian burial.” These particulars are from William of Newburgh. But that the threats achieved nothing and that the ardour of young men vainly coveting the glory of arms admitted no restraint is attested by the same author in the cited place. It is clear, therefore, what kind of fairs were instituted by Count Henry, son of Theobald the Great, Count of Champagne, and Robert, the King’s brother, who had returned from the Jerusalem expedition. See Letters 179, 288, and 363.]

—wherein Lord Henry, the Count’s son, and Lord Robert, the King’s brother, with reins loosed, are to rush upon and kill one another. Consider with what purpose they undertook the Jerusalem journey, if they returned with such a purpose.

[Col. 0581B]

How rightly may it be said of them: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed” (Jer. 51:9); “they were struck, and did not grieve; they were crushed, and refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5:3). After so many labours, after so many dangers by which they were afflicted with the tribulation of evils and pain, the kingdom is at peace and the Lord King is absent; yet through these two men the land may be especially shaken and disturbed.

I beseech and advise Your Highness, because you are the greatest prince in the kingdom, to oppose this with all your strength, whether by persuasion or by force, lest it take place; for this befits the honour of your person, your country, and the welfare of the Church of God. By force I mean what pertains to ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 0581C]

We are writing the same to the lord of Reims, the lord of Sens, the lord of Soissons, the lord of Auxerre, Count Theobald, and Count Ralph. Oppose such great evils, for the sake of the lord King and for the sake of the lord Pope, to whom belongs the guardianship of the kingdom.

## LETTER CCCLXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0582D] Otherwise Letter 359; what was formerly 377 is now 346. Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### TO THE SAME

He commends Suger’s zeal and concern for the common good, because he summoned an assembly of the kingdom for its safety, and exhorts him to conduct the public cause boldly.

To his dearest father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace—

[Col. 0582A]

—abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: the spirit of counsel and consolation.

1. Having seen certain letters of yours which Your Highness sent to the lord of Tours, we exulted and rejoiced—not with an ordinary joy, but with very great joy. May the Dayspring from on high visit you, who are planning to visit the kingdom of our most glorious King, so that it may thus be able to breathe again from the tribulation of evils and pain, which is already at the doors unless it is resisted with all strength.

Surely it was God’s counsel that you summoned the chief men both of the court and of the Church to counsel, so that all who inhabit the earth might know that there remains to the kingdom and its king a kindly friend, a wise counsellor, and a strong helper. To that king, I say, who serves the King whose kingdom is of all ages; who set nations and kingdoms in motion lest the King of heaven should lose his land—the land where his feet stood.

[Col. 0582B]

To that king, I say, who, though distinguished in glory, abounding in wealth, secure in peace, victorious in battles, and young in age, chose to go into exile from his own possessions in order to serve among strangers—yet to serve him is to reign. Who then would dare disturb his kingdom? Who would commit such great impiety against the Lord and against his anointed? My lord king, would that those who trouble you were cut off—those who seek evil both for you and yours, while you alone have remained among foreign peoples, lest that place which the Lord chose from all places on earth, that his name might be there, should remain deserted.

2. Therefore act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, for the Lord your God is with you in the protection of his King and exile. He who commanded the winds and the sea will easily calm the swelling waves. The whole Church of God will be with you, lest anyone rise up and cause Israel to sin; and it will bear with all its shoulders the whole burden, if indeed there is any burden.

[Col. 0582C]

For now is the time and the task for you to act according to the position you hold, the dignity in which you excel, and the power you have received, so that your memory may be held not only in blessing but also in admiration by this whole generation and those to come. Care must be taken, and great care taken, lest so great a portion of the Church of God be wearied without the greatest fruit; and something must here be determined which may either repel or crush all the malice of those who rise up.

It is our desire, when you are assembled in the Lord’s name, to send letters from our smallness to you; even if they do not help, they will at least show our affection.

[Col. 0583A]

May he who gave you this will also grant you the power and crush Satan under your feet, so that in this work the Lord may be glorified, the Church honoured, the kingdom established, and the mouth of those who speak and do wickedness stopped.

## 339. LETTER CCCLXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Otherwise Letter 360; what was formerly 378 is now 347. Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### TO THE SAME

He requests a supply of grain for religious persons in the archdiocese of Bourges.

[Col. 0583B]

To the most beloved lord SUGER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

Our brethren of the archdiocese of Bourges, of the House of God, lack bread. We have heard that the Lord King’s grain is abundant there and seems to be sold cheaply there. We therefore ask you to command that they be given from that grain whatever amount seems good to your prudence. For the lord King, while he was in this land, used to do them good.

## LETTER CCCLXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Otherwise Letter 361; what was formerly 379 is now 353. It is no. 93 among Suger’s letters. Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### TO THE SAME

He asks that assistance be given to a certain impoverished abbot.

[Col. 0583C]

To the lord and most beloved father SUGER, by God’s grace revered abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and devout prayers in Christ.

We send a poor abbot to a rich abbot, so that the poverty of one may in some measure be relieved from the abundance of the other. We certainly yield to you the more honourable part, in accordance with the saying of Truth, which declares it more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35). Nor do I doubt that you would extend your hand more willingly and generously to this poor man of Christ if his religious seriousness and integrity, and also the need he suffers, had become as well known to you as to us.

For he is weighed down by debts and suffers want of bread, because his fields have yielded him harmful weeds instead of wheat.

[Col. 0583D]

Since this barrenness has not affected your coffers, we beg and ask, by your mercy, that assistance be given him. Do not doubt in any way that whatever you are pleased to bestow upon him will be usefully invested and laid up.

## LETTER CCCLXXX

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Otherwise Letter 362; what was formerly 380 is now 360. Written in the year of Christ 1149.]

### TO THE SAME

Concerning the perilous condition of the Eastern Church.

To his most loving father and lord SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux:

[Col. 0584A]

greeting and such prayers as he can offer in the Lord.

I received the message brought by the master of the Temple and Brother John as gladly as something which I believed had come from God. For the Eastern Church itself now cries out so miserably that whoever does not sympathize with all his heart is not proved to be a child of the Church.

Yet, as glad as I was at the message, so grieved was I by the narrow time-limit, because I could not meet Your Belovedness. For I had promised to meet the bishop of Langres on that very day for a conference, which he had undertaken in reliance upon me concerning great and serious affairs. I have, however, indicated the time when, if you please, I shall gladly meet with the same bishop, who can be of great use to the discussion.

## 340. LETTER CCCLXXXI

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Otherwise Letter 364; what was formerly 381 is now 320. Written about the year 1150.]

### TO THE SAME

Though he thinks rightly of Suger himself, he warns that he nevertheless grieves because the evils of the kingdom are publicly imputed to him. He exhorts him to take care lest he be disgraced by association with those through whom these things are done.

[Col. 0584B]

To the revered father and our dearest friend SUGER, by God’s grace abbot of Saint-Denis, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and whatever prayers are ours.

The constraints of time compelled me to reply more briefly to the letter of Your Paternity. For it was already drawing toward evening on the day when I received that letter, and on the following day I had to set out for the Chapter at Cîteaux. [Col. 0584C] Therefore I reply briefly; and I wish this to be utterly far from you—that it should ever enter your heart that I have in any way believed the evils we lament to be done by your counsel and will. There was, however, one thing: driven by urgent zeal, I was laboring to express to you—indeed, to impress and urge upon you—that very zeal, so that the same feeling might inflame your Holiness as well. There was another: although I thought well of your conscience, I was nonetheless greatly saddened by the reputation and scandal existing in God’s Church. If they are unwilling to submit, especially in matters of this kind, what will you do among them? Why do they cloak themselves with you? Must you not utterly separate yourself from those sacrilegious persons and stand far from them, so that, secure in conscience, you may sing: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, [Col. 0584D] and I will not sit with the wicked” (Ps. 25:5); so that the whole church of the saints may know that your innocence is alien to their number and fellowship? Therefore remember the opening words spoken by the Lord in the Prophet, and you will find that blessed is the man who “has not walked in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. 1:1). But believe this: I have never thought ill of you. For I know you and your purity. Farewell, and pray for us.

## LETTER CCCLXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Elsewhere Letter 324; what had formerly been 382 is now 321. Written about the year 1150.]

TO LEONIUS, ABBOT OF SAINT-BERTIN. [Note: [Col. 0585D] The monastery of Saint-Bertin was discussed above in Letter 149. Concerning Thomas, compare Letter 108 addressed to him. Leonius the abbot is praised by Herman, monk of Laon, in Book Three of the *Miracles of Blessed Mary*, chapter 4, where he is called “a man most religious and most learned alike in secular and sacred literature.” [Col. 0586D] He presided from the year 1148 to the year 1163.] He gratefully acknowledges benefits received from him and his community. Thomas of Saint-Omer, wishing to transfer to Clairvaux, is not to be prevented.

[Col. 0585A]

To his beloved and venerable lord LEONIUS, abbot, and to the entire convent of the church of Saint-Bertin, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive.

1. We have received, dearest brothers, the letter of your Love, an indication of your wish and petition. I shall never forget the benefits which you extend to us and ours with a full hand, a cheerful mind, and a serene countenance. But what if I have not forgotten and am found ungrateful? Will memory alone leave me [Col. 0585B] excused? Indeed, it will accuse me more severely. I know how neither to show myself forgetful nor ungrateful to my friends. Yet if I have nothing with which to repay all that I have received from you—though I speak as one less wise—the Lord will repay on my behalf. I am generous with another’s resources, because I am needy and poor. How greatly I love the honor of your church and the beauty of the house of the Lord that is in you, he knows who enters more deeply into the human heart. Yet neither do I fear to tell the truth in this matter: I love those who love me. But in this I am not justified, for even the heathen do the same. There is not much praise in loving those who love me; but if I do not love them, I shall be judged wicked for wickedness. I loved you even before you deserved it; why, then, should I not love you after your merits? Those whom [Col. 0585C] it was right to honor even if no merits had preceded, not to honor after benefits is more than an injury. I shall always love you, dearest brothers, in the Lord, and with all affection shall serve you in him whose servants you are; indeed, I shall always honor in you Christ, whose members you are.

2. Yet, so that the service we render and the honor we owe you may be reasonable and irreproachable, it must be done prudently and cautiously, because “the honor of the king loves judgment” (Ps. 99:4). Concerning, therefore, what you write back to me, I reply to your Charity that neither do I dare, nor ought you, to prevent one who is able to do good. For what answer have we to the Apostle when he says, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19)? [Col. 0585D] For it is not safe to extinguish what, once extinguished, it is not in your power to kindle. And where is that saying: “Let each remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Cor. 7:20)? Thomas, I say, was called [Note: [Col. 0586D] Letter 108 addressed to him survives.] not by me, but by him “who calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4:17). Why do you look to us? Why do you regard us in this matter as though it were a human work and not God’s? This has been done not by a human being, nor [Col. 0586A] through a human being, but by the Lord. For it is not a human being but God who works in human hearts, inclining their wills wherever he wills. This, I say, has been done by the Lord; and therefore it ought to be not only wonderful but unchangeable in our eyes. For who, or what, is a human being, that he should assist the mind of the Lord or his Spirit? He who seeks the lost sheep knows both what he seeks and where he seeks it; and how and from where he recalls it, and where he places it, so that he may not lose it again. Therefore see that you do not recall one whom the Lord has called; do not bend down one whom God has raised up; nor place an obstacle before one to whom God extends his hand as he ascends.

3. But now we must consider what weight the point has which you make, that he was offered by his parents. Let your prudence see which has greater force and reason: that which was done concerning him by another while he himself did not know, or that which, knowingly and deliberately, he did concerning himself—not indeed he himself, but the grace of God, which goes before the unwilling so that he may will, and follows the willing lest he will in vain. But I say that his parents’ vow remains whole, and their offering is not made void but increased. For the same person is offered who was offered before; he is offered to the same one to whom he was offered before; and what had formerly been offered by the parents alone is now offered by the son. Moreover, I have no command to give you on this point; but I offer counsel. The word has gone forth from the Lord: do not hinder the course of God’s grace; do not repress the first fruits of a good will. For what has begun in him is from the Holy [Col. 0586C] Spirit. But do not fail to recognize the injury you inflict upon us, as though we had ever wronged you in this matter by wishing to take away from you the brothers whom God has sent to you. Let Thomas himself know that, if he makes void the vow for which he employed me as witness—and let any other person know, whoever he may be, who has impelled him to this—that I shall rise up against them and stand against them on the day of the Lord. But meanwhile it is better for him, for you, and for us to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0586D] Elsewhere Letter 342; what had formerly been 383 is now 361. Written about the year 1150.]

TO THE SAME ABBOT OF SAINT-BERTIN. He asks him to continue the acts of kindness hitherto shown to his brothers.

To his dearest friend LEONIUS, venerable abbot of Saint-Bertin [Col. 0586D], Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes salvation in him who sends blessings to Jacob.

Your charity has openly shown why I deservedly place confidence in you; having found an occasion to make itself known, it could not remain hidden under a bushel. I hold most gratefully those acts of kindness which you bestow upon our brothers [Note: [Col. 0586D] The monks of Clairmarais, near Saint-Omer, whose monastery Manrique dates to the year 1138.] who dwell near you. What you do for them, you do for me; indeed, you do it more truly for me than if you did it for me [Col. 0587A] directly. I therefore beseech you that this care of yours for them may continue, because they are far from us and we cannot assist them as we ought. Let it be the part of your kindness to take our place, so that you may be a father to them and they sons to you. If perhaps a time comes when we can respond to such great charity, visible proof will show that we are not ungrateful. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLXXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0587D] Elsewhere Letter 343; what had formerly been 384 is now placed before Letter 273. Written about the year 1150.]

TO THE MONKS OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT-BERTIN. He gives thanks for the beneficence hitherto rendered to his brethren, promising them an abundant recompense from God.

To all who are in the church of Blessed Bertin, beloved in Christ, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux [Col. 0587B], wishes them to serve the Lord in gladness.

Your merits call us to thanksgiving, to render the service of love. Since a benefit received should be impressed upon everlasting memory, I ought neither to be forgetful nor ungrateful for the benefits which you have bestowed upon our brethren—or rather, upon me. Whatever is bestowed upon mine is mine; whatever is poured into my very heart is given to me. I know in whom I have believed, and I am certain. I know that you love us not in word and speech, but in deed and truth. For, as evidence of the love and favor which our brothers have found in your eyes, not words but deeds proceed—deeds all the purer in God’s sight and more pleasing in human sight, because they arise from the grace of the giver alone, apart from the merit of the recipient. Therefore [Col. 0587C] we give thanks to your whole community for these things. For all these things we are indebted to you, if we are anything, if we can do anything—both we and our brethren. But lest it be too little for you to be acceptable to human beings, you are acceptable also to my God. For what you have done to one of his least ones, you have done to him (Matt. 25:40). And what of the fact that you have done it not merely to one but to several of his least ones? In all these matters I have no great recompense at hand, since I am needy and poor; but the Lord will repay on my behalf. May he who is the rewarder of all good things repay you, because you have gone before his poor in blessings of sweetness and in an example of charity. For the past we give thanks; for the future we pray that you may not grow weary in doing good. For in due season you shall reap from the seed of good work [Col. 0587D] sheaves of peace and glory. May God grant this to us. Amen.

## LETTER CCCLXXXV

[Note: [Col. 0588D] Elsewhere Letter 341; what had formerly been 385 is now 418.]

TO THE SAME. He congratulates them upon their stricter observance and encourages them to seek religious perfection and unceasing progress.

To the entire convent of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, most beloved to him in Christ, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes salvation and prayers.

1. Yes, I beg you, dearest brothers, do so. For a disciple who makes progress is the glory of his master. Whoever does not advance in Christ’s school is unworthy of his master’s teaching, especially where we are, where nothing remains in the same state; and not to advance is, without doubt, to fall away. Therefore let no one say, “It is enough; I wish to remain so; it suffices me to be as I was yesterday and the day before.” Such a person sits down on the road; he stops on the ladder, where the patriarch saw no one who was not ascending or descending (Gen. 28:12). Therefore I say: “Let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). The way is steep and narrow, and the many dwelling places are not here, but in the Father’s house (John 14:2). Thus, “he who says that he remains in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). For Jesus, as the Evangelist says, “grew and advanced in wisdom, age, and favor with God [Col. 0588B] and men” (Luke 2:52). Therefore he did not stand still, but “rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). And we too, if we are not foolish, shall run after him; we shall be drawn by the fragrance of his ointments. Otherwise, if he should happen to move far away, the way will be both more laborious and more dangerous for the sluggish soul, since it can neither be refreshed by the fragrance nor discern the sure footprints of one departing farther away.

2. Therefore run, brothers, so that you may obtain the prize (1 Cor. 9:24). This will indeed be so if you by no means judge that you have already obtained it, but, forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourselves toward what lies ahead (Phil. 3:13); if you lay hold of instruction, “lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way” (Ps. 2:12). Wisdom says: “He who eats me will still hunger, and he who drinks me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29), so that the sluggard, who is altogether deservedly stoned with ox dung (Ecclus. 22:2), may know that his distaste arises not from fullness, but from hunger.

3. Finally, since “all things work together for good to those who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8:28), let even the example of worldly desire move us. Whom have we ever seen who was ambitious, yet content with offices he had gained and not panting after others? Likewise, “the eye of every curious person is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” What of those who serve avarice, love pleasures, or pursue the empty praise of men? Do not even their insatiable desires rebuke [Col. 0588D] us for negligence and lukewarmness? Surely we ought to be ashamed to be found less eager for spiritual goods. Let the soul converted to the Lord blush to pursue righteousness with less ardor than it formerly pursued iniquity. For the cause too is very different: “the wages of sin is death; but the fruit of the Spirit is eternal life” (Rom. 6:23). Let us therefore be ashamed to go now more negligently toward life than formerly toward death, and to seek salvation with less zeal than the increase of perdition. For, that we may be wholly without excuse, on the way of life the faster one runs, the more easily one runs; and the Savior’s light burden, the more it increases, the more bearable it becomes. [Col. 0589A] Does not the very abundance of feathers or plumage lift little birds rather than burden them? Take these away, and the remaining body is carried downward by its own weight. So it is with Christ’s discipline, with the sweet yoke, with the light burden: the more we lay it down, the more we ourselves are weighed down, because it bears rather than is borne. The discipline of silence may seem burdensome to someone; but the prophet, seeing it to be strength rather than a burden, says: “In silence and hope shall be your strength” (Isa. 30:15). “In silence,” he says, “and hope,” because “it is good to wait silently for the Lord” (Lam. 3:26). Present consolation weakens the soul; expectation of future things strengthens it.

4. Therefore you did well, dearest brothers, to add something to the former rule of silence [Note: [Col. 0589D] It is remarkable how much Bernard attributed to silence in the pursuit of perfection, as in Letter 91 to the abbots assembled at Soissons, and elsewhere throughout his works. Indeed, it should seem remarkable to anyone that religion could stand without scrupulous observance of silence, which Bernard calls “the guardian of religion” in Sermon 2 after the Octave of Epiphany, no. 7.], since, as the aforementioned prophet testifies, it is the practice of righteousness [Col. 0589B] (Isa. 32:17). You did well in separating yourselves more and more from the affairs of this world, for this is pure and undefiled religion. For, brothers, “a little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (1 Cor. 5:6), and “dying flies spoil the oil of sweetness” (Eccl. 10:1). What profit is it to make the fruit of so great bodily and spiritual labor and exercise less acceptable—or even to put it at risk—by some utterly trifling consolation, or rather desolation? How greatly does the vapor of such trifles, arising for a brief time, impede the sweetness of inward consolation and the grace of divine visitation! Especially for us monks, whose life, whether we will or not, lies in labor: we are plainly more miserable than all people if we suffer such great losses for things so slight. What folly indeed—rather, what madness—is it that, having left greater things, we should hold lesser ones at such risk? If we have despised the whole world, if we have renounced the affections of relatives, if we have bound ourselves to the prison of monasteries; if, finally, we did not come to do our own will but “have set men over our heads”: what ought not to be done, lest perhaps all these things perish for us through our folly [Col. 0589C] and negligence?

5. Therefore act, dearest brothers, and be careful to persevere and abound even more in the things you have begun, so that the growth of the fruits of your righteousness may increase day by day. For “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings” (2 Cor. 9:6). And surely a small increase in seed is no small multiplication of harvest. Because we rejoiced and were delighted on hearing of your progress, brothers, we judged it fitting to write these things to your Charity, desiring that, having been admonished, you may receive and embrace with worthy devotion the holy observances which can save your souls. For you know that “God loves a cheerful giver” (ibid., v. 7). [Col. 0590A] May Christ preserve your whole community as it prays for us.

## LETTER CCCLXXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Elsewhere Letter 333; what had formerly been 386 is now 368. Written in the year of Christ 1150.]

FROM JOHN OF CASAMARI TO BERNARD, ABBOT. He consoles Bernard concerning the unhappy outcome of the expedition to the Holy Land.

To his beloved father and venerable lord BERNARD, by God’s will and grace most reverend abbot of Clairvaux, Brother JOHN, his servant, humble abbot of Casamari [Note: [Col. 0590D] Casamari, a distinguished abbey in the territory of Veroli in Italy, was founded in the year 1005 under the Order of Saint Benedict, with Benedict as its first abbot. Bernard is said to have visited it more than once; hence he formed a friendship with the most devout Abbot John, the author of this letter, who in 1140 united his monastery to the Cistercians under the line of Clairvaux. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. 1, col. 289.], wishes him to run successfully and, more successfully, to be brought to completion by Christ’s mercy.

1. Mindful of the kindness and familiarity which your compassion once extended to me, unworthy as I am, I presume to open the thoughts of my heart to your Paternity as though I were present before you, trusting more in your gentleness [Col. 0590B] than fearing offense. For I hope that the affection and love which I bear toward you are not hidden from your compassion; and even if I should say something foolish, I trust that you will kindly and gently forgive a son as a father. I have been told, dearest father, that you are greatly saddened over this matter—which did not turn out as favorably as perhaps you had wished, I mean the journey to Jerusalem—because the Church of God, or its glory, did not increase as you desired. Therefore I humbly suggest to you what God, as I believe, put into my heart after I had long reflected upon this, considering that the Lord often reveals something to some insignificant person which he by no means grants a great person, filled with many gifts, to see: just as Jethro, a foreigner, gave counsel to holy Moses, who spoke with God face to face [Col. 0590C] (Exod. 33:11; Exod. 18).

2. It seems to me, therefore, that almighty God brought much fruit from this expedition, though not in the order the travelers themselves imagined. For if they had wished to carry out what they began justly and devoutly, as Christians ought, the Lord would have been with them and would have accomplished great fruit through them. But since they fell into evils—and this could by no means have been hidden from the Lord, who had been the author of the expedition, from the beginning—so that his providence should not be thwarted in its own design, he turned their wickedness into an occasion for his mercy and sent upon them persecutions and afflictions, through which, purified, they might attain the kingdom. Finally, those who returned confessed to us that they had seen [Col. 0590D] many dying there who said that they gladly died and did not wish to return, lest they should relapse further into sins.

3. But lest what I say come into doubt, I disclose to my spiritual father as in confession that the patrons of our place, the blessed John and Paul, have often deigned to visit us. I caused them to be asked concerning this matter, [Col. 0591A] and they gave this judgment, saying that the multitude of fallen angels had been restored from those who died there. Know also this: they made much mention of you and foretold that your end would come soon. Since, therefore, the matter turned out well, though not according to human desire, yet according to God’s purpose, it will be for your prudence to find consolation in this matter in him whose glory alone you seek and desire. For this reason he gave you grace both to exhort and to act in this undertaking: because he foresaw the good which he would accomplish through it. May he therefore happily bring your course to its completion, and establish us with you in his glory.

## LETTER CCCLXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0591D] Elsewhere Letter 352; what had formerly been 387 is now 397. Written in the year of Christ 1150.]

TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY. After a preliminary declaration of sincere affection and love for Peter, he asks to be excused if he wrote anything too sharply in certain letters.

[Col. 0591B]

To his most reverend father and dearest friend PETER, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes salvation in the true Savior.

Would that, just as I can send you this letter, I could also send you my mind! Without doubt you would then read most clearly what the finger of God has written in my heart concerning my love for you, what he has impressed upon my inmost marrow. What then? Am I beginning once again to commend myself to you? Far be it. Long ago my soul was joined fast [Col. 0591C] to your soul; and the equality of charity made equal minds out of unequal persons. For what has my lowliness to do with your eminence, if condescension had not bowed down dignity? From that time it came to pass that my lowliness and your eminence were mutually mingled, so that neither could I be lowly without you nor could you be eminent without me. I say this because my Nicholas—indeed yours as well—was violently moved in spirit and moved me, asserting that he had seen our letter sent to you, in which words of bitterness were contained. [Note: [Col. 0591D] No extant letter corresponds to this. Peter mentions its substance in the following letter, no. 4. The Carthusians experienced similar agitation, as appears from Letter 270.] Believe one who loves you: nothing arose in my heart, nor was anything forced from my lips, that could irritate the ears of your Blessedness. The multitude of affairs is at fault, because while our secretaries do not retain our meaning properly, [Col. 0591D] they sharpen their pen beyond measure; nor can I see what I have instructed them to write. Pardon this once; for, whatever may be true of other letters, I shall see yours, and I shall not believe except my own eyes and ears. This common son of ours will report the rest to you more plainly and fully in person. Hear him as you would me, for he loves you not in word or speech, but in deed and truth. Greet for us that holy multitude of yours, and pray that they may pray for their child.

## LETTER CCCLXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0592D] Elsewhere Letter 353; what had formerly been 388 is now 348. Written about the year 1150.]

PETER THE VENERABLE TO BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX. He declines the titles and praises, clearly shows how highly he values Bernard and his friendship, and willingly accepts his satisfaction for the offense caused by the letters.

[Col. 0592A]

To the venerable and illustrious man in the members of Christ, Lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes him what he is after God and in God.

1. What shall I say? I am accustomed to speak, but now I have become mute. Why is this? Because your letter, which ought to have made me eloquent, has made me mute. Why? Because I read such great things in it, though it is brief, that if I tried to pour myself out in reply, I would seem more silent [Col. 0592B] than talkative. But I speak to a serious man, to a religious man. Therefore I must act as seriousness requires, as religion—if not mine, at least yours—demands. For is not what I say true? The letter is brief, but it supplies much matter for reply. Bear with me, I ask, if I say anything otherwise than I ought. For it belongs to true friendship not only to receive a friend’s savory things, but also either to season or to endure his unsavory ones. I have received from you, as I said, a letter: an exceptional letter, a letter displaying the sweetest love and an honor greater than is due to me. You call me most reverend, name me father, address me as dearest friend. I rejoice in these things; but, truth flowing into you from Christ being preserved, I do not know the first two and acknowledge the third. For I do not know that I am most reverend; I deny that I am your father; but that I am your friend, and your dearest friend, I profess not only with my mouth but acknowledge in my heart.

2. For, leaving aside the names “most reverend” and “dearest friend,” of which, as I said, I do not know one and acknowledge the other, concerning the name of father I write this to you, reverend brother, which the lord Guigo, Prior of the Carthusians, that singular and most illustrious flower of religion in his day, once wrote to me. I frequently wrote to him and often delighted in converse with him, whether in words exchanged face to face or in familiar letters; and in my letters I called him father. At first he tolerated this, thinking I would stop writing. But when he saw me persist and repeat the name of father in frequent [Col. 0592D] letters, that holy man finally burst forth in these words. For he wrote me a letter in which, among other things, he inserted this:

> “Therefore, through the love by which your heart burns toward us unworthy persons, we ask that, whenever your serenity deigns to write to our littleness, you think in such a way of your own edification that you do not inflate our weakness with dangerous exaltation.”

And immediately he adds:

> “And this, above all and before all things, we ask and beseech with knees fixed upon the ground: do not henceforth judge our vileness worthy of the name of father. It is enough and more than enough if one who is not deemed worthy even of the name of servant is called brother, friend, or son.”

[Col. 0593A] He wrote this to me; and I write this same thing to you. It is enough, and more than enough, if I may glory before you or concerning you in the name of brother, friend, dear one, or dearest one; or in some such title as befits you to send or teaches me to receive. This concerning the foregoing salutation.

3. But what of what follows? “Would that,” you say, “just as I can send you this letter, I could also send you my mind!” And immediately: “Without doubt you would then read most clearly what the finger of God has written in my heart concerning my love for you, what he has impressed upon my inmost marrow.” Truly these words, with the mystery of the greater meaning kept intact, are like “ointment upon the head, running down upon Aaron’s beard, to the edge of his garment”; truly they are like “the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion”; truly in this way “the mountains drip sweetness and the hills flow with milk and honey.” Do not wonder that I attend so carefully to your words and retain them. For I know that they have not been uttered by just any mouth, but by the mouth of one who knows how to speak only from a pure heart, a good conscience, and love unfeigned. I know this, I say; and the world knows with me that you are not among those who, according to the Psalm, “speak vanity to their neighbor”; that you are not among those whose lips are deceitful, who “speak with a heart and heart” (Ps. 11:3). Therefore, whenever it pleases your Holiness to write to me, I receive, read, and embrace your writings not carelessly or in passing, but diligently and affectionately. Who would not carefully read, and with great affection embrace, both what I have quoted and what follows? “Long ago,” you say, “my soul was joined fast to your soul, and the equality of charity made equal minds out of unequal persons. For what has my lowliness to do with your eminence, if condescension had not bowed down dignity? From that time it came to pass that my lowliness and your eminence were mutually mingled, so that neither could I be lowly without you nor could you be eminent without me.” Are words of this kind, then, to be read carelessly? Should they not hold fixed the reader’s eyes, seize the heart, unite souls? Consider, my dearest friend who wrote them, what you think of these words. I cannot think otherwise of them than what the letter says, than what I take to have been said by so great, so truthful, so [Col. 0593D] holy a man. Nor, as you yourself said, am I beginning again to commend myself to you. We began to love one another in Christ while still young; and shall we now, old men or nearly so, doubt a love so sacred and so long enduring? Far be it. Believe one who loves you, to use your own words: nothing has arisen in my heart, nor has anything proceeded from my mouth, that I should ever in any way doubt your words, if indeed they were spoken seriously. Hence I embrace, preserve, and guard what you wrote in the letter under discussion. A thousand talents of gold could more easily be stolen from me [Col. 0594A] than these words torn from my heart by any chance. But enough of this.

4. As to the matter on account of which your prudence thought I had been stirred, it was this. Concerning the affair, well known to you, of a certain English abbot, your letter contained these words [Note: [Col. 0593D] The letter does not survive.]:

> “It is as though judgment had been overthrown, justice had perished from the world, and there were no one to rescue the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the poor and destitute from those who despoil him.”

But, if you believe me, know that this stirred me just as the prophet says of himself—though I am no prophet: “But I, as a deaf man, did not hear; and as one mute, not opening his mouth”; and again: “I became as one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (Ps. 37:14–15). I was not offended by these words. But even if I had been offended, ample satisfaction was made when you said: “The multitude of affairs is at fault, because while our secretaries do not retain our meaning properly, they sharpen their pen beyond measure, nor can I see what I have instructed them to write. Pardon this once; for, whatever may be true of other letters, I shall see yours, and I shall not believe except my own eyes and ears.” Therefore I pardon, and readily grant forgiveness. With me, to say it humbly, it is not a great task, even in serious offenses, to forgive one who asks or grant pardon to one who seeks it. And if it is no task to forgive serious matters, how much less—or not at all—is it a task in slight ones?

5. Concerning the testament of Lord Baron, Roman subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0593D] See the notes to Letter 283.], which he is said, when dying, to have made for your churches of Clairvaux and Cîteaux [Col. 0594C] from the goods he had deposited with us: what certain persons, who said that this had been entrusted to them by him, wrote to me has been done. Yet I want you to know that, as certain witnesses whom I think truthful assert, you received more in these matters from the favor of the abbot of Cluny than from Baron’s testament. I know indeed, nor am I so ignorant of divine or human laws as not to know, that by a later testament both a legacy and a trust created in view of death are valid. Yet elsewhere I read: “Nothing is so consonant with natural law as that the will of an owner wishing to transfer his property to another should be held valid.” I say this because, as the witnesses just mentioned confess, he had given all that he had deposited at Cluny to Cluny, unless it should happen that Cluny received him before he ended his present life. Yet I did not wish to use this privilege; but what, according to their testimony, I believed to be mine, I granted to you and yours. Concerning the election of Grenoble [Note: [Col. 0594D] See the notes to Letter 270.], against which our Carthusians are acting, I have carefully reserved for disclosure to you, through the mouth of my dearest and your faithful Nicholas, what I think. Hear him, and believe without even the slightest hesitation that whatever he reports to you from my mouth is true. If any matters to be communicated have slipped my mind, when I remember them I shall communicate them to one most dear to me in Christ. Finally, [Col. 0595A] I ask and entreat as earnestly as I can—as I have already communicated through certain persons of your Order—that in this great assembly of holy men who have gathered at Cîteaux, you make mention of me, who am indeed yours, and earnestly commend me and the entire body of the Cluniac congregation to their prayers.

## LETTER CCCLXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Elsewhere Letter 354; what had formerly been 389 is now 413. Written in the year of Christ 1150.]

TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY. He says that Peter’s letter was exceedingly pleasant to him, but that, hindered by the weight of his occupations, he was unable to make a fuller reply.

To his dearest father and lord PETER, by God’s grace abbot of the Cluniacs, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes salvation and prayers.

[Col. 0595B] I read your letter in a brief moment, but not with a slight affection. I was occupied with such pressing business as you, most loving father, either know or can know. Yet I tore myself away and rescued myself from everyone’s requests and answers, and shut myself in with that Nicholas whom your soul loves. I read and reread the sweetness—great sweetness—which flowed from your letter. That letter breathed forth your affection and stirred my own. I was grieved because, though I was moved as I was, I could not write back. For the many evils of the day summoned me away. Indeed, a great multitude had assembled from nearly every nation under heaven. I had to answer them all, because, as my sins deserve, I was born into this world to be overwhelmed and [Col. 0595C] consumed by many and manifold anxieties.

Meanwhile I write this little to my own soul; but when I have time, I shall dictate a more careful letter, which will more clearly reveal the affection of one who loves. Concerning the Baron’s testament, which you sent us, we tell you truly that we received it not as something owed, but as a gift. I rejoice that I have learned the truth about the affair of Grenoble. [Note: [Col. 0595D] See the preceding letter, no. 5.] But know this: my heart grew exceedingly warm at the words of our common son which he conveyed to me on your behalf. I am ready, and I have not been troubled, to do your will wherever I can. At the Cistercian assembly, remembrance was made of you—as a special lord, father, and dearest friend—and of yours, both living and dead. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Such was the custom among monastic congregations bound together by a mutual fellowship of suffrages.] The bishop-elect of Beauvais greets you as his own; [Note: [Col. 0595D] Henry. See Letter 307 and the notes.] for he is yours. [Col. 0595D]

I, your Nicholas, greet you forever and beyond, and that household family which clings close to your side and spirit. [Note: [Col. 0595D] Nicholas, Bernard’s secretary, added this of his own accord.]

## LETTER CCCXC

[Note: [Col. 0595D] Otherwise Letter 314; what was formerly 390 is now 375. Written in the year of Christ 1152.]

### To Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, Legate of the Apostolic See in Denmark and Sweden

[Note: [Col. 0595D] The city of Lund, the metropolitan see of Denmark, then governed by Eskil, to whom Peter of Celle wrote several letters. At Eskil’s request he sent Carthusians into Denmark, as appears from Letter 23 of Book I, where he praises Eskil because “not only into grass, but into ears of grain, has the Cistercian or Clairvaux Order there grown through an increase of brethren, as likewise has the Premonstratensian religious order.” I find that Eskil was not only Archbishop of Lund in Denmark, but also Primate of Sweden by decree of Pope Adrian IV. He came from Denmark to visit St Bernard at Clairvaux. See the highly worthy account in Book IV, chapter 4, of the *Life of St Bernard*.]

He gratefully and humbly acknowledges Eskil’s love, and in return shows his own.

[Col. 0596A]

To his most loving father and lord ESKIL, by God’s grace Archbishop of Lund, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting in the true Saviour.

1. I received your writings and greetings—or rather, the affections of your heart—as gladly as I especially love you and am loved by you. Thus it is that, upon hearing of your troubles, I have made them not merely my own but have found them so; for I cannot but grieve when you grieve, sweetest father, nor can I hear of your distresses and anxieties except with distress and anxiety myself. Whatever vexes you touches and afflicts my heart; and whatever it is that persecutes you persecutes not you alone, but me with you. For whatever grace and affection absent friends can bestow upon one another, I think that I owe to you, and that you owe to me. I am bold, but not false; and the gracious condescension of your Sublimity has compelled me to this boldness. For when would I have presumed it? When would one so small have dared to hope for so great a favour from one so great? And if I cannot repay it, my recompense is not dead, for the Lord will repay on my behalf (Psalm 137:8). The Lord, I say, in whom and for whom you embrace us with such devotion and bind us with such affection. Blessed be your holy angel, who suggested this to your devout heart; [Col. 0596C] blessed be our God, who persuaded you. I glory in the privilege of your love; through our dearest brother, your son William, I have been refreshed by the abundance of sweetness in your heart. I have been refreshed by your messenger, refreshed by your letter, refreshed by all who can come from you to us or pass through us.

2. Would that it had been granted me from above to say these things rather than dictate them, so that I might disclose myself by speaking rather than writing! Certainly a living utterance would be more welcome than a written one; the tongue more effective than the letter. The eyes of one speaking would confirm his words, and the countenance would express affection better than the finger. But since I cannot do this in person, I satisfy you as far as I can through letters, [Col. 0596D] which take second place in such matters. We received your messenger with great rejoicing, and we supported your affair with the lord [Col. 0597A] Pope as far as we were able. [Note: [Col. 0597B] See Letter 280, no. 4.]

But concerning that secret matter [Note: [Col. 0597B] What was this secret? It would indeed be secret to me, unless Saxo Grammaticus, if I am not mistaken, reveals it. He says of our Eskil as follows, in Book 14 of his *History of Denmark*: “At the same time Eskil, exhausted by domestic affairs beyond his strength, while more earnestly seeking rest, with difficulty obtained leave to depart from the king and made for the noble Gallic monastery called Clairvaux.” Again in the same book: [Col. 0597C] “In a private conference Eskil earnestly begs King Valdemar not to interpret as untimely the confession of a secret which he wishes to entrust to him.” When he was told to state what he desired, he said that for a long time he had wished to lay down the episcopate, since age, its strength exhausted, had made him unequal to so great a burden. For he wished to withdraw not amid eminence, but as a private person, freed from administration, changing his former manner of life for a monastic one. Saxo immediately adds that, when Absalon, who succeeded him in the episcopate, asked why he so afflicted the people with grief, he replied: “Both his old age and the exile of his nephews had made office burdensome to him and his native country distasteful. To this was added the religious obligation of a vow, by which he had long ago promised Bernard of Clairvaux that he would voluntarily resign the episcopate and lead a private life free from honours.” This, then, is the secret. In the year 1178 Eskil came to Clairvaux, where, after spending four years piously and religiously, he died, namely in 1182. See Saxo Grammaticus, *History of Denmark*, Book [Col. 0597D] 14; also the *Book on the Illustrious Men of the Cistercian Order*, distinction 3, chapter 25; the *Life of St Bernard*, Book 4, chapter 4; Crantzius, Book 6 of his *Danish History*, chapters 41–42; and Henriquez, *Menologium*, 10 April. For Eskil’s withdrawal to Clairvaux, above all read the two letters of Peter of Celle: Book 7, Letter 17, and Book 8, Letter 1. The same author, in Book 1, Letter 23, praises him for resolving to plant throughout the province entrusted to him “new nurseries of every kind of sacred order,” and for having already accomplished this in great part by bringing in brethren not only from the Cistercian but also from the Premonstratensian Order, while Carthusians were to be established there as soon as possible.], your William will answer you on our behalf—the one who is yours, I say, and especially yours in the bowels of Jesus Christ. For I have put my words in his mouth, and in this matter you will hear him as myself.

Alas, I am torn away, snatched away! I may not continue. The evil of the day calls me off; the crowd of arrivals calls me back, and they break off the letter rather than bring it to an end. But because they make me write little, can they make me love little? They exclude the act, not the affection. That is always with you which is its own master; and it will be with you as long as it exists, father most devout and reverend, to be honoured by me with every right of friendship.

## LETTER CCCXCI

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Otherwise Letter 347; what was formerly 391 is now 326.]

### To the Abbess of Faverney

[Note: [Col. 0597D] Faverney, or Faverniacum, a monastery of the diocese of Besançon, situated in the county of Burgundy, was at first founded for nuns of the Order of St Benedict. Later, because dissensions and a freer manner of life among the nuns had opened the way, it passed in 1132 into the right and power of the monks of La Chaise-Dieu, as appears from the following charter, which we produce from the archives of La Chaise-Dieu.

ANSERIC, by God’s grace Archbishop of Besançon, to the venerable STEPHEN, Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, to the brethren serving God there, and to their successors in perpetuity. [Col. 0598C] From the pastoral care committed to us, we must provide with vigilant concern for the peace of churches and the increase of religion. Therefore we visited that noble church of Faverney, which in ancient times had flourished in the religious life of nuns, in order to offer some aid for its desolation. Having therefore assembled there the advocates of that place—namely Count Renaud, Guy of Junciville and his brother Henry, Theobald of Rougemont, Humbert of Jusliac, and his brother Louis—we found it estranged from every observance of religion and deserted by its inhabitants because of manifold disorder.

Accordingly, through our care and the exhortation of illustrious men, the discord which had devastated the aforesaid place was, by God’s working, pacified. For the reform of religion in the said place, the aforesaid advocates wholly surrendered, renounced (*vuerpiverunt*), and swore never again to reclaim the customs—whether just or unjust—which they possessed in the town of Faverney and within the bounds of its parish, into the hand of Count Renaud. [Col. 0598D] Likewise, they renounced into the hand of that same count and abjured all but what was due of the customs which they appeared to possess in villages belonging to Faverney. Richard of Montfalcherni likewise surrendered and renounced into our hand those same exactions beyond what was due in villages belonging to the church of Faverney. Count Renaud gave into our hand the customs deposited with him by the aforesaid advocates, and we offered them to God and Blessed Mary upon the altar.

When this had been accomplished through God’s mercy, the nuns, clergy, people, householders, and advocates, with one voice and consent, proclaimed that the church of Faverney should be united to the church of La Chaise-Dieu in such a way that, for all time, its abbot should be chosen from the chapter of La Chaise-Dieu, and that the church of Faverney should be governed by him according to the Order and custom of the church of La Chaise-Dieu. We therefore, yielding to the wishes of the said people, grant the church of Faverney with its appurtenances to be governed by the church of La Chaise-Dieu, saving episcopal right and the rights of its ministers. [Col. 0599D] We establish that correction of the abbot, should he offend against his Order, belongs to the Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu and his successors. But if his fault should be so grave that the abbot deserves deposition, after the fault has first been shown to us or to the archbishops succeeding us, if he proves rebellious and unwilling to amend, we grant to the aforesaid abbot the power to depose him.

That this present instrument may remain unshaken, we confirm it with the impression of our seal; and lest anyone should subsequently dare to violate it, we forbid this under the bond of anathema. Witnesses of this act are William of Arguel; Guy of Mertiniac, archdeacon; Peter of Treva, dean of Saint Stephen’s; Hugh, Archdeacon of Faverney; Wolbert, archdeacon; Hugh of Dole; Hugh, Abbot of Luxeuil; Guy, Abbot of Charo-Locus; Lambert, [Col. 0600D] Abbot of Clairfontaine; the Abbot of Morimond; Warin, chaplain; Count Renaud; Count Frederick of Fontenay; Guy of Junciville and his brother Henry; Theobald of Rougemont; Humbert of Vissiaco and his brother Louis. Given at Besançon, in the chapter-house of Saint John, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ 1132, the twelfth indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September]. See Letter 199.]

He exhorts her to restore not houses only but morals also, and to take diligent care of the hospital.

[Col. 0597B]

BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, to A., Abbess of Faverney: the title of chastity and grace.

These brethren, coming to our fatherhood for the counsel of their souls, have greatly gladdened us by reporting your good zeal in reforming the place over which, by God’s grace, you preside. [Col. 0598A] We exhort and beseech your devotion that, as you labour to restore buildings, so you may labour to renew morals. You must also take the most earnest care not only of the monastery but of the hospital, the house of God, in which the aforesaid brethren serve under your authority: namely, that you keep it safe and free from every exaction and harassment by your officers or retainers. And what, as we have heard, you took away from that house on the perverse advice of those men, though it had been granted to it by abbesses before you, we ask you to restore. For as it belongs to your care to destroy or correct the wrongs of others, so you ought not only to keep firm and undisturbed whatever good they have done, [Col. 0598B] but also to increase and multiply it.

Moreover, compel the priest who lives in that house, yet seems still to maintain his own property outside it, either to abandon what is his own or to leave the house. Farewell; and because of the good we have heard of you, trust familiarly in us, insofar as we have any power.

## LETTER CCCXCII

[Note: [Col. 0600D] A new letter; what was formerly 392 is now 327.]

### To Radulf, Patriarch of Antioch

He especially urges humility upon him.

[Col. 0599A]

To his lord and most reverend father R., by God’s grace Patriarch of the See of Antioch, Brother BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: whatever benefit may come from a poor man’s devotion and whatever power from a sinner’s prayer.

That I, a lowly little man, have dared to write to your Highness comes not from presumption but from confidence; for Brother Hatto suggested it and charity persuaded it. Therefore, having offered the brief yet faithful service of due reverence and greeting, I pray almighty God that he who has been deemed worthy of Peter’s chair may be judged worthy also of the crown. Yet, as your prudence knows very well, he will not be crowned unless [Col. 0599B] he has competed lawfully. Thus the blessed Apostle himself, whose words these are, when he wished to say that a crown of righteousness was laid up for him, first declared: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Timothy 4:7).

If human life upon earth is warfare (Job 7:1), what is the life of a pontiff, for whom there is surely a double cause of fighting: both for himself and for those entrusted to him? One must fight against the lust of the flesh, against the wickedness of the world, against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavens. And who is sufficient for these things? This threefold cord is not easily broken. The Chaldeans formed these three bands to plunder Job’s flocks: namely, the flesh with its vices and desires. “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Psalm 67:2). Let him arise, I say; it is necessary—for he said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). But with him, what then? “I can do all things,” he says, “in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

Be strengthened in him, then, father; be strengthened and be strong. Gird yourself, stand in battle, fight bravely for the flocks entrusted to you, which you must restore entire to their Owner. Fight also for yourself, because an account will be required of you concerning yourself. Take heed to yourself in the high place where you stand, lest perhaps—God forbid—you fall, and be shattered all the more grievously because you have fallen from a greater height. Hold your place fittingly, but do not “think highly,” as the Apostle says: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Romans 11:20). To a wise person a high place is not so much an occasion for exaltation as [Col. 0599D] a cause for fear. The Church indeed brings honour, but it also brings fear of falling; and it is not a high position, but a haughty brow, which is reproved. Who, indeed, sitting on high can have a lowered brow [Col. 0600A] unless he always keeps the precipice before his eyes? Fear of the precipice restrains the swelling of lordship.

“Whatever we wish men to do to us, let us do the same to them.” Who does not wish to receive deference from those subject to him? Would that we were equally willing to render deference to those set over us. Otherwise, “weight and weight, measure and measure, both are an abomination to God” (Proverbs 20:10). Therefore we are abominable to God if we do not render to our superiors with the same weight or measure that which we demand from those subject to us.

I cannot sufficiently marvel at the careful and humble faith and answer of the Centurion, who is recorded as having said to the Saviour: “For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me” (Luke 7:8). O prudent soul, truly humble in heart! When he was about to say that he was set over soldiers, he checked pride by confessing subjection; indeed, he placed his subjection first, so that what was beneath him was of greater account to him than what was under his command. He showed this by the very order of his words, and the sequence of well-ordered speech indicated the sound ordering of his mind.

I wished to pursue these matters more fully and distinguish them more clearly; but modesty intervenes. When I can write more, I shall do so without fear, provided I learn that these few things please you. 351 Finally, I beseech you that, if that place of favour which I am said to have with you truly remains, the soldiers of God who inhabit the Temple at Jerusalem may experience it in themselves, so that, for love of us, those whom we commend may henceforth be more commendable to you. By this you will indeed be more pleasing to God and more acceptable to men. [Col. 0600C]

## LETTER CCCXCIII

[Note: [Col. 0600D] A new letter.]

### To W., Patriarch of Jerusalem

[Note: [Col. 0600D] William, to whom Letter 175 is addressed; consult the notes there.]

He exhorts him to humility.

To his venerable lord and most beloved father W., by God’s grace Patriarch of Jerusalem, BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father.

1. Taking the opportunity offered by the faithful man and our friend who bears this letter, I write a few words, though occupied with many things, to you who are occupied with many. If this appears presumptuous to anyone, and I am judged on that account, it is nevertheless a pardonable presumption, because it descends from love. But lest I write much after promising little, let us come to the matter itself.

When God, Creator of all, was pleased to disclose the depth of his counsel concerning the salvation of humankind, [Col. 0601A] he so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son. Having become man for the sake of men, he will call to himself from among the children of men those whom he wills: elect from the rest and beloved above the rest. And one of these, as though chosen from among the chosen and beloved above the beloved, he set apart into the special favour of his love. Entrusting his own offices to him, when, already lifted up from the earth, he offered the evening sacrifice with hands raised, before commending his spirit into his Father’s hands, he commended, as brother to brother, Mother to virgin and Virgin to virgin. What is the meaning of such a beginning? Consider carefully.

2. The Lord chose many and made them princes in his people, that they might possess priestly dignity; but by a certain familiar grace he placed you in the house of David his servant. [Col. 0601B] To you alone, among all bishops of the whole world, has been entrusted that land which brought forth green grass and fruit according to its kind, from whose root arose the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. You alone, I say, has the Lord chosen above your companions, that you may be his familiar bishop, entering daily into his tabernacle and worshipping in the place where his feet stood.

We read that it was once said to holy Moses, when he received a command from the Lord to deliver to the children of Israel: “Take off the sandal from your foot, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). That place too was holy, but there it was a figure; here, however, the reality is shown in the sign of holiness. That place was holy, but this is holier. For what is comparable to reality? What likeness has that which is seen through a mirror and in an enigma to that glory which, now that the veil has been torn, is beheld with unveiled face? Yet, although all these things happened in figure and as types of things to come, it was said to Moses: “Take off the sandal from your foot, for the place where you stand is holy ground.” And I say to you: “Take off the sandal from your foot, for the place where you stand is holy ground.” If your affections are still in any respect wrapped up in dead works, take it off swiftly; for the place where you stand is holy ground.

O how fearful is that place in which the Dayspring from on high first visited us through the tender mercy of our God! O how fearful is that place in which the father first met the son returning from the far country, and, leaning over his neck, clothed him in the robe of glory! [Col. 0601D] O how fearful is that place in which the sweet and upright Lord poured wine and oil together into our wounds; in which the Father of mercies and God of all consolation established with us the covenant of his pact! Thanks to you, 352 Lord, thanks to you, because you have wrought a good work in the midst of the earth, making it known in the midst of the years of law and grace. For when you are angry, you will remember mercy.

Behold a place far holier and far nobler than that in which Moses stood: because it is the Lord’s place—the place, I say, of him who came through water and blood; not through water [Col. 0602A] only, as Moses did, but through water and blood. Behold the place where they laid him. “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place?” Only he should ascend who has learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be meek and humble of heart.

3. The humble person alone can ascend securely, because humility has no ground from which it may fall. The proud person, even if he ascends, cannot stand long, since he does not wish to stand upon his own feet, but has taken to himself a foot not his own—namely, that foot which the prophet, abhorring it, mentions: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Psalm 35:12). Pride has but one foot: the love of one’s own excellence. Therefore the proud person cannot stand long, because he rests on one foot alone. Who could stand on that foot [Col. 0602B] on which fell those who worked iniquity—the angel in heaven and the human being in paradise?

If God did not spare the natural branches—I mean the human being, whom he crowned with glory and honour and set over all the works of his hands; and the angel, who was the beginning of God’s ways, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty—how much more must I fear lest he not spare me when I am proud: me, who am now not in a place of delight, nor in the palace of heaven, but in the valley of tears. Therefore, that you may stand securely, stand in humility. Stand not on the one foot of pride but on the feet of humility, so that your footsteps may not be moved. Humility has two feet: consideration of divine power and consideration of one’s own weakness. O beautiful and firm feet, neither enveloped in the darkness of ignorance nor defiled by the slipperiness of lust!

You therefore, set in a high place, do not think highly, but fear; and humble yourself under the mighty hand of him who is accustomed by his own power to tread upon the necks of the proud and lofty. Know that the Church entrusted to you is not like a maidservant to her lord, but, to return to the beginning of the letter, like a mother to a son—like Mary to John—so that it may be said of you to her, “Woman, behold your son,” and of her to you, “Behold your mother” (John 19:26–27). Thus you will be able to go in and out safely, and to proceed at the command of him who, though he is high and dwells on high, yet regards the humble in heaven and on earth. [Col. 0602C]

## LETTER CCCXCIV

[Note: [Col. 0601D] A new letter.]

### To the Archbishop of Lyons

On behalf of the Abbot of Ainay at Lyons.

[Col. 0602D]

To the Archbishop of Lyons, [Note: [Col. 0601D] Peter, who died at Acre in Palestine, according to William of Tyre, Book XV, chapter 15, in the year 1139. Bernard writes of him in Letters 171 and 172.] legate of the Apostolic See, BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: to provide what is good before God and men.

If the gracious reputation and good odour which Mother Church has hitherto had of you—she in whose garden you sprang up like a lily—should be changed, I could not but grieve. As a cedar in Lebanon is exalted, so you are now in the Church of God: lovable, praiseworthy, and dear to all. Great are the things we already have from you, but we still expect greater. Hold fast meanwhile to what you have received: you will not give your reputation over to [Col. 0603A] corruption. For a good name is better than great riches.

What have you done with the Abbot of Ainay? [Note: [Col. 0603D] The monastery of Ainay, an ancient and illustrious monastery of the Order of St Benedict, is at Lyons, at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône.] He has already been judged, condemned, deposed; he has lost both the place and office of abbot. What was done to him was done swiftly, as in a moment and in the twinkling of an eye, as it will be at the resurrection of the dead. I speak to you confidently, because the fullness of love casts out fear. Yet what sin has the man committed? What evil, after all, has that man done whose praise is in the Church of God? We speak what we know, because he has a good testimony both from those outside and those within.
