Moreover, since it is not yet known whether the fault lies with him, and since, as it seems to us, he did not evade canonical examination, he should either still have remained in office or henceforth have fallen by canonical judgment. [Col. 0603B] What then? You condemned a man who had neither confessed voluntarily, nor been exposed by others, nor convicted by them! But you say to me: “While his case was in progress, he withdrew from the case.” For he could not produce those witnesses concerning whom I had written to him. Very well: because they did not stand up for him, they stood against him—as if they had been told, “Either you will stand against him, or he will be deposed.” Those witnesses, I say, he could not have; but he could have had others whose testimony would have been no less credible than that of those he could not obtain.

But let us now consider the case from another side. Suppose that he is guilty: in the midst of the case both his innocence and his case failed. Where then is the principle: “A defective case may nevertheless be restored by the remedy of appeal”? And if you did not wish to hear him as appellant, you nevertheless ought to have deferred to the appeal. It does not become [Col. 0603C] you for unconsidered words or precipitate judgments to proceed from your lips. No, I say, words of haste do not become a prince of the Church, especially words uttered not in darkness but in light.

I tell you: you have harmed many together with him, and many will grieve in his persecution. I will not conceal the matter from you. I was asked by the prayers of many to write on his behalf to the Apostolic See; it is not safe to disregard their prayers. But how could that be done until I had first conferred with my lord and dearest father? Therefore we approach you with peaceful words, as one whose honour has always been my concern, that you may recall that untimely sentence to its proper place and that the man may be restored to his former rank until his case is examined with greater caution. I write these things to you as your servant, especially for your sake. For I wish to stand not against you, but with you and for you, before God and before men. [Col. 0603D]

## LETTER CCCXCV

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Formerly Letter 325.]

### To Alvisus, Bishop of Arras

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Letter 65 was written to him when he was still abbot. He was bishop from 1131 to 1148, in which year he died at Philippopolis on 8 October, according to the necrology of Saint-Denis at Reims. His death is mentioned in Letter 22 of Louis the Younger among Suger’s letters. Compare Letter 339.]

His request is not sufficiently fair: Thomas of Saint-Omer, who had devoted himself to the brethren of Clairvaux, should not be surrendered to the monks of Saint-Bertin, who wished to claim him by a vow made by his parents.

[Col. 0604A]

To his venerable father and our friend ALVISUS, by God’s grace Bishop of Arras, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot: greeting and whatever prayers of ours may be worth.

1. You asked us on behalf of the church of Saint-Bertin, which you love and which we ourselves love, and have loved from the beginning. Yet what the venerable abbot of that monastery now asks—would that your prudence had more carefully considered what kind of thing this is, not merely to do, but even to request. For I do not doubt [Col. 0604B] that you would have rebuked him as one grievously at fault: both against us, his friends; against the man himself, whose soul he seeks; indeed, against God, whose counsel he attempts to change.

For what is this, lord father? Could you be persuaded to ask such a thing from your friend? God calls Thomas from heaven; he calls him to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s house, and to come to the place which he himself will show him. Who am I to prohibit the Spirit of God? Who am I to hinder him who calls his own sheep by name and himself goes before them, so that they may follow not another but him? Thomas has chosen poverty: shall I send him back to riches and pleasures?

2. Nor am I unaware that brethren at Saint-Bertin [Col. 0604C] can work out their own salvation; but those whom God has called there should remain there, so that each may remain in the calling in which he was called. [Note: [Col. 0603D] How great a guilt is incurred from profession itself, if so much follows even from vocation alone, as Bernard likewise teaches elsewhere in Letters 107 and 108; he also counts novices who abandon the Order among apostates in Sermon 63 on the Song of Songs, no. 6. If, without the crime of apostasy, one may not turn back to a more relaxed state, as Bernard also attests in the *Apology to William*, no. 30, is it permissible, even within the society of those who live strictly, to pursue lax and easier practices with impunity, to the scandal of the brethren and the injury of right order? Yet this is the religion of certain people, who suppose everything safe if, while disregarding all else, they preserve the essentials—as though violation of holy institution and right order were not a violation of profession, or as though the essentials could remain inviolate while the so-called accidental matters are corrupted in intention.]

I know, I know where I have read: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). I would by no means deprive my dearest son Thomas, and the soul entrusted to me by God, of this. Therefore I greatly wonder how it could have escaped so great a discernment to make such a request. For, because I presume upon your affection, as you know, I almost answer as the Lord said to the sons of Zebedee: “You do not know what you are asking” (Matthew 20:22). Except that I reflected that one ought not so to presume upon charity as not also to show deference to the priestly chair.

[Col. 0604D] 3. Therefore act according to your custom. Honour your ministry in this matter also, and manfully aid these brides of Christ, that they may deserve to enter, without hindrance and without [Col. 0605A] delay, the bridal chamber of the Bridegroom to whom they are called. Act, I say, as the Bridegroom’s friend, who stands and rejoices greatly at the Bridegroom’s voice. As you are accustomed rightly to help others, so help these also, that you may not merely refrain from quenching—God forbid—the Spirit of God, but may prove yourself his faithful fellow-worker. Let this be altogether certain to your Fatherhood: by my counsel or with my permission they will turn aside nowhere. For I know that I myself would sin, and make them sin, if I advised or allowed them anything else. Let them therefore pay the vows which their lips have uttered. Otherwise, let them themselves see whom they trust when people say, “Behold, here is Christ; behold, there.” For they will have to answer to me before Christ’s tribunal concerning their vow, of which I am witness.

## LETTER CCCXCVI

[Note: [Col. 0605C] Formerly Letter 365.]

### To Ricuin, Bishop of Toul

[Note: [Col. 0605C] This superscription was restored by the Corbie manuscript, written in Bernard’s lifetime; earlier editions read, “To a certain abbot.” The conjecture that the addressee was an abbot was not without basis, since the text of the letter speaks of a professed monk belonging to the person to whom Bernard writes, namely William, who was perhaps a monk of Saint-Èvre or Saint-Mansuy. Yet the address “Your Holiness” and the titles “holy and most reverend Father” suit a bishop better than an abbot. Letter 61 is likewise addressed to Ricuin.]

He excuses himself to Ricuin because, not knowing that William was Ricuin’s professed monk, he had received him.

[Col. 0605B]

To the venerable RICUIN, by God’s grace Bishop of Toul, Brother BERNARD, called of Clairvaux, with the little flock entrusted to him: well-being and peace.

We give thanks to the Author of salvation that we have been deemed worthy to receive a greeting from you. Yet, as much as your greeting gladdens us, so much does the obedience which you added burden us. Nevertheless, though burdened, we have done what you commanded. Before God and before your Holiness—and with the venerable brother William himself also as witness—we excuse ourselves: unknowingly, we received one who had declared himself to be yours [Col. 0605C]. If there is fault in his having been received by us in this way, it is his, not ours. After this true and unfeigned satisfaction on our part, may we deserve your favor and blessing. Farewell. We wish you, holy and most reverend father, to end your life, as full of virtues as of days, in a peaceful passing [Col. 0606A].

355. LETTER CCCXCVII  
[Note: [Col. 0605C] Previously letter 387.]

TO ODO, ABBOT OF MARMOUTIER NEAR TOURS  
[Note: [Col. 0605D] Geoffrey of Vendôme, in Letter 21 of Book IV addressed to him, dissuades him from a second journey to the holy places. Letter 26 of Book II also mentions him; there Geoffrey complains vehemently to Geoffrey of Chartres of the plundering and secular violence inflicted on his monastery, and of injuries done to the Archbishop of Tours, by the monks of Marmoutier. Yet at precisely this period Ulger, Bishop of Angers, highly commends their piety and religious life in a charter of 1131, in these words: “I, Ulger, Bishop of Angers, have given, in the year of the Incarnation 1131, the church of Bessé and the chapel of Belle-Fort to the church of Marmoutier and to my brethren, the venerable Abbot Odo and its monks—than whom I do not recall having known any more fervent in divine service,” etc. And in another document: “I, Ulger, Bishop of Angers, having learned that the most holy church of Marmoutier possessed no house of its own in the city of Angers, gave, with the consent of the chapter of Angers, the episcopal garden which I owned in the parish of Saint Stephen, not far from that church. For it was unfitting that so holy and religious a monastery—which everywhere has establishments distinguished for hospitality and is especially praised for this—in so populous a city and so near at hand should lack lodging . . . . In the reign of Louis, King of the Franks; Geoffrey, son of Fulk, King of Jerusalem; and Hugh, Archbishop of Tours.”

Moreover, Ulger’s successor Norman, in a charter granting the church of Ver, drawn up in the year of the Incarnation 1152, indiction 15 [Col. 0606D], bears no lesser witness to his affection and esteem for the monks of Marmoutier. “Whom,” he says, “because of the privilege of holy religious life in which they especially excel, and because they are good builders up and propagators of their order, I embrace with singular charity.”

Indeed, Ivo of Chartres vigorously defends the cause of the Abbot of Marmoutier—namely William, not his successor Odo, who held this office from 1124 to 1135—in Letter 108 to Paschal, against the accusations of Archbishop Ralph of Tours, though later, in Letter 234, he urges William to promise obedience to his metropolitan. For a similar dispute over tithes, the subject of this letter, see among others Peter the Venerable, Letter 28 of Book III, where he treats the question thoroughly.]

Monks disputing with clerics over certain revenues ought to abide by the decision of arbitrators.

To the most reverend father and lord ODO, by God’s grace Abbot of Marmoutier, and to the holy convent joined with him in Christ’s charity: HUGH of Pontigny and BERNARD of Clairvaux, that they may walk by the Spirit and never grow weary of seeking the face of the God of Jacob.

1. Charity, brothers, urges us to write to you and on your behalf; for although we are far from you in place, we are not far in spirit [Col. 0606B]. Indeed, the wonderfully fragrant reputation of your most renowned holiness, spreading everywhere, has easily fused our hearts into the same unanimity as your brotherhood. Yet since yesterday and the day before we have sorrowfully felt, within ourselves, a slight disturbance of our share in so great a serenity. For a cloud of rather dismal report suddenly arose—no doubt from the north—and shame covered our faces, because we heard concerning you something so unfamiliar, so discordant with your name.

We fear, therefore, that both your reputation and our glory in you may soon be gravely endangered unless the report that went out so swiftly vanishes with a more favorable breath. Thus, with brotherly concern, we take care by this letter to remind your Reverence that you must quickly correct the evil which flying rumor does not cease to spread from day to day [Col. 0606C]. We are indeed astonished that some of you—forbid that we should suspect all—have been so deceived by simplicity or blinded by greed that, sparing not your most celebrated name, they prefer the few revenues of one altar [Note: [Col. 0606D] By “altars” they meant parish churches with their tithes, such as at that time it was customary to confer upon monasteries even by laypersons. See Letter 375.] to the glory of the world.

Brothers, it is not right, it is not right [Col. 0607A], to value at any temporal gain the reputation which by the merit of your conduct you have acquired from of old—indeed from the beginning—even from those outside. But perhaps you say: “We wrong no one. We hold what is ours, ready, if anyone opposes us, to submit to judgment.” Correct. But what if another replies and says: “This itself is your fault—that you have lawsuits. Why do you not rather endure being defrauded?” (1 Cor. 6:7). What if another reads: “If anyone takes away what is yours, do not demand it back; indeed, to one striking your right cheek, offer the other also; to one taking your tunic, offer your cloak as well” (Luke 6:29–30)?

2. We should urge these and similar arguments upon you, except that we prefer to correct you rather than shame you. What we say is that for every Christian—and especially for a monk—it is safer to possess somewhat less in peace than more amid litigation [Col. 0607B]. For thus you sing: “Better is a little to the righteous than the great riches of sinners” (Ps. 36:16).

What is more, the dispute concerns an altar, and it is against the sons of Levi—that is, against clerics. It belongs to clerics to serve the altar and to live from the altar. Our profession and the example of the ancient monks prescribe for us sustenance from our own labor, not from the sanctuary of God. Moreover, the clerics alone serve the church now under dispute, while you share its benefice with those to whom you render no service.

Paul cries out on behalf of clerics—indeed Moses before him: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. 25:4). Likewise: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not eat of the flock’s milk?” (1 Cor. 9:7, 9) [Col. 0607C]. But, conversely, we address you: “With what boldness, O monks, do you presume to take either wine from a vineyard you did not plant or milk from a flock you do not tend? On what grounds do you exact there where you render nothing?”

Certainly, if you wish it so, baptize those who are born; bury the dead; visit the sick in bed; join those who marry; instruct the ignorant; correct offenders; excommunicate the defiant; absolve the repentant; reconcile penitents. Then, finally, let the monk open his mouth in the midst of the Church, though his office is to sit and keep silence. In that case perhaps the hired laborer will prove himself worthy of his wages. Otherwise, it is exceedingly invidious [Col. 0607D] to wish to reap where you have not sown; indeed, to gather what another has scattered is also unjust.

3. But grant it: let this too be allowed by a bishop’s gift, and let no wrong now be charged, since canonical investiture excuses it. Still, what are you doing about your agreement? For when the canons protested and complained of injury, you will not deny—unless we are mistaken—that you finally consented for your case to be placed in the hands of the Bishop of Chartres and Count T. [Note: [Col. 0607D] Theobald.], so that whatever should be determined by the equal agreement of both for settling the dispute should be held inviolably by both parties. This was plainly excellent and most prudent. For such mediators were chosen that you place confidence in their sufficiently proven equity and also, as we know well, in their private friendship with you [Col. 0608A].

Why then do you not observe, according to the agreement that preceded it, what good men—and your own friends—have unanimously, and doubtless faithfully, decided concerning the restoration of peace? Or are they thought not to have acted faithfully because the exchange appears unequal: a greater gain exchanged for a lesser? It indeed appears so—but only to one who seeks his own interests, who values coins above friends, money above justice, and earthly possession above brotherly love.

If you belonged to the world, and the world loved what was its own, this would appear as unsurprising as it would be customary. But now the children of light and peace prefer darkness to light and temporal things to peace. Such men are rightly lamented in the prophetic lamentation: “Those who were reared in scarlet have embraced dung” (Lam. 4:5) [Col. 0608B].

4. “Rightly,” they say, “we refuse to keep an agreement in which our party is found to be burdened.” What if the other party appeared to be burdened? Then, certainly, then the agreement would be judged fair and just. Yet this ought to have been stipulated before the agreement. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. But now the law of the agreement considers not advantage but what was agreed.

What do you say to this, you who object? While you pretend to be advisers, you show yourselves disturbers, equivocators, breakers of agreement. Either deny the agreement or fulfill it. What then? You do not indeed deny the convention, but you allege deception and lay the blame on the bishop, as though he had not dealt straightforwardly with you but had ensnared you by craft and fraud and induced you to enter the agreement [Col. 0608C] which you now regret. You may say this—but it is remarkable whom you expect to persuade, and remarkable that you should even suspect such a thing.

“Not at all,” they say; “but what was done without our counsel—that is, without the assent of the entire chapter—ought not to stand.” What? What the abbot has decided with the counsel of the elders ought not to stand if not all of you consent? Do you thus either fail to observe or despise the clear ruling on this in your Rule? It commands that brothers summoned to counsel should each give the opinion he judges right, yet not presume to defend what he has said; but after hearing the opinions of all, the abbot is to choose what he judges best, and all are to acquiesce in it without contradiction (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 3).

Therefore, since the Rule itself provides that the abbot’s authority has precedence in all arrangements, because every ordering of the monastery depends upon the abbot’s judgment, it is clear that you prove yourselves disobedient and rebellious in trying, against his will, to undermine the agreement which the abbot made [Col. 0608D]. Unless, perhaps, he too has spoken with a double heart, so that what he openly built by himself he might secretly destroy through his followers, thereby making himself also a breaker of agreement. Far be it from us to believe this; for even to suspect such a thing of so good a man is very bad.

We are not unaware of the scruple of certain persons who, more righteous than they ought to be, sought a knot in a reed, when they thought that exchanges of this kind between churches could not take place without simony [Col. 0609A]. But on this matter, we believe, your more careful inquiries have been answered by the replies of Catholic and learned men. Or, if this has not been done, it is even now easy to affirm on the authority of the canons that exchanges of ecclesiastical property may lawfully be made as appears expedient to the churches.

This is directed against those who, presumptuously interfering in matters in which they have no concern, are always ready to stir up injury [Note: [Col. 0609C] The Saint-Vaast manuscript concludes the letter thus: “Always ready to stir up injury for others, envy for their own people. But we advise you, Father, to use the counsel of better men and not to be led by the scandal of your predecessors into breaking the agreement of your lips, lest, in avoiding the scandal of a few evil men, you become, God forbid, a scandal to all good people.” MARTÈNE.].

LETTER CCCXCVIII  
[Note: [Col. 0609C] Previously letter 312.]

TO GUIDO, ABBOT, AND THE BRETHREN OF ARREMAR  
Asked by the brethren of Arremar to compose an Office for Saint Victor, their patron, he pleads his own insufficiency and the difficulty of the work, explaining what things publicly employed in divine worship ought to be like; he also sets forth rules for ecclesiastical chant.

[Col. 0609B]

To the venerable GUIDO, Abbot of Arremar [Note: [Col. 0609C] The monastery of Arremar, in the diocese of Troyes, of the Order of Saint Benedict, has as its patron Saint Victor the Confessor; his Acts from Bernard are found in Volume 3. Nicholas, Bernard’s secretary, mentioned above in Letter 298, was a monk of that place.], and to the holy brethren who are with him: BERNARD, servant of their Holiness, that they may serve the Lord in holiness.

1. You ask me, Guido, abbot most dear to me, and with you the brethren who are with you, to compose for you certain readings to be read solemnly, or chants to be sung, on the feast of Saint Victor, whose most sacred body rests among you. You press me when I hesitate; you urge me when I evade, overlooking my modesty, though it is justified. You even bring other petitioners to bear upon me, as though anything were more compelling for bending me to your will than your will itself [variant: “more fitting”].

But you [Col. 0610A], consulting even your own judgment, should have considered not your affection for me, but my place in the Church. The loftiness of the undertaking requires, surely, not a friend but a learned and worthy man—one whose authority is greater, life holier, and style more mature, so that his work may both adorn and accord with the saint’s holiness.

2. How small a person am I among the Christian people, that my writings should be read in churches? Or how small is my ability in intellect or expression, that festive and applauded compositions should be sought especially from me? What? Shall I begin anew on earth to praise him whom heaven holds praiseworthy and has praised? To wish to add to the praises of heaven is to detract from them. This is not because human beings ought no longer dare to praise those glorified by angels, but because, at a celebrated [variant: solemn] feast, what ought to be heard should not be novel or trivial [Col. 0610B], but certainly authoritative and ancient: things that build up the Church and breathe ecclesiastical gravity.

If, however, new compositions are desired and the occasion requires them, I should judge that those ought to be received which are made more welcome—and therefore more useful—to the hearts of hearers by both the dignity of their language and that of their author. Their meanings, moreover, should shine with undoubted truth, proclaim justice, commend humility, and teach equity; they should bring the light of truth to minds, a pattern to morals, a cross to vices, devotion to affections, and discipline to the senses.

If there is chant, it should be full of gravity [Note: [Col. 0609C] Bernard states these things most elegantly, and they therefore deserve careful consideration. If place and purpose allowed, Bernard’s words ought to be illustrated and strengthened with the statements of other holy Fathers, or at least their judgment concerning church chant and divine offices ought to be shown. But because their discipline may perhaps have been stricter and more rigorous than the customs and temperaments of the present age can bear, it is pleasant to hear a man wholly pious and religious, who has elegantly and eloquently discoursed on matters pertaining to the cultivation of piety and virtue in comparatively recent times.

“With your leave,” he says, “O musicians, a new kind of singing now dominates in churches, but it is excessive, broken up, dance-like, and certainly not very religious—more suited to the theater or dancing than to the temple. We pursue artifice and lose the old concern for prayer and song; we cater to curiosity but truly neglect piety. For what is this novel, prancing manner of singing but a comedy, in which the singers are like actors: now one comes forward, now two, now all appear together and converse in modulated voices; then once more a single living voice triumphs alone, the rest shortly to follow?”

And below: “In an earlier age there were outstanding musicians; but truly, as even you will testify, they sang differently and—if I may say it—more religiously. Yet your fastidiousness long ago buried their musical books. I beg that at least something of ancient religious feeling may revive in sacred music. If divine honor is dear to you and your concern, then do this, men; labor for this: that the words which are sung may also be understood. What use to me is varied sound in the church, or a manifold harmony, if it lacks a kernel, if I cannot grasp the meaning and words that are to be instilled by the harmony?” Thus Jerome Drexelius, *Rhetorica caelestis*, Book I, chapter 5.

But come: let us free this religious man of recent memory from the hostility which such criticism perhaps arouses against him among our musicians; or at least let us give him companions with whom, relying on greater men, he may more easily endure the hatred, that ill-fated offspring of truth. And here one from the school of our Bernard presents himself, who with a feeling and spirit equal to his master’s sharply rebukes the abuse of music: namely Aelred [Col. 0610D], Abbot of Rievaulx in England, much of whose work may be found in Volume V of Bernard’s Works. Thus, then, he speaks in *The Mirror of Charity*, Book II, chapter 2:

“To what purpose is that constriction and breaking of the voice? One voice sings beneath, another apart; one above, another divides and cuts certain middle notes. Now the voice is tightened, now broken, now struck, now spread out in a more diffuse sound. Sometimes—shameful to say—it is forced into the neighing of horses; sometimes, laying aside manly vigor, it is sharpened into the thinness of a woman’s voice; not infrequently, by some artful winding, it is twisted and retwisted. At times you may see a man with mouth open, as though his breath were cut off, expire rather than sing; and, by a ridiculous interruption of the voice, as though miming silence, now imitate the struggles of the dying, now the ecstasy of those in rapture.

“Meanwhile the whole body is agitated by certain theatrical gestures; lips are distorted, eyes roll, shoulders play, and every flexing of the fingers corresponds to each individual note. This ridiculous dissipation [Col. 0611B] is called religion; and where these practices occur more frequently, there it is loudly claimed that God is served more honorably. Meanwhile the crowd, trembling and astonished, marvels at the sound of bellows, the clatter [Col. 0611C] of cymbals, the harmony of pipes; but it watches the wanton gesturing of the singers and the courtesan-like alternations and inflections of their voices not without loud laughter and amusement. You would think that they had assembled not in an oratory but in a theater, not to pray but to watch.

“That dread majesty before which they stand is not feared; that mystical manger at which they minister is not reverenced—where Christ is mystically wrapped in swaddling clothes; where his most sacred blood is poured out in the chalice; where the heavens are opened and angels stand by; where earthly things are joined to heavenly and human beings are associated with angels. Thus what the holy Fathers instituted in order that the weak might be stirred to an affection of piety is employed there for illicit pleasure.

“For sound should not be preferred to meaning. Rather, sound with meaning should often be admitted to stimulate greater devotion. Therefore the sound ought to be such, so restrained and so grave, that it does not carry off the whole soul in delight in itself, but leaves the larger share to meaning [Col. 0611D]. For blessed Augustine says, *Confessions*, Book X, chapter 33: ‘The soul is moved to an affection of piety when it hears song; but if the desire of hearing seeks the sound more than the meaning, it is disapproved.’ Elsewhere he says: ‘When singing delights me more than the words, I confess that I have sinned culpably and would prefer not to hear the singer.’” Thus Aelred.

But let John XXII, supreme shepherd of the Church, put the finishing touch on this, and let us hear what he thinks—indeed, what he decrees—about music of this sort:

“A sweet sound indeed resounds in the mouth of those chanting psalms when they receive God in their hearts while they speak with words and kindle devotion toward him also through song. Therefore psalmody is commanded to be sung in the churches of God in order that the devotion of the faithful may be aroused. For this purpose the night and day office and the celebrations of Mass are constantly sung by clergy and people in a measured manner and with distinct gradation, so that by that distinction they may be pleased and by that moderation delighted.

“But some disciples of the new school, while they devote their attention to measuring time, attend to new notes: they prefer inventing their own to singing the old. Ecclesiastical chants are sung in semibreves and minims, and struck out with little notes. They interrupt melodies with hockets, make them glide in discants, and sometimes insert triple parts and vernacular motets; to such a degree that they sometimes disdain the foundations of antiphonary and gradual, do not know upon what they build, and are ignorant of the modes—which they cannot distinguish, indeed confuse. For by the multitude of their notes the modest ascents and measured descents of plainchant, by which the modes themselves are distinguished, obscure one another.

“They run and do not rest; they intoxicate the ears and do not heal them. By gestures they mimic what they utter; thereby the devotion that ought to be sought is neglected and the wantonness to be avoided is displayed. For Boethius himself does not say without reason: ‘A wanton mind either takes pleasure in more wanton modes or, through often hearing them, is softened and weakened by them.’ Therefore we and our brothers have long perceived that these things need correction; we hasten more effectively to banish—indeed, wholly cast out—and drive them from the same Church of God,” etc. Thus John XXII, *Extravagantes communes*, Book III, title *On the Life and Honor of Clerics*, sole chapter [Col. 0612D], where he also adds what kind of music and chant he wishes to be fitting for the Church of God.]

It should not sound of wantonness, nor of rusticity. It should be so sweet as not to be frivolous; it should soothe the ears so as to move the heart. It should relieve sadness and moderate anger [Col. 0611A]; it should not empty the meaning of the text but make it fruitful. It is no slight loss of spiritual grace to be drawn away from the usefulness of meanings by the frivolity of song, and to attend more to the winding of voices than to the communication of matters.

3. Behold what things ought to come before the hearing of the Church, and what their author ought to be. Am I such a person, or are the things I have prepared such? Yet, out of my poverty [358], because you knocked and troubled me, I rose—if not because you are a friend, then at least because of your persistence—and, according to the Lord’s saying, granted what you asked (Luke 11:8). I granted it, I say, not what would satisfy your wish, but what could come to my hand: according to my ability, certainly, not according to your desire.

Nevertheless, preserving the truth of the ancient writings which you sent me, I composed two sermons on the saint’s life [Note: [Col. 0612D] They are found in Volume III together with the Office of the saint.] in my own, such as it is, style [Col. 0611B], taking as much care as I could that neither brevity should make them obscure nor prolixity burdensome. Then, with regard to the chant, I composed a hymn, disregarding meter in order not to fail the meaning. I arranged twelve responsories with their twenty-seven antiphons in their proper places, adding one responsory assigned to First Vespers; likewise two other short pieces, to be sung on the feast day itself according to your regular custom—one at Lauds, the other at Vespers.

For all these things I ask a reward; I seek recompense. Why should I not seek it? Whether they please or do not please, it makes no difference to me, since I gave what I had. Therefore my reward is your prayer [Col. 0612A].

LETTER CCCXCIX  
[Note: [Col. 0612D] Previously letter 319.]

TO LELBERT, ABBOT OF SAINT MICHAEL  
[Note: [Col. 0612D] There are many monasteries of Saint Michael in Gaul: namely, Mont-Tombe, or Mont-Saint-Michel in the Peril of the Sea; Saint-Mihiel on the Meuse; Tonnerre in Burgundy; Saint-Michel-en-l’Herm among the Poitevins; and Saint-Michel de la Tréasse. Lelbert appears to have been abbot of the last named, whether he is Elbert, who granted the site of Fesmy to Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon, for building a Cistercian monastery in 1121, or his successor Gislebert, noted in the cartulary in 1130 and called another Plato of his age by Herman, Monk of Laon, in Book III of *The Miracles of Saint Mary*, chapter 19. After the death of Simon, Abbot of Saint-Nicholas—mentioned above in Letter 83—he was recalled to Saint-Nicholas, from which he had been taken. Innocent II granted a diploma in 1138 to Leo, his successor as abbot.]

Having dissuaded a certain monk from a misguided plan of pilgrimage, he sends him back to his monastery.

To his father and friend LELBERT, Abbot of Saint Michael: Brother BERNARD, unprofitable servant of the servants of God who are at Clairvaux, the affection owed by love.

This your son has returned to you after abandoning, on our advice, the pilgrimage which he had undertaken with your permission. For when we learned that he had sought that journey frivolously, and that you had consented because of his misconduct [Col. 0612B], we persuaded him to return after stern rebuke, as he deserved: as far as we could judge, repentant of his frivolity and misconduct, and promising amendment from now on. We judged it better that a monk, however guilty, should do penance in his own monastery than wander abroad through the provinces.

For the purpose of monks is to seek not an earthly but a heavenly Jerusalem, and to seek it not by advancing with their feet, but by advancing in their affections. But you, father, should not receive his return with displeasure, even if you regard his conduct with suspicion [Col. 0613A]. Rather, rejoice, because this your son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found (Luke 15:32). [Note: [Col. 0613C] Hildebert uses precisely the same words in Letter 23, which has the same subject as this one. Compare the opinion of Abbot Theodemir in the work of Jonas, Bishop of Orléans, against Claudius of Turin, concerning monastic pilgrimages.]

LETTER CD  
[Note: [Col. 0613C] Previously letter 326.]

TO THE ABBOT OF LAËTI  
He asks that Brother Robert be received and treated more kindly, and that the abbot’s decision be reported to him.

To the venerable father, the abbot of the monastery of Laëti [Note: [Col. 0613C] Some manuscripts read “of Lesci,” a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict on the borders of Hainaut and the Thiérache, then not undistinguished for the study of sacred letters, as Philip de l’Aumône attests in Letter 24, Volume III of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*; it was illustrious for the religious life and institutions of Louis of Blois, its most pious abbot. Thierry of Avesnes restored it from the foundations about the year 1080, as Herimann writes in Volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 413. Ganter, the first abbot, was succeeded after twelve years’ rule by Rainer, who died in 1124. He was followed by the most religious Abbot Wedric, who assembled a library and sought out pious and learned men from Hainaut. In 1147 Tescelin succeeded him; in 1153 Helgot, formerly a monk of Latiniac, was appointed in his place. Whether this letter concerns Wedric, let others judge. This letter, in an ancient manuscript of Saint Martin at Tournai, bears the following heading: “Bernard’s letter to Werric”—a name easily read as “Wedric”—“Abbot of Laëti, whose name until now has been unknown.” MARTÈNE.], and to his sons: Brother BERNARD, unprofitable servant of the servants of God who are at Clairvaux, that they may serve the Lord in fear and rejoice in him with trembling.

We have sent Brother Robert back to you, first asking for him and together with him that he be treated more gently upon being received than other fugitives who return are usually treated. For the penalty ought not to be the same where the cause differs [Col. 0613B]. Secondly, we ask that he be removed from the obedience [Note: [Col. 0614C] “Obedience”: a cell, priory, or estate to whose administration two, three, or more monks were customarily assigned. They are called *cellulae* in Letter 254, no. 1.] in which, as he says, he was long held unwillingly at danger to his soul, and transferred to another where he may live more safely and beneficially. Otherwise, considering the man’s intention, I fear that you may lose him irrevocably.

Moreover, we have heard that the lord abbot is seriously ill. We urgently ask that his life or death be reported to us swiftly, so that we may receive joy from his life, though mortal, or sorrow from his death, though life-giving—or, to speak more truly, both joy and sorrow from either. From his life, indeed, sorrowing for him [variant: “certainly sorrowing for him in his life”] because he is delayed, but rejoicing for ourselves because he is preserved for us; from his death, undoubtedly rejoicing with him for the reward obtained [Col. 0613C], but mourning for ourselves because we have been deprived of one necessary to us.

LETTER CDI  
[Note: [Col. 0614C] Previously letter 338.]

TO ABBOT BALDWIN OF CHÂTILLON  
He removes the fear arising from the imprudent statement of a certain person.

And by this I have known that you love us: because you feared for us. Yet rejoice, because the danger which you feared has not come upon us. The matter has been carefully investigated, as you advised [Col. 0614A], and deceit has been found in the mouth of the man who said these things to you. Do not doubt in the least one of two things: namely, that the man spoke either from malice or from suspicion. Without doubt his grief shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall descend upon his own crown. For he is guilty of the thing which he attempts to impute to another.

LETTER CDII  
[Note: [Col. 0614C] Previously letter 339.]

TO BALDWIN, BISHOP OF NOYON  
[Note: [Col. 0614D] The letter of the chapter of Noyon concerning his election appears as no. 44 among Suger’s letters. There several letters of Baldwin, now bishop, concerning the church of Compiègne are cited, namely nos. 157, 158, and 162. From the earlier Sugerian Letter 44 it is clear that this Baldwin is the same Abbot of Châtillon to whom Bernard’s Letter 279 and the present Letter 401 are addressed. He also subscribes Letter 426, below in the appendix.]

He wittily commends a boy to him.

To Lord BALDWIN, Bishop of Noyon: Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, better than he deserves.

I send you this boy, the bearer of the present letter, to eat your bread, so that I may test your avarice [Col. 0614B]—whether you will do it sadly. Do not mourn; do not weep: he has a small stomach and will be content with little. We shall nonetheless thank you if he leaves you more learned than fat. Let this manner [Note: [Col. 0614D] That is, “mode”; French *manière*.] of expression serve as a seal, because no seal was at hand—nor, indeed, was your Geoffrey.

LETTER CDIII  
[Note: [Col. 0614D] Previously letter 340.]

TO HENRY, ARCHDEACON  
[Note: [Col. 0614D] Henry, brother of Louis the Younger, was at this time Archdeacon of Orléans, according to the cartulary of Saint-Martin-des-Champs.]

Whether baptism conferred with the formula, “I baptize you in the name of God and of the holy and true cross,” is valid.

To his beloved HENRY, archdeacon: Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greetings and prayers.

1. We briefly answer you concerning the question proposed, [Col. 0614C] yet without prejudice to a wiser judgment. A child snatched from the womb, because of danger of death, was baptized, as you say, by a certain layman, who did not retain the customary form of words, but said: “I baptize you in the name of God, and of the holy and true cross.” You ask whether the child has been baptized, or rather, if he lives, must be baptized.

[Note: Bernard, when asked (if indeed this letter is his—for many deny it, though I should not readily say so) whether Baptism conferred under this form of words, “I baptize you in the name of God and of the holy cross,” were valid, replied in the affirmative, moved by a reasoning not altogether to be despised. Horstius has this; Mabillon thus: “This letter appears doubtful to some. Nevertheless, it is found in the old editions—the Lyons edition of 1520 and others following—and in the Sorbonne manuscript codex [Col. 0615D]; nor does its style differ from Bernard’s.” But this opinion is not accepted today by theologians, and is refuted by apostolic tradition, by the authority of other Fathers, and of St Augustine himself. They universally teach that the explicit invocation of the most holy Trinity, or the distinct expression of the three Persons, belongs to the essence of the form; consequently, Baptism conferred without it is invalid. Thus Canon 49 of the Apostles, interpreting, as it were, Matthew 27 concerning the form of words, rejects Baptism conferred “in the death of the Lord,” adding: “For the Lord did not tell us, ‘Baptize in my death,’ but, ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’” St Augustine’s view is very clear in Book VI against the Donatists, chapter 25: the Gospel words are certain, without which Baptism cannot be consecrated [Col. 0616D]. He says the same in Letter 23 to Boniface. There is a similar passage in Book XIX against Faustus, chapter 16. What those Gospel words are, he explains against the Donatists, Book III, chapter 15: “If Marcion consecrated Baptism with the Gospel words, ‘In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ the sacrament was complete.” See the same author, Book III against Maximinus, chapter 17; Letter 20; and Expositions on Psalm 86. Hence Cajetan’s opinion that Baptism conferred in the name of Christ is sufficient is also rejected.]

For my part, I truly consider him baptized; nor could the sound of the voice prejudice the truth of faith and the devoutness of intention. [Col. 0615A] For, to say nothing of the fact that by “the name of God” he expressed the one substance of the Trinity, in adding “of the holy and true cross” he manifestly commended the Lord’s passion. Unless perhaps we think that the Apostle, contrary to what he had said elsewhere—“Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31; 2 Cor. 10:17)—boasted in the material substance of the wood, rather than in the grace of the Crucified One, when he said: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). For when, in accordance with the common ordinance of the Church, we baptize saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” nothing else is to be understood than a confession of the Trinity. Moreover, confession of the holy cross is nothing but confession of the Crucified One. We read indeed [Col. 0615B] in the Acts of the Apostles that some were baptized not only “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” but also in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 10:48).

2. You go on to ask about the baptizer himself: whether he sinned, or whether others too may imitate this form. As though it followed that, if in what the man did his very simplicity appears to excuse him, so that there was either no sin or no great sin, those too must immediately be found excusable who, through their own rashness and contrary to the form of the Church, wished to introduce a new manner of baptizing. But if anyone maintains that he sinned, I would scarcely believe that it was such a sin as could prejudice either the salvation of the baptizer or that of the person baptized. For he seems not to have despised the ecclesiastical form, but, from a certain devotion of faith in haste, [Col. 0615C] to have burst forth into this utterance.

## LETTER CDIV

[Note: Previously Letter 345.]

### TO ALBERT THE RECLUSE

He advises him to take refreshment once a day, and never to admit women.

Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux, to brother ALBERT the recluse: fight the good fight.

You ask me to allow you, by my permission, to adopt a certain observance of fasting which you had requested from me within your cell, and conversations with little women, which, as you recall, I had likewise forbidden you; these, as you write, you cannot avoid because of poverty. I now claim no authority over you. [Col. 0616A] I gave you counsel, not a command: always to eat once a day only; wholly to admit neither visits from women nor conversations with them; to support yourself by the work of your hands; and many other things, which it would take too long now to enumerate. If you saw that resources for such expenses could in no way suffice for so costly an undertaking, you ought not to have begun what you could not complete. I considered this safe counsel for you. You are neither compelled to keep it as my command, nor will you alter it while it remains my counsel. Farewell.

## LETTER CDV

[Note: Previously Letter 346.]

### TO ABBOT G.

A certain brother has strength enough to live according to the community’s manner.

To Lord G., abbot, brother BERNARD: whatever he wishes for himself.

Know that brother G., since he came from La Crête, where he received medical treatment, has observed the Convent’s rule in every respect most steadfastly, like one of the stronger brethren; nothing in food beyond what was common was allowed him; and he has attended the vigils continually with the others. Henceforth, if he behaves otherwise among you, do not yield to him. For be certain that it is not bodily illness, but a malady of the soul. Farewell.

## LETTER CDVI

[Note: A new letter.]

### TO THE ABBOT OF SAINT NICHOLAS

To his sweetest friend and fellow abbot of Saint Nicholas—

[Note: Undoubtedly Simon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Nicholas in the forest of Vedogium, to whom Letters 83 and 84 are addressed.]

—brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: the spirit of devotion.

[Col. 0616C] The devil, Christ’s enemy, acted in his accustomed way by seducing a Christian; we too, to whom he happened to come, did what was ours, as far as we could, by correcting the man who had been seduced. It remains, therefore, for you also to do what is yours by receiving him now corrected; and thus let us all together hope that God too will someday do what is his: namely, render to each according to his works.

## LETTER CDVII

[Note: Previously Letter 348.]

### TO ODO, ABBOT OF BELLI-LOCUS

He warns that a deposit must be restored to a poor man without delay.

To his brother and friend ODO, abbot of the regular clerics of Belli-Locus, brother BERNARD, unworthy steward of the monastery of Clairvaux: greetings.

[Col. 0617A] This man’s deposit, which, as he says, he entrusted to you for safekeeping: what you retain is neither good nor honorable for you—if indeed you retain it.

[Note: On restoring a deposit, there is an excellent letter of Philip, abbot of L’Aumône, third in order, to Henry, Count Palatine, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, p. 241.]

For he came to make a loud complaint to me—

[Note: *Deplangere*: to lament greatly; *deplanctus*: many complaints.]

—because he had heard of the close and special friendship between you and me. Presuming upon that friendship, I say to you, with due respect: why did you not rather sell a chalice from the altar to silence such an importunate outcry, if you had no ox or horse to sell, so that he might recover what was his? Spare yourselves, I beg you; spare the good name of your house; spare this holy season of Lent; and let what is owed the poor man without excuse be restored without delay, before the matter is further disclosed and must then be paid with still greater [Col. 0617B] disgrace.

## LETTER CDVIII

[Note: Previously Letter 349.]

### TO W., ABBOT OF TROYES

[Note: William, abbot of Saint Martin at Troyes, of the Order of Saint Augustine.]

He commends to the abbot of Troyes a refined cleric renouncing the world, fearing that he would prove unequal to the austerity of Clairvaux.

To his friend and fellow servant, Lord W., abbot of the canons—

[Note: Here “canons” is used adjectivally for clerics, in the same sense in which the Premonstratensians are called “regular clerics” in the preceding letter. [Col. 0617D]]

—of the clerics of Troyes, brother BERNARD, unprofitable servant of the church of Clairvaux: greeting in the Lord.

I persuaded this cleric, who is leaving the world and wishes to remain with us, to take refuge instead in your Order, fearing that he might be broken by the difficulty of ours. We therefore commend him to you as one [Col. 0617C] well known to us, of honorable conduct, and learned in letters; finally, as a servant of God, whom I believe, by God’s grace, will become for you a faithful support. For we wish him to go to you not so much for his own sake as for yours, whom we love as ourselves. We would gladly [Col. 0618A] retain him because of the merit of his life, were it not that we fear to receive a refined cleric unaccustomed to labor. Farewell.

## LETTER CDIX

[Note: Previously Letter 350.]

### TO RORGO OF ABBATIS-VILLA

[Note: Rorgo of Abbatis-Villa, a town on the river Somme, is praised with his wife Elizabeth in an old breviary of the Library of Corbie, written five hundred years ago, on the day before the Ides of August, as founder of the place to which the breviary originally belonged: namely, the Priory of Saint Peter at Abbatis-Villa.]

He warns that bodily presence should not be highly valued, and asks that certain uncultivated land be granted to religious persons.

To the illustrious man RORGO of Abbatis-Villa, also dear to us, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and our prayers.

We have heard that it would please you if you could enjoy our presence and conversation, and that this is because your kindness believes me to be one of the servants of the Most High. And I tell you that, because of this humility of yours and the good report we have heard of your nobility, [Col. 0618B] your presence too would be welcome to me. Yet although this is a praiseworthy benefit of human affection among us, it is not perfect. For this vision is bodily, brief, and shared by us with the other living creatures. We ought rather to long for that most joyful vision of eternal fellowship, and to persist in good works so that we may attain it.

We ask your Belovedness to deign to grant as alms to the church of Auchy the land belonging to you in the parish of Currenni, concerning which our dear and familiar friend, the abbot of Auchy—

[Note: Auchy, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, then in the diocese of Thérouanne and now of Saint-Omer, founded among the Morini on the river Canche about the year 700, first for nuns, who were succeeded by monks after its restoration following the Northmen.]

—has spoken with you. It has lain deserted and uncultivated, useless to you and your predecessors until now; may this benefit avail before God for your soul and for the souls [Col. 0618C] of your predecessors and successors.

## LETTER CDX

[Note: Previously Letter 366.]

### TO GILDUIN, ABBOT OF SAINT VICTOR

[Note: He was made abbot in 1113 by Louis the Fat, founder of the abbey of Saint Victor, after William of Champeaux, who had begun to organize the place, was promoted to the see of Châlons, as stated in connection with Letter 3. Concerning Saint Victor, besides what Duchesne relates in his notes on Abelard, Alberic says in his Chronicle under 1129: “The house of Saint Victor at Paris, which had been a priory of the black monks of Marseille, after the aforesaid monks had been expelled, received a community of Regulars from Saint-Ruf at Valence, through Master Hugh, called of Saint Victor, and by the king’s authority. Thus religious life increased, and this Order possesses fully thirty abbeys and more than eighty priories.” James of Vitry narrates remarkable things concerning this Order of Saint Victor in chapter 24 of his *Western History*, saying among other things: “This holy congregation of those fighting in the camps of the Lord, worthy of every acceptance, is a refuge of the poor, consolation of mourners, support and, as it were, foundation of the weak, refreshment of the weary, raising up of the fallen, the most tranquil harbor of the schools . . . . From the beginning it was made illustrious by many Parisian masters, learned and honorable men, shining like stars and adorned as with precious pearls. Among them the most renowned and eminent was the minstrel of the Lord, the instrument of the Holy Spirit, Master Hugh, called of Saint Victor.” Therefore St Bernard always embraced this house with special affection. Clear evidence of this is provided by the following grant, made at his intervention, as the autograph still preserved in the charter treasury of Saint Victor attests. A copy of it was communicated to me by the learned and most friendly M. Tonnelerius, librarian. See below among Bernard’s charters.]

He commends P. Lombard.

To the reverend fathers and lords, and most dear friends, G., by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, and the whole holy community, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and such prayers as we can offer.

[Col. 0619A] We must make many requests because many requests are made of us; nor can we spare our friends, because we are not spared by other friends. The bishop of Lucca, our father and friend, commended to me the venerable man P. Lombard—

[Note: Peter, called “Master of the Sentences” from his theological books of *Sentences*, and “the Lombard” here from his native land. Coming to France from the school of Bologna, he was commended to Bernard by the bishop of Lucca, Hubert or Gregory—to whom the third letter of Nicholas of Clairvaux is addressed [Col. 0620D] in Bernard’s person—and through Bernard to Gilduin and the canons of Saint Victor.]

—asking that, during the short time he would remain in France for study, I should provide through our friends what was necessary for his sustenance. This I did while he was staying at Reims. Now that he is living at Paris, I commend him to your affection, because I presume more upon you, asking you to be pleased to provide him food for the short time he will remain here until the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Farewell.

## LETTER CDXI

[Note: Previously Letter 373.]

### TO THOMAS, PROVOST OF BEVERLEY

[Note: See Letter 107, to the same man.]

A most sweet and honeyed letter, in which he invites Thomas to religious life, despite whatever sins; nothing can be preferred in this world to a good conscience.

To THOMAS, young man of good hope and venerable provost of Beverley, brother BERNARD, servant of Christ’s poor at Clairvaux: in accordance with your name, an omen of apostolic inheritance.

1. Ivo, who knew you, urged me, though unknown to you, to write to you; charity persuaded me. He reported to us, as certainly known to himself, what he wished concerning you; charity, which “believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), could not hear it idly. I say, not idly—at least as regards us; for immediately upon hearing it, charity compelled us to write to you, exhort you, and pray for you. Whether it is fruitless for you, you must see.

I confess that what we have heard of you from those who know you pleases us: not nobility of blood, elegance of body, beauty of appearance, abundance of possessions, or lofty dignities. Such things and those like them are the glory of the flesh and the flower of grass. Rather, it is liveliness of intellect, nobility of character, and above all the love of holy poverty which, they say, you recently conceived amid riches. Thus, rejoicing greatly, we have conceived good hope concerning you; may it not be put to shame. May this joy of ours soon reach [Col. 0619D] even the angels, who await a joyous and festive banquet over your repentance and conversion, as over those of other sinners. Would that the flower of your youth and the promise of so great a natural endowment might come into my hands! Would that it might be granted to preserve for God what is excessive [perhaps read: diminished], unspoiled, and offer it as an odor of sweetness!

2. Yet perhaps your conscience will answer that I have spoken too late, because what you may feel you have stained with many crimes can no longer be kept unspoiled. [Col. 0620A] This does not frighten me; and, being a sinner, I do not shrink from a sinner. Nor do I despise one who is sick, since I know myself to be sick. But even if you consider me well, I do not refuse to become weak with the weak, that I may gain the weak; gladly heeding also Paul’s counsel: “You who are spiritual, restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). Nor do I reckon the enormity of the disease, when I consider the physician’s skill and his mercy, which I have often experienced in my own great illnesses.

However foul you may be with vices, however ugly the conscience you bear, however much you may feel that your youth has been defiled by dreadful crimes; though, made inveterate by evil days, you have rotted like a beast in its own dung: without doubt you will be cleansed, [Col. 0620B] made whiter than snow, and your youth will be renewed like an eagle’s. For I know him who says: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20). He is the good Physician, who heals all the soul’s infirmities, satisfying its desires with good things (Ps. 103:3, 5).

3. A good conscience is great wealth. And truly, what is richer or sweeter among earthly things? What is more peaceful and secure on earth? A good conscience does not fear loss of possessions, insults of words, or bodily torments; indeed, it is raised up rather than cast down even by death itself. What in earth’s goods, I ask, could you compare with so great a happiness? What such thing can a world flattering its lovers offer them? What like it can it promise, even falsely, to fools? If there are limitless estates, [Col. 0620C] vast palaces, pontifical mitres, and royal scepters—apart from the other hazards, which I pass over, without which such things can neither be acquired nor retained—when one death comes upon them, are not all abandoned at once? For it is written: “They slept their sleep, and all men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 76:6). But the good things of a good conscience grow green again; they do not wither in labors, nor disappear in death, but flower anew. They gladden the living, comfort the dying, refresh the dead, and never fail for eternity.

But why linger over words, when I am now prepared to fulfill words with deeds? You have it in your power, certainly, either to prove me a liar or yourself rich. Only come and see. With what joyful steps we shall run to meet the fugitive with loaves; with what joyful embraces we shall receive the younger son! Quickly the best robe will be brought out, a ring given for his finger, and it will be said: “This my son was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:24, 32).

## LETTER CDXII

[Note: A new letter.]

### TO T., A YOUNG MAN WHO HAD VOWED THE MONASTIC LIFE

To his most beloved son T., BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: go out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.

[Col. 0621A] 1. To speak to you in familiar terms: man is a rational, mortal animal. One thing the Creator’s grace gave us; another the sinner’s merit brought upon us. In one we share angelic nobility, in the other bestial weakness. Yet both should rouse and raise us to seek the Lord: both fear of death and the dignity of reason.

Remember your word, by which you gave me hope. I ask for the fruit of your promise; the time for demanding it has come. Do not tremble with fear where there is no fear. To serve the Lord in gladness is not a burden but an honor. I cannot grant you a reprieve: nothing is more certain than death, nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. But what shall we say of your tender age? Fruit is often plucked from trees before ripeness, by hand or by storm. What of your appearance [Col. 0621B] and beauty?

> O handsome boy, do not trust your color too greatly:  
> white privet falls, black bilberries are gathered.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues*, II.17–18.)

Go out, go out with Joseph from Pharaoh’s house, and leave your cloak to the Egyptian mistress—that is, to worldly glory. Go out from your land and from your kindred; forget your people and your father’s house, and the King will desire your beauty. The boy Jesus is not found among relatives and acquaintances. Go out from your father’s house to meet him, because he went out for your sake from his Father’s house. “His going forth is from the highest heaven.” Rightly did the woman find him who, having gone out from her own borders, cried out: “Have mercy on me, Son of David.” And he, because grace was poured out [Col. 0621C] upon his lips, quickly answered her: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you have asked” (Matt. 15:22, 28).

2. Satan can cast out Satan; but can the Spirit of truth be contrary to himself? I believe that it was he who spoke with me about your conversion through your own mouth. See, therefore, that you turn neither to the right nor to the left, but come to Clairvaux according to your word. I have written this to you briefly and secretly, sending it through our beloved son Gerard, your friend. Offer no excuse. If study is your reason, if you still wish to be taught and to be under a master: the Master is here and calls you, namely he in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden [Col. 0621D]. He it is who teaches man knowledge, makes the tongues of infants eloquent, opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens.

## LETTER CDXIII

[Note: Previously Letter 389.]

### TO ABBOT RAINALD

[Note: Of Fesmy, I think, to whom Letter 72 and those following are addressed.]

He asks that a novice, now firm in his purpose, be kindly received.

To Lord Abbot RAINALD, brother BERNARD: whatever spiritual grace he desires for himself.

I praise the prudence by which you feared to grieve a monk on account of a novice; but I approve still more the humility with which you so patiently endured an injury done to you—so great an injury. Incomparably [Col. 0622A] more, however, I value the charity by which, rather than allow a bruised reed to be broken, you took care to advise him to seek our counsel. O prudent humility and humble charity, thus sparing the offending monk without failing the wavering novice! Therefore, having confirmed him as much as I could, and finding him ready, as I think, to amend all the things for which he was reproved, I send him back to you. I appeal to your proven kindness and, if necessary, beg you that he may be received—provided, however, that the aforesaid brother, to whom I have accordingly sent letters of entreaty, be turned, if possible, from his former opinion. Farewell.

## LETTER CDXIV

[Note: Previously Letter 328.]

### TO ALARD, A MONK

On the preceding matter. He rebukes him because, after the aforesaid novice had been expelled and was already intending to return and amend his life, he opposed him too stubbornly.

[Col. 0622B]

To his beloved son ALARD, brother BERNARD: the affection of paternal love.

1. Brother Adamarus [otherwise Ademarus] complains that you have been excessively bitter toward him: not only because, through your action, he was expelled from the house, but because, through your opposition too, he cannot be reconciled. I would believe that you did this only from good zeal. But when I remember that obstinacy of yours which, as you know, I am accustomed often to reproach in you with the most friendly frankness, I fear that your zeal may not be according to knowledge.

For, to cite the Rule’s own words, how great an audacity it is for anyone to strike, excommunicate, much less expel, someone while the abbot is absent and [Col. 0622C] unaware! (*Rule of St Benedict*, ch. 70). Was it not rather an obligation of your humility not to do to another what you would not wish done to yourself? Indeed, your perfection ought rather to have imitated the Apostle saying, “I became weak to the weak, that I might gain the weak” (1 Cor. 9:22); and again: “You who are spiritual, restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

“But,” you will say, “the Prior expelled him, not I.” I know that myself; but it was on your persuasion and at your insistent urging. Hence, now that, as I have heard, the Prior himself, moved by pity, wishes to call him back, he is not allowed to amend what in his indiscretion he was compelled to do, because you persist in your hardness. I ask you: what security is this, that while all the rest take pity, and the lord [Col. 0622D] abbot himself is kindly disposed, you alone remain unyielding and cannot be bent to receive him? Have you not read: “Judgment without mercy is for the one who has shown no mercy” (James 2:13)? Have you forgotten what is elsewhere written: “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2)? Or do you despise what is promised to the merciful: “For they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7)?

2. “But,” you say, “you do not know how justly he was expelled.” Whether he was expelled justly or unjustly, I do not ask, nor do I now care. I complain only of this, make this my charge, and greatly wonder at this: that though he gives satisfaction humbly, [Col. 0623A] petitions insistently, endures patiently, and promises amendment, he still does not deserve to be heard, so that, according to the Apostle, love may be confirmed toward him (2 Cor. 2:8), and, according to our master, he may again be tested in all patience (*Rule of St Benedict*, ch. 58). Certainly, if he was expelled unjustly, it is just that he be recalled; if justly, it is merciful that he be received. Hence I judged this counsel of ours safe, though the case had not been examined, because by it one does not depart from the just and merciful God, whether through justice or through mercy. Therefore I ask you, most beloved son, that what he could not obtain from you by his own prayers, he may obtain through ours, which he has sought from so far away.

## LETTER CDXV

[Note: Previously Letter 393.]

### TO A CERTAIN BREAKER OF HIS PLEDGE

He urges him, having cast off the yoke of carnal pleasure, to carry out the promised vow of religious life.

[Col. 0623B]

Though you have forgotten yourself, I have not. I love you, and as much as I love you, so much I grieve. Love makes me grieve, and grief keeps me from forgetting. But alas—what a miserable and sorrowful memory! I wondered what prevented you from coming as you had promised. For I could not believe that you would lightly violate your pledge—such a pledge—unless there were a grave cause; for I had found you, even at a younger age, sufficiently faithful and truthful. Nor was my expectation deceived. For there is indeed a great and grave cause holding you back: the very cause that overcame most valiant David and deceived most wise Solomon. [Col. 0623C] What shall I say? Does one who falls not rise again?

O how much, and how necessary, I have to say to you! But it would take too long to write it. Therefore I say this briefly and intimately. If any spark of our former affection still lives in you; if any hope remains to you of escaping that most wretched captivity of yours; if, finally, you do not wish the confidence which they say you still place, even amid such a way of life, in the prayers and friendship of our congregation to be empty or false: do not delay to revisit Clairvaux—if you are sufficiently free and master of yourself to dare, at least for a time, to withdraw from that bloody beast which strives daily to pour out everything that is yours along with the blood of your soul.

Otherwise, know henceforth that you are entirely excluded from the familiar fellowship of our brotherhood, [Col. 0623D] and you will no longer be able, except vainly, to flatter yourself with the society of the good; for you judge yourself unworthy, surely, of the fellowship of those whose counsel you refuse to accept. But if you do not shrink from coming, I trust that by God’s mercy, before you depart from us, you will be freed from the chain of death in which you are held.

## LETTER CDXVI

[Note: A new letter.]

### TO AN UNKNOWN PERSON

He states that Count Theobald’s alms were not distributed by him.

The biting letter which you sent us some time ago, as is your custom, indicates that you suffer a bite of the heart. For [Col. 0624A] at first, supposing that you did not speak seriously in it but, as usual, wished to jest with us, we thought so. But a monk who happened to arrive from your region dispelled the cloud of that empty opinion of ours. For although he knew nothing beforehand about that letter except what he had heard from our own mouth, he interpreted it otherwise—but truthfully—though unknowingly. Thus we can no longer doubt that you truly suspect us ill, as though, in the distribution of the alms of the Count of Champagne—

[Note: Namely, Theobald.]

—we had not acted as friends toward friends who were absent. You feel this because you believe the matter was placed in our hands. But anyone who thinks that the aforesaid count, either himself or his possessions, is governed by our counsel, certainly knows either him or me insufficiently. Indeed, this has been proved. [Col. 0624B] For although I repeatedly and rather shamelessly begged him to give something to several monasteries—and especially to the bishop himself, about whom, lest we speak openly of you, you attacked me so sharply—I could not obtain it. The man therefore distributed from his own possessions as much as he wished and to whom he wished: partly while I watched, but did not divide; for the greater part, without my even seeing it, though not begrudging it. For perhaps we too could have extracted something, had we wished. But thanks be to God, who inspired us not even to accept what was offered.

Now, if you judge it fitting to believe me about myself rather than rumor, no occasion remains, I think, for you to judge either us—or the bishop—less worthy than usual of those customary favors of yours which you thought should be reproached to us. [Col. 0624C] Know, nevertheless, that we are prepared with equanimity to lack whatever we have not deserved to possess.

## LETTER CDXVII

[Note: A new letter.]

### TO THE ABBOT OF TRONC-BERENGER

He asks that Brother Dodo be humanely received by him.

To his most beloved brother and fellow abbot G. of Tronc-Berenger, brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: greeting in the Lord.

Brother Dodo came to consult our simplicity and carried back from us this counsel—or rather, judgment. Since he has brought forward no fitting reason why he should wish to abandon his place and Order, we saw no reason to permit his transfer elsewhere. For the vow which he says he made previously, from which he took the chief occasion for his scruple, was made by thought alone—or even by word, but with this alone actually done. It ought in no way to be preferred to this later vow, by which, though later, he seems to have bound himself by word, deliberation, habit, and profession; especially because that earlier thing which he vowed appears neither stricter nor more right than this. Therefore we do not believe that it is safe for you, who must render an account to Christ for his soul, to grant him permission in this matter, since it is written: “The Lord will lead away with evildoers those who turn aside into crooked ways” [Col. 0625A] (Ps. 125:5). Receive him, therefore, sweetly as a son; guard him diligently as one entrusted to you; for henceforth, unless I am mistaken, he will obey your commands and submit to your counsels.

## LETTER CDXVIII

[Note: A new letter, from the Savigny archive. Written about the year 1152.]

### TO HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

He asks the archbishop to confirm a donation made to Savigny.

To Lord and most beloved father HUGH, by God’s grace archbishop of Rouen, and to the whole Church of Rouen, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and such prayers as he can offer in the Lord.

We wish your kindness to know, and we bear sure witness to the truth, that Lord [Col. 0625B] Philip, bishop of Bayeux—

[Note: This was Philip of Harcourt. Concerning the land at Écrury, given to Savigny in 1124 by Robert de Tostes and confirmed by Richard I and Richard II, bishops of Bayeux, from whom it was held by beneficiary right, he had disputed for some time with the monks. At last he too confirmed it by his letters in November 1151, adding four acres of land.]

—granted, at our request and in our presence, to your sons and our brothers of Savigny, a cultivated plot situated before the grange of Écrury and containing four acres of land. The reverend father Lord Henry, now archbishop of York, Lord Guy, abbot of Cherlieu, and other brethren of ours were also present. Therefore we ask and earnestly entreat your beloved Piety in the Lord to provide for those aforesaid sons of yours with paternal solicitude and affection, lest they should hereafter be troubled concerning the same land. If anyone now or at any other time wishes either to raise a legal claim concerning this cultivated plot or to inflict violence upon them, [Col. 0625C] let it be for your charity to oppose yourselves as a wall for the house which is yours and to vindicate its right, so that it may possess it without disturbance. For this is the truth, and a certain truth, which we write to you.

## LETTER CDXIX

[Note: A new letter, from the cartulary of La Celle. Written in the year of Christ 1152.]

### TO PETER, ABBOT OF LA CELLE

He relinquishes a furnace to the monks of La Celle.

[Col. 0626A]

To PETER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Peter of La Celle, brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greetings and such prayers as he can offer in the Lord.

We grant and confirm to you and to your house the oven situated at Troyes, which belonged to our house of Mores. Since our brethren cannot retain revenues of this kind, those who built the said oven have, through our hand, after receiving the forty-four pounds which they had spent on its construction, transferred it to you and your house for free possession. We wish this to be held ratified [Col. 0626B] and confirm it by the impression of our seal. Witnesses are the brethren of your house: Peter the prior, Jocelin the subprior, Stephen the provost; also Walcher and Rainaud, our cellarers, and Fromund, who was building the place. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152.

EPISTLE 420 [Note: [Col. 0625D] A new letter, from the manuscript codex of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai.---Up to this point it was published without a numerical designation, under the title: “Fragment of a Letter.”]. (Fragment.) TO NICHOLAS, BISHOP OF CAMRAI.

To the venerable lord and dearest father N., [Note: [Col. 0626D] Nicholas de Chièvres, concerning whom see Letter 214.] bishop of Cambrai: Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes that you may provide what is good before God and men.

In an old friendship we seek a new proof, [Col. 0626C] not one that removes doubt, but one that produces certainty. For I am certain that you love me; but just as your very affection has made itself known to us in our own regard . . . [Note: [Col. 0626D] The remainder is lacking and occurs nowhere else.].

NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING THIRTY-SIX LETTERS, numbered 421–455 among the genuine letters and 461 among the spurious letters, first published, though without chronological indication, by Dom MARTÈNE in volume I, column 725, of the *Amplissima Collectio* [Note: [Col. 0626D] Letters 421–454 were supplied by the manuscript of Saint-Vaast at Arras; the following letter by the manuscript from Anchin; and the last letter, which is first in order among the spurious letters in the Appendix, by the Verdun codex. EDITOR.].

[Col. 0625]

Of the letters which we have published in large number in this volume, those which have Bernard as their author and have hitherto remained unpublished are of the greatest value, [Note: [Col. 0626D] Some nevertheless occur above, but addressed to others: namely, Letters 428, 430, 444, 452, and 453, which, with a few changes, are the same as those published under nos. 391, 316, 417, 86, and 413. EDITOR.] both because of the eminence of the holy doctor and because of the importance of the matters they treat. It is neither our purpose nor our leisure to examine each one here, although there is none among them which it is not greatly worthwhile to read with care and attention. We shall touch upon only one or two which seem especially conducive to elucidating the history of the holy abbot; and, on their occasion, we shall discuss some matters concerning that saint which have hitherto been less well known.

First to be considered is Letter 11, to Pope Innocent II, concerning the dispute of Philip and Hugh over the Church of Tours. Clearly, after Archbishop Hildebert died on 18 December 1134, [Col. 0627] while the canons, driven from their own seats by the violence of Count Geoffrey, lived in exile and ought to have provided for the vacant Church, some of them, against the ordinances of the sacred canons, elected a certain Philip, nephew of Gilbert, archbishop before Hildebert and, as St Bernard says (*Letter* 150), heir to his ambition. On the other hand, “Hugh, a prudent and noble man, was canonically elected by the sounder party of those same clerics,” as we read in the *Acts of the Bishops of Le Mans* (*Analecta*, vol. III). When the matter was brought before Pope Innocent, he committed the examination of both elections to appointed judges, granting them authority, after weighing the arguments of each side, to pronounce by definitive judgment who should be the lawful bishop. Among these judges St Bernard seems to have held the leading place. He informed Innocent II of the entire course of the proceedings in Letter 11, first published by us in this volume. From it we learn many things hitherto unknown, which remarkably illuminate both the history of the archbishops of Tours and the Life of St Bernard.
