A few years later Pope Eugenius III, formerly a disciple of St Bernard, entrusted to the holy abbot for settlement by an equitable and peaceful agreement that celebrated controversy which for more than two hundred years had been carried on between the Churches of Tours and Dol concerning primacy or metropolitan right. To execute the apostolic mandate, Bernard went to the appointed place with Geoffrey the notary and his brother Nivard. After examining the arguments of both sides, as a lover of peace he pronounced a decision favourable to the men of Dol. Its terms remain unknown to us. But the people of Tours—whose cause had previously been adjudged by the supreme pontiffs Nicholas I, John VIII, John XIII, Leo IX, Gregory VII, Urban II, and most recently Lucius II, who had invested Hugh, archbishop of Tours, with the bishoprics of Dol, Saint-Brieuc, and Tréguier by a wooden staff still preserved in the church of Tours—refused to abide by the sentence pronounced by St Bernard.

We learn this from the letter of Pope Anastasius IV to the archbishop of Tours, first published by us in volume III of the *Anecdota*, p. 897, in which he says:

> “Moved by the lamentations of the Church of Dol, our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory ordered, by his letters, Bernard, of holy memory, formerly abbot of Clairvaux, to labour for peace between you and the Church of Dol, and, according to the wisdom granted him from above, to soothe in brotherly charity the controversy long agitated on both sides. Since, therefore, after receiving assurance from you and from that Church that what he should establish between you would be observed, the same abbot, in the presence of our beloved sons G., a monk, and Nivard, brother of the same abbot, established between you what he saw to be expedient, we command your brotherhood by these present letters to descend from the rigour of your will, considering that charity seeks not its own things but those of others, and to observe that settlement.”

Innocent III likewise testifies to this in his definitive sentence against the people of Dol, published by us in the same place, p. 945. The men of Dol complained of the obstinacy of the people of Tours; yet they themselves fell into a like fault, refusing to abide by the settlement made by the abbot of Fontaines with the consent of the parties.

The writers of the Lives of St Bernard teach that the most holy abbot accompanied Innocent II on his return journey into Italy; yet nowhere do they report that he went to the monastery of Monte Cassino. Nevertheless, from the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* of Peter the Deacon we learn that he not only went there, but also addressed the chapter when Abbot Raynald was deposed by solemn judgment and Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, was substituted in his place. Shortly before, Wibald had avoided Cassino in order to escape so great a dignity. In Book IV, chapter 122, Peter writes:

> “On the following day they again ascended to the monastery and sat in chapter. After the sermon delivered by the abbot of Clairvaux, the cardinals, by apostolic authority, forbade Raynald to hold the abbacy of Cassino,”

etc.

It may have been in that place that St Bernard first became known to Abbot Wibald, who later heard him preach in Germany and admired him. Thus, in Letter 147 to Monegold, master of the school, Wibald presents Bernard as an outstanding example of the Christian orator in these words:

> “Yet there is sometimes in the Church an occasion suitable for matters in which the art of speaking is exercised without reproach, especially in the office of preaching; and in the primacy of this grace, in my judgment, is placed a man of our times, very illustrious—Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. I should not undeservedly call him an orator, whom rhetoricians define as a good man skilled in speaking. [Note: [Col. 0627] ‘Therefore let the orator whom we are training be the man whom M. Cato defines as a good man skilled in speaking.’ QUINTILIAN, Book XII, chapter 1.] For that good man, worn out by the long austerity of the desert, fasting, and pallor, and reduced to a certain thinness of spiritual form, persuades first by his appearance before he does by his hearing. He has been granted by God an excellent natural endowment, the highest learning, incomparable industry, vast practice, clear delivery, and bodily gesture suited to every mode of speech. Therefore it is no wonder that by the powerful force of such great gifts he awakens those who sleep—indeed, to say more, the dead—and, with the Lord cooperating and confirming the word, changes men and draws beneath God’s yoke as captives those who had been in Pharaoh’s chariots. You would truly call eloquent the man who does not destroy in deed what he preaches by word, who is not Nero within and Cato without. If you see him, you are taught; if you hear him, you are instructed; if you follow him, you will make progress.”

Since Bernard possessed such power and grace in speaking, it ought not at all to seem surprising that he preached everywhere with so great fruit, but especially in Germany, the Lord in particular cooperating and confirming the word by the signs that followed. His disciples, eyewitnesses, recorded in writing the miracles daily performed there by St Bernard. But it is pleasing here to repeat what Helmold writes about them in chapter 59 of the *Chronicle of the Slavs*:

> “About the time of those days there arose new things, astonishing to the whole world. For while the most holy Pope Eugenius presided, and Conrad III held the reins of the kingdom, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, shone forth; the fame of whose miracles was so renowned that crowds of people flowed to him from the whole world, desiring to see the wonders wrought through him. Entering the German land, he came to the celebrated court at Frankfurt, where King Conrad had then hastened with a great assembly of princes. When, therefore, the holy man was present in the churches and diligently applied himself to healing the sick in the Lord’s name, while the king and the highest authorities stood by, amid such multitudes of people it was uncertain what each person suffered or to whom help might perhaps be given. There was present our Count Adolf, wishing to know more certainly, by divine operation, the power of the man. Meanwhile a boy blind and lame was presented to him, whose infirmity admitted of no doubt. The most discerning man began carefully to seek whether he might perhaps obtain in this boy a proof of Bernard’s holiness. Providing a remedy for his unbelief, as though taught by God, the man of God ordered the boy, contrary to his usual practice, to be brought close to him; for he marked the others by word alone. Receiving this boy, however, when he was placed in his hands, he restored his sight by prolonged handling of his eyes. Then, taking hold of his contracted knees, he ordered him to run to the steps, giving plain evidence that both sight and the power of walking had been restored.”

In Letter 23 St Bernard dissuades a monk who wished to transfer to another monastery and wholly disapproves of his purpose. Indeed, it was always the settled and constant judgment of the most holy doctor that a monk established in a regular monastery ought not, under any pretext, to migrate to another monastery. He especially teaches this in Book *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 16, where he tries to turn from his purpose a monk who was considering, under the appearance of greater perfection, moving from the Cluniacs to the Cistercians, who were devoted to a stricter discipline.

Had Nicholas, monk of Arremar, observed this, he would never have plunged into that abyss of ruin which all upright men abhorred. Admitted at Clairvaux by Prior Rualen during Bernard’s absence, he was talented and yielding, but insufficiently steadfast in his own character. He insinuated himself into other men’s affections and had an excellent command of letters as occasion required. Soon after having professed stability at Clairvaux, he became St Bernard’s secretary. Abusing the indulgence and easy confidence of his most holy abbot in that office, he falsified Bernard’s seal for evil uses, committed certain shameful acts, and finally fell into dreadful apostasy. But after wandering here and there in various ways, after St Bernard’s death he returned to his fellow monks of Arremar, where he could then safely and securely remain. Mabillon observes and describes all this more fully at the beginning of the sermons of St Bernard, where he presents the Life of this same Nicholas composed by himself.

But who would believe what that learned man did not know? The same Nicholas, stained by so shameful a blot, afterwards gained such renown and bound to himself the affections of princes, bishops, and even supreme pontiffs, that he became dear to them. This is certainly clear from Pope Adrian IV’s letter to Samson, archbishop of Rheims, which we shall publish in volume II. There the supreme pontiff says:

> “Our beloved son Master Nicholas, a monk of the monastery of Arremar, who is very dear and acceptable to us, appearing before the Apostolic See, requested in our letters that your brotherhood be exhorted to support and receive his petitions in the affairs of that church. Therefore, by apostolic writing, we command your brotherhood diligently to love the same our son, who is sufficiently zealous and devoted in your affairs, for reverence toward St Peter and ourselves; to show him honour; and continually to concur with gracious assent in his petitions concerning the affairs of that church. Thus expend your favour and aid upon him in his causes, so that your brotherhood may appear commendable for accepting our requests.”

What is more, Alexander III honoured the same Nicholas with his own letter and even adorned him with not insignificant praise. Thus Letter 6, to the same Nicholas, to be published in volume II, begins:

> “We hold grateful and acceptable, and greatly commend in the Lord, the constancy of your devotion and the firmness of your faith toward the most holy Roman Church and our own person, which we know by many trials of events and by the actual effect of your work that you possess. For we know how you have spared yourself not at all and have laboured very much for the Church’s cause. Therefore we have the purpose and will to love your person, as a special son of the Church, with sincere charity in the Lord, and always to grant your petitions.”

He then exhorts Nicholas, just as he had begun well, to persevere steadfastly “in devotion and fidelity” both to the Church and to himself, “and to strive to lead and more earnestly confirm other persons, both ecclesiastical and secular, in the same.” Finally, he commends him to Hugh of Sens, Samson of Rheims, archbishops, and Henry, count of Troyes.

EPISTLE 421. TO MAR. AND HIS WIFE. He exhorts them to almsgiving and pious works.

[Col. 0629A]

Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to his beloved Mar. and his wife: may they so love one another that they know how to prefer Christ’s love mutually to their own.

Whatever you possess on earth, it is certain that you will someday lose, unless you take care to send it beforehand to heaven through the hands of the poor. Come then, beloved friends: store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth does not destroy, where thieves do not dig through or steal, and where, finally, the prince himself can take nothing from you. If you are concerned about a messenger, you have daily at your door not one but several [Col. 0629B] who will faithfully carry whatever you wish to send there. For this reason God has multiplied their afflictions in the present time: that you may have an opportunity to lay up treasure in a place of such happiness and security.

Take care to communicate this on your behalf to T., our brother and your good nephew, and to W., who has your niece; and to any others whom you know will not despise our most salutary counsel in this matter. Above all, I wish those who are in the house of God to feel the blessing of your forthcoming visitation.

EPISTLE 422. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. He excuses the brevity of his letter and sends back to him a young man whom he could by no means admit among his own brethren.

[Col. 0629C]

Whatever may concern himself.

I am not unaware that both the brevity and the dryness of our letters sent to you are accustomed to be troublesome. [Col. 0630A] But much occupation makes me brief, and scant devotion makes me dry. Bear with me; and now, pressed by the evil of the day, I am compelled to hasten [perhaps: “to prove”] to what is necessary. We persuaded this young man from your region, who came to us for the sake of his salvation, having for some reason passed you by, to return to you. Since, as you know, we cannot receive him, he will, I think, not be useless to you if you are willing to receive him—which I earnestly ask you to do.

EPISTLE 423. TO A CERTAIN BISHOP. He commends to him the cause of the monastery of Saint Martin.

Always to do what God wills.

[Col. 0630B] Does it please you that the poor church of St Martin should lose, perhaps through lack of friends rather than lack of justice, the relief of poverty bestowed upon it by God? Otherwise, if it is thought not to have a just cause, it is also expedient for it promptly to cease from an unjust complaint. We therefore wish you not to consider it burdensome carefully to investigate the matter, and to make an effort that it may be settled either justly or peacefully—that is, either by judgment or by agreement. Farewell; remember me, sweetest father.

EPISTLE 424. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. He excuses himself because he cannot go with him to the legate.

The reason why I myself did not come to you, as you directed, is [Col. 0630C] a serious one, and you must pity it, although for the moment you are not acquainted with it. I ask you simply [perhaps: “humbly”] to pray to almighty God for it. Therefore, what we were both to undertake together with the legate, accomplish alone as best you can.

EPISTLE 425. TO A CERTAIN JUDGE. He commends to him the cause of Fontenay Abbey. [Note: [Col. 0631D] Fontenay, a notable monastery of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Autun, not far from Montbard, founded about the year 1118 by relatives of St Bernard; the second daughter-house of Clairvaux. Its first abbot was Geoffrey. MARTÈNE.]

[Col. 0631A]

Until now I have had such confidence in you that, wherever I knew you to be in matters concerning us, I thought there was no need for me to be present. I wonder, therefore, how you have grown so lukewarm toward Fontenay Abbey, which we left in your keeping after God, and for which we often made requests to you in person while present. We have heard that in the pleas which you undertook before yourself on behalf of that church, you have not yet brought the matter to the end you determined. Know, however, that as long as you delay to do these things, and as long as you do not take care to console and visit the brethren otherwise than you are accustomed to do, you will always hear our complaints on their behalf [Col. 0631B].

EPISTLE 426. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. He commends to him the bearer of this letter.

To please God everywhere and in all things.

I commend to your Charity a man dear to me on account of his religious character, namely the bearer of this letter, who needs your patronage with the Count. I ask that in his cause, which he himself will relate to you, he may experience how much our humility can avail with you, and how much your Reverence can avail with the Count.

EPISTLE 427. TO THE BISHOP OF TROYES. He disapproves of his having given an archdeaconry to a boy.

[Col. 0631C]

To the venerable lord and father H. [Note: [Col. 0631D] Hatto, to whom there survive Letters 23 and 203 of this same St Bernard, and several of Peter the Venerable. EDITOR.] by God’s grace bishop of Troyes: Brother Bernard sends himself, insofar as he can.

Your gracious Dignity has made us presume without hesitation upon you whenever necessary. We have undertaken to make a request to you for your venerable son G.—indeed, to give you counsel for your own sake. We wonder, loving your good reputation as we do, on what grounds or by whose counsel you have considered utterly undoing what you had done well: namely, assigning the archdeaconry to the aforesaid son G., who can administer it excellently, rather than entrusting it to a boy who cannot govern even himself. [Note: [Col. 0631D] The holy doctor always took it ill that ecclesiastical dignities were bestowed upon boys. This appears both from Letter [Col. 0632D] 271, in which he rebukes Count Theobald because he wished to procure them for his underage son William, and from the treatise *On the Office of Bishops*, chapter 17, where he says: “Schoolboys and underage youths, on account of their birth, are promoted to ecclesiastical dignities and are transferred from beneath the rod to ruling priests; meanwhile they are happier that they have escaped the rods than that they have deserved authority.” See his third book *On Consideration*, chapter 5. EDITOR.] You have thought of bringing this to nothing so badly, in our view. For if you had built anything, you are again—God forbid!—destroying it. But enough has been said for one who understands. If you fear men, the Gospel teaches whom you ought rather to fear. If you wish to please men, yet it is better to obey God; render what you owe to Caesar, and also what you owe to God.

EPISTLE 428. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. He praises him and exhorts him to reform his monastery, and especially its hospital.

[Col. 0632A]

The title of chastity and grace.

These brethren, coming to our littleness for counsel concerning their souls, have greatly gladdened us by reporting your good zeal in reforming the place over which, by God’s grace, you preside. But we admonish and entreat your devotion that, as you labour to repair buildings, so you should labour to renew morals. You must take most diligent care not only of the monastery but also of the hospital, the house of God, in which the aforesaid brethren serve under your authority. In particular, [Col. 0632B] keep it safe and free from every exaction and harassment by your servants or retainers. We ask that you restore what, at their perverse counsel, as we have heard, you took away from that house though it had been bestowed upon it by abbots before you. For just as it belongs to your care to undo or correct the wrongdoings of others, so you ought not only to keep firm and unimpaired whatever good they have done, but also to increase and multiply it. Compel also the priest who lives in that house but still seems to retain property outside either to abandon what is his own or to leave the house. Farewell; and because of the good we have heard of you, place familiar confidence in us in whatever way we can be of help.

EPISTLE 429. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. He gives thanks to God for matters successfully accomplished.

[Col. 0632C]

I know that you wish to know what I now make known to you. Thanks be to him who has wrought all our works for us. We have cheerfully and successfully completed a great work and a difficult journey; we left the brethren joyful and at peace, abounding in resources and friends, and, as I judge, sufficiently pleasing to God and men. We could scarcely bring Brother G. back without offending both the bishop and the brethren. After harvest-time, which is now at hand, if you have need of him—indeed, because you will have need—you may have him.

EPISTLE 430. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. That ecclesiastical benefices are to be received not from a lay hand but from the bishop.

[Col. 0632D]

When laymen wish to relinquish churches or ecclesiastical benefices which they hold unlawfully, that is one good thing. But when they wish these to pass to the use of God’s servants, the good is doubled. Yet since this cannot be done except through the bishop’s hand, the bishop will prove himself responsible for a double evil or the author of a good, according as he withholds or gives his assent. What the knight asks you for, he ought himself to have asked of you. What then? Do you judge it better that the sanctuary of God should be possessed by the hereditary right of a military man than by the saints of God? It would be strange if all who hear this did not wonder. Do not, I beg you, do not act thus, lest the sons of uncircumcision hear and rejoice.

Suppose that you can rescue the captive Church from the hand of the powerful man and vindicate it for its proper right—which we do not at all suppose. Whom, I ask, would you choose more willingly as your heir and successor in respect of it: one who will from it serve the king’s armies, or one who will intercede for your sins? Do, therefore, what is just, what is worthy of you, what is pleasing to God and to good men, and finally what, even if nothing else supported it, I would confidently ask to be done out of love for me. [Col. 0633B]

EPISTLE 431. TO POPE INNOCENT II. Delegated by the supreme pontiff as judge to settle the suit between two contenders for the archbishopric of Tours, he declares Philip’s election null.

To decide the dispute at Tours, venerable Father, we assembled—and assembled at Blois, because that place was suitable to those conducting the proceedings by both proximity and security. There the opponents of Philip’s election [Note: [Col. 0633D] This Philip was the nephew of Gilbert, archbishop before Hildebert, and, as St Bernard says in Letter 150, the “heir of his ambition.” A letter of the same St Bernard, no. 151, survives addressed to him as an invader of the see of Tours. The book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans* says of him: “When Hildebert died, the canons of that Church were for a long time driven from their own seats by the violence of Count Geoffrey. When they ought canonically to elect a bishop, they were divided into parties. For some of them, against the ordinances of the holy canons and despite the protests of others, elected a certain Philip. Philip, indeed, not entering through the door into the sheepfold, but climbing up another way, went to his Peter—Peter, the firstborn of Satan’s Leo—and from him received, in place of honour, disgrace; in place of blessing, a curse; and in place of a sacrament, sacrilege. Returning swiftly, he occupied the see of Tours. Meanwhile Hugh, a prudent and noble man, was canonically elected by the sounder party of those same clerics. He was consecrated in the Church of Le Mans by Guy and the bishops of the province. When Philip learned this, he secretly fled, taking with him the ornaments of the church.” Moreover, since Hildebert died on 18 December 1136, these events could only have happened in the following year. From this you will correct Horst’s chronology, which dates Philip’s intrusion to 1133. MARTÈNE.] had accused him on many counts, which we omit for brevity’s sake. At last they brought two principal charges: that he was under age and that he had not been elected by those who ought to elect, [Col. 0633C] nor even by a sufficient number of them. For the senior persons of the church were absent at that time—indeed, expelled both from the church and from their own houses: namely, all the archdeacons, the dean and the chanter, together with all the priests of that church and a multitude of other clerics of various ranks.

They said, therefore, that the election of Hugh which they had made was sound and canonical, since those whose authority carried the greater weight in electing had consented to it. Nor did it harm it that it had, contrary to custom, been held outside the church or city, since necessity imposed by persecution compelled this. Nor did it prevent its validity that the other party had not been present, since, forewarned and summoned by the brethren, they had refused to attend. They said that the place had been assigned to them—the very place which both parties, by equal agreement, had chosen for conducting an election. But the others had anticipated the day, snatched away the election, and with stealthy rashness elected Philip while they were entirely unaware. No suffragan bishop had been awaited; whereas the bishops favoured their election more and had given it their assent.

To this Philip’s party replied: “We can easily and sufficiently answer the objections, provided only that another day convenient to us is appointed. It is not that we deny that the present day was given, but our elect was not specifically summoned. He should have been summoned by name, since the cause is known properly to concern him.”

Then the opposing party said: “Far from it! The dispute is not among the elected concerning a see, but among electors concerning elections. The cause is therefore that of the litigants, and they themselves ought to have been summoned to the case. If you contend that the elect is also one of the litigants, that is indeed serious and improper. It is sufficient, moreover, that he was summoned generally with the others. For no one belonging to the party was excluded from the letters of summons; although you cannot deny that it was plainly announced to you that he was being sought. He had gone away and could not be found, lest perhaps he should be detained and fail to be present on the appointed day. He therefore gains nothing by his absence; even if he did not come, the case would nevertheless be settled in his absence.

“If, as you say, it is his cause and it was necessary for the man to speak for himself, then the fact that he had no summons is the fault either of the man who disappeared or of you who neglected to inform him. What concern is it of those who sent common written summonses to your city and church if they did not reach one who withdrew himself—not only from the city, but also from his native land and from the kingdom, and for what purpose, let him himself consider? What still lacks to him of all that his case requires, if he does not distrust his justice? [Col. 0634C] We see the man surrounded by a multitude of wise persons and experts in legal cases, and also attended by a number of armed men, if there is need of them. He has bishops with him; he has an excellent advocate. Did he come so unprepared? Or what is the point of this great retinue of his necessary supporters if he was not going to proceed? What if his own people do not yet suffice him? The judge offers all the necessary assistants that he has.

“And we should say these things if it were truly established that Philip had not known the day appointed for the case. But since he cannot deny that the day and place were made known to him by the abbot of Clairvaux, who, nearly eighteen days earlier, happened to meet him in hiding while passing through the diocese of Cambrai, it is clear that you are not seeking peace, but delay.”

[Col. 0634D] After these arguments had been presented by the parties, it seemed just to us and to those with us—religious and wise persons, bishops, abbots, and clerics—to put an end [Col. 0635A] to the Church’s now long weariness, and no longer to tolerate the delays and postponements sought by those who seek their own interests and, under that pretext, ruin the Church of God. Therefore, after we had delivered judgment that justice required the case to proceed and that the excuse they had offered was not canonical, they, as usual evading the issue like men having little confidence in their cause, appealed.

Then, when the apostolic documents were produced, commanding both us to bring the case to an unexcusable conclusion and them to obey our judgment without resistance, they despised hearing them and departed. They were summoned and did not come; summoned a second time, they again refused. But we turned to the other side and nevertheless proceeded judicially in accordance with your mandate. Having received canonical proof concerning the two points mentioned, after examining witnesses and after the completion of the sacred rites, we annulled Philip’s election, relying on apostolic authority. But concerning Hugh, since it is clear that he was elected while below sacred orders, we reserved the matter, as was fitting, for your mercy. [Col. 0635B]

EPISTLE 432. TO THE LORD POPE. In favour of the bishop of Troyes.

We ask that the lord bishop of Troyes be heard concerning his right. We would also wish that, through the care of your kindness, such concord might be restored between him and his clerics that the clerics should no longer add unjustly to the harassment of an old man, though they cannot justly complain of the bishop in any matter. Among them is a certain youth, contemptible in age and insolent in his contempt, whose presumption we judge should rather be chastised than that the bishop should be trampled upon by him. The bearer of this letter will tell you who he is. Therefore may your discretion deign to provide concerning both this man and the others, so that the bishop, who loves your honour, may be honoured and may never be burdened in respect of his right. Care must be taken, however, that hatred for any person not harm one whom his innocence defends. [Col. 0635C]

EPISTLE 433. TO THE SAME. In favour of the bishop of Troyes.

[Col. 0635D] In the matter between the lord bishop of Troyes and the clerics, we ask that this precaution be observed: that the bishop, as is fitting, be honoured, and that the clerics not be deprived of their right. Let peace be restored between them, and let a curb be placed upon the malicious, so that hereafter they may never be able to rise up against their now aged shepherd.

EPISTLE 434. TO THE SAME. On the same subject.

You ought to be a friend to our friends and to assist Brother N. in the cause which he bears, yet with such discretion that, if possible, the clerics may be subject to their own shepherd, that they themselves may not be burdened in respect of their right, and that peace may henceforth exist between them.

EPISTLE 435. TO THE SAME. He commends to him the bearer of this letter.

[Col. 0636A]

As charity grows cold, few faithful persons are found today; and because everything dear is precious, the fidelity and affection of Lord N., who most faithfully conducted your affairs with us, ought to be bound with closer ties of favour and goodwill. Let it benefit him that we love him in spiritual charity as a ready bearer of letters and a faithful man.

EPISTLE 436. TO THE SAME. He commends to him a certain friend.

N., almost burned up by the flame of affairs continually transacted at Rome, [Col. 0636B] may I perhaps deserve to be refreshed by the welcome and pleasing sight of your writings. But alas! In all Clairvaux no scribes can be found for the work of your servant; enough has been said by a son to his father. May the sweetness of your goodwill hold dear, for his own sake and ours, our friend Lord N., a distinguished lover of both our person and the Order, who also faithfully conducts the affairs of his people.

EPISTLE 437. TO THE SAME. In favour of the bishop of Troyes.

The necessity of the lord bishop of Troyes, [Col. 0636C] a venerable old man and our friend, compels us to have recourse to the familiar fountain of mercy from which I and my friends have so often drawn. This, then, is what I desire to draw: that apostolic piety may not permit a man whose grey hairs now deserve rest to be unjustly harassed, and may deign to bring to effect the petitions which he makes through his messenger.

EPISTLE 438. TO THE SAME. In favour of the bishop of Troyes.

You increase your kindness toward me and multiply my honour when, out of regard for me, my friends find favour in your eyes; you have already made many who were dear to me dearer still. Yet I do not seek glory from man, but the kingdom of God and his righteousness, which, I think, are with the lord of Troyes. I confidently wish both to be commended to you: that is, both a just man and a friend; and not only these, but also the young man of good character sent by him, dear to us, the bearer of this letter, I commend equally to your charity.

### LETTER 439. TO THE SAME. On behalf of the bishop of Troyes.

May the cause of the lord of Troyes be commended to you along with our beloved messenger who carries it; uphold it, for, unless I am mistaken, it is just. The man himself is a friend of your friend. Take care not to listen to anyone against the lord of Troyes; rather, assist his cause and his messenger as far as you can.

### LETTER 440. TO AN UNNAMED PERSON. He urges him, preferring care for the soul to concern for the body, to renounce the world.

[Col. 0637A]

The lord of Avia has, I confess, done us a great kindness. [Note: [Col. 0637D] Ortelius identifies two places called Avia: one, according to Ptolemy, a city of the Vaccaei in Tarraconensian Spain; the other, a city of the Vestini in Italy, now destroyed, whose bishopric was transferred to Aquila. MART.] After granting us the much desired and welcome acquaintance of himself, he also mentioned your Belovedness, assuring and gladdening us concerning your wellbeing. Yet I would have received this news more gladly concerning your soul. For the bishop said of the body:

“I indeed love your body, but I love your soul more. I do not even love my own body except for the sake of my soul. Thus you may know that I love yours according to that rule: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself’ (Matt. 22:39). And just as I prefer my soul to my body, so I prefer your soul to your body. For take away the soul: what will the body be, except what was said of the whole body of humankind: ‘You are dust, and to dust you shall return’?” (Gen. 3:19.)

Moreover, it is better for the soul when it is released from the body—provided, however, that it has not been so burdened with sins that, when that which was taken from the earth returns to earth, the spirit cannot prevail, as it is written, “the spirit returns to the Lord who made it” (Eccl. 12:7). It is surely not right to love equally what is moved and what moves, what is governed and what governs, what is given life and what gives life; finally, that which is of earth and is earth, and that which comes from above, marked with the image of a higher nature.

Yet how greatly, alas, do they value this hay, and the foul-smelling flower of this hay—that is, the flesh and the goods of the flesh—not merely equally, [Col. 0637C] but even more highly than that rational creature capable of eternal blessedness and blessed eternity! But you, who think otherwise—for I know that you do, though I grieve that you do not yet live as you think—have mercy on your soul by pleasing God (Ecclus. 30:24). Why do you still join your life to those with whom you do not agree in judgment? Either change your life or conceal your opinion. Yet the better course is this: do not conceal in deed what you have already begun in reason and conceived in heart. The wise person does not despise wisdom’s counsel: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). What good is it to hold truth in your mind when you still cling to vanity in your manner of life?

Go, I beg you: withdraw from among the sons of strangers, whose [Col. 0637D] mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Let them call that people blessed who possess these things; but you, with the prophet, proclaim not so much in words as demonstrate in experience that “blessed is the people whose Lord is their God” (Ps. 143:11, 15). Let them delight in the world, since they are to perish with the world; but delight yourself in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart. Let it be good for you to cleave to him, so that you too may say with Jeremiah: “The Lord is good to the one who seeks him” (Lam. 3:25). And if he is good to one who seeks, how much more to one who finds!

### LETTER 441. TO A CERTAIN PRIOR. [Note: [Col. 0638D] Perhaps to the prior of Clairvaux.] He sends him a young man who requested admission into the Order.

[Col. 0638A]

Devout prayers.

I found at Châlons this young man who brought you these letters, awaiting me. When he saw me, he asked, simply enough and modestly, to be received into our Order and made a monk. He told me that, when Thomas of Marle, whose squire he had been, wished to make him a knight, he preferred the warfare of Christ to the warfare of the world and for this reason fled to us. Consult some of the brethren concerning these matters; and if they approve, and it seems right to you, receive and test him.

I inform you that I extracted from the bishop permission to winter near you—not in Clairvaux, however, but in the meadow of Dementin—not by my own prayers, [Col. 0638B] but by those of Lady Beatrice. [Note: [Col. 0638D] There survives Letter 118 of the same St Bernard to Beatrice, a noble and religious matron, in which he commends her obliging charity and solicitude. ID.] Meanwhile, keep watch; rouse the sluggish; restrain the excessive; comfort the faint-hearted. By becoming all things to all, make your virtues the virtues of all.

### LETTER 442. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT OF THE ORDER OF ST BENEDICT. He sends him two young men unequal to the strength required by the Cistercian Order, but perhaps not useless to him.

To love peace and charity.

We have taken care to send you these two young men. They indeed have good will, but their bodily strength is in no way sufficient for our Order; yet, if they persevere as we have found them, we trust that they will not be useless to you. Therefore receive them and test for yourselves whether our testimony is true. Let their profession not be hastened, so that their usefulness may first be discerned.

### LETTER 443. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND. Concerning a young man whose corrupt habits he describes, who sought marriage with the nobility.

I did what you wished, though it did not concern me at all except because you wished it. What have we to do with your lands, your lawsuits, your marriages? Moreover, we have always known that man, on whose behalf you compelled me to petition the duchess, to have been intent on evil from his youth and far removed from every good. [Col. 0638D] Therefore we believe that these misfortunes have befallen him not so much through the duchess’s will or desire as through God’s just judgment. We have never seen him, though he is a sinner, make a pilgrimage to any of the saints; we have never heard of his almsgiving, though he is rich; we have never known him, though he was for a long time a provost, to provide protection for an orphan or widow.

And now he does not cease to stretch himself beyond himself, even beyond his proper measure. Let you who are his friends know that association with nobles—whose sons and daughters he so eagerly seeks to unite in marriage with his own, without considering his own station—can scarcely, [Col. 0639A] if ever, bring him any benefit. Nevertheless, I wish, and greatly desire, that the thing which I undertook readily to request for your sake may turn out to his good.

### LETTER 444. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. Concerning a monk who wished to transfer to another Order; he disapproves of this.

When a certain brother came to seek counsel from our simplicity, he carried away from us this advice—or rather, judgment. Since he offered no fitting reason why he wished to leave his place and Order, no reason appeared for permitting him to transfer to another. For the vow [Col. 0639B] which he says he made previously, and from which he chiefly took occasion for scruple, is known to have been made merely in thought, or perhaps even in words, but only to himself. We do not think it ought to be preferred to this later commitment, by which he appears to have bound himself, not only in words and deliberation, but also by habit and profession—especially since what he had vowed seems neither stricter nor more right than this.

Therefore we do not believe it safe for you, who must render an account to Christ for his soul, to trust him in this matter or to grant him your permission in this matter, since it is written: “The Lord will lead away those who turn aside into obligations, with those who work iniquity” (Ps. 124:5). Receive him, therefore, kindly as a son; guard him carefully as one entrusted to you. Henceforth, unless I am mistaken, he will obey your [Col. 0639C] commands and submit to your counsels.

### LETTER 445. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. He commends to him L., a returning fugitive, and asks that he be received kindly.

I beseech you, by the mercy of God and by our mutual affection, kindly to receive Brother L., repentant of his error, desiring to return, and promising amendment. Moreover, in his reception and reconciliation let him be treated more mercifully and gently than is customary with other fugitives, so that he may feel the benefit of having taken care to commend himself to you through us and to fortify himself with our prayers.

### LETTER 446. TO AN UNNAMED PERSON. He writes that he has recovered from a severe illness and escaped the gates of death.

[Col. 0639D]

Whatever he wishes for himself.

Concerning the very concern which, as your letters indicate, makes you anxious, I too was long anxious. [Col. 0640A] For I could not be unaware of what you suffered when I considered in what condition you had left me. But until now an opportunity for a messenger was lacking, through whom, once I began by God’s mercy to improve in body, I might also make you better in spirit. Therefore now take courage: “The Lord has chastened me severely, but he has not handed me over to death.”

On the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent, I first approached the altar by myself, without another’s assistance, to receive Holy Communion. I myself dictated this letter. From these two signs you can judge how greatly, by divine kindness, I have recovered both in body and mind. I would gladly see you, if it could be done conveniently and without disturbance.

### LETTER 447. TO AMADEUS, ABBOT OF HAUTE-COMBE. He asks him to send messengers to Montpellier, where the Sicilian king’s ships were to arrive, so that they may excuse him before the king for not having sent brethren to Sicily.

[Col. 0640B]

To his beloved brother in the Lord, Amadeus, abbot of Haute-Combe: Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and love.

We ask that you send your father, or some other sensible and discerning messenger, on our behalf to Montpellier, so that he may be there during the Octave of the Assumption of Blessed Mary. On that very day and in that very place the messengers of the king of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0639D] Roger I, king of Sicily, to whom survive Letters 207, 208, and 209 of St Bernard. MART.] are to be present; they are crossing the sea in ships in order to bring the daughter of Count Theobald to the son of their lord. If by chance they bring ships for the use of our brethren and ask [Col. 0640C] about the abbey which we were to send, let your messenger excuse us in these words:

“The brethren indeed were ready, and the abbey was arranged; but Lord Alfanus, messenger of the lord king of Sicily, said that the king required only two brethren to go ahead of the others to inspect the site. When it pleases the lord king, he will signify to us his will concerning the whole abbey being sent together. For, as your prudence knows, it is dangerous to religious life and order for brethren to remain in a foreign land without discipline and without the guardianship either of an abbot or of their other brethren.”

[Note: [Col. 0639D] St Bernard afterwards sent brethren to found an abbey in Sicily, placing over them “Master Bruno, formerly for many days his inseparable companion, but then the father of many souls rejoicing in Christ,” according to Letter 209. That letter is said to have been written in 1139; consequently, this one appears to have been written either in that year or in the preceding year. ID.]

### LETTER 448. TO AN UNNAMED PERSON. He commends to him the abbot of Farfa, cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

[Col. 0640D]

We commend to you the abbot of Farfa, a man noble both in birth and character and a cardinal of the Apostolic See, [Note: [Col. 0640D] At first I suspected this to be Gerard, cardinal-deacon created by Innocent II, who afterwards became a monk of Clairvaux and was buried in its cloister. But since he lacks the rank of abbot, it is better to believe that he is Adinulf, abbot of St Mary of Farfa, of the Order of St Benedict, made cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church by Innocent II in 1130. ID.] that you may receive him honourably and amicably. He has come down from the side of the lord Pope to the court of the King, summoned by the latter; he bears to him confidential words concerning the common business of the kingdom and the Church.

[Col. 0641A] Receive honourably a man, and a man of good will; and in him honour alike the highest princes of the world—namely, him from whom he comes and him to whom he comes, Pope and Emperor. It is indeed presumptuous that I, so insignificant a person, dare to commend such a man to you; but the humility of the man himself, who requests this, dispels my embarrassment; and if I have become foolish, he has compelled me.

### LETTER 449. TO THE KING OF THE FRANKS. He excuses himself from accepting the dignity to which he had been elected.

To the king of the Franks, Brother Bernard.

I confess that I am pleased that you concern yourself with such sincerity in matters that belong to God. For, to pass over other things, you would never care so much about the promotion of a wretched man [Col. 0641B] if God were not involved in the matter. For what other advantage could make it so pleasing, since I am poor and destitute? Nor is it enough that you consent: you also urge me. You show favour, open wide the generous bosom of grace, and, lest I should shrink from the burden in weakness of heart, promise aid from royal protection.

What condescension in a king! What maturity in a young man! Yet I, excellent king, cannot at all consent to put my hand to mighty things: I am small in heart, broken in body, and have scarcely anything left except the grave. I utterly dare not approach holy things, unworthy and insufficient as I am. The authors of the election ought to have considered this. If they ignored it, I cannot ignore what I read: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24).

Or if they judged me fit on account of the religious habit which I wear, there is an appearance of holiness in the habit, not holiness itself. No one is better known to me than I am, and I am known to no one more than to myself. I certainly do not trust myself, against the testimony of my conscience, to those who see only the face and judge according to outward appearance. Behold, I and my little ones whom God has given me are here praying, though sinners, for your kingdom and your person. If you separate us from one another, that is difficult and cruel: you summon us not to prayer but to mourning.

Thus far concerning myself. Now, I beg you, deign briefly to consider what my heart labours to bring forth concerning the Church. The mistress of the churches sits in sorrow, and her tears are upon her cheeks. Her finest colour is changed; her ancient beauty has faded; that most precious ornament has been given over to trampling, nobility [Col. 0641D] to contempt, and freedom to slavery. I am tormented in this fire and find no counsel of refreshment until one comes to comfort her.

Therefore may reverence for her Bridegroom touch your heart: she has been redeemed by his blood, adorned with his likeness, endowed with his inheritance. Let your purpose endure, lest the beloved bride of our only Lord [Col. 0642A] be now, to the increase of her evils, committed to such a person as would displease his eyes. I tell you—and I tell you as one truly faithful—that it is wholly not expedient for you. May it be granted to you to govern the kingdom of the Franks in such a way that thereby you acquire the kingdoms of heaven, most excellent and illustrious king.

### LETTER 450. TO A FRIEND. He writes that he is at last recovering and has been snatched from the jaws of death.

The same as to himself.

You have laboured over a useful work and, as it seems to me, a Catholic one. Yet, if life endures, I have still once to read it through with you present and to discuss every point with you. Then, should anything perhaps be found that rightly gives offence, it will either be removed altogether or amended in such a way that it can no longer, and ought no longer, give offence.

For the rest, rejoice with me, because “the Lord has chastened me severely and has not handed me over to death” (Ps. 117:18). For when the axe had been set at the root of the fruitless tree and I feared that I was about to be cut down, I was restored through the prayers of friends. They promised that, with the most precious dung of their tears, they would make my barrenness fruitful, and obtained from the merciful Master of the household a reprieve for some time (Luke 13:6–9).

### LETTER 451. TO THE BRETHREN ***. He urges them to give alms in time of famine.

[Col. 0642C]

You know, brethren, who said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7); and: “Blessed is he who considers the needy and poor” (Ps. 40:2); and again: “If you see one naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh” (Isa. 58:7); and in holy Job: “You shall inspect your appearance [speciem], and you shall not sin” (Job 5:24). The reason for setting before you these few texts out of many, and weaving together the Scriptures in this manner, is that needy and wandering people are known to be in greater want than usual during this time of famine. [Note: [Col. 0641D] In the year 1146, according to the brief Chronicle of Châlons [Col. 0642D] in Labbe, “there was a severe famine everywhere in the lands, such as had never previously occurred.” If we believe the Chronicle of Lobbes, published by us in the third volume of the *Anecdota*, this famine began in 1143 and was severe for seven years. It is also mentioned by the chronicles of Münster, Mort-Mer, and Sens in the third volume of the *Anecdota*; by the Reims chronicle in Labbe; and by the Breton chronicle in Dom Lobineau, *History of Brittany*, vol. II, p. 3. ID.]

Therefore, if you have any bowels of mercy, any compassionate feeling, it is fitting that they should experience them in themselves. However wretched and contemptible they may be, they are your mouth and your flesh; and it is right that they should perceive that you do not think otherwise of them—not otherwise, I say, than through the benefit, if not of your goods, at least of your words. Namely, command your chaplain to take every care, both publicly and privately, to arouse and exhort the people to do them good.

### LETTER 452. TO A CERTAIN ABBOT. He urges him to receive a fugitive kindly and not to abandon the dignity of a superior.

[Col. 0643A]

To his own, that which is his own.

No one who reads this, if he knows whence I took the formula of salutation, should, I think, be angry with me because I presumed to place myself first in a better heading, and because I said that something inferior was mine, when I myself am rightly wholly his and wholly inferior to him. Yet we are accustomed not improperly to call “ours” not only things lower than ourselves but also, quite often, those whom we know to be above us, as in: “My portion, O Lord, in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6). This, indeed, is said of you, [Col. 0643B] but not to you.

Now I must reply briefly, as time permits, to your letter. When it came into my hands, the festal day of the birth of the soul of our Lady had dawned. The devotion which rightly claims me wholly for itself permitted me to think of nothing else. Moreover, the messenger, hurrying to return, barely waited until the next day for me, once relieved from the feast, somehow to write this reply.

I could do nothing better in the meantime than send the fugitive brother back to the place from which he had fled, after rebuking him harshly, as one hard of heart. According to our customs, I ought not to retain him at home without the consent of his abbot. You, however, should likewise rebuke him sharply and call him to humble satisfaction; then he should be strengthened by our letters sent on his behalf to his abbot.

Concerning our illness, I could at present state nothing more certain to one concerned than that I was ill and am ill—neither less than usual nor much more. As for not sending what I had intended to send, the reason is that I feared the scandal of many souls more than the danger to one body.

Now, lest I entirely pass over any of the matters you entrusted to me, and so that I may answer each point at least somewhat, I turn also to you. You wrote that you wished to hear what I, who surely know all about you, would have you do. But these things, unless I am mistaken, even if I were to say them now, you could not do, nor could I advise them. For I myself wish what you wish concerning yourself, as has not escaped me for a long time. Yet, setting aside equally, as is right, both my will and yours, I think it safer for me to advise you [Col. 0643D] to will what I think God wills concerning you; and, if I persuade you, it will not be disadvantageous to you.

Therefore, by my counsel, retain what you hold; remain where you are; and endeavour to benefit those whom you govern. Do not refuse to govern while you can benefit them. For woe indeed if you govern and do not benefit; but a graver woe if you fear to govern and refuse to benefit.

### LETTER 453. TO AN UNNAMED PERSON. He praises his prudence and humility.

[Col. 0644A]

Whatever spiritual grace he wishes for himself.

I praise the prudence by which you feared to grieve a monk for the sake of a novice; but I approve still more the humility by which you endured an injury done to you—and so great an injury. Yet incomparably more I value the charity by which, so that the bruised reed might not be allowed to be broken (Isa. 42:3), you took care to urge him to seek our counsel.

O prudent humility and humble charity, so sparing the monk an injury that you did not fail the wavering novice! Therefore, having strengthened him as much as I could, and finding him ready, I think, to amend all the matters for which he was reproved, I send him back [Col. 0644B] to you. I rely upon your proven kindness and, if necessary, entreat you that he be received—provided, however, that the aforesaid brother, to whom I have accordingly sent letters of petition, is first turned, if possible, from his opinion.

### LETTER 454. TO AN UNNAMED PERSON. He promises Stephen, if he perseveres, fruits worthy of repentance.

Who can sufficiently wonder at the ardour of your charity? But since it is not right that the charity whose concern we have learned should remain concerned for long, your Stephen, who is also ours, will, if he brings the beginnings of his way of life to a worthy end, if he diligently strives to offer the tail of the victim with devotion equal to that shown toward the head, receive this testimony from us: [Col. 0644C] he will produce fruits worthy of repentance.

### LETTER 455. TO THE AUNT OF THE EMPEROR OF SPAIN. He grants her the suffrages of the brethren and asks that the dispute between his people and the brethren of Careda be settled through the bishops.

To the illustrious lady G., queen and aunt of the emperor of Spain: Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting and prayers.

Having heard of your devotion from the report of our brother Nivard, [Note: [Col. 0644D] St Bernard’s youngest brother, said to have been the first abbot of the monastery of La Espina. ID.] we give thanks to God and pray that, according to the faith and trust you have in us, he may deign in his mercy to repay you. We gladly grant you the fellowship of our house and of our prayers, as you requested, [Col. 0644D] so that as much may be done for you as for any one of us, both in life and in death.

Furthermore, we have found it necessary to bring to your Excellency’s attention the brethren of Careda, [Note: [Col. 0644D] That is, Carracceda, of the Order of St Benedict, in the Asturian diocese. This monastery, founded around 990 by King Bermudo, was granted to the Cistercians by Alfonso VII, king of Spain. ID.] because they are bringing an accusation against us through your niece and in person. Concerning the monastery, [lacuna]. It is therefore necessary that we provide what is good not only before God but also before men; and in every respect [Col. 0645A] we wish to proceed in this affair so that our good may not be reviled and those men may have no occasion for detraction.

Accordingly, we have referred the matter to you, that you may strive to restrain this scandal. And if they refuse to desist otherwise, may you wish and cause this [Col. 0646A] controversy to be settled by the judgment, as is proper, of the lord bishop of Zamora and the lord bishop of Asturias. For once it is made known, either by their own confession or by the bishops’ judgment, that they have no grounds on which they can or ought to complain against us in this matter, we are ready, with God’s help, to arrange the place so that your devotion may rejoice and God be glorified in your work.

[Col. 0645] The following letters, collected into one body from various authors, are now for the first time added to the works of Saint Bernard. We have not wished to relegate the last, or four hundred and sixtieth, letter—though there are grounds for rightly doubting its authenticity—to an appendix, lest the order be disturbed. **EDITOR OF THE PATROLOGIA.**

## PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING LETTER

(Amaduzzi, *Literary Anecdota Extracted from Manuscript Codices*, vol. IV, p. 229. Rome: Antonio Fulgoni, 1783, octavo.)

[Col. 0645]

To Francesco M. Banditi of Rimini, archbishop of Benevento and most eminent cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Giovanni Cristoforo Amaduzzi.

Whoever devotes effort to letters and seeks to provide nourishment for the learned through certain established works takes especial care, first, to please everyone by variety of subjects, and then to make those things which concern each individual suitable to each. You see, most eminent Cardinal, that I have undertaken to engage and delight the various classes of men of letters with certain unpublished little works; and, in order to achieve this, I have long proposed to publish studies distinguished by diversity alike of language and style, age and subject-matter. Therefore, if there are works which ought especially to be brought to view—particularly in this corruption of the times, which has disgracefully mingled itself with the astonishing advances of letters and sciences—I judged that foremost among them should be those relating to sacred matters and displaying either the excellence of faith or purity of morals.

But what gratitude should I ever earn if I offered matters of this kind as a small gift to those accustomed to playful and frivolous trinkets?—for I do not trouble myself with the rest, who are occupied with impious and wicked inventions and are therefore altogether to be despised—when they nauseate every serious and austere thing to the point of disgust? Thus the thought naturally arises which has now especially prompted me to select you alone as the person to whom I might inscribe and dedicate a hitherto unpublished letter of the blessed Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.

You have diligently cultivated those studies which especially befit your office; for so many years you have directed your mind toward furnishing the library of the Canons Regular’s college at Rimini with every kind of writer; and you particularly pursue those authors who assist and encourage both your illustrious rank and your pastoral charge by precepts and examples. You will therefore most willingly receive the little work which I now resolve to offer you, composed by the most renowned and holiest son of the Cistercian Order. For Saint Bernard was such a man that he seems to have set before himself the instruction of every order of humankind by his letters. Inasmuch as he instructed and formed, according to their station, laypeople, monks, clerics, abbots, bishops, cardinals, and even supreme pontiffs themselves—namely Eugenius III—by his writings, furnishing each with highly suitable counsels for a more disciplined life.

The letter which I now bring forward is one in which he undertakes to instruct a layman in various precepts of human, yet upright and honorable, civil conduct. Since very many of these concern a private person—and every person ought always to recognize himself as such, however great his eminence in rank—each reader may readily claim and adopt those which he understands to suit him particularly.

Nowhere in the other letters or in any writings whatsoever of Saint Bernard the Abbot does there occur a mention of the man to whom we observe that this hitherto unpublished letter is addressed. Yet whoever has carefully read through both the letters and the other writings of this most holy Doctor of the Church, especially those which Mabillon put forward as genuine and distinguished from spurious works [Note: **[Col. 0645A]** Paris: Montalan, 1719, vol. IV], will readily discern here also the sweetness of style, the ardour of expression, the holiness of language, the weightiness of thought, and abundance of charm chiefly attributed to him. If anyone refuses to assert this, he will nevertheless be compelled to confess that the letter was written at least by an earnest imitator of the holy writer.

We obtained it from the most distinguished Angelo Maria Bandini, who transcribed it from a parchment codex of the early fourteenth century in the Medicean-Laurentian Library, over which he presides by reason of his merits, and generously permitted us to publish it. It also exists in two other codices of the same library, all of which he carefully described [Note: **[Col. 0645A]** See vol. II of the *Catalogus codicum manuscriptorum Latinorum Bibliothecae Laurentianae*, codex 15, pluteus 46, §2, col. 387; vol. III, codex 5, pluteus 78, §3, col. 159; and there, codex 138, pluteus 80, no. 8, p. 86, col. 697]. In first doing so, he seems to cast the authenticity of the letter into some doubt, perhaps in order to comply with the more rigorous rules of criticism, which learned men sometimes love rather excessively.

The library itself possesses other codices containing works of Saint Bernard, including works lacking from Mabillon’s edition. Since these are neither few nor insignificant, and require extensive examination and careful comparison, it is sufficient for the present to indicate them, relegating to a footnote the notices which may be useful to those who later wish to adorn this task [Note: **[Col. 0645A]** Pluteus 14, codex 18, §22: *Book on the Four Principal Virtues: Prudence, Magnanimity, Constancy, Justice.* Begins: “The kinds of the four virtues have been defined by the opinions of many wise men.” Ends: “If you shall have preserved [them] in living equitably.” See Bandini, catalogue, vol. I, col. 122. There, §27: *On the Offering of Praise.* Begins: “The offering of our praise, which we sacrifice to God,” etc. Ends: “divine martyrdom.” It consists of various brief sayings. See there, col. 123. There, §38: *On the immeasurable charity of God the Father, the wondrous obedience of the Son, and the kindness of the Holy Spirit.* Begins: “O immeasurable charity of God the Father, by which he so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Ends: “it is worse to read Salmon than to read Solomon.” See there, col. 124. Pluteus 16, codex 1, §17: *A Treatise on the Perfection of the Servants of God.* Begins: “The first thing to receive sinners is neglect of themselves, then curiosity about external things.” Ends: “and this is the perfection of the servants of God.” See there, col. 160. There, §24: *Sermon on the Eight Beatitudes in Dialogue Form, corresponding to the immediately preceding sermon.* Begins: “The kingdom of heaven is like a monk who is a merchant, who, hearing a report of the approaching fair...” Ends: “where he had such abundance and opportunity of gain.” See there, col. 161. There, §29: *On Meditating upon the Passion of the Lord in the Seven Canonical Hours.* Begins: “Seven times a day I have given praise to thee. You asked me to show you some method of contemplating the Passion.” Ends: “and you shall sit beside him at the tomb of the same Lord Jesus Christ, **[Col. 0647C]** who lives,” etc. See there, same column. There, §33: *On the Heavenly Glory toward Which We Must Hasten.* Begins: “Let us hasten to enter that holy city in which the Son of the Virgin is king.” Ends: “indeed, the perpetual and wholly unfeigned brightness of eternal life.” See there, same column. There, §34: *Mirror for Monks.* Begins: “Dearest brothers, this place in which we meet is a holy place.” Ends: “and may you deserve to rejoice, through the same our Lord, who with the Father,” etc. See there, col. 162. **[Col. 0648B]** There, §35: *Praise of the Lord Jesus Christ.* Begins: “How beautiful you are to your angels, Lord Jesus.” Ends: “Lord, who is like you?” It is very brief. See there, same column. Codex 3, §5, p. 65: *On the Love of God.* Begins: “Love is a great thing, by which the soul through itself...” Ends: “They do not cease to tell me that I should love my God.” See there, col. 165. There, §6, fol. 66v: *On the Excellence and Usefulness of Prayer.* Begins: “The Lord says in the Gospel that one ought always to pray,” etc. Ends: “and, to make a summary, the Lord Jesus Christ himself also prays,” etc. See there, same column. There, §8, fol. 68v: *How the Soul Falls Asleep and Rests in True Peace.* Begins: “In peace I shall sleep in the selfsame and rest. That peace, I say, through which and in which...” Ends: “who with such confidence sang, ‘In peace I shall sleep in the selfsame and rest.’” See there, same column. There, §9, fol. 70v: *The Life of Saint Bernard, Which He Gave to a Certain Monk for Living Well and Religiously.* **[Col. 0648C]** Begins: “If you wish fully to attain what you intend, two things must be done by you.” Ends: “but if not, ask God to forgive you, for he is merciful and gracious, blessed for ever.” See there, same column].

Moreover, elsewhere **[Col. 0647]** there are other works of our holy Doctor which are absent from the cited edition and which perhaps may be identical with those existing in the Medicean-Laurentian codices; this can certainly be determined only through diligent investigation. Thus the distinguished Martin Gerbert, Abbot of St. Blasien in the Black Forest, says in his *Iter Alemannicum* [Note: **[Col. 0648C]** pp. 175 ff.] that among the manuscript works of Saint Bernard preserved in the library of Augsburg there are some which do not occur at all in Mabillon’s edition and which demand examination. Further, in the same work [Note: **[Col. 0648C]** p. 216] he produces an exceedingly brief letter, taken from a thirteenth-century manuscript of the library of Ochsenhausen, written by Saint Bernard to G. de Stopho and sought in vain in the cited edition.

The works of that writer are not to be despised; rather, they deserve the highest esteem, since they complete ecclesiastical tradition and the succession of the Fathers, and happily precede the barbarism of the scholastics, which soon crept into religion, the sciences, and letters. Nor, most eminent Cardinal, will you be displeased if I add another letter: not one written by Saint Bernard, indeed, but written to him by a certain lady who depended upon his counsel and instruction.

You are certainly aware that our most holy Abbot maintained an exchange of letters with several most distinguished women, as his letters enumerated and published by Mabillon show: letters addressed to the Queen of Jerusalem; Matilda, Queen of England; Sancha, sister of the Emperor of Spain; the Duchess of Lorraine; the Duchess of Burgundy; a certain Ermengard, Countess of Brittany; Ida, Countess of Nevers; the Countess of Blois; Beatrice, a noble and religious lady; Sophia, a virgin; the Abbess of Faverney; and, finally, certain nuns. Perhaps through a copyist’s carelessness—unless another fault caused it—the name of the lady who wrote our letter has been withheld from us; nor have the investigations which we undertook on this point brought any light.

The aforementioned Bandini also communicated this letter to us. He took pains to extract it from another parchment codex of the fifteenth century in the Medicean-Laurentian Library [Note: **[Col. 0648C]** See vol. I of the *Catalogus codicum manuscriptorum Latinorum*, codex 2, pluteus 16, p. 234, col. 163], and granted us leave to publish it. Would that, just as I have now endeavoured to display my grateful and dutiful disposition toward you, you might receive this my goodwill and respect favorably! But what can I hesitate to promise myself from your ancient and altogether singular kindness? Although that kindness needs no spur and leaves no room for entreaty, nevertheless, most eminent Cardinal, allow me to judge that you ought earnestly to be asked continually to preserve it for me, as something both dearest and most admirable to me—something about which, like persons possessing precious objects, one ought to be concerned.

Farewell.

Given at Rome, on the Ides of August, in the year of Christ’s birth 1780.

## LETTER 456. TO RAYMOND, LORD OF CASTRUM AMBRUOSIUM

(Edited by John Christopher Amadutius from a parchment codex of the fourteenth century in the Medicean-Laurentian Library.)

**[Col. 0647A]**

367 10 To the gracious knight and fortunate RAYMOND, lord of Castrum Ambrosium, BERNARD, brought down into old age, greeting.

You ask to be instructed by us concerning the care and most useful management of household property, and how heads of households ought to conduct themselves; to this we reply. Although the condition and outcome of all worldly things are subject to fortune, the rule of life is not for that reason to be abandoned through fear. Hear, therefore, and attend.

If expenditure and income in your household are equal, an unforeseen event may destroy its condition. The house of a negligent man is in ruins. What is negligence in one who governs a household? A great fire kindled in the house. Examine carefully the diligence and intention of those who administer your affairs. It is less shameful to abstain while resources are declining, but have not yet fallen, than to fall. To review frequently what is yours and what condition it is in is great prudence. Think of food and drink for your animals; for they are hungry and do not ask.

Costly weddings bring loss without honour. Expenditure on military service is honourable; expenditure to assist friends is reasonable. Expenditure to assist spendthrifts is wasted. Feed your household on substantial, not delicate, food. One who has become gluttonous will scarcely change his habits except by death. Gluttony is the rot of a low and negligent person; gluttony is the consolation of a watchful and diligent person. During the Easter days feed your household abundantly, but not luxuriously.

Make the belly contend with the purse, and beware whose advocate you become. But if you become judge between belly and purse, give judgment more often, though not always, for the purse. For the belly proves its case by feelings, and thus by witnesses not under oath; the purse proves it plainly when strongbox and cellar have been emptied, or are shortly to be emptied. Then you judge badly against the belly when greed binds **[Col. 0649B]** the purse; greed will never judge rightly between belly and purse. What is greed? The murderer of its possessor. What is greed? Fear of poverty. You will always live in poverty. The miser lives properly for himself, not by wasting riches on himself, but by preserving them for others. It is better to preserve them for others than to waste them on oneself.

If you abound in grain, do not love the basket. One who loves the basket desires to be the murderer of the poor. Sell grain when it fetches a fair price, not when the poor person is unable to buy it. Sell to neighbours at a lower price—even to enemies; an enemy is conquered not always by the sword, but often by service. Pride toward a neighbour is a whale; you await thunder with an arrow. If you have a mortal enemy, you are placed in prison; if you have an enemy, seek your own eye as guardian. If you have an enemy, do not associate with strangers. Always reflect that a shrewd enemy considers the ways of his enemy. An enemy’s weakness is not a state of peace, but a truce for a time.

If you are not secure that your enemy does not think what you think, you expose yourself to danger. [Note: **[Col. 0649D]** Thus in the text.—Read: “If you are not secure,” etc.]

Regarding your suspected women, seek ignorance rather than knowledge of what they do. Once you have learned of your wife’s crime, no physician will cure you; you will then lessen the pain of a bad wife when you hear of other men’s wives. A noble and elevated heart does not inquire into women’s deeds; punish a bad wife rather with laughter than with a stick. A prostitute and an old man will destroy all riches; an old woman and a prostitute, if the law allowed it, ought to be buried alive.

Concerning clothing, note that expensive dress is proof of little sense. Dress that is too inconspicuous quickly causes neighbours annoyance: strive to please by goodness, not by clothing. The request of a woman who has clothes and seeks more clothes does not indicate constancy.

Concerning friends, hold this: a greater friend is one who gives his own goods than one who offers himself; of the latter kind there is a great abundance of friends. Do not consider him a friend who praises you in your presence. If you consult a friend, seek to please not him but reason. When advising a friend, say, “Thus it seems to me,” not, “This must absolutely be done.” Reproof after a bad outcome of counsel will follow more readily than praise after a good one.

I have heard that entertainers visit you; heed what follows. A man devoted to entertainers will soon have a wife whose name is Poverty. But who will be this wife’s son? Mockery. If an entertainer’s word pleases you, pretend not to hear and to be thinking of something else: one who laughs and rejoices at an entertainer’s words has already given him a pledge. Entertainers who utter reproaches deserve hanging. What is an entertainer who brings evil reproach? An animal carrying homicide with it. Instrumental entertainers have pleased God.

Hear concerning servants. Dismiss a servant of proud heart as a future enemy. Dismiss a servant who flatters your habits. Resist a servant and neighbour who praise you; otherwise each thinks he has deceived you. Love as a son a servant who is readily ashamed.

If you wish to build, let necessity, not desire, induce you. The desire to build is not removed by building; it produces an excessive and disorderly desire to build, and expects the sale of buildings. A completed tower and an emptied chest make a man wise only very late. If at some time you wish to sell, beware of selling a portion of your inheritance to someone more powerful than yourself; sell it instead, even at a lower price, to one less powerful than yourself. But sell the whole to the person offering more. It is better to suffer severe hunger than to sell inherited property; but it is better to sell a part than to subject yourself to usury. What is usury? A lawful robber, declaring beforehand what it intends.

Buy nothing in partnership with one more powerful than yourself. Patiently tolerate a lesser partner, lest he associate with you one more powerful. You asked about the use of wine. He who is sober amid diversity and abundance of wines is an earthly god. Drunkenness does nothing rightly except when it falls into mud. If you perceive wine, flee company. **[Col. 0650C]** If you perceive wine, seek sleep before conversation. He who excuses himself in words as drunk openly accuses his own drunkenness. It is ill-suited to a young man to know wines.

Avoid a physician full of knowledge but unproved in practice. Avoid a drunken physician. Beware of a physician who wishes to make trial on you of how he will cure others of a similar disease. Get rid of very small dogs. Guard-dogs are useful to clerics and queens. Dogs for hunting cost more than they yield. Do not appoint as steward of your goods a man who has children.

But you will say: “If fortune turns against us, what benefit is a rule of life?” Hear that in this matter I have seen fools abandon restraint and finally excuse themselves by fortune; and fortune sometimes comes, yet one who observes this teaching will rarely blame fortune. For you will rarely join diligence with misfortune, and more rarely separate misfortune from sloth. The lazy man waits for God to help him, though God commanded him to watch in the world. Therefore watch, and balance frivolity in spending with seriousness in earning.

Old age approaches. I advise you to entrust yourself to God rather than to your son. You make a bequest: I advise you first to order payment to servants rather than to priests. Do not entrust your soul to persons who love your person. Entrust your soul to one who loves his own soul. Dispose of your goods before illness; often one becomes the servant of illness, and a servant cannot make a will. Therefore make your will while free, before you become a servant. What has been said about wills is enough for you.

Hear concerning children. When their father has died, if they are nobles, they seek a division; often their scattering throughout the world is better than the division of an inheritance. If they are labourers, let them do what they wish. If merchants, division is safer than partnership, lest one person’s misfortune be charged to the others.

But perhaps their mother seeks to marry again. She acts foolishly; yet, in order that she may bewail her sins, would that she, being old, might take a young man: for he has sought not her, but what is hers. Having obtained these things, she will drink with him the cup of sorrow which she desired, until the end of her damnable old age brings her to this. Amen.

Thanks be to God.

(See below, among the letters of various persons to Saint Bernard, no. 477, the letter of a certain lady **[Col. 0651B]**.)

## LETTER 457. TO ALL THE FAITHFUL

On an expedition to the Holy Land. He appoints the feast of Saints Peter and Paul as the occasion for their assembly at Magdeburg. (Year 1147.)

[BOCZEK, *Codex diplomaticus et epistolaris Moraviae*. Olomouc, 1836, quarto, vol. I, p. 253, from a fourteenth-century Olomouc manuscript, marked CXXVI.]

367 11 To the reverend lords and fathers, archbishops, the other bishops and princes, and all God’s faithful: BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, [wishes] the spirit of strength and salvation.

I do not doubt that it has been heard in your land and spread abroad by public report how God has stirred the spirit of kings and princes to execute vengeance among the nations and to root out from the earth [text governing “of the Christian name” is missing] [lacuna]. A great good, a great abundance of divine mercy! Yet the Evil One sees this and, according to his custom, envies it. He gnashes his teeth and wastes away. He loses many of those whom he had held bound by various crimes and wickednesses: the most depraved turn back, departing from evil and ready to do good.

But he fears a far greater loss from the conversion of the nations, when he has heard that their fullness will enter in and that all Israel also will be saved.
