This time now seems imminent to him; and with every fraud his cunning malice strives to prevent so great a good. Accordingly, he has stirred up an evil seed, criminal pagan sons, whom—if I may say so without offence to your peace—the strength of Christians has tolerated too long, dissembling their destructive ambushes and not crushing their poisonous heads beneath its heel.

But because Scripture says, “Before ruin the heart shall be exalted,” it shall therefore come about, God willing, that their pride will be humbled more swiftly, and that the road to Jerusalem will not thereby be hindered. For since the Lord has committed this word of the cross to our littleness for proclamation, with the counsel of the lord king and of the bishops and princes assembled at Frankfurt, we announce that the strength of Christians is to arm itself against them and take up the saving sign, in order wholly to destroy—or at least convert—those nations. We promise them the same remission of sins **[Col. 0652A]** as is granted to those who have set out toward Jerusalem.

Many indeed were signed in that very place; moreover, we at the same time urged the others to this work, so that those Christians who have not yet been signed for the journey to Jerusalem may know that they will obtain the same indulgence by this expedition, provided that they perform their service in it according to the counsel of bishops and princes. We forbid altogether that they enter into any treaty with them for any reason—neither for money nor tribute—until, with God’s help, either their rite or their nation is destroyed.

We speak especially to you, archbishops and your fellow bishops: exert yourselves wholly, taking the greatest concern in these matters, and employ as much zeal and diligence as you can, so that it may be carried out manfully. You are ministers of Christ according to God, and therefore it is demanded of you with greater confidence that you keep watch over his cause, which pertains to you. We too earnestly ask and implore this of you in the Lord.

This army shall observe the same rule in garments, arms, trappings, and all other things as the other army, since the same reward protects them. It pleased all those assembled at Frankfurt that a copy of this letter be carried everywhere, and that bishops and priests proclaim it to God’s people and sign and arm them with the sign of the holy cross against the enemies of Christ’s cross, who are beyond *albi* (sic); all of whom must assemble at Magdeburg on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

## LETTER 458. TO VLADISLAUS, DUKE, THE MAGNATES, AND THE PEOPLE OF BOHEMIA

He invites all to the Jerusalem expedition and entrusts the same cause to the Bishop of Moravia. (Year 1147.)

[BOCZEK, as above, p. 255, from the same codex.]

To Duke VLADISLAUS, the other nobles, and all the people of Bohemia: BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, greeting in Christ.

I speak to you concerning Christ’s cause, in which true salvation also lies. I speak so that the authority of the Lord may excuse with you the unworthiness of the person writing; that consideration of your own advantage may excuse it; and that the intention of charity within us may excuse it. I am insignificant indeed, but I desire you all not insignificantly in the bowels of Jesus Christ. This zeal compels me to write what I would work more gladly to inscribe in your hearts by living voice, if, as will is not lacking, ability too were available.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. The corruptible body cannot obey the soul’s desire, nor can earthly mass keep pace with the spirit’s swiftness. But why should we complain of this? A part of us is absent from you; but the more useful part, our heart, is extended even to you, although the burdensome distance of lands holds back the body.

Therefore let your whole community hear a good word; let it hear the word of salvation; and let it embrace, with the devoted arms of the soul, the offered abundance of indulgence. For this time is not like the other times that have hitherto passed: a new abundance of divine mercy comes from heaven. Blessed are those whom the year acceptable to the Lord finds alive: the year of remission, indeed the year of jubilee! I tell you: the Lord has not done thus for every former generation, nor has he poured out upon our fathers so abundant a gift of grace.

See by what art he uses to save you; consider the abyss of his mercy and be astonished, sinners. He makes himself seem to be in need—or makes it so, or feigns it so—while he comes from heaven to assist your necessities. This design is not from a human being, but has proceeded from the heart of divine mercy. The earth was shaken and trembled because the Lord made his own land perish: his own, I say, **[supplied: in which]** he was seen and for more than thirty years **[Col. 0653B]** lived as a man among human beings. His own, which he honoured by his birth, illumined by miracles, consecrated by blood, and enriched by burial. His own, in which the voice of the turtledove was heard when the Son of the Virgin commended the pursuit of chastity. His own, in which the first flowers of resurrection appeared.

Wicked men have begun to occupy this land of promise; and unless there is someone to resist, they aim at the very sanctuary of our religion and strive to defile the very bed in which our Life fell asleep in death for us, and to profane the holy places—places, I say, made purple by the blood of the spotless Lamb.

Hear something further which ought to move even the hardest breast of a Christian person. Our King is accused of treachery; the charge is brought against him that he is not God, but falsely pretended to be what he was not. Whosoever among you is faithful to him, let him rise and defend his Lord against the disgrace of the alleged treachery. Let him enter a conflict without fear, where victory is glory and death gain.

Why do you delay, servants of the cross? Why do you disregard yourselves, you who lack neither bodily strength nor earthly resources? Take up the sign of the cross, and the supreme pontiff offers you full remission of all sins which you have confessed with a contrite heart—the vicar of him to whom it was said: “Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” Take up the gift offered, and let each hasten to outstrip the other toward the irrecoverable opportunity of indulgence.

I ask and advise that no one should wish to prefer his own affairs to Christ’s cause, nor, because of matters which could have been or may be undertaken at other times, omit that which can never again be recovered. And so that you may know when, by what route, and how you should go, hear briefly: at the coming Easter the Lord’s army will set out, and no small part has proposed to travel through Hungary.

It has also been decreed that no one should use garments of vair, grey fur, or silk; nor should anything of gold or silver be placed on horses’ trappings, except on the shields and wooden saddletrees they use. When they proceed to battle, those who wish may place gold or silver upon them, so that the sun may shine from them and the strength of the nations be scattered in terror.

These matters should have been treated more fully and at greater length, were it not that you have among you the lord Bishop of Moravia, a holy and learned man. We desire that he be asked to endeavour, according to the wisdom given him by the Lord, to exhort your entire community more diligently on this matter. We have also sent a copy of the lord pope’s letter; you ought to receive his admonition with most attentive ear and observe his decrees.

Farewell.

## LETTER 459. TO G. DE STOPHO

[... from GERBERT, *Iter Alemannicum*, 1765, octavo, p. 216.]

BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, to his beloved son in Christ, G. DE STOPHO: greeting and prayers.

Our dearest son, your brother Henry, turned aside to us and, by our counsel, did not abandon the purpose of the saving sign which he had received. Rather, he adopted something far better: having become poor for poor Christ, he has resolved to live under the religious habit in the house of Christ’s poor. This ought not to seem burdensome or harsh to you, because with Mary he has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from him; and he has assumed the countenance of one truly going to Jerusalem—not that Jerusalem which kills the prophets, but that whose “participation is in the selfsame.”

Take comfort, then, in these words, and remember what you most recently discussed together. Conduct yourself toward him in all things in such a way that you may obtain favour from us and from him, and mercy from God. Fare well, ever beloved.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Eugenius de LEVIS, priest, *Anecdota sacra, sive collectio omnis generis opusculorum veterum SS. Patrum*, etc. Turin, 178... quarto, p. 50.]

**[Col. 0653]**

From several historians, such as Charles Visch, and from the editors of the works of this same holy abbot, we have learned that many other works of Saint Bernard are preserved in manuscripts and still lie hidden here and there unpublished. Since this letter is read in one of our thirteenth-century parchment codices among various other works already published, as well as several works attributed to Saint Bernard that are doubtful or spurious—such as *On the Interior House*, *On Building Conscience*, and *A Sermon on the Teaching of Saint Bernard to One of His Monks*—we take care to publish it, lest it lie hidden in dust.

But who the brother N. may be, to whom Saint Bernard wrote this letter, we do not know, since we have been unable to ascertain in what place or to what monastery this N. is said to belong. We fear, however, that this is the work of some solitary, since it speaks of solitude in Instruction 11.

## LETTER 460. TO N...

[LEVIS, *Anecdota sacra*, p. 51.]

**[Col. 0653C]**

367 12 To his beloved brother N. in Christ, brother **[Col. 0654C]** BERNARD, in the Lord, [wishes him], having now put off the old man, to live for Christ and die to the world.

Because, my beloved brother in the Lord, you have most earnestly begged me—though I am still occupied in penitence—that I should henceforth visit you with some brief letters of spiritual exhortation, I know, brother, that in saying this you heap burning coals upon my head. Yet by pressing your request affectionately upon my hardness, you have overcome all my pride by your suppliant humility, so that I have now promised you what you desired—although it would have been more fitting for me to receive this from you than to send such things to you. Nevertheless, because the insistence of your devotion has compelled me to become foolish in this matter, I shall attempt, as best I can and however inadequately, what you urge. I shall write to you no spiritual matters other than those which, though rough and simple, I had intended to gather for myself.

Meanwhile I address your belovedness: for, as you know better, no one can serve God perfectly unless he takes care wholly to detach himself from the world. If we wish to follow God the Savior, we must hear the prophet’s voice: when the bonds of impiety have been loosed, let us undo the bundles that weigh us down; let us follow the Redeemer, because, according to the Apostle’s testimony, “No one serving as a soldier of God ought to entangle himself in worldly affairs” (cf. II Tim. II, 4). Therefore let us never allow our hearts to be anxious over any created thing, except insofar as such things stir in us the affection of divine love. For the manifold variety of passing things, pondered beyond due measure, not only interrupts the peaceful and pleasant repose of the mind by distracting the soul, but also, by generating phantasms of things, violently shakes the body with the troublesome agitation of disturbance.

Rather, once the burdensome load of attachment to all earthly things has been laid aside, let us run without the weight of recollection to him who invites us, in whom is abundant refreshment for souls and that supreme peace which surpasses all understanding. “Come,” he says, “to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” O admirable condescension of our God! O lovable gentleness! O ineffable charity! For which human being has done such things? Who has ever heard—or even seen—anything like them? Behold: he invites enemies, exhorts the guilty, draws the ungrateful: “Come,” he says, “to me; take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest” (Matt. XI, 19).

O sweetest words! O most gracious words! O divine words, sharper than every two-edged sword, laying open the inmost parts of the heart and, filled with excessive sweetness, reaching even to the division of the soul! Awake therefore now, Christian soul, to the love of such kindness, to the taste of such sweetness, to the fragrance of such delight. Surely, if I do not feel these things, I am sick—already near to death. Burn ardently, I beseech you, my soul; become rich; become sweet in the mercy of your God. Burn with fervor, grow rich in love, and become sweet through savor. Let no one prevent you from drawing him into yourself, holding him, and tasting him. What more do we seek? What do we await? What further do we desire? In this one thing we have every good.

But alas for our marvelous madness! O wretched weakness! O detestable frenzy! For we are called to rest, and we pursue toil; invited to delight, and we follow pain; joy is promised, yet we are ensnared by sorrow. Truly wretched weakness and most miserable perversity! We have now become almost senseless, almost worse than idols: having eyes before us and not seeing; ears and not hearing; reason and not discerning; making bitter sweet and sweet bitter. O God, what correction is there now for such perversity in us? Whence can there be satisfaction to you for so great an offense? Certainly nothing of the kind is found in us unless it is granted us by your gift. For you alone can make satisfaction for our offenses—you who alone know our fashioning—our salvation and redemption. You do this only in those who, seeing themselves to be wretched inwardly, trust that they can be raised up by you alone.

Let us thus lift the eyes of our mind straight toward God, and see where we now lie prostrate; for one who does not know his own fall cares less to rise. Therefore, knowing this, let us cry out strongly to God from the depths, that he may stretch forth to us the helping hand of his mercy, which has never been shortened so that it cannot save. Let us not, I beseech you, lose our confidence, which has a great recompense. Let us approach the throne of his grace with confidence, receiving the end of our faith, the salvation of our souls. Let no hesitation be in us: salvation now calls us, tribulation awaits us, and urges us to enter. What then are we doing? Why do we prolong delays? Let us hasten to enter that rest of eternal joy, heavenly festivity, and inward refreshment, where are great, unsearchable, and marvelous things without number.

Let Jerusalem rise above our heart. Let us sigh for our homeland; let us stretch upward toward our mother; let us enter into the powers of the Lord and behold our king, gentle and reigning over all; and our hearts will melt in his mercies. Let us give him thanks with our whole heart, who, considering our weakness, has not withheld from us the mercifulness of his compassion, granting us the desire to run after him—a desire which is not a gift to be rendered back as payment, but to be reckoned as grace. The eminent prophet declares that he desires this very thing: “My soul has longed to desire your justifications at all times” (Ps. CXVIII, 20). Without this desire itself, our negligent care grows weary through excessive lukewarmness.

I have thought to note down certain reminders that incite us, in which things to be avoided and things to be pursued may alike become clear. As we contemplate these daily with heartfelt affection, may we, having regained our former vigor, grow unweariedly in virtues and graces in divine charity, until there comes the perfect desire of the eternal hills. These, then, are certain innumerable virtues and saving ladders by which, without doubt, those faithfully stirred by them may ascend to the perfection and summit of virtues: namely, holy modesty in all their words and deeds; slowness in speaking; readiness in obeying; frequency in prayer; fleeing idleness; pure and frequent confession of one’s failings; willing service; avoidance of unprofitable company. These are certain shining pearls, which make their possessor pleasing to angels and human beings.

But when it pleases him who “set you apart from your mother’s womb” (Gal. I, 15) and called you through his grace, in order that he might reveal in you the image of his Son—transferring you from wretched Egyptian slavery into the freedom of the glory of the children of God—then, as it were, you will begin to set your foot upon the way of the new person, a path established between fear and love of humility. Then, ascending by that same way of humility to higher things, you will be able to exercise yourself in loftier matters. From these further reminders follow.

First of all, therefore, you who desire to follow the footsteps of the Savior must have your whole hope fixed in the Lord, and despair of all things belonging to this world.

Second, you must strive, so far as human nature permits, to reform yourself completely from all vices and evil desires, so that, having purged out the old leaven of all malice and wickedness, you may “walk in newness of life” (cf. I Cor. V, 7) after Christ. Unless you first break the chains of this iniquity, your soul, weighed down in darkness, cannot be raised to heavenly things.

Third, you must loosen from yourself every external bond, so that in mind you may be bound to the Lord.

Fourth, through love of the Most High, you must bear with equanimity all persecutions of the world, accepting all of them, if possible, according to your vow, solely as participation in Christ’s sufferings; refusing temporal joy, you must rejoice amid tribulations, reckoning them all prepared for you for the cleansing of sins and the mourning of your soul.

Fifth, since you know yourself indebted to your Creator, you must not demand that an account be given to you concerning any created thing.

Sixth, despising yourself and desiring to be held in contempt by everyone, and zealously preferring most holy poverty, you must maintain, in all things pertaining to you, as much harshness, lowliness, and frugality as you can. Yet do not require this in others; rather, be joyful and glad at every fraternal consolation, serving, ministering, and assisting them in every way when necessary, and reckoning all worthy of consolation—unless, which God forbid, some divine offense should be openly evident in someone, one that admits of no excuse. Yet even over this you should grieve from your inmost heart, as much as possible, with compassion and fear.

Seventh, living always in fear, flee with all your power the flatteries of this age, honors, glories, favors, and breezes of vainglory, which are deadly draughts; standing continually within yourself, have yourself under suspicion every hour. If you gain victory over your own self, no enemy, inward or outward, will harm you.

Eighth, through love of him who, though Lord of all things heavenly, earthly, and infernal, assumed for us the form of a most lowly servant, voluntarily subjecting himself as a man and humbling himself for sins: reckon every human being your lord, reckon yourself the lowliest servant of human beings, and in every matter toward all persons regard yourself as a servant. Thus, obtaining tranquility and peace with all, you will wholly avoid scandal.

Ninth, do not touch anything that does not touch you with spiritual profit; that is, do not concern yourself about any matter, nor entangle yourself in anything inwardly or outwardly in any way where you find no gain for your soul; nor permit anyone to entangle you in such matters.

Tenth, impose complete abstinence upon sight, mouth, and the other bodily senses, so that you strive to see, hear, or touch absolutely nothing except what is useful to your soul. Restrain your tongue perfectly also, so that you speak nothing at all unless questioned, compelled by necessity, or prompted by evident usefulness; and then speak briefly, reverently, fearfully, and with sweetness of spirit, humbly if possible—avoiding prolixity of words altogether and, as far as you can, cutting off their occasion.

Eleventh, possess welcome and holy solitude at all times; esteem the work of vigils precious; always offer your prayers to God with attentiveness to the words, fervor of devotion, and deep humility.

Twelfth, when you must celebrate the divine office, act in such a manner as to forget within yourself all earthly things, attending with a fixed and immovable mind to the heavenly mysteries; render them with such reverence, devotion, and fear that, placed among the companies of angels, you may chiefly offer praises in the divine presence together with them.

Thirteenth, holding the glorious Queen, the Mother of our Lord, in the highest affection of veneration at all times, turn to her confidently in every crisis and pressure of need, as to a singular and safest refuge, seeking the protection of her guardianship. Most devoutly receive her as your advocate and securely entrust your cause to her, for she is the Mother of Mercy. Strive daily to please her and to show her a spiritual and special reverence; let your devotion be acceptable to her and your reverence pleasing. With all your strength preserve in yourself the cleanness of her purity, unblemished in every virtue, in mind and body, and strive to follow the footsteps of her humility and gentleness.

Fourteenth, avoiding all women, young men, and beardless youths except for necessity or manifest usefulness, choose for yourself one father wherever you may be: discreet, holy, gentle, devout, learned through practical experience, and possessing loftiness of speech. By efficacious and fiery words and examples, he should instruct you in divine love; you should also be able to have recourse to him in all your necessities and receive spiritual consolation.

Fifteenth, driving away from yourself with the greatest diligence every chill of sadness or acedia, in which lies the way of confusion that leads to death, remain always serene both inwardly and outwardly. Contradict or resist no one in any way; rather, rest altogether in all things, provided that divine praise or the salvation of the soul is not obstructed.

Sixteenth, conform all your affections and wills to the divine will. Let everything in this world edify you through the grace of divine purity and innocence granted to you as a gift. Do not ever be disturbed beyond measure by the failings of others, lest, by adding iniquity to iniquity, you be polluted by other people’s filth. While desiring to free others from the sea, you may yourself fall more grievously into the depths. Therefore, those whom you cannot benefit without harm to yourself, cover with kindly charity and leave to that supreme Wisdom, which knows how to choose good out of whatever evils; thus, by God’s grant, you will be able to find spiritual progress alike in all good and evil things.

Seventeenth, guard your heart with every vigilance, devoting it only to spiritual exercises; let no images of visible things imprint their activity upon you, so that, free and estranged from all creatures, you may be at leisure for the Creator of all.

Eighteenth, contemplating the image and likeness of divine majesty in all human beings, love all with the inmost affection of charity, and care for everyone—especially the weak and all who are in need—provided that such care does not bring you spiritual harm or destruction; do so as a good mother loves and cares for her one dearly beloved son.

Nineteenth, keep your mind continually so ordered with God that every exercise of yours, whether of mind or body, may always be prayer. Perform all exercises and services, especially the lowlier and humbler ones, with such fervor of charity as though you were rendering them bodily to Christ; for you certainly can and ought truly to think this, because Christ says in the Gospel: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

Twentieth, render to all both the honor due and that of devotion; strive to preserve the most holy rule of obedience unharmed as the apple of your eye, not only in great and difficult matters but also in the least. Be obedient not only to superiors and prelates, but submit yourself to everyone, denying yourself for Christ in all things and, in matters of disagreement, strive more earnestly to do the will [reading uncertain]. Do not make yourself burdensome to anyone in any respect; rather, in the charity of Christ, loving all, make yourself generally pleasing to everyone. Flee singular affabilities, friendships, and intimacies. Above all beware lest by word, deed, or gesture you become, by any reason or means, either directly or through another, a cause or occasion of resentment, hatred, shouting, injury, disturbance, murmuring, detraction, scandal, flattery, or anything similar.

Twenty-first, strive, as far as possible, to conceal from all persons the virtues or spiritual graces which divine bounty deigns to work through you or in you, as well as tribulations, struggles for virtue, and similar things; except those which ought to be disclosed to your own priest in your personal confession of accusation—unless perhaps you reveal them to some spiritual and tested friend for a spiritual purpose, believing that his counsel or instruction may help you in this matter. Always be careful to steal time everywhere so that you may devote yourself to solitary prayer; and sit silent and solitary, lifted by desire toward heavenly things.

Twenty-second, freed from all things and desiring to hold nothing, now despising all things dear to you, direct the whole effort and fervor of your mind’s desire toward the Creator of all. Forgetting all lower things, whatever you do, wherever you stand, and in whatever business you are engaged, by day and by night, at every moment and every hour, always keep God in remembrance, believing and thinking most truly that you are always before him, and that he beholds you from every side. Think these things with the greatest reverence, with fear and trembling alike, with the highest discernment and most ardent love: now prostrate before the feet of his immeasurable majesty, seeking pardon for sins with a most bitter heart; now pierced by the sword of compassion at the most holy Passion of the Son of God, wounded before his cross, appearing with him tearful and weeping; now setting the whole course of your life before your crookedness as a line of rectitude; now considering in your mind his innumerable and immense benefits, persisting in thanksgiving; now pierced by the goads of some most ardent love, beholding him in all creatures; now attending to his power, now his wisdom, now his goodness and mercy, praising him magnificently in all his works; now drawn by desire for the heavenly homeland, panting with groaning sighs; now considering toward us the bowels of his inestimable charity, failing in heart and soul in Christ through joyful and most excellent wonder; now considering him catching you as you rush headlong and flee, then holding, lifting, and drawing you; now considering yourself altogether ungrateful, and, when the ineffable bowels of divine mercy have been opened to you, giving yourself wholly to him in excessive ardor of charity and dissolving in tears; now, indeed, carefully attending to the most hidden, deepest, most admirable, and highest mysteries and exceedingly stupendous judgments of his justice, reverently worshipping him before all things with utmost love and great fear, humbly and suppliantly; or maintaining a continual and living remembrance of his most holy Passion.

Twenty-third, keep watch at all times over your guard against the deceits of the ancient enemy, who often transforms himself into an angel of light and spreads snares and nets in every path of human beings in order to capture our souls. Flee the snares of the hunter with most careful vigilance, like a sparrow; and become so small through holy humility in your own eyes that even his most subtle nets cannot hold you. You will indeed be able to escape these unharmed when you have become Israel—continually seeing God with the eyes of your mind—for “he who guards you shall neither slumber nor sleep.”

Twenty-fourth, maintaining without weariness the strictness of the holy rule, and kindled by sacred ardors of heavenly desires, preserve undefiled the beauty of purity of mind and body, the purity of innocence, and the rectitude of conscience. Take the most diligent care never to relapse in any respect. In order to preserve this more diligently and purely, examine your life by daily scrutiny seven times a day; always see, after each canonical hour, whether you have walked worthily of God without blemish in righteousness and holiness. And since no one preserves righteousness and discipline so as to neglect or omit nothing whatever, it is necessary to have recourse to the bath of penitence and, with sorrow and groaning, to persist very frequently in your accusation. In this accusation—as in confession—recite fully, truthfully, and purely, without any veil of excuse or concealment, all your failings in order, as though speaking to God your priest with your own mouth: disclose and recount your own omissions in those things which concern God, especially your shortcomings in prayer, both mental and vocal, and in the observance of righteousness. After these, recount the commissions you have committed through poor custody of the senses and the affections and thoughts associated with the senses.

Such confession must always be accompanied by contrition and satisfaction. Grieve not only over grave offenses but also over slight ones; and in grieving, beware of repeating the fault, always striving to cut off the causes and occasions of sin, however much they may appear joined to you by love. According to the just judgment of the Savior, the eye that causes scandal must be torn out; indeed, occasions of sin, though they appear exceedingly pleasant to us, must be cut away, even if their removal greatly displeases our affections. Hence the struggle in this battle is exceedingly hard.

[Col. 0661]

## APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF ST. BERNARD

[Note: This Appendix contains certain doubtful or spurious letters of St. Bernard; also some written in his name by Nicholas of Clairvaux; then letters written to him by various persons; in addition, Bernard’s charters, together with certain other documents thought useful for elucidating Bernard’s letters. All are drawn partly from printed books and partly from manuscripts.]

### I. DOUBTFUL OR SPURIOUS LETTERS

## LETTER CDLXI. TO MATTHEW, BISHOP OF ALBANO

On the Gospel of Luke, chapter XVI, 1–9: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward.”

[Col. 0661B]

To his most reverend lord MATTHEW, venerable by the grace of God, bishop of Albano, Brother BERNARD—truly his servant in whatever respect, to his lord as servant and to his father as son.

[Note: We copied this letter from a manuscript codex of Verdun, where it appears after the Life and Miracles of St. Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux. Matthew, bishop of Albano, to whom it is addressed, was formerly a Cluniac monk; he became prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, was then created cardinal and bishop of Albano, and was legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul. St. Bernard’s Letter 21 is addressed to him. Servulus, or Serlo, mentioned at the beginning of the letter, was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Lucian at Beauvais. All these facts fit the period of St. Bernard. Nevertheless, we regard this letter as suspect and spurious; yet for that reason it was not to be omitted. It seems referable to the year 1133. MART.]

What your exalted greatness had commanded my smallness from Rome through our most beloved lord SERVULUS, abbot of Beauvais—namely, that I should transcribe for you those things which God had granted me to say upon the Gospel concerning the steward of iniquity—I now at last send, though late, and not without considerable fear lest something tasteless in it should offend you. Therefore I ask you, concerning this, to abound toward me in bowels of pity and charity: forgive me for delaying, and correct for yourself what I have offered uncorrected. I have reserved it for correction by the authority of your prudence, and humbly offer it. I send also a knife commonly called *Quinivers*, with an ivory handle, together with this little sheet, so that you may cut away with my sword the imposture which you judge worthy of excision. Moreover, I pray the abundance of your kindness not to forget me in your prayers, since I remember you daily without forgetting, especially where I more earnestly seek the mercy of God. Farewell.

Here ends the letter.

### READING FROM THE HOLY GOSPEL

At that time Jesus spoke this parable to his disciples, etc.

## LETTER CDLXII

[Note: Previously Letter 385.]

### TO CERTAIN RECENT CONVERTS

[Note: Although this letter is pious, it nevertheless has something strained and labored which does not savor of Bernard’s genius and ease of expression. In the very texture of the letter there is also something not sufficiently in accord with Bernard’s thought. We found it in a single Vatican codex, numbered 663, outside the order of the other letters, after the “Homily of Blessed Bernard on Contempt of the World,” under this title: “A Consolatory Letter of the Same.” We corrected certain passages here from that codex. Perhaps it belongs among those letters which Bernard’s secretaries sometimes wrote on their own initiative at Bernard’s command.]

He exhorts them to constancy in their purpose of religious life and not to allow themselves to be deterred by the sins of their former life.

[Col. 0662C]

1. At the good news concerning you which has sounded in our ears, my soul rejoiced greatly and my heart exulted in the Lord, who foreknew you and predestined you to be conformed to the image of his Son, and deigns to call you, that he may justify you in the present and glorify you in the future. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who commanded his light to shine in your hearts, so that, despising the false vanities and insanities of this age, you may draw sighs from the inmost marrow of your soul in exultation in the hope of the glory of the children of God, choosing and resolving to be lowly in the house of our God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners.

May God confirm in you the good purpose that he inspired, lest the ancient enemy of the human race be able either to turn you from your purpose or overthrow you within it: that is, lest the vain and senseless delight of this world, flattering you, summon your mind again to make provision for the flesh in its desires—which is to turn away from your purpose—or lest, at the very entrance into religion, outward consolations enticing your imperfection cause you to provide for the flesh rather than the spirit—which is to be overthrown in your purpose. For some who are about to renounce the world—if I may say so without offense to anyone—especially imitate the manner of life of those in whom the fragility of their flesh causes greater concern than the weakness of the spirit. Thus, although they have abandoned graver disgraceful acts, they nevertheless applaud gluttony and demand superfluity both of food and drink, not sufficiently observing that many things are lawful but not beneficial, because they gravely hinder the progress of one doing penitence.

2. On this matter, beloved ones, consult him who, in what was impossible for the observance of any law because it was weakened through the flesh, condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in those who do not walk according to the flesh. For whoever are in the flesh, whether wearing the religious habit or outside it, cannot please God—if the Apostle is true; indeed, because the Apostle is true (Rom. VIII, 8). He advances far short of progress—indeed, falls far below even imperfection—whose god is his belly.

Consult, I say, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, willing to heal not only our weaknesses but also our errors, came forth from his secret place into our public condition; and, bringing remedy to both, just as he abolished weaknesses by dying on the cross, so too he destroyed errors and instructed conduct while he lived in the flesh. For he, who could not sin and was Lord of all, although he could freely and justly have enjoyed the delights of this world, nevertheless embraced voluntary poverty so carefully that he did not even have a place where he might lay his head. In carrying out this poverty he showed such obedience to the Father that he denied to himself not only delights but even his own self, seeking in all things not his own will but that of the Father.

He had come to lead the person wandering in the wilderness and in a waterless land back into the straight way, so that he might go to the city of habitation. By the example of his own conduct he showed us the healthier and safer way of return: possessing nothing of his own in the world, obedient to the Father unto death. Therefore, following his example, we must flee delights and embrace the good of obedience with all the effort of mind and body, so that we who withdrew from God through disobedience may deserve to return through the law of obedience.

But some say: “Why should we afflict our souls in the misery of torments, since God takes no pleasure in sufferings and we can find salvation while using the world lawfully?” Children of men, to use the Apostle’s words to you: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 5–7). Therefore, if you think this concerning him—that although, by the just and equal prerogative of majesty, he could possess and display the form of God, he nevertheless laid it aside and put on the servant’s form, not to empty himself of something usurped but to repress our pride—if you think this concerning him, then on that very account empty yourselves also of your transitory happiness, repaying in return him who made himself wretched for us though he was not wretched: not by making yourselves into what you are not, but by showing in yourselves what you are, so that those whom the condition of necessity makes wretched may be acknowledged as wretched also by the devotion of their will.

4. Therefore, beloved ones, to return to you: if you are Christians, then in this valley of tears and miseries walk yourselves in the way in which Christ walked. “Woe to the person who enters upon two ways” (Ecclus. II, 14). For if flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God (I Cor. XV, 50), spiritual things plainly cannot be joined with fleshly consolations. Whoever makes himself debtor and provider for the flesh, so that he is more concerned to feed what is barren than to do good to the widow, finds no yoke of religion—however light, however sweet it may seem—tolerable. Hence it happens that he finds peace neither here, where he cannot be without murmuring, nor in the future, where he must endure the punishment for murmuring. But where peace is absent, God also is absent, because “his place has been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV, 3).

Yet God’s yoke is sweet and his burden light (Matt. XI, 30). But for whom? For those led by his Spirit (Rom. VIII, 14). Who are they? Not slaves of the flesh but children of God. Do you wish to know the children of God? They are those who mortify by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh, whose members are the temple of the Holy Spirit, whom they received from God, so that they are no longer their own and do not live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them: being bought at a great price, the precious blood of Christ. Therefore, bearing him and glorifying him in their body, they indeed honor him, because they confess him not only before God but also before human beings. “Whoever confesses me before human beings,” he says, “I also will confess before my Father” (Matt. X, 32).

5. It is good, then, to confess to the Lord in thanksgiving; it is also good to confess the Lord in the performance of works, so that Christ may confess us in the strict examination of each person, when we must be manifested before his tribunal, that each may receive according to the things done through the body, whether good or evil, according to what he has done in the body (II Cor. V, 10). If you wish to share in both confessions—both that by which a human being confesses God and that by which God confesses a human being—do not wander any longer abroad, dispersed among the vanities and insanities of the age. Rather, return to yourselves and enter into your heart, where undoubtedly the kingdom of God is. For “his kingdom is within you” (Luke XVII, 21).

What is this kingdom? The sound and free will of a human being, so conformed to God’s will that it wills nothing which it knows displeases him and refuses nothing which it knows pleases him. Seek first, therefore, the kingdom of God, so that your will may be freed and healed from the poison of the world with which it has been heavily imbued or corrupted; and all things necessary for the body shall be added to you. Do not be anxious about the body, which is the inheritance of worms; but be anxious for the soul, which was made in God’s image: how, with unveiled face, it may behold the glory of God and be re-formed and transformed into that same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.

6. What among bodily things is sweeter, my brothers, more pleasant, or holier than Christ’s body? And yet it was said to the Apostles: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come.” For while they delighted in seeing and hearing Christ’s bodily presence, the Holy Spirit was never given to them perfectly, but was always promised. For he says: “When I have been taken up, I will send him to you” (John XVI, 7). While Christ was still living in the flesh, did Peter not deny him at the voice of a maidservant? But after Christ had been taken up and the Holy Spirit sent, did not the Apostles go away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus? (Acts V, 41.)

The power of the Holy Spirit is therefore far more eminent and sweeter than the delight afforded by Christ’s body. If bodily delight in so excellent and blessed a body could turn the Holy Spirit away from the Apostles—without whose affection nothing good can be loved and without whose power no saving burden can be borne—judge for yourselves whether those who are about to enter religion but seek bodily delights are not wretched and insane. For those coming to religion ought not to consider the weakness of the flesh so that it may be delicately served, but should consider the hindrances to the fervor of the spirit so that they may be diligently fled.

7. Therefore hasten to become poor in spirit and needy in possessions, so that the Lord may take care of you. For the way of such poverty—voluntary, that is, and, by choice, necessary—is safe and straight; otherwise Christ would not have entered upon it. Other ways, although they may be good, are nevertheless full of robbers. The path of this poverty, because it is steep and few climb by it, is unaware of the ambushes of robbers. For robbers do not often lay ambushes where the passage of travellers is not frequent. I tell you in the truth which is God, and believe one who has experienced it: the narrower and more troublesome this way seems at its entrance, the more cheerful and delightful it is found in its progress. At the entrance it demands merit; in the progress it repays with reward. Indeed, you will possess not only eternal life in the world to come, but will also receive a hundredfold in the present—not only in spiritual goods, but in temporal goods as well—provided you do not set your heart upon them.

For temporal goods themselves are lawful if they are not loved; if they are loved, they are unlawful. But whether they are loved or not, they are of little advantage, because they quickly overthrow the possessor’s heart by a certain sweetness of their own. What occasion have you for doubt? You will leave a few things behind amid anxiety; you will take possession of the whole world without anxiety. For all things are yours: whether the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come—all, I say, are yours. Yet this may truly be added: “But you are Christ’s, as Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. 3:22–23); that is, if, just as Christ glorified his Father in all his works, so you also seek his glory in every action of yours.

8. For if Christ appears glorious in your works, whom have you to fear? He alone indeed holds our salvation and condemnation in his hand. If he condemns, blessed be his name, because we have deserved it.

> **Note [Col. 0665D].** We do not think Bernard would have said this; nor do we think that eternal condemnation—in which there will be no agreement of the human will with the divine, but rather an obstinate and detestable falling away from it—was, in Bernard’s judgment, among those things which we ought willingly to commit to the divine will. This is evident from Sermon 25 *On Various Matters*, where, distinguishing matters which ought to be sought from God conditionally from those which ought to be sought absolutely, he places within the latter class grace that makes one pleasing to God and future glory, no. 5. In Letter 42, to Henry of Sens, no. 13, he extends even to hell itself Moses’ excessive love, willing for his brothers’ sake to be blotted out from the book of life, and Paul’s wish to be accursed; but this is with a good conscience, which does not belong to the condemned persons mentioned in this letter.

If he saves, glorious be his name, because mercy has abounded beyond judgment. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son. Yet who is there that will condemn? Jesus Christ? Jesus, I say, gracious and sweet, who died for our offences; who rose again for our justification; who is at the Father’s right hand, where he also intercedes for us? Warring on earth and reigning also in heaven, he thirsts for nothing but our salvation—and will he bring confusion upon those who flee to him? Far be it!

However grievously the recollection of my crimes presses upon my memory, however greatly the dreadful consideration of my former life terrifies me, let others do what they judge expedient; I shall always think, in confidence in the goodness of my Lord Jesus Christ, of his sweetness; my eyes shall always be fixed upon his mercy. For I know—and have sometimes experienced in myself—that his sweetness is far more effective in consoling than the bitterness of my life is in desolating him; and that his kindness is much readier to pardon than my iniquity is to offend. I know indeed that there is no iniquity like my iniquity; but, conversely, there is no sorrow like his sorrow. If I have sinned beyond measure, I do not despair, because he in whom I breathe again suffered beyond measure. If God is angered by the enormity of my crime, he is beyond doubt appeased by the suffering of the satisfaction made by his Son. For the gentle and innocent Lamb hanging upon the cross—he who was silent before the shearer—does not reproach those standing around and raging against him; rather, he sweetly addresses those passing by on the road and looking upon him. For thus it is written: “O all you who pass by the way, look and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12). This he cries from the cross to those who pass by.

But whence do they pass? Out of the world, not along with the world. By what way, and toward what do they pass? By the way of momentary poverty, toward the riches of eternal blessedness. For “the momentary and light burden of our present tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high,” provided that we contemplate not the things which are seen, but those which are unseen (2 Cor. 4:17–18).

9. I do not write these things to you so that you may take more secure delight in sins. For the Most High, who is also Jesus Christ himself, hates sinners and has mercy upon penitents. If repentance—indeed, since repentance—is necessary for you, you do not lack a place and time for repentance. For behold, this is the acceptable time in which, although it is not the blood of martyrs, labour in Christ nevertheless triumphs over the craft of the ancient serpent and casts down his strength. Moreover, the place among us is fitting and pleasant, not for rejoicing, as in the world, but for mourning what was committed in the world. There, indeed, by the preaching of the elders we are very subtly and profitably instructed; but much more subtly and profitably by examination of their manner of life, we are both undone in respect of evil and trained for good.

May the God of all mercy and consolation make you companions of our community, so that you may share that inward consolation which may sometimes be felt in you, but can never be spoken of by us. Farewell.

## LETTER 463

> **Note [Col. 0667C].** Formerly Letter 367.

### To Alfonso, King of Portugal

> **Note [Col. 0667C].** Horstius assigned the following two letters to this place, and Bernard Brito-Lusitanus published in the first volume of his *Annals* letters otherwise issued as translated from the French language (if he is to be believed), namely letters of the Duchess of Lorraine to Bernard and of Bernard to her. But we desire another guarantor for letters of this kind. Certainly Bernard’s genius, style, and modesty seem lacking in them. Genuine are Bernard’s Letter 308 to King Alfonso, and also the eighth letter of Peter, Abbot of Clairvaux, to the King of Portugal, in which he thanks him for relieving the poverty of his brethren and for the gift of the monastery of Castineria; this is in Chesnius, vol. IV, p. 480. What follows are Horstius’s notes.

Having gained victory over the Saracens, the king was bound by a vow to establish a monastery for Cistercians. Bernard accordingly sends to Portugal the monks requested from Clairvaux.

To ALFONSO, most Christian and pious King of the Portuguese, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, the little that he is.

Blessed be God, and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who has comforted you in your tribulation by removing the reproach of the Saracens from your necks. The walls of Jericho have fallen; great Babylon has fallen; the Lord has destroyed the strongholds of his enemies and exalted the horn of his people. Even before this came to pass we learned of it, through the revelation of the Spirit, who breathes where he wills without the hearing of a voice. Therefore we afflicted our souls; both my littleness and my other brethren, prostrate before the Lord, while your hands were fighting, sought strength and courage.

> **Note [Col. 0667D].** See the event narrated at length by Henriquez, *Fasciculus*, book I, distinction 4, chapter 27; and in the *Menologium* for the twentieth day of August, p. 273. There you will see that Bernard, although living in Gaul, like another Moses with hands extended to heaven, supplied aid and victory to Alfonso in Portugal, like another Joshua, while he was besieging Santarém, the exceedingly fortified city of the Saracens. This occurred because Alfonso, stirred by Bernard’s fame alone, had implored his help despite so great a distance between them.

And because our sins did not hinder your success, we rejoiced exceedingly. We also learned of the great devotion by which, moved thereto, you vowed to the Most High to build a monastery. Therefore we send these sons, whom from the first beginnings of religious life we have nourished for Christ with the milk of doctrine, so that, commending ourselves to your Highness, they may bring your pious intention of fulfilling the vow to its due execution. They are to establish that monastery, in whose continuance and integrity you will have an indelible memorial of your reign; and when its revenues are divided, your crown shall be divided from you.

> **Note [Col. 0667D–0669B].** A memorable prophecy of Bernard, fulfilled by events in our own times. But I would rather have you learn it more fully from the authors of that nation itself. Hear, then, Angelus Manriquez, a Portuguese theologian of the Cistercian Order: “What he says there—‘when its revenues are divided, your crown shall be divided from you’—came to pass in our times. For when Sebastian perished miserably in Africa, Cardinal Henry obtained the kingdom. He assigned part of the revenues of the monastery of Alcobaça to a certain courtier; and the king shortly afterward died, leaving no heir. King Philip II of Spain entered upon the inheritance, and the ancient line of Portuguese kings became extinct. In the said monastery a thousand monks lived together, who day and night continually devoted themselves to divine praises. They were divided into groups of ten in such an order that perpetual praise was maintained in the choir. When the first group left the choir after completing matins, others succeeded them; when these also withdrew, others entered and sang the same offices, so that the choir was never seen without monks.” Thus the Reverend Father Angelus Manriquez explains this prophecy in his *Evangelical Laurel* and his *Annals*, and Henriquez after him in the *Fasciculus*, book I, distinction 4, chapter 27, and again in the *Menologium* for the twentieth day of August.
>
> Here there fittingly occurs another no less memorable counsel—or rather prophecy—concerning the same Henry, King of Portugal, though at that time still Cardinal and Archbishop of Évora. I remember reading it in the *Life of St Charles Borromeo*, and think it not irrelevant to add it here for the reader’s benefit:
>
> “When Sebastian, King of Portugal, died without children, his uncle Henry, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, was made king. The leading men of the kingdom, bishops, and peoples earnestly urged him to take a wife; for they hoped that, despite his advanced age, he would father one to succeed in the throne. They argued that this would bring consolation to the whole kingdom and be highly consonant with piety and religion, and would avert the discords, wars, and calamities which, after Henry’s death with no successor of the royal house left behind, would almost necessarily arise.
>
> “Henry, as a bishop, sought release from his religious obligation and permission from Pope Gregory to marry. At the same time he sent a letter to Charles at Milan, declaring that his Portuguese subjects had induced him to consent to marriage, as the one remedy through which peace might be secured for the realm; that this weighed very heavily upon him, and that he regarded it as a kind of sacrifice, in which he would offer himself for the salvation of his people; but that he had decided to yield to the public peace. He therefore earnestly begged Charles to endeavour, as far as he could, to persuade the Pope to grant the permission. Other leading men likewise petitioned Charles most insistently and entrusted the affair to his authority.
>
> “Charles replied to the petition of his most friendly and excellent king, not in accordance with what the king seemed to desire, but according to what he judged beneficial to the holy Church. It might indeed seem of great importance, he said, to seek for the Portuguese one who could lawfully succeed him in the kingdom without dispute; yet granting the power of marriage to so high a bishop seemed a matter of the utmost gravity, never conceded at any time. Permission for marriage had, it was said, sometimes been granted to persons dedicated to God in another order of life; but this was scarcely confirmed by the testimony of any sufficiently certain and approved author. The hoped-for results of such marriages, whether public tranquillity or succession, had by no means occurred; rather, very great public and private disadvantages had resulted from them, where great advantages had been expected. More worthy of approval and imitation, he said, was the continence of certain kings who, though married and lawfully able to have children, nevertheless, giving no thought to heir or successor, abstained from marital intercourse out of a singular devotion to chastity—how much more, then, should those who had professed the celibate life be unable to turn to marriage without some exceptional dispensation? He confirmed what he had said by adducing examples.
>
> “Finally, in a matter so great and difficult, he said that he could approve nothing other than that the reasons for which this permission seemed to be sought should be candidly presented to the Supreme Pontiff without any partisan pressure, and that whatever he should judge by his highest authority and divine inspiration should be accepted with an even mind and will. He wrote seriously to the Pope about the affair and made known what seemed best to him. No one is ignorant what the outcome was.”
>
> So writes the most weighty author of the *Life of St Charles Borromeo*, Charles of the Basilica, Bishop of Novara. In volume VIII of the *Spicilegium* there is a charter of John, King of Portugal, by which he gives the monastery of Cós to Menendo, Abbot of Alcobaça, dated in the era 1233.

May the Saviour of all preserve you and your illustrious queenly consort, and bless your offspring, so that you may see your children’s children rejoicing in your possessions.

## LETTER 464

> **Note [Col. 0670C].** Formerly Letter 368.

### To John Cirita

> **Note [Col. 0670C].** Otherwise, Zirita. He was abbot and founder of the monasteries of St John of Tarouca, St Christopher, and St Peter of Aquilis.

Having divinely learned of his zeal and desire, he sends monks from Clairvaux to establish a monastery in Portugal.

To the venerable brother, beloved of God and our companion in the way of this world, JOHN CIRITA, BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: greeting in the author of salvation.

By the permission of the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who does not allow the souls of sinners to be condemned by their sins, we have learned concerning your Brotherhood how you do not cease to strike at the divine breast with continual prayers for the forgiveness of sinners. And because you are a man of desires, the Lord has fulfilled your desire by making known to us that your prayers have been heard.

> **Note [Col. 0670D].** Henriquez, Horstius says, explains in the *Life of John Cirita* the manner in which the prayer was heard. Namely, on 24 June 1119, after the praises of the Vigils, while Blessed Bernard was persisting in prayer in the choir, St John the Baptist appeared to him and commanded him to send a colony of monks to the more remote regions of Spain, to a place which God would show as suitable for a monastery. Bernard accordingly chose eight of his own: Bohemund, Aldebert, John, Bernard, Cisinand, Roland, and Alan; and, having instructed them concerning the divine will, sent them into Spain. There they found John Cirita, through the sign given by St Bernard, and under his leadership and the auspices of the prince built the monastery of St John of Tarouca. See Henriquez, *Fasciculus*, book I, distinction 19, and Manriquez, *Annals*, year 1119, chapter 3.

And he who joined us with you in the same fellowship, who made himself companion to the two disciples going to Emmaus—we send these little sons, whom we have nourished for the Lord with the milk of evangelical doctrine. Wherever divine mercy shall appoint and some heavenly sign shall shine forth, establish a monastery; among them he has chosen you as standard-bearer and leader of the rest, so that you may both make the beginning and bring the work to its conclusion, and offer what has been led to God and to his Forerunner.

## LETTER 465

> **Note [Col. 0670D].** This letter, together with the following one, was published by Chesnius in volume IV; but neither has Bernard’s style.

### To the Abbot of Saint Benedict

To the lord Abbot of Saint Benedict, Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux: receive a holy blessing.

You must hasten at once to the lord King and set before him most fully our entire disgrace and how we have been betrayed, as before our gracious lord. And since we rejoice in part that his affair was the cause to us of this anxiety—for it was on his behalf that we gave counsel to the lord of Sens—he who had long before promised us that a day would be fixed has thus disgraced us, so avenging upon us the King’s love. Ask him also for most effective letters concerning this business, so that the lord Pope may by every means confirm what the obedient sons—namely, the two bishops—have done; for it is most pleasing to him and necessary to the Church. Nor should it do harm that the third has thus withdrawn himself, disobedient to the apostolic command and a despiser of the royal warnings. If he comes before the King, let him perceive that our injury—our particular injury—is displeasing to the King.

Greet our dearest chancellor, and ask him to write such letters on this matter as may demonstrate his own affection and be found to breathe the royal affection toward us, as we presume of both.

## LETTER 466

### To King Louis

To LOUIS, most excellent King of the Franks, his lord, BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: greeting.

You know, my lord, how both I and my affairs are placed under your protection. Therefore, trusting in your friendship, I commend by request to you this cleric J., bearer of the present letter, so that your Highness may, if necessary, commend him to the lord Pope, and may believe—upon my testimony—that his complaint concerning money entrusted to our bishop is true and just. Farewell.

## II. BY NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX, IN THE PERSON OF ST BERNARD

## LETTER 467

> **Note [Col. 0671D].** Written in the year of Christ 1146.

### Nicholas of Clairvaux to the Count and Barons of Brittany, in the Person of the Lord of Clairvaux, concerning the Affair of the Cross

> **Note [Col. 0671D].** Compare Letter 363, in imitation of which this was written.

1. The earth has been shaken and trembled, because the King of heaven has lost his land, the land where his feet stood. The enemies of his cross have with one accord made a covenant against him, and those who hate him have lifted up their head. Their kindred said together in their heart: “Let us possess his sanctuary as an inheritance.” They endeavour to overthrow the workshops of our redemption and seek to profane the places consecrated by Christ’s blood. Above all, they strive with every effort to tear away that badge of the Christian religion—the sepulchre, I mean, in which the Lord of majesty was buried, where his face was bound with a napkin. They shake their hands over the mountain of the daughter of Zion; and unless the Lord keeps it, they are near to breaking into the holy city Jerusalem, the city of the living God, over which his name has been invoked. Christian peoples are partly cast into chains and partly slaughtered like sheep for the slaughter. That great eye of providence sees and is silent, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God, whether there is one who grieves for his cause and restores his inheritance to him. Although he can do all things—for all power is subject to him whenever he wills—he nevertheless wishes to ascribe victory to the Christian name and to lay his hand upon those who afflict them.

2. Therefore, at the most urgent request of the lord King and by apostolic command, we came at the Paschal solemnity to the very celebrated place of Vézelay, where the lord King had assembled with the princes of the realm and a great multitude of people for the feast day. This lamentable grief was set forth before them all, and the letters of the lord Pope were read, a copy of which we send to all of you. The Holy Spirit softened their hearts; and immediately the King, with a great multitude of princes and innumerable people, was armed with the sign of Christ’s cross. This blessing spreads through the whole land, and all fly eagerly to receive the sign of salvation upon their foreheads and shoulders.

And because your land is fruitful in brave men and filled with martial youth, it is fitting that you be among the first, and with the first, to undertake so holy a work and to go up armed to serve the living God. Come then, most valiant soldiers, gird yourselves; and let him who has no sword buy one. Do not abandon your own king, the King of the Franks—indeed, the King of heaven—for whose sake he himself undertakes so great a journey and labour. The man of God, the lord of Chartres, comes to you, that he may instruct you more fully concerning what has been said and done, and may set forth the most generous remission contained in the letters of the lord Pope for those who have received the crosses. For him who deigned to die for you, defend the places of his death and of our redemption, lest the nations should say, “Where is their God?” May the Bridegroom of the Church, the Son of Mary, our Lord God, make you victorious on earth and glorious in heaven.

## LETTER 468

> **Note [Col. 0672D].** Written in the year of Christ 1146.

### By the Same Author to Manuel Comnenus, Emperor of Constantinople, in the Person of the Lord of Clairvaux

That he may make the son of Count Theobald a new knight.

> **Note [Col. 0672D].** This concerns Henry, to whom Letter 179 is addressed. For the rest, see Letter 363.

To the exalted and glorious MANUEL, Emperor of Constantinople, Brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux: greeting and prayers.

1. That I dare write to so great a majesty is not the insolence of rashness but the confidence of charity. For who am I, or what is my father’s house in Israel, that I should dare to anticipate by my letters an Emperor of so great a name? For I am poor, a person of no rank, removed from the presence of your Highness by a great expanse of lands and the intervening vastness of the sea. What, then, has such great exaltation to do with such great lowliness, unless the humility of Christ gave me confidence? In that humility, and from it, the kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and judges, glory. For even to us has come the magnificence and glory of your name, spread far and wide over the earth. In gratitude for this I bend my knees to the Father of spirits, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that you may be transferred from this kingdom into the kingdom of him whose kingdom is the kingdom of all ages.

2. Therefore, though no merits of mine precede me, I dare to send to the throne of your glory the bearer of this letter, a young man of great nobility, that you may admit him to the military oath and gird him with the sword against the enemies of Christ’s cross, who have lifted up their head against him. The young man indeed had access open to the courts of the great; but by a higher counsel we send him to the singular glory of your empire, that all the days of his life he may remember from whom he received the dignity of military discipline. I would by no means have undertaken these entreaties unless Christ were the cause, for whose sake he has undertaken so great a journey and labour. Whatever you do to him, or for his sake, is done to me.

3. Henceforth, most glorious Emperor, it is now time to show and extend the abundance of your kindness. The earth has been shaken and trembled, because the King of heaven has lost his land, the land where his feet stood. For the enemies of the Lord are near to breaking into his city, even into that glorious sepulchre where the virgin flower of Mary was laid with linen cloths and spices, and whence there rose the first and greatest flower that appeared in our land. Therefore, at the command of the lord Pope and at whatever exhortation we may offer, the King of the Franks and an innumerable multitude of princes, soldiers, and peoples will pass through your territories to the city of the living God.

It will be yours to receive them honourably. You must now act in a manner befitting the place you hold, the power you have received, the dignity in which you stand, and the riches in which you abound—befitting imperial excellence, the honour of your person, and the salvation of your soul for ever and ever. Among them, and before them, we most earnestly commend to you the son of the most illustrious Prince Count Theobald, not as one among the rest, but as one set above the rest. He is young, noble, and of good disposition; he has consecrated the first fruits of his knighthood not to wickedness but to justice. He is also the son of that man who, because of truth, gentleness, and justice, is loved and honoured among the princes of the earth. For all these reasons we make you a participant in all the benefits which are done and shall be done in our house. May the Bridegroom of the Church, the Son of Mary, our Lord God, make you victorious on earth and glorious in heaven.

## LETTER 469

### By the Same Author to the Bishop of Lucca, in the Person of the Lord of Clairvaux

An exhortation to courage.

> **Note [Col. 0673D–0674D].** We suppose this to be the bishop of Lucca in Italy who commended Peter Lombard to Bernard above in Letter 410—either Ubertus or Gregory, the former elected in 1140 and the latter in 1146, according to Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I.

To the venerable lord, the Bishop of LUCCA, BERNARD: to live in the light and die in the light.

1. You have been placed in a high position, and you need a lofty spirit to instruct you. For the chair which you have received is one of burden, not honour; of work, not title; finally, of virtues, not riches. Thus says that heavenly trumpet, in whose breast and from whose breast the word of the Lord resounded: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). A work, not a dignity.

Since, therefore, you have set your hand to mighty tasks, you need courage. Since you have been made a watchman for the house of Israel, you need prudence. You need the golden mean of temperance, because you are debtor to the wise and the foolish. Moreover, for the completion of the virtues, you must be clothed in justice, by which each person receives what is his own; as Scripture says, “Let your priests be clothed with justice” (Ps. 131:9). Blessed is this four-horse chariot, and blessed its charioteer who, presiding with the reins of humility, directs the wheels of the virtues according to his own driving and guidance.

2. Humility, mistress of the virtues, singular daughter of the highest King, descending from the highest heaven with the Lord of heavens, has established her eternal dwelling in heavenly minds. “Without humility, to choose through prudence what ought to be loved,” as the Wise Man says, “is mistaken discernment; to overcome adversities through courage is silent victory; to resist enticements through temperance is tumultuous sobriety; to persist in works of justice is pride veiled over.” Humility alone makes the virtues blessed and enduring. It takes the kingdom of heaven by force; it humbled the Lord of majesty unto death, even death on a cross.

For the Word of God, established on high, was first invited by humility to descend to us; truth compelled him, by which he had promised himself to come; the purity of the virgin womb received him; power brought him forth while preserving the Virgin’s integrity; obedience guided him in all things; patience sustained him; charity manifested him in words and miracles. This must be rooted and founded with a deep root in the heart of a bishop; when it gives way, the whole assembly of virtues is either crushed or collapses.

I have become foolish; you compelled me. It was not indeed my place to instruct a bishop; but it is both my duty, and the duty of all who know the truth of charity, to admonish a friend. Our common son there will report the rest to you more fully and plainly in person. For it ought not to be entrusted to letters, since it might instruct some but harm others.

## III. LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO ST BERNARD AND OTHERS

Those marked with the numbers 470, 473, 474, 475, and 477 are now published for the first time among the works of St Bernard. The Editors.

## LETTER 470

### King Alfonso to St Bernard

[MANRIQUE, *Annals of the Cistercians, or rather of Ecclesiastical History*, vols. I–IV, Lyons, 1642, folio, vol. II, p. 71.]

ALFONSO, by the grace of God King of the Portuguese, to the venerable father BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux.

Know that through God’s mercy we have acquired Santarém, which was a most strongly fortified city and a yoke upon our heads. We believe this came through your good prayers, because we first commended ourselves to you and promised that we would establish for you a monastery of your Order, which we are ready to build at our own expense. Send monks to us, and we will fulfil what we have said. Our household servant whom we send will tell you the rest—how matters happened and what occurred; believe him. And commend to God us, our queen and wife, and our only son, whom I have recently had, Henry.

## LETTER 471

### Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, to St Bernard

> **Note [Col. 0675D–0676D].** Suger wrote this letter when close to death, after receiving St Bernard’s Letter 266, in which the holy abbot encourages him to meet death fearlessly with these words: “Man of God, do not fear to put off that man who is of the earth . . . What have you to do with earthly spoils, you who are about to go to heaven and will soon be clothed with the glory of the robe?”

He gives thanks for the consolation bestowed upon him at the end of life and commends himself to Bernard’s prayers.

(Dom MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 424, from a manuscript of the Coislin Library.)

To his most loving lord and venerable father, BERNARD, by God’s grace Abbot of Clairvaux, SUGER, still the humble servant of Blessed Dionysius: greeting and the affection of sincere love.

You visited us by your letters; may the Dawn from on high visit you. You sent to me, a wretched sinner, your small gifts—indeed, your greatest gifts: a precious napkin, the bread of your blessing, and letters of consolation containing good and holy words, overflowing with honey and milk—and granted me the greatest consolation as I lay at the end. For if I had been able to see even once your angelic face before my death, I should depart more securely from this most wretched world. But know certainly that, even if I had deserved to live a thousand years or more, I would care for nothing except to remain in God’s good pleasure. For, trusting not in works of justice but in the mercy of God alone, which he always shows to those who hope in him, I desire with all the intention of my heart to return to him. I therefore devoutly commend my soul to your holy hands and, prostrate at the knees of your holiness, earnestly entreat you to obtain divine propitiation for my soul through your prayers and those of your holy communities.

## LETTER 472

### Everwin, Provost of Steinfeld, to St Bernard

Concerning the heretics of his time.

(From vol. IV of the works of St Bernard; formerly prefixed to Sermon 65 on the *Song of Songs*.)

To his reverend lord and father, BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux, EVERWIN, humble servant of Steinfeld: to be strengthened in the Lord, and to strengthen the Church of Christ.

377 1. “I will rejoice over your utterances, like one who finds abundant spoil” [Ps. 119:162]. In all that you say and write, you are accustomed to make us pour forth the memory of God’s abundant sweetness, especially in the Song of the Bridegroom’s and Bride’s love—that is, of Christ and the Church—so that we may truly say to that Bridegroom: “You have kept the good wine until now” [John 2:10].

He himself has appointed you for us as steward of this most precious wine. Do not cease to pour it out; do not hesitate: you will not be able to empty the jars. Nor, holy Father, may your weakness excuse you; for devotion accomplishes more in this ministry than bodily labor in building up the Church. Nor say that you are occupied: we know of nothing to be preferred to this most necessary common work. How much, most holy Father, you now have to pour out for us from the jar! From the first enough has been poured out, and it made them wise and strong against the teaching and assault of the Scribes and Pharisees; from the second, against the arguments and tortures of the Gentiles; from the third, against the subtle deceptions of heretics; from the fourth, against false Christians; from the fifth, against heretics who will come near the end of the age, [Col. 0676C] concerning whom the Spirit plainly says through the Apostle: “In the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving” [1 Tim. 4:1–3].

From the sixth they will be intoxicated, strengthening the faithful against him who will indeed be revealed in this falling away from the faith—namely, that son of sin, the man of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called or worshipped as God; whose coming is according to the working of Satan, in every power and signs and lying wonders, and in every seduction of iniquity [2 Thess. 2:3–10]. After this, the seventh will not be necessary [Col. 0676D], when the children of men shall be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and by the torrent of his delight.

O good Father, meanwhile you have poured out sufficiently for all of us from the fourth jar [Col. 0677A], for correction, edification, and perfection—for beginners, those making progress, and the perfect—so as to profit us to the end of the age against the lukewarmness and perversity found among false brethren. It is now time to draw from the fifth and bring it forth publicly against the new heretics, who are now bubbling up almost everywhere throughout all the churches from the pit of the abyss, as though their prince were already beginning to be loosed and the day of the Lord were at hand. Moreover, the passage in the bridal song of Christ’s and the Church’s love which, Father, as you yourself told me, you are now to expound—namely, “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” [Song 2:15]—suits this mystery and has brought you to the fifth jar. We therefore ask you, Father, to distinguish all the divisions of their heresy which have come to your knowledge and, by setting against them the arguments and authorities of our faith, to destroy them.

2. Recently, near Cologne, certain heretics were discovered among us, some of whom returned to the Church after making satisfaction. Two of them—one called their bishop, together with his companion—resisted us in an assembly of clergy and laity, in the presence of the lord archbishop himself and great noblemen, defending their heresy from Christ’s and the Apostle’s words.
