But when they saw that they could not proceed, they requested that a day be appointed on which they might bring men from among their own people, skilled in their faith. They promised that they would join themselves to the Church if they saw their teachers fail in answering; otherwise, [Col. 0677C] they would rather die than turn from this opinion.

When this had been heard, and they had been admonished for three days but refused to come to their senses, they were seized by a populace stirred by excessive zeal—though against our will—put into the fire, and burned. What is more astonishing, they entered into and endured the punishment of fire not only patiently, but even joyfully. Here, holy Father, had I been present, I should have wished to have your answer as to why these members of the devil possess such fortitude in their heresy as is scarcely found even among the very devout in Christ’s faith.

3. This is their heresy. They say that the Church exists among themselves alone, because they alone adhere to Christ’s footsteps and remain true followers of the apostolic life, seeking none of the things of this world and possessing neither house nor fields nor any private property, just as Christ possessed none and did not permit his disciples to possess such things. But you, they say to us, join house to house and field to field, and seek the things of this world. Thus even those among you who are regarded as most perfect, such as monks or regular canons, although they possess these things not as private property but in common, nevertheless possess all these things.

They say of themselves: “We are Christ’s poor, unsettled, fleeing from city to city like sheep among wolves; with the apostles and martyrs we suffer persecution. Yet we lead a holy and most strict life, persevering day and night in fasting and abstinence, in prayers and labors, seeking from these only what is necessary for life. [Col. 0678A] We endure this because we are not of the world; but you, lovers of the world, have peace with the world because you are of the world. False apostles, adulterating Christ’s word, sought what was their own and caused you and your fathers to stray beyond the bounds. We and our fathers, born apostles, have remained in Christ’s grace and shall remain until the end of the age. To distinguish us from you, Christ said: ‘By their fruits you shall know them’ [Matt. 7:16]. Our fruits are Christ’s footsteps.”

In their food they forbid every kind of milk, everything made from it, and whatever is begotten through sexual intercourse. This they put forward to us concerning their manner of life. In their sacraments they cover themselves with a veil. Yet they openly confessed to us that every day, when they eat at their table, they consecrate their food and drink into Christ’s body and blood by the Lord’s Prayer, after the pattern of Christ and the apostles, so that they may thereby nourish themselves as Christ’s members and body. But, they say, we do not hold the truth in the sacraments, but a certain shadow and human tradition.

They also openly confessed that, in addition to water, they baptize and have been baptized in fire and Spirit, adducing the testimony of John the Baptist, who baptized in water and said of Christ: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” [Matt. 3:11]; and elsewhere: “I baptize in water, but one greater than you stands among you, whom you do not know” [John 1:26]—as though he were going to baptize them with another baptism besides water. They tried to show that such baptism should be performed by the laying on of hands, from the testimony of Luke, who, in the Acts of the Apostles, describing Paul’s baptism which he received from Ananias at Christ’s command, makes no mention of water but only of the laying on of hands. Whatever is found, whether in the Acts of the Apostles or in Paul’s Epistles, concerning the laying on of hands, they wish to refer to this baptism.

They say that anyone thus baptized among them is one of the elect and has authority to baptize others who are worthy, and to consecrate at their table Christ’s body and blood. For they first receive him through laying on of hands from the number of those whom they call “hearers” among the believers; and then he may attend their prayers, until they have sufficiently tested him and made him one of the elect. [Col. 0678D] They care nothing for our baptism. They condemn marriage, but I was unable to discover their reason: either because they did not dare confess it, or, more likely, because they did not know it.

4. There are also certain other heretics in our land, altogether at variance with these; through their mutual disagreement and contention both groups were disclosed to us. These deny that Christ’s body is made at the altar, because all the priests of the Church are not consecrated. The apostolic dignity, they say, has been corrupted by entangling itself in secular affairs; and, not serving God in Peter’s chair as Peter did, it has deprived itself of the power of consecration which was given to Peter. Since it does not possess this power, the archbishops, who live secularly in the Church, do not receive it from it so as to be able to consecrate anyone. They cite Christ’s words: “The Scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ chair; therefore do what they tell you” [Matt. 23:2–3], as though such persons had been granted only the authority to speak and command, and nothing more.

Thus they nullify the Church’s priesthood and condemn the sacraments, except baptism alone; and this, in adults, whom they say are baptized by Christ, whoever may be the minister of the sacraments. They profess faith in infant baptism, except for the Gospel saying: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” [Mark 16:16]. They call every marriage fornication except that contracted between two virgins, male and female. They support this with the Lord’s words in answer to the Pharisees: “What God has joined, let no man separate” [Matt. 19:6], as though God joins such persons in likeness to the first human beings; and with his answer to their further objection about a bill of divorce: “From the beginning it was not so”; and likewise what follows there: “Whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery” [Matt. 19:6–9]; and the Apostle’s saying: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and the marriage-bed undefiled” [Heb. 13:4].

5. They do not trust in the intercessions of the saints. They maintain that fasts and other afflictions undertaken for sins are necessary neither for the righteous nor even for sinners, because on whatever day a sinner groans, all sins are forgiven him. They call superstitions the other observances in the Church which Christ and the apostles did not establish when they departed from it. [Col. 0679C] They do not admit a purgatorial fire after death, but hold that souls, immediately upon leaving the body, pass into either eternal rest or punishment, because of Solomon’s words: “Into whatever direction a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it shall remain” [Eccl. 11:3]. Thus they nullify the prayers or offerings of the faithful for the dead.

6. Against these many-shaped evils, holy Father, we ask that your vigilance may be aroused and that you direct your pen against the beasts of the reed. Nor let us be answered that the tower of David to which we flee has been sufficiently built with its bulwarks, that a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty. Rather, Father, we wish that this armor, gathered together by your diligence for the sake of us who are simpler [Col. 0679D] and slower, may be readier to find against so many monsters and more effective in resisting them.

Know also, lord, that those returning to the Church told us that they have a very great multitude scattered almost everywhere throughout the world, and that they include many of our clergy and monks. But those who were burned said to us in their defense that this heresy had remained hidden from the times of the martyrs until the present, and had persisted in Greece and certain other lands. These are the heretics who call themselves apostles and have their own pope. Others nullify our pope, yet do not confess that they have another besides him. These satanic apostolics have among them women whom they call continent—widows, virgins, [Col. 0680A] and their wives—some among the elect, some among the believers, as though after the pattern of the apostles, who were granted authority to lead women about with them. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CDLXXIII. HENRY OF RHEIMS TO BERNARD

[MANRIQUE, *Cistercian Annals*, vol. II, p. 135.]

377 1. To his father, from his son HENRY: whatever a son owes a father.

It is not presumption but confidence that makes me write to you, most kindly Father. I know that it is not for me to speak, like wounded N. and one sleeping in tombs; but zeal, I confess, burns my soul on behalf of this poor bishop, who, because he cultivated justice and desired equity, has been struck by the enemy’s blow with cruel chastisement. Because he wished to sit in his own seat and to render episcopal things to the bishop, this is accounted the greatest and first sin. Behold, this blood is required from his hand.

Therefore, if I have any power in the Father’s eyes—indeed, because I have great power—take up his cause, as you know best how it should be managed. As for the rest, I am cheerful and well, and I await the sight of your face as the face of God. For the day of my betrothal is near, on which I shall make a covenant with the Lord God through your hand and under your guardianship, that I may serve him day and night and all the days of my life, most beloved Father.

## LETTER CDLXXIV. JOHN, BISHOP OF ALETH, TO ST BERNARD

[MANRIQUE, cited above, p. 135.]

[Col. 0680C]

To his father and father of all good men, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, brother John, bishop of Aleth: that he may be honored here in his labors and there honored with the angels.

Would that I saw you rather than wrote to you, and that the sight of your sweetness might soothe and relieve my pain. For I have been saddened under my excommunication; although, according to the Wise Man, tribulation itself is for me consolation, while my conscience is not a scourge. For I know that those are happily miserable who plainly have not deserved what they endure. Therefore I write to you about the things concerning me, though briefly, lest a longer page detain eyes which you owe to the world.

After the sentence against me had been pronounced in accordance with your counsel, [Col. 0680D] I went to my lord, whom the Lord appointed lord of his household and ruler over all his possession. On entering his presence, I found more of a judge than of a father, less mercy than severity. For the men of the Greater Monastery had preceded me and had made themselves greater than I, making their voice a voice of power. They said that I had evaded the hearing of the bishops, into whose hands he himself had put me to be heard. Not only this, but everything whatever that they could gather from any source they brought against me, and they were heard with much calmness.

When I was prepared to rebut or refute what was being said, the judge of the whole body would not hear me—may this not be charged against him. Moreover, he added to the pain of my wounds by sending me back to those to whom he had sent me before, whom I had regarded with some suspicion; and his hand is still stretched out, because I went to him in suspense and left him in suspense.

Although I am conscious of none of the things which they maliciously fabricated against me, nevertheless I await judgment patiently, if not gladly. For I know that I have deserved things heavier than I suffer, as a servant working wickedly and deserving every indignation. Yet I, a man of the smallest resources, have undertaken a hard province: to assail and enter into a case with men who trust in their own strength and glory in the multitude of their riches. Therefore, placed among your men of Clairvaux, I await your counsel as God’s counsel; for no one will be able to rescue a poor bishop from the hand of those stronger than he unless your whole hand comes against those who harass and despoil him. [Col. 0681B]

Lord Father, I am ready and have not been troubled, to keep your commandments. Would that your will—if it is the Lord’s will—might not differ from mine. If you judge it fitting, communicate the good pleasure of your graciousness to your servant; for there is neither counsel nor help except with you and from you, most beloved Father.

## LETTER CDLXXV. M., BISHOP OF CRACOW, TO ST BERNARD: HE INVITES HIM TO THE CONVERSION OF THE RUTHENIANS

(G. Bernardus PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, part I, col. 360, from the Windberg manuscript.)

377 3. To B., by God’s grace abbot of Clairvaux, a venerable and reverend man, worthy of every proclamation of praise and distinguished by the merit of holiness; M., by the same grace bishop of Cracow, and Count . . . Peter: whom he makes to bear fruit.

We give thanks to our God—indeed, infinite thanks—who has raised you up such as you are, O ornament and glory of abbots, in our age: you whom concern for all the churches, like a vessel of election, never passes by, neither at any time nor in any place; whom others’ weakness compels to become weak with them; by whose merits God grants every good to an undeserving world; whose prayer softens the strict Judge, revokes the sentence, and suspends wrath, lest he strike sinners at once, so that he may spare them.

Your beloved son Master A. consulted us on your behalf whether anyone could extirpate the impious rites and observances of the Ruthenians. He could, lord, he could—but only that one man in whom powerful grace dwelt. We trust in the Lord Jesus that, if the abbot of Clairvaux were here, he could accomplish this good. That Ruthenian people, innumerable in multitude and equal, as it were, to the stars, does not observe the rule of orthodox faith and the ordinances of true religion, failing to heed that outside the Catholic Church there is no place of true sacrifice. Nor is it known to err shamefully only in the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, but also in the repudiation of marriages, in rebaptizing, and in the other sacraments of the Church. [Col. 0682A]

Thus, imbued from the beginning of its conversion with diverse errors—or rather with heretical perversity—it confesses Christ in name alone, but utterly denies him in deeds. It is willing to conform neither to the Latin nor to the Greek Church; separated from each and from both, the aforesaid people shares in the sacramental communion of neither. Yet, lord, your preaching, more penetrating than any two-edged sword, would cut away all this, if the Holy Spirit inspired you to visit it.

Nor only in Ruthenia, which is, as it were, another world, but also in Poland and Bohemia—or in Slavonia, the common designation which contains many provinces—you would produce fruit so great, so abundant, and so acceptable to God, that afterward you would hear from him: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” Or, most certainly, all of them—or almost all, as we hope—would obey you at the hearing of the ear.

Therefore deign, merciful Father, you who have enlightened others, to enlighten our darkness also. Deign to instruct the unformed Slavs in the way of morals and the principles of life. Deign to visit the frozen pole by your presence, so that, at the coming of our abbot, the dreadful cold of the North may be moderated by the grace of the South Wind and by Mulciber’s blast; that uncultivated barbarism may be cultivated by your moral teaching; that inhuman people may be softened by your instruction and become gentle under the Lord’s yoke.

For if famed glory places Thracian Orpheus and Theban Amphion in heaven and among the stars, if poetic genius celebrates them and song keeps them alive after death, because each softened woods and stones—that is, wild and stony-hearted people—by the songs of his lyre [Col. 0682C] and compelled them to endure law, how much more do we hope that the holy abbot will reconcile fierce and savage nations to Christ: he who is a herald of the Gospel, a lamp in the Lord’s house, an interpreter of the divine will, better than Orpheus, bright with heavenly knowledge, endowed with celestial understanding, and distinguished by the gift and grace of almost every charisma.

But how great and how ardent is the desire with which Count Peter—indeed a man most devoted to the worship of God, the Church, and religion—and I await your coming, merciful Father: he alone is our witness who sees the secrets of hearts. Nor do we alone desire the abbot of Clairvaux. Rich and poor together, noble and ignoble, young men and maidens, old men equally with the younger, all desire him. Every rank and age, every sex and condition, all the Poles, and the wishes of all, sigh for the abbot.

## LETTER CDLXXVI. THOMAS, FORMER ABBOT OF MORIGNY, TO ST BERNARD

[Note: This Thomas, formerly abbot of Morigny, had voluntarily relinquished his office and withdrawn to Saint-Martin-des-Champs. But when Alberic, bishop of Ostia, came to France as papal legate from Pope Lucius, and Ymarus of Tusculum to England, and when they learned, as the chronicler of Morigny attests, that the abbey lay in a ruinous condition, they deposed Abbot Ademar and put in his place Macarius, Alberic’s nephew and then abbot of Morigny, so that he might reform the place according to the customs of Cluny, which he had professed in the cell of Longpont. Thomas, already weary of his long leisure, hoped on that occasion to return to the abbey of Morigny. But disappointed in his expectation—perhaps because Alberic opposed him—and seeing Thevin, prior of Argenteuil, appointed in Macarius’s place, he attacked Alberic and his nephews, Macarius and Lancelin, with excessive violence. What he writes against them is demonstrably most false from the aforesaid chronicle of Morigny, whether carried away by excessive rancor or deceived by empty rumors. Whether Bernard answered this letter, and what he answered, is uncertain. But from the cited chronicle we learn that Thomas returned to the monastery of Coulombs, from which he had first been taken, and there died shortly afterward.]

(Printed in the 1719 edition of St Bernard’s *Works*, vol. I, appendix to the letters, col. 576.)

377 4. To the most beloved lord and one to be honored in Christ’s bowels, Bernard, by God’s grace abbot of Clairvaux, THOMAS, servant and son of his holiness: greeting.

The name of your place accords with the conduct of you and of those who serve beneath your standards. For you shine in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation like great lights, holding forth the word of life in the world; and you dwell in valleys which abound in that grain which God sent into Jacob and which fell in Israel. Seeing this, I, a small and lowly man in God’s house, have conceived confidence to write to your exaltedness concerning the disturbance which I suffer, though unwillingly, seeking from your holiness an antidote.

The cause is this. Alberic, an apostolic man and bishop of Ostia, while he traveled through Gaul under the office of Roman legation and went about the land performing miracles—of whose multitude and greatness we are silent—transferred his nephew Macarius, a man of damaged reputation, fat in body, double in heart, and double-tongued in speech, from a new, small, and poor abbey into the ancient, great, and wealthy abbey of Saint Benedict. He added this unheard-of agreement: that the Cluniac order should not be introduced there, and that none of those brothers should be sent to any place subject to Cluny. [Col. 0683B]

Whoever does not smell in this the deadly poison of simoniacal heresy surely lacks the gift of discernment and has in his spiritual nostrils the foulest polypus. For what is this except selling religion, justice, and truth, and not entering by the door? Thinking, therefore, that nothing could withstand him, the bishop strives by every effort to install another nephew, Lancelin, in the Church of Morigny. This Macarius, while he presided over the place, had not only promised to do but also sworn without doubt.

For this brood, taking its origin from a poisoned trunk, joins scale to scale, preoccupies the cultivation of the Church, and grows beneath the shadow and power of the aforesaid man, against the will of all. It acquires money and prebends by pardoning grave crimes and by the disgraceful redemption of persons. They hear their opponents’ outcries most gladly. But if the scattered bones of Bishop Albinus and Martyr Rufinus glitter, night is immediately turned into day, black turns white, Proteus plays upon the sea, and at once everything changes: those who wept laugh; those who laughed weep; and, as the common proverb says, fishers not of the Gospel but of Sidon cast their nets into troubled water and, though manifold in number, fill their purses with gold and silver.

The enormity of these exactions does not occur so that assistance may be given to the holy Roman Church, now disturbed by the sedition of its people, but so that a crooked and perverse generation may be sustained by the plundering of churches, enriched, raised to pride, dissolved in luxury, and strengthened for wickedness. [Col. 0684A] But bastard shoots shall not strike deep roots, because every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up.

Finally, in this matter too they were disappointed in their hope. For Lancelin was a wicked and unmanageable man, red of skin, lightning-like in face, bloody in mind—a second Phalaris of our age. For this reason he deservedly suffered rejection in the matter which he had long desired and to which he had aspired as disgracefully as openly. Of other things which rumor spreads, one must be silent. For, Seneca testifies, it is a fault to believe no one and everyone.

Yet the bishop, relying on his authority and knowing no defeat, pressed his designs vigorously; and if he could overwhelm me, who had long presided over the place and was now sought by monks, clergy, people, knights, and nobles, he believed that he would securely obtain what he desired. Therefore at Paris, in the palace, in an assembly of venerable persons, with the king and court present, he broke the rein of moderation and hurled many accusations against an absent friend who had served him and had procured for him Macarius’s installation as abbot. In anger he heaped together very many charges to which truth does not consent.

But when he could not calm his rage by these means and, to the weariness of certain persons whose sight was sounder and therefore clearer, repeated the same things, he saw that he was accomplishing nothing and almost failing. He then summoned the prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, under whom I had served and whom I had succeeded in a private place, and by the authority in which he excels commanded him, under oath, to declare before all what he thought of me. The prior, however, as he had contrived by agreement—for on the previous day he had also recalled from his journey the messenger whom the chapter was sending to me, that I might come to Paris as quickly as possible—asserted that I was so weakened in body that I could fulfill neither this obedience nor another. [Col. 0684C]

Here I withdraw my pen and lay my finger upon my mouth. For it is written: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people”; and, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay”; and, “A false witness shall not go unpunished.” How far this is from the truth, the matter itself, by God’s favor, shows. For from the infirmity in which your exaltedness visited me, your servant, I recovered sound and wholly unharmed in every limb, once the humors which I had contracted from the unhealthiness of the place where I had lived for about five years had been purged.

Immediately the bishop seized upon the statement; sternly and imperiously he ordered the monks to depart, and, without examination either of the election or of the person, commanded that another person be chosen in haste. For these and similar acts he will render account to the supreme and just Judge. Because of these things, my sweetest Father, the eye of my inner man has been troubled; and, as a film clouds the pupil, it trembles, gropes, and fails before the sight of the true light. [Col. 0685A]

Knowing, therefore, that I can no longer have peace at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, I waver, I confess, whether I should return to the monastery of Morigny, where I entered as a young man and vowed in the common chapter to become a monk, or to the church of Coulombs, in which, when certain causes arose, I put on the monastic habit and made profession, and to which I promised I would return if I left the abbey of Morigny. May God therefore rain upon me through you the heavenly dew; and may I deserve to receive a written reply of your consolation, which I devoutly desire and humbly request. Farewell.

## LETTER CDLXXVII. A CERTAIN LADY TO ST BERNARD

[AMADUZZI, *Literary Anecdota Unearthed from Manuscript Codices*, vol. IV, p. 251. Rome, 1783, octavo.—See the preface to Letter 456.]

[Col. 0685B]

I confess that I am distressed on every side, because love compels me to stir in words him whom my soul loves; impatient understanding bubbles forth and affection expands. Yet the restraint of silence represses me: the stammering tongue does not express the thought, paper fails, the pen is blunted, and my hand, not formerly sluggish, is delayed.

For, like cursed Eve, I labor in pain not bodily but spiritually; I am oppressed by Sarah’s great anxiety, Rebecca’s longing desire, Rachel’s rivalry, and Leah’s contempt. And would that Jael’s prudence, Ruth’s importunity, Judith’s boldness, and Hadassah’s (Esther’s) winning favor were granted me, so that I might cover Sisera with a cloak, make Boaz my friend, and deceive Holofernes as I approached him—attempting nothing else like theirs for this good end—and might approach Ahasuerus as he sits upon his throne, to seek remedies for my languishing soul.

O Magdalene’s unspeakable joy, O consolation, O exultation! Kissing Jesus’ feet, the fruit of virginity, watering them with tears, wiping them with her hair, and anointing them with ointment, she carried away the antidote of salvation. When I keep these things, I serve Jesus. If permission were given and propriety allowed, I would expend from abundance and conceive delights. I think I would become half alive through the greatness of joy.

I rejoice because I speak to one who knows the Law, to whom all things have their meaning as they sound, who understands and expounds both figures and enigmas. Why should my distress extend our letter to your fatherhood [Col. 0685D], when at your voice, long ago, a great fire of love, greater than all telling, flamed up within me, so that every thicket of vanity was burned away and I cried with the bride in one voice: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love” [Song 5:8]? Who will grant that you too may languish and drink the cup from which you give drink?

Indulge me, Father, indulge me: I have become foolish; you compelled me. The charity which is in Christ urges me; I am indeed full of words, and the spirit of my womb constrains me. Therefore, ending my words, I beseech in Christ Jesus your lordship, which is unique and singular to me, interceding for the wounds [Col. 0686A], that you may remember your handmaid—and, I pray, your daughter—who offers and presents, as a token of incorrupt faith and not as a gift, through the bearer of this letter, an *enxenium* [a complimentary present], longing and panting to be consoled by your presence before I die.

## LETTER CDLXXVIII. B. TO ST BERNARD

[Note: A new letter.]

[Note: Undoubtedly by Bernard, who was abbot of Saint Anastasius near Rome, mentioned at the end of the letter. Letters 343 and 344 are by the same writer.]

Concerning an undisciplined monk.

To his most beloved Father BERNARD, by God’s grace abbot of Clairvaux, brother B.: as a weaned child upon his mother, may he have a land flowing with milk and honey.

1. I had resolved to cover my injuries with silence, except that I judged it right for truth to forestall falsehood. 378 How often and how insolently Brother R. [Col. 0686B] disputed with me within and outside the monastery; how many and how great scandals he knowingly and deliberately set before the little flock; with what erect neck and outstretched throat he opposed regular discipline and customs—he who considers labor and pain is witness; the whole congregation of brothers is witness, in whose ears and before whose eyes his contention has been poured out; his own conscience is witness too, even if his tongue speaks otherwise.

I give thanks to my God because, so far as concerns injury to me—if there was any—my patience came from him. I heard many words which a monk may not speak, and I became like a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth. I begged the man with many prayers, in private and in public, alone and with others, to spare both himself and us; to have mercy on his conscience and also upon our reputation in a foreign land, lest so new a planting be shaken by some storm. I argued, entreated, rebuked, mingling gentleness with threats, lest he make us an object of mockery and derision to those around us. I poured wine and oil alike into the wounds of our half-dead man; but his pain was incurable.

2. When almost every means of correction had been exhausted and the wound would not come to a scar, I feared lest the scab and rottenness of one member should infect the remaining parts of the body. But because I feared my own works, I long held back, fearing that he who had transformed himself into an angel of light might provoke me, under pretense of zeal for justice and love of the Order, to avenge my injuries. Therefore, calling upon the Lord for aid, that he might not allow me to turn aside to right or left, I forbade the proud and contumacious man to intone psalm or antiphon until he had amended the scandal which he was setting against the children of his mother. [Col. 0686D]

In all this his anger was not turned away, but his hand remained stretched out. For he who had formerly refused to sing when asked, sang when forbidden; he intoned antiphons, the mute man spoke, and the crowds were astonished. On the next day I suspended the man from the table. When he came up in opposition and, standing against me on the other side of the chapter-house face to face, hurled many reckless words, I answered briefly: “If anyone wishes to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.” Thus I escaped his hands.

Deeply angered—for he proclaimed me a novice and himself an old hand in the Order—he leapt out of the cloister; leaving the monastery gate, he went away alone. For Rome had drawn him there, not from love of propagating the Order, but, as he himself shamelessly confessed to the abbot, for contemplation of himself. May God see and judge, because, so far as lay in him, he caused our Order to stink before the abbot and before his servants.

## LETTER CDLXXIX. HUGH METELLUS TO ST BERNARD, IN WHICH HE EXTENSIVELY SETS FORTH HIS PRAISES

[Col. 0687B]

To the reverend and Christ-blessed father BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, most shining lamp, HUGH METELLUS, once a bearer of trifles, now a bearer of Christ’s cross: may you enter the sanctuary of Holy Scripture, gather up its fragments lest they perish, and shake out what is within from the cold stone.

1. “Your name is oil poured forth,” fragrant as crushed spices. The fame of your most illustrious name, spread far and wide, has passed even to the ends of the earth; and by its most sweet fragrance it has refreshed sea and dry land, drawing very many to the place from which it breathes. For, drawn by the scent, they tasted from the very spice a life-giving flavor; and those whom Stygian taste had infected—or rather whom the stench of Acheron had enfeebled [Col. 0687C] and stripped of their humanity—have been remade by nectar-like taste.

“Your life is oil poured forth.” Your life is a most brilliant lamp: shining, it burns; and burning, it shines. It burns for itself; it shines for another. Your life is a lamp that not only gives light nearby, but also illuminates things afar off. For your manner of life, glowing with diffused radiance, is not shut in but sent forth; not confused, but modestly poured out. By good example it illumines darkness, supplies light, humbles mountains, irradiates, fills, and makes bright the valleys. You are also a burning coal, which kindles extinguished coals through the nearby bellows of your good manner of life. For the whole course of your life instructs very many by the example of good living, reforms what is misshapen, renews what has been restored, strengthens what has been stripped of its crust [Col. 0687D], and, giving forth the fragrance of sweetness not in darkness but in the sight of the sun, makes all things fragrant.

2. “Your word is oil poured forth.” The talent entrusted to you—the talent, I say, of speaking and persuading—you do not keep enclosed, but distribute by measure. Your words steam with the fire of charity and are sweetened with the nectar of gentleness. Your tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe. Your tongue is the tongue of an enchanter who charms wisely. You speak a new tongue—new, I say—when you sound forth sacred mysteries and proclaim the praises of the Creator.

Under your tongue are new things and old, body and shadow. Under your tongue are grace and law, not the examined dregs of the Law. Under your tongue are milk and honey, not deceit, not gall. Your tongue is a honeycomb distilling [Col. 0688A] honey. You do not beat the air in vain; you do not treat useless matters. You do not speak with your finger or make a clamor with your foot: you order all things with gentleness. For in your possession the wolf lies down with the lamb, the leopard with the kid, and a little child leads them.

“Your word is oil poured forth.” The law of clemency is in your speech. When you preach mercy, pardon to the fallen, consolation to the desolate, hope and counsel to the despairing, you pour forth oil. When you refresh with honeyed speech the athletes sweating in God’s arena and sinking beneath excessive toil, give them drink from a milky fountain, and anoint them with sweet discourse, you pour out oil. Your word is a dripping rain in which the sprouting seed rejoices; it is an intoxicating torrent, multiplying shoots. When, by the balance of discernment, you separate the honorable from the dishonorable and the useful from the useless, you strain [Col. 0688B] oil from lees in the press and separate chaff from grain in the winnowing basket. When you search out the spiritual meaning in the letter, you draw out, by the press of reason, oil from the case in which it lay hidden. Oil mixed with water rises above it; so the spiritual meaning which you seek rises above the literal. Oil mixed with wine seeks the higher place; so the mercy which you preach exalts itself above judgment, etc.

3. When I read your writings, they speak to me in your very voice and set forth those same salutary admonitions; but they do not yield to me, nor do they satisfy me. Speak yourself; kiss me yourself with the kiss of your mouth. I wish to see you with unveiled face, not through a mirror in an enigma. Kiss me yourself—not with your mouth by joining lips to lips, for I am unworthy, but with a kiss; not with the kiss of your writings [Col. 0688C], nor with those which preach good things concerning you, but with the kiss of your mouth: that is, with honeyed speech proceeding from your delightful mouth. For by speaking and exhorting, you will draw me after you: draw me, I say, not unwillingly, but voluntarily. Voluntarily: for although it be difficult to follow you—although Caucasus, Parnassus, and the Alps stand between you and me—still the fragrance of goodness draws me after you. Drawn, I shall run in the fragrance of your ointments, that by the fragrance I may reach the taste.

For you will introduce me into your storehouses, where are dishes of diverse kinds and cups seasoned with various flavors; fed by these and made drunk by these, I shall be brought into the chamber of the eternal King, where I may rejoice forever. I said, “I shall run after you,” but not “to you,” because I have not yet resolved within myself to exchange the angelic habit of the white Nazarites for another habit. It is good for me to remain thus, etc. What I have said above, venerable father, I have said specially to you, concerning you, and for your sake. Now I loosen my pen and invite others with you to hear what I shall say: in it I rebuke my errors, lament the misery of the world, and invoke the relief of your prayers, etc.

380. LETTER 480. OF THE SAME HUGH METELLUS TO ST BERNARD. He attempts to clear himself and his people from an accusation.

To BERNARD, most serene abbot of Clairvaux and blessed in Christ, HUGH METELLUS, once a member of Aristotle’s household, now a servant of Christ: may you ascend from Jericho to Jerusalem.

[Col. 0689A]

1. The beautiful places of the wilderness grow fat, and Clairvaux abounds in grain, on which the leopard feeds with the lamb and the lion with the calf; by whom the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and by whom the abominations of the Egyptians are sacrificed to the Lord God; where beasts become human beings, and angelic ways of life arise within human nature. May God’s generous right hand add ever more gifts to Clairvaux; may he make it, from bright, brighter, and from brighter most bright. Blessed assembly, blessed harmony, where the north wind does not blow, scorching the lands, but the rainy south wind nourishes beds of spices.

2. We send you, venerable father, our abbot: to see, to converse, and to be edified. For it is pleasant to see your angelic face, more pleasant to converse, and most pleasant [Col. 0689B] to be edified. We send you an innocent man, full of honey and without gall; for he has more honey than gall, more love than dread; prudent in simplicity and simple in prudence; a turtledove in chastity and a dove in simplicity.

3. It has been reported to us, reverend father, that it has been reported to you that the cloister which encloses us encloses few or no religious persons. If your informant reported “none,” he spoke falsely; if he reported “few,” he speaks truly and agrees with me. For we are few. But if he did not understand it in that way, but separates a few from the small number and places them at the left hand, this is not surprising, though it is pitiable.

For, to say nothing of present events and to recall earlier times, the ark of blessed Noah placed clean and unclean animals together in its bosom [Col. 0689C]. The house of the patriarch had one good member and another reprobate one. Finally, Christ’s school gathered eleven men of sound mind and endured one madman among the others; it also had other disciples whose names, according to present justice, he said were written in the book of life, but which, according to God’s foreknowledge, had been erased from that same book. Pride also ascended into the cloister of heaven, from which it fell disgracefully.

If, I say, your wicked informant separates a few reprobate persons from the number of the approved, let him see to it—let him take heed—with what eye he speaks. If it is dim, let him wipe and anoint his bleary eye with eye-salve, so that he may see more clearly and may not perceive another’s faults with such sharpness as an eagle [Col. 0689D] or an Epidaurian serpent, while viewing his own with bleary, anointed eyes. It is not safe, in doubtful matters, to offend God or one’s neighbor and to judge another’s servant. For I know the one who says: “Who are you, that you judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls” (Rom. 14:4).

Therefore, father, do not believe every spirit; let neither the tongue of flatterers and bleary-eyed men close your eye, nor the oil of the sinner make your head fat. For they seek your favor and their own glory through an imagined offense of others. I believe, father, that you possess the grace of discerning spirits and pour the oil of the seller upon the ground. Such runners are puncturers of other men’s thoughts, hunters of words and syllables. Such men have the form of eyes: they see others, but do not see themselves. But since the one perfection in human nature [Col. 0690A] is to know oneself imperfect—for “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)—“the best man is he who is troubled by the least things” (Horace, *Satires*, Book I, Satire 3, vv. 68–69). I recall a certain wise man who said and committed this memorable saying to writing: “I am not offended by a few blemishes where many things shine in an excellent body” (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, vv. 351–352).

4. I know, father, I know that, moved by charity and with the Apostle leading the way (1 Cor. 7:7), you wish all men to be like yourself. But it is a difficult labor to attain you, more difficult to follow you. For just as the sight of the outward man is dazzled by looking upon [Col. 0690B] the sun’s sphere, so the sight of the inward man is struck dumb at the sight of your virtues. Let the sated therefore stoop to the hungry, the healthy to the sick, the perfect to the imperfect; and let him pray that the hungry may be filled, the sick strengthened, and the imperfect made perfect. But almighty God, who made you when you were not and perfected you when you were imperfect—almighty, I say—has not become powerless; his arm has not been shortened, nor has his mercy been diminished.

LETTER 481. OF THE SAME HUGH METELLUS, IN THE PERSON OF HIS ABBOT, TO ABBOT WILLIAM. He excuses the fact that he answers rather harshly to the slanders of his Herbert.

To WILLIAM, venerable and beloved in Christ, abbot, [Col. 0690C] SIEBAUD, humble abbot of Saint-Leon: may you happily triumph over the roaring lion and the one prowling around Christ’s sheepfold.

1. Receive our letter with a devout and right hand, and read through whatever has been written in it. There is no salt in it, no bitterness, nothing to sadden your spirit. Our approach to you is peaceful; our speech bears an olive branch, not arms. Irritated by certain harsh reports, we were stirred against our brother Herbert because he had published harsh and vain things concerning us; and, stirred, we wrote harsh things against him in response to harsher ones. For we are human beings. No injury suffered by a person seems small to him; many also receive such injuries more seriously than is fair. Beyond this, the injury to our God, whose covenant he made void, provoked us much more than our own—although what is ours belongs to God, and what is God’s belongs to us.

Since, however, being angered and inwardly touched by zeal for God, we scattered harsh words against our brother, we did this neither without reason nor without the authority of Holy Scripture. Paul saddened the Corinthians, recently converted by him, by harsh and shameful words, and corrected them when saddened (1 and 2 Corinthians); he openly pronounced the bewitched Galatians such [Gal. 3:1]: had he addressed them more mildly, he would not have corrected them, etc.

2. But brother Herbert—if indeed he is a brother—described in his letter, not as was fitting, that I had sent a river after him to swallow him up. To say nothing of the fact that he contemptuously called me “the man,” suppressing the title of abbot [Col. 0691A], he also called me an archer in the same writing and armed my hand with a drawn bow. This indeed would be tolerable as a metaphor, if he had not added that I was shooting poisoned arrows. He returned like for like; he avenged his injury by our injury.

But let it be certain to your Charity, good father, that I mourn with paternal affection the lapse of our brother and await his resurrection with open bosom and outstretched hands. For I wait to see whether somehow he may recover his senses, whether somehow he may return to himself. As I declared at the beginning of my little document, so, while dictating, I poured forth harsh words against brother Herbert, and embittered both the brother and you in the brother. But because “the anger of man does not work the righteousness of God,” I did not kindle all my anger, but restrained it—indeed, extinguished [Col. 0691B] it—etc.

382. LETTER 482. OF HAIMO, ARCHDEACON OF CHÂLONS, TO BERNARD.

[Note: Guido, formerly dean of Laon, was elected bishop of Châlons in 1142, but was consecrated only in 1144. Concerning his election, see Bernard’s Letters 221 and 224. When he came to “his see, he immediately made, in the very first year of his consecration, a young cleric of the Church of Laon named Haimo—who had gone with him—archdeacon of that same see.” These words of Hermann of Laon, in Book III of *The Miracles of Blessed Mary*, chapter 25, are to be understood of this Haimo. We received the two letters of his printed here from the venerable N. of Saint-Remigius, likewise archdeacon of Châlons. Moreover, after Bartholomew, Guido’s successor, this same Haimo was himself made bishop of Châlons in 1152. [Col. 0691D; 0692D]]

To the reverend father and lord B., venerable abbot of Clairvaux by God’s grace, H., by the same grace humble archdeacon of the Church of Châlons: may you walk blamelessly before God and men.

Lord, behold, he whom you love is grievously ill. For he suffers from a quartan fever. I therefore ask you, father, since I burn with great fevers, to deign to help me by the great prayers of the saints who are with you. For I know—know knowingly—that if you bow down to the ground and touch the Lord Jesus with that strong touch of prayer which is your custom, power will go forth from him to heal, and [Col. 0691C] his Spirit will blow and melt away all my sickness. May your Holiness fare well in the Lord, my lord and most loving father. Would that I might deserve consolation and a reply from your hands, and receive from the bread of your refreshment, with God’s blessing and yours.

LETTER 483. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME.

To lord father B., worthily to be venerated, abbot of Clairvaux by God’s grace, H., by the same grace, what he is: the best portion in the lot of the saints.

Having received an occasion for requesting your Sermons on the *Song of Songs*, I have been compelled to write to you, reverend father; and I would not have presumed to do so without cause. What permission, indeed, has an unlearned young man such as I to trouble the ears of a most learned old man, whom the Lord Jesus has instructed in his doctrine as a man instructs his son? And who [Col. 0692A] am I, to question one who sees, whose eyes are in his head? Especially since I am a child and do not know how to speak, least among my brothers and a newly planted shoot in my youth. Far be it, my lord, far be it from the habits and training of my youth, that I should dare to speak to you without cause, much less carry on learned discourse with you.

But, as I said, an occasion has now presented itself for requesting your Sermons, which I have often sought through messengers, urging at the proper time and out of season; and now I press my request with still more importunate letters. Surely, if I were someone of consequence, would I not rightly have taken offense that this book of yours passes through the mouths and bosoms of everyone, yet escapes me alone? Why is this, my lord? Perhaps you have judged me unworthy. To this I reply: if you knew me to be unworthy and incapable [Col. 0692B] of understanding, why did you promise? But if you judged me upright and diligent, why do you delay? I beg you, lord, delay no longer what you promised. Announce also to me the good tidings which you have scattered among others concerning those spiritual nuptials, at which you have so often been present as best man. Break the bread of the word; set before me the honeycomb which your hands have distilled, so that I may have something by which to be refreshed during these days of fasting. May your Holiness fare well, my lord father, supreme arbiter of divine and human matters, teacher of Christ’s worshippers, chariot of the Church and its charioteer.

LETTER 484. [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1148.] G. TO ST BERNARD. To excuse the bishop of Amiens from the overseas expedition.

[Col. 0692C]

To the sweetest father and lord B., abbot of Clairvaux by God’s grace, brother G., what a son owes to a father.

Certain matters have been conveyed to the ears of our lord, the bishop of Amiens [Note: That is, Theodoric, who was first a monk of the monastery of Saint-Nicholas in the diocese of Laon; afterwards abbot of Saint-Eloi of Noyon; and finally bishop of Amiens, consecrated by Samson, archbishop of Reims, one year after the consecration of Guido of Châlons—that is, in 1145—according to Book III, chapter 26, of Hermann’s *Miracles of St Mary of Laon*. Theodoric’s letter to Suger, among the Sugerian letters, no. 24, replies to this letter; in it he declares that he is in no way adequate for the royal expedition. His letter no. 34 is likewise found there. Col. 0692D], which greatly terrified him. He is a humble man and thinks very little of himself; but what humility does not believe, frequent reports have brought into doubt. The king, he has been told, wishes to have him as companion on his pilgrimage, and is said to have the consent of the lord pope in this matter. It is a great dignity and sufficiently pleasant, if impossibility did not protest. He is poor and infirm, so that neither his body can meet the labor nor his money meet the need.

Those who know the matter know how necessary he is for restraining plunderers [Col. 0692D] and protecting Christ’s poor who are in his diocese; we ourselves know it, having learned the matter. We are therefore compelled by affection of charity humbly to entreat your compassion [Col. 0693A], that, if possible, you secure his excuse in this matter, having regard to the common welfare of the churches and contending against the grave illness by which he is afflicted. Farewell.

LETTER 485. [Note: Written about the year 1152.] OF SAMSON, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS, TO ST BERNARD. Concerning the status of the monastery of Mores, diocese of Langres.

SAMSON, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to his dearest and most heartfelt friend BERNARD, venerable abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux: greeting, and blessed perseverance in the purpose of holy religion.

Complying with the petitions of your Holiness with due diligence, we labored long and greatly with the abbot and canons of Saint Denis [Col. 0693B], that they might give us the church at Mores with all its appurtenances, in order that an abbey of the Order of Clairvaux might be established there; and this we could scarcely obtain. But at last, with the Lord’s favor, they gave us that church with all its appurtenances, on the condition, namely, that an abbey of the Order of Clairvaux should be made there. We therefore grant and give that church, with all its appurtenances, to you and to the holy congregation of Clairvaux, on the express condition that you establish there an abbey of the Order of Clairvaux without the hindrance of further delay. May your Holiness fare well in the Lord, and continually pray to the Lord for us and for the churches entrusted to us [Col. 0693C].

LETTER 486. [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1152.] OF HENRY, BISHOP OF TROYES, TO ST BERNARD CONCERNING THE ABBEY OF BOULANCOURT.

To the venerable and most reverend father BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, and to his successors regularly appointed, I, HENRY, bishop of Troyes, send perpetual greeting.

1. If we devote care and vigilance to monasteries and churches established in our bishopric, that they may make progress for the better, we hope for help from him who has care of all things and expect a reward. In our bishopric there was a church of canons called Boulancourt, having an abbot, canons, lay brothers, and women, all of whom had vowed a life of holiness. Since discipline had altogether failed there, insolence reigned, and propriety had perished, I came when summoned by the inhabitants of that place, who could no longer sustain themselves. There I was asked with many prayers by the abbot of that place and by all alike—canons, lay brothers, and women—to grant that church itself and all its possessions, which could no longer stand on their own, to God and the Cistercian Order, and especially to the venerable father and house of Clairvaux, to be reformed and possessed forever according to the custom of the Cistercian Order. The abbot of the aforesaid place resigned [Col. 0694A] the abbey into our hand and restored it for the use of Clairvaux.

2. Seeing therefore that almighty God had through your zeal, wisdom, and religious devotion almost illuminated and corrected the whole world, I give that church, with all its possessions, forever to the Cistercian Order, to your Paternity, and to the house of Clairvaux. Among these are the following, which we have thought fit to record by their proper names: the land adjoining the abbey; the grange of Frigid Fountain; Perta in Rosteria; Perta-Haymonis; Perta-Sicca; Domni-Peruclum; Brulia, with all the appurtenances and dependencies of those granges; and everything which the aforesaid church possessed in demesne. And lest this should be altered through the age of time or the perversity of any person [Col. 0694B], or should perish altogether, we have confirmed it by the protection of our seal. This was done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, while Louis the Younger was king of the Franks.

LETTER 487. [Note: Written in the year 1126. Previously Letter 465.] OF GEOFFREY, BISHOP OF CHARTRES, TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF PARIS. Concerning peace between him and Stephen of Garlande.

Concerning the restoration of peace between you and Stephen of Garlande, we spoke to you some time ago at his request. Now, however, because we have heard that, setting aside certain matters which he seemed to have against you, he desires peace with you, we counsel the discretion of your Holiness—whom we love from the affection of our heart and to whom we cannot give counsel except such as serves your honor [Col. 0694C]. We counsel and request, I say, that you appoint for him a suitable day and time on which, according to the consideration of reason, you may restore peace with him—the peace which he offers you for the knowledge and examination of your friends, namely the abbot of Clairvaux. For it does not become your fatherhood to reject the peace offered, which, even if not offered, you ought by every means to seek. For, following the example of the Lord and Savior, you ought to seek the wandering sheep and carry it back, even on your shoulders, to the fold of peace. If, as the Apostle says, we ought to have peace with all people, how much more with those for whom we must answer to the Lord? Therefore, God forbid, if you do not accept the aforesaid man’s satisfaction in accordance with the judgment of your friends [Col. 0694D], it is certain that you incur offense before God and bring shame upon your friends. Farewell.

LETTER 488. [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1153.] OF HUGH, BISHOP OF OSTIA [Note: He was formerly a monk of Clairvaux; Bernard’s Letters 287, 290, etc., are addressed to him.] TO THE CISTERCIAN CHAPTER. On the death of Pope Eugenius III.

To the fathers most beloved in Christ, GOSWIN, abbot of Cîteaux, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, and the entire Cistercian chapter gathered for God’s honor, [Col. 0695A] HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Ostia: the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

As sacred authority teaches, “all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40:6). The days of man are brief: man passes like a shadow and never remains in the same state. He vanishes like smoke and falls like a leaf carried off by the wind (Job 14:5, 2; 8:9; 13:25). The glory of the Church, father of justice, lover and patron of religion, who had trampled beneath his own strength the necks of the proud and exalted; who sat upon David’s throne and over his kingdom, to strengthen and establish the Church entrusted to him, which he had restored to an exalted state—our father and defender, Pope Eugenius of blessed memory, having put off the robe of flesh, passed, undefiled in flesh, to Christ on the eighth day before the Ides of July [8 July]. He went out to meet Christ in the air and so will always be with the Lord, following the Lamb wherever he goes.

Contrary to everyone’s expectation—for he had almost brought the senate to nothing—his funeral was celebrated by clergy and people for two days, beyond the customary manner, so that one would already have believed him reigning in heaven, who was honored so in death upon earth [Col. 0695B]. Oh, how great was everyone’s grief! How great especially the lamentations of orphans and widows! One would have said already that he was with God, who was so mourned by the people. Without doubt he was snatched from the snare of hunters: the snare was broken and he himself delivered, caught up—as we believe, who know his conscience—even to the third heaven, not leaving us orphans, as some suppose.

For he who is with God will pray for us to God the Father and the Only-Begotten with the Holy Spirit, who is God blessed forever. But you, from whose fellowship he was chosen to sit among princes and hold the throne of glory, pray for him; establish perpetual benefactions, that God may pardon him and increase for him the crown of glory. Pray likewise for our brother of good memory. And for us, who remain in this vale of misery, in this region of unlikeness, and in the midst of a crooked generation—and for the Roman Church, which in so brief a space has fallen from such a high rank into the depth of the abyss of hell—we likewise ask that you pray, lest it be sunk into the depths of this great sea, in which are creeping things without number [Col. 0695D].

Furthermore, we earnestly ask that, if our smallness has any weight in your eyes, you kindly and effectively hear the petitions which the bearers of this letter will make to you concerning the house of Saint Anastasius, the house of Fossanova, and the house of Casamari [Col. 0696A]. Otherwise, know that great scandal is felt on this account.

385. LETTER 489. [Note: Written about the year 1154.] OF BARTHOLOMEW, FORMER BISHOP AND NOW MONK, TO SAMSON, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS. He gives an account of his administration.

To the venerable and ever-beloved lord SAMSON, archbishop of Reims, and to the holy assembly gathered in his presence, brother BARTHOLOMEW, a poor monk at Foigny: to those who love mercy and truth.

1. The solemnity of this holy assembly commands my modesty to be silent; but the imminent danger to my reputation [Col. 0696B] opens my brow and urges me to speak openly. For I cannot conceal what common opinion has published among many, and what has even flown to the ears of the lord pope: namely, the report that I diverted episcopal revenues, a report to which the bishop of Laon gives more credence than is just. It is therefore for me to confess the truth concerning these matters; it will be for you to consider and defend what is just.

2. The see of Laon was sad and grieving when I first entered it, worn down by seditions and burned by fires. The property of the greater church itself was likewise distressed, and its revenues meager. If I extended my hand to it that it might rise, God knows, and the sons of the Church know. Nevertheless, I gave it nothing that belonged to the bishop’s revenues, except pigs, which our countrymen commonly call *verres* [boars], and which churches paid to the episcopal household table. These, I say, I granted for the prebend of the canons, because I could neither exact them without shame nor possess them without trouble.

Moreover, I found only five abbeys in our diocese [Note: Namely Saint-Vincent at the city; Saint-Michael in Thierache; Saint-Nicholas in the Wood; Saint Mary of Nouvion; and Saint-Nicholas in the Meadow—monasteries of men—besides the convents of Saint John in the city itself and of Aurigny in the same diocese. Col. 0695D], equally fallen into ruin in resources and religious discipline. In these, as the Lord God multiplied his mercy, the number of holy persons increased both in number and merit, and their possessions were enlarged. Moreover, nine monasteries of the new religious life were founded in various places in the same diocese [Note: Hermann of Laon lists these in Book III of *The Miracles*: namely, Prémontré; Saint-Martin in the city; Tenelles; Clairfontaine; and Cuissy, of the Premonstratensian Order; Foigny, Le Pin, and Val-Claire, of the Cistercian Order, for men. He added as the ninth Montreuil, at the foot [Col. 0696D] of the hill of Laon, for nuns of the same institution. Hermann judges that the Church of Laon ought to be preferred to others on account of this one monastery, since before it no abbey of women of this kind of religious life had existed. “Having laid aside all linen garments,” says the same author, “and furs, they used only woolen tunics; and, working continually and silently with their hands not only in spinning and weaving but also in digging fields, clearing woods, and pulling up thorns and briars, they sought their livelihood after the example of the monks of Clairvaux.”]. In their persons number almost exceeds number; their religious life is a model of religious life; their possessions are so great as to suffice abundantly for so many.

3. If I denied that I extended the hand of benefaction [Col. 0696D] to the old churches, that they might rise, and to the new ones, that they might stand up, I would lie. I indeed benefited almost all the churches, but neither as much as I wished nor as much as I ought. Pope Calixtus entrusted to our faith Lord Norbert, whose memory is blessed, [Col. 0697A] that I might give him a place and assist his purposes. I therefore granted him land belonging to the bishop, though it scarcely sufficed for two ploughs. One part lies at Versigny; another near Cuissy, though it had for many years lain uncultivated and barren. Of the things belonging to episcopal revenues, therefore, I do not recall having diverted anything further. Yet, with your favor and consent, certain persons gave lands to churches which they held from us as benefices; but I remitted to no one at all either the land-rent or the wine dues.

4. As for the advantage or honor that accrued thereafter to that see, I do not wish human judgment to pronounce upon it. But if in anything I sinned as a man, I do not refuse to be put to shame before men. I therefore wished to plead our case before you as judges and to make it known to you as witnesses; and in so doing I do not fear an accuser, since I speak the truth. Yet allow me [Col. 0697B] to venture something further before you; allow me to speak something human. Did no dignity and glory accrue to our see when it brought forth so many and such great churches, when it multiplied so many religious persons? Why then, as I hear, does the lord of Laon prepare war without witnesses [Note: Bartholomew was succeeded in 1151, after thirty-eight years of rule, by Walter, formerly the first abbot of Saint-Martin in the city. After three years Walter was succeeded by another Walter, called “of Mauritania,” formerly dean of the Church of Laon; he caused this lawsuit against Bartholomew, then a monk. How far this suit and controversy was carried, especially against the Premonstratensians, who had been among the first to experience Bartholomew’s benefactions, may be learned from the letters of Pope Adrian IV written to Louis the Younger, reported in the *Bibliotheca Praemonstratensis*. Col. 0697D; 0698D]? Why does he attempt what perhaps he is not permitted to accomplish? If I gathered together God’s children, if I received a righteous man in the name of a righteous man, let no one be angry with me; let another take care not to scatter what has been gathered. May the almighty Father preserve you for the honor of his name and, through you, strengthen the religious devotion and holiness of his Church.

LETTER 490. [Note: Written in the year of Christ 1132.] OF THURSTAN, ARCHBISHOP OF YORK, TO WILLIAM, BISHOP OF CANTERBURY [Note: For the subject of this letter, see Bernard’s Letters 94 and 313. Letters 95 and 319 were written to Thurstan; in the former Bernard congratulates him on this act.].

[Col. 0697C]

To the most reverend lord WILLIAM, archbishop of Canterbury by God’s grace and legate of the Apostolic See, THURSTAN, by the same grace archbishop of York, wishes progress in Christ and never failure.

1. The highest honour of ecclesiastical rank is to share one’s deepest counsels with the sons and leading men of the Churches amid the most difficult circumstances. Therefore, venerable lord and distinguished father, we have resolved to inform Your Paternity of an unusual occurrence which recently took place among us at York. For it is sufficiently well known and certain to many [Col. 0697D] how greatly the renowned monastery of Saint Mary at York has shone in the ears of all by the goodness and fame of its virtue. Within a few years it had increased exceedingly in resources and had laudably grown abundant in the number and religious observance of its brethren.

But since there can be no doubt that virtues flourish and endure less strongly amid wealth, some brethren of that monastery, nearly half a year ago, moved, I think, by divine prompting [Col. 0698A], began to be deeply troubled about the manner and condition of their way of life; and, as they themselves testify, their consciences reproaching them, they were distressed by many anxieties. Indeed, they feared that they were almost deceiving themselves if an undertaking worthy of so great a vow did not follow. The said York brethren were therefore struck with inexpressible dread because they saw that they seemed to fulfil the vow of their profession in no matters, or at least in the smallest matters; rightly fearing lest they might be running, or had run, in vain, if punitive vengeance did not condemn them as guilty of so great disobedience to their vow. For they believed it to be a crime—or rather madness—to carry the Rule of blessed Benedict, not for the advancement of salvation, but for a judgement of death.

Moved by these considerations, the aforesaid brethren endeavoured to make known to their prior, Richard by name, the grievous [Col. 0698B] agitations of their minds. Pleading fear of transgression, they begged for his support in reforming their vow; and, lest consideration of prosperity or fear of adversity should make him hesitate to help, they adjured him by the Spirit of God and in Christ’s name. He was alarmed at the novelty of the matter; and although among his own brethren he enjoyed every advantage of agreeable fortune, upon hearing of a better life he weighed the uncertain chances of declining prosperity, as it were with a censor’s intention. Shortly afterward, using, as the matter required, the counsel of inward virtue, he immediately distinguished and decided between the alternatives. He promised not merely assistance, but that he himself would be a companion in the same vow. In brief, soon their number grew to almost thirteen, who proposed to strive for the reform [Col. 0698C] of their manner of life according to the Rule of blessed Benedict—or rather, the truth of the Gospel [p. 387].

2. Therefore, on the vigils of the apostles Peter and Paul, our beloved brother Richard, the prior, upon whom almost the whole care of the monastery depended, took with him his subprior Gervase, a man named among his fellow monks as religious, and took care to explain familiarly to his lord abbot the matter that was under discussion. Thus the lord abbot—a man certainly upright and good according to his understanding and natural ability, but exceedingly simple and unlearned—was horrified at the marvel of this new report. He denied that he could alter in his own little place the ancient rites and customary usages which the general multitude had observed almost throughout the whole world.

But the lord prior, being well educated [Col. 0698D], said: “We are striving, father, to introduce nothing crude or new. We ought to take up and observe with all our strength, by grace, the true and ancient religious life of our blessed father Benedict—or rather, the most ancient Gospel of Christ, which precedes all religious observances and rules. We disparage none of the other monks; we do not begrudge their institutions. We know that in every place [Col. 0699A] service is rendered to one Lord and military service to one King, and that the grace of God has the same power in the marketplace and in the cloister. Job also proved stronger upon the dungheap than Adam in paradise. Finally, whatever blessed Benedict established was so wholly ordained by the providence of the Holy Spirit that nothing more useful, more holy, or more blessed could have been devised.

“And since he knew and proclaimed that idleness is hostile to the soul, he appointed fixed times for earnest reading and prayer, and fixed times also for labour and industry, so that in the one he might wholesomely exercise the soul, in the other the body, and in both remove weariness. He further says: ‘We condemn buffooneries, idle words, and speech provoking laughter to perpetual closure in all places, and we do not permit a disciple to open his mouth for such speech’ (*Rule of St Benedict*, ch. 6). And elsewhere he says: ‘Monks ought at all times to cultivate silence, but especially during the night hours’ (*ibid.*, ch. 42). How carefully this decree is observed is known to anyone who has become acquainted with our customs. For while some go to church after the conference, others in turn withdraw to trifles and useless, chattering talk. As though the evil of the day were not enough for itself, unless its own evil were also added to the night.”

3. He added much besides concerning the extravagance of foods, the pleasant and ceremonial succession of drinking-bouts, and the costly refinement of garments. “Our blessed father Benedict neither thought nor taught in this way. For with him it is not the colour of clothing but its warmth that is considered [Col. 0699C]; not the flavour of dishes that is sought, but necessity is met by sparingness in food. Blessed Benedict recognizes as his own only those who live in monasteries under a Rule and an abbot.

“Moreover, if it pleases you, venerable father, let us return to evangelical purity, evangelical perfection, and peace; and let us see how little, or scarcely at all, there shines in our morals or actions what Christ taught. We desire everything; we grow angry and quarrel; we seize what belongs to others and litigiously reclaim what is our own; we defend frauds and lies; we follow the flesh and its desires. We live for ourselves and please ourselves; we fear being conquered and boast of having conquered; we oppress others and avoid being oppressed; we envy others, glory in our own successes [Col. 0699D], jest, grow fat upon other people’s sweat, and the whole world is insufficient for our wickedness.

“Although the Gospel may seem dead and impossible in us, let us look at the monks of Savigny and Clairvaux, who recently came to us. How clearly the Gospel shone in them, so that, if it is permitted to say so, it is more useful to imitate them than to recite the Gospel. When their holy way of life is seen, the Gospel is judged, as it were, to come alive again in them. They alone do not reclaim what is theirs; they alone possess nothing by which they might strive to set themselves before their neighbours. They alone do not seek their neighbours’ loss. They are content with a modest cultivation of land and the use of livestock; indeed, they do not desire to possess even these except so long as God wills, because, when God wills them to be taken away, they would not seek what is unlawful.

“To them, I think, it belongs [Col. 0700A] to say: ‘The world has been crucified to us, and we to the world’ (Gal. 6:14). To them it belongs to say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors’ (Matt. 6:12), since they have no debtor from whom they wish to exact anything. Blessed is the race of men whose clothing, food, and entire manner of life savour of the Gospel. God alone is their portion. They alone are known fully, as far as human capacity permits, to fulfil love of God and neighbour; for, cleaving to God alone, they have so completely forsaken all temporal things except a modest and contemptible dress that they desire nothing for which their neighbour might reasonably be angry with them.

“Therefore, father, may it never seem impossible to keep the Rule of blessed Benedict [Col. 0700B], since God has supplied us with such examples, who have preceded us in holy virtues, that we may follow them. But if, because of the proximity and noise of peoples, we cannot wholly follow their purity, at least let us attend to the manner of life and profession prescribed by our Rule, because we are not monks but dead men.”

4. In this manner Lord Prior Richard spoke with his lord abbot Geoffrey about reforming his monastery. The lord abbot did not receive these words very pleasantly, because it is difficult to remove long-standing practices. Yet, confessing himself less discerning and unlearned, he asked that it might be made more fully known to him in writing how such practices could be carried on in his house. Richard willingly embraced this request and fulfilled the commission he had undertaken with no sluggish effort [Col. 0700C].

He wrote, then, that they should use no conversations, garments, or foods other than those which the Rule seemed to permit; and he described the site and arrangement of the monastery so carefully that one might have thought the Rule scarcely capable of being observed better in the desert than in a city. He also arranged its possessions as faithfully as one versed in secular affairs could do, so that one might think that in none of them had he in any way fallen short of evangelical justice. Concerning the revenues of churches or tithes—holdings for whose investiture monks are commonly regarded as particularly blameworthy—he prescribed that everything should be received and carried out under the lawful and canonical direction of bishops, and spent only for the use of the poor, pilgrims, or guests; but he decreed that monks should live from the lawful cultivation of land and the use of livestock.

When all this began to be remarked upon among the others by rumour, the sudden rage of the rest erupted into such envy that they assigned to such a man and his close associates nothing except exile or strict confinement [Col. 0700D].

5. Nevertheless, after many friendly arguments conducted on both sides, the lord abbot said that he could with difficulty change what his predecessors seemed to have maintained. Wishing to use sound counsel in the matter, he deferred his complete answer until after the Nativity of the Blessed Mary.

6. Meanwhile the other brothers, vainly fearing that they would be restrained more than usual by the strictness of the Rule, began to rage against the prior and the others with almost Pharisaic [Col. 0701A] envy. Had delay not intervened through the kindness of certain persons, the onset of internal persecution would have exceeded all bounds. Meanwhile, the rumour of internal sedition fluttered among the crowds outside. We heard the clamour of the populace, although the truth of the matter itself remained hidden. Then, behold, Prior Richard, having joined to himself the subprior and the secretary of his monastery, took care to disclose the whole matter to us as it stood. They asked for the mercy of blessed Peter and of ourselves, that we might not refuse benign assistance to enable them to observe what they had vowed. They declared that necessity was already imminent, especially because the brethren had now conspired that, if any of them so much as murmured anything concerning their profession, he should be excluded from communion. Even some of the prior’s companions, intimidated by fear, affection, or [Col. 0701B] frivolity, were already withdrawing; peace was restored to them only if they confessed as a fault that they had murmured anything about keeping their profession.

7. Therefore I, Thurstan, by God’s grace Archbishop of York, hearing that Christ’s servants wished, according to the command of blessed Benedict, to set nothing before the love of Christ, feared that I might offend Christ’s grace in them if I did not take care to help their just petition with episcopal compassion. For the height of that office consists both in providing for the religious peace of monks and in sympathizing with the oppressed in necessity. Accordingly, after taking the counsel of religious persons, I summoned Lord Abbot Geoffrey and Prior Richard with his subprior to a more suitable place, so that [Col. 0701C] in the presence of religious persons I might bring both the brethren’s petition and the abbot’s answer to a peaceful conclusion.

They sought nothing other than what they had previously sought with many tears: that they might follow the poor Christ in voluntary poverty, bear Christ’s cross in their bodies, and not be hindered from fully observing evangelical peace and the Rule of their blessed father Benedict. For this they sought the lord abbot’s permission and paternal assistance. But the lord abbot tearfully confessed that their work would be far too necessary to him, promising that, because their vow was holy, he would not obstruct it; yet he did not dare promise them the assistance they sought without the knowledge of his chapter.

8. Thus the lord abbot returned home with his monks, peace having meanwhile been given and a day appointed on which I should come to their chapter and discuss the matter with the abbot in the presence of religious persons. Meanwhile the remaining brethren strove to rise against them with all the greater cruelty as they more openly sought to fulfil their vow. The brethren of Marmoutier and Cluniac monks dwelling in our neighbourhood were summoned, so that, with these men present and assenting, Richard and his companions might be deprived of every office and responsibility in their monastery as deserters and violators of the common Order. For after the abbot the chief care of the monastery had been entrusted to their hands. But this by the way.

On the appointed day, very early in the morning, I prepared to come to the monks’ chapter; and I had almost set foot upon the threshold of the door [Col. 0702A], accompanied by wise and religious men, whose names are these: Hugh the dean; William, prior of the regular clerics of Gisborough; William the treasurer; Hugh the archdeacon; Serlo the canon; Alfred, my chaplain and canon; and Robert, priest of the hospital. Our horses remained outside the gate with a few attendants.

9. Finally, when we entered the chapter-house door, as stated, the lord abbot met us at the very entrance with the monks, who filled the chapter-house completely. Unless I removed some of the clerics coming with me, he forbade us to enter.
