I could scarcely reply that I ought not to enter upon so serious a matter without my clerics, who were good and wise men and friends of theirs, when suddenly the whole chapter resounded with such clamour and uproar that it seemed rather the tumultuous roaring of seditious, drunken, and riotous men than the humility of monks—which was there entirely absent. Many rose up and rushed forward with arms bared as though to wrestle; they shouted that they would go out if I entered.

Then I said: “May God be my witness that I came as a father and thought to bring you no harm, desiring only peace and Christian brotherhood among you. But since you are attempting to take from me what belongs to episcopal authority and office, I likewise take from you what belongs to your need. Let your church therefore cease [Col. 0702C].”

Then one of them, named Simeon, said: “We would rather that our church should cease for a hundred years.” All assented to him, crying in a frenzied voice: “Seize them! Seize them!” Laying hold of the prior and his companions, they were already beginning to drag them away, intending, as they had agreed among themselves, either to throw them into prison or drive them into exile. Having no other hope of escaping their hands, Richard and his companions embraced me with their whole arms, asking for the peace of blessed Peter and of ourselves. Thus we scarcely returned to the church, while they raged and shouted even into the church: “Seize the rebels! Arrest the traitors!” We therefore sat in the church, while the abbot and his remaining monks returned to their chapter-house.

[Col. 0702D] 10. Meanwhile men of the abbey stood by with the doors and entrances shut, keeping watch as though in ambush. Then we, to tell the truth, fearing the monks’ attack, caused the church door leading into the cloister to be barred from within. Meanwhile the rumour spread and the people gathered. Yet nothing evil was said or done outside. Since no agreement could be achieved among the monks, we returned home, taking with us the aforesaid twelve priests and one subdeacon. Several of them were well educated; all desired the full observance alike of the Rule, their profession, and the Gospel. Thus they lodged in the house of blessed Peter and in our own house, not to be frightened from their purpose by any adversity of violence. But the brethren of the abbey nevertheless continued to rage in their own community [Col. 0703A]; the abbot set out on a journey, I do not know to do what.

11. Therefore we beseech Your Paternity through Christ that you may be willing to defend by your authority the side of those who wish to pass to stricter and narrower observance. If their abbot should come to you, then by the authority and wisdom given you by God restore him to peace, and admonish him not to hinder the holy purpose of his sons. But if he has gone ahead and departed, we ask that through the present messenger you send him letters of exhortation, that he may not obstinately oppose them but rather furnish assistance and opportunity to those who desire truly to obey Christ’s Gospel and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

At least in this matter the abbot and his monks ought to imitate the Egyptians and Babylonians, who allowed the children of Israel profitably to return to the land of promise. Laban also, after cruelly pursuing Jacob as he fled secretly because of Laban’s obstinacy, allowed him to return to his father. Nor should those be reckoned deserters but providers who, leaving a place where freedom to sin is greater, desire to serve God more safely. Indeed Christ himself, who rebukes the Pharisees because they neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter, ought to deter them.

For it is known to all that the Rule of blessed Benedict, throughout almost the entire and, so to speak, common world of monks, has utterly lost its measure and proper condition in all things. So much so that no one can sufficiently wonder that anyone dares solemnly to promise before God and his saints what he himself [Col. 0703C] daily neglects—or rather, to speak more truly, is compelled not to observe. There falls upon them what the prophet says: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29:13); and, as the Apostle says, “They profess to know God in words, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16).

12. Yet perhaps, because many act in this way, common practice gives confidence. But—what I declare sorrowfully—the confidence of monks is deceived, utterly deceived; for a multitude of sinners does not make crimes unpunishable. Hence those who wish to observe the rule of their profession ought not to be hindered but protected; nor should those be reproached who for this reason hasten to change their place. For God is not chosen from a place, but a place is chosen from God. Blessed Benedict also plainly testifies that in every place one serves the one Lord God and fights for the one King (*Rule*, ch. 61).

In the *Conferences of the Fathers*, Joseph the hermit sufficiently explains that he more rightly preserves the faith of his profession who transfers himself to that place in which he can more fully fulfil the Lord’s commands of faith (Cassian, *Conference* 17). And someone says: “It helps us to seek holy opportunity, he who is a helper in untimely seasons, in tribulation.” But those, I think, should be judged Pharisees or heretics who neither fear nor allow others to fear what Truth says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.” For if an angel from heaven should preach otherwise than what has been preached [Col. 0704A], let him be anathema. For he preaches otherwise than Christ preached who hastens to hinder those wishing to observe the angelic peace and the rule of their profession.

Whoever he may be, he must be vigorously refuted, since Truth says: “If your right eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you” (Matt. 5:20, 29). For nothing is more painfully injured or more carefully protected in the body than the eye; yet when it obstructs, it must be spiritually torn out. For this is to be wise as the serpent: to withdraw the whole head—that is, the mind—from every deceit that harms the soul.

13. Nevertheless, because of the scandal of the weak, who understand truth less well, we ask Your Holiness, and all who may be willing to hear this petition [Col. 0704B] of ours, to endeavour to restore peace between the abbot of York and the often-mentioned brethren. Finally, we ought to remember that a similar departure of the monks of Molesme first established and founded the most perfect standard of Cistercian life, which almost the whole Church admires. The lord Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, of venerable memory, praised in Christian piety the character of their purity and faithfully embraced the renewal and most approved integrity of the holy Rule.

Finally, when the complaint of jealous opponents came to apostolic notice under Pope Urban II, a decretal command was issued: the abbot who had departed with them was to be restored alone to the governance of his abbey, while none of the others who wished to persevere in the full observance of the Rule should suffer any hindrance or molestation [Col. 0704C]. It is clearer than daylight how greatly the truth of the whole Gospel shines in their most excellent way of life.

We have used a lengthy and almost wearisome discourse because the condition of the other monks—which perhaps will not please them—seemed fit to be set forth for judgement, lest it be disseminated by the judgement of jealous opponents otherwise than it occurred. May Your Holiness fare well in Christ.

## LETTER CDXCI. FASTRED, THIRD ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, TO A CERTAIN ABBOT OF HIS ORDER

FASTRED, unworthy servant and abbot of the monks of Clairvaux, to Abbot N., greeting in Jesus Christ and the spirit of greater evangelical poverty.

[Col. 0704D] 1. From the report of one who pities your soul as much as you indulge bodily appetites, we have learned that, forgetful both of your Rule and of the example that you ought to set before the eyes of your monks, you set a table in the guest-house, indulging your own desires while guests go without; and that in clothing and beds you imitate the rich feaster rather than poor Lazarus, not remembering the punishment which God threatens to those who rely upon the felicities of this life.

Surely, son and brother, it matters little to wear this habit if one is thereby plunged into hell. Any other path by which you may walk lies more open and broader. Since, however, God has called you to this, attend to it, lest you lose your reward. For such clothing has never been fitting within a cloister or monastery; and the clothing which you are accustomed to wear there is not of the quality prescribed for us by our statutes. Since the etymology of “monk” is solitude and sadness, how can costly clothing, smelling of the world’s pomp, suit one who is solitary? And how do signs of joy and exultation accord with one who is sad?

It is enough, my son, for a monk to have what remained to the holy Apostle Paul: namely, food able to sustain nature and life, and clothing able to cover the body. Whoever seeks more will more properly be called among us a hypocritical Pharisee, seeking honour by dress, than a disciple and imitator of evangelical poverty.

2. This is not the life which our father and predecessor Bernard of happy memory taught you and me [Col. 0705B], nor the practice followed by the abbots and monks of our sacred Order. They nourished us on bread made from oats, vegetables cooked without oil and [fat?] (abdomine), beans and peas, even on the feast-day of Easter itself; and this austerity, or one like it, is observed in all houses of the Order. And do you, as though you did not belong to this Order, procure for yourself delicate and sumptuous foods in order to satisfy gluttony? If you are abbot, and rule and example to your men, how do you dare to eat rich meats, fresh fish variously prepared, and bread baked outside the monastery by women?

I say, not without shame, what nevertheless must be said: many on God’s way are more perfect as subjects under their abbot, sailors under a helmsman, and soldiers under a commander, than their abbot, helmsman, or commander. In your monastery many are found who, at the time when you spend the hours of night in rich and superfluous suppers [Col. 0705C], devote themselves to prayer and undertake disciplines for the expiation and remission of sins.

How far you are, my father and brother, from the perfection of our companion who died in his very year of novitiate, and whom the strictness of abstinence accompanied to the end! For, seized by severe nausea and desiring a cooked egg, he would not reveal it—lest he lose the merit of a denied wish and appetite—until the last moment of his life, when he was already giving up his soul, and only after the abbot had first promised that he would not be compelled to fulfil that desire.

3. Where, then, O abbot established in religion and a man set as an example to others, is your merit to be compared with that novice? If Christ fasts before preaching; if Elijah fasts in order to be lifted up in a fiery chariot; if the Ninevites redeem themselves from destruction by fasting; if Esther saves her people and appeases Ahasuerus’ wrath by fasting; if Saint John the Baptist spends his whole life fasting to prepare the way for the Gospel; and if the saints have walked by this way: what way to heaven do you prepare for yourself by entering upon a way so different?

By gluttony the innocence of our first parents perished. Drunken Noah uncovered his shame, and Lot committed incest. After the people ate, they rose up and worshipped the calf. Amnon was killed at a feast, and there Holofernes let himself go. While feasting, Belshazzar saw the writing that foretold his death. And finally, at a banquet, the head was displayed of that supernatural wonder, than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women [Col. 0706A].

4. Since, therefore, so many have perished badly, how can matters turn out well for you? In your defence you adduce pains of stomach and head, and say that ordinary foods harm you. You are wholly mistaken if you believe that a monk can follow the medical practices of secular people. [Note: [Col. 0705D] See Letter 345 and the notes there.] For we come to a monastery in order to seek bodily discomforts, not comforts and pleasures. If weakness gave strength to Saint Paul, why do you strive to drive from your house the means of so many goods and their cause?

Believe me, my father, I have often seen Saint Bernard, in order to warm his stomach, eat porridge made of flour with added oil and honey, but with scruple [Col. 0706B]. When I accused him of this austerity, he replied: “My son, if you knew a monk’s obligation, every morsel you eat would have to be watered with tears. For we enter this monastery in order to lament our own sins and those of the people; and, eating the bread which they have prepared by their labours, we eat their sins, that we may mourn them as our own.”

He further added: “Nor is it enough for a monk to plead weakness. For the holy fathers, our elders, sought out damp and sloping valleys for building monasteries, so that monks who were frequently ill and had death before their eyes might not live securely.” If, therefore, the saints seek the means of illness, why do you seek them in order to fare sumptuously? And if they bring this means of so many goods upon us as a cause, under what dispensation do you consume and squander the goods of the monastery, under the excuse of weakness, upon the comforts of your body?

The infirmity of your soul, my brother, is greater than that of your body. For if it were in God’s grace, your body would not be so weak, nor so friendly to earthly delights. Therefore amend your elaborate habits and avoid exquisite feasts. Although I do not examine your vein, I know by what remedy you must be healed. And if this brotherly admonition, proceeding from a companion, is not sufficient, it will be necessary for me, as a superior, to apply the remedy.

## LETTER CDXCII. PETER OF ROYA, A NOVICE OF CLAIRVAUX, TO C., PROVOST OF NOYON

*He enumerates the errors of his former life and praises the excellent institution of Clairvaux.*

[Col. 0706D]

Brother PETER, novice of Clairvaux by the mercy of God, to his beloved C., provost of the holy mother church of Noyon—perhaps for a year, but, if he wishes, for ever to be a servant of the King of heaven—greeting in the One Same.

1. It is the custom of friends joined by Christ’s love but separated by distances of place that, though they cannot see one another or speak face to face, they nevertheless frequently regard one another in pious remembrance in Christ and speak to each other with mutual affections; with the secret and friendly voice of the heart they inquire after one another and pray for each other with deep groanings before God.

According to this law of love, I think, you too sometimes inquire within yourself, in the secret of your heart, what is happening to me, your beloved friend: what my intention is, what my condition and dress, what my desire. Perhaps in friendly concern you fear for my shoulders, which you know to be slight and judge weak for bearing the burden and sustaining the yoke of the life I have chosen. My beloved, many have trembled with fear where there was no fear. Since, therefore, you love me in the good Jesus, you ought not to fear such things. For these matters belong to the Lord, whose yoke is sweet and burden light.

Although I am insufficient to weigh the multitude of blessings which, every day, the ears and eyes of my body report to my soul, yet, in order to assure your heart concerning my condition and desire [Col. 0707B], I shall endeavour to set down for your Love a few things about Clairvaux, the poor of Christ dwelling there, and their order and manner of life—men whom my soul longs to imitate with faithful sighs.

2. First of all, I shall describe for you some part and manner of my former life—“manner,” I say, if I can call it a manner where there was rarely or never any moderation. I want you carefully to observe in this description, for your own advancement, from how many and how great deaths the goodness of the Saviour has now delivered me, and to glorify him who truly does not cast out any sinner coming to him.

If you read anything in me which you happen to discover as blameworthy also in yourself, I faithfully advise your brotherhood and welfare to hasten without delay to correct it while you may, for you do not know what a coming day may bring. Therefore, my beloved, while I was at Noyon and sat alone in the windows of the episcopal residence—often with you too, and with others—I repeatedly considered the arrangement of that house, noticed the beauty which presented itself to the eyes, new yesterday and growing old today, and in secret directed the memory and gaze of my mind to that perfectly ordered heavenly house, whose glorious, unbounded, ever-new beauty transcends every human thought.

But far from its path, wretched that I was, I saw myself as most miserable, knowingly walking in the broadness of the worst road. Unless it is escaped by vigilant care, one runs quickly and without return by that road to a very different house: namely, the house of pain, the house of ultimate and infinite ugliness, where no order dwells but everlasting horror, together with the worm that does not die and everlasting fire [Col. 0707D].

How rightly, then, I anxiously considered lest, as it had begun, love of the world should drag me there, wandering as I was through its broad and foolish desires, slippery and insatiable, so drunk that, to the extent of my ability and opportunity, I resisted no pleasure of my flesh—except that I often remembered that I too must die, and, stupefied by the fleeting joys of this world, reflected upon the marvels of eternal ages.

3. For while, at the table of our lord bishop, our fellow citizen—indeed, my enemy—I was sweetly fed, as was customary, in silver vessels [Col. 0708A], and not unwholesomely, so far as the vessels themselves were concerned; and while with the hand of my body I selected pleasant delicacies for myself, I often silently read in those same vessels, with the hand of the heart, a very different food. But you, my beloved, though you reclined quite near me, did not know that I was reading this.

What then? Do I condemn daily festive dishes or blameless platters? Do I accuse that liquid whose colour gently smiled upon the eyes and whose flavour answered sweetly upon the palate, or the silver cups? Far from it. For neither food nor drink nor even silver vessels were at fault; rather, within my earthen vessel lay seeds from which I inwardly felt the heavy prickings of rising thorns, stirred by the breath of things heard or seen outwardly. Therefore, both at table and away from table, I often silently read in gold and silver, in the bishop’s household furniture, as costly as it was beautiful [Col. 0708B].

4. I also read in many other things of the world, at which my thieving eyes—transgressors of God’s commands—looked in order to desire them. And I read as follows:

“Peter, the things at which you look, in which you rejoice or desire to rejoice, are of the world. Therefore a time will come when they will no longer be; but you will be. Where will you be, Peter? For you, though an offender against the cross of Christ, in which alone you do not doubt that one ought to glory, desire to glory in worldly things, although you are certain that the world, with its desire, passes away daily as it perishes; and that, when a man dies, he shall not take all things with him, nor shall his glory descend with him.

“Peter, that most worthless tunic of flesh, which you value so highly that, for its care and desires, you forget not only yourself but—even more gravely and abominably—God also, you will shortly leave to worms and decay, made much more worthless still. Therefore, at this departure of yours, whose hour you do not know, when stripped of the tunic of flesh, where will you go? Whom will you meet? What will you answer? Where also will you be placed until you return to the tunic? For you will return, and you will truly put on that same tunic again. And you will rise either to life and joy or to death and mourning; and these will have no end.”

5. O my beloved, this was the lesson that I silently and frequently reread in the chamber of my heart; and the aforesaid questions often almost severed my spirit from every joy. Nor is this surprising. For my conscience reproached me [Col. 0708D] that in all my ways I deserved to make our Savior my condemner, since I was not afraid even to offend him in matters pertaining to his worship. O what astonishing, what bold and insane presumption! I was certain that the Lord is just and able to destroy me in hell; and, though fearing this, I nevertheless did not cease to offend him. Indeed, that the Lord might be my portion, I had received the sacrament of clerical office; but the enormity of my life had made me alien to the very reality of that sacrament. O what astonishing, then, what foolish and shameless arrogance! The words of the Lord are pure words; yet I presumed to utter and expound them from an unchaste breast through a polluted and deceitful mouth, knowing that the Lord had said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous ordinances, and take my covenant upon your lips?” [Col. 0709A] (Ps. 49:16 [Vulgate].) Whenever, for any reason other than the love and honor of God alone, I pronounced these same divine words in church by reading or singing them, I knew with complete certainty that I was bound by sacrilege, since I offered to vanity the worship owed to God. I was therefore not a servant of Christ, since on the one hand the Apostle says: “If I were pleasing men, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10); and on the other the prophet: “God will scatter the bones of those who please men” (Ps. 52:6 [Vulgate]). Yet often, in order to please men—or myself, rather than God—this was the intention of my inmost heart, or, to speak more truly, of my foolish heart.

6. I therefore, a worthless servant—why, or with what face, [Col. 0709B] did I occupy ground in God’s field, when in truth I was a bitter root, useful to no one, harmful to very many, yet most harmful to myself, producing no fruit but bitterness? What example did I give to the living, or what sacrifice did I offer for the dead, from whose sacrificial victims I ate the fat and drank the wine of libations? Whatever covering I might put on, I was a detractor from and plunderer of the Church’s goods, and squandered them upon wicked purposes. O how wicked and hateful to God was this perversity of mine! For I had heard blessed Jerome write: “All who misuse the goods of the Church for other purposes incur the sin of deceiving the Redeemer and of being guilty of the Savior’s blood.” Since, therefore, I was guilty both of misuse and [Col. 0709C] robbery in these and in many other things, whenever that true and fearsome declaration of the Apostle rang in my ears, “Robbers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10), there murmured in my heart, as if in reply, this hasty conclusion, full of fear, grief, and shame: “Therefore they themselves, seized and confined with unclean spirits, will burn without end in the fires of Gehenna!”

I called this conclusion hasty, both because of the logic of the argument and swiftly made inference, and especially because the day of the Lord, on which this shall happen, is drawing near swiftly. Hence it is written: “Yet a little while, and I will move heaven and earth” (Hag. 2:22 [Vulgate]); and elsewhere: “A great day, exceedingly bitter and very swift; there the mighty man shall be distressed” (Zeph. 1:14). It was therefore no wonder [Col. 0709D] if this and many similar things made me anxious and reflective, since I could not remember having lived from childhood even for a moment in which I had not committed either robbery or some other work of death. For I greatly loved gatherings and assemblies of vanity: entertainments, jokes, idleness, words suited to laughter rather than profit; rarely speaking truth, very often lying; swearing, perjuring myself, currying favor, flattering, and the like. Through a certain common and habitual practice, I did not regard all these as sins even on the surface, but as if they were witty expressions of affected sociability and worldly decency. Yet I knew that these very things, since they divide God and man, were vanities and false madnesses. I pass over greater matters: namely, the pride of the heart, jealousies, hatreds, dissensions, [Col. 0710A] slanders, shameful speech. I pass over the foulest mire and clay of thoughts and deeds, in which I was secretly and most wickedly occupied—wholly mud—while at every moment, so far as lay in me, I hurried by my deeds toward the punishment of eternal death. But the Father of mercies took pity on me at last, visited me, and drew me to the Son.

7. You see, therefore, how much the good Father has already done for the soul which, mercifully rescued from the rivers of Babylon, he has placed yet more mercifully at Clairvaux, beside the springs of the Savior. For Clairvaux, although in the appearance of its site it lies in a valley, has its foundations in the holy mountains; the Lord loves its gates more than many tents of Jacob. Glorious things have been said of it, because in it the glorious and wondrous God [Col. 0710B] works glorious wonders. There the old madmen return to their right mind; and although their outward person is wasting away, the inward is reborn and, in the Apostle’s words, “is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16), into the person created according to God (Eph. 4:24). There the proud are humbled; there the rich are made poor; there the poor receive the Gospel; and the darkness of sinners is changed into light.

Although a great multitude of blessed poor have come to this house from the ends of the earth, gathered from regions and nations, their heart and soul are one; so that it may fittingly be said particularly of this house: “Behold, foreigners and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there” (Ps. 86:4 [Vulgate]). Rightly, therefore, it is the dwelling of all who rejoice—not with empty joy. For they have found at Clairvaux a sure hope of everlasting joy and of their own ascent to heaven already begun: Jacob’s ladder, and angels upon it—some descending, who so provide for their bodies that they do not fail on the way; others ascending, who so govern their souls that afterwards their bodies too may be glorified with them.

8. But the more diligently, day by day, I observe the poor of this most blessed life, the more perfectly, I believe, do they follow Christ and think as he does in all things; and from sure signs I infer that in all they do they appear as true ministers of God. For when they devote themselves to prayer, they speak to God in spirit and truth; and both from their secret and intimate conversation with him and from their humble manner of comporting themselves, they plainly appear to be God’s [Col. 0710D] household members and friends. When, more openly praising God, they attend to psalmody, the entire bearing of their bodies, in every fear and reverence of holiness, shows how pure and fervent is the disposition of their minds toward this same end. Their deliberate articulation and their modulation in the psalms also show how sweet to their throats are God’s words, sweeter than honey to their mouths.

When I observe them thus chanting so holily and so tirelessly during the daytime hours and the night watches, from before midnight until the first hour of day, with only a brief interval, they seem to me little less than angels, and far more than human beings. That they possess such continuous, cheerful, and ever-fresh endurance, such fervor and merit, is not due to human strength but to a divine gift. When they are occupied in reading, they seem gently and abundantly to draw the waters of Siloam, flowing silently and springing up into eternal life. Their ordering and bearing show that they are all disciples of one master, teaching in their hearts and saying: “Hear, Israel, and be silent” (Prov. 1:5). For they are silent and hear, and become wiser, since “the wise hearer will be wiser.”

9. My beloved, what do you think these poor men of so blessed a life appear to be, or can be called, when they persist in the labors of their hands, when they go out to work or return? In all these things it is clear that they are led not by their own spirit but by the divine Spirit. Certainly, with such patient disposition, [Col. 0711B] such calm and unmoving expression, such holy and gentle order, they do everything that, though they exercise themselves very greatly in work, they can scarcely be perceived either to move or to be burdened by anything, however great their labors may be. Thus it is manifest that in them works that Holy Spirit who orders all things sweetly; in him they are refreshed and rest even while laboring.

Of these poor men, I hear that some were distinguished men of episcopal or consular rank, or of other dignities and much learning, and some outstanding young men. Yet now, by God’s grace, all regard for persons having died among them, the higher each thought himself in the world, the more he considers himself in this flock lesser than the least and altogether more abject. [Col. 0711C] As I observe them in the gardens with a hoe, in the meadows with a fork or rake, in the fields with a sickle, in the wood with an axe, and in other places of labor with other implements of work; and as I look back at what they were and consider their present condition, their tasks, their tools, their lowly persons, their ungainly and poor clothing—by the judgment of the outward eye they appear to me not as human beings, but as a foolish people, mute and tongue-tied, “the reproach of men and the despising of the people.” But sound and faithful understanding asserts in my heart that their life is hidden with Christ in heaven.

Among them I rejoice indeed to see Geoffrey of Péronne, Raynald of Morins, G. of Saint-Omer, and Walter of Lille—men whom, being older than all of them, I had known in the old man. [Col. 0711D] But now, by God’s grace, I perceive that not a trace of that oldness remains in them. In the old man I knew them to walk with heart exalted and eyes raised, amid things great and wonderful beyond themselves; but now I see them walking humbled under the merciful hand of God, amid things small and wonderful beneath themselves. In the old man I knew them to carry about with them tombs whitened on the outside, but within full of dead men’s bones; now, however, I believe them to bear the vessels of the Lord, which, though outwardly they seem contemptible, are inwardly full of the spices of heavenly fragrances.

When, therefore, this whole community goes out to its customary labor and returns, step by step and simply, one after another, as if in a straight battle line, humbly armed with the weapons of peace—do not the angels of God, seeing it advance in this fashion, newly converted to Christ from darkness, rightly sing in astonishment and joy: “Who is this that rises like the dawn, fair as the moon?” [Col. 0712A] (Song 6:9 [Vulgate]), and so forth? But the excluded devil is terrified and grieves exceedingly, seeing—would that he might always see and grieve—that their resurrection is no small ruin to his kingdom. Therefore he too arms himself with whatever sharper malice he can, so that those whom he could no longer hold by the allurements of this world, he may attack and entangle more fiercely through subtler arguments. Yet the enemy shall not prevail. For they have made the Most High their refuge: the cross of Christ, their beloved, which they embrace and bear with faithful longing, the one hope of those to be saved.

10. Again, my beloved, what do you think ought to be believed about these same poor men at mealtime, in their self-restraint and manner? At that time I believe that neither does God see anything displeasing, nor does man see anything for which he ought to accuse them. For there they comport themselves so modestly and so holily that they appear to be what they are: righteous people who fear God. On the one hand, they attentively receive the spiritual and chief dish, the word of life, for which they always hunger; on the other, they reverently eat and drink the other gifts of God set before them—not delicacies carefully sought out, but the fruits of their own manual labor: namely vegetables and cooked dishes. Their drink is beer; if they do not have it, they gladly drink plain water. They use wine rarely, and then mixed with much water.

Thus, rendering what is due to the body—not to gluttony, not [Col. 0712C] to the belly—they eat and drink only for natural need and for God, knowing what is written: “Food for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13). For “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy” (Rom. 14:17), and upon these their entire will and endeavor are directed. They have obedience as mistress and ruler of their whole life; and they follow it so faithfully in everything that they omit not even one portion of day or night which is not devoted among them to obedience and divine worship. Hence I also faithfully believe that they—leaving aside things of greater merit and reward—obtain, both in every step they take and in every movement [Col. 0712D] of their hands in the works assigned to them, either remission of sin or an increase of their crown in eternal life. And if they happen to fall sometimes, which they cannot wholly avoid while they bear fragile flesh, they are not dashed down, because the Lord upholds them with his hand.

11. Behold, my beloved, you have those few things which were promised to your love in the introductions to this letter concerning the poor of Clairvaux. There remain more, better, and best things; and since I am unable to suffice for describing them, let what has been said for the present suffice. My desire is that I may deserve to be joined to those aforesaid poor in Christ, in body and spirit, so that, assisted by their intercession, I may both practice repentance more fruitfully and more confidently cry to [Col. 0713A] the Lord: “Lord, I have fled to you; teach me to do your will. Deliver me from my enemies, O my God” (Ps. 142:9–10 [Vulgate]). “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul; my God, in you I trust; I shall not be put to shame” (Ps. 24:1–2 [Vulgate]); and similar words.

But I am still being tested and, by God’s grace, am being formed according to the rule and life of these poor men, so that when I have been joined to them I may know, together with them, how to keep watch and to dream only in the Spirit. For a kingdom is promised to the watchful person, and whoever sows in the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit. May I see myself, a participant in that life, and you and the whole Church of Noyon—my lady and mother—through God’s mercy happily made eternal with Christ and reigning with him. Amen. Farewell. If the Lord wills, on the Sunday immediately after the Ascension of the Lord, we shall receive the armor of our profession, by the grace and blessing of Jesus Christ; may that same Jesus Christ deign to grant it us through the merits of his Mother and your prayers. Amen. Farewell again; remember your last things, and have mercy on your soul.

398. LETTER CDXCIII. [Note: [Col. 0713D] This letter was written about the year 1155 against Godfrey, who called himself Abbot Geoffrey; see the notes on Letter 231.] FROM THE GENERAL CHAPTER OF THE BLACK MONKS TO ADRIAN IV. Concerning the removal of the abbot of Lagny.

To the most beloved father and lord Adrian, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman See: the humble assembly of abbots under the archbishopric of Rheims, united in one spirit for the honor of God, offers the services of sincere charity and the devout support of prayers.

[Col. 0713C] Since Your Holiness is present in the Church of the people and has deserved to be exalted in the chair of the elders, so that, by special grace, the keys of blessed Peter have been entrusted to you, to bind what must be bound and loose what must be loosed, we humbly lay our deliberations before the See of justice, compelled by zeal for the house of God; and we bring to your attention for your governance the lamentable afflictions and ruin of the monastery of Lagny. That man who appears to preside over the aforesaid monastery under the name of shepherd is proved not merely to be of no benefit, but indeed to be greatly harmful: for he does not direct his subjects according to the rule of religious life, and by living disgracefully he defiles and corrupts many of them by the example of his wicked life. This is sufficiently evident not only because he is held infamous throughout the cities of France, [Col. 0713D] but also because certain brethren dread his company as a deadly contagion and live in other monasteries under the rules of monastic profession.

Accordingly, that church of Lagny, once celebrated and renowned, appears to be left as “a shelter in a vineyard, and as a hut in a cucumber field.” Since we cannot but grieve over these things, yet are not permitted to put the sickle into another’s harvest, while it belongs to you to cut down the fruitless tree lest it occupy the ground [Col. 0714A] and to graft in one that bears fruit, we entreat and exhort your vigilance: by the authority in which you excel and the wisdom in which you are strong, pronounce against the plague which spreads like cancer such a sentence as the gates of hell shall by no means be able to resist; by it let the mouths of blasphemers be stopped, and in the gates of the daughter of Zion let the praises of the Lord be proclaimed. Farewell; and strengthen by your apostolic blessing our assembly, which Pope Innocent of blessed memory confirmed by a privilege of apostolic authority.

[Note: [Col. 0713D] From this it is evident that the origin of the general chapters of the Order of St. Benedict is to be referred to Innocent. The first seems to have been the one at Soissons, to whose abbots Bernard wrote Letter 91. Peter the Venerable calls them “great assemblies,” above, in Letter 229, no. 30. [Col. 0714D]]

LETTER CDXCIV. FROM THE SAME PERSONS TO ALEXANDER III.

To the most beloved father and lord Alexander, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman See: the humble assembly of abbots under the archbishopric of Rheims, gathered in one spirit for the honor of God, offers the service of sincere charity and due reverence with all submission.

1. Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies. For when, at the beginning of your election or consecration, the ship of the universal holy Church, entrusted in a special manner to blessed Peter alone, had no secure anchorage and was battered on every side by adverse waves, and was in such danger that, because of the greatness of the peril, we might have awakened the Savior as if sleeping, crying with the blessed disciples, “Lord, save us; we perish” [Col. 0714C] (Matt. 8:25), our cry entered the ears of him who saves from faintness of spirit and tempest; he made the storm a gentle breeze and led us into the harbor we desired.

For we desired, and anxiously longed for, that there should no longer be division; rather, with the most destructive error extinguished, kings and peoples should be gathered and assembled into one, to serve the Lord and honor only your blessedness, seated, that is, in the chair of the Prince of the Apostles. Since, therefore, we are no longer carried about by every wind of doctrine, nor hear deceivers saying, “Behold, here,” or “behold, there,” but cling immovably to that most firm Rock upon which the Pontiff of pontiffs founded his Church, we confidently take refuge in the protection of your apostolate amid our necessities, humbly asking that whatever things are beneficial in the house of God [Col. 0714D] you may confirm by the keys of blessed Peter, and whatever things are harmful you may repel.

2. And, to pass over many matters, there is one thing which especially disturbs us, disciples of blessed Benedict, not a little amid the peace that we enjoy under Your Sublimity: namely, that we now behold, not without tearful sorrow, the church of Lagny—once flourishing in holiness, religious observance, and abundance of resources—cast down from that condition and reduced to the keeping of an orchard. For the man who appears to preside, under the name of shepherd, over the aforesaid church is proved not merely to be of no benefit, but indeed to be greatly harmful: for he does not form his subjects according to the rule of religious life, but, leading a disgraceful and infamous life, miserably causes scandal and drags them down with himself into perdition. Since there is no one to protest, he has now broken out into such shamelessness that he has placed over the others as prior of the house one of the brethren, an accomplice in and privy to his own crime. How savage a plague thereby corrupts and destroys the Lord’s flock, [Col. 0715A] we refrain from writing; your prudence knows it better.

Finally, long ago we wrote to your predecessor, Pope Adrian of happy memory, concerning these evils and set forth our lamentable complaint; we devoutly urged him to put an end to the disastrous ruin of the aforesaid monastery. Wisely recognizing that this must be done, he sent letters to the venerable bishops Alan of Auxerre and Theobald of Paris, commanding them to examine the matter carefully in the presence of religious abbots and determine it by apostolic authority as justice required. When, on the appointed day at Lagny, they were prepared to obey the command of the lord Pope, the man who should not be called an abbot, insufficiently confident in his conscience and evading judgment, produced letters in public which, by some contrivance or surreptitious means unknown to us, he had procured. In them, by the authority of the aforesaid Pope Adrian, it seemed to be decreed that he, the abbot—as a son of the Roman Church—should not be harassed or burdened by the aforesaid bishops in any manner or judicial proceeding. [Col. 0715C] Thus the case remained unexamined from that time onward.

400. 3. Therefore, venerable Father, the viperous plague still spreads like cancer; and the report of the evil, vigorous in its swift movement, becomes widespread throughout the cities of France. Since we waste away with grief at seeing the laws of the Order transgressed, while we are forbidden to put the sickle into another’s harvest, and since it belongs to you to cut down the unfruitful tree—indeed, the one producing evil fruits—and to graft in one that bears good fruit, we entreat and exhort you: according to the power in which you excel and the wisdom in which you are strong, pronounce a judgment against the impending destruction which the gates of hell may not prevail against; and through it, the tongues of blasphemers being restrained, may the mouths of those praising the Lord’s name be opened in this work of yours. Farewell, and extend over us the right hand of apostolic majesty in blessings of sweetness.

LETTER CDXCV. TO THE ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF SS. AT RIETI.

To the most beloved and venerable lord, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of SS. at Rieti, from his A., consolation of the Paraclete Spirit.

[Col. 0716B] I have received Your Belovedness’s excessively brief and concise letter with due reverence, and my heart trembled at your words. For when I read at its head, “To the venerable lord father abbot,” since I am conscious of no such thing in myself, I confess that I blushed somewhat and wondered what that greeting meant. For who am I, or what is my father’s house? I am a little child, not knowing my going in and going out. I am wretched: though I am nothing in God’s sight, I am nevertheless great in your eyes, of whom there is some report, but no truth at all. Would that your letter had possessed as much truth as it had falsehood. Nevertheless, no one should be judged a liar who says what is false while believing it true; for, so far as he is concerned, he does not deceive, but is himself deceived.

For the rest, if the prayers of the poor have any power before the fountain of mercies, we trust in the Lord that the God of our salvation will make our way prosperous. We too beseech the ardor of your faith that you may hold us in the bosom of your remembrance when you enter into his tabernacle, when you worship in the place where his feet stood. May the angel of the Lord guard your going in and your going out, venerable and dearest lord father.

[Col. 0715]

CHARTERS OF ST. BERNARD.  
(Mabillon edition, passim.)

I. FOR THE ABBEY OF TRONCHIENNES-BERENGARII.

[Col. 0715D]

Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to all who shall inspect this present document.

It happened that the abbot of Tronchiennes [Note: [Col. 0715] He was then Goswin, abbot of the monastery of Tronchiennes near Ghent, from whose autograph this little document was extracted.] and Baldwin of Waas, going to Rome to settle their dispute, passed by us. Having heard their case and taken pity upon their labor and expense, with God’s help we settled them in peace and charity in this manner. The church of Tronchiennes shall possess forever, according to its privileges, Wervik and Saleghem with full parochial right. We also decreed that the church of Tronchiennes should give Baldwin twenty solidi annually on the feast of St. Remigius. At our request Baldwin likewise granted to that church the offerings which he held in the church of Tronchiennes. Simon, bishop of Tournai, judged likewise.

II. FOR THE MONASTERIES OF LUXEUIL AND SAINT-ÈVRE. [Note: [Col. 0717D] From the authentic record of Saint-Èvre. Written in the year of Christ 1140.] This is the settlement between the abbots of Luxeuil and Saint-Èvre concerning the church of Galdoncourt.

I, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, to whom the lord pope [Note: [Col. 0717D] Namely Innocent II.] committed for decision the case of the abbots of Luxeuil and Saint-Èvre [Note: [Col. 0717D] Joceran appears then to have presided over Luxeuil; over the monastery of Saint-Èvre, Peter—or Durandus?],] brought that case to an end by agreement in the following manner. It was decreed that those of Saint-Èvre should have the entire tithe of Galdoncourt; while the monks of Luxeuil should possess the church itself and everything belonging to it other than the tithes, relinquishing whatever right they held in the church of Boulogneville, which those of Saint-Èvre held. All annual payments owed by the church of Galdoncourt both to the bishop and to his officials shall be paid in full each year by those of Saint-Èvre. This was done on the advice of the venerable bishops Geoffrey of Langres and Hatton of Troyes, and of other religious men whom we summoned for this purpose, whose names are these: William, abbot of Saint-Martin of Troyes; Baldwin, abbot of Châtillon; Stephen, abbot of Trois-Fontaines; Baldwin, abbot of La Crête; and Guy, abbot of Cherlieu. [Note: [Col. 0718D] A seal had been appended to this charter, but it has been broken.]

III. SETTLEMENT MADE BETWEEN HUGH, BISHOP, AND WILLIAM, COUNT OF AUXERRE. [Note: [Col. 0718D] Letter 426 in the edition of 1690; 429 in the edition of 1729; 464 in the latest Paris edition, prepared by the brothers Gaume. EDITOR.]

400. 1. 1. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux. [Col. 0717C]

Having learned of the dispute that had arisen between Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and William, count of Nevers, over certain claims contested between them, I came to Auxerre; and with the equal consent and will of both, I caused those claims, brought into agreement, to be settled as follows. In the wood called the Bishop’s Bruyère (La Bruyère), the bishop and count shall jointly make an enclosure (*haia*) and jointly guard the enclosure so made. Each shall appoint his own officers to this guard, and each shall receive an oath of fidelity from both; and their oath shall include that no person or animal shall be seized in the enclosure on any pretext. Fines for offenses against the enclosure shall be received jointly, and are determined as follows. A pig, sheep, or cow running after bulls while in heat, if found there, shall pay no fine. For oxen, cows, horses, asses, goats, and similar animals, if found there without a keeper, one denarius shall be paid for each animal. If a keeper is present, he shall pay three solidi for himself. Nothing shall be exacted for smaller livestock. If a man is found cutting wood there, he shall pay fifteen solidi; if he causes a fire, sixty. Thus the aforesaid fines [Col. 0718A] for the enclosure shall never exceed the stated sums. The enclosure shall not extend more than forty arpent-rods in width. If at any time, whether through age or some other cause, the same enclosure should cease to exist, they may restore it jointly in the same place if they wish; but if they do not wish to do so, the land remaining—whether cultivated or uncultivated—shall revert to the bishop’s lordship. All other offenses committed outside the enclosure belong to the bishop, without any share for the count.

2. It was decreed concerning clerics that they shall be wholly free and immune from the count’s authority: the count shall exercise no right or lordship over them on any pretext, nor shall he or any of his officers be permitted in any way to lay hands on their goods, wherever they may be. But if a cleric is caught in the manifest offense of theft, he shall be delivered to the bishop or his officers without injury or dishonor to his clerical order; and thereafter, if the count, his officials, or his men bring a claim against him, the bishop shall render them satisfaction regarding him insofar as law and reason require.

3. Since the toll of the city and its suburbs is known to belong jointly to the bishop and count, if any offense is committed concerning it, the bishop shall receive his principal payment himself, together with the penalty prescribed by the law under which each person lives; and the count shall receive sixty solidi for the offense. If the count’s toll-collector or any retainer first seizes a person who has taken the bishop’s principal payment, he shall cause the bishop’s principal payment, with its legal penalty, to be restored; and if through his negligence that person escapes with that principal payment, he himself shall answer to the bishop for the principal and penalty.

4. The bishop’s servants and all his household shall never submit to justice through the count. All offenses committed in the precincts—namely, the precinct of Saint Stephen, that of Saint Mary, that of Saint Eusebius, Saint Peter, and Saint Amator—and those occurring in the places contained within the precincts, belong to the bishop’s jurisdiction. The count may exercise no authority in them; nor, for any offense by any person, shall he transfer to his own power goods located in the precincts. If a layman is caught in the precincts in theft, he shall be delivered to the count for justice to be done, with one item of whatever clothing is his. Outside the precincts, however, all lay thieves who are caught, both they and their goods, belong to the count, except for those goods contained in the named precincts, which belong properly to the bishop.

5. Concerning rent-paying lands, it is clear that the count or his man may never acquire those that are on the bishop’s demesne except through the bishop, nor may either acquire any tithe. All clerics and laypeople dwelling in the precincts shall observe the count’s ban for three days; once these have passed, they may sell freely. If the bishop purchases wine or grain, no gabelle or other customary due shall be exacted from him. The bishop shall summon the count’s servants and men, both personally and through ecclesiastical officials, in matters of Christian duty; and they shall answer to justice through him.

6. The count’s house and the fortified places of the castles which he is acknowledged to hold from the bishop—namely, Chastel-Neuf, Saint-Sauveur, Conada, and Mailliac—shall be handed over to the bishop at his pleasure; provided that, when he departs, they shall be restored intact to the count or his officials. In the count’s woods the bishop shall take what is necessary for himself and for the church of Saint Stephen.

7. It was declared and granted concerning the canons of Saint Stephen that they shall have their full right of use in the wood of Thul. The count acknowledged and granted that he may make no change or innovation at Auxerre without the bishop’s permission, since he acknowledges that he holds from the bishop in fief whatever he possesses at Auxerre and in its vicinity—except what lies within the city walls outside the precinct, which he holds from the lord king, and except the duke’s fief beyond the bridge.

8. The count must guard the bishop’s goods as his own. If anyone under his jurisdiction takes anything from the goods of the bishop or his men, the count shall have it restored or shall compensate from his own resources. At the bishop’s mills of Regenne, the channel shall be such that ships traveling upstream and downstream may pass through. From those who sell fish, [Col. 0719C] the count has four credit accounts, in which the bishop receives nothing. If, for the others, the bishop’s toll-collector arrives first and bargains first, he shall take only as much as the bishop’s household needs. The count’s toll-collector shall do likewise; if they arrive together, they shall share equally whatever they find. They shall act similarly concerning other provisions. The bishop has a credit account for forty days in all provisions thereafter; until he has paid, nothing shall be entrusted to him on credit by those to whom he is indebted.

400. 2. 9. It was decreed concerning merchants who sell in their homes that, every fifteen days or monthly, they shall render sales dues to the bishop’s toll-collector, if such dues are demanded from them. At the fair of the liberty of the Kalends of May, two parts of the tolls and sales dues belong to the bishop and one third to the count. Those who receive these revenues shall swear fidelity to the bishop and count.

10. The bishop shall establish a guard in his own vineyards and in rent-paying vineyards, if those whose vineyards they are wish it; if they do not wish it, they shall not be compelled. The count shall do likewise throughout Bruyère. Whatever the ownership or possession of the land, the hunting of the bishop and count is common, as are the fines pertaining to hunting.

[Col. 0720A] 11. Done at Auxerre in the year 1145 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the first year of the episcopate of Pope Eugenius III. Present at this transaction were the abbots Stephen of Réigny, Guy of Caro-loco, Baldwin of Châtillon, Geoffrey of Rupes; Raynaud the archdeacon; Geoffrey the cantor; Hugh, dean of Meaux; Andrew of Baldement; Landric, Bernard, Hugh of Châteaucensois, and Hugh of Toucy, priests. Geoffrey the cellarer, Master Anselm, Guy of Bichiaco, Stephen of Saint-Germain, canons. Knights: William, son of the aforesaid count; Hugh of Tilly; Humbert of Saint-Germain; Siguin of Tornelle; Odo of Toucy; Humbaud Tortus. Servants: Robert, the count’s provost; Humbaud the baker; Erveus, the bishop’s provost; Olannus [Col. 0720B] the cellarer; and many others on either side.

[Note: [Col. 0719D] The same dispute, having flared up again between Bishop Alan and Count William, was settled by Bishop Godfrey, formerly of Langres, then living as a private person at Clairvaux—that is, in the year 1164. He decreed that whatever Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, had settled between Bishop Hugh and Count William of Carthusia [Col. 0720D] should be inviolably observed.]

## IV. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT VICTOR IN PARIS

[Note: [Col. 0720D] This grant was made about the year 1150.]

I, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wish it to be known to all God’s faithful, both future and present, that, when I had once come to Paris, I asked Lord Odo, abbot of Saint Geneviève, and all the brethren assembled in the common chapter, that, out of regard for brotherly love, they should grant to Abbot Gelduin and the brethren of the church of Saint Victor permission to bring to their church the water called Benevim, taken from beneath the mill which is called Cupels, and thence to convey the water toward Paris into the Seine, upon payment of a suitable price to the successors of the men of Saint Geneviève [lacuna], they might convey the water.

[Col. 0720C] And that the aforesaid church of Blessed Victor might be permitted to build, within its walls, a mill upon this same water for its own use, and to construct at its own expense, both within those same walls and outside them, whatever small advantage it might be able to derive from that watercourse. Abbot Odo, with the common consent of his brethren and through our intervention, graciously granted all this, provided nevertheless that the mill of Saint Geneviève, mentioned above, should not be impeded by any contrivance of the works of Saint Victor or by any raising of the water. That this grant may remain ratified and firm in perpetuity for the church of Blessed Victor, we commend it to our seal and have judged it fitting that it be authenticated by the impression of our seal. It also pleased us to add the names of those who were then present at our request: Lord Godfrey, bishop of Langres; Lord John, bishop of Saint-Malo; [Col. 0720D] Master Bernard, archdeacon of Paris; and likewise our monks Gerard and Geoffrey.

## V. FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT AMANT

[Note: [Col. 0720D] From the cartulary of Buxia. Written in the year 1153.]

In the name of the Lord, I, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wish it to be known that I have granted to the church of Saint-Amant the place of Buxia [Note: [Col. 0720D] See notes on Epistle 299.] and whatever we possessed there by the gift of the Count of Angoulême, of the church of Angoulême, and of Peter of Austensium. [Col. 0721A] The witnesses were Hugh, bishop of Angoulême; Lord Junius, abbot of La Couronne; also Brother Philip, our prior; and Brothers Gerard and [Col. 0722A] Geoffrey, monks of our house.

Done at Clairvaux in the year 1153 from the Incarnation of the Lord.

# VOLUME TWO OF THE WORKS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, CONTAINING MORAL, DOCTRINAL, AND POLEMICAL TREATISES

(Collated with the Colbert, Saint-Denis, Cistercian, Saint-Germain, Marmoutier, Jumièges, Saint-Theodoric of Reims, and Compiègne manuscripts.)

[Col. 0721]

# PREFACE TO VOLUME II

Especially concerning the books *On Consideration*.

401–403 I. In the earlier editions of Horstius and in our own, the Sermons for the Seasons and the Saints, followed by the Sermons on Various Subjects, were placed in the second volume after Saint Bernard’s letters; the Sermons on the Song of Songs were in the third; and Bernard’s various Treatises followed in fourth place. But, upon more careful consideration, it seemed proper to place these Treatises immediately after the letters; and the natural order readily persuaded us to do so. For since treatises of this sort were written in epistolary form—and indeed some were transferred from letters into treatises—it followed that they should be placed not far after the letters.

This arrangement also has the advantage that, when the Sermons for the Seasons, for the Saints, and on Various Subjects are moved to the third volume, and the Sermons on the Song of Songs to the fourth, Gilbert’s continuation of the Exposition on the Song of Songs may be joined almost continuously to them at the beginning of the fifth volume. This continuation ought to follow Bernard’s Sermons on that same Song as closely as possible, as though it were their consequent appendix. For these and similar reasons, therefore, we have not thought it unsuitable to alter for a time Horstius’s customary order, in order to serve both the convenience of readers and the natural order of the material. These remarks concerning the arrangement of the works constituting the following volumes had to be repeated and prefaced here. Now a few words must be said concerning the order of the Treatises contained in the second volume.

II. In arranging the works in question, Horstius followed the order of dignity rather than chronology. For, if we follow chronological order, the first treatise is *On Humility*; then comes the treatise *On Loving God*; next, the *Apology to William*. They are enumerated in this order by Geoffrey in chapter 8 of book III of the *Life of Bernard*. Bernard himself suggests the first and third together in Letter 18 to Cardinal Peter, written about 1127; there he also mentions “a few letters to various persons,” under which designation I do not know whether he includes the treatise *On Loving God*.

After this must be listed Letter 42, addressed to Henry, archbishop of Sens, composed about the same year, 1127; then the treatise *On Free Will*, around 1128, as may be inferred from Letter 52 to Haimeric. Not long afterward the Sermon on Conversion, addressed to Clerics, was delivered. Before 1136 came the book addressed to the Knights Templar; it was during this period that Letter 77, to Hugh of Saint-Victor, was written. It is certain that in 1140 Letter 190, *On the Errors of Abelard*, was sent to Innocent. About the same year appeared the treatise *On Precept and Dispensation*, requested by Peter the Venerable after his return from Spain in 1143, in Letter 27 of Book IV. At the beginning of 1149 the book *On the Life of Saint Malachy* was completed; and in the same year the books *On Consideration* were begun, as we shall shortly say. These are the shorter works of which [Col. 0723] the fourth volume consists, excepting the Declamations, which we have relegated to the class of the preceding works, as foreign to Bernard; and the book *On Chant*, which we shall append to those already mentioned.

III. This, I say, is the chronological order in which the individual treatises were written. Yet it is preferable to preserve the order and dignity of their subject matter, assigning the first place to the books *On Consideration*; second, the Letter on the Conduct of Prelates, addressed to Henry of Sens; third, the Sermon on Conversion, addressed to Clerics; fourth, the treatise *On Precept and Dispensation*; fifth, the *Apology to William*—these two treatises concern monks; sixth, the book *In Praise of the New Knighthood*, [404] addressed to the Knights Templar. This is the first class, arranged according to the dignity of the persons concerned.

The second class concerns virtues: namely, seventh, the little book *On Humility*; eighth, *On Loving God*. The third class will concern doctrines: namely, ninth, the work *On Grace and Free Will*; tenth, the letter *On Baptism*, addressed to Hugh of Saint-Victor; eleventh, the letter *On the Errors of Abelard*, addressed to Innocent. Finally, twelfth, comes the historical book *On the Life of Saint Malachy*. To all these, in thirteenth place, will succeed the book *On Chant*. We have set out the order of the shorter works above, pp. 995–996, for the more convenient use of students.

IV. Among all these, none appears more worthy of Bernard than the five books *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius. If one considers the dignity of their subject and recipient, nothing is nobler; if their manner of treatment, nothing more elevated; if the majesty of their style and the weight of their thoughts, nothing more eloquent or forceful; finally, if the purity of their utterances and the discipline inherent in the sacred canons, nothing more fitting for a Catholic Doctor and most holy Father.

For what was more difficult for a man reared in solitude, removed from worldly affairs and business, than to lay down—and, as it were, prescribe—the rules of life for the supreme Pontiff, not to say for the whole Church? What was more difficult for a private man than to speak aptly, accurately, and concisely concerning the condition of the whole Church, the conduct of sacred ministers, and the offices, virtues, and vices of all; indeed, to pronounce a just judgment? What was wiser than so to identify, pursue, and chastise the vices, errors, and abuses of persons of however exalted station that one should not only avoid envy and the suspicion of fault-finding, but also win love and admiration? This, indeed, was Bernard’s skill—or good fortune—or divinely granted authority: as soon as his books *On Consideration* appeared publicly, everyone eagerly sought, repeatedly read, and loved them, even the supreme Pontiffs whom they most directly concerned.

V. Ernald, abbot of Bonnevaux, therefore rightly calls this work, in chapter 8 of Book II of the *Life of Bernard*, “a book of great usefulness, in which the holy man, pursuing with most penetrating inquiry both those matters which are about the Pontiff and those which are beneath him, and rising even to those which are above him, discoursed so greatly upon the divine nature that he seems to have been caught up into the third heaven, to have heard certain words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter, and to have seen the King in his beauty. In those matters which are below him and about him, the fellowship of manners, equality of nature, distinction of offices, consideration of merits, and judgment of advancement are distinguished with the utmost subtlety, and to each person self-knowledge in his own kind is imparted. In those things which are above humankind, he contemplates heavenly things—not in the manner of angels, who always cleave to God, but in the manner in which a person of pure heart and sincere mind can attain to the divine,” etc.

This is the division of the five books *On Consideration*: the first demonstrates the necessity and usefulness of consideration; the second considers what is in the Pontiff—that is, what sort of person the Pontiff himself is and ought to be; the third, what is beneath him—that is, the entire world; the fourth, what is about him—his household, cardinals, and bishops; the fifth, what is above him—God and the angels. In these books, “how unrestrained he is in speech, how eloquent, and how richly endowed in knowledge of things above and below, the diligent reader will recognize,” says Geoffrey in chapter 8 of Book III of his *Life*.

VI. It remains to note the time at which these books were written. The holy Father began to bring them forth in 1149; and he did not complete them in one continuous course, as Baronius thought, but sent them to Eugenius as they were written at different intervals. The first was sent in 1149 itself, for Nicholas, Bernard’s notary, writing to Peter the Venerable before his departure, says: “I am sending you the book of the lord Abbot of Clairvaux to the lord Pope.” This letter is found in Peter’s Book VI, Letter 7. Here “book” cannot mean the complete work, since these authors regularly speak in that way, as Ernald testifies when he calls all five books “a book of great usefulness.”

Bernard sent the second to Eugenius in 1150, after the unhappy outcome of the Jerusalem expedition, for which he sets forth an apology at the very beginning of the book. The third he sent in 1152, after the death of Hugh of Auxerre, as is clear from chapter 2, section 11; and specifically in the fourth year after the Council of Reims, celebrated in 1148, as appears from section 20. Finally, he completed the fourth and fifth shortly afterward, if not together with the third.

[405] VII. The aforesaid books were first published at Rouen, together with the *Apology to William* and the treatise *On Precept and Dispensation*, without indication of the year; then at Speyer in 1550. They were printed without any division into chapters, as is customary in ancient manuscripts. The same works were reprinted in 1520 and subsequently with Bernard’s other writings. Later they were revised under Pope Pius V by Antonio Carafa, the eminent cardinal, and separately printed at Antwerp by the Plantin press.

Finally, Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, at the request of the most devout John Vendeville, bishop of Tournai, undertook another revision. He collated them with eight manuscript codices and dedicated their separate Roman edition of 1594 to Clement VIII, employing the division into chapters which had been added to a copy made in 1450 for Pope Nicholas V. Concerning this edition Nicholas Faber, in a letter to Vossius himself, after praising his other works, says: “I pass over the books *On [Col. 0725] Consideration* of Blessed Bernard, on which perhaps you expended less oil than on the others; yet you displayed no less zeal for the house of God and for restoring its wavering discipline. For there you took care to publish books most suitable for this purpose, which an author not without merit, and nearly contemporary with Blessed Bernard, calls a “Deuteronomy of the supreme Pontiffs not without Dionysius” (*non ἀπροσδιόνυσον Deuteronomium summorum Pontificum*)—books sent forth where they were first intended by their most religious author, though perhaps where they were less frequently handled.”

VIII. After so many and such great men, we have again submitted the aforesaid books to critical examination. In our earlier recension we collated them with four copies; in this one, with two others from the Colbert Library, lent to us by the most distinguished Étienne Baluze. One of them, marked 3541, has a division into chapters entirely different from Vossius’s. Since these divisions were not the author’s own work, we have thought it best to retain the customary ones, so as to avoid confusion in citations.

IX. Moreover, the title of this work varies in the ancient books. The more probable title is that of Colbert manuscript 3964: “The prologue of Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to the book *On Consideration*, addressed to Lord Pope Eugenius, happily begins.” But titles of this kind are not of great importance, since they generally derive from the discretion of scribes. It is useful to append here what Horstius prefixed to the preface of this volume.

[Col. 0725]

# 406. NOTICE OF JACOB MERLON HORSTIUS TO THE READERS

This fourth volume presents various treatises of Saint Bernard—genuine and unquestioned ones, I mean; for others will have their place elsewhere. Foremost among them in order and excellence is the book *On Consideration*, addressed to Pope Eugenius III, a work altogether useful and necessary, if any other is, for bishops and prelates of the Church. In Book II, chapter 8, and likewise Book III, chapter 8, of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, you will find matters which I strongly recommend be read before these books. Add the following.

Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, separately published these books from the Vatican Library at Rome in 1594 and dedicated them to the supreme pontiff Clement VIII. In commending them, among other things he says:

> “How highly Nicholas V valued these books above others, he showed in deed, when, before the invention of printing, he caused these same books to be copied separately for his own and others’ use in so splendid and distinguished a script. Pius V also, pious both in fact and in name, burning with love and zeal for them, gladly used their reading at his table, pondered them, and held them in high esteem; and I understand that his successor in the pontificate, Gregory XIII, did likewise. Urban VII too is said to have made them very familiar to himself while bishop and afterwards cardinal, and to have carried them with him into the conclave in which he was proclaimed supreme pontiff. Gregory XIV, who followed him after his brief pontificate, likewise set great store by these same books of Bernard and often had them on his lips. He wished them to exist separately, so that they might more conveniently be carried about and read by all churchmen, but especially by prelates—as I learned from persons wholly worthy of trust concerning him while he was still a cardinal, and as I myself heard more than once from his own lips.”

Thus Vossius in his dedication to Clement VIII.

Moreover, among the Treatises you will find two transferred here from the Letters, and, I think, not without reason. Their length, the nature of their subject, and their manner of treatment seemed to require the name of Treatise. Ephraemius, in Photius, Codex 229, observes that pious labors of the Fathers frequently receive the title of Letter; and Baronius shows this by various examples under the year of Christ 584, when treating the letter written by Saint Gregory in the name of Pelagius II against the Three Chapters. Among the letters of Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine one encounters many which their authors themselves call Books. Later editors of the Fathers judged that works of this kind would more fittingly be entered and classified as treatises or books than as letters.

Nor do such editors appear entirely without authority, particularly since the precedent came from the Apostles themselves to commit even serious subjects to letters. Yet such letters are truly treatises concerning matters by no means private. Hence it seemed good to us to remove those two letters, the forty-second and the hundred and ninetieth, being very lengthy, from the number of the others; to divide them into chapters for the reader’s benefit; and to attach them to the Treatises. Nor does it matter that, being addressed to a single particular person, they frequently address that person specifically. Certainly, if sound treatises on some subject must receive the title of Letter merely because they are directed to one person, scarcely any book would not deserve the name Letter, since it is almost universally customary for authors to inscribe their works to someone. Indeed, Bernard’s *Apology to Abbot William* and several other of his shorter works are also classed among the letters.

We have nevertheless retained the accepted number and order of the Letters, lest our effort perhaps prove misleading to anyone if citations from earlier editions differed from ours. Any further points on which the reader may need warning will be found in their proper places, and at greater length in the Preface to the whole work.

[Col. 0727]

# THE FIVE BOOKS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, ON CONSIDERATION, ADDRESSED TO EUGENIUS III

## 407. PROLOGUE

[Col. 0727A] I am moved to dictate something which may either edify, delight, or console you, most blessed Pope Eugenius. But somehow my discourse, though cheerful, is slow to emerge: for majesty and love, opposing each other, vie to command it. Majesty presses; love restrains. Yet your graciousness intervenes: in it you do not command this of me, but ask it [Note: [Col. 0727B] Elsewhere: “Yet graciousness intervenes, in that you do not merely command this, but ask it.”], although it would better befit you to command. Since majesty thus graciously yields, why should modesty not yield as well?

For what if you have ascended the chair? Even if you walk upon the wings of the winds, you are not withdrawn from affection. Love does not know a lord; it recognizes a son, even amid the pontifical insignia (*infulae*). [Note: [Col. 0727B] By *infulae* he understands not only the mitre, but pontifical insignia generally. On these, see below at Book IV, chapter 3, section 6.] Of itself love is sufficiently subject: it serves willingly, obeys without payment, reveres freely. Others are not so, not so: rather, they are driven to such conduct either by fear or by greed.

[Col. 0727B] These are they who bless with their lips, but whose evils are [Col. 0728A] in their hearts; they flatter before one’s face, but fail in need. But charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). I, to speak the truth, have been released from a mother’s office, but not despoiled of a mother’s affection. Long ago you became rooted in my inmost being; you will not easily be torn out. [Note: [Col. 0728B] In other copies: “you will not be so easily withdrawn from my very marrow.”] Ascend into heaven; descend into the depths: you will not depart from me; I shall follow you wherever you go (Luke 9:57). I loved you poor; [Note: [Col. 0728B] The printed editions add “in spirit.” But *in spirit* is absent from most manuscripts. Indeed, the sense is more elegant without this word, although it is added below.] I shall love you as father of poor and rich alike. For, if I know you well, because you have become the father of the poor, you have not therefore ceased to be poor in spirit. I trust that this change has been made in you, not out of you; that promotion has not succeeded your former state, but has been added to it. Accordingly I shall admonish you—not as a master, but as a mother; plainly, as one who loves. I may seem more like a madman, but only to one who does not love and does not feel love’s force.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0727]

## 408. CHAPTER I. He sympathizes with the Pontiff, burdened by such varied occupations.

[Col. 0727C]

1. From where then shall I now begin? I should like to begin with your occupations, because in them I most deeply sympathize with you. I would say that I sympathize, provided that you too are in pain; otherwise I should rather have said that I grieve, because there can be no fellow-feeling where there is no one who suffers. Therefore, if you suffer, I suffer with you; if not, I nevertheless grieve—and deeply—knowing that the limb which has become numb stands farther from health, and that a sick person who does not feel himself sick suffers more dangerously.

[Col. 0728C] Far be it from me, however, to suspect this of you. I know what delights of sweet repose you enjoyed not long ago. You cannot have become unaccustomed to them so quickly, being so suddenly and recently removed from them without pain. A fresh wound is not without pain; nor has the wound yet grown callous, nor in so short a time become insensible. Yet, unless you are pretending, there is no lack for you of constant material for just sorrow from daily [alternative addition: losses and] setbacks.

Unwillingly, I suppose, you are torn away from the embraces of your Rachel; [Note: [Col. 0729C] It is customary among the Fathers and writers on mystical theology to denote the contemplative and active lives by the names Rachel and Leah. Both were Jacob’s wives, but one was distinguished by fruitfulness, the other by beauty; these qualities are commonly applied to the differing duties of the two lives. In the same sense, the names Martha and Mary are often used. Bernard therefore suggests that Eugenius, hitherto devoted to the pursuits of the contemplative life, descends reluctantly to the business of the active life, which variously distracts and almost overwhelms the mind, so that it can scarcely afterwards rise to things above and divine.

Indeed, the writings and deeds of the holy Fathers show how burdensome it is for devout and religious persons to be torn from the leisure of holy contemplation into worldly business, and drawn into dignities and honors liable to so many and such great occupations. I should like to cite one example from that loftiest rank, a man well acquainted with the sorrow and distress that the loss of religious repose and tranquility commonly brings.
