Saint Gregory the Great, most holy Pontiff, raised to that pinnacle of the highest honor in the Church, marvellously laments his lot and condition, comparing his former state with his present one. His words are most elegant and highly useful, and deserve to be repeatedly impressed upon those who are so far from shrinking from such cares and hindrances to contemplation that, like Ephraim, “a trained heifer loving to thresh,” they are avidly drawn toward them and count it a delight to live among thorns.

Let such persons hear Gregory groaning and complaining that, under the guise of the pontificate, he has been brought back to the world and now serves so many earthly cares as he cannot recall having served in lay life. “For,” he says, “I have lost the lofty joys of my repose; and while inwardly falling, I seem outwardly to have risen. Therefore I lament that I have been driven far from the face of my Creator,” etc. And shortly afterward: “On every side I am battered by the waves of cases and pressed down by storms, so that I may rightly say: ‘I came into the depths of the sea, and the tempest overwhelmed me.’ After legal cases I desire to return to my heart, but shut out from it by the vain tumult of thoughts, I cannot return. Thus what is within me has become far removed from me, so that I cannot obey the prophetic voice which says: ‘Return to the heart, you transgressors’; but, oppressed by foolish thoughts, I am compelled only to cry out: ‘My heart has forsaken me.’ I loved the beauty of the contemplative life, like Rachel—barren indeed, but clear-sighted and beautiful; though by its quiet it bears less fruit, it sees the light more subtly. But by what judgment I do not know, Leah, that is, the active life, has been joined to me in the night: fruitful, but bleary-eyed, seeing less, although bearing more abundantly. I hastened to sit at the Lord’s feet with Mary, to receive the words from his mouth; and behold, with Martha I am compelled to minister in outward matters and to be troubled about many things.”

Thus the truly most holy pontiff writes in *Register*, Book I, Letter 5. He says similar things there in Letters 6, 7, and especially 24, as well as 25 and 26. [Col. 0730D] But it is pleasing also to hear another pontiff of the same name and rank, speaking with the same mind and a similar anguish of spirit. For Gregory IX, writing to the Camaldolese monks, sets forth the anguish of his heart in the pontificate and asks their prayers; he speaks thus: “Since the troublesome insistence of bleary-eyed Leah frequently tears us away from the sweet embraces of clear-sighted Rachel, we cannot persist in prayer to God himself as we ought. You, who continually sit with Mary at his feet, and to whom from long ago we have been joined by the bitumen of charity, we have judged should be urged,” etc.]

—and whenever it happens that you endure this, your sorrow must necessarily be renewed. But when does it not happen? How often do you wish to act, and in vain? How often do you set things in motion, yet do not advance them? How often do you attempt something, and are not permitted to proceed; struggle, and do not bring forth; [Note: [Col. 0730D] Horstius: “you struggle and do not obtain; you are in labor and do not bring forth.” The old editions and most manuscripts prefer our reading. In some, however: “you struggle and do not go into labor.” But *bring forth* better suits the sense.] make an effort, and are torn away; and where you begin, there you fail; and while you are still setting out, they cut you down? “The children have come to the birth,” says the prophet, “and the woman in labor has no strength” (4 Kings 19:3).

Do you know this? No one knows it better than you. You are hardened in face, and like Ephraim, a trained heifer, have learned to love threshing (Hosea 10:11), if, with your leave [alternative: if I may say so], your situation is as described. Far be it: this is the portion of one who has been given over to a reprobate mind. From these things I desire peace for you, not peace with them. I fear nothing more for you than that peace. Do you wonder whether it can ever happen? Yes, I tell you: if affairs, as is customary, through habit come to be neglected.

[Col. 0729B]

## CHAPTER II. The force of habit in inducing wicked conduct and hardness of heart.

2. Do not place too much confidence in your present disposition. Nothing is so firmly fixed in the mind that it does not become worn away through neglect and time. A neglected, old wound is covered with a callus; and it becomes the more incurable as it becomes less perceptible. Finally, continuous and bitter pain does not permit itself to last long. For unless it is blunted from some other source, it must yield either to something else or to itself. Indeed, it will soon receive consolation either from a remedy or numbness from its persistence.

What does habit not overturn? What is not hardened by continual repetition? What does not yield to use? For how many people has what they formerly shuddered at because of its bitterness been turned by evil use itself into sweetness? Hear what the righteous man laments concerning such a condition: “The things my soul formerly would not touch have now become my food because of anguish” (Job 6:7). At first something will seem unbearable to you; with the passage of time, if you become accustomed to it, you will judge it not so grave; shortly afterward you will find it light; shortly afterward you will not even feel it; shortly afterward it will even delight you. Thus one goes gradually into hardness of heart, and from that into aversion.

So grievous and continuous pain, as I said, will soon have an end: either health, certainly, or insensibility.

3. From this cause, precisely from this, I have always feared and still fear for you, lest, when a remedy is deferred, you cannot endure the pain and, in despair beyond recall, plunge yourself into danger. [Note: [Col. 0730D] Thus the manuscripts with the old editions; Horstius: “either not feeling the pain or not enduring it.”] I fear, I say, lest amid your many occupations, while you despair of any end, you harden your brow and thus gradually deprive yourself, in a sense, of the feeling of just and salutary sorrow.

[Col. 0730B] It would be much wiser for you to withdraw from them, even for a time, than to allow yourself to be dragged along by them and gradually led, certainly, where you do not wish to go. Do you ask where? To a hard heart. Do not keep asking what that is: if you have not shuddered, it is yours. The only hard heart is the one which does not shudder at itself, because it does not feel itself. Why ask me? Ask Pharaoh. No one with a hard heart has ever obtained salvation, unless perhaps God, in mercy, removed from him, as the prophet says, the heart of stone and gave him a heart of flesh (Ezek. 36:26).

What, then, is a hard heart? It is that which [Col. 0731A] is not cut open by compunction, softened by pity, or moved by prayers; which does not yield to threats and is hardened by blows. It is ungrateful for benefits, unfaithful in counsel, savage [alternative: deaf] in judgments, shameless toward vile acts, fearless in dangers, inhuman toward human beings, reckless in [alternative: toward] divine things; forgetful of the past, negligent of the present, heedless of the future. It is that for which, of the past, nothing at all fails to pass away except injuries alone; of the present, nothing fails to perish; of the future, there is no foresight or preparation, unless perhaps for revenge. And, to gather briefly all the evils of this dreadful evil: it neither fears God nor reveres man.

Behold where these accursed occupations will lead you, if indeed you continue as you have begun, giving yourself wholly to them [Col. 0731B] and leaving none of yourself for yourself. You waste your time. If I may now present myself to you as another Jethro, you too will be consumed by foolish labor in these matters (Exod. 18:18), which are nothing but affliction of spirit, disembowelment of the mind, and emptying of grace. For what is their fruit but spiders’ webs?

## CHAPTER III. It is unworthy of Church leaders to be continually occupied with hearing and deciding litigious cases.

4. I ask you: what sort of thing is this—to litigate, or to hear litigants, from morning until evening? And would that the day’s own evil were enough! The nights are not free. Hardly enough is left for nature’s necessity to allow the little body its rest; and then one rises again for disputes.

[Col. 0731C] Day pours forth lawsuits to day, and night announces malice to night: so completely is there no breathing-space in good things, no opportunity to take up rest in alternation, not even occasional intervals of leisure. I do not doubt that you too lament these things; but this is vain unless you also strive to correct them. Meanwhile, however, I urge you always to do this: never become hardened to these things by any habit or continual repetition. “I struck them, and they did not grieve,” says God [alternative: the prophet] (Jer. 5:3). Let that not be true of you, or of them.

Rather, take to yourself both the feeling and the words of the righteous man who says: “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end [alternative: or what is my confidence], that I should be patient? My strength is not the strength of stones [alternative: of bricks], nor is my flesh bronze” (Job 6:11–12). Patience is a great virtue; but I would not wish it for you in these matters. At times it is more commendable [Col. 0731D] to be impatient. Would you approve the patience of those to whom Paul said: “You gladly endure fools, being yourselves wise”? If I am not mistaken, it was irony, not praise, but a rebuke of the mildness of certain people who, as though surrendering themselves bound hand and foot to false apostles by whom they had been deceived, most patiently allowed themselves to be drawn into all manner of strange and corrupt doctrines. Hence he adds: “For you endure it if someone reduces you to slavery” (2 Cor. 11:19–20).

It is not good patience, when you can be free, to allow yourself to be made a slave. I do not want you to disguise the slavery into which you are surely being reduced day by day, without your knowing it. It is a sign of a dull heart not to feel one’s own continual vexation. “Vexation gives understanding to hearing,” says someone (Isa. 28:19). It is true—but only if it is not excessive. For if it is, it gives not understanding at all, but contempt. “When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

Wake up, then. The yoke of most wretched slavery, now and again threatening—indeed, already pressing upon you not a little—do not merely beware of it: shudder at it. Is it because you do not serve one person, but everyone, that you are not [Col. 0732B] a slave? No slavery is more disgraceful or burdensome than that of the Jews, which they drag behind them wherever they go and in which they everywhere encounter [Note: [Col. 0731D] That is, “find.” In some manuscripts this gloss has entered the text.] their masters. You too, I ask, say where you are ever free, where secure, where your own master. Everywhere is noise; everywhere turmoil; everywhere the yoke of your slavery presses upon you.

## CHAPTER IV. What slavery is worthy, and what is unworthy, of the servant of the servants of God.

5. Do not now throw back at me [or: add] the Apostle’s saying: “Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all.” That is far from your case. Did he serve people in this way in order to obtain shameful gains? Did the ambitious, the greedy, simoniacs, sacrilegious persons, concubinaries, incestuous persons, and every such monster among men flock to him from the whole world, so that by his apostolic authority they might either obtain ecclesiastical offices or retain them? Thus the man for whom “to live was Christ, and to die gain” made himself a servant [or: you made yourself a servant] in order to gain more people for Christ, not in order to increase the gains of greed. Therefore do not seek support for your servile way of life [or: condition] from Paul’s most diligent industry and from his charity, as free as it was generous. How much more worthy of your apostolate, more salutary to your conscience, and more fruitful for God’s Church is it that you hear him elsewhere saying: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men” (1 Cor. 7:23)!

What could be more slavish or more unworthy—especially for the supreme Pontiff—than to toil over such matters and for such people, not merely every day but almost every hour? For when do we pray? When do we teach the peoples? When do we build up the Church? When do we meditate on the Law? Every day laws indeed resound through the palace—but Justinian’s, not the Lord’s.

> [Note: Col. 0731D] Abuse of the laws has caused holy men, ardent with zeal for justice, sometimes to pronounce a sharper censure upon laws. Yet they attack not so much the laws themselves as their abuse and those who abuse them. It is surely through the fault of these people that laws are often nothing but lawsuits, or sow lawsuits. Wine too turns into a vice, not through its own fault but through that of those who misuse it; nor would you therefore rightly blame wine. For what cannot be corrupted by abuse? Ambition and desire for profit especially corrupt the use of laws. Hence almost no cause, whatever it may be, lacks an advocate; hence those windings of lawsuits before one reaches the goal of the case, namely judgment. But the discussion will return to this in chapter X. Here Bernard calls the pontiff away from excessive preoccupation with Justinian’s laws and lawsuits.
>
> What prevents the same point from being extended to the other prelates of the Church as well—indeed, to all churchmen? We see many of them carried too eagerly toward the study of laws and legal rights, because these are thought to concern splendour, gain, and the comforts of life more directly. But what a perverse ordering of life and studies it is, that those whose whole will and delight ought to be in the Lord’s law should today be wholly occupied with Justinian’s laws! Do they not profess this by their very manner and rule of life, as clerics—that is, persons admitted into the Lord’s portion? [Col. 0733C] Do they not remind themselves of this every day when, following the Prophet’s lead, they declare blessed those whose will is in the Lord’s law and who meditate on his law day and night?
>
> Yet these people, strangers and foreigners in the divine Scriptures, alien to and disdainful of pious and spiritual books, occupy themselves with greater relish and pleasure in the Code and Digest, the Novels and Libelli, laws and lawsuits. They have no commerce with the book of the Gospels and the acts of the saints, except that they mutter the words of the Psalms hastily and hurriedly, and quickly discharge the task of the choir. From there they turn themselves to profane studies, to say nothing of vain ones. What meditation on the divine law is there here? What treatment of sacred matters suited to the ecclesiastical state? And yet every day they cry: “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long!” and so forth.
>
> It is surprising if they do not fear God, the witness of their heart—or at least their own conscience—lest they be charged with lying, when the testimony of both convicts them of loving nothing less than what they profess with their mouths. For why do we recite the Psalms daily? Is it not that we may put on affections corresponding to the words and meanings of the Psalms, and conform our manners to divine admonitions? But who would believe that they feel what they assert, or what they daily repeat as asserted through the mouth of the divine Psalmist, when they call blessed the person who searches and meditates upon the Lord’s law day and night?
>
> What wonder if we see such persons gradually deprived of the sap of true piety, animated by no infusion of divine things, drying up imperceptibly and at last dying altogether? Hence Peter of Blois, a most learned man and himself highly skilled in law: “The use of laws among clerics,” he says, “is a matter full of danger. For it so claims the whole person for itself that it suspends him from spiritual things and tears him away from divine things” (Letter 26). And elsewhere: “This treatment of laws is scarcely ever peaceable, because it is always litigating concerning contracts, or as if concerning crimes, or as if concerning the various forms of cases, concerning actions and obligations, judgments, sentences and appeals, and other matters which, though they ought to lull lawsuits to sleep, always stir up the ashes of lawsuits already asleep.”
>
> Thus he writes in the letter in which he calls a clerk of the king of England away from the study of jurisprudence to the study of sacred letters, as more suited to the ecclesiastical state: *In our Trumpets of Ecclesiastical Discipline*, trumpet 6, p. 553. Likewise, in Baronius, vol. XII, year 1165, no. 2, John of Salisbury dissuades Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury—who at last died a glorious martyr for the Church—from the study of laws, since they serve curiosity more than usefulness. “I would rather,” he says, “that you should chew over the Psalms and turn over the books of the blessed Gregory’s *Moralia*. Who rises contrite from reading laws and canons?”
>
> I read that the most holy prelate Charles Borromeo had a similar mind. “For,” says the writer of his Life, “he judged that the customary learning of jurists, with which he had been occupied as a young man, did not at all belong to his pastoral care. He knew theology and canon law only to the extent thought sufficient for a cardinal governing a great church. In theology he followed chiefly the divine Scriptures, then the ancient Fathers and those interpreters who embrace the sounder sense. That knowledge of canons was especially pleasing to him which, representing the character and acts of the Fathers, contains the method for shaping and ordering the Church. But grieving that by common practice only those canons were chosen for interpretation which served lawsuits and courts, he determined to preside over their exposition in such a way that the sacred institutions and rites of the forefathers, and the best form of administering the Church, might be drawn from them.” Book VII, chapter 11.
>
> Receive, moreover, all the foregoing with a grain of salt. No wise person condemns a sober knowledge and use of laws useful not for profit but for the defence of justice and truth. Sacred ministers are only warned to know the chief parts and duties of their state, to love studies worthy of and due to their calling, and to beware of being occupied in a disordered way: lest they neglect first of all to know what may increasingly advance the perfection of their state; lest they expend less care and industry upon what is chief, and more upon what is inferior and foreign. See Lindanus, bishop of Roermond, *On Flight from Impenitence*, where he asks why many clerics today value the study of jurisprudence more highly than theology.]

[Col. 0733A] Is this right as well? You must see to that. For certainly “the law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls” (Ps. 18:8). But these are not so much laws as lawsuits and quibbles, overturning judgment. You, then, pastor and bishop of souls, with what mind, I ask, do you endure that the one should always be silent before you and these others chatter? I am mistaken if this perversity does not trouble you with a scruple. I think that it sometimes even compels you to cry to the Lord with the Prophet: “The wicked told me tales, but not as your law” (Ps. 118:85).

Go on, then, and dare to profess yourself free under so heavy a burden of this impropriety—one from which it is not lawful for you to withdraw your neck. For if you can do so and will not, you are all the more a slave of this very perverse will of your own. Is not the person ruled by iniquity a slave? Most certainly. Unless perhaps you judge it more unworthy for a human being than for a vice to rule over you. What difference is there whether you serve willingly or unwillingly? For although compelled slavery is more pitiable, self-chosen slavery is more wretched.

“But what do you want me to do?” you ask. Spare yourself from these occupations. Perhaps you will reply that this is impossible, that it would be easier to bid farewell to the chair. You would be right, if I were urging you to break off these things rather than merely interrupt them.

## CHAPTER V. One must not undertake the care of others while neglecting and disregarding oneself.

[Col. 0734A]

6. Hear, then, what I rebuke and what I advise. If, in living and exercising judgment, you give your whole self to activity and nothing to reflection, do I praise you? In this I do not praise you. Nor, I think, would anyone who has heard Solomon: “He who lessens activity will gain wisdom” (Ecclus. 38:25). Certainly activity itself does not benefit from not being preceded by reflection.

Likewise, if you wish to be wholly everyone’s, after the example of him who “became all things to all” (1 Cor. 9:22), I praise your humility—but only if it is complete. How, however, is it complete when you are excluded? You too are a human being. Therefore, if humanity is to be whole and complete, let the embrace that receives everyone gather you also within itself. Otherwise, what does it profit you, according to the Lord’s word, if you gain everyone else while losing yourself alone? Therefore, since all possess you, be yourself also one of those who possess you. Why are you alone defrauded of the gift that is yourself? How long will you be “a spirit going forth and not returning” (Ps. 67:39)? How long will you fail to receive yourself also among others in your own turn?

You are debtor to wise and foolish alike; and do you deny yourself to yourself alone? Fool and wise person, slave and free, rich and poor, [Col. 0735A] man and woman, old and young, cleric and layperson, just and wicked—all alike share in you; all drink from the public fountain of your breast; and will you stand apart thirsty? If the person who makes his own portion worse is cursed, what of the person who renders himself wholly without a share? Let your waters indeed be poured out into the streets; let people, beasts of burden, and cattle drink from them; let even Abraham’s servants give drink to the camels. Yet, among the rest, drink also yourself from the fountain of your own well. “Let no stranger drink from it,” he says (Prov. 5:17). Are you a stranger? To whom are you not a stranger, if you are a stranger to yourself? Finally, “He who is wicked to himself, to whom is he good?” (Ecclus. 14:5).

Remember, therefore—not always, not often, but at least sometimes—to restore yourself to yourself. Make use of yourself too among the many, or at least after the many. What could be more indulgent? For I say this “by way of concession, not by way of command” [or: judgment] (cf. 1 Cor. 7:6). I think I am even more indulgent than the Apostle himself in this matter.

“So you say more than is fitting.” I do not deny it. But what if it is fitting? For you, as I trust, will not be content with our timid counsel, but will abound more richly. Indeed, it is fitting that you should be more abundant than I am bold. I too judge it safer for myself to risk before Majesty by timidity than by rashness. And perhaps a wise person ought to have been advised in no other way, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Give an occasion to a wise man, and he will be wiser” (Prov. 9:9).

## CHAPTER VI. Judicial authority belongs not so much to bishops as to princes.

[Col. 0735C]

7. Yet hear what the Apostle thinks about such matters. “Is there not among you,” he says, “a wise person who can judge between brother and brother?” And he adds: “I say this to your shame: appoint as judges those who are most despised in the Church” (1 Cor. 6:5, 4). Therefore, according to the Apostle, you, an apostolic man, unworthily usurp the office [variant: “judgment”; the ensuing text is corrupt/fragmentary: “vile, the rank of the despised”]. Hence the bishop too used to say, when instructing a bishop: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Tim. 2:4).

But I spare you. For I speak not of hard things but of possible ones. Do you think these times would endure it if, when people bound together over an earthly inheritance and demanding judgment from you, you replied in your Lord’s words: “O people, who appointed me judge over you?” (Luke 12:14) Into what a judgment would you immediately be drawn! What does that rustic and unlearned person say, ignorant of your primacy—

> [Note: Col. 0735D] In a certain Vatican codex, cited by Vossius, *personatum* occurs here, and likewise below everywhere in place of *primatus*; in the same place *personatus* is read, contrary to the authority of the other manuscripts and editions [Col. 0736D].

—dishonouring the supreme and exalted see and detracting from apostolic dignity? Yet, I think, those who said this would not show where any Apostle ever sat as a judge of men, or as a divider of boundaries, or distributor of lands. I read, indeed, that the Apostles stood to be judged (Acts 5:27); I do not read that they sat judging. That will be—

> [Note: Col. 0736D] Namely, that they may sit judging, according to Matthew 19:28: “You too shall sit,” etc.

—it was not.

Is a servant thereby diminishing his dignity if he refuses to be greater than his lord? Or a disciple if he refuses to be greater than the one who sent him? Or a son if he does not overstep the boundaries laid down by his fathers? “Who appointed me judge?” says that Lord and Master; and is it an injury to a servant or disciple if he does not judge everyone? Yet he seems to me no good assessor of things who considers it unworthy of Apostles or apostolic men not to judge concerning matters of this kind, when judgment in greater matters has been granted them. Why should those who will judge even angels in heavenly things not disdain to judge over people’s little earthly properties?

Your authority, then, is in crimes, not in possessions; because for the former, not for the latter, you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven: to exclude transgressors, certainly, not possessors. “That you may know,” he says, “that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins” (Matt. 9:6), [Col. 0736B] and so forth. Which seems to you the greater dignity and authority: forgiving sins, or dividing estates? There is no comparison. These weak and earthly matters have their own judges: the kings and princes of the earth. Why do you invade another’s boundaries? Why do you extend your sickle into another’s harvest? Not because you are unworthy, but because it is unworthy for persons such as you to persist in such concerns, occupied as you are with greater matters.

Finally, when necessity requires it, hear the Apostle’s judgment: “If the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?” (1 Cor. 6:2).

## CHAPTER VII. One must give oneself first to piety and consideration of eternal things.

[Col. 0736C]

8. But it is one thing to make an incidental excursion into such matters when a pressing cause demands it, another willingly to apply oneself to them as though they were great matters, worthy of the attention of a person such as you and of persons such as yourselves. I would say these things and countless others like them if I were saying hard things, right things, unvarnished things. But now, because “the days are evil” (Eph. 5:16), it is enough for the present to have advised you not to give your whole self, nor always, to activity, but to set apart for reflection some portion of yourself, your heart, and your time.

I say this in view of necessity, not equity—although yielding to necessity is not contrary to equity. For if what was fitting were permitted, irrefragable reason plainly shows that piety, which is useful for all things, ought in every respect and in all matters to be preferred, and either cultivated alone or above all else. Do you ask what piety is? It is to devote oneself to reflection.

Perhaps you will say that in this I disagree with the one who defines piety as the worship of God (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint). It is not so. If you consider carefully, I have expressed his meaning in my words, even if only in part [or: although perhaps in part]. For what is more pertinent to the worship of God than what he himself exhorts in the Psalm: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 44:11)? This is certainly foremost among the elements of reflection.

And what, finally [or: then], is more useful for all things than that which by a kind of generous anticipation makes even the parts of activity its own, somehow acting beforehand and arranging beforehand the things to be done? This is necessary, lest things that could have been usefully foreseen and premeditated be instead done rashly to one’s danger. I do not doubt that, if you recall it, this has often happened to you in the proceedings of cases, in great business affairs, and in counsels concerning great matters.

First, reflection purifies its very source, the mind from which it arises. Then it governs the affections, directs actions, corrects excesses, orders conduct, gives honour and order to life, and finally confers knowledge alike of divine and human things. It distinguishes what is confused, compacts what gapes open, gathers what is scattered, searches hidden things, tracks down truths, tests what is plausible, and investigates what is fabricated and disguised. It orders beforehand what must be done, and reconsiders what has been done, so that nothing may remain in the mind either uncorrected [Col. 0737B] or needing correction [variant: “unrebuked … rebuke”]. In prosperity it foresees adversity; in adversity it behaves as though it does not feel it. The former belongs to fortitude; the latter, to prudence.

## CHAPTER VIII. From piety and contemplation arises the most beautiful harmony and connection of the first four virtues.

9. There too it is most delightful for you to observe a certain harmony and interconnection of virtues, and how one depends on another. Thus in this passage you see prudence to be the mother of fortitude; for any venture not brought forth by prudence is not fortitude but rashness.

Likewise, prudence, seated as a kind of arbiter between pleasures and necessities, distinguishes their boundaries on either side by fixed limits, assigning and giving the latter what is enough, while judging excessive things in the former to be madness. Thus it forms a third virtue from the two, called temperance. For reflection itself judges intemperate both the person who stubbornly takes away what is necessary and the one who indulges superfluities. Temperance, therefore, does not consist only in cutting off superfluities; it also consists in admitting necessities.

The Apostle seems not merely a supporter but an author of this judgment, since he teaches that provision for our flesh should not be made “in desire.” By saying that provision for the flesh should not be made, he restrains superfluities; by adding “in desire” (Rom. 13:14), he does not exclude necessities. Hence he does not seem to me altogether absurd who defines [Col. 0737D] temperance as neither cutting off necessity nor exceeding it, in accordance with the philosopher’s saying: “Nothing in excess.”

10. Now concerning justice, which is one of the four: is it not plain that reflection first prepares the mind to shape itself by justice? For a person must first consider himself, so that he may draw from himself the norm of justice, neither doing to another what he would not wish done to himself nor refusing another what he would wish done to himself. For in these two points the complete character of justice is clear.

Nor is justice itself solitary. Consider with me now this virtue’s beautiful connection and coherence with temperance, and likewise that of both with the two higher virtues, prudence and fortitude. Since it is said to be a part of justice not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself, and its perfection is, as the Lord says: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7:12), neither of these will exist unless the will itself, from which the whole form is derived, has been so ordered that it neither desires anything superfluous nor superstitiously refuses anything necessary. This belongs to temperance.

Finally, temperance imposes a measure even upon justice itself, if justice is to be just. “Do not be excessively just,” says the Wise Man (Eccl. 7:17), thereby showing that justice not restrained by the moderating curb of temperance is by no means to be approved. Indeed, wisdom itself does not reject this curb of temperance, since Paul says, according to the wisdom given him by God, not “to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think unto sobriety” (Rom. 12:3).

Conversely, the Lord shows that justice is necessary for temperance when in the Gospel he rebukes the temperance of those who abstained in order to appear to people to be fasting (Matt. 6:16). There was temperance in food, but no justice in their minds, because their intention was to please people, not God. Again, how could either this virtue or that exist without fortitude? For it is plainly the work of fortitude—and no ordinary fortitude—to restrain one’s own willing and unwilling within the narrow bounds of too little and too much, so that the will may be content with that middle measure: bare, pure, solitary, constant in itself, equal to itself from every side, since it is equally cut away on every side. It is agreed that this alone is virtue.

11. Tell me, please, if you can, to which especially of these three virtues you think this inmost core ought to be assigned [Col. 0738C], since it borders so closely upon all of them that it seems peculiar to each individually. Or is it virtue itself and nothing else? But then virtue would not be manifold; all virtues would be one. Or rather, because without it there is no virtue, is it in some way the one innermost power and marrow of all virtues, in which they are so united that all consequently [or: equally] seem one? Especially since they do not share it by participating in it, but each possesses the whole of it entire.

For example, what is more characteristic of justice than measure? Otherwise, if it leaves anything outside measure, it does not truly render to each person what is his own—which is nevertheless justice’s own work. What is more characteristic, again, of temperance? It is surely temperance for no other reason than that it admits nothing immoderate. But, I think, you will grant that it is no less characteristic of fortitude, because fortitude especially powerfully draws out and secures that pure mean against vices rushing upon it and trying, as it were, to suffocate it from either side, establishing it upon a stable foundation of good and making it the seat of virtue.

Therefore, to keep measure is justice, temperance, and fortitude. But see whether they differ in this: that in justice it is a matter of disposition; in fortitude, its efficacy; and in temperance, its possession and use. It remains to show that prudence is not excluded from this communion. Is prudence not the one which first discovers and recognizes measure, long set aside through the mind’s neglect and, through the hostility of vices, shut away as it were in hidden places and covered with a certain darkness of age? Therefore I tell you: it is recognized by few, because prudence belongs to few.

Thus justice seeks it, prudence finds it, fortitude vindicates it, and temperance possesses it. My purpose here is not to dispute about the virtues; I have said these things to urge you to devote yourself to reflection, through whose benefit these and similar matters are recognized. Is it not to lose one’s life to devote no effort in life to leisure so pious and so useful?

## CHAPTER IX. Recent examples of Pontiffs should gradually be corrected; ancient examples should be imitated.

12. But what if you suddenly devote yourself wholly to this philosophy? Your predecessors were not accustomed to do so.

> [Note: Col. 0739C] Others punctuate differently: “But what? If you suddenly devote yourself wholly to this philosophy, your predecessors were not accustomed to do so.” Some read, “What then?”]

You will be burdensome to very many, as one who suddenly departs from the footsteps of the fathers; indeed, you will seem to be acting in censure of them. You will also be marked by the common proverb: “When someone does what no one else does, everyone marvels”—as though you wished to be an object of admiration. Nor can you at once and suddenly either correct all their errors or bring their excesses back to measure. When you have received the opportunity, you may gradually and fittingly apply yourself to this, according to the wisdom given you by God.

Meanwhile, make what good use you can of another’s evil. Yet, if we take examples from good things rather than novel ones, Roman pontiffs have not been lacking who found leisure for themselves amid the greatest affairs. The city was under siege, and the barbarian sword hung over the necks of its citizens; did that nevertheless terrify the blessed Pope Gregory—

> [Note: Col. 0739C] Gregory, amid the very din of arms, was intent upon sacred studies, like another Archimedes. In the preface to Book II of the *Homilies on Ezekiel*, he testifies that two difficulties disturbed him in his undertaking: the extreme obscurity of the visions and the terror of impending evils. “For,” he says, “we have learned that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, eager in every way for our siege, has crossed the Po. Consider, therefore, brothers, how far an unhappy mind, occupied by the disturbances of its own fear, can penetrate into dark and mystical meanings,” etc.
>
> Yet, as St Bernard says, at that time he expounded the most obscure and final part of Ezekiel with as much diligence as elegance. Let prelates of the Church and other ecclesiastical persons now see how, living in peace and tranquillity, they use the leisure granted them: for sacred studies, or for vain and secular business. Alas, how many may be seen occupied with matters foreign, idle, and unworthy! What difference is there, moreover, between being idle and being badly occupied? In former times holy prelates found leisure to devote themselves to God even in the gravest affairs; and those will find it now who exercise care and economy of time.]

—from writing wisdom in leisure? At that very time, as is clear from his preface [or: from his words], he expounded the most obscure and final part of Ezekiel as diligently as elegantly.

## CHAPTER X. He sharply rebukes the abuse of advocates, judges, and procurators, and their frauds.

[Col. 0740A]

13. But let it be so: another custom has become established; the days are different, people’s manners are different, and dangerous times do not merely threaten but are present. Fraud, deception, and violence have grown strong upon the earth. There are many false accusers and few defenders; everywhere the more powerful oppress the weaker. We cannot fail those who are oppressed or deny judgment to those suffering injury. Unless cases are brought forward and the parties heard, how can judgment be given between the parties [variant: “who can judge between the parties”]?

Let cases be brought, but as they ought to be. For the manner commonly practised is altogether detestable, and fit not merely for the Church but not even for a secular court [variant: “would be fit”]. I marvel that your religious ears can endure to hear such disputations of advocates and battles of words, which profit more for overturning than for discovering truth. Correct the evil custom; cut off vain-speaking [or: malicious-speaking] tongues and shut deceitful lips. These are the people who have taught their tongues to speak lies: eloquent against justice, trained for falsehood; wise in doing evil, articulate in attacking truth.

They instruct those from whom they ought to have been instructed; they construct assertions not verified but their own; from their own resources they build slanders against innocence; they destroy the simplicity of truth; they block the paths of judgment. Nothing makes truth so evident without labour as a brief and pure statement. Therefore I would have you decide carefully, but briefly, those cases that must come before you—for not all need to do so—

> [Note: Col. 0739D] He rebukes the arts and frauds of advocates, whose concern is so far from being to bring controversies to rest that they rather pour oil upon them. Lawsuits are sown from lawsuits; controversies succeed controversies; and no check can halt or restrain that course of quarrels. The resources of litigants are also worn down by expenses; and for many it would be more prudent to yield their legal right than, by trying the law, to add to the loss of a perhaps less favourable claim the waste of expenditure.
>
> Bernard therefore wishes cases to be decided briefly and all the windings of litigation cut away, since nothing makes truth so manifest without labour as a brief and pure statement. In accordance with this view, we read many enactments in decrees of various councils; but would that we saw them put into practice in courts and tribunals! Council of Trent, session 24, chapter 20, *On Reform*, and session 25, chapter 10, *On Reform*, where among other provisions it says:
>
> “The holy synod admonishes both ordinaries and all other judges whatsoever to strive to conclude cases with all possible brevity, and by every means to counter the devices of litigants for delaying proceedings, whether at the joinder of issue or at another stage of judgment, either by fixing a term or by another suitable method,” etc.
>
> See the Fifth Lateran Council, session 10; and in the *Clementines*, *Saepe*, on the meaning of words; *Finem litibus*, etc.; at the end, on dowry and marriage, chapter 2; on judgments, etc.; the constitution on procurators, chapter *Nonnulli*; on rescripts; Clementine *Dispendiosam*, on judgments; and elsewhere often.
>
> Cardinal Borromeo, a great champion of ecclesiastical discipline, diligently promoted observance of these canons. A memorable fact about him is that “the notaries and scribes of his court in his time almost unlearned the skill of those lawsuits concerning benefices which are so common among clerics elsewhere” (Book VII of the *Life*, chapter 36). Stapleton also testifies in his *Life* that Thomas More, martyr of England, was utterly averse to protracting cases in court. For he “so dispatched and cleared his tribunal of all cases and lawsuits that once, when a case had been completed and he ordered the next to be brought forward, he received the answer that none at all remained there.” Thus in his *Life*, p. 39.]

—and accustom yourself to cut off futile [Col. 0741A] and hunting delays. Let the widow’s cause come before you, the cause of the poor person, and of one who has nothing to give. You may entrust many other cases to others for decision, and judge very many unworthy even of a hearing. For what need is there to admit those whose manifest sins go before them to judgment? Such is the impudence of some that, though the entire face of their case bristles with the itch of manifest ambition, they are not ashamed to demand a hearing, exposing themselves to the consciences of many in a matter in which they could sufficiently have been put to shame by the judgment of their own conscience alone.

There was no one to blunt their worn-down foreheads; and so they became more numerous and more hardened. Moreover, I do not know how it is, but one vicious person does not recoil from another’s vicious conscience; and where all are filthy, one person’s stench is not perceived. For when, for example, did a greedy person blush before a greedy person, an unclean person before an unclean person, a sensual person before a sensual person? The Church is full of ambitious people. In the pursuits and schemes of ambition, there is now nothing to be horrified at—no more than in a den of robbers over the spoils of travellers.

## CHAPTER XI. Severe action must be taken against advocates and procurators who make profit from injustice.

14. If you are Christ’s disciple, let your zeal pardon me; let your authority rise against this impudence and universal plague. Look upon the Master acting thus, and hear him say: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12:26). He does not prepare ears to hear, but a scourge to strike. He neither speaks nor receives words. For he does not sit in judgment, but pursues in punishment. Yet he does not conceal the charge: namely, that they had made a house of prayer into a place of trade.

Therefore do likewise. Let such traders be ashamed before your countenance, if possible; if not, let them fear. You too hold a scourge. Let the money-changers fear; let them not trust in their money, but distrust it. Let them hide their money from you, knowing that you are readier to pour it out than to receive it. By acting in this manner diligently and steadfastly, you will gain many people, reclaiming followers of shameful profits for more honourable duties; and you will save many from even daring to attempt such things.

Add this point, which will contribute greatly also to the leisure I urge upon you. In this way you will redeem for yourself no small portions of time to devote to reflection: by not even hearing, as I have said, certain matters; by entrusting certain others to others; and by settling, through some faithful and suitable shortening of the matter itself, those cases that you judge worthy of your hearing. I intend to add something concerning this reflection, but under the beginning of another book. Let this be the end of this one, lest a less agreeable discourse burden you doubly if it is long.

# BOOK II

[Col. 0741]

## CHAPTER ONE. He undertakes an apology for the unfortunate outcome of the expedition undertaken to the Holy Land.

[Col. 0741C]

1. Mindful of my promise—which, as you see, I have for some time now been bound to fulfil for you, most excellent man, Pope Eugenius—I wish at last, though late, to discharge my obligation. I should be ashamed of the delay, if I were conscious of carelessness or contempt. But it is not so. Rather, as you yourself know, we have fallen upon a grievous time, which seemed almost to command even the ordinary business of living itself to cease, much less intellectual pursuits. For the Lord, provoked by our sins, seemed in a manner to have judged the whole earth before its time—indeed with justice, but as though forgetful of his mercy. He spared neither his own people nor his own name. Do not the nations say, “Where is their God?” (Ps. 113:2). Nor is this surprising. The children of the Church, those reckoned under the Christian name, have been laid low in the wilderness, slain by the sword, or consumed by famine. “Contention was poured out upon princes, and the Lord caused them to wander in a trackless waste, and not in a way” (Ps. 106:40). “Destruction and misery are in their ways” (Ps. 13:3); terror, grief, and confusion are in the inner chambers of their kings. How confounded are the feet of those proclaiming peace, proclaiming good things! (Isa. 52:7). We said, “Peace,” and there is no peace; we promised good things, and behold, turmoil. As though we had undertaken this work rashly or frivolously! We did indeed run in it, not as toward an uncertain goal, but at your command—rather, through you, at God’s command. Why then did we fast, and he did not regard it? We humbled our souls, and he did not know it? For in all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still outstretched. How patiently, meanwhile, he still hears sacrilegious voices and Egyptians blaspheming that he craftily led them out in order to kill them in the wilderness (Exod. 32:12)! And indeed, “the judgments of the Lord are true” (Ps. 18:10): who does not know this? Yet this judgment is so great an abyss that I seem to myself not without reason to pronounce blessed the person who has not been offended by it.

> **Note:** The expedition to the East, undertaken at St Bernard’s urging, ended unhappily. Hence arose murmurings and calumnies against the holy man. In this chapter he sets against them an antidote, or apology. Other writers do the same, lest one suppose that Bernard alone defended his own cause and innocence. See Geoffrey, *Life*, book III, ch. 4; Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, book I, ch. 60. After much philosophical discussion of this matter, Otto finally concludes: “That expedition, although joined with so great a slaughter of Christians, was good and salutary—not, perhaps, for an enlargement of territories or for bodily advantage, but at least for the salvation of many souls.” He adds: “And if we say that that holy Abbot, Bernard, was inspired by the Spirit of God to rouse us, but that we, through our pride and self-indulgence, failed to observe his salutary counsels and therefore deservedly suffered the loss of possessions and persons, this is not inconsistent with reason or ancient examples.” Thus Otto, who was present and was able to narrate more faithfully what he saw with his own eyes. See the letter of John, Abbot of Casa-Marii, among Bernard’s letters, no. 332 (now 386); and William of Tyre in Baronius under the year 1148, on the causes of the frustrated expedition. But it is pleasant to hear, above all others, a writer of that age of sound reputation and reliability explaining more carefully the causes of the unsuccessful war. This is William of Newburgh, *On English Affairs*, book I, ch. 20:
>
> “We read that in ancient times the exceedingly numerous army of the Lord was so defiled by the crime of one man sinning even secretly, and stripped of divine favor, that it appeared feeble and languid. When the Lord was consulted, he answered that the people had been polluted by the ban, and added: ‘The accursed thing is in your midst, Israel; you will not be able to stand against your enemies until the one contaminated by this crime is removed from among you.’ Now in that army of ours such evils, contrary both to Christian and even to military discipline, had increased that it is no wonder that divine favor did not smile upon them as polluted and unclean persons. For camps (*castra*) are so called from the castration of lust. But those camps of ours were not chaste; in them the passions of many breathed under a certain disastrous license. Moreover, presuming upon their multitude and the equipment of their forces, and thus proudly making flesh their arm, they trusted too little in the mercy and power of the Lord, for whom they seemed to be zealous. Thus it was made manifest in them that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Furthermore, in the land of the Christian Emperor, with whom they had made a treaty and by whose command goods for sale were either brought in or plentiful, they restrained themselves too little from plundering. Therefore the angered Emperor sent against them famine on the one side and the enemy on the other, not at all shrinking from the danger to so much Christian blood, though himself a Christian. Finally, when merchandise was prohibited and our men could not go out to gather provisions because of enemy ambushes, the army first wasted away with hunger; then, caught in the enemies’ snares, it either made the swords of the Turks drunk with blood or exchanged the condition of Christian liberty for the lot of a most shameful and miserable slavery. Nor did heavenly indignations fail in chastising the proud and unclean; and often, as is said, a downpour from untimely clouds, poured out from above, diminished our army more than the enemy sword. And so, after by far the greater part of two very great armies had been destroyed by diverse disasters and defeats, the two great princes came with the remnant to Jerusalem, scarcely escaping destruction; and, having accomplished nothing memorable, they departed without glory.”
>
> Thus Newburgh.

> **Note:** This passage is taken from Psalm 106:40, where in Bernard’s time *contentio* (“contention”) was read, as in William of Tyre, book XVI, ch. 21, instead of the reading now found, *contemptio* (“contempt”), which is more correct according to the Greek ἐξουδένωσις, “contempt.”

2. Yet how does human rashness dare to criticize what it is wholly unable to comprehend? Let us remember the judgments from on high which have existed from the beginning, if perhaps there may be consolation in this. For someone said: “I remembered your judgments from of old, O Lord, and was comforted” (Ps. 118:52). I speak of something unknown to no one, and now known to no one. Such, indeed, is the condition of mortal hearts: what we know when there is no necessity, we do not know in necessity.

Moses, about to lead the people out of the land of Egypt, promised them a better land (Exod. 3:17). For how else would a people that knew only one land have followed him? He led them out; yet he did not bring those whom he had led out into the land he had promised. The sad and unexpected outcome cannot be charged to the rashness of their leader. He did everything at the Lord’s command, with the Lord’s cooperation, and with the work confirmed by signs that followed. “But,” you say, “that people was stiff-necked, always acting contentiously against the Lord and Moses his servant.” Quite so: they were unbelieving and rebellious. But what of these people? Ask them themselves. Why need I say what they themselves admit? I will say one thing. What progress could those make who continually turned back while walking? Did not these too, throughout the whole journey, return in heart to Egypt? If those fell and perished because of their iniquity, do we wonder that these, doing the same things, suffered the same things? But was their fall contrary to God’s promises? Then neither was the fall of these. For God’s promises never prejudice God’s justice. Hear another example.

3. Benjamin sinned. The remaining tribes gird themselves for vengeance, and not without God’s approval. He himself finally appointed a leader for those about to fight. Thus they fought, relying on the stronger hand, the better cause, and—greater than these—the divine favor. Yet how terrible is God in his counsels over the children of men! (Ps. 65:5). Those avenging wickedness turned their backs before the wicked, and the more numerous before the fewer. But they return to the Lord. And the Lord says to them, “Go up.” They go up again, and again they are routed and confounded. Thus, with God first favoring and then commanding them, the righteous undertake a just contest and are defeated. But the more inferior they were in the struggle, the more superior they proved in faith.

What, do you think, would these people do to me if, at my urging, they went up again and were defeated again? If they heard me urging them a third time to repeat the journey, to repeat the undertaking in which they had already once and twice failed? Yet the Israelites, reckoning neither the first nor the second disappointment, obeyed a third time and prevailed (Judg. 20). But perhaps these people say: “How do we know that the word has gone forth from the Lord? What signs do you perform, that we may believe you?” I need not answer these things myself; my modesty must indeed be spared. You answer for me and for yourself, according to what you have heard and seen—or at least according to what God inspires in you.

> **Note:** What Bernard contributed to the undertaking of the expedition is shown by his letters 256, 288, and 386, and by book III of his *Life*, ch. 4.
>
> **Note:** He implies the miracles by which God confirmed Bernard’s preaching and exhortations to the holy war; see book IV of his *Life*, chapter following, and letter 242, to the people of Toulouse, with the notes there.

But perhaps you wonder that I pursue these matters when I had proposed another subject. I do so without forgetting my purpose, because I do not judge them foreign to that purpose. For, as I remember, I am speaking to Your Dignity about consideration. And surely these are great matters, requiring no small consideration. If great matters ought to be considered by great persons, to whom does this study belong as fittingly as to you, who have no equal on earth? But you will act in this matter according to the wisdom and power given you from above. It is not for my lowliness to prescribe that anything be done in this way or that. It is enough to have indicated that something ought to be done, so that the Church may be comforted and the mouths of those speaking iniquity stopped.

Let these few words be said by way of apology, so that your conscience, whatever its quality, may have from me grounds on which to regard me as excused, and you likewise—if not before those who judge deeds by their outcomes, at least before yourself. For each person, the complete and perfect defense is the testimony of his own conscience. It matters very little to me that I should be judged by those who call good evil and evil good, making light darkness and darkness light (Isa. 5:20). If one of two things must occur, I would rather that people’s murmuring be directed against us than against God. It is good for me if he deigns to use me as a shield. I willingly receive upon myself the slanderers’ malicious tongues and the blasphemers’ poisoned arrows, so that they may not reach him. I do not refuse to become inglorious, provided no assault is made upon God’s glory. Who will grant me to glory in that utterance: “For your sake I have borne reproach; shame has covered my face”? My glory is to become a companion of Christ, whose is that utterance: “The reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me” (Ps. 68:8, 10). Now let the pen return to its subject, and let the discourse proceed in its proper course to the matters we proposed.

## Chapter II. The distinction between consideration and contemplation

5. First, consider what I mean by consideration itself. I do not wish it to be understood as identical in every respect with contemplation: contemplation relates more to certainty about things, consideration to inquiry. In this sense contemplation may indeed be defined as the true and certain intuition of the mind concerning any matter, or an undoubting apprehension of truth. Consideration, however, is intense thought directed toward investigation, or the attention of a mind tracking down truth. Though both terms have customarily been used interchangeably and without distinction.

## Chapter III. He identifies four objects of consideration

6. As to the fruit of consideration, I think there are four things for you to consider as they occur: yourself; the things under you; the things around you; and the things above you. Let your consideration begin with yourself, lest you be fruitlessly extended toward other things while neglecting yourself. What does it profit you if you gain the whole world while losing yourself alone? (Matt. 16:26). Even if you are wise, you lack wisdom if you are not wise for yourself. How much do you lack? In my judgment, everything.

You may know all mysteries; you may know the breadth of earth, the height of heaven, and the depths of the sea; if you do not know yourself, you will resemble one building without a foundation, producing not a structure but a ruin. Whatever you build outside yourself will be like a heap of dust, exposed to the winds. Therefore one who is not wise for himself is not wise. A person wise for himself will be wise, and he himself will first drink from the spring of his own well. Therefore let your consideration begin with yourself; yet not only begin, but also end in yourself. Wherever it wanders, bring it back to yourself with the fruit of salvation. You are first for yourself; you are last.

Take an example from the Father of all, who both sends forth his Word from himself and retains it. Your word is your consideration: if it proceeds, let it not depart. Let it advance in such a way that it does not go out; let it go forth in such a way that it does not abandon you. In gaining salvation, no one is more closely related to you than your mother’s only child. Think nothing against your own salvation. I have said too little: I ought to have said, nothing apart from it. Whatever presents itself to consideration and does not in some way concern your own salvation must be rejected.

## Chapter IV. He embraces self-knowledge in a threefold consideration of oneself, and here expounds the first member of consideration

7. This consideration of yourself is divided into three points: consider what you are, who you are, and what kind of person you are. What you are by nature; who you are in person; what kind of person you are in character. What, for example, is a human being? Who are you? Pope, or Supreme Pontiff. What kind of person? Kind, gentle, or whatever else of that sort.

Although that first question belongs more to philosophical than apostolic inquiry, still it is contained in the definition of a human being, whom they call a rational, mortal animal. If you wish, you may examine this more carefully. It neither conflicts with your profession nor with your dignity; rather, it can bring benefit to salvation. For when one considers these two things together—rational and mortal—the fruit that comes to him is this: that what is mortal in him may humble what is rational; and, conversely, that what is rational may strengthen what is mortal. Neither point will be neglected by a prudent person. If the present place still requires further matters to be considered, they will be treated below, perhaps more usefully through comparison of the parts.

## Chapter V. He proposes the second member of self-consideration: namely, who he is and whence he comes

8. Now attend to who you are and from what you have been made. Although, as to my words “from what,” I think this should be passed over and left rather to your own knowledge. This I say: it is unworthy of you to deal imperfectly with so great a perfection which you have assumed. Why should you not blush to be found least among great persons when you remember that you were great among the least? You have not forgotten your first profession; what was taken up by your hand has not fallen from your mind, nor even from your affection. It will be useful to keep it before your eyes in every command, judgment, and ordinance of yours. This consideration makes you a despiser of honor even amid honor itself. And that is a great thing. Let it not depart from your heart: it is a shield against that arrow, “Man, though in honor, did not understand” (Ps. 48:13).

Say therefore to yourself: “I was lowly in the house of my God.” What is this—to be raised, from being poor and despised, above nations and kingdoms? Who am I, or what is my father’s house, that I should sit higher than the exalted? Surely the one who said to me, “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10), trusts that I shall be a friend. If I am found otherwise, it will not go well. He who raised me up can also cast me down. Too late will be the complaint: “By lifting me up, you dashed me down” (Ps. 101:11). Loftiness ought not to flatter where anxiety is greater. The former intensifies danger; the latter proves the friend. Let us gird ourselves for this, if we do not wish at last to take the lowest place in shame.

> **Note:** He warns that the memory of one’s former condition should keep a person within the bounds of modesty—certainly a fitting bridle for restraining and checking arrogance and swelling pride. Agathocles of Sicily gave a famous and outstanding example: born to a potter father of obscure station, he eventually gained the kingdom of Sicily. Yet, lest the appearance of honor should carry him beyond the limits of decency and make him forget whence he came and upon how slippery a place fortune had set him, he preserved the memory of his origin by using earthenware vessels, at the sight of which he recalled that he was the son of a potter. Ausonius expressed this elegantly in an epigram. Nicholas Serarius also recounts it in his *History of Mainz*, where he treats of Willegis, archbishop of that church. Though Willegis too was born in an obscure place and at length made archbishop, the greater he became, the more humbly he behaved; and so he endeavored repeatedly to recall the memory of his former condition. Since his father had been a wheelwright, he painted wheels—the craft of his father—everywhere on buildings and walls, adding this motto: “Willegis, Willegis, do not forget who you were.” He adopted this as his perpetual emblem, so that its sight might continually nourish remembrance of his origin. The city of Mainz preserves it even to the present day. See Serarius in the cited place, p. 723 in my copy, where he offers further symbolic observations about the wheel and not inappropriately philosophizes on the brevity of life and the mutability of fortune.

## Chapter VI. What ought to be the concern of the leaders of the Church

9. We cannot conceal the fact that you have been set above others; but we must by every means attend to the purpose for which this has occurred. It is not, I think, for ruling as a lord. For the prophet too, when he was similarly raised up, heard: “That you may root up and pull down, destroy and scatter, build and plant” (Jer. 1:10). What here sounds of pride? Spiritual labor is expressed under an image of rustic toil. Let us therefore, so that we may not think too highly of ourselves, recognize that a ministry has been imposed upon us, not a lordship granted us. I am not greater than the prophet; and though perhaps equal in authority, there is no comparison in merits.

Say these things to yourself and teach yourself, you who teach others. Think of yourself as one of the prophets. Is that not enough for you? It is more than enough. But by God’s grace you are what you are. What then? Be what a prophet is; are you anything more than a prophet? If you are wise, you will be content with the measure God has apportioned to you. For what exceeds it is from evil. Learn from the prophetic example to preside not so much for issuing commands as for doing what the times require. Learn that you need a hoe, not a scepter, in order to do the prophet’s work. Indeed, he went up not to reign but to uproot.

Do you suppose that you too will find something requiring labor in the field of your Lord? Very much indeed. The prophets were certainly not able to cleanse the whole field; they left something for their sons, the Apostles, to do; and your own fathers left something for you. But neither will you suffice for everything. You will certainly leave something to your successor, and he to others, and others to still others, until the end. Finally, workers are rebuked for idleness at the eleventh hour and sent into the vineyard. Your predecessors, the Apostles, heard: “The harvest indeed is great, but the workers are few” (Matt. 9:37). Claim your paternal inheritance. For if you are a son, you are also an heir (Gal. 4:7). To prove yourself an heir, awake to care; do not lie sluggish in idleness, lest it be said to you also, “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matt. 20:6).

10. Still less ought you to be found dissolved in luxuries or reclining amid pomp. Your testator’s documents assign none of these things to you. What then? If you are content with their tenor, you will inherit care and labor rather than glory and riches. Does the chair flatter you? It is a watchtower. From it you look out over all things, since you have been established as a watchman over all. For this outlook produces readiness for battle, not leisure. How can one delight in glory when one is not permitted to be idle? There is no place for idleness where the diligent care of all the churches presses upon one.

For what else did the holy Apostle leave you? “What I have,” he says, “I give you.” What was it? One thing I know: it was not gold or silver, since he himself says, “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). If it happens that you possess them, use them not at your pleasure but as the occasion requires. Thus you will use them as though not using them. In themselves, as regards the good of the soul, they are neither good nor evil; yet their use is good, their misuse evil, concern over them worse, and profit from them more shameful. Suppose you claim these things for yourself by whatever other right: it is not by apostolic right. For he could not give you what he did not possess. What he had, that he gave: care over the churches, as I have said. Did he give lordship? Hear him: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5:3). And lest you think this was said only in humility and not also in truth, the Lord’s voice in the Gospel says: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors”; and he adds, “But you are not so” (Luke 22:25). It is plain: lordship is forbidden to the Apostles.

11. Go then, and dare to claim for yourself either an apostleship exercised as a lord or lordship exercised as an apostolic man. You are certainly forbidden one or the other. If you wish to possess both at once, you will lose both. Otherwise, do not suppose that you are exempt from the number of those concerning whom God complains: “They reigned, but not through me; they became princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8:4). Now if it pleases you to reign without God, you have glory, but not before God. But if we acknowledge the prohibition, let us hear the command: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves.” This is the apostolic form: lordship is forbidden; service is commanded, and is commended by the example of the Lawgiver himself, who goes on to add: “But I am in the midst of you as one who serves” (Luke 21:26–27).

Who now can regard himself as inglorious in this title, when the Lord of glory first marked himself by it? Paul rightly glories in it, saying: “They are ministers of Christ—and I am too.” And he adds: “I speak as though less wise: I more so—in labors more abundant, in imprisonments more abundant, in stripes beyond measure, in deaths often” (2 Cor. 11:23). O splendid ministry! Is it not more glorious than a principality? If one must glory, the example of the saints is set before you, and the glory of the Apostles is proposed to you. Does that glory seem small to you? “Who will grant me to be made like those in the glory of the saints?” The prophet cries: “But to me your friends have been greatly honored, O God; their principality has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. 138:17). The Apostle cries: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6:14).

12. I desire that you should always glory in this, in the best kind of glory—the glory which the Apostles and Prophets chose for themselves and handed down to you. Recognize your inheritance in Christ’s cross and in abundant labors. Happy is the one who could say, “I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). It is glory, but there is nothing empty in it, nothing soft, nothing indolent. If labor terrifies, let the reward invite you. For each will receive a reward according to his labor. And though he labored more than all, he did not complete all the labor; there is still room.

Go out into the field of your Lord, and consider carefully how many thorns and thistles from the ancient curse still make it wild even today. Go out, I say, into the world: for the field is the world, and it has been entrusted to you. Go out into it, not as a lord but as a steward, to inspect and provide for that concerning which an account will be demanded of you. Go out, I would say, with certain steps of intent care and careful intention. For even those commanded to go into all the world did not traverse the world in bodily presence, but in the foresight of their minds.

Lift up, then, certain eyes of your consideration and see the regions, whether they are not more dry for fire than white for harvest. How many things that you thought were crops will, when carefully examined, appear rather as brambles! Indeed, not even brambles: they are ancient, decayed trees, certainly not fruitful—unless perhaps in acorns or husks, which swine eat. How long will they occupy the ground? If you go out and see these things, will you not be ashamed to let the axe lie idle? Ashamed to have received the apostolic sickle without purpose?

13. The patriarch Isaac once went out into this field, when Rebecca first met him; and, as Scripture says, “He had gone out to meditate” (Gen. 24:62). He went out to meditate; you must go out to uproot. Meditation ought already to have gone before you: the time for action is at hand. If you begin to hesitate—or to deliberate—now, it is too late. Earlier, according to the Savior’s counsel, you ought to have sat down; earlier you ought to have assessed the task, measured your strength, weighed your wisdom, compared your merits, and calculated the resources of your virtues.

Act, then; suppose that the time for pruning has come—provided meditation has preceded it. If you have stirred your heart, your tongue must now be stirred, and your hand must be stirred as well. Gird on your sword, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:17). Glorify your hand and right arm by executing vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples, binding their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles. If you do these things, you honor your ministry, and your ministry honors you. This is no mediocre principality: it is to drive evil beasts from your borders, so that your flocks may be led safely to pasture. You will tame wolves, but you will not lord it over sheep. You have undertaken to feed them, certainly, not to oppress them. If you have carefully considered who you are, you do not fail to know that these are the things you ought to do.

For to one who knows and does not act, it is sin (Jas. 4:17). You have not forgotten where you read: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do worthy things will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47). This is how the Prophets acted, and the Apostles. They were strong in battle, not soft in silks. If you are a son of the Apostles and Prophets, do likewise. Claim noble descent for yourself through similar conduct; for such descent is noble from no other source than nobility of character and strength of faith. Through this they conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises (Heb. 11:33).

This is the charter of your paternal inheritance which we have unfolded for you, so that you may see the portion—or substance—that falls to you. Put on strength, and you have inherited. Possess faith, possess devotion, possess wisdom—but the wisdom of the saints, which is the fear of the Lord—and you possess what is yours. You possess whole and intact your paternal estate, without fraud. Virtue is a most precious estate. Humility is a good estate, in which the whole spiritual building, constructed, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Through it some have even possessed the gates of their enemies. For what virtue can equally defeat all the pride of demons and the tyranny of men? Yet, although it is indiscriminately a tower of strength against the enemy’s face for every person, somehow its power is proved greater in the great and brighter in the illustrious. There is no gem more splendid, especially in the entire adornment of the Supreme Pontiff. For the higher he is above the rest, the more illustrious he appears through humility—and through it, more illustrious even than himself.

## Chapter VII. Returning to the earlier question, “Who is he?”, he examines it more carefully

15. Perhaps I shall be accused because, before sufficiently completing the first parts, my pen has somehow run on to the second, beginning to describe what sort of person you ought to be before more fully setting out who you are. I suppose that, blushing to see a man placed on the highest summit appear naked, it hastened to clothe him in his insignia. Without these, the more illustrious he appears to his equals, the more deformed he is. Can the desolation of a city set upon a mountain be hidden? Or can the smoke of a lamp extinguished upon a lampstand remain unseen? A monkey on a roof; a foolish king sitting on a throne.

Now hear my song, less pleasant indeed, but salutary. A monstrous thing: the highest rank and the lowest spirit; the first seat and the basest life; a high-sounding tongue and an idle hand; much speech and no fruit; a grave expression and frivolous conduct; great authority and wavering stability. I have held up a mirror: let the ugly face recognize itself in it. Rejoice if you find your own unlike it. Yet look into it yourself too, lest perhaps, even if you have reason to be properly pleased with yourself, there should not also be something by which you ought to be displeased with yourself. I want you to glory in the testimony of your conscience, but no less to be humbled by that same testimony.

Rare is the utterance: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4). You walk more cautiously amid good things if evil things also do not escape your notice. Therefore, as I said, know yourself, so that amid the anxieties which are not lacking you may enjoy the good of conscience; but more especially so that you may know what you lack. For who lacks nothing? The one who thinks that nothing is lacking to him lacks everything. What if you are Supreme Pontiff? Is it because you are Supreme Pontiff that you are supreme? Know that you are lowest if you think yourself highest. Who is supreme? The one to whom nothing can be added. You grievously err if you suppose that you are he. Far be it.

You are not among those who regard dignities as virtues. Virtue was yours before dignity. Leave that doctrine to emperors and others who did not fear to be worshiped with divine honors—for example, Nebuchadnezzar, Alexander, Antiochus, and Herod. But consider that you are called supreme not by consummation but by comparison. Do not suppose that I mean comparison of merits, but of ministries. Let a person regard you as a minister of Christ—and, without prejudice to anyone’s holiness, certainly the highest among ministers. Otherwise, I would have you strive toward the highest point, not think yourself supreme, or wish to be thought so before you are. For how do you advance if you are already sufficient to yourself? Therefore let it not be either burdensome for you to investigate what is lacking, or shameful for you to admit what is lacking. Say also in the voice of your predecessor: “Not that I have already received or am already perfected”; and again: “I do not consider that I have attained” (Phil. 3:12–13).

This is the knowledge of the saints, far removed from that knowledge which puffs up. He who adds this knowledge adds sorrow (Eccl. 1:18); but no wise person ever avoids this sorrow. It is a healing sorrow, by which that deadly numbness of the hardened and unrepentant heart is beaten out. Therefore he was wise who could say: “My sorrow is always before me” (Ps. 37:18). Now we must resume whatever remains of that passage from which we turned aside a little while ago.
