## Chapter VIII. He discusses the excellence of pontifical dignity and authority

15. Come, let us inquire still more carefully who you are, that is, what role you bear for the present in the Church of God. Who are you? A high priest, the Supreme Pontiff. You are the prince of bishops; you are the heir of the Apostles: Abel in primacy, Noah in governance, Abraham in patriarchal dignity, Melchizedek in order, Aaron in dignity, Moses in authority, Samuel in judgment, Peter in power, Christ in anointing. You are the one to whom the keys have been delivered and to whom the sheep have been entrusted. There are indeed other gatekeepers of heaven and shepherds of flocks; but you have inherited both names more gloriously inasmuch as you have inherited them more distinctively than the rest. They have their flocks assigned to them, each one a single flock; all have been entrusted to you, one flock to one person.

> **Note:** This reading is more pleasing than the other found in Vossius: “The one [Christ] entrusted all to you alone.”

You alone are the shepherd of all, not only of the sheep but also of the shepherds. You ask how I prove this? From the Lord’s word. To whom—not, I say, of bishops, but even of Apostles—were all the sheep entrusted so absolutely and without distinction? “If you love me, Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21:15). Which sheep? The peoples of this or that city, region, or particular kingdom? “My sheep,” he says. To whom is it not plain that he designated no particular sheep but assigned all? Nothing is excepted where nothing is distinguished. And perhaps the other fellow disciples were present when, in entrusting them to one, he commended unity to all in one flock and one shepherd, according to the saying: “One is my dove, my beautiful one, my perfect one” (Song 6:8). Where there is unity, there is perfection. The other numbers have not perfection but division, departing from unity.

Thus it is that the others each received a single people as their allotted share, knowing the mystery. Finally James, who seemed to be a pillar of the Church, was content with Jerusalem alone, yielding universality to Peter. He was fittingly placed there to raise up the offspring of his dead brother where that brother was killed; for he was called the brother of the Lord (Gal. 1:19). But when the Lord’s brother yielded, who else should intrude upon Peter’s prerogative?

[Col. 0752B] 16. Therefore, according to your canons, others are called to share in the burden of responsibility [Note: [Col. 0751D] Nor is this reading pleasing, from the codex of Nicholas V: “to share in the burden of responsibility or authority, yet subject to you”; the words “or authority, yet subject to you” are absent from all the others.], whereas you are called to the fullness of power. The authority of others is confined within fixed limits; yours extends even over those who have received authority over others. If cause should arise, can you not close heaven to a bishop, depose him even from the episcopate, and hand him over to Satan? Your privilege, then, stands unshaken for you, both in the keys given and in the sheep entrusted.

Receive another point which likewise confirms your prerogative [variant: “itself”] for you. The disciples were sailing, and the Lord appeared upon the shore—and, more joyfully still, in his risen body. Peter, knowing that it was the Lord, cast himself into the sea and thus came to him, while the others arrived by boat (John 21). What does this mean? Surely it is a sign of Peter’s singular pontificate [Col. 0752C]: by it he undertook to steer not one ship—as each of the others did his own—but the very world. For the sea is the world, and the ships are the Churches. Thus, on the other occasion when he walked upon the waters in the likeness of the Lord, he designated himself as Christ’s sole vicar [Note: [Col. 0752D] Yet Bernard also calls bishops vicars of Christ in the following treatise, no. 36. See the notes there on no. 31 and on Epistle 183.], one who ought to preside not over one people but over all; for “many waters” are “many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). Thus, while each of the others has his own ship, one most immense ship has been entrusted to you: the universal Church itself, made up of all and spread throughout the whole world.

## CHAPTER IX. He commends consideration of one’s own nature.

17. Behold who you are. But do not forget also what you are. For neither have I forgotten that I promised to return to this at a suitable point. How fittingly, when you consider what you were before along with what you are [Col. 0752D] now! What do I mean, “were”? You are it even now. Why cease to look upon what you do not cease to be? There is indeed one consideration of what you have been and what you are; another of what you have become. The latter ought not, in the examination of yourself, to drive out page 423 the former. For, as I said, you are still what you were; and you are no less this than what you became afterwards—perhaps even more so. For you were born that, but borrowed this; you were not changed into this. The former was not discarded, but the latter added.

[Col. 0753A] Let us treat both together; for, as I remember having said beforehand, the two matters, compared with one another, will become more useful. I said above that, when one considers what one is, the nature by which one is a human being presents itself—for you were born a human being. But if one asks who you are, the name of your office answers: that you are a bishop. This you became; you were not born it. Which of these seems to you to be purely your own and more fundamentally to belong to you: what you became, or what you were born? Surely what you were born. Therefore I advise you to consider above all that which you most are—namely, a human being, which is also what you were born.

18. You must attend not only to what you were born, but also to what sort of being you were born, if you do not wish to be cheated of the fruit and benefit of your self-examination. Remove, then, these hereditary loin-coverings, cursed from the beginning. Tear away [Col. 0753B] the covering of leaves that conceal shame but do not heal the wound. Wipe away the cosmetic of this fleeting honor and the sheen of ill-colored glory, so that you may consider the naked man nakedly, because “naked you came forth from your mother’s womb” (Job 1:21).

Did you emerge wearing a mitre? Glittering with gems? Resplendent in silks? Crowned with feathers? Laden with metals? If you disperse and blow away all these things from before your consideration, like morning clouds swiftly passing and soon to pass away, there will meet you a human being naked, poor, wretched, and pitiable: a human being grieving that he is human, ashamed that he is naked, weeping that he has been born, murmuring that he exists; a human being “born for toil” (Job 5:7), not for honor; a human being born of [Col. 0753C] woman, and therefore bearing guilt; living for a short time, and therefore in fear; “filled with many miseries” (Job 14:1), and therefore with tears. And truly with many: those of body and soul together.

For what calamity is absent from one born in sin, with a frail body and a barren mind? Truly he is filled, upon whom bodily weakness and folly of heart are heaped together with inherited impurity and bondage to death. It is a salutary conjunction that, when you consider yourself Supreme Pontiff, you should at the same time observe that you were not, but are, the most worthless dust. Let thought imitate nature; let it imitate also, what is worthier, the Author of nature, joining the highest and the lowest. Did not nature, in the person of man, bind the breath of life to vile clay? Did not the Author of nature, in his own person, blend the Word and clay? Thus take your pattern both from the composition [Col. 0753D] of our origin and from the mystery of redemption, so that, sitting high, you may not think high things, but may think humbly of yourself and agree with the humble.

## CHAPTER X. He expounds the third part of self-consideration, namely, what sort of person one is.

19. Therefore, if you consider how great you are, consider also—and especially—what sort of person you are. This consideration indeed holds you within yourself and does not allow you to fly away from yourself, to walk in great things or in things too wonderful for you. Stand within yourself. Do not cast yourself down below; do not raise yourself above; do not escape farther away; do not spread yourself more broadly. Hold the middle, if you do not wish to lose measure. The middle place is safe. The middle is the seat of measure, and measure is virtue. Every dwelling beyond measure [variant: “habitation”] the wise person counts as exile.

[Col. 0754A] Therefore it is not for him to dwell in what is long, because that is beyond measure; nor in what is broad, because that is outside it; nor, again, in what is high or low, because the one is above and the other below it. For length commonly has banishment, breadth division, height ruin, and depth engulfment. I say this more plainly, lest you think that I am speaking of the length, breadth, height, and depth which the Apostle urges us, with all the saints, to comprehend (Eph. 3:18); that belongs to another discussion and another time (below, Book V, chapters 13–14).

Here, however, I call it “long” when a person promises himself a longer life; “broad” when the mind is stretched out toward superfluous cares; “high” when one presumes too much about oneself; and “deep” when one casts oneself down too much. He, therefore, who measures out for himself [Col. 0754B] long periods of time surely enters upon the road of banishment, passing beyond the bounds of life through prolonged anxious care. Hence people, exiles from themselves in the present through forgetfulness, migrate through vain anxiety into other ages—ages that will not benefit them, indeed that will not even exist.

Likewise, a mind stretched out into many things must be torn by many cares. Excessive extension produces attenuation, and excessive attenuation produces tearing. Further, what is high presumption but a ruinous plunge? For you have read: “Before ruin the heart is lifted up” (Prov. 18:12). Conversely, what is the descent of excessive faintheartedness but a certain despairing engulfment? The courageous person will not be cast down into this. The prudent person will not be drawn away by the uncertainty of a longer life. The moderate person [Col. 0754C] will regulate his cares, restrain himself from superfluities, and not fail in necessities. The just person, moreover, will not presume things higher than himself, but will speak with the just man: “Even if I were righteous, I would not lift up my head” (Job 10:15).

## CHAPTER XI. He earnestly commends to the Pontiff an earnest examination of himself.

20. Therefore, in this consideration of yourself, walk cautiously and conduct yourself with complete fairness, so that you neither attribute more to yourself than is true nor spare yourself more than is just. Moreover, you attribute more than is true not only by arrogating to yourself good that you do not possess, but also by ascribing to yourself the good that you do possess. Carefully distinguish what sort of person you are from yourself and what sort you are by God’s gift; and let there be no deceit in your spirit. Yet there will be, unless, faithfully apportioning, you return what is yours to yourself and what belongs to God to God, without fraud.

I do not doubt that you are persuaded that evils come from yourself and good things from the Lord. Indeed, while considering what sort of person you are, you must also call to mind what sort you have been. Later things must be compared with earlier. Have you advanced in virtue, wisdom, understanding, and sweetness of character, or have you perhaps—may it not be so!—fallen away from them? Are you more patient or more impatient than usual, more irascible or gentler, more arrogant or humbler, more approachable or harsher, more easily entreated or more difficult, more fainthearted or more magnanimous, more grave or somewhat more lax, more fearful or perhaps more confident than you ought to be?

How broad a field lies open to you in this kind of consideration! I mention a few things, putting forward, as it were, certain seedbeds; I do not myself sow, but give seed to the sower. Your zeal, your clemency, and also the discernment that governs those virtues must become known to you [Col. 0755A]: namely, what sort you are in forgiving injuries, what sort in avenging them, and how observant in both cases you are of due measure, place, and time. These three things must certainly be considered in exercising these virtues, lest they cease to be virtues when found apart from them. For virtues of this kind are made virtues not by nature but by use; they are known to be indifferent in themselves. It is yours either, by abusing and confusing them, to make them vices, or, by using them rightly and in order, to make them virtues.

When the eye of discernment is clouded, they commonly steal one another’s places and occupy one another’s limits. There are two causes of this clouding: anger and a softer affection. The latter weakens the rigor of judgment; the former precipitates it. How can either the compassion of clemency or the rectitude of zeal not be endangered by one or the other? An eye disturbed by anger sees nothing mercifully; an eye suffused with a certain weak and womanish softness [Col. 0755B] of mind does not see what is right. You will not be innocent if you either punish one whom perhaps you ought to spare, or spare one who ought to have been punished.

## CHAPTER XII. The mind must neither be relaxed too greatly in prosperity nor fail in adversity.

21. I do not want you to conceal from yourself what sort of person you find yourself to be in tribulations. If you are steadfast in your own troubles and compassionate in those of others, rejoice. This belongs to an upright heart. The opposite belongs to one altogether perverse: if, perhaps, you find yourself impatient in your own troubles, yet are found not to sympathize at all with those of others.

What of prosperity? Is there nothing there to stir self-consideration? Certainly there is, if you carefully observe how rare it has always been to find one who has not, even [Col. 0755C] slightly, relaxed his mind’s guard and discipline in prosperity. When has prosperity not been, for the incautious, to discipline what fire is to wax, what the ray of the sun is to snow or ice? David was wise, Solomon wiser; yet when favorable circumstances excessively flattered them, one partly and the other wholly lost his wisdom. Great is the person who, falling into adversity, does not fall away even a little from wisdom; nor is he less great whom present happiness, if it smiles upon him, does not mock.

Yet you will more easily find those who retained wisdom when fortune was adverse than those who did not lose it when it was favorable. That person is to be preferred and is great [variant: “among the great”] in whom, amid prosperity, not even an unbecoming laugh, a haughty word, or an excessive concern for clothing or bodily appearance has crept in.

## CHAPTER XIII. He dissuades the Pontiff from idleness, trifles, and empty talk.

22. Although the Wise Man rightly urges that wisdom be written “in leisure” [Col. 0756B] (Ecclus. 38:25), one must guard against idleness even in leisure. Idleness must therefore be avoided, the mother of trifles and the stepmother of virtues. Among secular people, trifles are trifles; in a priest’s mouth, they are blasphemies [Note: [Col. 0755C] He commands trifles and idle tales to be driven from the mouth of a priest—how much more from that of a Pontiff? He wishes it to be open only to serious and useful matters, namely, a mouth consecrated to the Gospel and not to be profaned by empty talk, even if others disguise it under the more polished name of wit.

A wholly similar example of ancient and strict virtue was left by Blessed Peter Damian, who seems to have derived—or at least sharpened—from this his weariness of public life and his desire for quiet and solitude: namely, that the manners, witticisms, jokes, or, to use Bernard’s word, trifles of courtiers did not suit him well. Let us hear him in the letter in which he excuses himself before the pope and cardinals for having resigned the bishopric of Ostia:

> “There was once a time—there was—but it has now passed away, when the modesty of shame, the badge of mortification, worthy severity, and the discipline proper to a priestly character could be maintained. For, to rebuke myself alone as I deserve, you yourselves see that as soon as I come among you, behold: sallies of wit, pleasantries, charms, urbanities, sharp sayings, volumes of questions, and every pest of empty words burst forth without restraint. They show us no longer as priests, but rather as orators and rhetoricians, or—even more disgracefully—as buffoons.
>
> “For as soon as we begin exchanging words, certain allurements of reciprocal conversation gradually creep in, improperly softening all the mind’s rigor and dissolving the strength of seriousness into uncontrolled laughter and shameful jokes. Thus the mind, scattered outside itself, is thrown into confusion; the eye of the heart is blunted; the light of divine love is extinguished; reverence for the priesthood and its power to inspire awe in others are lost; and, more dangerously still, the rule of right living, which ought to have been proposed to others as an example, is not maintained.
>
> “But if we disdain to bend toward these things either through shame or through fear, we are immediately judged inhuman, rigid, and [Col. 0756C] as though born of Hyrcanian tigers—made of stone. I restrain my pen, for I blush to add still more shameful absurdities: hunting, bird-catching, moreover the frenzies of dice or of chess,” etc.

Such is his testimony. Here you see how well he agrees with Bernard, and what kinds of trifles he detests in priests—trifles which many churchmen today, not to mention prelates, so far from judging to be blasphemies with Bernard, do not even regard as venial sins.

The fault of empty speech, against which Bernard here warns Eugenius, another most holy Pontiff, Gregory, long ago rebuked gravely and movingly, proposing his own example as though he himself were guilty. For, when reflecting upon Ezekiel’s words, “Son of man, I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel,” he weighed the burden of his calling and burst out in words that deservedly strike our hearts as well. We shall excerpt a little; read the whole passage in its place, Homily II on Ezekiel:

> “Oh, how harsh these things are that I say! For in speaking I strike myself … I who am often entangled in idle words, and, sluggish and negligent, refrain from exhorting and edifying my neighbors! Before the sight of God I have become mute and wordy: mute in necessary things, wordy in idle things, etc. … And indeed, while I was in the monastery, I was able both to restrain my tongue from idle talk and to keep my mind almost continually intent upon prayer. But after I placed the shoulder of my heart beneath the burden of pastoral office, my mind cannot continually gather itself back to itself, because it is divided among many things … And because the necessity of my position often joins me to secular men, I sometimes relax the discipline of my tongue. For if I maintain myself in the continual rigor of my own strictness, I know that the weaker flee from me, and that I never draw them toward what I seek. Thus it happens that I often patiently listen even to their idle words. But because I too am weak, drawn for a little while into idle speech, I begin gladly to say those things which I began unwillingly to hear. And where I was weary of falling, I delight to lie,” etc.

Saint Ambrose, when treating of duties, considers the discipline of joking, customarily handed down by secular men, to be something he ought to pass over. “For although,” he says, “honorable and pleasant jokes may sometimes occur, they nevertheless depart from the ecclesiastical rule.” Book I, chapter 23.

Those sacred speakers, indeed, who—to use Bernard’s words—have consecrated their mouths to the Gospel, ought here to be cautious lest they slip into trifles and amusements, whether privately or publicly [Col. 0757D]. I am angry with preachers who, from the pulpit, repeatedly bring forward jokes, witticisms, and amusing little stories—such as I see even in recently published sermons of a certain religious. Let them read Chrysostom on chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Ephesians, where he shows how fitting it is for Christian seriousness to abstain from ridiculous things. Whoever reads this, says Charles Régis, S.J., in *The Christian Orator*, cannot fail to wonder how far most preachers to Christian people “depart from that seriousness which that very wise man justly demanded even from the people themselves.” Thereupon he presses the present passage of Bernard upon them.

Accordingly, he prudently warns that a preacher must avoid a manner of speaking more suited to courtiers than to religious men, characteristic of those who live more by the spirit of this world than by the Spirit of God, and savoring more of certain habits which today we call political than of evangelical simplicity. “Of this kind,” he says, “is a light and youthful freedom in familiar intercourse: under the pretext of a certain cheerful and more pleasant conversation, mixing in ridiculous sayings and deeds and amusing stories, so as in this manner to keep friends and noblemen engaged in familiar talk.”

So says that writer, most suitable for forming a sacred orator [Col. 0758D], and worthy to be kept in the hands of every preacher. Book II, chapter 16.]. Yet if such things happen to arise, they may perhaps sometimes be endured; they must never be repeated. One should rather intervene cautiously and wisely in such trifling. One must indeed break out with something serious, which they will hear not only profitably but willingly, and thus cease from idle talk.

You have consecrated your mouth to the Gospel; to open it now for such things is unlawful, and to grow accustomed to them is sacrilege. “The lips of the priest,” he says, “guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth” (Mal. 2:7), certainly not trifles or tales. A scurrilous word, which they disguise under the name of witty or urbane speech, is not sufficiently banished from the mouth; it must be relegated far from the ear as well. You are shamefully moved to loud laughter; more shamefully, you move others to it. Moreover, whether it is more damnable to speak ill of another or to listen to one speaking ill, I would not easily say.

## CHAPTER XIV. Partiality in judgments must be avoided above all.

[Col. 0757A]

23. There is no need for me to weary your attention [Note: [Col. 0758D] Vossius notes that some manuscripts read *animum* (“mind”). But this is the explanation of a certain shallow scholar. Bernard wrote *intuitum* (“attention,” “consideration”), referring to the consideration with which the whole book is concerned. Nor would it be worth noting this, were it not for similar passages: thus, in Book III, no. 16, some codices cited by Vossius have *animam* (“soul”) instead of *sanguinem* (“blood”), which is a gloss.] regarding avarice, since you are said to regard money as chaff. There is absolutely no reason to fear it in your judgments. But there is something which is accustomed to lie in wait for judges no less often and no less harmfully; and I do not wish you to remain ignorant of what may lurk concerning it in your conscience. You ask what it is? Partiality toward persons.

Do not consider yourself guilty of a small sin if you show partiality to sinners rather than judge cases according to their merits. There is another fault too, from which, if you find yourself free, you will sit, in my judgment, solitary among all whom I have known to ascend the thrones; because, truly and uniquely, you have raised yourself above yourself, according to the prophet (Lam. 3:28). This is the ease of credulity, from whose most cunning little fox none, so far as I have discovered, has guarded sufficiently against the wiles of the great. Hence great anger against them for nothing; hence the frequent condemnation of the innocent; hence prejudgments against the absent.

Yet I congratulate you—for I do not fear to incur with you the charge of flattery. I congratulate you, I say, that up to now you preside with little complaint of all these things. Whether also without fault, you must see. Now consideration must turn to the things beneath you. But this belongs to another beginning; for a briefer discourse better suits your occupations.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0757]

426 ## CHAPTER I. The Pontiff’s task is not so much to subject all to his dominion as to bring all, as far as possible, to the bosom of the Church.

[Col. 0757B]

1. The end of the preceding book provides the beginning of this one. Therefore, according to that book’s promise, the things beneath you must be considered. What those things are, most excellent Eugenius among priests, you should not think must be asked of me; perhaps you should more properly ask what things are not. Whoever wishes to investigate what does not belong to your care would have to go beyond the world.

Your fathers were appointed to conquer not certain regions, but the world itself: “Go into all the world” (Mark 16:15) was said to them. They, indeed, sold their tunics to buy swords: a fiery word and a mighty spirit, weapons powerful through God. Where did those famous conquerors, sons of the cast-off [uncertain], not arrive? Where did the sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals, not reach? (Ps. 119:4.) “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5) [Note: [Col. 0758D] Not so much by bodily presence as by the providence of the mind; above, Book II, no. 12.]. Those words, kindled with the fire which the Lord sent upon earth (Luke 12:49), penetrated [Col. 0758B] and set aflame. The most valiant warriors fell, but did not yield; even in death they triumphed. “Their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. 138:17); “they were appointed princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17).

You succeeded them in the inheritance. Thus you are heir, and the world is the inheritance. But how far this portion concerns you, or concerned them, must be weighed by sober consideration. For I do not think that possession of it was granted to you at all; rather, as it seems to me, its stewardship was entrusted to you only to a certain extent. If you proceed to usurp possession too, he contradicts you who says: “The world is mine, and its fullness” (Ps. 49:12). You are not he of whom the prophet says: “And the whole earth shall be his possession” (Ps. 103:24).

This is Christ, who claims possession for himself by the right of creation, by the merit of redemption, and by the gift of the Father. To whom else was it said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2:8)? Yield possession and lordship to him; you are to have care of it. This is your portion. Do not stretch out your hand farther.

2. “What?” you ask. “Do you not deny that I preside, and yet forbid me to rule?” Precisely so. As though he did not preside well who presides in care. Is not an estate subject to its steward, and a minor master to his tutor? Yet the one is not master of the estate, nor is the other master of his master. So you too must preside in order to provide, take counsel, manage, and safeguard. Preside so as to benefit; preside as the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household. For what purpose? “To give them food at the proper time” (Matt. 24:45): that is, to administer, not to command.

Do this, and do not, being a human being, desire to dominate human beings, lest all injustice dominate you [Col. 0759B]. But this has been more than sufficiently made known above, when the question of who you are was discussed. Yet I add this: I fear for you no poison and no sword more than the lust for domination. Certainly, to grant you much, unless you are greatly deceived, you think that you have received nothing more than the great Apostles.

Remember now that saying: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Rom. 1:14). And if you think this debt is not undue for you, remember at the same time that the troublesome name of debtor suits a servant rather than a master. The servant in the Gospel hears: “How much do you owe my master?” (Luke 16:5). Therefore, if you recognize yourself not as the master but as the debtor of the wise and the foolish, you must take the utmost care and consider with complete vigilance how those who are not wise may become wise and those who have become foolish may return to soundness of mind. Now no kind of foolishness is, so to speak, more foolish than unbelief. Therefore [Col. 0759C] you are debtor also to unbelievers: Jews, Greeks [variant: “Greeks omitted”], and Gentiles.

3. It is therefore your concern to make every effort you can that unbelievers may be converted to faith; that those converted may not turn away; that those turned away may return; moreover, that the perverse may be ordered toward uprightness, those subverted recalled to truth, and subverters convicted by invincible arguments—so that they themselves may be corrected, if possible, or, if not, may lose the authority and ability to subvert others. Nor should you wholly neglect even this worst kind of foolish people. I mean heretics and schismatics: for these are the subverted and the subverters, dogs for tearing apart and foxes for deceit. Such people, I say, must especially be either corrected through your effort, lest they perish, or restrained, lest they destroy others.

Suppose that the time excuses you regarding the Jews: they have their own appointed end, which cannot be anticipated [variant: “passed over”]. The fullness of the Gentiles must come first. But what answer do you give concerning the Gentiles themselves? Rather, what answer does your consideration give when it asks you this: What seemed good to the Fathers in setting a limit to the Gospel and suspending the word of faith while unbelief endures? For what reason, we may suppose, did the swiftly running word come to a halt? (Ps. 147:15.) Who first checked this saving course? Perhaps some cause unknown to us, or necessity, could have stood in their way.

4. What reason have we for overlooking it? With what confidence, with what conscience, do we fail even to offer Christ to those who do not possess him? Do we hold back the truth of God in unrighteousness? Yet the fullness of the Gentiles must at some time be reached. Do we wait for faith to fall upon them? Who ever happened by chance to believe? “How shall they believe without a preacher?” (Rom. 10:14). Peter was sent to Cornelius, Philip to the eunuch (Acts 10:20; 8:26); and, if we seek a more recent example, Augustine, sent by blessed Gregory, handed on the form of faith to the English.

Consider these matters thus with yourself. I add also the obstinacy of the Greeks, who are with us and are not with us, joined in faith but divided in peace, although even in faith itself they have limped away from right paths [Col. 0760B]. I add likewise the heresy which creeps secretly almost everywhere and openly rages among some. For it hastens everywhere and publicly to swallow up the Church’s little ones [Note: [Col. 0759D] The Henrician and Cologne heretics wished to exclude little children from baptism; see Epistle 241 and Sermons 65 and 66 on the Song of Songs. Or perhaps those people, spread from Aquitaine even into Spain, which land is called “the South” below because it lies southward for us Gauls.].

You ask where this is? Your men [variant: “men”], who so often visit the land of the South, behold, they know and can tell you. They go and return through the midst of those people, or pass alongside them; but what good they have yet done among them, we have not heard. And perhaps we would have heard, had the salvation of the people not been valued less than the gold of Spain. It is your task also to provide a remedy for this plague.

5. But there is a foolishness which has now almost made foolish even the wisdom of faith itself. How has this poison infected almost the whole Catholic body too? For while each of us, even within it, seeks what is our own [Col. 0760C], we become envious of one another, provoke one another, are exercised toward hatreds, encouraged toward injuries, armed for lawsuits, sharpened for deceits, carried away toward slanders, and burst forth into revilings; we are oppressed by the stronger and oppress the weaker.

How worthily and laudably is the meditation of your heart occupied against so pestilential a kind of foolishness, which you observe to have occupied Christ’s very body, that is, the multitude of believers! O ambition—the cross of aspirants! How, while tormenting all, do you please all? Nothing tortures more bitterly; nothing disturbs more painfully; yet among miserable mortals, nothing is more celebrated in its affairs. Does not ambition now wear down the thresholds of the Apostles more than devotion? Does not your palace resound all day long with its clamors? Does not the whole discipline of laws and canons toil over its profits? Does not all Italy’s insatiably greedy rapacity gape after its spoils?

Why is this so? Or rather, what else has not merely interrupted but cut off your own spiritual pursuits? How often has this restless and disturbing evil caused your holy and fruitful leisure to miscarry? One thing is what the oppressed appeal to you concerning; another is what ambition strives to make reign in the Church through you. You must neither fail those people nor give any assent to this ambition. Yet it is unjustly fostered, while they are despised; and you are debtor to both: to them, that you may raise them up; to the others, that you may restrain them.

## CHAPTER II. What moderation ought to be observed in appeals to the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0761A]

6. And since the subject of appeals has arisen, it will not be inappropriate to pursue it somewhat further. Great and pious consideration is needed in these matters, lest what was provided out of great necessity [variant: “utility”] be rendered useless through bad use. It seems to me that appeals may bring about much ruin if they are not conducted with the highest moderation [Note: [Col. 0761D] On the use of appeals, compare Epistle 178 and its notes, and also Hildebert’s Epistle 82.].

Appeals are made to you from the whole world. This indeed testifies to your unique primacy. But if you are wise, you will not rejoice in primacy, but in its fruit. The Apostles were told: “Do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you” (Luke 10:20). Appeals are made to you, as I said; and would that they were as fruitful as they are necessary. Would that, when the oppressed cries out, the oppressor might feel it, and the wicked might not boast in that by which the poor man is inflamed. What could be so fitting as that, at the invocation of your name, the oppressed should flee to safety and the crafty should not take refuge [Note: [Col. 0761D] That is, should not flee for refuge, as in Volume V, Guerric’s Sermon 1 on the Assumption, no. 1, and elsewhere among reputable authors. Hence *refugium*, “refuge.”]? Conversely, what could be so perverse, so alien to rectitude, as that the one who has done wrong should rejoice and the one who has suffered it should be wearied in vain?

You are most inhuman if you are not moved toward the person whose pain has been increased by the injury inflicted, the labor of the journey, and the loss of expenses. Yet you are no less cowardly if you are not moved against the one who has been partly the author and partly the cause of so many calamities for him. Awake, man of God, when these things occur: let your compassion be stirred, and let your indignation be stirred as well. You owe the one to the injured person, the other to the injurer. Let the former be consoled by recovery of his losses, satisfaction for his injuries, and an end to vexatious litigation [Col. 0761C]; let the latter be dealt with so that he repents of doing what he did not fear to do, and does not laugh at the sufferings of the innocent.

7. I think that the person who perhaps appealed without cause ought to suffer the same. This rule of justice is set before you both by the divine, unchangeable principle of equity and, if I am not mistaken, by the very law of appeals: an unlawfully made appeal must neither benefit the appellant nor harm the appellee. Why should a person have been wearied in vain? How full of justice it is that he should harm himself rather than his neighbor [Note: [Col. 0761D] Others add *laedere* (“harm”) by way of explanation. Then: “To appeal unjustly is unjust; for one who appeals unjustly to go unpunished is a tinderbox for unjust appeals.” Vossius thinks this reading should be inserted into the text. But our reading is constant in our manuscripts and, in my judgment, better. Most prudently, the Council of Trent, Session 13, chapter 1, *On Reform*: “Since those accused of crimes, in order mostly to avoid punishment and evade the judgments of bishops, pretend complaints and grievances and, by the evasions of appeal, impede the judge’s proceedings, lest they abuse for the defense of wrongdoing a remedy instituted for the protection of innocence, and so that provision may be made against their cunning and evasion, it decrees as follows,” etc.] whom he wished to harm? To appeal unjustly is unjust; for one who appeals unjustly to go unjustly and unpunished is a tinderbox for unjust appeals.

Every appeal is unjust which is not compelled by lack of justice. It is permissible to appeal, not in order that you may burden another, but if you have been burdened. Appeal must be made from a judgment. Before judgment, an appeal is wholly improper unless it is undertaken because of a manifest grievance. Therefore, one who appeals without having been aggrieved plainly intends either to burden another or to buy time. Appeal is not an evasion, but a refuge.

How many do we know who have appealed after being summoned [Col. 0762A], so that meanwhile they might be allowed what is never allowed? We know that some, for as long as they lived, were enabled by the support of an appeal to commit wicked deeds—for example, incest and adultery. What sort of thing is this: that what ought especially to have been feared by the shameless should patronize shamefulness? How long do you either ignore or fail to notice the murmur of the whole earth? How long do you sleep? How long will your consideration not awaken to such confusion and abuse of appeals?

They are made contrary to law and justice, contrary to custom and order. Neither place, manner, time, cause, nor person is distinguished. They are lightly undertaken everywhere, and most often wickedly. Were not those who wished to act maliciously especially accustomed to fear them? Now, through them, they become a terror to the very people who ought to be protected—and this harms the good. The antidote has been turned into poison. This is not a change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.

8. Good people are appealed against by bad people so that the good may not do good; and, fearing, they refrain from the voice of your thunder. Thus bishops are appealed against lest they dare dissolve or prohibit unlawful marriages. They are appealed against lest they presume in any way to punish or restrain robberies, thefts, sacrileges, and such things. They are appealed against lest they be able to exclude or remove unworthy and infamous persons from sacred offices or benefices.

What remedy do you find for this disease, lest what was found as a remedy be found to bring death? The Lord was zealous for the house of prayer when it was made a den of thieves (Matt. 21:13); do you, his minister, ignore the refuge given to the wretched when it becomes [Col. 0762C] weapons for injustice? You see everywhere the cause of the oppressed snatched away, while those not so much burdened as wishing to burden others burst forth to appeal. What mystery is this? It is yours to consider, not mine to comment upon.

“And why,” you ask, “do those wrongly appealed against not come, to show their innocence and convict malice?” I say what they are accustomed to say in reply: “We do not wish to be harassed in vain. There are persons in the curia who more readily favor appellants and encourage appeals. It is better to yield at home than to yield at Rome.”

9. I confess that I do not wholly disbelieve these things. [Note: [Col. 0762D] Others read “disbelieve,” as in Epistle 158, to Innocent.] Among the very frequent appeals made today, show me one person who has refunded even a penny to someone whom he may have appealed against, for the expenses of the journey. Yet it would be strange [Col. 0762D] if all the appellants were just, and all those appealed against were found guilty upon your examination. “Love justice, you who judge the earth” (Wis. 1:1), he says. It is little merely to uphold justice unless you also love it. Those who uphold it, uphold it; those who love it, are zealous for it. A lover of justice investigates justice and pursues it; moreover, he persecutes every injustice. Have nothing to do with those who regard appeals as hunting expeditions. One is ashamed of the saying which among the pagans has already become proverbial: “We have started two fat stags.” [Alternatively: “We have known two fat stags.”] To speak more mildly, there is more wit than justice here. If you love justice, you do not seek appeals, but endure them. Yet what benefit does the justice of one man bring to the churches of God where the prevailing judgment is that of men otherwise disposed? But this will belong to that part of the subject when the matters around you begin to be considered (below, IV.5).

10. Now do not suppose that you may idly neglect this consideration: namely, that you should restore appeals, if possible, to their lawful use. And if my view is sought—or rather, if it is to be given attention—I say that appeals are neither to be despised nor, on the other hand, to be used indiscriminately. [Col. 0763B] Which of these two I should judge more insolent, I could scarcely say—unless it be that abuse seems to create a certain necessity for contempt, and therefore perhaps ought to be attacked more sharply, since it does greater harm. Or is not what is evil in itself, and worse in its offspring, truly more harmful? Is it not this very abuse that either weakens or destroys even the law of nature itself? For it often not merely diminishes, but takes away, the value attached to even the most precious things.

What is more acceptable than the Sacraments? Yet, when they are usurped by the unworthy or treated unworthily, they are by no means acceptable. They rather bring condemnation, because they do not receive the reverence due to them. I confess that appeals are a great good, universal to the world, and as necessary to mortals as the sun itself. Indeed, they are in some sense a sun of justice, bringing to light and reproving works of darkness. They must certainly be fostered and upheld—but those appeals which necessity has compelled, not cunning devised. All appeals of this kind are abusive: they do not come to the aid of necessity, but assist injustice. Why should they not fall into contempt? How many people, in order that they might even defer to such appeals, have surrendered their own right rather than weary themselves with a long and fruitless journey?

[Note: [Col. 0763D] Relevant here are the words above, no. 8: “It is better to yield at home than to yield at Rome.” In a similar case Juvenal, *Satire* 8:

> It is madness, after everything, to lose the fare as well.]

Yet many, unable to bear losing what was theirs, have treated ill-timed appeals—and exalted titles—with too little respect.

11. Let me give an example relevant to the matter. A certain man had publicly betrothed a wife to himself. The celebrated day of the wedding arrives; everything is ready, and many have been invited. Then behold: a man coveting his neighbour’s wife suddenly raises the cry of an appeal, [Col. 0763D] asserting that she had previously been given to him and therefore ought rather to be his. [Alternatively added: “What more need be said?”] The bridegroom is stunned; all stand motionless; the priest does not dare proceed; the entire preparation comes to nothing. Everyone returns home to eat his own dinner, and the bride is withheld from both the bridegroom’s table and bed until a return has been made from Rome. This happened at Paris, the noble royal city of Gaul.

Again, in the same city, a man who had betrothed a wife to himself fixed the day for the marriage. In the meantime an accusation arose, some saying that they ought not to be joined. The case was brought before the judgment of the Church; [Col. 0764A] but before sentence was awaited, an appeal was made without cause, without grievance, solely for the sake of delaying the matter frustratively. But he, unwilling either to lose what he had prepared or to be deprived for so long of the society of his beloved, nevertheless carried out what he had planned, disregarding—or overlooking—the appeal.

What of the recent presumption of a certain young man in the church of Auxerre? After the holy bishop had died, [Note: [Col. 0764D] Namely Hugh, whom Bernard likewise calls holy, without naming him, in Epistle 276.] and the clergy wished, according to custom, to elect another for themselves, he intervened, appealing and forbidding it to be done until he had gone to and returned from the City. Yet he himself did not defer to that appeal. For when he saw himself being disregarded—as one who had appealed without reason—he summoned such persons as he could, and on the third day after the election made by the others, held his own election. [Note: [Col. 0764D] Bernard treats this whole affair at length in Epistles 275, 276, and 280.]

[Col. 0764B]

12. Since, therefore, from these examples and innumerable others like them it is clear that abuse is not born from contempt, but contempt from abuse, consider what it means that your zeal almost continually punishes contempt while overlooking abuse. Do you wish to restrain contempt more perfectly? See that the wicked shoot is choked in the very womb of its most wicked mother. This will happen if abuse is punished with a penalty worthy of correction. Remove abuse, and contempt has no excuse. Moreover, inexcusable conduct will expel boldness. Let there be no abuser, and there will be no contemner—or at least a very rare one.

You do well when, denying the support—indeed the refuge—of appeals, you remit many cases to those competent to hear them, or to those who can learn the facts more quickly. For where knowledge is more certain and more readily obtained, judgment can be safer and swifter. How full of grace this is, and how many people you thereby spare alike labour and expense! But to whom you entrust cases in this way is something you must attend to in every respect. I could usefully add much more on this same point; but, mindful of my purpose and content for the present to have supplied an occasion, I pass on to other matters.

## CHAPTER III. Church prelates are appointed not so much to preside and feed themselves as to benefit others.

13. And first, what occurs to me I think should by no means be passed over. You preside—and uniquely so. For what purpose? I tell you, this requires consideration. Is it that you may grow from your subjects? By no means, but that they may grow through you. They made you their ruler, but for themselves, not for you. Otherwise, how do you regard yourself as superior [Col. 0764D] to those from whom you beg a benefit? Hear the Lord: “Those who have authority over them are called benefactors” (Luke 22:25). But this concerns those outside. What has it to do with us? You are falsely called this unless you intend not merely to be set over benefactors, but to be a benefactor yourself.

It is the mark of a mean and abject mind to seek from subjects not their advancement but one’s own gain. Nothing is more shameful, especially in the chief ruler of all. The Teacher of the Gentiles rightly judged that parents ought to lay up treasure for their children, not children for their parents (2 Cor. 12:14). That repeated saying of his is a word of no small glory: “I seek not the gift, but the fruit” (Phil. 4:17).

But let us now pass from this also, lest anyone construe my delay upon these matters as imputing avarice to you. How far this vice is from you I testified in the preceding book (ch. 4), knowing how great are the things you have refused, and in how great need you have refused them. Thus I have written these things to you, but not because of you. For what is written to you ought not benefit you alone. This passage censures avarice, a vice from which your reputation is sufficiently free; whether your conduct is also free, you must see for yourself. Yet we have seen—leaving aside offerings from the poor [alternatively, “poorer persons”], which you refuse to touch—German money-bags return emptied, [alternatively, “held back”], 431 but in price, not in weight. Silver was reckoned as hay; packhorses, though their loads were not lightened, returned home laden nevertheless, and against their will.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] *Summarii*: packhorses, commonly called *sommiers*, from *summa*, or σάγμα (*sagma*, “a load”).]

A new thing! When until now has Rome disgorged [alternatively, “fled from”] gold? And we do not believe that this was done by Roman counsel. Two men came, both wealthy and both accused. One was from Mainz, the other from Cologne.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] Henry I, Archbishop of Mainz, burdened by the accusations of his own canons and appealing to the Apostolic See, was absolved. Bernard writes for him in Epistle 302; see the notes there. The other, from Cologne, was Arnold, elected archbishop in 1138 after having been provost of St Andrew’s; some years later he was accused of simony. Concerning this Arnold, the author of the *Great Belgian Chronicle*, a canon regular of St Augustine near Neuss, testifies that he was accused of simony at the Council of Reims in the presence of Eugenius, and received a sentence of deposition together with the Archbishop of Mainz. When the said archbishops went to Rome to seek reconciliation, Henry of Mainz obtained favour, but Arnold of Cologne could not obtain reconciliation, though he had offered very much in order to secure it.]

To one favour was restored freely; the other, I suppose, as unworthy to have favour restored, heard: “With the garment in which you entered, you shall depart in the same.” O magnificent saying! A saying truly of apostolic freedom! How is it inferior to that saying, “Your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20)? Except that the former sounds more zealous, the latter more restrained.

What of that man from overseas regions, running almost from the ends of the earth by land and sea for a bishopric, buying it again with his own resources and those of others?

[Note: [Col. 0766D] He seems here to speak of William intruded into the see of York; see Epistles 235, 238, and those following. Add what John of Salisbury reports concerning Eugenius in *Polycraticus*, Book V, ch. 15, where Eugenius is praised because “he received absolutely no gift from a litigant, or from anyone whom he believed to have litigation impending.”]

For he had already bought it once before. He brought much, [Col. 0765C] but took back much—though not everything. The wretch fell into other hands, more powerful [alternatively, “more ready”] to receive than to give. You did well, keeping your own hands innocent in both cases, consenting neither to lay a burden on the ambitious man nor to bow before unjust Mammon. You did not similarly withhold from a poor bishop, giving what he might give lest he be thought ungenerous; he received secretly what he gave openly. Thus his honour was preserved by provision from your purse; and, while also complying with the custom of the Curia, by your kindness he escaped the odium of those who love gifts. You cannot hide it: we know both the deed and the person. Does it distress you to hear it? I proclaim it all the more gladly because you hear it more reluctantly: if this is expedient for you, it is expedient for me as well. It is no more fitting for me to keep silent about Christ’s glory than for you to seek your own. And if you still continue to murmur, the Gospel will answer you: “The more he commanded them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it, saying: ‘He has done all things well’” (Mark 7:36–37).

## CHAPTER IV. The ranks of orders and dignities in the Church must not rashly be confused or disturbed. From this he censures the abuse of seeking privileges and exemptions.

[Col. 0766A]

14. Hear something else—if indeed it is something else. For someone might perhaps say that it belongs to the same matter. Let your consideration judge this. It seems to me that one does not differ far from the truth who perhaps thinks it should be classed among forms of avarice. I shall not deny that it is either a form of avarice or has its appearance. It belongs to your perfection to avoid both evil things and likewise evil appearances. In the one case you provide for conscience; in the other, for reputation. Suppose that you may not do—even though on other grounds you perhaps might lawfully do—anything that carries an evil appearance. Ask your elders, [Col. 0766B] and they will tell you: “Abstain from every appearance of evil” (1 Thess. 5:22).

Let the servant of the Lord imitate the Lord, for he himself says: “Whoever serves me must follow me” (John 12:26). And of him you have: “The Lord reigns; he has put on majesty; the Lord has put on strength” (Ps. 92:1). You too, then, be strong in faith and splendid in glory, and you will prove yourself an imitator of God. Your strength is the confidence of a faithful conscience; your splendour is the brightness of a good reputation. Therefore, I beg you, put on strength; for “the joy of the Lord is your strength.” Moreover, he delights in your appearance and beauty as in his own likeness. Put on the garments of your glory; be clothed doubly, as that strong woman was accustomed to clothe her household (Prov. 31:21). Let there be no wavering weakness of little faith in your conscience, nor blemish of evil appearance in your reputation; then you will be clothed doubly, the bridegroom will rejoice over your soul as over his bride, and your God will rejoice over you.

You wonder where this is tending, still unaware of what I mean to say. I will not detain you longer. I speak of the murmur and complaint of the churches. They cry out that they are being cut short and dismembered.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] For the exemptions Bernard approves or disapproves, see here no. 18, and compare Epistle, or Opuscule II, to Henry of Sens, ch. 9, below.]

There are either no churches, or very few indeed, which neither feel nor fear this wound. You ask: what wound? Abbots are withdrawn from bishops, 432 bishops from archbishops, archbishops from patriarchs or primates. Is this a good appearance? It would be remarkable if even the action could be excused. By acting thus you prove that you possess plenitude of power, but perhaps not so much plenitude of justice. You do this because you can; but whether you ought to do it is the question. You have been set in place to preserve for each his own rank and order of honours and dignities, not to begrudge them, [Col. 0767A] as one of your own has said: “Render honour to whom honour is due” (Rom. 13:7).

15. The spiritual man who “judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15) will anticipate every action of his by a threefold consideration. First, whether it is lawful; next, whether it is fitting; and finally, whether it is expedient. For although in Christian philosophy it is certainly established that nothing is fitting unless it is lawful, and nothing expedient unless it is fitting and lawful, it does not follow that everything lawful is fitting or expedient.

Come, let us apply these three tests, if we can, to this action. But how is it not unfitting for you to use your will as law, and because there is no one to whom you may appeal, to exercise power while neglecting reason? Are you greater than your Lord, who said: “I have come not to do my own will” (John 6:38)? Indeed, it is no less the mark of an abject than of a proud mind to act as though devoid of reason—not according to reason, but according to whim; to be led not by judgment but by appetite. What is more bestial? And if it is unworthy of any rational being to live like cattle, who can endure in you, the ruler of all, so great an insult to nature and injury to honour? By such degeneration—may it never be!—you make a universal reproach particular to yourself: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Again, what is more unworthy of you than that, while possessing the whole, you are not content with the whole unless you somehow strive still to make your own certain trifles and small portions of the whole entrusted to you—as though they were not yours? Here I would have you remember [Col. 0767C] Nathan’s parable of the man who had many sheep

[Note: [Col. 0767D] Alternatively, “who had a hundred sheep.” But the parable in 2 Kings 12 has “very many sheep.” “A hundred” was introduced by some unskilled person from the Gospel parable of the hundred sheep, Luke 15.]

yet coveted the one belonging to a poor man (2 Kings 12). Let the deed—indeed, the crime—of King Ahab also be brought to mind: he possessed the totality of things, yet coveted one vineyard. May God avert from you what that man heard: “You have killed and taken possession” (3 Kings 21).

16. But do not allege to me the benefit of this emancipation itself. There is none, except that bishops become more insolent, and monks more lax. And what is more, poorer as well. Examine more carefully everywhere the resources and lives of such freedmen, and see whether you do not find in the one shameful poverty, and in the other worldliness. These are the twin offspring of the noxious mother, liberty. Why should a wandering and improperly free populace not sin more licentiously, when there is no one to rebuke it? Why too should unarmed religion not be more freely plundered and despoiled, when there is no one to defend it? To whom can they flee? Surely not to bishops who grieve at the injury? They look on with laughing eyes, both at the wrongs they do and at those they suffer. What benefit, finally, is there in this blood? I fear it is that which God threatened through the prophet: “He shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood at your hand” (Ezek. 3:18).

For if the person withdrawn becomes proud, and the person from whom he is withdrawn burns [alternatively, “murmurs”], how is the one who withdraws him innocent? This is too little: we involve him in fire; hear more plainly. If the one who murmurs is dead [Col. 0768A] in respect of his soul, how does the instigator live? How indeed is he not guilty of the death of both—and of his own as well—who gave the sword by which both might die? This is what I said: “You have killed and taken possession.” Add that those who hear are scandalized, indignant, slanderous, and blasphemous—that is, wounded unto death. A tree producing such fruits is not good: insolence, laxity, waste, quarrels, scandals, hatreds, and, what is more grievous, serious enmities and enduring discords among churches. You see how true that saying is: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. 10:22). What if perhaps they are not even lawful? Forgive me: I am not easily persuaded that what brings forth so many unlawful things is lawful.

[Col. 0768B]

17. Do you finally judge it lawful for yourself to mutilate churches of their own members, confuse their order, and disturb the boundaries established by your fathers? If it belongs to justice to preserve to each person what is his own, how can taking away what is his from anyone accord with a just man? You are mistaken if you think that your apostolic power is established by God not only as supreme, but as the only power. If you think this, you dissent from him who says: “There is no power except from God.” Therefore what follows—“Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance”—though it applies to you principally, does not apply to you exclusively. For the same man says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13:1–2). He does not say “to the higher power,” as though there were one, but “to the higher powers,” as though there were many. Therefore, your power alone is not from the Lord; there are intermediate powers, [Col. 0768C] and there are lower ones.

And just as those whom God has joined are not to be separated (Matt. 19:6), so those whom he has subordinated are not to be made equals. You make a monster if, removing the hand, you make the finger hang from the head, superior to the hand and beside the arm. Such is the case if you arrange the members in Christ’s body differently from the way he himself arranged them. Unless you think that another is meant by him who “set some in the Church as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as teachers and pastors, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body” (Eph. 4:11–12). And Paul himself, portraying this body for you in truly apostolic language, and fitting it most aptly to its head, declares it to be wholly joined and knit together through every joint of supply, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, making the body grow for its own edification in charity [Col. 0768D] (Eph. 4:16).

Do not regard this form as lowly because it is on earth: it has its pattern from heaven. For “the Son can do nothing except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19), especially since under Moses’ name it was said to him: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40).

18. He had seen this who said: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, prepared by God” (Rev. 21:2). For I think it was said because of the resemblance: just as there Seraphim and Cherubim, and all the others down to Angels and Archangels, are ordered under one head, God; so here also, under one supreme pontiff, are primates or patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, priests or abbots, and the rest in this manner. It is no small matter that this has God as its author and derives its origin from heaven. If a bishop says, “I do not wish to be under an archbishop,” or an abbot, “I do not wish to obey a bishop,” this is not from heaven. Unless perhaps you have heard some angel say, “I do not wish to be under the Archangels,” or someone from any other lower order refusing to be subject to anyone except God.

“What,” you ask, “do you forbid dispensations?” No: I forbid dissipation. I am not so ignorant as not to know that you have been appointed dispensers, [Col. 0769B] but for building up, not for destruction (2 Cor. 13:10). For among stewards it is required that one be found faithful (1 Cor. 4:2). Where necessity presses, a dispensation is excusable; where advantage invites, a dispensation is praiseworthy.

[Note: [Col. 0769C] Bernard’s opinion concerning dispensations should be noted: namely, that dispensations are to be granted only where necessity presses and [Col. 0769D] the common good recommends it. I now fear that dispensations are too often made where necessity and utility either do not exist or are merely private. But what, in Bernard’s sense, is to dispense here, if not to dissipate? And these words of the same holy Father are rightly pressed upon us: “Why does anyone vainly flatter you concerning apostolic absolution when the divine sentence holds his conscience bound?” Epistle 1, to Robert. Likewise: “And you too, not unreasonably fearing this and insufficiently confident of your own cause, have attempted to soothe consciences reproaching and biting you with an apostolic sentence. O altogether frivolous remedy! It is nothing other than, after the manner of the first parents, covering cauterized consciences with fig-leaves: that is, for a covering, not a cure. ‘We sought,’ they say, ‘and obtained apostolic permission.’ Would that you had sought not permission, but counsel—not that it might be permitted, but whether it was permitted,” etc. Thus Bernard in Epistle 7, where matters highly worthy of notice concerning dispensations occur from no. 7 through no. 10.

[Col. 0770C] John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, Book 4, ch. 7: “Yet I do not withdraw the dispensation of law [Col. 0770D] from the hands of authorities; but I by no means judge provisions containing a perpetual command or prohibition to be subject to their will. Thus a dispensation of the words is admitted only in matters that are mutable, yet in such a way that through compensation of honesty or utility the measure of the law is kept whole.” Read also Book 7, ch. 17, in the same author.]

I mean common advantage, not private advantage.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] Vossius notes in the margin, “not yours,” as though *private* should be referred to the pontiff, not to the person to whom the dispensation is granted.]

For when neither is present, it is plainly not a faithful dispensation but a cruel dissipation. Yet who does not know that certain monasteries situated in different bishoprics have belonged more particularly, from their very foundation, to the Apostolic See, in accordance with their founders’ wishes? But one thing is granted by devotion; another is contrived by ambition impatient of subjection. And enough has been said about these matters.

## CHAPTER V. The supreme pontiff is charged with ensuring throughout the world the observance of apostolic decrees and the institutions of the fathers.

[Col. 0769C]

19. It remains that your consideration should attend generally to the entire state of the Church: whether lay people are subject to clerics, clerics to priests, and priests to God in the humility proper to each; whether order is maintained and discipline kept watchfully in monasteries and religious houses; whether ecclesiastical censure flourishes against evil deeds and doctrines; whether the vineyards flourish through the integrity and holiness of priests; whether the flowers produce the fruits of obedience [alternatively, “obedience produces the fruits”] among the faithful peoples; [Col. 0770A] and finally, whether your own apostolic commands and ordinances are observed with the diligence they deserve, so that nothing in the field of your Lord may be found either uncultivated through neglect or usurped through fraud.

Do not doubt that such things may be found. I can readily show, to pass over many innumerable matters lying neglected everywhere, some things even among those planted by your own right hand which have been torn up. Did not your mouth promulgate the following chapters at the Council of Reims? Who observes them? Who has observed them? You are mistaken if you think they are observed. If you do not think so, you yourself have sinned: either by establishing provisions that would not be observed, or by overlooking their non-observance.

“You said: ‘We command that neither bishops nor clerics offend the eyes of those who behold them—though they ought to be a model and example to such observers—by excess, an indecorous variety of colours, slashing of garments, or their tonsure; but rather that in their conduct they should condemn faults and display love of innocence by their manner of life, as befits the dignity of the clerical order. If, after being warned by their bishops, they do not comply within forty days, they shall be deprived of ecclesiastical benefices by the authority of those same pontiffs. Bishops, however, who neglect to inflict the prescribed [alternatively, “aforementioned”] penalty, since the faults of inferiors are to be imputed to none more than to slothful and negligent rulers, shall abstain from the pontifical office until they impose upon the clerics subject to them the penalty established by us’” (Canon 2).

“You also said: ‘We considered it necessary to add that no one shall be appointed archdeacon or dean unless he is a deacon and priest. Archdeacons, [Col. 0770C] deans, and provosts who are below the aforesaid orders, if they scorn to be ordained in obedience, shall be deprived of the honour received. We also prohibit those aforesaid honours from being granted to young men or to men below the sacred orders, unless they are distinguished by prudence and the merit of their life’” (Canon 9).

20. These are your words; you enacted them. What has been put into effect? Young men are still promoted in the Church; so too are men below the sacred orders. As for the first chapter: luxury of dress has been forbidden,

[Note: [Col. 0770D] In Bernard’s age, most people judged that luxury and softness in clerical dress spread more widely and almost without punishment because many men of the highest nobility had then been admitted to the clergy. Long accustomed to elegance, they found it hard to adapt themselves to the modesty and frugality worthy of the sacred estate; indeed, they wished in this way to preserve their former splendour and the eminence of their rank by a distinctive manner of dress, lest perhaps they should seem to have been taken from the common people like the rest. But what prudent person could approve such a disposition in them? For together with their estate and way of life, their habits and dress ought to have changed; or at least they ought to have resolved that the chief honour and adornment of a person consecrated to God is virtue, [Col. 0771D] modesty, and piety. But because the opinion of very many was generally mistaken and corrupt in this matter, holy and religious men always took care to prick sharply with the pen that swelling sore which daily grew toward the common ruin. Decrees of various Church prelates and councils were also issued to restrain the luxury of dress; yet St Bernard laments and complains that they were not observed. See below, *Treatise on the Morals and Office of Bishops*, against luxury of dress among clerics, etc., ch. 2.]

but it has not been restrained; a penalty has been laid down, but it has by no means followed. It is now the fourth year since we heard the mandate given, [Col. 0771A] yet we have seen no cleric deprived of a benefice, no bishop suspended from office, for luxury of dress. But what followed is worthy of the bitterest grief. What was it? Impunity, the offspring of negligence, mother of insolence, root of shamelessness, and nurse of transgressions. Blessed are you if you strive with every care to guard against negligence, the first parent of all evils. But you will give attention to this.

Then lift up your eyes and see whether, as before, a variegated fabric still discolours the sacred Order; whether, as before, an enormous slit almost lays bare the groin.

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Sacred decrees strictly provide that clerics must not wear striped, parti-coloured, or checkered garments. Our forefathers called them *fractilatae* garments, lavish and ostentatious clothes. See the *Chronicle of Windesheim*, Book II, ch. 47. They seem to have been garments cut up with very broad, gaping slits, such as we see in the breast-coverings worn by the French in summer; thus they seemed half-naked and, to speak with Peter Chrysologus, “clothed in artful nakedness,” Sermon 122. St Bernard calls this an “enormous slit” that almost lays bare the groin, because formerly not only breast-coverings were pierced and gaping in that way, but even the breeches were broadly slit, as ancient paintings show. [Col. 0772D] Thus, when clerics outside the choir wore a shorter garment, the shamefulness of this clothing met everyone’s eyes and offended the eyes and minds of modest people. So approximately Cressollius in *Mystagogus*, Book IV, ch. 13, §5. There he also adds that this disease raged dreadfully in Germany, though prelates exerted great vigilance lest it spread more freely and widely. He then adduces several prelates of Cologne who endeavoured by pastoral care and censure to restrain the growing abuse. Such were Conrad in 1260, Walram in 1337, and William in 1353 and 1360, who, among other things, said: “We warn all and each individual cleric that henceforth they shall not wear parti-coloured, striped, cut, checkered, etc., garments; or garments entirely red, entirely green, blue-green, buttoned, knotted, etc.” I omit the rest.]

They commonly say: “Does God care about clothes and not rather about morals?” But this fashion of clothing is evidence of deformity in minds and morals. [Col. 0771B] What does it mean that clerics wish to be one thing and appear another? This is certainly less chaste and less sincere. For in dress they present soldiers, in gain clerics, but in conduct [Col. 0772A] neither. They neither fight as soldiers nor preach the Gospel as clerics. To what order do they belong? Since they desire to belong to both, they abandon both and confuse both. “Each one,” he says, “will rise in his own order” (1 Cor. 15:23). In what order will these rise? Will those who sinned without order perish without order? Or, if the supremely wise God is truly believed to leave nothing unordered from the highest point to the lowest, I fear that these will be ordered nowhere except where no order exists, but everlasting horror dwells.

O pitiable bride entrusted to such bridegrooms’ friends! Assigned to her care, they do not blush to retain her possessions for their own profit. They are certainly not the bridegroom’s friends, but his rivals. Enough has been said concerning those beneath you—not in proportion to the abundance of material, which is very great, but certainly for my present purpose. We must now examine the matters around you; but the fourth book will open the door to them.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0771]

## CHAPTER I. He treats of the matters surrounding the pope himself.

[Col. 0771B]

1. If I had known more fully, most beloved Eugenius, how you received the earlier matters, I would accordingly have proceeded with greater confidence in what remains, or more cautiously, or perhaps have stopped altogether. But since, because of the distance between places, this is not granted to me, do not wonder if [Col. 0771C] a more restrained and hesitant discourse comes forward, I confess, modestly into the midst. Having dealt with the first parts of consideration in the earlier books, I now have in hand to add something concerning the matters surrounding you. These indeed are under you; but because they are nearer, they are more troublesome to you. Things placed before one’s eyes admit neither negligence, nor dissimulation, nor forgetfulness. They press more forcefully and rush in more turbulently; there is reason to fear that they may overwhelm you.

I do not doubt that your own experience has sufficiently taught you how sober and attentive a consideration is required in such matters. Otherwise, if cautious and timely consideration does not intervene, occupation will continue without end, vexation will have no limit, and anxiety no conclusion. There will be no free time and no unburdened heart: more labour and less benefit. I mean those daily demands upon you—arising from the city, the Curia, and your own household church. These, I say, are the things around you: your clergy and people, over whom you are specifically bishop and consequently owe a special debt of care. Also those elders of the people, judges of the world, who attend you daily; and those of your household and table—chaplains, chamberlains, and all ministers assigned to different offices for your service. These visit you more familiarly, knock more frequently, and trouble you more insistently. These are the people who do not hesitate to awaken the beloved before she herself wishes it.

## CHAPTER II. He discusses the character of the Roman clergy and people, and the care and vigilance of pastors of old.

[Note: [Col. 0772D] See Baronius under the years 1144, no. 3; 1145, nos. 3 and 7; and 1152, nos. 1–2.]

2. First, that clergy ought to be exceedingly well ordered, since from it especially the pattern of clergy spread through the whole Church. Next, whatever is done wrongly in your presence is more shameful for you. It concerns the glory of Your Holiness that those before your eyes should be so ordered and trained that they themselves may be the mirror and model of every propriety and order for the whole Church. Above all others they ought to be prompt in duties, fit for the Sacraments, diligent in instructing the people, and watchful in preserving themselves in every chastity.

What shall I say of the people? They are the Roman people. I could not more briefly, nor yet more explicitly, disclose what I think of your parishioners. What has been so well known through the ages as the Romans’ insolence and pride [alternatively, “stubbornness”]? A race unaccustomed to peace and accustomed to tumult; a race harsh and untamable even now, knowing not how to submit except when unable to resist. Behold the wound: this care lies upon you, and you may not overlook it. Perhaps you laugh at me, persuaded that it is incurable. Do not despair; what is required of you is care, not cure. For you have heard: “Take care of him” (Luke 10:35), not “Cure” or “Heal him.” A certain man spoke truly:

> It is not always within the physician’s power that the sick person be relieved.  
> (Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus* 1.10.)

But I prefer to set before you what concerns yourself. Paul says: “I labored more than all of them” (1 Cor. 15:10). He does not say, “I benefited more than all,” or, “I bore more fruit than all,” devoutly avoiding an unusual expression. Elsewhere, however, the man 436 taught by God knew that “each shall receive according to his own labor” (1 Cor. 3:8), [Col. 0773C] not according to the outcome. For this reason he thought one should glory in labors rather than successes, as you also find him saying elsewhere: “In very many labors” (2 Cor. 11:23).

Thus, I beg you, do what belongs to you; for God will adequately attend, without your anxious concern, to what belongs to Him. Plant, water, take care: you have discharged [Latin *explicuisti*; variant: *explevisti*, “fulfilled”] your part. Certainly God, not you, will give the increase where He wills. Should He perhaps not will it, nothing is lost to you, Scripture saying: “God will render the reward of the labors of His saints” (Wis. 10:17). Labor is secure when no failure can render it void. And I say this without prejudice to the divine power and goodness. I know that the heart of this people is hardened; but God is able to raise children of Abraham from [Col. 0773D] these stones. Who knows whether He may return and forgive, convert and heal them? Yet it is not my purpose to prescribe to God what He ought to do; would that I could persuade you of what ought to be done, and how it ought to be done.
