3. But here the ground is doubtful, and an anxious discussion arises. For where am I to begin saying what I think? I see clearly enough what threatens. It will be cried that it is unprecedented; for it cannot be denied that it is just. Yet I would not even concede that it is unprecedented. Certainly, I know that it was customary, and therefore could have fallen out of use; but it cannot become unprecedented again. Or can anyone deny that something was customary [Col. 0774A] which is known not merely to have been done once, but to have been done repeatedly for some time? I shall say what it is, and it will do no good. Why? Because it will not please the satraps, who favor grandeur more than truth.

Before you there were men who devoted themselves wholly to feeding the sheep, glorying in the work and name of shepherd, counting nothing beneath them except what they judged contrary to the sheep’s welfare; seeking not their own interests, but spending themselves. They spent their care, their substance, and themselves. Hence one of them says: “And I myself will be spent beyond measure for your souls” (2 Cor. 12:15). And as though they said, “We have not come to be served, but to serve,” they offered the Gospel freely whenever necessary. Their one gain from their subjects, their one display, their one delight, was that somehow they might prepare them for the Lord as a perfect people. This they strove for in every way, even amid much contrition of heart and body, in labor and hardship, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness.

4. Where now, I ask, is this custom? A very different one has entered in; pursuits have been changed far in another direction—and would that it were not for the worse. Yet care, anxiety, rivalry, and solicitude, I admit, remain. They have been transferred, not diminished. I bear you witness that you spare neither your possessions, any more than formerly. But a different expenditure makes the difference. A great abuse! A few look to the mouth of the lawgiver; all look to his hands. Yet not without reason. Those hands conduct every papal affair. Whom can you show me in this greatest of cities [Col. 0774C] who received you as Pope without payment, or hope of payment, intervening? And then they especially wish to rule when they have professed servitude. They pledge themselves faithful in order more conveniently to injure those who trust them. Hence you will have no counsel from which they do not think themselves excluded, no secret into which they do not intrude. If, while any one of them stands before the door, the doorkeeper delays even a little, I would not then wish to be in that man’s place [variant: I would not wish it]. And now try me briefly, that I may know whether I too have understood, at least somewhat, the character of this people.

Before all else, they are wise in doing evil, but do not know how to do good. They are hated by earth and heaven: 437 they have laid hands upon both—upon earth and heaven, as is shortly explained.

[Note: That is, upon earth and heaven, as he explains immediately. These disturbances occurred at the instigation of Arnold, who persuaded the Romans to attempt the restoration at Rome of the ancient constitution of the Republic, leaving to the Pope alone the care of sacred matters. These things are treated fully in Letter 243 and in Baronius under the year 1152.]

They are impious toward God, rash toward sacred things, seditious among themselves, [Col. 0774D] hostile toward their neighbors, inhuman toward strangers. Since they love no one, no one loves them; and because they seek to be feared by all, all must necessarily fear them. These are men who cannot bear to be subject and do not know how to preside; faithless to their superiors and unbearable to their inferiors. Shameless in asking, brazen in refusing.

[Note: So in Letter 198, “brazen” in the sense opposed to shame, no. 1.]

They are importunate in receiving, restless until they receive, ungrateful when they have received. They have taught their tongue to speak grand things while doing paltry ones. Most lavish in promises and most sparing in performance; most flattering in adulation and most biting in detraction; most artful in concealment and most malicious in betrayal. [Col. 0775A] We have ranged thus far because we thought you ought to be warned more fully and explicitly in this respect about those surrounding you.

5. Let us now return to the order of our argument. What is this: those who say to you, “Well done, well done,” are bought [variant: buy] with the spoils of churches? The life of the poor is sown in the streets of the rich. Silver gleams in the mud; people run together from every side, and it is taken not by the poorer man but by the stronger, or perhaps by the one who runs ahead more quickly. Yet this custom—or rather, this death—did not begin with you; would that it might end in you.

But let us continue the rest. Meanwhile you proceed as shepherd, gilded and surrounded by such great magnificence. What do the sheep gain? If I dared say it: these are pastures more fit for demons than for sheep. Did Peter act so? Did Paul play such games? You see all ecclesiastical zeal [Col. 0775B] burning only for the defense of rank. Everything is devoted to honor; nothing, or little, to holiness. If, when a cause requires it, you attempt to act somewhat more humbly and to conduct yourself more companionably, they say: “Far be it! It is not fitting.”

[Note: See whence comes the corruption of princes and prelates: namely, from evil counselors and intimates. They know only how to suggest flattering things and to say nothing except what pleases. Hence Seneca elegantly says: “I shall show you what great eminences lack, what is absent to those who possess everything: namely, someone to tell them the truth. . . . Do you not see how extinguished freedom and loyalty reduced to slavish compliance drive them headlong into ruin, while no one advises or dissuades according to his own judgment, but there is a contest in flattery, and the single duty and rivalry of all friends is to see who can deceive most pleasantly?” (On Benefits, Book VI, chapter 30.)

Hence St. Ambrose, though he knew the Emperor Theodosius’s keen temper and vehement impulse, feared this less than the counsels of his intimates. Therefore, writing to the emperor in Letter 28, he earnestly asks him to entrust the governance of the movements of his mind—however sharp and lively they might be—to himself rather than to others. “Would,” he says, “that if no one softens them, no one inflames them! I willingly leave the impetuosity of your nature to you: you yourself call yourself back and, through zeal for piety, overcome the impulse of nature.” And rightly so: for although one could not but fear a prince’s vehement disposition, one had more to fear from wicked intimates. The facts recorded by Baronius regarding the once most flourishing empire of Theodosius confirm Ambrose’s judgment, vol. VI, A.D. 446. Thus indeed Theodosius’s empire, governed according to the will of courtiers rather than the reason of counsel, perished; so great a mass collapsed. It remains, therefore, that princes should examine carefully whom they admit among their intimates. Let them hear—indeed, observe and follow—the example of David. Behold his excellent and truly royal word and deed: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house; he who speaks iniquity did not direct his way before my eyes” (Ps. 100).]

“It does not suit the times; it does not befit majesty; consider the person you bear.” God’s good pleasure is mentioned last; there is no hesitation at the loss of salvation. Unless something is lofty, we do not consider it salutary; and whatever smells of glory, that we deem just. Thus everything humble is considered shameful among courtiers, so that you will more readily find one who wishes to seem humble than one who wishes to be humble. Fear of the Lord is reckoned simplicity—indeed, folly. They slander a prudent man, a friend of his own conscience, as a hypocrite. Further, one who loves [Col. 0775C] quiet and occasionally attends to himself they call useless.

## CHAPTER III. The splendor of dress must be curtailed, and zeal is necessary for the Pope.

6. What then of you? Are you still awake to these men who have surrounded you with snares of death? I beg you, bear with me a little and support me. Rather, pardon one who speaks these things not so much rashly as timidly. I am jealous for you with a good jealousy, and would that it were as useful as it is vehement. I know where you dwell: unbelievers and subverters are with you. They are wolves, not sheep; yet you are the shepherd of such men. It is a useful consideration by which perhaps you may discover how, if possible, to convert them, lest they themselves subvert you. Why should we despair that they can return to being sheep, when they were able to be changed from sheep into wolves? Here—here—I do not spare you, that God may spare you. Either deny that you are shepherd to this people, or show yourself to be one. You will not deny it, lest he whose seat you occupy deny you as heir. Here is Peter, who is not known ever to have gone forth adorned with jewels or silks; not covered with gold, not riding a white horse,

[Note: Observe that it was then customary for the Pope to ride a white horse, as Suger also proves in his book *On the Life of Louis the Fat*, p. 318.]

nor attended by soldiers, nor surrounded by noisy servants. Yet without these things he believed that the saving command could sufficiently be fulfilled: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John 21:15). In these things you have succeeded not Peter, 438 but Constantine. I advise that they be endured for the time, not desired as a duty. Rather I urge you to those things [Col. 0776B] of which I know you are debtor. Though you proceed in purple,

[Note: Peter Damian attributes a “red cape” to the Pope in Book I, Letter 20. Adrian IV, in John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*, Book VIII, chapter 23, says that “the crown and phrygian cap” (which is elsewhere called the “kingdom”) “rightly appear bright, because they are fiery.” See below, no. 5, and Book II, no. 18.]

though you proceed gilded, still, heir of the Shepherd, you need not dread pastoral work or care; you need not be ashamed of the Gospel. Indeed, if you preach the Gospel willingly, there is even glory for you among the Apostles. To preach the Gospel is to feed. Do the work of an evangelist, and you have fulfilled the work of a shepherd.

7. “You urge me,” you say, “to feed dragons and scorpions, not sheep.” Precisely for this reason, I say, approach them all the more—but with the word, not the sword. Why do you attempt again to wield the sword which you were once commanded to put back into its sheath? Yet anyone who denies that it is yours does not seem to me sufficiently to heed the Lord’s saying: “Put your sword into its sheath” (John 18:11). It is yours, then, and perhaps to be drawn at your nod, though not by your hand. Otherwise, if it in no way concerned you, when the Apostles said, “Behold, here are two swords,” the Lord would not have answered, “It is enough” (Luke 22:38), but, “It is too much.” Both swords, then, are the Church’s: the spiritual sword, namely, and the material; but the latter is to be wielded for the Church, the former also by the Church. The one is in the priest’s hand; the other in the soldier’s hand, but indeed at the priest’s nod and at the emperor’s command.

[Note: He says nearly the same, with slightly altered words, concerning the two swords in Letter 256. John of Salisbury, *Polycraticus*, Book IV, chapter 3: “The prince therefore receives this sword from the hand of the Church, although the Church herself does not possess the sword of blood. Yet she possesses this also, but uses it through the prince’s hand.” Compare chapter 2 of the book *To the Knights Templar*. St. Bernard teaches that both swords belong to the Church, namely spiritual and material; but the former is to be wielded by the Church, the latter for the Church; the former by the priest’s hand, the latter at his nod, but by the soldier’s hand and at the emperor’s command.

For a long succession, political writers—not to mention sectarians—and indeed many theologians and canonists have used these words, who formerly, perhaps even today, have assisted emperors and princes armed against the Pope. While elsewhere men fought with the sword, these writers pursued the matter no less with the pen. They contend that the material sword does not belong to the Pope, but that, as supreme head of the Church, he can require the emperor, as a more worthy and powerful member of the Church, and by the same reasoning other princes, to lend arms to the Church and defend her against enemies; but that he cannot initiate war on his own authority. To this end they rely on the present passage of Bernard, who wishes the temporal sword to be wielded not by the Pope’s hand but only at his nod and by the emperor’s command.

They advance similar words of his from Letter 256 to the same Eugenius: “Now both swords must be wielded, while Christ suffers anew where He suffered on the other occasion. But through whom, if not through you? Both belong to Peter: the one to be drawn by his nod, the other by his hand, whenever necessary. For of that concerning which there seemed less certainty, Peter was told: ‘PUT YOUR SWORD BACK.’ Therefore it was his, but certainly not to be drawn by his own hand,” etc. But see the Gloss on the chapter *Unam sanctam*, where the present passage of Bernard is fittingly explained. See also the letter of Gregory IX, from Vossius’s edition, which treats expressly of the Pope’s two swords and the use of each. Also Peter Damian, Book IV, Letter 6, where he seems not to permit the material sword to the Church; but an unknown author of the annotation—perhaps Constantine Cajetan himself, who published it—supplies a rather lengthy antidote. Also read Baronius, A.D. 1053. But above all let the reader consult Sixtus of Siena, a most learned man of the Order of Preachers, Book VI of the *Sacred Library*, annotation 72, where he explains Bernard’s words at length and vindicates them from the sinister interpretations of Calvin and the Ferialians. It will suffice to have indicated these matters to the reader; for there is no leisure now to discuss them more extensively, since I see these notes growing beyond their intended scope.]

And of this elsewhere. But now take up the sword entrusted to you for striking, and wound for salvation—if not all, if not even many, at least those whom you can.

8. “I am not,” you say, “better than my fathers.” Which of them had a provoking household which, I do not say, listened to him, but did not mock him? Therefore persist all the more, in case they may hear and cease; persist even against those who resist. In saying this, perhaps I shall be called excessive. Is that not our own voice: “Insist in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2)? If you dare, call him excessive. The prophet is commanded: “Cry out, do not cease.” To whom, except the wicked and sinners? “Declare,” he says, “to my people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. 58:1). Observe prudently that they are called both criminals and the Lord’s people. Judge the same of these men. Though they are criminals, though unjust, take care lest you hear: “What you did not do for one of the least of mine, [Col. 0777B] you did not do for me either” (Matt. 25:45).

I admit that this people has thus far shown itself hard of face and untamed of heart; but whether also unconquerable, I do not know how you can know with certainty. What has not yet been may come to be. If you despair, yet with God no word will be impossible (Luke 1:37). If they are hard of face, harden yours in return. Nothing is so hard that it does not yield to something harder. The Lord says to the prophet: “I have made your face harder than their faces” (Ezek. 3:8). One thing absolves you: if you have dealt with that people so that you can say, “My people, what ought I to have done for you that I did not do?” If you have done so and have made no progress, then at last there is something for you to do and say: “Depart from Ur of the Chaldeans,” and say, “I must preach the Gospel to other cities also” (Luke 4:43). I think you will not regret the exile, having exchanged a city for the world. [Col. 0777C]

## CHAPTER IV. What sort of associates and assistants the Pope should employ; concerning the virtues of prelates.

[Col. 0778A]

9. Let us come to your associates

[Note: John of Salisbury, in Book V, chapter 10, discusses the “sides” of powers—that is, those who ought to assist princes.]

and assistants. These are your diligent attendants; these are your intimates. Therefore, if they are good, they are especially yours; if bad, they are equally yours to an even greater degree. Do not call yourself sound while your sides ache; that is, do not call yourself good while leaning upon bad men. Or if you are good, what benefit can your goodness alone produce? As I remember having said in the preceding book (Book III, no. 9), what advantage, I ask, does the righteousness of you alone bring to the churches of God, where the judgment of men otherwise disposed prevails? Nor is your well-being, besieged by evil men, safe for you any more than health is safe with a serpent nearby. There is no escape from domestic evil. [Col. 0778B] Conversely, a domestic good is greater because it helps more often.

But whether they relieve or burden you, to whom can this more rightly be imputed than to you, who either chose or admitted such persons? I do not speak of all; for some were not chosen by you, but chose you. Yet they have no power except what you have either bestowed or allowed them. We return, therefore, to the same point. Attribute to yourself whatever you suffer from one who can do nothing without you. With these exceptions, all others are to be selected or gathered for this ministry, as you see, with careful consideration. It is yours, wherever they may be found, to summon and associate with yourself, after the example of Moses, elders (Num. 11:16), not young men; but elders not so much in age as in character—men whom you know to be elders of the people. [Col. 0778C] Should they not be chosen from the whole world, who are to judge the world?

[Note: Here he most usefully admonishes and instructs the Pope concerning the election of cardinals, and wishes them to be chosen not from one people or nation, but from the whole world. The Council of Basel, session 23, established the same, and lastly Trent did so in the same words, session 24, chapter 2, *On Reform*: “The most holy Roman pontiff shall, so far as it can conveniently be done, choose cardinals from all the nations of Christendom, according as he finds suitable men.”

The chief reason is necessity in investigating cases and matters arising throughout the whole Church, and in becoming acquainted with the condition of all peoples. For no graver errors are committed in government than through ignorance of the condition of the commonwealth. Yet foreigners can scarcely have all matters fully in view, or care as they ought for things pertaining to the instruction, reconciliation, and governance of other peoples. Further, since dealings must take place with the princes, commonwealths, and kings of all nations, it is expedient that the leading men of every people should be in the council, through whose assistance affairs and business may be managed more successfully. Finally, lest national partialities and rivalries be felt in the consistory and judgment of the Church, which ought to be the most impartial of all, when some nation believes itself despised and therefore complains that it lacks advocates and patrons.]

Certainly, no petitioner should intrude himself into this matter. [Col. 0779A] It must be managed by counsel, not petition. There are matters in our power in which either a petitioner’s importunity extorts something from us, or necessity deserves it. But that is in matters that are ours. Where I am not permitted to do what I wish, what place is there for a petitioner? Unless perhaps the person who petitions me is petitioning that I may be permitted to will what he wills, rather than that I should will it.

[Note: Horstius reads, “rather than that I should will it,” but incorrectly; and a little earlier Vossius has, “that what he wills may be permitted to me.”]

One petitions for another; another perhaps petitions for himself. Let the man for whom you are asked be suspect; he who himself petitions for himself is already judged. Nor does it matter whether someone petitions in person or through another. Know that a cleric frequenting the court,

[Note: Other princes also rightly considered clerics frequenting courts suspect of ambition, and therefore unworthy of the honors they seek. Thus Philip II, king of Spain, had designated a certain cleric as bishop; but as soon as he learned that the man was present at court, he revoked the appointment, tearing up the letters already prepared concerning it. See Peter Damian and Peter of Blois against court clerics; also the learned Espencaeus, excursus on the Epistle to Timothy, Book II, chapter 10.

But this is still more unworthy and less tolerable when bishops and prelates, neglecting residence and abandoning their sheep, linger at courts and make themselves retainers of kings and nobles. Those who retain such men without cause, or do not send them back to their own charges, may perhaps be no less culpable. Considering the indignity of this matter, Gentianus Hervetus, writing in the Canons of the Council of Chalcedon, speaks thus: “All good men at Rome judge it certainly a pitiable, pitiable spectacle when crowds of bishops are seen who prefer, by following cardinals, to bind themselves to their service rather than serve Christ in their own dioceses by performing their office. If the supreme pontiff”—a harsher judgment—“drove such men by whips, not out of the Church, but out of the city of Rome to their own churches, he would seem to me duly to perform the office of Christ’s vicar.” So he.]

even if he is not a courtier, belongs, you should know, to the same class of aspirants. Regard a flatterer, and one who speaks to please everyone, as one of the petitioners, even if he has asked for nothing. What you need fear in a scorpion is not in its face; it stings with its tail.

[Col. 0779B] 10. If you feel your heart, as commonly happens, softening under the flatteries of such men, remember what is written: “Every man first serves the good wine; but when they have become drunk, then that which is worse” (John 2:10). Weigh equally the humility of one who fears and of one who hopes. It is characteristic of a shrewd and deceitful man to feign humility when he wishes to obtain something; of such men Scripture says: “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit” (Sir. 19:23).

Take from yourselves an obvious and familiar example of this judgment. How many men whom you admitted as suppliants did you afterward endure as troublesome, insolent, contumacious, rebellious? Their beginnings conceal the inward evil; their later conduct reveals it. Regard a talkative young man, eager for eloquence yet empty of wisdom, [Col. 0780A] as nothing other than an enemy of justice. Concerning false brethren of this kind the Master tells you: “Lay hands suddenly on no one” (1 Tim. 5:22).

11. Having therefore excluded this whole pestilential class of men, let it be your chief concern to introduce those whom you will not afterward regret having introduced. It is shameful for you repeatedly to retract what you have done, and it does not become you frequently to put your judgment at risk. Therefore consider carefully within yourself, and with those who love you, everything that must be done. Deliberate before acting, because reconsideration after action is too late. The counsel of the wise is: “Do everything with counsel, and after the deed you will not repent” (Sir. 32:24).

And persuade yourself of this: those who are to be admitted can scarcely be tested in the court; therefore, if possible, tested men must be chosen, not men requiring testing. In monasteries we receive everyone in the hope of improving them; but the court is accustomed more readily to receive good men than to make them. And if we have proved that more good men have failed there than bad men have improved, we must certainly seek those from whom neither failure is feared nor improvement hoped for, since they are already perfect.

12. Therefore admit not the willing or the eager,

[Note: He commands that only worthy men be admitted; but only those who flee are worthy. For why do very many desire honors so greedily? Because they do not consider the burdens. To those who imagine them, honors are alluring; but to those who weigh the burdens, honors are objects of dread and fear. Who could believe that those who have obtained honors will duly perform them when they neither know nor care about their burdens or duties?

Yet in holy men it has always been observed that they came to honors and dignities unwillingly and under compulsion. Nevertheless, the more reluctantly they accepted imposed dignities, the more worthily and faithfully they discharged them. Those who flee honor, of course, look not to the flattering outward appearance but to the inward sting concealed within; terrified by this, they hold back and flee. But when, though resisting, they cannot escape submitting themselves to divine providence and the obedience of their superiors, and placing their shoulders beneath the burden, necessity becomes for them a spur and incentive to virtue and labor. They feel that this rests upon them: that by every means they must strive to prove equal to the office undertaken.

Thus they quickly put their hands to difficult things, recognizing that they have been summoned to labor; therefore they have no wish to be idle or self-indulgent, but take care to preside so as to benefit others and to be able one day to answer for the talent entrusted to them. Such was Heliodorus, whom Jerome commends for refusing the priesthood: “By refusing, he deserved what he did not wish to be; and he was the more worthy because he declared himself unworthy.” Such also was Pope Cornelius, whom Cyprian praises as having not, like some, used force to become bishop, but suffered force in order to accept the episcopate (Letter 52).

Leo the Emperor therefore most beneficially decreed, about A.D. 469, law 31, *On Bishops and Clergy*: “Let a bishop be ordained not by payment but by prayers. He ought to be so far removed from canvassing that he must be sought in order to be compelled, withdraw when asked, and escape when invited; necessity alone should plead for excusing him. For indeed he is unworthy of the priesthood unless he is ordained unwillingly.” For the remaining qualifications of those to be chosen as cardinals, see the Lateran Council under Leo X, session 9, *On Reform*, beginning *cur . . .*; also chapter *Bonae*, *On the Postulation of Prelates*; chapter *Exsecrabilis*, *Extra*, *On Benefices*; Antoninus of Florence, third part of the *Summa*, title 21, chapter 2, §2; and Jerome Platus, the separate book *On the Condition of Cardinals*, whose teaching can easily be adapted also to other prelates and ecclesiastical men.]

but those who hesitate and refuse; even compel them and 440 force them to enter. In such men, I think, your spirit will find rest: men not of worn-down shamelessness, but modest and God-fearing; men who fear nothing but God and hope for nothing except from God. Men who attend not to the hands of those who come, but to their needs. [Col. 0780C] Men who stand courageously for the afflicted and judge with equity for the meek of the earth. Men formed in character, approved in holiness, ready for obedience, gentle in patience, subject to discipline, strict in correction, catholic in faith, faithful in stewardship, harmonious for peace, conformed to unity. Men upright in judgment, prudent in counsel, discerning in command, diligent in ordering, vigorous in action, modest in speech, secure in adversity, devout in prosperity, sober in zeal, not lax in mercy, not idle in leisure, not disorderly in hospitality, not excessive at table, not anxious in managing their own household, not covetous of another’s, not prodigal with their own—circumspect everywhere and in all things.

Men who, whenever needed, do not refuse when commanded to serve as ambassadors for Christ, yet do not seek the task when uncommanded. Men who do not refuse more obstinately what they modestly excuse themselves from doing. Men who, when sent, do not pursue gold but follow Christ; who do not regard an embassy as profit and seek not a gift but fruit. Men who show John to kings, Moses to Egyptians, Phinehas to the sexually immoral, Elijah to idolaters, Elisha to the greedy, Peter to liars, Paul to blasphemers, Christ to merchants. Men who do not despise the common people but teach them; do not flatter the rich but strike fear into them; do not burden the poor but cherish them; do not fear the threats of princes but despise them. Men who do not enter with a crowd or depart in anger; who do not despoil churches but restore them. Men who do not empty purses but refresh hearts and correct crimes; who provide for their own good name without begrudging another’s. [Col. 0781C] Men devoted to prayer and practiced in it, who in every matter trust prayer more than their own skill or labor. Whose entrance is peaceful and whose departure is grievous,

[Note: Thus most manuscripts. Some, together with the printed editions, read “not grievous.” But we prefer the other reading: that is, men whose departure brings sorrow. Vossius has one reading: “modest.”]

whose speech builds up, whose life is righteous, whose presence is welcome, whose memory is blessed. [Col. 0782A] Men who make themselves lovable not by word but by deed; who make themselves worthy of reverence by conduct, not pomp. Men humble with the humble, innocent with the innocent; who sternly rebuke the hard, restrain the malicious, and repay the proud as they deserve. Men who do not hasten to enrich themselves or their own from the dowry of a widow

[Note: See the notes to Letter 271; the Council of Trent, session 25, chapter 1, *On Reform*, where Bernard’s words are finely confirmed; the Apostolic Canons, canons 39 and 75; the Council of Antioch, chapter 25; Carthage IV, chapters 15 and 31; Mâcon, chapter 13; Spain I, chapter 1.

If anyone wishes, let him see Cornelius on Ezekiel 44, where, on the occasion of the divine command by which the high priest is forbidden to mourn for the dead, not even for father or mother, he says: “These were priests of the Old Testament, bound by wives and children. What then should priests and bishops of the New Testament do, whom God wished to be celibate and without children, in order that they might transfer their minds from earthly cares to heavenly things and fix them wholly upon God and eternal goods? Therefore St. Basil wisely admonishes in the *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 23: ‘Knowing, then, the intolerable harm of this affection toward relatives, let us flee their care as a diabolical weapon for attacking us.’

“But behold,” says the wise teacher, “Satan, envying them, lays snares at their side, substituting relatives for children and suggesting that they ought to be cared for and gradually advanced from the lowest to the highest ranks of wealth and dignity; that the family must be exalted and perpetuated in them, and the name preserved and celebrated among posterity. Thus indeed:

> When the Maker of things deprived the clergy of offspring,  
> A multitude of nephews succeeded according to Satan’s wish.

“This is the devil’s fraud; this is his snare; this is the rock of stumbling against which not a few otherwise good men strike, allowing themselves to be conquered and bound by affection for relatives. With continual and endless care and effort they heap wealth and rank upon them—even from the goods of the Church—with grave danger to their own souls and salvation and those of their kin. For this greed swells, creeps, and grows like hidden fire; the more it is indulged, the more it finally becomes insatiable and turns into a monstrous conflagration. Thus priests, who ought to be heavenly, become earthly, and the highest become lowest. Thus those who ought, with lofty mind, to despise all human things, rise above them, and teach others the same, are turned toward them, fall downward, and press their exalted minds down to these lowest things.”

> O souls bowed down to earth and empty of heavenly things!

How far these men degenerate from the virtue of Christ and the ancient Fathers! See these things and much more to the same effect in Cornelius à Lapide on Ezekiel 44, verse 25.]

and the inheritance of the Crucified; men giving freely what they freely received, dispensing justice freely to those suffering injury, executing vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. Men who may be seen to have received of your spirit, after the manner of Moses’ seventy elders (Num. 11:16–17), and who, whether absent or present, strive to please you by pleasing God. Men who return to you tired indeed, but not laden with baggage; [Col. 0782B] rejoicing at the same time, not because they have brought back every curious or precious thing from the lands, but because they have left peace to kingdoms, law to barbarians, tranquility to monasteries, order to churches, discipline to clerics, and to God a people acceptable and zealous for good works.

## CHAPTER V. Abstinence from gifts commended by examples; and the arrogance of the Pope’s ministers rebuked.

13. I think it worthy to bring forward the deed of our Martin, of sweet memory.

[Note: He was made cardinal-priest by Innocent in 1130. Bernard calls him “ours,” not because he belonged to Clairvaux—for Ernaldus does not number him among the prelates taken from there in Book II of the *Life*, no. 8—but either because he was a particular friend of Bernard, or because he was a Frenchman, or because he belonged to the same, that is, Cistercian, order. Manrique does not venture to assert the latter. This embassy of Martin to Denmark is placed in 1132. John of Salisbury praises this deed of Martin from Bernard in *Polycraticus*, Book V, chapter 15, as also the following deed of Geoffrey of Chartres. Other examples occur there in chapter 16.]

This you know; but whether you remember it, I do not know. This cardinal-priest, 441 having once discharged an embassy in Dacia,

[Note: Thus the printed and manuscript texts consistently read; Manrique reads “Dania.”]

returned so poor that, with his expenses and horses nearly exhausted, he scarcely reached Florence. There the bishop of the place gave him [Col. 0782C] a horse, on which he traveled as far as Pisa, where we then were. On the next day, I believe, the bishop followed—for he had a case against an adversary and the day for conducting it was at hand—and began to seek the assistance of his friends. When they were canvassed one by one, they came to Martin. His confidence in him was greater, since Martin could not be forgetful of the recent favor. Then Martin said: “You deceived me. I did not know that business was pressing upon you. Take your horse; behold, it is in the stable.” And that very hour he gave it back to him. What do you say, my Eugenius? Is it not a deed belonging to another age: for an envoy to return from the land of gold without gold; to pass through a land of silver and not know silver; and, beyond this, to reject at once a gift that could have been suspect?

14. But oh, a pleasant occasion has arisen for me to remember and name a man of most sweet fragrance: I mean Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, who vigorously carried out, at his own expense, a legation in the regions of Aquitaine for several years. [Note: [Col. 0783D] On this legation to Aquitaine against the Henricians, see Book II of the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 6, and Book III, chapter 6. Various letters of Bernard to this same Geoffrey may be found in the first volume.] I speak of something that I myself saw. I was with him in that country when a fish, commonly called a sturgeon, was presented to him by a certain priest. The legate asked what it had cost. “I will not accept it,” he said, “unless you take back its price.” And he returned five solidi to the man, though he was unwilling and embarrassed. Likewise, when we were in a certain town, the lady of that town offered him, out of devotion, two or three handsome dishes together with a towel—wooden ones, however. The man of scrupulous conscience looked at them for some time, praised them, but did not consent to accept them. How would he have accepted silver dishes when he refused wooden ones? There were none who could say to the legate: “We have enriched Abraham” (Gen. 14:23). Rather, like Samuel, he spoke freely before all: [Col. 0783C] “Speak concerning me before the Lord and before His Christ: whether I have taken anyone’s ox or ass; whether I have slandered anyone; whether I have oppressed anyone; whether I have accepted a gift from anyone’s hand; and today I shall despise it and restore it to you” (1 Sam. 12:3). Oh, if an abundance of such men as those whom we have just sketched were granted! What could be happier for you, what more delightful than that age? Would not the blessedness of those times seem to you second only to eternity itself, when, wherever you went, you saw yourself surrounded by so illustrious a company of blessed men?

15. If I know you, you sigh, drawing a deep breath [variant: “spirit”], and say to yourself: “Do you suppose that what is said can come to pass? Shall we be here until these things happen? [Col. 0783D] Who would grant us life, that we might live to see it? Oh, if in my lifetime I saw the Church of God supported by such pillars! Oh, if I beheld the bride of my Lord entrusted to such fidelity, committed to such purity! What could be happier or safer for me, when I saw men of this kind around me, both guardians and witnesses of my life? To whom I might safely entrust all my secrets and communicate my counsels; to whom I might pour out my entire self, as to another self. If I wished in any measure to go astray, they would not permit it; they would check me when rushing headlong and rouse me when asleep. [Col. 0784A] Their reverence and freedom would restrain me when I became proud and correct me when I exceeded bounds; their constancy and fortitude would steady me when wavering and raise me when distrustful; their faith and holiness would urge me toward everything holy, honourable, pure, lovely, and of good report.”

And now, Eugenius, turn your eyes back to the present condition of your court or of the Church, and to the pursuits of the prelates, especially of those around you.

16. But enough of these matters. I have merely felt the wall, not dug through it. [Note: [Col. 0783D] A proverbial expression taken from Ezekiel 8; as though he said: “I have touched the matter only lightly, incidentally, and, as it were, with my fingertips. It is yours to investigate more deeply [Col. 0784D] and examine what vices disfigure the Church.”] You may dig through and see, as the son of a prophet. I am not permitted to proceed further. I say only what lies on the surface. Ridiculously, your ministers try to rank themselves above your fellow-presbyters. Reason does not support this, antiquity has not maintained it, [Col. 0784B] and authority does not agree with it. Even if a charge is fabricated against their customary practice, surely it is better that it be so accused than that the highest Order be despised.

Yet the ground upon which they chiefly wish to establish this claim is quite frivolous. “We,” they say, “stand more closely beside the lord Pope at every ceremony; we sit nearer while he is seated; when he proceeds, we precede behind him.” [Note: [Col. 0784D] The manuscripts now restore the passage thus, and correctly: according to Roman custom servants precede their master, the more honourable persons being in the rear rank. The printed editions read: “we follow him first as he proceeds.”] All this is not a privilege of rank but a duty of diligence, the very administration of the office interpreting the name “deacon.” Finally, while the presbyters surround the majesty in an ordered sitting, you sit at his feet. You stand nearer so that he may have you more ready at hand. We read in the Gospels that contention arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be greatest (Luke 22:24). You would be blessed [Col. 0784C] if all the rest were held in the same way around you.

## CHAPTER VI. It does not become the pontiff, occupied as he is with weightier matters, to attend to domestic affairs; these should therefore be entrusted to another, namely a steward

17. I am weary now of the court; we must leave the palace. At home they await us. These persons are not merely around you but, in a sense, within you. Consideration is not superfluous when you intend to order your household and provide for those who are in your bosom and upon your lap. Indeed, I say it is necessary. Hear Paul: “If anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how shall he care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. 3:5). Again: “If anyone does not provide for his own, especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith [Col. 0784D] and is worse than an unbeliever” (ibid. 5:8).

In saying this, I do not urge you, occupied with the highest concerns, to attend to the lowest and become, as it were, petty; to spend upon trifles what you owe to the greatest matters. Why entangle yourself in that from which God has delivered you? “All these things,” He says, “shall be added unto you” (Matt. 6:33). Yet these too must be done, and the others not neglected. But while you do the latter yourself, you must also yourself ensure that others provide for you in the former. For if one servant is not by himself sufficient both to guard the beasts of burden and to tend the tables, how can you personally attend [Col. 0785A] both to your own household and to that of the Lord, of which it is written: “O Israel, how great is the house of God!” (Baruch 3:24).

The mind that is occupied with such great and numerous matters must be wholly free from concern for lesser and worthless affairs. It must be free, claimed by no violent occupation. It must be noble, drawn downward by no unworthy desire. It must be upright, diverted aside by no perverse purpose. It must be cautious, entered by no stealthy suspicion. It must be watchful, drawn away from itself by no alien and curious thought. It must be steadfast, shaken by no sudden disturbance. It must be unconquered, wearied by no unceasing tribulation. It must be expansive, narrowed by no loss of temporal property.

[Col. 0785B] 18. Do not doubt that you will be deprived of these goods and struck by evils if, dividing your mind, you wish to distribute it both to the concerns of God and to your own little affairs. A manager must be procured to whom you may entrust such matters, who may grind for you. I say “for you,” not “with you.” Some things you will do by yourself; some through yourself and others together; some through others and without yourself. “Who is wise, and shall understand these things?” Your reflection must not sleep amid them.

For my part, I would judge that the business of your household should be placed under the last category that I have mentioned. You will do it through another, as I said. But if he is not faithful, he will defraud you; if he is not prudent, he will be defrauded. Therefore seek a faithful and prudent man to place over your household. Yet he is still useless if a third thing is lacking. Do you ask what it is? Authority. For what profit is it for him to be willing and to know [Col. 0785C] how to arrange everything as necessity requires, if he cannot do what he knows and wills? He must therefore be given freedom to act as he sees fit.

If you think this is done to the prejudice of reason, remember that he is faithful and will nevertheless wish to act rationally; consider that he is prudent and will nevertheless know how to act rationally. But faithful and competent willingness will then be of use when he has an abundant supply by which his whole purpose can be freely brought into effect, with all obeying without hesitation. All, therefore, must be subject to him. He should suffer no opponent. There must be no one to say, “Why have you done this?” Let him have power to exclude and admit whom he chooses, to change ministers, and to transfer offices to whom and when he chooses. Thus let him be a source of fear to all, so that he may also be of benefit. Let him preside over all so that he may benefit all, and [Col. 0785D] be accountable for all.

Do not receive secret and whispered denunciations against him; rather, judge them to be slanders. And I would have you establish this as a general rule: regard as suspect anyone who fears to say openly what he has spoken in your ear. If, when you order him to say it in that man’s presence, he refuses, judge him a denouncer, not an accuser.

19. Thus let one man assign tasks to all, and let all answer to one. Put faith in him, remaining free for yourself and for the Church of God. If it is impossible to find someone both faithful and prudent, entrust the matter rather to a faithful man. Certainly this is safer of the two. Indeed, if no suitable man is found, I advise you rather to tolerate one who is less faithful than to plunge yourself into this labyrinth. Remember that the Saviour had Judas as steward (John 12:6).

[Col. 0786A] What is more unbecoming in a bishop than to devote himself to his furniture and little property: to search through everything, inquire into every item, be gnawed by suspicions, and be disturbed at every loss or neglect? I say this to shame certain men of this sort, who daily scrutinize all their possessions, count each item, and demand an account of trifles and farthings. The Egyptian did not act thus: having entrusted everything to Joseph, he did not know what he possessed in his own house (Gen. 39:4, 6). Let a Christian blush to refuse to trust his possessions to a Christian. A man without faith nevertheless had faith in his servant, appointing him over all his goods; and this man was a foreigner.

20. A remarkable thing! Bishops have more than enough people at hand to whom they entrust souls, yet cannot find anyone to whom they may entrust [Col. 0786B] their small resources. Excellent assessors of values, plainly: they take great care of trifles and little or none of the greatest matters. But, as may plainly be understood, we endure Christ’s loss more patiently than our own. We check daily expenses by daily scrutiny, yet do not know the continuous losses of the Lord’s flock. There is daily discussion with servants concerning the price of food and the number of loaves; there is very seldom a conference with priests concerning the sins of the people. An ass falls, and someone is there to raise it; a soul perishes, and no one takes notice.

Nor is this surprising, since we do not even perceive our own continual failings. Do we not grow angry, burn inwardly, and become anxious at each such accounting? How much more tolerably we should endure loss of possessions than loss of souls! [Col. 0786C] “Why,” he says, “do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” (1 Cor. 6:7). I beg you, teacher of others, teach yourself—if indeed you have not already taught yourself—to value yourself more highly than your possessions. Make these transient things, which can in no way remain with you, pass away from you rather than through you. A stream hollows the ground through which it flows; so the passage of temporal concerns gnaws away the conscience. If a torrent can run through fields without damaging what has been sown, then believe that you too can handle these things without injury to the mind. In every way I advise you to strive to turn their rush away from yourself. Be ignorant of many matters, overlook very many, forget some.

21. Yet there are things of which I would not have you remain ignorant: the character and pursuits of each person. It is not right that you should be the last to know the faults of your [Col. 0786D] household; we know that this has happened to very many. Therefore, as I said, let another administer the higher matters; but provide for discipline yourself, and entrust that to no one. If a speech more insolent than is fitting is heard in your presence, or an unbecoming manner of dress appears, let your hand be upon such a person: exact satisfaction yourself for the injury done to you. Impunity produces boldness, and boldness excess.

A bishop’s household ought to possess holiness, modesty, and propriety; discipline is their guardian. Household priests are either more honourable than others or the subject of everyone’s mockery. In the face, clothing, and gait of those about you, permit nothing shameless or indecent to remain. Let your fellow-bishops learn from you not to keep with them long-haired boys and elaborately groomed youths. Certainly it is not fitting that curled-haired persons run about among men wearing mitres. And remember the warning of the Wise Man: [Col. 0787A] “Have you daughters? Do not show them a cheerful countenance” (Ecclus. 7:26).

22. Yet I do not urge harshness upon you, but gravity. Harshness drives away the weaker; gravity restrains the frivolous. The former, if present, makes one hated; the latter, if absent, makes one contemptible. In all things, however, moderation is better. I would have you neither too severe nor too lax. What is more pleasing than this moderation, so that you may neither burden others by severity nor be despised for familiarity?

In the palace show yourself Pope; at home, head of a household. Let your household love you; if not, see that they fear you. Guarding one’s mouth is always useful, provided that it does not exclude the grace of affability. Therefore the reckless tongue must everywhere be restrained, but especially at table. This is the more fitting bearing: be indeed serious in conduct, serene in countenance, measured in speech. Let the chaplains [Col. 0787B] and those who are continually present with you at the divine offices not be without honour. It is yours to provide such persons for yourself as are worthy. Let all serve them as though they were serving you. Let them receive necessities from your hand. Let them be content with what you have provided for them; see that they do not lack anything.

If you discover that one of them seeks something additional from arrivals, judge him a Gehazi (2 Kings 5:20–27). The same is to be decreed concerning the doorkeepers and the other officials. But this is said in abundance, for we remember that you established this standard long ago. What is more worthy of your apostolic office? What more conducive to conscience, more honourable to reputation, more useful as an example? An excellent canon is one that casts avarice out not only from conscience but from the very suspicion of extortion.

## CHAPTER VII. Epilogue, or summary of the qualities required in a pontiff

[Col. 0787C]

23. I should now like to close this book also; but at [Col. 0788A] its conclusion I wish either to repeat in summary some things already said, or to add things omitted. Consider before all else that the holy Roman Church, over which you preside by God’s appointment, is the mother of the Churches, not their mistress; and that you are not the lord of bishops, but one of them; moreover, the brother of those who love God and a fellow-participant with those who fear Him.

Henceforth consider that you ought to be: a pattern of justice, a mirror of holiness, an exemplar of devotion, a defender of truth, a champion of faith, a teacher of the Gentiles, a leader of Christians, a friend of the Bridegroom, the Bride’s attendant, an organizer of the clergy, a shepherd of peoples, a teacher of the ignorant, a refuge of the oppressed, an advocate of the poor, a hope of the wretched, a guardian of orphans, a judge of widows, an eye for the blind, a tongue for the mute, [Col. 0788B] a staff for the aged, an avenger of crimes, a terror to the wicked, a glory to the good, a rod for the powerful, a hammer of tyrants, a father of kings, a moderator of laws, a dispenser of canons, salt of the earth, light of the world, priest of the Most High, vicar of Christ, the Lord’s anointed, and, lastly, a god to Pharaoh.

Understand what I say: the Lord will give you understanding. Where malice is joined to power, you must assume something above the merely human. Let your countenance be set against evildoers. Let him who does not fear a man and does not dread the sword fear the spirit of your anger. Let him who has despised admonition fear prayer. Let the person with whom you are angry think not that a man, but God, is angry with him. Let him who has not listened to you fear that God will hear and will act against him.

What remains is discussion of [Col. 0788C] the things above you. With God’s help, I hope to complete that in one book, and at the same time to discharge my promise.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0787]

## CHAPTER ONE. He begins a consideration of the things above us—that is, God and divine matters—to which we now rise through created things

[Col. 0787C]

1. Although the preceding books are entitled *On Consideration*, they nevertheless contain a great deal of action mixed in, because they teach or urge certain matters not merely to be considered but to be done. But the book now in hand will be occupied with consideration alone. [Note: [Col. 0787D] Other texts read “as indeed is evident”; but *instat* should be read, that is, “this alone remains now to be carried out.”] For the things above do not require action but contemplation. You need not busy yourself with things that exist in one manner always and forever, and some of which exist from eternity.

And I would have you note this carefully, most discerning Eugenius: your consideration goes into exile as often as it turns away from those things to these lower and visible things—whether they are to be viewed for knowledge, desired for use, or ordered and managed as a duty. Yet if it is occupied with these in such a manner as to seek those things through them, it is not far exiled. Thus to consider is to return to one’s homeland. [Note: [Col. 0787D] There is a variant reading here: some manuscripts have *appropinquare est*, “it is to draw near”; others, *repatriare est*, “it is to return to one’s homeland.” Horstius, with a few manuscripts, has both. “To return to one’s homeland” better suits the sense, as it is contrasted with exile, as below in section 2: “This will be to have returned to one’s homeland,” etc.]

This is a higher and worthier use of present things: that, according to the wisdom of Paul, [Col. 0788D] “the invisible things of God are perceived by understanding through the things that have been made.” The citizens of that realm do not need this ladder, but exiles do. The author of this statement himself saw this, for when he said that invisible things are seen through visible things, he significantly added: “from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1:20). Truly, what need has one who already possesses the throne of ladders? That heavenly creature has immediately at hand a better means by which to contemplate these things. It sees the Word, and in the Word the things made through the Word. It does not need to beg knowledge of the Maker from things that have been made.

For it does not descend to these things in order that it may know them, since there it sees them where they are far better than in themselves. Hence it does not require bodily sense as an intermediary for them: it is itself its own sense, perceiving itself through itself. The best manner of seeing is, if you have no need of anyone else for whatever you wish [variant addition: “to know”], to be content with yourself. Otherwise, to be aided from elsewhere is to become dependent: this is less perfect and less free.

2. What then? Do you need even lower things? Is this not backward and unworthy? Certainly it is in some sense an injury to higher things to require the service of lower things. No human being will be perfectly freed from this injury until each has entered into the liberty of the children of God. For all these shall be taught by God (John 6:45), and, with no creature intervening, shall be made blessed by God alone. This will be to have returned to one’s homeland: to have departed from the country of bodies into the region of spirits. God Himself is our greatest Spirit, the greatest dwelling-place of blessed spirits. And lest bodily sense [variant addition: “or imagination”] here arrogate anything to itself, He is truth, wisdom, power, eternity, and the highest good.

For the present we are absent from Him [variant addition: “from whom”]; and where we are is a valley of tears, in which sensuality reigns and consideration is exiled. There bodily sense indeed freely and powerfully asserts itself, but the entangled spiritual eye is darkened. What wonder, then, if a stranger needs the help of a native? Happy, according to the conditions of the present time, is the traveller who has been able to turn into service the assistance of citizens, without which he cannot pass through: using it, not enjoying it; demanding it, not begging for it; acting as a claimant, not a suppliant.

## CHAPTER II. He assigns various degrees of consideration

[Col. 0789C]

3. Great is the person who strives to expend the use of the senses, as though they were resources of fellow-citizens, administering them for his own salvation and that of many others. Nor is he lesser who, by philosophizing, establishes for himself this step toward invisible things; except that the latter is clearly sweeter, the former more useful; the latter happier, the former stronger. But greatest of all is the person who, despising even the use of things and senses themselves, so far as human frailty allows, is accustomed sometimes to fly away in contemplation to those sublime things—not by ascending steps but by unexpected transports.

I think that Paul’s transports belong to this final class. They were transports, not ascents, for he himself declares that he was caught up rather than that he ascended (2 Cor. 12:1–4). Hence he said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (ibid. 5:13). These three states occur when consideration, although in the place of its pilgrimage, is made superior by the pursuit of virtue and the help of grace, and either restrains sensuality lest it become insolent, compels it lest it wander, or flees it lest it defile. In the first case it is more powerful, in the second freer, in the third purer. For that flight is made on the twin wings of purity and eagerness.

4. Do you wish these kinds of consideration to be distinguished by names of their own? Let us call the first, if you please, administrative; the second evaluative; the third speculative. Definitions will explain the rationale of these names. Administrative consideration uses the senses and sensible things in an ordered and social manner in order to merit God. Evaluative consideration prudently and carefully investigates [Col. 0790A] and weighs each thing in order to trace out God. Speculative consideration gathers itself into itself and, insofar as it is divinely assisted, withdraws from human affairs in order to contemplate God.

I think you attentively observe that this last is the fruit of the others; and that the rest, if not referred to it, may seem to exist, but do not truly exist as what they are called. The first, indeed, without the contemplation of this one sows much and reaps nothing; the second, unless it directs itself to this one, goes forward but does not arrive. Therefore what the first prepares, the second smells, and the third tastes. Yet the others also lead to this taste, though more slowly: the first arrives more laboriously, the second more quietly.

## CHAPTER III. The things above us—namely God and the angels—are investigated by opinion, faith, and understanding

[Col. 0790B]

5. “You have said enough,” you say, “about the means of ascent; do you also have something to say about the goal to which we must ascend?” You are mistaken if you expect that: it is ineffable. Do you suppose that I can speak of what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and has not entered into the human heart? “God,” he says, “has revealed it to us through His Spirit” (1 Cor. 2:9–10). Therefore the things above are not taught by sight but revealed by the Spirit.

But what speech does not explain, let consideration seek; let prayer ask for; let life merit; let purity attain. When you are exhorted to consider the things above, do not suppose that I am sending you to look upon the sun, moon, and stars, or even the firmament, or the waters above the heavens. All these things, although higher in place, are lower in worth and in dignity of nature; for they are bodies. Your portion is spirit, and you seek in vain something higher than yourself which is not spirit.

Moreover, God is spirit; holy angels also are spirits, and these are above you. God is superior by nature, the angels by grace. The single highest element in you and in an angel is reason; but God does not possess some highest thing belonging to Himself: He is wholly the one highest good. He, and the blessed spirits who are with Him, are to be traced by our consideration in three ways, as by three paths: opinion, faith, and understanding. Understanding rests upon reason; faith upon authority; opinion supports itself upon likelihood alone. The former two possess certain truth: faith possesses it closed and wrapped up, understanding naked and manifest. Opinion, however, possessing nothing certain, seeks truth through what is plausible rather than apprehending it.

6. In these matters confusion must wholly be avoided, lest faith establish what is uncertain in opinion, or opinion call back into question what is firm and fixed in faith. Know this: opinion, if it asserts, is rash; faith, if it hesitates, is weak; likewise, understanding, if it attempts to break into what faith has sealed, is deemed a breaker-in and a searcher into majesty. Many have taken their own opinion for understanding and have erred.

Indeed, opinion may be thought to be understanding; understanding cannot be thought to be opinion. Why does this occur? Certainly because the former can be mistaken and the latter cannot; or, if it could be mistaken, it was not understanding but opinion. True understanding possesses not only certain truth but knowledge of the truth. We may define each as follows: [Col. 0791A] faith is a voluntary and certain foretaste of truth not yet disclosed. Understanding is certain and manifest knowledge of any invisible reality. Opinion is, as it were, holding something to be true while not knowing that it is false.

Therefore, as I said, faith has nothing ambiguous; if it does, it is not faith but opinion. In what, then, does it differ from understanding? In this: although it has no uncertainty any more than understanding does, it nevertheless has an envelopment which understanding does not have. Finally, once you have understood something, there is nothing further to seek about it; if there is, you have not understood it. Yet we desire to know nothing more than what we already know by faith. Nothing will remain to be added to blessedness when the things now certain to us by faith shall likewise be nakedly manifest.

## CHAPTER IV. How angels are to be considered

[Col. 0791B]

7. With these points settled, let consideration now be directed toward that Jerusalem above, our mother; and let us cautiously and attentively trace what may be investigated through all three of the aforementioned paths—as far as is permitted, or rather as far as it is granted to us. First, we learn by reading and hold by faith that the citizens there are mighty, glorious, and blessed spirits: distinct in persons, arranged in ranks, standing from the beginning in their own order, perfected in their kind, ethereal in body, everlasting by immortality, incapable of suffering, not uncreated but made—that is, such by grace, not by nature—pure in mind, kind in affection, devout in religion, whole in chastity, indivisible in unity of mind, secure in peace, created by God, and devoted to divine [Col. 0791C] praises and services.

[Note: [Col. 0791D] Compare Sermon 5 on the *Song of Songs*, where angelic bodies are discussed, together with the notes there.]

Yet concerning their bodies, some people’s opinion hesitates not only as to what sort they are, but whether they exist in any degree. Therefore, if someone judges that this should rather be placed among matters of opinion, I do not dispute it. But that they are endowed with understanding we apprehend not by faith, nor by opinion, but by understanding itself, because they cannot lack this and at the same time participate in God.

Certain names are likewise known to us by hearing; through them, the offices, merits, ranks, and orders belonging to these blessed beings—even those which the hearing of mortals has not clearly perceived—can somehow be conjectured and distinguished by us. But what is not received by hearing is no longer received by faith, for “faith comes by hearing” (Rom. 10:17). Therefore, we shall speak of these things by way of opinion. For why have the names of heavenly beings been made known, if faith may not safely permit us even to form opinions concerning the realities whose names they are? Angels, Archangels, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Dominations, Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim: these are the names. What are the things signified by them? Is there no distinction among those spirits who are simply called Angels and those called Archangels?

8. What, then, does this gradated distinction mean? [Note: [Col. 0791D] That there are nine orders of angels, neither more nor fewer, distinct among themselves by rank and dignity, is an opinion handed down with the consensus of many Fathers. Thus Ignatius thinks in his Letter to the Trallians; Dionysius, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 6, where he treats the matter expressly, establishes three angelic hierarchies and subdivides each into three orders. They are followed by Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels; Jerome, Book II of the *Apology against Rufinus*; Chrysostom, Homily 4 on Genesis; Rupert, Book III, *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 6; and our Bernard, besides the present passage, in the Sermon on Saint Martin and Homily 8 on the *Song of Songs*.

Nevertheless, the Fathers differ in arranging these orders and do not appear to have had a fixed principle of placement. On this matter see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, I, question 108, article 6. Further, observe that Bernard speaks of this subject with considerable restraint and more by conjecture than by assertion. For how many orders of angels there are, and by what respective properties they are distinguished, is a matter far removed from the senses and experience of mortals. Therefore, in a dark and obscure place one must not set one’s foot rashly: one must not decide on the basis of human reasoning, but proceed cautiously, as far as the authority of Holy Scripture and the Church sheds light for us.

Hence the holy Fathers also thought that the matter should be treated sparingly and soberly, as may be seen in Hilary, *Exposition of Psalm* 129; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 58, where he frankly confesses that he does not know the constitution of that most blessed and supreme society, or what distinctions of persons are there. The same Augustine declares this in his book to Orosius against the Priscillianists and Origenists, but says that no danger lies in such ignorance. Indeed Dionysius himself, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 6, when undertaking his treatment of angelic orders, prefaces it by saying that God and the angels alone know how many orders there are and what the orders of heavenly natures are. But see Saint Thomas, in the place cited, articles 5 and 6, and the commentary there.] Let us suppose—unless you have discerned something more fitting—that Angels are so called because they are believed to be assigned individually to individual human beings, sent for ministry, according to Paul’s teaching, on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation (Heb. 1:14); and concerning them the Saviour says: “Their angels always behold the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10).

Let us suppose [Col. 0792B] that Archangels preside over them, being aware of the divine mysteries and sent only for especially important and great causes. Among these the great archangel Gabriel is read to have been sent to Mary (Luke 1:26), surely for a cause than which none could be greater. Let us suppose that above these are Virtues, at whose command or by whose operation signs and wonders appear in the elements or arise from the elements for the admonition of mortals. Perhaps this explains why, when you read in the Gospels, “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars,” a little later you find, “For the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Luke 21:25–26): namely, those spirits through whom signs are wrought.

Let us suppose that Powers are higher than these, by whose strength the power of darkness is crushed and the malice of this air is restrained, lest it harm as much as it wishes, lest it be able to act maliciously except in a way that benefits. Let us suppose that Principalities are set over these also, through whose governance and wisdom every principality on earth is established, governed, limited, transferred, curtailed, and changed. Let us suppose that Dominations rise so far above all the aforesaid orders that, in comparison with them, all the others seem ministering spirits, and that the governments of Principalities, the protections of Powers, the operations of Virtues, the revelations of Archangels, and the care and providence of Angels are referred to these as to lords.

Let us suppose that Thrones have flown away from these to an even more exalted distance: they are called Thrones because they sit, and they sit because God sits in them. [Col. 0793A] For He could not sit in those who did not themselves sit. Do you ask what [variant: “how”] I understand that sitting to be? Supreme tranquillity, most peaceful serenity, the peace which surpasses all understanding. Such is the Lord of hosts who sits upon the Thrones, judging all things in tranquillity: most peaceful, most serene, most at peace. And He establishes as His Thrones beings like Himself.

Let us suppose that Cherubim drink from the very fountain of wisdom, from the mouth of the Most High, and pour back streams of knowledge upon all their fellow-citizens. Consider whether this may be the one of whom the prophet spoke: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). Let us suppose that Seraphim, spirits entirely kindled by the divine fire, kindle all things, so that the individual citizens are individual lamps burning and shining: burning with charity, shining with knowledge.

9. O Eugenius, how good it is for us to be here! How much better it will be if at some time we wholly follow where we have partly gone before! We go before in mind—and not even with our whole mind, but with a portion far too small. The affections lie weighed down by bodily mass and clinging desires like mud; meanwhile consideration alone, dry and slender, flies ahead. Yet from the little already granted, we delight to cry: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of Your house and the place where Your glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8).

What if the soul gathers its whole self and, withdrawing its affections from all the places where they are held captive—fearing what ought not to be feared, loving what is not fitting, grieving vainly, rejoicing more vainly still—takes flight in complete freedom with them, beats with the force of the spirit, and pours itself into the richness of grace? When it begins to range through the luminous dwellings, to search more curiously into that bosom of Abraham, and to visit again beneath the altar—whatever that altar may be—the souls of the martyrs, patiently awaiting the second robe while clothed in the first, [Note: [Col. 0793D] These words show that Bernard, in Sermon 2 for the feast of All Saints, did not so understand that altar as though its meaning were certain to him by understanding or faith; he merely expressed his opinion. [Col. 0794D] These matters are discussed more fully in the preface to Volume III.] then surely it will speak with the prophet still more earnestly: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may behold the will of the Lord and visit His temple” (Ps. 26:4).

Why should the heart of God not be seen there? Why should it not be proved there what the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God is? Good in itself, pleasing in its effects, well-pleasing to those who enjoy it, perfect for the perfected who seek nothing further. The depths of mercy lie open; thoughts of peace lie open; riches of salvation [Col. 0793D] lie open; the mysteries of good will and the secrets of kindness—things closed to mortals and uncertain even to the elect. This is beneficially so, lest they cease to fear while they are not yet found fit to love worthily.

10. It is to behold, in those who are called Seraphim, how he loves who has nothing from which to love, yet is he who hates none of the things he has made: how he cherishes, advances, embraces those whom he made to be saved; and how that consuming fire purges away the sins of chosen youth and the chaff of its ignorances, rendering it utterly pure and most worthy of his love. [Note: [Col. 0794D] In some copies, “neglected youth,” but wrongly; for the discussion here concerns the elect.] It is to behold, in the Cherubim, who are said to be the fullness of knowledge, that God is the Lord of all knowledge: he alone knows no ignorance; he is wholly light, and there is no darkness in him; he is wholly eye and is never deceived, because he is never closed; he does not seek outside himself a light to be brought near him so that he may see—he himself sees, and he himself is the source from which he sees. It is to behold, in the Thrones, how the judge of all innocence sits in them beyond suspicion: he does not wish to deceive and cannot be deceived, since he so loves and so sees. Nor is his sitting idle: it is the mark of tranquillity. “May my judgment come forth from such a countenance,” I pray: may love be present in it, error absent, and disturbance absent. [Col. 0794B] It is to behold, in the Dominions, how great is the majesty of the Lord, at whose nod authority stands firm, and for whose authority the universe and eternity are boundaries. It is to behold, in the Principalities, the beginning from which all things are, and how, as a door is governed from its hinge, so the universe is governed by him. It is to behold, in the Powers, how powerfully that same Prince protects those whom he rules, warding off and driving back contrary powers. It is to behold, in the Virtues, that one power is everywhere equally at hand, through which all things are: life-giving, effective, invisible, and immovable, yet moving all things beneficially and holding them firmly. When this power breaks forth among mortals in less usual effects, they call them miracles or portents. Finally, it is to behold and marvel, in Angels and Archangels, at the truth and experience [Col. 0794C] of that saying: “For he himself cares for us” (1 Peter 5:7); for he does not cease to delight us with the visits of beings so great and of such a kind, to instruct us by revelations, to warn us by promptings, and to console us by their diligent care.

## CHAPTER V. The graces and endowments of the Angels are derived into them from God.

11. He who created those spirits, the one and same supreme Spirit, bestowed all these things upon them, distributing to each as he willed. He works these things in them; he granted them also to work them, but differently. The Seraphim burn, but with God’s fire—or rather, with God as fire. What is chief in them is that they love; but not as much as God, nor in the same way. The Cherubim shine and excel in knowledge, but by participation in truth; and therefore not as Truth itself, [Col. 0794D] nor to the same degree. The Thrones sit, but by the benefit of him who sits upon them. They too judge in tranquillity, but not according to the measure or manner of the peace that gives peace, the peace that surpasses all understanding. The Dominions rule, but rule under the Lord; at the same time, they serve. What is this compared with supreme, everlasting, and unique dominion? The Principalities preside and govern; but they themselves are governed, so that they would no longer know how to govern if they ceased to be governed. Strength excels in the Powers; but they owe their strength to another, and another is strong in a different manner and more strongly; nor are they as strong as Strength itself. The Virtues, [Col. 0795A] in accordance with their ministry and power, strive to stir the sluggish hearts of human beings by the renewal of signs; but the power abiding in them itself performs the works. They too perform them, but in comparison with it they do not perform them. Indeed, the difference is so great that the prophet seems to say of him alone: “You are God, who alone works wonders” (Psalm 75:15); and likewise: “Who alone performs great wonders” (Psalm 136:4). Angels and Archangels are present; but he is more intimately related to us, for he not only is present, but is within us.

12. If you say that an angel too can be within us, I do not deny it. I remember the words written: “And the angel who spoke in me” (Zechariah 1:14). Yet there is a difference even here. An angel is within, suggesting good things, not implanting them; urging toward good, not creating the good. God [Col. 0795B] is within in such a way that he affects, pours in—or rather, is poured in and shared—so that one need not fear to say that he is, as it were, one spirit with our spirit, although not one person or one substance. [Note: [Col. 0795] See Sermon 5 on the Song of Songs, no. 8, and the note there.] For you have: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17). Therefore the angel is with the soul; God is in the soul. The angel is in it as a companion dwelling with the soul; God as its life. Thus, as the soul sees in the eyes, hears in the ears, smells in the nostrils, tastes in the throat, and touches in all the rest of the body, so God works different things in different spirits: for example, showing himself loving in some, knowing in others, doing other things in others, “as the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for profit” (1 Corinthians 12:7). Who is this one, so common in words and so far removed in reality? How does he [Col. 0795C] whom we speak of in our words, hidden in his own majesty, wholly escape both our sight and our affections? Hear what he himself says to human beings: “As the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts” (Isaiah 55:9). We are said to love, and so is God; we are said to know, and so is God; and there are many such expressions.
