But God loves as charity, knows as truth, sits as justice, rules as majesty, governs as principle, protects as salvation, works as power, reveals as light, stands by as mercy. All these things Angels do, and we do them also; but in a far inferior way—not by a good that we are, but by one in which we participate.

## CHAPTER VI. The character of being principle and essence properly belongs to God alone.

[Col. 0795D]

13. Now pass beyond these spirits, if perhaps you too can say with the Bride: “When I had passed a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 3:4). Who is he? Surely no answer occurs more fittingly than: “He who is.” This is what he himself willed to be given in answer concerning himself; this he taught when Moses said to the people, by his command: “He who is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3:14). Rightly so. Nothing is more fitting to eternity, which is God. If you call God good, great, blessed, wise, or anything else of that kind, all is restored in this word, [Col. 0796A] “is”: he is. For to be is precisely to be all these things. Even if you add a hundred such predicates, you have not departed from being. If you state them, you have added nothing; if you do not state them, you have taken nothing away. Now if you have seen that this being is so singular and so supreme, do you not judge that, in comparison with it, whatever is not this is rather not than is? Again, what is God? He without whom nothing is. Nothing can be without him any more than he can be without himself. He is being for himself; he is being for all things. And thus, in a certain manner, he alone is, who is both his own being and the being of all things. What is God? The Principle; and he himself gave this answer concerning himself (John 8:25). Many things are called principles among created things, but only in relation to what comes after them. Otherwise, if you look to something preceding them, you will assign that rather as their principle. Therefore, if you seek [Col. 0796B] a true and simple principle, you must find that which has had no principle. That from which the universe began certainly did not itself begin. For if it began, it necessarily began from something else. Nothing began from itself. Unless perhaps someone thinks that what did not exist could have given itself the power to begin to exist, or that something existed before it existed. Since reason admits neither, it is clear that nothing was a principle to itself. What had another principle was not the first principle. Therefore the true principle did not begin at all, but all things began from it.

14. What is God? He to whom the ages neither came nor departed, though neither are they coeternal with him. What is God? “From whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things” (Romans 11:36). From whom are all things: by creation, [Col. 0796C] not by propagation from seed. Through whom are all things: lest you suppose one author and another craftsman. In whom are all things: not as in a place, but as in power. From whom are all things, as from the one principle, the author of all. Through whom are all things, lest another principle be introduced as artificer. In whom are all things, lest a third be introduced as place. From whom are all things, not out of whom; for God is not matter. He is an efficient cause, not a material cause. Philosophers seek matter in vain: God had no need of matter. He did not seek a workshop or a craftsman. He made all things through himself. From what? From nothing. For if he made them from something, he did not make that thing, and therefore did not make all things. Far be it that he should have made from his own incorrupt and incorruptible substance so many things which, though good, are nevertheless corruptible. [Col. 0796D] You ask: if all things are in him, where is he himself? I find nothing less applicable than that question. What place could contain him? You ask where he is not? I would not say that either. What place is without God? God is incomprehensible; yet you have grasped no little if you have learned this concerning him: that he is nowhere in the sense that he is not enclosed by place, and nowhere not in the sense that he is not excluded by place. But in his own exalted and incomprehensible manner, as all things are in him, so he himself is in all things. Thus, as the Evangelist says, “He was in the world” (John 1:10). Yet, where he was before the world was made, there he is. There is no need to ask further where he was: apart from him, nothing existed. Therefore he was in himself.

## CHAPTER VII. God is both simple and triune.

[Col. 0797A]

15. What is God? That than which nothing better can be thought. If you approve this, you ought not to grant that there is something by which God is God, [Note: [Col. 0797D] An altogether necessary correction from two Colbert manuscripts, where earlier editions read, “that God is.” The reason is clear from what follows.] and which is not God. For that would undoubtedly be better. How could that not be better than God, if it is not God and yet gives God his being? Rather, we confess that the divinity by which they say God is God [Note: [Col. 0797D] Namely Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, and his followers, condemned at the Council of Rheims in 1148; concerning this, see Geoffrey, Book III of the Life of St Bernard, no. 15. The same Geoffrey published a treatise on the proceedings of the Council of Rheims against Gilbert, [Col. 0798D] concerning which see Sermon 80 on the Song of Songs.] is nothing other than God himself. Therefore there is nothing in God except God. “What?” they ask. “Do you deny that God has divinity?” No; but what he has, that he is. “Do you deny that God is God by divinity?” [Note: [Col. 0798D] Others wrongly read “divinity” in the accusative. The same correction is made in Sermon 80 on the Song of Songs, no. 15.] No; but not by a divinity other than what he himself is. Or if you have discovered another, may the Trinity, God, help me: against that other [Note: [Col. 0798D] The printed editions add “or a quaternity,” but this is absent from the manuscripts.] I rise in complete defiance. [Col. 0797B] A quaternity marks out the world; it does not mark divinity. God is Trinity; God is each of the three persons. If you choose to add a fourth divinity, meanwhile I am convinced that it, since it is not God, must not be worshipped. I think you too agree. For: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Luke 4:8). A glorious divinity indeed, which would not dare claim divine honour for itself! But we wholly reject this fourth thing more fittingly than receive it without honour. Many things are said to be in God, and rightly and catholically; but the many are one. Otherwise, if we consider them diverse, we have not a quaternity but a hundredfold multiplicity. For example, we say that he is great, good, just, and countless other things; but unless you consider all these as one in God and with God, you will have a composite [Col. 0797C] God.

16. Yet I can readily think of something better than such a God of yours. You ask what? Pure simplicity. By sound judgment, a simple nature is preferred to one that is composite. I know what they usually answer to this. “We do not assert,” they say, “that many things, but only one divinity—which is all those things—gives God his being.” Then you assert, even if not a multiple, at least a double God; and you have not arrived at the purely simple, nor at that than which nothing better can be thought. That which is subject even to one form is no more simple than a virgin who has known even one man. I speak without fear: even one who is merely double will not be my God. For I have a better one. Grant that I prefer him to a God that is manifold and multiple; yet in comparison with the simple I plainly despise him. My God is himself wholly. He no more has “this and that” than he has “these and those.” He is “he who is,” not “that which is.” Pure, simple, whole, perfect, constant to himself: drawing nothing into himself from times, places, or things, and laying down nothing from himself in them; having nothing to divide into number, [Col. 0797D] nothing to gather into one. For he is one, but not united. He is not composed of parts, as a body is; he is not varied by affections, as a soul is; he is not subject to forms, as everything made is; nor is he subject even to a form, as those men have thought. Surely it is high praise for God that he should escape formlessness by being content with one form! That is to say: other things owe what they are to several forms, but God to only one. What then? He by whose benefit things are what they are—will he, for his own being, depend upon another’s benefit? [Note: [Col. 0798D] Some, with Horstius, read “another’s benefit.” But the clearer sense is “another benefactor,” as in the purer manuscripts.] Such praise, as the common saying goes, amounts to blasphemy. Is it not greater to need none than to need one? Have reverence for God, and attribute to him what is greater. If your heart has been able to ascend thus far, how will you place your God below it? He himself is his own form; he himself is his own essence. At this point, for the present, I contemplate him; and if another, more excellent, should appear, I would assign that one instead. [Col. 0798B] Must one fear that thought may fly beyond him? However far it advances on high, he is beyond it. To seek the highest beneath what a human being can think is ridiculous; to place it there is impious. He must be sought beyond, not short of, thought.

17. Ascend still higher, if you can, into the heart on high, and God will be exalted. God is not formed: he is form. God is not an affection: he is affection. God is not composite: he is pure simplicity. And that you may clearly know what I call simple: it is the same as one. God is as simple as he is one. But he is one, and in such a way that there is nothing else. If it may be said, he is most-one. The sun is one because there is no other sun; the moon is one because likewise there is no other moon. God too is one in this sense, but more. What more? He is one even to himself. Do you wish this [Col. 0798C] explained? He is always the same and in one manner. The sun is not one in this way, nor the moon. Each proclaims that it is not one to itself: the sun by its movements, the moon by its wanings. But God is not merely one to himself: he is one in himself. He has nothing in himself except himself. He has no temporal alteration, no diversity in substance. Hence Boethius says of him: “This is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing in it other than what it is; for it cannot become a subject, since it is form.” Compare with this One everything that can be called one, and it will not be one. Yet God is Trinity. What then? Do we destroy what has been said of unity because we introduce Trinity? No: rather, we establish unity. We name the Father, we name the Son, we name the Holy Spirit; yet not three Gods, but one God. What does this number—if I may so speak—without number mean? If there are three, how is there not number? If one, where is the number? “But,” you say, “I have something to count and something not to count. The substance is one; the persons are three.” What is remarkable or obscure in this? Nothing, if the persons are conceived separately from the substance. But since those three persons are that substance, and that one substance is [Col. 0799A] those three persons, who can deny number? For they are truly three. Yet who can count them? For they are truly one. Or if you think it easy to explain this by saying “three,” tell me what you have counted. Natures? There is one. Essences? There is one. Substances? There is one. Divinities? There is one. “Not these,” you say, “but I count the persons.” Persons which are not that one nature, that one essence, that one substance, that one divinity? You are Catholic: you will certainly not grant this.

## CHAPTER VIII. The plurality of persons in God arises from properties; nevertheless the essence is one and simple.

18. Catholic faith confesses that the properties of the persons are nothing other than the persons; and that the persons themselves are nothing other than the one God, the one divine substance, the one divine nature, [Col. 0799B] the one divine and supreme majesty. Therefore count, if you can, either the persons without the substance which they themselves are, or the properties without the persons which they themselves are. Or if anyone should attempt to separate either the persons from the substance or the properties from the persons, I do not know how he could profess himself a worshipper of the Trinity when he has proceeded to so great a multiplicity of things. Let us therefore say “three,” but without prejudice to Unity; let us say “one,” but without confusion of Trinity. For these are not empty names, nor meaningless, futile sounds. Someone asks how that which we call catholic can be [variant addition: how this can be]. Let it suffice him to hold that it is so. And this is not transparent to reason, yet not doubtful to opinion, but assured to faith. This is a great sacrament, and indeed one to be reverenced, not scrutinized. How plurality is in unity—and in this unity—or unity itself in plurality: to scrutinize this is rashness; to believe it is piety; to know it is life, and eternal life. Therefore, if you think it worthwhile, O Eugenius, let reflection now range over many things called one, so that the eminence of this singular One may become more evident. There is a unity that may be called collective: for example, when many stones make one heap. There is also constitutive unity, when many members constitute one body, or many parts constitute any whole whatsoever. There is also conjugative unity, by which two are now not two but one [Col. 0799D] flesh. There is native unity, by which soul and flesh give birth to one human being. There is unity of power, by which a person of virtue strives to be found neither unstable nor unlike himself, but always one with himself. There is concordant unity, when through charity many people are one heart and one soul. There is also votive unity, when the soul, cleaving to God with all its vows, is one spirit. And there is dignifying unity, by which our clay was assumed by the Word of God into one person.

19. But what are all these compared with that supreme and, so to speak, uniquely One, where consubstantiality makes unity? If you liken any one of them to this One, it will in some manner be one; if you compare it, it will be nothing. Therefore among all things rightly called one, the Unity of the Trinity holds the summit, by which three persons are one substance. In second place excels that unity by which, conversely, three substances are one person in Christ. But sound and sober reflection proves that this unity and whatever other things can be called one are called one by imitation, not comparison, with that supreme unity. Nor are we drawn away from the profession of this unity by affirmation of the Three, since in this Trinity we admit neither multiplicity, just as we admit no solitude in unity. Therefore, when I say “One,” the number of the Trinity does not disturb me, for it does not multiply, vary, or divide the essence. Again, when I say “Three,” the contemplation of unity does not convict me, for it neither forces those three things, or those three persons, into confusion [Note: [Col. 0799] Horstius adds “of nature,” but this is absent from the other printed editions and manuscripts.] nor reduces them to singularity.

## CHAPTER IX. As in God one simple nature exists in three persons, so conversely in Christ several natures coalesce into one person.

[Col. 0800B]

20. I confess that I think the same concerning that unity to which, among things called one, I gave second honour after the former. I say that in Christ the Word, soul, and flesh are one person without confusion of essences, and yet, without prejudice to personal unity, remain in their own plurality. Nor would I deny that this belongs also to that kind of unity by which soul and flesh are one human being. For it was fitting that the sacrament established for humanity should accord more familiarly and more closely with the constitution of a human being. It was also fitting that it should accord with the supreme unity, which is in God and is God, [Col. 0800C] so that, as there three persons are one essence, here, by a most fitting kind of contrast, three essences might be one person. Do you see how beautifully this unity is placed between the two others, in him who was established as mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus? It is, I say, a most beautiful correspondence: the saving sacrament answers both the saviour and the saved through a fitting resemblance. Thus this unity, standing between two unities, is known to yield to the one and excel the other: as much lower than the higher as it is higher than the lower.

21. Finally, that person in whom God and man are one Christ displays in itself so great and so manifest a force of union that, if you predicate either of the two of the other, you do not err, truly and catholically declaring God to be human and the human being to be God. But you cannot similarly predicate flesh of soul or soul of flesh except most absurdly, though soul and flesh are likewise one human being. Nor is it surprising if the soul cannot, by its life-giving though not feeble power of concentration, bind and unite flesh to itself as divinity can bind to itself that human being who was predestined Son of God in power. Divine predestination is a long and strong chain for binding, for it is from eternity. What is longer than eternity? What is stronger than divinity? Hence, even when death intervened, this unity could in no way be cut off, although flesh and soul were separated from one another. [Col. 0801A] Perhaps this is what he understood who declared himself unworthy to loosen the strap of this shoe [variant: his shoe] (Mark 1:7).

## CHAPTER X. The parable in Matthew concerning three measures is applied to the person of Christ.

22. Those three measures from the Gospel (Matthew 13:33), mixed and leavened into one loaf, seem to me not inappropriately referred by anyone to these three. How well that woman leavened them, so that even when flesh and soul were divided, the Word was not divided from flesh or soul! The inseparable unity remained even in separation. For the separation that occurred in part could not override the unity remaining in all three. Whether the two were joined or separated, personal unity nevertheless persevered in the three. Christ remained equally one, and one person—Word, soul, and flesh—even when the human being was dead. This mixing and leavening took place, in my judgment, in the Virgin’s womb; and she herself was the woman who mixed and leavened. For perhaps it would not be improper to call Mary’s faith the leaven. Truly blessed is she “who believed, because the things spoken to her by the Lord were fulfilled in her” (Luke 1:45). They would not have been fulfilled unless, according to the Lord’s word, the whole had been leavened, and perpetually leavened—preserving for us, in death as in life, alike one and entire mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, together with his divinity.

23. In this wondrous sacrament, according to the number of the measures, one may observe degrees of a remarkable and most fitting distinction: new, ancient, eternal. New: the soul, believed to have been created from nothing when it was infused; ancient: the flesh, known to have been transmitted from the first human being, that is, from Adam; eternal: the Word, asserted by undoubted truth to have been begotten from the eternal Father as coeternal with him. And in these three, if you observe carefully, is a threefold kind of divine power: that something is made from nothing; something new from the ancient; and something eternal and blessed from what was condemned and dead. What has this to do with our salvation? Much, in every way. First, because we who were reduced to nothing through sin have in some manner been created anew through this, so that we may be some beginning of his creature. [Col. 0801D] Next, because we have been transferred from ancient slavery into the freedom of God’s children, walking in newness of spirit. Finally, because we have been called from the power of darkness into the kingdom of eternal brightness, in which he has already made us sit in Christ. Far from us be those [Note: [Col. 0801] Horstius adds “Novatians,” but this is a marginal lemma.] who try to alienate Christ’s flesh from us, impiously asserting that it was newly created in the Virgin and not taken from the Virgin. Long beforehand the prophetic Spirit admirably opposed this opinion—indeed, this blasphemy—of the impious: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from his root” (Isaiah 11:1). He could have said, “And a flower from the shoot”; but he preferred, “from the root,” to show that the flower derived its origin from the same source as the shoot. Therefore the flesh was taken from the source from which the Virgin sprang: it was not new in the Virgin, since it came forth from the root.

## CHAPTER XI. Continuation of the reflection upon God.

24. Perhaps you are somewhat impatient because we still continue to ask, “What is God?”—both because it has now been asked so often and because you doubt whether he will be found. I tell you, Father Eugenius: God alone can never be sought in vain, even though he cannot be found. Let your own experience teach you this; or, if not, believe one who has experienced it—not me, but the saint who says: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lamentations 3:25). What, then, is God? With respect to the universe, the end; with respect to election, salvation; with respect to himself, he himself [Col. 0802B] knows. What is God? Almighty will; most benevolent power; eternal light; unchangeable reason; highest blessedness: creating minds for participation in himself, enlivening them for perception, moving them to desire, expanding them for reception, justifying them for merit, kindling them for zeal, making them fruitful for fruitfulness, directing them toward equity, forming them toward benevolence, regulating them toward wisdom, strengthening them toward virtue, visiting them for consolation, enlightening them for knowledge, perpetuating them for immortality, filling them for happiness, surrounding them for security.

## CHAPTER XII. God is both the merciful rewarder of good works and the most just avenger of crimes.

25. What is God? No less the punishment of the wicked [Col. 0802C] than the glory of the humble. For he is a certain rational, unwavering, and undeviating direction of justice, reaching everywhere; against it all crookedness must necessarily be shattered. Why should not everything swollen or distorted strike against it and be crushed? Woe to everything that perhaps meets this rectitude, which does not know how to yield; for it is strength as well. What is so contrary and opposed to unrighteous wills as always to strive, always to strike against it, and in vain [variant: to be frustrated]? Woe to opposing wills, which assuredly receive only the punishment of their own turning away. What is so penal as always to will what will never be? What is so condemned as a will bound to this necessity of willing and unwilling, so that it can now move in either direction only perversely and therefore only miserably? It will never obtain what it wants; and what it does not want, it will nevertheless endure forever. Most fittingly indeed: one who is never inclined toward anything becoming should never attain anything pleasing. Who does this? The Lord our God, who is upright and “is perverse with the perverse.” The upright and the crooked will never agree. For they oppose one another, though they do not harm one another. Harm belongs to the latter; far be it from God. “It is hard for you,” he says, “to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:5): that is, it is hard not for the goad but for the one kicking. God is the punishment of the shameful, for he is light. And what is so hateful to obscene and criminal minds? [Col. 0803A] “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). But I ask: will they not be able to turn aside? Not at all. He shines everywhere, although not for all. For “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). The Light sees the darkness, for to it seeing is shining; but, conversely, it is not seen by darkness, because darkness does not comprehend it (77). Therefore they are seen, that they may be confounded; and they do not see, that they may not be consoled. Nor are they seen only by the light: they are seen in the light. By whom, or by what beings? By everyone who sees, so that their shame is great in proportion to the multitude of observers. Yet among so many beholders, no eye is more painful to each person than his own. There is no gaze, either in heaven or on earth, which a darkened conscience more desires to escape and is less able to escape. Darkness does not conceal even itself. [Col. 0803B] It sees itself, though it sees nothing else. The works of darkness follow it, and there is nowhere it can hide from them—not even in darkness. This is the worm that does not die: remembrance of past things. Once introduced—or rather, born in through sin—it clings firmly and can never afterward be torn away. It does not cease to gnaw the conscience; feeding upon it, upon food that is indeed inexhaustible, it perpetuates its own life. I shudder at the biting worm and the living death. I shudder at falling into the hands of living death and dying life.

26. This is the second death, which never kills once for all, but always kills. Who would grant them to die once, that they might not die eternally? Those who say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” [Col. 0803C] and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30)—what do they desire except, by the benefit of death, either to end or escape death? “They will call upon death,” he says, “and it will not come” (Revelation 9:6). Consider this more clearly. The soul is certainly immortal, and can never live without its memory, lest it somehow cease to be a soul. Thus, while the soul endures, memory also endures. But what sort of memory? Foul with shameful acts, dreadful with crimes, swollen with vanity, rough with contempt and neglect. The former things have passed, and have not passed. They have passed from the hand, but not from the mind. What has been done cannot become not done. Therefore, though doing it belonged to time, having done it remains forever. That which outlasts times does not pass with time. Therefore it must torment you forever that you will forever remember having acted wrongly. This will be to experience the truth of that saying: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Psalm 49:21). The Lord has spoken, and everything opposed must necessarily oppose itself, so that the complaint comes too late: “O guardian of men, why have you set me against you and made me burdensome to myself?” (Job 7:20). Thus it is, O Eugenius. Nothing can be contrary to God and remain joined to itself; rather, whoever is rebuked by God will also be rebuked by himself. At that time there will certainly be no possibility either for reason to disguise the truth or for the soul to turn away from the sight of reason, when it has been torn from bodily members and gathered into itself. What purpose would that serve, when the senses through which it used more inquisitively to go out from itself and turn toward this passing form of the world are stilled and shut up in death? [Col. 0804A] You see that nothing is lacking for the shame of the shameful when they are brought forth to become a spectacle to God, Angels, human beings, and themselves. O how wretchedly all the wicked are situated—set against this torrent of upright justice and exposed to this light of manifest truth [variant: set against it]. Is this not to be continually beaten and continually confounded? “Crush them with a double crushing,” says he, “O Lord our God” (Jeremiah 17:18).

## CHAPTER XIII. He discusses profoundly and elegantly the length, breadth, depth, and height of God.

27. What is God? Length, breadth, height, [Col. 0804B] and depth. “What?” you ask. “We have caught you as a professor of the quaternity which you have denounced.” Not at all. I have denounced it, and I denounce it. I seem to have set forth several things, but it is one. The one God is designated according to our capacity, not according to his state. Here he is divided in our apprehension, not in himself. The words are different, the paths many; but through them one thing is signified and one is sought. In this fourfold expression there are not divisions of substance; not dimensions such as we discern in bodies; not personal distinction such as we adore in the Trinity; not a number of properties such as we confess belong to the persons themselves, though they are not other than the persons. Otherwise each one of these in God would be what all four together are; and the four themselves would be what each one [Col. 0804C] is. But because we cannot contend with God in simplicity while striving to grasp the One, it meets us as though fourfold. This is produced by the mirror and riddle through which alone, for the present, he allows himself to be seen. But when we see face to face, we shall see him as he is. Then the frail sight of our mind, however intensely directed, will no longer rebound or break apart into its own plurality. Rather, it will gather itself, become one, and be conformed to his unity—or rather, to that Unity—so that one face may answer the face of the One. For “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Blessed vision! For it the one who said, “My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, will I seek” (Psalm 26:8), rightly longed. Since the matter is still one of seeking, meanwhile let us mount this four-horse chariot, as weak and feeble people needing such a vehicle, in the hope that even thus we may grasp that in which we have been grasped—that is, the meaning of this very vehicle. For we have this instruction from the charioteer himself and the first exhibitor of this chariot: that we should strive to comprehend with all the saints “what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Ephesians 3:18). [Col. 0804D] He said “comprehend,” not “know,” so that, not content with the curiosity of knowledge, we may direct all our concern toward its fruit. The fruit lies not in knowledge but in comprehension. Otherwise, “to one who knows the good and does not do it,” as someone says, “it is sin” (James 4:17); and Paul himself elsewhere says: “Run so that you may comprehend” (1 Corinthians 9:24). What it is to comprehend, I shall explain below.

28. What, then, is God? Length, I say. And what is length itself? Eternity. It is so long that it has no limit, in place no more than in time. There is also breadth. And what is that? Love. By what boundaries could this too be confined in God, who hates none of the things he has made? For he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). Thus that bosom encloses even enemies. Nor, content even with this, does it fail to extend into infinity. It surpasses not only every affection but also every knowledge, as the Apostle adds when he says: “To know also the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge” [Col. 0805B] (Eph. 3:19). What more shall I say? It is eternal—unless perhaps it is more to say that it is eternity. Do you see that its breadth is as great as its length? Would that you might see, not that it is so great, but that it is itself: that the one is the other; not less one than two, nor more two than one. God is eternity; God is love: length without extension, breadth without diffusion. In both alike he transcends the restrictions of place and time, but by the freedom of his nature, not by an excessive magnitude of substance. In this way he who made all things in measure is immeasurable; and, although immeasurable, this is nevertheless the measure even of his immensity.

[Col. 0805C] 29. What else is God? Height and depth: in the one, above all things; in the other, beneath all things. It is plain that equality nowhere falters in the Godhead; it stands firm on every side and remains immovably consistent with itself. Consider height as his power, depth as his wisdom [or, “being”]. These too correspond to one another equally, since height is known to be unattainable and depth equally unsearchable, as Paul marvels and cries: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

We too may delight to cry out with Paul, beholding, insofar as we can, these things in God and, along with them, his utterly simple unity: “O mighty Wisdom, reaching everywhere mightily! O wise Power, ordering all things sweetly!” (Wis. 8:1). [Col. 0805D] The reality is one; its effects are manifold and its operations diverse. And that one reality is length because of eternity, breadth because of love, height because of majesty, depth because of wisdom.

## Chapter XIV. He shows how we may comprehend the foregoing things according to the Apostle.

30. We know these things. But do we therefore suppose that we have comprehended them? It is not disputation but holiness that comprehends them—if, indeed, that which is incomprehensible can in any way be comprehended. Yet, unless it could be, the Apostle would not have said: “That we may comprehend with all the saints” (Eph. 3:18). Therefore the saints comprehend. Do you ask how? If you are holy, you have comprehended and know; if not, become holy, and you will know by your own experience.

A holy affection makes one holy, and this affection is twofold: holy fear of the Lord and holy love. The soul perfectly moved by these, as by two arms of its own, comprehends, embraces, clasps, holds fast, and says: “I have held him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4). Fear corresponds to height and depth; love, to breadth and length. What is so fearful as power, which you cannot resist, or wisdom, from which you cannot hide? God might be feared less, were he lacking either. But now you must fear him perfectly: he lacks neither an eye that sees all things nor a hand powerful over all things. [Col. 0806A] Again, what is so lovable as love itself, by which you love and by which you are loved? Yet eternity joined to it makes it more lovable: because it does not fail, it casts out suspicion.

Therefore [Col. 0806B] love steadfastly and patiently, and you possess length; extend your love even to enemies, and you hold breadth. Be also fearful in every concern, and you have grasped height and depth.

31. Or, if you prefer to match four things of your own equally with the four divine things, you do so if you marvel, fear, burn with zeal, and endure. The height of majesty is indeed to be wondered at; the abyss of judgments is to be feared. Love requires ardour; eternity, the perseverance of endurance. Who marvels except one who contemplates God’s glory? Who fears except one who examines the depth of wisdom? Who burns except one who meditates on God’s love? Who endures and perseveres in love except one who emulates the eternity of love? [Col. 0806C] Certainly perseverance presents a certain image of eternity. Finally, it alone is repaid with eternity—or rather, it is what restores a human being to eternity—as the Lord says: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22).

32. And now observe four kinds of contemplation in these four things. The first and greatest contemplation is admiration of majesty. This requires a purified heart, free from vices and relieved of sins, so that it may readily rise to things above; and so that, at times, it may hold the one who marvels suspended for a while in astonishment and ecstasy.

The second is necessary to this: it is the contemplation of God’s judgments. By this truly fearful sight, while it shakes the beholder more forcefully, [Col. 0806D] it drives out vices, lays the foundation of virtues, initiates one into wisdom, and preserves humility. For humility is a certain good and stable foundation of virtues. Indeed, if it wavers, the accumulation of virtues is nothing but ruin.

The third contemplation is occupied—or rather, at leisure—with the remembrance of benefits; lest it leave a person ungrateful, it urges the remembering person to love the benefactor. Of such things the prophet says when speaking to the Lord: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness” (Ps. 144:7).

The fourth, forgetting the things behind, rests in the expectation of promises alone. Since this is meditation upon eternity—for the things promised are eternal—it nourishes long-suffering and gives strength to perseverance. I think it is now easy to assign these four things of ours to the Apostle’s four: meditation on the promises comprehends length; [Col. 0807A] remembrance of benefits, breadth; contemplation of majesty, height; examination of judgments, depth.

There still remained one to be sought, who has not yet been sufficiently found and cannot be sought too much; [Col. 0808A] but perhaps he is sought more worthily by praying than by disputing, and found more easily. Therefore let this be the end of the book, but not the end of seeking.

[Col. 0807]

# A Treatise, or Letter XLII, of Saint Bernard, Abbot, On the Conduct and Office of Bishops, to Henry, Archbishop of Sens

459–460. Prefatory Notice to the Following Letter, or Little Work II.

[Col. 0807] 1. The books *On Consideration*, addressed to the Supreme Pontiff, are appropriately followed by the treatise *On Ordering the Conduct of Bishops*, which is the first of Bernard’s five letters to Henry, Archbishop of Sens, and is forty-second in order. According to Hugh, the chronicler of Auxerre, he was surnamed Aper; according to others—if the published indexes are not mistaken—Gilbert. Having been a canon, he was elected bishop of Sens after Daimbert in 1122. When he conducted himself rather laxly in this dignity, he was encouraged to more diligent care for his office, chiefly through the efforts of Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, together with Burchard of Meaux, and especially through the confirmation given by Saint Bernard. Bernard also served as his protector against the attacks of Louis VII, as Letter XLIX to Pope Honorius attests.

2. These storms, however, were raised against both Henry and Stephen, Bishop of Paris, by their withdrawal from court and their adoption of a better way of life. Thus those who formerly, as is read in the aforesaid letter, “had been honoured, exalted, judged faithful, and regarded as intimates in secular dress and conduct,” afterward “became enemies because they lived in a manner worthy of their priesthood and in every respect honoured their ministry.” Hence King Louis attempted “to weaken the constancy of the lord of Sens.” This is further illustrated in the Notes to Letters XXII and XLV.

3. Yet Henry did not so order his conduct that he avoided ecclesiastical censure for unjustly harassing a certain archdeacon of his church. Bernard testifies in Letter CLXXXII to the same Henry that he deprived this man of his rank, though he had “not merely not been convicted by judgment, but had not even been accused in word.” Hugh, the chronicler of Auxerre, reports under the year 1136 that Henry was suspended; and this is confirmed by the *Acts of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 55, where it is said concerning Bishop Hugh: “Since, owing to the suspension of Lord Henry, metropolitan, he had no place of consecration in the church of Sens, he was consecrated at Ferrières by Lord Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, about the feast of Saint Vincent.” It is highly likely that this suspension befell Henry because of the unjust deposition of his archdeacon. But the bishop, at length released from this censure, held a synod at Sens in 1140, at which the errors of Peter Abelard were condemned. The joint synodal letter of the Fathers concerning this matter to Pope Innocent survives as Bernard’s Letter CXCI. In that letter they state that they had set out the whole affair briefly, “especially because the same matter was contained more fully and at greater length in the letter of the lord of Sens.” These letters seem to be none other than Bernard’s Letter CXC to Innocent, included among these treatises. Henry died in 1144, on the fourth day before the Ides of June [10 June], and Hugh the precentor succeeded him.

4. Moreover, that this letter was written immediately after Henry’s conversion is demonstrated especially by its words in section 2: “Lately, however, a more favourable breeze has begun to blow to us from your region. For more recent reports have announced concerning you things more cheerful than usual, not by the uncertain voice of rumour but from the truthful mouth of the venerable Bishop of Meaux.” That is, Henry had reformed his life through the counsel of Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, as Bernard shortly declares. But it is certain that this change in Henry occurred during the pontificate of Honorius II, and therefore before 1130: both from Bernard’s Letter XLIX to that same Honorius, in which he commends Henry to him, and from the very cause of the attacks, which was nothing other than Henry’s departure from court and from the courtly mode of life, and consequently his adoption of a more upright life, as is clear from what precedes.

5. This letter was therefore written about the year 1126, when Burchard presided over the Church of Meaux. Bernard says that he received “more cheerful than usual” reports of Henry’s conversion from Burchard’s account. I say Burchard, not Manasses II, who—as has hitherto commonly been believed—did not succeed Burchard before 1133. This is proved by Manasses’s authentic letters concerning Choisy for the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, containing this clause: “These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1135, in the thirteenth indiction, in the sixth year of the ordination of Lord Innocent II, pope, and in the second year of our ordination”; and by another of his charters concerning Mauregard, issued “in the year of the Incarnation 1140, in the seventh year of our ordination.”

Orderic supports this calculation in Book VI, p. 627, where Stephen, Bishop of Paris, and Burchard of Meaux are recorded as having admonished the monks of Rebais to grant the relics of Saint Ebrulf to the monks of Ouche, regarding which Bernard had written a letter to those of Rebais. Orderic places this event in 1130; therefore Burchard, not Manasses, administered the Church of Meaux in that year. Hence the dates in Duchesne’s notes on Abelard must be corrected, where Manasses is said to have begun to govern the Church of Meaux in 1125. This is disproved by his letters concerning Choisy, which, as we have observed above, were issued ten years later, in the second year of Bishop Manasses. What gravity of character and counsel Burchard possessed is shown by the fact that Bernard, in this letter, congratulates Henry on having him together with Geoffrey as counsellor. In Vatican manuscript 663 the letter is divided into seven chapters. Yet it seemed preferable to retain the now accepted divisions of Horstius.

461. Prologue.

[Col. 0809A]

To the venerable lord HENRY, Archbishop of Sens, Brother BERNARD: whatever a sinner’s prayer may avail.

It has pleased Your Eminence to request from us some new composition. We are burdened by the weight of your dignity, yet rejoice in the gift of your gracious condescension. The favour of one requesting is flattering, and the obligation of the request is daunting. For who are we, that we should write to bishops? Yet again, who are we, that we should not obey bishops? Thus I am compelled, both to grant and to refuse, what is asked of me. To write to one of such high rank is beyond me; not to obey that same person is against me. There is danger on either side; but the greater danger seems to threaten if I do not obey. Therefore, taking the path by which danger appears less, I do what you command. [Col. 0809B] For the kindly granted familiarity of your very rank gives boldness, and the authority of the one commanding excuses presumption.

## Chapter I. The office of bishop is arduous and dangerous; therefore he needs good counsellors.

1. Therefore, from the time when, by God’s appointment, you received the keys of the kingdom of heaven entrusted to you, and, according to the pattern of that strong woman, began to put your hand to mighty tasks (Prov. 31:19), whenever we heard that you had either done things you ought not to have done or suffered things you would not have wished to suffer, we grieved for you in doing the former and sympathized with you in enduring the latter.

Meanwhile I recalled those verses: “They that go down to the sea in ships, doing business in great waters, rise up to the heavens [Col. 0809C] and go down to the depths. Their soul wasted away in evils; they were troubled and moved as a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up” (Ps. 106:23, 26–27). And therefore I did not judge, as people commonly do; rather, such a thought moved me to compassion: If, I said, the life of every human being upon earth is temptation (Job 7:1), to how many perils do you think the life of a bishop lie open, who must necessarily bear the temptations of all?

If therefore I, hidden in a cave and, as it were, under a bushel—not indeed shining, but smoking—am nevertheless unable even so to avoid the assaults of the winds, but, worn down by continual and diverse impulses of temptations, am carried to and fro like a reed shaken by the wind, what must be the condition of one set upon a mountain, [Col. 0810A] set upon a lampstand? I alone must be guarded; yet I myself alone am a source of scandal to myself, weariness to myself, burden and danger to myself, so that I must often be angry with my own appetite, stomach, and offending eye. By what troubles, then, is he distressed? By what injuries is he assailed—he for whom, even if personal troubles cease, there are nevertheless never lacking “fights without and fears within” arising from the troubles of others?

2. Lately, however, a more favourable breeze has begun to blow to us from your region. More recent reports have announced concerning you things more cheerful than usual—not by the uncertain voice of rumour, but from the truthful mouth of the venerable Bishop of Meaux [Note: [Col. 0809C] Undoubtedly Burchard, not Manasses II; see the Prefatory Notice, no. 5.]. When asked how you were, he answered with cheerful countenance and as one confidently informed about the matter asked: “I think that this man will now submit himself [Col. 0810B] to the counsels of the Bishop of Chartres.”

I received this answer from him with as much joy as I was certain that the man’s counsels would be most trustworthy. In no way could he have more effectively commended to us the purpose of your heart, or given a surer hope of your progress in the Lord. Safely, I think, you may entrust both yourself and your affairs to the two men named above. By employing such counsellors, you will preserve for yourself both a good reputation and a good conscience. Thus it befits a priest of God, thus a bishop of so great a city, not to be governed by childish or secular counsels.

All men—even enemies—are to be loved, according to the Lord’s command (Luke 6:27); but only those who seem both prudent and well-disposed should be chosen for counsel [Note: [Col. 0809C] In printed editions, including that of 1494, the words “without prudence and goodwill there are no perfect counsels” are inserted here. This is a marginal lemma that entered the text and is absent from the better Colbert manuscripts 1038 and 1410.]. Therefore the Lord rejected both the imprudent counsel of a disciple and the unfaithful counsel of his brothers. To the imprudent man he replied, [Col. 0810C] “You do not understand the things of God” (Mark 8:33); and to the ill-disposed men, “You go up to this feast; but I will not go up” (John 7:8). He thought that he ought entrust himself neither to their malice nor to that man’s imprudence.

Finally, seeking one to whom he might entrust himself, to whom he might safely commit the stewardship of his mysteries, and finding such a person, as it were, with difficulty, he asks in wonder: “Who do you think is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household?” (Matt. 24:45). Accordingly, when about to entrust the care of the sheep to Peter, he first took pains to test his goodwill, asking him three times whether he loved him (John 21:15–17). He also tested his prudence when men were mistaken and thought him to be one of the prophets; but Peter, discerning the truth wisely, confessed him rather to be the God of the prophets: “You are the Christ, the Son of God” (Matt. 16:16).

Woe to our race because of its imperfection! Among a multitude of people you will scarcely find one perfected in both graces. For you will not readily discover either goodwill in the prudent or wisdom in the faithful. But innumerable are those who are plainly devoid of both gifts.

3. You have therefore wisely considered that the priestly burden, episcopal work, and pastoral care cannot be worthily administered without counsel. Hence Wisdom herself, the mother of chaste counsels, speaks of herself: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel.” But in what kind of counsel? In just any sort? “And,” she says, “I am present in learned thoughts” (Prov. 8:12). And, through the mouth of Solomon, she warns in this manner that untrustworthy counsels are to be avoided: “Conduct your case with your friend, and reveal no secret to a stranger” (Prov. 25:9). Likewise, through another wise man, when he advises that nothing should be done without counsel but recognizes the scarcity of men fit for counsel, he says: “Let many be your friends, but let one out of a thousand be your counsellor” (Ecclus. 6:6).

“One,” he says, “out of a thousand.” I would therefore not doubt that divine goodness has shown favour to you, since amid such scarcity among mortals it has granted you not one but two men, and men sufficiently fit: prudent, well-disposed; and, that they may be readily at hand, fellow provincials; and, that they may serve freely, bound by the right of subjection. By resting in their counsels, [Col. 0812A] you will be neither rash in judgment nor violent in punishment; neither too lax in correcting nor too severe in sparing; neither faint-hearted in waiting; neither excessive in food nor remarkable in dress; neither quick to promise nor slow to fulfil; nor lavish in giving.

Their counsel will always keep far from you that evil which is ancient in time but new to cupidity—simony—and its mother, avarice, which is the service of idols. And, to sum up everything in a brief word: if you trust these men, in all things, following the Apostle’s example, you will honour your ministry [Col. 0812B] (Rom. 11:13)—your ministry, I say, not your dominion. You will therefore honour it, not yourselves; for whoever seeks what is his own desires that he himself, not the ministry, be honoured.

## Chapter II. The honour and dignity of ecclesiastical office consist not in outward splendour, but in the adornment of character and virtues.

4. You will honour it, however, not by sumptuous dress [Note: [Col. 0811B] Thus the Fourth Council of Carthage, at which Saint Augustine was present, canon 15: “Let a bishop have plain household goods, a poor table and fare, and seek the authority of his dignity through faith and the merits of his life.” The Council of Trent repeats these words, confirms them by the weight of its new authority, and exhorts bishops first of all so to order their conduct that others may seek from them examples of frugality, modesty, self-restraint, and holy humility. After citing the words of the Council of Carthage, it further requires that, in their remaining manner of life and throughout their household, they take care that nothing appear which is alien to this holy institution, and which does not display simplicity, zeal for God, and contempt for vanities: Session 25, chapter 1, *On Reform*.

A perverse opinion has taken possession of many minds: that outward splendour, pomp, and magnificent display are appropriate—even necessary—to ecclesiastical leaders, so that they may maintain the dignity of their rank. But the authority of canons and councils, the unanimous teaching of the Fathers, the examples of holy bishops, and reason itself overthrow this persuasion. It would be easy to demonstrate this point in detail, if the plan of the present work allowed. It will be treated at length elsewhere, when *Zeal for the House of God*, a book under that title concerning the discipline of ecclesiastical life, now nearly finished, is published.

Meanwhile, read these authors: Bartholomew of the Martyrs, Dominican Archbishop of Braga, in the most useful book entitled *The Shepherds’ Goad*, part 2, chapter 6. There you will find added the most elegant treatise *On the Conduct of Prelates* by Father Louis of Granada, of the same Order, a most celebrated preacher, who treats the same subject learnedly and elegantly in chapter 11. Antonio Molina, *Instruction for Priests*, treatise 2, chapter 13—a book that I wish were worn out in the hands of every churchman! Lindanus, Bishop of Roermond, *Treatise to All Churchmen on Avoiding Impenitence*, Book II, p. 115. Henry Cuyck, likewise Bishop of Roermond, Letter 2, exhortatory to the clergy of his diocese. Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, vol. II, treatise *On the Temperance of Prelates*, in my copy pp. 543 ff.; and vol. I, p. 202, *On the Signs of the Ruin of the Church*. To these Bellarmine, *On the Office of Christian Princes*, Book I, chapter 5; Platus, *On Cardinals*, chapter 16; and Rodriguez, part II of the *Exercises*, treatise III, chapter 29, should deservedly be added. There, on the testimony of Saint Francis Xavier, he teaches [Col. 0812B] how authority is acquired and preserved, and why it has today so greatly declined in prelates.

All these authors teach with one voice, and establish by the weightiest reasons and examples, that honour and reverence are gained more through true and solid virtues than through outward splendour; that the supports of honour on which most people lean are exceedingly weak; and that these things rather hinder authority and finally turn into contempt. This applies especially to an ecclesiastical prelate, as the examples of holy bishops readily show. For, passing over countless others, how great were the authority, dignity, and glory of Saints Basil, Martin, Augustine, and Chrysostom! Yet on what did they rest? Certainly, if they had sought those aids to maintaining authority which are now the sole concern of many, their memory would long ago have perished with a noise, and their names would lie buried in darkness and perpetual oblivion. But now they are exceedingly honoured throughout the whole Church and will always be blessed, because in the days of their flesh they honoured their ministry—not by silver or gold, not by costly garments and the goods of this age, but by contempt for such things, diligent care for their office and calling, and earnest pursuit of humility, modesty, love, and the other virtues.

But you will read these matters treated more fully and elegantly by the authors cited, whose words we gladly use in this kind of subject, so that truth, supported by such great authorities, may carry more weight and fear envy less. Yet those who lie low and are sluggish in the pursuit of a higher life commonly plead the difference of times. Despairing of being able to acquire and maintain honour and authority by virtues, they resort to these base and feeble supports and maintain that different times demand different customs. To such persons it is pleasing to propose a most holy bishop of our own age, whose authority and reverence were the greater because his moderation of life was rarer, his frugality greater, and his renunciation of all splendour more complete.

Jerome Platus writes of him in *On the Office of Cardinals*, chapter 16: “This is the surest and best way of acquiring veneration among people: that virtue shine forth, that integrity, seriousness, religion, and piety stand out so that they may be seen by people.” He confirms this with the example of Saint Nicholas, Bishop of Myra, and then adds: [Col. 0813B] “But why recall ancient things? Cardinal Borromeo—so that no one may plead the times—it is well known how he removed from himself all household furnishings of any value, canopies, curtains, and other things of that sort. In outward garments he dressed as a cardinal; but beneath them he wore simple cloth and linen. Indeed, even his night garment was of ash-coloured, rough, thick cloth, and he never changed that garment throughout fourteen whole years. He steadily maintained until death many other practices of this sort, which need not be reported because they are well known and recent.

“What, then, did any of these things diminish from his distinction? Rather, it added much. For many possess splendid things, and this is not virtue but wealth, which may fall to a foolish person and often does. But to despise such things is wisdom, and therefore produces admiration and praise.” Thus Platus.

Charles of the Basilica of Saint Peter, Bishop of Novara, “the most eloquent writer of the Life of Saint Charles Borromeo,” agrees with him, in Book VII, chapter 6. He says that there were those who criticized Charles’s small retinue and certain other features pertaining to the virtue of Christian humility, complaining that his supreme dignity was in some degree thereby diminished. The matter was even reported at one time to Pope Pius V himself. Charles explained the reason for his conduct in such a way that the excellent Father had nothing to disapprove. He said that the dignity and reputation of those who are ministers of God [Col. 0813D] consist not in human ornaments but in religious virtues. The event itself made this clear, and the matters narrated above demonstrate it: Charles’s simplicity of life, joined to gravity of character and holiness, was always held in such honour by the highest and lowest alike as no ornaments of earthly splendour could have obtained.”], [Col. 0813A] not by the ostentation of horses, not by spacious buildings, but by well-ordered conduct, spiritual pursuits, and good works.

How many act otherwise! In some priests one sees an excessive elegance of dress, but no virtues, or very few. If I remind such persons of that apostolic saying, “Not in costly dress” (1 Tim. 2:9), I fear that they may take offence, since they will perhaps think it unworthy that a saying first directed to the weaker sex and order should be applied to them. As though physicians did not use the same knife to cut kings as they do ordinary people; or as though the head were injured if its overgrown hair were cut with the same scissors that have trimmed the superfluities of nails.

Yet if they disdain to be struck by the same judgment as little women—not by me, indeed, but by the Apostle—they should also disdain to be involved with them in the same fault. Let them now despise the garments of weavers or furriers, and not glory in works of their own. Let them also shrink from putting reddish skins of mice—called *gulae*—around hands consecrated and consecrating the dread mysteries [Note: [Col. 0813D] A twofold explanation of this word may be given. First, with a change of letter, it may quite suitably be used for *guna*, from the Greek γούνα (*gouna*), meaning a shaggy garment made from skins. Hence Guibert, in his letter to Bishop Lullus: “I have sent your brotherhood a *guna* made from otter skins.” Nor is it unprecedented for the letter *n* to be changed into *l*: thus Varro has *vallus* for *vannus*, and Pliny, Book XVIII, chapter 10, has *evallere* for *evannere*, as Dausque noted in his *Orthography*.

Second, it may refer to animal skins dyed a blood-red colour, in the manner in which some suppose that the French word *gueule* was introduced into heraldic usage to designate red. The metaphor was presumably taken from the bloody skins, or *gulae*, of animals that strangled one another in the amphitheatres by fighting with mutual bites. Therefore the skins of which Bernard speaks here were perhaps those of Pontic mice, or other similar animals, to which either their reddish colour or shaggy fur gave the name *gulae*.

As for their use here assigned by Bernard, it is considerably illustrated by a mutilated parable inserted in certain editions of Bernard’s works, though it does not attain the gravity of his style and genius. To explain this passage it is enough to excerpt a few words from it: “But did such and so great a bridegroom come to his bride empty-handed? By no means: he brought gifts and distributed what he brought. Because he came in winter, he first gave the bride winter garments: namely, a lambskin garment and a cloak, both of which are made from a lamb. But one, namely wool, from which the cloak is made, is taken without pain to the lamb; the other, namely the skin, from which the fur garment is made, is not obtained from the lamb without serious pain. This bridegroom is the Lamb … [lacuna] From his wool he made a cloak for his bride when he taught humility in words. He gave her a fur garment when, by vigils, fasts, and the other afflictions of his flesh, and finally by the passion of the cross, he showed his bride the mortification of the flesh. A fur garment, which is made from dead animals, signifies mortification. These things are for winter. But at Easter he gave her an ermine (*d’hermine*) fur garment about the neck and the hand, furnished with red *gulae*. Thus the bride’s fur garment is made of ermine, which is white, signifying spiritual joy in the hope of the future resurrection; it is ornamented with red *gulae* about the neck, down over the breast, and about the hand, because she preaches with her mouth, feels in her heart, and attests in her works the passion of Christ. At Easter Christ also gave his bride two Cordovan [leather shoes],” etc. See *Declamations*, no. 10, Letter 2, no. 11.

Further, for how customary the use of fur garments was in Bernard’s age among clerics and monks, indeed among laypeople and women themselves, see Duchesne, notes on Peter the Venerable, Letter 28, Book I. Benedict XII seems to speak of *gulae* in the bull *Ad decorem*, in these words: “We also prohibit the said canons henceforth from wearing trimmings of the bellies of variegated animals or squirrels mixed with their backs; rather, they are to be of plain, simple, white, black, or grey civilian fur,” etc.], around sacred hands that administer the dread mysteries. Let them reject placing upon the breast what the jewel of wisdom adorns more fittingly. Let them be ashamed to weave around the neck [Col. 0814A] what is more honourably and sweetly subjected to Christ’s yoke. These are not the marks of Christ which such men bear about their bodies after the example of martyrs. Rather, they are known to be feminine ornaments, which women are accustomed to provide for themselves with greater curiosity and expense, thinking, of course, of the things of the world—how they may please men.

5. But you, priest of the most high God: whom do you desire to please by these things—the world or God? If the world, why are you a priest? If God, why should the priest be like the people? For if you desire to please the world, what profit is the priesthood to you? You cannot serve two masters. Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God (Jas. 4:4); and the prophet says: “God shall scatter the bones of those who please men; they have been confounded, because God has despised them” [Col. 0814B] (Ps. 52:6); and the Apostle: “If I were pleasing men, I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). Therefore, if you desire to please men, you do not please God; if you do not please him, you do not appease him. Why then, as I said, are you a priest?

But if, as I added, you intend to please not the world but God, why should the priest be like the people? Indeed, if the priest [Col. 0815A] is a shepherd and the people are sheep, is it fitting that the shepherd should appear in no respect unlike the sheep? If, like me, who am a sheep, my shepherd also walks bent over, with his face directed downward, always looking at the earth, and, fasting in mind only for his belly, seeking fodder—how are we distinguished? Woe if the wolf comes! There will be none to foresee, none to meet him, none to rescue. Does it become a shepherd, after the manner of cattle, to devote himself to bodily senses, cling to low things, and hunger after earthly things? Should he not rather stand upright as a human being, lift his mind toward heaven, seek and savour the things above, not those upon the earth?

6. Moreover, he is angry with me if I dare even to make a gesture, and orders me to put my hand over my mouth, saying that a monk ought not to judge bishops. [Col. 0815B] Would that you would also close my eyes, so that I might not even see what you forbid me to criticize! Is it really such great presumption if, being a sheep, I see the most savage wolves—vanity and curiosity—rushing upon my very shepherd, and roar, so that perhaps, at my bleating, someone may come against those bloodthirsty beasts and bring aid to one who is perishing? What will they do to me, a little sheep, when they leap even upon the shepherd himself with such ferocity? And indeed, if he does not wish me to cry out for him, may I not at least bleat for myself? Yet, even if I keep silence, lest I seem to set my mouth against heaven, the Church nevertheless cries aloud: “Not in costly apparel.” This cry is directed especially to women, so that a bishop may be ashamed to be found guilty of what he hears reproved even in the weaker [Col. 0815C] sex. Or is no shame to be feared if I alone cease to whisper? Even if I do not speak, does not each person’s conscience speak to him? What if someone bolder than I should introduce—not something from the Apostle, as I do, not from the Gospel, not from the prophet, nor indeed anything ecclesiastical, but merely that pagan saying: “Tell me, priests,” not “in the sanctuary,” but “on the bridle,” “what is gold doing?” How much more tolerable it appears in the sanctuary than on a bridle! Even while I am silent, if not the court of kings, at least the poverty of the poor cries out. Reputation may be silent, but hunger is not. Reputation is indeed silent, because the world cannot hate you. For how will the world accuse sin, when rather the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked man is blessed?

[Col. 0815D]

7. But the naked cry out, the hungry cry out; they complain and say:

> “Tell me, priests, what is gold doing on a bridle?”  
> (Persius, *Satires* 8, verse 69.)

Does gold on a bridle ward off cold or hunger? While we suffer miserably from cold and hunger, what do so many changes of apparel, whether spread upon poles or folded in bags, contribute to us? What you squander is ours; what you spend vainly is cruelly withheld from us. For we too are God’s handiwork, and we too have been redeemed by Christ’s blood. We, therefore, are your brothers. See what it means to feed your eyes from a brother’s portion. Our life is turned into your superfluous [Col. 0816A] abundance. Whatever is added to your vanities is taken away from our necessities. In short, two evils proceed from the one root of greed: you perish through self-display, and you kill us by despoiling us. Beasts of burden go laden with jewels, while you take no care for our bare legs with even a pair of boots. Rings, little chains, bells, and certain studded straps [Note: [Col. 0815] Studded straps: reins interwoven with studs of gold, purple, or other colours.], along with many such things—beautiful in colour as well as costly in weight—hang from the necks of mules; but you do not pity your brothers’ sides enough even to put half-girdles upon them.

To this is added that you have procured none of these things either by mercantile enterprise or by the labour of your own hands, nor do you possess them by hereditary right—unless perhaps you too have said in your hearts: “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance” (Ps. 82:13). And these things [Col. 0816B] the poor presently say only before God, to whom hearts speak. For they do not dare openly to complain against you, since for their very lives they must meanwhile rather entreat you. But in the future they will stand with great steadfastness against those who oppressed them, for the Father of orphans and Judge of widows will stand for them. For then his voice will be: “As long as you did not do it for one of these least ones of mine, neither did you do it for me” (Matt. 25:45).

## Chapter III. The chief and worthiest ornaments of bishops: chastity, charity, and humility

8. But you, most reverend father—you, I say—far be it from you to think that your ministry should be honoured by such things. They seem honourable indeed, but to the eye [Col. 0816C] that sees what is on the surface, not to the eye that sees what is hidden. For the things seen in secret appear in no painted colours, yet they are lovely; they are seasoned with no flavours, yet exceedingly sweet; they are raised by no lofty pinnacles, yet they are exalted. Chastity, charity, and humility have no colour, to be sure, but they are not without beauty—indeed, not without such beauty as can delight even divine eyes. What is more beautiful than chastity, which makes a man, conceived from unclean seed, an angel from a human being, a member of God’s household from an enemy? A modest man and an angel differ from one another in blessedness, indeed, [465] not in virtue. And although the angel’s chastity is more blessed, the man’s is known to be stronger.

Chastity alone, in this place and time of mortality, represents a certain condition of immortal glory. Alone amid the solemnities of marriage it claims the manner of that blessed region in which “they neither marry nor are given in marriage”; in some way it provides on earth an experience already of that heavenly manner of life. The fragile vessel that we bear, in which we are frequently endangered, chastity keeps—as the Apostle teaches—“in sanctification” (1 Thess. 4:4), and like fragrant balm by which embalmed bodies are preserved incorrupt. It restrains and binds the senses and limbs [*constringit*: “binds tightly”], lest they be dissolved in idleness, corrupted by desires, or rot away in pleasures of the flesh—as we read of some, that “they rotted like beasts in their dung” (Joel 1:17).

I should therefore rightly say that this ornament of such great beauty [Col. 0817A] honours the priesthood, because it makes the priest beloved by God and men; his memory is then not in bodily succession but in spiritual blessing, and it renders him like the saints in glory, although he is still situated in this region of unlikeness.

9. Yet however greatly chastity may seem distinguished by its own beauty, without charity it has neither value nor merit. Nor is this surprising. For what good thing is accepted without charity? Faith? Not even if it moves mountains. Knowledge? Not even that which speaks with the tongues of angels. Martyrdom? “Not even if,” he says, “I should deliver my body so that I might be burned” (1 Cor. 13:1–3). Without charity no good whatever is accepted; with it, no good however small is rejected. Chastity without charity [Col. 0817B] is a lamp without oil. Remove the oil: the lamp does not shine. Take away charity: chastity does not please. But how beautiful is, as the Wise Man cries, “a chaste generation with charity” (Wis. 4:1)—with that charity, I say, which the Apostle describes as proceeding “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

10. Purity of heart consists in two things: seeking God’s glory and the neighbour’s benefit; so that in all his deeds and words a bishop may seek nothing of his own, but only God’s honour, or the salvation of his neighbours, or both. In doing this he will fulfil not only the office of bishop but also the etymology of his title, making himself a bridge between God and neighbour. This bridge reaches as far as [Col. 0817C] God through the confidence by which it seeks not its own glory but his; it reaches as far as the neighbour through the compassion by which it desires to benefit him, not itself.

A good mediator offers God the prayers and vows of the people, bringing back to them from God blessing and grace. He entreats the Majesty concerning the offences of sinners; he vindicates God’s injury against those who sin. He reproaches the ungrateful with the benefits of mercy; to those who despise, he makes known the severity of power. Yet he strives nevertheless to appease the wrath of the offended One toward both alike: now by setting forth human weakness, now the greatness of divine mercy. Finally, whether he is beside himself for God or sober for us, he always seeks, so far as lies in him, either to serve [variant: *placere*, “to please”] God or to serve [variant adds: *praestare*, “to serve”] us, seeking not what is useful to himself, [Col. 0817D] but what is useful to many.

11. Faithful is the bishop who, looking with a dove-like eye upon all good things that pass through his hands—whether divine benefits to human beings or human vows to God—keeps nothing of them back for himself. He seeks not the people’s gift but their gain, nor does he appropriate God’s glory for himself. He does not bind up the talent entrusted to him in a napkin, but entrusts it to bankers, from whom he receives interest, not for himself but for the Lord. He has no den like the foxes, no nest like the birds, no money-bags like Judas, nor finally, like Mary, a place in an inn. He indeed imitates him who had nowhere to lay his head; for the present he becomes like a vessel cast away, though without doubt he will one day become a vessel for honour and not for dishonour. Finally, [Col. 0818A] he loses his life in this world so as to keep it for eternal life.

No one can truly glory in this great good of inward purity unless he has perfectly rejected outward [466] little glories. For one cannot purely seek either God’s gain or the neighbour’s gain if one has not despised one’s own. Only the person who can say with the Lord, “If I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54); with the Apostle, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21); and with the prophet, “I have been given over to oblivion, like one dead from the heart” (Ps. 30:13)—that is, dead to one’s own will—is not deprived of the glory of inward purity.

Blessed oblivion, if you do not know yourself in order that you may benefit your neighbour. And well is one dead from the heart, if one no longer strives to live for oneself but for him who died for one. Well is one dead [Col. 0818B] from the heart who says: “Now it is no longer I who live.” Yet if dead to himself, he is not dead to Christ, for it follows: “But Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). This death which takes place from the heart is inflicted by charity, of which the Bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by charity” (Song 4:9). For love is strong as death (Song 8:6), and it kills death in us, not life. Hence it boldly threatens: “O death, I shall be your death” (Hos. 13:14). It extinguishes sin, which had expelled the soul’s life, and restores the soul to innocence.

11. But if charity prevails over death so that it can kill death in the encounter, why is it called “strong as death,” rather than stronger than death? Perhaps because it too is death, and cannot be stronger than itself. It is a good death—not of life, but of death. It is a good death, and by no means to be shunned: although it takes life away, it does not destroy it. It takes it away indeed, but only for a time; it will be restored in time and endure beyond time. Finally, “You have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, shall appear, then you too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4). I shall therefore gladly lack it for a time, in order to possess it eternally.

And this is enough concerning what is written: “Charity from a pure heart” (1 Tim. 1:5). Certainly, amid such great self-forgetfulness, it is necessary for the heart to have a good conscience, so that it may more securely extend itself outward for others’ gain, after leaving its conscience secure within itself. For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world [Col. 0818D] but suffers loss to his own soul? (Matt. 16:26).

## Chapter IV. Concern for sincere faith and unfeigned charity, especially necessary for a bishop

13. The order of reason also requires that one who is commanded to love his neighbour according to his own measure should first know how to love himself. Thus there are chiefly two things that make the conscience good: repentance for evils, and abstaining from evils—that is, to use the words of blessed Gregory, “to weep for sins committed and not to commit things to be wept for” (*Homily* 34 on the Gospels, after the middle). Neither of these alone suffices. For if the first sufficed without the second, David would vainly exhort us, saying, “Turn away from evil” (Ps. 36:27); and Isaiah, “Cease to act perversely” [Col. 0819A] (Isa. 1:16); and God himself to Cain: “You have sinned; cease” (Gen. 4:7, according to the Septuagint).

Again, if the second of itself were sufficient after sin to restore a good conscience, the penitent would cry without cause in the Psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1); and: “See my humility and my labour, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24:18); and in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). A soul well assured of both virtues may now securely abandon and, in a certain manner, lose itself in order to gain others. Let it become weak with the weak, burn with those who are scandalized; let it even, if necessary, become a Jew to the Jews. With such a conscience, let it fear nothing: following the example of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, [Col. 0819B] let it fear neither captivity with transgressors in Egypt or Chaldea (Jer. 43:6; 4 Kings 24), nor becoming, with holy Job, a brother of dragons and companion of ostriches (Job 30:29); nor, with Moses—which is more grave—being blotted from the book of God (Exod. 32:32); nor, with Paul, being anathema from Christ for its brothers (Rom. 9:3). With such a conscience, should it be necessary, let it even enter Gehenna itself; securely penetrating the midst of the flames, let conscience sing joyfully: “Even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because you are with me” (Ps. 22:4).

Let us compare, if you please, the treasures of kings and the heights of kingdoms with such confidence. Will not all their prosperity be judged misery beside the riches of so great a good [variant: “such great goods”]? [467] And charity from a pure heart and a good conscience produces this confidence.
