14. There remains “unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5); and likewise the other saying that comes to mind, “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20). These two statements lead us to a threefold division of faith: faith is called dead, feigned, or proven. The Apostle defines dead faith as that which is without works—that is, faith which does not work through love, as though it had no soul, namely that love by which it is animated [variant adds: “soul”] and moved to works.

But I think that feigned faith is faith which, having indeed received life from charity, begins to be moved to good works, but, not persevering, fails and dies like an untimely birth. [Col. 0819D] I would call it “feigned” in the sense in which we call a potter’s vessels *fictilia*, “fashioned things”: not because they are not useful while they last, but because, being fragile, they do not last long. I think that those in the Gospel are marked by this feigning of faith: “They believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away.”

I ask those who say that charity, once received by someone, can never afterward depart: Truth says of some, “These have no roots, because they believe for a time and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke 8:13). From where, and to where, do they fall away? Certainly from faith to unbelief. Again I ask: Could they be saved in that faith, or could they not? If they could not, what injury is done to the Saviour, or what joy to the tempter, by their departing from a place where salvation is not? For the Saviour desires nothing but [Col. 0820A] salvation, and the evil one envies nothing but salvation. But if they could be saved, how are they without charity while they remain in that faith, when salvation cannot exist without charity? Or, in abandoning faith, how do they not also abandon charity, when charity and unbelief cannot exist together?

Therefore some do fall away from faith, because Truth affirms it; consequently, also from salvation, because the Saviour reproves it. From this we infer that they also fall away from charity, without which salvation could not have existed [variant: “cannot exist”]. “And these,” he says, “have no root.” He does not deny that they possess something good; rather, he charges that they are not rooted in the good.

15. Finally, he continues and says: “Because they believe for a time.” It is good, but would that it might endure. For it is not one who has begun, but one who has persevered to the end, who will be saved (Matt. 10:22). Yet they [Col. 0820B] do not endure, because in the time of temptation they fall away. Blessed would they have been if they had meanwhile been snatched away before wickedness changed their hearts. But now, “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days”—that is, to those bearing tender offspring, easily driven out of newly begun life amid dangers. Such are souls that possess charity still small and tender; and therefore their faith, although living, is feigned, and must fail in temptation.

“The furnace tests the potter’s vessels,” he says, “and temptation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27:6): namely, those who live by faith. “For the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17), but by a faith that lives. A dead faith cannot give life. The faith of demons is not brought to examination; empty of charity, it is dead. They believe indeed and tremble, but fear is not [Col. 0820C] in charity. Therefore they are not in the labour of men, nor are they scourged with men; for no testing is now owed to extinguished faith, but rather reprobation. Thus only the faith of the righteous—that is, the living faith of the living—is admitted to the furnace of temptations for examination.

But not every righteous person’s righteousness endures forever, because there are those who believe for a time and fall away in the time of temptation. Tribulation proves the character of anyone’s faith. If one’s faith fails—for it fails when one does not persevere in charity—it is known to be feigned; if one’s faith perseveres, it is judged proven and perfect.

16. From these points it is sufficiently clear, I think, that not all who have had charity also have perseverance in charity. Otherwise the Lord would vainly have admonished the disciples, saying, “Remain in my love” (John 15:9). For either, if they did not yet love, he ought not to have said, “Remain,” but “Be in my love”; or, if they already loved, there was no need to admonish them about perseverance, of which, according to these people, they could not be deprived. Let the good and faithful servant therefore take care, by unfeigned [Col. 0820D] faith, to preserve charity from a pure heart and a good conscience, valuing the life of the soul more highly than that of the body, and dreading the death of the flesh less than the death of faith.

## Chapter V. On the virtue of humility, necessary to all but first of all to prelates

17. Of the three things proposed above, humility alone, unless I am mistaken, remains to be discussed. It is so necessary to the two preceding virtues that without it they scarcely appear to be virtues at all. [Col. 0821A] For humility merits the gift of chastity or charity, because “God gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Humility, therefore, receives the other virtues. It preserves those received, because the Spirit of the Lord rests only upon one who is quiet and humble (Isa. 66:2). It perfects those preserved, for virtue is made perfect in weakness—that is, in humility (2 Cor. 12:9). It overcomes pride, the enemy of every grace and the beginning of every sin, and drives away its proud tyranny both from itself and from the other virtues.

For while pride is accustomed to gain an increase of its strength from any other good things, humility alone—the bulwark and, as it were, tower of all virtues—strongly withstands its malice and confronts presumption. [Col. 0821B] Finally, it alone is the virtue of which Mary, full of every virtue, thought herself worthy to boast. For when she heard from the angel, “Hail, full of grace,” as though she recognized in herself from that fullness only humility, she is recorded as rendering and returning only this in acknowledgment of grace: “God has looked upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:28, 48).

18. What then of Christ, the author and giver of virtues, in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, in whom all the fullness of divinity also dwells bodily? Did not he too glory in humility as in the summit of his teaching and virtues? “Learn from me,” he says—not that I am sober, chaste, prudent, or anything of that sort—but “because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). “Learn from me,” he says. I do not send you to the teaching of the patriarchs [Col. 0821C] or to the books of the prophets; I offer myself to you as an example, myself as the pattern of humility. An angel and a woman envied the height that I possess with the Father: he, my power; she, my knowledge. But you, “seek the better gifts,” learning from me that I am meek and humble of heart.

19. I think it useful to investigate something also concerning pride, so that the beauty of this virtue may appear more clearly from the vice opposed to it. Pride is the desire for one’s own excellence. It is divided into two kinds: blind pride and vain pride. These may also be called, by other names, obstinacy and vanity. The former is a defect of the understanding; the latter, of the will. For by the former the eye of reason is deceived, and by the latter the desire of the will is wrongly disposed. We shall show this better from the definitions of each.

[Col. 0821D] Blind pride, or obstinacy, is the vice by which someone, thinking either that he is good when he is not, or that what he is comes from himself, glories in himself and not in the Lord. Vain pride, or vanity, is the vice by which someone delights more in his own praises than in God’s, whether concerning what he is or concerning what he is not. Having set this out, let us now fit the opposites to humility, setting each against each. Humility is contempt for one’s own excellence. Contempt is opposed to desire. Moreover, two forms of humility are opposed to the two forms of pride: against blind pride, that a person may know how to think humbly of himself; against vain pride, that he may not agree with those who think otherwise. For one who knows how to think humbly of himself cannot be deceived [Col. 0822A] in either judgment concerning himself: either by thinking himself something greater than he is, or by thinking that what he is comes from himself. And so, patiently lacking what he knows to be absent from himself, he humbly glories—not in himself, but in the Lord—in what he is certain is present in him.

20. Against thinking himself something higher than he is, the truly humble person is accustomed, lest he become insolent, continually to turn over in meditation: “Do not be wise in high things, but agree with the humble” (Rom. 12:16); and: “I have not walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me. If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul” (Ps. 130:1–2); and again: “Whoever thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Against thinking that what he is comes from himself, he carefully questions himself: “What do you have that you have not received? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

[Col. 0822B] Likewise, one accustomed perfectly to despise human praise, when he perceives that he is praised for something he knows is not in him, in no way assenting to it, recalls to himself: “Those who call you blessed lead you into error” (Isa. 3:12). He also remembers the verse: “Yet the sons of men are vain, the sons of men are false upon the scales; in order to deceive, they together are from vanity” (Ps. 61:10). Accordingly, he carefully strives to imitate the Apostle speaking thus of himself: “But I refrain, lest anyone think of me above what he sees in me or hears from me” (2 Cor. 12:6).

But when he finds himself praised for a good that he perhaps knows he possesses, nevertheless, as far as he can, he takes care to ward off from himself with the shield [Col. 0822C] of truth the dart of favour, giving glory to God and saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). And, repelling every suspicion from himself, he says to the Lord: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9). For he fears that, if he acts otherwise, he may perhaps hear from him: “You have received your reward” (Matt. 6:5); and again: “You seek glory from one another and do not desire the glory which is from God alone” (John 5:44). Therefore, taking refuge also in this in the Apostle’s counsel, he proves his own work, so that he may have glory in himself and not in another (Gal. 6:4).

He is the faithful guardian of himself who keeps for himself, without deception, the oil of favour, lest when the bridegroom comes the lamp of conscience, empty, be extinguished. “Not in another,” I say. For he judges it unsafe to commit his glory to human lips [Col. 0822D]—to a chest without key or bolt, not shut at all against anyone who wishes to harm it. It is plainly not safe, but foolish, to place one’s treasure where one cannot recover it when one wishes. If you place it in my mouth, it is no longer in your power but in mine, since at my own pleasure I may either praise you or disparage you.

## Chapter VI. Praise and true glory are to be stored in each person’s conscience; yet not without fear, because God searches and judges hearts

21. Conscience is a sound and unshaken vessel, suitable for keeping secrets, open to no snares and yielding to no violence; for it is accessible to no eye or hand, except only to the Spirit who searches [Col. 0823A] even the depths of God. Whatever I store in it, I am secure that I shall not lose it: it will keep it while I live and restore it when I have died. For wherever I go, it goes with me, carrying with it the deposit it has received for safekeeping. It is present while I live; it follows me when I die. Everywhere glory or shame, according to the quality of the deposit, remains inseparable from me.

Blessed are those who can say truthfully: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). Only the humble can say this: those who, according to the common proverb, are accustomed both to fear the eyes of the open field and always to suspect the ears of the woods. For “blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14). The arrogant and presumptuous person cannot say it. Boldly displaying himself, he is carried everywhere and in every place into glory, as though walking across an open field; he glories [Col. 0823B] even when he has acted wickedly and exults in the worst things. He thinks himself unseen because he has more imitators than reprovers—a blind guide of the blind. But this field surely has the eyes of the holy angels, whom undisciplined conduct is accustomed continually to offend.

The hypocrite will not say: “My glory is the testimony of my conscience.” Even if he deceives the opinion of those who judge by appearances through a counterfeit word, face, or bearing, he neither deceives nor escapes the judgment of him who searches hearts and reins; for God is not mocked.

22. Let such a person therefore also fear the ear of the forest. Though tongue and hand are at rest, nevertheless, in the ever-present ear [Col. 0823C] the heart speaks from every thicket of hidden duplicity and thorny cunning, silent and motionless; thought makes confession. “The heart of man is crooked and inscrutable” (Jer. 17:9), so that no one knows the things that are in a person except that person’s spirit within him—and not even that spirit fully.

For when the Apostle said, “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day,” he added: “But neither do I judge myself.” Why? “Because,” he says, “I cannot even myself pronounce a settled sentence about myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified.” I do not wholly entrust myself even to my own conscience, since it cannot itself comprehend me wholly; and one who does not hear the whole cannot judge the whole. “But the Lord is the one who judges me” (1 Cor. 4:3–4).

[Col. 0823D] The Lord, he says, whose knowledge does not fail to reach, whose judgment does not pass over, even what lies hidden from one’s own conscience. God hears in the heart of one who thinks what even the thinker does not hear. The ear of the prophet, though absent, was present to the mouth secretly asking for money (4 Kings 5:22); and shall I, while plotting in however hidden a manner either wickedly to harm my neighbour or shamefully to harm myself, not fear an ear that is nowhere absent? It is indeed a dreadful and reverend ear, for which rest never ceases and silence is never silent. Finally, he says: “Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (Isa. 1:16). But what does he mean by “from before my eyes”? Does God not only hear but also see our secrets?

What sort of eyes behold thoughts? Thoughts have no colour, so as to be seen; nor do they make a sound, so as to be heard. They are accustomed [Col. 0824A] to be felt by the thinker, not heard by the listener or seen by the observer. Yet rightly the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain. Why should he not know what he both hears and sees? In these two senses especially—sight and hearing—no one thinks faith ought to be denied. We firmly maintain that we know what we have seen and heard. Therefore the Lord Jesus had no need for anyone to bear witness concerning a person, for he himself knew what was in a person. “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” he says (Matt. 9:4). He answered not words but thoughts; he heard those who did not speak and saw things that did not appear.

23. I tremble altogether, O Lord Jesus, contemplating as far as I can your majesty, [Col. 0824B] especially when I remember how greatly I have at times been its despiser. But even now, when I have fled from the face of majesty to the knees of mercy, what more do I do? I fear lest I who was once opposed to majesty may now be found ungrateful to mercy. For what if my hands cease, but my breast does not cease? What if my mouth is now silent, but my heart has not yet come to rest? If every unlawful movement of my mind is a distinct insult against you, O God—for example, a movement of anger against gentleness, of envy against charity, of luxury against frugality, of impurity against chastity, and innumerable similar things which, even now, incessantly boil up from the filthy pool of my itching breast, overflow, and strike against the serenity of your brilliantly shining countenance—what great thing have I done in restraining the limbs alone [Col. 0824C] and correcting my outward actions?

If you observe these and similar iniquities—which, though outwardly inactive, I nevertheless do not cease inwardly to perform—who, O Lord, will endure? Or perhaps I no longer do them but suffer them? They are indeed done in me, but are not done by me, if I do not consent. Certainly, if they have not ruled over me, then I shall be undefiled, and undefiled before him—not only if I lack them, but if I keep myself from my iniquity. I call it mine not because I do it, but because I endure it. I bear a body of death and flesh of sin. For the present, it is enough for me if sin does not reign in my mortal body. Thus neither the body nor the sin dwelling in it is counted as guilt, provided that I do not take pleasure in it and do not present my members as weapons to iniquity.

For this every saint will pray to you, O merciful One, at the fitting time [Col. 0824D] (Ps. 31:6): a suppliant, indeed, because he feels the evil; and nevertheless holy, because he does not consent—suppliant because of danger, holy because of virtue. Truly holy and blessed is the person who delights in the law of God according to the inward man and, because he feels evil to be so present in the body that he cannot be rid of it without at the same time being rid of the body, rightly consoles himself and says: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin which dwells in me” (Rom. 7:17).

24. Yet who understands transgressions? For if I could say with Paul—far be it from me—“I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4), I ought not therefore glory as though I were justified. [Col. 0825A] “For it is not the person who commends himself who is approved, but the person whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:18). If the human day applauds my righteousness, I make little of it, because it shines only upon the face. “For man sees what is before the eyes, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). For this reason Jeremiah was not greatly moved by popular judgments, like rays of a human day, but confidently spoke to God: “You know that I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. 17:16). “If my day smiles upon me,” he says, “neither do I judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3), because I do not sufficiently understand even myself.

He alone is rightly appointed Judge of the living and the dead who fashioned the hearts of all individually and understands all their works. I attend only to the Judge whom I recognize also as the only Justifier. [Col. 0825B] “The Father gave him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:27). Shall I, the servant, arrogate to myself even over myself the Son’s authority, and number myself among those of whom he is accustomed to complain: “Men have taken judgment from me”? “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid., 22); and shall I presume for myself what not even the Father claims for himself? Whether I wish it or not, I must stand before him and render account to him for the things I have done in the body—to him whom no word escapes and no thought evades.

Under so equitable a weigher of merits, under so inward a scrutinizer of secrets, who will glory that he has a pure heart? Humility alone, which is not accustomed to glory, does not know presumption, and is not accustomed to contend, will find grace in the eyes of mercy. [Col. 0825C] For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). The truly humble person does not contend in judgment or put forward righteousness, but says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. 142:2). He refuses judgment and asks for mercy, trusting that he can obtain pardon more easily than establish his righteousness. He knows the divine nature to be naturally merciful, one which in no way shrinks from our [variant: “your”] humility.

That Majesty does not despise a contrite and humbled heart in our human nature, having not disdained to assume a body from humility itself. I do not know how, but divinity is always accustomed to draw nearer to humility in a more familiar way. Finally, it clothed itself in humility so as to appear to human beings. [Col. 0825D] It bore a humble substance, form, and condition, commending to us the excellence of that very virtue which it willed to honour with its special presence.

## Chapter VII. He censures the ambition of ecclesiastics, the promotion of younger men, and the plurality of benefices
25. But for you, most beloved, for you especially, I judge this [humility] to be necessary all the more because you are known to possess greater material for pride. Birth, age, learning, a chair, and—what is greater still—the prerogative of primacy [Note: The primacy of the metropolitan of Sens is traced back to John VIII, who entrusted his vicariate in Gaul and Germany to Archbishop Ansegisus. There is an individual work on this subject by Jean-Baptiste Driot, canon of Sens. See the letter of Louis VI to Callixtus II, in vol. 3 of the *Spicilegium*, p. 147.]: for whom would these not be fuel for insolence, an occasion for self-exaltation? Yet they can also be occasions of humility. To those who contemplate them, honours are alluring; but to those who weigh their burdens, they are wearisome and frightening. Yet not all receive this saying. Many would not run toward honours with such confidence and eagerness if they perceived that burdens were attached to them as well. They would certainly fear being weighed down, and would not seek the mitres of whatever dignities at such labour and peril. But now, because glory alone is considered and not punishment, it is considered shameful in the Church simply to be a cleric; and those who have not been raised to some more eminent position are regarded by themselves as base and inglorious.

[Col. 0826B] Schoolboys and beardless youths are promoted, on account of nobility of blood, to ecclesiastical dignities [Note: Compare Letter 271, to Theobald, Count of Champagne, whom Bernard gravely and kindly restrains when he wishes to procure ecclesiastical dignities for his underage son William.]; and they are transferred from beneath the rod to presiding over priests. In the meantime they are happier that they have escaped the rods than that they have deserved authority; what delights them is not so much the mastership they have obtained as the mastership taken away from them. This is so at first. But as time goes on, gradually becoming insolent, they quickly learn to claim altars [Note: Scribes of that age wrote *vendicare* (“to claim”), for which some manuscripts have *vendicate*. The former reading is preferable, since the verb corresponds to ambition, discussed immediately below; avarice is another branch, concerning the emptying of subjects’ purses.], to empty the purses of their subjects—using ambition and avarice as exceedingly suitable masters in this discipline. Yet however cautiously you may seem, by whatever industry, to acquire gains for yourself; however watchfully you may be able to preserve your own property; however diligently you may strive to win for yourself the favour of kings and princes—we nevertheless say: “Woe to the land whose king is a child, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. 10:16).

26. Nor do we say that any age is premature for God’s grace, just as none is too late; since we see many younger persons understanding more than elders, making their days old by character, forestalling time by merit, and compensating by virtues for what their age lacks. Good boys are those who strive to be children in malice just as they are in age—malice, I say, but not understanding—of whom, according to the Apostle’s admonition, “let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:12). Young people of good disposition are better than those grown old in evil days. “A child of a hundred years is accursed”; and, conversely, “venerable old age is not that which lasts long, nor is it reckoned by the number of years” (Wis. 4:8).

[Col. 0826D] Good was the boy Samuel, who stood ready as a listener when God spoke, saying: “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:9); as though he said: “I am ready and am not troubled, that I may keep your commandments” (Ps. 118:60). Jeremiah too was good: sanctified before he was born, when he excused himself on account of youth, he was nevertheless appointed over nations and kingdoms (Jer. 1:6). [Col. 0827A] Daniel likewise was good, whose spirit God stirred up in order to convict unjust judgments and deliver innocent blood (Dan. 13:45–64). In short, “the gray hairs of humanity are understanding, and a spotless life is old age” (Wis. 4:8–9). Wherever a boy-old-man of this sort is found promoted, it is God’s work: to be admired by those who are not such, not imitated.

27. But throughout the clergy persons of every age and rank, learned and unlearned alike, rush toward ecclesiastical *curae*—“cures,” pastoral charges—as though, once they have reached the charges, each were henceforth to live without cares [Note: Hence the common use of the name *curae* to signify the benefices of those called curates.]. Nor is this surprising in those who have not yet experienced such things in themselves. For, seeing those who have already placed their own shoulders beneath the desired burden, not merely failing to groan as under a load, but even desiring [Col. 0827B] to be more heavily burdened, they are not deterred by dangers—which, blinded by desire, they do not see—but are further provoked by the favours which they envy in them.

O ambition always boundless, and avarice insatiable! When they have attained the first steps of honour in the Church—whether by merit of life, or by money, or even by the prerogative of flesh and blood, which shall not possess God’s kingdom—their hearts do not therefore rest. They are ever agitated by a twofold desire: to be extended more and more into greater things, and raised to higher ones. For example, when someone has become dean, provost, archdeacon, or something of this kind in any church, he is not content with one office in one church, but strives to acquire for himself several honours—indeed, as many as he can—in one church as well as in many. [Col. 0827C] Yet, should opportunity arise, he would gladly prefer to all these the dignity of one bishop. But will he thus be satisfied? Once made bishop, he wishes to be archbishop. Having perhaps attained this, and dreaming again of something higher—I know not what—he resolves, through laborious journeys and costly intimacies, to frequent the Roman court, thereby securing for himself certain profitable friendships. If they do this for the sake of spiritual gain, their zeal deserves praise; but their presumption needs correction.

28. Some, unable to do these things, turn to another kind of ambition, in which they nevertheless disclose the desire to dominate that they possess. For when they preside over very populous cities and enclose, as it were, whole countries within the circuit of their own diocese, then, finding an occasion in any ancient privilege, they strive to subject neighbouring cities to themselves, so that two places—which two bishops could scarcely govern—may be reduced beneath one bishop [Note: This perhaps refers to the bishop of Noyon, who scarcely at last allowed the church of Tournai, long united to his see, to enjoy its own bishop—namely Anselm, formerly abbot of Saint-Vincent at Laon—whom Eugenius III, at Bernard’s request, granted to the people of Tournai. Compare *On Consideration*, book III, nos. 14 and 16.].

[Col. 0828A] I ask: what is this so hateful presumption? What is this great passion for dominion upon earth? What is this unbridled desire to rule? Certainly, when you were first drawn to the episcopal chair, you wept, you fled, you complained of compulsion, declaring that the office was far too great for you, indeed altogether beyond you; crying out that you were wretched and unworthy, unfit for so holy a ministry and unequal to such great cares. Why then, now that modest fear has been cast away, do you voluntarily seek greater things? Indeed, with irreverent boldness, why, not content with your own possessions, do you invade those of another? Why do this? Perhaps in order to save more peoples? But to send your sickle, which is yours, into another’s harvest is an injury. Is it in order to serve your own Church? But the Bridegroom of the Churches is not pleased by such an increase of one church as becomes the loss of another. Cruel and incredible ambition—if the eyes did not establish its truth! Their hands scarcely refrain from literally fulfilling what is read in the prophet: “They have cut open the pregnant women of Gilead, in order to enlarge their borders” (Amos 1:13).

29. Where is that dreadful threat: “Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field” (Isa. 5:8)? Is this woe to be feared only in those small matters, and not when cities are joined to cities or provinces to provinces? Let them indeed answer, if they wish, that they imitate the Lord Christ, themselves making both one, themselves bringing flocks from different pastures so that there may be one shepherd and one fold. To achieve this they do not shrink from frequently wearing down the thresholds of the Apostles, where they will find—as is more grievous—persons who favour their wicked desire: not because the Romans greatly care to what end the matter is brought, but because they greatly love gifts and follow recompense.

[Col. 0828C] I speak nakedly of naked things; I do not uncover shameful matters, but refute shameless ones. Would that these things happened privately and in chambers! Would that we alone saw and heard them! Would that even those who spoke of them were not believed! Would that the modern Noahs had left us something by which they might in some measure be covered by us! But now, when the whole world beholds the spectacle, shall we alone be silent? My head has been shattered on every side, and shall I think it ought to be covered while blood boils all around? Whatever covering I apply will be stained with blood; and the shame will be greater for having wished to conceal what could not be concealed.

## Chapter VIII. He commends humility and moderation to a bishop.

30. Good is the humility which, even in the present life, keeps the mind quiet amid such biting cares, and makes the conscience secure from threatening punishments in the life to come. May this restrain, Father, your minds from the ruinous emulation of all these things. Hear rather the Prophet, warning against such people in these words: “Do not emulate evildoers, nor be jealous of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 36:1). Rather, the Apostle should be emulated: he does not boast beyond measure, nor stretch himself beyond himself; nor does he dare, as he himself confesses, to compare himself with certain persons who commend themselves, but compares himself with himself and measures himself according to the measure of the rule which [Col. 0829A] God has measured out to him (2 Cor. 10:12–13).

When one also hears from his mouth, “Do not defraud one another” (1 Cor. 7:5), one will be pleased to be content with one’s own possessions. He also, while urging humility, will not hesitate to address to an archbishop, for his welfare, that saying of his: “Do not think highly of yourself, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). For one placed on high, not to think highly is difficult and altogether unusual; but the more unusual it is, the more glorious. Fear concerning an elevation already attained will make higher things tiresome rather than pleasing. Therefore do not consider yourselves happy because you preside; but if you do not benefit others, consider yourselves unhappy.

31. In order that you may preside securely, do not disdain also to be subject, if you owe subjection to anyone. For disdain of subjection renders one unworthy of precedence. The counsel is that of the Wise Man: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20). The precept is that of Wisdom: “Let the greater among you become as the lesser” (Luke 22:26). If it is expedient even to be subject to inferiors, how may one despise the yoke of superiors? Let your subjects see in you what they ought to render to you. You understand what I mean: “honour to whom honour.” “Let every soul,” he says, “be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13:1). If every soul, then yours also. Who exempts you from the universal whole? Whoever attempts to exempt you attempts to deceive you.

Do not yield to the counsels of those who, although Christians, count it a disgrace to follow Christ’s deeds or obey his words. They are the people accustomed to say to you: “Preserve the honour of your see. It was indeed fitting that the Church entrusted to you should grow through you; [Col. 0829C] but at least let it remain in the dignity in which you received it. Are you less capable than your predecessor? If it does not grow through you, let it not diminish through you.” So they speak. Christ both commanded and acted otherwise. “Render,” he says, “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Mark 12:17). What he said with his mouth, he promptly took care to fulfil in deed. The Creator of Caesar did not hesitate to render tribute to Caesar; for he gave you an example that you too should do likewise. When would he deny due reverence to God’s priests, he who took care to show it even to secular authorities?

Moreover, if you diligently attend the successor of Caesar—that is, the king—in his courts, counsels, affairs, and armies, would it be unworthy of you to render such service to any vicar of Christ [Note: That is, the pope or Roman pontiff, whom Bernard was among the first to call “Vicar of Christ” as a proper title, here and in Letter 251, no. 1. Compare the note to Letter 183. Yet he also calls a bishop “Christ’s vicar,” according to ancient custom, below, no. 36; the pope, however, uniquely, in *On Consideration*, book II, no. 16, and book IV, no. 23.] as has from ancient times been ordered among the Churches? “For,” says the Apostle, “the things that are, have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1). Let those who dissuade you from this supposed disgrace consider what it is to resist God’s ordinance. It is very disgraceful for the servant to be as his lord, or for the disciple to be as his master! They think they are showing you great deference when they attempt to prefer you to Christ, though he himself protests and says: “A servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle than he who sent him” (John 13:16). What the master and Lord did not disdain—and such a master and Lord—will a good servant and devoted disciple judge unworthy of himself?

32. How beautifully spoke that blessed centurion, whose faith had no equal found in Israel: “I also,” he says, “am a man under authority, having soldiers under me” (Luke 7:8). He did not boast of the authority which he stated neither alone nor first. For, intending to say, “having soldiers under me,” he prefaced it with: “I am a man under authority.” He recognized himself as a man before he recognized himself as powerful. This Gentile recognized himself as a man, so as to show that there was now fulfilled in him what David had long before said: “Let the nations know that they are men” (Ps. 9:21). “I am a man,” he says, “and under authority.” [Col. 0830B] Whatever you add afterward, we no longer suspect boasting. Humility has been put first, lest loftiness should cast him down. Arrogance finds no place where so bright a badge of humility has preceded it.

You acknowledge weakness [alternative reading: humility], you confess subjection; now you may safely profess that you also have soldiers under you. Truly, because he was not ashamed of subjection, he deserved rightly to be honoured for precedence. He did not blush at authority above him, and therefore was worthy to have soldiers beneath him. His mouth spoke from the abundance of his heart; and, according to the order he had established among his affections within, he fittingly arranged his words without. He first gave honour to those set over him, so that he might now justly receive it from those subject to him. He knew that he received from his superiors [Col. 0830C] what he was to confer upon inferiors, and that through experience of his own subjection he would better learn to govern his own commands with moderation.

Perhaps he did not fail to know that God subjected all things beneath the feet of the human being subject to him; but when that human being offended him, he made them hostile. The one whom he had established, humble, over the works of his hands, was, through the guilt of pride, compared to senseless beasts and made like them. Perhaps he also knew that the human spirit, when subject to its Creator, possessed the flesh subject to itself; but, when rebellious, found it rebellious; and, having become a transgressor of the higher law, began to perceive another law in its members, opposing the law of its mind and taking it captive under the law of sin.

## Chapter IX. Abbots who perversely seek exemptions are rebuked.

[Col. 0830D]

33. I am astonished that certain abbots of monasteries in our Order violate this rule of humility with hateful contention, and under a humble habit and tonsure—which is worse—think so proudly that, although they do not allow their subjects to transgress even a single little word of their commands, they themselves disdain to obey their own bishops. They despoil churches in order to be emancipated [Note: Bernard does not elsewhere disapprove such monastic exemptions when, from the very foundation of a monastery, it belonged especially to the Apostolic See by the founders’ intention. “For,” he says, “one thing is granted by devotion, another is contrived by ambition impatient of subjection.” *On Consideration*, book III, no. 18.]; they ransom themselves in order not to obey. Christ did not act thus. [Col. 0831A] He gave his life so as not to lose obedience; whereas these men, in order to be without it, expend nearly all the livelihood of themselves and their communities.

What is this presumption, O monks? For because you are set over monks, you are not therefore no longer monks. It is profession that makes a monk; necessity that makes a superior. Therefore, lest necessity prejudice profession, let prelation be added to monasticism, not take its place. Otherwise, how will this be fulfilled: “Have they made you their leader? Be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. 32:1). How can you be as one of them while proud among the humble, rebellious among the subject, harsh among the meek? That we may think you one of them, let us see you as ready to render obedience as to demand it; let us see you as willingly obeying superiors when subject [Col. 0831B] as commanding subjects when superior. But if you always wish to have obedient persons and never to be one yourself, you prove that you are not as one of them, since you refuse to be one of the obedient. By proudly separating yourself from them, we plainly perceive with whose fellowship you are associating yourself. And though you either shamelessly despise or foolishly ignore this, know that you are certainly reckoned among those of whom it is written: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens, and lay them upon men’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. 23:4).

Which fellowship, then, do you judge more unworthy of you: that of luxurious masters, whom Truth rebukes, or that of obedient monks, whom he calls his friends? For he says: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). You see, then, how serious it is to command what you have not done yourself, or to refuse to do what you have taught.

34. Further, not to mention what is in the Rule, where Saint Benedict commands you to show by your deeds that those things which you teach your disciples to be contrary are not to be done; and likewise to pass over the fact that he expressly defines the third degree of humility as this: that, for the love of God, one submit oneself in all obedience to one’s superior (*Rule*, chapters 2 and 7)—observe in the rule of Truth those of whom it is written: “Whoever shall break one of these least commandments of mine and teach people thus shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). Accordingly, you who teach and refuse to obey are convicted both of teaching and breaking not Christ’s least commandment, but his greatest. Therefore, as teacher and breaker of the commandment, you are to be called least in the kingdom of heaven.

If, then, you consider it an injury to your priorate to appear inferior to the highest priests, should it not be considered more unworthy to be called least in the kingdom of heaven? If you are greatly proud, be more ashamed to be called least than inferior. For it is a lesser humiliation to appear inferior than least; but it is far more excellent to be subject only to bishops than to the whole multitude.

35. “But,” he says, “I do this not for my own sake, but I seek [Col. 0832A] the liberty of the church.” O liberty more slavish, if I may so speak, than every slavery! May I patiently abstain from a liberty of this kind, which subjects me to the servitude of the worst pride. I fear the teeth of the wolf more than the staff of the shepherd. For I, a monk and an abbot of monks of whatever sort, am certain that if I should ever attempt to shake from my own neck the yoke of my bishop, I immediately subject myself to Satan’s tyranny. For that bloodthirsty beast, who goes about seeking someone to devour, perceiving the watch withdrawn—alas!—at once leaps upon the presumptuous man. Rightly indeed he does not hesitate to rule over the proud man, since he justly glories in himself as king over all the children of pride.

Who will grant me that a hundred shepherds be appointed for my protection? The more numerous those whom I perceive to care for me, the more safely I go out into the pastures. Astonishing madness! I do not hesitate to gather crowds of souls for myself to guard, yet I am displeased to have one guardian over myself! Certainly, my subjects make me anxious concerning the account I must render for them; but those who preside over me themselves, as Paul says, keep watch all the more diligently, as persons who will render an account for me (Heb. 13:17). Those men, even when they honour me, burden me; these do not so much press upon me as protect me. I know that I have read: “A most severe judgment is for those who preside, but mercy is granted to the lowly” (Wis. 6:6–7).

Why then, O monks, does the authority of priests burden you? Do you fear oppression? But if you suffer anything for righteousness’ sake, you are blessed. Do you disdain worldliness? Yet none was more worldly than Pilate, before whom the Lord stood to be judged. “You would have no authority over me,” he says, “unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). Already then he spoke concerning himself, and experienced in himself, what later he proclaimed through the apostles in the churches: “There is no authority except from God,” and “whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:1–2).

36. Go now, then: resist Christ’s vicar, though Christ did not resist even his own adversary; or say, if you dare, that God does not know the ordinance of his own bishop, though Christ acknowledges that even the authority of the Roman governor over himself had been ordained from heaven. But some of them plainly reveal what they think when, after acquiring apostolic privileges at great labour and expense, they claim pontifical insignia for themselves by means of those privileges, themselves using, in the manner of bishops, mitre, ring, and sandals [Note: Such ornaments first began to be granted to abbots in the tenth century. Our Paul Langius, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1398, likewise rebukes abbots who coveted these insignia. Lucius III imposed them upon Lantelmus, abbot of Casa Dei, in connection with obedience. In the church of Besançon, Leo IX granted to priest, deacon, and subdeacon the use of mitre, ring, and sandals on certain feast days, as is recorded in the evidences of the history of Tournus, pp. 358 and 362.].

Certainly, if the dignity of the things is considered, the monastic profession rejects them; if their ministry is considered, they plainly suit bishops alone. They plainly desire to be what they are eager to appear; and rightly they cannot be subject, since already by desire itself they compare themselves with bishops. What if the authority of privileges could confer the name upon them as well? With how much gold, do you think, would they buy the right to be called bishops? Where is this leading, O monks? Where is the fear of the mind? Where the shame of the face? Which approved monk ever taught such a thing in word or left it as an example? Your Master sets forth twelve degrees [Col. 0833A] of humility and distinguishes them by specific descriptions (St Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 7): in which of them, I ask, is a monk taught or permitted to delight in this pomp or seek these dignities?

37. Labour, seclusion, and voluntary poverty: these are the insignia of monks; these are what ordinarily ennoble monastic life. But your eyes behold every lofty thing; your feet go around every forum; your tongues are heard in every council; your hands plunder every inheritance belonging to another. Yet, if it must be so—that, emancipated from subjection to bishops, you should be exalted with equal glory to the successors of the Apostles, with an equal chair and the same insignia of solemn vestments—why do you not also celebrate the sacred orders and give blessings among the people [Note: Both later came into use, as regards blessings and the conferral of minor orders. Indeed, the first five abbots of the Cistercian Order sometimes even confer the subdiaconate.]?

How much I am moved to say against this most shameless presumption! But this consideration restrains my impulse: remembering that I write for ears already occupied, I fear that I may become burdensome to an archbishop by too long a reading; and because the matter is so manifest that the multitude of those who rebuke it seems only to have hardened its shamelessness. But if these very remarks too are seen to exceed the agreeable limits of brevity, pardon me, my lord: you have compelled me, even in this matter, to disclose my own lack of skill, since I have not known how to preserve the customary manner and measure in writing.

[Col. 0833]

# Sermon, or Book, of Saint Bernard, Abbot, On Conversion Addressed to Clerics

## Prefatory Notice

[Col. 0833] The title of the following little work varies. In its first edition, namely the Speyer edition of 1501, it is entitled “A Little Book on Conversion, Addressed to Scholars,” without division into chapters. In the editions of 1520 it is entitled, “A Sermon on Conversion, Addressed to Clerics”; this we judge to be the genuine title. Bernard himself calls it a sermon, no. 31: “We have wearied you by the length of the sermon,” etc. Some manuscripts give the heading, “To the Clerics of Paris.” The Cistercian *Exordium* supports this in book seven of the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 13:

> Moreover, on one occasion, when Bernard, the man of God, was at Paris because necessity required it, he entered, at the clerics’ request, their schools according to custom; and, showing them the pattern of true philosophy, he admonished them earnestly concerning contempt of the world, etc.

Geoffrey relates the event in book five of the same *Life*, no. 10:

> Once, when the holy father was travelling through the region of Paris, Bishop Stephen and all the others who were present together earnestly begged him to turn aside into the city itself, but could not obtain this. For, unless some serious cause compelled him, he avoided public gatherings with great zeal. Although he had arranged his journey otherwise on the evening before, in the morning, as soon as he had spoken to the brothers, he ordered the bishop to be told: “We shall go to Paris, as you asked.” Therefore, when an exceedingly large body of clergy had assembled—as they were always accustomed to request from him the word of God—three of them were immediately pierced with compunction and, turning from vain studies to the cultivation of true wisdom, renounced the world and attached themselves to God’s servant, etc.

This sermon is grave and impassioned against clerics who aspire to ecclesiastical dignities and rashly approach sacred orders. We have retained the division into chapters as used in the editions from 1520 onward.

## Chapter I. That no one can be converted to the Lord unless first anticipated by God’s will and by his voice crying inwardly.

[Col. 0833B]

1. You have assembled, as we believe, to hear God’s word. For no other cause of this your eager gathering presents itself to us. We certainly approve this desire and rejoice in such praiseworthy zeal. For blessed are those who hear God’s word, provided that they keep it (Luke 11:28). Blessed are those who remember [Col. 0834B] his commandments, provided that they do them (Ps. 102:18). Surely he has words of eternal life; and the hour is coming—would that it were so now also—when the dead will hear his voice, and those who hear will live (John 5:25), since life is in his will.

And, if you wish to know it, our conversion is his will. Hear him himself at last: “Is the death of the wicked my will,” says the Lord, “and not rather that he turn and live?” (Ezek. 18:23). From these words we plainly recognize that our true life exists only in conversion, nor is entrance to it opened otherwise, as the Lord likewise says: “Unless you are converted and become as little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Rightly indeed, little children alone enter; for the little child leads them, he who was born and given to us for this very purpose.

I therefore seek the voice which the dead hear and, having heard it, live; perhaps indeed it is necessary to preach the gospel even to the dead. Meanwhile there occurs to me a brief but full saying which the Lord’s mouth uttered, as the prophet testifies: “You have said”—speaking, without doubt, to the Lord his God—“Turn back, children of men” (Ps. 89:3). Nor is conversion without reason required of the children of men, since it is certainly necessary for sinners. For to the spirits above is enjoined rather the praise befitting the upright, as the same prophet sings: “Praise your God, Zion” (Ps. 147:12).

2. But what he says—“you have said”—in my judgment should neither be passed over carelessly nor heard simply. For who would dare compare what God is said to have spoken with human utterances? Surely the word of God is living and effective (Heb. 4:12), and his voice is in magnificence and power (Ps. 28:4). For “he spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). He said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3). He said, “Turn back, children of men,” and they turned back. Thus the conversion of souls is the work of the divine voice, not of a human one.

Simon son of John, called and appointed by the Lord to be a fisher of human beings, nevertheless labours in vain all night and catches nothing, until, casting his net at the Lord’s word, he can enclose a great multitude. Would that we too today might cast the net of the word in this word, and experience what is written: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power” (Ps. 67:34). If we speak falsehood, that is plainly from ourselves. Even then, perhaps, our voice will be judged ours and not the Lord’s, if we seek what is ours rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ. But even if we speak God’s righteousness and seek God’s glory, it is nevertheless necessary to hope for and ask the effect from him alone: that he may join to his voice a voice of power.

Therefore we urge you to raise the ears of your heart to this inward voice, so that you may strive to hear God speaking within rather than a human being speaking outwardly. For that voice of magnificence and power [Col. 0835D] shakes deserts, searches hidden places, and rouses souls from torpor.

## Chapter II. That the Lord’s voice offers itself to all and presents the unwilling soul to itself.

3. Certainly, one need not labour to attain hearing of this voice; rather, the labour is to stop one’s ears so as not to hear it. The voice itself offers itself; it presses itself upon us; nor does it cease meanwhile to knock at each person’s door. “For forty years,” he says, “I was near to this generation, and I said: These always go astray in heart” (Ps. 94:10). He is still near to us, still speaks, and perhaps there is no one who hears. Still he says, “These go astray in heart”; still Wisdom cries in the streets: “Return, transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. 46:8).

This indeed appears to be the Lord’s beginning of speech; this word seems to have preceded all who turn to their heart, not only recalling them, but bringing them back and setting them before his face. For it is not merely a voice of power, but also a ray of light, at once declaring to human beings their sins and illuminating the hidden things of darkness. Nor is there any difference between this inward voice and light, since one and the same is the Son of God, the Word of the Father, and the radiance of glory. The substance of the soul too, in its own kind, is likewise spiritual and simple, without any distinction of senses; yet the whole soul—if it may indeed be called whole—seems at once both to see and to hear.

For what is effected by that ray or word except that it may know itself? The book of conscience is opened; the miserable course of life is turned over; a sad history is unfolded; reason is illumined; and memory, unrolled, is displayed, as it were, before certain eyes of the soul. Yet both reason and memory are not so much possessions of the soul as the soul itself: so that it is the same thing both inspecting and inspected, set before its own face and compelled, by certain violent officers—that is, the thoughts sent in—to stand before its own tribunal for judgment. Who can endure such a judgment without tribulation? “My soul was troubled within me,” says the prophet of the Lord (Ps. 41:7); and do you wonder that you cannot be set before your own face without rebuke, disturbance, and shame?

## Chapter III. That by God’s voice the soul’s reason can, as in a book, discover, reprove, judge, and distinguish all evils.

[Col. 0836C]

4. Do not expect me to tell you what reason discovers in your memory, what it reproves, what it judges, what it decides. Apply your hearing within; turn back the eyes of your heart; and by your own experience you will learn what is going on. “For no one knows what belongs to a human being except the human spirit that is within him” (1 Cor. 2:11). If pride, envy, avarice, ambition, or some similar plague lies hidden there, it will scarcely escape this examination. If fornication, robbery, cruelty, any deceit, or any sin has been committed, the guilty person himself will not remain hidden from this inward judge, nor will he deny it before him. For all that itching desire of wicked pleasure has swiftly passed away, and the whole enticement of enjoyment has soon come to an end; yet it has imprinted certain bitter marks upon the memory [Col. 0836D], and has left foul traces behind. Into that storehouse, indeed, as into a kind of bilge, all abomination runs down and all uncleanness flows. It is a great volume, in which all things are inscribed, certainly by the stylus of truth. The belly now bears bitterness, though in passing it seemed to have delighted the wretched throat for a short time by some trifling sweetness. “I grieve for my belly, wretch that I am; I grieve for my belly.” Why should I not grieve for the belly of memory, where so much corruption has been heaped up?

Which of us, brothers, if he were suddenly to see this outer garment by which he is covered smeared everywhere with obscene spittle and polluted with every sort of most disgusting filth, would not recoil violently, cast it off quickly, and throw it away in indignation? Therefore, he who finds, not a garment, but himself within the garment to be such, ought to grieve all the more [Col. 0837A] and be dismayed in spirit, because he bears more closely what he recoils from. For a defiled soul cannot cast off itself as it casts off its tunic. Finally, who among us has such patience and strength that, if perhaps—as is read of Miriam, Moses’ sister (Num. 12:10)—he saw his flesh made horribly white by a sudden [variant: subcutaneous] leprosy, he could stand calmly and give thanks to the Creator? Yet what is this flesh except a perishable tunic with which we are clothed? And what should this bodily leprosy be reckoned among all the elect except a fatherly rod of correction and a cleansing of the heart? There, there is fierce tribulation and the most just cause for grief: when, awakened from the sleep of miserable pleasure, a person begins to discover the inward [Col. 0837B] leprosy which he himself sought with much zeal and labour. For although no one hates his own flesh, the soul will be still less able to hate itself.

## Chapter IV. That one who loves iniquity hates both his soul and his flesh; and concerning fruitless repentance after death

5. But perhaps someone may be troubled by that saying of the Psalm: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). But I say: he hates his flesh as well. Does he not hate it, for whom he daily purchases heaps of Gehenna, and who, “through his hardness and impenitent heart,” stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath? Yet this hatred of both flesh and soul is found not so much in intention as in effect. Thus a madman also hates his own flesh when, with rational deliberation lulled to sleep, he strives to lay hands upon himself. Is any madness judged more grievous than an impenitent heart and an obstinate will to sin? For he lays wicked hands upon himself, and tears and gnaws away not his flesh but his mind. If you have seen a man scratch his hands and rub them until they bleed, you have before you an evident likeness of the sinful soul. For that pleasure gives way to pain, and torment succeeds the itching. He was not ignorant of this, but disregarded it while scratching. Thus with our own hands we tear, thus we ulcerate our unhappy souls—only with so much greater gravity as the spiritual creature is more excellent [Col. 0837C] and more difficult to heal. Nor do we do this from deliberate hostility, but through a kind of stupor of inward insensibility. For the soul poured outward does not feel inward losses, because it is not within, but perhaps in the belly or below the belly. Indeed, the minds of some are found in dishes, and those of others in money-boxes. “Where your treasure is,” he says, “there your heart is also” (Matt. 6:21). What wonder, then, if a soul does not feel its own injury when, forgetful of itself and wholly absent from itself, it has gone into a far country? But it will feel it when, returning into itself, it recognizes how cruelly, under the pretext of miserable hunting, it has disembowelled itself. For it could not feel this while, greedily pursuing the worthless prey of flies, it seemed, like a spider, to weave nets out of its own entrails.

6. This return will doubtless occur, at least after death [Col. 0838A], when all the bodily doors through which the soul had been accustomed to go forth, wandering outside and uselessly occupying itself with the passing form of this world, are shut, so that it must remain within itself, having no longer any exit from itself. But that return will be most ruinous, and a misery everlasting, when repentance may be possessed but cannot be performed. For where the body is lacking, there can be no action. And where there is no action, no satisfaction can be found. Accordingly, to have repentance is to grieve; but to perform repentance is the remedy for grief. One deprived of hands will no longer be able to lift up his heart to heaven together with his hands. Whoever, therefore, before the death of the flesh has not returned to himself must remain in himself for eternity.

But in what sort of self? Such as he has made himself in this life, such will he find himself when he departs this life—except that perhaps he will sometimes be worse; for he will never be better. For he has this very thing, the body which he now lays aside, to receive again one day, yet not for repentance but for punishment. There, indeed, the condition of sin and of flesh will seem in a certain way alike: just as guilt can always be punished and can never be expiated, so bodily torments can never end, nor can the body itself be consumed by its torments. Justly, indeed, will vengeance rage forever, because guilt can never be erased; and the substance of the flesh will not fail, lest the affliction of the flesh should thereby also be forced to end. This, my brothers: whoever fears it, avoids it; whoever neglects it, falls into it [Col. 0838C].

## Chapter V. That the worm of conscience must be felt and stifled in the present, not cherished and nourished unto immortality

7. Therefore, to return to the voice from which we began: it is surely expedient for us to return to the heart, while there is still a way there by which he may show us his salvation—the one who, with such zeal of mercy, calls transgressors back to it. Meanwhile, let it not weary us to feel the bites of the inward worm. Let no dangerous tenderness [variant: bitterness] of spirit or destructive softness persuade us to wish to ignore the present discomfort. It is best for the worm to be felt while it can also be stifled. Let it therefore bite now, so that it may die; and, dying, gradually cease to bite. Let it gnaw meanwhile at the corruption, so that by gnawing it may consume it and itself be consumed together with it, lest it begin to be nourished unto immortality. “Their worm,” he says, “shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24). Who could endure the face of those bites?

For manifold consolation now lightens the torment of a reproving conscience. God is gracious: he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, nor does he permit this worm to rage beyond measure. Especially at the beginning of conversion he anoints wounds with the oil of mercy, so that neither the extent of the sickness nor the difficulty of its cure becomes known beyond what is expedient. Rather, a certain ease seems to smile upon one; but later it vanishes, when perhaps a contest is granted to a person whose senses have now been exercised, so that he may conquer and learn that wisdom is stronger than all things. Meanwhile, one who hears [Col. 0839A] the Lord’s voice, “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. 46:8), and discovers so many obscenities in the inner chamber, strives to investigate each one and curiously explores through what entrance they flowed in. Nor is the opening difficult to see—indeed, the openings—to one who looks. Yet no small grief is added to him from this consideration, when he discovers that this death has entered through his own windows. For the licentiousness of the eyes seems to have admitted much, the itching of the ears much, and likewise the pleasure of smelling, tasting, and touching much. But the carnal person still examines spiritual vices, which we mentioned above, only with difficulty and not as they truly are. Hence it happens that he feels the more serious sins little, or not at all, and is stung less by the recollection of pride or envy than by that of disgraceful or criminal acts [Col. 0839B].

## Chapter VI. A vivid representation of the difficulty of conversion and of the struggle of one preparing to come to his senses

8. And behold, again a voice from the clouds says: “You have sinned; be still.” The meaning of this saying is as follows. A brimming bilge pollutes the whole house with an intolerable stench: it is useless for you to drain it while filth is still flowing in; while you do not cease from sinning, it is useless to repent. For who would approve the fasts of those who fast for quarrels and disputes and strike wickedly with the fist, while their own wills and pleasures are found among them? “This is not the fast that I have chosen,” says the Lord (Isa. 58:5). Close the windows, bar the entrances, carefully stop up the openings; and then at last, when no new filth enters, you will be able to clear away the old.

A person judges the command given to him easy to fulfill, as one ignorant of spiritual discipline. “Who,” he says, “will prevent me from commanding my members?” He therefore imposes fasts upon the throat, forbids excess in eating, commands the ears to be stopped lest they hear bloodshed, turns away the eyes lest they see vanity; he stretches out his hands, not toward greed, but rather toward almsgiving; perhaps he wishes to impose labour upon them, forbidding theft, as it is written: “Let him who stole steal no longer; but rather let him labour, working with his hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one in need” (Eph. 4:28) [Col. 0839C].

9. But while he proclaims laws and sets forth decrees in this manner for each of his members, they suddenly interrupt the voice of the one commanding and shout with one impulse: “Whence comes this new religion? You command us to do whatever you please. But someone will be found to oppose these new decrees, to contradict these new laws.” “Who is that?” he asks. And they reply: “Indeed, she herself, who lies paralyzed in the house and is grievously tormented. For she is the one to whose service you long ago assigned us, if you do not know it, to obey her desires.” At this voice the wretched man grew pale and, confounded, fell silent. For his spirit was distressed within him.

The members immediately go to that most unhappy mistress of theirs, in order cruelly to intercede against the Lord and complain of the harsher commands. The throat laments that a measure of moderation has been imposed upon it and the pleasure of gluttony forbidden. The eye complains that tears have been enjoined and licentiousness prohibited. As they pursue these and similar complaints, the will, aroused and fiercely exasperated, says: “Is what you tell a dream or a tale?” Then the tongue, finding the suitable time for its own complaint, says: “It is altogether as you have heard. For I too have been commanded to be silent about tales and falsehoods, and henceforth to say nothing except what is serious—indeed, wholly necessary” [Col. 0840A].

10. Then the old woman leaps up in fury and, forgetting all her sickness, advances with hair standing on end, torn garment, bared breast, scratching her sores, gnashing her teeth, parched, and polluting the very air with venomous breaths. What remains of reason could fail to be confounded at such an encounter and assault by miserable will? “Is this,” she says, “the whole fidelity of your marriage? Is this how you sympathize with one suffering grievously? Have you spared so little as to add to the pain of my wounds? Perhaps something ought to have been taken away from my immoderate dowry; but when this is removed, what remains? You bestowed this alone upon a wretched sick woman; and you have at last learned how all her services are distributed.

“Now perhaps the threefold malignity of this most grievous sickness by which I suffer has slipped your mind; but not mine. For I am pleasure-loving, inquisitive, and ambitious; and from the sole of my foot to the crown of my head there is no soundness in me from this threefold wound. Thus the throat and the indecent parts of the body have been assigned to pleasure—since it is apparently necessary to recount every detail anew. For a wandering foot and an undisciplined eye serve curiosity. But ear and tongue serve vanity: through the former the oil of the sinner fattens my head; through the latter I myself make up what others seem to have done too little in praising me. For I take great pleasure both in receiving praise from others and, when I suitably can, in passing my praises on to others, always desiring to be extolled by my own mouth and by another’s. Your own ingenuity also commonly furnishes abundant fuel to this particular disease.

“As for the hands themselves, whose movement is free in every direction, we do not assign them specifically to any one task; rather, they give quite diligent service now to vanity, now to curiosity, now to pleasure. With these things so arranged, all of them together could never satisfy me even in one respect [Col. 0840D], ‘for the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.’ Would that, while looking, my whole body might at some point become an eye, or, while dining, all my limbs be transformed into a throat! Then would it be a small consolation to me, miserable as I am, somehow to steal away so much?” She spoke; and withdrawing in indignation and fury, she said: “I hold fast, and I shall hold fast for a long time.”

11. Now the very affliction gives understanding to reason; now the difficulty of this business becomes somewhat known; now presumed ease vanishes. For reason sees the memory full of filth; it sees ever more abundant filth flowing in; it sees that the very windows open to death cannot be completely shut; and it sees that the sickly ruling will still holds sway [Col. 0841A], from whose sores all the discharge has flowed. Finally, the soul sees itself contaminated, not through another but through its own body, and from no other source than itself. For there is something in the soul which, like memory, is infected, and something which, like will itself, infects. Indeed, the whole soul is nothing other than reason, memory, and will. But now reason is found deficient and in a sense blind, because it did not previously see these things; utterly weak, because it is unable even to restore [variant: restrain] what it has recognized; memory is equally foul and fetid; and the will is sickly, flowing everywhere with horrible sores. And lest anything belonging to the human being should remain unaffected, the body itself is rebellious: each member is a separate window by which death enters into the soul, and confusion itself continually overflows [Col. 0841B].

## Chapter VII. The breath of consolation for the poor in spirit, that is, for the soul that recognizes its misery

12. Let any soul of this kind therefore hear the divine voice, and hear it with astonishment and wonder saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Who is poorer in spirit than one who finds no rest in his whole spirit, who finds nowhere to lay his head? This also is a counsel of mercy: that the one who displeases himself may please God, and that one who hates his own house—a house full indeed of filth and misery—may be invited into the house of glory, the house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens [Col. 0841C].

Nor is it surprising if he trembles at the greatness of this condescension, if he finds this report hard to believe, if he marvels with intense astonishment and says: “Then does misery make a human being blessed?” Yet whoever you are that are such, do not despair. Misery does not make one blessed, but mercy does; yet misery is mercy’s proper dwelling place. Or indeed misery itself may make one blessed, when humiliation passes into humility and necessity into virtue. “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance; and it was weakened, but you have made it perfect” (Ps. 67:10). Weakness is wholly useful when it calls for the physician’s hand; and he who fails of himself in a salutary way is made perfect by God.

But because there is no way to the kingdom of God without the first-fruits of the kingdom, and one cannot hope for the heavenly kingdom when he has not yet been granted to rule even over his own members, the voice follows, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matt. 5:4)—as though it said more plainly: “Tame the wild impulses of the will, and take care to make the cruel beast gentle. You are bound: strive to loosen what you are altogether unable to break. She is your Eve [variant added: life]. You will in no way prevail either to use force or, so far as that goes, to offend me.”

## Chapter VIII. That carnal pleasures and riches are altogether vain, deceptive, and momentary

13. Without delay, the person takes breath amid these words; and, judging this also easier, though shamefacedly, he approaches and tries to soothe the inflamed viper. He rebukes the allurements of carnal life and accuses the consolations of worldly frivolity as paltry and unworthy [Col. 0842A], as well as very brief and harmful to all their lovers. “Confess this yourself also,” he says, “to this worthless and useless servant of yours. For you cannot deny that not even in a small measure could all her services ever satisfy you. The pleasure of the throat, so highly valued today, scarcely occupies the width of two fingers; and what anxiety is required for so slight a pleasure of so small a part, and what trouble does it subsequently produce? From this the loins and shoulders are monstrously enlarged; from this swollen bellies are not so much fattened as made pregnant with ruin; and while the bones cannot bear the burden of the flesh, various diseases are generated.

“Likewise, at what cost of labours and losses—sometimes even at the peril of reputation, honour, or life itself—is the enticing abyss of lust acquired? It is gained so that for a brief moment a sulphurous, burning vapour may drive mad persons with its stings, and so that a pair of flying bees, after pouring forth ill-pleasing honey, may wound hearts struck by their excessively clinging bite. Its desire is known to be full of anxiety and madness, its act of abomination and disgrace, its outcome of repentance and shame [Col. 0842B].”

14. But empty spectacles, I ask, what do they give the body, or what do they appear to contribute to the soul? Certainly you will find nothing in a human being to which curiosity is beneficial. It is altogether frivolous, empty, and trifling consolation. I do not know what harsher curse I could utter against it than that one who, fleeing the peace [variant: leisure] of pleasant rest, delights in restless curiosity should always have something to seek. Surely it is clear from this very fact that there is no pleasure in all these things, whose passing alone gives enjoyment. Moreover, how utterly nothing “vanity of vanities” is may be judged still more plainly from the name itself. Vain, indeed, is labour undertaken [variant: spent] in the pursuit of vanity. “‘O glory, glory,’” says the wise man, “‘among thousands of mortals you are nothing but an empty swelling of ears!’” (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book III, prose 6.)

Yet how great a misery, do you suppose, is produced by this not so much happy vanity as vain happiness? From it comes blindness of heart, as it is written: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you into error” (Isa. 3:12). From it comes the stiff-necked fury of pride, the anxious labour of suspicion, the cruel torment of envy, and the more wretched suffering of burning jealousy. From it comes an insatiable love of riches, which torments the soul much more by desire than it refreshes it by use; for their acquisition is found to entail labour, their possession fear, and their loss full grief [Col. 0842D]. Finally, where there are many riches, there are also many who consume them (Eccl. 5:10); the use of the riches belongs to others, while only their name and anxiety fall to the rich. And amid all these things, to think lightly, for things so small—or rather, not even small but nothing at all—of that glory “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart,” which God has prepared for those who love him, seems to be [variant: is recognized as] not so much folly as unbelief.

15. And not without reason this world, which is “set in evil,” deceives by its vain promise souls forgetful of their own condition and nobility: souls not ashamed to be yoked to swine in service and associated with them in desire, and yet not satisfied even by so wretched a food. For whence comes such great faintheartedness and so pitiable an abasement, that an excellent creature, capable of eternal blessedness and of the glory of the great God—formed by his inspiration, marked by his likeness, redeemed by his blood, endowed with faith, adopted by the Spirit—does not blush to bear miserable servitude beneath this corruption of bodily senses? Rightly, surely, can one who deserts such a bridegroom and follows such lovers not even obtain the husks. Rightly does one hunger for husks and receive none, who preferred feeding swine to being satisfied with his father’s feast (Luke 15:16). For it is mad labour to feed a barren woman who does not bear children, while refusing to do good to a widow [Col. 0843B]; to neglect the care of the heart and provide for the flesh in its desires; to fatten and pamper a rotting corpse, which without doubt will shortly become food for worms. For who does not know that to serve mammon, cultivate avarice—which is the service of idols—or pursue vanity is plainly a mark of a degenerate soul?

16. Suppose nevertheless that the things which the world appears for the moment to distribute to its lovers are great and honourable: who does not know that they are unreliable? Their brevity is certain, while even the end of that brevity is uncertain. They often abandon a person while living; and they not infrequently follow him when dying. What in human affairs is more certain than death, and what is more uncertain than the hour of death? It does not pity poverty, does not respect riches, spares neither rank nor character nor, finally, age itself—except that for old persons it stands at the doors, but for young persons in ambush [Col. 0843C].

Unhappy, therefore, is the person who, trusting in the darkness and slipperiness of this life, expends labour on what will perish and does not notice that it is a vapour appearing briefly, and vanity of vanities. Have you finally obtained, ambitious man, the office you had desired for so long? Keep what you have. Have you, wealthy man, filled your money-boxes? Be anxious lest you lose them. Has your field yielded abundant crops? Tear down your barns so as to build larger ones; replace square ones with round ones; say to your soul: “You have many goods laid up for many years.” For there will be one who says: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:19–20) [Col. 0843D].
