17. And would that only the amassed possessions perished, and that their gatherer did not perish more grievously as well. It would surely be more tolerable to labour for what perishes than for what destroys. But now “the wages of sin is death,” and “he who sows in the flesh will from the flesh reap corruption.” For our works do not pass away as they appear to do; rather, all temporal things are sown like seeds of eternity. The fool will be astonished [variant: corrupt “will be proud”] when from this small seed he sees a copious harvest arise, good or evil according to the differing quality of the sowing. Whoever considers this judges no sin at all to be small, because he values the coming harvest rather than the seed. People therefore sow while they do not know it, and sow while they conceal the mysteries of iniquity, hide counsels of vanity, and walk about in darkness amid works of darkness [Col. 0844A].

## Chapter IX. That it is impossible for a sinner to remain hidden

18. “There are walls all around,” he says; “who sees me?” Suppose no human being sees you: still, it is not true that no one sees you. An evil angel sees you; a good angel sees you; and God, greater than both good and evil angels, sees you. The accuser sees you; a multitude of witnesses sees you; the Judge himself sees you, before whose tribunal you must stand. To will to sin beneath his eyes is as mad as it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. Do not be secure: hidden snares lie in wait, and you cannot escape them. The snares, I say, are hidden; and just as you yourself cannot discover them, so you yourself cannot avoid being discovered. “He who planted the ear surely hears; and he who formed the eye surely sees” (Ps. 93:9). A stone wall, which he himself created, does not keep the rays of that Sun from him; nor does even the wall of this body exclude the sight of truth. All things are naked before his eyes; he is more penetrating than a two-edged sword. He not only sees but distinguishes the very paths of thoughts and the inmost parts of affections.

Finally, unless he looked before himself into the whole abyss of the human heart and whatever lies hidden in it, that man who was conscious of nothing against himself would not so greatly fear the judgment of the Lord who judges him. “It is a very small thing to me,” he says, “that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified. The one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:3–4) [Col. 0844C].

19. If you boast that, behind the cover of a wall or the pretext of any disguise, you can frustrate human judgments, be certain that he who is accustomed even to accuse falsely will not pass over real crimes. If you so greatly fear the conscience of your neighbour, who perhaps nevertheless respects you, much less should you despise those to whom iniquity is more hateful and corruption far more detestable. Finally, if you do not fear God and reverence only human eyes, remember that Christ as man cannot be ignorant of human deeds. What you would not dare at all to attempt in my presence, dare still less before him; and what, I do not say would not be permitted, but would not even be safe to presume in the sight of a fellow-servant, utterly shrink from even thinking when the Lord is looking on [Col. 0844D].

Otherwise, if you fear the eye of flesh more than the sword that has flesh to devour, the fear which you fear will also come upon you, and what you dread will happen to you. “Nothing is covered that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known” (Luke 12:2). The works of darkness, brought forth from darkness into light, will be reproved. The one who knows all things will make known to all, not only the abominable secrets of obscenities, but also the unjust commercial covenants of sellers, the fraudulent whisperings [variant: sighings] of those devising deceits, and those overturning judgments, when that searcher of heart and kidneys begins to search Jerusalem with lamps.

## Chapter X. That salvation is obtained not only by turning away from evil, but also by doing good

20. What then will those who have committed crimes do—or rather, what will they suffer—when they hear, “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41), because they did not perform works of mercy? When will one be admitted to the wedding feast who neither girded his loins to abstain from evil nor held a lamp to do good? When neither the integrity of virginity nor the brightness of lamps will be able to excuse a lack of oil? Or what torments should we suppose await those who in this life commit not merely evil deeds but perhaps the worst deeds, if those who here received good things are so tortured that, with their tongues burning amid the flames, they cannot obtain the refreshment of even the smallest drop [Col. 0845B]?

Let us therefore avoid evil deeds, and not, trusting in the enclosing net, sin freely within the Church. Let us know that not all whom the net draws will be received into the fishermen’s vessels; but when they reach the shore, “they will gather the good into vessels, but throw the bad outside” (Matt. 13:48). Nor, content with girding our loins, should we fail to light our lamps also and work diligently at what is good, remembering that every tree—not merely that which produces bad fruit, but also that which fails to produce good fruit—will be cut down and thrown into the fire: namely, that eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

21. Yet let us so turn away from evil and do good that we seek peace and do not pursue glory [Col. 0845C]. For glory belongs to God, and he will not give it to another. “My glory,” he says, “I will not give to another” (Isa. 42:8). And the man after God’s heart said: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:1). Let us remember also the Scripture which says: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4, according to the Septuagint). Brothers, this division of ours is right; let no one reject it. Otherwise, if perhaps it pleases anyone less, let him know that it is not ours but the angels’. For the angels first sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Let us therefore preserve oil in our vessels, lest perhaps—God forbid—when the doors of the wedding feast have already been shut, we knock in vain and hear the bitter word, while the bridegroom answers us from within: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Yet death is set not only beside iniquity, barrenness, and vanity, but also beside the entrance of pleasure itself. Therefore courage is needed against the temptations of sin, that we may resist the roaring lion, strong in faith, and bravely repel his fiery darts with this very shield. Justice is needed, that we may do good. Prudence is needed, lest we be rejected with the foolish virgins. Finally, temperance is needed, lest by indulging pleasures we someday hear what that wretched man, after the splendour alike of feasts and clothing had ended, heard when he begged for mercy: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:25).

Truly God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men [Col. 0846A]! Yet, if he is terrible, he is also found merciful, because he does not conceal the pattern of the coming judgment. “The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18:4); the branch that does not bear fruit shall be cut off (John 15:2); the virgin who lacks oil shall be shut out from the wedding feast (Matt. 25:12); and one who receives good things in this life shall be tormented in the life to come. If perhaps these four things are found together in any one person, that is indeed utter despair.

## Chapter XI. Those seeking conversion are more fiercely tempted by their customary vices, and mourning is necessary for them

22. Reason therefore suggests these and similar things inwardly to the will, all the more abundantly as it is more perfectly instructed by the illumination of the Spirit. Happy indeed is the person whose will yields and acquiesces so to reason’s counsel that, conceiving through fear, it is thereafter cherished by heavenly promises and gives birth to the spirit of salvation. But perhaps a rebellious and obstinate will may be found—one not merely impatient, but made worse by admonitions, harder through threats, and more bitter through applied caresses. Perhaps one may be found who, unmoved by reason’s suggestions, indeed stirred by fierce rage, answers: “How long am I to endure you? Your preaching finds no place in me. I know that you are cunning; but your cunning has no place in me.” Perhaps it even summons each member and commands it more than usual to obey its customary desires and serve wickedness. From this comes what we learn by daily experience: those who resolve to convert are more fiercely tempted by the desire of the flesh [Col. 0846C] and more heavily pressed in works of mud and brick, as they endeavour to leave Egypt and escape Pharaoh’s rule.

23. But may one who is such turn away from impiety and beware that terrible depth of which it is written: “When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). For he is treated with a very strong potion and easily comes into danger unless, with much care, he strives to obey the physician’s counsels and observe his commands. The temptation is violent and near to despair unless he gathers his whole affection and turns it toward pity for his own soul, which he sees to be so wretched and pitiable, and hears the voice saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5) [Col. 0846D].

Let him mourn abundantly, because the time for mourning has come; and these considerations suffice for swallowing continual tears. Let him mourn, but not without an affection of piety and the prospect of consolation. Let him consider that he finds no rest in himself, but all things full of misery and desolation. Let him consider that there is no good in his flesh; and that in the wicked world there is nothing but vanity and affliction of spirit. Let him consider, I say, that neither within, nor below, nor around himself does he encounter consolation, so that he may finally at least learn that it must be sought above and hoped for from above. Meanwhile, let him mourn, lamenting his pain; let his eye pour forth streams of water, and let his eyelid have no rest. For the eye, formerly dim, is cleansed by tears and the sight is sharpened, so that it may gaze into the brightness of the most serene light [Col. 0847A].

## Chapter XII. How the will is gently to be led toward loving and desiring heavenly things
24. From this point, let him look up through the opening, gaze through the lattice, follow with his eyes that most sweet ray; and, as a diligent imitator of the Magi, seek light by light. For he will find the place of the wondrous tabernacle, where man eats the bread of angels; he will find the paradise of delight planted by the Lord; he will find a garden blooming and most pleasant; he will find a seat of refreshment, and will say: “Oh, if that wretched will would hear my voice, so that, entering, it might see good things and visit this place! Here indeed it will find [Col. 0847B] more ample rest, and it will trouble me the less as it is itself less troubled.” For he does not lie who said: “Take my yoke upon you, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). In faith in this promise, let him gently address her when she is embittered, and, approaching her in a spirit of gentleness with a certain feigned cheerfulness, say: “Let your indignation utterly cease. I am not one who can offend you. The body is yours, and I myself am yours also. There is nothing for you to fear, nothing for you to dread.” Nor should it surprise him if she perhaps returns an even more bitter answer and says, “Many thoughts have driven you mad.” Let him meanwhile bear this patiently and wholly conceal what is being done, until, introducing one matter after another in conversation, he may at some suitable time [Col. 0847C] add, saying: “Today I found [another reading: entered] a most beautiful garden and a most pleasant place. It would be good for us to be there; for it harms you also to lie in this bed of sickness, upon this couch of pain, to be pierced in this your bed with a heavy heart.” The Lord will be present to one who seeks him, to the soul that hopes in him; he will be present to suppliant prayers and will give efficacy to her words. The will’s desire will be aroused, so that it may gradually long not merely to see the place, but also to enter it and make its dwelling there.

## CHAPTER XIII. Converts are refreshed by the wondrous sweetness and delights of the devout and spiritual life.

25. Do not, however, suppose that this paradise of inward delight is a bodily place. One enters this [Col. 0847D] garden not with one’s feet but with one’s affections. It is not an abundance of earthly trees that is commended to you, but the pleasing and beautiful planting of spiritual virtues. It is a locked garden, where a sealed fountain is led forth into four heads, and from the one vein of wisdom a fourfold virtue proceeds. There too the most splendid lilies bloom; and when the flowers appear, the voice of the turtledove is heard as well. There the bride’s nard gives forth its most fragrant scent, and the other spices also flow forth, while the south wind blows and the north wind is driven away. There in the midst is the tree of life, that apple tree of the Song, more precious than all the trees of the forests; its shade refreshes the bride, and its fruit is sweet to her throat (Song 2:3). There the brightness of continence and the contemplation of unfeigned truth irradiate the eyes of the heart; and the most sweet voice of the inward Comforter gives joy and [Col. 0848A] gladness to the hearing also. There, into certain nostrils of hope, flows the most delightful scent of a full field which the Lord has blessed. There the incomparable delights of charity are tasted beforehand with the greatest eagerness; and, after the thorns and briars by which it was formerly pierced have been cut down, the mind, suffused with the anointing of mercy, happily rests in a good conscience.

These things are reckoned not among the rewards of eternal life, but among the wages of this temporal warfare; they belong not to the future promise, but rather to the promise of the Church which now is. For this is the hundredfold given in this world to those who despise the world (Matt. 19:29). Nor should you expect it to be commended to you by our speech. The Spirit alone reveals it: you consult the page in vain; seek experience rather. [Col. 0848B] It is wisdom whose price man does not know. It is drawn from hidden things, and this sweetness is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly. It is indeed the sweetness of the Lord: unless you have tasted, you will not see. “Taste,” he says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9 [Vulgate]). It is hidden manna; it is a new name which no one knows except the one who receives it. Learning does not teach it, but anointing; knowledge does not comprehend it, but conscience. It is holy; they are pearls; and he who began both to do and to teach will not himself do what he forbids (Matt. 7:6). For he no longer regards as dogs or swine those whom, after they have renounced their former crimes and shameful deeds, he consoles even through the Apostle, saying: “Such indeed you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (1 Cor. 6:11). Only let him beware lest [Col. 0848C] the dog return to its vomit, or [another reading: or] the washed sow to the wallowing in mire.

## CHAPTER XIV. In earthly things there is no satiety except one joined with disgust; but desires for heavenly things always increase through experience.

26. At the entrance of this divine paradise, a voice of gentle whisper is heard: a most sacred and secret counsel, hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones. The hearing of this voice is now grasped not by reason alone, but is gladly shared with the will as well. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). A most lofty counsel indeed, and an inestimable [Col. 0848D] mystery. It is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, which has come to us from heaven, from the royal seats.

For a grievous famine has arisen in the land, and we have all begun not merely to lack, but have come to utter want. At last we have been compared with senseless beasts and made like them; we hunger insatiably even for the husks of swine. He who loves money is not satisfied; he who loves luxury is not satisfied; he who seeks glory is not satisfied; in short, he who loves the world is never satisfied. I have known people filled with this world and nauseated by every remembrance of it. I have known people filled with money and filled with honours, filled with pleasures and the curiosities of this world—filled not moderately, but even to disgust. And it is easy for each of us to obtain this satiety [Col. 0849A] through God’s grace. For abundance does not produce it, but contempt. Thus, foolish children of Adam, in devouring swine’s husks you feed not your hungry souls, but the very hunger of your souls. Your want is nourished by this food alone; hunger alone is fed by unnatural food.

To state this more plainly by an example, taking one thing among the many desired by human vanity: human hearts will not be filled with gold before bodies are filled with air. Let not the miser take offence: the same judgment applies to the ambitious and the luxurious, and even to the criminal. If anyone perhaps does not believe me, let him believe experience—his own or that of many others.

27. Who among you, brothers, wishes to be satisfied and desires that his longing be fulfilled? Let him begin to hunger for righteousness, and he cannot fail to be satisfied. Let him desire those loaves [Col. 0849B] which abound in the father’s house, and he will immediately find himself disgusted by the swine’s husks. Let him strive to experience even a small taste of righteousness, so that by that very taste he may desire more and deserve more, as it is written: “He who eats me shall still hunger; and he who drinks me shall still thirst” (Sir. 24:29). For this desire, being more congenial and more natural to the spirit, takes a stronger hold on the human heart and vigorously drives out its other desires. Thus the stronger overcomes the armed strong man; thus one nail is usually driven out by another.

Therefore, blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled—not yet indeed with righteousness itself, by which man shall not be sated and live, but with all the other things previously desired insatiably. Thus the will, ceasing to claim the body for service to its former desires, [Col. 0849C] may wholly yield it to reason; or rather, may itself strive to serve righteousness unto sanctification with no less zeal than it had formerly shown in serving iniquity unto iniquity.

## CHAPTER XV. Memory must be cleansed of the defilements of sins through trust in divine mercy.

28. But now, even though the will has been changed and the body reduced to slavery—as though the fountain had already been somewhat dried up and its opening stopped—there remains a third task, and the gravest of all: namely, cleansing the memory and draining the bilge. For how will my life pass out of my memory? A cheap, thin parchment has perhaps completely absorbed the ink: by what art will it thereafter be erased? For it has not been dyed merely on the surface; it has been saturated through and through. I would strive in vain to scrape it away: the paper will be torn before the inscribed characters are erased.

Perhaps forgetfulness could erase memory itself, so that, having lost my mind, I might not remember what I have committed. But if memory remains whole and the stains themselves are erased, what razor could accomplish this? Surely only the living and efficacious word, sharper than every two-edged sword: “Your sins are forgiven you.” Let the Pharisee murmur and say: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:5, 7). For he who speaks this to me is God, “and none shall be compared with him,” who “found out all the way of instruction, and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved” (Bar. [Col. 0850A] 3:37); afterward he was seen upon earth and conversed with men.

His forgiveness blots out sin, not so that it falls from memory, 490 but so that what formerly both remained in memory and polluted it may henceforth remain in memory without discoloring it at all. For we now remember many sins which we know were committed either by ourselves or by others; but our own defile us, while those of others do us no harm. Why is this, except because in these we are uniquely ashamed and fear that these are uniquely to be imputed to us? Remove condemnation, remove fear, remove shame; and full forgiveness removes all these things. Then they will not merely do no harm, but will even work together for good, so that we may render devout thanks to him who forgave.

## CHAPTER XVI. Divine mercy is obtained first by showing mercy to oneself, then to one’s neighbour.

[Col. 0850B]

29. Now to one who entreats for it, there is fittingly answered: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Therefore have mercy on your soul, if you desire God to have mercy on you. Every night wash your bed; remember to water your couch with your tears. If you have compassion on yourself, if you labour in the groaning of repentance—this is the first degree of mercy—you will surely obtain mercy.

But if perhaps you are a great and frequent sinner, and seek great mercy and a multitude of mercies, labour also to make and multiply your own mercy great. Be reconciled [Col. 0850C] to yourself; for you had become burdensome even to yourself, because you had set yourself in opposition to God. From this point, once peace has been restored in your own house, it must first be extended toward your neighbours, so that at last he himself may kiss you with the kiss of his mouth and, as it is written, you may have peace with God, being reconciled (Rom. 5:1). Forgive those who have sinned against you, and what you yourself have sinned will be forgiven you, when with a secure conscience you pray to the Father and say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

If perhaps you have defrauded anyone, restore even the principal; give what remains to the poor, and by showing mercy you will obtain mercy. “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as the crimson worm, they shall be as white wool” (Isa. 1:18). So that you may not be ashamed over all your devices by which you have transgressed and in which you now blush: give alms, if not from earthly possessions, then from good will; and all things will be clean—not only your enlightened reason and corrected will, but memory itself will also be clean. Thus you will henceforth be called to the Lord and hear the voice saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5:8).

## CHAPTER XVII. The eyes of the heart must continually be cleansed so that God may be seen.

30. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (ibid.). A great promise, my brothers, and one to be pursued with every desire. For this vision is confirmation, as the apostle John says: [Col. 0851A] “Now we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). This vision is eternal life, as Truth himself says in the Gospel: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

Hateful is the stain that deprives us of this blessed vision, and execrable the negligence by which we meanwhile neglect the cleansing of that eye. For just as bodily sight is hindered in us either by an inward moisture or by dust cast in from outside, so spiritual vision is sometimes disturbed by the enticements of one’s own flesh, sometimes by worldly curiosity and ambition. [Col. 0851B] This is taught us no less by our own experience than by the divine page, where it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15).

Yet in both cases, sin alone is what dulls and confuses the sight; and nothing else appears to separate the eye from light, or God from man. For as long as we are in this body, we are away from the Lord. The fault is not, of course, the body which we bear, this body of death; rather, it is that the flesh is a body of sin, in which there is no good but rather the law of sin. Yet sometimes the bodily eye seems to remain dim for a while, even when the speck no longer remains but has already been removed or blown away; and this too is often experienced by the inward eye of one who walks in the spirit. For when you have drawn out the iron, the wound is not at once restored to health; rather, then it is first necessary to apply poultices and attend to treatment. Therefore let no one, having cast out the bilge, suppose himself immediately cleansed; rather, let him know that he still needs many purifications. He must not only be washed with water, but also cleansed and tested by fire, so that he may say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65:12 [Vulgate]). “Blessed, therefore, are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”: now indeed through a mirror in an enigma, but in the future face to face, when the cleansing of our face has been completed, so that he may present it to himself glorious, without spot or wrinkle.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Peacemakers are deservedly blessed with the name of sons of God.

[Col. 0851D]

31. Here there appropriately follows at once: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). For there is a peaceable person who, returning good for good, wishes, so far as lies in him, to harm no one. There is another, patient person, who, not returning evil for evil, is even able to endure one who harms him. And there is also a peacemaker who, returning good for evil, is ready even to benefit one who harms him.

The first is indeed a little child and is easily scandalized; nor can one of this sort easily attain salvation in this wicked age, full of scandals. The second, as it is written, possesses his soul in patience (Luke 21:19). But the third not only possesses [Col. 0852A] his own soul, but gains the souls of many. The first has peace, insofar as lies in him; the second holds peace; the third makes peace. He is therefore deservedly blessed with the name of son, because he has fulfilled a son’s work: after his own reconciliation, for which he is not ungrateful, he reconciles others also to his Father. For “he who has ministered well acquires a good degree for himself” (1 Tim. 3:13); and in the Father’s house no degree should be thought better than that of son. For if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Rom. 8:17), so that, as he himself says, where he is, there his servant also may be (John 12:26).

We have wearied you by the length of our discourse and detained you longer than was fitting. From this point, the hour itself seems to command an end to our talkativeness, which modesty does not command. Yet remember the Apostle, whom you read once prolonged the word of preaching until midnight. Would that you might still, to use his own words, bear with a little of my folly. For “I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy” (2 Cor. 11:1–2).

## CHAPTER XIX. He sharply rebukes ambitious men who rashly and unworthily usurp the sacred offices of the Church.

32. Little children, who will show you how to flee from the wrath to come? For no one deserves wrath more than an enemy who pretends to be a friend. Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? You, a man of one mind with me, who together with me took sweet food, who dipped your hand with me in the dish! You have no share in that prayer by which he prays to the Father and says: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

Woe to you who take away the key not only of knowledge but also of authority! You yourselves do not enter, and in many ways hinder those whom you ought to have brought in. For you take up the keys without receiving them. Of such the Lord complains through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not through me; they have become princes, and I did not call them” (Hos. 8:4). Whence comes such burning desire for pre-eminence, such shamelessness of ambition, such madness of human presumption? Would any of you dare, without the command—or even against the prohibition—of some earthly prince, to seize his offices, snatch away his benefices, or administer his affairs? Nor should you suppose that God approves what, in his great house, he endures from vessels of wrath fitted for destruction. Many indeed come, but consider who is [Col. 0852D] called.

Attend to the very order of the Lord’s saying. “Blessed,” he says, “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”; and then, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:8–9). The heavenly Father calls those pure in heart who do not seek what is their own, but what is Jesus Christ’s; not what is useful to themselves, but what is useful to many. “Peter,” he says, “do you love me?” “Lord, you know that I love you.” “Feed,” he says, “my sheep” (John 21:17). For when would he entrust sheep so loved to one who did not love them? Surely this is required among stewards: that one be found faithful.

Woe to faithless ministers, who, not yet reconciled, undertake the business of reconciling others, as though they were persons who had practised righteousness. Woe to children of wrath who profess themselves ministers of grace. Woe [Col. 0853A] to children of wrath who do not fear to usurp for themselves the ranks and titles of peacemakers. Woe to children of wrath who falsely claim to be faithful mediators of peace, so that they may devour the sins of the people. Woe to those who, walking in the flesh, cannot please God and yet presume to wish to appease him.

33. Brothers, we who grieve for the Church’s present condition are not surprised; we are not surprised that a basilisk rises from the serpent’s root. We are not surprised if one who transgresses the path ordained by the Lord harvests the Lord’s vineyard. For a man shamelessly occupies the rank of peacemaker and the office of son of God, though he has not yet even heard the first voice of the Lord calling his heart back; or, if he has perhaps begun at some time to hear it, recoiling, he flees to the leaves in order to hide himself among them.

Therefore he has not yet ceased to sin but still draws out a long rope; [Col. 0853B] he has not yet become a man seeing his own poverty, but says, “I am rich and lack nothing,” though he is poor, naked, wretched, and pitiable. He possesses nothing of the spirit of gentleness by which he might instruct those overtaken in a fault, considering himself lest he too be tempted. Knowing nothing of tears of compunction, he rather rejoices when he has done evil and exults in the worst things. He is surely one of those to whom the Lord says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25). He desires money, not righteousness; his eyes behold everything lofty. He hungers insatiably for dignities and thirsts for human glory. The bowels of mercy are far from him; rather, he rejoices to rage and display himself as a tyrant; he considers gain to be godliness.

What should I say of purity of heart? Would that he had not given it over to oblivion as one dead in heart! Would that he were not “a deceived dove without a heart”! Would that at least what is outward were clean, and that the garment of the body were not found stained, so that he might obey even in this respect the saying: “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11).

## CHAPTER XX. He rebukes incontinent men who do not fear shamelessly to profane the sacred Orders.

34. We do not accuse the whole body, but neither can we excuse the whole body. The Lord has reserved many thousands for himself. Otherwise, unless their righteousness excused us and the Lord Sabaoth had left us that holy seed, we should long ago have been overthrown like Sodom and likewise perished like Gomorrah. [Col. 0853D] For the Church seems to have been enlarged; the most sacred Order of the clergy itself; the number of brethren has been multiplied beyond number [Note: [Col. 0853D] The reading of this passage varies in printed editions and manuscripts. The Speyer edition of 1501 has: “the most sacred order has been multiplied beyond number.” The edition of 1520 has our reading, in which “brethren” perhaps means the cardinals, as in Epistle 48.]. Yet though you have multiplied the nation, O Lord, you have not magnified its joy, since there appears to have been no less decline in merit than increase in number. 493

Men run everywhere to sacred Orders, and human beings take hold without reverence or reflection of ministries venerable even to angelic spirits. For those in whom avarice reigns, ambition commands, [Col. 0854A] pride rules, and iniquity and luxury also hold sway, do not fear to seize the badge of the heavenly kingdom or wear the crown of that dominion. In them too perhaps the foulest abomination may appear within the walls, if, following Ezekiel’s prophecy, we dig through the wall (Ezek. 8:8), in order to see horror in the house of God. For after fornications, adulteries, and incests, even disgraceful passions and shameful deeds are not lacking among some. Would that things so utterly unfitting did not occur—things such that [another reading: would that] neither the Apostle needed to write of them (Rom. 1 and Eph. 5), nor we to speak of them! Would that one were not believed when speaking of them—that such an abominable desire had ever possessed a human mind!

35. Were not those cities, mothers of this filth, long ago condemned beforehand by divine judgment and destroyed by fire [Col. 0854B] (Gen. 19)? Did not the flame of Gehenna, tolerating no delay, anticipate the removal of that execrable people because their own peculiar sins were manifestly going before them to judgment? Did not fire, sulphur, and the blast of storms consume the very earth itself, made complicit in such great shame? Was not the entire soil reduced to a dreadful lake? The five heads of the hydra were cut off, but alas, innumerable heads have arisen. Who rebuilt the cities of disgrace? Who enlarged the walls of shame? Who extended the poisonous shoots?

Woe, woe! The enemy of humankind scattered far and wide the unhappy remains of that sulphurous fire; he sprinkled the body of the Church with that execrable ash, and splashed even some of her ministers with a most foul and stinking discharge. Alas! Chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, people of possession: who, amid those beginnings of yours so divine, and at the birth of the Christian religion abounding in spiritual gifts, could have believed that such things could ever be found in you?

36. With this stain they enter the tabernacle of the living God; with this stain they inhabit the temple, polluting the Lord’s sanctuary. They will receive a manifold judgment, because they bear consciences burdened with such grievous matters and nevertheless thrust themselves into God’s sanctuary. Such persons not only do not appease God but provoke him all the more, since they seem to say in their hearts: “He will not require it.” They indeed provoke him and make him hostile to themselves—I fear, in the very matters in which they ought [Col. 0854D] to have rendered him propitious.

Would that those who are about to begin building a tower would sit down and calculate whether they have the means to finish it. Would that those unable to live continently would fear rashly to profess perfection or to enroll themselves in celibacy. For the tower is costly and the saying great, which not everyone can receive. It would undoubtedly be better to marry than to burn, and to be saved in the humble rank of the faithful people than both to live more wickedly in the eminence of the clergy and to be judged more strictly.

For many—not all indeed, but certainly many, and they cannot remain concealed because of their multitude, nor do they seek concealment because of their shamelessness—appear to have made the liberty in which they were called an occasion for the flesh: abstaining from the remedy of marriage and thereafter pouring themselves out into every shameful deed.

## CHAPTER XXI. He earnestly exhorts to repentance.

37. Spare yourselves, I beseech you, brothers; spare the blood that was shed for you. Beware the dreadful danger; turn aside from the fire that has been prepared. Let there at last be a profession of perfection that is not a mockery; let power also be shown in the appearance of godliness. Let not the form of celibate life be empty, nor truth void. How can chastity fail to be endangered amid pleasures, humility amid riches, godliness amid business, truth 494 amid much speaking, charity in this wicked age? Flee [Col. 0855B] from the midst of Babylon; flee, and save your souls. Fly together to the cities of refuge, where you may both do penance for past sins, obtain grace in the present, and confidently await future glory.

Let not consciousness of sins delay you, for where they have abounded, grace has been accustomed to abound more greatly. Let not even the austerity of repentance frighten you. For the sufferings of this present time are not comparable to the past guilt which is forgiven, nor to the present grace of consolation which is infused, nor to the future glory promised to us. In short, no bitterness is so great that the prophet’s meal cannot sweeten it (4 Kings 4:41), or wisdom, the tree of life, make it savoury (Exod. 15:25).

38. If you do not believe words, believe works; accept the examples [Col. 0855C] of very many. Sinners run to repentance from every side, and persons softened alike by nature and habit count external harshness as nothing, in order that their embittered consciences may be soothed. Nothing is impossible to believers; nothing difficult to those who love; nothing harsh is found by the gentle, nothing arduous by the humble—those to whom grace brings aid and the devotion of obedience makes command gentle.

How long will you walk in things great and wonderful above you? It is indeed something great and wonderful to be a minister of Christ and steward of God’s mysteries. The order of peacemakers is far above you, unless perhaps, with the steps set before you omitted, you prefer to leap rather than climb. Yet would that whoever enters in this way, if it were possible, might minister as faithfully as he thrust himself in confidently. But it is difficult, perhaps impossible, for the sweet fruit of charity to proceed from the bitter root of ambition.

I say—if you wish to hear—or rather not I, but the Lord: “When you are invited to a wedding, recline in the lowest place; for everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:10–11).

## CHAPTER XXII. It belongs to good shepherds to teach, and not to flee persecutions for righteousness’ sake.

39. “Blessed,” he says, “are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). Consider carefully that it is not *pacidici* (“peace-sayers”) but *pacifici* (“peace-makers”) who are commended. For there are those who speak but do not act. Certainly, just as hearers of the law are not righteous but doers, so it is not proclaimers [Col. 0856A] of peace who are blessed but makers of it.

Yet would that any among our present-day Pharisees—or perhaps some such exist—even if they did not act, would at least say what they ought. Would that those unwilling to set forth the Gospel without payment would at least set it forth for payment; would that they would at least preach the Gospel in order to eat. “The hired hand,” he says, “sees the wolf coming and flees” (John 10:12). Would that all who are not shepherds today would be willing to show themselves hired hands to the flock, not wolves; would that they did not themselves injure it; would that they did not flee when no one persecutes; would that they did not expose the flock until the wolf was seen coming.

They should indeed be tolerated, if they could be found—especially in a time of peace—receiving their wage and at least labouring to guard the flock for the sake of their wage, provided that they did not themselves disturb the flock and gratuitously turn it away from the pastures of righteousness and truth. For persecution unquestionably separates and distinguishes hired hands from shepherds. For when will one who pursues temporal gain not fear transitory losses? When will one who seeks earthly wages more than righteousness endure earthly persecution for righteousness’ sake? “Blessed,” he says, “are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This blessedness belongs to shepherds, not to hired hands—much less to robbers or wolves. So far are they from enduring persecution for righteousness’ sake that they prefer to endure persecution rather than righteousness. Indeed, righteousness is opposed to their deeds and is burdensome even for them to hear.

[Col. 0856C] 495

40. But for greed or ambition you may see them ready to undergo every danger, stir up scandals, endure hatreds, conceal reproaches, and disregard curses; so that the boldness of such people is no less ruinous than the cowardice of hired hands. Therefore their Shepherd, the good Shepherd who did not spare to lay down his life for his sheep, says to true shepherds: “Blessed shall you be when men hate you, and when they separate you, and cast out your name as evil for the sake of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day and exult, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5:10–12).

For those who store up treasure for themselves in heaven have nothing to fear from thieves. Nor have they reason to complain of manifold tribulation when they consider the multiplication of their reward. Rather, as is fitting, let them rejoice all the more because not so much the persecution as the reward is increased; and let them exult more abundantly the more they suffer for Christ, so that a more abundant reward may accordingly await them with him. Why are you fearful, you of little faith? The saying is faithful and founded on irrefutable truth: no adversity will harm where no iniquity rules (*in the prayer, or collect, of the Church*). Yet it is too little merely not to harm: it will even benefit, and benefit more abundantly, provided that righteousness is in the intention and Christ in the cause, with whom the patience of the poor shall not perish forever. To him be glory now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0857]

# THE BOOK OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT, ON PRECEPT AND DISPENSATION

## 946. PREFATORY NOTICE TO OPUSCULE IV

1. Among those who follow the observances of monastic life, it commonly happens that the more religious a person is, the less he considers the binding force of his Rule than its meaning; nor does he seek so much the opinions of casuists as the intention of his legislator. For, being wholeheartedly devoted and subject to the Rule prescribed for him, he desires nothing more than to follow it as his guide in all things, even if there were no necessity of obedience.

For religious persons disposed in this way, no law has been laid down; nor is the reading of the following book as necessary for them as for others, who are more affected and troubled by questions about the obligation of the Rule than by its true and genuine meaning and practice. Nor do the latter consult teachers with any other purpose than that they may lessen the burden of the Rule and, so far as may be done without fault, withdraw with impunity from its exact—or, as they think, scrupulous—observance. Such persons should fear nothing more than falling among teachers who accommodate an unsound will; following their advice, they may adopt a laxer path and thence gradually fall into neglect of their Rule, then contempt for it, and finally hatred of their own state—which is the condition of certain damnation.

2. Yet, in my judgment, among all whom they can consult, they can consult no one who will instruct them more beneficially and safely than Bernard. For he possessed the qualities that make a teacher most upright: piety far from ordinary, doctrine infused from heaven, and distinguished experience in monastic affairs. Hence his judgment in these matters cannot possibly be suspect, but is wholly devout, sure, and to be embraced by all followers of the same institute. Indeed, if we were offered the choice that someone descended from heaven should confirm it, we ought to wish to listen to no author rather than this one.

But now we owe this gratitude to the monks of Saint Peter at Chartres, who obtained the judgment and teaching of the most holy Father on the matter proposed. It is worth investigating on what occasion and at what time this happened.

3. While Udo was abbot of this monastery, its monks wrote to consult Bernard as to what was the obligation of the Rule of Saint Benedict and of its enactments. They pressed the hesitant Bernard with repeated letters (for Bernard mentions two, below, nos. 57 and 60), and, it seems, without consulting their abbot. This was why the holy man, who at length yielded to their request, addressed his book not to Geoffrey—whom the common indices wrongly insert here—but to Roger, abbot from 1131 to 1158, and to the monks of Coulombs, of the same diocese and observance: so that his response should not reach the hands of the monks of Chartres without their abbot’s knowledge, as the Rule forbids. Bernard had intended to answer two letters with two letters; but as the subject grew, a letter became a book. “Therefore,” he says in no. 60, “call it a Book, if you please; call it a Letter, if you please.” And in the prefatory letter to the monks of Coulombs: “Let it be regarded as a Book, if you judge so, not as a Letter. And because, among the many questions which I resolve there, this in particular is treated more subtly and usefully—what commands may be dispensed with, by whom, and to what extent—let it bear the title *On Command and Dispensation*, unless perhaps some other title seems more suitable to you.” From these words—indeed, from the whole book—we understand that it is especially necessary for those set over monasteries, not only that they may instruct their subjects, but also that they themselves may know what authority of dispensation they possess.

4. What occasion impelled the monks of Chartres to consult Bernard is unknown to us. For throughout Abbot Udo’s entire administration, which lasted from 1128 to about 1150, we find no disturbances among them. Indeed, from his acts it may be inferred that Abbot Udo and his monks were in harmony. His election—to note this in passing—was confirmed by solemn decree in 1128 not only by that great Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, but also by Matthew, cardinal of Albano and legate. Geoffrey himself, bishop surnamed de Leugis, determined the dues owed to the monastery of Saint Peter, to the abbey of Saint John in the Valley, and to the lepers, from the church of Saint Martin in the Valley outside the city; Innocent II and Count Theobald approving, and in the presence of Udo, abbot of Saint Peter; likewise Andrew of Baldament, “of whom more than once in Bernard’s letters”; Hugh, abbot of Saint John in the Valley; Lord Bernard of Clairvaux; Walter, prior of Saint Martin in the Valley; Goslen de Leugis, brother of Bishop Geoffrey; and Goslen de Leugis, his nephew. “In the year 1141, indiction IX, epact XX, concurrent III, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February [18 January].” There was also another Hugh de Leugis, provost of the church of Chartres.

Moreover, when Abbot Udo of Saint Peter observed that the books of the armarium, or library, had been almost destroyed by age and that many had been gnawed by moths, he judged it “dishonourable and [497] unseemly” that “a monastery of great nobility should have a library of such poverty.” With the chapter’s consent, he undertook to renew it, assigning revenues from each of the monastery’s obediences so that the librarian—for that was what they called the keeper of the library—might have each year the means to restore old books or add new ones to the old. This was done and confirmed in 1145, by which time Bernard had already composed the following book.

5. For Peter the Venerable, lately returned from Spain, requested it from Bernard in the twenty-second letter of his fourth book, corresponding to Bernard’s Letter 227, written about the year 1143, as has been demonstrated in its proper place. I here transcribe Peter’s words from the end of that letter:

> “Please send, by the bearer of this letter or by another, that letter of yours, sent, as I think, to certain monks of Chartres, replying about the precepts of the Rule and the various practices of the monastic Order. I once read it at Cluny, but afterwards was never able to obtain it for rereading.”

In this work Geoffrey, in Book III, chapter 8, of the *Life of Bernard*, deservedly praises the holy Doctor’s “vigilant” and “circumspect discernment.” Anyone who reads this book with an impartial mind and compares it with the teaching of Saint Thomas Aquinas will readily be persuaded of this.

6. Bernard’s teaching is not, as it may seem to some, excessively severe, but sincere and most exact; this could readily be shown from other sources, if the authority of its author did not support it more solidly. The most devout Father sets forth four principal points concerning the bodily observances, as he calls them, of Saint Benedict’s Rule.

First: bodily observances—not indeed the grave ones, such as abstinence from meat and nocturnal silence, so strictly prescribed by the most holy lawgiver, but, for example, “imposed silence”—when accompanied by a superior’s command, if not observed, “are reckoned as sin, though not as a crime, provided that the transgression occurs through inadvertence or forgetfulness, not through contempt” (no. 17). Thus, “even these cannot be neglected without fault, nor despised without crime”; and they “make one liable to sin, though not grave sin, if contempt is absent” (ibid.). Finally, “they are scarcely reckoned as sin” (no. 18), especially when they are healed “by the remedy of penance.” Thus the monk keeps himself within the limits of the Rule, which is divided into “Commands and Remedies” (no. 32).

Second: such transgressions become mortal sins through contempt. For the arrogance of one who despises, and the obstinacy of one who refuses repentance, even in the smallest commands, makes the fault far from small, and turns “the rather light blemish of a simple transgression into the grave crime of rebellion” (no. 26).

Third: contempt differs from neglect in that “neglect is a certain languor of sloth, whereas contempt is a swelling of pride” (no. 18), “a proud resistance of the will” unwilling to submit to command (no. 26). Finally, “if we can and will not, we are proud” (no. 31), and therefore guilty of contempt in the matter. “Therefore,” he says in no. 26, “not every passing-over of a command makes disobedience criminal, but resistance, but unwillingness to obey,” especially where both the command and the penal remedy are rejected.

498

7. This is altogether the teaching of Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 186, article 9, both in the body of the article and in the reply to the first objection. It has three parts: the first concerns the observances of Saint Benedict’s Rule; the second, observances whose transgression by agreement obliges to venial sin; the third, the statutes of the Order of Preachers, which by a certain special constitution oblige only to a penalty.

The first part reads:

> “Therefore, to the first objection it must be said that one who professes a Rule does not vow to observe everything contained in the Rule; rather, he vows the regular life, which also consists in the three principal vows mentioned above. Hence in some religious orders some persons make their profession more cautiously: they profess not the Rule itself, but to live according to the Rule—that is, to strive to form their conduct according to the Rule, as according to a certain model. And this is destroyed by contempt.”

This is also the proper character of Saint Benedict’s Rule, as Bernard likewise testifies in no. 10.

The second character is expressed thus:

> “But in some religious orders they profess obedience according to the Rule with still greater caution, so that nothing is contrary to the profession unless it is contrary to a precept of the Rule”—

that is, a precept properly so called, which imposes an obligation:

> “But transgression or omission of other matters obliges only to venial sin; because, as has been said, such dispositions are ordered to the principal vows, and venial sin is a disposition toward mortal sin.”

Thus, in Saint Thomas’s judgment, transgressions of lesser observances dispose one toward transgressions of the principal vows and are consequently venial faults.

8. But let us even grant that Saint Benedict’s Rule, in lesser observances, obliges only to a penalty. Let us see how Saint Thomas explains his judgment on this point:

> “Yet in one religious order, namely that of the Friars Preachers, such transgression or omission does not by its nature oblige to fault, either mortal or venial, but only to the bearing of the assigned penalty; because they are bound in this manner to observe such things. Nevertheless, they can sin venially or mortally through negligence, lust, or contempt.”

Therefore, even according to Saint Thomas, in statutes which oblige only to a penalty, one may incur venial fault “through negligence or lust,” and indeed mortal sin “through contempt.” In a word, the character of such offences depends upon the disposition of the mind, whose negligence or corrupt inclination can be excused by no constitution—especially when it is directed not against one particular observance but against the whole body of regular observance.

9. To elucidate this teaching, the reply to the third objection is necessary. There he explains contempt thus: “A person commits or transgresses through contempt when his will refuses to submit to the ordinance of law or rule”—which is precisely Bernard’s teaching—and from this proceeds to act contrary to law or rule. But when, conversely, he is induced by some particular cause, such as desire or anger, to do something contrary to the enactments of law or rule, he does not sin through contempt, but from some other cause, even if he frequently repeats a similar sin from the same or another cause. So Augustine also says in *On Nature and Grace* that not all sins are committed through the contempt of pride. Yet frequent sin disposes one toward contempt.

499

10. Therefore, according to the mind of blessed Thomas, a habit or custom of such faults progresses into contempt. Bernard seems entirely to agree with him, though he says in no. 26 that such lapses are “turned by contempt into use and custom”—as though contempt were a step toward custom, not custom toward contempt. “And then,” he says, “the kind of sin”—that is, whether it is lighter or graver—“is not weighed, but the intention of the sinner.” He explains the same judgment more fully in chapters 20 and 21 of his book *On Humility*.

Yet the two may properly be reconciled if we say that Bernard is to be understood as speaking of a hardened custom, from which a person is unwilling to withdraw, neither by returning himself to the command nor by consenting to undergo the penalty for his fault; and this state can be reached only through contempt. Thomas, however, is to be understood as speaking of a habit arising from weakness and the movement of passion, which someone would willingly cast off from his heart but cannot overcome because of infirmity. Nevertheless, this habit gradually draws him toward contempt, unless he finally resists it courageously.

But I have gone on too long—yet, I think, neither idly nor inappropriately. I conclude with the saying of John of Salisbury in Letter 282: “Small things, when observed, obtain life and often merit the glory of martyrdom; but when neglected, through the crime of disobedience and contempt they bring eternal death.” Moreover, the following little work was first printed at Rouen before the year 1500, without a date, together with the books *On Consideration* and the *Apology to William*, as we have noted elsewhere.

500

## LETTER TO THE ABBOT OF COULOMBS, CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

[Col. 0859D]

To the Lord Abbot of Coulombs, Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux: abiding welfare in the Lord.

I have taken care first to send to you, as I promised, my reply to the letters of certain monks of Chartres [Col. 0860D]; in this I have also fulfilled what you commanded. For when I had resolved to write briefly and had begun by wishing to return merely a letter for letters, at your encouragement I have extended my pen, as you see, to the length of a book [Col. 0861A], so that more people may be edified in more respects.

When you have read this work, let it then be delivered, not to those for whom it was made, but first to their abbot; and only afterwards may it reach them, if the abbot commands. For they are monks, and the law of their Rule forbids them, without their abbot’s permission, both to give and to receive letters that have been sent (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 54). This too was the principal reason why, as you know, although often entreated by them, I delayed long in answering: because, as it appeared to me, they had presumed to write and send those letters without their abbot’s knowledge. Nor was I wrong in suspecting this, as I afterwards clearly discovered.

I had given the work I began—which will indeed be apparent to its readers—the name of a Letter. But because, contrary to your command, I did not keep the measure suited to that name, as I had promised, let it be judged a Book, if you think fit, not a Letter. And because, among the many questions which I solve there, this in particular is treated more subtly and usefully—what commands may lawfully be dispensed with, by whom, and to what extent—let it be given the title *On Command and Dispensation*, unless perhaps another title seems more fitting to you.

## PREFACE TO THE MONKS OF CHARTRES TO THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

With what disposition of mind shall I now be silent? Yet with what face shall I speak? By repeated letters and messengers you compel me either to betray my own lack of learning or to refuse the office of charity. But I would rather be found without that which puffs up than without that which builds up. Conquered at length by your prayers [Col. 0861C], I set my tender nails to hard knots—knots which, I fear, will do nothing but wear them down.

But this excuse is vain. For, as you write and prescribe, both my writings while absent and my words when present convict me when I make excuses. For what room is now left to me for pleading impossibility, especially before you, who believe that from my mouth and heart you hold sufficiently certain knowledge of what I can do in such matters? Trusting therefore in your faith, not in my own ability, I enter the abyss of questions, not knowing—God knows—how I shall emerge. Charity will be at hand; may truth be so as well. If it is not, let deficiency of ability rather excuse the result; you will certainly not blame my will.

I shall attempt, if I can, to compress these same small questions into the brevity proper to a letter, though not into a short letter. For it is not surprising [Col. 0861D] if I prove longer in expounding them, since you, merely in proposing them, composed two letters, both of them quite long.

## CHAPTER I. Whether the enactments of the monastic Rule are commands, or merely counsels

I. The first question, then, concerns our Rule, from which, unless I am mistaken, all the others—or nearly all—arise. You ask in what manner and to what extent that regular institution is to be assessed for those who profess it: whether everything it contains is to be considered commands, and consequently destructive to one who transgresses; or merely counsels or admonitions, and therefore whether their profession is of no weight, or not of great weight, and violation of them a fault of no kind or no grave kind; or whether some things are to be assigned to commands and others regarded as counsels, so that it is lawful in part, and wholly unlawful in part, to pass them over.

And if this last is granted, you ask me at last to distinguish definite and proper limits for each part, lest someone perhaps be given occasion to wander too freely among diverse opinions of his own understanding; and so it may happen that he strains out a gnat and swallows a camel, if he does not know how much care or effort he owes to each observance. This, as I recall, is the whole meaning, though not the wording, of that division of yours.

What you add, and continue to inquire about concerning obedience—by what degrees it is distinguished and by what limits it is bounded—I judge to belong to the same division, since obedience is held to be principal among regular decrees. And I think that when sufficient answer has been given regarding the former, nothing concerning the latter will remain doubtful.

2. Therefore, in my judgment, Saint Benedict’s Rule is offered to every person, but imposed on none. It benefits if it is devoutly received and kept; yet it does no harm if it is not received. What rests in the will of the recipient, not in the power of the one offering it, I rightly call voluntary, not necessary. Yet this very thing which I call voluntary, if someone of his own will has once accepted it and promised thereafter to keep it, he certainly converts it for himself into a necessity. He is no longer free to abandon what he was nevertheless free not to accept in the first place. [Col. 0862C] Therefore what he received voluntarily, he will keep necessarily [variant addition: “now”], because it is altogether necessary for him to render the vows which his lips have uttered, and to be now either condemned or justified by his mouth.

But, as one of the saints says, happy is the necessity that compels toward what is better (Saint Augustine, Letter 127). Accordingly, all Saint Benedict’s enactments—except, certainly, some concerning spiritual matters, such as charity, humility, and gentleness, which it is clear were instituted not so much by him as by God, and which therefore must not at all be changed—whereas all the rest [Note: [Col. 0861D] He calls them “bodily observances” in no. 3 and following.] are to be regarded for those who have not professed them as mere admonitions or counsels, and do not burden them if unobserved. Yet for those who have professed them, they become commands; for transgressors, crimes—or, to use your own language in reply to you, for the former voluntary or made by agreement, and for the latter necessary and, as it were, natural. I call them necessary in such a way, however, that this does not at all prejudice necessary and reasonable dispensations.

## CHAPTER II. When, and by whom, dispensations are to be made in the constitutions of the Fathers

3. But dispensation in such matters has not been entrusted to everyone, but only to those who can say with the apostles: “Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Cor. IV.7). The faithful and prudent servant, whom the Lord has set over his household, knows that he may exercise dispensation only where he can have a good recompense. For this is required among stewards: that a person be found faithful. And perhaps the same faithfulness is no less required of subjects in obeying as of superiors in dispensing.

From what has been said, it is clear that your division is complete and sufficient, provided that persons and times are distinguished: for subjects, every regular institution, insofar as it concerns bodily observances, is voluntary before profession and necessary after profession; but for superiors it is partly voluntary, as things devised by man, and partly necessary, as things instituted by God.

4. For this reason, perhaps the same division will appear especially fitting and clearer if the member called “necessary” is subdivided again into these three: Stable, Inviolable, Immutable. I call Stable that which is necessary in such a way that it is not lawful for every person to alter it, but only for stewards of the mysteries of God—that is, superiors—such as, for example, the Rules of Saints Basil, Augustine, and Benedict, the authentic canons, and any other ecclesiastical institutions of worthy authority. Since these were handed down by saints, they remain established with stability, and no subject is at all permitted in any manner to vary or change them.

Nevertheless, because they are from human beings, they may also lawfully and harmlessly be dispensed with through human beings—those who succeed to their place and office through canonical election—for reasons arising from persons, places, and times. Let the reader here attend carefully that I do not say that even these persons may lightly change such things at will, but that they must faithfully dispense with them according to reason. They can admit this kind of change by such persons because they are not naturally or intrinsically good.

5. They were devised and instituted, not because it was unlawful to live otherwise, but because this way was more expedient; and plainly for no other purpose than the gain or safeguarding of charity. Therefore, so long as they serve charity, they remain fixed immovably and cannot be changed without fault, not even by superiors. But if, conversely, they should sometimes appear contrary to charity, then to those alone to whom it has been granted to perceive this and entrusted to provide for it, is it not plainly most just that things devised for charity should likewise, for charity’s sake, where expedient, be omitted, interrupted, or perhaps changed into something more advantageous? Conversely, it would beyond doubt be unjust if enactments established for charity alone were kept against charity.

Therefore, things derived from the Stable Necessary retain fixed, firm, and immovable force even for superiors, but only insofar as they serve charity. Do I alone hold this view, or say it first? Did Pope Gelasius not hold precisely this view? For he says: “Where there is no necessity, the decrees of the holy Fathers are to remain unaltered.” Pope Leo likewise says: “Where there is no necessity, the enactments of the holy Fathers are in no way to be violated”; and he adds: “Therefore, where necessity exists, let the person who has authority dispense with them for the Church’s benefit. For a change of law is made from necessity.”

## CHAPTER III. Dispensation in divine law is reserved to God alone; but what belongs to eternal law is altogether immutable even for God

6. Next, by the Necessary which I call Inviolable, I mean that which was not handed down by man but promulgated by God, and which cannot at all be changed except by God who gave it; for example: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. XX.13–15), and the other ordinances of that table of the law.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] That is, if there are other matters whose inward act can be separated from a disordered disposition of mind, as in theft and homicide, where the deed itself admits divine dispensation, though the corrupt inclination of mind does not. Otherwise Bernard would disagree with himself, since in the following number he counts as immutable the entire teaching delivered by the Lord in the Sermon on the Mount; in that sermon, corrupt desire for any woman is forbidden. False testimony belongs to the same category.]

Although these admit no human dispensation whatever, and it neither has been nor will be lawful for any human being in any way to release anyone from any of them, nevertheless the Lord himself released from them whatever he willed, when he willed: whether when he commanded the Hebrews to despoil the Egyptians (Exod. III.22), or when he commanded the prophet to join himself to a prostituted woman (Hos. I.2). The former, certainly, would be regarded as nothing other than the grave crime of theft, and the latter as nothing other than the shamefulness of disgrace, if the authority of the one commanding had not excused both acts.

Certainly, where something similar is ever read to have been undertaken by holy persons, while Scripture does not indicate that God commanded it, we must either admit that they sinned as human beings, or else that, as prophets, they received God’s intimate counsel. I give one example that occurs to me: Samson, who brought down the building upon himself together with his enemies and killed them (Judg. XVI.30). If that act is defended as not having been a sin, it must beyond doubt be believed that he had a private divine counsel, even though we do not have this from Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] What the holy Doctor says—that Scripture does not state that Samson’s deed was done by divine counsel—is true, inasmuch as it is nowhere expressly stated, although it is not obscurely inferred from Hebrews, chapter 11, verse 32. Estius discusses the matter thus in his commentary: “I come to Samson. Augustine answers for him in *The City of God*, Book I, chapters 21 and 26, saying that when Samson brought the house down upon himself with his enemies, he did so at the hidden prompting of the Spirit who worked miracles through him. Nor may we believe otherwise, for his lost strength was divinely restored to him in order that he might perform this deed. For he says: ‘Lord God, remember me and restore to me my former strength, that I may avenge myself upon my enemies.’ Most others rightly follow this answer. Nor is it an objection that he says, ‘that I may avenge myself upon my enemies,’ as though he desired to avenge a private injury. For Samson’s injury was a public injury, since he was judge of the people and fought for their safety. His mockery too was mockery of the God of Israel, in insult of whom the Philistines, because Samson had been captured, gave solemn thanks to their gods in the temple.” [Col. 0865D]

“Yet, even if Samson’s deed be granted to have been done without divine counsel, Francis of Vitoria nevertheless contends, at the end of his *Relection on Homicide*, that it was not therefore a sin, as Saint Bernard here thinks. ‘For,’ he says, ‘Samson did not kill himself intentionally; rather, he wished to crush and kill his enemies, from which his own death followed. Otherwise, he would have wished to destroy them while remaining safe himself, if that could have been done. This is lawful without a new revelation.’ This is confirmed by the example of Eleazar, recorded in 1 Maccabees VI, whom Scripture seems to praise, and whom Ambrose praises splendidly in *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 40. Finally, Estius, in the cited place, judges that Samson himself should be numbered among the saints.”]

[Col. 0865A]

7. Now what do I mean by Necessary Immutable? Nothing, in my view, is more suitable than that which is established by divine and eternal reason so firmly that it can in no circumstance be changed in any respect, even by God himself. Under this category falls the whole spiritual teaching of the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, and whatever is handed down as to be spiritually observed concerning love, humility, gentleness, and the other virtues, both in the New and in the Old Testament. These are indeed such things that it is neither lawful nor expedient ever not to possess them. For, being immovably good because naturally good, they are never commanded or observed except innocently and beneficially. At every time and for every person, if despised they bring death, but if kept they bring salvation. Therefore the first necessity is made personal to each by the will in promising; the second, by the authority of the one commanding; the third, by the worthiness of the command.

8. As has already been said, these three necessities differ from one another in certain degrees, and not all are attended by the same firmness of immutability. What results from the first, though not altogether immutable, is nevertheless plainly scarcely changeable: it may be changed only by superiors, and then only through faithful and prudent dispensation. What results from the second, which is greater, is now almost immutable. As was shown above, it can be changed by God alone. But what results from the last, as from the greatest of all, is altogether immutable, since not even God himself is free to change it.

Therefore, what no human being may change except superiors alone may appropriately be called scarcely changeable; what God alone may change may be called almost immutable; and what not even he may change is to be called altogether immutable.

## CHAPTER IV. What is lawful for superiors concerning dispensation from the Rule

9. Since these things are so, to return to the principal matters in question: it is clear that a great part of regular tradition is subject to the one who presides—not, however, to his will, but certainly to his discernment. Yet you say: What then remains for necessity? Listen: very much.

First, whatever is handed down in the Rule concerning spiritual matters is by no means left in the abbot’s hands, as was noted above. Secondly, even the remaining part, consisting in bodily observances, is not placed so much at his will that it should serve his will, but rather charity. For the abbot is not above the Rule, to which he too once submitted himself by voluntary profession—although, as cannot be denied, charity, God’s rule, is rightly set above Saint Benedict’s Rule.

Therefore, although at times the letter of the Rule may yield for a time to charity when necessity requires it [Note: [Col. 0866D] The printed editions add “or charity,” which is absent from the manuscripts and seems superfluous; for the ground of necessity itself arises from charity. Thus below, no. 11: “Necessity has no law and therefore excuses dispensation,” etc.], yet far be it from being subjected to any person’s will. The man chosen abbot is set over the brethren’s transgressions, not over the Fathers’ traditions: a keeper of commands and an avenger of vices.

For I judge that those holy observances have been entrusted to the prudence and faithfulness of superiors, not subjected to their will. Hence, in matters which the same lawgiver left to the abbot’s dispensation, he nowhere, as I recall, cautiously uses the word “will,” but instead “consideration,” “arrangement,” “forethought,” or “judgment,” or some such term. He plainly intends the dispenser to be prudent and faithful, following the judgment of reason where he happens to dispense, rather than the pleasure of his own will. Therefore he tells him more than once that he will render account to God for all his judgments.

10. I indeed read in the Rule: “Let this consideration belong to the abbot”; and that this or that is in the abbot’s foresight, judgment, or arrangement (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 3). But I do not recall reading there that he may change anything according to his own will. On the contrary, he says: “In all things let all follow the Rule as their mistress, and let no one rashly depart from it.” Therefore not even the abbot. “Let all,” he says, “follow the Rule as their mistress.” Therefore no one is to follow his own will; and here I think the abbot is not excepted.

You see how much is attributed to necessity and withdrawn from will. What more? Does not the very regular profession by which the junior freely subjects himself to the prior equally bind the prior also?

[Note: [Col. 0866D] The sense is that by one and the same monastic profession both the superior or abbot and the monk making profession are bound: the former by a duty of faithful care, namely to direct his subject toward the observance of the Rule; the latter by a duty of humble obedience.]

I consider both to be held by an equal necessity arising from a common covenant, and by one person’s pledge to become mutually debtors to the other: the one owing faithful care, the other humble obedience. What then is left to will, where even the superior is held by the necessity of a debt?

Moreover, the superior’s will is no little restricted also by this: the one who professes promises obedience, indeed, but not unrestricted obedience; rather, obedience determined according to the Rule, and according to no Rule other than Saint Benedict’s. Therefore the superior must not loosen the reins of his own will over his subjects, but must know that a measure has been fixed for him by the Rule, and must accordingly moderate his commands only within what has been established as right—not just any right thing, but only what the aforesaid Father instituted, or what accords with what he instituted.

For the profession runs thus: “I promise,” not indeed “the Rule,” but “obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” [Col. 0867A] “Therefore not according to the superior’s will. Accordingly, if my abbot should perhaps attempt to impose on me, as one professed according to that Rule, something else which is not according to the Rule, or even something not according to these institutions—for example, those of Basil, Augustine, or Pachomius—what necessity, I ask, threatens me in this matter to obey? For I judge that only what I promised can be demanded of me.”

[Note: [Col. 0867C] This is a difficult passage, from which one might infer that a superior’s command does not exceed its measure if it accords with Saint Benedict’s Rule, or even with the institutions of Basil and others; and therefore that one professed under Saint Benedict’s Rule is bound by them if they are commanded by his superior. But this is by no means Bernard’s view. A little earlier he said that such a professed monk had promised obedience according to the Rule, and according to no Rule other than Saint Benedict’s; and therefore the superior’s commands must be moderated in accordance with what is right which the aforesaid Father instituted, or which accords with what he instituted.

I therefore think the passage should be restored thus: “which is not in the Rule, or even which is not according to that Rule; the institutions, for example, of Basil,” etc. Certainly, two manuscripts of good authority, those of Compiègne and Saint-Theodoric, indeed also the Vatican manuscript and the first Rouen edition, have *secundum istam* (“according to that [Rule]”), not *ista* (“these”), as in the others; although in the first member, with the other manuscripts and editions, they read *secundum Regulam* (“according to the Rule”), for which I do not doubt that *in Regula* (“in the Rule”) should be read.
