Yet if anyone contends for the common reading [Col. 0868C], I do not object, provided he agrees that the argument is from greater to lesser: as though he said that a follower of Saint Benedict is not bound by commands of his superior that are not according to the Rule; much less is he bound by the institutions of Basil and others, in which there may be an honourable ground for commanding, but no necessity for the subject to obey. Just as a Christian may be said not to be bound to do things which are not according to God’s commands, and much less things which are not according to counsels, by which he is not bound.]

## CHAPTER V. The law of obedience is not to be extended by superiors beyond the limits of profession, nor contracted short of them
11. You now see, then, the limits of obedience which you require. If the measure of obedience is the tenor of one’s profession, and the authority of the commander can extend no further than the vow of the professed person reaches, surely I should regard “around,” [Col. 0867B] “beyond,” and even “contrary to” as certain limits of obedience, enclosing that virtue within its own boundaries. Therefore, whoever has made profession in any form of saving life ought neither to be compelled beyond the law of obedience [Note: [Col. 0868D] The manuscript of Saint-Theodoric rightly has *lege* (“by the law”), not *legem* (“the law”), as in the other editions. Peter of Celle rightly says, in Book II, Letter 7, to the abbot of Molesme: “Do nothing apart from God; command nothing apart from Benedict.”] nor restrained short of what his own profession appears to embrace. How much less may he be compelled contrary to it? Thus the intermediate manner of life, fixed by a vow and confirmed by profession, like the tree that was in the midst of Paradise, will alone, without doubt, be subject to law and liable to command.

Therefore a superior’s command or prohibition must not pass beyond the bounds of profession. It can neither be extended beyond them nor contracted short of them. Let no superior forbid me any of the things I have promised, nor demand more than I have promised. [Col. 0867C] Let him neither increase my vows without my consent nor diminish them without clear necessity. For necessity has no law, and therefore excuses a dispensation. But the will, because it alone deserves recompense, rightly claims for itself alone a higher degree. Otherwise, a relaxation of a vow without necessity is not dispensation but prevarication; and restriction against the will is murmuring, not advancement. Let superiors, therefore, set the boundary of their subjects’ obedience from the vows of the subjects’ own lips, not from the superiors’ desires: exhorting them, not compelling them, toward higher things; accommodating themselves to them, when necessary, in less exacting matters; not falling together with them.

## Chapter VI. A religious person eager for perfection ought not to confine obedience within the fixed limits of profession.

[Col. 0868A]

12. Yet a subject should know that such obedience, confined within the bounds of a vow, is imperfect. Perfect obedience knows no law and is not confined by limits. Not content with the narrowness of profession, it is borne by a more generous will into the breadth of charity; and, freely undertaking everything commanded, with the strength of a liberal and eager spirit, it does not consider the measure, but extends itself into boundless freedom.

This is that obedience of which the Apostle Peter speaks pointedly: “Purifying your hearts in obedience of charity” (1 Peter 1:22). By this expression he aptly distinguishes it from that sluggish and, as it were, servile obedience, which is not ready for charity [Col. 0868B] but subject to necessity. This belongs especially to that righteous person “for whom the law is not made” (1 Tim. 1:9): not because even a perfect person ought to live without law, but because he is not under the law. For he is by no means content with the vow of whatever profession he has made, but surpasses it through the devotion of his spirit.

Nor has the Rule itself been silent on this point, when it directs that, if impossible things are commanded to a brother, “trusting in the help of God, he should obey out of charity” (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 68). [Note: [Col. 0868D] It is a slight matter that we here restore *ista* (“these things”) from the same manuscript in place of *istam* (“this”). The Gemeticensis manuscript adds *obedientiam* (“obedience”). But *ista* must be read in the plural, that is, “the things just mentioned.”] Finally, in the same Rule the third degree of humility is described thus: “that in all obedience the monk submit himself to his superior” (ibid., ch. 7). For by saying “in all,” he does not wish us, in obeying, to be satisfied with the measure of profession, to attend to the obligation of what was promised, or to derive our measure from a compact; but to go joyfully [Col. 0868C] beyond even the vow and obey in all things.

There is indeed a limit to obedience according to time: namely, the very end of time, so that the boundary of obedience is also that of life. The example of the Only-Begotten Son of God especially commends this to us: he became obedient to the Father unto death. Whenever this obedience is interrupted, therefore, it is called disobedience, sin, and transgression or prevarication.

## Chapter VII. How the degrees of obedience and the gravity of disobedience are to be known, according to the distinctions already stated.

13. Yet it certainly matters for what cause, with what disposition, with what [Col. 0869A] intention, at whose command, and in what command this evil is committed. I say indeed that no disobedience whatever should be regarded as insignificant; yet not every disobedience should be assessed as carrying equal danger.

For God’s command is: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13). Suppose, then, that there are two murderers: one committed the crime out of a desire for plunder, the other from the necessity of defending himself. [Note: [Col. 0869] What Bernard thinks of a murderer of this sort he himself explains below, in treatise 6, *To the Knights Templar*, no. 2.] Does not the difference of cause here plainly distinguish leprosy from leprosy, making the guilt of one and the same transgression greatly unequal? What if sudden anger drove one to the same crime, while deliberate malice or longstanding hatred drove the other? Must what is clearly done from such unlike dispositions be weighed by a similar judgment?

Again, nothing was more incestuous or shameful than those daughters of Lot who engaged in intercourse with their father (Gen. 19:32–36); and yet who does not see how greatly the piety of their intention, and the intention of their piety, removed or lessened the guilt of that base and abominable crime? Likewise, concerning the one who commands and that which is commanded, a distinction of this kind must be drawn according to reason: the more reverent the authority that bears upon us among those who command, the more grievous must its offence be feared; and the transgression of any greater command must be judged more condemnable.

For it is better to obey God than human beings; and among human instructors themselves, it is better to obey teachers than fellow pupils; and among teachers, one’s own rather than strangers. Those whom it is more fitting to obey are, without doubt, also more detestable to disobey.

[Col. 0869C]

14. The same applies to commands. Greater service and care are due to greater commands; lesser service and care to lesser ones. And from contempt for them, according to the same consideration, a graver or lighter offence is incurred. By greater and lesser commands I mean according as the one who commands—whether human or divine—is shown to will them more or less.

For example, there is the command, “You shall not steal” (Exod. 20:15), and there is the command, “Give to everyone who asks of you” (Luke 6:30). Both are great, since both are divine; but the command against stealing is greater. Who does not know that the supremely just God is not equally displeased by the grasping and by thieves; that, of two evils, he prefers us to keep what is ours rather than take what belongs to another; and that one who does not give what is his own sins less [Col. 0869D] than one who steals what is not his own?

15. Nor is equality commonly found in human commands. For, in view of the differing necessities or advantages of things to be done, the intention of those who command varies; and what they judge more right or more useful, they desire and require to be observed more strictly. Thus both the character of commands and the authority of those commanding set the boundary of obedience and define the guilt of disobedience. For, as has been said, the more diligent care in obeying is owed to superiors of greater authority and to their commands of greater usefulness, the graver also is the guilt incurred through contempt.

[Col. 0870A]

16. Once these distinctions have been observed, both the measure of obedience and the weight of disobedience are easily discovered. By these degrees one distinguishes not only day from night—that is, the good of obedience from the evil of disobedience—but also day from day and night from night: the good from the better, and the evil from the worse.

A good degree of obedience is when, according to the teaching of our master, someone obeys for fear of hell or because of the holy profession which he has made (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 5). Better, however, is obedience from love of God. The former obedience is of necessity; the latter, of charity. [Col. 0870B] But I should call that the best degree of obedience in which the commanded work is received with the same disposition with which it is commanded. For when the intention of the person executing depends upon the will of the person commanding, the subject’s effort to fulfil what is commanded is not confusedly spent upon lesser matters more than greater, or upon greater matters less than lesser, as often happens. Rather, with a mind regulating each command according to its dignity, he knows how to preserve measure in both respects: in observing commands and in avoiding prohibitions.

This does not mean that he considers even the least thing commanded to be contemptible; rather, he considers the least to be least only in comparison with greater things. The truly humble and obedient person knows both not to despise the least and to give the greatest care to what is greatest, discerning with the inward savour of a devoted and sincere heart to which commands he should in some manner respond, by his own actions, with the prophet: “You have commanded your commandments to be kept exceedingly” (Ps. 118 [119]:4).

Since he does not say “all” without qualification, we must understand only those commands [Col. 0870C] which, because they are violated on any occasion only with great guilt, are forgiven when violated only with great punishment—such as “You shall not kill,” and others of this kind. Their observance can never be unjust or evil, nor can their transgression ever be good or lawful merely by a human dispensation.

## Chapter VIII. Contempt of laws is a more grievous sin than neglect.

17. Other matters, which admit dispensation by superiors [Col. 0870D] and are punished more lightly when neglected, are called lighter. Of this kind, for example, are a forbidden laugh or an imposed silence. If these do not violate a command, they are not sins. Once a command is added, failure to observe them is counted as sin, though not as a crime—provided that their transgression occurs through inadvertence or forgetfulness, not through contempt.

For they are intermediate matters, from which arise those commands that you call artificial, bearing, so far as they are concerned, a necessity far unlike that of natural commands. Yet even these cannot be neglected without offence or despised without crime, when imposed by those alone to whom it is properly said: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Although the nature of the commanded act is in itself harmless, the weight of the authority attached makes the person liable to the command, and the command liable to sin—though not to great sin, unless contempt is present.

[Col. 0871A]

18. Let this, therefore, be the general rule for all matters which are neither good nor evil in themselves or for their own sake, and which are not fixed by divine institution or by each person’s own profession: when not commanded, they may lawfully either be done or omitted; when commanded, they must not be neglected without guilt or despised without crime. For everywhere neglect is blameworthy and contempt condemnable.

They differ, however, in that neglect is a certain [perhaps: *quidam*] weakness of sluggishness, while contempt is the swelling of pride. Contempt, in every class of commands, is equally grave in weight and commonly condemnable. Neglect, however, is more serious in fixed commands and more tolerable in changeable ones. Adultery, in whatever manner and with whatever intention you commit it, is a shameful deed and a criminal sin. But a light word, perhaps slipping out through forgetfulness at a time or place of silence, or a laugh shaken out by an impulse rather than presumptuously uttered against a command—though this surely indicates a negligent mind or undisciplined spirit—more easily merits pardon, precisely because it is scarcely even reckoned a sin.

What then, if the tongue is deliberately and knowingly loosened into idle words, although silence has not been imposed? Can anyone deny that this is committed against the rule of Truth? Therefore an account must surely be rendered at the future judgment, when the Judge himself most fearfully threatens: “Human beings will render an account on the day of judgment for every idle word” (Matt. 12:36). Alas for us! What account can be rendered for idleness? Otherwise, it is not idleness if it is not wholly devoid of reason. Yet who does not know how greatly one word of detraction outweighs even countless such words—that is, idle words—in guilt and in deserving condemnation? Why is this? Because there is discrimination among commands and, consequently, among faults: thus, as I said, the transgression of greater [Col. 0871D] commands is judged more grievous and that of lesser commands lighter.

## Chapter IX. A superior must be obeyed as God.

19. But this is not so with those who command. Whether God or a human being who is God’s vicar gives any command, it must surely be obeyed with equal diligence and received with equal reverence, [Note: [Col. 0871] See and compare nos. 21, 22, and 29, and Sermon 42 on the Song of Songs, no. 2.] provided that a human being commands nothing contrary to God. If this happens, I advise that one turn without hesitation to the judgment of the Apostle Peter: “We must obey God rather than human beings” (Acts 5:29). Either this must be answered with the apostles, or one must certainly hear with the Pharisees: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God [Col. 0872A] for the sake of your traditions?” (Matt. 15:3).

If a human master grieves that he is despised in preference to the one who teaches human beings knowledge, let him take comfort from the saying of Samuel, which you also cited and which appears to distinguish leprosy from leprosy: “If a man sins against a man, God may be merciful to him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25). If, therefore, I find myself pressed by this dilemma—that I must offend either God or a human being—I gladly choose not to offend God; and this is safer and more just.

For from the present passage of the prophet I have consolation when a human being is injured: namely, God’s propitiation. But if God is offended, who will pray for me? If I flee to a human being, Scripture does not advise it; indeed, it says: “Cursed is the one who puts his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5). And rightly so. If one sins against God—even if “because of a human being” is understood—who, he says, will pray for him? Neither party, indeed. For both the one by whom God is offended and the one for whose sake he is offended have their prayer decreed equally abominable before the one offended, that is, before God. Thus someone fit to make propitiation must be sought for prayer.

Moreover, whatever fault there may be when a human being is offended because one does not obey him, a better cause greatly lessens it or wholly removes it. Therefore, when it is said, “If a man sins against a man,” one must understand, “because of God.” Injury to any neighbour—much less to a superior—is by no means excused from guilt if God alone is absent from the cause. Otherwise this contradicts Paul, who says: “Thus, sinning against the brethren, you sin against Christ” (1 Cor. 8:12). And concerning superiors we have the certain testimony of Truth itself, speaking to them: “He who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). And concerning any brother: “Do not despise one of these little ones”; and, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble” (Matt. 18:10, 6)—may God avert from us what follows.

[Col. 0872D]

20. Yet the scandals of all persons are not to be weighed on an equal scale. The scandals of the little ones must be understood differently from those of the Pharisees. When the apostles feared and reported that the Pharisees had been offended by the word of truth, the answer was: “Leave them; they are blind and leaders of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). The scandal of the former arises from ignorance, that of the latter from malice. The former are scandalized because they do not know the truth; the latter because they hate it.

I think those people are called little ones because, though they possess good will, they have not great knowledge: they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. The scandals of such persons commonly provoke care, not anger, in spiritual persons alone, as Paul teaches: “You who are spiritual, instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1). For it is most unworthy that those who so readily obtain divine mercy should deserve human indignation.

Even those who crucified the Lord, though great sinners, were small in understanding; and though on one account they deserved wrath, did they not on the other deserve pardon? [Col. 0873A] Blessed indeed would they have been had they not been scandalized in him, according to the Lord’s word (Matt. 11:6). As it was, they were nothing but miserable—yet still to be pitied. This is shown by that pious prayer of the suffering, yet nevertheless compassionate, Christ upon the cross: “Father, forgive them.” And as though the reason for forgiveness were sought in so horrible a deed, it follows: “For they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). It is as though he said: They are worthy of pardon because they are little in knowledge. I forgive them because I am not recognized by them. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

There are others whom I do not thus forgive: namely, those whom I know to have both seen and hated both me and my Father. Concerning one little in knowledge of this kind, Paul terrifies the person who possesses knowledge but does not know how to accommodate himself to the weaker: “And through your knowledge the brother for whom Christ died will perish” (1 Cor. 8:11).

21. If, then, the scandals of little ones must be so carefully avoided, how much more those of superiors? God has deigned in some manner to make them equal to himself in both respects, attributing to himself both their reverence and their contempt, and expressly testifying to them: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me.” Does not our Rule itself finally declare this when it says: “The obedience rendered to superiors is offered to God” (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 5)?

Therefore whatever a human being commands in God’s place, provided it is not certainly displeasing to God, must be received no differently [Col. 0873C] than if God commanded it. For what difference is there whether God makes his will known to human beings directly or through his ministers, whether human beings or angels?

“But,” you say, “human beings can easily be mistaken in discerning God’s will in doubtful matters and can deceive others when commanding.” But what does this matter to you, when you are not aware of it? Especially since you hold from Scripture that “the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

They seek, I say, a law not one handed down by any authoritative Scripture or proved by manifest reason—for in such matters no commander need be awaited and no prohibitor heeded—but one known to be so hidden [Col. 0873D] or obscure that doubt may arise whether God perhaps wills it one way or another, unless certainty is supplied from lips preserving knowledge and from the mouth of the angel of the Lord of hosts. From whom, finally, should divine counsels rather be sought than from the one entrusted with the stewardship of the mysteries of God? We must therefore hear as God the one whom we regard as God, in matters that are not plainly contrary to God.

22. Nor do we speak contrary to the holy prophet Samuel, as though in this respect we attributed divine authority to human beings, whereas in the passage mentioned above he plainly seems to distinguish between the two. For what we affirm concerning doubtful matters, he denies concerning manifest matters. Thus, when he says, “If a man sins against a man,” one must understand, “because of God,” whose commands human beings frequently presume to impose upon human beings in manifest opposition.

But taking from this a subject or occasion for argument, you maintain that, if it is established that human commands or institutions of any sort must be weighed with the authority of divine authority, a person under another person can scarcely, or not at all, be saved: since amid so great a multitude [Note: [Col. 0873] Since our manuscripts agree in the word *populo* (“multitude”), it seemed right to restore it in place of *cumulo* (“heap”), as in earlier printed editions.] of commands, which superiors often impose even through carelessness, it appears either very difficult or wholly impossible not sometimes to transgress.

## Chapter X. Obedience is not grave and burdensome except to the imperfect, unwilling, and carnal; to others it is sweet and easy.

[Col. 0874B]

23. I do not deny, indeed, that so great perfection contains difficulty; but only when it is undertaken with an imperfect heart. The mark of an imperfect heart and a thoroughly weak will is to scrutinize too carefully the ordinances of elders, to hesitate over each particular command, to demand a reason for everything, and to suspect ill intent in every command whose reason is hidden. Such a person never obeys willingly, except when he happens to hear what he perhaps wishes, or what clear reason or unquestioned authority shows cannot otherwise be allowed or expedient.

Such obedience is excessively delicate—indeed, excessively burdensome. It is certainly not the obedience handed down by the Rule: “Obedience without delay” (Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 5). To dispute in this way is surely to obey with the craftiness of the heart, not with the hearing of the ear. Therefore a carnal soul of this kind must be not merely burdened but crushed by the weight of the perfection it has presumed to undertake. Weak flesh cannot bear what the willing spirit alone experiences as a sweet yoke and a light burden. Christ’s yoke is indeed a yoke and a burden, and wholly unendurable except by Christ’s Spirit equally present.

If you say, therefore, that the law of the Rule entered for this person so that transgression might abound, you speak truly. Yet the fault lies not in the law given or in the lawgiver, but in the one who makes profession without foresight and transgresses wickedly. The commandment is holy and just; but recognize yourself as carnal, sold under sin [Col. 0874D] (Rom. 7:12, 14). You ought, however, to have foreseen this before laying the foundation of this evangelical tower, before first sitting down and calculating whether you had the resources to finish it. But now what remains except either that, corrected, you obey the elders, or that, ashamed, you hear from mockers: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14:28–30)?

24. But perhaps you say: “Then is anyone found so perfect that not even the least thing sometimes slips from him among the many minute matters imposed here and there by negligent superiors?” I would certainly not grant this of anyone, since even the apostles confess of themselves: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2); and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8).

But we do not perish immediately because we overlook something, especially since Scripture consoles us, saying: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2). The prophet also testifies concerning him that he prayed for transgressors, so that they might not perish (Isa. 53:12). It should be noted, however, that while he is said to have prayed for transgressors, he is not said to have prayed for despisers. But how can those perish for whom the Saviour prays that they may not perish?

Therefore I do not see why you have thought every disobedience and transgression, even of the slightest commands, so exaggerated that you exclaimed: “What sin, then, can now be venial or light for a monk, when the crime of disobedience lies in wait for his entire conduct?” You evidently believe this follows because it is asserted that as much must be attributed to the commands of superiors as if they were delivered by God himself. As though even evangelical commands did not greatly differ from one another, both in the merit of their observance and in the danger of their transgression.

## Chapter XI. Commands, and consequently transgression, are unequal.

25. But just as it is evident that not all things are of one necessity, usefulness, or dignity, so one judgment is not passed concerning the transgression of all things, nor do unequal faults retain equal dangers. What is not commanded with equal care is not neglected with equal fault, and consequently is not punished with equal penalty.

The Gospel condemns both the shameful excess of gluttony and the ugliness of fornication. But which of the two evils would one not more greatly shrink from: being defiled by shamefulness, or being sated with food? Does not Truth itself distinguish grave and light faults of disobedience in the Gospel under the names of a beam and a speck (Matt. 7:4)? Does not Truth itself, while reasoning—indeed, while determining—distinguish for us by degrees the penalty due to each guilt, declaring one person liable to judgment, another to the council, and another even to Gehenna? (Matt. 5:22.)

What necessity of inference, then, compels us to think that, if divine authority is given to masters in their commands, no light or venial sin can any longer be found for a monk, and that the crime of disobedience lies in wait for his entire conduct? Let it be a crime to which that penal Gehenna or Gehenna’s punishment is assigned. What kind of crime, I ask, shall we define that to be which, in Truth’s judgment, makes one liable only to judgment? Yet we shall not deny that there is liability, since it makes one liable even to this extent. And if liability, then sin; moreover, every sin is presumed to be against God’s command. But what is presumed against a command is called disobedience.

[Col. 0876A]

26. From this it follows that being angry with a brother is both disobedience and not a crime. Here is one light and venial sin found for a monk, making him a transgressor not of a human command but of a divine command. In this class of transgression are certain foolish or empty utterances, and whatever is said, done, or thought idly. Such things are never committed except against a command—and against God’s command. They are sins, for God forbids every sin; yet they are counted venial, not criminal, except when through contempt they are turned into practice and habit. Then the species of sin is not weighed, but the intention of the sinner.

For the arrogance of the contemptuous person and the obstinacy of the unrepentant make guilt in even the smallest commands not small, and turn the very light stain of a simple transgression into the crime of grave rebellion. Observe, finally, in Samuel what unquestionably constitutes the crime of disobedience: “To resist,” he says, “is like the sin of divination; and to refuse to submit is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15:23). He does not say, “Not to submit,” but “to refuse to submit,” so that not simple transgression of the command but the proud contention of the will [Note: [Col. 0875] So read our three manuscripts; the printed editions have *contemptio* (“contempt”). *Contentio* (“contention”) must certainly be read, as is shown below by the phrase “a recalcitrant and contentious will.”] is reckoned the crime of idolatry.

For not willing to obey and not obeying are not the same thing. The latter sometimes arises from error and sometimes from weakness; the former from hateful stubbornness or intolerable contumacy. This itself is to resist and oppose the Holy Spirit; and if it endures unto death, it is blasphemy, unforgivable either in this age or in the age to come. Therefore the omission of any sort of command does not make criminal disobedience; rather, resisting and refusing to obey do so. But how many disobey without that most wicked and rebellious will? How, then, does the crime of disobedience lie in wait for a monk, if he transgresses without crime as often as such a recalcitrant and contentious will is absent from the transgression?

[Col. 0876C]

27. Some, as you say, compare every sort of disobedience in vain with that ancient disobedience committed in Paradise, which was powerful enough not only to bind the person but also to corrupt nature. Yet I think that even this first and most grievous prevarication was judged most grievous either only for this reason, or especially because of the rebellion of self-defence which followed. For when God asked the cause of their sin, in order to summon sinners to repentance—for he did not will their death, but rather that they should turn and live—they preferred to turn their hearts toward words of malice, “to make excuses for excuses in sins.”

And the sinner’s malice was twofold: first, because he did not even have mercy on himself by confessing his own fault and being healed; second, because, in order to excuse himself deceitfully, he cruelly accused his wife (Gen. 3:1–13).

28. What is this that you finally say: that in every action the crime of disobedience lies in wait for a monk, as though it crept in secretly without his knowledge, happened by some unhappy accident, or as though an accusation of crime were devised from an impossibility against one unable to fulfil what is commanded? Does the crime of disobedience, I ask, thus lie in wait for a monk? Even that ancient, so well-known and so harmful prevarication would, it is believed, easily have obtained pardon, provided confession, rather than self-defence, had followed. For, as has been said, the transgression of the simple act, though deliberate, harmed them less than the obstinacy, undertaken with forethought, of the excuse added to it.

## Chapter XII. In the Rule, as in divine law, disobedience has degrees.

29. But perhaps this consideration of graver and lighter disobedience ought indeed to be maintained in divine law, though not in our Rule? Yet who would say that more should be attributed to human than to divine traditions, or that what God commands through his servants should be esteemed more highly than what he commands in person? Do not distinct and separate rulings occur in Saint Benedict himself, one concerning lighter faults and another concerning graver ones? (Rule of Saint Benedict, chs. 24–25.) What is a lighter fault except lighter disobedience?

Therefore superiors sometimes give lesser commands, whose transgression produces lighter sins according to the Rule; and nevertheless transgression against God occurs whenever an abbot’s command is passed over. For commands uttered from the mouth of God himself are not equal, and therefore all are not to be observed with equal vigilance. [Col. 0877C] One kind of care must certainly be given to what he himself calls the first and greatest commandment (Matt. 22:38), another to those which he distinguishes elsewhere when he says: “Whoever breaks one of these least commandments” (Matt. 5:19).

What then? We have heard from the Rule of graver and lighter faults; we read in the Gospel of greatest and least commandments. Shall we say that all transgressions of commands are equally greatest? Thus I need not concede what you say: either that everything received from a human master which is not contrary to God is not attributed to God, or that no light or venial sin can be found for a monk. For although he is, as must be admitted, proved disobedient to God as often as he transgresses the command of the human being set over him in God’s place—a command not opposed to justice—still, as equal care is not required in their execution, so equal guilt is not incurred through transgression.

For although the one offended is one, what is commanded is not all of one weight; nor should the transgression of all commands be judged to involve one and the same danger. Hence Father Benedict says: “According to the measure of the fault, let the measure of excommunication be extended” (Rule, ch. 24).

[Col. 0877D]

30. In vain, therefore, as you see, are you frightened, or try to frighten others, concerning the promise of obedience made in regular profession, as though it ought not to be promised because it is known neither to be capable of complete observance nor of being passed over without crime, since whatever God’s minister, a human being, does not wrongly command is evidently to be attributed to God.

In vain, I say, do you on this occasion exaggerate the evil of disobedience so greatly as to frighten people away from the very necessary good of promising obedience. Although disobedience, slipping in everywhere [manuscripts: “stealing in”] or lying in wait, as you say, amid the many and innumerable commands imposed by elders is difficult to avoid, what is commanded is not always left undone damnably or criminally.

For although every disobedience is inexcusably blameworthy, none is eternally condemnable unless the remedy of repentance does not heal it; and none is lethally criminal unless it does not avoid the contempt of pride. Great, then, is the security of the children of obedience, and truly there is peace for people of good will. For in every disobedience only impenitence is condemned, and one who loves God does not know it; only pride is charged as a crime, and one who fears Gehenna readily avoids it.

But what we say will appear more clearly through examples. If, when an elder commands me to be silent, a word perhaps slips from me through forgetfulness, I acknowledge myself guilty of disobedience, but venially so. If knowingly, deliberately, and willingly I burst into speech out of contempt and break the law of silence, I make myself a transgressor—and criminally so. And if I persist unrepentant unto death, I have sinned damnably.

## Chapter XIII. He refutes monks who greatly exaggerate the difficulty, or even the impossibility, of religious obedience.

31. Might this also perhaps seem harsh? For these, if I recall correctly, are your words when, considering the difficulty—or, as you think, impossibility—of maintaining obedience or avoiding disobedience [Col. 0878C], you cry out against the monastic life in this fashion: “Is this that path to God, the safer the narrower it is, the more certain the more arduous it is, such that a monk, scarcely able through common human weakness to fulfil even things naturally good, must nevertheless exercise no less caution in avoiding or observing whatever his superior may wish either to prohibit or command?” And you add: “Since this is believed by many, though observed completely by few or even none, what else does belief in such an opinion accomplish than that liberty of eating things sacrificed to idols which the Apostle so strongly censured?” (1 Cor. 8:7.)

Nothing whatever, if matters were as you say [Col. 0878D]. For one who believes himself not to fulfil what he believes himself bound to fulfil cannot possibly have a good conscience. You therefore believe—to sum up briefly the sense of your words—that God’s commandments can scarcely be observed completely, while an abbot’s cannot be observed at all; although Truth itself testifies that not even one iota shall pass away (Matt. 5:18). But one who thinks thus seems to me, if you will permit me to say so, not yet to have tasted how sweet the Lord is; still to groan under the yoke of the Law, not yet to breathe under grace; never to have experienced Christ’s sweet yoke; and therefore certainly still to be weakened by the flesh, because the Spirit does not help his weakness.

32. But what can that distinction mean—that you admit that God’s commands can scarcely be kept, but those of a human superior cannot at all [Col. 0879A] be kept by everyone? As though the former could be fully observed without the latter. Yet, if you attend to it, God’s command concerning even wickedly living superiors is: “Do what they say” (Matt. 23:3). Therefore one who does not do so plainly proves a transgressor not only against a human being but also against God.

So then, does no one perfectly carry out his master’s commands? Why do you think so? Because we will not, or because we cannot? But if we will and cannot, we are secure. If we can and will not, we are proud. Now, for avoiding pride, I readily grant that the caution you mention is truly necessary, lest one incur the guilt of disobedience. But if you think it impossible never [Col. 0879B] to resist the commands of superiors through the contempt of pride, know that not merely a few but innumerable people think entirely otherwise, having learned nothing but this from their own experience.

But if you think it not impossible, yet difficult, not to despise one’s masters; and if, because you are burdened by it, you agree not to be proud in disposition, yet murmur against the law of obedience, declaring it dangerous to promise what is so laborious to observe: to this I answer—indeed, not I, but the Lord: “Let him who can accept it, accept it” (Matt. 19:12). For this is what I said a little earlier: before beginning the building, you should have provided the means for finishing it. But now, as someone says, “Either you should not have attempted it” [thus the manuscripts; variant: “do not attempt it”], “or else complete it” [Col. 0879C].

Nevertheless, no one who professes cautiously promises that he will never again transgress in anything—that is, never again sin. Otherwise, either the person who swears this commits perjury, or he is holier than the one who says: “In many things we all stumble” (Jas. 3:2). But if the latter consequence seems false, we must examine the antecedent as well: perhaps the law given to restrain transgressions not only does not restrain them, but actually increases them by the crime of perjury, if we believe that in our profession we promise what certainly cannot be kept.

33. Therefore this whole regular observance must be divided into two parts: namely, Commands and Remedies. By the Commands, life is established against sin; by the Remedies, innocence is restored after sin. Thus our profession embraces both, so that when someone who has professed commits a fault in one of the regular commands, if he has recourse to an equally regular remedy, then, though he is proved a transgressor of the command, he is not a violator of the covenant [Col. 0879D].

I would therefore judge that only the person has broken his vow, violated his purpose, and transgressed the covenant who has despised both the command and the remedy. For I certainly call that man secure who, even if he sometimes exceeds the boundary of obedience, does not reject the counsel of repentance. He does not escape the regular limits, even though he sins often, who does not evade the discipline of the censure derived from the Rule. For regular correction is itself part of the Rule; and in it are found not only instruction in good living but also correction of bad living. In it are found both the commands of obedience and remedies for disobedience, so that one does not depart from the Rule even by sinning. I indeed admit that it is impossible for any mortal not sometimes to offend, even venially, against the commands of obedience; but there is now no complaint about impossibility, since even what happens to be committed criminally may be corrected according to the Rule [Col. 0880A].

Therefore, what you say—that no one can fully observe whatever masters command—is true; but the fault of disobedience is slight, and an easy remedy for it is found in the Rule, provided the transgression is without contempt. But if you contend that even contempt itself cannot sometimes be absent, that indeed is false; yet regular diligence does not leave even such disobedience without a remedy [Col. 0880B]. And although it needs the medicine of a stronger cure, it lacks the disease of covenant-breaking unless that medicine itself also happens to be despised.

34. Since this is so, we who profess the Rule complain in vain of impossibility; in vain we flatter ourselves with the necessity of sinning, so as to think that the just commands of superiors are not to be imputed to God but to be despised as merely human—lest our profession seem to contain an impossible requirement if we maintain that as much obedience is owed under it to human beings as to God. For to whom, even after making such a profession, is it impossible—indeed, through God’s grace, not very easy—to avoid covenant-breaking, where it is not disobedience but impenitence that makes one a covenant-breaker? For, as I have said, no one who professes promises [Col. 0880C] that he will sin no more. Therefore, merely because someone fails in some respect to obey, he does not thereby make himself a covenant-breaker—unless perhaps he falsely supposes that this is what he professed, as you assert that not a few do.

Of such persons, if any exist as you say, what you add is also true: that such belief of theirs—or rather cruelty—produces in their own consciences nothing other than that harmful liberty of those reclining in an idol-temple produces in the consciences of others. For one who is of this sort must perish by his own judgment, just as the Apostle cries out that the weak brother perishes through that other man’s knowledge (1 Cor. 8:11). And just as he himself likewise declares that nothing is unclean when received with thanksgiving, except for the person who thinks something to be unclean (Rom. 14:14; 1 Tim. 4:4), so regular profession, in itself, is not condemnable except to the one who considers it condemnable [Col. 0880D]. How far it ought to be considered so, I think I have sufficiently shown above.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why an erring conscience does not convert evil into good in the same way as it converts good into evil.

35. We must now answer the small question which has arisen for you from the occasion of the present apostolic passage. You ask whether Paul’s statement about things sacrificed to idols—“I think that nothing is unclean in Christ except to the one who thinks something unclean: to that person it is unclean”; and again, “If he eats, he is condemned, because he does not act from faith” (Rom. 14:14, 23)—may be extended into a general rule, so that any good action a person performs becomes evil for him if he believes it evil, and evil to the degree that he believes it to be so [Col. 0881A].

If I grant this, you go on to ask why, conversely, what a person does is not good for him to the degree that he thinks—even falsely—that it is good. It seems strange to you, indeed unjust, that human judgment of intention should have more power in evil than in good. If I answer that concerning evils this is rightly believed because of the evil eye, you will answer that, no less rightly, the same ought likewise to be thought concerning good things because of the single eye. For he who said that bodily darkness is measured by an evil eye also indicated that bodily light is likewise approved by a single eye (Matt. 6:23).

But consider whether an eye that is deceived is truly single. For both the person who regards good as evil and the person who regards evil as good are deceived [Col. 0881B]. You know that neither escapes that prophetic “Woe”: “Woe to those who call good evil, and evil good” (Isa. 5:20). Yet no one will wish to avoid this curse if that intention is the single eye—

> [Note: Col. 0881D. The passage is obscure, but constant in the printed and manuscript witnesses, although Horstius thinks that *quin hoc velit* should be read. The other reading must be retained, since it supplies the other member of the dilemma. Bernard here proves that a good intention, which is the light of an action, does not have equal force in evil and in good. His reasoning is approximately this: an intention concerning evil either is a single eye or is not. If it is, he says, it nonetheless incurs the prophetic “Woe,” uttered against those who call evil good; and, on the other hand, no one will wish to avoid this curse if that intention is the single eye praised by Truth.]

—which Truth declares to be the source of light—

> [Note: Col. 0882D. This must certainly be read as in two manuscripts, not *lux* (“light”), as in the editions hitherto published, so that the sense is that the single eye is the *argumentum*, that is, the origin and cause, of the light of the whole body, that is, of the action.]

—of the whole body, that is, of the action. But far be it that the herald of Truth should cry out against Truth, or curse what Truth has approved!

36. For my part, I judge that two things are necessary if the inward eye is truly single: charity in intention and truth in choice. For if one loves what is good but does not choose what is true, one indeed has zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; and I do not see how simplicity can be true in the judgment of Truth when it is joined to falsehood. Therefore Truth herself, the teacher, wishing to instruct her disciples in true simplicity, says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). Thus she set prudence first, knowing that without it no one could be sufficiently simple.

How, then, can the eye be truly single when it is ignorant of truth? Or how can simplicity be called true when Truth is unknown to the simple person? For it is written: “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). It is clear, then, that that praiseworthy simplicity praised by the Lord does not exist without these two goods, goodwill and prudence: so that the eye of the heart may be not only devout, unwilling to deceive, but also cautious, incapable of being deceived [Col. 0881C].

37. Conversely, just as these two goods make the eye single—love of the good and knowledge of the true—so two corresponding evils make the eye evil: blindness, by which it fails to recognize truth; and perversity, by which it loves iniquity [Col. 0881D]. Between these two goods, which permit neither deceiving nor being deceived, and those two evils, which cause both deception and being deceived, are two intermediate conditions: one a good, by which the inward eye, although it may be deceived through ignorance of the true, nevertheless through zeal for the good [Col. 0882A] wholly refuses to deceive; the other an evil, which, though it does not hinder knowledge of the true, nevertheless does not feel love of the good in preference to malice.

38. And because every matter is better understood by division, let us, following this twofold evil and likewise twofold good, divide the eye of the heart in four ways: into good and better, evil and worse. Let us add examples. There is a person who loves good and does evil unknowingly. His eye is good because devout, but it is not single because blind. And there is one who both willingly does good and prudently understands it. I would rightly call this person’s eye single, since neither good is lacking to it—neither good zeal nor knowledge. This is indeed the eye God seeks when he looks upon the children of men, “to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 13:2) [Col. 0882B].

Conversely, there is a person who does not love good and is perverse through malice, but is “wise to do evil”; he is not blind through ignorance. I would not yet call him evil-eyed, because one good—though to his own harm—is not lacking to him, namely knowledge.

39. But there is one who perhaps unknowingly does the good that he does not love. To him I should fittingly assign the designation “evil-eyed,” because he lacks neither evil—neither blindness nor perversity. For he is called *nequam* (“evil,” “worthless”), as if *nequaquam* (“in no way”); so that only the one should be called *nequam* who is in no way—that is, in absolutely nothing—seen to be good, but is empty of both goods, namely both knowledge of the truth and goodwill [Col. 0882C].

Thus one eye is devout—not ready to deceive, but, as has been said, liable to be deceived—of which the prophet says: “Ephraim is like a deceived dove, without heart” (Hos. 7:11). Another is that which the Lord calls single, neither readily deceiving nor readily deceived, and concerning which the Apostles are instructed when they are told: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.”

40. Again, there is one eye that is simply evil, gladly deceiving but not easily deceived: such, indeed, as those have whom the Lord declares to be wiser in their generation than the children of light. And there is another which we have defined as evil-eyed because it is evil in two ways: malice produces [Col. 0882D] ignorance in it, and ignorance conceals malice, so that often, without knowing, it neither does the evil it wishes nor does the good it does not wish. The foolish heart of persons of this sort has been darkened; and, as if already given over to a reprobate mind, they are wholly unable either to love or to recognize good. Of such it is written: “When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3).

For a person of this sort certainly does not wish to avoid evil even if he can; nor does he know how, even if he wishes to [Col. 0883A]. Therefore in the preceding division I judged this eye deservedly worse than the other, not because it is more malicious but because it is more dangerous. For ignorance makes one more secure, and security more sluggish, not more evil. Yet it is unquestionably worse in this respect: the other has only one evil, an evil intention; this one has also a false judgment. The former lacks one of the two goods, good zeal; the latter lacks true judgment as well. Therefore, of this most evil eye, which has neither good, and likewise of that best eye, which lacks neither good, Truth must be understood to have spoken when she said that the whole body is either covered in darkness or filled with light. For the remaining two eyes, neither of which has both goods or both evils, can indeed partly, but cannot wholly, give either light or darkness to the body [Col. 0883B].

41. Therefore, to return now to the proposed question: if the truly evil eye is one that, being at once perverse and blind, does good and believes it evil, then by acting rightly but judging wrongly it turns good into evil for itself—and into as much evil as it believes it to be—since, according to the Lord’s judgment, the evil eye makes the whole body dark. What remains for light where neither devout intention nor true opinion is found?

But it does not follow that a person who, conversely, does evil and considers it good likewise finds it so according to his faith. Why? Because that is not the single eye which, in Truth’s judgment, makes the whole body full of light [Col. 0883C], namely the eye we defined above. For darkness has not altogether disappeared where ignorance of the truth obscures the light of good will [variant: *bona* (“good”) is absent]. Since, therefore, the former eye has both evils while the latter does not have both goods, does not reason require that the former should harm more than the latter benefits? For it does not follow that one good has as much force toward good as two evils have toward evil.

Indeed, I would call even devout intention alone worthy of praise; and good will itself will certainly not be defrauded of a fitting reward, even in an action that is not good. Yet simplicity that is deceived will not be without some evil. Why, you ask? Is it not from faith? Certainly it is from faith, but false faith; or rather, it is not from faith, because false faith is not faith [Col. 0883D]. For I think the Apostle said, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), of true faith, not false. But what is evil is not believed good from true faith; for it is false. Therefore it is sin.

The present passage thus embraces both blind malice and deceived innocence: because, in what is done by an ignorant person, a wicked intention wholly condemns even a good act, while a right intention does not wholly excuse an evil act. Whether, then, you consider good the evil that you perhaps do, or evil the good that you perform, both are sin, because neither is from faith. Yet the sin is certainly far lighter where, with sound intention, only the outward action appears blameworthy than where a malicious intention lies hidden even in an action that is not evil [Col. 0884A; variant, corruptly: “in an evil action”].

But what is not without even the least sin is not pure good. How, then, can good that is not pure be compared with pure evil in efficacy—that is, so as to have as much efficacy toward good as the latter has toward evil? Let this suffice concerning this question. For I think the earlier questions have also been sufficiently answered above. You repeatedly return to and reconsider the same doubts; but it is not my concern to repeat their solutions so many times. It is enough to have resolved once what has been more frequently raised in question.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether disobedience has as much force for demerit as obedience has for merit.

42. While asking about the weight of obedience or the distinction of disobedience, you are incidentally led to ask about the merit of each: namely, whether in every command disobedience weighs as heavily as obedience avails, so that, for example, Abraham concerning the sacrifice of his son (Gen. 22), or some other man concerning the likewise exposure of his son to the flames of a furnace (*Teaching of the Holy Fathers*, book *On Obedience*, no. 6), would have incurred as much divine anger and vengeance had they not obeyed as they received praise and grace because they obeyed [Col. 0884B].

This seems to you both harsh and necessary. But it is not so. For it is clear that some things cannot be done without glory and can be left undone without fault; hence, if done, they deserve rewards, but if left undone they do not deserve punishments [Col. 0884C]. For not touching a woman is a merit of no small kind; yet embracing one’s own wife is no sin at all. Such are all the things that may accord with that evangelical passage: “Let him who can accept it, accept it” (Matt. 19:12).

43. Conversely, some things, if neglected, incur offense, but if fulfilled do not merit glory [variant: grace]; they condemn the despiser, but do not glorify the doer. Such are all things imposed upon human beings by divine public law, without which they cannot be saved. Hence the saying in the pagan poet:

> “I have committed no theft. You shall not feed ravens on the cross.”  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.16.46)

And in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? And if you greet only your brothers, what more do you do?” (Matt. 5:46–47) [Col. 0884D]. Finally, universally: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10).

It is as though he said: If you are content solely with the commands and traditions of the imposed law, and do not freely also devote yourselves to the counsels and exhortations of perfection, you are indeed free from debt, but not glorious through merit: you have escaped punishment, but have not gained a crown. What necessity, then, compels us to fear equal vengeance for transgressing every imposed command and to expect equal reward for observing it? Therefore in such matters let this general rule be observed: in harder acts, obedience is to be judged more pleasing than transgression is grievous; in easier and less burdensome matters, contempt is to be considered more damnable than the act is praiseworthy [Col. 0885A].

## CHAPTER XVI. To what extent transfer and change of monastery are to be approved.

44. And now, if enough has been said on this, let us see to what extent that stability of place which is customarily confirmed in profession must be maintained, and for what causes—if indeed for any—it may be lawful or expedient for someone to break it. You say that you doubt concerning this as well.

For the moment I answer confidently: it is not lawful to withdraw from a good that one has once vowed; and I do not at all advise anyone to change the place he has chosen for himself and to which he has bound himself by his own will and word [Col. 0885B]. Nor does the holy Pope Gregory advise it. For he says: “All who are perfect carefully examine themselves with great subtlety of discernment, lest they ever decline to worse things either in action or in thought.” But what the apostolic man understood by this, the Apostle boasts that he himself fulfills: “Forgetting,” he says, “the things behind, and stretching forward to those things which are before” (Phil. 3:13).

Did not the prophet Ezekiel signify the same when he said of the holy living creatures: “They did not turn back as they went, but each one went straight ahead”? (Ezek. 1:12.) And all these, in thinking this, followed nothing other than the judgment of their Master, who says in the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit [Col. 0885C] for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

Let the covenant of stability, therefore, prohibit every subsequent lax decline, contentious departure, wandering and inquisitive roaming, and, in short, every lightness of instability; but let it not prohibit the things that follow in the sequence of profession, namely conversion of manners and obedience according to the Rule. For if these cannot perhaps be obtained there because of the wickedness and irreligion of those living together, I unhesitatingly advise a person, led by the spirit of freedom, to move to another place where he is not prevented from rendering to God the vows his lips have uttered. Indeed, “with the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted.”

45. But from religious and well-ordered monasteries no professed monk, even out of desire for a stricter life, should leave without his superior’s permission [Col. 0885D].

> [Note: Col. 0885. See Bernard’s Letter 395, no. 2, where he states the same concerning the monastery of Saint-Bertin.]

Yet if he leaves and finds and chooses something better, I nevertheless advise him not to return to the inferior good which he left and despised in favor of the better—especially if that better course appears compatible with his first profession. Let him himself see for what reason or with what intention he presumed to undertake higher or stricter things; but, on my advice, he must by no means apostatize to lower or laxer things—unless he is recalled by the vicinity of his former place, since a person cannot regularly be retained from a nearby monastery or received without his abbot’s consent (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 61) [Col. 0886A]. Take a clearer explanation of this judgment from examples.

46. Perhaps someone wishes to bind himself from Cluniac observances to Cistercian poverty, choosing, that is, the purity of the Rule over those customs. If he asks my advice, I do not advise it, unless he undertakes it with his abbot’s consent. Why? First, because of the scandal to those whom he leaves. Second, because it is not safe to leave certainties for uncertainties: perhaps he can maintain this but will not be able to maintain that. Third, I suspect fickleness—the fickleness by which we often desire easily what we have not tested, but once we have experienced it, do not want it; desiring and rejecting the same thing almost in a single moment, as lightly as irrationally.

We very frequently find not a few people of this sort [Col. 0886B]: scarcely lasting one hour in one intention, driven by the breeze of fickleness, they reel this way and that like drunkards, wandering and unstable. They change their judgment by experiment—or rather, wavering and agitated without judgment, they form as many plans about themselves as places they visit; always desiring what they do not have and despising what they do have.

47. “But how,” someone asks, “can I, having professed the Rule, live according to the Rule with a good conscience? For if I vow and do not pay, what do I do but commit perjury?” As though you would not have much greater reason to complain elsewhere too, once you began to live purely according to the Rule. Certainly then you would say: “And with what conscience can I endure to live outside my former house, which received me when I fled from the world, initiated me into good, and marked me for salvation [Col. 0886C]—being burdensome to the brothers, disobedient to my superior, moreover violating the covenant of stability, and making my first pledge void?”

Nevertheless, neither complaint is justified. For one who thinks himself perjured because he does not observe the Rule to the letter [variant: “to the point”] seems to me not to pay sufficient attention to what he swore. For when anyone makes profession, he does not promise the Rule itself; rather, each person promises specifically to direct his conversion according to the Rule and thereafter his manner of life. This is, indeed, the common profession of nearly all monks of our time.

And although God is served in different monasteries by different observances, nevertheless so long as each person carefully maintains the good customs of his own place, there is no doubt that he lives according to the Rule, since good customs do not conflict with the Rule. Whoever therefore observes what he finds to be good where he makes profession plainly lives as he promises, because no one promises anything other than what the devout life of those with whom he intends and chooses thereafter to live appears to possess [Col. 0886D].

48. For what? Do the Cluniac customs at Marmoutier, for example, or perhaps the practices of those monks, or both groups of Cistercians, profess literal strictness? Yet all profess according to the Rule. Everywhere there is one verbal promise [Col. 0887A]; but because the intention of heart is not one and the same for all, a diversity of observance in practice may undoubtedly be maintained everywhere without harm to salvation or damage to profession.

For just as not all good Christians observe every precept found in the Gospel, yet all live according to the Gospel—for those who are content with permitted marriage do not therefore believe that they have departed from the Gospel because they have not chosen the elevated evangelical counsel of a celibate life, provided they conduct themselves lawfully and faithfully in that lower state—so also those who resolve to live according to the Rule do not depart at all from regular profession, even if they do not preserve the whole Rule to the fingernail, as the saying goes, and even if, according to the usage of their cloister, they alter or omit certain matters, provided they do not cease to live soberly, justly, and devoutly according to their customs [Col. 0887B].

Finally, the Rule itself lays down the eighth degree of humility: “that a monk do nothing except what the common Rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge” (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 7).

49. Therefore, except for Cistercians and perhaps those who, following their rite, take care not so much to live according to the Rule as to observe the Rule itself wholly, purely, and literally—as they certainly consider themselves to have professed—in other monasteries let no one living obediently be troubled by the regular and solemn profession, in which no promise is made concerning the whole Rule, provided that order and discipline with good customs are preserved there [Col. 0887C].

Thus each person’s profession remains intact in well-ordered cenobitic communities, provided only that the intention is sound. But one who is restless and cannot believe this, and who, believing otherwise and yielding to his pricking conscience, leaves and seeks a place where he may discharge what [variant: *solvat vota sua quae*, “may discharge his vows, which”] in his own place he had, in his own judgment, vowed but not fulfilled—just as I do not praise his departure, so I do not advise his return, provided he has moved to a remote and unknown monastery.

Why so? First, because of Paul’s statement, by which he plainly pronounces blessed the one “who does not judge himself in what he approves” (Rom. 14:22); then because of the authority of our Master, who commands that such a person be received and retained, that a good and useful person once found be drawn by persuasion and bound by profession. “Finally,” he says, “let him be persuaded to remain” (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 61) [Col. 0887D].

And lest, remembering his former monastery, with conscience gnawing at him as it commonly does, he should begin anew to trouble himself over broken stability—

> [Note: Col. 0887D. Such were the monks transferred to Pontigny, to whom Peter of Celle wrote a notable letter in volume II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 447; see there also the two following letters.]

—he offers a general consoling statement concerning such a scruple: “For everywhere one God is served, one King is fought for.” But what he commands concerning a stranger, he prohibits concerning one from nearby [Col. 0888A]: lest proximity between monasteries become fuel for scandal and material for quarrels, if they consent to receive one another’s monks without mutual consent.

> [Note: Col. 0887D. Bernard’s various letters show how many quarrels such receptions caused him: namely Letters 3, 32, 33, 65 with the following three; also 253, 293, 313, 395, and 396. Compare Letters 94 and 371, and especially Cassian, *Conferences* 14, ch. 5 and following.]

We experience this as often as the reception of monks of this kind is anywhere undertaken plainly only against the decree of the Rule.

50. But if, after these matters, remembrance of the scandal that a brother regularly received in this way caused, when leaving, to the brethren he deserted should perhaps disturb his mind more anxiously, and if he thinks that what he did wrong by departing ought to be repaired by his return, let the person thinking this prudently observe that scandal is not properly repaired by scandal. For what kind of repair will it be if, in removing scandal from some, you scandalize others? Indeed [Col. 0888B], that former scandal is more tolerable and more venial, having been done with the intention of making progress toward something better, than the scandal you contemplate committing by apostatizing to something worse.

And even previously, though not without scandal, you certainly followed your conscience more safely toward what you thought better than you would have remained in the former good and place against conscience, although you could have done so securely—if, that is, you could in this respect have made your own conscience secure.

51. Therefore let us apply, in concluding this little discussion, what the Apostle decides concerning the eater and the non-eater (Rom. 14:3): let the person who, prompted by his own conscience, leaves his place lest he abandon what he thinks to be his vow, not despise the person who does not leave; and let the person who, with a secure conscience and fearing scandal to his brethren, does not abandon the brethren, not judge the one who leaves [Col. 0888C]. Take this, then, as my answer concerning these matters—what I think—without prejudice to anyone who thinks more soundly.

## CHAPTER XVII. He answers certain doubts proposed from the Fathers.

52. You likewise ask me to explain why blessed Gregory not only did not compel a certain Venantius—who had devoutly received and impiously discarded the monastic habit—to resume it, but is also said to have granted him full communion while he persisted as an apostate (*Book* 1, Letter 33; *Book* 9, Letters 25, 31); or why Saint Augustine in some way subjects the vow of continence to the law of marriage, so that in his book *On Virginity* [Col. 0888D] he seems to assert that even the resolve of a celibate life cannot override a marital union so as to prevent a marriage from remaining indissoluble, even when it has been contracted by continent persons after their vow of holiness was broken through the devil’s deception.

> [Note: Col. 0887D. That this question was debated in Bernard’s age is clear both from Abelard, who charges a certain Burgundian master, p. 1067, with asserting that monks and nuns, even after the public vow of their profession and the bond of blessing or consecration, can contract marriage; and from the Council of Reims under Eugenius III, where canon 7 defines such marriages, even among professed converts, to be invalid and null. Long before this, Gregory the Great commands that monks who had taken wives be recalled to the monastery, in Book 1, Letter 40; and the Council of Chalcedon likewise excommunicates them, canon 16. Bernard’s Letter 76 has a somewhat different subject: a certain man who, after a long life in the house and habit of religion, though his resolve had not yet been confirmed, had entered a second marriage.]

For the present, nothing more certain or briefer occurs to me in answer to these matters than this: the holy bishops thought thus. Whether rightly, let them see [Col. 0889A]. For I am certainly cautious, in the opinions and acts of illustrious Fathers, to judge nothing other than what, according to the testimony of the blessed Apostle, is now required among stewards: namely, that a person be found faithful (1 Cor. 4:2). For I am certain that, whether they abounded in their own judgment or in the Spirit of God, they were faithful in both respects, as in other things: the former in administering what was before him, the latter in writing what he had thought.

53. Finally, as to what you ask concerning certain bishops whom the same holy Pope Gregory is said to have confined for a time in monasteries on account of their offences—whether meanwhile they lived with the monks in their own episcopal dress or in monastic habit—I do not know, except that it seems more credible [Col. 0889B] that they did not assume the distinctive habit of religion, which they were not going to wear permanently, but merely sought quiet in the seclusion of monasteries and an opportunity for repentance.

54. You also wish to hear from me why, among the other institutions of penance, monastic discipline has deserved this prerogative, namely, to be called a second baptism. [Note: [Col. 0889C] The same author, in Sermon 11 *On Various Subjects* and in Epistle 411, no. 2. Blessed Peter Damian, *Opuscule* 16, addressing a bishop who was recalling monks to the world, says: “Tell me, I beg you, have you ever read that the monastic profession of life is a second Baptism?” But since this is plainly found in the sayings of the Fathers, it is no longer permissible to deny it, etc. See the passage cited, chapter 8. See also Jerome, Epistle 25, where he consoles Paula over the death of Blaesilla: “Indeed,” he says, “if untimely death had snatched her away while she was thinking of worldly desire and—may God avert it from his own—of the delights of this life, she ought to have been mourned. But now, by Christ’s favour, nearly four months ago she washed herself in a certain manner in the second baptism of her purpose; and thereafter lived in such a way that, trampling the world underfoot, she always had the monastery in mind,” etc. The same writer, to Demetrias: “Now,” he says, “because you have left the world and, at the second stage after Baptism, have entered into a covenant with your adversary, saying to him, ‘I renounce you, devil, and your world, and your pomp, and your works,’ keep the covenant that you have made.” Add to these Odo, Abbot of Cluny, *Conferences*, book II, chapter 7, and Theodore the Studite’s testament in Baronius, volume IX.

The reason, therefore, why profession of the religious life is reckoned as a kind of [Col. 0890C] Baptism is this. For just as Baptism accomplishes our complete death to the old life and rebirth to the new (see Romans VI, Colossians III, Ephesians II, and elsewhere), so that the person emerging from Baptism is not the same person who entered it, but plainly another: it follows that the sins of that former person ought no more to be imputed to this newly born person than my sins to another, or another’s to me. Precisely so does the matter stand in the profession of Religion. For the religious dies to the world and its works, and in addition to himself and his own will; and he dies in such a way that he may no more use the world, its delights, or his own will than if he were utterly dead and buried. Since, therefore, the religious too, as in Baptism, cease to be what they were before and begin to be, as it were, new persons, devoted to new pursuits, a new life, and wholly different delights and thoughts, it is no wonder if the guilt and punishments owed by that old person die together with him and no longer concern this second person. Thus, approximately, Jerome Platus, *On the Good of the Religious State*, book I, chapter 13. Hence, as Renatus Choppinus also observed, *On Monasticism*, book I, title 2, no. 17, just as those reborn in Baptism, so those professed in Religion, as new persons, are given new names—especially among Italians and Belgians, as he says, and also among the French Feuillants and Capuchins.]

I think it is because of the perfect renunciation of the world and the singular excellence of the spiritual life. This manner of life, surpassing 521 every kind of human life, makes its professed adherents and lovers like angels and unlike human beings; indeed, it restores the divine image in man, configuring us to Christ after the pattern of Baptism. And, as it were, we are baptized a second time when, through [Col. 0889C] mortifying our members which are upon the earth, we put on Christ anew, being once again planted together in the likeness of his death. Moreover, just as in Baptism we are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of eternal light, so too in this holy second regeneration of purpose we escape from darkness—not merely from that of one original sin, but from that of many actual offences—into the light of virtues, [Col. 0890A] applying anew to ourselves the Apostle’s words: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12).

## Chapter XVIII. Those professed may not change their place on the death of the abbot.

55. You ask also to be informed whether a change of abbot gives any warrant to monks wishing to change their monastery; that is, whether, at the death or deposition of their superior, a greater measure of liberty is granted to subjects, so that they may more freely depart at that juncture, before another has yet been appointed. To this I answer: by no means. For when the promise of profession is customarily made in the oratory, it takes no limit from the abbot’s life, but only testimony from his presence. [Col. 0890B] Therefore the professed person’s measure is to be his own life, not another’s. Let him consider, finally, what the Lawgiver himself has not only thought but handed down: “If at any time,” he says, “he does otherwise”—that is, otherwise than he promises—“let him know that he is condemned by God, whom he mocks” (*Rule of St Benedict*, chapter 58). Again, he says that the novice will no longer have power even over his own body; and again: “Persevering in the monastery until death” (*ibid.*, Prologue). Therefore, saving the exceptions touched upon in the foregoing discussion, from then on no occasion permits a monk, on his own authority, to abandon the place in which he has professed before his death. Otherwise he is a transgressor, under condemnation because he has made void his first pledge of faith.

56. But you continue to inquire further and say: [Col. 0890C] What if he cannot remain there except with lasting resentment of heart, owing, namely, to an abbot’s election that is less regular or less agreeable? The saying of the disciples in the Gospel now comes to mind; when the Lord taught them concerning the law of marriage, they answered: “If this is so, it is not expedient to marry” (Matt. XIX, 10). Truly, this is a great strait. If he keeps what he hates, nothing is more burdensome; if he dismisses what he is unwilling to dismiss, nothing is more unchristian. Is not he [Col. 0891A] bound by a similar necessity who can neither leave the place, lest he break his vow, nor remain in the place, lest he live in resentment and lose his life? What shall I advise such a man? That he depart? Profession does not permit it. That he remain? Resentment makes it inadvisable. You propose to me two things equally unsuitable and equally dangerous, so that whatever I answer will benefit you very little. For you ask which of two alternatives is safer for the monk: to remain in his own monastery under one irregularly elected, in resentment; or to move elsewhere in order to live more peacefully. I take this no differently than if you asked by what death I should advise one who perhaps wishes to kill himself: by fire or by a fall from a height. For truly, he who remains in hatred is burned; and he who breaks his purpose falls headlong. Yet you easily release me from [Col. 0891B] this difficulty of counsel when you go on and explain the sense in which you wish this very thing you call “irregular” to be understood: especially if the irregularity of the election is so involved and entangled that, although there is no doubt of it before God, it can scarcely, or not at all, be proved before men.

Now too comes to mind the maxim of the Wise Man: “He seeks an occasion who wishes to withdraw from a friend” (Prov. XVIII, 1). In what sense do you call irregular an election which cannot regularly be annulled or rejected?
