Indeed, it is written: “What cannot be proved is, for me, undone.” But you say: “And who should knowingly obey one unworthy, even if he is not manifestly so?” Brothers, have you not read both in your Rule and in the Rule of Truth: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; do what they say, but do not do according to their works” (Matt. XXIII, 2–3; *Rule of St Benedict*, chapter 4).

## Chapter XIX. He answers briefly certain other doubts.

57. Now receive brief counsel concerning changing clothes or washing after a nocturnal emission. I advise each person in such matters to follow the custom of his own place, since it is certain that they are observed in different ways in different monasteries. Concerning those who make profession in more than one monastery—which I had almost forgotten—I think sufficient answer was given above when the stability of place was discussed; there is no need for me to repeat it. I also pass over certain matters concerning canons which [Col. 0891D] you ask about, both because such matters do not concern us who are monks, and because you yourselves can easily find them in books, if you do not begrudge the effort of looking.

58. I come to the three matters contained in your other letter. First you ask what I would advise a man who has been angered against someone, yet not so much that he himself wishes to harm him, but enough that he would gladly welcome it if the other should somehow happen to be harmed from elsewhere: namely, whether it is safe for one so stirred to approach the altar, or whether he ought to withdraw for the time being until the disturbance is restrained. May it never happen to me to approach the sacrifice of peace while troubled; to receive the Sacrament amid anger and dispute, in which God is undoubtedly reconciling the world to himself. Certainly no offering of mine which I bring to the altar is accepted unless I have first appeased a brother whom I remember I may have injured; how much less if I have not first made peace with myself?

## Chapter XX. He reconciles two apparently conflicting sayings of Paul.

59. Next you ask concerning the apparent contradiction between those two sayings of Paul: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20), and “As long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II [Col. 0892B] Cor. V, 6): namely, how the soul can at the same time be away from the Lord in the body and yet be in heaven with the Lord. The Apostle himself resolves this when he says elsewhere: “We know in part and prophesy in part.” Insofar as we know, contemplating as though things present, we are already with the Lord. Insofar as we still prophesy as though concerning future things—believing what we do not understand and hoping for what we do not see—we are away from God and in the body. But when that which is perfect comes, that is, the fullness of glory which is to come in the resurrection, then what is in part will be done away with (I Cor. XIII, 9–10): namely, all corruption of the body, from which without doubt arises this present sojourn in the body that still remains in part. This is what he laments miserably in himself, groaning and saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII, 24). He does not complain of the body alone, but of “the body of this death,” that is, of the corruption which still endures; showing that not the body, but the body’s afflictions, are the cause of this sojourn. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul.” [Note: [Col. 0891D] In our three manuscripts, “weighs down the soul” is lacking, though these words are necessary for the [Col. 0892D] connection. Perhaps the copyist omitted them as familiar to everyone.] (Wisdom IX, 15). Not simply the body, but the corruptible body: so that the body’s corruption, not its nature, is the burden. Hence those who groan within themselves await “the redemption of their body” (Rom. VIII, 23), not its loss. Therefore, rightly burdened by the body’s necessity, not by its companionship, we desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I, 24), 523 so that what still remains in part, [Col. 0892D] namely exile, may end, and the heavenly dwelling which has already begun in part may be completed.

60. Or certainly our commonwealth is in heaven, in the sense in which the Apostle says: “For by hope we were saved” (Rom. VIII, 33). By hope, therefore, we already dwell in heavenly places, while in actual fact we still journey on earth and in the body. Or again: we have that whereby we cleave both to the body and to the Lord—by animating and giving sensation to the former, and by believing and loving the latter. For our spirit is not more present where it gives life than where it loves—unless one supposes it is more where it is held unwillingly and by necessity than where it is borne willingly and gladly [Col. 0893A] by the will. Finally, “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. VI, 21). Again, if the soul that loves God lives from him, as the body lives from the soul, how, I ask, can it be asserted to be more present where it gives life than where it receives life? For love is the fountain of life; nor would I call that soul alive which has not drawn from it. But how can it draw unless it is present at the fountain itself, which is love, which is God? Therefore the one who loves God is present to God insofar as he loves. Insofar as he loves less, he is certainly absent. But he is shown to love God less in that he is still occupied with the necessities of the flesh. And what is that occupation about the body but a certain absence from God? And what is absence but sojourning? Thus we are away from the Lord and journey in the body, [Col. 0893B] whose miseries hinder our intention and whose cares weary our love.

61. At the end of the second letter you ask what, in my judgment, ought to be thought of the Gospel’s promise to us: “Behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke VI, 23). You are particularly puzzled that Saint Augustine said on this passage that these visible and bodily heavens ought not to be understood, lest our reward seem to be placed among movable and changeable things; spiritual firmaments, therefore, must be understood, concerning which, as you say, you do not know what even to conjecture. But if you consider what you have read: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21); and that Christ dwells [Col. 0893C] “by faith in your hearts” (Eph. III, 17), [Col. 0894A] as a king, surely, in his kingdom; and “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18)—not “revealed to us,” as though something external, but “in us,” as though already abiding within, though not yet appearing; and again, “All the glory of the king’s daughter is from within” (Ps. XLIV, 14); and “Man shall ascend to the lofty heart” (Ps. LXIII, 8); and “he has arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII, 6); likewise, “The soul of the just is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom VII, according to the Septuagint), whose voice undoubtedly says, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI, 1)—if, I say, you attend to these and many similar passages in Scripture, you will surely strive, in seeking the kingdom of God and his righteousness, to enter rather into yourselves than to go outwards or ascend above.

[Col. 0894B] Yet I would indeed say “above” or “outside” in terms of spatial position, just as heaven occupies a position outside the earth, and the sun, moon, and stars a higher one. For these very realities which are within us through the invisible subtlety of their nature are also above us through the loftier excellence of their dignity, and outside us through the immensity of their majesty. But these matters are very profound and require both more careful discussion, a more learned disputant, and a longer work. For I had thought that in treating these questions I would by no means exceed the measure of letters; but the discourse, as I see, has extended farther than I hoped. Therefore, if you please, call it a Book; if you please, an Epistle. For whether in few matters or many, I owed—and have endeavoured—to satisfy [Col. 0894C] your wish.

[Col. 0893]

# The Apology of Saint Bernard, Abbot, to William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry

[Note: [Col. 0895] How greatly the discipline of the Cluniac Order flourished under the government of Saint Hugh is too clear to require proof. Peter Damian, that strict censor of morals, in Epistle 4 of book VI calls Cluny a Paradise watered by the streams of the four Gospels, a garden of delights, a spiritual field where heaven [Col. 0896] and earth meet, and, as it were, an arena of contest, where, in the manner of a spiritual wrestling-school, frail flesh struggles against the powers of the air. And in Epistle 5 he asserts that the Cluniac manner of life and Order contain not the pursuit of human invention but the instruction of the Holy Spirit.

But when Saint Hugh was taken to heaven in 1109, Pons succeeded him. According to Peter the Venerable, *On Miracles*, book II, chapter 12, although Pons lived sufficiently modestly and soberly in the first years of his appointment, in the course of time he changed his habits; and there is no doubt that, following his example, the fervour of his subjects too grew lukewarm. Yet Peter the Venerable, chapter 11 of the same book, does not assign the whole cause of this relaxation to him; he says that through the fault or negligence of certain persons—whom, he says, “I do not wish to name”—things needing to be cut back, or rather uprooted, had grown up.

After Pons resigned [Col. 0897C] his office and went to Jerusalem, Hugh II was appointed in 1122; after about five months Peter the Venerable succeeded him. While these things stood thus, a serious dispute arose between the Cluniacs and Cistercians concerning the Rule of the holy father Benedict, observed with differing habit and religious practice. Since Saint Bernard was accused on this account as either the author or supporter of these divisions, William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, out of reverence and affection for this most holy man—on which see the notes to Epistle 86—induced him to defend himself and at the same time to examine what he judged worthy of correction among the Cluniacs. This *Apology* therefore contains two parts: in the first, having cleared himself of the accusation, he rebukes his own Cistercians for speaking against the Cluniacs; in the other, he attacks Cluniac excesses.

It is of no small importance to know about what year this *Apology* was written by the holy Doctor. Until now all except one, Manrique, have been convinced that it was composed while Peter Mauricius was abbot. It appears, first, to have been written after 1120, when, as the notes to Epistle 85 prove, William was made Abbot of Saint-Thierry. Although the heading of the letter prefixed to this work calls him only “Venerable Father,” I do not doubt that the term expresses the dignity of abbot, since before the thirteenth century scarcely any religious person besides abbots was styled “Father.” Thus the venerable Guigo modestly refused the title “Father,” as was said in the note to Epistle 11; and Saint Bernard addresses Epistle 317 to Godfrey, Prior of Clairvaux, as “Brother Godfrey,” in the same manner in which Epistle 87 greets Ogerius, a regular canon, although he had formerly held the dignity of abbot.

Nevertheless, I judge this little work to have been written before Peter the Venerable’s administration, although he later devoted himself to extinguishing the sparks of this dispute when they were from time to time rekindled, as we shall see below. For Saint Bernard testifies in Epistle 277 to Eugenius that [Col. 0898B] Peter of Cluny, almost from his accession, improved that Order in many matters—for example, in the observance of fasts, silence, and costly, elaborate clothing. This is also clear from Peter himself, *On Miracles*, book II, chapter 11, where he writes that at the very beginning of his appointment he summoned Matthew, Prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, so that together they might provide for restoring regular discipline.

Orderic Vitalis also mentions another reform under the year 1132. At Peter of Cluny’s command, he says, two hundred priors and one thousand two hundred and twelve brothers assembled at Cluny on the third Sunday of Lent. At that gathering Peter, emulating the Cistercians, increased fasts, abolished conversations, and removed certain aids for bodily weakness which the moderate clemency of venerable Fathers had until then allowed them.

Who then can say that Bernard, fully aware of the things Peter had begun from the outset of his administration, intended to assail him for his monks’ excesses? Nor does Peter’s letter—the first which he wrote to Saint Bernard, *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, book I, Epistle 28—in which he answers certain objections of the Cistercians, appear, as is commonly thought, to be a response to this *Apology*. This is clear from the respective chapters of the two writings. Bernard, in this little work, criticizes approximately four things among the Cluniacs: first, excess in food and drink, especially freer use of meat; second, ostentation in clothing; third, superfluous adornment of churches; fourth, the luxury of abbots. Yet Peter the Venerable answers the objections in twenty chapters, scarcely any of which touches anything that Bernard had here alleged. For he says nothing there about wine and spiced casks, monstrous fish, fried eggs, or varied seasonings; nothing about the rest; and, although he touches upon clothing, [Col. 0898D] he raises a question only about fur garments, which Bernard scarcely even mentions here. Therefore Peter’s letter does not answer this *Apology* of Bernard, but the complaints of the Cistercians, as is also plainly inferred from the opening and conclusion of Peter’s letter itself.

But whether this *Apology* was written under Abbot Pons, as we contend, or under Peter, one should recall what William wrote concerning Saint Bernard in book I of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 8: “If an excess of holy fervour is reproached in him, this excess nevertheless has its own reverence among devout minds; and all who are led by the Spirit of God greatly fear to rebuke in God’s servant this excessive excess. It also readily finds excuse among men, since scarcely anyone dares condemn one whom God justifies, working with him and through him so many and such sublime things. Happy the man to whom alone it is imputed as a fault what others commonly dare to claim for glory.”]

[Col. 0893]

# Notice on Little Work V

524. 1. Nothing has stirred up greater hostility toward Bernard than this book, published against the monks of Cluny. For their reputation at that time was such that anyone who attempted to criticize them seemed to be undertaking, as it were, the censure of the whole world; and their extent and numbers were such that he aroused against himself a host of adversaries. Even now there are some who accuse Bernard’s zeal in this matter as excessive, not sufficiently considering that the holy Doctor was so fashioned and appointed by God as to wipe away the blemishes of the Church and restore the integrity and splendour of the monastic Order by declaring war upon the vices which in his time disfigured its purity. It is therefore important now to know under what title and in what year Bernard published this work; whether the matters he criticizes among the Cluniacs were actually vices or tolerable observances; and, if vices, whether real or alleged.

2. As regards the title, Bernard calls it an Epistle in the following book, no. 15: “But now the Epistle, in order to remain an epistle, had to be brought to an end,” etc. But at the end of the book he calls it a Little Work, where he speaks of Ogerius, who did not wish to leave Bernard “without a recent Little Work.” Geoffrey, in book III of Bernard’s *Life*, chapter 8, calls it an *Apologetic*: “If one wishes to read his fervent zeal against the vices of his own people or of others, let him read that which he calls an Apologetic.” Certainly the holy man uses the name *Apology* in Epistle 18, where, listing his writings to Cardinal Peter, he says: “And likewise an Apology to a certain friend of ours, in which I discussed certain observances of the Cluniacs and our own—that is, the Cistercians.” We shall therefore retain the familiar title *Apology*, consecrated by the author himself.

3. From the same Epistle 18, written about 1127, the time when the *Apology* was composed may be understood. Indeed, from the enumeration made to Cardinal Peter, it is clear that this book was one of Bernard’s earliest little works, and in fact the third: before the *Apology* he mentions only two works, namely, the book *On Humility* and the Homilies on the praises of the Virgin Mother in *Missus est*; immediately after them he places the *Apology*, together with a few letters. Thus the *Apology* was composed around 1125, that is, at the beginning of the rule of Peter the Venerable, who succeeded Hugh II in 1122, a year and a half after Pons, under whom the regular discipline of the Cluniac Order had been greatly relaxed. It is therefore unsurprising that Bernard noted certain matters worthy of criticism, and committed them to writing at the request of William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, who belonged to the Cluniac Order.

For since almost all the monasteries of the Black Monks followed Cluniac customs, after the Cistercian congregation arose with different practices, they were called the Cluniac Order, though they were not incorporated into it. This is evident even from the following *Apology*, where Bernard, addressing William, calls it “your Order” in nos. 1 and 30, and in the same no. 30 assigns the monastery of Saint Nicholas in the diocese of Laon to that Order. Bernard therefore writes this *Apology* at the request of William, a Cluniac; he writes, I say, at a time when Cluniac religious observance was more relaxed. Yet he composes the booklet so as first—and indeed more severely—to rebuke his own people, the Cistercians, who, under the appearance of a stricter life, disparaged Cluniac institutions and thereby violated the holier laws of religion. Thus the most holy Doctor, in order to reconcile the two parties, sincerely sets forth in this book what seemed to him blameworthy in each, believing that “he was arguing not against the Order but for the Order, if he reproved not the Order in human beings, but human vices,” from no. 15.

525. 4. Nor ought it to be doubted that what Bernard noted among the Cluniacs was true. No one should fail to grant that he had been accurately informed about these matters and was therefore free from every suspicion of a false accusation. The truth of his statements, however, is proven by the Statutes of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, who, having convened a general chapter at Cluny, attempted to correct most of these very abuses, as his Statutes clearly show; we shall refer to them in notes at their appropriate places. Orderic Vitalis, who himself was present, speaks of this chapter under the year 1132, in book XIII, p. 896:

> “Peter, Abbot of Cluny, then sent messengers and letters throughout all his Cells, and summoned all the Priors of the Cells from England, Italy, and other kingdoms, ordering them to be at Cluny on the third Sunday of Lent, to hear precepts for monastic life stricter than those which they had hitherto observed. Those archimandrites accordingly obeyed his commands, and two hundred Priors came to Cluny at the appointed time. On that day one thousand two hundred and twelve brothers were present there . . . But he”—Peter—“increased fasts, abolished conversations, and removed certain aids for bodily weakness which the moderate clemency of venerable Fathers had previously allowed them. The brothers, accustomed always to obey their master and unwilling, contrary to the religious custom, to resist him, accepted indeed harsh commands; yet they reasonably showed that the venerable Hugh and his predecessors Maiolus and Odilo had followed the narrow way of life . . . But the austere instructor . . . emulating the Cistercians and other followers of novelties, persisted in untried measures and was at the time ashamed to withdraw from what he had begun. Afterwards, however, softened, he consented to the judgment of his subjects,” etc.

Compare Epistle 28 of book I of the same Peter the Venerable, and another letter included among Bernard’s letters as no. 229.

5. From these facts it is apparent that what Bernard criticizes among the Cluniacs was true; but not everyone counted it as vice, indeed it was regarded as a necessary moderation of human weakness. This may seem plausible in some matters, such as the ornamentation of churches and similar things that offer plausible reasons; but the very reading persuades one that most of these practices cannot be tolerated among monks even moderately disciplined. But, you ask, what of the magnificence and adornment of churches? Did not the Cistercians, and Bernard himself, construct churches of the greatest size and ornament? When I hear this, I think of that first Oratory which Bernard built at Clairvaux. Good God! How slender, how mean in appearance, yet how venerable precisely in its mean appearance! He did indeed begin another, very large one, sufficient to contain seven hundred monks and other persons; but it was devoid of every adornment except the majesty of the building itself. The Cistercians at first entirely forbade “sculptures or paintings” in their churches or monastic workshops, “because, while attention is directed to such things, the benefit of good meditation or the discipline of religious seriousness is often neglected.” They did, however, have painted crosses, provided that they were “wooden.” Finally, even in the chapter of 1213, they rejected “notable superfluities and curiosities in sculptures, buildings, pavements, and other similar things, which disfigure the ancient propriety of the Order and do not accord with poverty,” according to *Cistercian Institutes*, part I, chapter 20.

6. But to leave these matters aside, great benefit certainly followed from the ensuing little book. Not only the Cluniacs, but also other monasteries separated from their association, were brought by reading it to better conduct—above all the monastery of Saint-Denis, through the influence of Suger. Finally, following the Cistercian example, general chapters of the Black Monks, apart from the Cluniacs, began to be convened, in which the correction of monastic vices was considered. That this began under Pope Innocent II and was approved by him is clear from the letter of the general chapter of the abbots of the province of Reims to Adrian III against the Abbot of Lagny, reported above, col. 813.

526. 7. But this is enough to elucidate the following *Apology*, which we may divide into two parts. In the first the Cistercians are reproved for disparaging Cluniac institutions; in the second the superfluities of the Cluniacs are censured. Hence the codex of Marmoutier calls it two letters and bears this heading: “Here begins the Apologetic of Lord Bernard, Abbot, against Cistercian disparagements, addressed to Abbot William; and he divides the treatise into two letters.” Epistle 84 is prefixed as a kind of brief preface, a designation Bernard gives it in Epistles 85 and 88. This little work was first published at Rouen, together with the treatise *On Precept and Dispensation* and the books *On Consideration*, without indication of a year, under the title: “Here begins the little book of Bernard, Abbot, on the harmony of the religious states that existed in his time.” Under the same title the book is sometimes cited by William the Monk in his *Book of Flowers from Saint Bernard*.

## Brief Preface

I gladly accept your command that I undertake this work, by which scandal may be removed from the kingdom of God; but how you wish it to be done is not yet sufficiently clear to me. For, while sweetly reading and rereading your most sweet letter—for repeated reading made it more pleasing [Col. 0897A]—I understood that you wish me to satisfy those who complain of us as detractors of the Cluniac Order, so that it may be known that what they have hitherto thought, or wished to think, ill of us is untrue. But if, after making this defence, I should then wish, as you direct, to criticize the excessiveness of their food and clothing and the other matters you add, I would seem to contradict myself, and I do not see how I could do so without scandal. Unless perhaps I should say that the Order is praiseworthy, that the Order’s detractors are blameworthy [variant: “show them blameworthy”], and nevertheless criticize its superfluities. If you wish this method, or judge another more expedient, command more plainly; and pray more earnestly that I may do what you wish in the manner you wish. [Col. 0897B] Yet know that I suffer no slight loss from writings of this kind, [Col. 0898A] because much devotion is thereby taken from me when my application to prayer is interrupted—especially since I have neither the means for dictation nor leisure.

527. ## Chapter I. He declares that he and his brethren are wholly removed from disparagement of the religious Order.

To the venerable father WILLIAM, Brother BERNARD, unprofitable servant of the brothers at Clairvaux, greeting in the Lord.

1. Until now, if you ordered me to write anything, I complied either reluctantly or not at all—not because I neglected what I was commanded, but lest I presume to do what I did not know how to do. Now, however, a new necessity pressing upon me has put my former diffidence to flight; and, skilfully or unskilfully, I am compelled to give satisfaction to my grief, necessity itself giving me confidence. [Col. 0898B] [Col. 0899A] For how can I hear in silence this complaint of yours concerning us: namely, that we, the most wretched of men, clad in rags and half-girded, coming forth from caves—as the Apostle says (Heb. XI, 38)—are said to judge the world; and, what is more intolerable than all else, to disparage even your most glorious Order, shamelessly to slander the saints who live laudably within it, and from the shadow of our own obscurity to insult the lights of the world? Is it then that, beneath sheep’s clothing, we are not indeed ravening wolves, but biting fleas—nay, devouring moths? Because we dare not openly attack the life of good men, do we secretly gnaw at it, uttering not even the cry of invective, but the whisper of detraction? If this is so, why are we slain all day long, accounted as sheep for the slaughter? [Col. 0899B] (Ps. XLIII, 22.) If, I say, we despise other people with Pharisaic boasting—and, more proudly still, those who are better than ourselves—what profit is there for us in such restraint and austerity in food, such conspicuous poverty and difference in clothing, daily sweat in manual work, continual exercise in fasting and vigils, and, finally, a certain singular and more austere manner of life throughout our whole existence? Unless perhaps we do all our works in order to be seen [variant: “that they may be seen”] by men. But Christ says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 5). Are we not, if in this life only we have hoped in Christ, more miserable than all men? (I Cor. XV, 19.) Or do we not hope in Christ only in this life, if from Christ’s service we seek merely temporal glory? [Col. 0899C]

2. Wretched little man that I am, who with so much labour and industry strive not to be—or rather, to appear—not to be like other people, yet am to receive less, indeed to suffer more severely, than any other person. Was there then no path for us, so to speak, more tolerable on the way to hell? If it was necessary for us to descend there, why did we not at least choose that broad path by which many walk, the path that leads to death, so that we might pass to mourning from joy, rather than from mourning? How much happier are those “whose death is without regard, and whose wound is firm; who are not in the labour of men, nor are they scourged with men” [Ps. LXXII, 4–5]: who, though sinners and condemned to everlasting torments for temporal pleasures, at least obtained abundant riches in this world (Ps. LXXII, 12). Woe to those who bear the cross, not as the Saviour bore his own, but as that Cyrenian bore another’s (Matt. XXVII, 32). Woe to minstrels playing the harp, not like those in the Apocalypse upon their own harps (Apoc. XIV, 2), but truly, like hypocrites, upon the harps of others. Woe once, and woe again, to proud poor men. Woe, I say, once and woe again, to those who bear Christ’s cross and do not follow Christ: for though they share his sufferings, they neglect to imitate his humility. [Col. 0899D]

3. For such men are crushed by a twofold contrition: here they afflict themselves temporarily for temporal glory, and hereafter, for inward pride, they are dragged to everlasting punishments. [Col. 0900A] They labour with Christ, but do not reign with Christ; they follow Christ in his poverty, but do not attain him in glory; they drink from the torrent on the way, but shall not lift up their heads in their homeland; they mourn now, but then shall not be comforted. And rightly so: what has pride to do beneath the rags of Jesus’ humility? Does human malice have no means of cloaking itself except that in which the Saviour’s infancy was wrapped? And how does counterfeit arrogance confine itself within the Lord’s manger, and in place of innocence’s cries mutter there the evil of detraction? Are not those most proud men in the Psalm, “whose iniquity proceeded from their fatness,” far more safely covered in their iniquity and impiety (Ps. LXXII, 5–6) than we are concealed beneath another’s holiness? For who is more impious: one who professes impiety, or one who pretends holiness? Is it not he who, adding falsehood, doubles his impiety?

And what shall I say? I fear that perhaps I too may be held suspect—not by you, Father, not by you, to whom, certainly, I know that I am known as far as one human being can be known by another amid this darkness; and I know especially that you are not ignorant of my opinion in this matter. But for the sake of those who have neither known me as you have nor heard me speak as I am accustomed to speak with you on this subject, I write to you what you have often heard: so that, since I cannot go to each person and satisfy each one, you may have from me the means of persuading them most truthfully on my behalf concerning what you know most certainly about me. For I am not afraid to write before the eyes of all what I have spoken into your ear concerning this matter. [Col. 0900B–C]

## CHAPTER II. Saint Bernard clears himself and commends the Cluniac Order

4. Who has ever heard me argue against that Order openly, or whisper against it in secret? Whom from that Order have I ever seen except with joy, received except with honour, addressed except with reverence, exhorted except with humility? I have said, and I say: its manner of life is holy, honourable, adorned with chastity, outstanding in discretion, established by the Fathers, ordained beforehand by the Holy Spirit, and by no means unfit for the salvation of souls. Shall I condemn or despise that which I praise in such terms? I remember that I was once received as a guest in some monasteries of that Order. May the Lord repay his servants for the kindness which, when I was ill, they showed me even beyond what was necessary; and for the honour with which they deigned to treat me as one more worthy than I was. I commended myself to their prayers and took part in their conferences. Often I spoke with many of them about the Scriptures and the salvation of souls, both publicly in chapters and privately in rooms. Whom have I ever tried, secretly or openly, either to dissuade from that Order or persuade to come to ours? Have I not rather restrained many who wished to come, and turned away those who came and knocked? Did I not send Brother Nicholas back to Saint-Nicholas [Note: [Col. 0901D] The monastery of Saint-Nicholas of the Wood, in the diocese of Laon; Nicholas, mentioned in Letter 84, was its monk.] and, as you yourself can testify, two of your own men back to you? And as for two abbots of the same Order [Note: [Col. 0902D] One of these two was William himself, according to Bernard’s Letter 86.], whose names I will not disclose—you know them very well, and know also how closely they are joined to me in friendly familiarity—did not our counsel nevertheless oppose their desire, known also to you, to move to another Order, when they were already on the point of deciding; and did it not cause them not to abandon their own seats? Why, then, am I thought or said to condemn an Order in which I advise my friends to serve, to which I return its monks when they come to us, and from which I so anxiously request and so devoutly receive prayers for myself? [Col. 0900D–0901A]

## CHAPTER III. The diversity of religious orders ought not to prejudice the bond of charity

5. Or am I suspected on this account: that I seem to live according to another Order? But by the same reasoning, all of you who live differently disparage ours. Thus continent persons and married persons must be thought mutually to condemn one another because each lives in the Church according to its own laws. Monks and regular clerics must likewise be said to disparage one another because they are separated by distinct observances. We should also suppose that Noah, Daniel, and Job could not endure one another in the same kingdom, though we know that they did not arrive there by one and the same path of righteousness. Finally, Mary and Martha would necessarily either both, or one of them, displease the Saviour, though both strove to please him by such different forms of devoted service. [Col. 0901B–C]

By this reasoning there will be no peace, no concord whatever, in the whole Church—which, as the queen in the Psalm is said to be “clothed round with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 10), is diversified by so many and such different orders. What secure rest, what safe condition can be found in it, if any one person, choosing any one Order, either despises others living differently or suspects that they despise him, especially since it is impossible for one person to embrace all Orders or for one Order to contain all people?

I am not so dull as not to recognize Joseph’s coat—not the Joseph who delivered Egypt, but he who saved the world, and saved it not from bodily famine but from the simultaneous death of body and soul. It is well known to be *polymita*, that is, marked by a most beautiful variety; and it is seen to be dipped in blood—not the blood of a goat, signifying sin, but of a lamb, signifying innocence: that is, his own blood, not another’s. He is indeed the most meek Lamb, who became silent before not one shearing him but one killing him; who did not commit sin, but took away the sins of the world. Those who sent it said to Jacob: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s coat or not” (Gen. XXXVII, 32). Do you also see, Lord, whether this is the garment of your beloved Son. [Col. 0901D–0902A]

Acknowledge it, almighty Father: the *polymita* garment which you made for your Son Christ, giving some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, and all the other things which you fittingly set in its wondrous adornment, for the perfecting of the saints, until they meet in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness (Eph. IV, 11–13). Deign also, O God, to recognize the purple of the most precious blood with which it is sprinkled, and in that purple the splendid mark and most glorious evidence of obedience. “Why then is your garment red?” “I have trodden the winepress alone,” he says, “and of the nations there was not a man with me” (Isa. LXIII, 2–3).

6. Therefore, since he became obedient to the Father as far as the winepress of the cross, which he indeed trod alone—for his own arm alone helped him, according to that other saying: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. CXL, 10)—now, O God, exalt him and give him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee may bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II, 9–10). Let him ascend on high, lead captivity captive, and give gifts to men (Eph. IV, 8). What gifts? Let him leave to his bride, the Church, the pledge of her inheritance: namely, his own garment, the *polymita* garment, seamless and woven from above throughout; *polymita* because of the manifold distinction of the many Orders in her, but seamless because of the indivisible unity of indissoluble charity. “Who,” he says, “shall separate me from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. VIII, 35.) Hear how it is *polymita*: “There are divisions of graces,” he says, “but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of operations, but the same Lord.” Then, after enumerating diverse charisms, as though the various colours of the garment by which it is shown to be *polymita*, he adds, to show that it is also seamless and woven from above throughout: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (I Cor. XII, 4–5). [Col. 0902B–C]

For charity is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5). Therefore let it not be divided; rather, let the Church inherit it whole and entire by hereditary right, for of her too it is written: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round with variety” (Ps. XLIV, 10). Thus, while different persons receive different gifts, one in this way and another in that—whether Cluniacs, Cistercians, regular clerics, or faithful laypersons; indeed, every Order, every language, every sex, every age, every condition, in every place and through all time, from the first human being to the last—the garment is said to be full-length (*talaris*) because it reaches to the end. For the prophet says: “There is none that can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. XVIII, 7). This is fitting for him for whom it was made, who, as another Scripture testifies, “reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1). [Col. 0902D–0903A]

## CHAPTER IV. He embraces all other Orders in charity, but one by profession

7. Let us all therefore come together into one garment, and let one garment consist of all. One from all, I say. For though it consists of many and diverse members, “my dove, my beautiful one, my perfect one, is one” (Song VI, 8). Otherwise neither am I alone, nor are you without me, nor is he without both of us; rather, we are all together that one, provided that we are diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Not only our Order, I say, nor yours alone, belongs to that one; but ours together with yours—unless perhaps, which God forbid, we envy, provoke, bite, and consume one another (Gal. V, 15), so that the Apostle cannot present us to that one husband to whom he betrothed us, a chaste virgin to Christ (II Cor. XI, 2). Yet that one says in the Song: “He ordered charity in me” (Song II, 4): so that though she is one in charity, she is nevertheless divided in ordering.

What then? I am a Cistercian: do I therefore condemn the Cluniacs? Far from it! Rather, I love them, praise them, and magnify them. Why then, you ask, do you not embrace that Order if you praise it so? Listen. Because of what the Apostle says: “Let each remain in the calling in which he was called” (I Cor. VII, 20). If you ask why I did not choose it from the beginning, knowing it to be such, I answer: because the Apostle again says, “All things are lawful to me, but not all things are expedient” (I Cor. X, 22). Not, indeed, that the Order is not holy and righteous; but because I was carnal, sold under sin (Rom. VII, 14), and felt such a weakness in my soul as required a stronger remedy. Different diseases require different medicines, and stronger ailments stronger ones. Suppose two people suffering from fevers, one from a quartan and the other from a tertian fever. Let the one suffering from quartan fever recommend water, pears, and every cold thing to the man with tertian fever, while he himself abstains from these and takes wine and other warming things as suited to his own condition. Who, I ask, could rightly blame him for this? If the other said, “Why do you not drink the water that you praise so highly?” would he not rightly answer: “I faithfully prescribe it to you and beneficially withhold it from myself”? [Col. 0903B–D]

8. Finally, someone may ask [variant: “you ask”] me why, when I praise all Orders, I do not embrace them all. I praise and love all wherever people live piously and justly in the Church. I embrace one in practice, the rest in charity. Charity will bring it about, I say confidently, that I shall not be deprived even of the fruit of those whose institutions I do not follow. I shall say something stronger. Take care for yourself. For it can happen that you have laboured in vain; but it cannot happen at all that I have loved in vain the good that you do. O, the great confidence of charity! One person works without loving, while another loves without doing anything. The former loses his work, but the latter’s charity never fails.

And what wonder if, in this exile, while the Church still journeys, there is a kind of plural unity, so to speak, and a unified plurality, when perhaps even in that homeland, when the Church herself shall reign, there will nevertheless be some such unequal equality? For it is written there: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV, 2). As there are many dwelling places there in one house, so here there are many Orders in one Church; and as here there are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit (I Cor. XII, 4), so there there are distinctions of glories, but one house. Unity, both here and there, consists in one charity; diversity here consists in the manifold division of Orders or activities, while there it consists in a certain most evident and yet most orderly distinction of merits. [Col. 0903D–0904B]

Understanding this, its own discordant concord—or concordant discord—the Church says: “He led me along the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake” (Ps. XXII, 3). By using “paths” in the plural and “righteousness” in the singular, she neither omits the diversity of activities nor the unity of those who act. Foreseeing also that ordered unity to come in heaven, she joyfully sings with deepest devotion: “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold, and in all your lanes Alleluia shall be sung” (Tob. XIII, 22). When you hear of streets and lanes, understand diverse crowns and glories. In the gold, the single metal with which that city is described as adorned, and in the single Alleluia said to be sung, observe the similar beauty of differing kinds and the one devotion of many minds. [Col. 0904B–C]

9. Therefore one path alone is not travelled, because there is not one dwelling place to which people proceed. Let each person take care, whichever path he travels, that through diversity of paths he does not depart from the one righteousness. For whoever reaches any dwelling place by his own path will not be excluded from the one house of the Father. Yet, “as star differs from star in glory, so,” he says, “will be the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41–42). Though the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father, some will do so more than others according to the diversity of their merits.

We should understand, however, that merits cannot in this world be as easily discerned by human beings as in that world, since here only deeds are seen, whereas there nothing prevents hearts also from being seen. For when the Sun of righteousness shines everywhere, “the hidden things of hearts” will be made manifest (I Cor. IV, 5); and as now there is none who can hide from his heat (Ps. XVIII, 7), so then there shall be none who can conceal himself from his splendour. Judgement concerning deeds is often uncertain and therefore dangerous, since those who do more often have less righteousness. [Col. 0904C–D]

## CHAPTER V. He sharply attacks envious critics and detractors among religious of other Orders

10. For this reason I must now address certain persons of our Order who, contrary to that saying, “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illumine the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV, 5), are said to disparage other Orders; wishing to establish their own righteousness alone, they are not subject to God’s righteousness. Of such people—if any such exist—I would more truly say that they belong neither to our Order nor to any other. Though they may live orderly lives, they speak proudly and make themselves citizens of Babylon, that is, confusion; indeed, sons of darkness and of Gehenna itself, “where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells” (Job X, 22).

To you, therefore, brothers, who even after hearing that parable of the Lord concerning the Pharisee and the Publican, presume upon your own righteousness [variant: “your own institute”], despise others, and say, as people say you do, that you alone among men are righteous, or holier than all others; that you alone among monks live according to the Rule, while the rest are rather transgressors of the Rule—to you I speak. [Col. 0905A–B]

11. First, what is it to you concerning another’s servants? They stand or fall before their own master. Who appointed you judges over them? Next, if you presume, as is said, upon your Order, what sort of order is it for each person, before removing the beam from his own eye, to search so curiously for specks in his brothers’ eyes? You who glory in the Rule, why do you slander contrary to the Rule? Why, contrary to the Gospel, before the time, and contrary to the Apostle, do you judge other people’s servants? (Rom. XIV, 4.) Does the Rule not agree with the Gospel or the Apostle? Otherwise the Rule is no longer a rule, because it is not straight.

Listen and learn order, you who contrary to order disparage other Orders. “Hypocrite,” he says, “first cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matt. VII, 3–5). Do you ask what beam? Is not pride a great and massive beam, by which, thinking yourself something when you are nothing, you most madly rejoice in yourself as though sound, and, bearing a beam, most vainly insult others over their specks? You say: “I thank you, God, that I am not like other men—unjust, robbers, adulterers” (Luke XVIII, 21). Continue, then, and say: “slanderers.” For this is no small speck among the rest. Why, when you enumerate the others so carefully, are you silent about this one? If you consider it nonexistent or insignificant, hear the Apostle: “Neither revilers,” he says, “shall possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI, 10). Hear also God’s threat in the Psalm: “I will rebuke you,” he says, “and set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX, 21). That he speaks this to a detractor is clear from what precedes. And indeed, the one who turns his face from himself and is accustomed to investigate the evils of others more curiously than his own must justly be turned back upon himself and compelled to look at himself. [Col. 0905B–D]

## CHAPTER VI. He rebukes those who rashly judge and condemn the Cluniacs’ manner of life

12. “But,” they say, “how do those men keep the Rule who dress in furs; who, though healthy, eat meat or fat extracted from meat [Note: [Col. 0905D] Peter the Venerable moderated the former Cluniac practice of using fat or grease extracted from meat to season vegetables on any day, by forbidding it on Fridays in statute 10 and on every day of Advent except the first Sunday, in statute 15.]; who allow three or four cooked dishes in one day, although the Rule forbids this (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 39); who do not perform the manual labour which it commands (ibid., ch. 48); and who, in short, alter, add, or subtract many things according to their own pleasure?”

Correctly so. These things cannot be denied. But attend to God’s rule, with which Saint Benedict’s institution certainly does not disagree. “The kingdom of God,” he says, “is within you” (Luke XVII, 21): that is, it lies not outwardly in clothing or bodily food, but in the virtues of the inward person. Thus the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. XIV, 17); and again: “The kingdom of God is not in word, but in power” (I Cor. IV, 20). Therefore you construct accusations against brothers over bodily observances, while leaving aside the greater matters of the Rule, namely its spiritual institutions; you swallow the camel and strain out the gnat.

What a great abuse! The greatest concern is that the body should be clothed according to rule, while the soul is left naked in garments contrary to the Rule. With such effort a tunic and cowl are provided for the body, so that one lacking them will not be thought a monk; why are piety and humility, which are surely spiritual garments, not similarly provided for the spirit? Clothed in tunics and puffed up with pride, we abhor furs—as though humility wrapped in skins were not better than pride clothed in a tunic. Especially since God made coats of skin for the first human beings (Gen. III, 21); John girded his loins in the wilderness with a leather belt (Matt. III, 4); and the very founder of tunics clothed himself in the desert, not with tunics, but with skins. [Col. 0906A–C]

Then, having filled our belly with beans and our mind with pride, we condemn rich foods—as though it were not better to consume a little fat for use than to be stuffed to belching with windy legumes. Particularly since Esau was reproved not for meat but for lentils (Heb. XII, 16); Adam was condemned for a tree, not for meat (Gen. III, 17); and Jonathan was sentenced to death for tasting honey, not meat (I Sam. XIV, 29). Conversely, Elijah ate meat without harm (III Kings XVII, 6); Abraham most acceptably fed the angels with meat (Gen. XVIII, 7); and God commanded sacrifices to be made from such things (Exod. XXIX, 1).

It is also better to use a little wine because of infirmity than to gulp down much water through greed. Paul advised Timothy to use a little wine (I Tim. V, 23); the Lord himself drank, so that he was called a wine-drinker (Matt. XI, 19); he gave his Apostles wine to drink, and moreover instituted from it the sacrament of his blood (Matt. XXVI, 27). By contrast, he did not allow water to be drunk at the wedding feast (John II, 3–9); he severely punished the people’s murmuring at the waters of contradiction (Num. XX); David was afraid to drink the water that he had desired (II Sam. XXIII, 16); and those men of Gideon who, because of greed, lay flat and drank from the river with their whole bodies were not worthy to go to battle (Judg. VII, 5–7). [Col. 0906C–0907A]

And why do you glory in manual labour, when Martha, who was working, was reproved and Mary, who rested, was praised (Luke X, 41–42)? Paul openly says: “Bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety for all things” (I Tim. IV, 8). The best labour is that of which the prophet said: “I laboured in my groaning” (Ps. VI, 7), and elsewhere: “I remembered God and was delighted, and I was exercised.” And lest you understand this exercise bodily, he adds: “And my spirit failed” (Ps. LXXVI, 4). Where it is not the body but the spirit that is wearied, the labour must without doubt be understood as spiritual. [Col. 0907A]

## CHAPTER VII. Spiritual exercise is more fruitful than bodily exercise

13. “What then?” you ask. “Do you commend those spiritual matters in such a way as also to condemn these bodily observances which we have from the Rule?” By no means. Those spiritual things ought to be done, and these bodily observances not omitted. Yet when either the bodily observances or the spiritual things must be omitted, the bodily observances ought rather to be omitted than the spiritual things. For as much as the spirit is better than the body, so much more fruitful is spiritual than bodily exercise.

Therefore, when you are puffed up by the observance of these things and disparage others who do not observe them in the same way, do you not show yourself the greater transgressor of the Rule? For while observing certain lesser things, you avoid the better matters, concerning which Paul says: “Be zealous for the better charisms” (I Cor. XII, 31). By slandering brothers, in what you exalt yourself you lose humility; in what you humble others you lose charity. These are undoubtedly the better charisms. You wear down your body with many excessive labours and mortify your members that are upon the earth with the Rule’s austerities. You do well. But what if the person whom you judge because he does not labour in the same way has only a little of this bodily exercise, which is useful for a little, but more than you have of that which is useful for all things, namely piety? Which of you, I ask, keeps the Rule better? Is it not the better person? And who is better: the humbler person or the more exhausted? Is it not the one who learned from the Lord to be meek and humble in heart (Matt. XI, 29), and who, with Mary, chose the best part, which shall not be taken from him? (Luke X, 42.) [Col. 0907B–C]

14. But if you think that the Rule must be kept literally by everyone who has professed it, so that you permit no dispensation at all, I say boldly that neither you nor he keeps it. For although he offends in many respects concerning bodily observances, it is impossible that you too should not transgress in at least one matter. You know that whoever offends in one point is guilty of all. But if you allow that some things may be changed by dispensation, then without doubt both you and he keep it, though differently: you more strictly, he perhaps more discerningly.

I do not say this because outward matters should be neglected, or because anyone who has not exercised himself in them thereby immediately becomes spiritual. On the contrary, spiritual things, though better, are scarcely or never acquired or attained except through these, as it is written: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterwards that which is spiritual” (I Cor. XV, 46). Nor did Jacob deserve to attain Rachel’s desired embrace unless he had first known Leah. Hence again in the Psalm: “Take the psalm, and give the timbrel” (Ps. LXXX, 3): that is to say, take spiritual things, but first give bodily things. The best person, however, is the one who does both these and those things discerningly and fittingly. [Col. 0907D–0908A]

15. Now, if this letter is to remain a letter, it ought to have ended here, since I have sufficiently rebuked with my pen, as far as I could, our own men—concerning whom, Father, you complained that they disparaged your Order—and have also cleared myself, as I ought, of this false suspicion. But since, while sparing our own men least of all, I may seem to indulge too much some of yours where it is not fitting, I judge it necessary to add a few matters which I know displease you also and which I do not doubt ought to be avoided by all good people. Though they may appear to occur in the Order, far be it that they belong to the Order. For no order admits anything disordered; and what is disordered is not order. I should therefore be considered to argue not against the Order but for it, if I rebuke, not the Order in people, but people’s vices.

I do not fear that those who love the Order will find me troublesome in this matter; indeed, they will doubtless receive it gratefully if I pursue what they themselves hate. But if anyone is displeased, he thereby reveals that he does not love the Order, since he does not wish its corruption—that is, its vices—to be condemned. To such persons I reply with the saying of Gregory: “It is better that scandal arise than that truth be abandoned.” (Homily 7 on Ezekiel.) [Col. 0908A–B]

## CHAPTER VIII. He censures Cluniac vices concealed under the names of virtues

16. It is said, and truly believed, that the holy Fathers established that way of life and, in order that more might be saved within it, tempered the Rule’s severity even for the weak, rather than destroyed the Rule. But far be it from me to believe that they commanded or permitted the vanities and excesses, so great as I see in very many monasteries. I wonder whence such lack of restraint in eating and drinking, in clothing and bedding, in riding horses and building edifices, could have grown among monks—so that the place where these things are done more eagerly, more luxuriously, and more lavishly is said to observe the Order better, and is thought to possess greater religious devotion.

For thrift is considered avarice, sobriety is thought harshness, silence is reckoned sadness. Conversely, laxity is called discretion; lavishness, generosity; talkativeness, affability; laughter, cheerfulness; softness of garments and display in horses, respectability; excessive adornment of beds, cleanliness. And when we confer these things upon one another, it is called charity. Such charity destroys charity; such discretion confounds discretion. This kind of mercy is full of cruelty: the body is served in such a way that the soul is slaughtered. For what charity is it to love the flesh and neglect the spirit? What discretion is it to give everything to the body and nothing to the soul? What mercy is it to refresh the maidservant and kill the mistress? [Col. 0908C–0909A]

Let no one hope, because of such mercy, to obtain the mercy promised to the merciful in the Gospel, where the mouth of Truth says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7). Rather, let him most certainly expect the punishment which holy Job invokes—more in prophecy than in desire—upon such an impious merciful person, so to speak: “Let him not be remembered, but let him be broken like an unfruitful tree.” He immediately adds a fully adequate reason for this worthy recompense, saying: “For he fed the barren woman, who does not bear, and did no good to the widow” (Job XXIV, 20–21).

17. It is indeed disordered and irrational mercy to be vigilant in fulfilling the desires of barren and fruitless flesh—which, according to the Lord’s word, “profits nothing” (John VI, 64), and, according to the Apostle, “shall not possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. XV, 50)—while neglecting the most salutary counsel of the Wise Man concerning the soul’s care, who admonishes and says: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX, 24). It is good mercy to have mercy on your soul; and that mercy, by which you please God, cannot fail to deserve mercy.

Otherwise it is not mercy, as I have already said, but cruelty; it is not charity, but iniquity; it is not discretion, but confusion: to feed the barren woman who does not bear—that is, to serve the desires of useless flesh—and to do nothing good for the widow, that is, to give no effort to cultivating the soul’s virtues. Although she is for the time being widowed from her heavenly Bridegroom, she nevertheless does not cease to conceive and bear immortal offspring from the Holy Spirit—offspring capable of inheriting an incorruptible and heavenly inheritance, if only they have a devout and diligent cultivator. [Col. 0909A–C]

18. Under this abuse, however, these practices are now almost everywhere maintained as though they were the Order itself, and almost everywhere observed by all without complaint or reproof—though not in the same manner. For some use all these things as though not using them, and thus do so either without fault or with very little. Some do these things from simplicity, some from charity, some from necessity. Some simply observe them because they are so commanded, being ready to act otherwise if commanded otherwise. Some do so lest they live discordantly with those among whom they dwell, pursuing in these matters not their own pleasure but the peace of others. Others do so because they cannot resist the multitude of opponents, who defend these things openly as though they were for the Order’s sake; and whenever the former begin, as reason dictates, to restrict or change any of them, the latter immediately resist them with all their authority. [Col. 0909C–D]

## CHAPTER IX. He compares their lack of restraint with the frugality of the ancient monks
19. Who at the beginning, when the monastic Order first arose, would have believed that monks would fall into such idleness? How far we are from those who were monks in the days of Antony! For when they visited one another from time to time in charity, they received from one another with such eagerness the bread of souls that, wholly forgetting bodily food, they often spent the entire day with their stomachs fasting, but not their minds. And this was right order, when service was first rendered to the worthier part; this was the highest discernment, when that which was greater received more; this, finally, was true charity, where souls—for whose love Christ died—were refreshed with such solicitude. But when we come together, to use the Apostle’s words, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper (1 Cor. 11:20). For there is no one to seek the heavenly bread, nor anyone to distribute it. Nothing is discussed from the Scriptures, nothing about the salvation of souls; but trifles, laughter, and words cast into the air are produced. During the meal, as much as the throat is fed with dishes, so much are the ears fed with gossip; and, wholly absorbed in this, one cannot know moderation in eating.

[Col. 0910B]

20. Meanwhile dish is added to dish; and in place of the meats from which they abstain, great bodies of fish are doubled. When you have been satisfied with the first courses, if you touch the second, you will think that you have not yet tasted the former courses [variant: “fish”]. For everything is prepared with such care and culinary art that, after four or five dishes have been devoured, the first do not impede the last, nor does fullness diminish appetite. The palate, seduced by novel seasonings, gradually unlearns familiar tastes and, as though still fasting, eagerly renews its desire for exotic flavors. The stomach indeed works while it does not know [variant: “feeds”], but variety removes disgust. Because we disdain foods pure as nature created them, while different things are blended with others in manifold ways, and, rejecting the natural tastes which God implanted in things, gluttony is provoked by certain adulterated flavors, the boundary of necessity is certainly passed, though delight has not yet been overcome. For who could adequately describe in how many ways—to say nothing of the rest—eggs alone are turned and tormented; with what care they are overturned, inverted, liquefied, hardened, diminished; now fried, now roasted, now stuffed, now served mixed together, now separately? Why all this, except to make provision solely against disgust? Then care is taken that the very appearance of foods should be externally such that sight is delighted no less than taste. And although the stomach now declares by repeated belching that it is full, curiosity is not yet satisfied. But while the eyes are enticed by colors and the palate by flavors, the unhappy stomach—to which colors do not shine and flavors give no pleasure—is compelled to receive everything, and is more overwhelmed and crushed than refreshed.

21. And what shall I say about drinking water, when even watered wine is by no means admitted? Clearly, ever since we became monks, we all have weak stomachs; and we rightly do not neglect the Apostle’s necessary counsel about using wine—yet, for some reason, omitting the word “a little,” which he first added (1 Tim. 5:23). Would that we were content even with wine alone, when it is pure! It is shameful to tell of it—but it should be still more shameful to do it; and if it is shameful to hear, it should not be shameful to correct. At one meal you may see a half-full cup carried back three or four times, so that, by a discriminating trial and quick judgment, among various wines more smelled than drunk, more touched than swallowed, one at last may be selected from many as the stronger.

What, moreover, is this practice which some monasteries are said to observe by custom: namely, on great feast days, to drink in the community wines sweetened with honey and sprinkled with powders of spices? [Note: [Col. 0911D] Peter abolished the use of such spices by Statute 11, except at the Lord’s Supper.] Shall we say that this too is done because of weakness of the stomach? I see that it serves no other purpose than that more may be drunk, or that it may be drunk more pleasantly. But when the veins have been filled with wine and throb throughout the head, what does one rising from table desire except sleep? And if you compel one who is undigested to rise for vigils, you will draw forth not song but rather groaning.

22. But when I have come to bed full, I complain of discomfort—not of the sin of gluttony, but of my inability to eat. Yet I do not think it should be passed over in silence—ridiculous though it may be, if it is true—what has been reported to me by several people who said they knew it for certain. They say that healthy and robust young men are accustomed to leave the community and place themselves in the house of the sick, though they are not sick; and by eating flesh—which, by the Rule’s discernment, is scarcely permitted except to the truly sick and wholly feeble, for the restoration of strength [Rule of St Benedict, chs. 31, 39]—they do not restore the ruins of an ailing body in its distress, but fulfill the care of luxuriant flesh in its desire. [Note: [Col. 0911D] Peter also corrected this by Statute 12. But on this subject one should read his weighty letter, Book VI, Epistle 15, to the Priors and Guardians of the Order, in which he is more forceful and severe than Bernard in condemning this perverse abuse.]

I ask: what sort of security is this—to cast away one’s arms amid the flashing spears and flying missiles of enemies raging on every side, as though the war were already ended and the adversary conquered, and either to devote oneself to prolonged meals or to roll naked upon a soft bed? What idleness is this, good soldiers? While your companions are engaged in bloodshed and slaughter, do you love delicate food or prolong your morning sleep? While others, I say, night and day with wakeful care hasten to redeem the time, because the days are evil, do you, on the contrary, consume long nights in sleeping and spend idle days in talk? Or do you say, “Peace,” when there is no peace? Why are you not ashamed before the reproach of apostolic indignation? “You have not yet resisted unto blood,” he says (Heb. 12:3). Indeed, why do you not now awake at the thunder of that same most dreadful threat? “When they shall say,” he says, “Peace and security, then sudden destruction shall come upon them, as travail upon a woman with child; and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3). It is a treatment excessively delicate: to be bound up before being wounded; to lament a limb that has not been struck; to apply the hand before the blow has yet been received; to soothe with ointment where there is no pain; to apply a plaster where there is no cut.

23. Then, in order to distinguish the healthy from the unwell, those called sick are ordered to carry staffs in their hands—quite necessary, of course—so that the supporting staff may falsely attest the infirmity which pallor of face and thinness do not reveal. Shall I call such absurdities laughable or lamentable? Did Macarius live thus? Did Basil teach thus? Did Antony institute thus? Did the fathers in Egypt conduct themselves thus? Did, finally, the holy Odo, Maiolus, Odilo, and Hugh—whom they glory to have as leaders and teachers of their Order—either practice this or judge it should be practiced? But all these men, if they were holy—indeed, because they were holy—did not disagree with the holy Apostle, who speaks thus: “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Tim. 6:8). But for us, abundance is food; and we seek not clothing, but adornment.

537

## CHAPTER X. He attacks the adornment and luxury of their clothing.

24. For clothing one seeks not what is more useful, but what may be found more finely woven; not what repels cold, but what compels pride; not, finally, as the Rule says, “what can be obtained more cheaply” (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 55), but what may be displayed more handsomely—indeed, more vainly. Alas for me, whatever kind of monk I am! Why do I still live to see our Order brought to this: that Order which was first in the Church—indeed, from which the Church began; than which none on earth was more like the angelic orders, none nearer to Jerusalem our mother which is in heaven—whether for the beauty of chastity or for the ardor of charity; whose founders were the Apostles, and whose beginners were those whom Paul so often calls saints?

Indeed, among them, since no one retained anything as his own, distribution was made, as it is written, to each according to his need—not according to what each might childishly crave [variant: “wear”]. Certainly where only what was needed was received, nothing idle was admitted beyond doubt; how much less anything curious? How much less anything proud? “What was needed,” he says: that is, with respect to garments, what covered nakedness and repelled cold. Do you suppose that anyone there sought a galabrunum or an isembrunum [Note: [Col. 0911D] Peter the Venerable decreed in Statute 16 that none of the brethren should be clothed in fabrics called galabruni or isembruni. He gives this reason for the statute: “Many of ours,” he says, “were adorning themselves no differently from secular persons in varied silken or gray kinds of dress.” These were therefore silken garments of darkish color. The Corbie manuscript reads *rasenbrunum*.], or that a mule worth two hundred solidi was procured for anyone to ride? Do you suppose, I say, that anyone there covered his little bed with a cat-skin coverlet [Note: [Col. 0912D] The same most pious abbot also prohibited such coverlets made of foreign cat skins by Statute 17, allowing in their place skins of *putois*, or *vesons*; whereas previously the Cluniacs, scorning French cat skins, used bed-coverings made from the skins of Numantine, or Zamoran, cats. Compare Epistle 1.] or with a many-colored *barricanus* [Note: [Col. 0912D] *Barricani* were likewise abolished by Statute 18, which reads: “Let no one possess scarlet cloths, barracans, or precious burels made at Regensburg, nor straw mats dyed in any manner, but only haircloth, with merely two cloths laid over it, one white and one black.” The mats were multicolored, called from *barria*.], where only as much was distributed to each as each needed? I do not think that there was much concern there about the price, color, or embellishment of garments, where there was such tireless zeal for harmony of conduct, union of hearts, and progress in virtues. “The multitude of believers,” he says, “was of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32, 35).

25. Where now is that practice of unanimity? We are dissipated outwardly; and, abandoning the true and enduring goods of the kingdom of God which is within us, we seek outwardly a vain consolation in vanities and false insanities. Now we have lost not merely the virtue of ancient religion, but do not even retain its appearance. For behold, our very habit—which I say with grief—once used to be the badge of humility, but is worn by monks of our time as a mark of pride. In our provinces we can scarcely now find anything worthy for us to wear. Soldier and monk divide between themselves, from the same cloth, hood and cloak. Any man of the world, however distinguished—even if he were a king, even if he were an emperor—would not shrink from our clothes, if they were prepared and fitted in his own style.

26. “But,” you say, “religion is not in the habit, but in the heart.” Well said. But when, intending to buy a cowl, you inspect cities, go round markets, run through fairs, search the houses of merchants, turn over every individual’s entire stock, unfold great heaps of cloth, handle them with your fingers, bring them before your eyes, hold them to the sun’s ray; whatever is coarse or pale that you encounter, you reject; but if anything pleases you by its purity and brightness, you immediately strive to secure it for yourself at whatever price: I ask you, do you do this from the heart, or simply? Finally, when contrary to the Rule you seek with the greatest care not what is cheaper when encountered, but what, because it is rarer, is bought more dearly—do you do this in ignorance, or deliberately? Whatever outward manifestations of vices appear, they undoubtedly proceed from the treasury of the heart. A vain heart imposes upon the body the mark of vanity; and outward excess is evidence of inward vanity. Soft clothing indicates softness of soul. Such care would not be taken over bodily adornment unless the mind, uncultivated in virtues, had first been neglected.

## CHAPTER XI. On why superiors do not correct the faults of their subjects. He censures the luxury and splendid equipment of prelates.

[Col. 0913D]

27. Yet I wonder, since the Rule says that whatever faults are committed by disciples concern the master (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 2), and the Lord threatens through the prophet that he will require at the shepherds’ hands the blood of those who die in sin (Ezek. 3:18), how our abbots tolerate such things being done—unless perhaps, if I dare say it, no one confidently rebukes a fault in which he does not trust that he himself is blameless. For it belongs to human nature that no one is greatly angry with others over what he permits himself. I shall speak, I shall speak: I shall be called presumptuous, but I shall speak the truth. How has the light of the world been darkened? How has the salt of the earth become tasteless? Those whose life ought to have been for us the way of life, while they display in their deeds an example of pride, have become blind guides of the blind.

For what example of humility is it, to say nothing of other things, to proceed with such pomp and mounted retinue, attended by so many long-haired servants, so that the retinue of one abbot would suffice for two bishops? I lie if I have not seen an abbot lead sixty horses, and more, in his train. [Note: [Col. 0913D] This is thought to have been said of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis; see Epistle 78. Peter the Venerable issued a statute in chapter 40 that no prior should take with him more than three mounts, or, if he were a prior of the Order, four.] If you saw them passing, you would say they were not fathers of monasteries, but lords of castles; not rulers of souls, but princes of provinces. Then cloths, cups, basins, candlesticks, and bags stuffed not with bedding but with bed ornaments are ordered to be carried. Indeed, hardly anyone goes four leagues from his own house unless with his entire household equipment, as though he were going to war or crossing a desert where necessities could not be found.

Could not hands be washed with water and wine drunk from the same vessel? Could a burning lamp not give light except in the candlestick you carry—and that of gold or silver? Could one not sleep except upon a varied bedspread or beneath a foreign coverlet? Could not one attendant both tether a beast, serve at table, and prepare a bed? Why then, for the sake of such a multitude of servants and pack animals, do we not carry necessities with us, at least to relieve the evil, so that we may not burden our hosts?

## CHAPTER XII. He rebukes luxury and abuse in building, decorating, and painting churches and oratories.

[Col. 0914C]

28. But these are small matters. I shall come to greater ones, which seem smaller only because they are more customary. I omit the immense height of oratories, their immoderate length, superfluous breadth, costly polishing, curious paintings—things which, by turning the gaze of those who pray toward themselves, impede devotion and in some manner represent to me the ancient rite of the Jews. But let it be: let these things be done for the honor of God. Yet I ask monks the question which the pagan poet asked pagans:

> “Tell me, priests,” he says, “what does gold do in a sanctuary?”  
> (Persius, *Satires* II.69)

But I say: “Tell me, poor men”—for I attend not to the verse but to its sense—“tell me, poor men, if indeed you are poor, what does gold do in a sanctuary?” The case of bishops is one thing, that of monks another. For we know that bishops, being debtors to wise and foolish alike, stir up the devotion of a carnal people through bodily ornaments because they cannot do so through spiritual ones. But we, who have already gone out from the people; who for Christ’s sake have left behind every precious and beautiful thing in the world; who have regarded as dung, that we might gain Christ, everything that shines beautifully, soothes by sound, smells sweetly, tastes pleasantly, pleases the touch—in short, every bodily delight: whose devotion, I ask, do we intend to stir up by these things? What fruit, I say, do we seek from them? The admiration of fools, or the offering [variant: “pleasure”] of the simple? Or, because we are mingled among the nations, have we perhaps learned their works and still serve their carved images?

28. And, to speak openly, does avarice—which is the service of idols—do all this? Do we seek not fruit, but a gift? If you ask how: in a marvelous way, I say. Money is scattered by a certain art so that it may be multiplied. It is spent in order that it may increase; expenditure produces abundance. For by the very sight of costly yet astonishing vanities, people are more inflamed to offer than to pray. Thus wealth draws wealth, thus money draws money: because, by some inexplicable means, where greater riches are seen, there offerings are made more willingly. Eyes are fed by relics covered with gold, and purses are opened. The most beautiful form of some saint or holy woman is displayed, and it is believed to be the holier the more brightly colored it is. People run to kiss it; they are invited to give; and they admire beautiful things more than they venerate sacred things.

Then there are placed in the church jeweled wheels—not crowns [Note: [Col. 0915D] Concerning crowns of this sort—one of which remains at Reims in the church of St Remigius, having seventy-two little candles—the often-praised Abbot Peter decreed that those great crowns, most elegantly made of bronze, gold, and silver, which hang in the middle of the choir supported by a strong chain, should have lighted candles placed upon them only on the five principal feasts, etc. He calls the smaller crowns *erzas*.]—but wheels, encircled with lamps and no less radiant with gems set into them. We also see, in place of candlesticks, certain trees erected, fashioned with great weight of bronze and marvelous workmanship, shining not more from lamps placed upon them than from their own gems. What, do you suppose, is sought in all these things? The contrition of penitents, or the admiration of spectators? O vanity of vanities—yet not more vain than mad!
