The church gleams in its walls and is needy in its poor. It clothes its stones with gold and abandons its children naked. From the expenditures needed by the poor, provision is made for the eyes of the rich. The curious find something in which to delight; the miserable find nothing by which to be sustained.

Why at least do we not reverence the images of saints, when the pavement itself—which is trampled underfoot—abounds with them? The face of an angel is often spat upon; the face of some saint is often beaten by the feet of passersby. And if these sacred images are not respected, why are beautiful colors at least not spared? Why adorn what is soon to be defiled? Why paint what must be trampled? What use are lovely forms there, where they are continually stained by dust? Finally, what have these things to do with the poor, with monks, with spiritual men? Unless perhaps the prophetic response may here be made against the poet’s verse already mentioned: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of thy house, and the place where thy glory dwells” (Ps. 25:8). I agree: let these things too be allowed in churches, because although they are harmful to the vain and avaricious, they are not harmful to the simple and devout.

29. But in cloisters, before brethren who are reading, what is the purpose of that ridiculous monstrosity, that marvelous sort of misshapen beauty and beautiful deformity? What are those unclean apes doing there? What those fierce lions? What those monstrous centaurs? What those half-men? What those spotted tigers? What those fighting soldiers? What those hunters sounding horns? Under one head you may see many bodies, and again, upon one body, many heads. On one side, a four-footed creature has a serpent’s tail; on another, a fish has the head of a quadruped. Here a beast presents the forepart of a horse while dragging behind it half a goat; there a horned animal bears the hindquarters of a horse. Finally, so great and so marvelous a variety of diverse forms appears everywhere that one would rather read the marbles than the books, and spend the entire day wondering at each individual thing than meditating upon the law of God. Good God! If men are not ashamed of such follies, why are they not at least grieved by the expense?

## CHAPTER XIII. He briefly gathers the means and measures for fostering mutual charity and peace; finally, he censures unstable deserters.

30. Abundant material suggested many other things to be added; but both my own sufficiently anxious occupation and your excessively hasty departure, brother Oger [Note: [Col. 0916D] This is Ogerius, a regular canon, to whom Epistle 87 and those following are addressed. Bernard submitted this book to the judgment of him and likewise of William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, in Epistle 88.], draw me away. For you consent neither to stay longer nor yet to leave without a fresh little work. I therefore do what you wish: I let you go, and shorten my discourse—especially because a few useful things in peace are better than many things with scandal. And would that I have written even these few things without scandal! For in criticizing vices I know that I offend the vicious. Yet, God willing, it may happen that some whom I fear I have exasperated will rather be pleased—if they cease to be vicious: that is, if the stricter cease to be detractors, and the more relaxed cut off their superfluities; if each holds firmly the good that he holds without judging another who holds something else; if one who has attained goodness does not envy those who are better; if one who seems to himself to act better does not despise another’s good; if those able to live more strictly neither despise nor rival those unable to do so; and if those unable to do so admire those who can, without rashly imitating them. For just as those who have perhaps vowed something greater may not descend to what is less, lest they become apostates, so it is not expedient for everyone to pass from lesser goods to greater ones, lest they fall headlong.

31. For I know that some have flown from other congregations and observances to our Order: they have knocked and entered. By doing this, they have left scandal among their own and brought it to us no less, troubling them by their rash departure and us by their wretched manner of life. And because they proudly despised what they held and rashly presumed upon what they could not sustain, God at last revealed their cowardice by a fitting outcome: for they shamelessly abandoned what they had imprudently undertaken, and shamefully returned to what they had lightly forsaken. Since they sought our cloisters rather through impatience with their own Order than through desire for ours, they show what they are when, flying with unstable fickleness from you to us and from us to you, they cause scandal to us, to you, and to all good people.

Although we know some among them who, by God’s help, began bravely and, under his protection, persevere still more bravely, it is nevertheless safer to persevere in the good which we have begun than to begin something in which we shall not persevere. Let us all equally strive for this: that, according to the Apostle’s counsel, all our things may be done in charity (1 Cor. 16:14). This is our judgment about our Order and yours; this is what I am accustomed to say to ours and yours—about you not in your absence, but to you yourselves. No one will be a better witness for me than you, or anyone else who knows me as you do. Whatever is praiseworthy among you, I praise and proclaim. If there are things deserving rebuke, I customarily urge you and my other friends to amend them. This is not detraction, but attraction. I pray and earnestly beseech that this may always be done to us by you. Farewell.

[Col. 0917]

# BOOK OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT, IN PRAISE OF THE NEW KNIGHTHOOD, ADDRESSED TO THE KNIGHTS OF THE TEMPLE

541

## NOTICE ON TREATISE VI

1. In ancient manuscripts the following book bears this title: “Here begins the prologue of Saint Bernard, abbot, in the little book addressed to the Knights of the Temple”; and after the prologue: “Here begin the chapters concerning the praise of the new Knighthood.” There are thirteen of them in all, as in our editions, where we have retained the titles according to the author’s intention. Geoffrey, in Book III, chapter 8, of the *Life of Bernard*, calls this book an “Exhortatory discourse addressed to the Knights of the Temple.” “How faithful,” he says, “he was as a commender and helper of every devout manner of life is shown by the exhortatory discourse addressed to the Knights of the Temple.” Accordingly, the title of this book may be given as follows: “Book Addressed to the Knights of the Temple, in Praise of the New Knighthood.”

2. The prologue, however, is addressed to “Hugh, soldier of Christ and master of Christ’s Knighthood”; but to dedicate the book to the Master of the Knighthood is effectively to dedicate it to all the Knights. They were called Brothers of the Temple because, by permission of King Baldwin, they first took up residence beside the Temple of the Lord, as William, archbishop of Tyre, testifies in Book XII, chapter 7, where he describes their origin under the year 1118:

> “In the same year certain noble men of the knightly order, devoted to God, religious, and fearing God, committed themselves in the hand of the lord patriarch to Christ’s service; after the manner of regular canons they professed that they wished to live perpetually in chastity, obedience, and without private property. Among them the first and chief were the venerable men Hugh of Payns and Godfrey of Saint-Omer. Since they had neither church nor fixed dwelling, the king granted them for a time a lodging in the palace situated beside the Temple of the Lord on its southern side. Their first profession, and the duty imposed upon them by the lord patriarch and other bishops for remission of sins, was that they should, as far as their strength allowed, protect roads and routes, especially for the safety of pilgrims, against the ambushes of robbers and raiders.”

This is the origin of the Knights of the Temple, whose first Master was the aforesaid Hugh of Payns; the same William of Tyre calls him the first Master of the Knighthood of the Temple in Book XIII, chapter 26. The second letter of Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, is addressed “to Hugh, Prior of the holy Knighthood.” This is the Hugh to whom Bernard dedicated the following book, and he must of course be distinguished from the other Hugh, who, formerly Count of Champagne, became a Knight of the Temple, as Bernard’s thirty-first letter addressed to him testifies. Further, Hugh of Payns, first Master of the Knighthood, was succeeded by “an outstanding knight, valiant in arms, noble in birth and character, Lord Robert, surnamed Burgundian, an Aquitanian by nation,” about the year 1136, as may be gathered from William of Tyre, Book XV, chapter 6, who also discusses him at the beginning of Book XVII. Robert appears to have been succeeded by Ebrard, to whom Peter the Venerable writes the letter which is Book VI, Epistle 26.

542

3. I cannot easily say in what year this book was written. It is certain that it was composed when the Order had already greatly increased and the number of knights had multiplied. Bernard’s words at no. 10 prove this:

> “These things are done at Jerusalem, and the world is stirred. The islands hear, and peoples from afar give heed; and they pour forth from East and West . . . And what is seen more joyfully and done more advantageously is that, in so great a multitude of men, you see very few flocking there except the wicked,” etc.

Yet before the Council of Troyes—that is, before 1127—there were only nine Knights of that institution, as we shall shortly see from William. Therefore this book can scarcely be said to have been composed before 1132, but nevertheless before 1136, the approximate year in which Robert succeeded Hugh as Master.

4. Miraeus published the Rule of the Templars from a Victorine manuscript and inserted it in the *Cistercian Chronicle*, “as dictated,” he says, “by Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, as is clear from the prologue.” This Rule consists of as many chapters as the Rule of Saint Benedict—from which it is for the most part taken word for word—namely, seventy-two chapters. Before the prologue it bears this title: “Rule of the Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon.” Manrique, under the year 1128, chapter 2, attributes this Rule to Bernard as author together with Miraeus, and in proof brings forward two passages from the prologue.

The first passage reads thus:

> “Although indeed the very great number of religious Fathers who assembled in that council by divine prompting commend the authority of our composition, we should not pass over in silence the fact that, while they looked on and set forth true opinions, I, John of Michelsberg, by order of the council and of the venerable abbot of Clairvaux—to whom this was entrusted and due—by divine grace was deemed worthy to be the humble scribe of this present document.”

But these words do not signify that Bernard composed any Rule for the Templars; rather, they signify that he transferred to John of Michelsberg the scribal office laid upon himself. Nothing further follows from the subsequent words, which, after the Fathers of the Council of Troyes have been enumerated, are related as follows:

> “The Master of the Knighthood himself, Hugh by name, was indeed not absent, and he had with him some of his brethren, namely Brother Godfrey, Brother Rorval, Brother Geoffrey Bisol, Brother Pagan of Montdidier, and Archambaud of Saint-Aignan. This Master Hugh, with these disciples, communicated to the above-named Fathers, according to what his memory knew, the manner and observance of the small beginning of his military Order, which took its origin from him who says, ‘I am the beginning, who also speak to you.’ It therefore pleased the council that the decision there carefully examined by the file of counsel and consideration of the divine Scriptures should nevertheless be committed to writing and inviolably observed, with the approval of the Roman Pope and the Patriarch of Jerusalem, and also with the assent of the chapter of the poor fellow-soldiers of the Temple which is in Jerusalem.”

From these words we understand only that the Fathers decreed that a Rule should be prescribed for the Knights by their agreement, after consultation with the Roman Pontiff and the Patriarch of Jerusalem; Bernard is by no means asserted to be its author. Indeed, Alberic of the Cistercian Order writes that the Rule of Saint Augustine was imposed upon these Knights. Thus in the *Monasticon Anglicanum* they are referred to the Order of Saint Augustine. It would be very strange if Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, a Cistercian monk not far from Clairvaux, had been ignorant of this Rule of Bernard and had attributed another Rule to Knights who survived in his own time.

William, bishop of Tyre, in the already-mentioned Book XII, chapter 7, reports that the same Knights, who before the Council of Troyes “were only nine,” received, “by command of Pope Honorius and Stephen, patriarch of Jerusalem, a Rule and a white habit,” whereas earlier they had used ordinary dress. “Later, in the time of Pope Eugenius, it is said that they began to sew crosses of red cloth upon their mantles,” both the knights “and their brethren who are called Servants. Their possessions grew so enormously that today,” says William, “they have more or less three hundred knights in their convent, clothed in white cloaks, apart from the Brethren.”

From these last words we infer that the Rule attributed to Bernard as author was written only after William of Tyre. For in chapter 21 certain “false brethren from beyond the mountains, falsely claiming to be of the Temple” are noted, and certain things which “have arisen among the Knights without discernment and counsel of the common chapter, and must be wholly cut off” are criticized—for example, “formerly servants and squires had white clothing, whence intolerable harms resulted.” But there was no general chapter of the Templars before the Council of Troyes; before then they had no distinctive habit, but ordinary dress. White was granted to them by the Fathers of the council, with Servants excepted. From these words alone it is entirely clear that at least this chapter was added long after the time of the council.

Chapter 7 not only does not praise “standing to hear the divine office,” but even condemns it, decreeing that it should be heard while seated; such a decree would surely never have entered Bernard’s mind. Chapter 56 decrees “that sisters shall no longer be admitted,” which shows that the institution was not recent. I leave it for others to judge whether John of Michelsberg was the author of this Rule. One point in it not unworthy of notice is that *collatio* is used in chapter 16 for the light meal on fast days.

544

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0921A]

To HUGH, soldier of Christ and Master of Christ’s Knighthood, BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux in name alone: may you fight the good fight.

Once, twice, and three times, if I am not mistaken, you asked me, dearest Hugh, to write for you and your fellow-soldiers a discourse of exhortation, and to brandish the pen against hostile tyranny because I was not permitted to wield the lance; asserting that it would be no small help to you if I could encourage by letters those whom I could not encourage by arms. I delayed for some time—not because the request seemed contemptible, but lest a rash and superficial assent be blamed, if I, unskilled as I am, presumed to undertake what someone better might more adequately perform, and so perhaps rendered a most necessary matter less useful through my own inadequacy.

[Col. 0921B]

But when I saw myself frustrated for long enough by this sort of waiting, lest I might now seem unwilling rather than unable, I finally did what I could. Let the reader judge whether I have satisfied the request. Yet even if what I have written should perhaps please someone very little, or prove insufficient, it is no concern of mine, since I did not fail to conform my judgment to your will rather than my own.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the praise of the new knighthood
1. A new kind of knighthood has lately arisen on earth, and in that region which the Dayspring from on high once visited in bodily presence: so that, from the very place where he then by the strength of his hand drove out the princes of darkness, he may now also destroy their minions—the sons of unbelief—scattered and put to flight by the hand of his strong ones, accomplishing even now the redemption of his people and once more raising up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant. I say, a new kind of knighthood, untried through the ages: in which battle is tirelessly waged at once on two fronts, both against flesh and blood and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

[Note: [Col. 0921C] Peter the Venerable says almost the same in Book VI, Letter 26: “Who would not rejoice,” he says, “who would not exult that you have gone forth not to a simple but to a [Col. 0922C] double conflict,” etc.? “You are monks in virtues, soldiers in deeds.”]

Where bodily strength alone stoutly resists a bodily enemy, I judge this neither so extraordinary as to be uncommon. And when war is declared by strength of spirit against vices or demons, I would not call this miraculous either, though it is praiseworthy, since the world is seen to be full of monks. But when each of the twofold persons is powerfully girded with his own sword and nobly distinguished by his own belt, who would not judge this worthy of all admiration, since it is plainly so unusual? Surely that soldier is fearless and secure on every side who, as his body is clothed in iron, so his soul is clothed in the breastplate of faith. Fortified, indeed, with both kinds of arms, he fears neither demon nor human being. Nor does he dread death, since he desires to die. For what can he fear, whether living or dying, whose life is Christ and whose death is gain? He stands confidently and willingly for Christ; yet he desires more earnestly to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is better. Go forth, therefore, in security, soldiers, and with undaunted spirit drive back the enemies of Christ’s cross, certain that neither death nor life can separate you from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus; repeating indeed with yourselves in every danger: “Whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. 14:8). How gloriously victors return from battle! How blessedly martyrs die in battle! Rejoice, brave athlete, if you live and conquer in the Lord; but rejoice and glory still more if you die and are joined to the Lord. Life is indeed fruitful and victory glorious; but holy death is rightly preferred to either. For if those who die in the Lord are blessed, how much more those who die for the Lord?

2. Indeed, whether one dies in bed or in war, the death of his saints will without doubt be precious in the sight of the Lord. But in so great a war it is surely more precious insofar as it is more glorious. O secure life, where conscience is pure! O secure life, I say, where death is awaited without fear—indeed desired with sweetness—and received with devotion! O truly holy and safe knighthood, altogether free from that double danger in which that class of men is accustomed frequently to be imperiled, provided only that Christ is not the cause for which they fight. For whenever you who pursue worldly military service engage in battle, there is every reason to fear that either you may kill your enemy in body while you yourself are killed in soul, or perhaps that you may be killed by him both in body and in soul. For a Christian’s danger or victory is assessed from the disposition of the heart, not from the outcome of the war. If the cause of the combatant is good, the result of the fight cannot be an evil result; just as the end will not be judged good where no good cause and no right intention have preceded it. If, while intending to kill another, it happens that you are instead killed, you die a murderer. But if you prevail and perhaps kill a human being with the intention of conquering or avenging yourself, you live as a murderer. Yet it is not advantageous, whether dead or alive, victor or defeated, to be a murderer. It is an unhappy victory when, by overcoming a person, you are overcome by vice. And if anger or pride rules you, you glory in vain over a defeated person.

There is, however, one who kills a person neither from zeal for vengeance nor from the arrogance of conquest, but solely as a means of escape. Yet I would not call even this a good victory, since, of two evils, to die in body is lighter than to die in soul.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Bernard therefore judges with Augustine and Ambrose that, without loss to the soul, it is not permissible for a person to kill an assailant while defending himself. Compare *On Precept and Dispensation*, no. 13. Notable on this subject is Letter 60 of Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, concerning a priest who had killed a robber. The passage from Ambrose is in Book III of *On Duties*, chapter 4; those of Augustine are in Book I of *On Free Choice of the Will*, chapter 5, and Book 22 of *Against Faustus*, chapter 74, as well as in the letter [Col. 0924D] to Publicola.]

It is not, however, because the body is killed that the soul also dies; rather, “the soul that sins, it shall die.”

## CHAPTER II. On worldly knighthood

[Col. 0923B]

3. What, then, is the end or fruit of this worldly—not to say military service, but evil service—if both the killer sins mortally and the slain person perishes eternally? For, to use the Apostle’s words, “He who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit” (1 Cor. 9:10). What astonishing error, then, O soldiers, what intolerable madness is this: to serve in arms at such expense and labor, with no wages except death or crime? You cover horses in silks and put over your coats of mail I know not what dangling little cloths; you decorate lances, shields, and saddles; you adorn bridles and spurs with gold, silver, and gems.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] This is forbidden in chapter 38 of the Rule of the Templars: “Let there be no covering on shields and lances, on surcoats and lances,” etc. The same Rule rejects gold and silver on bridles and spurs in chapter 37.]

And with such pomp you rush toward death in shameful frenzy and impudent folly. Are these military insignia, or rather feminine ornaments? Will an enemy’s sword perhaps reverence gold, spare gems, or be unable to pierce silk? Finally, as you yourselves experience more often and more surely, three things are especially necessary to a combatant: namely, that a vigorous, skillful soldier be watchful in preserving himself, unencumbered in moving about, and ready to strike. You, on the contrary, after a womanly fashion nourish your hair as a burden to your eyes; with long and flowing shirts you entangle your own footsteps; and you bury delicate, tender hands in wide, hanging sleeves. Over and above all this is the fact that the cause for which such a perilous military service is undertaken is one that terrifies the armed man’s conscience more: namely, a cause wholly slight and frivolous. Certainly nothing else among you moves wars and raises quarrels except either the motion of irrational anger, the desire for empty glory, or greed for some earthly possession. For such causes it is safe neither to kill nor to fall.

## CHAPTER III. On the Soldiers of Christ

[Col. 0924A]

4. But the soldiers of Christ fight the battles of their Lord in safety, fearing neither sin from the slaughter of enemies nor danger from their own death; since death, whether endured or inflicted for Christ, has no guilt and merits very great glory.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] Hence John of Salisbury, speaking of the brethren of the Temple in *Polycraticus*, Book 7, chapter 21, says: “Almost alone among men, they wage lawful wars.”]

For in the one case a man is gained for Christ, and in the other Christ himself is gained: he willingly accepts the enemy’s death as vengeance, and more willingly gives himself to the soldier as consolation. The soldier of Christ kills in safety; he dies in still greater safety. He benefits himself when he dies; he benefits Christ when he kills. For not without cause does he bear the sword. He is God’s minister, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Indeed, when he kills an evildoer, he is not a murderer but, so to speak, an “evil-killer” (*malicida*), and is plainly regarded as Christ’s avenger upon those who do evil and as defender of Christians. But when he himself is killed, he is understood not to have perished but to have arrived. Thus the death he inflicts is Christ’s gain; the death he receives is his own gain. In the death of a pagan the Christian glories, because Christ is glorified; in the death of a Christian the King’s generosity is revealed, when the soldier is brought forth to receive his reward. Concerning the former, “the righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance.” Of the latter a person will say: “Surely there is fruit for the righteous; surely there is a God judging them on earth” (Ps. 57:12).

Indeed, pagans ought not to be killed if they could in some other way be restrained from excessive assault or oppression of the faithful. But now it is better that they be killed than that the rod of sinners should be left over the lot of the righteous, lest perhaps the righteous stretch out their hands to iniquity.

5. What then? If it is never lawful for a Christian to strike with the sword, why did the herald of the Savior command soldiers to be content with their wages (Luke 3:14), rather than forbid them all military service? But if, as is true, it is lawful for all who have been divinely appointed precisely for this task and have professed nothing better—by whose hands and strength, I ask, more fittingly than by those through whom Zion, the city of our strength, is held as a defense for us all? Thus, when the transgressors of the divine law have been driven out, the righteous nation that keeps truth may enter in safety. Therefore let the nations that desire war be scattered in security; let those who trouble us be cut off; and let all workers of iniquity be destroyed from the city of the Lord, those who are eager to seize the inestimable riches of the Christian people stored in Jerusalem, to defile holy things, and to possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance. Let both swords of the faithful be drawn upon the necks of the enemies, to destroy every height raised against the knowledge of God—which is the faith of Christians—lest the nations ever say, “Where is their God?” (Ps. 113:2).

[Note: [Col. 0925D] That is, the spiritual and the material sword; on both, see Letter 256 and Book IV of *On Consideration*, chapter 3, no. 7.]

6. When these have been expelled, he himself will return to his inheritance and his house, concerning which he said angrily in the Gospel: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23:38); and through the prophet he laments: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance” (Jer. 12:7). And that prophetic utterance will be fulfilled: “The Lord has redeemed his people and delivered them; and they shall come and rejoice upon Mount Zion and delight in the good things of the Lord” (Jer. 31:11–12). Rejoice, Jerusalem, and now know the time of your visitation. Rejoice and praise together, desolate Jerusalem, because the Lord has comforted his people and redeemed Jerusalem; the Lord has made bare his holy arm before the eyes of all nations. Virgin Israel, you had fallen, and there was no one to lift you up. Rise now; shake yourself from the dust, virgin captive daughter of Zion. Rise, I say, stand on high, and see the joy that comes to you from your God. You shall no longer be called forsaken, and your land shall no more be called desolate, because the Lord has taken pleasure in you and your land shall be inhabited. Lift up your eyes all around and see: all these have gathered; they have come to you. This help has been sent to you from the Holy One. Through these men, beyond all doubt, that ancient promise is now being fulfilled for you: “I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from generation to generation; you shall suck the milk of nations and nurse at the breasts of kings” (Isa. 60:15–16); and again: “As a mother comforts her children, so I will comfort you, and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted” (Isa. 66:13).

Do you see by how frequent a testimony of the ancients this new knighthood is approved, and how, as we have heard, so we see in the city of the Lord of hosts? Provided, indeed, that the literal interpretation does not prejudice spiritual meanings, so as to prevent us from hoping eternally for whatever we draw from the words of the Prophets as signifying this present time; lest, through what is seen, what is believed should vanish, the poverty of the thing itself diminish the riches of hope, and the testimony of present things become the nullification of future things. Otherwise, the temporal glory of the earthly city does not destroy heavenly goods, but confirms them—provided that we do not doubt at all that this city bears the figure of that one which is in heaven and is our mother.

## CHAPTER IV. On the manner of life of the Soldiers of Christ

7. But now, for the imitation or the shame of our soldiers, who devote their property and life not to God at all but to the devil, let us briefly describe how Christ’s soldiers conduct themselves in war and at home, so that it may be clear how greatly the knighthood of God and that of the world differ from one another. First, discipline is lacking in neither condition, and obedience is by no means despised; for, Scripture testifies, “an undisciplined son shall perish” (Ecclus. 22:3), and “to resist is the sin of divination, and unwillingness to obey is as the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15:23). They go and return at the command of the one set over them; they wear what he has given them, and receive neither clothing nor food from elsewhere. In food and clothing every superfluity is avoided, and necessity alone is provided for. They live plainly in common, in a pleasant and sober fellowship, without wives and without children. And, lest anything be lacking from evangelical perfection, they live without any private property, of one way of life in one house, careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. You might say that the whole multitude has one heart and one soul: thus each person strives not at all to follow his own will, but rather to obey the commander. At no time do they sit idle or wander about inquisitively. Rather, whenever they do not go forth—which happens rarely—lest they eat bread for nothing, they mend torn arms or clothing, repair what is worn out, put in order what is disordered, and do whatever the master’s will and common necessity require. No person is treated with partiality among them: deference is given to the better man, not the nobler-born. They outdo one another in showing honor; they bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. An insolent word, a useless action, immoderate laughter, even a slight murmur or whisper, when discovered, is never left uncorrected. They detest chess and dice.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] In some writings, *cacos*; commonly *échecs* [chess]. This game is so called either from the Arabic or Persian word *scach*, meaning “king,” which is the principal piece in the game; or from the German *schach*, that is, “robber” or “little robber,” whence “the game of little robbers.” On this see Du Cange’s *Glossary* and John of Salisbury’s *Polycraticus*, Book I, chapter 5.]

They abhor hunting and do not delight, as is customary, in that playful capture of birds.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] This is clear from chapters 46 and 47 of the Rule. In the former, hunting with a bird is forbidden; in the latter, striking a wild beast with bow or crossbow.]

They reject and abominate mimes, magicians, storytellers, vulgar songs, and theatrical spectacles as vanities and false insanities. They cut their hair, knowing from the Apostle that it is dishonorable for a man to grow it long.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] A statute on this matter is found in chapters 28 and 29 of the Rule of the Templars.]

They are never well groomed, rarely washed; rather, with neglected hair they are rough, foul with dust, darkened by mail and heat.

8. When battle is imminent, they arm themselves inwardly with faith and outwardly with iron, not with gold, so that armed rather than adorned they may strike fear into their enemies, not provoke their greed. They desire horses that are strong and swift, but not brightly colored or richly caparisoned; for they think of battle, not display, of victory but not glory, and strive to inspire fear rather than admiration. Further, they do not arrange themselves rashly, turbulently, or with headlong impetuosity born of levity, but deliberately and with every caution and foresight, setting themselves in order and drawing up their battle line, as is written of the fathers. They go forth to war as true Israelites, yet peaceable men.

But when they have come to the contest, then at last putting aside their former gentleness, as if they said: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and pine away because of your enemies?” (Ps. 138:21), they rush upon their adversaries and regard their enemies as sheep. Though very few in number, they fear neither savage barbarity nor a multitudinous host. For they know not to presume upon their own strength, but to hope for victory from the power of the Lord of hosts. They trust that it is easy for him, according to the saying of the Maccabee, to shut up many in the hands of few, and that before the God of heaven there is no difference between saving by many and by few; “for victory in war does not lie in the multitude of an army, but strength is from heaven” (1 Macc. 3:18–19). They have experienced this very often, so that frequently one has seemed to pursue a thousand and two to put ten thousand to flight.

Thus, in a wonderful and singular way, they are seen to be gentler than lambs and fiercer than lions, so that I am almost uncertain whether they should rather be called monks or soldiers—unless perhaps I should more fittingly call them both, since neither is found lacking in them: neither the monk’s gentleness nor the soldier’s courage. What can be said of this except: “This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes”? God has chosen such men for himself and gathered from the ends of the earth ministers from among the bravest of Israel, that they may vigilantly and faithfully guard the true bed of Solomon, namely the sacred sepulcher, all holding swords and most skilled [or: bravest] in war.

## CHAPTER V. On the Temple

[Col. 0927C]

9. There is, moreover, a temple in Jerusalem in which they live together. In structure it is indeed inferior to that ancient and most famous temple of Solomon, but not inferior in glory. For the whole magnificence of the latter consisted in perishable gold and silver, in the squared arrangement of stones and the variety of woods; but all the beauty and pleasing splendor of this one consists in the devout religious life and the most orderly conduct of its inhabitants. The former was admirable for its various colors; this one is venerable for its diverse virtues and holy deeds. “Holiness befits the house of God” (Ps. 92:5), who delights not so much in polished marbles as in well-ordered morals, and loves pure minds more than gilded walls.

[Note: [Col. 0927] Thus the Colbert manuscript; others read: “he loves pure minds more than walls overlaid with gold.”]

Yet the face of this temple too is adorned—but with arms, not gems. Instead of the ancient golden crowns, the wall is covered with shields hanging round about; instead of lamps, censers, and vessels, the house is fortified everywhere with bridles, saddles, and lances. All these things plainly demonstrate that the soldiers burn with the same zeal for God’s house as their Commander of old, who, most vehemently inflamed, entered the temple with that holy armed hand—yet not with iron, but with a whip which he had made of cords [or: ropes]—drove out the merchants, poured out the money-changers’ coins, and overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2:15). He judged it altogether unworthy that a house of prayer should be defiled [or: infested] by such worldly commerce.

Moved, therefore, by the example of their King, the devout army judges it far more unworthy and intolerable that holy things should be defiled by unbelievers than that they should be profaned by merchants. Having driven from that holy house, and from the other sacred places, every filthy and tyrannical rage of unbelief, they remain there with horses and arms; and day and night they are occupied in it with offices both honorable and useful. They vie in honoring God’s temple with diligent and sincere services, continually offering there in devotion—not, indeed, according to the ancient rite, the flesh of beasts, but truly peace-offerings: brotherly love, devoted submission, voluntary poverty.

[Col. 0928B] 10. These things are done in Jerusalem, and the world is stirred. The islands hear, and peoples from afar give heed; and they pour forth from East and West like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations, and like the rush of a river making glad the city of God. What is more pleasant to see and more beneficial in its effect is that, amid so great a multitude of people, you see very few flocking there except criminals and wicked persons, robbers and sacrilegious people, murderers, perjurers, and adulterers. From their departure, surely, a kind of twofold good results, and so joy is doubled: since by their departure they gladden their own people, while by their arrival they gladden those whom they hasten to help. For they are useful in both places: not only in protecting these people, but also in ceasing now to oppress the others.

Thus Egypt rejoices at their departure, while Mount Zion nonetheless rejoices in their protection and the daughters of Judah exult. The former rightly boasts that it is delivered from their hand; the latter rather boasts that it is delivered by their hand. Egypt gladly loses its most cruel ravagers; Zion joyfully receives its most faithful defenders. What most sweetly consoles the latter, equally and most beneficially desolates the former. Thus Christ knows how to take vengeance on his enemies: not only from them, but also through them, he is often accustomed to triumph all the more gloriously as he triumphs more powerfully. It is delightful indeed and fitting that he who long endured them as attackers should now begin to have them as defenders, making an enemy into a soldier—as once he made Saul the persecutor into Paul the preacher (Acts 9). Therefore I do not wonder if that heavenly court also, according to the Savior’s testimony, rejoices more over one sinner doing penance than over many righteous persons who have no need of repentance, since the conversion of a sinful and malignant person surely benefits to the degree that his former manner of life had harmed.

11. Hail, then, holy city, which the Most High himself sanctified as the dwelling place for himself, so that so great a generation might be saved in you and through you. Hail, city of the great King, from which new and joyful miracles for the world have almost never been absent from the beginning. Hail, mistress of nations, ruler of provinces, possession of Patriarchs, mother of Prophets and Apostles, initiator of faith, glory of the Christian people. God has always allowed you to be assailed from the beginning, in order that strong men might find in you an occasion both for virtue and salvation.

Hail, land of promise, which once flowed with milk and honey only for your inhabitants, but now offers remedies of salvation and the nourishment of life to the whole world. Land, I say, good and most excellent, which, receiving in your most fruitful bosom the heavenly grain from the ark of the Father’s heart, have brought forth from the heavenly seed such abundant harvests of martyrs; and which, from the remaining stock of all the faithful, as fertile soil have likewise produced over all the earth fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. Thus those who have seen you, most pleasantly satisfied and most richly nourished from the great abundance of your sweetness, everywhere pour forth the memory of your abundant delights; and to those who have not seen you they proclaim, even to the end of the earth, the magnificence of your glory and recount the wonders done in you. Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God; but now, from the delights with which you abound, let us also bring forth a few things for the praise and glory of your name.

## CHAPTER VI. On Bethlehem

[Note: [Col. 0929] From this point to the end of the treatise, he draws mystical meanings from the holy places.]

12. Before all else, for the refreshment of holy souls, you possess Bethlehem, the house of bread, in which he who had descended [or: descends] from heaven first appeared as living bread, born of the Virgin. There the manger is shown to devout beasts, and in the manger hay from the virginal meadow, so that even thus the ox may know its owner and the ass the manger of its Lord. For all flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay (Isa. 40:6). Since, however, through not understanding the honor in which he was made, man “was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13), the Word, the bread of angels, became fodder for beasts, so that he who has wholly unlearned to feed on the bread of the Word may have the hay of flesh to chew—until, restored through the God-man to his former dignity and changed again from a beast into a human being, he can say with Paul: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him thus no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

I do not think, indeed, that anyone can truly say this unless he has first heard with Peter from the mouth of Truth those further words: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life; but the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64). Otherwise, one who finds life in Christ’s words no longer seeks flesh, and belongs among the blessed who “have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29). A cup of milk is needed only by a little child, and fodder of hay only, surely, by a beast. But the person who does not stumble in word is a perfect man, plainly fit to eat solid food; and though he eats the bread of the Word in the sweat of his brow, he does so without stumbling. He also speaks God’s wisdom safely and without scandal only among the perfect, comparing spiritual things with spiritual; yet, in regard to infants or beasts, he is careful to set forth, according to their capacity, only Jesus Christ—and him crucified. Nevertheless, the one and same food from heavenly pastures is sweetly chewed by the beast and eaten by the human being, providing strength to the adult and nourishment to the child.

## CHAPTER VII. On Nazareth

13. Nazareth is also seen, which is interpreted “flower.” There God, who was born in Bethlehem, was nourished as fruit growing together in a flower, so that the fragrance of the flower might precede the taste of the fruit, and the holy liquid might flow from the nostrils of the Prophets into the mouths of the Apostles; thus refreshing Christians with substantial taste, while the Jews were content with a faint scent.

Nathanael, however, had perceived that this flower breathed a fragrance sweeter than all spices. Thus he said: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” But, not content with fragrance alone, he followed Philip, who answered him, “Come and see” (John 1:46). Indeed, delighted by a copious sprinkling of that wondrous sweetness, and having through a draught of the good fragrance become desirous of taste, he hastened without delay, led by the scent itself, to reach the fruit: wishing to experience more fully what he had faintly sensed, and to taste in presence what he had smelled in absence.

Let us look also at Isaac’s sense of smell, lest perhaps it may signify something relating to the very matters now in hand. Scripture speaks of him thus: “And as soon as he perceived the fragrance of his garments”—undoubtedly Jacob’s—“he said: ‘Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed’” (Gen. 27:27). He perceived the fragrance of the garment but did not recognize the presence of the wearer. Delighted outwardly by the smell of the garment alone, as though by that of a flower, he did not taste the sweetness of the inward fruit, since he remained deprived both of knowledge of the chosen son and of the sacrament.

What does this mean? The garment of the Spirit is surely the letter and the flesh of the Word. But even now the Jew does not know the Word in flesh, or divinity in the human being; nor does he discern the spiritual meaning beneath the covering of the letter. Feeling externally the skin of the goat, which represented the likeness of the greater—that is, the first and ancient—sinner, he does not reach naked truth. He appeared not indeed in sinful flesh, but “in the likeness of sinful flesh,” since he came not to commit sin but to take it away, for the reason which he himself did not conceal: “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

Deceived, then, by this likeness, the Prophet is blind to this day: he blesses him whom he does not know, since he is ignorant in miracles of the one whom he reads in books; and though he handles him with his own hands—binding, scourging, striking him with the fist—he nevertheless does not understand him even as rising again [or: by rising again]. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Let us run through the remaining holy places in brief discourse, and, if not all of them, at least some; for, since we cannot admire them one by one, we wish at least briefly to recall the more notable among them.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Mount of Olives and the Valley of Jehoshaphat

14. One ascends the Mount of Olives and descends into the Valley of Jehoshaphat, so that you may contemplate the riches of divine mercy without in any way concealing from yourself the terror of judgment. For though in his many mercies he is abundant in forgiveness, his judgments are nevertheless a great deep, by which he is known to be utterly terrifying over the children of men. David, indeed, who points out the Mount of Olives by saying, “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord; how you have multiplied your mercy, O God,” also recalls the valley of judgment in the same psalm, saying: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35:7, 12). He confesses that he wholly dreads its precipice when, praying in another psalm, he says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118:120).

The proud person falls and is shattered in this valley; the humble person descends and is not endangered at all. The proud person excuses his sin; the humble person accuses it, knowing that God does not judge twice concerning the same thing, and that if we judged ourselves, we would surely not be judged (1 Cor. 11:31).

15. But the proud person, not considering how terrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God, easily bursts out into wicked words, making excuses for excuses in sins. Truly great wickedness: not to have mercy on oneself, to repel from oneself the sole remedy after sin, namely confession, to wrap fire in one’s bosom rather than shake it out, and not to heed the counsel of Wisdom, which says: “Have mercy on your soul by pleasing God” (Ecclus. 30:24). Therefore, one who is evil to himself, to whom is he good?

“Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12:31)—that is, from your heart, if by humbling yourself you judge yourself. The judgment of heaven will come when he himself “shall call heaven from above, and the earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 49:4). In that judgment you must surely fear being cast out with him and his angels, if you are found unjudged. Otherwise, the spiritual person, who judges all things, is himself judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15). Therefore judgment begins with the house of God, so that when the Judge comes he may find his own people, whom he knows, already judged, and may then have nothing left to judge in them—when those are to be judged who “are not in the labor of men and are not scourged with men” (Ps. 72:5).

## CHAPTER IX. On the Jordan

16. With what joyful embrace does the Jordan receive Christians, since it boasts that it was consecrated by Christ’s baptism! That Syrian leper plainly lied when he preferred I know not what waters of Damascus to the waters of Israel (4 Kings 5:12), since the Jordan’s devoted service to God has so often been proved: whether in the time of Elijah, or in the time of Elisha (4 Kings 2), or, to recall something more ancient, when it wonderfully checked its current and provided a dry passage through itself for Joshua and all the people together (Josh. 3).

Finally, what river is more eminent than this one, which the Trinity itself consecrated by a kind of manifest presence? The Father was heard, the Holy Spirit was seen, and the Son was baptized. Therefore, by Christ’s command, the whole faithful people also experience in soul the very power which Naaman, advised by the prophet, experienced in his body (4 Kings 5:14).

## CHAPTER X. On the Place of Calvary

17. One also goes out to the place of Calvary, where the true Elisha, mocked by senseless children, imparted eternal laughter to his own children, of whom he says: “Behold, I and my children whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. 8:18). Good children, whom the Psalmist, in contrast with those malignant ones, rouses to praise, saying: “Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 112:1), so that praise might be perfected in the mouth of holy infants and sucklings—the praise that had failed in the mouth of the envious, those of whom he complains: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2).

Thus our bald one ascended the cross, exposed to the world for the world; and, with face unveiled and brow uncovered, making purification for sins, he was no more ashamed of the disgrace of a shameful and cruel death than he shrank from its punishment, in order to rescue us from everlasting reproach and restore us to glory. Nor is this surprising. For what would he blush at, he who washed us from sins not as water does, cleansing while retaining impurity, but as a ray of sunlight, drying and preserving purity? For the wisdom of God reaches everywhere because of its purity.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Sepulcher
18. Among holy and desirable places, the sepulchre holds, as it were, a certain primacy; and one senses I know not what greater devotion where the dead man rested than where he lived and moved about; and the memory of death moves one to piety more than the memory of life. I suppose that the former appears harsher, the latter sweeter; and that the repose of sleep is more soothing to human weakness than the labor of active life, and the security of death than the uprightness of life. [Col. 0932D] Christ’s life has been for me a rule of living; his death, redemption from death. The one instructed life; the other destroyed death. His life was indeed laborious, but his death precious; yet both were altogether necessary. For what good could Christ’s death do one living wickedly, or his life one dying damnably? Does Christ’s death even now free from eternal death those who live wickedly unto death? Or did the holiness of life of the holy fathers who died before Christ free them? As it is written: “What man shall live and not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” (Ps. 88:49 [Vulgate])?

Therefore, since both were equally necessary for us—to live piously and to die securely—by living he taught us to live, and by dying he made death secure: for he died as one who was to rise again, and gave the dying the hope of rising. [Col. 0933A] But he added also a third benefit, when he forgave sins, without which the other things certainly had no efficacy. For what could any uprightness or length of life avail, so far as true and supreme blessedness is concerned, one who remained bound even by original sin alone? Sin indeed came first, so that death might follow; and if man had avoided sin, he would never have tasted death.

19. Thus by sinning he lost life and found death; for God had so foretold, [Col. 0933B] and it was certainly just that, if man sinned, he should die. What could be more just than to receive retribution in kind? God is the life of the soul; the soul is the life of the body. By voluntarily sinning, he voluntarily lost the power of living; unwillingly, let him lose the power of giving life also. Of his own accord he rejected life when he refused to live; let him not be able to give it to whom or in whatever measure he wishes. The soul refused to be ruled by God: let it be unable to rule the body. If it does not obey its superior, why should it command its inferior? The Creator found his creature rebellious against himself: let the soul find its handmaid rebellious against itself. Man was found a transgressor of the divine law: let him likewise find another law in his members, resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive to the law of sin (Rom. 7:23).

Moreover, sin, as Scripture says, separates between us [Col. 0933C] and God (Isa. 59:2); therefore let death also separate between our body and us. The soul could not be divided from God except by sinning, nor the body from the soul except by dying. What harsher penalty, then, could it suffer than to endure from its subject precisely what it had presumed to do against its Author? Nothing, indeed, is more fitting than that death should work death: spiritual death, bodily death; culpable death, penal death; voluntary death, necessary death.

20. Therefore, when man had been condemned to this twofold death according to each nature—the one spiritual and voluntary, the other bodily and necessary—God-man mercifully and powerfully met both by his one bodily and voluntary death; and by that one death of his condemned both deaths of ours. Rightly so: for of our two deaths, one was reckoned to us [Col. 0933D] as the due of guilt, the other as the debt of punishment; but he, taking punishment and knowing no guilt, by dying willingly and only in the body, earned for us both life and righteousness. Otherwise, if he had not suffered bodily, he would not have paid the debt; if he had not died voluntarily, that death would have had no merit. But now, if, as has been said, sin is the merit earning death, and death the debt owed for sin, then with Christ forgiving sin and dying for sinners, there is plainly no longer any merit, and the debt has been paid.

21. But how do we know that Christ can forgive sins? Beyond doubt from this: that he is God, and can do whatever he wills. But whence do we know that he is God? His miracles prove it. For he performs works which no other could perform—to say nothing of the oracles of the prophets, [Col. 0934A] and likewise the testimony of the Father’s voice descending from heaven upon him from the majestic glory. “If God is for us, who is against us?” God who justifies—who is he that condemns? If he is the one, and no other, to whom we daily confess, saying, “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50:6 [Vulgate]), who can better forgive—or rather, who else can forgive—that which is sin against him? Or how can he be unable, who is able to do all things? In short, I can, if I wish, forgive what is done wrong against me; and shall God be unable to forgive what is committed against himself? Therefore, since the Almighty can forgive sins, and he alone can forgive them, because sin is against him alone, blessed indeed is the one to whom he does not impute sin. Thus we know that Christ was able, by the power of his divinity, to remit sins.

22. Further, who can doubt his will? He who both put on our flesh and underwent death—do you suppose that he will withhold his righteousness from us? [Col. 0934B] Having voluntarily become incarnate, voluntarily suffered, voluntarily been crucified, will he keep righteousness for himself alone? What he was able to do by his divinity, then, he was shown by his humanity also to have willed. But again, whence are we confident that he took away death? Clearly from this: he endured it, though he had not deserved it. For on what grounds could that be demanded of us again which he has already paid for us? He took away the merit of sin by giving us his righteousness; he paid the debt of death and restored life. Thus life returns when death has died, just as righteousness returns when sin has been removed. Death is put to flight in Christ’s death, and Christ’s righteousness is imputed to us.

But how could one who was God die? Because he was also man. Yet how could the death of that man avail for another? Because he was righteous. Certainly, since he was man, he could die; since he was righteous, he ought not to die without cause. A sinner cannot pay the debt of death for another sinner, since each dies for himself. But one who has no need to die for himself—should he not die for another, and not in vain? Indeed, the more undeservedly one dies who did not merit death, the more justly does the one for whom he dies live.

23. “But,” you ask, “what justice is there in an innocent man dying for the ungodly?” It is not justice, but mercy. If it were justice, he would die not gratuitously but as a debt. If as a debt, then he himself would die; but the one for whom he died would not live. Yet if it is not justice, it is nevertheless not contrary to justice. Otherwise, no one could be both just and merciful at once. [Col. 0934D] But even if a righteous man can justly satisfy for a sinner without acting unjustly, how can one do so for many? For it would seem sufficient for justice if one, dying for one, restored life. Let the Apostle answer this:

“For as through the trespass of one man [judgment came] upon all men unto condemnation, so also through the righteousness of one [man it came] upon all men unto justification of life. For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. 5:18–19).

But perhaps one man could restore righteousness to many, yet could not restore life. “Through one man,” he says, “came death, and through one man life. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22). [Col. 0935A] What then? One man sinned, and all are held guilty; and shall the innocence of one be reckoned to only one [variant: to one innocent person]? The sin of one worked death for all, and the righteousness of one will restore life to only one? Has God’s justice been more powerful to condemn than to restore? Or could Adam accomplish more in evil than Christ in good? Shall Adam’s sin be imputed to me, while Christ’s righteousness does not belong to me? Did that man’s disobedience destroy me, while this man’s obedience will not benefit me?

24. “But,” you say, “we all rightly contract Adam’s offence, because we all sinned in him: for when he sinned, we were in him, and we are born from his flesh through the lust of the flesh.” Yet we are born much more genuinely from God according to the spirit than from Adam according to the flesh; according to that spirit we were also in Christ long before we were in Adam according to the flesh—if indeed we confidently count ourselves among those of whom the Apostle says: “He chose us in him” (that is, doubtless, the Father in the Son) “before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4).

[Col. 0935B] The evangelist John also bears witness that they are born of God, saying: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John 1:13). Likewise he says in his Epistle: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, because the heavenly generation preserves him” (1 John 3:9). “But,” you say, “carnal desire bears witness to the propagation of the flesh; and the sin which we feel in the flesh plainly proves that according to the flesh we descend from the flesh of a sinner.” Yet that spiritual generation is likewise felt—not in the flesh, indeed, but in the heart—by those only who can say with Paul: “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Cor. 2:16). In this they perceive that they have progressed so far that they too may say with all confidence: “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8:16); and: “But we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things granted to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12).

[Col. 0935C] Therefore, through the Spirit who is from God, charity has been poured out into our hearts, just as through the flesh which is from Adam the lust implanted in our members flows forth. And as this latter, which descends from the progenitor of bodies, never departs from the flesh during this mortal life, so the former, proceeding from the Father of spirits, never falls away from the intention of perfect children alone.

25. If, therefore, we are born of God and chosen in Christ, what justice is it that human and earthly generation should harm more than divine and heavenly generation can avail; that carnal succession should overcome God’s election, and that lust derived in time through flesh should set limits to his eternal purpose? Rather, if death came through one man, why should life not come much more through one man—and that man? And if in Adam we all die, why shall we not much more powerfully all be made alive in Christ? Finally, “the gift is not like the trespass. For judgment from one [trespass] was unto condemnation; but grace from many trespasses unto justification” (Rom. 5:15–16). [Col. 0936A] Therefore Christ was able to forgive sins because he is God; to die because he is man; by dying to pay the debt of death because he is righteous; and, being one, to suffice for all unto righteousness and life, since both sin and death proceeded from one to all.

26. Yet this also was altogether necessarily provided: that, death having been delayed, he deigned to live for a time among men, in order that by frequent and truthful utterances he might raise them to invisible things, establish faith by wonderful works, and instruct them by upright conduct. Thus God-man lived before men soberly, justly, and piously; spoke truth; worked wonders; suffered indignities. What then is lacking to us for salvation? Add also the grace of forgiveness of sins—that he forgives sins freely—and the work of our salvation is surely complete. [Col. 0936B] Nor need we fear that God lacks power to pardon sins, or that he who suffered—and suffered so greatly for sinners—lacks the will, provided that we are found diligently and worthily, as we ought, to imitate his examples, reverence his miracles, not disbelieve his teaching, and not prove ungrateful for his sufferings.

27. Therefore everything about Christ availed for us; everything was saving and necessary; nor did his weakness benefit us less than his majesty. For although by the power of his divinity he removed the yoke of sin by command, by the weakness of his flesh he shook the claims of death by dying. Hence the Apostle rightly says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1:25). [Col. 0936C] And that folly of his by which he pleased to save the world, in order to refute the world’s wisdom and confound the wise—namely, that, though he was in the form of God and equal with God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; that though rich, he became poor for our sake; from great became little, from lofty lowly, from powerful weak; that he hungered, thirsted, was weary on the journey, and endured the other things voluntarily, not from necessity—was not this particular folly of his for us a way of prudence, a pattern of righteousness, an example of holiness? For this reason the Apostle again says: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25).

Thus death delivered from death, life from error, and grace from sin. Death accomplished victory through its righteousness: because the righteous one, by paying what he had not taken, justly recovered what he had lost. [Col. 0936D] Life, for its part, fulfilled its office through wisdom, becoming for us a teaching and mirror of life and discipline. Grace, moreover, by that power of which it was said, forgave sins—the power by which he did everything whatever he willed. Therefore Christ’s death is the death of my death: for he died so that I might live. How indeed can one for whom Life dies fail henceforth to live? Or who, with Wisdom as guide, will now fear to go astray in the path of conduct or in the knowledge of things? Or by what means will one whom Righteousness absolves still be held guilty? In the Gospel he himself declares that he is Life, saying, “I am the life” (John 14:6). [Col. 0937A] The Apostle testifies to the other two, saying: “Who was made for us righteousness and wisdom from God the Father” (1 Cor. 1:30).

28. If, therefore, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed us from the law of sin and death, why do we still die and not immediately put on immortality? Certainly, in order that God’s truth may be fulfilled. Since God loves mercy and truth (Ps. 83:12 [Vulgate]), man must indeed die, because God foretold it; yet he must rise from death, lest God forget to show mercy. Thus, although death does not rule perpetually, it nevertheless remains in us for a time because of God’s truth; just as sin, although it no longer reigns in our mortal body, is not altogether absent from us. [Col. 0937B]

Accordingly Paul boasts that he has been freed in part from the law of sin and death; yet he complains in turn that in part he is nonetheless burdened by each law: whether when he cries wretchedly against sin, “I find another law in my members” (Rom. 6:23 [as cited]), and the rest; or when, groaning under a burden—doubtless the law of death—he awaits the redemption of his body (Rom. 8:23).

29. Whether, therefore, these thoughts or any others of this kind, according as each abounds in his own understanding in such matters, are suggested to Christian minds by the occasion of the sepulchre, I think no small sweetness of devotion is poured into one who views it close at hand; nor is there little profit in seeing with bodily eyes the bodily place of the Lord’s rest. Though now empty of the sacred limbs, it is nevertheless full of sacraments that are ours and exceedingly delightful. [Col. 0937C] Ours, I say, ours—if only we embrace as fervently as we hold without doubt what the Apostle says:

“For we were buried with him through Baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall likewise be in the likeness of his resurrection” (Rom. 6:4–5).

How sweet it is for pilgrims, after the weariness of a long journey, after the many dangers of land and sea, finally to rest where they recognize that their own Lord also rested! I think that, through joy, they no longer feel the labour of the road or count the expense burdensome; but, as though they had gained the reward of their toil or the prize of their course, [Col. 0937D] according to the saying of Scripture, “they rejoice exceedingly when they find the grave” (Job 3:22). Nor should it be thought that the sepulchre acquired this so celebrated name by chance or suddenly, or as by the fickle acclaim of popular favour, when Isaiah himself so plainly foretold this very thing so many ages before: “In that day,” he says, “the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples—to him the nations shall make petition, and his sepulchre shall be glorious” (Isa. 11:10). We therefore truly see fulfilled what we read as prophesied: new to the beholder, yet ancient to the reader; so that delight in its novelty is present without authority from antiquity being absent. And let this suffice concerning the sepulchre.

# Chapter XII. On Bethphage

30. What shall I say of Bethphage, the village of priests, which I had almost passed over, where both the sacrament of confession and the mystery of priestly ministry are contained? For Bethphage is interpreted “House of the Mouth.” [Col. 0938A] Now it is written: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30:14). Remember to have the word not in one only, but in both together. The word in the heart of the sinner works saving contrition; but the word in the mouth removes harmful shame, lest it hinder necessary confession. For Scripture says: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory” (Ecclus. 4:25).

Good is the shame by which you are ashamed to have sinned, or even to be sinning; and although perhaps every human judge is absent, you nevertheless reverence the divine gaze more shamefacedly than the human, by as much as you conceive God to be more truly pure [variant: more present] than man; and you regard him as more grievously offended by the sinner, since every sin is known to be farther removed from him. Such shame beyond doubt puts reproach to flight and prepares glory: for it either prevents sin altogether, or, if it has been committed, punishes it by repentance and expels it by confession—provided that this too is our glory, the testimony of our conscience.

But if someone is ashamed to confess even that by which he is pierced with compunction, such shame brings sin and loses the glory of conscience. For the evil which compunction strives to expel from the depth of the heart, foolish shame, by keeping the gateway of the lips shut, does not permit to go out; whereas he ought rather, after David’s example, to say: “I will not restrain my lips, Lord; you know” (Ps. 39:10 [Vulgate]). [Col. 0938B] Rebuking himself, I think, for such foolish and irrational shame, he says: “Because I kept silence, my bones grew old” (Ps. 31:3 [Vulgate]). Hence he also desires a door to be set around his lips (Ps. 140:3 [Vulgate]), so that he may know both how to open the gate of his mouth to confession and to close it against self-defence.

Finally, openly praying for this very thing, he asks it of the Lord, knowing indeed that “confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. 110:3 [Vulgate]). For not keeping silence about our wickedness and, equally, about the magnificence of divine goodness and power, is the great good of a twofold confession; but it is God’s gift. [Col. 0938C] Thus he says: “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4 [Vulgate]).

For this reason priests, as ministers of the word, must carefully and anxiously keep watch over both matters: namely, that they may apply the word of fear and contrition to the hearts of offenders with such moderation that they do not frighten them away from the word of confession; that they open hearts without shutting mouths. Yet neither should they absolve even one who is contrite unless they see him also confessing, since “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Otherwise, “from one dead, as though he were not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17:26). [Col. 0938D] Therefore whoever has the word in his mouth but not in his heart is either deceitful or empty; whoever has it in his heart but not in his mouth is either proud or fearful.

# Chapter XIII. On Bethany

31. Certainly, even though I am hurrying greatly, I ought not pass over in silence the house of obedience—Bethany, that is—the village of Mary and Martha, where Lazarus was raised; where, indeed, are commended the image of each life, God’s wonderful mercy toward sinners, and the power of obedience together with the fruits of repentance. Let it suffice to state briefly here that neither zeal for good action, nor the leisure of holy contemplation, nor the tears of the penitent can be acceptable outside Bethany to him who valued obedience so greatly that he preferred to lose life itself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death. [Col. 0939A]

These indeed are the riches which the prophetic word promises in the Lord’s name: “The Lord,” it says, “will comfort Zion, and will comfort all her ruins; and he will make her wilderness like delights, and her desert like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51:3). [Col. 0940A] Therefore these delights of the world, this heavenly treasure, this inheritance of the faithful peoples, are entrusted to you, beloved, to your faith, prudence, and courage. But you will be sufficient to guard the heavenly deposit safely and faithfully only if you presume nowhere upon your own prudence or strength, but everywhere upon God’s help alone, knowing that “a man shall not be strengthened by his own power,” and therefore saying with the prophet: “The Lord is my strength, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Ps. 17:2 [Vulgate]); and: “I will keep my strength for you, because God is my protector; my God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:10–11 [Vulgate]); and again: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9 [Vulgate]); [Col. 0940B] so that in all things he may be blessed who “teaches your hands for battle and your fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1 [Vulgate]).

# Saint Bernard, Abbot: Treatise on the Degrees of Humility and Pride

## Prefatory Notice to Opuscule VII

1. The following little book, entitled “On the Degrees of Humility,” is Bernard’s first fruit, and it is called his first both by Bernard himself and by the monk Geoffrey, writer of his Life. Bernard’s words are found in his eighteenth letter, to Cardinal Peter: “And that you may know what you ask, I know that I have written a little book entitled *On Humility*, and four homilies,” etc. This letter was written about the year 1127. Geoffrey, moreover, says in Book III, chapter 8, of his *Life*: “If anyone wishes to know how diligently, from the beginning, he examined and scrutinized himself, let him inspect his first work, *On the Degrees of Humility*.”

The holy man gives the reason for this title in the Censure or Retraction of the book, which he wished to have placed at the beginning of the work. For, since a certain expression, as though drawn from Holy Scripture, had escaped him, and he had advanced a certain exposition concerning the Seraphim which he had not read in the Fathers, once he discovered this he did not hesitate immediately to correct his own judgment. So great was the holy Doctor’s love of truth; so great his reverence for the Fathers. Here Manrique earnestly admonishes, by Bernard’s example, certain mystical and theological authors “who introduce, and even profess, novelties both in literal senses and in the loftiest meanings of sacred theology: whereas Bernard, endowed with divinely infused theology, regards with suspicion in a mystical sense what he had not received from the Fathers, and does not sufficiently trust what his own conscience has produced until he retracts the notion he had devised.”

Although elsewhere he allowed himself something more—namely, at the end of the homilies on *Missus est*, where he says: “If anything has been said beyond the Fathers which is not contrary to the Fathers, I think it ought not to displease either the Fathers or anyone else.” And in his seventy-seventh letter: “Certainly let each person abound securely in his own understanding where what he thinks conflicts neither with certain reason nor with authority not to be despised.” Thus the holy Doctor qualifies his earlier statement, condemning not so much new interpretations when guided by reason as the affected pursuit of them.

2. We infer the date of the writing of the book *On the Degrees of Humility* from the aforesaid eighteenth letter, written about 1127. For at that time Bernard had composed only four little works, together with some letters; and since the first of these works was *On Humility*, it must be said to have been written before 1125. Certainly it was addressed to Godfrey, Prior of Clairvaux and Bernard’s kinsman, afterwards bishop of Langres, to whom Letter 320 is addressed. Here, at no. 24, Bernard calls him “son, brother, companion, and participant in his progress.” In the Colbert manuscript, numbered 3964, this title of the book occurs after the books *On Consideration*: “Here begins the book of the same author, *On the Degrees of Humility*, addressed to Godfrey, then Prior at Clairvaux and afterwards bishop of the city of Langres.” The Retraction, which is prefixed to the book in four other manuscripts, is absent from this codex. It therefore seemed proper to restore it here; Horstius had relegated it to the end.

## Saint Bernard’s Retraction of the Treatise on the Degrees of Humility

In this little work, when I brought forward, in order to confirm and strengthen a certain proposition, the statement from the Gospel that the Lord said that he did not know the day of the last judgment (chapter 1, no. 1), I unwisely inserted something which I afterwards discovered is not written in the Gospel. For the text has only, “nor does the Son know”; but I, deceived rather than wishing to deceive—forgetful, indeed, of the wording but not of the sense—said: “Not even the Son of Man knows.” Consequently, when beginning the whole following discussion, I attempted to prove a true assertion from something I had not stated truthfully.

But because I discovered this error of mine long after the same little book had been published by me and copied by many people, and could not pursue the falsehood scattered throughout so many copies, I judged it necessary to have recourse to the remedy of confession. In another place also (chapter 10, no. 35), I proposed a certain opinion concerning the Seraphim which I had never heard and nowhere read. There, let my reader observe that I consequently said, with moderation, “I think,” wishing only that what I could not establish as certain from the Scriptures should be regarded as an opinion.

The very title, too, which is inscribed *On the Degrees of Humility*, may perhaps be criticized because degrees of pride rather than humility seem here to be distinguished and described. But this criticism will arise only from those who either understand or attend too little to the reason for the title, which I myself have taken care briefly to indicate at the end of the work.

## [First Part]

## Preface

Brother Godfrey, you asked me to expound for you in a fuller treatise the things I had said before the brethren concerning the degrees of humility. Wishing to satisfy your request as worthily as it deserved, yet fearing that I could not do so, I remembered the evangelical counsel and, I confess, did not dare begin before I had sat down and calculated whether the resources would suffice to complete it (Luke 14:28).
