But when charity had cast out the fear by which I feared being mocked for leaving the work unfinished, another, contrary fear entered: I began to fear more gravely the danger of glory if I completed it than the disgrace if I failed. [Col. 0941B]

Thus, placed as though at a crossroads between fear and charity, I long hesitated to which road I might safely entrust myself: fearing either that, while speaking usefully about humility, I myself might not be found humble; or that, while keeping silent humbly, I might become useless. And when I saw that neither road was safe, though I had to take one or the other, I chose rather to share with you whatever fruit of discourse I could than to secure myself alone in the harbour of silence. At the same time I had confidence that, if I should perhaps say anything you approve, your prayers would enable me not to be proud; while if—as I think more likely—I should achieve nothing worthy of your zeal, I could not be proud of nothing.

# Chapter I. Christ Is the Way of Humility by Which One Comes to Truth

1. Since I am to speak about the degrees of humility, which blessed Benedict proposes not to be counted but climbed (Rule, ch. 7), I shall first show, if I can, what must be reached by them, so that, on hearing the fruit of arrival, the labour of ascent may weigh less heavily. The Lord therefore sets before us the labour of the way and the reward of the labour: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). He calls humility the way which leads to truth. The one is labour; the other is the fruit of labour. [Col. 0941C]

“You ask, ‘How do I know that he spoke there of humility, when he said without qualification: “I am the way”?’” Hear more plainly: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Therefore he sets himself before us as an example of humility and a pattern of gentleness. If you imitate him, you do not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life (John 8:12). And what is the light of life except truth, which, enlightening every person coming into this world, shows where true life is? Therefore, after saying, “I am the way and the truth,” he added, “and the life,” as if he said: I am the way which leads to truth; I am the truth which promises life; I am the life which I give.

“For this,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (Matt. 17:3). Or thus, as though you said: I consider the way—that is, humility; I desire the fruit—truth. But what if the labour of the way is so great that I cannot reach the gain I seek? He answers: “I am the way,” that is, the provision by which you are sustained on the way. Thus he cries to those who are wandering and do not know the way: “I am the way”; to those who doubt and do not believe: “I am the truth”; to those already climbing but growing weary: “I am the life.” [Col. 0942A]

I think it has been sufficiently shown from the passage of the Gospel set forth that knowledge of truth is the fruit of humility. Receive another proof: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things”—doubtless the secrets of truth—“from the wise and prudent,” that is, the proud, “and have revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21), that is, to the humble. In this it appears that truth, which is hidden from the proud, is revealed to the humble.

2. A possible definition of humility is this: humility is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes lowly in his own eyes. This belongs to those who, having set ascents in their heart, advance from strength to strength—that is, from degree to degree—until they reach the summit of humility, where, as though placed in Zion, that is, in contemplation, they behold truth. “For,” he says, “the lawgiver will give a blessing” (Ps. 83:8 [Vulgate]): because he who gave the law will also give the blessing; that is, he who commanded humility will lead to truth. [Col. 0942C]

Who is this lawgiver except the Lord, sweet and upright, who “gave a law to those who transgress in the way” (Ps. 24:8 [Vulgate])? For those transgress in the way who abandon truth. But are they abandoned even thus by the gracious Lord? Therefore the gracious and upright Lord gives them the law, the way of humility, by which they may return to the knowledge of truth. Because he is gracious, he gives an opportunity to recover salvation; yet not without the discipline of law, because he is upright. He is gracious because he does not permit them to perish; upright because he does not forget to punish.

# Chapter II. By What Fruit the Degrees of Humility Are Climbed

3. Blessed Benedict therefore orders this law, by which one returns to truth, through twelve degrees: so that, as one comes to Christ through the ten commandments of the law and the twofold circumcision—whereby the number twelve is fulfilled—so, having climbed these twelve degrees, one may attain truth. [Col. 0943A] What else does the Lord, appearing supported above upon that ladder shown to Jacob as a figure of humility (Gen. 28:12–13), signify to us except that knowledge of truth is established at the summit of humility?

For the Lord looked down from the top of the ladder upon the children of men as Truth, whose eyes neither wish to deceive nor can be deceived, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. Does he not seem to cry to you from on high and say to those seeking him—for he knows who are his—“Pass over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled from my fruits” (Ecclus. 24:26); and again, “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28)? “Come,” he says. Where? To me, Truth. By what way? Through humility. With what fruit? “I will refresh you.” [Col. 0943B]

But what is this refreshment which Truth promises to those who climb and gives to those who arrive? Is it perhaps charity itself? For to charity, as blessed Benedict says, the monk will immediately come once all the degrees of humility have been ascended (Rule, ch. 7, degree 12). Charity is indeed sweet and delightful food: it relieves the weary, strengthens the weak, and gladdens the sorrowful. Finally, it makes the yoke of Truth sweet and its burden light.

4. Charity is good food. Standing in the middle of Solomon’s couch (Song of Songs 3:9–10), it refreshes the hungry by the fragrance of diverse virtues, like the perfume of spices of different kinds, and delights those whom it refreshes. There are set forth peace, patience, kindness, long-suffering, joy in the Holy Spirit; and, if there are any other offspring of truth or wisdom, they are prepared [variant: set forth] there. Humility too has its fare upon the same couch: namely, the bread of sorrow and the wine of compunction, which Truth first offers to beginners, to whom it is said: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Psalm 126:2). There also contemplation has, from the fat of wheat, the solid food of wisdom, together with the wine that gladdens the human heart; to these Truth invites the perfect, saying: “Eat, my friends, and drink; and be inebriated, my beloved” (Song of Songs 5:1). “He paved the middle with charity,” he says, “for the daughters of Jerusalem” (ibid. 2:10): that is, for imperfect souls, which, while they are still less able to receive that solid food, must meanwhile be nourished with the milk of charity instead of bread, and oil instead of wine. It is rightly described as being in the middle, because its sweetness is not yet available to beginners, being prevented by fear; nor is it enough for the perfect, because of the more abundant sweetness of contemplation. The former, still needing to be cleansed from the harmful humors of carnal pleasures by the most bitter draught of fear, have not yet tasted the sweetness of milk; the latter, already weaned from milk, delight more gloriously in feasting at the threshold of glory. It belongs only to those in the middle—that is, to those making progress—who have already tasted certain honeyed sips of charity, so that meanwhile they may be content with these in proportion to their tenderness.

5. Therefore the first food is that of humility: purifying, with bitterness; the second, that of charity: consoling, with sweetness; the third, that of contemplation: solid, with strength. Alas for me, Lord God of hosts! How long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant? Will you feed me with bread of tears, and give me tears to drink? Who will invite me to that middle and sweet banquet of charity, where the righteous feast in the presence of God and delight in joy, so that I may no longer speak in the bitterness of my soul and say to God, “Do not condemn me”; but, feasting on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, may joyfully sing in the ways of the Lord, “for great is the glory of the Lord”? Yet the way of humility is good: by it truth is sought, charity is acquired, and the offspring of wisdom are shared. For as Christ is the end of the Law, so the knowledge of truth is the perfection of humility. When Christ came, he brought grace; Truth gives charity to those to whom it becomes known. But it becomes known to the humble; therefore he gives grace to the humble.

## CHAPTER III. In what order the degrees of humility lead to the proposed prize of truth; and how Christ learned mercy through suffering.

6. I have said, as I could, with what fruit the degrees of humility ought to be ascended. I shall say, as I can, in what order they lead to the proposed prize of truth. But since the knowledge of truth itself also consists in three degrees, I shall briefly distinguish them, if I can, so that it may become clearer from this to which of the three degrees of truth the twelfth degree of humility reaches.

For we seek truth in ourselves, in our neighbors, and in its own nature: in ourselves, by judging ourselves; in our neighbors, by having compassion on their evils; in its own nature, by contemplating with a pure heart. Observe both the number and the order. Truth itself must first teach you that it ought to be sought first in neighbors rather than in its own nature. Afterwards you will learn why it ought to be sought first in yourself rather than in neighbors. For in the number of beatitudes which the Lord set out in his discourse, he placed the merciful before the pure in heart (Matthew 5:7–8). The merciful quickly apprehend truth in their neighbors, as they extend their own affections toward them; by charity they so conform themselves to others that they feel their goods and evils as their own. “They are weak with the weak, and burn with those who are scandalized” (2 Corinthians 11:29). They have learned to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). With the sight of the heart purified by this brotherly charity, they delight in contemplating truth in its own nature, for love of which they endure the evils of others.

But those who do not thus unite themselves with their brothers, but on the contrary either mock those who weep or disparage those who rejoice—because they do not feel in themselves what is in others, being not similarly affected—how can they apprehend truth in their neighbors? That common proverb suits them well: “The healthy person does not know what the sick person feels, nor the full person what the fasting person suffers.” And the sick have compassion on the sick, and the fasting upon the fasting, more intimately in proportion as they are nearer to them. For as pure truth is seen only by a pure heart, so a brother’s misery is more truly felt by a miserable heart. But in order to have a miserable heart over another’s misery, you must first recognize your own, so that you may find your neighbor’s mind in your own and learn from yourself how to help him: following the example of our Savior, who willed to suffer in order that he might know how to suffer with others; to become miserable, in order that he might learn to have mercy. Thus, as it is written of him, “He learned obedience from the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8), so also he learned mercy. Not that he did not know how to have mercy before, he whose mercy is from everlasting and unto everlasting; but what he knew by nature from eternity, he learned by temporal experience.

7. But perhaps it seems hard to you that I have said that Christ, the wisdom of God, learned mercy—as though he through whom all things were made had at some time been ignorant of anything among the things that are. This is especially so since the passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews which I cited to establish this may be understood in another, less apparently absurd sense: namely, that the word “learned” is not referred to the Head himself in his own person, but to his body, which is the Church. Thus the sense is: “He learned obedience from the things which he suffered”—that is, he learned obedience in his body from the things which he suffered in the Head.

For that death, that cross, the reproaches, spittle, and scourging which Christ our Head underwent—what were they to his body, that is, to us, except most noble lessons in obedience? “Christ,” Paul says, “became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). By what necessity? Let the apostle Peter answer: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow,” he says, “his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21)—that is, that you may imitate his obedience. Therefore, from the things which he suffered, we learn how much we, who are merely human, ought to endure for obedience, since he who was also God did not hesitate to die for it.

In this way, you say, it will not be unfitting to say that Christ learned obedience, mercy, or anything else in his body, provided that nothing which had previously been hidden from him is believed to have accrued to him in his own person over time. Thus he himself is both the one who teaches mercy or obedience and the one who learns, because Head and body are one Christ.

8. I do not deny that this understanding is correct. But from another passage in the same Epistle the former interpretation seems to be confirmed, where it says: “For he does not take hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham; therefore he had to be made like his brethren in all things, that he might become merciful” (Hebrews 2:16–17). I think these words must be referred to the Head in such a way that they cannot at all be fitted to the body. It is certainly said of the Word of God that he did not take hold of angels—that is, did not assume them into one person with himself—but the seed of Abraham. For it is not written, “The Word became an angel,” but “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14); and that flesh was of the flesh of Abraham, according to the promise first made to him.

Therefore, from that assumption of the seed, he had to be made like his brethren in all things: that is, it was fitting and necessary that, being passible like us, he should pass through every kind of our misery except sin. If you ask, by what necessity? “That he might become merciful,” it says. And you ask why this cannot rightly be referred to the body? But hear what follows shortly afterward: “For in that he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to aid those who are tempted” (Hebrews 2:18). I see no better understanding of these words than that he willed to suffer and be tempted, and to share all human miseries except sin—which is to be made like his brethren in all things—so that by experience he himself might learn to have mercy and compassion on those who suffer and are tempted in like manner.

9. By this experience, I do not say that he became wiser, but that he appeared nearer, so that the weak children of Adam—whom he did not disdain to make his own and call brethren (ibid. v. 11)—might not hesitate to entrust their infirmities to him: one who could heal them as God, willed to do so as one near to them, and knew them as one who had suffered the same things. Hence Isaiah calls him “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity” (Isaiah 53:3); and the Apostle says: “For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our infirmities.” Explaining whence he can do this, he adds: “But tempted in all things in like manner, without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

For blessed God, the blessed Son of God, in that form in which he did not deem equality with the Father a thing to be seized, was undoubtedly impassible before he emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). As he had not experienced misery or subjection, so he did not know mercy or obedience by experience. He knew indeed by nature, but not by experience. But when he was made lower not only than himself, but also a little lower than the angels—who are themselves impassible by grace, not by nature—even to that form in which he could suffer and be subjected, which he certainly could not be in his own form, then in suffering he experienced mercy and in subjection obedience.

Yet by this experience, as I have said, knowledge did not increase for him, but confidence increased for us: through this wretched kind of knowledge, he from whom we had wandered far became nearer to us. For when would we have dared to approach him while he remained in his impassibility? But now, at the Apostle’s urging, we are instructed to approach with confidence his throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16), since we know, as it is written elsewhere, that he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4), and do not doubt that, in what he himself suffered, he can sympathize with us.

10. Therefore it should not seem absurd if Christ is said not indeed to have begun to know something which he had once not known, but to have known mercy in one way eternally through divinity, and in another way to have learned it in time through flesh. Consider whether the saying that the Lord answered inquirers that he did not know the last day may be spoken in a similar manner. For how did he not know that day, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge? (Colossians 2:3). Why then did he deny that he knew what certainly he could not fail to know? Did he perhaps wish falsely to conceal from them what could not usefully be made known? Far be it. As he could be ignorant of nothing, because he is Wisdom, so neither could he lie, because he is Truth. But, wishing to restrain his disciples from the curiosity of useless inquiry, he denied that he knew what they were asking—not absolutely, but in a certain manner in which he could truthfully deny it.

For though by the insight of his divinity, surveying equally all things—past, present, and future—he had that day plainly before him, he had not known it by experiencing it through any of the senses of his flesh. Otherwise he would already have slain Antichrist by the spirit of his mouth; already he would have heard with the ears of his body the archangel crying aloud and the trumpet sounding, at whose sound the dead are to be raised; already he would have seen with the eyes of his flesh the sheep and the goats who are to be separated from one another.

11. Finally, so that you may understand that he professed not to know that day only by the knowledge which comes through flesh, when answering attentively he did not say, “Nor do I know,” but, “Not even the Son of Man knows” [Note: See the Retraction at the beginning of this treatise, cols. 939–940.] (Mark 13:32). What is “Son of Man” but the name of the assumed flesh? By this name it is made clear that, when he says he does not know something, he speaks not according to what he is as God, but according to man.

For elsewhere, when speaking of himself according to his divinity, he is accustomed more often to say not “the Son” or “the Son of Man,” but “I” or “me,” as there: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:58). “I am,” he says; not, “The Son of Man is.” Nor is there any doubt that he spoke of that essence by which he is before Abraham and without beginning, not that by which he was made after Abraham and from Abraham.

Again, when asking the disciples what people thought of him, he said: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?”—not “me,” but “the Son of Man” (Matthew 16:13). Asking the same men again what they themselves thought of him, he said not, “Whom do you say the Son of Man is?” but, “Whom do you say that I am?” In asking the judgment of the carnal people concerning his flesh, he used the name of the flesh, properly “Son of Man”; but in asking his spiritual disciples concerning his divinity, he significantly said not “the Son of Man,” but “me.” Peter, understanding this, made clear in his reply what they had been asked by the word “me”: “You are,” he says, not Jesus son of the Virgin, but “Christ, the Son of God” (Matthew 16:13–16). Had he answered otherwise, he would nonetheless have spoken truth; but wisely perceiving the questioner’s meaning in the words of the question, he answered fittingly and precisely what had been asked: “You are Christ, the Son of God.”

12. Therefore, since you see that Christ has in one person two natures—one by which he always was, the other by which he began to be—and that according to his eternal being he always knows all things, but according to his temporal being has experienced many things temporally, why do you hesitate to confess that, as he began in time to be from flesh, so he also began to know the miseries of flesh, at least by that mode of knowledge which the weakness of flesh teaches? The first-created humans would more wisely and more happily have lacked that kind of knowledge, since they could attain it only foolishly and miserably.

But God their Maker, seeking what had been lost, mercifully pursued his work, himself descending to the place into which they had miserably fallen. He willed to experience in himself what they deservedly suffered by acting against him—not with like curiosity, but with wondrous charity—not so that he might remain miserable with the miserable, but so that, having become merciful, he might free the miserable. He became merciful, I say, not with that mercy which he possessed from eternity while remaining blessed, but with that which he found, by means of misery, in our condition.

Moreover, the work of loving-kindness which he began through the former mercy he completed through the latter—not because the former alone could not complete it, but because it could not suffice for us without the latter. Both were necessary; but this latter was more fitting for us. O ineffable contrivance of loving-kindness! When could we conceive that wonderful mercy which is not shaped by preceding misery? When could we recognize, unknown to us, that compassion which, not preceded by suffering, endures together with impassibility? Yet unless the mercy which knows no misery had first gone before, it would not have come to this mercy whose mother is misery. If it had not come, it would not have drawn us; if it had not drawn us, it would not have drawn us out. And from where did it draw us out, except “from the pit of misery and the mire of filth”? (Psalm 39:3). Yet it did not abandon that mercy, but implanted this one; it did not change, but multiplied it, as it is written: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord, according as you have multiplied your mercy, O God” (Psalm 35:7–8).

## CHAPTER IV. The first degree of truth is first to attend to oneself, or to recognize one’s own misery.

13. But let us now return to our subject. If he who was not miserable made himself miserable in order to experience what he already knew, how much more must you—not, I say, make yourself what you are not, but attend to what you are, because you are truly miserable—and thus learn mercy, which you cannot know otherwise! Otherwise, if you consider your neighbor’s evil and do not attend to your own, you may be moved not to compassion but indignation; not to help but to judgment; finally, not to correction in a spirit of gentleness but to destruction in a spirit of anger.

“You who are spiritual,” says the Apostle, “correct such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” It is the Apostle’s counsel, indeed command, that you assist a sick brother with a gentle—that is, the same—spirit in which you desire assistance when you are sick. And, that you may know how you can become gentle toward an offender: “Considering yourself,” he says, “lest you also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

14. It is pleasing to consider how well the disciple of Truth follows the order of the Master. In the beatitudes mentioned above (§6), just as the merciful are pronounced before the pure in heart, so the gentle are pronounced before the merciful (Matthew 5:4, 7–8). And when the Apostle exhorted the spiritual to correct the carnal, he added, “in a spirit of gentleness.” The correction of brothers belongs to the merciful; the spirit of gentleness, to the gentle. It is as though he said: No one can be counted among the merciful who is not gentle within himself.

See: the Apostle plainly shows what I promised above (§6) to demonstrate—that truth must be sought first in ourselves, and then in our neighbors. “Considering yourself,” he says: that is, how easily you may be tempted, how prone to sin, so that by considering yourself you may become gentle and thus come to help others in a spirit of gentleness. Otherwise, if you do not heed the disciple who warns you, fear the Master who rebukes you: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye; and then you shall see to cast the mote out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5).

The large and thick beam in the eye is pride in the mind. By a certain empty bulk of its own, swollen rather than sound, puffed up rather than solid, it darkens the eye of the mind and overshadows truth. Thus, if it has taken possession of your mind, you can no longer see yourself; you can no longer perceive yourself as you are or as you can be. Instead, as you love yourself to be, so you either think that you are or hope that you will be. For what else is pride but, as a certain saint defines it [St Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, Book XI, §§24–25, and elsewhere], “love of one’s own excellence”? We may therefore say, conversely, that humility is contempt for one’s own excellence.

But love, no more than hatred, knows the judgment of truth. Do you wish to hear the judgment of Truth? “As I hear, so I judge” (John 5:30)—not as I hate, not as I love, not as I fear. There is a judgment of hatred, as in: “We have a law, and according to our law he ought to die” (John 19:7). There is also one of fear: “If we let him go on thus, the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11:48). And there is a judgment of love, as David concerning his parricidal son: “Spare,” he says, “the young man Absalom” (2 Samuel 18:5).

I know that human laws have decreed, and that both ecclesiastical and secular cases observe, that the special friends of litigants should not be admitted to judgment, lest they either deceive or be deceived by love for their own people. If love for a friend either lessens or altogether conceals his fault from your judgment, how much more does self-love deceive your judgment against yourself!

15. Therefore, whoever endeavors fully to know truth in himself must, having removed the beam of pride that keeps the eye from light, set in order ascents in his heart by which he may seek himself within himself, and so, after the twelfth degree of humility, reach the first degree of truth. When truth has been found in himself—or rather, when he has been found in truth—he may say: “I believed, therefore I spoke; but I was greatly humbled.” Let the human being ascend to the lofty heart, that truth may be exalted; and, reaching the second degree, let him say in his ecstasy: “Every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:10–11).

Do you suppose David did not maintain this order? Do you suppose the Prophet did not perceive what the Lord, what the Apostle, and what we also after and through them perceive? “I believed,” he says, Truth saying: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). Therefore I believed by following, and for that reason spoke by confessing. What did I confess? The truth which I knew by believing. But after I both believed unto righteousness and spoke unto salvation, “I was greatly humbled,” that is, completely. It is as though he said: Because I was not ashamed to confess against myself the truth known in me, I advanced to perfection in humility.

For “greatly” may be understood as “completely,” as there: “He will delight greatly in his commandments” (Psalm 111:1). But if anyone contends that here “greatly” means “very much,” not “completely,” since commentators also seem to maintain this, neither does this conflict with the Prophet’s meaning, if we understand him to have said: “While I did not yet know truth, I thought myself to be something when I was nothing. But after I came to know truth by believing in Christ—that is, by imitating his humility—truth itself was exalted in me through my confession; but I was greatly humbled, that is, I became very contemptible to myself by considering myself.”

## CHAPTER V. The second degree of truth is, from the recognition of one’s own weakness, to have compassion on a neighbor’s misery.

16. Therefore, humbled in this first degree of truth, as he says in another psalm, “In your truth you have humbled me” (Psalm 118:75), let the Prophet attend to himself and from his own misery judge the common misery of all. Then, passing to the second degree, let him say in his ecstasy, “Every human being is a liar.” In what ecstasy? Undoubtedly in that by which, going beyond himself and clinging to truth, he judges himself. Therefore in that ecstasy let him say, not in indignation or mockery, but in pity and fellow-feeling: “Every human being is a liar.”

What does “Every human being is a liar” mean? Every human being is weak; every human being is miserable and powerless, unable to save either himself or another. As it is said, “A horse is deceptive for salvation” (Psalm 32:17), not because a horse deceives anyone, but because the person who trusts in its strength deceives himself; so every human being is called a liar—that is, fragile and changeable, from whom neither one’s own salvation nor another’s may be hoped for. Rather, one incurs a curse who puts one’s hope in a human being (Jeremiah 17:5). Therefore, advancing humbly under truth’s guidance, the Prophet, seeing in others what he mourned in himself, adds sorrow as he adds knowledge, and says generally but truthfully: “Every human being is a liar.”

17. See how very differently that proud Pharisee thought of himself. What did he utter in his ecstasy? “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humankind” (Luke 18:11). While exulting singularly in himself, he insolently mocks others. David, however, does otherwise. For he says: “Every human being is a liar.” He excepts no one, lest he deceive anyone, knowing that all have sinned and all lack the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The Pharisee deceives himself alone, whom alone he excepts while condemning the rest.

The Prophet does not except himself from the common misery, lest he be excepted from mercy; the Pharisee spurns mercy because he conceals misery. The Prophet affirms concerning all, including himself: “Every human being is a liar.” The Pharisee affirms concerning all except himself: “I am not,” he says, “like the rest of humankind.” And he gives thanks not because he is good, but because he is alone; not so much for the good that he possesses as for the evils he sees in others. He had not yet cast the beam out of his own eye, and he counts the motes in his brothers’ eyes. For he adds: “Unjust, extortioners” (Luke 18:11). I have not, I think, made this digression from the subject without cause, if you have understood the difference between the ecstasies of the two.

18. We must now return to our subject. Those, therefore, whom truth has already caused to know themselves and thereby to become contemptible in their own eyes must necessarily find bitter all the things that they were accustomed to love. Setting themselves before themselves, they compel themselves to see themselves as they are ashamed even to be seen by themselves. And, displeased by what they are and sighing for what they are not—which they despair of becoming by themselves—they deeply mourn themselves. Their sole consolation is to be severe judges of themselves: hungering and thirsting for justice out of love of truth, they exact from themselves the strictest satisfaction, even to self-contempt, and thereafter amendment.

But when they see that they cannot suffice for this—for even when they have done all things commanded them, they call themselves unprofitable servants (Luke 17:10)—they flee from justice to mercy. In order to obtain mercy, they follow Truth’s counsel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). This is the second degree of truth, by which they seek it in their neighbors: from their own sufferings they investigate the needs of others; from the things which they endure, they know how to have compassion on those who endure.

## CHAPTER VI. The third degree of truth: cleansing the eye of the heart for contemplation of heavenly and divine things.

19. Therefore, if they persevere in these three things which have been mentioned—that is, in the mourning of repentance, in the desire for justice, and in works of mercy—they cleanse the sight of the heart from the three hindrances contracted through ignorance, weakness, or deliberate purpose, so that by contemplation they may pass to the third degree of truth. These are the ways which appear good to human beings—excepting only those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things (Proverbs 2:14), and cover themselves with weakness or ignorance in order to make excuses for sins (Psalm 140:4).

But those who willingly remain ignorant or weak in order to sin more freely flatter themselves in vain concerning weakness or ignorance. Do you suppose it benefited the first human being, though he did not sin willingly, that he defended himself by his wife, as though by the weakness of the flesh? (Genesis 3:12). Or will the stoners of the first martyr be excusable through ignorance because they stopped their ears? (Acts 7:56). Therefore, those who feel themselves alienated from truth by deliberate purpose and love of sin, weighed down by weakness and ignorance, should turn deliberate purpose into groaning and love into grief; conquer the weakness of the flesh by zeal for justice; and drive away ignorance by generosity. Otherwise, if now they do not recognize Truth when needy, naked, and weak, they may recognize her too late, with shame, when she comes in great power and might, terrifying and rebuking; and may answer vainly with trembling: “When did we see you in need and not minister to you?” (Matthew 25:44).

Certainly the Lord will be known when he executes judgments (Psalm 9:17), though now he is not known while seeking mercy. Finally, they shall look upon him whom they pierced (John 19:37); likewise the greedy shall see him whom they despised. Therefore the eye of the heart is cleansed from every stain contracted through weakness, ignorance, or deliberate purpose, by weeping, by hungering for justice, and by persevering in works of mercy. To this eye Truth promises to show herself in her purity: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Since, then, there are three degrees or states of truth, we ascend to the first through the labor of humility; to the second through the affection of compassion; to the third through the ecstasy of contemplation. In the first, truth is found severe; in the second, gracious; in the third, pure. Reason leads to the first, by which we examine ourselves; affection brings us to the second, by which we have mercy on others; purity carries us away to the third, by which we are raised to invisible things.

## CHAPTER VII. How the Holy Trinity works these three degrees of truth within us.

20. Here there shines forth to me a certain wonderful and distinct operation of the indivisible Trinity—if, indeed, a human being sitting in darkness can in any way grasp that ineffable distinction of the persons who work together. In the first degree the Son seems to me to work; in the second, the Holy Spirit; in the third, the Father. Do you wish to hear of the Son’s operation? “If I, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet,” he says, “how much more ought you also to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:14). The Master, the Truth, handed on to his disciples the pattern of humility by which truth would first become known to them in the first degree.

Observe also the work of the Holy Spirit: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). Charity is the gift of the Holy Spirit. By it those who, under the Son’s discipline, have already progressed through humility to the first degree of truth, reach the second through compassion for their neighbor, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

Hear also concerning the Father: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17); and: “The father will make his truth known to the children” (Isaiah 38:19); and: “I confess to you, Father, because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25). Do you see that those whom the Son first humbled by word and example, and upon whom the Holy Spirit afterwards poured charity, the Father finally received into glory? The Son makes disciples; the Paraclete consoles friends; the Father exalts children.

But since not only the Son but also the Father and the Holy Spirit are truly called Truth, it is evident that one and the same Truth, preserving the distinctive character of the persons, performs these three works in the three degrees: first teaching as Master; second, consoling as friend or brother; third, binding them to himself as a father does children.

21. For the Son of God, namely the Word and Wisdom of the Father, first finds that power of our soul which is called reason depressed by the flesh, captive to sin, blinded by ignorance, and devoted to outward things. Mercifully taking it up, powerfully raising it, wisely instructing it, drawing it inward, and wonderfully using it as a deputy on his behalf, he appoints it judge over itself. Thus, out of reverence for the Word to which it is joined, it fulfills the office of Truth against itself as its own accuser, witness, and judge. From this first union of the Word and reason, humility is born.

Then the Holy Spirit graciously visits the other part, called the will, which is indeed infected by the poison of the flesh but has now been examined by reason. The Spirit fights sweetly and moves it ardently, making it merciful. Like a skin which, when anointed, is stretched out, it too, drenched with heavenly anointing, is expanded in affection even to enemies. Thus charity is produced from this second union of the Spirit of God and the human will.

Finally, the Father joins both parts to himself as a glorious bride: reason, instructed by the word of truth, and will, breathed upon by the Spirit of truth; the former sprinkled with the hyssop of humility, the latter kindled by the fire of charity. The soul is now perfect, without spot because of humility and without wrinkle because of charity; neither does the will resist reason nor does reason conceal truth. It is not permitted to reason to think about itself, nor to will to think about its neighbor; the blessed soul delights only to say: “The King has brought me into his chamber.”

Certainly it is worthy: having first learned, under the Son as teacher, to enter into itself in the school of humility, in accordance with the warning addressed to it, “If you do not know yourself, go forth and feed your kids” (Song of Songs 1:3, 7), it is worthy, then, to be led by the Holy Spirit from that school of humility into the wine-cellars of charity—which are, of course, to be understood as the breasts of neighbors—through affection. From there, supported by flowers and surrounded by fruits, that is, by good habits and holy virtues, it is finally admitted to the King’s chamber, for whose love it languishes.

There, when silence has been made in heaven for a little while, as it were half an hour, it rests sweetly amid the longed-for embraces. It sleeps indeed, but its heart keeps watch; in the meantime it searches out the secrets of truth, and upon returning to itself is afterward immediately nourished by their remembrance. There it sees invisible things and hears ineffable things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak. For they surpass all that knowledge which night declares to night; yet day pours forth speech to day, and among the wise it is permitted to speak wisdom and to compare spiritual things with spiritual.

## CHAPTER VIII. The same degrees are illustrated in the rapture of Saint Paul.

22. Do you suppose that Paul had not passed through these stages—he who testifies that he was caught up even to the third heaven? (2 Cor. 12:2.) But why “caught up,” rather than “led”? So that, if so great an Apostle says that he was caught up to a place to which he neither knew how to go by instruction nor could go by being led, I—who am without doubt less than Paul—may presume that I can reach the third heaven by no strength or labor of my own [Col. 0954B]; lest I either trust in my own strength or despair because of labor.

For one who is taught or led is shown to labor precisely because, in following the teacher or guide, he himself does something in order to be drawn to the appointed place or understanding; so that he may say: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). But one who is caught up, supported not by his own powers but by another’s, is borne he knows not where; and he boasts neither wholly nor partly in himself, where he works neither by himself nor together with another.

Thus the Apostle could ascend to the first or middle heaven by being led or assisted; but to reach the third he had to be caught up. For the Son is said to have descended in order to call and help those who were to ascend to the first; and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0954C] to have been sent in order to bring them through to the second. The Father, although always working together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is nevertheless never said either to have descended from heaven or to have been sent to the earth.

Certainly I read that “the earth is full of the Lord’s mercy” (Ps. 32:5), and, “Heaven and earth are full of your glory,” and many such sayings. I read also of the Son: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4). And the Son himself says of himself: “The Spirit of the Lord sent me” (Isa. 61:1). And through the same prophet: “And now,” he says, “the Lord has sent me and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). I read also of the Holy Spirit: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26); and, “When I have been taken up, I will send him to you” (John 16:7)—undoubtedly the Holy Spirit. But the Father, in his own person, though he is nowhere absent, I find nowhere except in heaven: as in the Gospel, “And my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:9); and in the prayer, “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

23. From this I plainly infer that, because the Father does not descend, the Apostle could not ascend to the third heaven in order to see him; nevertheless, he recalled that he was caught up there. Finally: “No one ascends into heaven except the Son of Man who descended from heaven” (John 3:13). And lest you suppose this is said of the first or second heaven, David tells you: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18:7).

To this heaven he was not suddenly caught up, nor secretly borne away; rather, “while they were watching,” that is, while the Apostles watched, [Col. 0955A] “he was lifted up” (Acts 1:9). Not like Elijah, who had one witness (4 Kings 2); not like Paul, who had none—for he could scarcely have had even himself as witness or judge, as he himself declares: “I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12:2). But as the Almighty, who descended when he willed and ascended when he willed, he awaited, according to his own decision, witnesses and spectators, place and time, day and hour; and, while those watched whom he deemed worthy of so great a vision, he was lifted up.

Paul was caught up; Elijah was caught up; Enoch was translated (Ecclus. 44:16). But our Redeemer is said to have been lifted up—that is, raised by himself, not helped from elsewhere. Finally, no vehicle of a chariot, no assistance of an angel, but a cloud received him, supported by his own power, from their sight (Acts 1:9). Why was this? Did it aid one who was weary? Did it urge one who was sluggish? Did it support one who was falling? Far from it. Rather, it received him from the carnal eyes of the disciples, who, although they had known Christ according to the flesh, were no longer to know him so. Therefore, those whom the Son calls through humility to the first heaven, the Spirit gathers in the second through charity, and the Father exalts to the third through contemplation.

At the first stage they are humbled in truth, and say: “In your truth you have humbled me” (Ps. 118:75). At the second they rejoice together with truth, and sing: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1). For it is written of charity: “It rejoices together with the truth” (1 Cor. 13:6). At the third they are caught up to the secrets of truth and say: “My secret is for me, my secret is for me” (Isa. 24:16).

## CHAPTER IX. The groanings and sighs of Saint Bernard, panting after Truth.

[Col. 0955C]

24. But why do I, wretched man, range over the two higher heavens more by superfluity of speech than by vitality of spirit, when I still labor beneath the lower one, crawling on hands and feet? Yet already, with the help of him who calls me, I have set up for myself a ladder to it. For there is the way by which he may show me the salvation of God. Already I look up at the Lord leaning down from above; already I leap at the voice of truth. He called me, and I answered him: “You will stretch out your right hand to the work of your hands” (Job 14:15).

You indeed, Lord, count my steps; but I, a slow climber and weary traveler, seek byways [Col. 0955D]. Woe to me if darkness overtakes me, or if my flight takes place in winter or on the Sabbath, while I delay to set out now toward the light, in this acceptable time and day of salvation. Why do I linger? Pray for me, son, brother, companion, and fellow-partaker in my progress, whoever you may be in the Lord. Pray to the Almighty that he may so strengthen this sluggish foot that the foot of pride may nevertheless not come upon me. For although a sluggish foot is not fit to climb to the degree of truth, it is still more tolerable than that foot which cannot stand there, as you have it: “They are cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35:12–13).

25. This, indeed, concerns the proud. But what of their head? What of him who is called “king over all the children of pride”? (Job 41:25.) “He too,” it says, [Col. 0956A] “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44); and elsewhere: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Why was this, except because of pride?

Woe to me if he who knows the lofty from afar sees me also growing proud, and thunders over me that terrible voice: “You indeed were a son of the Most High, but you shall die like a man, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:6–7). Who would not tremble at the sound of this thunder? O how much more healthful was it that Jacob’s sinew in his thigh withered at the angel’s touch (Gen. 32:25), than that the sinew of the proud angel swelled, vanished, and fell! Would that an angel might touch my sinew also, so that it may wither; perhaps from this weakness I may begin to make progress, since from my own strength I can only fail.

For I read indeed: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” [Col. 0956B] (1 Cor. 1:25). Thus the Apostle too, complaining of his own sinew, which was buffeted by an angel not of the Lord but of Satan, heard the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you; for strength is made perfect in weakness.” What strength? Let the Apostle himself answer: “I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, that the strength of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9).

But perhaps you do not yet understand what he said especially, since Christ possessed all virtues. Yet, though he possessed them all, above all he commended to us one virtue in himself, namely humility, when he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

26. Therefore I too, Lord Jesus, will gladly boast, if I can, in my weakness, in the contraction of my sinew, so that your strength—that is, humility—may be made perfect [Col. 0956C] in me. For your grace is sufficient for me when my own strength fails. Planting firmly the foot of grace, and gently drawing mine, which is weak, I shall safely climb the ladder of humility until, cleaving to truth, I pass over into the breadth of charity. Then I shall sing with thanksgiving and say: “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (Ps. 30:9).

Thus the narrow way is traveled more cautiously, step by confined step; thus the steep ladder is climbed more safely, little by little; thus, in a wonderful way, though more slowly, one climbs more steadily toward truth by limping. But alas for me, “because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119:5)! Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly more swiftly to truth and at last rest in charity? (Ps. [Col. 0956D] 54:7.) Since I lack these wings, lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth, and truth will set me free.

Woe to me because I descended from it. For unless I had first descended lightly and vainly, I would not have labored so long and heavily in ascending. But what do I say—“I descended”? Perhaps it would be more correct to say, “I fell.” Unless perhaps, just as no one becomes supremely good all at once, but each ascends by stages, so no one becomes utterly worst all at once, but descends gradually. Otherwise how would this stand: “The wicked man is proud all the days of his life”? (Job 15:20.) Finally, there are ways that seem good to people and yet lead to evil.

27. Therefore there is a way of descent as well as of ascent. There is a way to good, and there is a way to evil. Avoid the evil way; choose the good. If you cannot do so by yourself, pray with the prophet and say: “Remove from me the way of iniquity.” How? “And in your law have mercy on me”—that law, namely, which you gave to those who stray in the way, that is, who abandon truth; among them I am one, for I truly fell from truth.

But does one who falls not rise again? Therefore I have chosen the way of truth, by which I shall ascend humbled, from where I descended in pride. I shall ascend, I say, and sing: “It is good for me, Lord, that you have humbled me; the law of your mouth is good for me above thousands of gold and silver pieces” (Ps. 118:29, 30, 71, 72).

David seems to have set before you two ways, but know that they are one and the same. Yet he calls it by different names, and distinguishes it according to those who travel it: the way of iniquity for those descending, and the way of truth for those ascending. For the same are the steps of those ascending a throne and of those descending; the same is the way of those approaching a city and departing from it; and one door [Col. 0958A] belongs both to those entering a house and to those going out. Thus angels ascending and descending appeared to Jacob upon one ladder (Gen. 28:12).

What is the point of this? If you wish to return to truth, you need not seek out a new way which you do not know, but the familiar way by which you descended. Following your own footprints with steps retraced, you may climb humbled by the same stages through which you descended in pride: so that the twelfth stage of pride for one descending becomes the first stage of humility for one ascending; the eleventh becomes the second; the tenth, third; the ninth, fourth; the eighth, fifth; the seventh, sixth; the sixth, seventh; the fifth, eighth; the fourth, ninth; the third, tenth; the second, eleventh; and the first, twelfth. Once these stages of pride are found—or rather recognized—in you [Col. 0958B], you need no longer labor to seek the way of humility.

## THE SECOND PART OF THE TREATISE ON THE TWELVE DEGREES OF PRIDE.

[Col. 0957]

## CHAPTER X. On the first degree of pride, which is curiosity.

> [Note: [Col. 0957] The twelfth degree of humility is opposed to this: namely, modesty, especially of the eyes.]

[Col. 0957B]

28. The first degree of pride, then, is curiosity. You will detect it by such signs as these. If you see a monk, formerly deserving your confidence, beginning, wherever he stands, walks, or sits, to let his eyes wander [Col. 0957C], to hold his head erect and his ears attentively raised, recognize from the movements of the outer person that the inner person has been changed.

“For the perverse man winks with his eye, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger” (Prov. 6:12–13); and from an insolent movement of the body a newly arisen disease of the soul is detected. When the soul, through negligence of itself, grows sluggish in watching over itself, it makes itself curious about others. Because it does not know itself, it is sent outside to pasture its kids (Song 1:7).

I would rightly call the eyes and ears “kids,” which signify sin, because, as death entered the world through sin, so it enters the mind through these windows. The curious person occupies himself in pasturing these, while he takes no care to know in what condition he has left himself within. And truly, if you, O man, attended vigilantly to yourself, it would be remarkable if [Col. 0957D] you ever attended to anything else.

Hear Solomon, O curious man; hear the Wise Man, O fool: “Keep your heart with all watchfulness” (Prov. 4:23), so that all your senses may keep watch to guard that from which life proceeds. For where do you go away from yourself, O curious man? To whom do you meanwhile entrust yourself? Why dare you lift your eyes to heaven—you who have sinned against heaven? Look upon the earth, so that you may know yourself. It will present you to yourself, because you are earth and shall go into earth.

29. Yet there are two causes for which you may lift your eyes without blame: either to ask for help or to give it. David lifted his eyes to the mountains in order to ask (Ps. 120:1); and the Lord lifted his eyes over the crowds in order to give (John 6:5). The one did so pitiably, the other mercifully; both without blame.

You also, if, considering place, time, and reason, you lift your eyes because of your own need or your brother’s, I not only do not blame you but praise you highly. Misery excuses the one; mercy commends the other. But otherwise I shall call you an imitator not of the Prophet or of the Lord, but of Dinah or Eve—indeed, of Satan himself [Col. 0958C].

For Dinah, when she went out to pasture the kids, was herself ravished, and her virginity taken from herself (Gen. 34:1–2). O Dinah, what need was there for you to see foreign women? What necessity? What benefit? Was it curiosity alone? Although you look idly, you are not looked upon idly. You gaze curiously, but are gazed upon still more curiously. Who would then have believed that your curious idleness—or idle curiosity—would afterward prove not idle, but so ruinous to you, to your family, and to your enemies?

30. You also, O Eve, were placed in paradise so that you might work and guard it with your husband. If you fulfill the command laid upon you, you will one day pass to a better place, where you need neither be occupied in any work nor be anxious about guarding anything [Col. 0958D]. Every tree of paradise is granted you for food, except that which is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:15–17). For if the others are good and taste of good, what need is there to eat from a tree that tastes also of evil? “Do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise” (Rom. 12:3). For to taste evil is not wisdom but folly.

Guard what has been entrusted to you; await what has been promised; beware of what has been forbidden, lest you lose what has been granted. Why do you gaze so intently upon your death? Why do you cast your wandering eyes so often upon it? Why do you desire to look upon what you may not eat?

“You say, ‘I direct my eyes, not my hand. I am forbidden not to eat, not to look. May I not raise my eyes wherever I wish, since God has placed them [Col. 0959A] under my power?’” To this the Apostle replies: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable” (1 Cor. 6:12). Even if it is not a fault, it is an indication of fault. For unless the mind guarded itself less curiously, your curiosity would have no idle time. Even if it is not a fault, it is nevertheless an occasion of fault, an indication of fault already committed, and a cause of one yet to be committed.

For while you are intent on something else, the serpent meanwhile creeps secretly into your heart and speaks soothingly. By blandishments it restrains reason; by lies it suppresses fear. “You shall not die at all,” it says (Gen. 3:4). It increases concern while exciting appetite; it sharpens curiosity while suggesting desire. At last it offers what is forbidden and takes away what was granted: it extends the apple and steals paradise. You drink poison, doomed to perish, and you will bear children doomed to perish. Salvation perished; childbearing did not cease [Col. 0959B]. We are born, we die; and therefore we are born to die, because first we die in order to be born. For this reason a heavy yoke lies upon all your children until this present day.

31. But you also, “the seal of likeness,” were placed not in paradise but “in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28:12–13). What more ought you to seek? Therefore, being full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, do not seek things higher than yourself, nor search out things stronger than yourself. Stand within yourself, lest you fall from yourself, if you walk amid things great and wonderful above you.

But why meanwhile do you cast a sidelong glance toward the north? I see you now; I perceive you, searching with curiosity into certain heights above yourself. “I will place my throne in the north,” you say (Isa. 14:13). While the other inhabitants of heaven stand, you alone desire to sit; you disturb the concord of the brethren, the peace of the whole heavenly country, and, so far as lies in you, the repose of the Trinity itself.

Where, wretched one, does your curiosity lead you, that by singular presumption you do not hesitate to cause scandal to your fellow-citizens and injury to the King? “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10), where no one is said to sit except he alone who sits upon the Cherubim and is served by the others. And you, by perceiving I know not what above others more distinctively, by inquiring more curiously, by intruding more irreverently, place a throne for yourself in heaven in order that you may be like the Most High?

To what end? With what confidence? Measure your powers, foolish one; weigh the end; devise a limit. Do you presume with the Most High knowing it, or not knowing it? Willing it, [Col. 0959D] or unwilling? But how could he either will or fail to know whatever evil you devise, he whose will is most good and whose knowledge is perfect? Or do you perhaps have no doubt that he knows and does not will it, but suppose that he cannot resist? Yet unless you doubt that you were created, I cannot believe that you doubt the omnipotence, complete knowledge, and goodness of the Creator, who was able, knew, and willed to create you such and so great from nothing. How then do you think God consents to what he does not will and is able to prevent?

Or perhaps I see fulfilled in you—indeed, first initiated by you—what is commonly said on earth after you and through you by those like you: “A private lord keeps rash retainers” [or: “rash satellites,” added in some texts]. Is your eye wicked because he is good? Since you take impious confidence from his goodness [Col. 0960A], you have become shameless against his knowledge and bold against his power.

32. For this, impious one, is what you think; this is the iniquity you meditate upon your bed, when you say: “Do you suppose that the Creator will destroy his work? I know indeed that no thought of mine, whatever it may be, is hidden from God, for God is God. Nor does such a thought please him, because he is good. Yet even if he wished it, I could not escape his hands, because he is powerful. But must I therefore fear? For if, being good, my evil cannot please him, how much less can his own evil please him? I call it mine to will something against his will; but his, if he should avenge himself. Therefore he can no more will to avenge any crime than he can will, or be able, to be deprived of his own goodness.”

You deceive yourself, wretched one; you deceive yourself [Col. 0960B], not God. You deceive yourself, I say: iniquity lies to itself, not to God. You act deceitfully, indeed, but in his sight. Therefore you deceive yourself, not God. And because, from his great good toward you, you devise a great evil against him, rightly “your iniquity is found unto hatred.”

For what iniquity is greater than that the Creator should be despised by you precisely on account of that for which he deserved to be loved more? What iniquity is greater than this: though you do not doubt God’s power—that he who could create you can also destroy you—yet, trusting in his abundant sweetness, because you hope that he will not avenge himself even though he can, you repay evil for good and hatred for love?

33. This iniquity, I say, is worthy not of momentary wrath but of everlasting hatred: you desire and hope, although he is unwilling, to be made equal to your most sweet and most high Lord, so that he may always see what grieves him—having you as companion when he does not will it, and not casting you down when he can. Rather, as you suppose, he chooses to grieve himself rather than allow you to perish; he can indeed cast you down if he wishes, but, because of sweetness, is incapable—as you think—of willing it.

Certainly, if he is such as you suppose, you act all the more wickedly in not loving him. And if he endures something to be done against himself rather than himself do anything against you, what malice it is that you should not spare him who does not spare himself in sparing you! Yet far be it from his perfection that, because he is sweet, he should not also be just—as if he could not at once be sweet and just. For just sweetness is better than indulgent sweetness; indeed, sweetness without justice is not a virtue.

Therefore, because you prove ungrateful for God’s gratuitous goodness, by which you were made freely, and do not fear justice because you have not experienced it; and because you boldly commit the sin for which you falsely promise yourself impunity—behold, you will feel him just whom you know to be good, falling into the pit which you prepare for your Maker. That is, while you devise for him such a punishment as he could escape if he wished, but—as you suppose—cannot will to escape, and therefore cannot lack that goodness by which you have never known him to punish anyone: the just God will most justly turn back upon you such a punishment, since he neither can nor ought to allow his goodness to be offended with impunity. Thus he tempers the sentence in vengeance so that, if you are willing to repent, he does not refuse forgiveness; yet, according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are unable to will it, and therefore unable to be free from punishment.

[Col. 0961A]

34. But now hear the accusation: “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1). He did not say, “the East,” or “the West,” or some single region of heaven; but, “The whole heaven is my throne.” Therefore you cannot sit in a part of heaven when he has chosen the whole for himself. You cannot remain on earth, because it is the footstool of his feet. For earth is the solid place where the Church sits, founded upon the firm rock. What will you do? Driven from heaven, you cannot remain on earth. Choose therefore for yourself a place in the air—not for sitting, but for flying—so that you who attempted to shake the state of eternity may feel the punishment of your own instability.

While you thus fluctuate between heaven and earth, the Lord sits upon a high and exalted throne, and the whole earth is full of his majesty (Isa. 6:3), so that you find no place except in the air [Col. 0961B].

35. For the Seraphim, flying on some of the wings of their contemplation from throne to footstool and from footstool to throne, while with other wings they veil the Lord’s head and feet, seem to me to have been set there for this purpose: that, just as entrance into paradise is forbidden to sinful man through the Cherubim, so a limit may be imposed through the Seraphim upon your curiosity.

> [Note: [Col. 0961] See the Retraction at the beginning of this treatise, cols. 939–940.]

Thus you may no longer search the mysteries of heaven more impudently than wisely, nor know the mysteries of the Church upon earth; but may be content only with the hearts of the proud, who do not deign to remain on earth like other people, nor to fly to heaven like angels. Yet although both the head in heaven and the feet on earth are hidden from you, something intermediate is permitted you to see, though only so that you may envy it [Col. 0961C]: while suspended in the air, you behold angels descending through you and ascending; but what they hear in heaven or announce to earth you do not know at all.

36. O Lucifer, who once arose in the morning—indeed, now no longer light-bearer (*lucifer*), but night-bearer (*noctifer*), or even death-bearer (*mortifer*)—your proper course was from east to south, and do you, in reversed order, turn toward the north? The more eagerly you hasten upward, the more swiftly you decline toward the west. Yet, O curious one, I would inquire more closely into the intention of your curiosity. “I will set my throne in the north,” you say (Isa. 14:13).

I understand neither this north as bodily nor this throne as material, since you are a spirit. But I think that by “the north” rejected human beings are designated; by “the throne,” authority over them. Foreseeing them in God’s foreknowledge—as you were nearer to him, and therefore more discerning than the rest—you found, as it were, an empty place: shining with no ray of wisdom and burning with no love of the Spirit. You desired dominion over them, that you might suffuse them with some brightness of your own cunning and inflame them with the heats of your malice; so that, just as the Most High presided by his wisdom and goodness over all the children of obedience, you too might be established as king over all the children of pride and rule them by your cunning malice and malicious cunning, thereby becoming like the Most High.

But I wonder: when, in God’s presence, you foresaw your own principality, why did you not at the same time foresee [Col. 0962A] your fall? For if you did foresee it, what madness was it to desire to rule amid such misery—to prefer presiding wretchedly to being subject happily? Was it not better to share in those luminous ranks than to be prince of these darknesses?

But it is more believable that you did not foresee it: either for the reason I stated above, because, attending to God’s goodness, you said in your heart, “He will not require it” (Ps. 10:13), by which you, impious one, provoked God; or because, when you saw the principality, a beam immediately grew in the eye of pride and, intervening, prevented you from seeing your fall.

37. Thus Joseph, although he foresaw his exaltation (Gen. 37:7–9), nevertheless did not foreknow his being sold, though the sale was nearer than [Col. 0962B] the exaltation. Not that I believe so great a patriarch fell into pride; rather, his example shows that those who foresee future things through the spirit of prophecy, though they do not foresee everything, should not for that reason be thought to have foreseen nothing.

If anyone contends that, when he was still a youth and told his dreams whose mystery he then did not understand, vanity can be detected in him, I judge that it should be attributed rather to the mystery or simplicity of the boy than to vanity. Yet any vanity that there may have been could have been expiated through the things which he is recorded to have suffered.

For sometimes pleasant things about themselves are shown to some persons by revelation. Although the human mind cannot know these without some vanity, what is shown will nevertheless occur; yet the vanity by which a person exults, even slightly, at the greatness of the revelation or promise concerning himself does not go unpunished. Just as a physician uses not ointment alone but also fire and iron, in order to cut away and burn whatever excessive growth has arisen in healing a wound, lest it hinder the health produced by the ointment, so God, the physician of souls, provides temptations and sends tribulations to such a soul, so that, afflicted and humbled, it may turn joy into mourning and think revelation an illusion. Thus it becomes free from vanity, while the truth of the revelation does not perish.

Thus Paul’s exaltation is restrained by the thorn in the flesh (2 Cor. 12:7), while he is raised up by frequent revelations. Thus Zechariah’s unbelief is punished by the binding of his tongue (Luke 1:20), while the truth of the angel, to be manifested in its own [Col. 0962D] time, is not altered. Thus saints make progress through glory and dishonor, when, amid the singular gifts they receive, they feel themselves assailed by the common vanity of human beings, so that, while through grace they perceive something above themselves, they do not forget what they are.

38. But what have revelations to do with curiosity? The occasion for this digression arose because I wished to show that the reprobate angel, before his fall, could have foreseen the dominion over reprobate human beings which he afterward received, while nevertheless not foreknowing his own condemnation. Having raised certain little questions about him rather than resolved them [Col. 0963A], the sum of the whole little discussion is this: through curiosity he fell from truth, because he first looked curiously upon what he illicitly desired and presumptuously hoped for.

Therefore curiosity rightly claims the first place among the degrees of pride, since it is also found to be the beginning of every sin. But unless it is checked promptly, it soon slips down into levity of mind, which is the second degree.

## CHAPTER XI. On the second degree of pride, which is levity of mind.

> [Note: [Col. 0963D] The eleventh degree of humility is opposed to this: namely, to speak few and reasonable words, in a gentle rather than a loud voice.]

39. For when a monk neglects himself and curiously looks about at others, he looks up to some as superiors and down on others as inferiors. In some he sees what he envies, in others what he mocks. Thus, because of the restlessness of his eyes, his mind is made light, being weighed down by no care of itself [Col. 0963B]; now by pride it raises itself to heights, now by envy it sinks to depths; now it wastes away wickedly through envy, now it is childishly exhilarated through self-excellence. In the one state he is wicked, in the other vain; in both proud, because the love of his own superiority makes him grieve at being surpassed and rejoice in surpassing.

Such alternations of the mind are shown by words now few and biting, now many and empty; now full of laughter, now of lamentation, but always irrational. Compare, if you wish, these first two degrees of pride with the highest two degrees of humility, and see whether curiosity is not restrained in the last degree and levity in the next to last. You will find the same thing in the remaining degrees if the opposing terms are compared. But now let us come to the third by instruction, not by descent.

## CHAPTER XII. On the third degree of pride, which is foolish merriment.

> [Note: [Col. 0963D] The tenth degree of humility is opposed to this, [Col. 0964D] namely, not to be quick or ready to laugh.]

[Col. 0963C]

40. It is characteristic of the proud always to seek pleasant things and avoid sad ones, according to the saying: “The heart of fools is where there is merriment” (Eccl. 7:5). Hence the monk who has already descended two degrees of pride, passing through curiosity to levity of mind, finds that the joy he always seeks is frequently interrupted by sadness, which he derives from another’s good. Impatient of his own humiliation, he flees to the counsel of false consolation.

From that quarter in which his own lowliness and another’s excellence are shown to him, he restrains his curiosity, so that he may transfer himself wholly to the opposite quarter. There he notes more curiously whatever seems to make himself excel; whatever makes another excel, he continually ignores. Thus, avoiding what is thought sad, he keeps up his merriment. And so, whereas joy and sorrow had alternately claimed him for themselves, foolish merriment alone begins to possess him.

Now that you have been placed upon this third degree, learn by what signs you may detect it in yourself or another. You will never, or rarely, hear such a person groaning or see him weeping. If you observe him, you might suppose him either forgetful of himself or washed clean of faults. Buffoonery appears in his gestures, cheerfulness in his face, vanity in his walk. He is inclined to jesting, quick [Col. 0964A] and ready to laugh.

For, having erased from his memory all that he knew to be contemptible in himself, and therefore sad, and having gathered together—or imagined before the eyes of his mind—whatever good he perceives in himself, he thinks of nothing but what pleases him and does not consider whether it is lawful. Consequently, he can no longer restrain laughter or disguise foolish merriment.

For as a bladder, swollen with collected wind and pierced by a tiny puncture, crackles as it is squeezed and deflates—the escaping wind, not pouring out diffusely but issuing in a narrow stream, makes repeated sounds—so, when a monk has filled his heart with vain and buffoonish thoughts, and, because of the discipline of silence, finds no fuller outlet for the wind of vanity, it bursts out in laughs through the narrow passage of his throat. Often, ashamed, he hides his face, closes his lips, and clenches his teeth; he laughs unwillingly and guffaws against his will. And when he has blocked his mouth with his fists, he is still heard sneezing through his nostrils [Col. 0964B].

## CHAPTER XIII. On the fourth degree of pride, which is boastfulness.

> [Note: [Col. 0964D] The ninth degree of humility is opposed to this: silence until one is questioned.]

41. But after vanity has begun to grow and the bladder to become large, the windiness must needs be belched forth through a wider opening, as its folds are loosened; otherwise it will burst. So, when a monk’s foolish merriment overflows and laughter or gestures do not suffice to reveal it, he breaks out into the words of Elihu: “Behold, my belly is like wine without a vent, which bursts new wineskins” (Job 32:19). Therefore he will either speak or burst. For he is full of words, and the spirit of his belly constrains him [Col. 0964C].

He hungers and thirsts for hearers before whom he may parade his vanities, pour out everything he thinks, and make known what sort of man and how great a man he is. Once an occasion for speaking has been found, if discussion of literature arises, he brings forward the old and the new; maxims fly about and bombastic words resound. He anticipates the questioner and answers one who has not asked. He himself asks and himself solves, cutting short his interlocutor’s unfinished words.

When the signal is struck and the conversation must be interrupted, he complains that the hour is long and the interval brief. He asks permission to return to his tales after the hour, not in order to edify anyone, but to display his knowledge. He can edify, but does not intend to edify. He does not care to teach you, or himself to be taught by you what he does not know; rather, he wants to be known to know what he knows.

If religion is discussed, visions and dreams are immediately brought forward. In short, he praises fasts, commends vigils, exalts prayers above all; he argues most fully, but most vainly, about patience, humility, and each individual virtue, so that, on hearing him, you may say that “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,” and that “a good man brings forth good things from his good treasure” (Luke 6:43). If conversation turns to amusements, the more practiced he is in them, the more talkative he proves. On hearing him, you would call his mouth a stream of vanity, a river of buffoonery [Col. 0965A], so that it stirs even serious and grave minds to frivolous laughter.

And, to gather everything briefly: recognize boastfulness in much speaking. Here you have the fourth degree both described and named. Flee the thing, and retain the name. With the same caution now approach the fifth, which I call singularity.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the fifth degree of pride, called singularity.

> [Note: [Col. 0965D] The eighth degree of humility is opposed to this: to keep the common rule of the monastery.]

42. It is shameful for one who boasts himself above others if he does not do something more than the rest, by which he may appear superior to them. Accordingly, the common rule of the monastery, or the examples of the elders, do not suffice for him. Yet he does not strive to be better, but to seem so. He is eager not to live better, but to seem to live better, so that he may say: “I am not like the rest of men” (Luke 18:11). He flatters himself more over one fast which he keeps while the others are dining than if he had fasted seven days with the others. One little private prayer seems more advantageous to him than the entire psalmody of a single night. During meals he is accustomed frequently to cast his eyes about the tables, so that, if he sees anyone eating less, he may grieve that he has been outdone, and begin cruelly to deny himself the very thing which he had foreseen ought to be allowed as necessary nourishment, fearing a loss of glory more than the torment of hunger. If he notices anyone thinner or paler, he counts himself contemptible and never rests. Since he cannot see his own face—that is, what appearance he presents to those looking at him—he looks at his hands and arms, feels his ribs, touches his shoulders and loins, in order to judge the pallor and complexion of his face according as he finds the members of his body more or less sufficiently thin.
