In short, he is energetic in everything of his own, lazy in what is common. He keeps awake in bed; he sleeps in choir. And while the others sing psalms at the night offices, he sleeps through the whole night; after the vigils, while the others rest in the cloister, he alone remains in the oratory. He spits, coughs, groans, and with sighs fills from his corner the ears of those sitting outside. And when, through these things which he does singularly but vainly, his reputation has grown among the simpler brethren—who indeed approve the works they see, but do not discern whence they proceed—they call the wretch blessed and lead him into error (Isaiah 3:12).

## CHAPTER XV. On the sixth degree of pride, that is, arrogance

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Opposed to this is the seventh degree of humility: To regard oneself as inferior to all.]

[Col. 0965D]

43. He believes what he hears, praises what he does, and gives no heed to what he intends. He forgets his intention while embracing his reputation. And whereas in every other matter he believes himself more than he believes others, concerning himself alone he believes others more than himself: so that he no longer merely prefers his own religious observance in words or in the mere display of works, but inwardly believes with the affection of his heart that he is holier than all others; and whatever praise of himself he learns of, he arrogantly attributes not to the ignorance or goodwill of the one praising him, but to his own merits. Thus, after singularity, arrogance rightly claims the sixth degree for itself. After this comes presumption, in which the seventh degree consists.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the seventh degree of pride, which is presumption

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Opposed to this is the sixth degree of humility: To confess oneself unworthy and useless for everything.]

44. For one who thinks himself superior to others—how can he fail to presume more of himself than of them? He sits first in assemblies and answers first in councils. Uninvited he approaches; without command he thrusts himself in. He rearranges what has been arranged and remakes what has been done. Whatever he has not himself done or ordered, he judges neither rightly done nor properly ordered. He judges those who judge and prejudges those who are about to judge. If, when the time comes, he is not promoted to the priorate, he judges his abbot either envious or deceived. If some comparatively humble obedience is enjoined upon him, he is indignant and rejects it, thinking that he ought not be occupied with lesser matters when he feels himself suited to greater things. But one who is accustomed so readily to thrust himself into everything, more rashly than freely, cannot possibly avoid erring at some time. Now it belongs to the superior to rebuke one who errs. But how will a man confess his fault when he neither thinks that it exists nor permits himself to be thought blameworthy? Therefore, when fault is imputed to him, it grows rather than is cut away. If, then, when he has been rebuked, you see his heart turning aside into words of malice, know that he has fallen into the eighth degree, called the defense of sins.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the eighth degree of pride, which is the defense of sins

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Opposed to this is the fifth degree of humility, namely, the humble and frank disclosure of sins and evil thoughts.]

45. Excuses for sins are made in many ways. For either the one excusing himself says, “I did not do it”; or, “I did do it, but I did well”; or, “If badly, not very badly”; or, “If very badly, not with a bad intention.” But if he is convicted even of that, like Adam or Eve he tries to excuse himself by another’s persuasion. But one who brazenly defends even manifest faults—when would he humbly reveal to the abbot the hidden and evil thoughts which come into his heart?

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the ninth degree of pride, which is feigned confession

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Opposed to this is the fourth degree of humility: To embrace patience in hardships through obedience.]

[Col. 0966D]

46. Although these kinds of excuse are judged evil insofar as they are called, in the prophetic phrase, “words of malice” (Psalm 140:4), nevertheless a deceitful and proud confession is far more dangerous than a stubborn [variant: brazen] and obstinate defense. For when some people are reproved for more open faults, knowing that they would not be believed if they defended themselves, they find a subtler argument for defense, answering with words of deceitful confession. For, as it is written, “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, and his inward parts are full of deceit” (Sirach 19:23). Their faces are lowered and their bodies prostrated; they squeeze out a few tears for themselves, if they can; they interrupt their speech with sighs and their words with groans. Nor does such a person merely fail to excuse the charges brought against him: he even exaggerates his fault, so that, when you hear from his own mouth something impossible or unbelievable added to his guilt, you may disbelieve even what you had thought certain; and, because you do not doubt that what he confesses is false, what had been held almost certain may come into doubt. While they assert what they do not want believed, they defend their fault by confessing it, and conceal it by exposing it. Confession has a commendable sound on their lips, while iniquity is still hidden in their hearts, so that the hearer may suppose them to confess more from humility than from truth, applying to them that saying of Scripture: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself in his speech” (Proverbs 18:17). They prefer to endanger truth before men rather than humility, though before God they endanger both. Or if the fault is so manifest that no artifice whatsoever can conceal it, they nevertheless assume the voice, not the heart, of a penitent, so as to erase their discredit rather than their guilt, compensating for the notoriety of their manifest transgression by the elegance of a public confession.

[Col. 0967C]

47. Humility is a glorious thing, since pride itself desires to cloak itself with it lest it become contemptible. But this evasion is soon detected by the superior if he is not easily swayed by this proud humility to conceal the fault more completely or postpone its punishment. “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels,” and tribulation distinguishes those who truly repent. For one who truly repents does not shrink from the labor of penance; whatever is enjoined upon him for the fault which he hates, he embraces patiently with a silent conscience. In obedience itself, when hard and contrary matters arise, enduring whatever injuries are inflicted upon him, he does not grow weary, and thus shows that he stands in the fourth degree of humility. But one whose confession is feigned, when challenged by a single slight insult or a small punishment, can no longer either feign humility or conceal the pretense. He murmurs, gnashes his teeth, and grows angry; and he is shown not to stand in the fourth degree of humility, but to have fallen into the ninth degree of pride, which, as described above, may rightly be called feigned confession. How great, do you think, is then the confusion in the proud man’s heart, when his fraud is exposed, peace is lost, praise diminished, and guilt not washed away? At last all take note of him; all judge him. And all are the more violently indignant in proportion as they perceive everything they had formerly thought of him to have been false. Then the superior must consider that he ought to spare him the less, because he would offend everyone the more were he to spare one man.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the tenth degree of pride, which is rebellion

[Note: [Col. 0967D] Opposed to this is the third degree of humility: For the love of God willingly to submit oneself to a superior.]

48. Unless heavenly mercy looks upon him at this point—which is very difficult for such persons—he does not silently acquiesce in the judgments of all. Soon becoming shameless and impudent, he falls all the more disastrously, because more desperately, into the tenth degree through rebellion: for previously he had secretly contemned the brethren in arrogance; now, openly disobedient, he contemns even his master.

49. It should be understood that all the degrees which I have divided into twelve can be gathered into only three groups: in the upper six, contempt for the brethren is accomplished; in the next four, contempt for the master; and in the two remaining degrees, contempt for God is consummated. It should also be observed that these last two degrees of pride—which, in ascending humility, are found to be the first—must be ascended outside the community and cannot be descended within the community. That they must first be ascended is plainly understood from what is read in the Rule concerning the third degree: “The third degree,” it says, “is that a man, for the love of God, submit himself in all obedience to a superior” (Rule 7.31). Therefore, if subjection is placed in the third degree—and this undoubtedly occurs when a novice is first joined to the community—it follows that the two preceding degrees are understood to have already been passed. Finally, when a monk despises the concord of the brethren and the judgment of his master, what does he do further in the monastery except cause scandal?

## CHAPTER XX. On the eleventh degree of pride, which is freedom to sin

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Opposed to this is the second degree of humility: Not to delight in fulfilling one’s own will.]

50. Therefore, after the tenth degree, called rebellion, when he has been expelled or has departed from the monastery, he is immediately received by the eleventh. Then he enters ways which seem good to men, whose end—unless perhaps God hedges them in for him—will plunge him into the depth of hell, that is, contempt for God. “When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Proverbs 18:3). The eleventh degree may be called freedom to sin, through which the monk, now seeing neither a master whom he fears nor brethren whom he reveres, delights in fulfilling his desires all the more securely because more freely—desires from which, in the monastery, he had been restrained both by shame and by fear. Yet although he no longer fears either the brethren or the abbot, he is not yet wholly without fear of God. Reason, still murmuring faintly, sets this fear before his will; and he performs his first unlawful acts not without some hesitation. But like one testing a ford, he enters the whirlpool of vices little by little, not at a run.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the twelfth degree of pride, which is the habit of sinning

[Note: [Col. 0969] Opposed to this is the first degree of humility: continual fear of God.]

[Col. 0969A]

51. But after impunity follows the first crimes by the terrible judgment of God, pleasure once experienced is willingly repeated, and when repeated becomes alluring. As desire revives, reason falls asleep; habit binds. The wretch is drawn into the depth of evils and delivered captive to the tyranny of vices, so that, swallowed by the abyss of carnal desires and forgetful of his own reason and of divine fear, the fool says in his heart: “There is no God” (Psalm 13:1). Now he uses what pleases him as though it were lawful without distinction; now mind, hand, and feet are not restrained from thinking, perpetrating, or seeking unlawful things. Whatever comes into his heart, mouth, or hand, he devises, babbles, and does—malicious, empty-talking, criminal. Finally, just as, after ascending all these degrees, the righteous man, with heart now joyful and without labor, runs toward life because of good habit, so the wicked man, having descended them, governed not by reason and restrained not by the bridle of fear because of evil habit, rushes fearlessly toward death. Those in the middle are weary and distressed: now tortured by fear of Gehenna, now held back by former habit, they labor in descending or ascending. Only the highest and the lowest run without hindrance and without labor. The one hastens to death, the other to life; one more cheerful, the other more headlong. Love makes the one cheerful; desire makes the other headlong. In the one, love; in the other, numbness does not feel the labor. Finally, perfect love in the one, consummated iniquity in the other, casts out fear. Truth gives security to the former, blindness to the latter. The twelfth degree, therefore, may be called the habit of sinning, by which the fear of God is lost and contempt for him is incurred.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whether and how one should pray for those who despair and are dead in soul

52. “For such a one,” says the apostle John, “I do not say that anyone should pray” (1 John 5:16). But do you say, Apostle, that anyone should despair? Rather, let him who loves that person groan. Let him not presume to pray, yet let him not cease to weep. What am I saying? Does any refuge of hope perhaps remain where prayer finds no place? Hear one who believes, hear one who hopes, and yet does not pray. “Lord,” she says, “if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” Great faith, by which she believed that the Lord by his presence could have prevented death had he been there. But now what? Far be it that she should doubt that he can raise the dead when she believed that he could have preserved him alive. “But now,” she says, “I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.” Then, when asked where they had placed him, she replies: “Come and see.” Why so? O Martha, you offer us great proofs of your faith; but how, with so great a faith, do you despair? “Come,” you say, “and see.” Why, if you do not despair, do you not go further and say, “And raise him”? But if you despair, why do you trouble the Master without cause? Does faith perhaps sometimes receive what prayer does not presume to ask? Finally, you prevent him from approaching the corpse and say: “Lord, by now he stinks, for he has been dead four days” (John 11:21, 22, 34, 39). Do you say this in despair or in dissimulation? For the Lord himself, after the resurrection, pretended to be going farther, though he wished to remain with his disciples (Luke 24:28). O holy women, intimates of Christ: if you love your brother, why do you not implore mercy from him whose power you cannot doubt and whose compassion you cannot mistrust? They reply: Thus we pray better as though not praying; thus we trust more effectively as though doubting. We display faith and bear witness to affection; he who has no need to be told anything knows what we desire. We know indeed that he can do all things; but this miracle, so great, so new, so unheard of, though within his power, greatly exceeds all the merits of our humility. It is enough for us to have given power a place and compassion an occasion; we prefer patiently to await what he wills rather than presumptuously to ask what perhaps he does not will. Finally, perhaps modesty will supply what is lacking in our merits. After Peter’s grievous fall I see indeed a tear, but I do not hear a prayer; yet I do not doubt his forgiveness.

53. Learn also from the Mother of the Lord to have great faith in marvelous works, and in great faith to retain modesty. Learn to adorn faith with modesty and restrain presumption. “They have no wine,” she says (John 2:3). How briefly, how reverently, she suggested the matter about which she was lovingly concerned! And so that you may learn in such circumstances rather to groan piously than to ask presumptuously: the shade of modesty tempered the heat of compassion, and she modestly suppressed the confidence in prayer which she had conceived. She did not approach boldly; she did not speak openly, saying audaciously before all: “I beg you, Son, the wine is gone; the guests are saddened; the bridegroom is put to shame. Show what you can do.” Yet though her heated breast and fervent affection may have spoken these or many more things, the pious mother approached her mighty Son privately, not testing his power but exploring his will. “They have no wine,” she says. What could be more modest? What more faithful? Faith did not fail her compassion, gravity her speech, or effectiveness her wish. Therefore, if she, though a mother, forgetting that she is a mother, does not dare ask for the miracle of wine, with what face do I—a worthless servant, for whom it is a very great thing to be a household servant of both Son and Mother—presume to ask for the life of one dead four days?

54. We read also in the Gospel of two blind men: one received sight, the other recovered it—the latter what he had lost, the former what he had never possessed; one, that is, had been blinded, the other was blind from birth. But the one who had been blinded merited marvelous mercy by pitiful and extraordinary cries; whereas the one born blind nonetheless experienced the benefit of his illuminator, anticipated by no prayers of his own, all the more mercifully because more marvelously. To the former, finally, it was said: “Your faith has saved you”; but not to the latter (Luke 18:35–43; John 9). I also read that two recently dead persons and a third already dead four days were raised; yet only the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, still lying in the house, was raised at her father’s prayers, whereas the other two were raised by an unanticipated greatness of compassion (Mark 5:35–42; Luke 7:11–15; John 11).

55. In like manner, if it should happen—may God avert it—that one of our brethren dies, not in body but in soul, while he is still among us, I too, a sinner of whatever sort, will knock at the Savior with my prayers and with the prayers of the brethren. If he revives, we shall have gained a brother. But if we do not merit to be heard, when he can no longer either endure the living or be endured by the living, but begins to be carried out, I indeed still groan faithfully, but no longer pray with such confidence. I do not dare openly to say, “Come, Lord, raise our dead man”; yet with anxious heart I do not cease to cry inwardly and tremblingly: “Perhaps, perhaps, perhaps the Lord will hear the desire of the poor; his ear will hear the preparation of their heart”; and: “Will you work wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them, and will they praise you?” And concerning the man dead four days: “Will anyone declare your mercy in the grave, and your truth in destruction?” (Psalm 87:11–12). Meanwhile, if he wills, the Savior can meet us unexpectedly and suddenly and, moved by the tears of those carrying him—not by prayers—restore the life of the dead man to the living, or at least call back one already buried from among the dead. I call that man dead who, defending his own sins, has already fallen into the eighth degree. For from a dead man, as from one who is not, confession perishes (Sirach 17:26). After the tenth degree—which is the third from the eighth—he is carried out into freedom to sin when he is expelled from fellowship in the monastery. But after he has passed through a fourth degree, he is rightly called four-days-dead, since, falling into the fifth, he is buried through habit.

56. Yet far be it from us, even for such persons, though we do not presume openly, to cease praying even in our hearts, since Paul also mourned those whom he knew to be dead without repentance (2 Corinthians 12:21). For though they exclude themselves from the common prayers, they cannot altogether exclude themselves from affections. Let them see, however, in what danger they stand, for whom the Church does not dare pray openly—she who confidently prays even for Jews, heretics, and Gentiles. For although on Parasceve [Good Friday] prayer is made by name for all kinds of evil persons, nevertheless no mention is made of the excommunicated.

57. Perhaps you say, Brother Godfrey, that I have at last delivered something other than what you asked and what I myself promised, since I seem to have described the degrees of pride instead of the degrees of humility. To this I answer: I could teach only what I had learned. I did not think it fitting for me to describe ascents, since I know more of descending than ascending. Let blessed Benedict set before you the degrees of humility which he first set in order in his own heart; I have nothing to set before you except the order of my descent. Yet if it is carefully examined, perhaps a way of ascent will be found in it. For if a man coming from Rome met you as you were making for Rome, and you asked him the way, what could he do better than show you the way by which he had come? As he names the castles, villages, cities, rivers, and mountains through which he passed, by relating his own route he foretells yours to you; so that you recognize in going the same places which he traversed in coming. In this manner, perhaps in our descent you will find the ascending degrees; you will read them better in ascending within your own heart than in our book. Amen.

[Col. 0971]

# THE BOOK OR TREATISE OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT, ON LOVING GOD, ADDRESSED TO HAIMERIC, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

## 582. INTRODUCTION TO OPUSCULE VIII

1. Although the following little work is one of the earliest books composed by Bernard, I think that scarcely any was written by him either more worthy of Bernard or more useful to religion. For what is more worthy of a Catholic teacher, or more useful to the Christian commonwealth, than to preach, impress, indeed defend, the first and greatest commandment, on which the rest depend and without which the rest are of no use—that commandment, I mean, which self-love, greed, and perverse human interpretations daily attack and endeavor to undermine? Hence the Apology of Berengar, that rash disciple and defender of Abelard, deserves perpetual darkness. He insolently attacks Bernard for publishing his treatise *On Loving God*, since, he says, “No one doubts this”—not any little woman, nor any utterly ignorant person. Yet divine love has always had its adversaries. Although Christians do not deny its commandment in words, most deny it in deeds; indeed, some reduce it to nothing by evil interpretations to such an extent that today one may even raise the question, and with impunity doubt, whether God—best and greatest, creator, preserver, and redeemer—ought to be loved by any Christian with any special act of love, even once in a lifetime. Bernard therefore did not undertake in vain, in this little work, to commend this divine commandment to Cardinal Haimeric as something worth the labor, teaching in chapter 2, section 6, that God must be loved “without measure,” and that everyone, “even an unbeliever, is inexcusable if he does not love the Lord his God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength.” Further, faith enjoins that God be loved all the more as each person understands that God is to be valued more highly than himself. “But if,” he says in chapter 5, section 15, speaking in the person of all, “I owe my whole self for having been made, what shall I now add for having been remade—and remade in this way?”

2. In this book, therefore, the most holy herald and teacher of divine love describes accurately and feelingly its measure, causes, origin, degrees, and obligation. Its measure: that it be loved “without measure,” that is, in every best way in which we can love. Its causes: God’s merit and our advantage. Its origin: from self-love into the love of God, even to the forgetting and contempt of self. Its degrees: love of self; love of God for one’s own sake; then love of God for his own sake; and finally chaste and pure love—that is, self-interested, mercenary, filial, and beatific love. Finally, its obligation extends to Gentiles, Jews, but most of all Christians. The whole treatise concerns love consisting in affection. Though Bernard says that this cannot be perfectly fulfilled in this life so as to exclude all fear and desire, he nevertheless says that it is the end and goal toward which we are bound to be carried unceasingly and without remission. Finally, he teaches that this love itself comes to us from God’s gift, not from an inborn disposition. Thus he cries out in chapter 6, section 16: “My God, my helper, I will love you for your gift and according to my measure—indeed, less than is right, but certainly not less than I am able. Although I cannot love you as much as I ought, I cannot go beyond what I can do. I shall be able to do more when you deign to give more; yet never shall I do so as you deserve.” Such is the teaching and arrangement of this entire little book.

3. Bernard inculcates the same teaching in other places as well, for example in the sermon *On the Fourfold Debt*, which is the twenty-second among the miscellaneous sermons. Nor does he teach otherwise in the fiftieth sermon on the Song of Songs, where he distinguishes a twofold charity, one “in act” (*in actu*), the other “in effect” (*in effectu*). “Of that which consists in works,” he says, “a law has been given to men and a commandment laid down. But who possesses charity in affection as it is commanded? Therefore the former is commanded for merit, the latter for reward.” That is, charity or love of God is commanded with all the heart, all the soul, and all the strength, so that love may be perpetual, unfailing, perfect, neither hindered nor diminished by anything created. This will not occur except in the other life. Charity “in effect,” however, aims at referring all our actions to God. Bernard’s meaning is so far from excluding love of affection from charity in effect that it includes it. For Bernard does not approve an “effective,” as it is called, love that is dry, empty, merely external, and Jewish; rather, he requires an inward love joined to work: inward, because it is charity and love; joined to work, because it is in effect. The words that follow there plainly show this to be Bernard’s meaning. “I do not say this,” he says, “so that we may be without affection and merely move our hands to works. Among other things which the Apostle writes are evil and grievous evils of men, I read this too listed among them: namely, being without affection.” The kind of affection required for works of charity the holy man at once teaches, after first stating that there are three kinds of affection: the first “which flesh produces”; the second “which reason governs”; the third “which wisdom seasons.” He then adds: “Through the second, therefore, works are done, and charity is in it; yet not that affective charity which, seasoned with the salt of wisdom and becoming rich, brings to the mind a great abundance of the Lord’s sweetness, but rather a certain active charity. Although it does not yet refresh with that sweet love, it is nevertheless vehemently kindled by love of love itself.” This is the charity in effect which Bernard says is commanded by God, inferior indeed to the third, or beatific, charity, which “removes the first and rewards the second,” as he says in the same place. “Thus, then, a love surpassing every other obligation ought, as it were, to reign alone in us, so that it may claim for itself whatever is owed to others and we may do everything from love,” says the holy man in Sermon 12 on Psalm 90, section 7. This is enough concerning the subject of the following little book.

4. Bernard addressed it to Haimeric or Aimeric, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, as all manuscript codices state, except one Colbert manuscript, which has “Ascelin,” but erroneously, as is attested even by Berengar, Abelard’s apologist, who gives “Aimeric.” The book was written under the pontificate of Honorius II, by whom Haimeric was made chancellor. Geoffrey, in Book III of the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 8, says: “If one seeks the religious devotion of a pious mind, one must proceed to the homilies on the Praises of the Virgin Mother, and to the book which he published *On Loving God*.” Haimeric was a Frenchman from the town of Castra near Bourges; he was made cardinal by Callixtus II in 1121, chancellor by Honorius II about 1126, and died in 1141. From other letters he is known as a particular friend of Bernard.

## 584. PREFACE

[Col. 0973A]

To the illustrious lord HAIMERIC, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the Roman Church, BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes life in the Lord and death in the Lord.

You have been accustomed to ask prayers from me, not questions; and I indeed am confident that I am fit for neither. Yet my profession enjoins the former, though my manner of life does not equally do so; while for the latter, to tell the truth, I see that I lack the things which would seem especially necessary: diligence and ability. Yet I confess that I am pleased that you seek spiritual things in place of carnal things, if only you had chosen to do this with one richer than I. But since it is equally customary for learned and unlearned people in matters of this kind to make excuses, and it is not easy to know which excuse proceeds truly from incompetence and which from modesty unless obedience in an imposed task proves it, receive from my poverty what I have, lest by remaining silent I be thought a philosopher. Yet I do not promise to answer every question. I shall answer only what you ask concerning loving God, as he himself gives. For this subject is sweeter to savor, safer to treat, and more profitable to hear. Reserve the rest for more diligent persons.

## CHAPTER I. Why and how God ought to be loved

1. You wish, then, to hear from me why and how God ought to be loved? And I answer: The reason for loving God is God; the measure is to love without measure.

[Note: [Col. 0973A] Severus, bishop of Milevis, has the same words in his letter to Augustine, among the Augustinian letters, no. 109: “No measure of loving is imposed upon us, when the measure itself is to love without measure.” John of Salisbury imitates Bernard here in *Polycraticus*, Book VII, chapter 11. Away with Berengar, that most shameless apologist of Abelard, who dares attack this golden saying.]

Is this enough? Perhaps certainly for the wise. But since I am debtor also to the unwise (Romans 1:14), where enough has been said for the wise, they too must be accommodated. Therefore, for the slower minds, I shall not hesitate to repeat the same thing more diffusely than profoundly. For a twofold reason, then, I say that God should be loved for his own sake: either because nothing can be loved more justly, or because nothing can be loved more profitably. For when it is asked of God why he should be loved, the question produces a twofold meaning. One may doubt what precisely is being asked: whether God ought to be loved because of his own merit, or certainly because of our benefit. To each question I shall give the same answer: I find no cause worthy of loving him other than himself. Let us first consider his merit. He has indeed greatly merited from us, who gave himself to us even when we were undeserving. For what better thing could he himself give than himself? Therefore, if God’s merit is sought when the reason for loving him is sought, this is chief: that he first loved us. He is surely worthy to be loved in return, especially if one considers who loved, whom he loved, and how greatly.

For who was it? Was it not he to whom every spirit confesses: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Psalm 15:2)? And such is the true charity of majesty, since it does not seek its own things. But to whom is such purity shown?

[Note: [Col. 0975] That is, the purity of charity which does not seek its own things, as above. Most printed editions read *charitas* (“charity”), but the manuscripts have *puritas* (“purity”).]

“For while we were still enemies,” he says, “we were reconciled to God” (Romans 5:10). Therefore God loved freely, and loved enemies. But how greatly? As John says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16); and Paul: “He did not spare,” he says, “his own Son, but delivered him up for us” (Romans 8:32). The Son himself likewise says of himself: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Thus the righteous merited love from the ungodly, the highest from the lowest, the omnipotent from the weak. But someone says: “Yes, from human beings; but not so from angels.” That is true, because there was no necessity. Yet he who aided human beings in such necessity preserved angels from such necessity; and he who, by loving human beings, made them such that they would not remain as they were, likewise by loving gave angels the grace not to become such.

## CHAPTER II. How greatly God deserves to be loved by humanity, because of the goods both of body and soul; and how these are to be recognized and possessed without wronging the giver

[Col. 0975D]

2. To those for whom these matters are clear, I think it is also clear why God ought to be loved—that is, by what he has deserved to be loved. But if unbelievers do not know these things, God nevertheless has at hand innumerable benefits of his, supplied for human use and manifest to human perception, by which to confound the ungrateful. For who else provides food for everyone who eats, light for everyone who sees, breath for everyone who breathes? Yet it is foolish now to wish to enumerate things which I said not long ago were innumerable. For an example, it is enough to bring forward the chief: bread, sun, and air. I call them chief not because they are more excellent, but because they are more necessary; for they belong to the body. Let a person seek his higher goods in that part of himself by which he is superior to himself, namely in the soul: dignity, knowledge, and virtue. By dignity in a human being I mean free choice, through which he has been granted not merely to excel other living creatures, but to rule over them. By knowledge I mean that through which he recognizes this dignity in himself, yet recognizes that it is not from himself. By virtue I mean that through which he then both seeks without sloth the one from whom it comes and, when he has found him, holds fast to him steadfastly.

3. Thus each of these three appears to be twofold. For human dignity is shown not only by nature’s prerogative, but also by the power of dominion: in that the terror of man is ordained to hang over all the living creatures of the earth [Col. 0976B]. Knowledge likewise will be twofold if we know both that this dignity itself, or any other good whatever, is in us, and that it is not from us. Virtue too will similarly be recognized as twofold, if we consequently seek its author and, having found him, cling to him inseparably. Therefore dignity without knowledge is of no benefit; and knowledge itself is harmful if virtue [variant: “this”] be lacking. The reasoning set forth below demonstrates both points. For what glory is there in possessing something when you do not know that you possess it? Further, to know that you possess it, but not to know that you do not possess it from yourself, has glory—but not before God. To one who glories in himself the Apostle says: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. 4:7). He does not simply say, “Why do you glory?” but adds, “as though you had not received it,” in order to declare blameworthy not the person who glories in possessions, but the one who glories in them as though they had not been received. Such glory is rightly called vain, since it lacks the solid foundation of truth. He distinguishes true glory from this as follows: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. 1:31), that is, in truth. For the Lord is truth.

4. Therefore you must know both what you are and that you are not from yourself, lest you either not glory at all or glory vainly. For “if you do not know yourself,” he says, “go forth after the flocks of your companions” (Cant. 1:7). And indeed this is what happens. Man, made in honour, when he does not understand that very honour, is deservedly compared, because of such ignorance of his own, to beasts—fellow sharers, as it were, in his present corruption and mortality [Col. 0976D]. Thus it comes about that the creature, distinguished by the excellent gift of reason, by failing to recognize itself begins to be joined to herds of irrational creatures; ignorant of its own inward glory, it is drawn outward by its own curiosity, to be conformed to sensible things. And it becomes one among the rest, because it understands that it has received nothing above the rest.

This ignorance, then, by which perhaps we think too little of ourselves, must be guarded against most carefully. But no less—indeed, even more—must that ignorance be avoided by which we attribute too much to ourselves: this occurs when, deceived, we suppose that any good whatsoever is both in us and from us [Col. 0977A]. Yet more to be shunned and abhorred than either ignorance is that presumption by which, perhaps knowingly and deliberately, you dare to seek your own glory from goods that are not yours, and, though certain that you are not your own source, nevertheless do not fear to seize another’s honour from those goods. The former ignorance has no glory; the latter indeed has glory, but not before God. But this third evil, now committed knowingly, usurps glory even against God.

Indeed, this arrogance appears so much graver and more dangerous than the latter ignorance, inasmuch as by that ignorance God is not known, whereas by this he is also despised. And it is so much worse and more detestable than the former, that through the former we are associated with beasts, but through this also with demons. For it is both the greatest pride [Col. 0977B] and a grave offence to use bestowed things as though innate, and in benefits received to usurp for oneself the glory due to the benefactor.

5. Therefore dignity and knowledge require virtue as well—the fruit of them both—by which he is sought and held fast who, as the author and giver of all things, ought rightly to be glorified for all things. Otherwise, “the one who knows and does not do what is worthy will receive many blows.” Why? Certainly because “he did not wish to understand, so as to act well; rather, he meditated iniquity upon his bed” (Ps. 25:4–5), while the impious servant strives to appropriate—indeed, to snatch for himself—the glory of the good Lord from goods which, by the gift of knowledge, he has learned with complete certainty are not from himself.

It is clear, therefore, both that dignity without knowledge is utterly useless, and that knowledge without virtue is damnable [Col. 0977C]. But the man of virtue, for whom neither harmful knowledge nor fruitless dignity remains, cries out to God and frankly confesses: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9). That is: We attribute nothing to ourselves, O Lord, from knowledge; nothing to ourselves from dignity; but we assign everything to your name, from whom everything comes.

6. But we have wandered almost too far from our purpose while striving to show that even those who do not know Christ are sufficiently admonished, through the natural law and through the goods they have received in body and soul, that they too ought to love God for God’s own sake. For, to repeat briefly what has been said on this point: what unbeliever can fail to know that, in this mortal life, the necessities mentioned above—by which his body subsists, sees, and breathes—are supplied to him by none other than him “who gives food to all flesh” (Ps. 135:25), “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45) [Col. 0977D]?

Likewise, what impious person could suppose that there is any author of the human dignity that shines in the soul other than the very one who says in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)? Who could judge anyone else the giver of knowledge except likewise him who “teaches man knowledge” (Ps. 93:10)? Who, again, could suppose that the gift of virtue has been given him from elsewhere, or hope that it will be given him from elsewhere, than from the hand of the Lord of hosts?

God therefore deserves to be loved for his own sake even by the unbeliever; for though he does not know Christ [Col. 0978A], he nevertheless knows himself. Thus every unbeliever too is without excuse if he does not love the Lord his God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength. For the justice innate in reason, and not unknown to it, cries out inwardly that he ought to love wholly him to whom he knows he owes his whole self.

Yet it is difficult—indeed impossible—for anyone, by the powers of free choice received once from God, to turn that choice wholly toward God’s will, rather than twist it toward his own and retain it for himself as though it were his own. For it is written: “All seek the things that are their own” (Phil. 2:21); and again: “The thoughts and inclinations of man are prone to evil” (Gen. 8:21).

## CHAPTER III. How much greater are Christians’ incentives to love God than those of unbelievers.

[Col. 0978B]

7. In contrast, the faithful fully know how utterly necessary Jesus—and Jesus crucified—is to them. As they marvel at and embrace in him the love surpassing knowledge, they are ashamed not to return, in exchange for so great love and condescension, even that little which they are. Accordingly, those who understand that they have been loved more, love more readily; but the one to whom less has been given loves less.

Certainly neither Jew nor pagan is stirred by such goads of love as the Church experiences when she says, “I am wounded by love”; and again, “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Cant. 2:4–5) [Col. 0978C]. She sees King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him (Cant. 3:11); she sees the Father’s Only-Begotten carrying the cross for her; she sees the Lord of majesty beaten and spat upon; she sees the author of life and glory fastened with nails, pierced with a lance, filled with reproaches, and finally laying down his beloved life for his friends.

Seeing these things, her own soul is yet more transfixed by the sword of love, and she says: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love.” These indeed are the pomegranates which the bride, having been brought into the garden of her Beloved, plucks from the tree of life: deriving their flavour from the heavenly bread and their colour from Christ’s blood. Then she sees death dead and the author of death conquered [Col. 0978D]. She sees captivity led captive from the lower world to earth, from earth to heaven, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10). She observes that the earth which, under the ancient curse, had brought forth thorns and thistles, has been renewed by the grace of the new blessing and has blossomed again. And amid all these things, recalling that verse, “My flesh has blossomed again, and of my own will I shall praise him” (Ps. 27:7), she desires to flourish [variant: “be joined”] by the fruits of the Passion that she has taken from the tree of the cross, and by the flowers of the Resurrection, whose fragrance especially invites the Bridegroom to revisit her more frequently.

8. Finally she says: “Behold, you are fair, my beloved, and comely; our bed is flowering” (Cant. 1:15). In showing the bed, she sufficiently reveals what she desires; and in declaring it flowering, she sufficiently indicates from what she hopes to obtain what she desires [Col. 0979A]. It is not from her own merits, but from the flowers of the field which God has blessed.

Christ delights in flowers—Christ, who willed both to be conceived and reared at Nazareth. The heavenly Bridegroom delights in such perfumes, and readily and gladly enters often into the chamber of the heart when he finds it filled with fruits of this kind and strewn with flowers. That is, wherever he sees, through diligent meditation, either the grace of his Passion or the glory of his Resurrection being considered, there indeed he is present, attentive and willing.

Recognize in the memorials of the Passion fruits as it were of the past year: namely, of all the preceding ages passed under the dominion of sin and death, finally appearing in the fullness of time. But understand the marks of the Resurrection as new flowers of the time that follows, flourishing anew in the new summer of grace; their fruit the general resurrection to come will bring forth at the end, to remain without end [Col. 0979B]. “For now,” he says, “winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land” (Cant. 2:11–12). He signifies that summer has arrived with him who, having thawed from death’s frost into a kind of spring mildness of new life, says, “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). His flesh, sown in death, blossomed again in the Resurrection; and at once, at its fragrance, the dry places in the field of our valley grow green again, the cold are warmed, and the dead return to life.

9. By the newness of these flowers and fruits, and by the beauty [variant: “fullness”] of the field breathing forth a most sweet fragrance, the Father himself also delights in the Son who makes all things new [Col. 0979C], so that he says: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27). It is well called full, “for from his fullness we have all received.” Yet the bride, more intimately, gathers flowers for herself from it whenever she wishes and plucks fruits, with which she may sprinkle the inner chamber of her own conscience, so that the bed of her heart may smell sweetly when the Bridegroom enters.

For if we wish Christ to be our frequent guest, we must always keep our hearts fortified with faithful testimonies both of the mercy of him who died and of the power of him who rose again. David spoke thus: “These two things have I heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to you, O Lord” (Ps. 61:12–13). For the testimonies of both things have been made exceedingly credible: Christ died for our offences [Col. 0979D], rose again for our justification, ascended for our protection, sent the Spirit for our consolation, and will one day return for our consummation. In his death he displayed mercy, in his resurrection power, and in each of the remaining acts both together.

10. These apples and these flowers, by which the bride asks meanwhile to be surrounded and strengthened, I think she does so because she feels that the force of love within her can easily grow lukewarm and, in some way, languish unless it is continually nourished by such incentives—until she is at last brought into the chamber, received in long-desired embraces, and says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand has embraced me” (Cant. 2:6).

For then she will feel and prove that all the testimonies of love which she had received in his first coming, as from the left hand of her Beloved, are, in comparison with the abundance of sweetness in the embrace of his right hand, to be despised and now to be regarded as altogether beneath her [Col. 0980A]. She will feel what she had heard: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (John 6:64). She will prove what she had read: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than honey and the honeycomb. My memory is unto generations of ages” (Ecclus. 24:27–28).

The latter statement means that, so long as this present age visibly endures—in which one generation comes and another passes away—the elect will not lack the consolation of remembrance, since full refreshment from the Presence has not yet been granted them. Hence it is written: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness”—without doubt those whom a little earlier he had called, “Generation after generation shall praise your works” (Ps. 144:7, 4) [Col. 0980B]. Thus remembrance belongs to the generations of the ages; presence belongs to the kingdom of heaven. From the latter the election already taken up is glorified; by the former the generation still on pilgrimage is consoled.

## CHAPTER IV. Which persons draw consolation from the remembrance of God, and which are better fitted for his love.

11. But it matters which generation draws comfort from the remembrance of God. It is not the perverse and provoking generation, to which it is said: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6:24), but that which can truly say: “My soul refused to be comforted.” We certainly believe this generation if it adds consequently: “I remembered God, and was delighted” (Ps. 86:3–4) [Col. 0980C].

For it is just that those who are not delighted by present things should have the memory of future things at hand; and that those who disdain to be consoled by any abundance of passing things should be delighted by the recollection of eternity. This is the generation that seeks the Lord, seeking not its own things but “the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. 23:6). Thus those who seek and long for God’s presence have meanwhile a sweet remembrance close at hand—not one by which they are satisfied, but one by which they hunger more intensely for that with which they may be satisfied.

The food himself testifies this concerning himself, saying: “He who eats me shall hunger still” (Ecclus. 24:29). And one fed by him says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Yet blessed even now are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because one day they—and not others—shall be filled (Matt. 5:6) [Col. 0980D].

Woe to you, perverse and distorted generation! Woe to you, foolish and senseless people, who both disdain remembrance and dread presence! And deservedly so. For you do not now wish to be freed from the snare of those who hunt, since “those who wish to become rich in this age fall into the snare of the devil” (I Tim. 6:9); nor then will you be able to be freed from the harsh word. O harsh word, O hard saying: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41).

This is certainly harsher and more bitter than that saying which is daily repeated to us in the Church in remembrance of the Passion: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” That is: whoever remembers my death and, following my example, mortifies his members that are upon the earth has eternal life. That is: “If you suffer, you shall also reign” [Col. 0981A]. Yet even today most recoil and withdraw from this saying, answering not in word but in deed: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John 6:55, 61).

Thus the generation “which did not set its heart aright, and whose spirit was not faithful to God” (Ps. 77:8), but rather hopes in the uncertainty of riches, finds the word of the cross burdensome now and judges the memory of the Passion oppressive. But how will it bear, in the Presence, the weight of that saying: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels”? Upon whomever this stone falls, it will crush him.

But “the generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111:2): those who, with the Apostle, whether absent or present, strive to please God [Col. 0981B] (II Cor. 5:9). For they shall hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34), and so forth. Then that generation which did not set its heart aright will learn, though too late, how sweet Christ’s yoke and light his burden had been in comparison with that pain; yet it had proudly withdrawn its stiff neck from them as though they were heavy and harsh.

You wretched servants of Mammon cannot both glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ and hope in the treasures of money; you cannot pursue gold and prove how sweet the Lord is. Therefore, since you do not experience him as sweet in remembrance, you will without doubt experience him as harsh in presence.

12. But the faithful soul both eagerly longs for his presence and sweetly rests in remembrance; and until it is fit to behold with unveiled face the glory of the Lord [Col. 0981C], it glories in the shame of the cross. Thus, indeed, the bride and dove of Christ rests and sleeps meanwhile “between the lots,” having already received, from the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord Jesus, silvered wings—that is, the brightness of innocence and chastity. And she hopes besides to be filled with joy in your countenance, where “the hinder parts of her back” also may become “in the pale glow of gold” (Ps. 67:14), when, brought with joy into the splendours of the saints, she will be more fully illumined by the radiance of wisdom.

She rightly glories even now and says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Cant. 2:6). In the left hand she places the memory of that love than which none is greater: that he laid down his life for his friends. In the right hand, however, she places the blessed vision which he promised his friends and the joy of the presence of majesty [Col. 0981D]. That divine and deifying vision, that inestimable delight of the divine presence, is rightly reckoned in the right hand, of which it is sung with delight: “Delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). That marvellous love, recalled and ever to be recalled, is rightly placed in the left hand, so that, until iniquity passes away, the bride may recline and rest upon it.

13. The Bridegroom’s left hand is rightly under the bride’s head, upon which, as she reclines, she may support her head—that is, the attention of her mind—lest it incline and bend toward carnal and worldly desires. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15) [Col. 0982A].

For what else does so great and so unmerited mercy, so gratuitous and so proven a love, so unexpected a condescension, so unconquered a gentleness, so astonishing a sweetness—what, I say, do all these things, carefully considered, accomplish except to snatch the mind of the one who considers them wonderfully away from every perverse love, move it deeply, and make it despise in comparison with themselves whatever cannot be desired except by despising them? Thus, in the fragrance of these ointments the bride runs eagerly and loves ardently; and, loved in this way, even when she has spent her whole self in love, she thinks she loves too little.

And not without reason. For what great thing is repaid to a love so great and of one so great, if a little dust gathers its whole self to love in return, while that Majesty, preceding it in love, is seen wholly intent upon the work of its salvation [Col. 0982B]? “For God so loved the world that he gave his Only-Begotten” (John 3:16): without doubt this is said of the Father. Likewise, “He delivered his soul unto death” (Isa. 53:12): without doubt this speaks of the Son. And he says of the Holy Spirit: “The Paraclete Spirit, whom the Father sends in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 14:26).

God therefore loves, and loves with his whole self, because the whole Trinity loves—if “whole” can be said of what is infinite and incomprehensible, or at least of what is simple.

## CHAPTER V. How great is the Christian’s obligation of love.

[Col. 0982C]

14. Reflecting on these things, I think one sufficiently recognizes why God ought to be loved—that is, what makes him worthy to be loved. But the unbeliever, not having the Son, consequently has neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit. For “he who does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him” (John 5:23), nor the Holy Spirit whom he sent. It is therefore no wonder if he loves less one whom he knows less [Col. 0982D]. Yet he too knows that he owes his whole self to him whose authorship of his whole self he does not fail to know.

What then of me, who acknowledge my God not only as the gratuitous giver of my life, its most generous provider, its loving comforter, its watchful governor, but further as its most abundant redeemer, eternal preserver, enrich­er, and glorifier? As it is written, “With him is abundant redemption” (Ps. 129:7); and again, “He entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:12). And concerning preservation: “He will not forsake his saints; they shall be preserved for ever” (Ps. 36:28). And concerning enrichment: “They will give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6:38). And again: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. 2:9). And concerning glorification: “We await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21). And: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18) [Col. 0983A]. And again: “That which is presently our momentary and light tribulation works in us, beyond all measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are not seen” (II Cor. 4:17–18).

15. “What shall I render to the Lord for all these things?” Natural reason and justice urge a person to give his whole self to him from whom he has his whole self, and to love him with his whole self. Faith surely commands me to love him so much more as I understand that he is to be valued more highly than myself: for I recognize him as the giver not only of myself but also of himself.

For the time of faith had not yet come; God had not yet been made known in the flesh, died on the cross, come forth from the tomb, and returned to the Father [Col. 0983B]. He had not yet, I say, commended to us his great love—the love of which we have already said much—when man was already commanded to love the Lord his God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength (Deut. 6:5), that is, with all that he is, knows, and can do.

Yet God was not unjust in claiming his work and gifts for himself. Why should a work not love its maker, when it had the means by which it could do so? And why should it not love him with all its power, when it could do nothing at all except by his gift? Furthermore, that it was made from nothing, gratuitously, and in such dignity, both makes the debt of love more manifest and shows the demand more just.

But how much benefit, we may think, was added when he saved humans and beasts—how God multiplied his mercy (Ps. 35:7–8)! I mean us, who “changed our glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay” (Ps. 105:20), being through sin compared to senseless beasts (Ps. 48:13) [Col. 0983C]. If I owe my whole self for having been made, what shall I add now for having been remade—and remade in this manner? For I was not remade as easily as I was made. Of me, and indeed of everything made, it is written: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). But he who made me, so great a thing, and did so by speaking once, in remaking me certainly both spoke much, performed wonderful deeds, and endured hard things—not only hard, but also undeserved things.

“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12). In the first work he gave me to myself; in the second, he gave himself; and where he gave himself, he restored me to myself [Col. 0983D]. Given and restored, I owe myself for myself, and I owe myself twice over. What shall I render to God for himself? For even if I could repay myself a thousand times over, what am I in comparison with God?

## CHAPTER VI. Brief recapitulation and summary of what has been said.

16. Here first observe in what way—or rather, how without measure—God has deserved to be loved by us. For he, to repeat briefly what has been said, first loved us: so great a one, loving so greatly, gratuitously, such small creatures and such creatures as we are. This is what I remember saying at the beginning: that the measure of loving God is to love without measure.

For since love directed toward God is directed toward the immeasurable [Col. 0984A], directed toward the infinite—for God is both infinite and immeasurable—what end or measure, I ask, ought there to be to our love? Moreover, our love is no longer offered gratuitously, but is rendered as a debt. Immeasurable Being loves; Eternity loves; Love surpassing knowledge loves; God loves, “whose greatness has no end” (Ps. 144:3), “whose wisdom has no number” (Ps. 146:5), and whose peace “surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7): and shall we render a return by measure?

“I will love you, O Lord, my strength, my firm foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Ps. 17:2–3)—and, finally, whatever can be called mine that is desirable and lovable. My God, my helper, I will love you for your gift and according to my measure: less indeed than is just, but certainly not less than I can. Although I cannot do as much as I ought, I cannot do more than I can [Col. 0984B]. Yet I shall be able to do more when you deign to bestow more; but never in proportion to your worthiness. “Your eyes saw my imperfection; yet all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138:16): all who do what they can, though they cannot do what they ought.

I think it sufficiently clear both in what manner God ought to be loved and by what merit of his. By what merit, I say; for to whom is clear how greatly he deserves it? Who can say it? Who can comprehend it?

## CHAPTER VII. God is not loved without fruit and reward; earthly things do not satisfy the appetite of the human heart.

[Col. 0984C]

17. Let us now see for what benefit of ours God ought to be loved. Yet how slight is even our seeing in this matter in comparison with what it is! Nevertheless, what is seen ought not to be left unsaid, even if it is not seen wholly as it is.

Above, when the question was why and how God should be loved, I said that the question “Why?” yields a twofold understanding: it may seem to ask either by what merit of his or for what benefit of ours he ought to be loved. Therefore, having spoken of God’s merit—not as is worthy of him, but as it has been granted to me—I must now speak of the reward likewise to be given.

For God is not loved without reward, although he ought to be loved without regard to reward. True love cannot be empty, yet it is not mercenary, since it “does not seek its own things” (I Cor. 13:5) [Col. 0984D]. It is an affection, not a contract; it is neither acquired by agreement nor makes acquisitions. It moves freely and makes one free. True love is satisfied with itself. It has a reward, but that reward is what is loved.

For whenever you seem to love something for the sake of something else, you plainly love that toward which the end of love is directed, not that through which it is directed. Paul does not preach the Gospel in order to eat; rather, he eats in order to preach the Gospel, because he loves not food but the Gospel (I Cor. 9:18). True love does not demand a reward, but deserves one. A reward is indeed proposed to one who does not yet love, owed to one who loves, and rendered to one who perseveres.

In urging lesser goods, we invite the unwilling, who are not spontaneous, by promises or rewards. For who would think that a man ought to be rewarded for doing what he already desires voluntarily [Col. 0985A]? No one, for example, hires a hungry man to eat, a thirsty man to drink, or a mother to nurse the little child of her womb. Or would anyone think that someone must be prompted by request or payment to fence his own vineyard, dig around his own tree, or erect the structure of his own house? How much less does a soul loving God seek, as the reward of its love, anything besides God? And if it seeks something else, certainly it does not love God.

18. It is naturally implanted in everyone who uses reason always to seek, according to his own judgement and intention, what is better, and to be content with nothing which he judges inferior to something lacking. Thus, for example, the man who has a beautiful wife looks with wanton eye or heart at one more beautiful; he who is clothed in an expensive garment desires one more expensive; and one who possesses great wealth envies one wealthier [Col. 0985B].

You may see men whose estates and possessions have already expanded greatly still day after day adding field to field and, in boundless covetousness, extending their boundaries. You may also see those who live in royal houses and spacious palaces nevertheless daily joining house to house, and, in restless curiosity, building, demolishing, and changing squares into circles. And what of people exalted in honours? Do we not see them striving with insatiable ambition, with all their strength, more and more toward higher positions?

There is no end to all these things because in them nothing is found that is supremely and uniquely good. And what wonder if one is not content with inferior and worse things when he cannot rest short of the highest or best? But it is foolish, and the height of madness, always to seek things which can never, I do not say satisfy, but not even moderate appetite. For whatever things of this sort you have, you nevertheless covet what you do not have, and restlessly pant after whatever is lacking.

Thus the wandering mind, running through the various deceptive delights of the world in vain labour, is wearied but not satisfied [Col. 0985C]. Whatever the hungry person greedily swallows, he reckons little compared with what remains to be devoured; and he always desires what is absent no less anxiously than he joyfully possesses what is present. For who can obtain everything? Yet even the little that anyone gains with labour is possessed with fear: he is uncertain when he will lose it with sorrow, but certain that he will lose it at some time.

Thus the perverse will, by a straight course, strives [variant: “when it strives”] toward the best, hastening toward that by which it may be fulfilled. Or rather, in these winding paths vanity plays with itself and iniquity lies to itself. If you wish to fulfil what you wish—that is, if you wish to attain that upon attaining which you would wish for nothing more—why need you try all the rest? You run through byways, and you will die long before you arrive at the object of your desire by this circuitous route [Col. 0985D].

19. It is in this circuit that the wicked walk, naturally seeking that by which they may end their appetite, yet foolishly rejecting that by which they might draw near to the end: I mean the end not as destruction, but as completion. Therefore those who delight more in the appearance of things than in their author hasten not to be completed by a blessed end, but to be consumed in empty labour [Col. 0986A]. They wish first to traverse all things and test each separately by experience, rather than take care to arrive at the Lord of the universe himself.

And they would indeed arrive there if they could ever obtain what they desire—if, that is, some one person could possess all things except the source of all things. For by the law of his own desire, according to which amid other things he used to hunger after what he did not possess in preference to what he did, and despise what he possessed for what he did not possess, once he had obtained and despised everything in heaven and on earth, he would finally without doubt run to him who alone remained lacking: God, the God of all. And there he would rest, because just as no rest calls him back short of that point, so no unrest would trouble him beyond it.

He would certainly say: “But for me, it is good to cleave to God.” He would say: “For what have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” And again: “God is the God of my heart and my portion for ever” (Ps. 72:28, 25, 26) [Col. 0986B]. Thus, as was said, every covetous person would reach what is best, if he could first attain what he desires short of it.

20. But since shorter life, weaker capacity, and the greater number of fellow seekers make this utterly impossible, those who wish to attain everything they desire toil over a long journey and fruitless labour, unable to reach the end of all desirable things. Would that they wished to reach all things in mind rather than in experience! For this they could do easily and not in vain.

For the mind, being swifter and more penetrating than bodily sense, has been given for this purpose: to anticipate sense in all things, and to permit sense to touch nothing unless the mind, running ahead, has first approved it as useful [Col. 0986C]. I think this is why it was said: “Test all things; hold fast what is good” (I Thess. 5:21): namely, that the mind may provide for sense, and that sense may pursue its desire only according to the mind’s judgment.

Otherwise, “you shall not ascend the mountain of the Lord, nor stand in his holy place, because you have received your soul in vain” (Ps. 23:3–4)—that is, the rational soul—while you follow sense like a beast, reason lying idle and resisting nothing. Those, therefore, whose reason does not anticipate their steps run, but run outside the way; and so, having despised the Apostle’s counsel, they do not run “so that they may obtain” (I Cor. [Col. 0986D] 11:24). For when will they obtain him, whom they do not wish to obtain except after all things? It is a distorted path and an endless circuit to wish first to attempt everything.

21. But the righteous man is not so. For, hearing the reproach of the many who linger in circuits (for many are those who travel the broad way that leads to death), he chooses for himself the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left. Thus, as the prophet testifies: “The path of the righteous is straight; the tracks of the righteous are straight for walking” (Isa. 26:7). These are they who, by a saving shortcut, prudently avoid this burdensome and fruitless circling: choosing the abbreviated and abbreviating word—not to desire everything they see, [Col. 0987A] but rather to sell what they possess and give to the poor. “Blessed indeed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). “All run” (1 Cor. 9:24), certainly; but among those running, a distinction is made. For “the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly shall perish” (Ps. 1:6). Therefore “a little that the righteous man has is better than the many riches of sinners” (Ps. 36:16), because, as the Wise Man says and the foolish man discovers, “he who loves money shall not be satisfied with money” (Eccl. 5:9); but “those who hunger and thirst for righteousness shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

For righteousness is the vital and natural food of a spirit that uses reason; whereas money no more diminishes the soul’s hunger than wind diminishes the body’s hunger. Indeed, if you saw a starving man, his mouth open, drawing in air with puffed cheeks [Col. 0987B] as though to relieve his hunger, would you not think him mad? So it is no less madness to suppose that a rational spirit is puffed up by any bodily things whatsoever no more than it is satisfied by them. For what have bodies to do with spirits? Bodies certainly cannot be refreshed by spiritual things, nor spirits, conversely, by bodily things. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things” (Ps. 102:1, 5). He fills it with good things: he awakens it toward the good, holds it in the good; he goes before it, sustains it, fulfills it. He himself makes you desire; he himself is what you desire.

22. I said above: God is the cause of loving God. I spoke truly: for he is both the efficient cause and the final cause. He himself gives the occasion; he himself creates the affection; he himself brings desire [Col. 0987C] to completion. He made—or rather, became—one to be loved; he himself is hoped for, most happily as one to be loved, lest he be loved in vain. His love both prepares and rewards ours. It precedes more kindly, is repaid more justly, and is awaited more sweetly. He is rich toward all who call upon him; yet he has nothing better than himself. He gives himself as the merit; he reserves himself as the reward; he sets himself before the souls of the saints for their refreshment; in redemption he expends himself for captives.

“You are good, O Lord, to the soul that seeks you” (Lam. 3:25): what, then, to the soul that finds you? Yet here is the wonder: no one can seek you unless he has first found you. Thus you wish to be found that you may be sought, and sought that you may be found. You can indeed be sought and found, but not anticipated. For even if we say, “In the morning my prayer shall anticipate you” [Col. 0987D] (Ps. 87:14), there can be no doubt that every prayer is lukewarm which inspiration has not first anticipated. It must now be said whence our love begins, since where it is consummated has been stated.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the first degree of love, by which a person loves himself for his own sake

23. Love is one natural affection among four.

> **Note:** [Col. 0987D] Bernard, following ancient writers, including pagan ones, commonly recognizes only four principal affections: [Col. 0988D] love, fear, joy, and sorrow; as in Sermon 2 for the beginning of Lent, no. 3, and frequently elsewhere.

They are well known; there is no need to name them. Since, then, what is natural ought first of all to serve the Author of nature, it was said: the first and greatest commandment is, “You shall love the Lord [Col. 0988A] your God” (Matt. 22:37), etc. But because nature is frailer and weaker, it is first compelled by necessity itself to serve itself. And this is carnal love, by which before all things a person loves himself for his own sake, as it is written: “First that which is animal, afterward that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46). It is not imposed by commandment, but implanted by nature: for who has hated his own flesh? (Eph. 5:29).

But if that same love begins, as usually happens, to be too inclined or excessive, and, not content at all with the channel of necessity, is seen to overflow broadly and occupy even the fields of pleasure [p. 594], its excess is immediately checked by the opposing commandment: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39). Most justly, indeed, lest one who shares in nature should be excluded from grace—[Col. 0988B] especially from that grace which is implanted in nature. If a person finds it burdensome to provide, I do not say for a brother’s necessities, but for his pleasures, let him discipline his own pleasures, if he does not wish to be a transgressor. Let him indulge himself as much as he wishes, provided he remembers that he must equally extend the same amount to his neighbor.

A bridle of temperance is laid upon you, O man, by the law of life and discipline: lest you follow your lusts and perish; lest, from nature’s goods, you become a slave to the enemy of the soul—that is, lust. How much more justly and honorably do you share these goods with your fellow participant, that is, your neighbor, than with your enemy? And indeed, if, following the counsel of the Wise Man, you turn away from your pleasures (Sir. 18:30), and, according to the Apostle’s teaching, are content with food and clothing (1 Tim. 6:8), and do not count it burdensome to suspend your love for a little while from carnal desires, which [Col. 0988C] “wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2:11), surely you will not find it burdensome to impart to your fellow in nature what you withdraw from the enemy of your soul. Then your love will be both temperate and just, if what is withheld from one’s own pleasures is not denied to a brother’s necessities. Thus carnal love becomes social when it is extended into common possession.

24. But if, while you share with your neighbor, even the necessities of life should perhaps fail you, what will you do? What indeed, except ask with all confidence of him “who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach” (Jas. 1:5), who “opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing” (Ps. 144:16)? For there is no doubt that he readily provides what is necessary, since he does not fail many even in superfluities [Col. 0988D]. Thus he says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Luke 12:31). He promises voluntarily to give necessities to one who restrains superfluities and loves his neighbor.

For this is to seek first the kingdom of God: to call for help against the tyranny of sin, to take upon oneself the yoke of chastity and sobriety rather than permit sin to reign in one’s mortal body. Moreover, this also belongs to righteousness: not to have divided from another the gift of nature, when nature itself is shared with him.

25. Yet, if love of neighbor is to be perfect righteousness, [Col. 0989A] God must be included as its cause. Otherwise, how can one love one’s neighbor purely if one does not love him in God? And one cannot love in God unless one loves God. Therefore God must first be loved, so that one’s neighbor may be loved in God. Thus God also causes himself to be loved, he who brings about all other goods as well. And he does so in this way. He who created nature also protects it. For it was created so as continually to require the protector whom it had as its Creator: so that what could not exist except through him could not subsist at all without him.

And lest the creature be ignorant of this concerning itself and therefore arrogantly—as may it never be—claim for itself the Creator’s benefits, the same Creator wills, by a lofty and salutary design, that man be exercised by tribulations: so that when man fails and God comes to his aid, [Col. 0989B] as man is delivered by God, God may, as is fitting, be honored by man. For this is what he says: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). This therefore comes about in such a way that the animal and carnal man, who had known how to love no one besides himself, begins to love even God for his own sake, because he has often experienced that in God he can do all things which it is beneficial for him to be able to do, while without him he can do nothing.

## CHAPTER IX. On the second and third degrees of love

26. He now loves God, then, but still for his own sake, not for God’s sake. Yet there is a certain prudence in knowing what you can do by yourself and what by God’s help, [Col. 0989C] and in keeping yourself unoffending toward him who keeps you unharmed for yourself. But if frequent tribulation comes upon him, causing frequent conversion to God and, in turn, frequent deliverance from God, will not even [p. 595] a breast of iron or a heart of stone, so often delivered, necessarily be softened by gratitude toward its deliverer, so that a person may love God not only for his own sake, but also for God’s sake?

For through the occasion of frequent necessities God must necessarily be frequently approached by a person through repeated petitions; by frequent approach he is tasted; by tasting he is proved to be sweet—the Lord’s sweetness is known. Thus the sweetness of God, now tasted, draws a person more strongly to love God purely than personal necessity presses him to do so.
