Thus, following the example of the Samaritans, who said to the woman announcing that the Lord was present: “We no longer believe because of your word; for we ourselves have heard and know that he is truly the Savior of the world” [Col. 0989D] (John 4:42), so too, I say, let us address our flesh after their example and rightly say: “We no longer love God because of your necessity; for we ourselves have tasted and know that the Lord is sweet.”

For necessity is a kind of language spoken by the flesh, and the benefits which it proves by experience it proclaims by enjoyment [variant: “by tasting”]. Thus disposed, a person will no longer find it difficult to fulfill the commandment concerning love of neighbor. For he truly loves God and, through this, what belongs to God. He loves chastely, and he is not burdened by obedience to a chaste commandment; rather, as it is written, he purifies his heart “in obedience to love” (1 Pet. 1:22). He loves justly and gladly embraces the just commandment [Col. 0990A].

This love is deservedly pleasing because it is gratuitous. It is chaste because it is rendered not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. It is just because it returns love as it receives it. For one who loves in this way undoubtedly loves just as he has been loved; he too seeks in return, not his own interests, but those of Jesus Christ, just as Christ sought ours—or rather, sought us—and not his own. Thus does he love who says, “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117:1). Whoever gives thanks to the Lord, not because he is good to him, but because he is good, truly loves God for God’s sake and not for his own. He does not love in the manner of the man of whom it is said: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19). This is the third degree of love, in which God is now loved for his own sake.

## CHAPTER X. On the fourth degree of love, when a person does not love even himself except for God’s sake

[Col. 0990B]

27. Blessed is he who has deserved to reach even the fourth degree, so that a person loves not even himself except for God’s sake. “Your righteousness, O God, is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7). This love is a mountain, a high mountain of God. Truly, “a mountain curdled, a rich mountain” (Ps. 67:16). “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” (Ps. 23:3). “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7). “This place has been made in peace, and this dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3). “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119:5).

When can flesh and blood, an earthen vessel, an earthly habitation, attain this? When can it experience [Col. 0990C] such an affection—that the mind, intoxicated with divine love, forgetful of itself and made to itself like a lost vessel, should pass wholly into God and, cleaving to God, become one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17), and say: “My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (Ps. 72:26)? I would call blessed and holy one to whom it is granted in this mortal life to experience something such as this rarely and only at intervals, or even once—and that itself swiftly, within scarcely the span of a single moment.

For to lose yourself in some manner, as though you did not exist; to have no awareness whatever of yourself; to be emptied of yourself and almost reduced to nothing—is the affection of heavenly life, not of human life. And if any mortal is admitted to this, swiftly, at intervals, and for a moment (as was said), the wicked world immediately resents it; the day’s evil troubles him; the body of death weighs upon him; the necessity of the flesh harasses him; the failure of corruptibility cannot sustain it; and what is more forceful than these, brotherly love recalls him. Alas! He is compelled to return to himself, to fall back into his own concerns, and miserably cry: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me” [Col. 0990D] (Isa. 38:14); and: “Wretched man that I am, who [p. 596] will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24).

28. Yet because Scripture says that God made all things for himself, it will surely come about that creation will one day conform and accord itself to its Author. Accordingly, we must at some time pass into the same affection: so that, just as God willed all things [Col. 0991A] to exist for himself, we too may will neither ourselves nor anything else to have existed or to exist except equally for him, namely for his will alone and not for our own pleasure. We shall indeed delight not so much in our own necessity, whether calmed, or in happiness bestowed upon us, as in seeing his will fulfilled in us and concerning us. This is what we ask daily in prayer when we say: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. 6:10).

O holy and chaste love! O sweet and delightful affection! O pure and clarified intention of the will! It is certainly the more clarified and pure because nothing of one’s own is now left mixed within it; and the more sweet and delightful because all that is felt is divine. To be so disposed is to be deified. As a small drop of water poured into much wine appears wholly to lose itself, taking on both the wine’s taste and color; and as heated, glowing iron becomes very like fire, stripped of its former and proper shape; and as air flooded with sunlight is transformed into the same brightness of light, so that it seems not so much illuminated as itself to be light: so then, in the saints, every human affection must in some ineffable way melt away from itself and be wholly poured into the will of God [Col. 0991B].

Otherwise, how will God be all in all if anything of man remains in man? The substance will indeed remain, but in another form, another glory, and another power. When will this be? Who will see it? Who will possess it? “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3). “O Lord my God, my heart said to you: My face has sought you; your face, O Lord, I shall seek” [Col. 0991C; 0992A] (Ps. 26:8). Do you think that I shall see your holy temple?

29. I think that the commandment, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37), will certainly not be perfectly fulfilled until the heart itself is no longer compelled to think of the body, the soul ceases in this state to attend to enlivening and animating the body, and its strength, relieved of burdens, is strengthened in God’s power. For it is impossible

> **Note:** [Col. 0991C] He treats of the commandment of love, by which we are commanded to love God with the whole heart, and says that it cannot be fulfilled perfectly by a mortal person, or one in the present state of life. He asserts the same in Sermon 50 on the Song of Songs. St Augustine says similar things in various places: *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, ch. 22; *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, ch. 8, where he says that this commandment is to be fulfilled in the fullness of the charity of the future life. For while anything of carnal concupiscence remains, or is restrained by continence, God is not loved altogether with the whole soul. And again: “Why then should this perfection be commanded to a person, even though no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run rightly if one does not know where one ought to run. But how would that be known if it were not shown by commandments?” Likewise, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, final chapter, recalling the commandment of love for God and neighbor, he says: “We shall fulfill this in that life, when we shall see face [Col. 0991D] to face; but this is commanded us even now so that we may be reminded what to seek by faith, toward what to send hope ahead, and, forgetting what lies behind, toward what lies ahead we ought to stretch ourselves,” etc.

> But beware lest you suppose that these statements favor the Sectarians who teach that no one, even if regenerated, can fulfill God’s law in the present state of life. Against this error see the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 11 and canon 18. To explain this point of difficulty briefly, it should be noted that the totality prescribed by the law when it says “with all your heart,” etc., can be understood in three ways. First, as meaning that our whole heart, without remainder, is to be given to loving God alone, and that love is to be directed toward no other object than God alone. In this sense love of God is not commanded; otherwise it would not be permissible to love one’s neighbor. Second, as signifying that our heart ought to be carried into love of God with as great an effort as possible, or that it should love him as much as he is lovable in himself. Third, as meaning that a thing is done “with the whole heart” when someone places in it his chief care and effort, as when we say that someone is wholly occupied with letters. [Col. 0992C]
>
> Therefore the totality contained in the commandment of love must be said not to be understood in the first way, since then one could not love one’s neighbor; nor in the second, although, if it were commanded in that sense, it could be kept; but in the third, which occurs when nothing is preferred to God in love, so that we offend God through no love or fear of any creature. The Apostle expressed this meaning in Romans 6: “No creature shall be able to separate us from the charity of God”; and Christ himself in Matthew 10: “He who loves father or mother,” etc.—that is, whoever prefers love for parents to love for God does not love God above all things. In this sense Abraham is praised because he put aside love for his only son in favor of love for God.
>
> Therefore Saints Augustine and Bernard do indeed understand totality in the first and second senses, and in that sense assert that the commandment of love cannot be fulfilled in this life; but they also imply that a commandment so understood is not imposed upon frail humanity under penalty of sin, but is set forth only as a goal and end toward which one ought to strive, advance, and eventually arrive: that is, the perfection of righteousness hoped for in the age to come. Hence, in the cited passage of *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “For if so great a love of God as is owed to that full and perfect knowledge cannot yet exist, it is not therefore to be counted as guilt. For it is one thing not yet to have attained all charity; another to pursue no desire.” See St Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, II–II, question 44, articles 6 and 8. [Col. 0992D]

for all these powers to be wholly gathered to God and fixed upon the divine countenance as long as they must necessarily be occupied and distracted in serving this frail and wretched body.

> **Note:** [Col. 0992D] The commandment which prescribes the end and perfection of love is not therefore immediately impossible: we must always and unceasingly strive toward it, but are not bound to attain it at once. Thus absolute perfection of charity is not commanded in this life, but the pursuit of that perfection: that, insofar as human circumstances allow, we may be occupied with thought of God, love of God, union with God, and God’s will.

Therefore, in a spiritual and immortal body—in a whole, tranquil, pleasing body [Col. 0992B], wholly subject to the spirit—the soul may hope to attain, or rather to be attained by, the fourth degree of love. For it belongs to God’s power to grant it to whomever he wills, not to human effort to achieve it. Then, I say, it will easily obtain the highest degree, when, as it hastens most readily and eagerly into the joy of its Lord, no enticement of the flesh will any longer delay it and no affliction disturb it.

But might we suppose that the holy martyrs attained this grace even in part while they still dwelt in those victorious bodies? Truly, love’s great power had drawn those souls inwardly in such a way that they could expose their bodies outwardly and despise torments. Yet the sensation of most acute pain could not but disturb their serenity, although it could not overthrow it [Col. 0992C].

## CHAPTER XI. This perfection of love does not belong even to the souls of the blessed after their release, before the resurrection

[Col. 0993A]

30. What, then, of souls already released from their bodies? We believe that they are wholly immersed in that immeasurable sea of eternal light and luminous eternity. But if, as cannot be denied, they would wish to have recovered their bodies, or at least desire and hope to recover them, it is undoubtedly clear that [p. 597] they have not yet been wholly changed away from themselves. For something of their own still remains, toward which their attention is turned, however slightly. Therefore, until death is swallowed up in victory and everlasting light invades and occupies the boundaries of night on every side, so that heavenly glory also shines forth in their bodies, souls cannot wholly abandon themselves and pass into God [Col. 0993B]. For even then they are bound to their bodies, not indeed by life or sensation, but certainly by natural affection, so that without their bodies they neither wish nor can be consummated.

Therefore, before the restoration of their bodies, that self-loss of minds which is their perfect and highest state will not occur; nor indeed would the spirit still require fellowship with the flesh if it could be consummated without it. In truth, the body is neither laid aside nor resumed without the soul’s advancement. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). If death is precious, what is life—and that life? Nor is it strange if the body now seems to contribute glory to the spirit, since it is certain that, even while weak and mortal, it has powerfully aided it.

O how truly spoke he who said that “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). A weak body benefits a soul that loves God; a dead body benefits it; a resurrected body benefits it: first for the fruit of repentance, secondly for rest, lastly for consummation [Col. 0993C]. Rightly, then, the soul does not wish to be perfected without that body which it perceives has served it for good in every state.

31. Flesh is indeed a good and faithful companion to a good spirit: either, if it burdens the spirit, it helps it; or, if it does not help it, it is laid aside as a burden; or certainly it helps and does not burden it at all. The first state is laborious but fruitful; the second restful but not tedious; the third also glorious. Hear the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs inviting us to this threefold progress: “Eat, friends,” he says, “and drink; and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5:1). He calls those laboring in the body to food; he invites those resting after laying aside the body to drink; and he urges those resuming their bodies also to become intoxicated. These he calls “most beloved,” namely, those most full of charity.

For even among the others, whom he calls not “most beloved” but “friends,” there is a difference: those who still groan while burdened in the flesh are held dear for the charity they have; but those already released from the fetter of flesh are the dearer because they have become readier and freer to love [Col. 0993D]. But above both, those who have already received the second robe—that is, their bodies resumed with glory—are deservedly named and are “most beloved”; for they are carried into God’s love with greater freedom and gladness, insofar as nothing of their own remains to trouble or delay them in any degree. Neither of the other states claims this for itself: in the first, the body is borne with toil; in the second, it is awaited with a certain personal desire.

32. [Col. 0994A] Thus at first the faithful soul eats its bread—but alas, in the sweat of its face. For while it remains in the flesh, it still walks by faith, which must work through love, since, if it does not work, it is dead. The work itself is food, as the Lord says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). Then, once stripped of flesh, it is no longer fed upon the bread of sorrow; rather, after its food, it is permitted to drink more fully the wine of love. Yet not pure wine, but as we read in the Song of Songs under the Bridegroom’s name: “I drank my wine with my milk” [Col. 0994B] (Song 5:1).

For even then the soul mixes into the wine of divine love the sweetness of natural affection, by which it desires to recover its own body and have it glorified. Thus it now burns with the wine of holy charity that it has drunk, yet certainly not to the point of intoxication; for the admixture of this milk tempers that ardor for the time being. Intoxication, after all, commonly overturns minds and makes them wholly forgetful of themselves. But a soul is not entirely forgetful of itself while it is still thinking about the resurrection of its own body. But once it has attained that which alone was lacking, what then prevents it in some way from departing from itself and passing wholly into God, and from becoming wholly unlike itself to the degree that it is granted to become like God?

Then at last, admitted to Wisdom’s cup, of which it is written, “My intoxicating cup, how excellent it is!” [p. 598] [Col. 0994C] (Ps. 22:5), what wonder if it is intoxicated with the abundance of God’s house, when, with no anxious concern biting at anything of its own, it securely drinks that pure, new wine with Christ in the kingdom of his Father?

33. Wisdom celebrates this threefold banquet and completes it from one charity: she herself feeds those who labor, she herself gives drink to those at rest, she herself intoxicates those who reign. And just as, at a bodily banquet, food is served before drink, because nature requires this order, so it is here as well. Before death, while in mortal flesh, we first eat the labor of our hands, chewing with toil what must be swallowed. After death, however, in spiritual life [Col. 0994D], we drink, filtering with a certain most sweet ease what is received. Finally, when our bodies live again, in immortal life we are intoxicated, overflowing in wondrous fullness.

This is the meaning of the Bridegroom’s words in the Song of Songs: “Eat, friends, and drink; and be intoxicated, most beloved.” Eat before death; drink after death; be intoxicated after the resurrection. Rightly are they then most beloved, who are intoxicated with charity; and rightly are they intoxicated, who deserve to be brought to the marriage-feast of the Lamb, eating and drinking at his table in his kingdom, when he presents to himself a glorious Church, “not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Eph. 5:27). Then indeed he intoxicates his most beloved; then he gives them drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35:9): for in that most close and chaste embrace [Col. 0995A] of Bridegroom and bride, “the rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5).

I believe this is none other than the Son of God, who passes by and ministers, as he himself promised (Luke 12:37), so that the righteous may now feast and exult in God’s presence and delight in joy (Ps. 67:4). Hence comes that satisfaction without weariness; hence that insatiable curiosity without restlessness; hence that eternal and ineffable desire which knows no lack; hence, finally, that sober intoxication, drinking deeply of truth, not of wine; not drenched with wine, but burning with God. From this point the fourth degree of love is possessed forever, when God alone is loved supremely, because we no longer love even ourselves except for his sake: so that he himself may be the reward of those who love him, the eternal reward of those who love eternally [Col. 0995B].

## CHAPTER XII. On charity, from a letter written to the Carthusians

34. I remember that long ago I wrote a letter to the holy Carthusian brothers, and in it discussed, among other things, these same degrees (Letter 11). Perhaps I spoke there of charity in other, though not unrelated, terms; and therefore I think it not useless to append some of those remarks to this discourse as well—especially since it is easier at hand to transcribe what has already been dictated than to dictate something new again.

That charity is true and sincere, and must altogether be confessed to proceed from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith, by which we love our neighbor’s good equally with our own [Col. 0995C]. For one who loves his own good more—or only his own—is proved not to love the good chastely, since he loves it for his own sake and not for the good’s own sake. Such a person cannot obey the prophet who says: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117:1). He gives thanks, indeed, perhaps because God is good to him, but not because God is good in himself. Therefore let him know that the reproach of the same prophet is directed at him: “He will praise you when you have done him good” (Ps. 48:19).

One person gives thanks to the Lord because he is powerful; another because he is good to him; and another because he is simply good. The first is a servant and fears for himself; the second is a hireling and desires for himself; the third is a son and pays honor to his father. Thus the one who fears and the one who desires both act for themselves. Charity alone—the charity found in the son—“does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). Therefore I think it is said of charity: “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls” (Ps. 18:8), because charity alone can turn the mind from love of self and of the world and direct it to God.

For neither fear nor private love converts the soul. They sometimes change its face or its action, but never its affection. A servant may indeed [p. 599] sometimes do God’s work; but because he does not do it willingly, he is known to remain in his hardness. A hireling does it too; but because he does not do it freely, he is shown to be drawn by his own greed. But where there is possessiveness, there is isolation; where there is isolation, there is a corner; and where there is a corner, there is undoubtedly dirt or rust. Let the servant, then, have his own law—namely, the fear by which he is constrained; let the hireling have his own greed, by which he too is held fast, when he is tempted, drawn away, and enticed [Col. 0996A]. But none of these is either without stain or able to convert souls. Charity, however, converts souls, making them willing.

35. Moreover, I would call it undefiled because it is accustomed to retain nothing of its own for itself. For one who possesses nothing as private property has, beyond doubt, everything he possesses from God; and what belongs to God cannot be unclean. Charity, then, is the undefiled law of the Lord: it seeks not what benefits itself, but what benefits many. It is called the law of the Lord either because he himself lives by it, or because no one possesses it except by his gift. Nor should what I have said—that God himself lives by the law—seem absurd, since I have said that this law is nothing other than charity.

For what preserves the supreme and ineffable unity in that highest and blessed Trinity [Col. 0996B] except charity? Charity, therefore, is a law, and the law of the Lord: it somehow holds the Trinity together in unity and binds it with the bond of peace. Yet let no one suppose that I take charity here to be a quality or an accident—for then I should be saying, God forbid, that there is in God something which is not God—but rather that divine substance itself. This is neither new nor unusual, since John says, “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). Therefore it is rightly called charity, God, and God’s gift.

Accordingly, charity gives charity: the substantial gives the accidental. Where the term signifies the giver, it is the name of a substance; where it signifies the gift, it is the name of a quality. This is the eternal law, creator and governor of the universe. For all things were made through it in weight, measure, and number [Col. 0996C], and nothing is left without law, since even this law of all things is not itself without law—yet it has no law other than itself, by which, though it did not create itself, it nevertheless governs itself.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the law of self-will and greed in servants and hirelings
36. But the slave and the hired servant have a law—not from the Lord, but one they have made for themselves: the former by not loving God; the latter by loving something else more. They have, I say, not the Lord’s law but their own, though their law remains subject to the Lord’s. Each was able indeed to make his own law for himself; yet none was able to withdraw it from the unchangeable order of the eternal law. I shall say that each has made his own law when he has preferred his private will to the common and eternal law, perversely wishing to imitate his Creator: so that, just as God is a law to himself and under his own jurisdiction, so he too might govern himself and make his will his own law.

This is a heavy and unbearable yoke, alas, pressing upon all the children of Adam and bowing down our necks, so that “our life has drawn near to hell” (Ps. 87:4). “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24)—by which I am weighed down and almost crushed, so that, unless the Lord had helped me, “my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17). Beneath this burden groaned the one who said: “Why have you set me as your opponent, and I have become a burden to myself?” Where he said, “I have become a burden to myself,” he showed that he himself was a law to himself, and that no one but he himself had brought this about. Yet, in speaking to God, he first said, “You have set me as your opponent”; thus he indicated that he had not escaped God’s law.

For it belonged to God’s eternal and just law that one unwilling to be gently governed by God should be governed punitively by himself; and that one who voluntarily cast off the sweet yoke and light burden of love should unwillingly bear the unbearable burden of his own will. Thus, in a wonderful and just manner, the eternal law both made its fugitive opposed to itself [variant: “opposed to that same person”] and retained him in subjection: that is, he neither escaped the law of justice which his deserts incurred; nor yet did he remain with God in God’s light, rest, and glory—subject to power and excluded from blessedness.

“Lord my God, why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?” (Job 7:20–21), so that, having cast off the heavy load of my own will, I may breathe freely beneath the light burden of love; that I may no longer be restrained by slavish fear or enticed by a hired servant’s desire for reward, but may be led by your Spirit, the Spirit of freedom, by whom your children are led, and who bears witness to my spirit that I too am one of the children (Rom. 8:14–16), when the same law is mine as is yours, and “as you are, so am I also in this world.” For those who do what the Apostle says—“Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. 13:8)—are without doubt, as God is, themselves in this world: neither slaves nor hired servants, but children.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the law of love belonging to children

[Col. 0997C]

37. Therefore children too are not without law—unless someone thinks otherwise because it is written, “A law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1:9). But it must be understood that one law is promulgated by the spirit of slavery in fear; another is given by the Spirit of freedom in sweetness. Children are not compelled to be under the former, nor are they permitted to be without the latter.

Do you wish to hear that no law is laid down for the righteous? “You have not received,” he says, “the spirit of slavery again in fear.” Do you wish to hear that they are nevertheless not without the law of love? “But you have received,” he says, “the Spirit of adoption as children” (Rom. 8:15). Finally, hear a righteous man confessing both of himself: that he is not under law, yet is not without law. “I became,” he says, “to those under the law as though I were under the law, although I myself was not under the law; to those without law as though I were without law, although I was not without the law of God, but was under the law of Christ” (1 Cor. 9:21).

Hence it is fittingly not said, “The righteous have no law,” or, “The righteous are without law,” but, “A law is not laid down for the righteous”: that is, it is not imposed upon them as unwilling persons, but freely given to those who are willing, because it is sweetly inspired. Thus the Lord beautifully says, “Take my yoke upon you” (Matt. 11:29), as if he were saying: I do not impose it upon the unwilling; rather, take it if you wish. Otherwise you will find not rest but labor for your souls.

38. Love, then, is a good and sweet law. Not only is it borne lightly and sweetly; it also makes the laws of slaves and hired servants bearable and light. It does not, to be sure, destroy them, but brings about their fulfillment, as the Lord says: “I came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). It moderates the one, adorns the other, and lightens both.

Love is never without fear, but it is chaste fear; never without desire, but it is ordered desire. Love therefore fulfills the slave’s law when it instills devotion; it fulfills the hired servant’s law when it orders desire. Devotion mingled with fear does not abolish fear itself but makes it chaste. Only punishment is removed, without which fear could not exist while it remained slavish; and fear remains forever chaste and filial. For where it is written, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), punishment is to be understood—the punishment which, as we have said, never fails slavish fear—by that manner of expression in which the cause is frequently put for its effect.

Further, desire is rightly ordered by love when it comes upon it: evil things are wholly rejected; better things are preferred to good things; and good things are desired only for the sake of better things. When this has been fully attained through God’s grace, the body and all bodily goods will be loved only for the soul’s sake; the soul for God’s sake; but God for his own sake.

## CHAPTER XV. On the four degrees of love, and the blessed state of the heavenly homeland

39. Yet because we are carnal and born from the desire of the flesh, our desire or love must begin with the flesh. If it is directed in right order, advancing through its certain stages under grace’s guidance, it will finally be perfected in the spirit. For “not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterward that which is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46). And first we must bear the image of the earthly man, then that of the heavenly.

At first, therefore, a person loves himself for his own sake, for he is flesh and cannot have any understanding beyond himself. When he sees that he cannot subsist by himself, he begins through faith to seek and love God as necessary to himself. Thus at the second stage he loves God, but for his own sake, not for God’s. But when, because of his own need, he begins to worship and frequent God—through reflection, reading, prayer, obedience, and a certain familiarity of this sort—God gradually and little by little becomes known to him and consequently becomes sweet. Having thus tasted how sweet the Lord is, he passes to the third stage, loving God now not for himself but for God’s own sake.

Certainly one remains a long time at this stage; and I do not know whether the fourth is perfectly attained by anyone in this life: namely, that a person should love himself solely for God’s sake. Let those who have experienced it affirm this if they can; to me, I confess, it appears impossible. But it will without doubt occur when the good and faithful servant is admitted into the joy of his Lord (Matt. 25:21) and made drunk with the abundance of God’s house (Ps. 35:9). For then, as if in some wonderful way forgetful of himself and wholly failing, as it were, from himself, he will pass entirely into God; and thereafter, cleaving to him, he will be one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17).

I think the Prophet perceived this when he said: “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone” (Ps. 70:16). He knew surely that, upon entering into the Lord’s spiritual powers, he would be stripped of all weaknesses of the flesh, so as to have nothing of the flesh left to think upon, but wholly in spirit to remember the righteousness of the Lord alone.

40. Then each member of Christ will certainly be able to say of himself what Paul said of the head: “Even though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). No one there will know himself according to the flesh, for flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God. Not that the substance of flesh will not be there, but that every carnal relation will be absent; love of the flesh will be swallowed up in love of the spirit; and the weak human affections that now exist will be transformed into certain divine affections.

Then the net of love, which now, drawn through this great and broad sea, does not cease gathering fish of every kind, when it has been brought to shore, will cast out the bad and keep only the good (Matt. 13:47–48). In this life, indeed, the net of love encloses within the bosom of its breadth fish of every kind. For a time it conforms itself to all, takes into itself the adversities and prosperities of all, and in some sense makes them its own; it is accustomed not only to rejoice with those who rejoice but also to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15).

But when it reaches the shore, casting out, like bad fish, everything painful that it endures, it will retain only what can be pleasing and joyful. For will Paul then, for example, either be weak with the weak or burn for those who are scandalized (2 Cor. 11:29), where scandals and weakness will be far away? Or will he mourn those who do not [variant: “have”] repent (2 Cor. 12:21), where it is certain that there will be neither anyone sinning nor anyone repenting?

Far be it that in that city he should lament and weep even for those assigned to eternal fires with the devil and his angels—that city which “the rush of the river makes glad,” whose gates the Lord loves above all the tents of Jacob. For in tents, although there is sometimes joy over victory, there is nevertheless toil in battle and frequent peril to life; whereas in that homeland no adversity or sorrow at all is admitted, as it is sung of her: “The dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 86:7); and again, “Everlasting joy shall be theirs” (Isa. 61:7). Finally, how will one remember mercy where one will remember the righteousness of God alone? Therefore, where there will no longer be room for misery or time for mercy, there can certainly be no feeling of compassion.

[Col. 0999]

# TREATISE OF ST BERNARD, ABBOT, ON GRACE AND FREE CHOICE, ADDRESSED TO WILLIAM, ABBOT OF SAINT-THIERRY

## 602 NOTICE ON LITTLE WORK IX

Bernard composed this little work before the year 1128—that is, before the thirty-eighth year of his life. It treats of Grace and Free Choice, prompted by a discussion with some man unknown to me, to whom the holy Doctor seemed to attribute too much to grace, as though he left free choice no part in human actions. The principal purpose of the book, therefore, is to determine the respective roles of grace and free choice in the business of salvation.

Here much is taught concerning the free choice of God, angel, and human being—humanity in its original integrity, fallen humanity, and humanity made blessed—as also concerning the grace of the first human being before and after the fall. It is a small book, but one containing more substance and solid teaching than large volumes of books that treat this theological subject. Its style is vigorous, full of lively intellect and illumination; its words are apt and suited to its subject; its speech is easy, not laboriously artificial but, as it were, natural; neither bloated nor thin, but rich and sinewy; elegant, harmonious, and pleasing; not languishing in the commonplace vocabulary of the schools, nor barbarous or unpolished.

It is not so compressed as to flow sparingly, drop by drop; yet neither is it so profuse as to burst forth like a torrent, as though a dike had broken and its channel run dry. Rather, flowing uniformly with steady course and grave majesty, it shows an unfailing spring, filled not from another source but from its own—or rather from God’s gift and continual meditation upon Scripture, especially the Apostle [see no. 48].

Speaking of this treatise in book three, chapter eight, of his *Life of Bernard*, Geoffrey says: “How far from ungrateful he was to the grace of God is clear from what he discussed, both faithfully and subtly, concerning Grace and Free Choice.” Nor should the words of Letter 52, to Cardinal Haimeric, written about the year 1128, be omitted: “The aforementioned bishop, Geoffrey of Chartres, asked me for some of our little works to send to you; but I had nothing at hand that I considered worthy of your study. Yet I have recently published a little book on Grace and Free Choice; I shall gladly send it to you when I know that you wish it.”

The little book was addressed to William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, Bernard’s singular friend, to whom the *Apology* printed above and several letters are also addressed. The older manuscripts have no division into chapters, but the more recent ones do. It seemed preferable to retain the customary and received division.

## 603 PREFACE

[Col. 1001A]

To Lord WILLIAM, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, Brother BERNARD.

The little work on Grace and Free Choice which, for the reason you know, I recently undertook, I have completed as best I could, with the help of that same grace [variant: “God”]. Yet I fear either that I may be found to have spoken of great matters with too little worthiness, or that I have unnecessarily reconsidered matters already treated by many. Therefore read it first, and, if you judge so, read it alone, lest, if it is brought into public, the writer’s rashness perhaps be more widely proclaimed than the reader’s love be edified.

But if you judge it useful for it to be made public, then, should you notice anything said too obscurely which, in an obscure matter, could have been said more plainly while preserving fitting brevity, do not be reluctant either to correct it yourself or to return it to me for correction, if you do not wish to be deprived of that promise of Wisdom which says: “Those who make me clear shall have eternal life” (Ecclus. 24:31).

## CHAPTER I. For the merit of a good work, free choice’s consent concurs with God’s grace

1. Once, while I was speaking before others and commending God’s grace in me—namely, because I recognized that by it I had been anticipated in good, felt myself advanced by it, and hoped to be brought to completion—one of those standing by said: “What then do you yourself do, or what recompense or reward do you hope for, if God does everything?”

“What counsel, then,” I asked, “do you give?”

“Give glory to God,” he said, “who freely anticipated, roused, and initiated you; and henceforth live worthily, so that you may prove yourself neither ungrateful for benefits received nor unfit for those yet to be received.”

“And I,” I said, “say that you give good counsel—but only if you also give the power for it to be kept. For it is not equally easy to know what should be done and to do it. To give guidance to a blind person differs from providing transport to one who is weary. Not everyone who points out the road also supplies provisions for the traveler. One thing is given to prevent him from straying; another, to prevent him from failing on the way. Thus not every teacher immediately becomes the giver of whatever good he teaches.

“Now I need two things: to be taught and to be helped. You, a human being, rightly counsel my ignorance; but, if the Apostle speaks truly, ‘the Spirit helps our weakness’ (Rom. 8:26). Indeed, the one who provides me with counsel through your mouth must also provide help through his Spirit, so that I may be able to fulfill what you counsel. For behold, through his gift, willing is already present to me, but I do not find the power to accomplish it (Rom. 7:18); nor do I trust that I shall ever find it unless he who gave the will also gives accomplishment according to the good will” (Phil. 2:13).

“Where then,” you ask, “are our merits, or where is our hope?” Listen: “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3:5). What then? Did you perhaps suppose that your merits created you, or that you could be saved by your own righteousness—you who cannot even say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3)? Have you so forgotten who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and, “It depends not on one who runs nor on one who wills, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16)?

[Col. 1002B]

2. “What then,” you ask, “does free choice do?” I answer briefly: it is saved. Take away free choice, and there will be nothing to be saved; take away grace, and there will be nothing by which it may be saved. This work cannot be accomplished without two parties: one by whom it is done, the other to whom, or in whom, it is done. God is the author of salvation; free choice is only capable of receiving it. Salvation can be given only by God, and it can be received only by free choice. Therefore what comes from God alone and is given to free choice alone cannot occur without the consent [variant: “be accomplished”] of the recipient, any more than it can occur without the grace of the giver.

Thus free choice is said to cooperate with grace working salvation when it consents—that is, when it is saved. For to consent is to be saved. The spirit of a beast, however, cannot receive salvation of this kind, because it lacks voluntary consent by which it might gently obey God who saves: acquiescing when he commands, believing when he promises, and giving thanks when he bestows.

Voluntary consent, indeed, is one thing; natural appetite another. The latter we share with irrational creatures; entangled by the enticements of the flesh, it cannot consent to the Spirit. Perhaps this is what the Apostle elsewhere calls “the wisdom of the flesh,” when he says: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. 8:7). We share this appetite, as I have said, with beasts; voluntary consent distinguishes us from them. For it is a disposition of the mind, free in its own regard. It is not compelled or extorted. It belongs to will, not necessity; it neither refuses itself nor presents itself to anyone except voluntarily. Otherwise, if it can be compelled against its will, it is violent, not voluntary. But where there is no will, there is no consent; for consent is only voluntary. Where consent is, therefore, there is will; and where there is will, there is freedom. This, I think, is what is called free choice.

## CHAPTER II. What free choice is, or wherein freedom consists

3. But that what is said may become clearer, and that we may more fittingly reach our purpose, I think we must begin a little further back. In natural [variant: “material”] things, life is not the same as sensation; sensation is not appetite; nor is appetite consent. This will appear more clearly from their respective definitions.

In any body, life is an inward and natural motion, active only within. Sensation is a vital motion in a body, active both outwardly and inwardly. Natural appetite is a power in a living creature assigned to its senses for moving them eagerly. But consent is the spontaneous assent of the will; or, certainly—as I remember having said above—a disposition of the mind free in its own regard.

Will, moreover, is a rational motion presiding over both sensation and appetite. Wherever it turns, it always has reason as its companion and, as it were, attendant—not because it is always moved by reason, but because it is never moved without reason. Thus it often acts through reason against reason itself: that is, as though through reason’s service, against its counsel or judgment. Hence the saying: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16:8); and again: “They are wise to do evil” (Jer. 4:22). For prudence or wisdom cannot exist in a creature, even in evil, except through reason.

4. Reason is given to will to instruct it, not to destroy it. Yet it would destroy it if it imposed any necessity upon it that prevented it from turning freely according to its choice: either by consenting to appetite or to a wicked spirit for evil, so as to become animal, not receiving—or even persecuting—the things of God’s Spirit; or by following grace toward the good and becoming spiritual, judging all things while itself judged by no one.

If, I say, will were unable to do any of these things because reason prohibited it, it would no longer be will. For where necessity is, there is no will. If just or unjust, evil or good actions could occur by necessity and without the consent of one’s own will [Note: “[Col. 1003] So our three manuscripts; the printed editions: ‘without the consent of will, evil or good actions could occur’”], then a rational creature ought either in no way to be miserable or could not at all be blessed, since in either case it would lack that which alone makes it capable of misery or blessedness—namely, will.

For the other things mentioned above—life, sensation, or appetite—do not in themselves make one miserable or blessed. Otherwise trees by life, and beasts by the latter two faculties, could be either subject to misery or capable of blessedness, which is altogether impossible. Therefore, while we share life with trees, and sensation, appetite, and likewise life with beasts, what is called will distinguishes us from both. Its consent, being voluntary and not necessary, makes persons just or unjust and thus, according to merit, blessed or miserable.

Such consent, therefore, because of the inalienable freedom of will and the unerring judgment of reason which it always and everywhere carries with it, may fittingly, I think, be called free choice: free in its own regard because of will, and judge of itself because of reason. Judgment rightly accompanies freedom, because what is free in its own regard surely judges itself precisely where it sins. And it is judgment because, if it sins, one rightly suffers what one does not wish, since one sins only by willing.

5. But what is known not to be free in its own regard—how can either good or evil be imputed to it? Necessity excuses both. Where necessity exists, freedom does not; where freedom does not exist, neither merit exists and therefore neither does judgment—excepting, indeed, original sin in every respect, which plainly has a different rationale.

Apart from that, whatever lacks this freedom of voluntary consent is undoubtedly without both merit and judgment. Everything belonging to a human being apart from will alone is free from both, because it is not free in its own regard. Life, sensation, appetite, memory, intelligence, and whatever else is of this kind are subject to necessity precisely because they are not completely subject to will.

But because it is impossible for will not to obey itself in respect of itself—for no one either does not will what he wills, or wills what he does not will—it is also impossible for it to be deprived of its freedom. Will can indeed be changed, but only into another will, and so never loses freedom. It can no more be deprived of freedom than it can be deprived of itself. If a human being could at any time either will absolutely nothing or will something without willing it, then will could also lack freedom.

Hence nothing that they do, whether good or evil, is imputed to the insane, infants, or sleepers; for, just as they are not masters of their own reason, so they retain no use of their own will, and consequently no judgment of freedom. Since will has nothing free except itself, it is rightly judged only from itself. For neither slow intelligence, faulty memory, restless appetite, dull sensation, nor languishing life makes a person guilty in itself, any more than their opposites make one innocent; and this for no other reason than that these are shown capable of occurring necessarily and apart from will.

## CHAPTER III. The threefold freedom: of Nature, Grace, and Glory

6. Therefore will alone, because through its innate freedom it is compelled by no force and no necessity either to dissent from itself or to consent apart from itself to anything, rightly makes a creature just or unjust, worthy and capable of blessedness or misery, according as it consents to justice or injustice.

Accordingly, I think that this voluntary and free consent, upon which all judgment of oneself depends, as has been said, is fittingly what we defined above as usually called free choice: *free* referring to will, *choice* to reason. Yet it is not free with the freedom of which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). That is freedom from sin, as he says elsewhere: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free in relation to righteousness. But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:20–22).

Who, while in the flesh of sin, can claim freedom from sin? Therefore I do not think that free choice is rightly so called with this freedom. There is likewise freedom from misery, of which the Apostle also says: “The creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:21). But does anyone presume to possess even this in mortal life? Therefore we also rightly decline to call free choice free with this freedom.

There is, however, a freedom which I think suits it better, which we may call freedom from necessity, because necessity seems contrary to what is voluntary. What is done from necessity is no longer done from will, and conversely likewise.

7. Since, then, as far as we have thus far been able to see, three freedoms are set before us—freedom from sin, from misery, and from necessity—the last named was bestowed on us in the condition of nature; by grace we are restored to the first; the middle freedom is reserved for us in our homeland. Let the first freedom therefore be called that of Nature; the second, that of Grace; the third, that of Life or Glory.

For first we were created with free will and voluntary freedom, a creature noble before God; second, we are re-formed into innocence, a new creature in Christ; third, we are raised into glory, a creature perfected in the Spirit. The first freedom, then, possesses much honor; the second, very great virtue as well; the last, fullness of delight. By the first we surpass other animals; by the second we subject the flesh; by the third, death. Or rather, just as by the first God subjected beneath our feet sheep, oxen, and cattle of the field, so also by the second he equally strikes down and crushes beneath our feet the spiritual beasts of this air, of whom it is said: “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. 73:19). Finally, by victory over corruption and death, he will more fully subject us ourselves to ourselves in the last freedom, when death, the last enemy, will be destroyed and we shall pass into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. Christ will free us by this freedom when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father.

Of this freedom, and likewise of that which we have called freedom from sin, I think he spoke to the Jews when he said: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free” (John 8:36). He indicated that free choice needs a liberator—one who would liberate it, indeed, not from necessity, which will, being will, did not know at all [Note: “[Col. 1005D] In the printed editions and certain manuscripts, *voluntatis* (‘of will’); but *voluntas* (‘will’) better suits the sense.”], but from sin, into which it had fallen as freely as voluntarily, and at the same time from the punishment of sin, which it had incurred through lack of caution and bore unwillingly. It could not at all be liberated from either evil except through him who alone among human beings “became free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), free, that is, from sin among sinners.

8. For among the children of Adam, he alone claims freedom from sin who “did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). He likewise possessed freedom from misery, the punishment of sin, but in power rather than in actual exercise. For no one took his life from him; he himself laid it down (John 10:18). Indeed, as the prophet testifies: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7); just as, when he willed, he was born of a woman and made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4–5).

Thus he too was under the law of misery; but he was so because he willed, in order that, free among the miserable and sinful, he might shake both yokes from the necks of his brothers. He therefore possessed all three freedoms: the first from both his human and divine natures; the remaining two from divine power. Whether the first human being had the latter two in paradise, and how and to what extent he had them, we shall see later.

## 607 CHAPTER IV. What freedom belongs to holy souls released from the flesh; and what freedom is common to God and every rational creature

9. This, however, must be known beyond doubt: both freedoms are fully and perfectly present in perfected souls released from the flesh, together with God, his Christ, and the angels above the heavens. For holy souls, though they have not yet received their bodies, lack something of glory but have absolutely nothing of misery.

Freedom from necessity, however, belongs equally and without distinction to God and to every rational creature, evil as well as good. It is neither lost nor diminished through sin or misery; it is no greater in the righteous than in the sinner, nor fuller in an angel than in a human being [Note: “[Col. 1005D] That is, so far as it is in itself; see below, and no. 24: ‘Free choice therefore remains even after sin: though miserable, still intact,’ etc. For it does not belong to free choice, insofar as it is in itself, nor has it ever belonged to it, to be able or to be wise—that is, the will’s conversion toward good (no. 19)—but only to will. And in no. 28 he gives the reason why free choice suffers absolutely no failure or diminution in itself: namely, because in it is seen chiefly to be impressed a certain substantial image of the eternal and unchangeable divine essence; whereas in the other two freedoms there is a more accidental likeness of divine wisdom and power superimposed upon the image. Compare Sermon 81 on the *Song of Songs*, from no. 6.”].

For just as the consent of human will, converted toward good through grace, makes a human being freely good and free in the good precisely because it becomes voluntary and is not drawn unwillingly, so one who of his own accord falls into evil is likewise made both free and spontaneous in evil: led by his own will, not compelled from elsewhere to be evil. And just as the heavenly angel, or even God himself, remains freely good by his own will and not through some external necessity, so the devil equally freely both fell into evil and persists in it, by his own voluntary inclination and not another’s impulse.

Freedom of will therefore remains even where there is captivity of mind: as complete in the evil as in the good, but more ordered in the good; as intact in its own manner in the creature as in the Creator, but more powerful in the Creator.

10. When people customarily complain and say, “I want to have a good will, but I cannot,” this in no way derogates from this freedom, as though will suffered force or necessity in this respect. Rather, they testify that they lack the freedom called freedom from sin. For one who wishes to have a good will proves that he has will, since he cannot wish to have a good will except by will. And if he has will, he also has freedom—but freedom from necessity, not from sin.

Certainly, in being unable, even when he wills, to have a good will, he feels that freedom is lacking to him; but it is freedom from sin that he lacks, from the sin by which he grieves to be oppressed—not freedom of will as though it were destroyed. Indeed, in some sense he already has a good will when he wishes to have it. For what he wills is good, and he could not will the good except by a good will, just as he could not will evil except by an evil will. When we will good, will is good; when we will evil, will is evil. In either case there is will, and everywhere freedom; for necessity yields to will. But when we cannot do what we will, we feel indeed that freedom itself is in some manner made captive or miserable by sin, but not lost.

11. Therefore we believe that free choice receives its name only from this freedom: that the will is free to judge itself good if it consents to good, or evil if it consents to evil—for it recognizes that it consents to neither except by willing. From the freedom called freedom from sin it might perhaps more fittingly be called free counsel; likewise, from the freedom called freedom from misery, it might better be called free delight than free choice.

For choice is judgment. As it belongs to judgment to distinguish what is permitted and what is not permitted, so it belongs to counsel to discern what is expedient and what is not expedient; and to delight to experience what pleases and what does not please. Would that we took counsel for ourselves as freely as we judge concerning ourselves: so that, just as through judgment we freely determine what is permitted and forbidden, so through counsel we might freely choose permitted things as advantageous and reject forbidden things as harmful. Then we would be not only of free choice but undoubtedly also of free counsel, and therefore free from sin.

But what if we were to take delight only and wholly in what was expedient or permitted? Would we not rightly also be called free in delight, since we would feel ourselves thereby free from everything that can displease—that is, from all misery? But now, although through judgment we determine that many things ought either to be done or omitted, we nevertheless do not through counsel choose or reject them according to the rightness of judgment. Again, we do not willingly embrace as pleasing everything that we prudently observe as right and advantageous; rather, we also persist in bearing some things, as harsh and burdensome, scarcely with equanimity. It is clear, therefore, that we possess neither free counsel nor free delight.

12. Another question is whether we possessed it even before sin, in the first man; this will be discussed in its proper place. Most certainly, however, we shall possess it when, through God’s mercy, we obtain what we pray for: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” For this will be fulfilled when that freedom from necessity which now seems common to all rational creatures everywhere [Col. 1008B], as has already been said, will in the elect also be guarded against sin and secure from misery—as it already is in the holy angels. Then, through the blessed experience of the threefold freedom, they will at last prove what is the good will of God, pleasing and perfect.

But since this is not yet so, the sole full and unimpaired freedom that remains in human beings for the present is freedom of choice. For freedom of counsel exists only in part, and only in a few spiritual persons, who have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires, so that sin may no longer reign in their mortal body. Freedom of counsel causes sin not to reign; but the fact that sin is not altogether absent is the captivity of free choice. When, however, “that which is perfect has come, then that which is in part shall be done away” [Col. 1008C]: that is, when freedom of counsel is full, there will no longer be any captivity of choice.

And this is what we ask daily in prayer when we say to God: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10). This kingdom has not yet come into us wholly. Yet it comes daily by degrees, and little by little extends its boundaries ever more widely—only in those whose inward person is renewed day by day through God’s help. Insofar as the kingdom of grace expands, the power of sin diminishes. But insofar as there still remains less of it, because the body of death weighs down the soul, and because the necessity of earthly dwelling surely depresses the mind that is full of thoughts, even those who seem more perfect in this mortality must confess and say: “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2); and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8) [Col. 1008D]. Therefore they too pray without ceasing: “May your kingdom come.” It will not be consummated even in them until sin not only does not reign in their mortal body, but neither exists at all nor can exist in their now immortal body.

## CHAPTER V. Whether freedom from misery, or freedom of delight, is given in this age

13. What, then, shall we say of freedom of delight in this evil age? Here scarcely does the day’s own evil suffice; here “the whole creation groans and travails in pain until now,” being “subjected to vanity unwillingly” (Rom. 8:22, 20) [Col. 1009A]; here “the life of man is a trial upon earth” (Job 7:1); here even spiritual men, who have already received the firstfruits of the Spirit, “groan within themselves, awaiting the redemption of their body” (Rom. 8:23). Is there any place amid these things for such freedom? What freedom, I ask, remains for our delight, where misery seems to occupy everything? For neither innocence nor righteousness can here be safe from misery, any more than from sin, where the righteous man cries: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7:24); and again: “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4).

Where nights and days are continued in sorrow [Col. 1009B], no interval of time is left free for delight. Finally, those who wish to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution all the more (2 Tim. 3:12), because judgment begins with the house of God. This is also what he commands: “Begin,” he says, “with my own” (Ezek. 9:6; 1 Pet. 4:17).

14. But perhaps, if virtue is not secure, vice at least is secure; perhaps it can meanwhile enjoy delight in some measure and avoid misery. Far from it. For those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things act as madmen do when they laugh. No misery is truer than false joy. Indeed, what appears to be happiness in this age is so greatly misery that the Wise Man says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3).

There is indeed some pleasure in bodily goods: in eating, drinking, warming oneself, and other such comforts or coverings of the flesh [Col. 1009C]. But are even these in any degree free from misery? Bread is good to one who is hungry; drink delights one who is thirsty. Indeed, when one is full, food and drink are no longer pleasant but burdensome. Take away hunger, and one will not care for bread; take away thirst, and one will regard the clearest spring as though it were a marsh. Likewise, no one seeks shade except when overheated; no one cares for the sun except when chilled or in darkness. Otherwise none of these things will please unless pressing need has preceded them. If that need were wholly removed from things, even the pleasure that seems to be in them would immediately turn into weariness and annoyance.

We must therefore confess that misery occupies every aspect of this present life [Col. 1009D], except that, amid the continual tribulations of graver labours, the lighter ones are a kind of consolation.

> [Note: This is the sound reading of this passage in two Colbert manuscripts: the printed editions have “consolations of whatever sort.” But “lighter” refers not to the consolations [Col. 1010D], but to the tribulations: the lighter tribulations are a kind of consolation in this life.]

And when, perhaps according to changing times and events, heavy and light troubles succeed one another in alternation, the experience of lesser evils seems to provide some interruption of misery; thus, when after undergoing many very grievous things one happens to fall into something less troublesome, it is thought to be happiness.

15. Nevertheless, we must admit that those who, through the ecstasy of contemplation, are at times carried away in spirit and can taste, however little, something of the sweetness of heavenly happiness [Col. 1010A], are free from misery whenever they are thus transported. Such persons plainly—even in this flesh, though rarely and fleetingly—enjoy freedom of delight: those who, with Mary, have chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from them (Luke 10:42). For those who already possess what cannot be taken away surely experience what is to come. But what is to come is happiness; and happiness and misery cannot coexist at the same time. Therefore, whenever they share in the former through the Spirit, they do not feel the latter.

Thus in this life only contemplatives can in any manner enjoy freedom of delight; and this only in part, in a very small part, and on very rare occasions. Freedom of counsel, however, is enjoyed also by all righteous persons—indeed in part, but not in a small measure. Freedom of choice, on the other hand, as was clearly shown above, belongs equally to all who use reason [Col. 1010B]: it is no less, so far as it is concerned, in the evil than in the good; as full in this age as in the age to come.

## CHAPTER VI. Grace is altogether necessary for willing the good

16. I think it has also been shown clearly enough that this very freedom is in a sense held captive so long as the other two freedoms do not accompany it at all, or do so less fully. Nor does our deficiency, of which the Apostle says, “So that you do not do the things that you will” (Gal. 5:17), arise from any other source. For willing is ours through free choice, but not the ability to accomplish what we will. I do not mean willing good [Col. 1010C], or willing evil, but simply willing. To will good is progress; to will evil is decline. But willing simply is that which either progresses or declines. In order that it might exist, creating grace made it; in order that it may progress, saving grace brings this about; in order that it may decline, it casts itself down.

Thus free choice makes us willing; grace makes us well-disposed. From the former comes our willing; from the latter, our willing the good. Just as it is one thing simply to fear and another to fear God, one thing simply to love and another to love God—for “to fear” and “to love,” stated simply, signify affections, but with the addition they signify virtues—so too it is one thing to will and another to will the good.

17. Simple affections are naturally in us, as though from ourselves [Col. 1010D]; the additions come from grace. Nor is this anything other than grace ordering what creation has bestowed: thus virtues are nothing other than ordered affections. It is written of some that “there they trembled with fear, where there was no fear” (Ps. 13:5). There was fear, but it was disordered. The Lord wished to order it in the disciples when he said: “I will show you whom you ought to fear” (Luke 12:5); and David says: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 33:12).

Likewise, he rebuked people for disordered love when he said: “I came as light into this world, and men loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19) [Col. 1011A]. Therefore the bride asks in the Song of Songs: “Order love within me” (Song 2:4). Likewise they were rebuked for disordered willing when they were told: “You do not know what you ask.” But they were taught to bring their distorted will back to the line of uprightness when they heard: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Mark 10:38). At that time he taught them to order their will by word; afterwards, also by example, when, praying at the imminent passion that the cup might pass from him, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will” (Matt. 26:39).

Therefore we received from God, in the condition of nature, willing, as also fearing and loving, in order that we might be some creature [Col. 1011B]. But in the visitation of grace we receive willing the good, as also fearing God and loving God, in order that we may be God’s creature.

18. Created, in a certain sense, as our own through free will, we become, as it were, God’s through good will. He who made it free makes it good; and he makes it good in order that we may be a kind of firstfruits of his creation, because it would surely be better for us never to have existed at all than to remain our own. For those who wished to be their own—as gods, knowing good and evil—became not merely their own, but the devil’s. Thus free will makes us our own; evil will, the devil’s; good will, God’s.

This pertains to the saying: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). For to those who are not his he says: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12) [Col. 1011C]. Therefore, when through evil will we are the devil’s, in some sense we are not then God’s; just as, when through good will we become God’s, we cease to be the devil’s. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24).

Yet whether we are God’s or the devil’s, we do not in the same way cease to be our own. For in either case freedom of choice remains, and through it the ground of merit remains: so that we may deservedly be punished as evil, because as free beings we become such through our own will; or glorified as good, because we cannot be so unless equally voluntary. Certainly, our own will enslaves us to the devil, not his power; God’s grace subjects us to God, not our will. For our good will—this must be confessed [Col. 1011D]—is created by the good God; yet it will not be perfect until it is perfectly subject to its Creator.

Far be it from us to attribute its perfection to itself, while attributing only its creation to God, since it is certainly far better to be perfect than merely to have been made. It seems impious even in the saying itself to attribute to God what is lesser and to ourselves what is more excellent. Finally, the Apostle, knowing what came from nature and what he expected from grace, said: “Willing is present to me; but I do not find the accomplishing” (Rom. 7:18). He knew indeed that willing was in him through free choice; but that, in order to possess that willing in perfection, he needed grace [Col. 1012A]. For if willing evil is a certain defect of the will, then willing good will surely be its progress; and being sufficient for every good thing that we will is its perfection.

19. Therefore, in order that our willing, which we possess through free choice, may be perfect, we need the twofold gift of grace: namely, true Knowing, which is the turning of the will toward the good; and full Ability, which is the strengthening of that same will in the good. Perfect turning toward the good is to desire nothing except what is fitting or permitted; perfect strengthening in the good is that nothing which one desires should now be lacking. Only then will the will be perfect, when it is wholly good and well-filled.

For it has a twofold good within itself from its beginning. One is general, from creation alone: since it could not have been created except good by the good God, according to the words, “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31) [Col. 1012B]. The other is special, from freedom of choice, in which it was formed according to the image of him who created it. If to these two goods a third is added—namely, conversion to the Creator—it will deservedly be judged perfectly good: good in its universality, better in its kind, best in its ordering.

> [Note: [Col. 1011] The printed editions read: “in its ordering to God.” But “to God” is redundant, as is understood from the following clause.]

Now ordering is the complete conversion of the will to God and its voluntary and devoted submission of itself wholly to him. To this most perfect righteousness fullness of glory is due—indeed, joined—because these two accompany one another in such a way that righteousness cannot be perfect except in full glory, nor can glory be full without perfect righteousness. Such righteousness deservedly will not be without glory, because true glory exists only in such righteousness. Hence it is rightly said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6) [Col. 1012C].

20. These, then, are the two things we mentioned above: true Knowing and full Ability—Knowing referring to righteousness, Ability to glory. But “true” and “full” have been added: the former in distinction from the wisdom of the flesh, which is death (Rom. 8:6), and likewise from the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God (1 Cor. 3:19)—the wisdom by which people are wise in their own eyes, wise, I say, “to do evil” (Jer. 4:22); the latter in distinction from those of whom it is said: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:7).

For true Knowing or full Ability are found nowhere at all unless those two things previously mentioned are already joined to free choice: namely, free counsel and free delight. I should indeed call that person alone truly wise and fully powerful for whom willing is not merely present through free choice, but who through the other two freedoms also finds accomplishment [Col. 1012D]: because he can neither will what is evil nor lack what he wills. The former comes from freedom of counsel—that is, true Knowing; the latter from freedom of delight—that is, full Ability.

But who among human beings is such and so great as to glory in this? Or where, or when, is this attained? Is it in this age? But if anyone were such, he would be greater than Paul, who confesses: “I do not find the accomplishing.” Was Adam such in paradise? But if he had possessed this, he would never have been exiled [variant: “would have been an exile”] from paradise [Col. 1013A].

## CHAPTER VII. Whether the first human beings in paradise were endowed with that threefold freedom, and what happened after sin

21. Now it is time to consider what we deferred above: whether the first human beings in paradise had all three freedoms of which we spoke—freedom of choice, counsel, and delight; or, by other names, freedom from necessity, sin, and misery [Col. 1013B]—or only two, or one alone.

There is no longer any question about the first, if we remember how clearly the preceding argument has taught that it belongs equally to both righteous and sinners. The question properly concerns the two remaining freedoms: whether Adam ever possessed them, whether both or even one. For if he possessed neither, what did he lose? He always retained freedom of choice unshaken, both before and after sin. If, then, he lost nothing, how did being cast from paradise harm him? But if he possessed either one of them, how did he lose it? For it is certain that from the moment he sinned he was free neither from sin at all nor from misery while remaining in the body.

Yet he could by no means lose whichever of them he had once received [Col. 1013C]. Otherwise it is proved that he did not possess perfect Knowing or Ability, as these two were defined above: for he was able to will what he ought not, and to receive what he did not wish. Or should we say that he possessed them in a certain way, but, because not fully, could lose them? For each has two grades, a higher and a lower. The higher freedom of counsel is inability to sin; the lower is the ability not to sin. Likewise, the higher freedom of delight is inability to be troubled; the lower is the ability not to be troubled.

Thus, in his creation, man received the lower grade of each freedom together with full freedom of choice, and he fell from both when he sinned. He fell from the ability not to sin into inability not to sin, losing freedom of counsel altogether [Col. 1013D]. Likewise, he fell from the ability not to be troubled into inability not to be troubled, losing freedom of delight altogether. Freedom of choice alone remained, as a punishment; through it he lost the others, though he could not lose it itself. For by his own will, having become the servant of sin, he deservedly lost freedom of counsel. And having through sin become liable to death, how could he retain freedom of delight?

22. Therefore, of the three freedoms which he had received, by misusing that called freedom of choice, he deprived himself of the others. He misused it in this: receiving it for glory, he turned it to his disgrace [Col. 1014A], according to the testimony of Scripture: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

Among living creatures, only human beings were given the ability to sin, because of the prerogative of free choice. But it was given not so that they might sin, but so that they might appear more glorious if they did not sin though able to do so. For what could have been more glorious for them than that Scripture might say of them: “Who is this, that we may praise him?” Why is he so worthy of praise? “For he has done wonders in his life.” What wonders? “He could have transgressed,” it says, “and did not transgress; he could have done evil and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:9–10).

He preserved this honour as long as he was without sin; he lost it when he sinned. He sinned because it was free to him [Col. 1014B]; and it was free to him from no other source than freedom of choice, through which he had the possibility of sinning. Yet the fault was not the giver’s, but the abuser’s: he turned to the practice of sin the very capacity which he had received for the glory of not sinning. For although he sinned through the ability he received, he sinned not because he could, but because he willed. Indeed, when the devil and his angels transgressed, others did not transgress: not because they could not, but because they would not.

23. Therefore the sinner’s fall is to be ascribed not to the gift of capacity, but to the defect of will. Yet, though he has freedom to fall through his will, he no longer has equal freedom to rise through his will. For although the will was given the power to stand so as not to fall, it was not given the power to rise if it fell [Col. 1014C]. It is not as easy for someone to get out of a pit as to slip into it. By will alone man fell into the pit of sin; but his will does not suffice to enable him to rise again, since he now, even if he wishes, cannot avoid sinning.

## CHAPTER VIII. Freedom of choice remains after sin

24. What then? Has free choice perished because man cannot avoid sinning? By no means. Rather, he has lost free counsel, through which he formerly had [variant: “had”] the ability not to sin.
