Likewise, his present inability to avoid disturbance comes to the wretched man because he has also lost freedom of delight [Col. 1014D], through which he formerly had the ability not to be disturbed.

Therefore free choice remains even after sin: miserable indeed, but unimpaired. And the fact that a person is not sufficient by himself to shake off sin or misery does not show the destruction of free choice, but the deprivation of the other two freedoms. For, so far as it is concerned, free choice neither pertains nor ever pertained to Ability or Knowing, but only to willing.

> [Note: [Col. 1013] This is to be read disjunctively, so that *posse* (“Ability”) and *sapere* (“Knowing”), discussed above in §19, are distinct.]

It does not make the creature powerful or wise, but merely willing. Thus free choice should not be thought lost if a creature has ceased to be powerful or wise, but only if it has ceased to be willing. Where there is no will, there is no freedom [Col. 1015A]. I do not mean if a creature has ceased to will the good, but if it has ceased to will altogether. It must be confessed without contradiction that, where goodness no longer comes from the will, but the will itself has wholly perished, free choice too has perished.

But if willing the good alone is no longer possible [variant: “alone perishes”], that is a sign that he lacks not free choice but free counsel. If, however, he lacks not willing but Ability for the good which he already wills, let him know that he lacks free delight, not that free choice has perished. Therefore, if free choice follows the will everywhere in such a manner that, unless the will wholly ceases to exist, it is not absent; and if the will endures equally in evil as in good; then free choice also surely remains equally unimpaired in evil as in good.

And just as the will, even when placed in misery, does not cease to be will, but is called and is a miserable will, just as it may be a blessed will, so no adversity or necessity can destroy or, so far as it is concerned, diminish free choice in any degree [Col. 1015B].

25. Yet though it remains everywhere equally, without diminution of itself, it cannot equally return by itself from evil to good as it was able by itself to fall from good into evil. And what wonder if, lying fallen, it cannot rise by itself, when, while standing, it could not by any effort of its own advance to something better? Indeed, while it still retained the other two freedoms with it in some measure, it could not rise from their lower grades [Col. 1015C]—from the ability not to sin and the ability not to be disturbed—to the higher grades, inability to sin and inability to be disturbed. If, assisted in some manner by those freedoms, it still could not extend itself from good to better, how much less, once wholly deprived of them, can it emerge by itself from evil into the good which it formerly possessed?

26. Therefore humanity needs Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God: so that, insofar as he is wisdom, he may pour true Knowing back into humanity, restoring freedom of counsel; and, insofar as he is power, may restore full Ability, repairing freedom of delight. Thus through the former humanity may become perfectly good and know sin no more; through the latter fully blessed and feel nothing adverse. But this perfection must certainly be awaited in the life to come [Col. 1015D], when both freedoms now lost will be restored in full [variant: “fully”] to free choice—not as they are given to any righteous person in this age, however perfect; nor as they were given even to the first human beings in paradise; but as the angels now possess them in heaven.

Meanwhile, in this body of death and this evil age, it is enough, through freedom of counsel, not to obey sin in its desire; and through freedom of delight, not to fear adversity for righteousness’ sake. In this flesh of sin and this day of evil, it is no small Knowing not wholly to be free from sin, but certainly not to consent to it; and it is no small Ability [Col. 1016A], though not yet to be altogether beyond feeling adversity in happiness, nevertheless to despise it courageously for the truth.

27. We must therefore learn here for the present, through freedom of counsel, not to misuse freedom of choice, so that we may one day fully enjoy freedom of delight. Thus we restore in ourselves the image of God; thus, by grace, we are prepared to recover that ancient honour which we lost through sin. Blessed is the person who deserves to hear said of himself: “Who is this, that we may praise him? For he has done wonders in his life: he could have transgressed and did not transgress; he could have done evil and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:9–10).

## CHAPTER IX. The image and likeness of God, according to which we were made, consist in the threefold freedom

[Col. 1016B]

28. I think that in these three freedoms are contained the very image and likeness of the Creator according to which we were made: the image, indeed, in freedom of choice; and in the other two a certain twofold likeness is marked out. Perhaps this is why free choice alone suffers absolutely no loss or diminution of itself: because in it there seems to be imprinted especially a certain substantial image of the eternal and unchangeable divinity. For although it had a beginning, it knows no end; nor does it receive increase from righteousness or glory, nor loss from sin or misery. What is more like eternity, while not itself eternity?

In the other two freedoms, however, since they can not only be diminished in part [Col. 1016C] but also wholly lost, there is recognized, superimposed upon the image, a more accidental likeness of divine wisdom and power. For we lost them through fault and recover them through grace; and daily, some more and some less, either advance in them or decline from them. They may also be lost in such a way that they can no longer be recovered; and they may be possessed in such a way that they can neither ever be lost [variant: “in any way”] nor diminished.

29. In paradise humanity was created in a grade of this twofold likeness to the wisdom and power of God—not the highest grade, but one nevertheless nearest to it. For what is nearer to inability to sin or be troubled—in which it is beyond doubt that the holy angels now stand [note: [Col. 1015] other witnesses read “the holy and the angels now stand”; but the conjunction *and* is absent in three manuscripts], and God always is [Col. 1016D]—than the ability not to sin and not to be troubled, in which humanity was certainly created?

From that condition humanity fell through sin—indeed, we fell in and with Adam. By grace we have again received not that same grade, but a lower grade in its place. For here we cannot be entirely without sin or misery; yet, with the help of grace, we can avoid being conquered by sin or misery. Scripture does, however, say: “Everyone born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9). But this is said of those predestined to life: not that they do not sin at all, but that sin is not imputed to them, because it is either punished by worthy repentance [Col. 1017A] or hidden in love.

> [Note: Bernard proves that love can be lost in *Opusculum* 2, §14. Yet the sin of a predestined person is said to be hidden in love—namely, in the subsequent love of the person who is later again to be justified, just as it is washed away through subsequent repentance. Indeed, it is also hidden in the love of God who predestines, because the love of their Father covers a multitude of sins; see Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs, §15. Another explanation of this passage is given in Sermon 4 *On Various Subjects*, where one born of God is said not to sin because he does not persist in sin. Compare the notes on Sermon 1 for Septuagesima.]

“For love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8); and, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered”; and, “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31:1–2).

Therefore the highest angels hold the highest grade of the divine likeness; we hold the lowest; Adam held the middle; demons none. The heavenly spirits have been granted to endure without sin and misery; Adam, to be without them, but not also to remain so; we, not even to be without them, but only not to yield to them. The devil and his members, however, just as they never wish to resist sin, so they can never avoid the punishment of sin.

[Col. 1017B]

30. Therefore, since these two freedoms—counsel and delight—through which true wisdom and power are supplied to the rational creature, are varied by God’s dispensation as he wills, according to particular causes, places, and times, so that they are possessed slightly on earth, fully in heaven, moderately in paradise, and not at all in hell; whereas freedom of choice is not altered in any degree from the state in which it was created, but is always possessed equally, so far as it is concerned, in heaven, on earth, and in hell: the former are rightly assigned to likeness, the latter to image.

And Scripture’s authority testifies that in hell both freedoms which are said to belong to likeness have perished. For that true Knowing which is conceived from freedom of counsel is plainly absent there, as is shown by the passage: “Whatever your hand can do, do earnestly [variant: ‘steadfastly’], because there is neither work nor reason nor wisdom in hell, whither you are hastening” (Eccl. 9:10) [Col. 1017C]. Regarding the power given through freedom of delight, the Gospel says: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13). For what is the binding of hands and feet except the utter removal of all power?

31. But someone says: How is there no Knowing there, where the evils suffered compel people to repent of the evils they have done? Can anyone in torments fail to repent, or can repentance for evil fail to be wisdom? This objection would be correct if only the act of sin and not also the evil will were punished. For no one doubts that a person in torments takes no pleasure in repeating the act of sin. Yet if the will remains evil even amid torments, what weight does the renunciation of the act have, such that someone should be thought wise because he no longer wishes to indulge lust in the midst of flames?

Finally: “Wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4) [Col. 1017D]. How shall we prove that evil will persists even in punishments? Certainly, to omit other points, they would not wish to be punished at all. Yet one who has done things deserving punishment ought justly to be punished. Therefore they do not will what is just. But the will of one who does not will what is just is not just. Thus the will is unjust, and therefore evil, because it does not accord with justice.

Two things demonstrate an unjust will: either pleasure in sinning, or pleasure in having sinned with impunity. Those, therefore, who took pleasure in sinning while they could, and who, now that they can no longer sin, wish the sins they committed to remain unpunished—what evidence of true wisdom or good will appears in them? But grant that they repent of having sinned: do they not nevertheless, if the choice were given, still prefer to sin rather than endure the punishment of sin? Yet the former is unjust; the latter just [Col. 1018A]. When would a good will choose what is unjust rather than what is just?

Moreover, those do not truly repent who grieve not so much that they have lived for themselves as that they are now unable to do so. Finally, what occurs within is displayed outwardly. For as long as the body lives in the flame, it is clear that the will persists in wickedness. Therefore in hell there is absolutely nothing, nor can there be anything, of the likeness contained in freedom of counsel and likewise in freedom of delight; yet the image remains even there unmoved through free choice.

## CHAPTER X. The likeness of the divine image is re-formed in us through Christ

32. But neither could likeness be found anywhere equally in this age. The image would still lie here foul and deformed, unless that woman of the Gospel lit her lamp—that is, unless Wisdom appeared in the flesh—swept the house, namely of vices, and sought her drachma which she had lost (Luke 15:8) [Col. 1018C]: that is, her image, stripped of its native beauty, defiled beneath the skin of sin, and lying hidden as though in dust. Having found it, she wiped it clean and lifted it from the region of dissimilarity; re-forming it to its former appearance, she made it like herself in the glory of the saints—or rather, would one day render it in every respect conformed to herself—when that saying of Scripture was fulfilled: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

And indeed, to whom could this work more fittingly belong than to the Son of God [Col. 1018D], who, being “the brightness of glory” [variant: omits “of glory”] and “the figure of the Father’s substance,” upholding all things by his word, appeared readily equipped from both sources: with that by which he might reform what was deformed and that by which he might strengthen what was weak. By the brightness of his figure, driving away the darkness of sins [variant: “vices”], he made it wise; and by the power of his word, he made it strong against the tyranny of demons.

33. Therefore the Form itself came, to which free choice had to be conformed [Col. 1019A]; for, in order that it might receive its former form again, it had to be re-formed from that by which it had also been formed. Now the Form is Wisdom; conformity is that the image may do in the body what the Form does in the world. For she “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). She reaches from end to end—that is, from the highest heaven to the lowest regions of the earth, from the greatest angel to the least worm. And she reaches mightily, not by mobile movement, or local extension, or merely the official administration of a subject creature, but by a certain substantial power present everywhere, by which she moves, orders, and governs all things most powerfully. And she is compelled by no necessity of her own to do all these things. For she labours in none of them with any difficulty [Col. 1019B], but orders all things sweetly by a tranquil will.

Or, certainly, she reaches from end to end—that is, from the origin of the creature to the end appointed by the Creator: whether it be the end toward which nature presses, which causation hastens, or which grace grants. She reaches mightily, since none of these things occurs which she has not powerfully preordained according to her will by providence.

34. Thus, then, let free choice endeavour to preside over its own body as Wisdom presides over the world, reaching it also mightily from end to end: namely, commanding each sense and limb so powerfully that it does not permit sin to reign in its mortal body, nor yield its members as weapons to unrighteousness, but presents them to serve righteousness. And then a person will no longer be a slave of sin, when he does not commit sin. Once freed from it [Col. 1019C], he will begin to recover freedom of deliberation and to claim his own dignity, when he has clothed the divine image within himself in a likeness worthy of it—or rather, has restored its ancient beauty.

But let him take care to do these things no less sweetly than mightily: that is, not from sorrow or necessity, which is the beginning, not the fullness, of wisdom; but with ready and cheerful will, which makes an acceptable sacrifice, since “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Thus in every respect he will imitate Wisdom, resisting vices mightily and resting sweetly in conscience.

35. Yet we need the help of him whose example summons us to such things, so that through that very Form we may be conformed to him and transformed into the same image [Col. 1019D], “from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). Therefore, if it is from the Spirit of the Lord, it is no longer from free choice. Accordingly, let no one suppose that free choice is so called because it moves between good and evil with equal power or ease. For it was able by itself to fall, but not to rise again except through the Spirit of the Lord.

Otherwise neither God nor the holy angels—since they are so good that they cannot be evil—nor likewise the fallen angels—since they are so evil that they can no longer be good—would be said to possess free choice [Col. 1020A]. But we too shall lose this after the resurrection, when some of us will assuredly be inseparably joined to good things and others to evil things.

Yet neither God nor the devil lacks free choice. For God’s inability to be evil results not from a weak necessity, but from a will firm in goodness and voluntary steadfastness; and the devil’s inability to breathe again toward the good results not from violent oppression imposed from outside, but from his own will obstinately fixed in evil and from voluntary obstinacy. Thus free choice is rather so called because, whether in good or evil, it makes the will equally free; for no one should be called—or can be—either good or evil except willingly. By this reasoning, then, it is not unfittingly said to have itself equally toward good and evil: namely, that in either case there is equal freedom of will for it, though not equal ease in choosing [Col. 1020B].

> [Note: [Col. 1019D] This is freedom of power, or the elective faculty capable of turning toward good and evil; but its exercise and application toward good depend upon grace. For its efforts toward good are both ineffective if they are not aided by grace [Col. 1020D], and nonexistent if they are not stirred up; see below, no. 42.]

## CHAPTER XI. That grace and temptation take nothing away from free choice

36. By this prerogative of dignity, as has been said, the Creator singularly distinguished the rational creature [Note: [Col. 1020D] Two manuscripts read “the prerogative of divine dignity”; one Dionysian manuscript, “the prerogative of divinity in the flesh.”]: just as he himself was his own master and was good by his own will, not by necessity, so that creature too should in some fashion be its own master in this respect: that it should become evil and be justly condemned only by its own will, or remain good and be deservedly saved. This does not mean that its own will could suffice for salvation, but that it could by no means attain salvation without its own will. [Col. 1020C] For no one is saved unwillingly.

For what is read in the Gospel, “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44), and likewise elsewhere, “Compel them to come in” (Luke 14:23), presents no obstacle. For although the gracious Father, “who wills all to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), may seem to draw or compel however many persons to salvation, he nevertheless judges no one worthy of salvation whom he has not first found willing. For this is his purpose when he terrifies or strikes: to make persons willing, not to save them unwillingly; so that, when he changes the will from evil to good, he transfers freedom rather than removes it.

Still, we are not always drawn unwillingly. A blind or weary person, for example, is not grieved when drawn. And Paul was led by the hand to Damascus, certainly not unwillingly (Acts 9:8). Finally, she especially wished to be drawn [variant: “spiritually”], who earnestly begged this very thing in the Song: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3).

37. Again, it is written on the other hand: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1:14); and: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15); and likewise the Apostle says: “I find another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and leading me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). All these statements may seem to compel the will and rob it of freedom.

But however greatly one may be pressed by temptations within or without, the will will certainly always remain free insofar as choice is concerned; for it judges freely by its own consent nonetheless. But insofar as deliberation or satisfaction is concerned, while the desire of the flesh and the misery of life resist it, it feels itself less free indeed; yet it is not at all evil, so long as it does not consent to evil. Thus Paul, who complains that he is led captive into the law of sin, undoubtedly suffers from a less complete freedom of deliberation. Yet he glories that his consent is sound and already in large part free in the good [Col. 1021B]: “Now it is no longer I,” he says, “who do it.”

Why are you confident of this, Paul? “Because,” he says, “I consent to the law of God, because it is good”; and again: “For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man” (Rom. 7:16, 22). With the eye being single, he expects the whole body to be full of light. Though drawn by sin in respect of consent, or captive in respect of misery, he does not hesitate to profess himself free in the good. Hence he confidently concludes in general: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1).

## CHAPTER XII. Whether one who denies the faith through fear of death and punishments is excused from guilt or deprived of free choice; with an examination of Peter’s denial

38. But let us consider those who have been compelled by fear of punishments or death to deny the faith merely in words [Col. 1021C], lest perhaps, according to this argument, either there was no fault in their verbal denial, or even the will could be compelled into fault—so that a person might will what he was known not to will—and free choice thus perish. Since this was impossible (for willing and unwilling the same thing at the same time was impossible), the question arises why evil had to be imputed to persons who by no means willed evil.

For this is not like original sin, by which one not only does not consent, but is often even unaware, yet is bound for another reason while not yet reborn through baptism. Let the apostle Peter be brought forward as an example. He seems to have denied the Truth against his own will, since it was necessary either to deny or to die [Col. 1021D]. Fearing death, he denied. He did not wish to deny, but he wished still less to die. Thus, unwilling though he was, he nevertheless denied, lest he should die.

But if a man was compelled to say with his tongue, and not with his will, what he did not wish, he was not thereby compelled to will anything other than what he willed. His tongue was moved against his will; but was his will changed too? What, then, did he will? Plainly this: to be Christ’s disciple. What did he say? “I do not know the man” (Matt. 26:72). Why so? He wished to escape death. But what fault was there in that? We find two wills in the apostle: one, by which he wished not to die, wholly blameless; the other, by which it pleased him that he was a Christian, highly praiseworthy [Col. 1022A]. In what, then, is he to be blamed? Is it because he preferred to lie rather than die? This will was indeed worthy of rebuke, because [variant: “by which”] he wished to preserve the life of his body more than that of his soul. For “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

Thus he sinned, and not without the consent of his own will—weak and wretched indeed, but plainly free. Yet he sinned not by despising or hating Christ, but by loving himself too much. Sudden fear did not compel his will into this perverse self-love; it only exposed it. Undoubtedly he was already such, though he did not know it, when he heard from him from whom he could not be hidden: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26:34). Thus the weakness of his will was made known, not brought into being, by the fear that struck him; it disclosed how far he loved himself and how far he loved Christ. It was made known not to Christ, but to Peter. For Christ already knew what was in a human being.

Insofar, therefore, as he loved Christ, that will certainly suffered violence—this must not be denied—so that it spoke against itself; but insofar as he loved himself, it unquestionably consented voluntarily, so that it spoke for itself [Col. 1022B]. Had he not loved Christ, he would not have denied unwillingly; but had he not loved himself more, he would not have denied even to some extent. We must therefore acknowledge that the man was compelled, not indeed to change his own will, but to conceal it: compelled, I say, not to withdraw from the love of God [Note: [Col. 1021] That is, by an act contrary to love. For he sinned, as stated above, not by despising or hating Christ, but by loving himself too much.], but to yield somewhat to self-love.

39. What then? Has the entire preceding assertion concerning freedom of will perhaps been overthrown, since the will has in fact been found capable of being compelled? It certainly has—if it could be compelled by someone other than itself. But if it compelled itself, being both compelled and compelling, then where it seemed to lose freedom, there it also received it. For the violence which it inflicted upon itself, it suffered from itself. But what the will suffered from itself came from the will. What came from the will was no longer from necessity but voluntary. And if voluntary, then free.

Thus, the one whom his own will compelled to deny was compelled because he willed it; indeed, he was not compelled, but consented—not to another’s power, but to his own will, namely that will by which he wished at all costs to escape death. Otherwise, how could the voice of a servant-girl have prevailed to form the sacred tongue into impious words [Col. 1022D], if the will, mistress of the tongue, had not assented? Finally, when later he restrained himself from that excessive self-love and began, as he ought, to love Christ with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, no threats or punishments could thereafter extort from his will [variant: “the will”] any yielding of the tongue as a weapon of unrighteousness; rather, he boldly made it serve the truth: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

40. There are indeed two kinds of compulsion, according as we are compelled either to suffer something or to do something against our own will. The passive kind—for the first is rightly so called [Col. 1023A]—can sometimes occur without the voluntary consent of the sufferer, but the active kind never can. Therefore evil done to us, or done concerning us, is not to be imputed to us, provided that we are unwilling. But what is done by us is no longer without fault of the will. We are plainly shown to will what would not be done if we did not will it.

There is, then, also a kind of active compulsion; but it has no excuse, since it is voluntary as well. The Christian was compelled to deny Christ, and indeed grieved, but not except willingly. He greatly wished to avoid the sword of the one striking him; and that very will, ruling within, opened his mouth—not the sword that appeared outside. The sword exposed, but did not compel, that will to be such. Therefore it was his will, not the sword, that drove him into guilt.

Finally, those whose will was sound could be killed but could not be bent. This is what had been foretold to them: “They will do to you whatever they wish” (Mark 9:12)—but to their limbs, not their hearts. You will not do what they wish; rather, they will do it, and you will suffer it. They will torture the limbs, but will not change the will; they will rage against the flesh, but will have nothing they can do to the soul.

> [Note: [Col. 1023D] Thus read the Dionysian and Cistercian manuscripts, and two others. Horstius reads otherwise: “This is what was said of John: ‘They did to him whatever they wished.’ Did they do what he wished? So they did to the other martyrs as well—not what the martyrs wished, but what they themselves wished. They did, I say, to them what they wished, but to their limbs, not their hearts. They tortured the limbs, but did not change the will. They raged against the flesh, but had nothing they could do to the soul.” The same is found in the Colbert manuscript.]

Though the body of the sufferer may be in the torturer’s power, the will is free. If it is weak, they will discover this by raging; they will not compel it to be weak if it is not. Its weakness, indeed, is from itself, but its health is not from itself, but from the Spirit of the Lord. And it is healed when it is renewed.

41. It is renewed when, as the Apostle teaches, by beholding the glory of God it is transformed into the same image [Col. 1023C], “from glory to glory,” that is, from virtue to virtue, “as from the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). Between this divine Spirit and the appetite of the flesh, that which in a human being is called free choice—that is, the human will—occupies a sort of middle position. Like something hanging on the steep side of a very high mountain between the two, it is so weakened in its appetite through the flesh that, unless the Spirit diligently aids its weakness through grace, it is unable not only to ascend, from virtue to virtue, and attain the summit of righteousness—which, according to the prophet, is like “the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7)—but also, continually rolling downward by its own weight from vice into vice, falls headlong. It is weighed down [Col. 1023D] not only by the law of sin originally implanted in the members, but also by the habit of earthly dwelling customarily ingrained in its affections.

Scripture briefly recalls both burdens of the human will in one verse: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). And just as these two evils of mortality do not harm but exercise those who do not consent [Col. 1024A], so they do not excuse but condemn those who consent; so that neither salvation nor condemnation can in any way be had without preceding voluntary consent, lest freedom of choice appear to be prejudiced in any respect.

## CHAPTER XIII. Human merits are pure gifts of God

42. Therefore, what is called free choice in a creature is either justly condemned, since no external force prejudices it toward sin; or mercifully saved, since no power of its own suffices for righteousness [Note: [Col. 1024D] Some manuscripts read, “no force”; the Dionysian manuscript: “its own power by no means suffices for righteousness.”]. In all this, however, let the reader understand that the case of original sin is entirely excepted. Apart from that, one should seek neither outside free choice the cause of condemnation, since it is now condemned only by its own fault; nor from free choice itself the merits of salvation, since mercy alone saves [Col. 1024B]. For its efforts toward good are both ineffective if grace does not help them and nonexistent if grace does not stir them up.

But toward evil, Scripture says, “The senses and thoughts of humankind are prone” (Gen. 8:21). Therefore merits should be thought to descend to it not from itself, as has been said, but rather from above, from the Father of lights—provided that, among the good gifts and perfect donations, the very things through which eternal salvation is gained are deservedly reckoned merits.

43. For God our king, when before the ages he worked salvation in the midst of the earth, divided his gifts, which he gave to human beings, into merits and rewards: so that present gifts might meanwhile become our merits through free possession, while future gifts we might await—or rather, seek—as things due by gratuitous promise. Paul recalls both: “You have,” he says, “your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22); and again: “We ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan, awaiting the adoption of the children of God” (Rom. 8:23). He calls sanctification—that is, the virtues—“the firstfruits of the Spirit,” by which we are now sanctified by the Spirit so that we may deservedly receive adoption [Col. 1024C].

Again, in the Gospel the same things are promised to one who renounces the world: “He shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29). Thus salvation belongs not to free choice but to the Lord; indeed, he himself is salvation and is also the way to salvation, who says, “I am the salvation of the people” (Ps. 34:3), and likewise testifies, “I am the way” (John 14:6). He who was salvation and life made himself the way, so that no flesh might boast [Col. 1024D].

If, then, merits are the good things of the way, just as salvation and life are the good things of the homeland; and if David’s saying is true, “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:3)—except, namely, that one of whom it is likewise said, “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18)—then both our works and God’s rewards are undoubtedly God’s gifts. He who made himself a debtor in those rewards also made us deserving through these works. Yet in establishing these merits [Col. 1025A], he deigns to employ the ministries of creatures, not because he needs them, but so that through them, or from them, he may benefit them.

> [Note: [Col. 1025D] This argument is treated excellently in Sermon 5 on the Song of Songs.]

44. Therefore he works the salvation of those whose names are in the book of life: sometimes through a creature without that creature itself; sometimes through a creature against that creature; sometimes through a creature together with that creature. Many things beneficial to human beings are certainly done through the insensible, and likewise through the irrational, creature. I said that these are done without the creature itself because, lacking intellect, it cannot even be conscious of them.

God also performs many things useful to the salvation of many through evil persons, whether human beings or angels; but because they are unwilling, he works against them. For while they help by wishing to harm, as much as the useful action benefits others, so much does their perverse intention harm themselves. But those through whom and with whom God works are good angels or human beings, who both do and will what God wills [Col. 1025B]. For those who assent in will to the good which they carry out in deed are made participants in the work which God accomplishes through them.

Thus Paul, after recounting many good things which God had done through him, says: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10). He could have said “through me”; but, because that was less, he preferred to say “with me,” claiming that he was not only the minister of the work in its effect, but in some manner also the companion of the worker through consent.

45. Let us now see, according to the threefold operation of God which we have set forth, what each creature merits for its ministry. What can that creature merit through which, and without which, what is done is done? What can that creature against which it is done merit except wrath? And what can that creature with which it is done merit except grace? Thus no merits are gained in the first case, evil merits in the second, and good merits in the last [Col. 1025C].

For cattle, when any good or evil is done through them, do not merit anything good or evil. They have no means by which to assent to good or evil. Stones do so still less, since they do not even perceive. But the devil or an evil person, since they possess and exercise reason, indeed merit—but only punishment, because they dissent from the good. Paul, however, who preaches willingly—lest, if unwillingly, only a stewardship be entrusted to him (1 Cor. 9:17)—and all who think similarly, because they obey by consent of the will, trust that a crown of righteousness has been laid up for them [Col. 1025D].

God therefore uses irrational and likewise insensible creatures for the salvation of his own as a beast of burden or an instrument; once their work has been completed, they will be nowhere. He uses the rational but ill-disposed creature as a rod of discipline, which, when the son has been corrected, he will cast into the fire like a useless branch. And he uses angels and human beings of good will as his fellow-soldiers and helpers, whom, victory accomplished, he will reward most generously. Finally Paul confidently declares concerning himself and those like him: “For we are God’s fellow-workers” (1 Cor. 3:9) [Col. 1026A]. Therefore God graciously appoints merits for a human being where he deigns to undertake some good work through that person and with that person. Hence we presume that we are God’s fellow-workers, co-workers of the Holy Spirit, and those who deserve the kingdom, because through voluntary consent we are joined to the divine will.

## CHAPTER XIV. What is to be attributed to grace and what to free choice in the work of salvation

46. What then? Is all this, therefore, the work of free choice? Is its only merit that it consents? It is indeed. Not, however, because even the consent itself, in which all merit consists, comes from it; for we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think—which is less than to consent—anything as from ourselves (2 Cor. 3:5). These are not my words but the Apostle’s, who attributes to God, not to human choice, every possible good thing: namely, thinking, willing, and accomplishing according to the good will (Phil. 2:13).

If, then, God works these three things in us—good thinking, willing, and accomplishing—he does the first without us, the second with us, and the third through us. By imparting a good thought, he goes before us; by changing even an evil will, he joins it to himself through consent; by supplying the consent with ability [Note: [Col. 1026D] Some manuscripts add “or ease,” because the copyists were uncertain of the reading in this passage.], the inward worker makes himself known outwardly through our manifest work. Certainly we cannot in any way go before him. But he finds no one good, and saves no one whom he has not first gone before.

Thus the beginning of our salvation is undoubtedly from God, neither through us nor with us. But consent and work, though not from us, are nevertheless no longer without us [Col. 1026C]. Therefore neither the first stage, in which we do nothing, nor the last, which is often extorted by useless fear or blameworthy pretence, is reckoned to us as merit; only the middle stage is. Good will alone sometimes suffices; the other things do not profit if it alone is absent. I say they do not profit the doer, not the observer. Intention, therefore, avails for merit; action, for example; and the thought that precedes both avails only to arouse [variant: “to exercise”].

47. We must therefore take care that, when we sense these things being carried on invisibly within us and with us [Col. 1026D], we attribute them neither to our own will, which is weak, nor to God’s necessity, which does not exist, but to grace alone, with which he is full. Grace awakens free choice when it sows the thought; heals it when it changes the affection; strengthens it so as to bring it to action; preserves it lest it suffer failure.

Yet grace works with free choice in such a way that it goes before it only in the first stage, and accompanies it in the rest—going before it, indeed, so that free choice may thereafter cooperate with it. Nevertheless, what is begun by grace alone is completed by both together [Col. 1027A]: mixed together, not separately; simultaneously, not alternately; they work in every individual advance. Grace does not do one part and free choice another, but each performs the whole work undividedly. The whole is done by grace, and the whole by free choice; yet, as it is wholly in free choice, so it is wholly from grace.

48. We trust that the reader is pleased that we never depart from the Apostle’s meaning; and wherever our discourse may wander, we frequently return almost to his very words. For what else do our words say than this: “Therefore it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16)? He does not say this as though someone could will or run in vain, but because the one who wills and runs ought to glory not in himself but in him from whom he received both willing and running. Thus he says: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

You are created, healed, saved. What of these, O human being, comes from yourself? What of these is not impossible to free choice? You who did not exist could not create yourself; you, a sinner, could not justify yourself; you, dead, could not raise yourself—leaving aside the other good things either necessary for the healing or laid up for the salvation of persons [Col. 1027B]. What we say is clear concerning the first and the last; but no one doubts it concerning the middle either, unless, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish his own, he is not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3).

What then? Do you acknowledge the power of the Creator and the glory [variant: “grace”] of the Saviour, yet not the righteousness of the healer? “Heal me,” he says, “and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise” (Jer. 17:14). This man acknowledged God’s righteousness, from whom he equally hoped both to be healed from sin and to be delivered from misery; and therefore he rightly set up God, not himself, as his praise [Col. 1027C].

For this reason David also repeats: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:9), because he expected from God both garments: that of righteousness and that of glory. Who is ignorant of God’s righteousness? The one who justifies himself. Who justifies himself? The one who claims merits for himself from some source other than grace.

But he who made what he might save also gives that by which he saves. He himself, I say, grants the merits, who made those to whom he would grant them. “What shall I render,” he says, “to the Lord for all—not the things which he gives, but the things which he repays—to me?” He confesses that both his existence and his righteousness are from God, lest, by denying either, he lose both: losing, that is, the source by which he is righteous, and thus condemning what he is [Col. 1027D]. Yet, as a third response, he finds something to render in return: “I shall take,” he says, “the cup of salvation.” The cup of salvation is the blood of the Saviour.

Therefore, if you entirely lack anything of your own with which to repay even God’s secondary gifts, whence do you presume salvation for yourself? “I shall call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13), he says; for whoever calls upon it will be saved (Rom. 10:13).

49. Thus those who think rightly confess a threefold operation, not of free choice but of divine grace in it or concerning it. The first is creation; the second, reformation; the third, consummation. First, we were created in Christ into freedom of will; second, we are re-formed through Christ into the spirit of freedom; then we are to be consummated with Christ in a state of eternity [Col. 1028A].

For what did not exist had to be created in him who existed; what was deformed had to be re-formed through the Form [Note: [Col. 1027D] Thus our three manuscripts read. Horstius reads: “what did not exist had to be created in him; what existed had to be re-formed from the Form”; but the reading and punctuation are corrupt.]; and the members cannot be perfected except with the head. This will assuredly be fulfilled when “we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13), when, Christ our life appearing, we too shall appear with him in glory (Col. 3:4).

Since consummation is to take place concerning us, and even in us, but not from us; and since creation took place without us: reformation alone, which in some manner takes place with us because of our voluntary consent, is reckoned to us as merit. These are our fasts, vigils, continence, works of mercy, and the other exercises of virtue [Col. 1028B], through which our inward person is plainly renewed day by day: while an intention bent down by earthly cares gradually rises from the depths to things above; an affection languishing amid desires of the flesh slowly gathers strength for love of the Spirit; and a memory made foul by the shamefulness of former deeds grows daily brighter and more joyful through new and good actions.

For inward renewal consists in these three things: uprightness of intention, purity of affection, and the remembrance of good action, through which memory, conscious that it has acted well, shines brightly.

50. But since it is certain that these things are carried on in us by the divine Spirit, they are God’s gifts; yet because they occur with the assent of our will, they are our merits. “It is not you,” he says, “who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). And the Apostle says: “Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). If Christ or the Holy Spirit speaks in Paul, does he not likewise work in him? “For,” he says, “I do not speak of anything which God does not accomplish through me” (Rom. 15:18).

What then? If both the words and works belong not to Paul but to God speaking in Paul or working through Paul, where are Paul’s merits? How can he say so confidently: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” [Col. 1028D] (2 Tim. 4:7–8)? Does he perhaps trust that a crown has been laid up for him because those things were done through him? Yet many good things are done through evil angels and evil persons, but they are not reckoned to them as merits. Is it rather because they were done also with him—that is, with his good will? “For if I preach the Gospel unwillingly,” he says, “a stewardship is entrusted to me; but if willingly, there is glory for me” (1 Cor. 9:17).

51. But if even the will itself, upon which all merit depends, is not from Paul, in what way does he call the crown which he expects to be laid up for him a crown of righteousness? Is it because whatever is freely promised is rightly demanded, and therefore due [Col. 1029A]? Thus he says: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit” (2 Tim. 1:12). He calls God’s promise his own deposit; and because he believed the promiser, he confidently claims the promise. It was promised from mercy, but must now be paid from righteousness.

The crown which Paul expects, therefore, is a crown of righteousness—but of God’s righteousness, not his own. For it is just that God should pay what he owes, and he owes what he has promised. This promise of God is the righteousness in which the Apostle glories, lest, despising it and wishing to establish his own righteousness, he should not be subject to God’s righteousness. Yet God willed him to share in that righteousness of his, so as to make him deserving of the crown. For God made him a participant in righteousness and deserving of the crown [Col. 1030A] when he deigned to make him a fellow-worker in the works for which that crown had been promised.

Moreover, God made him a fellow-worker when he made him willing—that is, consenting to God’s will. Thus the will is an aid, and the aid is reckoned as merit. If, therefore, the will is from God, so is the merit. And there is no doubt that both willing and accomplishing according to the good will are from God. God, then, is the author of merit, since he applies the will to the work and carries out the work for the will [variant: “of the will”].

Otherwise, if what we call our merits are properly so called, they are seeds of hope, incentives to love, signs of hidden predestination, foretastes of future blessedness, the way to the kingdom—not the cause of reigning. Finally, “those whom he justified,” not those whom he found righteous, “he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

[Col. 1029]

# LETTER OR TREATISE OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT, TO HUGH OF SAINT VICTOR, ON BAPTISM AND OTHER QUESTIONS PROPOSED BY HIM

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO OPUSCULUM X

624. 1. This letter, which was formerly numbered seventy-seven, was placed among the treatises by Horstius. In old books it is entitled, “To Master Hugh of Saint Victor.” At the same time there were two Hughs in the abbey of Saint Victor near Paris. One, renowned for his writings, was called Hugh of Saint Victor; this letter was addressed to him. He was called Lotharingian or Ypresian, not Saxon, in the fragment which I cited in the first volume of the *Analecta*. He died in 1142, and thus before the pontificate of Eugenius III.

The other Hugh was praised by Eugenius himself in his letter to Suger, which is letter sixty-eight among the letters of Suger. These are Eugenius’s words: “Since, therefore, our beloved son Hugh, canon of Saint Victor, is returning to us, we ask your goodwill to grant him one mount and sufficient expenses for it and its rider on his return.” I return to the first Hugh, whose letter, which occasioned this one, is lacking from his published works.

2. The subject of this letter is directed against a certain unnamed person, whose opinion was: first, that the commandment of Baptism became binding from the moment when the Lord Christ first said to Nicodemus, “Unless one is born again,” etc.; secondly, that no one could in any way be saved without Baptism, or at least martyrdom in its place; thirdly, that the Fathers of the Old Testament possessed as clear a knowledge of the Incarnation as Christians do; fourthly, that there is no sin arising from ignorance; fifthly, that Bernard erred when, in his homilies on *Missus est*, he wrote that the angels were ignorant of God’s plan concerning the Incarnation.

3. It is not easy to guess who this unnamed person was. Some think him to have been John, Archbishop of Seville, to whom Hugh of Saint Victor wrote a letter arguing that faith must be confessed not only with the heart but also with the mouth—a faith which John himself had denied with his mouth. Yet nothing in that letter establishes this conjecture. In the third volume of the Works of Hugh of Saint Victor, Book I of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 8, it is said that it would be more probable to identify this anonymous person with Hugh Farsit, whose views on the Sacraments are plainly shown to have been somewhat unsound by Bernard’s thirty-fifth letter, addressed to him:

> “Because among friends there ought to be no timid flattery against the truth, since flattery is dangerous, I confess that this has moved me and still moves me: you have endeavoured, at the beginning of the aforesaid little work, to defend and establish the discussion formerly held between us concerning the Sacraments. In that discussion, if you remember well the substance of your opinion, consider whether it accords with the ecclesiastical understanding. It belongs, however, to your candid humility not to blush at correction, if at any time you have thought otherwise.”

But since Bernard, at the request of Hugh of Saint Victor, answered the assertions of an opposing author whose name Hugh had concealed and Bernard himself did not know, some may think that the following letter concerns someone other than Hugh Farsit, whose views and name Bernard did know. It may, however, be replied that the discussion of which Bernard speaks in the thirty-fifth letter was perhaps later than this seventy-seventh letter: when Bernard wrote the latter, he had not yet learned who was the author of the opinion which he attacks here. In any event, this letter is not against Abelard, whose name Hugh would not have spared; although Abelard held certain views akin to those censured here by Bernard. Concerning the date of the letter, we can affirm only that it was written before 1142, the year in which Master Hugh of Saint Victor died.

625

## PREFACE

[Col. 1031A]

If I seem to you to have replied rather late, know that I also received late the matter to which I was to reply. For what you had sent did not immediately reach me, but was held for a long time beforehand at Pontigny. When I received it, however, I made no delay in replying. Yet I have done so more briefly than perhaps your purpose required, though not wholly as briefly as my occupations allowed. Still, I took care that you should not in any way remain unaware of what I thought concerning the questions asked, leaving it to your leisure and ability to establish these same opinions of mine more fully, should you judge it appropriate. Nor do I doubt that you have at hand sound arguments and fitting authorities by which you can easily do this.

Therefore let him whose assertions you command me to answer—and whose name you conceal—know that I have stated to you what I think concerning the matters consulted, not contradicted him, even if we think otherwise than he does. For if we think rightly, truth contradicts him, not we. But if he is not ashamed to acquiesce in truth, then truth thinks with him, and so do we. If not, nevertheless the servant of God ought not to quarrel, but rather to be patient toward all men (2 Tim. 2:24). Therefore we do not seek battles of words; and, according to apostolic teaching, we also avoid novelties of expressions. We merely set against him the opinions of the Fathers and bring forward words that are not our own; for we are not wiser than our fathers. Let him abound in his own opinion as much as he wishes, provided that he permits us to abound in the meanings of the Scriptures, as the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything [Col. 1031C] from ourselves, as though it came from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

## CHAPTER I. Baptism did not become binding from the time when it was said to Nicodemus: “Unless one is born again.”

1. You write, then, that someone asserts—I do not know whom, since you do not name him—that from the moment when it is first recorded that the Lord said, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), no one could in any way be saved without receiving that actual visible sacrament, or martyrdom in its place; and that even if someone should seek it with true faith and contrition of heart, but, prevented by the point of death, were unable to obtain what he desired, he would nevertheless be wholly condemned.

First, this fixing of the time seems excessively harsh and severe: that a word still hidden should already openly harm, and that the judge should strike before he threatens; that what the Saviour meanwhile speaks in darkness and in the ear should not yet save, because it has not yet appeared, and yet should already fill the world with persons condemned. Was it then that the word of salvation and commandment of life could restore life no sooner than it inflicted death—and inflict it upon those who were innocent precisely because they did not yet know their Lord’s will? Was God bound to destroy an ignorant and righteous nation—if we may speak with the Gentile? (Gen. 20:4). Who thinks thus? Certainly it accords not with the Author of life to employ, at the very beginning of his ways, to the detriment of a world still wholly ignorant of the freshest heavenly decree, the death which he came to destroy. It is indeed wicked to think of the giver of all good things that, upon his coming, he gave so evil a beginning. I certainly would never assent to any such view of Christ—a view more fittingly to be feared from Antichrist, who too “has prepared his arrow in his quiver, that he may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.”

2. For how many unbaptized persons meanwhile die throughout the whole world, undoubtedly ignorant of what Jesus discusses by night and in secret with Nicodemus? What then? The law has not yet been promulgated, and already transgressors are held guilty? “And how,” he says, “shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:14–15). The preaching has not yet been enjoined, published abroad, or heard; and, according to the judgment of the slothful and wicked servant, is the Lord so hard that he already wishes to reap where he has not sown and gather where he has not scattered? Far be it.

Rather, hear the truth of the matter. He who is the one Teacher in heaven and on earth was, in a familiar and private conversation, delivering to one who was only a teacher in Israel what that teacher was to hand on; teaching what he was to teach, not what he was to exact from those absent, nor what he was to prescribe for those who had not heard. For obedience is demanded very unjustly where hearing has not first preceded it. This is not like what the natural law does not allow one to be ignorant of even without promulgation—for example: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16). It is, in a certain sense, a positive rather than a natural commandment. For what nature or reason teaches that no mortal can receive inward and eternal salvation unless his body has outwardly been washed with a visible element? The sacrament of God Most High must be received, not investigated; revered, not judged; obtained by faith, not innate; established by tradition, not devised by reason.

Moreover, hearing must necessarily precede faith, as the Apostle says: “Therefore faith comes from hearing.” How then, I ask, could that which could not possibly be done [variant: known] unless it was heard be required before it was heard? See, moreover, how the Apostle resorts to this point and convicts unbelievers on the basis of hearing alone. “But I say,” he says, “have they not heard?” (Rom. 10:17–18), as if to say: they could have been excused if they had not heard. For where there is no law, neither is there transgression. But now, since “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” [Note: [Col. 1033D] The manuscript of Compiègne adds: “who preach faith to the nations.”], because hearing can no longer be ignored, contempt is certainly inexcusable.

3. Many things that ought to be known are not known, either through negligence in seeking knowledge, laziness in learning, or shame in asking. Ignorance of this sort indeed has no excuse. But is this perhaps something that can be learned by human instruction if it is sought out? One human being understands another’s thought only when that person discloses it; how much less can anyone investigate the divine counsel unless God himself chooses to reveal it? Hear him himself, finally: “If I had not come,” he says, “and spoken to them, they would not have had sin.” He does not say simply, “And I had not spoken”; but, inserting “to them,” he says, “and had not spoken to them,” plainly showing that they are not reckoned inexcusable for contempt before the command reaches their knowledge. For if he had indeed spoken, but not to them, ignorance would nevertheless excuse them from the fault of disobedience. “But now,” he says, “because I have spoken, and have spoken to them, they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

Hence he also said: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have spoken nothing in secret” (John 18:20). Not that he did not teach his own household many things secretly and privately, but because he considered such teaching, in the meantime, as nothing, and judged that what he delivered in secret would produce neither punishment nor reward [Note: [Col. 1034D] Thus all manuscripts together with the early editions; later editions: “increase.”], until it was brought forth from concealment and came out into the light. Finally, he said: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light” (Matt. 10:27), so that, once the things were publicly proclaimed, he might rightly ascribe either the merit of obedience or the guilt of contempt to those hearing them. Again: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me”—as though he said: My judgment between those who obey and those who despise will depend not upon my secret instruction, but upon your public preaching.

4. But perhaps someone will say that those who did not hear are indeed not judged for contempt, yet are condemned on account of original sin, from which they could certainly not be cleansed except through the washing. But who does not know that, in ancient times, remedies besides Baptism were not lacking against original sin? To Abraham and his seed the sacrament of circumcision was divinely given for this very purpose (Gen. 17:10). Among the nations, wherever faithful persons were found, we believe adults were cleansed by faith and sacrifices; while for little children the faith of their parents alone was beneficial—indeed, sufficient. This, moreover, endured until the time of Baptism; once Baptism alone had been instituted in its place, the others ceased to have effect.

5. We therefore ask when the time of Baptism began. “From the time,” he says, “when it was first said: ‘Unless one is born again,’ etc.” Then hold firmly that this was said to Nicodemus, certainly a friend of Jesus, but concealed because of fear of the Jews; and that he sought that hidden conversation by night. Yet how many thousands of circumcised persons do you suppose died in the meantime—not to mention the Gentiles—while what was then said in darkness concerning Baptism had not yet come forth into the light? What then? Do we say that all of them were condemned because they were not baptized? An injury is therefore done to that earlier commandment of God if, when the new commandment stealthily arrives, as it were, but has not yet come to help, the old one is thought suddenly to have vanished so completely that it could thereafter be of no benefit.

And how much later, do you suppose, was this publicly preached and proclaimed upon the housetops: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2)? How, further, will this stand: “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence” (Matt. 11:12), if it is established that especially at that time there occurred such a violent exclusion from the kingdom as had neither occurred before nor was to occur afterward? For after the decree of the new mystery had been established but was still secret, what access, I ask, lay open to the kingdom for those who died in the meantime? The old was already failing, because it was excluded by the new; yet the new did not come to their aid, because, while unknown, it was not received. O most unhappy times, which alone, throughout all ages, passed entirely without every remedy of salvation! Circumcision, which had prevailed until then, did not dare to benefit them because Baptism was secretly supplanting it; and Baptism, because it was still hidden, did not help them. Perhaps God slept at that time, and there was meanwhile none to redeem, nor any to save.

## CHAPTER II. The obligation of Baptism began only after its sufficient promulgation; nevertheless, in a case of necessity, Baptism received by faith and desire, as also martyrdom, suffices.

6. From these considerations it sufficiently appears, I think, that the condemnation of the unbaptized, the frustration of the circumcised, and the nullification of sacrifices—which perhaps the ancient rite observed as remedies against original sin—did not generally begin at the time when it was secretly said to Nicodemus: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). Nor did it begin when the Apostles were openly commanded: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). Rather, only from the time when the commandment itself could have reached a person’s knowledge without excuse did the old observance begin to be of no avail to that person, and every unbaptized person become guilty of the new commandment.

Certainly, in the case of little children and those not yet possessing reason, since only the contagion of sin, and not transgression of the commandment, is believed to harm them, the ancient sacraments must be believed to have retained their efficacy as long as they had not plainly been forbidden. Whether this extended further is God’s concern, not mine to define. But whoever, at a more mature age, after the remedy of Baptism has been proclaimed everywhere, now refuses Baptism, adds to the general and original stain the guilt of personal pride, carrying with him a double cause of most just condemnation if he should depart from the body in that condition.

Yet if, before death, he comes to his senses, wishes and asks to be baptized, but perhaps is unable to obtain it because the moment of death forestalls him—provided that right faith, devout hope, and sincere charity are not lacking—may God be merciful to me, for on account of water alone, if it is absent, I cannot at all despair of that person’s salvation, nor believe his faith empty, nor put his hope to shame, nor think his charity has failed—provided only that water is withheld not by contempt but, as I have said, by impossibility alone. If anyone thinks otherwise, let him see by what means he has persuaded himself of what he asserts. I confess that I do not readily assent unless a stronger reason leads me to understand it, or a stronger authority to believe it.

7. But I am greatly astonished if this new inventor of novel assertions and assertor of inventions can discover in this matter a reason hidden from the holy Fathers Ambrose and Augustine, or an authority stronger than theirs. For if he does not know it, both undoubtedly held the same view which we confess that we hold. Let him read Ambrose’s book *On the Death of Valentinian* [Note: [Col. 1035D] Abelard’s shamelessness in this matter is remarkable. Although he held that catechumens can be saved solely by martyrdom in place of Baptism, as in his *Letter to the Romans*, p. 564, and Letter 7 to Heloise, p. 129, he says that Ambrose wrote here against the faith, in order to mitigate the grief of Valentinian’s sisters over his death.], if he has not read it; let him recall it if he has read it; let him not dissemble if he recalls it. Without doubt, he will see that the saint confidently hopes for salvation through faith alone for an unbaptized man who has died, and unhesitatingly attributes to good will what ability lacked [Col. 1035D] (*On the Death of Valentinian*, near the end).

Let him also read Book IV of Augustine’s work *On the One Baptism*, and either acknowledge that he has been imprudently deceived or prove himself shamelessly obstinate. “Blessed Cyprian,” Augustine says, “draws no slight proof from the thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said, ‘Today you shall be with me in paradise’ (Luke 23:43), that suffering sometimes supplies the place of Baptism.” And he adds: “Considering this again and again, I find that not only suffering for the name of Christ can supply what was lacking from Baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if, in the constraints of time, one cannot obtain assistance for celebrating the mystery of Baptism.” And below: “How much even without the visible sacrament of Baptism the Apostle’s saying, ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Rom. 10:10), avails, is shown in that thief. But this is then invisibly fulfilled when the mystery of Baptism is excluded not by contempt for religion but by an emergency of necessity” (*On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book IV, ch. 22, no. 29).

I do not indeed fail to know that Augustine retracts the testimony he had cited concerning the thief and acknowledges it to be less suitable for proving that view, since it is uncertain whether the thief had been baptized (*Retractions*, Book II, ch. 18, 55). Nevertheless, he pursues the opinion boldly and confirms it in many ways; nor, unless I am mistaken, will you find that he ever retracted it. Elsewhere Augustine, after mentioning certain persons whom Scripture records as sanctified invisibly, though not visibly, finally concludes: “From these things,” he says, “it is gathered that invisible sanctification was present and beneficial to some without visible sacraments, which have changed according to the diversity of times: some existed then, and others exist now.” Shortly afterward he says: “Yet the visible sacrament is not to be despised at all; for one who despises it cannot be sanctified invisibly” (*Questions on Leviticus*, question 84). Here he plainly shows that a believer converted to the Lord is deprived of the fruit of Baptism not if he has been unable, but if he has scorned, to be baptized.

8. From those two pillars—Augustine and Ambrose, I mean—believe me, I am not easily torn away. With them, I say, I confess that I either err or think rightly. I too believe that a person can be saved by faith alone, together with the desire to receive the sacrament, if death coming beforehand or any other irresistible force prevents the devout desire for its fulfilment. Consider also whether perhaps for this reason the Saviour, when he said, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved,” did not carefully and deliberately add, “But he who is not baptized”; but said only: “He who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16:16), thus indicating that faith alone sometimes suffices for salvation, and that without it nothing suffices.

Therefore, although martyrdom is granted to be able to supply the place of Baptism, it is not suffering itself that accomplishes this, but faith itself. For what is martyrdom without faith except suffering? Then shall that which gives martyrdom the pre-eminence whereby it is unquestionably reckoned in place of Baptism be so weak and feeble in itself that, though it can give this to another, it cannot obtain it by itself? Indeed, the shedding of blood for Christ is an unquestionable proof of great faith—not to God, however, but to human beings. But if God needs no tests whatever to prove what he wishes to know, does he not see in the heart of one dying in peace an equally great faith, not put to the test by martyrdom but nevertheless fit for martyrdom?

If a person remembers that he has not yet received the mystery of salvation, and sorrowing and repentant seeks it with his whole desire, but is unable to attain it because death comes too swiftly beforehand—will God condemn his faithful servant? Will he condemn, I say, a person ready even to die for him? Paul says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). Shall we then say that one who, at the point of death, not only calls upon the Lord Jesus but also seeks his sacrament with his entire desire either does not speak in the Holy Spirit, and the Apostle is false, or is condemned together with the Holy Spirit? He has the Saviour dwelling through faith in his heart and through confession on his lips—and will he be condemned with the Saviour?

Certainly, since martyrdom obtains its privilege of being securely received in place of Baptism solely from the merit of faith, I do not see why faith itself should not have equal power before God without martyrdom, since it undoubtedly becomes known to him without the testing of martyrdom. It can have equal power, I would say, in regard to the attainment of salvation, though not in regard to the increase of merit, in which martyrdom unquestionably excels. We read: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15); and again: “Whoever looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). What could be clearer than that the will is reckoned as the deed where necessity excludes the deed? Unless perhaps one thinks that, with God who is charity, the will is found more effective in evil than in good, and that the merciful and compassionate Lord is readier to punish than to reward.

Just as one who, perhaps at the point of death, remembers that he is bound by another’s debt, but lacks the means to repay it, is believed nevertheless to obtain pardon by repentance alone and contrition of heart, so that he is no longer condemned for it; so faith alone and the mind’s turning toward God, without shedding of blood or washing with water, unquestionably works salvation for one who wishes but is unable to be baptized because the point of death prevents it. And just as no repentance remits that person’s sin if, when he can, he does not restore what he has taken away, so no faith will profit this person if, when he can, he does not receive the sacrament. Indeed, he is proved not to possess perfect faith if he neglects it. For true and full faith embraces all the commandments, and this is one—and the chief—of the commandments. Hence whoever refuses obedience will deservedly be reckoned not merely unbelieving but plainly rebellious and contemptuous. For how is one faithful who scorns God’s sacrament?

9. Certainly, infants, because age prevents them from possessing this faith—that is, the heart’s turning toward God—consequently cannot have salvation if they die without receiving Baptism. This does not mean that, when they are baptized, they are altogether without faith, without which it is impossible even for them to please God. They too are saved through faith, though not their own faith but another’s. It is fitting, and belongs to God’s goodness, that grace should be allowed to benefit by another’s faith those to whom age denies their own. For the justice of the Almighty does not judge their own faith to be required from those whom he knows to have no personal guilt. Yet another’s faith is needed because they are not born without another’s stain, so that what is said generally of all may not be inapplicable to little children: “cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). Nor is there any doubt that a stain contracted from others can and ought also to be cleansed by the faith of others. These are the judgments of divine justice; rejoicing in them, holy David said: “I remembered your judgments of old, O Lord, and was comforted” (Ps. 118:52). Thus far concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER III. The righteous of the Old Testament did not possess as clear a knowledge of the future mysteries of faith as we possess of things past.

[Col. 1038B]

10. Furthermore, as you say, the person of whom you speak asserts that all the righteous of old—namely, all who preceded Christ’s coming—had altogether as much foreknowledge of future things as we who come after have knowledge of things past. Thus, no one, even among the simple righteous, was entirely ignorant of any of the things which Gospel history now discloses to us: the incarnate Word, the virgin birth, the Saviour’s teaching, miracles, cross, death, burial, descent into hell, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. All these things, he says, were foreknown both openly in their entirety and distinctly in every particular by all the righteous of those times, just as they were afterward manifested in their proper time and are now known to us. Indeed, he holds that those to whom all these things were not thus clear and evident were neither righteous nor saved. This is false.

11. Yet you appear to have included so much in your letter to refute this [variant: “you have exerted yourself so greatly in your letter”] that I think nothing at all need be added; indeed, I can scarcely discover what could be added. Nevertheless, concerning the man who says these things, I shall briefly state what I think, with his leave. He seems to me more eager for novelty than devoted to truth, and burdened by having to think with others about every matter and to say what either no one else has said or he himself has said first. Hence it comes about that in the things he thinks or says he either does not know, or pretends not to know, how to observe any measure.

For in this assertion, while he makes all those who hoped for things to come equal in knowledge to those who read things past, he portrays God as either excessively sparing or excessively lavish, opening the eye of discrimination on neither side. Either he reduces the number of the elect of that time to the small number of the rarest spiritual persons—those whom Scripture records as conspicuous and distinguished in those times by the particular excellence of their holiness, and as certainly able through the singular gift of the Spirit to foresee each thing as it was to come—and thus he excessively shortens the hand of God, by thinking that no one but those few most perfect persons could then be saved; or, if he does not deny that those times also had a multitude of persons to be saved besides them, he asserts that a great but unheard-of abundance of the divine gift was bestowed upon the ancient people, if it is established that the whole multitude clearly foreknew all the matters listed above concerning the mystery of our redemption.

For, since it is plain that some of these things were then neither plainly written nor publicly preached, it remains for us to acknowledge that everything was revealed by the Spirit to everyone. Thus all were spiritual, all perfect, all prophets—every righteous and saved person from the advent of the Lord backward. Therefore, in ancient times salvation was either exceedingly rare, or perfection excessively numerous; to hold either opinion is to pass beyond the bounds of discernment.

12. But if it appears more tolerable—indeed, more worthy [variant: more just] in relation to God—to have filled and enriched those ages with a multitude of perfect persons than to have been content with so scant a number of the saved, so that not few were then saved and all nevertheless, filled with a prophetic spirit, penetrated mysteries not yet revealed—if, I say, this is accepted, we indeed bless God in his gifts. But we do not see what is reserved for the age of grace, unless, according to this opinion, that age should rather be called the age of grace in which such numerous and great riches of the Spirit flowed to the people of God that what Moses desired seemed fulfilled in altogether incredible felicity when he said: “Who will grant that all may prophesy?” (Num. 11:29).

I ask: what comparable thing did the Gospel bring? Paul boasts in vain of the firstfruits of the Spirit, which he thought he had received with his fellow Apostles, since he could have experienced nothing of this kind in his own day. Finally, he said: “Are all prophets?” (1 Cor. 12:29). In vain, I say, does he boast of his Gospel, because he received it neither from man nor through man, but, as by a certain special prerogative, through a revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1), when it had previously been revealed by the Holy Spirit even to the peoples. Nor should the Apostle Peter have applied to his own times that prophetic saying: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon your sons and daughters, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Acts 2:17; Joel 2:28), if a more abundant outpouring of the Spirit had already preceded it in earlier ages. Or surely the Prophet—or rather God speaking in the Prophet, if he truly beheld those apostolic times when he spoke—should not have said, “I will pour out,” but rather, “I will withdraw my Spirit.” For what follows?
