If we make all the righteous of old equal to the children of the Gospel in knowledge, must we not consequently acknowledge them superior in grace, since they were taught concerning everything not by reading or preaching, as we are, but by the anointing itself?

13. Let it be so, nevertheless. Let us endure the injury done to ourselves, and the Apostles theirs as well, so that even the least of the ancient righteous may be compared with them in knowledge and preferred to them in grace. But there is something we cannot endure in any way, and rightly so: namely, that the Lord of glory should be thought ever to have been deceived or to have wished to deceive. He himself testified that among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist had arisen (Matt. 11:11). See whether we are not compelled truly to admit that this testimony of Truth is false, if we attribute so much to the ancients as we cannot claim even for John. It is certainly no injury to John if he is believed or said to have been ignorant of something which he himself does not deny; but if we give to another, contrary to the proclamation of Truth, what we deny to the herald of Truth, this is not only an injury but blasphemy, and plainly contradicts not John but Truth.

What then? The friend of the bridegroom doubts and asks, “Are you he who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Matt. 11:3), while by our falsehood we assure thousands of people of certainty concerning all things.

14. We may briefly observe that the ancients themselves did not think thus of themselves. Moses writes that God, speaking to him, said: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai” (Exod. 3:6; 6:3)—that is, as I have to you. He thus shows that he received something additional concerning the knowledge of God beyond what the earlier Fathers received. David likewise boldly claims for himself a gift of understanding above his teachers and elders, saying: “I have understood beyond all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation”; and again, “I have understood beyond the elders” (Ps. 118:99–100). The prophet Daniel also says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4), likewise promising a fuller knowledge of things to later generations.

Therefore, if, as holy Pope Gregory also says, the knowledge of spiritual fathers grew according to the progress of times, and the nearer they were to the advent of the Saviour, the more fully they perceived the mystery of salvation (*Homily 17 on Ezekiel*), there is no doubt that the manifestation of the things themselves and the presence of him who manifested them bestowed far more upon those who were actually present. For they hear: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23); and again: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15). “Many kings and prophets,” he says, “desired to see the things that you see and did not see them, and to hear the things that you hear and did not hear them” (Luke 10:24). Why? So that they might receive more clearly and abundantly what they had scarcely foreseen, faintly and obscurely.

Otherwise, what need was there to see the flesh outwardly and hear the flesh’s words, if they had already been perfectly instructed inwardly by the Spirit concerning everything? Especially since the Lord says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (John 6:64). But if the Prophets and those who seemed more illustrious among that people could not all know all things clearly and equally, but some more and others less, according as the Spirit gave to them, distributing to each as he willed—and this without prejudice to their holiness and perfection—how much more could the simpler righteous, without detriment to salvation, remain ignorant of the time, manner, and order of salvation, which nevertheless they most firmly held by certain hope and faith, as it had been promised?

15. How many even today among the Christian people undoubtedly believe, hope for, and ardently desire eternal life and the world to come, yet do not know how even faintly to conceive its form and condition! In the same way, many before the Saviour’s coming, holding and loving Almighty God as the gratuitous promiser of their salvation, believing him faithful in his promise, and hoping for a most certain Redeemer, were saved in this faith and expectation, though they did not know when, how, or in what order the promised salvation would come to pass.

Finally, Bede plainly teaches that not all things which were to happen concerning Christ were openly known to everyone, a testimony which you too included in your letter:

> “The one and same trophy of the Lord’s cross was known and preached by the Prophets and Moses before the Apostles; but the Prophets sometimes preached it in figurative and veiled language, whereas the Apostles and the successors of the Apostles always preached it openly in the unveiled light of the Gospel. Thus now the whole Christian people ought to know and confess the faith which, in that time, very few—and only the more perfect—knew, although the whole people of God even then bore the mysteries of the same faith typologically in the legal ceremonies.”

Many things support these points, but the limits of a letter do not allow everything, nor is it necessary. For I think, as I said above, that even if I had not replied, the things contained in your letter on this matter could have sufficed. But I have added this [variant: “these things”], lest I leave untouched anything among all that you asked.

## CHAPTER IV. He shows, against the proponent of the contrary opinion, that sin can arise through ignorance.

16. Now, against the third assertion, I think we need not labour much: both because it bears an all too manifest falsehood upon its face, and because its very inventor, in his preceding opinion, sufficiently attacks it by itself, contradicting himself. For when, concerning that nocturnal and private conversation of the Lord with Nicodemus, he weaves a snare of public condemnation for those throughout the whole world who were ignorant of it—thinking, namely, that no one from that hour could be saved unless baptized—does he not openly admit a sin of ignorance, and [Col. 1041D] a damnable sin? Unless perhaps he is so obstinate as to suppose that God condemns men without fault.

Nevertheless, lest, if a fool is not answered even briefly according to his folly, he may perhaps imagine it wisdom and more securely scatter the seed-bed of madness into the ears of the foolish, so that there may now be no number to his folly: let the manifest lie be refuted by a few clear testimonies of truth. Perhaps he who maintains that one cannot sin through ignorance never prays for his ignorances, but rather mocks the prophet praying and saying: “Remember not the offences of my youth and [Col. 1042A] my ignorances” (Ps. 24:7). Perhaps he will also rebuke God for requiring satisfaction for a sin of ignorance. For in Leviticus He speaks to Moses, saying: “If a soul shall sin through ignorance and do one of those things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and, being guilty of sin, recognize his iniquity, he shall offer to the priest an unblemished ram from the flocks, according to the measure and assessment of the sin.” And again: “He shall pray for him concerning what he did unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him, because through error he sinned against the Lord” (Lev. 5:17–19).

17. If ignorance is never sin, why is it said in the Epistle to the Hebrews that, into the second tabernacle, the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own and the people’s [Col. 1042B] ignorance? (Heb. 9:7.) If there is no sin of ignorance, then Saul did not sin in persecuting the Church of God, since he did this in ignorance, remaining in unbelief. Thus he acted well in being a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent man; in breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of Jesus; and indeed in this very thing being exceedingly zealous for the traditions of his fathers (Gal. 1:13–14). Therefore he ought not to have said, “I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13), but rather, “I received my reward,” since ignorance rendered him immune from sin, and zeal moreover judged him worthy of recompense.

If, I say, there is never sin through ignorance, why then do we complain against the murderers of the Apostles, when they not only did not know that killing them was evil, [Col. 1042C] but moreover supposed, in doing it, that they were rendering service to God? (John 16:2.) And the Saviour prayed in vain upon the cross for His crucifiers, since, as He Himself testified, they did not know what they were doing (Luke 23:34), and therefore were in no way sinning. For it is by no means permissible to suspect that the Lord Jesus lied when He openly testified that they did not know what they were doing; even if someone perhaps doubts the Apostle, on the ground that, favouring his own flesh, he might have lied as a man when he said: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Do not these things sufficiently show in how great darkness of ignorance he lies who does not know that one can sometimes sin through ignorance? But enough of this.

## Chapter V. He defends from calumny a certain statement of his that has been misconstrued: namely, that the counsel of the Lord’s Incarnation was unknown to the angels.

[Col. 1042D]

18. At the end, you intimate to me—certainly in a friendly manner—that some are disturbed by a certain statement of mine, in which, while expounding the Gospel [Note: namely, the Gospel of Luke, chapter 1, “He was sent,” and specifically Homily 1, below, vol. III.], I said that God’s counsel was revealed to no one, even among the blessed angels, before it was revealed to the Virgin. First, I think they may observe from this that they are not quite justly disturbed: for I do not assert that proposition unqualifiedly, but with reservation, suspending it under a disjunctive [Col. 1043A] particle: “Or perhaps for this reason,” I say, “it is said, ‘by God.’” For after setting forth one reason which seemed to me to explain why the Evangelist, when he said, “The angel Gabriel was sent,” added expressly, “by God” (Luke 1:26), I also added another, cautiously and under a disjunction—so that neither would I be bound by a necessity of defending it, nor would the reader lack the freedom to choose 634 whichever of the two he wished [variant: preferred]. If, therefore, either one can stand, why am I reproached concerning the other, when I affirm neither and rather leave both to the judgment of the reader?

And yet, even if I had stated as my settled opinion that God’s counsel had remained unknown to the holy angels until then—not indeed that God’s purpose was at some time to work salvation in [Col. 1043B] the midst of the earth through the mystery of the incarnate Word (for this was granted to many mortals both to know beforehand and to foretell), but rather what time, what place, and what manner, and above all which virgin, God had chosen for accomplishing His purpose—if, I say, I had thought and written that even the holy angels were ignorant of this counsel of God, not concerning the work itself but concerning its time, place, manner, and person, I certainly do not see why this should seem incredible. Indeed, each person securely abounds in his own judgment where what he thinks does not conflict either with sound reason or with an authority not to be despised.

19. For what reason or authority compels me to think that even that time had been known to the angels from of old, of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, made [Col. 1043C] of a woman, made under the law”? (Gal. 4:4.) It perhaps seems more credible that, just as they are wholly ignorant, on the Lord’s own testimony, of the day of His future coming (Matt. 24:36), so too they did not know beforehand the time of His former coming. For who knows whether, in that spiritual manner, the Wisdom of God spoke to the angels concerning His first advent what He is read to have answered the Apostles, through the mouth of assumed flesh, concerning His second: “It is not for you,” He said, “to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in His own power”? (Acts 1:7.)

What necessity compels me further to believe that the angels had already noticed the city of Nazareth before they saw the archangel sent there to greet the Virgin and announce the divine birth? For Bethlehem had been preselected for the Nativity and Jerusalem for the Passion; this was openly [Col. 1043D] foreknown and foretold by the Prophets. But that Nazareth was likewise foreseen for the conception is not, I think, similarly proved by any evident testimony from the Scriptures to have been foreseen by the Prophets. For when it is read, “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matt. 11:23 [sic]), the Evangelist, who takes this from the prophet, shows clearly enough that it refers not so much to the conception as to His upbringing: namely, because He was brought back there from Egypt and brought up there.

Finally, the Jews say to Nicodemus: “Search and see, for no prophet arises from Galilee” (John 7:52). They were speaking, indeed, to one who knew the law, a teacher in Israel, who would scarcely be ignorant of anything; and nevertheless they insisted with complete confidence, showing that the Scriptures did not say that Christ would come from Galilee, in which Nazareth is known to be a city. Yet the testimony from the prophet, by which they immediately answered “Bethlehem” when the king asked the place of the birth, was more readily available to them. Thus Christ was born at Bethlehem (Matt. 2:1) and suffered at Jerusalem; and it is evident that the Prophets openly foretold both. He was likewise conceived in Nazareth, a city of Galilee; yet nothing appears to have occurred even to Nicodemus by which he might show that either Galilee or Nazareth had anything whatever to do with Christ’s advent.

20. Likewise Nathanael, himself learned in the law, when Philip announced Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, immediately answered in wondering question: “Can anything good come [Col. 1044B] from Nazareth?” (John 1:46.) He was plainly astonished that Christ was announced as coming from Nazareth, since he recalled this from no Scripture at all. Or, if it is maintained that he replied not interrogatively but rather affirmatively, remembering, no doubt, the aforementioned testimony, “He shall be called a Nazarene,” nevertheless it would not thereby follow that he knew Jesus had been conceived in Nazareth, since many other reasons might have occurred for which the prophet foretold this. Therefore the divine counsel concerning the place of conception could have been unknown to the angels as well as to the Prophets.

635 21. Then that utterly incomprehensible manner, concerning which even the Virgin anxiously asked—how, I ask, can I be taught that it was foreknown by the angels? It seems to me, indeed, that not even the angel who announced it knew it [Col. 1044C] (if I may say so without offence); and he himself admits this, if we carefully observe his words. For when he answers, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” does he not openly refer her to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, by whose anointing she is to be taught concerning all things of which he himself does not presume knowledge, and is to learn by experience what she could not learn by hearing? Finally he adds: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35), more expressly indicating the utterly secret manner of an incomprehensible and ineffable mystery: namely, that in a manner as though in shadow, with the Virgin alone and in the Virgin alone, the Trinity alone would accomplish the divine conception.

The great John also confesses himself less suited to investigate this mystery when he declares himself unworthy to loosen the strap of the sandal. And concerning the Virgin herself, [Col. 1044D] I ask: how will it be proved that the angels had previously known her by name or face, that she was the one whom God had chosen as His mother—except only the archangel, to whom she must be believed to have been entrusted for protection from the beginning? Moreover, if the devil did not recognize her even after the conception, being deceived by her betrothal to Joseph, one may believe that it was not known even beforehand to the holy angels that she herself would become the Mother of God. For indeed the reprobate spirits, although deprived of participation in spiritual grace, are not deprived of the liveliness of natural shrewdness.

22. Do you see how many things, without injury to faith and the truth of Scripture, the angels could have been ignorant of in the divine counsel—especially so that the prerogative of revealing these things might be reserved for the Virgin Mother? First is the time; second, the place; third, the manner; fourth, the choice of the virginal person. Give this answer to the brethren who reproach me because I said, to the Virgin’s praise, that “by God” was added for this reason: lest God be thought perhaps to have revealed His counsel to anyone, [Col. 1045A] [Col. 1046A] even among the blessed angels, before revealing it to the Virgin—except only the archangel Gabriel. By “His counsel” I meant not the work itself, but the time of the work, its place, its manner, and also the election of the person.

Farewell.

[Col. 1045]

# [Articles of the Heresies of Peter Abelard]

## Notice on Little Work XI

636 1. The following letter, which among Bernard’s letters is one hundred and ninetieth in order, Horstius placed among the treatises because of the letter’s length and the dignity of its subject matter. It was written on the occasion of Abelard’s errors being condemned at the Synod of Sens, which we have said in the notes to the one hundred and eighty-seventh letter was held in 1140, with a large gathering of Gallican bishops and in the presence of King Louis the Younger. In the synodal letter—which is the one hundred and ninety-first among Bernard’s letters—and in another which is now number three hundred and thirty-seven, the Fathers inform Pope Innocent that Abelard’s errors had been condemned by them, while the author himself remained untouched because he had appealed to the Apostolic See; and they state that the articles of error “are more fully contained in the letters of the lord of Sens.” We believe these letters to be none other than the following letter of Bernard, in which such articles are reported and briefly refuted. They are the same articles which William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry and then a monk of Igny, sent to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and to Bernard, as appears from his letters published above among Bernard’s letters.

2. In his *Apology*, Abelard complained that some of these articles had been falsely attributed to him; others he acknowledged as his own and corrected. In that work he repeatedly attacks Bernard, as his sole adversary, as a malicious or careless informer. Bernard’s defence against these calumnies was undertaken by two former associates of Abelard himself, who had at last recovered from his errors: Geoffrey, later Bernard’s secretary; and an anonymous abbot of the “Black Monks.” Chesnius had identified both in his Notes on Abelard; but both their works have now been printed in volume IV of the *Cistercian Library*. There the learned editor Bertrand Tissier observes that this anonymous abbot was not William of Saint-Thierry. The abbot, moreover, was in Francia—that is, in the metropolitan province of Sens or of Reims, as Geoffrey testifies, as we shall shortly see—and dedicated three books written by himself against Abelard to Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. At the beginning of the second book he calls him “his lord,” and likewise “the most illustrious lamp of Rouen”: “You,” he says, “who think concerning your God with a Catholic heart, speak with a Catholic mouth, and write more excellently than others with a Catholic hand.”

3. Some of the articles of error imputed to Abelard are lacking from his published works. Hence some seize an occasion to accuse Bernard, as though he had attributed false errors to Abelard and fought against masks and shadows. Yet it is established that very many errors are found even in the published writings, as we shall show in their places; and, if any others no longer exist, William of Saint-Thierry, Geoffrey, and that anonymous abbot—a former disciple of Abelard, who knew his teacher’s doctrine and cites his very words—had once read them in Abelard himself, as did William, both from Abelard’s *Apology* and from his *Theology*, which do not appear in the editions. Indeed Abelard himself, in the second book of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 554, reserves for treatment in his *Theology* certain matters of which there is no mention in the printed text, which ends thus: “The remainder is missing.” It is thus apparent that the *Theology* in the editions is mutilated.

4. Therefore those who, in order to acquit Abelard, accuse Bernard of having been impelled, as they say, by blind zeal, deserve very ill of the Christian religion, let alone of Bernard. At least they must ultimately acknowledge, with Abelard himself and his defender Berengar, that he erred in certain things. For Abelard acknowledges himself guilty in some respects, though not sufficiently from the heart, in his *Apology*, where he says: “Perhaps I wrote certain things in error which I ought not to have written; but I call God as witness and judge upon my soul that, in those matters of which I am accused, I presumed nothing through malice or pride.” Let it then be granted that malice, and even heresy, may be removed from him; yet one may not disguise at least some errors, a pursuit of novel terms, frivolity, perhaps even pride and an itch for disputes. But in the end Innocent, by a rescript sent to the bishops, ordered the man confined and his books burned; and he ordered them consigned to the flames at Rome, as Geoffrey testifies. Peter, however, finally came to his senses and abandoned his appeal through the counsel and exhortation of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, who highly praises his final conduct in a letter to Heloise.

637 5. It did not cost Bernard nothing that he pursued Abelard both in writing and in speech. For not only Abelard, impatient of censure, but also Berengar, his disciple and defender, finally dared to allege, by a notable fabrication, certain erroneous things in Bernard’s writings. “You truly erred,” says Berengar, addressing Bernard, “when you asserted that the origin of souls is from heaven,” p. 310. And on p. 315: “You make up stories that the origin of souls is from the heavens, where I recall you speaking as follows”—namely, in Sermon 17 on the Song of Songs—“The Apostle rightly said: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven.’ Your words, subtly examined, taste of heresy to the palate of a Christian mind.”

Away with the mad and shameless charlatan. Near the end of Book II, the anonymous abbot sets forth another calumny of Abelard against Bernard: “It is a wonder to me that, for so long a time and by so many men—whose learning shines in the Church as the moon by the sun—no answer has been given to our Abelard, who charges the Abbot with saying that God and the man assumed by God are one person in the Trinity; whereas man is a corporeal thing, composed of limbs and liable to dissolution, but God is neither a corporeal thing nor composed of limbs so as to be dissoluble. Therefore neither God is to be called man nor man God,” etc. Thus Abelard plays the Nestorian while impudently accusing Bernard of error.

William of Saint-Thierry rightly says on this subject in chapter 8 against Abelard: “And we likewise say that Christ, the Son of Man, is in the very nature of His humanity—but not from that nature, according to the union which He has with God—the third person in the Trinity; because, just as the incarnate God became Son of Man on account of the assumed man, so the assumed man became Son of God on account of the assuming God.”

6. Besides the articles which Bernard refutes expressly, in no. 10 he recounts several together, being content to have [Col. 1047] expounded those which are likewise refuted by others, namely by William and the anonymous abbot. Concerning the accidents which Abelard taught remained in the air after consecration in the Eucharist, William says thus: “It seems to us—if it also seems so to you,” addressing Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Bernard, “that those accidents, or the former form of the substance—which, I suppose, is nothing but a harmonious concurrence of accidents into one—if it is there, are in the body of the Lord, not forming it, but, by the power of God’s Wisdom working in them, fitting and modifying it, so that according to the rite of the mystery and the mode of the sacrament, that which could not be so in its own form may become fit for use, capable of being handled, and capable of being tasted in an alien form.”

Likewise, in the work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, addressed to Rupert, chapter 3: “But contrary to every reasoning and understanding of secular philosophy, the substance of bread having been changed into another substance, He so transferred unchanged, for a certain service of the mystery, certain accidents that adhered to it, that the body of the Lord, although whiteness is present, does not become white, nor round on account of roundness; but He so preserved all accidents of this sort that, although they truly are present to the body of His humanity, they are nevertheless not in it, nor do they stain or affect it,” etc.

638 7. Moreover, just as Abelard did not think rightly, or at least did not speak rightly, concerning the Incarnation, so neither did he concerning the grace of Christ, which he reduced to reason given by God alone, to the admonition of the Scriptures, and to examples; and he said that it was therefore common to all. “It must therefore be said that man, through reason indeed given by God, can adhere to the grace set before him; nor does God do more for the man who is saved, before he adheres to grace, than for him who is not saved. But just as one who displays precious stones for sale and arouses in those who see them the desire to buy, so He sets His grace before all, counsels through the Scriptures, and recalls by examples, so that men may adhere to grace through the freedom of choice which they possess. And below: This quickening is attributed to grace, because the reason by which a man discerns and understands that he must abstain from evil and do good is from God. And therefore he is said to act by God’s inspiration, because God, through the reason which He gave to man, causes him to recognize sin itself.”

William cites these and other things from Abelard’s writings, undoubtedly from his *Theology*, which perhaps for this and very many other reasons was mutilated by later generations. Nor may credit be denied in this matter to William, a man otherwise learned and most devout, especially since, in Book IV on the Epistle to the Romans, Abelard teaches the same pernicious doctrine on p. 653 and following, where the following words are found in many copies: “What grace, then, must necessarily precede in order to kindle our desire for God and make us long for the heavenly kingdom, except that the blessedness to which He invites us and the way by which we can arrive there be explained and imparted? This grace He bestows equally upon reprobate and elect alike, instructing both equally in this matter, so that from the same grace of faith which they have received one may be stirred to good works and another, through the negligence of his own sluggishness, may be rendered inexcusable.” And shortly afterward: “Nor is it necessary that, through each of the new works that arise daily, God should set forth another grace besides faith itself, by which, namely, we believe that for what we do we shall obtain so great a reward.”

We mention these things so that all may finally understand how impiously Abelard, if he did not think, at least wrote concerning the Incarnation and the grace of Christ; and how rightly Bernard said in Letter 192: “When he speaks of the Trinity, he savours of Arius; when of grace, he savours of Pelagius; when of the person of Christ, he savours of Nestorius.” The latter two charges are established from what has been said and from the following letter. Concerning the third, whoever wishes to know it should read near the end of Book III of Abelard’s *Theology*, where he will find the author himself saying that “those who recoil from our expressions concerning the faith are easily convinced when they hear that God the Father and God the Son are joined to us in the sense of the words.”

In what way? “Let us ask them,” he says, “whether they believe in the Wisdom of God, concerning which it is written: ‘You have made all things in wisdom’; and they will immediately answer that they believe.” This, he says, is to believe in the Son; just as to believe in the Holy Spirit is nothing other than to believe in God’s goodness. If these statements are taken strictly, they seem to savour of more than Arianism—that is, of Sabellianism. Although, to confess frankly, he rejects this error later, on p. 1069. Yet it matters not only to think rightly, but also—especially where faith is concerned—to speak and write rightly.

Therefore William of Saint-Thierry, in chapter 3 of his book against Abelard, after citing Abelard’s words concerning the bronze and the seal, power and a certain power, says: “As regards the destruction of the persons, it is Sabellian; as regards dissimilarity and inequality, it goes on foot into the opinion of Arius.” We mention these things, I say, so that those who detest these errors may be ashamed to take Abelard’s cause against Bernard, whom they are not ashamed still to accuse of rash judgment concerning Abelard and excessive rancour. William of Conches explains the mystery of the Trinity in almost the same way as Abelard; and William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, likewise refutes his errors in a letter to Bernard. So true is it that nothing can turn out more unhappily for religion than when philosophers attempt to explain the mysteries of our faith by reason alone.

8. Geoffrey, secretary of Saint Bernard, speaks thus in a letter to Henry, cardinal and bishop of Albano, concerning the whole affair of Abelard: “I have also heard that, concerning the condemnation of Peter Abelard, your diligence desires more fully to know the truth likewise. The booklets of this man were condemned to a public burning in the city of Rome and in the church of Saint Peter by the lord Pope Innocent II of pious memory, who by apostolic authority declared him a heretic. For many years earlier a venerable cardinal and legate of the Roman Church, named Cono, formerly a regular canon of the church of Saint Nicholas of Arrouaise, had likewise burned his *Theology* while holding a council at Soissons, accusing Peter himself in person and, upon conviction of heretical depravity, condemning him. Therefore, if it please your desire, satisfaction will be provided through the booklet *On the Life of Saint Bernard* and through his letters sent to the Curia.

“Yet I found at Clairvaux a booklet by a certain abbot of the Black Monks, in which the errors of the same Peter are noted, and which I remember having seen formerly. But for many years, as the guardians of the books affirm, after a careful search, the first quire could not be found. Therefore we intend to send into Francia to the monastery of which the man who composed that book was abbot; and, if I can recover it, to have the whole codex copied and sent to you. For I believe that this ought to suffice for your inquiry: that you may know what things were condemned, in what way, and why.”

Thus far Geoffrey, from Chesnius’s Notes on Abelard. We pass over what is mentioned in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, pp. 478 and following, concerning a vision of Henry, canon of Tournai, reported to the Fathers of the Synod of Sens and to Bernard.

9. After I had written these things, our John Durand, who was then staying at Rome, sent me from a faulty Vatican codex, marked 663, the *Articles of the Heresies of Peter Abelard*, placed before the following letter. These are doubtless the very articles which Bernard signifies at the end of this letter that he collected and sent to the Pope. For that reason, it seemed appropriate to place them here beforehand for the illumination of the letter itself.

# Here Begin the Articles of the Heresies of Peter Abelard

[Col. 1049]

640 I. A dreadful comparison of a bronze seal, and of species and genus, with the Trinity.

[Col. 1049A]

“Since the Wisdom of God is a certain power, just as a bronze seal is a certain bronze, it is plainly evident that divine Wisdom has its being from divine power, according to that likeness by which a bronze seal is said to be that which its material is; or a species from its genus, which is said to be, as it were, the matter of the species—for example, animal in relation to man. For just as, from the fact that something is a bronze seal, it necessarily follows that it is bronze, and from the fact that something is a man, that it is animal, but not conversely: so divine Wisdom, which is the power of discernment, requires that it be divine power, but not conversely.” And shortly afterward: “Goodness itself, which is indicated by the name Spirit, is not power or wisdom in God.”

II. That the Holy Spirit is not from the substance of the Father.

[Col. 1049B]

“Therefore, since both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father—the former begotten, the latter proceeding—generation itself differs from procession in that he who is begotten is from the very substance of the Father, since Wisdom itself, as has been said, has this very being: that it is a certain power.” And shortly afterward: “But although the Spirit is of the same substance as the Father and the Son, whence the Trinity itself is also proclaimed *homoousion*, that is, of one substance, He nevertheless is not from the substance of the Father or of the Son; for that would be to be begotten from the Father or the Son. Rather, He has from them the proceeding which is God’s extending Himself through love toward another. For in some manner each person proceeds from himself to another through love, since, properly speaking, as has been said, no one is said to have charity toward himself, so as to be kind to himself, but toward another; most of all God, who needs no one and cannot be moved by an affection of kindness toward Himself so as to bestow anything upon Himself from kindness, but only toward creatures.”

III. That God can do, or leave undone, only those things which He does at some time, and only in the manner and at the time in which He does them, not otherwise.

[Col. 1049C]

“By the reasoning which proves that God the Father begot the Son as good as He could—otherwise He would be guilty of envy—it is also clear that He makes all things that He does as excellent as He can, and is unwilling to withhold any benefit which He can confer.” And shortly afterward: “In all things which God does, He so attends to what is good that He may be said to be inclined to make each thing by the worth of the good itself rather than by the pleasure of His own will.” Likewise: “Thus from these considerations, gathered both from reason and from Scripture, it is established that God can do only what He does at some time.” And shortly afterward: “If He could restrain the evils that occur—and if He did so, only suitably, since He can do nothing unsuitably—I do not see how He would not be consenting to sins. For who is to be said to consent to evil except one through whom it could also suitably be restrained?” Likewise: “Therefore, from the foregoing arguments and solutions of objections, I think it is clear to all that God can do, or leave undone, only those things which He does, and only in the manner and at the time in which He does them, not otherwise.”

[Col. 1049D]

641 IV. That Christ did not assume flesh in order to free us from the yoke of the devil.

“Know that all our teachers after the Apostles agree on this: that the devil had dominion and power over man, and possessed him by right.” And shortly afterward: “The devil never had any right over man, but possessed him by right, by permission, as a jailer; nor did the Son of God assume flesh [in order that He might free him] from the yoke of the devil.” [Col. 1050B] And shortly afterward: “How does the Apostle say that we are justified or reconciled to God through the death of His Son, when God ought to have been so much the more angry against man, inasmuch as he sinned more greatly in crucifying His Son than in transgressing His first command by tasting one fruit? For how would it have been more just? But if Adam’s sin was so great that it could not be expiated except by the death of Christ, what expiation will that very homicide have which was committed against Christ—the many and such great crimes committed against Him or His own? Did the death of the innocent Son so please God that through it He was reconciled to us, who committed this sin through which the innocent Lord was killed? And could He not forgive even a lighter sin unless this greatest sin occurred, nor do so great a good except after evils had been multiplied, by which we were made more just through the death of the Son of God than we were before, so that we ought now to be freed from sins?”

[Col. 1050C]

Likewise: “To whom does it not seem cruel and unjust for someone to require the blood of an innocent person and some payment, or in any way to be pleased that an innocent person be killed—much less for God to have accepted His Son’s death so as to be reconciled through it to the whole world? These and similar points raise no slight question, not only concerning our redemption but also concerning our justification through the death of our Lord Jesus Christ. But it seems to us that we are nevertheless justified in the blood of Christ and [Col. 1050D] reconciled to God through this singular grace shown us: that His Son assumed our nature and, in that nature, instructed us both by word and example even unto death, binding us more closely to Himself through love, so that, inflamed by the benefit of divine grace, your charity may not fear to endure anything for His sake. We do not doubt that this benefit likewise inflamed the ancient fathers, who awaited it through faith, into the highest love of God, as men of their own time.” And below: “I think, therefore, that the counsel and cause of the Incarnation was to illumine the world with the light of His wisdom and kindle it to His love.”

[Col. 1051A]

V. That neither God-and-man nor the man—the person who is Christ—is the third person in the Trinity.

“When I say, ‘Christ is the third person in the Trinity,’ I mean that the Word, which from eternity was the third person in the Trinity, is the third person in the Trinity; and I think that this expression is figurative. For if we said it were proper, since this name Christ signifies the same thing as God and man, the meaning would then be: ‘God and man is the third person in the Trinity.’ This is wholly false.” And shortly afterward: “It must be known that, although we concede that Christ is the third person in [Col. 1051B] the Trinity, we nevertheless do not concede that this person, which is Christ, is the third person in the Trinity.”

VI. That God does no more for the person who is saved, before he adheres to grace, than for the person who is not saved.

“Thus again that question is commonly raised which is stated by some, namely, whether all human beings are saved so entirely by mercy alone that no one can have a good will unless the grace of God goes before, moves the heart, inspires a good will, multiplies it when inspired, and preserves it when multiplied. But if it is so, that a human being can do no good of himself, or cannot in any way, by free choice and without the assistance of grace, raise himself to receive divine grace, as was said above, then no reason appears [Col. 1051C] why, if he sins, he should be punished. For if he cannot of himself do anything good, and is so made as to be more inclined toward evil than toward good, then surely, if he sins, he is free from blame; and is God, who made him so weak and of such frail nature, to be praised for such a creation? Indeed, if this were so, would he not rather seem blameworthy?” And shortly afterward: “But if it were so that a human being could not raise himself to receive divine grace without another’s grace, no reason appears why the human being should be blamed; and his not having God’s grace would seem rather to be attributed to its author. But this is not so; rather, it must be stated very differently, as the truth of the matter requires. It must therefore be said that a human being can, by reason bestowed by God, adhere to the grace set before him; nor does [Col. 1051D] God do more for the one who is saved, before he adheres to grace, than for the one who is not saved. For God deals with human beings as a merchant who has precious stones for sale: he displays them in the marketplace, offers them equally to all, and by showing them arouses in them a desire to buy. The prudent person, knowing that he needs them, works to obtain them: he acquires money and buys them. But the idle and slothful person, even if he has the desire, nevertheless does not work because he is lazy, even though he may be physically stronger than another; and so he does not buy them, and it is therefore his own fault that he lacks them. Similarly, God sets his grace before all and gives counsel through the Scriptures and eminent teachers, so that, by freedom of choice, the prudent person may adhere to grace, providing [Col. 1052A] for his future through that freedom of choice by which he adheres to this grace. But the slothful person, entangled in carnal desires, even if he desires to be made blessed, nevertheless never wishes to labor by restraining himself from evil; instead he neglects this, although through free choice he can adhere to grace. And thus he is neglected by almighty God.”

## VII. That God ought not to prevent evils

“First one must consider what it is to consent to evil, and what it is not. A person is said, indeed, to consent to evil when, although he ought to prevent it and can do so, he does not prevent it. But if he ought to prevent it and cannot; or conversely, if he can and ought not to prevent it, he is not guilty. If, however, he neither ought nor can prevent it, he must much less be judged guilty. And therefore God is free from consent to evils, since he neither ought nor can prevent evils. [Col. 1052B] He ought not, because, since a thing comes to pass through his goodness in the best way in which it can, he ought by no means to will this otherwise. Nor can he, because his goodness cannot, once a lesser good has been chosen, place any impediment before that which is greater.”

## VIII. That we contracted from Adam not guilt, but punishment

“It must be understood that when it is said, ‘Original sin is in infants,’ this is said with reference to the temporal and eternal punishment owed to them on account of the guilt of the first parent.” And shortly afterward: “Likewise it is said, ‘in whom all sinned’ (Rom. 5:12), namely because the seed of all was in him who sinned. Yet it does not follow from this that all who did not yet exist had sinned; and one who does not exist does not sin.”

## IX. That the Lord’s body does not fall to the ground

[Col. 1052C]

“Concerning the appearances of bread and wine, the question is asked whether they are now in Christ’s body, as formerly they were in the substance of bread and wine, which was changed into Christ’s body; or whether they are in the air. But it is more plausible that they are in the air, since Christ’s body has its own outlines and its own appearance, like other human bodies. These appearances, namely of bread and wine, come into being in the mouth in order to conceal and cover Christ’s body.” And shortly afterward: “Here, moreover, the question is raised concerning that which seems to be a multitude . . . whence it is also commanded that it be kept from Sabbath to Sabbath, as is read to have been done with the loaves of presentation; it also seems to be gnawed by mice and to fall from the hand of priest or deacon [Col. 1052D] onto the ground. The question is therefore asked why God permits these things to happen to his body. 643 Or perhaps they do not happen thus to the body, but he merely makes them so appear in the appearances? To this we answer that this truly is not so in the body; rather, God causes it to be so in the appearances themselves in order to restrain the negligence of ministers, while he places and preserves his own body as he pleases.

## X. That a human being is made neither better nor worse by works

“It is commonly asked what is rewarded by the Lord: the work, the intention, or both. Authority seems, however, to maintain that works are eternally rewarded by God; for the Apostle says, ‘God will render to each according to his works’ (Rom. 2:6). And Athanasius says, [Col. 1053A] ‘They will render an account of their own deeds.’ And shortly afterward he says: ‘Those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire’ (Matt. 25:46; John 5:29). But we say that works are eternally recompensed by God, whether for good or for evil; and a human being is not made worse or better on account of works, except insofar as, while acting, perhaps his will is increased in some respect. Nor is this contrary to the Apostle or to other authorities; for when the Apostle said, ‘He will render to each,’ and so forth, he put the effect for the cause, namely the work for the will or intention.”

## XI. That those who crucified Christ in ignorance did not sin; and that whatever is done through ignorance is not to be imputed as guilt

“He raises an objection concerning the Jews who crucified Christ, [Col. 1053B] and others who, in persecuting martyrs, thought that they were rendering service to God; and concerning Eve [lacuna] who did not act against her conscience, because she was deceived, and yet it is certain that she sinned. To this we say that those simple Jews did not truly act against conscience, but rather persecuted Christ out of zeal for their law; nor did they think that they were doing wrong, and therefore they did not sin. Nor were any of them damned on this account, but because of preceding sins, by the just desert of which they fell into this blindness. And among them were those elect persons for whom Christ prayed, saying, ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23:34). Nor did he pray that this sin might be forgiven them, since it was not a sin, but rather their preceding sins.”

## XII. On the power of binding and loosing

[Col. 1053C]

“That which is read in Matthew, ‘Whatever you bind on earth’ (Matt. 16:19), and so forth, must be understood thus: ‘Whatever you bind on earth,’ that is, in the present life, ‘will be bound also in heaven,’ that is, in the present Church.” And shortly afterward: “The Gospel seems to oppose this opinion of ours, by which we say that God alone forgives sins; for Christ says to his disciples, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them’ (John 20:22–23). But we say that this was said to the Apostles alone, not to their successors.” And immediately it is added: “Yet if anyone should say that this applies to their successors, it is proper to explain this also in the manner of the authority mentioned above.”

## XIII. On suggestion, pleasure, and consent

“It must also be understood that suggestion is not a sin in the person to whom the suggestion is made; nor is the pleasure consequent upon suggestion—which pleasure arises from weakness and [Col. 1054B] from the memory of the pleasure that lies in the fulfillment of the thing which the adversary suggests. Rather, consent alone, which is also called contempt of God, is that in which sin consists.” And shortly afterward: “Nor do we say that the will to do this or that, nor even the act itself, is sin; rather, as was said above, sin is contempt of God arising from some act of will.”

## XIV. That omnipotence pertains properly or specially to the Father

“If we refer power both to the knowledge of subsisting and to the efficacy of acting, we find that omnipotence pertains properly or specially to the personal property of the Father: not only because he can accomplish all things equally with the other two persons, but also because he alone has existence from himself and not from another; and as he has existence from himself, so also he has power from himself.” [Col. 1054C]

These are the Chapters of Peter Abelard’s *Theology*—or rather, his *Foolishology*.

[Col. 1053]

# LETTER CXC OF ST BERNARD, ABBOT, AGAINST CERTAIN CHAPTERS OF ABELARD’S ERRORS, OR TREATISE ADDRESSED TO POPE INNOCENT II

644

## PREFACE

[Col. 1053D]

To the most beloved father and lord INNOCENT, supreme pontiff: Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux, offers the little that he is.

Every danger and scandal arising in the kingdom of God, especially those that concern the faith, ought to be referred to your apostolic office. For I judge it fitting that injuries to the faith be repaired above all there where faith cannot suffer deficiency. This indeed is the prerogative of this See. For to whom else was it ever said, [Col. 1054D] “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail”? Therefore what follows is required of Peter’s successor: “And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). This is indeed necessary now. It is time, most loving Father, that you acknowledge your primacy, prove your zeal, and honor your ministry. You truly fulfill Peter’s role—whose see you hold—if by your admonition you strengthen hearts wavering in the faith, and by your authority crush corrupters of the faith.

## CHAPTER I. He recounts and denounces Abelard’s impious doctrines concerning the Holy Trinity

[Col. 1055A]

1. In France we have a new theologian from an old master, who from his earliest youth played at dialectic and now raves in the holy Scriptures. He strives to revive doctrines long condemned and put to sleep, both his own and those of others; moreover, he adds new ones. While he deigns to be ignorant of nothing that is in heaven above or on earth beneath, except “I do not know”:

> [Note: [Col. 1055C] In other editions, “I do not know what”; but in the manuscripts simply “I do not know,” and more correctly, so that the meaning is that Abelard refuses to stick at any question or confess his ignorance. [Col. 1055D]]

he sets his mouth in heaven and investigates God’s heights; returning to us, he reports ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter. And while he is prepared to give an account of all things, he presumes even concerning things above reason and against reason, and [Col. 1055B] against faith. For what is more contrary to reason than to attempt by reason to transcend reason? And what is more contrary to faith than to refuse to believe whatever one cannot attain by reason? Finally, wishing to expound the saying of the Wise Man [or Solomon], “Whoever believes quickly is light-minded” (Ecclus. 19:4), he says: “To believe quickly is to give faith before reason”:

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] This is the sense of *Introduction to Theology*, book II, which hereafter we shall call simply the *Theology*. The words occur on p. 1060: “But one believes quickly or easily who, indiscriminately and without due consideration, assents to what people say before he investigates, as far as he can, by a reason previously unknown to him, whether faith ought to be given to what is being urged upon him.”]

although Solomon speaks not of faith in God but of credulity among ourselves. For blessed Pope Gregory plainly denies that the faith which is in God has merit if human reason supplies it with proof; but he praises the Apostles because, at the sound of a single command, they followed the Redeemer (*Homily 26 on the Gospels*). He knows, surely, that this was said in praise: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Ps. 17:45); and that, conversely, the disciples were rebuked for believing too slowly (Mark 16:14). Finally, Mary is praised because she anticipated reason by faith; and Zechariah is punished because he tested faith by reason (Luke 1:45, 20). Again Abraham is commended because, “against hope, he believed in hope” (Rom. 4:18).

645

2. But our theologian, on the contrary, says: “What profit is there in speaking for instruction, if what we wish to teach cannot be explained so as to be understood?”

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] This likewise gives the sense of the same work, p. 1063: “What profit is there in integrity of speech which is not followed by the hearer’s understanding?” etc.]

And so, while promising understanding to his hearers, even in those loftier and holier matters contained in that profound [Col. 1056A] recess of sacred faith, he posits degrees in the Trinity, modes in majesty, and numbers in eternity. Finally, he maintains that “God the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, the Holy Spirit no power; and that the Son stands in relation to the Father as a certain power to power, species to genus, the materialized to matter, man to animal, a bronze seal to bronze.”

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] Abelard complains in his *Apology*, p. 331, that this was ascribed to him through malice or error, and says that he abhors and detests it as something diabolical. Yet his former disciple and later opponent, the anonymous author published in vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, accuses Abelard of lying here, p. 209: “And first,” he says, “I ask why he accuses an abbot of holy religious life and great reputation of having spoken falsely, because he wrote in his *Theology* that the Son is a certain power and the Spirit no power,” etc. He then proves that Abelard said this by reporting his words as if from the *Apology*, where they are now not found, just as neither are the words reported by the same anonymous author on p. 242. But in his *Theology*, concerning the Son, Abelard teaches in book I, p. 991: “Divine Wisdom is therefore a certain divine power,” etc.; and in book II concerning the Son and Holy Spirit, as we shall shortly observe. [Col. 1056C–D]]

Is he not here more than Arius? Who can bear such things? Who would not close his ears to sacrilegious utterances? Who would not shudder at profane novelties alike of words and meanings? He also says that “the Holy Spirit proceeds indeed from the Father and Son, but is by no means of the substance of the Father or Son.”

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] These are Abelard’s words in book I, p. 1085: “Since both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father—the former begotten, the latter proceeding—generation differs from procession in this: he who is begotten is from the Father’s very substance, since he has Wisdom itself, that is, being itself, and is thus a certain power; whereas the affection of love pertains more to the benevolence of mind than to power. Hence the Son is rightly said to be begotten from the Father, that is, properly said to be from the Father’s very substance,” etc. Abelard therefore wrongly—indeed, not to say shamelessly—denies in his *Apology* that he uttered this, and attributes it to malice or ignorance.]

From where, then? Perhaps from nothing, like all things that were made? [Col. 1056B] For the Apostle himself does not deny that these things are from God, nor does he fear to say, “From whom are all things” (Rom. 11:36). What then? Shall we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son in no manner different from all things—that is, not essentially, but as a creature—and is accordingly created like all things? Or will the man who always seeks novelties and invents what he does not discover, affirming things that are not as if they were, find for himself a third manner by which he produces him from Father and Son? “But,” he says, “if he were of the Father’s substance, he would surely be begotten, and the Father would have two sons.” As though everything which is from a substance must immediately have as its begetter the very thing from which it is. Are lice, nits [Col. 1056C] [or *lentes*], or phlegm sons of flesh, or are they not from the substance of flesh? Or are worms that come forth from rotten wood from anything other than the substance of the wood, although they are not sons of wood? Moths, too, have their substance from the substance of garments, but not their generation; and there are many things of this kind.

3. I wonder how a man acute and learned in his own estimation, while confessing the Holy Spirit to be consubstantial with the Father and Son, nevertheless denies that he proceeds from the substance of Father and Son. Unless perhaps he wishes them to proceed from the Spirit himself: [Col. 1057A] a thing unheard of and impious. But if neither the Spirit is of their substance nor they of his, where, I ask, is consubstantiality? Therefore, either let him confess with the Church that the Holy Spirit is of the substance of those from whom he does not deny that he proceeds; or at least, with Arius, let him deny consubstantiality and openly proclaim creation. Further, if the Son is of the Father’s substance and the Holy Spirit is not, they must necessarily differ from one another—not only because the Holy Spirit is not begotten, while the Son is, but also because the Son is of the Father’s substance whereas the Holy Spirit is not. This latter difference Catholic [faith]:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] Printed editions add the word “faith,” which is absent from the manuscript codices. The expression is familiar to Augustine for signifying Catholic faith or the Church, throughout the *Confessions*—for example, book V, ch. 14; book VI, ch. 4; book VII, ch. 1—and in *Against Lying*, ch. 7. Compare Bernard, *On Consideration*, book III, no. 3; and *Sermons on the Song of Songs* 64 and 65, no. 8, and 66, no. 4. [Col. 1058D]]

has not known until now. If we admit it, where are the Trinity and the Unity? For when Holy Spirit and Son differ from one another by a new multiplicity [Col. 1057B] of differences, unity is shattered—especially since the difference which this man attempts to introduce is plainly substantial. Moreover, when the Holy Spirit departs from the substance of Father and Son, there remains not a Trinity but a duality. For it is not fitting to admit into the Trinity a person who has nothing in substance common with the rest. Let him therefore cease to separate the procession of the Holy Spirit from the substance of Father and Son, lest by a double impiety he both diminish the number belonging to the Trinity and attribute it to the Unity. Christian faith rejects both. And lest I seem to rest in so great a matter on human arguments alone, let him read Jerome’s letter to Avitus; he will certainly see, among the other blasphemies of Origen which Jerome refutes, that he also detests Origen’s assertion that the Holy Spirit is not of the substance [Col. 1057C] of the Father. Blessed Athanasius speaks thus in his book *On the Unity of the Trinity*: “When I mentioned God alone, I did not indicate the person of the Father alone; for I did not deny that the Son and Holy Spirit are of this one very substance of the Father.” Thus Athanasius.

## CHAPTER II. That no inequality is to be admitted in the Trinity, but complete equality

4. Your Holiness sees how, when this man is not disputing but raving, the Trinity does not cohere and the Unity hangs in suspense; and this certainly does not occur without injury to majesty. Whatever God is, indeed, is without doubt that than which nothing greater can be conceived:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] Anselm especially establishes this notion of God in the *Monologion* and the *Apologeticus*, at their very beginning.]

If, therefore, in this one and supreme majesty we admit, in considering the persons, even a slight defect, while more is given to one and taken away from another, then the whole is surely less than that than which nothing greater can be conceived. For what is wholly greatest is without doubt greater than what is greatest only in part. But the person who, according to his ability, worthily esteems divine magnificence conceives in it nothing unequal, where all is supremely great; nothing separate, where [Col. 1058A] all is one; nothing gaping, where all is whole; finally, nothing imperfect or lacking, where all is all. For the Father is wholly what the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are; the Son is wholly what he himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit are; and the Holy Spirit is wholly what he himself, the Father, and the Son are. And this whole is one whole, neither excessive in the three nor diminished in each. For they do not divide among themselves, as particular shares, the true and supreme good which they are; since neither do they possess it by participation, but are it essentially. For the fact that one is truly said to be from another, or one in relation to another, is indeed the designation of persons, not a division of unity. Although in this ineffable and incomprehensible essence of the Godhead “one” and “another” are said soberly and catholicly—because the properties of the persons require it—yet there are not there one thing and another thing, but a simple one. Thus confession of the Trinity does not prejudice Unity, nor does a true assertion of Unity exclude personal properties. Let that abominable comparison—indeed, dissimilarity—of genus and species be as far from our minds as it is from the rule of truth:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] Read chapter 2 of William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, *Against Abelard*.]

and likewise that comparison of bronze and a bronze seal. For since genus and species, in their mutual relation, are the one superior and the other inferior, whereas God is one, they can never suitably correspond—so great is the equality in one case and the inequality in the other. The same judgment applies again to bronze and a certain bronze thing, namely a bronze seal, since it is employed in the same sort of comparison. Since, as I said, species is less and inferior to genus, far be it from us to conceive this diversity in Father and Son; far be it from us to assent to one who says that the Son is to the Father as species to genus, man to animal, a bronze seal to bronze, or some power to power. All these things are, by the reciprocal relation of their natures, superior and inferior to one another; and for that reason no comparison at all may be admitted from them to that in which nothing is unequal and nothing dissimilar. You see from what great ignorance or impiety the invention of these comparisons descends.

## CHAPTER III. He attacks Abelard’s absurd doctrine that assigns absolute and essential names properly and specially to one person

[Col. 1058D]

5. Observe still more clearly what he thinks, teaches, and writes. He says that power pertains properly and specially to the Father, wisdom to the Son. This is false. For the Father is most truly wisdom and the Son power, and they are most soundly so called; what is common to both cannot be proper to each singly. Those names are different which are not said of themselves but reciprocally of one another; [Col. 1059A] and therefore each has what is his own and not common with the other. For he who is Father is not Son, and he who is Son is not Father. The Father is designated by the name “Father” not as he is in himself, but as he is relative to the Son; likewise, by the name “Son” is expressed not what the Son is in himself, but what he is relative to the Father. Power and wisdom, and many other things said of themselves, are not so: both Father and Son possess them, not each separately in relation to the other. “No,” he says, “but we find that omnipotence pertains properly or specially to the personal property of the Father, not only because he can accomplish all things equally with the other two persons, but also because he alone has existence from himself and not from another; and as he has existence from himself, so also he has power from himself.” (*Abelard’s Theology*, book I, p. [Col. 1059B] 990.) O second Aristotle! By the same reasoning, if it were reasoning, would not wisdom and benevolence also pertain properly to the Father, since the Father has being wise and benevolent equally from himself and not from another, just as he has being and power? If he does not deny this—and he cannot deny it on his own reasoning—what, I ask, will he do with his noble division, by which he assigned power properly and specially to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and benevolence to the Holy Spirit? For one and the same thing cannot properly belong to two persons, that is, be proper to each. Let him choose what he wishes: either let him give wisdom to the Son and take it from the Father, or attribute it to the Father and take it from the Son; and again assign benevolence either to the Holy Spirit without the Father or to the Father without the Holy Spirit. Or else let him stop making common names proper, and because the Father has power from himself, let him not therefore dare to concede that it is proper to him, lest his own reasoning compel him likewise to assign to the Father as proper both benevolence and wisdom, which he possesses from himself no less.

648

6. But let us wait a little longer and see with what theory our theologian contemplates the invisible things of God. As I said, he declares omnipotence to pertain properly to the Father, and places its completeness and perfection in acting and discerning:

> [Note: [Col. 1059] Walter, bishop of Laon, attacks Abelard in almost the same manner in his letter to him, vol. II of the *Spicilegium*, p. 473.]

To the Son, as has already been said, he assigns wisdom, and defines it as not simply power, but a certain power in God—that is, only the power of discerning. Perhaps he fears to injure the Father if he gives the Son as much as the Father, and to one to whom he does not dare give entire power he grants half-power. What he says he illustrates with clear examples, maintaining that the power of discerning, which is the Son, is a certain power just as man is a certain animal and a bronze seal a certain bronze thing; and that the relation of the power of discerning to the power of acting and discerning—that is, of the Son to the Father—is that of man to animal and bronze seal to bronze. “For just as,” he says, “from the fact that something is a bronze seal it necessarily follows that it is bronze, [Col. 1060A] and from the fact that it is a human being, that it is an animal, but not conversely; so divine wisdom, which is the power of discerning, requires that it be divine power, but not conversely” (*Abelard’s Theology*, book II, p. 1083). What then? Do you wish, according to your comparison and after the pattern of the preceding cases, that from the fact that he is Son it should also follow that he is Father—that is, that whoever is Son is Father, although not conversely? If you say this, you are a heretic; if you do not say it, the comparison is pointless.

7. For why do you borrow this comparison by such a circuit from remote and less suitable things, assemble it with such labor, repeat it with such empty multiplication of words, and extol it with such praise, if it does not accomplish the purpose for which it is introduced—namely, that members may be correlated to members in fitting proportions? [Col. 1060B] Is this not your work, this your labor: to teach us through it the relation between Father and Son? Yet under your teaching we understand that animal is predicated when man is posited, but not conversely, according to the rule of your dialectic: when the genus is posited, the species is not thereby posited, but when the species is posited, the genus is. Therefore, since you refer the Father to genus and the Son to species, does not the rationale of the comparison require you similarly to show that when the Son is posited, the Father is posited, and that this is not reciprocal? Thus, just as whoever is human is necessarily an animal, but the proposition is not reversible, so too whoever is Son must necessarily be Father, and the proposition must equally not be reversible. But Catholic faith contradicts you in this, for it rejects both claims: that whoever is Son is Father, and that whoever is [Col. 1060C] Father is Son. For Father is undoubtedly other than Son, although the Father is not something other than the Son. Through *alius* (“another person”) and *aliud* (“another thing”), the piety of faith knows how carefully to distinguish between the properties of the persons and the indivisible unity of essence, and, holding the middle course, to proceed by the royal road: neither turning to the right by confusing the persons nor looking to the left by dividing the substance. If, however, by simple being you say that it truly follows that if there is a Son, there must necessarily be a Father, this does not help you, since the logic of relation necessarily requires reciprocity and the same truth to accompany the converse. This does not suit your adduced comparisons of genus and species, or of bronze and a bronze seal. For it is not as it is with simple being alone, of which it is most truly said: [Col. 1060D] if there is a Father, there is a Son; and if there is a Son, there is a Father. We can similarly construct a genuinely reciprocal consequence between man and animal, or between bronze seal and bronze. For although it is true to say, “If there is a human being, there is an animal,” the converse, “If there is an animal, there is a human being,” is not true. Likewise, if there is a bronze seal, it necessarily follows that there is bronze; but if there is bronze, it does not necessarily follow that there is a bronze seal. But let us now proceed to the remainder.

649

8. Thus, according to this man, we have omnipotence in the Father and a certain power in the Son. Let him tell us [Col. 1061A] what he thinks also concerning the Holy Spirit. “Benevolence itself,” he says, “which is signified by the name ‘Holy Spirit,’ is not power or wisdom in God” (*Abelard’s Theology*, book II, p. 1085). “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). Thus he ought to fall who walks in things great and wonderful beyond himself. You see, holy Father, what ladders—or rather, what precipices—this man has prepared for his ruin: omnipotence, half-power, no power. I shudder at the very hearing of it, and I think the shudder itself sufficient refutation. Nevertheless, I offer a testimony which occurs to me in this disturbance, to remove the injury done to the Holy Spirit. Isaiah reads: “Spirit of wisdom, Spirit of strength” (Isa. 11:2). By this, surely, this man’s audacity, if not [Col. 1061B] restrained, is nevertheless convicted. O boastful tongue! Grant that injury to the Son or Father may be forgiven you; but what of blasphemy against the Spirit? The angel of the Lord remains to cut you in two; for you have said, “The Holy Spirit is not power or wisdom in God.” Thus the foot of pride falls when it rushes in.

## CHAPTER IV. He refutes Abelard’s definition of faith, by which he says faith is an estimate or opinion

9. Nor is it surprising if a man who does not care what he says, rushing into the mysteries of faith, invades and tears apart with such irreverence the hidden treasures of piety, when he thinks neither piously nor faithfully about the piety of faith itself. For at the very threshold of his *Theology*—or rather his *Foolishology*—he defines faith as an estimate or opinion (*Theology*, [Col. 1061C] book I, pp. 977 and 1061). As though everyone were permitted in it to think and say whatever he pleased; or as though the mysteries of our faith hung uncertainly amid wandering and diverse opinions rather than subsisting in certain truth. If faith wavers, is not our hope empty? Our martyrs were therefore foolish, enduring such bitterness for uncertainties and, with no doubt amid uncertainty about the reward, entering through a hard and prolonged death into a long exile. But far be it from us to suppose that anything in our faith or hope hangs, as he thinks, on doubtful estimation; rather, all that is in it is supported by certain and solid truth, divinely commended through oracles and miracles, established and consecrated by the Virgin’s childbirth, the Redeemer’s blood, and the glory of his resurrection. These testimonies have been made exceedingly credible. And if anything further is needed, the Spirit himself finally bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God. How then does anyone dare call faith an estimate, unless he has not yet received this Spirit, or does not know the Gospel, or considers it a fable? “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain,” cries the Apostle (2 Tim. 1:12); and you hiss in my ear, “Faith is an estimate”? You babble to me of uncertainty where nothing is more certain. But Augustine says otherwise: “Faith,” he says, “is held in the heart of the person who has it, not by conjecture [Col. 1062A] or opinion, but by certain knowledge, with conscience bearing witness.” Far be it, then—far be it—that Christian faith should have these boundaries. Such estimates belong to the Academics, whose practice is to doubt everything and know nothing. But I go confidently with the judgment of the Teacher of the Gentiles, and I know that I shall not be put to shame. I confess that I like his definition of faith, although this man covertly attacks it as well. “Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1). “The substance,” he says, “of things hoped for”—not the empty fantasy of conjectures. You hear “substance.” You are not permitted in faith to suppose or dispute as you please, to wander here and there through vain opinions and byways of error. By the name “substance,” something certain and fixed is set before you; you are enclosed within definite boundaries and confined by definite limits. For faith is not estimation, but certainty.

10. But observe the rest. I omit his saying that the spirit [650] of the fear of the Lord was not in the Lord; that chaste fear of the Lord will not exist in the age to come; that after the consecration of bread and chalice, the remaining former accidents hang in the air; that demons’ suggestions in us occur through contact with stones and herbs, insofar as their cunning malice knows the various powers of these things to suit the stirring and kindling of diverse vices; that the Holy Spirit is the soul of the world; and that, according to Plato, the world is an animal so much more excellent as it has the Holy Spirit for a better soul. In striving hard to make Plato a Christian, [Col. 1062C] he proves himself a pagan. All these things, I say, and not a few other such trifles of his, I pass over. I come to graver matters—not because I shall answer all these things, for volumes would be needed; I speak of what cannot be passed over in silence.

## CHAPTER V. He charges Abelard with preferring his own opinions or dreams to the unanimous judgment of the Fathers, especially where he says that Christ was not incarnate in order to free humankind from Satan’s power
11. In a certain book of his *Sentences*, and likewise in a certain exposition of his Epistle to the Romans, I read that this rash investigator of majesty, at the very opening of his disputation on the mystery of our redemption, says that all ecclesiastical doctors hold one and the same opinion on this matter; and he states it, rejects it, and boasts that he has a better one. He is not afraid to transgress, against the precept of the Wise Man, the ancient boundaries which our fathers set up (Prov. 22:28).

> “It must be known,” he says, “that all our doctors after the Apostles agree in this: that the devil had dominion and power over man, and possessed him by right—namely because man, through the freedom of choice which he possessed, voluntarily consented to the devil. For they say that if someone conquers another, the conquered person is by right made the servant of the conqueror. Therefore,” he says, “as the doctors say, the Son of God was incarnate by this necessity, so that man, who could not otherwise be set free, might by the death of the innocent one be lawfully delivered from the devil’s yoke. But, as it seems to us,” he says, “the devil never had any right over man, except perhaps by God’s permission, like a jailer; nor did the Son of God assume flesh in order to free man.”

[Note: Col. 1061D. Abelard touches on this argument in Book II of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, first question; then, on pp. 553–554, he adds: “If anything is lacking to completeness, we reserve it for the treatment of our Theology.” But the published *Theology* of Abelard is mutilated. In it, at Col. 1062D, I do not find the words which Bernard shortly reports, although the irreverent statements against the Fathers here ascribed to Abelard are found almost verbatim in Book II of the *Theology*, p. 1118, where he treats of God’s power; and are stated explicitly in Abelard’s Chapter IX, above Col. 1437.]

What in these words should I judge more intolerable: the blasphemy or the arrogance? What more condemnable: the rashness or the impiety? Would it not be more just for a mouth uttering such things to be beaten with rods than refuted by arguments? Does not a man whose hand is against all men deservedly provoke every hand against himself? “All,” he says, “think thus—but I do not.” What then are you? What better thing do you offer? What subtler thing have you discovered? What more secret revelation do you boast has been given you, which has passed by so many saints and escaped so many wise persons? I suppose this man will set before us stolen waters and hidden bread.

12. Yet speak: say whatever it is that seems right to you and to no one else. Is it that the Son of God put on humanity not in order to free man? Certainly this seems right to no one except you; you may seem right wherever you are seen. For you received this neither from a wise man, nor from a prophet, nor from an apostle, nor finally from the Lord himself. The Teacher of the Gentiles received from the Lord what he also handed on to us (1 Cor. 11:23). The Teacher of all confesses that his teaching is not his own: “For,” he says, “I do not speak from myself” (John 7:16; 14:10). But you hand down to us something of your own, something received from no one. “He who speaks a lie speaks from his own resources” (John 8:44). Therefore let what is yours belong to you. I listen to prophets and apostles; I obey the Gospel—but not the Gospel according to Peter.

[Note: Col. 1063D. Abelard.]

Are you composing a new Gospel for us? The Church does not receive a fifth evangelist. What else do the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and apostolic men proclaim to us than what you alone deny: namely, that God became man in order to free man? And if an angel from heaven should preach another gospel to us, let him be accursed.
