13. But you do not accept the doctors who came after the Apostles—you, a man who have understood above all those who teach you. Indeed, you are not ashamed to say that all think against you, though they do not disagree among themselves. It would therefore be useless for me to set before you the faith and teaching of those whom you have already proscribed. I shall take you to the Prophets.

Speaking under the figure of Jerusalem to the people of his possession, not the prophet but the Lord in the prophet says: “I will save you and deliver you; do not fear” (Zeph. 3:16–17). You ask: from what power? For you do not want the devil to have, or to have had, power over man. I confess that neither do I wish it. Yet he does not lack it because you and I do not wish it. If you do not confess this, neither do you know it; but those redeemed by the Lord know it and say it—those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy. You too would by no means deny it, if you were not under the enemy’s hand. You cannot give thanks with the redeemed, since you are not redeemed. For if you were redeemed, you would acknowledge the Redeemer and would not deny redemption. Nor does one seek to be redeemed who does not know himself to be captive.

But those who knew cried to the Lord, and the Lord heard them and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. And so that you may understand who this enemy is: “Those whom he redeemed,” he says, “from the hand of the enemy, he gathered them from the regions” (Ps. 106:2, 6 [Vulgate]). But first recognize this gatherer. Caiaphas prophesies concerning him in the Gospel that Jesus would die for the nation; and the narrator continues: “Not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11:51–52). Where were they scattered? Into every region. Therefore, those whom he redeemed he gathered from the regions. He would not gather them unless he redeemed them. For they were not merely scattered, but also captive. He redeemed and gathered them; and he redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. He does not say, “of enemies,” but “of the enemy.” One enemy; many regions. For he gathered them not from one region but from regions—from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea (Ps. 106:3 [Vulgate]). Who is this one master so powerful that he ruled not one region but all? No other, I think, than he whom another prophet says “swallows up the river,” that is, the human race, “and does not wonder”; yet he is confident that the Jordan—that is, election itself—will flow into his mouth (Job 40:18 [Vulgate]). Blessed are those who so flow in as to flow out, who so enter as to depart.

14. But perhaps you do not yet believe the Prophets, who harmonize so completely concerning the devil’s power over man. Come with me also to the Apostles. You said, of course, that you do not agree with those who came after the Apostles. At least assent to the Apostles, if perhaps what one of them says about certain persons may happen to you: “Lest at any time,” he says, “God give them repentance for the acknowledgment of the truth, so that they may return to sobriety from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive at his will” (2 Tim. 2:25–26). It is Paul who asserts that men are held captive by the devil at his will. You hear “at his will,” and yet deny his power?

If you do not believe Paul either, come now to the Lord himself, so that perhaps you may hear and be still. He himself calls the devil “the prince of this world” (John 14:30), “the strong man armed” (Luke 11:21), and possessor of the vessels (Matt. 12:29); and do you say that he has no power over men? Unless you think that “courtyard” here means something other than the world, and “vessels” something other than human beings. But if the world was the devil’s courtyard, and human beings his vessels, how did he not rule over men?

The Lord also says to those seizing him: “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53). That power was not hidden from him who said: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his brightness” (Col. 1:13). Thus the Lord did not deny the devil’s power even over himself, any more than he denied Pilate’s power, Pilate being a member of the devil. For he says: “You would have no power over me at all unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). If this power, given from above, so raged against the green wood, how would it not dare to touch the dry? Nor, I think, will this man claim that a power given from above was unjust. Let him therefore learn that the devil had not only power over men, but just power; and consequently let him see that the Son of God came in the flesh precisely in order to free human beings.

Yet although we call the devil’s power just, we do not call his will just. Hence it was not the devil who invaded, nor man who deserved it, but the just Lord who handed him over. For a person is called just or unjust not because of power, but because of will. This, therefore, was a certain right of the devil over man: although not acquired lawfully but wickedly usurped, it was nevertheless justly permitted. Thus man was justly held captive; yet justice was in neither man nor devil, but in God.

## Chapter VI. In the work of human liberation, not mercy alone but justice also shines forth

15. Therefore man was justly condemned, but mercifully set free—yet so mercifully that a certain justice was not lacking even in the liberation itself. For this too belonged to the mercy of the liberator: that, as was fitting to the remedies of liberation, he should employ justice against the invader rather than power.

For what could man, a slave of sin and bound by the devil, do of himself to recover the justice once lost? Another’s justice was therefore assigned to him who lacked his own; and it is thus: the prince of this world came and found nothing in the Savior. Yet when he nevertheless laid hands upon the innocent one, he most justly lost those whom he held, because he who owed nothing to death, having endured the wrong of death, lawfully released the one who was liable both to the debt of death and to the devil’s dominion. By what justice, indeed, could man have demanded this a second time? For it was man who owed, and man who paid. “For if one died for all,” he says, “then all died” (2 Cor. 5:14): so that the satisfaction of one might be credited to all, just as that one bore the sins of all; and that no different person might be found to have committed the offence and another to have made satisfaction, because Christ, head and body, is one.

[Note: Col. 1065. That is, “offended” or “sinned,” as though *foras facere*, “to act outside,” that is, outside reason; from Cange’s Glossary and others.]

The head therefore made satisfaction for the members, Christ for his own body, when—according to Paul’s Gospel, by which Peter’s lie is convicted—having died for us, he made us alive together with himself, forgiving us all trespasses, blotting out the written decree that stood against us and was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross, stripping principalities and powers (Col. 2:13–14).

[Note: Col. 1065. Abelard.]

16. Would that I might be found among those spoils by which the hostile powers were despoiled, and be carried over with them into the Lord’s possession! If Laban, pursuing me, should accuse me of having departed secretly from him, let him hear that I secretly came to him, and for that reason departed secretly. A more hidden cause of sin subjected me to him; a more hidden rationale of justice withdrew me from him. Or if I was sold for nothing, shall I not be redeemed for nothing? If Assyria has falsely accused me without cause, it demands without cause a ground for my escape. And if it says, “Your Father has condemned you,” I shall answer, “But my brother has redeemed me.” Why should justice not come from another source, when guilt comes from another? One made me a sinner; another justifies me from sin—one in seed, the other in blood. Is sin in the seed of the sinner, but not justice in Christ’s blood?

“But,” he will say, “let justice belong to whom it belongs: what has it to do with you?” Granted. But let guilt likewise belong to whom it belongs: what has it to do with me? Shall the justice of the just man be upon him, but the wickedness of the wicked man not be upon him? It is not fitting that a son should bear his father’s iniquity and be excluded from his brother’s justice. Now, therefore, through a man came death, and through a man life. “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22), because I am not joined to the former in such a way as not also to be joined to the latter. If I belong to the former through flesh, I belong to the latter through faith; and if I have been infected from the former by original concupiscence, I have also been filled with Christ’s spiritual grace.

Why is more imputed to me from the transgressor? If there is generation, I set regeneration against it—except that this is spiritual and that carnal; nor does the principle of equity permit them to contend on equal terms. Rather, spirit must conquer flesh, and the cause whose nature is superior must be more effective; so that the second generation may profit more than the first harmed. Certainly sin has reached me, but grace too has reached me. And “the gift is not like the trespass. For judgment from one offence resulted in condemnation; but grace, from many offences, in justification” (Rom. 5:16). From the first man sin flowed forth; from highest heaven came forth grace. Both came from a parent—the former from the first, the latter from the highest. Earthly birth destroys me; and shall not heavenly generation, far more, preserve me? Nor do I fear that, having thus been snatched from the power of darkness, I shall be rejected by the Father of lights, since I have been freely justified in the blood of his Son. Surely, “it is God who justifies; who is he that condemns?” He will not condemn the just person who had mercy on the sinner.

I would call myself just—but by his justice. What justice is that? “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). Finally, he “was made for us righteousness from God the Father” (1 Cor. 1:30). Is the justice which was made mine not mine? If transmitted guilt is mine, why should forgiven justice not be mine? Indeed, justice given is safer for me than justice inborn. The latter has glory, but not before God; the former, because it is effective for salvation, has no ground for boasting except in the Lord. “Even if I were just,” he says, “I would not lift up my head” (Job 10:15), lest I receive the answer: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

## Chapter VII. He censures Abelard for impiously and rashly investigating and diminishing God’s mysteries

17. This is the righteousness of man in the blood of the Redeemer. The man of perdition, blowing scornfully upon it and mocking it, strives so far to empty it of force that he thinks and argues that all this—that the Lord of glory emptied himself, was made lower than the angels, was born of a woman, lived in the world, experienced the lowest things, suffered indignities, and finally returned to his own through the death of the cross—must be reduced to this alone: that by living and teaching he might give human beings a pattern of life, and by suffering and dying might set before them the goal of love.

So he taught righteousness but did not give it; he displayed love but did not pour it into us; and thus returned to his own? Is this, then, the whole of that great mystery of godliness: “manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, received up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16)? An incomparable teacher indeed, who, opening even the depths of God to himself and making them clear and accessible to whomever he wishes, by his falsehood renders the highest sacrament and mystery hidden from ages so plain and open to us that anyone, even an uncircumcised and unclean person, may pass lightly through it—as though God’s wisdom either did not know how, or neglected, to guard against what it itself forbade; as though it itself gave what is holy to dogs and pearls to swine.

But it is not so. For although it was manifested in the flesh, it was nevertheless justified in the Spirit, so that spiritual things may be compared with spiritual, and the natural man may not receive the things of the Spirit of God, and our faith may not rest in the wisdom of words but in the power of God. Hence the Savior says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). And the Apostle says: “Even if my Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who perish” (2 Cor. 4:3).

18. Finally, observe the man mocking the things of the Spirit of God because they seem folly to him; insulting the Apostle who speaks of God’s wisdom hidden in a mystery; attacking the Gospel and blaspheming the Lord. How much wiser it would be for him to deign to believe what he cannot comprehend, rather than daring to despise or trample underfoot a sacred and venerable mystery. It would take long to answer all his absurdities and calumnies, which he constructs against the divine counsel. Yet I shall bring forward a few, from which the rest may be judged.

> “Since Christ freed only the elect, how did the devil possess them, whether in this world or, still more, in the world to come, than he does now?”

[Note: Col. 1067D. These statements occur indeed in Abelard, Book II on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 550; but he proposes them as questions, not assertions, as also those which follow.]

We answer: on the contrary, because the devil possessed God’s elect—by whom, as the Apostle says, they were held captive at his will (2 Tim. 2:26)—a liberator was necessary for the fulfillment of God’s purpose concerning them. They had to be set free in this world, so that they might be free in the world to come.

He then adds:

> “Did the devil torment even that poor man who rested in Abraham’s bosom, just as he did the condemned rich man? Or did he have dominion even over Abraham himself and the other elect?”

No; but he would have had it, had they not been liberated by faith in the One to come. Thus it is written of Abraham himself: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6); and again: “Abraham rejoiced to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56 [the printed text reads John 18]). Therefore already then Christ’s blood was sprinkling even Lazarus, so that he would not feel the flames, because he too had believed in him who was to suffer. The same must be thought of all the elect of that time: they too were born, as we are, under the power of darkness because of original sin; but before they died they were delivered, and only in Christ’s blood.

For it is written:

> “The crowds that went before and those that followed cried out, saying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 21:9).

[Note: Col. 1067D. Abelard also adduces this passage for the same purpose, p. 555.]

Therefore Christ, coming in the flesh, was blessed by the crowds of the blessed, both before he came and afterward; although those who went before had not yet attained the full blessing, that prerogative being reserved, of course, for the time of grace.

## Chapter VIII. Why Christ undertook so grave and laborious a means of freeing us, when his will or command alone would have sufficed

19. Then, laboring to teach and persuade that the devil could not and ought not to claim any right over man except by God’s permission, and that God could lawfully reclaim his fugitive if he wished to show mercy, and could rescue him by a word alone without wronging the devil—as though anyone denied this—after much discussion he eventually adds:

> “What necessity, then, what reason, what need was there, when divine mercy could free man from sin by its command alone, that for our redemption the Son of God, having assumed flesh, should endure so many and such great fasts, reproaches, scourges, spitting, and finally the shameful and most bitter death of the cross, so that he might endure the gibbet with the wicked?”

[Note: Col. 1068D. These same words are found in Abelard at the same place, p. 552, but in interrogative form; although his solution which follows does not depart from this teaching. Bernard therefore recognized such questions as malicious.]

We answer: it was our necessity—the hard necessity of those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death. The work was equally ours, God’s own, and that of the holy angels: ours, that the yoke of our captivity might be removed; God’s, that the purpose of his will might be fulfilled; the angels’, that their number might be completed. The reason for this deed was the gracious condescension of its doer.

Who denies that other and still other means of our redemption, justification, and liberation were at the Almighty’s hand? Yet this does not prejudice the efficacy of the means which he chose out of many. And perhaps this one is preferable, by which in the land of forgetfulness, heaviness, and our fall we are more powerfully and vividly reminded, through the many and great burdens borne by the Restorer, of our fall. Besides, no human being knows, nor can fully know, what good for grace, what fitness for wisdom, what beauty for glory, what advantage for salvation the unfathomable depth of this venerable mystery contains in itself. Considering it, the prophet was terrified but did not penetrate it (Hab. 3:2, according to the Septuagint); and the Lord’s forerunner judged himself unworthy to penetrate it (John 1:27).

20. But though it is not permitted to search out the sacrament of the divine will, it is permitted to perceive the effect of the work and receive the fruit of its benefit. And what we are permitted to know we are not permitted to conceal: because “it is the glory of kings to conceal a word, and the glory of God to investigate a saying” (Prov. 25:27 [the note indicates that the Vulgate now reads this passage in the opposite sense]). This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance: “while we were still sinners, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:10). Where there is reconciliation, there is forgiveness of sins. For if, as Scripture says, “our sins separate between us and God” (Isa. 59:2), reconciliation does not exist while sin remains.

Where, then, is forgiveness of sins? “This cup,” he says, “is the new testament in my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:28; Luke 22:20). Therefore where reconciliation is, there is forgiveness of sins. And what is that except justification? Whether, then, it be reconciliation, forgiveness of sins, justification, redemption, or liberation from the devil’s bonds—by whom we were held captive at his will—we obtain it through the intervening death of the Only-Begotten, being freely justified in his blood. In him, as the same Apostle says, “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace” (Eph. 1:7).

“Why,” you ask, “through blood, when he could have done it through a word?” Ask him. I may know that it is so; I may not know why it is so. Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it, “Why have you formed me thus?”

21. But these things seem foolish to him; he cannot restrain his laughter. Hear his guffaws:

> “How does the Apostle say that we are justified or reconciled to God through the death of his Son, when God ought to have been all the more angered against humankind because human beings sinned more greatly by crucifying his Son than by transgressing his first command through the tasting of one fruit?”

[Note: Col. 1069D. All the matters here reported from Abelard are questions, pp. 552–553. Bernard rightly represents them as Abelard’s opinions, since in his solution Abelard does not dissolve them but appears to approve them. The theologians of Paris judge likewise at the beginning of Abelard’s works. Indeed, Abelard did not deny that this had been his thought, nor did he claim, as he often does in other cases, that it had been maliciously imputed to him; rather, he corrected it in his *Apology* by an opposing testimony, in these words: “I confess that the Son of God alone was incarnate in order to free us from the servitude of sin and the yoke of the devil, and by his death to open the entrance to the higher life.”]

As though, in one and the same event, the iniquity of the wicked could not displease God and the piety of the sufferer please him. And he says:

> “If Adam’s sin was so great that it could not be expiated except by Christ’s death, what expiation will there be for the homicide committed against Christ himself?”

We answer briefly: the very blood which they shed, and the intercession of him whom they killed.

He further adds:

> “Did the death of the innocent Son please God the Father so greatly that through it he was reconciled to us who, by sinning, committed the act on account of which the innocent Lord was killed? And unless this greatest sin had occurred, could he not have forgiven that much lighter sin?”

It was not the death, but the will of the one freely dying, that pleased God—the will which by that death blotted out death, brought salvation to effect, restored innocence, triumphed over principalities and powers, despoiled hell, enriched heaven, made peace between things in heaven and things on earth, and renewed all things. And because this death, so precious and voluntarily to be undertaken against sin, could nevertheless not take place except through sin, God was not delighted by the wickedness of criminals, but made good use of it; by death he condemned death, and through sin condemned sin.

And the greater their iniquity, the holier and more powerful was his will to save; so that, by the intervention of so great a power, that ancient sin, although great, must nevertheless yield to the sin committed against Christ, as the lesser to the greater. Yet this victory is not attributed to sin or sinners, but to him who made good use of sin, bore sinners steadfastly, and turned to the use of mercy whatever the cruelty of the impious dared against him.

22. The blood that was shed was abundant enough to forgive even the greatest sin by which it came to be shed; and thereby it left no doubt at all about the removal of that ancient sin, being the lighter one. Then this man says:

> “To whom, indeed, does it not seem cruel and unjust that someone should demand the blood of an innocent person as a price, or should in any way be pleased that an innocent person be killed—much less that God should have found the death of his Son so acceptable that through it he was reconciled to the whole world?”

God the Father did not demand the blood of his Son, but he accepted it when offered—not thirsting for blood, but for salvation, because salvation was in the blood. Salvation indeed, and not—as this man thinks and writes—a mere display of love. For he thus concludes all his calumnies and invectives, which he has vomited forth against God as impiously as ignorantly:

> “The whole purpose of God’s appearing in flesh was our formation by his word and example”—or, as he subsequently says, “our instruction”; “the whole purpose of his suffering and dying was the manifestation or commending of his love toward us.”

[Note: Col. 1070D. I find these statements, and those which follow, in sense in the solution on pp. 553 and 584, though not in the same words.]

## Chapter IX. Christ came into the world not only for our instruction but also for our liberation

23. But what good is it that he instructs us if he does not restore us? Or are we instructed in vain unless first the body of sin is destroyed in us, so that we may no longer serve sin? If all that Christ accomplished was a display of virtues, it remains to be said that Adam too harmed us merely by displaying sin; for the remedy was brought in accordance with the nature of the wound. “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). Therefore the one is as the other.

If the life which Christ gives is nothing but his instruction, then the death which Adam gave will likewise be nothing but his instruction: so that Adam formed human beings toward sin by his example, while Christ formed them by example and word toward living well and loving himself. Or, if we assent to the Christian faith rather than the Pelagian heresy, and confess that Adam’s sin—and through sin, death—was transmitted to us by generation, not instruction, we must also confess that righteousness—and through righteousness, life—has been restored to us by Christ, not through instruction but regeneration: “as through one offence condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one man’s righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:18).

And if this is so, how can he say that “the counsel and purpose of the incarnation was to illuminate the world with the light of his wisdom and kindle it to his love”? Where, then, is redemption? From Christ, as he deigns to confess, come illumination and a summons to love; but redemption and liberation—from whom?

24. Suppose that Christ’s coming benefits those who can conform themselves to him in life and return to him love in return. What of infants? What light of wisdom will he give to those scarcely yet catching the light of life? From what source will they be kindled [variant: “will ascend”] to love of God, when they do not yet know how to love even their mothers? Will Christ’s coming benefit them in nothing? Does it do nothing for those planted together with the likeness of his death through Baptism, because their age prevents them from knowing or loving Christ?

> “Our redemption,” he says, “is that supreme love in us through Christ’s passion.”

Therefore infants have no redemption, because they do not have that supreme love. Or, just as they do not have the means by which to love, do they likewise lack the means by which to perish, so that regeneration in Christ is unnecessary for them because generation from Adam has done them no harm? If this is his thought, he is foolish with Pelagius.

Whatever of these things he thinks, it is clear how greatly he begrudges the sacrament of human salvation; how greatly, so far as he can, he empties the dispensation of the profound mystery—he who attributes all salvation to devotion and nothing to regeneration; who locates the glory of our redemption and the fullness of salvation not in the power of the cross, not in the price of blood, but in the progress of our conduct. But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 6:14), in which are our salvation, life, and resurrection.

25. I behold three principal things in this work of our salvation: the pattern of humility, in which God emptied himself; the measure of love, which he extended unto death, even death on a cross; and the sacrament of redemption, by which he abolished the death that he endured. The first two without the last are as though one were painting on emptiness. The example of humility is indeed great and most necessary; the example of love great and worthy of all acceptance. But they have no foundation and consequently no stability if redemption is absent.

With all my strength I desire to follow humble Jesus; I desire, with the arms of responsive love, to embrace him who loved me and gave himself for me. But I must also eat the Passover Lamb. For unless I eat his flesh and drink his blood, I shall not have life in myself. To follow Jesus is one thing; to hold him is another; to eat him another. To follow is wholesome counsel; to hold and embrace is solemn joy; to eat is blessed life. For his flesh is truly food, and his blood is truly drink. He is the bread of God who came down from heaven and gives life to the world (John 6:56, 33). What stability can joy or counsel have without life? Surely no more than a painting without a solid ground. Therefore neither examples of humility nor tokens of love are anything apart from the sacrament of redemption.

26. These things, Lord Father, such as they are, you hold from the labor of your servant’s hands, against a few chapters of the new heresy. Even if you recognize nothing in them but my zeal, I have nevertheless satisfied my own conscience for the time being. Since there was nothing I could do regarding the injury to the faith that grieved me, I judged it worthwhile to warn the man whose weapons are mighty through God for the destruction of contrary assertions, for destroying every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and for bringing every understanding captive into obedience to Christ. There are also in his other writings many other, and no less evil, chapters, to which neither the brevity of time nor of a letter permits a reply. Yet I do not think it necessary, since they are so manifest that they are easily refuted by the common faith itself. Nevertheless, I collected some and sent them.

## [Col. 1073] Book of Saint Bernard, Abbot, on the Life and Deeds of Saint Malachy, Bishop of Ireland

[Note: Col. 1073. St Malachy died in the year 1148, on the second day of November.]

658. Preface to Abbot Congan.

[Col. 1073A]

1. It has always been worthwhile to describe the illustrious lives of the saints, so that they may serve as a mirror and example, and as a kind of seasoning for the life of humankind upon earth. For in this way they somehow live among us even after death, and summon and recall to true life many who, though living, are dead. But this is especially required now by the scarcity of holiness and by our age, plainly barren of great men. We feel that this poverty has prevailed over us so greatly that no one can doubt that the saying strikes us: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). And, as I suppose, he of whom it is written, “Want will go before his face” (Job 41:13), is either present or near at hand. Unless I am mistaken, that is Antichrist, whom hunger and barrenness of every good thing both precede and accompany. Whether, therefore, want is the messenger of one already present or the herald of one soon to come, it is plainly before our eyes.

I pass over the common crowd; I pass over the base multitude of the children of this age. I wish to raise my eyes to the very pillars of the Church. Show me one among those who seem appointed as a light to the nations, who smokes from his height no more than he burns. “And if the light that is in you,” he says, “is darkness, how great is that darkness!” (Matt. 6:23). Unless perhaps—you will not, I think, say so—they are shining who consider godliness a means of gain, who, in the inheritance of the Lord, seek not what belongs to the Lord but rather what belongs to themselves.

What do I say, “what belongs to themselves”? Let him who seeks and retains his own things be perfect and holy, provided that he keeps both heart and hand from the property of others. Yet let the man who thinks he has perhaps reached this point remember that the same degree of holiness is demanded even of a pagan. Are not soldiers commanded to be content, perhaps, with their own wages, that they may be saved? (Luke 3:14). It is a great thing indeed for a teacher of the Church if he is like one of the soldiers; or at least—according to the prophet’s reproach of them—if “as is the people, so is the priest” (Isa. 24:2)! O deformity! Shall he be reckoned supremely worthy because, falling from the highest rank, he barely clings to the lowest lest he be swallowed by the abyss? Yet how rare even such a man is among the clergy! Again, whom can you show me content with necessities and despising superfluities? Yet the Apostles prescribed a law for the successors of the Apostles: “Having food and clothing,” they say, “let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8). Where is this pattern? We see it in books, but not in men. Of the righteous man, however, you have: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36:31), not in a manuscript.

Nor is this the degree of perfection. The perfect person is ready to lack even necessities. But this is given freely. Would that a limit were set to superfluities! Would that we did not desire without end! But what? Perhaps you will find someone able to do this? That indeed is difficult; but consider what we have come to. We were looking for an excellent man, a deliverer of many; and behold, we struggle to find one who can save himself. The best man today is he who is not excessively bad.

2. Therefore, since “the saint has failed from the earth,” I think it not superfluous to bring forth into public notice from among those “purchased from the earth” Bishop Malachy, a man truly holy and, indeed, of our own times, of singular wisdom and virtue. He was a lamp burning and shining; yet it has not been extinguished but only moved aside. Who can justly be angry with me if I set it forward again? Indeed, the people of my own age, and every succeeding generation to come, ought not to be ungrateful to me if I recall by my pen one whom his condition has taken away; if I restore to the world one of whom the world was not worthy; if I preserve for human memory a man whose memory may be a blessing to all who deign to read; if, when I awaken a sleeping friend, the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land, saying: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Moreover, he is buried among us: this work therefore rests especially upon us. And what more? That holy man counted me among his particular friends, and to such a degree that I believe no one was second to me in this share of his favor. Nor is such intimacy with so great a saint without recompense for me: I have already received the first-fruits. He lay at the end—indeed, at the beginning—according to the saying, “When a man has been brought to completion, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18:6). I hastened to him, that the blessing of the dying man might come upon me. And he, though he could no longer move his other limbs, was strong enough to give a blessing: raising his holy hands over my head, he blessed me. I possess that blessing as an inheritance; and how could I be silent about him?

Finally, you, Abbot Congan, venerable brother and my dear friend, lay this charge upon me; and together with you—as you write from Ireland—that whole church of saints which is yours. I obey willingly, especially since you require not eloquence but narration. I shall endeavor to make it pure and clear: instructing the devout without burdening the fastidious. Certainly, the truth of the narrative is secure with me, having been communicated by you, who undoubtedly attest nothing other than what you yourselves have established with complete certainty.

## Chapter I. The childhood and youth of Saint Malachy

1. Our Malachy was born in Ireland among a barbarous people; there he was brought up, and there he was taught letters. Yet he drew nothing from his native barbarism, any more than the fish of the sea derive salt from their mother. How delightful it is that uncultivated barbarism produced for us so polished a citizen of the saints and member of God’s household! He who brings forth honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone did this.

His parents, indeed, were distinguished in rank and power, according to the standard of the great who are upon earth. But his mother, more noble in mind than in blood, took pains, at the very beginning of his ways, to make known to the little boy the paths of life, judging this of greater worth for him than the windy knowledge of secular letters. Yet he did not lack aptitude, beyond his years, for either. At school he was taught letters; at home, the fear of the Lord. By daily progress he satisfactorily answered both his teacher and his mother.

For from the beginning he received a good spirit, through which he was a teachable boy, very lovable, and wonderfully pleasing to all in every respect. Instead of milk he drank from his mother’s breast the waters of saving wisdom, and daily became wiser than himself. Shall I say wiser, or holier? If I say both, I shall not regret it, for I shall speak the truth. In morals he acted the old man while still a child in years, free from childish wantonness. And though this made him an object of reverence and amazement to all, he was not thereby found more presumptuous, as commonly happens; rather, he was more quiet and submissive in all gentleness. He was not impatient of instruction, did not avoid discipline, was not weary of reading, and finally did not desire games—the thing that age especially finds sweet and familiar.

He advanced beyond all his contemporaries in the learning suited to his age. But in moral discipline and progress in virtues he soon shone above all who taught him—not so much through his mother as through the anointing that was his teacher. Under its prompting he diligently exercised himself also in divine matters: seeking solitude, anticipating the watches, meditating upon the law, taking food more sparingly, and praying more frequently. Because he neither had leisure to frequent church on account of his studies nor wished to do so openly through modesty, wherever he could do it secretly he lifted pure hands to heaven. Even then he was careful to avoid the poison of virtues: vain glory.

2. Near the city in which the boy studied was a village to which his teacher was accustomed often to go, with Malachy alone as companion. While they were both travelling there together, Malachy himself, as he later related, would draw back his foot, stop his pace, and, standing behind his teacher without the latter’s noticing, stretch his hands to heaven and swiftly, as it were, shoot forth a prayer. Then, concealing this, he again followed his teacher. By such a pious theft the boy often deceived at once his companion and teacher.

It would be impossible to tell all the things which adorned his beginnings with the appearance of a good disposition; we must hasten to greater and more useful matters. Yet I shall mention one further incident which, in my judgment, supplied in the boy a mark not only of a good but even of a great hope. Once stirred by the reputation of a certain teacher—for he was famous in the disciplines called liberal—he went to him out of a desire to learn. For, having now reached the end of childhood, he was eager for those studies. But upon entering the house, he saw the man playing with an awl and repeatedly tracing lines upon the wall in some strange and conspicuous fashion. The boy, offended merely by the sight, since it smelled of frivolity, recoiled from him, and thereafter did not care even to see him. Thus, though exceedingly studious of letters, as a lover of virtue he despised them for the sake of what was honorable.

By such a prelude the boy was being prepared for the conflict awaiting him in stronger age; and already he himself challenged the adversary. Such, indeed, was Malachy’s childhood. His youth, moreover, he passed with similar simplicity and purity, except that as his age increased, wisdom and grace before God and men increased with it.

3. From this point—that is, from the beginning of his youth—it began to appear more openly what was in the man, and that the grace of God in him was not idle. For the diligent young man, seeing how “the world lies in the evil one” (John 5:19), and considering what manner of spirit he had received, said within himself:

> “This is not the spirit of this world. What has this spirit to do with that world? They have no fellowship with one another, any more than light has with darkness. Mine is from God, and I know what has been given to me in it. From it I have, for the present, innocence of life; from it the glory of continence; from it hunger for righteousness; from it also that glory of mine which is all the safer because it is more hidden—the testimony of my conscience. None of these things is safe for me under the prince of the world.
>
> “Moreover, I have this treasure in an earthen vessel. I must fear lest it strike against something and be broken, and the oil of gladness which I bear be poured out. And indeed it is exceedingly difficult not to strike against the rocks and cliffs of this crooked and winding road and life. Shall I in one moment lose together all the blessings of sweetness with which I have been anticipated from the beginning?
>
> “Rather I shall surrender both them and myself to him from whom they come; for I too am his. I shall lose my very soul for a time, lest I lose it eternally. And what I am, and all that I have—where are they equally safe for me except in the hand of their Author? Who is so solicitous to preserve, so powerful to retain, so faithful to restore? He will preserve safely and restore at the proper time. Without reservation I give myself to serve him with his own gifts. Nothing of all that I expend upon the work of mercy can perish for me. Perhaps I may even hope for something more. He who gives freely is accustomed to repay with interest. So it is. He will even heap up and multiply virtue in my soul.”

These things he thought and did, knowing that the thoughts of men are vain without action.

## Chapter II. His apprenticeship in the religious life

4. There was in the city of Armagh—the very city in which Malachy was reared—a man who was holy and of an exceedingly austere life, an unrelenting chastiser of his own body, possessing a cell beside the church. There he lived, serving God with fasts and prayers day and night. To this man Malachy went, to receive from him a pattern of life, from one who had condemned himself while alive to such a burial.

Observe his humility. From his earliest age, in the holy art, he had had God as teacher—of this there is no doubt—and behold, the man meek and humble of heart became again the disciple of a man. If we did not know it before, by this alone he proved it to us. Let those read this who try to teach what they have not learned, who heap up disciples for themselves though they have never been disciples, blind leaders of the blind. Malachy, taught by God, nevertheless sought a human teacher—and did so prudently and wisely.

What comparable example, I ask, could he offer, in which he could equally give and receive proof of his progress? If the example of Malachy means little to them, let them attend to Paul’s practice. Did he not judge that his Gospel, which he had received not from man but from Christ, should nevertheless be compared with men, lest perhaps he should run, or have run, in vain? (Gal. 1–2). Where he was not secure, neither am I. Whoever thinks that he knows this should take care lest his security be not security so much as rashness. But these matters belong to another time.

5. Now news of what had happened spread through the city, and everyone was stirred by the unexpected novelty. All were astonished and admired his virtue, all the more because it was less customary among a savage people. You could then see the thoughts of many hearts revealed. Most, judging the deed by human feeling, mourned and grieved that a youth beloved and cherished by all had bound himself to such harsh labors. Others, suspecting youthful fickleness because of his age, despaired of his perseverance and feared a fall. Some blamed rashness, were angry with him, and murmured because he had inconsiderately undertaken a difficult task beyond his age and strength.

But he did nothing without counsel. For he had counsel from the Prophet, who says: “It is good for a man if he has borne the yoke from his youth,” and adds: “He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has lifted himself above himself” (Lam. 3:27–28). The young man sat at the feet of Imar—for that was the man’s name—and either learned obedience or showed that he had learned it. He sat quietly, gently, humbly. He sat and was silent, knowing, according to the prophet, that “silence is the cultivation of righteousness” (Isa. 32:17). He sat as one persevering; he was silent as one modest, except that through this very silence he spoke in God’s ears with holy David: “I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your justifications” (Ps. 118:141).

Meanwhile he sat alone, because he was without companion and without example. Who before Malachy would even have thought of attempting that most strict purpose of life? It was indeed regarded by all as marvelous, not imitable. Malachy persuaded men that it was imitable, merely by sitting and keeping silent. Within a few days he had no few imitators, drawn by his example. Thus he who first sat alone, the only son of his father, now became one among many; from an only-begotten son he became firstborn among many brethren. And as he was foremost in conduct, so he was more exalted in conduct; having come before all, he shone, in everyone’s judgment, above all in virtue. He was judged worthy by both bishop and teacher to be promoted to the rank of deacon. And they compelled him.

## Chapter III. Initiated into orders, he performs the bishop’s duties

6. From this point the Levite of the Lord publicly girded himself for every work of piety, but especially for matters in which some wrong appeared. Thus he took greatest care in burying poor people who had died, because this seemed to him to savor no less of humility than of humanity. Nor did temptation fail our new Tobias, revived through a woman—indeed, through the serpent by means of a woman. His sister, horrified at what seemed to her the indignity of the office, said: “What are you doing, madman? Let the dead bury their own dead.” And every day she reproached him with this and pressed it upon him.

But the woman was answered with folly according to her folly: “Wretched woman, you have the voice of chaste speech, but you do not know virtue.” Thus he held devotedly and exercised tirelessly the ministry to which he had been compelled to come. Hence they judged that the priestly office also ought to be laid upon him, and it was done. When he was ordained priest, he was about twenty-five years old.

If in either of his ordinations something appears to have occurred contrary to the form of the canons—as indeed it seems to have occurred, since he received the Levitical ministry before his twenty-fifth year and the dignity of the priesthood before his thirtieth—

> **[Note: Col. 1077D]** It was provided in the Councils of Neocaesarea, Agde (506), Arles IV, and others that a man should not be made a priest before thirty years of age. Canon 17 of Agde: “Let none of the metropolitans presume to ordain a priest or bishop before thirty years of age—that is, before they have reached the age of a complete man—or deacons before twenty-five,” etc. This is the reading in Bochellus; in Sirmond the passage concerning deacons, to which Bernard here refers, is absent. In Bernard’s time this law was still in force, as appears from the following words. Bishops nevertheless often granted dispensations, especially for devout men.

—this should certainly be attributed both to the zeal of the ordainer and to the merits of the ordained. But I advise neither that this be reproved in a saint nor that it be presumed upon by one who is not a saint.

Nor was the bishop—

> **[Note: Col. 1078D]** Namely Celsus; see below, no. 19.

—content even with this: he entrusted his own duties to Malachy, that he might sow holy seed among an unholy people and give to a rude population, living without law, the law of life and discipline. Malachy received the commission with complete eagerness, being fervent in spirit: he did not bury his talents, but desired gain. And behold, with the hoe of his tongue he began to root up, overthrow, and scatter, daily making crooked things straight and rough places into level ways. He rejoiced like a giant to run everywhere. You would have called him a burning fire consuming the brambles of sins. You would have called him an axe or hatchet felling evil plantations: uprooting barbarous customs and planting ecclesiastical ones. He abolished all inveterate superstitions—for they were not few—and every kind of wickedness, wherever he found it introduced by evil angels.

7. Whatever he found disordered, unseemly, or distorted, his eye did not spare; but as hail knocks unripe figs from fig trees and the wind scatters dust from the face of the earth, so he strove with all his strength to drive such things wholly from before him and wipe them out from his people. In place of all these things, as an excellent lawgiver, he gave heavenly laws: laws full of justice, moderation, and honor. He also established in all the churches apostolic ordinances, decrees of the holy Fathers, and especially the customs of the holy Roman Church.

Hence it is that even today, in those churches, the canonical hours are sung and psalms chanted according to the custom of the whole world. For this had not been done at all before, not even in the city. Malachy himself had learned singing in his youth, and in his monastery he promptly caused singing to be introduced, when they did not yet know, or wish, to sing either in the city or throughout the bishopric. He also newly instituted the most salutary practice of confession, the sacrament of confirmation, and the contracting of marriages—all things that they either did not know or neglected. Let these examples suffice regarding these matters. For throughout the course of the history, in the interest of brevity, we omit very many things.

## Chapter IV. He attaches himself to Bishop Malch in order to be more fully instructed

8. Since he had the greatest zeal and concern for the worship of divine things and reverence for the sacraments, lest perhaps he should establish or teach anything concerning these contrary to the rite of the universal Church, he resolved to go to Bishop Malch [variant: Malach], that the latter might instruct him more fully in everything. This was an old man full of days and virtues, and the wisdom of God was in him. Irish by birth, he had lived in England in monastic habit and profession in the monastery of Winchester. From there he was taken to be bishop in the city of Lismore in Munster, itself more noble than the other cities of that kingdom. There such grace was bestowed upon him from above that he shone not only in life and doctrine but also in signs.

I shall set down two of these by way of example, that all may know what kind of teacher Malachy had in the knowledge of the saints. He healed, during confirmation with holy unction, a boy whose mind was disordered, one of those called lunatics. This was so well known and certain that he immediately made the boy porter of his house; and the boy lived unharmed in that office until manhood. He restored hearing to a deaf man; and in this case the man confessed the following marvel: when the saint had inserted his fingers into both ears from either side, he felt two little pigs, as it were, come out of them.

As his fame spread by these and similar deeds, he gained a great name, so that Scots and Irish flocked to him and all revered him as the one father of all. Therefore Malachy, having received Father Imar’s blessing and having been sent by the bishop, came prosperously to him and was kindly received by the old man. He remained with him for several years, so that by this delay of time he might drink more fully from an aged breast, knowing what is written: “Wisdom is in the aged” (Job 12:12).

Nor do I think that this too was without purpose: the great Provider of all things willed that his servant Malachy should become known to everyone in so famous a place, since he was to benefit everyone. For he could not fail to be pleasing to those who came to know him. Meanwhile one event occurred through which he made manifest to men, at least in some measure, what was known to God concerning him.

9. A quarrel arose between the king of Munster—which is the southern part of Ireland—and his brother; and the brother gained the upper hand. The king—

> **[Note: Col. 1079D]** Cormac; see below, no. 18.

—was driven from his kingdom and fled to Bishop Malch. Yet he did not do so that he might recover the kingdom by the bishop’s aid. Rather, the devout prince gave place to wrath and turned necessity into virtue, choosing to lead a private life. When the bishop prepared to receive the king with due honor, he refused, saying that he preferred to be like one of the poor brethren attached to the bishop: he would lay aside royal splendor and be content with their common poverty; he would await the Lord’s will rather than recover the kingdom by force; and he did not wish, for the sake of his earthly honor, to shed human blood that might cry against him from the ground to God.

On hearing this, the bishop rejoiced; admiring the man’s devotion, he granted his request. Why say more? A poor house was assigned to the king as a dwelling, and Malachy was given to him as teacher; his food was bread with salt and water. Yet the presence, life, and teaching of Malachy were sufficient delicacies for the king, so that he said to him: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103). Furthermore, every night he drenched his bed with tears; and by a daily bath in cold water he extinguished in his flesh the lust that burned improperly. Praying, the king said with the King: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Ps. 24:18).

God did not remove his prayer or his mercy from him. His prayer was heard, though otherwise than he himself intended. For he was concerned for his soul; but God, the avenger of innocence, wishing to show men that “there is a remnant for the peaceable man,” meanwhile prepared to execute judgment for one suffering wrong—a thing which he did not at all expect. God stirred the spirit of a neighboring king; for Ireland is not one kingdom but divided into several. Seeing what had happened, this king was filled with zeal. On the one hand he was indignant at the freedom of the robbers and the insolence of the proud; on the other, he pitied the desolation of the kingdom and the king’s humiliation. He came down to the poor man’s little cell and urged him to return, but did not persuade him. Still he persisted: he promised aid, urged him not to doubt success, promised that God would be present, against whom none of his adversaries could stand. He also set before him the oppression of the poor and the devastation of his country; but he made no progress.

10. Yet when the bishop’s command and Malachy’s counsel were added—upon whom the king wholly depended—he at last, though reluctantly, consented. King followed king; and according to the word of the king, as the will had been in heaven, the robbers were driven out with complete ease, and the man was restored to his own people amid their rejoicing and reinstated in his kingdom.

From that time the king loved and always revered Malachy; and he did so more devotedly because he had more fully discovered in the holy man what was worthy of reverence and love. For one who had experienced such intimacy with him in adversity could not remain ignorant of his holiness. Therefore in prosperity he honored him with enduring friendship and devout services, gladly listened to him, and, having heard him, did many things. But enough of this. Yet I do not think it happened by chance that the Lord thus already magnified him in the sight of kings, but because he was a chosen vessel, destined to bear God’s name before kings and princes.

## Chapter V. He aids his deceased sister by the offering of the sacrifice

11. Meanwhile that sister of his, of whom we have spoken, died. Nor should the visions he saw concerning her be passed over. The saint had abhorred her fleshly life, and with such zeal that he had vowed not to see her while she lived in the flesh. But when she was released from the flesh, the vow was released, and he began to see in the spirit one whom he had not wished to see in the body.

One night, in a dream, he heard a voice telling him that his sister stood outside in the courtyard and that, behold, for thirty whole days she had tasted nothing. When he awoke, he quickly understood from hunger for what food she was wasting away. Carefully examining the number of days he had heard, he discovered that it was precisely the time since he had offered for her the living Bread from heaven. Then he who hated not his sister’s soul but her sin resumed the charitable act which he had interrupted—and not in vain.

Not long afterward he saw her reach the threshold of the church, though she was not yet able to enter; she also appeared in a dark garment. As he continued his efforts, taking care that she should not lack on any day the customary offering, he saw her a second time, clothed in a somewhat whitish garment. She had indeed been admitted within the church, but was not permitted to touch the altar. Finally, the third time, he saw her joined to the company of those in white, and in a white garment.

You see, reader, how great is the power of the persistent prayer of the righteous. Truly, “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.” Does not Malachy’s prayer seem to you in some fashion to have played the role of a breaker-in at the gates of heaven, when a sinful woman obtained by her brother’s arms what was denied to her own merits? This violence, good Jesus, you who endure it also cause it: mighty and merciful to save, showing mercy and power in your arm, and preserving in your Sacrament those saints who are on the earth until the consummation of the age. This Sacrament indeed has power to consume sins, defeat opposing powers, and bring into heaven those returning from earth.

## Chapter VI. He restores the ruined monastery of Bangor

12. Thus in the region of Lismore the Lord was preparing his beloved Malachy for the glory of his name. But those who had sent him, no longer able to bear his absence, summoned him back by letters. When he returned to his own people, now more fully instructed in all that was necessary, behold: there was a work prepared and reserved by God for Malachy.

A rich and powerful man, who held the place of Bangor and its possessions, inspired by God, immediately gave into Malachy’s hand all that he had, and himself as well. He was Malachy’s uncle. But the kinship of the spirit mattered more to Malachy than that of the flesh. The prince also gave him the very place of Bangor—

> **[Note: Col. 1081D–1082D]** Bangor is called *Banchor* in the Acts of Saint Columbanus. It was situated in the province of Ulster in Ireland and must be distinguished from another monastery of the same name, situated in Wales, a region of Britain.

—from which he was named, to build a monastery there, or rather to rebuild it. For it had formerly been most renowned under its first father, Congell, producing many thousands of monks and serving as the head of many monasteries. It was a place truly holy and fruitful in saints, bearing fruit for God in the greatest abundance, so that one of the sons of that holy congregation, named Luan, is said alone to have founded a hundred monasteries. I mention this so that the reader may infer from this single case how vast the remainder of the multitude was.

Indeed, its offspring filled Ireland and Scotland so completely that the following verses of David seem especially to have been sung beforehand of those times:

> “You visited the earth and made it drunk;  
> you multiplied to enrich it.  
> The river of God is filled with waters;  
> you prepared their food, for such is its preparation.  
> Make its streams drunk; multiply its offspring;  
> in its showers it shall rejoice, springing forth.”  
> (Ps. 64:10–11)

And so likewise the verses that follow. Nor did those swarms of saints pour themselves out, as if in a flood, only into the regions mentioned above, but into foreign regions as well. From them Saint Columbanus came to these regions of ours in Gaul and built the monastery of Luxeuil, becoming there a great nation. It is said to have become so great that, as choirs relieved one another in succession, the divine offices continued without interruption, so that not even a moment of day or night was free from praises.

13. Let this be said concerning the ancient glory of the monastery of Bangor. Once destroyed by pirates, Malachy embraced it—because of the outstanding dignity of its former greatness—as though he were going to replant a kind of paradise, and because many bodies of saints slept there. For, to say nothing of those buried in peace, it is reported that nine hundred were slain together by pirates on a single day.

The place possessed great estates. But Malachy, content with the holy site alone, yielded all its possessions and lands to another. For from the time when the monastery was destroyed, there had never been lacking someone to hold it together with its possessions. Men were even appointed by election and called abbots, preserving in name, though not in reality, what had formerly existed. Although many advised him not to alienate the possessions but to retain everything together for himself, this lover of poverty did not consent. Rather, retaining the place for himself and his own, as stated above, he caused someone to be elected according to custom to hold the estates. Perhaps it would have been wiser, as later appeared, had he retained the whole undivided; but he looked more to his humility than to peace.

14. Therefore, at Father Imar’s command, he took with him about ten brothers and came to the place, where he began to build. One day, while he was cutting with an axe, one of the workmen accidentally, as Malachy swung the axe into the air, carelessly stepped into the place toward which the blow was directed. The axe fell upon the man’s spine with as much force as Malachy had been able to strike. The man fell. Everyone ran up, thinking either that he had been struck to death or was dead. His tunic, indeed, was torn from top to bottom; but the man himself was found unharmed, with the skin only so slightly and superficially grazed that scarcely a trace appeared on its surface. The man whom the axe had struck down stood uninjured, while those around him looked on in amazement.

As a result they became more cheerful and afterward more ready for the work. This was the beginning of Malachy’s miracles. The oratory was completed within a few days: made of smoothed timber, suitably and solidly joined together, a Scottish work and quite beautiful. From that time God is served there as in ancient days, with similar devotion, though not with equal numbers.

Malachy presided over that place for some time, Father Imar having so appointed him. He himself was the ruler; he himself was the rule of the brothers. They read in his life how they should live, and he himself went before them in righteousness and holiness before God. Except that, beyond the common observances, he did many things individually, in which he outstripped all; and no one among the others could follow him in such arduous practices.

At that time and in that place, a certain man fell ill. The devil stood beside him and, speaking openly, urged him never to believe Malachy’s counsels, but, should Malachy enter, to attack and kill him with a knife. Those attending the sick man learned this from the man himself and carried word to Malachy in warning. But Malachy, taking up his customary weapons of prayer, fearlessly attacked the enemy and drove away both the illness and the demon.

The man’s name was Malch. He is the brother according to the flesh of our Christian, abbot of Mellifont. Both are still alive, now more truly brothers in spirit. For when Malch was delivered, he immediately showed himself not ungrateful: in that same place he was converted to the Lord and changed both habit and disposition. The brothers recognized that the evil one envied their good works; and they were edified, becoming thereafter more watchful.

## Chapter VII. He heals a man suffering from dysentery

15. A cleric named Michael, suffering desperately from dysentery, was healed in the same place when Malachy sent him something from his table. A second time he healed the same man, who had been seized by a most grievous illness, both in body and mind. For Michael immediately attached himself to God and to Malachy, God’s servant, fearing that something worse might happen to him if he were again found ungrateful for so great a benefit and miracle.

Now, as we have heard, he presides over a certain monastery situated in the regions of Scotland; and this is the last of all those founded by Malachy. Because of such deeds, Malachy’s reputation and community increased daily, and his name became great within and without—though not greater than the reality. For, having become a bishop, he remained there because the place was near the city.

## Chapter VIII. He accepts the bishopric of Connor, though unwillingly
16. At that time the episcopal see was vacant, and had long been vacant, because Malachy had refused his consent, although they had elected him. Yet, as they persisted, he at last yielded [Col. 1084B], when the command of his master, no less than that of the metropolitan, was added to compel him. In about the thirtieth year of his life, Malachy was consecrated bishop and installed at Connor—for that is the name of the city. But when he began to act in accordance with his office, the man of God then understood that he had been sent not to men but to beasts. Nowhere, even amid however great barbarism, had he yet encountered such people; nowhere had he found persons so insolent in character, so savage in their customs, so impious toward the faith, so barbarous toward the laws, so stiff-necked under discipline, so foul in life. Christians in name, pagans in fact. There was no giving of tithes or firstfruits; no contracting of lawful marriages; no making of confessions; nor could anyone at all be found either to request or to impose penances. There were very few ministers of the altar [Col. 1084C]. But what need was there of more, when even this small number was almost idle among the laity? They had nothing to reap from their offices among so wicked a people. For in the churches neither the voice of a preacher nor that of a singer was heard. What was the athlete of the Lord to do? He must either yield shamefully or fight at peril. But, knowing himself to be a shepherd and not a hireling, he chose to stand rather than flee, ready, if need were, to give his life for the sheep. And although all were wolves and there were no sheep, the fearless shepherd stood among the wolves, ingenious in every way as to how he might make sheep out of wolves. He exhorted publicly, rebuked privately, wept for individuals; he approached them now sternly, now gently, according as he saw expedient for each [Col. 1084D]. For those among whom he had made less progress by these means, he offered a contrite and humbled heart on their behalf. How often did he spend entire nights awake, stretching out his hands in prayer! And when they would not come to church, he met them unwillingly in streets and lanes; going about the city, he searched eagerly for someone whom he might win for Christ.

17. Nor did he less frequently traverse the countryside and towns outside, accompanied by that holy company of his disciples, who were never absent from his side. He went and distributed—even to the ungrateful—the measure of heavenly wheat. He did not ride a horse, but went on foot, proving himself in this also an apostolic man. Good Jesus! How much your warrior suffered for your name at the hands of wicked children! How much he endured from those very persons to whom and for whom [Col. 1085A] he spoke good things to you! Who can worthily express amid how many troubles he was harassed, with what insults he was assailed, by what injuries he was provoked, how often worn down by hunger, how often afflicted by cold and nakedness? Yet, with those who hated peace, he was peaceful, nevertheless pressing the matter in season and out of season. When blasphemed, he entreated; when wronged, he opposed the shield of patience and overcame evil with good. Why should he not have overcome? He persevered in knocking, and, according to the promise, at last it was opened to him that knocked (Luke 11:9). How could what Truth had foretold would follow fail to follow? The right hand of the Lord wrought mightily, because the mouth of the Lord spoke truth. Hardness gave way; barbarism was quieted; and the provoking house gradually began to soften, gradually to admit correction and receive discipline. [Col. 1085B] Barbarous laws disappeared from among them, Roman laws were introduced; ecclesiastical customs were everywhere received and their opposites rejected; churches were rebuilt, and clergy appointed in them. The solemn rites of the sacraments were duly celebrated; confessions were made; the people gathered at church; concubinage was dignified by the public celebration of marriages. Finally, all things were so changed for the better that today the word spoken by the Lord through the prophet suits that people: “Those who were not my people are now my people” (Hosea 2:24).

## CHAPTER IX. He builds the monastery of Ibrac

18. Some years later, it happened that the city was destroyed by the king of the northern part of Ireland, because “from the north every evil is opened” (Jeremiah 1:14). And perhaps that evil was good for those who used it well. For who knows whether God intended, by such a scourge, to wipe out the ancient evils of his people? Compelled by this necessity, Malachy also departed with the crowd of his disciples. Nor was his departure idle. On this occasion the monastery of Ibrac was built, Malachy going there with his one hundred and thirty [alternatively, twenty] brethren. There King Cormac met him. This was the man who, long before, when driven from his kingdom, had received under Malachy’s care consolation from the mercy of God. That place lay within his kingdom. The king rejoiced at seeing Malachy, placing himself and all that he had at Malachy’s disposal, and at the disposal of those with him, as one neither ungrateful for nor forgetful of the benefit received. Many animals were immediately brought for the brethren’s use, and much besides in gold and silver was bestowed, with royal generosity, for the expenses of the buildings [Col. 1085D]. The king himself also diligently and helpfully went in and out with them: a king in dress, but in spirit Malachy’s disciple. And the Lord blessed that place for Malachy’s sake. In a short time it became great in resources, possessions, and persons. There, as though beginning anew, the bishop and master himself bore more than others the rule and discipline which he imposed on others. In his turn in the order, he served in the kitchen; he ministered to the brethren as they reclined at table. Among the brethren succeeding one another in singing or reading in church, he did not allow himself to be passed over, but energetically fulfilled his own duty in his proper place, as one of them. He showed himself not merely a participant in holy poverty, but its leader [Col. 1086A], being above all others its more abundant imitator.

## CHAPTER X. He becomes archbishop, or primate, of Ireland

19. While these things were happening, Archbishop Celsus fell ill. He was the one who had ordained Malachy deacon, priest, and bishop. Knowing that he would die, he made something like a testament: Malachy was to succeed him, because no one else seemed more worthy to hold the episcopal office in the chief see. He laid this charge upon those present, sent it to those absent, and especially commanded it, by the authority of Saint Patrick, to the two kings of Munster and the leading men of the land. Because of the reverence and honor due to Patrick, as apostle of that people, who had converted the whole country to the faith, that see—in which he had presided while living and rests after death—has from the beginning been held in such veneration by all that not only bishops, priests, and clerics, but even the whole body of kings and princes, is subject to the metropolitan in every obedience, and he alone presides over all [Col. 1086B].

But through the devilish ambition of certain powerful men, a most evil custom had grown up: the holy see was to be held by hereditary succession. They would permit no one to become bishop except one from their own tribe and family. Nor had that execrable succession advanced only a little: by then almost fifteen generations had passed in this iniquity. The evil and adulterous generation had so firmly established for itself this perverse claim—indeed, this outrage deserving every death—that, although clerics of that blood sometimes failed [Col. 1086C], bishops never did. In fact, before Celsus there had already been eight married men, without orders, though educated. From this came that dissolution of ecclesiastical discipline throughout all Ireland, mentioned above; that weakening of correction; that emptying of religion. From this came everywhere, in place of Christian gentleness, a cruel barbarism introduced—or rather, a kind of paganism brought in under the Christian name. For, a thing unheard of from the very beginning of Christianity, bishops were changed and multiplied without order or reason at the metropolitan’s pleasure, so that one bishopric was not content with one bishop, but nearly every church had its own bishop [Col. 1086D]. Nor is this surprising: for how could the members be healthy when the head was so diseased?

20. Grieving deeply over these and similar evils of his people—for he was a good and God-fearing man—Celsus took every means to secure Malachy as his successor, trusting that through him the badly rooted succession could be uprooted. Malachy was beloved by all, admired by all, and the Lord was with him. Nor was Celsus disappointed in his hope. When he died, Malachy was appointed in his place—yet not at once, nor easily. For behold, from the wicked seed came one to occupy the place, named Maurice. For five years, relying on secular power, he oppressed the Church, not as a bishop but as a tyrant. The wishes of the devout, however, were more inclined toward Malachy. They accordingly urged him to undertake the burden according to Celsus’s ordinance. But he, who avoided every high position no differently than his own downfall, thought he had found a good occasion for excuse: at that time his entrance could not be peaceful. All pressed him toward so holy a work and urged him on—especially two bishops, Malchus and Gilbert [Col. 1087A]. The former was the elder of Lismore mentioned above (ch. 4); the latter, they say, had first fulfilled the apostolic legation of the Holy See throughout all Ireland. When three years had now passed during this usurpation by Maurice and Malachy’s forbearance, they could no longer endure the Church’s adultery and Christ’s disgrace. They summoned the bishops and princes of the land and, with one mind, came to Malachy ready to use force.

At first he refused, alleging the difficulty of the undertaking: the number, strength, and ambition of that noble lineage. It was too much for him, a poor man, to set himself against so many, so great, such men, so deeply rooted—men who had possessed the sanctuary of God as an inheritance for almost two hundred years and had even now seized it in advance. They could not be uprooted, not even by the deaths of men. It was not his concern that human blood should be shed on his account. Finally, he was joined to another bride, whom he was not permitted to leave [Col. 1087B].

21. But as they, on the contrary, continued to press him and cry that the word had gone forth from the Lord; as they commanded him with all authority to undertake the burden and threatened him with anathema, he said: “You are leading me to death; yet I obey in the hope of martyrdom, upon this condition: if, according to your faith, the matter turns to the better and God vindicates his inheritance from those who plunder it, then at last, when all is accomplished and the Church has peace, I may be allowed to return to my former bride and beloved, poverty, from which I am torn away; and to put another in my place there, if someone fit may then perhaps be found.”

Observe, reader, the man’s virtue and purity of intention: he neither sought honor nor feared death for Christ’s name. What could be purer or stronger than this spirit, which exposes itself to danger and labor while yielding to another the fruit—security and peace in the place of primacy? He does this while retaining by agreement the freedom to return to poverty, once the Church’s peace and liberty are restored. When they had promised, he finally yielded to their will—or rather to God’s will. For he remembered that long ago there had been foreshown to him what was now being done to him, though he grieved at it [alternatively, willed it] [Col. 1087D].

For when Celsus was already ill, a woman of tall stature and venerable appearance appeared to Malachy, who was far away and knew nothing of it. When he asked who she was, he was told that she was Celsus’s wife. Handing him the pastoral staff she held in her hand, she disappeared. A few days later, as Celsus was dying, he sent his staff to Malachy as to his successor. When Malachy saw it, he recognized it as the very staff he had seen. The remembrance of this vision especially frightened Malachy: he feared that if he continued to refuse what he had long enough put off, he might appear to resist the divine will. Nevertheless, he did not enter the city while that usurper lived, lest anyone should die on that account among those to whom he had come chiefly to minister life. Thus for two years—for so long the man survived—he remained outside the city, energetically performing the episcopal work throughout the whole province.

## CHAPTER XI. He escapes unharmed from plots, while their wicked authors perish

[Col. 1088A]

22. When that man was swiftly removed by death, another, named Nigellus—indeed truly blackest—again seized the see. Maurice, while still alive, had provided for his own soul in this as well: he had secured this man as his heir, so that he who went forth to condemnation might persist in adding deeds deserving condemnation. For he too was of that condemned stock, a kinsman of Maurice [Col. 1088B]. Yet the king, bishops, and faithful people of the land nevertheless gathered to install Malachy. And behold, the counsel of the wicked on the other side. One of the sons of Belial, ready for evil, powerful in iniquity, knowing the place where they had determined to assemble, secretly occupied with many followers a neighboring high hill opposite. While the others discussed other matters, they would rush suddenly upon the unsuspecting and kill the innocent. They had agreed to slaughter both the king and the bishop, so that no one might remain to avenge righteous blood.

The affair became known to Malachy. Entering a church nearby, he lifted up his hands and prayed to the Lord; and behold, clouds and darkness, and dark water in the clouds of the air, turned day into night.
