Lightning also, thunder, and dreadful storm-winds threatened the Last Day, while all the elements menaced imminent death [Col. 1088C].

23. And so that you may know, reader, that Malachy’s prayer shook the elements: the storm overtook only those who sought his life; the dark whirlwind enveloped only those who had prepared works of darkness. Indeed, the very leader of so great an evil was struck by lightning and perished with three others; those who had shared the crime became companions in death. On the following day their bodies were found half-burned and decayed, clinging to the branches of trees where the lifting wind had dashed each one. Three others were found half alive; all the rest were scattered in every direction. But those with Malachy, although nearest in place [Col. 1088D], were not touched by the storm at all, nor did it cause them any distress.

In this event we receive a fresh proof of the truth of that saying: “The prayer of the righteous pierces the heavens” (Ecclus. 35:21). We also see a new instance of the old miracle by which, when all Egypt was plunged in darkness, Israel alone remained in light; as Scripture says: “Wherever Israel was, there was light” (Exodus 10:23). I am reminded too of the deed of holy Elijah, who at one time drew clouds and rain from the ends of the earth (3 Kings 18:45), and at another called down fire from heaven upon blasphemers (4 Kings 1:10). In a like manner God was then glorified in his servant Malachy.

## CHAPTER XII. By strength of mind and steadfast faith in God, he softens and reconciles enemies or rivals armed against him

[Col. 1089A]

24. In the thirty-eighth year of his life, poor Malachy, after the usurper had been expelled, entered Armagh as pontiff and metropolitan of all Ireland. When the king and the others who had brought him in returned to their own homes, he remained in God’s hand; and battles remained for him without, fears within. For behold, the viper’s brood, gnashing and shouting that they were being disinherited, stirred itself up wholly within and without against the Lord and against his Christ.

Nigellus, seeing that flight was imminent, carried away certain insignia of that see: namely, the Book of the Gospels which had belonged to blessed Patrick, and a staff covered with gold and adorned with very precious gems, which they call the Staff of Jesus, because the Lord himself, according to popular report, had held and fashioned it with his own hands [Col. 1089B]. These objects were of the highest dignity and veneration among that people. For they were very well known and famous among the populace and held in such reverence by everyone that the foolish and ignorant people considered whoever seemed to possess them to be the bishop himself. That wandering man, another Satan, went about the earth and traversed it, carrying the sacred insignia around. Displaying them everywhere, he was everywhere received for their sake; by them he gained the affections of all, and turned from Malachy as many as he could. Such was he.

25. There was a certain prince among the more powerful men of that wicked stock. Before leaving the city, the king had compelled him to swear that he would keep peace with the bishop, and had also taken many hostages from him. Yet after the king’s departure he entered the city and took counsel with his relatives and friends on how they might seize and kill the saint by deceit; but they feared the people. Having conspired for Malachy’s death, they appointed a place and day, and the traitor gave them a signal. On that day, as the bishop was already celebrating the evening office in church with all the clergy and a multitude of people, the wicked prince sent to him deceptively with words of peace, asking that he would deign to come down to him to make peace. Those standing by answered that he ought rather to come to the bishop; the church was a more fitting place to establish peace, for they had perceived the plot [Col. 1089D].

Those who had been sent added that this would not be safe for the prince: he feared for his life and did not trust the crowds, which had nearly killed him a few days earlier on the bishop’s account. While they disputed in this manner, the one party urging him to go and the other not to go, the bishop—eager for peace and unafraid of death—said: “Let me be, brethren; let me imitate my Master. I am a Christian in vain if I do not follow Christ. Perhaps I may bend the tyrant by humility; and if not, I still conquer by showing, as a shepherd to a sheep and a priest to a layman, what he ought to have shown me. And by such an example I build you up, so far as lies in me, not a little. For what if I should be killed? I do not refuse to die, so that you may retain from me an example of life. A bishop, as the Prince of bishops says, ought not to lord it over the clergy, but to become an example to the flock (1 Peter 5:3) [Col. 1090A]. Certainly no example other than that which we have received from him who humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death. Who will grant me to leave this example to my children, marked with my blood? You shall surely discover whether your priest has learned worthily enough from Christ not to fear death for Christ.”

Rising, he began to go, while all wept and begged him not to desire so greatly to die for Christ that he would leave so great a flock of Christ desolate.

26. But placing all his hope in the Lord, he went with full eagerness, accompanied by only three disciples, who were ready to die with him. As soon as he crossed the threshold of the house, he suddenly came into the midst of armed men, himself fortified with the shield of faith. The faces of all fell, because fear fell upon them, so that the bishop could say: “My enemies who trouble me, they themselves were weakened and fell” (Psalm 26:2). This saying was true. You might have seen the victim standing, with executioners all around him, their hands armed with swords; yet no one was there to sacrifice him. You would have thought their arms were benumbed [Note: [Col. 1089D] You have similar examples in Ambrose against Maximinus; in Basil against Valens; [Col. 1090D] in Leo the Great against Attila; in Chrysostom against Gainas, etc.], for there was no one who stretched out his hand. Even he who seemed the chief of the wickedness rose to greet him rather than rose against him. Where, man, I ask, was the signal you had given for the bishop’s death? This was rather a sign of honor than an indication of death. It was an act of deference, not an infliction of death.

A marvelous thing! Those who had prepared murder offered peace [Col. 1090C]. He could not refuse it, since he had sought it even at the risk of his life. Peace was therefore made, and so firm a peace that from that day the priest had his former enemy not merely peaceful, but subject and devoted. When this was heard, all the faithful rejoiced that on that day not only had innocent blood been saved, but that the souls of many guilty persons had, through Malachy’s merits, escaped unto salvation. Fear seized all around when they heard how God had so suddenly overthrown two of his enemies who appeared fiercer and stronger in their generation: I mean this one now in hand and the one mentioned above. One he punished terribly in body, the other he changed mercifully in heart; both he wonderfully caught in the counsels which they had devised [Col. 1090D].

27. After these things had been done, the bishop began in the city to arrange and order with complete freedom all matters pertaining to his ministry, though not without continual danger to his life. For although there was now no one to harm him openly, neither place was sufficiently safe for the bishop from ambushes nor any time free from danger. Armed men were assigned to guard him night and day [671], but he trusted more in the Lord.

There was a plan to pursue the aforesaid schismatic, because he was deceiving many by means of the insignia he carried, persuading everyone that he ought to be bishop [Col. 1091A], and thus stirring up the people against Malachy and against the unity of the Church. And this was done. By the grace given him from the Lord and by his influence with all, Malachy quickly and without difficulty blocked every way of that man, so that the wicked man was forced to surrender, return the insignia, and thereafter remain quiet in complete submission. Thus Malachy, though through many dangers and labors, prospered day by day and was strengthened more and more, abounding in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIII. God punishes Malachy’s detractors

28. God corrected not only Malachy’s evildoers, but also his detractors. For example, a certain man enjoyed the favor of princes and powerful men, even of the king himself, because he was a flatterer, a chatterer, and powerful in speech. In every respect he favored Malachy’s opponents and insolently defended their side. He resisted the saint openly and in person, and slandered him in his absence, confronting him irreverently everywhere, especially where he knew Malachy was attending more notable gatherings [Col. 1091B]. But he soon received a fitting reward for his insolent tongue. His malicious tongue swelled and rotted; worms swarmed from it and poured out through his whole blasphemous mouth. For almost seven days he vomited them continually, and at last, with them, expelled his wretched soul.

29. Once, while Malachy was speaking publicly and exhorting the people, an unhappy woman dared to interrupt his sermon with shameless cries, showing no reverence for the priest or for the Spirit who spoke. She belonged to the impious stock and had “spirit in her nostrils”; she spewed blasphemies and insults against the saint, calling him a hypocrite and invader of another’s inheritance, and reproaching him with his baldness [Col. 1091C]. He answered her nothing, being truly modest and gentle; but the Lord answered for him. By the Lord’s judgment she was driven mad; repeatedly shouting that Malachy was choking her, she finally paid for the sin of blasphemy by a dreadful death. Thus the wretched woman took up against Malachy the reproach cast upon Elisha (4 Kings 2:24), and truly discovered him to be for herself another Elisha.

30. Moreover, because of a plague that had arisen in the city, Malachy had solemnly led outside the multitude of clergy and people with the relics [alternatively, memorial] of the saints. This also must not be passed over: when Malachy prayed, the plague immediately ceased. From that time there was no one to murmur against him; those of the seed of Canaan said: “Let us flee Malachy, because the Lord fights for him.” But this came too late, because the zeal of the Lord, meeting them everywhere, pursued them to extermination [Col. 1091D]. How, within a few days, did their memory perish with a crash? How were they made desolate, suddenly failed, and perished because of their iniquity! The very swift destruction of that generation still works a great miracle today, especially for those who knew their pride and power.

There were indeed many other signs by which God glorified his name and strengthened his servant amid sweat and dangers [Col. 1092A]. Who can worthily recount them? Yet we do not pass over all, though we are not equal to all. But lest the sequence of the narrative be interrupted, we reserve until the end certain things which we shall mention.

## CHAPTER XIV. He resigns the metropolitan see after restoring it to peace

31. Therefore, within three years, Malachy had rendered recompense to the proud, restored the liberty of the Church, driven out barbarism, and everywhere reformed the morals of Christian religion. Seeing all things at peace, he began to think also of his own peace. Remembering his purpose, he appointed Gelasius in his place, a good man and worthy of such honor. The clergy and people consented—or rather endured it because of the agreement; for otherwise it would have seemed wholly harsh [Col. 1092B]. When Gelasius had been consecrated and carefully commended to kings and princes, Malachy himself, illustrious in miracles and triumphs, returned to his own diocese—not, however, to Connor.

Hear the reason, worthy of narration. That diocese is said in ancient times to have had two episcopal sees and to have constituted two bishoprics. This seemed better to Malachy. Therefore, what ambition had fused into one, Malachy restored to two, yielding part to another bishop and retaining part for himself. For this reason he did not come to Connor, because he had already ordained a bishop there; rather, he went to Down, dividing the dioceses as in ancient days. O pure heart! O dove-like eye! He gave up the place where he himself had sat to the new bishop, who seemed more ready and was considered more eminent [Col. 1092C]. Where are those who quarrel over boundaries, carrying on everlasting hostilities with one another for a single little village? I do not know whether any class of people is more directly touched than they by the ancient prophecy: “They ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead, that they might enlarge their borders” (Amos 1:13). But of this elsewhere.

32. Made bishop of Down, Malachy immediately, according to his custom, took to himself for consolation a community of regular clergy from among his own sons. And behold, he again girded himself, like a new recruit of Christ, for spiritual battle; he again put on the arms powerful through God: the humility of holy poverty, the rigor of monastic discipline, leisure for contemplation, and persistence in prayer. Yet he was able long to retain all these more in desire than in practice. For all flocked to him: not merely persons of middling rank, but nobles and powerful men hastened to entrust themselves to his wisdom and holiness, to be instructed, corrected, and governed [Col. 1092D]. He too sometimes went out to sow his seed, ordering and determining ecclesiastical affairs with full authority, as though one of the Apostles. And no one said to him, “By what authority do you do these things?” since all saw the signs and wonders he performed, and that “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

## CHAPTER XV. He decides to go to Rome to seek the pallium from the Pope

33. Yet he thought that these things were not conducted with sufficient security without the authority of the Apostolic See, and he decided to go to Rome. This was especially because the metropolitan see still lacked, and had lacked from the beginning, the use of the pallium, which is the fullness of honor [Col. 1093A]. He thought it good if the Church for which he had labored so greatly should obtain, through his care and labor, what it had not possessed hitherto. There was also another metropolitan see, newly established by Celsus, yet subject, as to a primatial see, to the first see and its archbishop. Malachy likewise desired a pallium for this see also, and that the prerogative which it had deserved to obtain by Celsus’s favor should be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See. When his intention became known, it displeased the brethren, as also the nobles and people of the land. All considered the long absence of their pious father intolerable and feared for his death.

[Col. 1093B]

34. Meanwhile his brother, a good man named Christian, full of grace and power, died. He was a bishop, second to Malachy indeed in public renown, but perhaps not inferior in holiness of life and zeal for righteousness. His death frightened everyone still more and made Malachy’s departure more distressing. They said that they must by no means consent to the pilgrimage of their only protector, lest the whole land be left desolate if deprived at one moment of two such pillars. Thus all alike opposed him. They used force, while he threatened divine vengeance. Yet they did not desist until, by casting lots, the will of God should first be consulted on this question. Although he forbade it, they nevertheless cast them; but the lot was found to have answered three times in Malachy’s favor. They were not satisfied with one casting, being eager to keep him [Col. 1093C]. At last, yielding, they let him go, though not without much weeping and lamentation.

But lest he leave anything unfinished, he began to consider how he might raise up seed to his deceased brother. Summoning three of his disciples, he anxiously considered which seemed more worthy or useful for this work. Looking carefully at each one, he said: “You, Eadan”—for that was the name of one—“take up the burden.” When he hesitated and wept, Malachy said: “Do not fear. You have been designated for me by the Lord, because I have already foreseen on your finger the golden ring by which you are to be espoused.” The man consented, and Malachy, after consecrating him, set out.

[Col. 1093D]

35. When he had departed from Scotland and arrived at York, a priest named Sycarus saw him and recognized him. He had not seen Malachy’s face before; but, possessing the spirit of prophecy, he had long previously received a revelation concerning him. Now, without hesitation, pointing him out with his finger to those standing around, he said: “This is the man of whom I said that a holy bishop would come from Ireland, who knows the thoughts of men.” Thus the lamp could not remain hidden under a bushel, for the Holy Spirit who had lighted it disclosed it through Sycarus’s mouth. Sycarus also told him many hidden things concerning Malachy himself and his companions, all of which Malachy recognized to be or to have been so.

When Malachy’s companions asked about his return, Sycarus answered without hesitation—an answer later proved by the event—that very few of that number would return with the bishop [Col. 1094A]. On hearing this, they suspected death; but God fulfilled it otherwise. For, on his return from Rome, Malachy left some with us and others elsewhere to learn the pattern of religious life; and, according to Sycarus’s word, he returned to his homeland with very few. So much concerning Sycarus.

36. In the city of York itself, a man noble according to the world, named Wallenus, came to him. At that time Wallenus was prior at Kirkham [alternatively, Kirkstead] of the regular brethren; now he is a monk and father of monks in the monastery of Melrose of our order. Devoted to Malachy, he humbly commended himself to his prayers. Seeing that the bishop had many companions and few horses—for besides attendants and other clerics there were five priests with him, while there were only three horses—he offered him the horse he himself rode, saying only that he regretted that it was a rough-gaited nag. He added: “I would more gladly have given it, if it had been better; but, if you deign, take it with you as it is.”

“And I,” said the bishop, “accept it all the more gladly because you declare it inferior; for nothing which so precious a goodwill has offered can be worthless to me.” Then, turning to his companions, he said: “Saddle this one for me, for it will be convenient enough and sufficient for the journey” [Col. 1094B].

When this had been done, he mounted. At first he found it hard, as it was; afterward, by a marvelous change, he found it very comfortable and moving pleasantly. And lest the word he had spoken fall to the ground, until the ninth year, when Malachy himself died, it did not fail him, having become an excellent and most valuable palfrey. And, what made the miracle more evident to those who saw it, it began to turn white from darkish-black, and before long scarcely any horse whiter than it could be found [Col. 1094C].

## CHAPTER XVI. On his way to Rome and on his return, he visits Clairvaux

37. On this journey I too was granted to see the man; and by the sight and speech of him I was refreshed and delighted as with every kind of wealth. And I in turn, though a sinner, found favor in his eyes from then onward until his death, as I stated in the preface. He also deigned to turn aside to Clairvaux. On seeing the brethren, he was moved to compunction [Col. 1094D], and they were greatly edified by his presence and speech. Embracing the place and ourselves, and gathering us into his innermost affection, he bade us farewell and departed. Crossing the Alps, when he came to the Italian city of Ivrea, he immediately healed the little son of his host, who was gravely ill and about to die.

38. At that time Innocent II, pope of blessed memory, held the Apostolic See. He received him graciously, showing him much human sympathy after so long a pilgrimage. First, Malachy, with many tears, begged for what he had most deeply fixed in his heart: permission, with the leave and blessing of the supreme Pontiff, to live and die at Clairvaux. He asked this not forgetting the purpose for which he had come, but drawn by the longing for Clairvaux with which he had come. But he did not obtain it, because the Apostolic Man judged that he should be employed in more abundant gains. Yet he was not altogether disappointed of his heart’s desire: he was granted to die there, though not to live there. He spent a full month in the City, visiting and frequenting the holy places for prayer. During this time the supreme Pontiff often and carefully inquired of him and of those with him concerning his native country, the customs of its people, the condition of its Churches, and how great were the works God had accomplished in that land through him. As Malachy was now preparing to return home, the Pope entrusted his own authority to him, appointing him legate throughout all Ireland. For Bishop Gilbert, who, as we mentioned above, had then been legate, had informed him that because of old age and bodily weakness he could no longer administer his stewardship. After this, Malachy asked that the establishment of the new metropolitan see be confirmed, and that the pallia of both sees be given to him. He immediately received the privilege of confirmation. “But concerning the pallia,” said the supreme Pontiff, “this must be dealt with more solemnly. When bishops, clergy, and the leading men of the land have been assembled, you shall celebrate a general council; then, with the consent and common vote of all, you shall seek the pallium through honourable persons, and it shall be given to you.” Then, taking the mitre from his own head, he placed it upon Malachy’s head; and he also gave him a stole and maniple, which he himself was accustomed to use during the offering. Having greeted him with the kiss of peace, he dismissed him, strengthened by apostolic blessing and authority.

39. Returning by way of Clairvaux, he bestowed upon us for the second time his blessing. Drawing deep sighs because he was not permitted to remain according to his desire, he said: “Meanwhile, I ask you to keep these men for me, so that they may learn from you what they may afterwards teach us.” And he added: “They shall be to us for seed; and in this seed the nations shall be blessed—those nations which from ancient days have indeed heard the name ‘monk,’ but have not seen a monk.” Leaving four men from his own company, he departed; they were tested and found worthy, and became monks. After some time, when the Saint was already in his own land, he sent others, and the same was done with them. When these had for some time been instructed and educated in wisdom of heart, we sent them out, giving them as father the holy brother Christian, one of their own number, and adding from among our brethren as many as were needed to make up the number for an abbey. That abbey conceived and bore five daughters; and thus, as the seed multiplied, the number of monks increases daily, in accordance with Malachy’s desire and prophecy. Now let us resume the order of the narrative.

## Chapter XVII. Various benefits of healing bestowed through him

40. Departing from us, Malachy arrived safely in Scotland. He found King David, who is still alive today, in one of his castles; the king’s son was mortally ill. Malachy entered, was honourably received by the king, and humbly entreated to heal his son. He sprinkled the young man with water which he had blessed, looked upon him, and said: “Take courage, son; you shall not die this time.” He said this, and on the following day, according to the prophet’s saying, health followed his word; the father’s joy followed health, along with the cry and commotion of the whole rejoicing household. The report spread everywhere; for what had happened in the royal house, to the king’s son, could not remain hidden. Behold, everywhere thanksgiving resounded and voices of praise arose, both for the lord’s recovery and for the novelty of the miracle. This was Henry; for he is still alive, his father’s only son, a strong and prudent knight, resembling his father, as they say, in pursuing justice and in love for the man. Both loved Malachy as long as he lived, as one who had recalled him from death. They begged him to remain for some days; but he declined the glory and would not endure delay, setting out in the morning.

As he passed through a village named Crugeldum, a mute girl met him. At his prayer the bond of her tongue was loosed, and she spoke plainly. Then he entered the village called the church of Saint Michael. Before all the people he healed a frenzied woman brought to him bound with ropes; and, leaving her unharmed, he proceeded on his way. When he reached the harbour of Laperasper, he waited there for a crossing for several days; but the delay was by no means idle. Meanwhile an oratory was built from woven branches, at his command and with his own work alongside the others. When it was completed, he enclosed it with a rampart and blessed the intervening space as a cemetery. The miracles said to be performed there even to this day sufficiently declare the merits of the one who blessed it.

41. Hence people customarily bring to him from neighbouring places the sick and afflicted, and many are healed. A woman whose limbs were wholly disabled was carried there in a cart and returned home on her own feet, having waited only one night in the holy place, not vainly, for the Lord’s mercy. Another woman was spending the night there in prayer. A barbarous man happened to find her alone; inflamed by lust and no longer master of himself, he rushed furiously upon her. She turned, trembling, looked up, and perceived the man filled with a diabolical spirit. “Hey, wretch,” she said, “what are you doing? Consider where you are; reverence these holy things; show respect to God, show respect to his servant Malachy; spare yourself also.” But, driven by wicked madness, he did not desist. And behold—horrible to tell—a poisonous, swollen creature called a toad was seen crawling out from between the woman’s thighs. What more need be said? Terrified, the man recoiled, and with leaps sprang hastily out of the oratory. He withdrew in confusion, while she remained untouched: a great miracle both of God and of Malachy’s merit. Fittingly, a foul and abominable monster intervened in a foul and abominable deed. No other means was more fitting for extinguishing bestial lust than the coldest of creeping things; nor for restraining a reckless audacity and frustrating its attempt than a vile and useless little beast. Let these few instances among many suffice concerning this place; now let us pursue what remains.

## Chapter XVIII. Returned to his homeland, he devotes himself wholly to pastoral care and reform

42. Malachy boarded a ship and, sailing safely, came to his monastery at Bangor, so that his first sons might receive the first grace. What joy, do you think, did they feel when their father, safe from so long a journey—and such a father—was restored to them? Nor is it surprising that their whole hearts poured themselves out in joy at his return, when swift report immediately carried incredible gladness even to surrounding foreign peoples. Indeed, people came out to meet him from cities, castles, and villages; wherever he turned aside, he was received with the rejoicing of the whole land. Yet honour did not delight him. The work of the legation was carried out: many assemblies were held in many places, so that no region, or part of a region, might be deprived of the fruit and benefit of the legation. He sowed beside all waters; there was none who could hide from the work of his care. Neither sex, age, rank, nor profession was overlooked. Everywhere the saving seed was scattered; everywhere the heavenly trumpet sounded. Everywhere he hastened, everywhere he broke in, drawing the sword of his tongue to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples. His terror fell upon evildoers. He cried to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly”; and to sinners: “Do not raise up the horn” (Ps. 74:5). Religion was everywhere planted, propagated, and fostered. His eyes were upon them, and his care attended to their needs.

At the councils held everywhere, ancient traditions were reaffirmed—traditions which had been proved good but had been abolished through the negligence of priests. Not only were old things restored: new ones were also established; and whatever he promulgated was received, observed, and committed to writing for the remembrance of posterity as though issued from heaven. Why should they not be believed to have been sent from heaven, when so many heavenly miracles confirmed them? To establish confidence in my words, I shall touch briefly on a few. For who could enumerate everything? Yet, I confess, I would rather linger over deeds to be imitated than wonders to be admired.

## Chapter XIX. The marks of his virtues and manners worthy of a true bishop

43. In my judgment, the first and greatest miracle he performed was himself. To say nothing of his inward person, whose beauty, strength, and purity were sufficiently displayed by his conduct and life, he bore even his outward person always in one and the same manner, and that most modest and becoming, so that absolutely nothing appeared in him which could offend those who looked upon him. “Whoever does not offend in word is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2). But in Malachy, who ever detected—even with the most searching observation—not merely an idle word, but an idle gesture? Who saw hand or foot moved purposelessly? Rather, what was there in his walk, glance, bearing, or countenance that did not edify? Sorrow did not darken the cheerfulness of his face, nor did laughter make it frivolous. Everything in him was disciplined; everything bore the mark of virtue, a pattern of perfection. He was grave in all things, but not harsh; sometimes relaxed, never undisciplined; negligent in nothing, though for a time he often passed over many matters. Often quiet, but never idle.

From the first day of his conversion until the end of his life, he lived without property. He possessed neither male nor female servants, estates nor hamlets, nor indeed any ecclesiastical or secular revenues, even while bishop. Nothing whatever was fixed or assigned to the episcopal table from which the bishop might live. For he did not even have a house of his own. He travelled almost continually through all the parishes, serving the Gospel and living by the Gospel, as the Lord ordained for him: “The labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10:7). Except that, more often, he offered the Gospel itself without charge and, from his own labours and those of his companions, brought what was needed to support himself and those who laboured with him in the work of ministry. If at times he needed rest, he did so in the holy places which he himself had scattered throughout all Ireland; and wherever he wished to stay, he conformed himself to their customs and observances, content with their common life and table. In food and clothing there was nothing by which Malachy could be distinguished from the other brothers: so completely, though he was greater, did he humble himself in all things.

44. Finally, when he went out to preach, he himself went on foot with those who went on foot—bishop and legate though he was. This is the apostolic pattern, and it was all the more remarkable in Malachy because it is exceedingly rare in others. Surely this man is a true heir of the Apostles, since he does such things. But observe how he divides the inheritance with his brothers, those equally the descendants of the Apostles. They lord it over the clergy; he, though free from all, made himself the servant of all. They either eat without preaching the Gospel, or preach in order to eat; Malachy, imitating Paul, eats in order to preach the Gospel. They regard pride and gain as godliness; Malachy claims as his inheritance work and burden. They believe themselves happy if they enlarge their boundaries; Malachy glories in enlarging charity. They gather into barns and fill vats, so that they may burden their tables; Malachy gathers in deserts and solitudes, so that he may fill heaven. Though they receive tithes, firstfruits, offerings, and, in addition, tolls, taxes, and countless other revenues through Caesar’s beneficence, they are nevertheless anxious about what they shall eat and what they shall drink. Malachy, possessing none of these things, nevertheless enriches many from the storehouse of faith. Their covetousness and anxiety know no end; Malachy desires nothing, yet does not know how to think about tomorrow. They exact from the poor what they may give to the rich; he solicits the rich for the support of the poor. They empty the purses of their subjects; he heaps altars with vows and peace offerings for their sins. They raise lofty palaces, lifting towers and walls to the heavens; Malachy, having nowhere to lay his head, does the work of an evangelist. They mount horses amid a crowd of men who eat bread freely—and not their own bread; Malachy, surrounded by a fellowship of holy brothers, journeys on foot, carrying the bread of angels with which to satisfy hungry souls. They do not even know their people; he instructs them. They honour powerful men and tyrants; he punishes them. O apostolic man, made illustrious by so many and such great marks of his apostolate! What wonder, then, if he worked wonders, being himself so wonderful? Indeed, not he, but God in him. For, as Scripture says: “You are God, who work wonders” (Ps. 76:15).

## Chapter XX. He frees those possessed and tormented by demons

45. There was a woman in the city of Culratim [variant: Cultatim] who had a demon. Malachy was summoned. He prayed for the woman enslaved by it, pressed the invader, and it departed. But its malice not yet satisfied, it invaded a poor woman who happened to be standing nearby. Malachy said: “I did not take her from you so that you might seize this one. Depart from her also.” It obeyed, but returned to the first woman. Driven out again, it fled to the other. Thus, for some time, it tormented them alternately, fleeing back and forth. Then the saint, indignant that he should be mocked by the demon, gathered his spirit, roared in anger, and, making an assault upon the enemy with all the strength of faith, drove it from both women—indeed, no less tormented itself than those whom it had tormented.

But, reader, do not suppose that the delay imposed upon the saint was owing to any lack of power; it was rather by divine dispensation, so that both the presence of the evil one and Malachy’s victory might be more clearly shown. Hear, then, what he did elsewhere—not in his personal presence. Surely he could do in presence what he accomplished in absence.

46. In a region of northern Ireland a sick man lay in a house, doubtless through the evil working of demons. For one night he heard them speaking, one saying to the other: “See that this wretch does not touch the bed or bedding of that hypocrite, and so escape from our hands.” The man understood that they meant Malachy, whom he remembered had spent a night in that same house not long before. The bedding was still in place. Taking courage, and with whatever effort he could, he began to crawl, weak in body but strong in faith. And behold, there was a cry and shouting in the air: “Stop him, stop him! Hold him, hold him! We are losing our prey.” But the man whom faith and the desire to escape carried onward, the more they cried out, the more he supported himself on knees and hands and hastened to the remedy. Reaching it, he climbed onto the bed and rolled in the bedding. He heard the howls of their lamentation: “Alas, alas! We ourselves betrayed ourselves; we have been deceived; he has escaped.” More swiftly than speech, the demonic terror and horror he suffered departed from him, together with all his illness.

In the city of Lismore, a man tormented by a demon was freed through Malachy. Likewise, once when he was travelling through Leinster, an infant possessed by a demon was brought to him and carried back well. In the same region he ordered a frenzied woman, bound with ropes, to be loosed and washed in water which he had blessed. She was washed and healed. He also healed another woman in the district of Saul in Ulaid, who was tearing her own limbs with her teeth, by prayer and touch. Friends and relatives brought to the man of God a madman, who foretold many future things, firmly bound with ropes because his very frenzy had made him powerful and dangerous in doing harm. Malachy prayed; immediately the sick man was healed and loosed. This happened in a place whose name we suppress because it sounds too barbarous, like many others. At another time in the aforementioned city of Lismore, the parents of a mute girl presented her to Malachy as he passed through the middle of the street, earnestly begging him to deign to help her. Malachy stopped; after praying, he touched her tongue with his finger, put spittle into her mouth, and sent her away speaking.

## Chapter XXI. Benefits bestowed upon the dying and women in childbirth

47. Leaving a certain church, he met a man with his wife, who could not speak. Asked to have mercy upon her, he stood in the doorway with the people gathered around; having pronounced a blessing over her, he ordered her to say the Lord’s Prayer. She said it, and the people blessed the Lord. In the city named Oenthreb [variant: Onereb], a certain rich man lay upon his bed, deprived of the use of speech for twelve days. At the command of the saint who visited him, he recovered speech and received the Eucharist; thus strengthened, he breathed his last in a good confession. O fruitful olive tree in the house of God! O oil of gladness, anointing and shining! By the splendour of the miracle he enlightened the healthy, and by the sweetness of the benefit he anointed the sick man, who was soon to die, obtaining for him the saving opportunity of confession and communion.

One of the nobles entered, having something to say to him. While speaking, full of faith, he piously stole three reeds from the bed on which Malachy sat and took them with him. Through this theft of piety God worked many things, by the man’s faith and the holiness of the bishop. Malachy happened to come to the city called Duevania. As he sat at table, a nobleman of that city came in and humbly begged for his pregnant wife, who had already exceeded every customary time of childbirth, so that all marvelled and no one thought anything but danger to her life imminent. Nehemiah, bishop of that city, who sat beside him, joined in the request; and so did all the others reclining at table. Then Malachy said: “I pity her, because she is a good and modest woman.” Handing the man a cup over which he had pronounced a blessing, he said: “Go; give her this to drink. Know that, once she has drunk the blessed draught, she will give birth without delay and without danger.” What he commanded was done, and that very night what he promised followed.

He was seated in a field, discussing certain matters with the Count of Ulaid, and a large crowd was about them. A pregnant woman came, truly heavily burdened. She stated that, contrary to all the laws of nature, she had retained the child in the womb for fifteen months and twenty days. Malachy, moved with compassion at this new and unheard-of affliction, prayed, and the woman gave birth. Those present rejoiced and marvelled. For all saw with what ease and speed she gave birth in that very place, and how the sad danger of a withheld birth was transformed by miracle into a happier outcome.

## Chapter XXII. He foretells destruction to an obstinate concubinary

48. In the same place something occurred equal in miracle, but different in outcome. Malachy saw a man said publicly to be keeping his brother’s concubine; he was a knight, an official of the count. Meeting the incestuous man openly, Malachy showed himself to him as another John: “It is not lawful for you,” he said, “to have your brother’s concubine.” But the man, making himself another Herod in return, not only would not listen but answered arrogantly and swore before all that he would never abandon her (Mark 6:17–28). Then Malachy, moved as he was by a vehement zeal for justice, said: “May God separate you from her even against your will.” The man thought little of it and went away at once in anger.

Coming upon a woman standing not far from the crowd, he violently assaulted her, being wholly given over to Satan, to whom he had shortly before been delivered. The crime did not remain concealed. The maidservant accompanying the woman ran home—for the house was not far from the place—and, breathless, announced the harm that had been done. At this report her brothers, who were at home, jealous for their sister’s violated chastity, rushed there in all haste. Finding the enemy of her honour in the very place and act of his crime, they killed him, piercing him with many wounds. The assembly had not yet dispersed when his armour-bearer announced what had occurred. All marvelled that Malachy’s sentence had taken effect so swiftly. Every shameful person who heard of this word—for there were many in the land—was afraid; and, terrified, they were cleansed, washing their hands in the sinner’s blood.

## Chapter XXIII. Various benefits of healing granted to various persons

49. Malachy sharply rebuked Count Diarmait, who had lain sick in bed for a long time, because he was a bad man, serving his belly and appetite too excessively. After sprinkling him with blessed water, he made him rise without delay, so strong that he immediately mounted a horse—certainly beyond the expectation both of himself and of his household. In the city of Cashel, a man came before him with his paralysed son, asking that he be healed. Malachy prayed briefly and said: “Go; your son will be healed.” The man went and returned the next day with his son, who had not been healed at all. Then Malachy rose and, standing over him, prayed for a long time; and the boy was healed. Turning to the father, he said: “Offer him to God.” The man agreed, but did not keep his promise. After some years, when the boy was already a young man, he fell again into the same condition, doubtless because of his father’s disobedience and breach of covenant.

Another man came from far away while Malachy was in the borders of Munster, bringing his son, wholly deprived of the use of his feet. When asked how this had happened, he said: “As I suspect, through the malice of demons.” He added: “While he was playing in a meadow, they caused sleep to come upon him, I suppose; and when the little boy awoke, he found himself as he is.” Saying this, he poured out his prayer with tears and urgently sought help. Malachy took pity on him, prayed, and ordered the sick boy meanwhile to sleep there upon the ground [perhaps *solum*; the text has *solium*, “seat/throne”]. He slept and rose well. Since he had come from afar, Malachy kept him for some time in his company, and he walked with him.

50. At the monastery of Bangor, a poor man was supported by the alms of the brothers. Receiving a daily allowance, he performed some small service in the bakehouse. He had been lame for twelve years; crawling on the ground with his hands, he dragged behind him his lifeless feet. One day Malachy found him sad and grieving before his cell and asked the cause. The man said: “You see how long I have been miserably afflicted, and how the hand of the Lord is upon me. And now, to crown my misery, the people who ought to have pitied me mock me instead, reproaching me with my suffering.” When Malachy heard him, he was moved with compassion, looked up to heaven, and raised his hands. After a brief prayer, he entered his cell, and the man rose. Standing upon his feet, he wondered whether what he experienced was real, since he had almost thought it a dream. Yet he began to move slowly, for he scarcely believed that he could walk. At last, as though waking from a heavy sleep, he recognized the Lord’s mercy upon him. He walked firmly and returned to the bakehouse, leaping and rejoicing and praising God. Those who had formerly seen and known him were filled with amazement and ecstasy, thinking it an apparition. Malachy likewise healed a man suffering from dropsy by prayer; the man immediately remained in the monastery and became a shepherd of sheep.

51. A city in Ireland called Corcagia [variant: Coreava] lacked a bishop. An election was discussed, and factions disagreed, each—as commonly happens—wanting to appoint its own bishop, not God’s. Malachy came there after hearing of the disagreement. Gathering clergy and people, he laboured also to unite the hearts and wishes of those who were divided. Having persuaded them that the whole matter ought to be entrusted to him, since the chief responsibility for that Church, as also for the other Churches throughout Ireland, rested upon him, he immediately named for them not one of the nobles of the land, but rather a poor man whom he knew to be holy and learned. This man was a foreigner.

They sought him and were told that he lay in bed, so weak that he could by no means come out unless carried in the hands of attendants. Malachy said: “Let him rise in the name of the Lord; I command it. Obedience will make him well.” What could he do? He wished to obey, but felt himself unprepared. Even if he could walk, he feared being made a bishop. Thus, though he was willing to obey, two enemies struggled against him: the burden of sickness and fear of the honour [variant: burden]. Yet willingness to obey prevailed, aided by the hope of recovery. He tried; he moved himself; he tested his strength; he found himself stronger than usual. Faith increased together with strength, and faith, made stronger again, in turn increased his strength. Now he was able to rise by himself; now to walk rather better; now not even to feel weariness while walking. Finally, vigorous and cheerful, he came to Malachy without human help. Malachy received him and placed him in the episcopal chair, to the acclaim of clergy and people. This was done peacefully, because the others did not dare oppose Malachy’s will in anything, seeing the sign he had performed; nor did the man hesitate to obey, being made more certain of the Lord’s will by so evident a proof.

52. A certain woman suffered from a flow of blood. She was noble and very dear to Malachy, yet more because of the nobility of her character than of her birth. Wholly failing, no doubt because her strength was exhausted with her blood, and already at the point of death, she sent to the man of God so that he might help what remained of her soul, since she thought she would not see him again in the body. Malachy heard and was distressed, because she was a woman of virtue, whose life was fruitful in deed and example. Seeing that he could not arrive quickly enough in time, he summoned Malch, a young and active man—this is the one mentioned above (No. 39), brother of Abbot Christian—and said: “Hurry. Take her these three apples, over which I have invoked the name of the Lord. I trust in him that when she has tasted them, she will not taste death before she sees us, though we shall follow somewhat slowly.”

Malch hastened in obedience to the command and, arriving, entered to the dying woman, making himself another of Elisha’s servants (2 Kings [4 Kings] 4:29), except that this man’s work was more effective. He ordered her to accept the blessing sent by Malachy and to taste it, if she could in any way manage it. Cheered at hearing Malachy’s name, she signified by a gesture that, in order to obey, she wished to be raised a little; she could not speak. She was raised and tasted it; after tasting, she was strengthened, spoke, and gave thanks. The Lord sent sleep upon her, and she rested most sweetly in a sleep from which she had long been deprived, as also from food. Meanwhile the bleeding stopped; soon she awoke and found herself well, except that she was still weak from long fasting and loss of blood. The desired arrival and sight of Malachy on the following day completed her recovery.

## Chapter XXIV. He raises a woman who had died without the sacrament of Extreme Unction

53. A nobleman lived near the monastery of Bangor. When his wife fell mortally ill, Malachy was asked to come down before she died, in order to anoint the sick woman with oil. He came down and entered to her. At the sight of him she rejoiced, her hope of recovery revived. When he was preparing to anoint her, it seemed best to all to defer it until morning, for it was evening. Malachy consented. Having pronounced a blessing over the sick woman, he went out with those who were with him.

Shortly afterward there suddenly arose cries, lamentation, and great commotion throughout the whole house: word had spread that she was dead. Hearing the uproar, Malachy ran in, followed by his disciples. Coming to the bed and learning certainly that she had breathed her last, he was deeply distressed, blaming himself because she had died deprived of the grace of the sacrament. Raising his hands to heaven, he said: “I beseech you, Lord: I acted foolishly. I, I have sinned, because I delayed—not she, who wished it.” Saying this, he declared before all that he would receive no consolation and grant no rest to his spirit unless he were permitted to restore the grace which he had taken away. Standing over her, he laboured throughout the night in his groaning. In place of the holy oil, he poured abundant rain of tears over the dead woman, rendering her such a substitute for the anointing as he could. For his own part, this he did; but to his companions he said: “Watch and pray.” Thus they spent the wakeful night: they in psalms, he in tears.

At morning the Lord heard his saint, because the Spirit of the Lord was making intercession for him—the Spirit who intercedes for the saints with unutterable groanings. What more need be said? She who had been dead opened her eyes. Like people waking from heavy sleep, she rubbed her forehead and temples with her hands, raised herself upon the bed, recognized Malachy, and bowed devoutly in greeting. Mourning was turned to joy, and amazement seized all who saw or heard. Malachy too gave thanks and blessed the Lord. He then anointed her nonetheless, knowing that sins are remitted in this sacrament and that “the prayer of faith will save the sick person” (Jas. 5:14–15). After this he left, and she recovered. Having lived in health for some time, so that the Lord’s glory might be manifested in her, she completed the penance Malachy had imposed upon her, then again fell asleep in a good confession and passed to the Lord.

## Chapter XXV. Other various benefits bestowed upon various persons

54. There was also a woman so dominated by a spirit of anger and fury that not only her neighbours and relatives avoided her company, but even her own children could scarcely endure to live with her. Wherever she was, there were shouting, bitterness, and violent storm. Bold, fiery, and reckless, dreadful in tongue and hand, intolerable and hated by everyone. Her sons, grieving both for her and for themselves, dragged her into Malachy’s presence and made their tearful complaint with weeping. The holy man, pitying both the mother’s danger and the sons’ distress, called her aside and carefully asked whether she had ever confessed her sins. She replied, “Never.” “Confess,” he said. She obeyed. Imposing penance upon her as she confessed, and praying over her that almighty God might give her a spirit of gentleness, he commanded her in the name of the Lord Jesus to be angry no more. Such gentleness followed that it was plain to all that this was nothing other than the wonderful change wrought by the right hand of the Most High. She is said still to be alive and to possess such patience and mildness that she who formerly used to provoke everyone can now be provoked by no injury, insult, or affliction.

If I too may, according to the Apostle, “be fully convinced in my own mind” (Rom. 14:5), let each take it as he wishes; for my part, I judge this miracle superior to that earlier miracle of the dead woman restored to life, because there the outward person, but here the inward person, was brought back to life. And now let us hasten on to what remains.

55. A man honourable in the world and God-fearing before God came to Malachy and complained of the barrenness of his soul, begging him to obtain from almighty God for him the grace of tears. Malachy smiled, because he was pleased to find in a worldly man a spiritual desire; affectionately joining his own cheek to the man’s cheek, he said: “Let it be to you as you have asked.” Thereafter such copious and almost unceasing streams of water flowed from the man’s eyes that the saying of Scripture seemed applicable to him: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters” (Song 4:15).

There is an island in the sea in Ireland, anciently fruitful in fish, and the sea there is very rich in fish. The accustomed abundance was removed, it is believed, because of the sins of the inhabitants. The island, which had many children, became weak and withered entirely from so great a source of its prosperity. While the inhabitants grieved and the people bitterly endured the heavy loss, it was revealed to a certain woman that a remedy could be obtained through Malachy’s prayers; she herself made this known to all. By God’s direction Malachy happened to be present. For as he travelled about and filled the region with the Gospel, he turned aside there to impart the same grace to them. But the barbarians, whose greater concern was for fish, pressed him with every urgency to look instead upon the barrenness of their island. He answered that he had not come for this purpose, desiring rather a catch of human beings than of fish. Yet seeing their faith, he bent his knees upon the shore and prayed to the Lord that he would not deny to those unworthy people, who sought with such faith, the benefit once granted. The prayer rose, and the multitude of fish rose also—perhaps more abundantly than in ancient days—and that abundance has remained with the people of the land even to the present day. What wonder if the prayer of a righteous person, which penetrates the heavens, penetrated the depths also and called forth so great a multitude of fish from the deep sea?

56. Once three bishops came to the village of Fochart [variant: Fochaut], said to be the birthplace of the virgin Brigid; Malachy was the fourth. The priest who had received them as guests said to him: “What shall I do, since I have no fish?” When Malachy answered that he should ask the fishermen, the priest said: “For two years fish have not been found in the river. Thus the fishermen have entirely dispersed and have even abandoned their trade.” Malachy said: “Command that nets be cast in the name of the Lord.” This was done, and twelve salmon were caught. They cast a second time, and twelve salmon were caught. They cast a second time; the same number being caught, they brought to the table an unexpected dish—and a miracle. To make it clearly evident that this was granted through Malachy’s merits, the same barrenness nevertheless continued through the following two years also.

## Chapter XXVI. He defends the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist
57. There was a certain cleric at Lismore, of reputable life, it is said, but not equally so in faith. Wise in his own eyes, he presumed to say that in the Eucharist there is only the sacrament and not the reality of the sacrament—that is, sanctification alone and not the reality of the Body. Malachy summoned him privately, and often, concerning this matter, but in vain. He was then called before an assembly, though apart from the laity, so that, if possible, he might be healed rather than put to shame. Therefore, in a gathering of clerics, the man was given an opportunity to answer for his opinion.

With all the strength of an intellect in which he was by no means unskilled, he tried to assert and defend his error. But Malachy disputed against him and refuted him; overcome in the judgment of all, he left the assembly ashamed indeed, but not corrected. Yet he said that he had not been conquered by reason, but oppressed by the Bishop’s authority.

“And you, Malachy,” he said, “have today shamed me without cause, speaking truth, assuredly, against the truth, and against your own conscience.”

Malachy grieved for a man so hardened, but grieved still more for the injury done to the faith. Fearing danger, he summoned the church: publicly he rebuked the erring man and publicly warned him to come to his senses. When, despite the exhortations of the bishops and the whole clergy, he would not yield, they pronounced an anathema upon the obstinate man, declaring him a heretic. Not even then did he awaken.

“You all,” he said, “favor the man rather than the truth. I do not accept persons so as to abandon the truth.”

Indignant at these words, the saint said: “May the Lord make you confess the truth, even by necessity.”

When he answered, “Amen,” the assembly was dismissed. Branded with such a cautery, he contemplated flight, unable to endure being infamous and dishonored.

[Col. 1106B] Immediately he gathered his belongings and was leaving, when suddenly seized by illness, he stopped short; his strength failed, and there in the same place he threw himself, panting and exhausted, upon the ground. By chance a wandering madman came to that spot, encountered the man, and asked what he was doing there. He answered that he was afflicted by a severe illness and was unable either to go forward or to return.

“That illness,” said the other, “is nothing but death itself.”

He did not say this of himself; rather, the Lord fittingly rebuked through a madman the one who had refused to yield to the sound advice of sensible persons. And he added: “Return home; I will help you.”

Accordingly, with the man himself as guide, he returned to the city; he returned to himself and to the Lord’s mercy. That very hour the Bishop was summoned; the truth was acknowledged and error rejected. Having confessed his guilt, he received absolution; he asked for the Viaticum and was reconciled. Thus, in almost a single moment, faithlessness was renounced by his mouth and washed away by death. Thus, to the amazement of all, Malachy’s saying was swiftly fulfilled, together with the Scripture which says: “Affliction gives understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28:19).

## CHAPTER XXVII. He wonderfully reconciles peace and concord among those at variance.

58. At one time a serious discord arose between the peoples of certain regions. Malachy was appealed to for the making of peace among them; but, being occupied elsewhere, he entrusted this task to one of the bishops. The bishop excused himself and refused, saying that Malachy, not he, had been requested; he would be despised, and he did not wish to labor in vain.

“Go,” said Malachy, “and the Lord will be with you.”

“I consent,” said the bishop, “but if they do not listen to me, know that I shall appeal to your Fatherhood.”

Malachy smiled. “So be it,” he said.

Then the bishop summoned the parties and laid down terms of peace. They agreed and were reconciled to one another; mutual pledges were given, and peace was established. Thus he dismissed them. But one side, seeing that their enemies had become secure and unprepared, since after peace had been made they suspected no evil, spoke among themselves; and one man said to his neighbor: “What have we done? Victory is in our hands, and vengeance upon our enemies.” And they began to pursue them.

The bishop learned what was happening. Running up, he confronted their leader about the injustice and treachery, but was despised by him. [Col. 1107A] He invoked Malachy’s name against him, and it was treated as nothing. Mocking the bishop, the leader said: “Do you suppose that because of you we ought to let go our wrongdoers, whom God has delivered into our hands?”

Then the bishop recalled the words he had exchanged with Malachy; weeping and lamenting, he turned his face toward Malachy’s monastery:

“Where are you, man of God? Where are you? Is this not, my father, what I told you? Alas, alas! I came that I might do good and not evil; and behold, through me they perish in body, and these in soul!”

In this manner he spoke much, lamenting and grieving, as though he were summoning and addressing Malachy in person against the evildoers. Meanwhile the impious men, with whom they had made peace, did not cease pursuing them in order to destroy them. And behold, there was a lying spirit in the mouths of certain men, to deceive them. Men met them on the road, announcing that their adversaries had invaded their lands; that everything was being consumed by the sword and their goods plundered, while their wives and children too were being seized and carried off.

On hearing this, they hurried back. Those behind followed those ahead, not knowing where they were going or what had happened; for not all had heard the men speaking. When they arrived and found none of the things reported, they were put to shame, caught in their own wickedness. They recognized that they had been given over to a spirit of error because they had deceived Malachy’s messenger and despised his name. The bishop, hearing that the traitors had been thwarted in the iniquity they had devised, joyfully returned to Malachy and related in order all that had happened to him.

59. Knowing that peace had been disturbed on such an occasion, Malachy, when he found a suitable time, took care personally to restore peace among them anew and to strengthen the restored settlement by pledges and oaths given and received on both sides. But those whose peace had previously been broken, remembering the injury, disregarded Malachy’s agreement and command and plotted retaliation. All gathered together and went out to take their opponents unprepared and repay upon their heads the evil which they themselves had intended to do.

They forded with great ease a large river lying between them; but at a little stream which they encountered not far beyond it, they were stopped. For it no longer appeared a little stream, but plainly a great river, everywhere denying passage to those who wished to cross. All wondered that it was now so great when they knew it had been so small before; and they said among themselves: “Whence comes this flood? The sky is clear, there has been no rain, nor do we remember any recently. Even if it had rained heavily, which of us has ever remembered it swollen in any inundation whatsoever to such a degree that it covered the land and overflowed the fields and meadows? This is the finger of God, and the Lord has hedged up our ways because of his saint Malachy, whose agreement we have violated and whose command we have transgressed.”

Thus these men too, their enterprise undone, returned to their homes equally ashamed. The report was spread throughout the whole region; and they blessed God, who catches the wise in their own cunning and, breaking the horns of sinners, exalts the horn of his Christ.

[Col. 1108A] 60. One of the nobles, hostile to the king, was reconciled through Malachy’s mediation. For the man did not trust the king sufficiently to make peace with him unless Malachy, or someone whom the king equally revered, stood between them. And not without reason, as later became apparent. For the king seized the man when he was secure and no longer on his guard, and cast him into chains—himself more seized by his old hatred.

The man was demanded from the mediator by his own people, for his friends expected nothing but death. What could Malachy do? There was nothing possible except to have recourse to his customary refuge, available to everyone. Gathering a very strong army—a great crowd of his disciples—he approached the king and demanded the prisoner; he was refused.

“You act unjustly,” said Malachy, “against the Lord, against me, and against yourself, by violating your agreement. Though you may dissemble, I shall not. The man trusted himself to my good faith. If he should die, I have betrayed him; I am guilty of his blood. What did you mean by making me a betrayer and yourself a covenant-breaker? Know that until he is released I shall taste nothing, nor shall these men.”

Having spoken thus, he entered the church and, by the anxious groans of himself and his companions, implored almighty God to deign to rescue the unjustly condemned man from the hand of the faithless and wicked covenant-breaker. That day and the following night they continued in fasting and prayer.

The king was informed of what was happening. His heart was hardened all the more by that through which it ought to have been softened. Like a carnal man, he began to flee, fearing that, if he remained nearby, he would not be able to withstand the force of prayer. As though prayer could not find one hidden, or reach one far away! Do you set boundaries, wretch, to the prayers of saints? Is prayer an arrow shot that you can flee from the bow? Where will you go from the Spirit of God who bears it, and where will you flee from his presence?

At last it pursued the fugitive and found him in hiding: “You shall be blind and unable to see, so that you may see better and understand that it is hard for you to kick against the goad.” At last, feel even now that the sharp arrows of the Mighty One have reached you. Though they rebound from your heart because it is stony, they do not rebound from your eyes. Would that through the windows of your eyes they might at least reach the heart, and that affliction might give understanding to blindness.

It was possible to see Saul again led by the hand and brought to Ananias (Acts 9)—the wolf, that is, to the sheep—in order to restore his prey. He restored it, and received his sight, because Malachy was so completely a sheep that he showed mercy even to the wolf.

[Col. 1108D] Observe carefully from these things, reader, among what people Malachy lived: what rulers and what peoples they were. How was he not also “a brother of dragons and a companion of ostriches”? (Job 30:29.) Therefore the Lord gave him power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron chains. Hear, finally, what follows.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. While planning a sacred building, he suffers opposition, but his adversary is soon struck by divine vengeance.

61. The man to whom the possessions of the monastery of Bangor had passed was ungrateful for the benefit. From that time forward he always behaved with the greatest insolence toward Malachy and his followers: hostile in everything, laying snares everywhere, and slandering his deeds. But this did not go unpunished.

He had an only son who, imitating his father, also dared something against Malachy; in that same year he died. His death occurred thus. Malachy considered that a stone oratory ought to be built at Bangor, like those which he had seen erected in other regions. When he began to lay the foundations, all the natives were astonished, because in that land no buildings of this kind had yet been found. But that wicked man, presumptuous and insolent as he was, did not marvel, but was indignant. From indignation he conceived grief and gave birth to iniquity. Becoming a whisperer among the people, he now slandered in secret, now blasphemed openly; he criticized the frivolity, recoiled from the novelty, and exaggerated the expense.

[Col. 1109B] With poisonous words of this kind he incited and persuaded many to prevent the work. “Follow me,” he said, “and let us not permit that to be done against us which can only be done through us.” Accordingly, with many whom he had managed to persuade, he went down to the place. Finding the man of God, he addressed him first, being the leader in speech and the origin of the evil:

“Good sir, what has made you think fit to introduce this novelty into our regions? We are Scots, not Gauls. What frivolity is this? What need was there for a work so superfluous, so proud? How can you, poor and needy as you are, have the resources to finish it? Who will see it completed? What presumption is this—to begin what you will not be able, I do not say to complete, but even to see completed? Indeed, it is more the act of a madman than of one who presumes [or, of a prudent man] to attempt what exceeds measure, surpasses strength, and exceeds resources. Stop, stop; desist from this madness, otherwise we shall not permit it, we shall not endure it.”

He said this, revealing what he wished, without considering what he was able to do. For those in whom he had trusted and whom he had brought with him, on seeing the man, changed their minds and no longer went along with him.

62. The holy man replied with complete freedom: “Wretch, the work which you see begun and begrudge will without doubt be completed, and many will see it completed. But you, because you do not wish it, will not see it; and because you do not wish it, you will die. Take heed to yourself, lest you die in your sin.”

So it was. The man died and the work was completed; but he did not see it, for, as we have said, he died in that same year. Meanwhile, when the father promptly heard what the holy man had predicted concerning his son, knowing that his word was living and effective, he said: “He has killed my son.” And, at the devil’s instigation, he blazed with such fury against Malachy that before the duke and leading men of Ulidia he did not hesitate to accuse as false and deceitful the man who was most truthful, both disciple and lover of truth. He even insulted him, calling him an ape.

But Malachy, instructed not to return curse for curse, was silent and did not open his mouth while the sinner stood against him. Yet the Lord had not forgotten his word: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32:35). That same day, when the man returned home, he paid for the recklessness of his unbridled tongue, punished by the very one at whose instigation he had loosed it. The demon seized him and threw him into fire; he was quickly pulled out by those standing by, but a part of his body was burned and his mind was deranged.

[Col. 1110A] While he raved, Malachy was summoned and came. He found the slanderer twisting his foam-covered mouth, terrifying everyone with horrible cries and movements, his whole body convulsed and scarcely able to be restrained by many men. The man of complete perfection prayed for his enemy and was heard—but only in part. For as soon as the saint prayed, the man opened his eyes and recovered his senses. Yet there remained to him an evil spirit from the Lord, to buffet him, so that he might learn not to blaspheme.

We believe that he is still living and, down to these times, is paying for the great sin which he committed against the saint; though they say that at certain times he is lunatic. As for the aforementioned possessions, when he could no longer hold them because of his weakness and uselessness, they returned peacefully to the place from which they had come. Malachy did not refuse them, at last, after much vexation, for the sake of peace.

63. But now let the account return to the work of building which Malachy undertook. Malachy did not have the means, I do not say to complete it, but even to do anything at all. Yet his heart had confidence in the Lord. The Lord provided that, although he did not hope in treasures of money, money should not be lacking. For who else caused a treasure to be deposited in that place and, once deposited, not discovered until the time and work of Malachy?

God’s servant found in God’s purse what was lacking in his own. And deservedly so. For what could be more just than that the man who had nothing of his own for God should enter into partnership with God and that both should have one purse? For to a faithful man the whole world is riches. And what is the world but a certain purse of God? Thus he says: “The earth is mine and its fullness” (Ps. 46:12).

Therefore Malachy did not put back the many pieces of silver he found, but brought them out. For he ordered the whole gift of God to be spent on God’s work. He did not consider his own needs or those of his followers, but cast his care upon the Lord, to whom he did not doubt he must turn whenever necessity required it.

Nor is it doubtful that this was God’s work, which Malachy foresaw by God’s revelation. He had first discussed the work with the brethren, and many, because of their poverty, assented less readily. Hence, anxious and uncertain what to do, he began in prayer earnestly to inquire what God’s will might be. One day, returning from a journey when he was already approaching the place, he looked ahead in the distance. Behold, there appeared a great stone oratory, exceedingly beautiful. Examining its position, form, and construction carefully, he undertook the work confidently, having first disclosed the vision to the elder brethren, though only to a few.

He observed with such care everything that he had attentively noticed concerning its site, fashion, and character that, when the work had been completed, the thing made appeared most like the thing seen—as though he too had heard with Moses: “See that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40). By the same kind of vision, the place situated at Saballinum was shown to him beforehand before it was built—not only its oratory but the whole monastery.

## CHAPTER XXIX. He is distinguished by the spirit of prophecy and every grace of miracles.

[Col. 1111A]

64. As Malachy was passing through a certain city, while a large crowd ran together to him, he happened to notice among the others a young man curious to see him. The young man had climbed upon a stone and, standing on tiptoe, stretched out his neck and directed his eyes and mind toward Malachy, presenting to him a new Zacchaeus. It did not escape Malachy—by revelation of the Holy Spirit—that he had truly come in the spirit and power of Zacchaeus (Luke 19:2–9). Nevertheless, he concealed this at the time and passed on in silence.

That same night at the lodging he told the brethren how he had seen the young man and what he had foreseen concerning him. On the third day, behold, the young man came with a certain nobleman, his lord. The nobleman disclosed the young man’s vow and desire and asked that Malachy would graciously receive one commended by him and henceforth keep him among his own.

[Col. 1111B] Recognizing him, Malachy said: “There is no need for a man to commend one whom God has already commended.” Taking him by the hand, he handed him over to our abbot Congan, and Congan to the brethren. The young man himself—if I am not mistaken—still lives as the first lay convert of the monastery of Surius; all bear witness that he lives a holy converted life among the brethren according to the Cistercian order. The disciples recognized that Malachy possessed the spirit of prophecy in this matter as well, and not only here, but also in what we shall relate next.

65. While he was offering the Sacraments, and a deacon came near him to perform something belonging to his office, the priest looked at him and groaned because he sensed that the deacon harbored something unfitting. After the sacrifice had been completed, Malachy questioned him privately about his conscience. The deacon confessed and did not deny that he had been deceived in a dream that very night.

Imposing penance upon him, Malachy said: “You ought not to have ministered today. Rather, you should modestly have withdrawn from the sacred rites and shown reverence to mysteries so great and so divine, so that, purified by this humility, you might afterward minister more worthily.”

On another occasion, while Malachy was celebrating the sacrifice and praying at the hour of sacrifice with his customary holiness and purity of heart, the attendant deacon saw a dove enter through the window in great brightness. The priest was entirely bathed in its light, and the whole rather dark basilica shone. After circling for some time, the dove finally settled upon the cross before the priest’s face.

[Col. 1111D] The deacon was astonished. Afraid both because of the novelty of the light and of the bird—for that bird is rare in that land—he fell upon his face and, scarcely breathing, did not dare raise himself except when the necessity of his office required it. After Mass, Malachy called him aside and commanded him, under peril of his life, never to reveal the secret of what he had seen for as long as Malachy himself lived.

Once, when he was at Armagh with one of his fellow bishops, he rose at night and began to visit in prayer the memorials of the saints, of which there are many in the cemetery of Saint Patrick. Behold, they saw one of the altars suddenly burn. Both saw this great vision and both were astonished. But Malachy, understanding it as a sign of the great merit of the person or persons whose bodies rested beneath that altar, ran forward and plunged himself amid the flames; with outstretched arms he embraced the sacred altar. What he did there or what he felt, no one knows; but I think there is no one of the brethren who were then with him who does not know that he came forth from that fire more inflamed than usual by heavenly fire.

66. These things have been said—few among many, but many for the present time. For these are not times of signs, according to the saying: “We have not seen signs; there is no longer a prophet” (Ps. 73:9). From this it sufficiently appears how great my Malachy was in merits, since he was so abundant in signs, and in so great a rarity of signs. For in what kind of the miracles of the ancients did Malachy not shine? If we consider carefully even the few things which have been said, he lacked neither prophecy nor revelation, neither the punishment of the wicked nor the grace of healings, neither the changing of minds nor, finally, the raising of the dead.

Blessed be God in all things, who so loved and adorned him, who magnified him in the sight of kings and gave him a crown of glory. Love is proved in merits; adornment in signs; magnification in the punishment of enemies; glorification in the recompense of rewards. You have, devoted reader, in Malachy what to admire, and you also have what to imitate. Now attend diligently to what you ought to hope from these things. For their end is a precious death.

## CHAPTER XXX. He foretells the place and day of his death, and again undertakes a journey to Pope Eugenius for the sake of the pallium.

67. Once, when asked in what place, if he were given the choice, he would prefer to spend his last day—for the brethren were discussing among themselves which place each would choose—he hesitated and did not answer.
