When they pressed him, he said: “If I depart from here, nowhere would I more gladly be than where I may rise again with our Apostle.” He meant Saint Patrick. “But if I must live as a pilgrim, and God so permits, I have chosen Clairvaux.”

Asked also about the time, he named the solemn day of All Souls. If this is considered a simple wish, it was fulfilled; if a prophecy, not one iota failed. As we heard, so we saw, both concerning the place and concerning the day. Let us briefly recount in what order, and on what occasion, this came about.

He was greatly distressed that Ireland had until then lacked a pallium, being zealous for the sacraments and unwilling that his people should be wholly deprived of any one of them. Remembering that Pope Innocent had promised it to him, he grieved all the more that, while Innocent was still alive, it had not been sent for. When he found an opportunity because Pope Eugenius held the supreme governance and was reported to have come at that time as far as France, he rejoiced that he had found an occasion to make the request.

He was confident concerning Eugenius, as a man of such character and from such a profession; but even more because he had been a special son of his Clairvaux, and Malachy did not fear that he would encounter any difficulty with him. Therefore the bishops were summoned and a council convened. For three days they discussed matters pressing at the time; on the fourth day a proposal was made to request the pallium. It pleased them, provided it were requested through someone else. Yet because the journey was shorter and therefore seemed more bearable, no one presumed to oppose his counsel and wish.

[Col. 1113A] When the council had been dissolved, Malachy set out. The brethren who had assembled accompanied him to the shore, though not many, since he himself had expressly forbidden it. One of them, named Catholicus, spoke to him with tearful voice and countenance:

“Alas, you are leaving, and you know in what almost daily affliction you abandon me; yet you do not take pity and bring me help. If I deserve to suffer, what sin have the brethren committed, who are scarcely permitted to have a single day or night free from the laborious care and watchfulness required by me?”

By his words and tears—for he was weeping—the father’s heart was moved. Malachy embraced and comforted him, and, making the sign of the cross upon his breast, said: “Be assured that you will suffer nothing of this kind until I return.”

The man was epileptic and fell frequently, sometimes suffering not once but several times in a day. He had endured this dreadful disease for six years, but by Malachy’s word he was completely healed. From that hour he suffered nothing of the kind; and, as we trust, he will suffer nothing of the kind thereafter, because Malachy will not thereafter return.

68. As he was actually boarding the ship, two of those who adhered to him more intimately approached, daring to ask something of him.

“What do you want?” he said.

“We shall not tell you,” they replied, “unless you promise to grant it.”

He promised.

They said: “We want your graciousness to promise us certainly that you will return safely to Ireland.”

All the others also urged him. Then Malachy deliberated for a while, first regretting that he had bound himself, finding no way out. He was pressed on every side, as nothing occurred to him that would be safe from either danger: either that of the vow or that of the promise. At last he judged that he must choose what was more urgently required at present and entrust the remainder to divine providence. He consented, sorrowful indeed, yet more unwilling to grieve them; and, promising as they wished, he boarded the ship.

When they had almost completed half the sea voyage, a sudden contrary wind drove the ship back and brought it again to the land of Ireland. Disembarking, he spent the night in one of his churches in that very harbor. Joyfully he gave thanks to the counsel of divine providence, by which he had now fulfilled his promise. In the morning he boarded the ship; that same day he crossed with favorable sailing and came to Scotland.

On the third day he reached the place called Greenlake, which he had caused to be prepared for the establishment of an abbey. Leaving there a community of monks and an abbot from among his own sons—our brethren, whom he had brought with him for this very purpose—he bade them farewell and departed.

69. As he traveled, King David met him, received him joyfully, and kept him for several days. Having accomplished many things pleasing to God, Malachy resumed his journey. Passing through Scotland, he turned aside, upon entering England, to the church of Gisborough, where religious men lived a canonical life. They had long been dear to him because of their religious devotion and integrity.

[Col. 1114A] There a woman suffering from the disease commonly called cancer, dreadful in appearance, was brought to him, and he healed her. For when the places of the ulcers were sprinkled with water which he had blessed, she felt no pain; and on the following day the ulcers were scarcely visible.

Leaving there, he came to the sea, but was denied passage. The reason, I think, was a certain quarrel that had arisen between the supreme pontiff and the king of England. The king suspected—I know not what evil—of that good man should he cross, for he allowed no other bishops to cross either. Although this impediment opposed Malachy’s will, it did not oppose his desire. He was grieved that he was delayed from his desire, not knowing that through this very delay it would be more fully fulfilled. For if he had crossed immediately, he would have had to pass through Clairvaux as well in order to follow the supreme pontiff. Eugenius had already departed and was in Rome or near Rome. But now, through the intervening delay, it came about that, crossing later, he arrived at the place and hour of his most holy death at the fitting moment.

## CHAPTER XXXI. He comes again to Clairvaux, to die in the place and at the time he had desired.

70. He was received by us as the true “Dayspring from on high,” coming from the West to visit us. O how greatly that sun of brightness, shining upon our Clairvaux, increased its radiance! What a joyful festal day dawned for us at his entrance! “This is the day which the Lord has made” [variant: “given”]; let us rejoice and be glad in it! How quickly, though trembling and weak, I myself hastened to meet him! How joyfully I rushed into his kisses! With what joyful arms I embraced the grace sent to me from heaven! With what eager face and heart, my father, I brought you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who conceived me! How festively afterward I spent days with you—yet few!

And what, in return, was he to us? Our pilgrim showed himself cheerful and gracious to all, incredibly welcome to all. What a good and pleasant guest he was among those whom, indeed, he had come from the ends of the earth to see—not to hear Solomon, but to present him! We heard his wisdom, we possessed his presence, and we still possess it.

Four or five days of this our festivity had passed when, behold, on the feast day of the blessed evangelist Luke, after he had celebrated Mass in the community with that holy devotion of his, he was seized by fever and took to his bed—and all of us with him. Sorrow seized the end of our joy, though more moderately because the fever at first seemed slight.

You could see the brethren hurrying about, eager either to give or to receive. To whom was it not sweet to see him? To whom was it not sweeter to minister to him? Both were delightful; both were salutary. It was an act of humanity to render service, and it was each person’s own spiritual gain when he received grace in return. All stood by; all were attentive to the abundant service: seeking medicines, applying remedies, urging him more frequently to take nourishment.

To them he said: “What you are doing is unnecessary, but out of love for you I do whatever you prescribe.” [Col. 1115A] For he knew that the time of his departure was near.

71. When the brethren who had come with him pressed him more confidently, saying that he ought not to despair of life, since no signs of death appeared in him, he said: “Malachy must leave the body this year.” And he added: “Behold, the day approaches which, as you know very well, I always wished to be the very day of my release. I know in whom I have believed, and I am certain: I shall not be disappointed of the remainder of my desire, since I already possess part of it. He who in his mercy brought me to the place I sought will not refuse me the end which I likewise wished. As for this little body, here is my rest; as for the soul, the Lord will provide, he who saves those who hope in him. Nor is there a little hope laid up for me on that day when such great benefits are bestowed by the living upon the dead.”

That very day was not far off when he spoke these things. Meanwhile he ordered himself to be anointed with the holy oil. When the gathering of brethren came out so that this might be performed solemnly, he did not allow them to come up to him; he himself went down to them. For he lay in an upper room on the upper story of the house. He would not wait for them to come up to him, but himself went down to them. He was anointed and received the Viaticum; commending himself to the brethren’s prayers and the brethren to God, he returned to bed. He went down the stairs from the upper room on his own feet and likewise went back up on his own feet; yet he said that death was at the doors.

Who would have believed this man was about to die? He alone and God could know it. His face did not seem paler or thinner; his brow was not wrinkled, his eyes were not sunken, his nostrils were not sharpened, his lips not drawn tight, his teeth not darkened, his neck not wasted and slender, his shoulders not bent, nor was the flesh depleted from the rest of his body. Such was the grace of his body and the glory of his countenance, which did not fade even in death. Such as he appeared while living, such he appeared dead—more like one alive.

72. We have run thus far; but now we halt, because Malachy has finished his course. He stands still, and we stand still with him. For who willingly runs toward death? Above all, toward yours, holy father—who can recount it? Who would wish to hear it? Yet we loved one another in life; in death we shall not be separated. Brothers, let us not abandon in death the one whom we accompanied in life. From the furthest Scotland he ran here to death; let us also go and die with him.

We must, we must speak of what we were compelled to see. Everywhere the bright festival of All Saints is at hand; but, according to the old saying, “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” (Sirach 22:6). We are present and sing, though unwillingly. We sing while weeping and weep while singing. Though Malachy does not sing, he does not weep: for what should one weep over who approaches joy? Grief remains to us who are left behind; Malachy alone keeps festival.

For what he cannot do with his body, he does in his mind, as it is written: “The thought of man shall praise you, and the remnant of thought shall keep a feast for you” (Ps. 75:11). Since the instrument of his body fails him, the organ of his mouth is silent, and the function of his voice has ceased, it remains for him to celebrate with the rejoicing of the mind. Why should not the saint celebrate, who is being led to the festival of the saints? He offers them what will shortly be due to himself. A little while longer, and he himself will be one of them.

73. At nightfall, when the day’s celebration had somehow been completed by us, Malachy was drawing near—not to twilight, but to dawn. Was it not dawn for him, whose night had preceded and whose day drew near? Thus, as the fever intensified, burning sweat began to break forth from his inmost parts over his whole body, so that, as one passing through fire and water, he might be brought into refreshment. His life was now despaired of; each person reproached his own judgment; no one any longer doubted that Malachy’s pronouncement would prevail.

We were summoned; we came. Raising his eyes toward those around him, he said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you. I give thanks to the heavenly goodness: I have not been disappointed of my desire.”

Do you see a man secure in death, and not yet dead, already certain of life? Nor is this surprising. Seeing that the night which he had awaited was at hand, and that in it dawn was breaking for him, he seemed, as it were, to triumph over the night and taunt the darkness, saying in some manner: “I shall no longer say, ‘Perhaps darkness will trample me,’ because this night is illumination for me in my delights.”

And gently consoling us, he said: “Take care of me; I shall not forget you, if it is permitted. And it will be permitted. I have believed in God, and all things are possible to one who believes. I have loved God; I have loved you; and charity never fails.”

Looking up to heaven, he said: “God, preserve them in your name—not only these, but also all who through my word and ministry have bound themselves to your service.”

Then, laying his hands upon each one and blessing them all, he commanded them to go and rest, because his hour had not yet come.

74. We go; we return about the middle of the night, for at that hour light is announced as shining in darkness. The house is filled; the whole assembly is present, and many abbots who had gathered. With psalms and hymns and spiritual songs we accompany our friend as he returns to his homeland. In the fifty-fourth year of his age, in the place and at the time which Malachy, bishop and legate of the holy Apostolic See, had chosen beforehand and foretold, he happily fell asleep in the Lord—as though taken from our hands by angels.

And truly he fell asleep. His peaceful face was a sign of his peaceful departure. Indeed, everyone’s eyes were fixed upon him; yet no one could have noticed when he departed. The dead man was thought to live, and the living man dead: so completely did nothing intervene to distinguish one condition from the other. The same liveliness of countenance remained, the same serenity as is usually seen in one asleep. You would have said that death had taken away none of these things, but had rather greatly increased them. He was not changed; rather, he himself changed everyone. In a marvelous way the grief and groaning of all suddenly ceased: sorrow was changed into joy, and song banished lamentation. He is borne forth; voices are borne heavenward; upon the shoulders of abbots he is carried into the oratory. Faith has prevailed, affection triumphs, the matter has returned to its proper state: everything is done in order, everything proceeds according to reason.

691 75. And indeed, what reason is there for mourning Malachy without measure [Col. 1117A], as though his death were not precious; as though it were not sleep rather than death; as though it were not the harbor of death and the gate of life? Our friend Malachy sleeps, and shall I mourn? This grief defends itself by custom, not by reason. If the Lord has given sleep to his beloved—and such a sleep, in which are the inheritance of the Lord, children as a reward, the fruit of the womb—what in all this seems to call for weeping? Shall I weep for one who has escaped weeping? He rejoices, he triumphs, he has been brought into the joy of his Lord; and shall I lament him? I desire these things for myself; I do not begrudge them to him.

Meanwhile the funeral rites are prepared; the sacrifice is offered for him; all things are completed according to custom with the utmost devotion. At a distance stood a boy whose withered arm hung at his side, more a hindrance than a use to him. When this became known, I motioned for him to approach; taking his shriveled hand, I laid it upon the Bishop’s hand, and [Col. 1118A] he restored it to life. Surely the grace of healings lived in the dead man; and his hand was to the dead hand what Elisha was to the dead man (IV Kings 13:21). That boy had come from far away, and returned to his homeland with the hand which he had brought hanging limp restored to health.

When all things had duly been performed, he was committed to burial in the very oratory of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in which Malachy had taken great pleasure, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1148, on the fourth day before the Nones of November [2 November]. Your deposit, good Jesus, is that which has been entrusted to us; your treasure is that which is laid up among us. We keep him to be claimed back at the time when you judge that he should be required of us—only let him not go forth without his companions, but let us have as our leader him whom we had as a guest, that we may reign together with you and with him for ever and ever. Amen.

> [Note: [Col. 1117A] You have two sermons of Bernard on St Malachy in the third volume.]

[Col. 1117]

## HYMN ON ST MALACHY

(Martène, *Amplissima collectio*, vol. I, col. 746, from the manuscript of Vieux-Mont.)

[Col. 1117]

Noble in signs, gentle in character,  
holy in merits, illustrious in triumphs,  
today, relieved of the body’s burden,  
the bishop departed.

Nor is the name Malachy without significance for the man:  
sounding “angel,” it signifies that he was  
like the angels in purity of life  
and their equal in glory.

Our angel, restored to the desires of his fellow citizens  
and joined to their choirs,  
excels many and is equalled with the highest—  
and deservedly so.

His sober manner of life, perpetual chastity,  
faith, teaching, and gains for souls  
join him, equal in merits,  
to the company of the apostles.

In deed he held their office, in spirit their virtue,  
this bishop and legate;  
and therefore he rightly  
claims their honor also for himself.

[Col. 1118]

If you seek signs, who could recount them?  
Yet this I say: sufficiently evident  
was how great his glory was in this respect—  
the dead rose again.

Do we suppose that Christ now reigning has any care  
for us whom he formerly loved—  
the poor whom he cherished, the humble in spirit—  
he himself being humble?

Far be it from that fountain of mercy,  
now raised to a higher lot, to flow more sluggishly;  
far be it that the blessed father  
should despise his miserable orphaned children.

O Malachy, your Clairvaux,  
made more illustrious by the treasure of your body,  
humbly asks that, under your protection,  
it may enjoy everlasting peace.

Glory to the Father and to his Son;  
glory to you, Spirit of them both.  
One majesty be yours,  
because the Three are One.

[Col. 1117]

## NOTICE TO OPUSCULUM XIII: ST BERNARD, ABBOT, ON THE ANTIPHONARY OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER

692 1. The book *On the Theory of Chant*, attributed to Bernard, was once supplied to me by John Bona, of pious and venerable memory—at that time Abbot General of his congregation and later cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. A letter is prefixed to the book which I judged to be Bernard’s; but the treatise itself should be assigned to those associates whom he enlisted to assist in this undertaking, as the letter itself clearly indicates.

In the Fesny codex the same opusculum is attributed to Guy, Abbot of Cherlieu, under this title: “Letter of Lord Guy, Abbot of Cherlieu, on Chant.” It begins with these words [Col. 1119]: “The chant which the churches of the Cistercian Order have been accustomed to sing,” etc. The treatise, however, begins: “But we wish those especially to be forewarned,” etc.

Guy of Cherlieu, abbot in the diocese of Besançon, is the man for whose benefit Bernard wrote Letter 197 and the two following letters. What prevents me from being wholly convinced that he was the author of this treatise is that, near the end, the author calls the churches of Reims, Beauvais, Amiens, and Soissons “fellow-provincials.” Further, when mentioning the Antiphonary of Soissons, he adds, “which you have, as it were, at your door.” From this it seems more probable that the author was a monk or abbot of Longpont, not far from the city of Soissons. Perhaps he was the book’s author together with Guy, Abbot of Cherlieu; for Bernard employed several associates for this work. Might he be Gerard, Abbot of Longpont, praised in Book VII of the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 11? Or perhaps another Guy was then abbot of Cherlieu near Senlis?

2. Some doubt whether this treatise was in fact written during Bernard’s lifetime, because certain opening words of the letter and treatise imply that these writings were composed long after the beginnings of the Cistercian Order. Yet a treatise of this sort, recently put together, was preserved in the copy of the Bible corrected by Stephen, third Abbot of Cîteaux, according to whose standard all Bibles of the same Order were commanded to be corrected; and the same thing was prescribed concerning the Antiphonary. Such was the care and concern of the first members of that Order for sacred matters.

This treatise, I say, was attached to that original corrected copy of the Bible, but later torn from it, as I myself discovered from the table of contents and from the vacant space. Certainly this opusculum is understood to have been composed in those first times of the Order from its beginning, where mention is made of the Cistercians who then “held the truth,” that is, the purity, “of the Rule,” “passing over the dispensations of others.” This must be understood of the earliest period.

Moreover, in the book of Cistercian Institutes—believed to have been compiled in 1134 by Rainard, Abbot of Cîteaux—the Antiphonary is assigned in chapter 12 among the books necessary for newly founded monasteries; this treatise was prefixed to it in the Cistercian codex. But all doubt is removed by the *Life of Stephen, Abbot of Obazine*, written by his contemporary and recently published by the learned Baluze in volume IV of the *Miscellanies*. In chapter 13 of Book II the following words occur:

> “It should be known that the books which the Cistercians first used in the divine offices were very corrupt and faulty, and remained so until the time of St Bernard. Then, by the common decree of the abbots, they were corrected and amended by that holy abbot and his cantors, and arranged as they are now held.”

Nothing more explicit than this testimony can be offered.

3. In the *Supplement of the Fathers*, published at Paris in 1684 by the Augustinian Reverend Father Jacques Hommey, a treatise *On the Method of Singing the Gradual* is appended to the booklet *On the Method of Singing the Antiphonary*. Since Bernard’s letter makes no mention of it, but only of the Antiphonary, one may rightly doubt whether it should be attributed to Bernard or to his associates in this work; and still more so concerning the other pieces in Hommey, which we do not think belong to Bernard.

Here should be appended the notice concerning this opusculum sent to me by the late most devout John Bona, as follows.

693 “Dom John Bona, Abbot General of the Reformed Congregation of St Bernard of the Cistercian Order, greetings to the reader.

“In the celebrated Cistercian monastery of Saint Saviour on Mount Amiata, in the diocese of Siena, there is an old Antiphonary of the same Order, which the monks brought with them from Cîteaux when the Cistercian reform was first introduced into that monastery by the Venerable Abbot Rayner in the year of the Lord 1231. This treatise, attributed to Dom Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, is prefixed to that Antiphonary. Nor do I doubt that other copies of it are found in other abbeys of the Order.

“Charles de Visch, in his *Cistercian Library*, mentions one in these words: ‘In the monastery of Loos in Flanders there is preserved an unpublished letter of the same St Bernard on the theory of chant, whose beginning is: “Bernard, humble abbot of Clairvaux.”’ Possevino, in Book XV, chapter 6, of his *Selected Library*, counts St Bernard among the other writers who have written on music.

“Angelo Picittonese, a Friar Minor, published at Venice in 1547 *Two Books of the Angelic Flower on Plainchant and Figured Song*. In the first book he cites much from this treatise, especially in chapter 29: ‘St Bernard proves this in his *Music*, saying, where it is appropriate to produce a softer sound: B-flat is sometimes placed, yet secretly, lest the chant seem to assume the likeness of another mode.’ Likewise in chapter 46, on the endings of the modes: ‘St Bernard, most learned both in divine and human sciences, sets down these letters in his carefully weighed *Music*, where he says that the letters D, E, F, G are the final notes of chants.’ And in chapter 47, on the ascent and descent of the modes: ‘Every mode,’ he says, ‘can have ten notes, as St Bernard, no less truthful than learned, plainly sets forth in the carefully considered prologue to his *Music*, assigning three principal reasons: namely, the authority of the Psalter, equality of dignity, and the necessity of notation.’

“Since all these matters occur exactly in this treatise, it follows sufficiently clearly that Bernard is its author. Nor does the style conflict with this attribution, insofar as the special terminology of music permits. Musicians commonly use the barbarous word *maneria* or *maneries* [‘mode’], which is frequently repeated here. It is also found in the little treatise *On Practical Music*, attributed to Bede; but the musical signs, nearly three hundred years later than Bede, prove that attribution mistaken, as do many matters there taken word for word from the *Doctrinal* and the *Micrologus* of Guido of Arezzo. Bernard himself also used the word in Letter 402, to Baldwin.

“From these facts it is evident how diligently our forebears took care that, with every impropriety and novelty removed from the divine offices, ecclesiastical gravity and majesty might be preserved both in chant and in words. I had intended to elucidate this treatise with fuller notes; but after more mature consideration I refrained, for they would be superfluous to those skilled in musical theory and useless to the unlearned. Meanwhile, see what I discuss concerning ecclesiastical chant and the modes in chapter 17, §§3–4, of my *Harmony of the Singing Church*.”

## LETTER OR PROLOGUE

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121A] 694 BERNARD, humble Abbot of Clairvaux, to all who shall copy this Antiphonary or sing from it.

Among the other matters in which our fathers—the founders, that is, of the Cistercian Order—were most laudably zealous, they also took the most diligent and devout care that in the divine praises they should sing what was found to be more authentic. Accordingly, men were sent to copy and bring back the Antiphonary of the Church of Metz, for it was said to be Gregorian. They found the matter far different from what they had heard. Therefore, when it had been examined, it displeased them, because both its chant and its text were found faulty, excessively ill-arranged, and almost wholly contemptible.

Yet because they had once begun with it and had used it, they retained it down to our own time [Col. 1121B]. At length, since our brethren, the abbots of the Order, could no longer endure it and had resolved that it should be changed and corrected, they entrusted the task to our care. I therefore summoned from among our brethren [Col. 1122A] those found more instructed and expert in the art and practice of singing. From many and diverse materials we at last compiled into the volume below a new Antiphonary, irreproachable, as we believe, both in chant and in text. Indeed, its singer, if knowledgeable, will approve it.

Therefore we will that, as it has finally been altered and is contained in this volume, it be henceforth observed throughout our monasteries both in text and in notation. We forbid anyone whatever to alter it in any respect, by the authority of the whole chapter, by which it was unanimously adopted and confirmed by all the abbots. But anyone who wishes to know the cause and rationale of this alteration more clearly and fully should read the prefatory statement set below, which the aforementioned examiners of the old Antiphonary took care to place before this work, [Col. 1122B] so that, once the faults in its chant and text had been openly shown, the necessity and usefulness of the revision and correction might appear more clearly.

## PREFACE OR TREATISE ON CHANT, OR ON THE CORRECTION OF THE ANTIPHONARY

[Col. 1121]

[Col. 1121C] 1. Although serious and manifold absurdity obscured the chant which the churches of the Cistercian Order had been accustomed to sing, the authority of those singing it nevertheless commended it for a long time.

> [Note: [Col. 1121] Cicero, *On the Laws* II; Plutarch, *On Music*; and others teach that chant cannot be changed without a change of morals.]

But since it seemed altogether unworthy that those who had undertaken to live according to a rule should sing God’s praises irregularly, you will find that, with their consent, the chant has been so corrected that, once the filth of falsehood has been removed and the unlawful liberties of the unskilled expelled, it is supported by the whole truth of the rules and is more convenient than the chants of others—by which it had been inferior—for notation and singing.

For it is fitting that those who hold to the truth of the Rule, passing over the dispensations of others, 695 should also possess a correct knowledge of singing, rejecting the liberties of those who attend more to resemblance than to nature in chants: they separate things that belong together and join opposites; and thus, confusing everything, they begin and end, lower and raise, compose and arrange chant as they please, not as is permitted. Therefore no one should be surprised or offended if he finds that chant, heard otherwise than hitherto, has been changed in many places. For there either the progression is irregular, or an opposition resists the progression or arrangement [variant: “composition”], or an opposition dissolves an opposition. Since all these are defects of the rules, destroying perfection rather than defining it, they are wholly far from those who know how to cut off defects rather than dispense with them.

Finally, since music is the correct knowledge of singing, all chants of this sort are excluded from music, because they are sung not correctly but irregularly and disorderly. The excuse for altering the text is easy, unless we are mistaken [Col. 1123A]. We found it in many places so sparse and restricted that the same verse was repeated three or four times in the same historia, as if nothing could be found in the whole Old and New Testament which might be fitted in equally appropriately. In many histories also we found Postcommunions placed as Responsories by those who do not understand the simplicity of Antiphonary chant; the verses attached to them cohere so miserably that they could not be notated as their pronunciation required.

2. We have therefore taken pains that no verse should occur more than once in any historia; indeed, unless we are mistaken, you will scarcely find three verses in the whole Antiphonary which occur even twice. We removed certain Postcommunions and put in their place customary and authentic responsories. In other cases we retained the text as holy and evangelical, but overlaid it with the grace and beauty of chant, everywhere preserving music that is nevertheless restrained and modest.

Finally, in many places we discovered the text of the old Antiphonary to be so slack and disordered that, sprinkled with many falsehoods or with the trifles of apocryphal writings, it produced not merely weariness but even hatred in its readers. Thus novices who had been trained under ecclesiastical discipline, finding the Antiphonary distasteful and unfamiliar both in text and notation, became slower and sleepier in the divine praises.

But we especially wish those who are to notate books to be forewarned not to separate linked neumes or join separated ones [Col. 1123C], because through such variation a serious dissimilarity of chants can arise. Furthermore, they should strive to end each chant on its own proper final notes; for through their thoughtless alteration such confusion has arisen in chants that many belong to one *maneria* [mode] and are assigned to another.

3. There are four distinctions, or *maneriae*, of chants, within which all their multiplicity is contained. Among the Greeks these are called *protos* [first], *deuteros* [second], *tritos* [third], and *tetradus* [fourth]. They are opposed to one another and differ by definite properties. The first *maneria* is that which, from the note on which it ends, rises by a tone after a semitone and descends by a tone. It has only two finals, D and A [Col. 1123D], each of which has immediately above it a tone and then a semitone, and immediately below it a tone.

The second *maneria* is that which rises from the note on which it ends by a semitone and a tone, and descends by a tone. It likewise has two finals, E and B-square, at which you naturally find precisely that ascent and descent. The third *maneria* rises by two tones and descends by a semitone; it likewise has two finals, F and C, as capable of such properties. The fourth rises by two tones and descends by a tone, and has only one final, G.

The first *maneria* contains two modes, commonly called tones: namely, the first and second. The second contains two, the third and fourth; the third, two, the fifth and sixth; and the fourth [Col. 1124A], two, the seventh and eighth. The pairs of tones contained under each *maneria* are not distinguished from each other by a difference of finals, which they have entirely in common, but by progression and composition. Of these, one determines quantity and the other quality.

Therefore, you who are to notate books, impress carefully upon your memory that all chants of the first *maneria* which have been made, or which can regularly be made, ought to end only on D and A; and every chant that can be placed upon either of these is certainly of the first *maneria*, that is, of the first or second tone.

“You will say that both assertions are false: for not all chants of the first *maneria* can end only there, since through B-round they also place their ending on G; nor are all chants which end there of the first *maneria*, because the antiphons ‘Blessed are you in …’ and ‘Peter, do you love me?’ and many similar ones can end only on A, and yet they are of the second *maneria*, assigned to the fourth tone.”

This opinion has already deceived many, having been introduced through the addition of B-round, by which the presumption of the unskilled has stained music with many errors. Certainly the property of finals is distinguished not according to something added accidentally, but according to the original and proper arrangement of the letters, upon which the principal and greatest judgment concerning chant rests.

In the natural reckoning of the letters you will find seven which are called low notes. These were doubled in order that chant might range more freely; some were even tripled. In the doubling you find the high notes, and in the tripling [Col. 1124C] the highest notes. If you consider the relations of each letter to the neighboring letters placed on either side, you will assuredly find none except D and A which rises by a tone and a semitone and descends by a tone. Hence these alone are finals of the first *maneria*, whose proper characteristic is to rise and descend in this fashion. G is therefore excluded, because in the natural order of the letters—both where it is first placed and where it is repeated—it rises directly not by a tone and semitone but by two tones.

4. In this order of letters B-round is not counted. For it is obvious to all that it is not one of the low notes, since it is nowhere placed among them; nor is it one of the high notes, since it is joined to none of the low notes by a doubled proportion [octave]. It was invented not to determine the property of finals but to preserve euphony in many chants, which the tritone ending at B-square would diminish or destroy.

Therefore, in any *maneria*, wherever it is appropriate to make a softer sound, B-round is sometimes placed in place of B-square, but furtively and briefly, lest through it the chant acquire the likeness of another mode. For B-round occupies no line or space in books as determined by any letter, unless it is actually added. And if B-square occurs once, every trace of B-round is erased from the book until the aforesaid necessity requires it again.

If, therefore, through it you were to end some chant of the first *maneria* on G [Col. 1125A], you would be acting wholly against its invention and opposing the establishment of finals; for no chant ought to end outside the final of its *maneria*. If you say that G is a final of the first *maneria* through B-round, I answer that this cannot be. For in order to be a final of the first *maneria*, it would be necessary for it to rise by tone and semitone according to the natural arrangement of the letters, and neither B-round nor anything else can confer this upon it.

Although, then, it may be conceded that chants of the first *maneria* can somehow be notated or sung on G through B-round, it must by no means be conceded that G, in this way or any other, is its final, because of the necessity mentioned above. What advantage, then, or what skill is there in notating a chant incidentally on an alien final when you can notate it on its natural and proper one—with greater security because more irreproachably, greater praise because more carefully, and greater pleasure because more truthfully?

For this reason, lest you be found faulty or superfluous, take care to place B-round where necessity requires it, since necessity devised it. No chant which can be notated without it ought to be notated by means of it. Which chants cannot be notated without it? Those which, at the same letter, have now a tone and now a semitone. Yet because imperfect singers are less familiar with the highest letters and those adjoining them, custom, yielding to their weakness, notates some chants lower through B-round which could more conveniently be notated without it at the aforementioned letters.

But we, wishing that the upper notes as well as the lower [Col. 1125C] should be in use and known—for otherwise they would be had in vain—have ended on the lower notes every chant which nature assigns to them. Those chants are ended on the upper notes which naturally have them as finals. The same must be understood concerning the antiphon “Blessed are you,” and similar chants, which can end only on A: according to this arrangement they are undoubtedly of the first *maneria*, and should be assigned not to the fourth tone but to the second.

For see: this antiphon “Blessed are you” at one point naturally has, above its final, a tone and then a semitone through B-square; elsewhere it has first a semitone and then a tone through B-round. What discernment, I ask, is this in judging to which *maneria* a chant belongs: preferring an accident to nature, and judging it to be of the second *maneria* according to an accidental arrangement when it is of the first according to the natural one?

To make you wonder and recoil still more from such foolishness, examine the antiphon “Peter, do you love me?” and many others of this sort. You will certainly find that they naturally have, above the final, a tone and a semitone through B-flat, and nowhere a semitone and a tone through B-round. Why, then, are they judged to be of the second *maneria*? Likewise, the antiphon “We who live,” as it is sung almost everywhere, properly and principally ought to end on D and is of the second tone; yet wicked transgressors notate it on G through B-round and solemnly affirm that it is of the eighth tone, although at G through B-round a chant of the first *maneria* rather than of the fourth is ended among them [Col. 1126A]. What musician, I ask, could patiently endure that a chant having D as its proper and natural final should be assigned to the eighth tone, while one having A as its proper and natural final should be included under the fourth tone?

5. These chants ending on A, in which resemblance stifles nature, therefore require correction. For, rendered incoherent by an addition which contaminates the parts of their composition, they suggest one tone at the beginning and another at the end. In the most ancient libraries of great monasteries there is found a very elegant compendium of musical art which begins thus: “Since there are few …”; I read part of it, but do not recall reading the author’s name [Col. 1126B]. In it, if I remember correctly, chants of this sort are called *nothi*, that is, spurious and illegitimate, because, as is read there, they begin in the seventh tone, preserve it in the middle, and near the end degenerate, some ending in the first tone and others in the fourth: in the first, as “From the time when she was made”; in the fourth, as “Blessed are you.”

Accordingly, with their endings suitably changed, you will find all chants of this sort reduced to the seventh tone. There are two kinds of these chants. Some rise cheerfully from the letter on which they begin to the fifth and rest on it. Unless beneath that note there were first a tone, then a semitone, and afterwards three tones—which arrangement can be found only beneath the letter which is the fifth above the final of the seventh tone—the remaining parts of those chants could not be notated there. You may see this in “Blessed are you” and similar chants, which use this arrangement both at their beginning and throughout their whole body, and which, by changing the semitone near the end through B-round, properly receive the nature of the second tone and the likeness of the fourth. Therefore, because they require alteration near the end, they have been corrected in that part.

Others are those which are immediately lowered by a tone from the letter on which they begin and, returning to the fourth, rest upon it; this seems more characteristic of plagal modes, as in “The Lord rules me” and “After childbirth.” You will therefore find these altered not only at the end but also at the beginning, so that they may conform everywhere to the seventh tone.

Again, you must be forewarned concerning the finals of the third and fourth *maneriae*, where a great confusion is likewise found [Col. 1126D]. There are certain most wretched chants which possess the property of no *maneria* and can end equally on C and G, which are finals of different *maneriae*. Some who have examined this matter more carefully say—and say correctly—that all chants which are distinguished by the certainty of no *maneria* are irregular. They judge that the progression of all these chants ought either to be extended or their composition varied, so that they can in no way end on finals of different *maneriae*.

Accordingly, you will find that their uncertainty has been removed from these most wretched chants lightly and briefly, so that you will no longer be doubtful to which finals you ought to assign each of them. Therefore end all chants of the first *maneria*, that is, of the first or second tone [Col. 1127A], as we have said, on D or A. End all of the second *maneria*, that is, of the third and fourth tone, on E or B-square. Although B-square is naturally capable of receiving both authentic and plagal chants, you will find no authentic chant in the Antiphonary which you can end on it. For if it is a responsory, the verse of that authentic mode cannot suit it, since it has a semitone under the sixth letter at which it begins; but if it is the antiphon *Saeculorum* [“of the ages”], it cannot receive the same authentic mode for the same reason.

6. For you cannot end on B-square a chant which rises by a diapente [fifth] and a semitone to the sixth, because B-square does not have a diapente above it.

> [Note: [Col. 1127D] More recent writers deny that the third and fourth tones can end on B-flat, because the tritone and the semidiapente stand in the way.]

For this reason they did not find in the third tone a verse, neume, and *saeculorum* altogether suitable [Col. 1127B]. Yet perhaps they considered both the barrenness of B-square and its suitability: its barrenness, in composing the verse, neume, and *saeculorum*, which are suitable only for chants ending on E; and its suitability, by using the sixth in place of the fifth, so that if fruitfulness should ever succeed the barrenness of that final, a letter would be ready to receive its authentic elevation.

Among us, however, you will find an authentic chant ending on B-square, namely “As they were going” [variant addition: “and you, God the Father”]; it cannot end elsewhere. It has neither the common verse nor can have it, but has one proper to itself.

Moreover, end all chants of the third *maneria*, that is, of the fifth and sixth tone, on F or C—assigning F to the greater part of authentic chants, and C to almost all plagal chants [Col. 1127C]. But you must end all chants of the fourth *maneria*, that is, of the seventh and eighth tone, on G alone.

Know that among these seven letters not one is more and another less, but all are equally principal and proper finals, possessing both the elevation of authentic and the descent of plagal chants. They begin at low D and end at high C; for above or below these you will find none which does not lack the completeness either of elevation or of descent. In order that each might excel in fullness of progression, musicians arranged the letters from Greek Γ (*gamma*) to the highest *ee*.

> [Note: [Col. 1127D] In the manuscript this letter is H, which signifies [Col. 1128D] E—that is, E-la in Guido’s monochord.]

They did this not because they preferred excess to deficiency, but because they wished neither to exceed nor to fall short, making an arrangement which could not be narrower without inconvenience or longer without superfluity [Col. 1127D]. Why indeed would you add anything, when this arrangement suffices for the fullness stated above? Conversely, if you removed anything from it, you would certainly deprive some final of the dignity of that same fullness.

7. Moreover, there are many chants in which you will find a sesquialteral (*hemiolia*) or sesquitertian (*epitritus*) descent subtracted from the double ascent which they normally possess.  
[Note: [Col. 1128D] *Hemiolia* is a ratio of 3:2; *epitritus*, of 4:3.]  
Such are “Cornelius,” “Holy Paul,” and many others. For all chants of this sort are double and irregular: double because they are partly authentic and partly plagal.  
[Note: [Col. 1128D] Tones of this sort are called mixed.]  
That they thus rise and fall contrary to rule is admitted even by the teachers of error themselves; but they say that this happens by licence, confusing the rules in order to retain defects, rather than cutting away defects in order to preserve the rules. What sort of licence is this, which traverses the realm of dissimilarity, brings in the confusion of uncertainty, is the mother of presumption and refuge of error, suppresses truth, and disturbs judgment? What, I say, is this unlawful licence, which joins opposites and crosses natural boundaries, inflicting upon nature an injury as much as it produces an unseemly conjunction?

For it is clearer than daylight that a chant is badly and disorderly composed when it is either lowered so far that it cannot be heard as it ought to be, or raised so far that it cannot be sung. It ought therefore to be arranged so that it has a hearer in its lower notes and a singer in its higher ones. Some have wished the span of this moderation to consist of eight notes, others of nine, considering not the possibility of shouting voices, but of ordinary voices. Yet, according to those whose opinion seems more exact, a chant may extend to ten notes, because of the authority of the Psalter, which is ten-stringed; and so that the individual notes of the octave, which are eight, may be equal in dignity: thus the outermost notes, like the middle ones, may have a double capacity—namely, to rise and to fall—when two notes are placed on either side, one above and the other below. [Col. 1128C] For chants have scope through only eight notes, and not more; therefore the octave is sufficient for the regular course of chants. Although, with the two notes placed on either side as stated, ten notes are found in the course of a chant, the chant nevertheless runs not through ten notes but only through the eight middle notes; it may reach the notes placed at either side, but it must not proceed or return through them.

And, what is more, according to the arrangement of tones and semitones used by musicians—who assign a tone above and below to the first, fourth, and seventh letters; a tone below and a semitone above to the second and fifth; and conversely, a tone above and a semitone below to the third and sixth, sometimes employing rounded B (*B rotundum*) because of the harshness of the tritone—according to this arrangement, I say, no chant of ten notes or fewer can be made which cannot be notated; but an eleven-note chant can be made which cannot be notated. For make a chant authentic of the third *maneria*, and give its arrangement a tone in one place and a semitone in another; then raise that chant through ten notes, so that there are eleven, adding the note which lies in the descent. You may be sure that such a chant cannot be notated, because it cannot end below high C; since in its descent below the final it has now a tone, now a semitone, and neither can it end there, because the chant exceeds superacute *ee*.

8. There are therefore three reasons why ten notes are assigned to chants: the authority of the Psalter, equality of dignity, and the necessity of notation. In accordance with this sufficiency of ten notes, musicians considered the fullness of melodic progression; because of it they extended the aforementioned arrangement, which was to be assigned to each final, from Greek Γ (*gamma*) to *ee*. Otherwise the scheme would be insufficient and would not give each final a complete ascent.

Plagal modes order these ten notes differently in their course. We call authentic those of greater authority—the first, third, fifth, and seventh—which refuse to be weighted down or depressed, but, light in leaps and agile in movement, frequent the fifth letter and those above it. Beneath their final, which is one of the ten notes, they place one note, and above it eight. Plagal modes are those of lesser dignity—the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth—which rarely touch or pass the fifth, but prefer to linger weightily below it. Setting their finals, as it were, in the middle, they place four notes below and five above them, by a fair plausibility of reason: that by as many notes as they are surpassed in ascent, they may surpass the authentic modes in descent. Therefore no plagal mode ought to rise beyond the sixth, and no authentic mode ought to descend by more than one note. Clearly, then, those are mad who presume to raise a plagal mode through an octave, or to lower an authentic mode through a fifth [*diapente*] or fourth [*diatessaron*]. Why indeed are such chants made or retained—burdensome to notate, more burdensome to sing, varying their lines, tormenting the vocal passages, having a cauterized [variant: “cavernous”] progression, now rising to heaven, now descending to the abyss?

Indeed, lest chants of this kind should be made, Wido testifies that it was deliberately arranged that each of the four modes—*protus*, *deuterus*, *tritus*, and *tetradus*—should be divided in two, that is, into authentic and plagal, and that, with rules distributed, high things should accord with high things and low with low. For since chants of this sort are low and plain in one part of themselves, but high and elevated in another, verses and psalms sung in one and the same manner cannot suitably be fitted to them in different ways. What follows, if it is low, does not suit the high; if high, it disagrees with the low. The same Wido also forbids this abuse of ascent and descent in antiphons and responsories, to whose chants psalms and verses must be fitted. For when the chant is mixed and double, while the verse and the “of the ages” (*saeculorum*) are sung either wholly authentically or wholly plagal, they cannot properly be adapted to the chant of that mode; for there are many chants in which lowliness and height are so confused that one can scarcely perceive to which they should rather be assigned, that is, to the authentic or the plagal.

[Col. 1130A] 9. Since the necessary boundaries of nature prohibit it, it is impossible for more than four *maneriae* to be found. These themselves are expressed in eight modes according to the descent of the plagal and the ascent of the authentic modes. Each pair—namely, an authentic mode and its plagal—agrees entirely in *maneria*, but differs on the one hand in the descent and ascent of melodic progression, and on the other in the brightness and gravity of composition: the authentic modes claiming ascent and brightness, the plagal retaining descent and gravity.

10. In order to distinguish these from one another, “neumes” were devised to be appended to individual antiphons. Among some they are called “stivae”; among the Greeks they are indicated by the words “Hoa nocane” and “nocais,”  
[Note: [Col. 1129D] Thus in the manuscript. Elsewhere: *noe anc* and *noe ais*.]  
and similar expressions. These indeed signify nothing, but were invented by the Greeks solely so that, through their wonderful diversity of different and dissimilar sounds, the mode might be apprehended at once by ear and mind. They ought so to express the *maneria* and composition of their modes that, after they have been more carefully impressed upon your memory, and after you have for some time practised the diverse chants, you may easily recognize by hearing which chants they suit.

Each of them, therefore, must be sufficiently distinctive for its own mode: sufficient in that it can suit any final of its mode, distinctive in that it cannot suit a chant of another mode. For neumes would not have been suitably devised for distinguishing modes from one another unless each were sufficient for its own mode and plainly distinguished that mode from the others. It must therefore express both the common and the proper *maneria* and form of its mode: the *maneria* through disposition, the form through composition. For the present, let us pass over the neumes of the plagal modes, which seem suitably devised, being sufficient for their modes and distinctive.

Concerning the neumes of the authentic modes, it must be known that all have been badly devised, or corrupted after their invention, except the neume of the first tone. Thus you will find that the neume of the fifth tone was unsuitably devised, because it is neither sufficient nor distinctive for its mode. For though it rises through two tones and a semitone, and although it naturally has C as its final, it cannot end in F except accidentally. Hence it is not sufficient, because it should naturally suit either final, rather than through rounded B, which is altogether excluded from distinguishing the properties of tones. It is indeed very absurd that, among the letters in which a chant is wholly contained, the neume which ought to reveal its nature cannot be admitted; yet this happens in this mode in chants rising through the tritone.

Again, it is not distinctive, because it naturally and properly ends in G, which is the final of the fourth *maneria*. Consider the neume of the seventh tone and compare this with it: you will find both to have exactly the same arrangement and nearly the same composition, so that you may assign this to the seventh tone and that to the fifth with the same care with which you could assign this to the fifth and that to the seventh. Hence this neume of the seventh tone too was irrationally devised, since it can suit the final of the third *maneria*. There is another very improper feature in both neumes: each has, at its beginning, a plagal ascent, rising through a tone and a semitone and dwelling on the fourth, just as you find precisely in the neume of the eighth tone, which is plagal. Therefore neither expresses the common composition of the authentic modes or the proper composition of any authentic mode; nor could either less appropriately be assigned to the eighth tone, which is plagal.

For this reason you will find both changed, so that each may be sufficient and distinctive for its own mode and may not employ a superfluous circuit. Likewise, the neume of the third tone is insufficient, because it cannot suit authentic modes which may end on square B (*B quadratum*); therefore you will find the semitone removed below the sixth. Know that these refined properties of neumes are highly necessary for distinguishing certain authentic modes from their plagal counterparts. For this antiphon, “The Law was given through Moses” [variant: “Sit at my right hand”], which touches the fifth only once and gathers itself wholly below it, would be entirely plagal unless it possessed the proper composition of its authentic mode, which you will find in its neume: namely, to descend from the final through a tone [variant: “a whole tone”] to B, then rise from there through a fourth, consisting of two tones and a semitone; afterwards to ascend through two tones to the fifth; and then, through certain intervening movements, to return to the final. Run through any antiphons of the first tone: you will find this composition in almost all of them. The same may be found in the neumes of the other authentic modes.

Let all who wish to possess a perfect knowledge of the distinction of chants beware lest, from a desire for brevity, they pass over these neumes as superfluous. The advantage gained by brevity would not be worth as much as the loss caused by the forfeiture of usefulness.

[Col. 1132A] 702 11. By these and other plausible arguments we have been compelled to correct this Antiphonary, contrary to the practice of all Churches—emulating nature rather than usage. Nor was this suggested merely by presumption: obedience commanded it. Therefore, if we are reproved for having made a work singular and different from all Antiphonaries, this consolation remains to us: reason made ours different from the others; but chance, not reason—or something else no weightier in explanation than chance—made the others differ among themselves. For though they nearly all agree in their defects, they disagree so greatly in matters in which they might reasonably agree that not even two provinces sing the same Antiphonary.

It may therefore seem surprising that false things have possessed greater authority and more common recognition than true ones, defective things more than sound ones. To speak of neighbouring churches: take the Antiphonary of Rheims and compare it with that of Beauvais, Amiens, or Soissons, which you have, as it were, at your door; if you find identity, give thanks to God. We do not wish later generations to be unaware that, at the urging of our lords and Fathers, we retained many things from the old Antiphonary which are tolerable indeed, but could be much better. Yet we left two matters uncorrected, though wholly deserving correction: the formula of the fourth tone and that of the seventh. Although we corrected these in the Gradual, we could not correct them in the Antiphonary because of the use of the psalms, our same Fathers objecting; with their assent and blessing we carried out the rest to the best of our ability.

The reason why the aforesaid formulas are defective is readily at hand. The psalm tone of the fourth mode, solely because of its formula, cannot be fitted to any antiphon ending on square B; while the formula of the seventh tone pauses on a letter upon which that tone takes no beginning—a thing permitted to no tone. Every tone ought to pause on those letters from which it most frequently begins.

## Appendix to the Moral and Doctrinal Treatises

[Col. 1131]

### On the Hymn: “Jesus, Our Redemption”

### Notice on the Following Short Work

Whether this little commentary is truly by St Bernard, certainly Bernard of Clairvaux, or not, I would not venture to affirm positively. Yet the manuscript Melk E. 42, although no earlier than the fifteenth century, directs us to think so; in it this work immediately follows Eckbert’s *Stimulus of Love*. Certainly you will find in it nothing at all unworthy of Bernard.

### St Bernard: On the Hymn “Jesus, Our Redemption”

(R. P. Bernard Pez, *Bibliotheca ascetica antiquo-nova*, vol. VI, Regensburg, 1725, 12mo.)

[Col. 1134]

So great was his love! If Christ, the Son of the living God, had as many members as there are stars in the firmament of heaven, and each member had its own body, Christ would have exposed them all to suffering before leaving a single soul unredeemed in the jaws of the devil. O what and how great is the Lord’s mercy!

What mercy has conquered my Jesus Christ, who loves the converted sinner no less than one who has never contracted the stain of sin.

For example: the conversion of a sinner is the food and drink of the Saviour.

“Penetrating the barriers of hell.” Let a human being boldly say: “I have sinned!” Let neither the wrath of the Prince, nor fear of the Devil, nor the punishment of hell, nor despair over an enormous sin terrify you. For Judas was condemned more by despair than by the sin which he committed.

“May mercy itself compel you.” We sinned, and he spared us; we offended, and he still remains appeased.

“You are our joy.” O good Jesus, forgive two things in me: the nature which you made and the sin which I added. I confess that through fault I have disfigured nature. Remember that I am a spirit that goes and does not return. By myself I went into sin; by myself I cannot return. Come then, most gracious Jesus: take away from me what I have made, so that what you have made may remain, lest that which you redeemed by your precious blood on your cross should perish. Amen.

[Col. 1133]

## Two Short Works

[Col. 1133]

### Notice on the Two Following Short Works

We publish the following book from a parchment manuscript of the thirteenth century. It treats of the Passion of Christ and the sorrows and laments of his Mother. It is written in dialogue form, and we do not know whether it is by Bernard of Clairvaux or another Abbot Bernard; nevertheless we make it public because it is very devout.

It was necessary to transcribe the second treatise, entitled *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, from another quarto paper manuscript, as it is called, of the fourteenth century. We saw this treatise or book in the library of the convent of St Mary Magdalene of the Order of Preachers at Asti, shelf-mark N. A. B. C., number not supplied. Whether it is by the same author or another monk who excerpted the works of that author, let critics judge.

## Book on the Passion of Christ and the Sorrows and Laments of His Mother

(D. Eugenius de Levis, *Anecdota sacra*, p. 60. Turin, 178… 4to.)

[Col. 1133A] 702 2 Who, ever reigning above in heaven or dwelling below on earth, on hearing or pondering in mind how the Lord of angels himself became “a reproach of men” (Ps. 22:7), and the Son of God the Father “an outcast of the people” (ibid.), could restrain tears—or to whom indeed would it be impossible to weep? Yet you, rejoice with great joy in him, now glorious in heaven,  
[Note: [Col. 1133B] I believe that he himself is also glorified.]  
you who were transfixed in mind by the most bitter nails of his most merciful death: grant me, I beseech you, those tears which you had in his Passion, so that I may shed them more abundantly.

Let us speak together concerning the Passion of your Son and my Lord.

You must fulfil the promise which you previously made us. I remember that, at the beginning of our discourse, you spoke to me concerning the sorrows which you yourself bore at the death of your only-begotten Son; and because, as I heard it, I began to ask, not a little disturbed, grieving over what those words of yours might mean.

To him she herself said: “What words are these? Meanwhile reflect in the bitterness of your soul. We shall speak together concerning these things in what follows.”

Tell, I beg you, the order of truth, you who are the mother of truth. To him she replied:

“You ask that which is the head and beginning of great sorrow. But because I, being glorified,”  
[Note: [Col. 1134D] “Glorified,” that is, glorious; elsewhere, “made glorious.”]  
“cannot weep, write with tears what I myself endured with great sorrows.”

To her I said: “I earnestly desire to weep, and nothing else pleases me. Give what you command and provide what I desire.”

Listen, and let my Lady speak to her servants. Tell me whether you were in Jerusalem when your Son was seized, bound, and brought to Annas?

But she said: “I was in Jerusalem when I heard this, and, weeping, I came by whatever pace I could to my Lord. When I saw him struck with fists, beaten with slaps, his face spat upon, crowned with thorns, and made the reproach of men, all my inward parts were moved (Gen. 43:30), my spirit failed within me (Ps. 76:4), and I had almost neither voice nor sense. My sisters and many women were also with me, lamenting him with me as an only son. Among them was Mary Magdalene, who grieved above all the others except the one now speaking with you.

“And while Christ God, as the herald cried out and Pilate gave the order, was dragged to punishment carrying his cross, and a crowd of peoples went after him—some lamenting over him, others mocking him and laughing—his most sorrowful Mother followed him as best she could, with the women who had followed from Galilee and ministered to him. They drew her along and held her up as though lifeless, until they came to the place where they crucified him. Before her eyes he was raised upon the cross and fixed to the wood with cruel nails; and he, like a lamb before the one who shears it, uttered no sound and did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

“The handmaid looked upon her Lord; the mother beheld her Son hanging on the cross, dying a most wicked death. Her mind was afflicted with such grief as no speech could express. Nor is it surprising: his blood ran from four places, watering the bare wood; his hands and feet were fastened with nails; all beauty had flowed away from his countenance. He who was ‘beautiful beyond the sons of men’ (Ps. 44:2) seemed the most disfigured of all. I saw that the prophetic judgment was fulfilled in him: ‘He had neither form nor beauty’ (Isa. 53:2), because the bruising of unjust men’s blows had marred his countenance. I saw myself abandoned by him whom I bore; no one else remained to me, because he was my only one. Therefore my grief could find no room within me. Almost all my voice had perished; yet I uttered groans and sighs of sorrow.

“I wished to speak, but grief broke my words. For when a word already conceived in the mind stretched toward formation in the mouth, grief drew it back to itself incomplete. No hostile voice of the sad heart sounded outwardly to declare the wound of the mind. Love gave words which sounded hoarse; the tongue, mistress of speech, had lost the use of utterance. As I spoke, I saw dying him whom my soul loved, and I melted wholly from the anguish of sorrow. He too looked with a most gracious countenance upon me, his weeping Mother, and wished to console me with a few words. But I could not be consoled by them; I wept as I spoke, and spoke as I wept:

“‘My son, my son, who will grant that I may die for you? The Son dies: why does his wretched Mother not die with him? My only love, my sweetest Son, do not abandon me; draw me after yourself to yourself (Song 1:3), so that I may die with you. You die badly alone; let this your Mother perish with you in death. O death, do not spare me, wretched as I am. You alone, pleasing to me above all things, exert your strength; slay the Mother and destroy her together with the Son.

“‘Son and my only sweetness, the singular joy of my life and soul and every desire, make me, who bore you unto death, now die with you. Do not die without your Mother. Recognize me, your wretched Mother, and hear my prayer; for it is fitting that a son should hear his mother. Hear me, I beseech you; receive me upon your gallows, so that we who live in one flesh may perish in one flesh.

“‘O Jews, do not spare me, you who have crucified my child. Crucify the Mother, or destroy me by whatever other cruel death. Let me end together with my Son; he dies badly alone. O death, you deprive the world of its ray, lest I see my Son—my joy, my sweetness! My life, my salvation, is killed, and my hope is taken from the earth. Why then does the Mother live in grief after her Son? Take the Mother and hang her with her pledge. You do not spare the child: spare me also not. Death, be my servant.’

“Then I would rejoice supremely if I could die together with my sweet Christ, and, wretched, die with him. But the death I desire retreats. Woe is me, unhappy one! O Jesus, death conquers your commands. For me, to die by death is better than the sweet life of death; but death flees from me, wretched as I am, and leaves me unhappy, though death itself would now be desired by me.

“‘O dear Son, O gracious, most exalted child, receive the prayers of your wretched Mother. Cease now to be hard toward your Mother, you who have always been gracious in all things. Receive your Mother with you in death, that she may live with you forever after death. Nothing is sweeter to me in life than to die and live with you. Nothing is more bitter in life than for me to live after your death.

“‘You were father to me, mother to me, spouse to me, son to me; you were all things to me. Now I am bereaved of father and mother, widowed of my spouse, and desolated above all; I lose everything. O my Son, what shall I do further? Woe is me! Come, Son. Where shall I go? Where shall I turn, sweetest one? Who will henceforth give me consolation, most merciful one? Who will thereafter give me help and counsel, dearest Son? All things are possible for you. But if you do not wish me to die with you, kindly leave me some counsel. Lord, to whom do you nod so anxiously with eyes and countenance upon the cross?’”

Concerning John, he said: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26). John himself was present, sad in countenance and ever weeping with tears, as though he said:

“O frail little human being [manuscript: *homulus*], prone to weeping and to grief! You know that I came for these things and took flesh from you, so that through the gibbet of the cross I might save the human race. How shall the Scriptures be fulfilled? You know that I must suffer for the salvation of the human race; but on the third day I shall rise for you, openly appearing to you and to my disciples. Cease to weep; lay aside grief, because I go to the Father and ascend to receive the glory of the Father’s majesty. Rather, rejoice with me, because I have now found the wandering sheep whom I had lost for so long a time. One dies, and so that the whole world may recall him: through Christ’s merit all sinners are now saved, through the merit of one alone. What pleases God the Father, how does it displease you, beloved Mother? Do you not wish me to drink the cup which the Father gave me? (John 18:11). Do not weep, woman; do not weep, sweetest Mother. I do not cast you aside; I do not abandon you. I am with you; I shall be with you through every age of the world. Though according to the flesh I am subject to the power of death, according to divinity I was, am, and always shall be immortal and incapable of suffering. You know well whence I proceeded and came. Why then are you sad if I ascend to the place from which I descended? It is time for me to return to him who sent me; and where I go, you cannot come now, but you will come later” (John 13:36).

“Meanwhile John, who is your nephew but will be regarded by you as a son, will care for you and will be your most faithful consolation.” Then, looking at John, he said: “Behold your mother” (John 19:27). “Serve her; care for her. I entrust her to you. Receive my Mother; receive your mother—or rather, receive mine.”

These two virgins were silent. Both were unable to speak or answer a word because of grief, for they saw him as though dead. They were as if dead, so that their spirits could not exhale voices. They heard and were silent because grief prevented speech. Their spirit had failed and they had lost the power of speaking; grief alone, anxious mourning, remained to them, loving to weep and weeping bitterly. They wept bitterly because they grieved bitterly. For Christ’s sword pierced the souls of both. It pierced them cruelly and destroyed each; the more it loved, the more feeble it became in the Mother. The Mother felt Christ’s sorrows. The Virgin who bore him endured the sword of grief; the wounds of dying Christ were the Mother’s wounds, and Christ’s sorrows were torturers in the Mother’s soul. The Mother was a mother uplifted by the death of her pledge;

By death she was a martyr, struck by the spear-point with which the servants unjustly pierced Christ’s limbs; she was held by great grief. Immense sorrows had grown within her mind and could not be poured out outwardly. The more cruelly raging pains within wounded the Mother’s soul like a sword. In the flesh Christ paid the debt of death; but for the Mother’s soul this was more grievous than dying.

Meanwhile Christ said to his Mother and John: “I thirst” (John 19:28), and those who crucified him gave him vinegar mixed with gall. When he had tasted it, he would not drink (Matt. 27:34), and he said, “It is finished” (John 19:30); and he cried with a loud voice and said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). And saying this he expired (Matt. 27:30).

Then the earth trembled; then the sun closed its lights;

The heavens mourned, and all the stars mourned;

Losing its lights, it lost all its radiance;

Every brightness departed from on high in lamentation.

Hard rocks were split, and the pinnacles of the temple were split.

Many arose when the tombs of the sepulchre were opened, publicly confessing with their voices that Christ was God.

702 4 It is fitting to consider how great was the Mother’s grief, when she grieved thus, she who was so sensitive. Neither tongue could speak nor mind conceive how great a grief then held the soul of Mary. By Christ’s cross stood the Virgin almost dead, she who as a virgin had conceived him by the Holy Spirit. There was no voice; grief had taken away her strength. Rather, lying prostrate, she grew pale as though dead: living, she lived; dying, and yet alive, she died; and she could not die, because while living she was dead. In her soul grief raged cruelly. She desired to die rather than to live after Christ’s death, for in living she was then miserably dead.

There she stood grieving, consumed by cruel sorrow, awaiting the removal of Christ’s body from the cross. She wept, saying, and weeping she said: “Wound me, wretched one, even in my lifeless body. You have fulfilled your desires. Take him down, extinguished. Mother, rather join me to him by a like death, so that with his sorrows my infinite sorrows may perish. Give him to me, that I may have with me his lifeless body; it will be a consolation to me, though only dead.”

Mary stood by the cross (John 19:25), gazing with a loving face upon Christ hanging on the wood of the cross, on the cruel trunk. With feet bent and hands joined, she raised herself on high, embracing the cross as she fell, and kissed Christ wherever the blood watered his bare flesh. Wishing to embrace Christ, though she could not, she stretched her hands upward. Love hopes for many things which are rarely, or never, granted. Impatient love believes everything. She wished to embrace Christ hanging on high; but her hands, stretched out in vain, returned to fold around herself. Raising herself from the ground, she lifted herself toward Christ; and because she could not touch him, she fell wretchedly to the ground. There she lay cast down, oppressed by the immensity of grief; but the force of great love compelled her, inflamed as she was, to rise. In the impulse of love she rose, longing with outstretched hands to touch Christ. For she was truly tortured by great grief and was compelled once more to seek the ground.

O how grievous was her condition then! It was more grievous for her to live such a life than to be cruelly slain by the sword of death at the hands of the wicked. The pallor of death had filled her mind; yet her face, cheeks, and mouth were reddened with Christ’s blood. With her mouth she touched the falling drops of blood, kissing the earth which the flood of blood had watered.

Meanwhile a noble man named Joseph, who was his disciple (Matt. 27:57), though secretly, confidently entered Pilate’s presence and asked that the body of our Lord Jesus be given to him. When this was granted, he summoned a certain wise man, a doctor of the Law and likewise a secret disciple of Christ, named Nicodemus. They came to the place where the Lord had been crucified, bringing with them tools by which they might pull out the nails and take him down from the cross. When his Mother saw that they wished to take him down, she rose from death, as it were; her spirit revived a little, and she gave whatever assistance she could. One drew the nail from his hands; another supported the body lest it fall lifeless. Mary too stood with arms raised on high, so that she herself might draw Christ’s hanging head and hands upon her breast. When she could touch him, she rushed upon her beloved, and could not be satisfied with kisses and embraces of him, though extinguished. When the body had been taken down from the cross to the ground, she fell upon it; through the unrestrained force of grief and immensity of love she stood as though dead.

Mary, the Mother, stood at the head of her lifeless Son, watering his face with tears. She was inwardly tormented by varied sighs; she repeatedly kissed his forehead, cheeks, eyes, nose, and everything else. She wept with such abundance of tears that you would think all her flesh and spirit were dissolved in tears. She watered with tears the exposed lifeless body of her Son when it had been laid upon the stone, which she moistened, and on which, they say, her tears still appear. She recalled his deeds to mind.

Who and what had he been whom the Virgin herself conceived without seed and bore without pain? He was her all, everything which she saw; yet he was her God and Lord and her only Son. Thus grievous was her condition, because he who could do all things also suffered. Let anyone who wishes to speak say, if he can, how great was the wretched grief which held Christ’s Virgin Mother. I do not believe that such sorrow can be narrated. Yet her love maintained a right and restrained measure: she did not despair, but mourned devoutly and justly for him whom she, a virgin, had borne, condemned to an unjust death; nevertheless she hoped that he would rise on the third day.

702 5 The holy women also wept, with the foremost group of them, and a few men, who mourned Christ together with the Virgin Mother.
