Angels too were with her in sorrow—if they were able to grieve—grieving devoutly and with righteous sorrow. In Christ’s death they suffered with him in grief, yet rejoiced that the human race was redeemed. I think they wept most bitterly, their minds troubled, because they saw Christ’s Mother held by such grief. O which angel or archangel there would not have wept contrary to nature? Indeed, contrary to nature, the immortal God lay dead as a human being. They saw Christ’s body so ill-treated by the wicked, lying wounded and lifeless; and Mary stained with his blood—she who was devout, holy, wholly good, wholly beloved, wholly sweet, wholly beautiful, wholly delightful: their most blessed Mary, their Mother—tormented by such sobs, filled with the sorrows of love, and weeping so bitterly that they could not restrain their own tears. Mourning, lamentation, and sorrow wept through the angels present there, as grief instructed the kindly spirits. Indeed, be astonished if all the angels did not weep even in that blessedness where it is impossible to weep. I believe, for the reason I state, that they grieved if they were capable of grief: just as it was possible for God to die through the humanity he assumed, so it was possible for the blessed angels to grieve at the death of their Lord.

Joseph of Arimathea, a holy and just man, who with Nicodemus had taken Christ’s body down from the cross, as the Gospel bears witness concerning him, laid him, wrapped in a clean linen cloth and embalmed with most precious spices (John 19:39), and laid it in a new tomb [Col. 1140A] which he had made for himself, eagerly and devoutly. Then, at his funeral rites, thousands upon thousands of angels sang, because they had all gathered for the burial of their Lord. They raised praises to heaven. Mary wept bitterly beside the tomb while Joseph and Nicodemus placed God in the tomb. The grieving mother wished to be buried with him. She was bent over her beloved, embracing him with all love, kissing him most sweetly, and saying: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you who are my friends” (Job 19:21). “Leave him to me a little while, dearest ones, so that I may have some consolation in seeing him; so that I may still be able to contemplate his face under a roof, or his soul. Do not commit him to burial so quickly. Give him to his wretched mother, [Col. 1140B] that I may have him with me, even if dead; or, if you place him in the tomb, lay me, wretched as I am, down with him. I should prefer it, for what will remain for me afterward?”

They were placing Christ in the tomb, while she was drawing him toward herself. She wished to keep him with her, while they wished to commit him to burial; and thus there arose this loving dispute and pitiable contention among them. Yet every person wept so bitterly that none of them could fully form words. They saw the mother enter, deprived of every consolation, and they made lament rather over her than over her dead son, our Lord. Their grief at the mother’s grief was greater than it had been at their Lord’s death. Therefore all wept, groaning in compassionate sorrow, and thus they gave the Lord of life to the burial of death [Col. 1140C]. When the Lord had been buried, his mother embraced the tomb with all her heart and, in such voice as she could, blessed her son. Sitting beside the tomb, with her head uncovered, she stretched her hands over it, kissing it, and mourned the Lord with exceedingly bitter sobbing.

John came, he to whom Christ had entrusted her; weeping himself, he raised her up as she wept. For, worn out by groans, exhausted by grief, afflicted by weeping, she could scarcely stand on her feet. Yet, thus borne along, helped by the holy women, with all weeping together, she entered Jerusalem. Many women who saw her, moved with pity at her sufferings, turned to bitter mourning; and some of them, walking behind her, lamented also. [Col. 1140D] Those who wept kept weeping, and many grieved with Mary. For her grief made many grieve. Hardly anyone who saw her weeping could restrain tears. She wept so tenderly and suffered so bitterly that, by her compassionate weeping, she drew even unwilling people into mourning; wherever she passed, lamentations arose.

Mary herself wept; those walking with her wept; many who came to meet her wept. Thus she was escorted by weeping people, while weeping, until they came to John’s house. There she sat down and remained in the house where John kept her, loving her in his heart as his own mother.

O happy, O blessed John, to whom the Lord entrusted such a treasure. May the Lord repay you [Col. 1141A] for the love which you always bore toward his mother, entrusted to you by himself. Blessed are you by Christ. Blessed are you by his mother, whom you loved with a pure and clean heart. Blessed are all who love her.

[Col. 1142A] And may her son Jesus Christ our Lord always be blessed, who lives and reigns with God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TREATISE IN PRAISE OF THE GLORIOUS VIRGIN MOTHER

(Eugenius de Levis, *Anecdota sacra*, p. 70.)

[Col. 1141B] **702.6** Syllables full of heavenly mysteries restrain in me both love and reverence because of my polluted mouth: for I am a man of unclean lips (Isa. 6:5); I have an unclean heart and a polluted tongue, blackened by the rust of defilement, like a moth. My conscience is sick, and the moth gnaws it toward the vengeance of corruption. Therefore, in speaking of this greeting, I profess not only weakness of speech but silence as well. Fire has fallen upon me, so that I cannot behold this sun in its ray—or rather the ray from which the true sun proceeds. I believe that the syllables of this greeting, full of heavenly mysteries, were taken from that book which Isaiah saw sealed, and which, if given to one who knows letters or to one who does not, neither will be able to read (Isa. 29:11).

This is the Queen of Heaven of whom we strive to speak; but as Mother of Mercy [Col. 1141C] she terrifies on this account, and comforts on that. Yet because the Mother of Mercy was made the gate of Heaven for sinners, confidence in mercy presumes what the height of mercy dissuades. I know indeed that my teeth are broken in number. I know certainly that splendid praise is not in the mouth of a sinner; and though I have not presumed to take up a psalm, so that my drum may give forth its sound, like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal (1 Cor. 13:1), yet, although my voice disagrees with my life, I know that a word concerning the queen is more glorious because it comes from on high. Let us therefore say: “Hail, Mary, full of grace” (Luke 1:28).

O greeting new and touched with heavenly nectar! O greeting truly worthy of proclamation! “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind” (Song 4:16): breathe upon us the syllables of this greeting [Col. 1141D] in sweetness, so that her spices may flow forth. In this greeting every syllable breathes the fragrance of paradise, because these words are truly sweetened with heaven’s honey; and because, proceeding from the throne, they are pilgrims in this valley of tears, they scarcely dwell in houses of clay so as to be understood by the sons of Eve. “Nard with saffron, and saffron with fragrant cane, and cinnamon, myrrh, and aloe, with all the trees of Lebanon” (Song 4:14).

In this greeting the grammatical polisher of words, the dialectical reasoner, and the rhetorical ornamenter breathe together in mutual sweetness; and they are astounded by these words, because the wondrous greeting proceeding from the throne has flashing lamps, that it may perceive and illumine the lamp of the breast. This greeting [Col. 1142B] was inscribed by the finger of God in the sanctuary of the Trinity. Having taken its origin from the majesty’s decree in the council chamber of the heavenly palace, it was entrusted to one of the palace’s mightiest servants for delivery. For “Gabriel” is interpreted by the Hebrews as “strength of God.” Thus Gabriel the archangel is sent, and he goes forth from the King to the Queen, from the Emperor to the Empress, from the citizens of heaven to the co-lord of the palace. He enters to the Virgin chosen above all by the King, and perhaps all the more eagerly because, although the angels formerly had a King, they were now to have a Queen also; and so that sinners might enter the way of paradise to make good the fall of the angelic order, the Mother of Mercy, Queen of Angels, might become the gate of Heaven. Therefore, when the angel entered, he said: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.”

It delights one to gaze upon, to embrace, to admire [Col. 1142C] in this greeting the titles of our Empress shining in her diadem, and to contemplate its gems. Look at the syllables of this most lofty greeting, and you will find in the seal of our Empress, as though characters of spiritual grace impressed by the ring of authority. It seems to me that I see in this seal, as it were, four gems of most powerful light, gleaming by their mutual reflection. The first is “Full of grace”; the second, “The Lord is with you”; the third, “Blessed are you among women”; the fourth, “Blessed is the fruit of your womb.” Gabriel brought three of these from heaven; the fourth he uttered as the Holy Spirit spoke through the mouth of Elizabeth prophesying.

Above these four, as though on the front of the seal, shines the starry name of the Virgin—namely, “Star of the Sea”—because it sheds rays of inward light upon those following amid mortal light [Col. 1142D]. This Star of the Sea is set above the stormiest deep of this world, so that it may guard from rocks, rescue from waves, defend from pirates, and bring to port. All the children of Eve groan over how many and how great are the dangers of this most troubled sea, whether they sigh for rewards or lament exile. For the whole present life is temptation; and anyone who does not fear being overcome is overcome too easily. In this great and wide sea there are as many creeping things as vices, as many shipwrecks as transgressions. O faithful soul, in every shipwreck lift your eyes to the ray of this most shining star. Look upon the star; call upon Mary. Fix the gaze of your mind upon this most serene [Col. 1143A] light. If you fall, you will rise. If you are submerged, you will be raised. If you ask, you will receive. If you go on, you will escape. Did not Theophilus, wrapped in contemplation of this most shining star, swim forth from the abyss of eternal damnation? Did not Basil, heard in prayer through contemplation of this most serene brightness, receive consolation? This Star of the Sea adorns the heavens, illumines the lands, lights the sea, and penetrates the abyss. O singular remedy for all who bore Eve as mother both in the cause of their origin and of their condemnation; who, cast down into these outer, lower darknesses, are discovered by the brightness of so great a star after the shadow of so great a death! If you look upon this star with sick eyes, it heals; if you are advancing, it strengthens. This star truly has medicinal rays: it drives away [Col. 1143B] darkness, burns up vices, increases virtues, and the more closely you look upon it, the more it illumines. If you are in the deep, look up to this star; if you have never seen it, look at it; if you have failed, look back to it; if you wish to be more illumined, look intently upon it. This star lifts from the deep, shows the way—indeed, brings one safely into port.

Lord Jesus Christ, sun of eternal light, who willed that your mother should be the Star of the Sea: through that star, I ask, illumine my darkness. This Star of the Sea has rays wondrous to heaven, terrible to hell, and salutary to earth. The morning stars marvel at and praise this most bright constellation, and all the sons of God rejoice. At the newness of this star, I believe the whole brotherly multitude cries out: “Who is she that ascends?” (Song 3:6). And she is terrible at the gates [Col. 1143C] of hell because of the excellence of the virtues over which she preeminently presides. She is terrible to the Jew, terrible to the Manichaean, because of unheard-of fruitfulness. Terrible, I say, to heretics who confuse either the nature or the person in the Son of the Virgin. Surely she is terrible to all who, dulled by natural conjectures concerning the Virgin’s birth, scoff at and gnaw away the heavenly mystery through earthly argumentation. At this heavenly ray the Jew grows bleary-eyed, the heretic is blunted, and the Christian is illumined. For the light which delights healthy eyes offends diseased ones.

**702.7** But for you, O faithful soul, the ray of this star illumines the mind’s sight and drives away blindness. For she is full of grace—full, I say, of sweetness, full of every delight. For the inventor [Col. 1143D] of all graces, the distributor of gifts, the Paraclete, prepared her in the resting-place of the whole Trinity as a royal palace with wondrous adornment. God’s Wisdom built a house for himself in her and, by spiritual work, raised in her seven pillars, when the Virgin bore in her womb him in whom all the beauty of divinity dwelt bodily. If vessels of spices preserve for a long time the fragrance of aromatics and retain long the scent they first received, how much more did the storehouse of all graces—in which the heavenly perfumer placed himself with all his ointments and reclined with every delight—give forth its fragrance? “The nard of the Virgin gave its scent” (Song 1:11), drew the King from the resting-place of glory, and filled the sanctuary of the virginal hall with the fullness of angels.

O inviolate lily [Col. 1144A] of chastity! Most blessed Virgin Mary, you are the living temple of the living God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the chamber of spices, the bridegroom’s bridal chamber, the golden couch of the living Solomon, the bed of heavenly nuptials, the gathering-place of aromatics, the paradise of every delight. You are full of grace, from whom grace, fully full, flowed forth to us—the grace through which the Father with the Son gave us all things. And rightly you are fuller than the rest, because the Lord is with you: with you in heart, with you in womb, with you in deed, with you in word; with you to sanctify you, with you to preserve you, with you to dwell in you, with you to make you mother from daughter, queen from handmaid, heaven from earth. The Lord is with you who sent me; the Lord is with you who speaks in me; the Lord is with you who went before me.

The angel ran under the authority of him who had sent him [Col. 1144B], but he went before minds, because his word ran swiftly. God is indeed in every creature; in a certain way the preposition signifies this when he is said to have been “in Mary the Virgin.” He was in prophets and apostles by indwelling grace, but far otherwise in the Virgin, who became, by the grace of the One dwelling in her, the dwelling-place of grace itself, and offered the Word God an inviolate lodging in both natures. The Lord is with you: the Father with the Son; the Lord is with you: the Son with the Paraclete, in the undivided work of the Trinity.

And therefore: “Blessed are you among women”—you who are of singular merit; “Blessed are you among women”—you who are a woman-savior; “Blessed are you among women”—you who are mother and virgin. O woman truly blessed above women! O chosen one, blessed above all blessed women! O unique one truly chosen above all chosen women! O truly inestimable gem brought forth from the treasury of heavenly wisdom and inseparably adorned by the artistry of the whole Trinity! O mother and glory of mothers! O singular woman in childbirth, at whose giving birth even Roman faith is astonished, nature marvels, and custom flees! For both are beyond reason; belief in both is the merit of faith: that she is both mother and virgin, and that he is both God and man.

Mother Eve, mother of sorrow, who condemned your children before you bore them: embrace, with all your daughters, the feet of this new mother; for she removes the old bitterness, removes reproach, tears up the bond of condemnation, and erases the proscription.

O Virgin, noble rod, rod of Jesse, through whom in the branch that which had perished in the root grew strong. The root [Col. 1144D] of bitterness is Eve; the root of eternal sweetness is Mary. This is the wondrous and most profound dispensation of wisdom: that such a rod should be born from such a root, such a daughter from such a mother, such a free woman from such an outlawed woman, such an empress from such a captive, so flourishing a rose from so dry a thorn! Your mother scarcely possessed innocence, and lost it. She scarcely stood, and fell. She had not yet borne children, and condemned those who were to be born. But the most blessed Virgin Mary was made a royal antidote against the deadly poison of persuasion, so that from her womb she might prepare the secret of heavenly medicine. You are truly blessed among women, because you are a wondrous medicine, the honor of virgins, the mirror of innocence, the example of chastity, the pattern of integrity, “that virgins may be brought to the king; the virgin mother serves them first, and her companions [Col. 1145A] after her bring joy and exultation” [cf. Ps. 44]. For if the daughters of the king are in exultation, in honor of the bridegroom, if the daughters of Tyre enter (Ps. 44:13) the wedding feast, how much more do you, Virgin, Mother of the Bridegroom, Queen of Virgins, “in a garment embroidered with gold, surrounded by variety” (ibid., v. 10), adorn all the choirs of heavenly spirits.

You are therefore the adornment of the heavenly court, the astonishment of angels: wholly one miracle, wholly one inestimable novelty. You are the short way to heaven, the pledge of faith, the ark of hope in the hearts of the faithful. You are, between God and man, the living tabernacle of the living covenant. You are the propitiatory, which not only overshadows the cherubim but is indeed the holy of holies of the entire Trinity. Therefore you are truly blessed among women, because your name is blessed. Blessed is [Col. 1145B] your motherhood, blessed your words, blessed your chastity, blessed your humility, blessed your fullness, blessed your integrity. And hence it is justly said: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb.” He is the fruit of life—indeed, life’s life—scenting all the delights of paradise with the essence of such sweetness. By the scent of this fruit, a human being is drawn from earth to the homeland. An angel is satisfied in that homeland. The fragrance of this fruit is not, as with Jacob, “the fragrance of a full field” (Gen. 27:27), but the fullness of the common good, fully intoxicating and fully satisfying, not declining through age, because “delights are at his right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). In this fruit of your womb the soul embraces the tree of life transplanted from paradise into the valley and grafted with the precious shoot of balsam, where the inward nobility of the sweet tree gives forth its scent in a kind of double sweetness.

**702.8** Therefore, blessed Virgin, you are a scent like the thread of precious balsam; indeed, the Word of the Father in your womb is as the tree of life. When that happy sinner poured ointment over Jesus’ feet, “the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (Luke 7:38; John 12:3). How much more does the house of the chaste breast give forth its fragrance, poured over with the chrism of every grace through the illumination of the Holy Spirit. “Your name is ointment poured out,” Virgin Mary (Song 1:2). The bridegroom’s name is ointment—he who was born from you. Draw us after you, that we may run in the fragrance of your womb, because the young women who love the bridegroom love you. Make us enter the bridegroom’s wedding feast, where friends drink and are intoxicated with light, [Col. 1145D] and are satisfied with the mysteries of figures: that is, the page on which so many preceding signs indicated the novelty of virginal birth. Thus Moses’ vision of the burning bush is revered (Exod. 3); Aaron, in the dry rod, reveres the flowers of one mystery; Gideon marvels at the dry ground, as though in Midian (Judg. 7); in the gate Ezekiel marvels at the passage of the King alone through the closed gate (Ezek. 44:2). Solomon also made a throne of ivory, which he clothed with the purest gold of his chastity and love—the Virgin signifying the privilege of her mother.

Yet Gabriel the angel illumines more fully the day of this greeting, while the preceding figures, like lesser stars, sparkle with its flashing rays, saying: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.” You have become beautiful and sweet in your delights, holy Mother of God, because everything that the garden of fragrance possesses, or the treasury of spiritual delights in the chamber and in the gardens of aromatics, breathes forth your perfumes [Col. 1146A]. O blessed Virgin, unique among the blessed: from the bridal chamber of your unstained chastity the mysteries of our redemption were ordained. You are the praise and glory of the human race, the advocate of peace and of humankind upon earth, the wonder of angels, the ornament of nature, the lamp of the sun—indeed, the sun of the sun—marvelously illuminating the tabernacle from the everlasting mountains.

From you light ineffably rose in the vessel of our flesh, so that heavenly wisdom might restore the drachma long lost to the choirs of angels. Secondly, since you, most serene Virgin, are flooded by the living sun with so many rays of grace, you shine as the Star of the Sea, illumining not merely the northern pole but heaven and earth throughout the whole world. And because, as you ministered, the light of divinity entered the vessel of our flesh through the finding of the tenth drachma, this increased the angels’ joy: they possessed not only joys from heaven but found on earth a fuller occasion for rejoicing in the conversion of sinners [Col. 1146B].

O most merciful Virgin Mary: he who created you reigns in you, and the potter does not disdain bodily to dwell in his own fashioned work. Therefore Mount Zion will joyfully say: “Man, and man, was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her”; and, “the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you,” holy Mother of God. Therefore we shall exult and rejoice in you, remembering your breasts. Your ointments, O Zion, are better than every aromatic. “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Ps. 86 [citation as printed]). Therefore, since it is fittingly said that nothing can be denied you when you pray, cause us to be brought with you into the wine-cellar, where the King ordered his love in you; where John the Evangelist was assigned as your guardian; where Gabriel, the bridegroom’s friend, marvels at your fullness; where, amid the manifestations of the heavenly host, choirs of virgins follow you as their queen; where you are the true Star of the Sea, as though holding the same circuit as the whole sun; where you are light knowing no eclipse; where immortal love is between you and your Son. “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3), Mother of God, seat of all grace, lamp of eternal light. For if “the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Wis. 3:7), how much more you, who brought forth light from light, light from the Father of lights, light [Col. 1146D] of all the stars.

O most serene Star of the Sea, look upon me, a sinner; pray humbly to your sun, that I may be able to see this star with its sun among the angelic contemplations of those beholding such great brightness. My God, illumine my darkness. O blessed Virgin, sincere Christian devotion embraces with the arms of pure faith the Son of God descending into you. Whatever nature reports as frail in other mothers, all this passed into mystery in you, so that the human heart should in no way presume to reach the inestimable secret of your giving birth—unless perhaps, by a dissimilar likeness, it says that the Word of the Father entered the bridal chamber of the generative court as dew into wool, passing through a mirror by the sun’s ray. Not in fire, not in the shaking of the house, but in the breath of a gentle breeze; and in it [Col. 1147A] the house trembles, as does the people in the desert whom flashes and lightning terrify. But finally, in the presence of light, the sun offered himself to be seen from the Virgin, though with the loving cloud of flesh set before him.

**702.9** Rejoice, blessed Virgin, whose joy in this life is always unfailing in the contemplation of light, while you nurse on earth him who fed the angels in heaven. O joy of a mother, transcending joys in comparison with a mother, whose Son raises the dead, triumphs over death, and penetrates the heavens! These two names, “Mother” and “Virgin,” materially opposed, come together wondrously in you, blessed Virgin; and, as by a doubled light, fittingly pour into you both a saving and a wonderful perpetual brightness. For Christian devotion most fully believes that a certain gratuitous participation in divinity was bestowed upon you by the Lord your Son, such as the Virgin Mother could receive or endure [Col. 1147B]. For as God the Father said to no angel, “You are my Son,” except to the Only-Begotten (Ps. 2:7), so among the daughters of Eve he said to none, “You are the Mother of my Son,” except to you, most blessed Virgin.

But if cherubim and seraphim are so inflamed by the ardor of love that perhaps a creature then passes into the state of divinity as far as it can, how much more are you, Virgin Mother, united to your Son; and the multitude of angels adores your flesh deified in the Son. Although Christian devotion is aided by the patronage of all the saints, nevertheless the fullness of grace shines forth more abundantly upon the human race from your intercession, like a well of living waters from heavenly Lebanon. For your exalted dignity persuades us—indeed compels us—to believe that through angels and angelic ministries you often aid those devoted to you and finally bring them to the kingdom of your Son. For if the angel of angels is sent, the devout Christian ought confidently to believe that the Empress of Angels has angels all the more at her service, inasmuch as through him she inherited a name more excellent (Heb. 1:14 [citation as printed]). But if cherubim and seraphim, drinking undeservedly from the fountain of life, reveal certain secrets from the counsel of the palace to the lower orders of angels, so that “the rush of the river makes glad the whole city” (Ps. 86 [citation as printed]), how much more do you, glorious *theodotos* [Sic; perhaps Greek *theotonos* (θεοτόνος)], pour out more abundantly to angels and human beings the mysteries of your Son, tasted in his embrace from hidden things.

What shall we say of you, O illustrious mother among women? If we call you sun, you are more splendid; if [Col. 1148A] rose, you are more flowering; if cinnamon and balsam, aromatic species, you strike with fragrance. For we believe that the privileges granted you are marvelous not only to humans but also to angels. If Moses’ face was made radiant by companionship with the Lord’s word (Exod. 34:29), how glorious among all saints do we believe is the light of your countenance—you who are one flesh with your Son through wondrous birth, and one spirit with him in one most ardent love. If Joshua, leader of Israel, amid bloodshed commanded the sun to stand still in Gibeon, how should not all the stars run at the will of the glorious Empress?

Look, therefore, most blessed Virgin, upon us, the exiled and proscribed children of Eve, in whom the first-fruits of calamity, the shares and dues of death, and the taxes of sin still condemn us. The woe which Eve gave us to drink still condemns us. We are still in battle. The serpent still attacks Eve, and Eve the man. Sensuality still attacks reason; the promptings of reason still trouble the lower part. Still, in the same house, five are divided against three and three against two, and “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7:6). Therefore, that we may have steadfastness in their conflict, send us that eminent prince of the heavenly court, your bridegroom’s friend Gabriel, who, as in name so also in power, may in his kindness be willing to send us divine strength.

O Mother of Mercy, if you withdraw, there is no one in the whole communion of saints to speak for us, to intercede for us with your Son. But when you intercede, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, raising their voices, fall [Col. 1148C] before the throne before the Lamb (Rev. 4), and the whole multitude of saints confidently undertakes prayer for us. Moses prays in the presence of the Lord his God; praying for his people, he asks him to remember the oath made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the Lord was appeased. But you, most gentle Virgin, ask your Son to remember the everlasting covenant which the Word established in flesh taken from you, which the Word pledged in the shedding of blood, and which he sealed by an indissoluble bond in the mysteries of our redemption. Therefore, we who flee under your protection: bring our prayer before our judge, your Son, so that you, O salvation, who began our salvation by bringing him forth, may complete it by interceding. Amen.

[Col. 1147]

## [ON THE BODY OF THE LORD]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING WORK

In manuscript no. 19 of the Greater Augustinian convent, the following treatise displays this title: “Here begins a certain treatise of blessed Bernard, *On the Body of the Lord*”; and at the end: “Here ends the book of blessed Bernard, *On the Body of the Lord*.” Let faith be placed in the manuscript. In it, it is noteworthy that the meditations published under the name of Saint Bernard extend only as far as the fourteenth chapter and end with these words: “And the more he loves God, the more nearly he will see him, whom to behold is an end without end.” But the editions have: “The more nearly he will see him, whom he desires to behold,” etc. The same manuscript supplies me with a much enlarged book of Isidore of Seville, *On the Rule of Living*, under the title *Formula of the Honorable Life*; but of these matters elsewhere.

## TREATISE ON THE BODY OF THE LORD

(Hommey, *Supplementum Patrum*, vol. I, p. 147.)

[Col. 1149]

[Col. 1149A] **702.10** Recalling the mercies of God, let us give thanks to him who, through the bowels of his mercy, “visited us, the Dayspring from on high” (Luke 1:38 [citation as printed]). For if, God forbid, we prove ungrateful to him who made us for his own sake and redeemed us for his own sake, we shall be cast out of the house as useless servants and uprooted from the land of the saints as an unfruitful tree. Therefore, abhorring every ingratitude because we are children of grace, let us behold the overflowing love and superabundant mercy which that Majesty displays daily to sinners. Do you think that God came to you once and then left you; that he visited the earth once and thereafter did not look upon it? Has God’s hand been shortened, or his power weakened, or has God forgotten to show mercy, so that he who [Col. 1149B] once made himself known has now departed entirely? By no means. “Behold,” he says, “I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). It is Truth who speaks, and Truth speaks truth; he does not deceive you, O human being, for he loves you greatly and does not wish to be deceived by you. He does all this for you.

He wishes to remain with us, so that we may be with him—indeed, we are not so with him that he could truly say to us: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip?” etc. (John 14:6 [citation as printed]). Therefore he says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). Behold, he comes to us daily, appearing humble, and we do not recognize him; every day he descends from the bosom [Col. 1149C] of the Father onto the altar in the priest’s hands, and we do not know him. Each day he humbles himself as when he came from royal seats into the Virgin’s womb, and we, hardened, do not consider it. O human being, do you believe that this is the Son of God? Certainly I believe and confess it. And how do you not utterly fail, not utterly dread, not utterly tremble, when he whom angels tremble before and every heavenly order adores daily casts himself down for you, earth and ashes? I suspect that you confess with voice alone what you do not hold in your heart and contradict by your deeds. For if you do not believe, you are already judged; but if you believe as you say and act so irreverently, you are foolish and most arrogant toward so great a sacrament, and “your iniquity is found unto hatred” (Ps. [Col. 1150A] 35:3).

For he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 55:57 [citation as printed]). How do you abide in him whom you dishonor by wicked deeds and provoke by depraved conduct, when he is truly holy and cannot abide except in what is holy? Or how does he abide in you when you are proud, he who rests only upon one who is humble and quiet (Isa. 66:7 [citation as printed])? Therefore, if he does not abide in you, you do not eat his flesh nor drink his blood; but if you do not eat, you cannot be saved at all, as he himself says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 40–54 [citation as printed]).

Do you therefore wish to eat the flesh of the Son of Man, that you may have eternal life? To be worthy, gather together [Col. 1150B] the things he suffered for you, and commit the sufferings of your soul and the needs of your body to the continual recollection of your memory. Review each and every thing, even to the death of the Cross. Thus, by his example and imitation, offer your body and soul as a living, holy sacrifice pleasing to him, so that you may offer your whole self to him as an acceptable sacrifice, a sweet-smelling offering, just as he spent his whole self in your redemption.

Finally, believe firmly, without any scruple of mind, that the holy bread and holy wine upon the altar, according to the form of holy Church, become his true body and blood in the priest’s hand; and receive him with fitting reverence, holy fear, a good conscience, pure love, and unfeigned faith. Remember that, just as he appeared to the holy apostles in true flesh, so now he shows himself to us in the holy bread; and just as they, by the sight of his flesh, saw only his flesh but believed him to be God, contemplating with spiritual eyes, so we too, seeing bread and wine, should believe them to be his body and blood, and that he is living and true [Col. 1150C].

For this reason—yes, for this reason—divine kindness appeared: that the humble man might appear glorious in divinity. For we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is through his glory, which is most full, most sufficient, and most abundant eternally in all who love him in truth. To him alone be honor and glory in the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 1151]

## TREATISE ON CHANTING THE GRADUAL

Prefixed as a kind of prologue to the Cistercian Gradual.

[Hommey, *Supplementum Patrum*, I, p. 27.]

[Col. 1151A] **702.11** As we have instructed beforehand those who are to notate antiphonaries, so we instruct beforehand those who are to notate graduals. We beg and implore both of them not to separate joined notes or join separated ones, so that identity may be preserved, both in the chant and in its manner of delivery, as regards pauses and divisions. Only those letters are called, and are, finals which are supported by the fullness both of the descent of the plagal modes and of the ascent of the authentic modes: that is, those which have four notes below them and seven above them. The first is low D, and the last high C. Apart from these, and only those which naturally lie between them, you will find none above or below which does not lack either fullness of descent or perfection of ascent.

But that you may be made certain about each one, you should know that the first [Col. 1151B] mode, namely the *protus*, which contains the first and second tones, has two finals: low D and high A. Therefore, for chants of this manner which have a tone above the fifth, low D is the necessary final, since it naturally has a tone above the fifth. But for those which have not a tone but a semitone above the fifth, high A is the proper final, since there it has not a tone but a semitone. It is likewise necessary for those which descend two tones below the final. Therefore, having carefully considered this property, you will not wonder that chants which were accustomed to end on D are naturally notated through B on high A; nor will it seem to you superfluous or tiresome to imitate this.

The second mode, namely the deuterus, which contains the third [Col. 1151C] and fourth tones, likewise has two finals: low E and square B. The latter is the proper and necessary final for those chants of this mode which have a semitone below the sixth. The other, however, properly serves those chants which have not a semitone but a tone below the sixth, and likewise those which descend three tones below the final. Note that many authoritative churches—among which, I think, are the churches of Amiens and of Thérouanne—have psalms in their postcommunions, as in their introits. Although you may find few introits among them, you may find many postcommunions. Those which can end only on square B can by no means admit the chant of the Psalm-tone of the third or fourth tone [Col. 1151D], since the psalms of those tones have a tone above the fourth, whereas square B has not a tone but a semitone above the fourth. We too, like them, have many introits which should naturally end on square B, since they everywhere have a semitone above the fourth [Col. 1152A]; but because there they cannot receive a psalm which, as we have said, has a tone above the fourth, they are transferred to the lower final through round B. For this reason you will find the Psalm-chants of the third and fourth tones so altered that they can serve either final.

The third mode, namely the tritus, which contains the fifth and sixth tones, likewise has two finals: low F and high C, for those which at that point have not a semitone but a tone. But since we have no introit which can end on C, you will find the Psalm-chant altered in the fifth tone, although it cannot be adapted to both finals.

The fourth mode, that is, the tetrardus, which contains the seventh and eighth tones, has only one final, G. You will find the chant of the Psalm of the seventh tone altered only in its metrum, because it makes its pause where it cannot begin—which is permitted to no chant. For a chant can pause only on those letter-notes on which it can begin, especially on those which most frequently and suitably serve as beginnings of chants.

With the superfluous multiplicity of differences excluded, each tone retains only one difference: namely, that one which, ending on its final, identifies its mode either in itself or in its metrum. For this reason, in the eighth tone the difference has been retained which, turning back as far as low D, returns through F to the final G; for by this means it cannot end on the final of another mode.

[Col. 1152C] Whereas the differences of six tones end on their proper finals, the differences of only two, namely the third and fifth tones, did not end on their own finals; and therefore they could be assigned to other tones just as suitably as to those. These have been brought into conformity with the rule and end on their proper finals. Moreover, there are certain responsories—namely, *Christus factus est*, *Ecce sacerdos*, *Exiit sermo*, and the like—of which there is a large number.

In these the responsory is in the sixth tone, but the verse in the fifth; although you would attach the verse far more suitably to its responsory if it were in the same tone as it, as it is in the other responsories of this Gradual. In the responsory which is in the sixth tone there is also the fault of opposition [Col. 1152D]: for its progression is plagal, but its composition authentic, and this must not occur. For this reason you will find these responsories quite suitably reduced to the fifth tone. Although such corrections may seem contrary to custom, yet because nature prevails over custom [Col. 1153A], let the alteration of custom displease you no more than the integrity of the observed natural order pleases you; so that you who have refused to allow dispensation in the rule of living may not permit falsehoods or faults in the rules of singing—faults which ought rather to be cut away than dispensed.

[Col. 1153]

# TONARY OF ST BERNARD

*Ecclesiastical writers on music, especially sacred music, brought to public light by Martin Gerbert, Abbot of St Blaise in the Black Forest. Printed at St Blaise, 1784, quarto, vol. II, p. 265.*

## Notice

From a thirteenth-century manuscript of St Blaise we publish this Tonary, as it occurs there anonymously; Homeyo, however, attributes it to St Bernard of Clairvaux in the *Supplementum Patrum*. Certainly, if it cannot be attributed to Bernard himself, it may at least be attributed to one of the correctors of Cistercian chant and antiphonary under St Bernard’s direction. See also Mabillon’s notice in St Bernard’s treatise *On the Correction of the Antiphonary*, published by him in vol. II of the latter’s works, p. 691.

702 12

## HERE BEGINS THE TONARY

[Col. 1153]

[Col. 1153B]

**Disciple.** What is a tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the nature and form of regular chants.

**D.** In what is nature recognized, and in what form?

**M.** Nature consists in disposition; form, in composition and progression.

**D.** What do you call disposition, progression, and composition?

**M.** Disposition is the direct arrangement of tones and semitones according to the natural placement of the letter-notes. Progression is ascent and descent. Composition, however, consists in lightness and gravity, extension and turning back, various windings, and the many varieties of melodic byways. Thus you recognize the nature of a chant if you know to what disposition [Col. 1153C] or mode it belongs; you recognize its form when you know whether it progresses or is composed authentically or plagally.

**D.** How many modes are there?

**M.** Four.

**D.** How do they differ from one another?

**M.** The first ascends from the final through a tone and a semitone, and descends through a tone. The second ascends from the final through a semitone and a tone, and descends through a tone. The third ascends from the final through two tones, and descends through a semitone. The fourth ascends from the final through two tones, and descends through a tone.

**D.** What do you call a final?

**M.** Finals are the notes on which chants end.

[Col. 1153D]

**D.** How many finals does each mode have?

**M.** The first has two: D and high a. The second has two: E and square B. The third has two: F and high c. The fourth has only one, namely G.

**D.** Are there as many tones as modes?

**M.** There are four modes, but eight tones contained under the modes. The odd-numbered tones—namely, the first, third, fifth, and seventh—are called authentic, as being of greater dignity. The even-numbered—the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth—are called plagal because they are of lesser dignity. Each mode contains one authentic tone and its plagal counterpart: the first contains the first and second; the second, the third and fourth; the third, the fifth and sixth; the fourth, the seventh and eighth.

**D.** What is the difference between authentics and plagals?

**M.** An authentic may ascend beyond the note which is sixth from the final; a plagal may not. A plagal may descend more than one note below the final; an authentic may not.

[Col. 1154C]

**D.** By how many notes does the authentic exceed the plagal in ascent, and by how many is it exceeded by it in descent?

**M.** By three.

**D.** How many notes, then, does a chant comprise?

**M.** Ten.

**D.** Why?

**M.** Because, according to the arrangement of tones and semitones employed by musicians, no chant can be made within ten notes or fewer which cannot be notated; but a chant of eleven notes can be made which cannot be notated. Therefore it is unnecessary for a chant to extend below or above as far as that uncertainty.

**D.** What sort of arrangement do musicians employ?

**M.** The first, fourth, and seventh letters have a tone on either side; the second and fifth have a tone below and a semitone above; the third and sixth, conversely, a tone above and a semitone below. They sometimes employ round B, so as to avoid the harshness of the tritone.

[Col. 1154D]

**D.** I ask about those chants which do not ascend beyond the sixth nor descend beneath the first note below [Col. 1155A] the final: are they authentic or plagal?

**M.** Some are authentic and some plagal.

**D.** What distinction is there between them?

**M.** They are distinguished not by progression but by consideration of composition. For every chant of this diminished and restricted progression is authentic if it begins on the fifth, or, frequently using it, pauses there; or if, beginning on the final, it leaps to the fifth. In the third tone, however, the sixth is substituted for the fifth. But every chant which does not exceed the fourth is unquestionably plagal. If it sometimes exceeds it but immediately draws itself back below it, making its pauses and turns beneath it, it is again plagal—unless it is evident that it possesses the proper composition of some authentic tone.

[Col. 1155B]

**D.** What are these proper compositions?

**M.** Examine the *neugma* of the first tone, and in the *neugma* you will find its proper composition; unless the antiphon *Lex per Moysen*, and many similar ones, possessed this, they would be altogether plagal. The same holds in the other authentic tones. Again, every chant of this diminished progression is plagal if, at its beginning, it ascends from the final to the fourth through a fully formed diatessaron, then quickly returns to the final and pauses there. I define this on account of certain beginnings of the seventh tone, which, although they ascend through a diatessaron, nevertheless turn it back and immediately leap to the fifth. By this rule the antiphon *Petrus Apostolus* is plagal, though it seems to possess the proper composition of its authentic [tone].

[Col. 1155C]

**D.** It remains for you to indicate what chant is regular.

**M.** To comprehend it for you by a proper and reciprocal definition: a regular chant is one which, being perfectly consonant with itself, identifies its own mode in itself.

**D.** This definition is brief indeed, but obscure and in need of explanation.

**M.** A chant is perfectly consonant with itself when its progression is not unsuitable; when its composition is not unlike its progression or disposition; and when opposition does not disrupt its composition.

**D.** Give an example of each.

**M.** A chant has unsuitable progression [Col. 1155D] when plagal descent is joined to authentic ascent. Such a chant, progressing without judgment and transgressing its due limits in both directions, attaches a horse’s tail to a human head. These responsories are marked by the disfigurement of this fault: *Sancte Paule*, *Cornelius*, and many other chants; in order that we might enter upon them without blemish, we have “done righteousness.” A chant also progresses unsuitably when it has too restricted an ascent; for just as there are limits beyond which it ought not to ascend, so there are notes to which it must ascend. It is certain of every authentic that it must ascend to the fifth. A plagal must ascend to the fourth, or at least to that note on which its *Saeculorum* begins.

[Col. 1156A] Take, for example, this antiphon, *Clamavi*, as it is sung in the fourth tone. When it is finished, if you begin its *Saeculorum*, you will make a ridiculous and dissonant leap. For that antiphon ascends no higher than low F, whereas the *Saeculorum* begins on high a. For this reason we have given a longer ascent to certain antiphons defective in this respect, namely *Dele Domine*, *Omnis terra*, *Si iniquitates*, and similar ones.

**D.** Continue, so that like clarity may illuminate what follows.

**M.** Composition contradicts progression in that chant which, having authentic composition throughout, inserts plagal descent somewhere; such were *Deus omnium*, *Sint lumbi*, and many others, both antiphons [Col. 1156B] and responsories. There are other chants in which composition agrees with progression but disagrees with disposition: according to the natural disposition of their letters they belong to one mode, but by similarity of composition they seem and are said to belong to another mode. Such is *Benedicta tu*, and many similar antiphons, which among almost everyone suffer from this fault: according to their natural disposition they belong to the first mode, yet by similarity of composition they are said and believed to belong to the second. The composition of that chant, however, is disrupted by opposition when its parts are composed dissimilarly, so that in one part it seems to belong to one tone and in another to a different tone; such were *Beata Caecilia*, *Videntes Joseph*, and *Dedisti, Domine*.

[Col. 1156C]

**D.** Which chants fail to identify their own mode in themselves?

**M.** Those which so lack the characteristic of any mode that they can end alike on the finals of different modes and belong to different tones. Among these were *Ecce sacerdos magnus* and many other chants of the seventh tone; *Visita nos* and many of the eighth; *Nazaraeus vocabitur* and many of the fifth; *Miserere mei Deus* and many of the sixth.

**D.** I should like you to state for me those characteristics of the modes by which chants are supported, so that they cannot waver between different finals.

[Col. 1156D]

**M.** If those who composed chants defectively—or later corrupted well-composed chants by notating or singing them badly—had known the characteristics you seek, so many improprieties of chants would not have emerged. To answer your questions briefly: in no chant of the first or second mode ought the semitone nearest the final ever to be absent, so that it is found somewhere at least once; and thus the finals of those modes cannot be interchanged. Likewise all chants of the fifth tone must have either a semitone below the final or below the fifth, or a tone above the sixth; while all chants of the sixth tone require a semitone below the final or below the fifth. All chants of the seventh tone must have a semitone below the fourth, and besides this either a tone below the final or a semitone above [Col. 1157A] the sixth; its plagal requires a semitone below the fourth and a tone below the final.

**D.** Having set out what appears necessary for knowledge of the tones, you can more conveniently proceed to establish teaching about each individual one.

**M.** I have answered your questions as briefly as I could; I shall answer any others you have with the same care.

**Disciple.** What is the first tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the authentic of the first mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant authentically ascending or composed, and ending on D or high a, is an authentic [Col. 1157B] of the first mode. What authentic ascent or composition is has been stated above.

**D.** What if some chant ascends authentically but has not authentic composition, but plagal composition?

**M.** Ancient irregularity lays claim to it as its own; it is wholly alien both to the novelty of our practice and to the present discussion.

[Col. 1158A]

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** Once the superfluities of multiple differences sung by others have been excluded, three differences seem necessary to some: the first serving mature and grave beginnings; the second, light and high ones; the third, middling ones. Yet, through the importunity of certain persons who indiscreetly emulate brevity, the one properly suited to grave beginnings, and sung in the first tone—namely, *A-men*—has been abandoned; we use the remaining two in this tone, as the formula below shows. For the third difference, adapted to the antiphon *Nos qui vivimus*, has been retained more by will than by reason. Since they have rejected the other, which is not only so proper but also lighter and more customary, on what grounds have they retained this one for a single psalm only? Yet would that they had been content in the first tone with this alone, since it expresses the characteristic of the first tone and cannot serve another tone. Neither statement is true of the other two differences.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Pri-mum quae-ri-te reg-num De-i* [First seek the kingdom of God.]  
A. *A-ve Ma-ri-a* [Hail, Mary.]  
A. *Mu-li-e-res* [Women.]  
A. *Ec-ce no-men* [Behold the name.]  
A. *An-ge-li Do-mi-ni* [Angels of the Lord.]  
A. *Ve-nit lu-men* [The light came.]  
A. *Ad-ju-to-ri-um* [Help.]  
A. *Spe-ci-o-sus* [Beautiful.]  
A. *Chri-sti vir-go* [Virgin of Christ.]  
A. *I-sti sunt* [These are.]  
A. *Bidu-o vi-vens* [Living for two days.]  
A. *O quan-tus luc-tus* [O how great the mourning.]  
A. *Eu-ge ser-ve* [Well done, servant.]  
A. *In me-di-o* [In the midst.]  
A. *Cum sub-le-vas-set* [When he had raised up.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Vi-di Do-mi-num* [I saw the Lord.]  
A. *Ec-ce ve-re* [Behold, truly.]  
A. *A-per-tis* [When opened.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]  
A. *Nos qui vi-vi-mus* [We who live.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]

[Col. 1157B]

**Disciple.** What is the second tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the plagal of the first mode.

[Col. 1158B]

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant descending or composed plagally, and ending on D or high a, is a plagal [of the] first mode. What plagal descent or composition is has been stated above.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

[Col. 1160]

**M.** Only one, serving all its beginnings quite suitably, as appears in what follows:

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Se-cun-dum au-tem si-mi-le est hu-ic* [But the second is like it.]  
A. *I-sti sunt sanc-ti* [These are holy.]  
A. *O sa-pi-en-ti-a* [O Wisdom.]  
*In u-ni-ver-sa ter-ra* [Throughout the whole earth.]  
A. *In om-nem ter-ram* [Into all the earth.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1159]

**Disciple.** What is the third tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the authentic of the second mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant authentically ascending [Col. 1160] or composed, ending on E or [square B, omitted in the source], is an authentic of the second mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** Two: one assigned quite suitably to lower beginnings, the other to higher beginnings, as the formula below shows.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Ter-ti-a di-es est quo haec fac-ta sunt* [The third day is when these things were made.]  
A. *Cum for-tis ar-ma-tus* [When the strong man, armed.]  
A. *Ni-gra sum* [I am black.]  
A. *Ma-los ma-le* [The wicked badly.]  
A. *Quo-ni-am* [Because.]  
A. *Do-mi-ne* [O Lord.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Qui de ter-ra est* [He who is of the earth.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1159]

**Disciple.** What is the fourth tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the plagal of the second mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant descending [Col. 1160] or composed plagally, ending on E or [square B, omitted in the source], is plagal of the second mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** Two: one suitable to the beginnings of chants proceeding gravely, the other appropriate to all the rest, as the description below shows.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Quar-ta vi-gi-li-a ve-nit ad e-os* [At the fourth watch he came to them.]  
A. *Lau-da-bo* [I shall praise.]  
A. *Nos sci-en-tes* [We, knowing.]  
A. *Rubum quem vi-[Col. 1161]de-rat* [The bush which he had seen.]  
A. *Ste-tit An-ge-lus* [The angel stood.]  
A. *I-ste cog-no-vit* [This man knew.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *O-cu-li me-i* [My eyes.]  
A. *In pro-le ma-tris* [In the mother's offspring.]  
A. *Ni-si di-li-gen-ter* [Unless diligently.]  
A. *In do-mum* [Into the house.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1161]

**Disciple.** What is the fifth tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the authentic of the third mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant authentically ascending [Col. 1162] or composed, ending on F or C, is an authentic of the third mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** Only one, suitable to all its beginnings, as is shown below.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Quin-que pru-den-tes in-tra-ve-runt ad nup-ti-as* [The five prudent virgins entered the wedding-feast.]  
A. *Con-fi-te-bor Do-mi-no* [I shall confess to the Lord.]  
A. *In con-spe-ctu an-ge-lo-rum* [In the sight of the angels.]  
A. *In so-le po-su-it* [He set [it] in the sun.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1161]

**Disciple.** What is the sixth tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the plagal of the third mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant descending [Col. 1162] or composed plagally, ending on F or C, is plagal of the third mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** One, agreeable to all its beginnings, as the formula below declares.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Sex-ta ho-ra se-dit su-per pu-te-um* [At the sixth hour he sat upon the well.]  
A. *O ad-mi-ra-bi-le com-mer-ci-um* [O wondrous exchange.]  
A. *Be-ne-di-ctus Do-mi-nus* [Blessed be the Lord.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1161]

**Disciple.** What is the seventh tone?

[Col. 1162]

**Master.** A rule determining the authentic of the fourth mode.

[Col. 1163]

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant authentically ascending or composed, ending on G, is an authentic of the fourth mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

[Col. 1164]

**M.** Two: one serving beginnings made on, or leaping to, the fifth; the other suitable to beginnings which ascend from the final through certain steps to the fifth, as appears below.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Sep-tem sunt spi-ri-tus an-te thro-num De-i* [Seven spirits are before the throne of God.]  
A. *Om-nes si-ti-en-tes* [All who thirst.]  
A. *Ve-te-rem ho-mi-nem* [The old man.]  
A. *Ar-gen-tum* [Silver.]  
A. *Vi-vit Do-mi-nus* [The Lord lives.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Di-xe-runt dis-ci-pu-li* [The disciples said.]  
A. *Ie-ru-sa-lem* [Jerusalem.]  
A. *Be-ne-di-cta-tu* [Blessed are you.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1163]

**Disciple.** What is the eighth tone?

**Master.** A rule determining the plagal of the fourth mode.

**D.** What is that rule?

**M.** Every regular chant descending [Col. 1164] or composed plagally, ending on G, is plagal of the fourth mode.

**D.** How many differences does it have?

**M.** Two: one serving the beginnings of chants which begin on the fourth above the final; the other assigned to all its other beginnings, as the following show.

*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Oc-to sunt be-a-ti-tu-di-nes* [There are eight beatitudes.]  
A. *Scri-ptum est* [It is written.]  
A. *Nup-ti-ae* [Wedding-feast.]  
A. *Ad-o-ra-te Do-mi-num* [Worship the Lord.]  
A. *Dum me-di-um* [While the middle.]  
*Glo-ri-a se-cu-lo-rum a-men* [Glory for ever. Amen.]  
A. *Ec-ce an-cil-la* [Behold the handmaid.]  
A. *Do-mi-nus di-xit* [The Lord said.]  
A. *De pro-fun-dis* [Out of the depths.]  
A. *In ae-ter-num* [For ever.]  
*Glo-ri-a Pa-tri et Fi-li-o et Spi-ri-tu-i sanc-to* [Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.]

[Col. 1163]

**D.** I remember that you said above, concerning the two differences of the first tone, that they do not express the characteristic of their mode and can be adapted to another tone. Are the differences set out above for the remaining modes, I ask you, proper ones?

**M.** Some of them are proper and suitably devised, such as the difference of the second tone and the first difference of the fourth, which are of the same tone as their antiphons. But the differences of the third tone are sung in the second tone and can be adapted far more suitably to chants of the second than to chants of the third, since they end on the same finals. The difference of the fifth, however, is sung in the fourth tone, and likewise the difference of the seventh in the second. The differences of the sixth and eighth tones do not express the characteristics of their own modes. Therefore all these are reckoned faulty by the Peripatetics among musicians; for the difference assigned to a mode ought to belong to that mode, so that difference and antiphon are of the same mode and the psalm is sung in the same mode. Have you understood all this?

[Col. 1165B]

**D.** Certainly I have understood it, and what you say seems most true. For it is a mystery hidden from the ages, and a wondrous sacrament which it is not lawful for a human being to utter, that the differences of the third and seventh tones are sung in the second tone, and the difference of the fifth in the fourth.

**M.** In this matter invention certainly sinned, or forgetfulness corrupted the invention.

**D.** I likewise wonder concerning the verses of responsories, why they do not have to end on the same finals as their responsories and are shown to belong to another tone, except for the verses of the sixth and eighth tones.

[Col. 1166A]

**M.** The usual answer is this: if the chant of the versicle is judged by itself, it truly belongs to another mode; but it ought not to be judged without that portion of the responsory which is repeated, so that the versicle and the repetition form one chant. In responsories there are many phrases which, if judged by themselves, would be found both badly composed and of another mode. Accordingly, just as the whole responsory is one chant, although it consists of different phrases belonging to different modes, so the versicle and repetition together are one chant, composed from the one and the other. For this reason the repetition of the responsory must agree with the versicle both in lettering and in melody.

**D.** Unless I am mistaken, this opinion is slippery and seems a certain evasion, lacking solid truth. But now, speaking from your own judgment, set forth what you think concerning metra, differences, and versicles.

[Col. 1166B]

**M.** What you ask is not the business of the present work, since, by prohibition of the holy Cistercian chapter, it is no longer permitted to alter anything in Guido’s Antiphonary. Seek out, however, the music treatise of Guido of Augsburg, which he writes to his most holy master, Lord William, first abbot of Rievaulx. There you will be able to receive sufficient instruction about such matters.

## Order of Matters Contained in the Earlier Part of This First Volume

[Col. 1165]

# ST BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1165]

## General Preface

§ I.—On the various editions of the works of St Bernard, where are explained both the causes and reasons of this most recent edition and its advantages and usefulness. 15

§ II.—On Bernard’s holiness, learning, and authority in the Church. 25

§ III.—On Bernard’s success in reforming the morals of clergy, monks, and laity. 29

§ IV.—On the schism of Anacletus, suppressed through St Bernard. 33

§ V.—On the errors of Peter Abelard and Gilbert of Poitiers, refuted by St Bernard. 41

§ VI.—On the Henricians and other heretics repressed by St Bernard. 47

§ VII.—On the preaching of the holy expedition carried out by St Bernard, and its unhappy outcome. 53

**Bernardine Chronology.** 57

# Volume One of the Works of St Bernard—Letters
EPISTLE I.—To his nephew Robert, who had passed from the Cistercian to the Cluniac Order.—He recalls Robert, his kinsman, who, whether induced by dread of the stricter rule, by the attraction of a more relaxed life, or even by the flatteries and crafty whisperings of others, had gone over from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs, with remarkable charity and more-than-paternal affection. 67

EPISTLE II.—To the boy Fulk, who afterwards became Archdeacon of Langres.—He earnestly and seriously admonishes Fulk, a regular canon whom his uncle had drawn back into the secular world by blandishments and promises, to obey and cleave to God rather than to his uncle. 79

EPISTLE III.—To the regular canons of Aildicourt.—He says that their praises alarm him rather than flatter him. Then, that certain canons of Saint Augustine received by him ought not to be hindered. 87

[Col. 1166]

EPISTLE IV.—To Arnold, Abbot of Morimond.—He recalls Arnold, an abbot wandering abroad after rashly abandoning his monastery, to the care of the monastery, setting forth the scandals among the brethren and the dangers to the flock. 89

EPISTLE V.—To the monk Adam.—He dissuades him from attaching himself to Arnold, Abbot of Morimond, or making himself the companion of his pilgrimage—or rather, his vagrancy. 91

EPISTLE VI.—To Bruno of Cologne.—He wishes certain wandering monks of the Abbot of Morimond to be brought back to the monastery through Bruno’s efforts. 92

EPISTLE VII.—To the monk Adam.—He urges Adam to return at last, even now that the abbot is dead, to the monastery; he shows that in such a case there had been no bond of obedience. Finally, he answers why he receives religious from other Orders. 93

EPISTLE VIII.—To Bruno, Elect of Cologne.—When Bruno consulted Bernard concerning acceptance of the bishopric of Cologne, Bernard replies so as to keep him in suspense—indeed, to alarm him with the weight of so great an office—admonishing him to seek God’s counsel through prayer. 105

EPISTLE IX.—To the same, now Archbishop of Cologne.—He induces Bruno, newly made Archbishop of Cologne, to fear. 107

EPISTLE X.—To the same.—He stirs Bruno to a just zeal in correcting others. 108

EPISTLE XI.—To Guigo the Prior and the other religious of the Grande Chartreuse.—He devoutly discusses at length the law, signs, effects, and degrees of true and sincere charity, whose perfection is reserved for the homeland. 108

EPISTLE XII.—To the same.—He commends himself to their prayers. 115

EPISTLE XIII.—To Pope Honorius.—He requests that Alberic’s election to the bishopric of Châlons be ratified. 116

EPISTLE XIV.—To the same Pope Honorius.—He commends the cause of the Church of Dijon to the Supreme Pontiff. 117

[Col. 1167]

EPISTLE XV.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—On the matter above. 118

EPISTLE XVI.—To Peter, Cardinal-Priest.—On the matter above. 119

EPISTLE XVII.—To Peter, Cardinal-Deacon.—He excuses himself for not having come when summoned, and answers concerning the writings requested of him. 119

EPISTLE XVIII.—To the same.—He strives to dispel the reputation for holiness attributed to him, and promises to share the little books he had written. 120

EPISTLE XIX.—To the same.—He commends the delegates from Rheims. 122

EPISTLE XX.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—On the matter above. 123

EPISTLE XXI.—To Matthew, Legate.—He offers a most graceful excuse for not coming when summoned to conduct business. 123

EPISTLE XXII.—To Humbald, Archbishop of Lyons and Legate.—He commends the cause of the Bishop of Meaux. 124

EPISTLE XXIII.—To Atto, Bishop of Troyes.—He consoles and praises Bishop Atto, who, while ill and expecting death, had distributed all his possessions among the poor, but had been restored to health. 125

EPISTLE XXIV.—To Master Gilbert Universal, Bishop of London.—He praises Gilbert because, having become a bishop, he cultivates poverty. 128

EPISTLE XXV.—To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—He exhorts Hugh to strive to be both patient and peaceable among his people of Rouen, and to moderate his zeal with discretion. 129

EPISTLE XXVI.—To Guy, Bishop of Lausanne. 130

EPISTLE XXVII.—To Arducius, Elect of Geneva.—He admonishes him to attribute his election to divine grace and thereafter to strive diligently to cooperate with it. 130

EPISTLE XXVIII.—To the same, now bishop.—Meanwhile he exhorts him to adorn, at least by merits following, the dignity which he obtained without preceding merits. 131

EPISTLE XXIX.—To Stephen, Bishop of Metz.—He congratulates Stephen upon the restoration of peace to the Church, which ought to be attributed solely to the benefit of the one God. 132

EPISTLE XXX.—To Albero, Primicerius of Metz.—He admonishes that a certain matter which Albero was pressing should be accomplished according to God’s good pleasure, seeking not so much the gift as its fruit. 132

EPISTLE XXXI.—To Hugh, Count of Champagne, who had become a Knight of the Temple.—He congratulates Hugh upon his embracing holy knighthood, and promises remembrance of his benefactions. 135

EPISTLE XXXII.—To the Abbot of Saint-Nicaise at Rheims.—He consoles the abbot over the departure and transfer of the monk Drogo to another monastery, and exhorts him to patience. 136

EPISTLE XXXIII.—To Hugh, Abbot of Pontigny.—He states his mind more plainly concerning the reception of Drogo, and dispels every adverse suspicion concerning himself. 138

EPISTLE XXXIV.—To Drogo, Monk.—He congratulates Drogo for passing to a stricter observance, and exhorts him to perseverance. 139

EPISTLE XXXV.—To Master Hugh Farsitus.—He commends to him the cause of a certain Humbert, and admonishes him not to be ashamed to correct himself in a certain erroneous judgment. 141

EPISTLE XXXVI.—To the same.—He answers Hugh’s letters and advises him to desist from attacking the judgment of the bishop now deceased. 142

EPISTLE XXXVII.—To Theobald, Count of Champagne.—He wonders that, in Humbert’s cause, while asking what is just and equitable, he suffers rejection; and he admonishes Theobald, in view of the supreme Judge, not to deny aid and mercy to a wretched man. 143

EPISTLE XXXVIII.—To the same.—On the matter above. 145

EPISTLE XXXIX.—To the same.—He commends various causes to Theobald. Finally, he exhorts him to conduct himself honorably and reverently toward the bishops assembled in his city for the council. 146

EPISTLE XL.—To the same.—He commends a poor religious man to Theobald. 147

EPISTLE XLI.—To the same.—He commends an elderly religious man. 148

EPISTLE XLII.—To Henry, Archbishop of Sens.—This letter more properly deserved the name and place of a treatise; accordingly, having removed it from its position, we transferred it to Volume II among the treatises, under this title: *Letter 42, or Treatise, On the Morals and Office of Bishops, to Henry, Archbishop of Sens.* 148

EPISTLE XLIII.—To the same Henry.—He writes for the liberty of the Church of Molesme. 148

[Col. 1168]

EPISTLE XLIV.—To the same.—On the matter above. 148

EPISTLE XLV.—To King Louis of France.—The Cistercians sternly and freely rebuke King Louis, hostile and injurious toward the Bishop of Paris, declaring that they will plead the bishop’s cause before the Roman Pontiff unless the king desists from his wrongful course. 149

EPISTLE XLVI.—To Pope Honorius II.—On the matter above.—They complain to the Pontiff that, by surreptitiously obtaining relaxation of the interdict, the King of France, formerly inclined toward peace, has become more obstinate. 153

EPISTLE XLVII.—To the same, in the person of Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres.—He lays before the Pontiff the case of the Bishop of Paris, unjustly oppressed by King Louis. Compelled by an interdict imposed by the French bishops, the king had promised restitution; but after obtaining absolution from Honorius, he became more contumacious and did not fulfill it. 153

EPISTLE XLVIII.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—On the matter above, and against detractors. He answers complaints made against him and asks for the capacity to remain in solitude and thirst for it. 154

EPISTLE XLIX.—To Pope Honorius.—For Henry, Archbishop of Sens. 157

EPISTLE L.—To the same.—On the matter above.—He asks that the archbishop be permitted to appeal to the Apostolic See. 158

EPISTLE LI.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—On the matter above. 158

EPISTLE LII.—To the same.—The Bishop of Chartres had not sought a journey to Jerusalem. He asks to be released from public causes and affairs. 159

EPISTLE LIII.—To the same.—He presents two religious men, including himself, to Haimeric. 159

EPISTLE LIV.—To the same.—He commends Abbot Vivian and admonishes him to take serious care for his soul. 160

EPISTLE LV.—To Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres.—He asks Geoffrey to protect and assist a certain enclosed monk who had deserted his institute but had now repented. 160

EPISTLE LVI.—To the same.—He is uncertain about Norbert’s pilgrimage to Jerusalem; he does not assent to Norbert’s opinion concerning Antichrist. He also commends Humbert’s cause. 162

EPISTLE LVII.—To the same.—Greater goods ought not to be impeded by lesser vows. This appears, unless I am mistaken, to have been written in the case of the monk mentioned above in Letter LV. 163

EPISTLE LVIII.—To Ebalus, Bishop of Châlons.—He exhorts Ebalus to take care to appoint a suitable man over the monastery or church of All Saints. 165

EPISTLE LIX.—To Guilencus, Bishop of Langres.—He exhorts him to cede to the Church of Saint Stephen at Dijon certain property vacant through the death of Garnier, so as to remove an occasion for scandals and accusations. 166

EPISTLE LX.—To the same.—He intercedes for the Church of Molesme. 167

EPISTLE LXI.—To Ricuinus, Bishop of Toul.—He sends back to him for care a man who had come, by order of the Bishop of Toul, to undergo penance. 167

EPISTLE LXII.—To Henry, Bishop of Verdun.—He commends to the bishop a woman burdened with many sins, but now repentant. 168

EPISTLE LXIII.—To the same.—He clears himself of a rash act of which he had been accused; he desires to learn about it; he commends Guy to him. 168

EPISTLE LXIV.—To Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln.—Philip, wishing to travel to Jerusalem, happened to turn aside to Clairvaux and resolved to remain there. Bernard requests Alexander’s consent to this. He commends to him the business concerning Philip’s creditors. Finally, he exhorts him not to put too much trust in worldly glory. 169

EPISTLE LXV.—To Alvisus, Abbot of Anchin.—He praises Alvisus’s fatherly gentleness toward Godwin. He excuses himself concerning the admission and asks forgiveness. 170

EPISTLE LXVI.—To Geoffrey, Abbot of Saint-Médard.—He asks his assistance in reconciling Abbot Alvisus to himself, and consoles him in his tribulations. 173

EPISTLE LXVII.—To the monks of Flavigny.—He defends his reception of Brother B., who had left a monastery hitherto unknown to him, for just reasons. 175

EPISTLE LXVIII.—To the same.—On the matter above. 176

EPISTLE LXIX.—To Guy, Abbot of Trois-Fontaines.—He instructs Guy, who through the negligence of the ministers had erred in consecrating the chalice because of a shortage of wine. 179

EPISTLE LXX.—To the same.—He teaches what mercy ought to be in a pastor, and admonishes him to reconsider the sentence pronounced against a transgressing monk. 182

EPISTLE LXXI.—To the monks of the same place.—He says that he had postponed his visitation so far, not through negligence but in expectation of a suitable opportunity; he consoles them concerning the death of Abbot Roger. 183

[Col. 1169]

EPISTLE LXXII.—To Rainald, Abbot of Foigny.—He shows how far he is from praises. Christ’s yoke is light. He declines the title of father, being content to be called brother. 184

EPISTLE LXXIII.—To the same.—He instructs Rainald, excessively anxious and complaining about the office of prelate entrusted to him; he admonishes him to bestow help and consolation on his own people rather than demand them from those people. 187

EPISTLE LXXIV.—To the same.—Bernard had wished Rainald to refrain from troublesome complaints; now he directs that he himself be informed of Rainald’s affairs. 188

EPISTLE LXXV.—To Artald, Abbot of Preuilly.—He dissuades him from founding a monastery in Spain. 189

EPISTLE LXXVI.—To the Abbot of the Canons of Saint Peter of the Mount.—What ought to be done with a man who, after long continuance in a religious house and habit, had gone over to the secular world and to a second marriage. 190

EPISTLE LXXVII.—To Master Hugh of Saint-Victor.—(This letter too, removed from this place, was assigned a place among the treatises in Volume II.) 190

EPISTLE LXXVIII.—To Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—He praises Suger for unexpectedly turning away from pomp and outward splendor to the care of modesty and religious discipline. He sharply censures a cleric devoted rather to court life than to the ministry of God. 191

EPISTLE LXXIX.—To Abbot Luke.—He admonishes that cohabitation with women is to be avoided, and discusses what should be done concerning a brother fallen into crime. 199

EPISTLE LXXX.—To Guy, Abbot of Molesme.—He consoles him in affliction caused by a grave wrong, but says that vengeance should be tempered with mercy. 201

EPISTLE LXXXI.—To Gerard, Abbot of Pultaria.—He clears himself against an unjust accusation. 202

EPISTLE LXXXII.—To the Abbot of Saint John at Chartres.—He dissuades him from relinquishing pastoral care and from a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. 202

EPISTLE LXXXIII.—To Simon, Abbot of Saint Nicholas.—He consoles him in persecution. Pious endeavors do not always attain their desired results. He discusses what a prelate devoted to stricter discipline should do with his subjects. 204

EPISTLE LXXXIV.—To the same.—He sends back an erring monk, but advises that, upon his return, he be treated more gently and mildly. 205

EPISTLE LXXXV.—To the same William.—He gently reproves William, who complained that Bernard was not responding with equal offices of love. 206

EPISTLE LXXXVI.—To the same.—He sends back a fugitive monk who has been, and should be, severely rebuked. But he advises William himself, who was considering a change or a private life, to persevere. 210

EPISTLE LXXXVII.—To Ogerius, Regular Canon.—He disapproves the relinquishment of pastoral care, even when done from love of pious repose. Nevertheless, he instructs him how thereafter he ought to live as a private person in a religious community. 211

EPISTLE LXXXVIII.—To the same.—He says that, hindered by many occupations, he has thus far been unable to satisfy Ogerius’s wishes and is now compelled to write more sparingly. He forbids the publication of a certain work of his unless revised. 217
