EPISTLE LXXXIX.—To the same.—He excuses the brevity of his writing on the ground of the sacred season, to which silence is more fitting; likewise on the ground of his profession and lack of learning, so that he does not dare to usurp the office of teaching. 220

EPISTLE XC.—To the same.—Sincere love has no need of lengthy letters or many words; he is recovering from a state in which he had almost despaired of his health. 221

EPISTLE XCI.—To the abbots assembled at Soissons.—He urges the abbots to handle vigorously the business for which they have assembled. He earnestly commends zeal for progress: there must be no delay if certain lukewarm and dissolute persons perhaps refuse and murmur. 222

EPISTLE XCII.—To Henry, King of England.—He asks the king’s favor for monks sent by him to build a monastery. 224

EPISTLE XCIII.—To Henry, Bishop of Winchester.—He offers him a respectful greeting. 225

EPISTLE XCIV.—To the abbot of a monastery in Yorkshire, from which a prior had departed with several brethren. 226

EPISTLE XCV.—To Thurstan, Archbishop of York.—He praises his charity and beneficence toward religious persons. 228

EPISTLE XCVI.—To Richard, Abbot of Fountains, and his companions, who had passed from another Order to the Cistercian.—He praises them for the renewal of religious discipline. 229

EPISTLE XCVII.—To Duke Conrad.—He dissuades him from making war on the Count of Geneva, lest he provoke God the avenger against himself. 229

EPISTLE XCVIII.—On the Maccabees; but to whom it was written is unknown.—He answers the question why, among the righteous of the Old Law, the Church has decreed a feast day for the Maccabees alone. 230

EPISTLE XCIX.—To a certain monk.—Anxious because a certain monk had departed from his monastery, he writes that the monk’s letter has freed him from adverse suspicion. 234

EPISTLE C.—To a certain bishop.—He praises the bishop’s favor and beneficence toward poor religious persons. 235

EPISTLE CI.—To religious persons.—He asks that a monk who had departed without permission be kindly received upon his return. 236

EPISTLE CII.—To a certain abbot.—The reform of a certain unruly monk must be attempted by every means; but if he is incorrigible, he must be expelled, lest more persons be corrupted by association with him. 236

EPISTLE CIII.—To the brother of William, monk of Clairvaux.—After a notable commendation of religious poverty, he reproves in him an excessive attachment to earthly goods, joined with harm to the poor—indeed, to himself—since he would prefer to yield his possessions to death rather than to the love of Christ. 237

EPISTLE CIV.—To Master Walter of Calvomont.—He exhorts him to flee the world, warning that the cause of Christ and of the soul is weightier than that of parents. 238

EPISTLE CV.—To Romanus, Subdeacon of the Roman Curia.—He presses upon him the resolve of religious life, inculcating remembrance of death. 240

EPISTLE CVI.—To Master Henry Murdac.—He urges him to embrace the state of religious life, briefly setting forth its delights. 241

EPISTLE CVII.—To Thomas, Provost of Beverley.—This Thomas had vowed himself to the Cistercian Order at Clairvaux. Bernard exhorts him, while delaying, to fulfill his vows. But that he sang to a deaf man will be shown by the following letter, which recounts Thomas’s unhappy end. In this letter, however, the whole economy of salvation is described with the greatest profundity. 242

EPISTLE CVIII.—To Thomas of Saint-Omer, after he had broken his promise to come to conversion.—He exhorts him to abandon his studies and enter religious life, setting before him the unhappy end of Thomas of Beverley. 249

EPISTLE CIX.—To the illustrious young Geoffrey of Péronne and his companions.—He praises the noble young men for their purpose of religious life and exhorts them to perseverance. 251

EPISTLE CX.—A consolatory letter to the parents of the same Geoffrey.—They have no cause to mourn their religious son as though lost, nor even to fear some wrongdoing on his account. 253

EPISTLE CXI.—In the person of the monk Elias, to his parents.—He exhorts them not to try to hinder or draw back one wishing to serve God: it would be unworthy and futile. 253

EPISTLE CXII.—To Geoffrey of Lisieux.—He grieves that Geoffrey has abandoned his resolve of religious life and returned to the secular world, and exhorts him to repentance. 255

EPISTLE CXIII.—To Sophia, a virgin.—He praises her for despising worldly glory; and, after setting forth the praises, privileges, rewards, and adornments of religious virgins, exhorts her to perseverance. 256

EPISTLE CXIV.—To another nun.—She had borne, under a religious habit, a heart devoted to the world. He now praises her repentance and exhorts her not to neglect grace. 259

EPISTLE CXV.—To another nun of the monastery of Saint Mary at Troyes.—He dissuades her from the hermitage, which she was rashly and imprudently seeking. 261

EPISTLE CXVI.—To Ermengard, formerly Countess of Brittany.—He gently and intimately conveys the affection of his heart and the power of religious love. 262

EPISTLE CXVII.—To the same.—He praises her eagerness in divine service and indicates his desire to see her. 263

EPISTLE CXVIII.—To Beatrice, a noble and religious matron.—He commends her dutiful charity and solicitude. 263

EPISTLE CXIX.—To the Duke and Duchess of Lorraine.—He gives thanks for the tolls remitted thus far, but wishes care taken lest the favor of princes be thwarted by the actions of their servants. 264

EPISTLE CXX.—To the Duchess of Lorraine.—He gives thanks for the offered benefits and deters her from an unjust war. 265

EPISTLE CXXI.—To the Duchess of Burgundy.—He endeavors to placate Hugh’s anger and seeks from her consent to a certain marriage. 266

EPISTLE CXXII.—From Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours, to Abbot Bernard.—Moved by the renown of Bernard’s name and holiness, he seeks his friendship. 266

EPISTLE CXXIII.—Abbot Bernard’s reply to Hildebert, Archbishop of Tours.—He returns praise for praise. 267

EPISTLE CXXIV.—To the same Hildebert, who had not yet received Pope Innocent.—He exhorts him to acknowledge Innocent, exiled in France because of the schism of Peter Leo, as the legitimate Pontiff. 268

EPISTLE CXXV.—To Master Geoffrey of L’Oratoire.—He seeks his assistance in upholding Innocent’s pontificate against the schism of Peter Leo. 269

EPISTLE CXXVI.—To the bishops of Aquitaine against Gerard of Angoulême.—He ably defends Innocent’s cause as legitimate Pontiff against Gerard of Angoulême, who was acting for the schismatic party; he depicts Gerard’s character and exposes his evasions. 270

EPISTLE CXXVII.—To William, Count of Poitou and Duke of Aquitaine, in the person of Hugh, Duke of Burgundy.—He exhorts William, who favored the antipope Anacletus, to receive Innocent as the true Pontiff. 281

EPISTLE CXXVIII.—To the same.—He earnestly exhorts him to restore to the Church the clerics whom he had expelled. 282

EPISTLE CXXIX.—To the Genoese.—He exhorts them steadfastly to retain and defend the peace which he had formerly negotiated in their presence. 283

EPISTLE CXXX.—To the Pisans.—He praises the Pisans for their zeal and support for Pope Innocent, who, with Rome occupied by the antipope Anacletus, had gone into exile at Pisa. 285

EPISTLE CXXXI.—To the Milanese.—Although the Milanese had been reconciled to Innocent, they seemed to waver in duty and obedience; he urges them to preserve their constancy, recalling the recent benefits of the Roman Church toward them. 286

EPISTLE CXXXII.—To the clergy of Milan.—He congratulates the Milanese clergy, through whose efforts the city, abandoning Anacletus’s schism, had returned to the unity of the Church. 287

EPISTLE CXXXIII.—To all the citizens of Milan.—Invited to make peace, he rejoices that his assistance is sought for this work. 288

EPISTLE CXXXIV.—To converts newly entered at Milan.—He congratulates the Milanese novices upon their conversion and promises to visit them after the council is finished. 289

EPISTLE CXXXV.—To Peter, Bishop of Pavia.—He refers the praises offered to him back to God. He praises the bishop for works of mercy. 289

EPISTLE CXXXVI.—To Pope Innocent.—He wishes Dalfinus, ready to make satisfaction for injuries inflicted, to be treated more mildly. 290

EPISTLE CXXXVII.—To the Empress of the Romans.—The Milanese were not received into favor by the Pontiff before they themselves had received Emperor Lothair. Accordingly, he commends them to the empress’s clemency. 291

EPISTLE CXXXVIII.—To Henry, King of England.—He seeks the king’s help for Pope Innocent. 292

EPISTLE CXXXIX.—To Emperor Lothair.—He urges the emperor to repress the schismatics. He commends the cause of a certain church situated near Toul. 293

EPISTLE CXL.—To the same.—He commends to Lothair the Pisans, supporters of the Pontiff. 295

EPISTLE CXLI.—To Humbert, Abbot of Igny.—He sharply reproves him for rashly and without counsel abandoning the office of prelate. 296

EPISTLE CXLII.—To the Alpine monks.—He commends and consoles the Alpine monks, who had joined themselves under the Cistercian Order to the brethren of Clairvaux, concerning the absence of their father, who had been raised to a higher rank. He therefore instructs them about electing a new abbot. 297

EPISTLE CXLIII.—To his own brethren of Clairvaux.—He excuses the length of his absence, which was no less—indeed, more—burdensome to himself than to his brethren. Meanwhile he briefly reminds them of their duty. 298

EPISTLE CXLIV.—To the same.—He expresses the pain of his prolonged absence from beloved Clairvaux and his most tender affection and longing for his sons. Nevertheless, he declares the consolation he finds in such great labors for the Church. 300

EPISTLE CXLV.—To the abbots assembled at Cîteaux.—He wishes them to be aware of his labors and sufferings, perhaps thus excusing his absence. He certainly wishes to die not abroad but among his own. 302

EPISTLE CXLVI.—To Burchard, Abbot of Balerne.—He rejoices that his labors in forming Burchard have not been fruitless; yet a happy result must be attributed to God alone. 303

EPISTLE CXLVII.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.—Peter had consoled Bernard, laboring abroad amid varied and difficult affairs for the Church, by sending Gebuin, Archdeacon of Troyes. Bernard therefore recalls Peter’s benevolent spirit most affectionately and proclaims the happier condition of the Church now that the schism has been extinguished. 304

EPISTLE CXLVIII.—To the same.—He answers Peter briefly, reserving more for another occasion. 305

EPISTLE CXLIX.—To the same.—He admonishes him to cease laboriously claiming the monastery of Saint-Bertin for himself. 306

EPISTLE CL.—To Pope Innocent.—He praises the Pontiff for various right actions and stirs his zeal against the ambition of Philip, who was attempting to seize the see of Tours by unlawful means. 306

EPISTLE CLI.—To Philip, invader of the Church of Tours.—He expresses his profound grief over Philip, who was seeking the prelacy of the Church of Tours by improper means. 310

EPISTLE CLII.—To Pope Innocent, for the Bishop of Troyes.—The insolence of clerics is nourished by bishops’ indolence; but the Bishop of Troyes is oppressed because he had corrected clerics. 311

EPISTLE CLIII.—To Bernard de Portes, of the Carthusian Order.—Asked for an exposition of the Song of Songs, he pleads his own inadequacy for so great a work and for others’ expectation. 312

EPISTLE CLIV.—To the same.—Business had prevented him from keeping his promise to visit the Carthusians. He sends the requested sermons on the Song of Songs. 313

EPISTLE CLV.—To Pope Innocent, for the same man when he had been elected.—Bernard de Portes, appointed bishop in Lombardy, was indeed worthy of that honor, but less suitable for such a place; he should therefore be reserved more fittingly for another. 314

EPISTLE CLVI.—To the same, for the clerics of Orléans. 314

EPISTLE CLVII.—To Haimeric, for the same persons. 315

EPISTLE CLVIII.—To Pope Innocent, concerning the murder of Master Thomas, Prior of Saint-Victor at Paris. 315

EPISTLE CLIX.—To the same, in the person of Stephen, Bishop of Paris.—On the matter above. 319

EPISTLE CLX.—To Haimeric, Chancellor, in the person of the same bishop.—On the matter above. 320

EPISTLE CLXI.—To Pope Innocent.—Against the perpetrators of the murder of Archembald, Subdean of Orléans. 320

EPISTLE CLXII.—To Haimeric, Chancellor, concerning the same. 321

EPISTLE CLXIII.—To John of Crema, Cardinal-Priest, concerning the same. 321

EPISTLE CLXIV.—Pleading of the cause of the Church of Langres before Pope Innocent.—Bernard complains that the election of a bishop for the Church of Langres has been attempted deceitfully and contrary to a pledge given. 322

EPISTLE CLXV.—To Fulk, Dean, and Guy, Treasurer, of the Church of Lyons.—On the matter above. 325

EPISTLE CLXVI.—To Pope Innocent.—On the matter above. 326

EPISTLE CLXVII.—To the same.—For the same business. 327

EPISTLE CLXVIII.—To the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Curia.—On the matter above. 327

EPISTLE CLXIX.—To Pope Innocent.—Why he detained the summoned clerics of the Church of Langres, and to whom the office of electing ought to be entrusted. 328

EPISTLE CLXX.—To Louis the Younger, King of France.—He attempts to vindicate the election of his Prior Geoffrey as Bishop of Langres, an election which the king seemed to oppose. 329

EPISTLE CLXXI.—To Pope Innocent.—For Fulk, Archbishop-Elect of Lyons. 331

EPISTLE CLXXII.—To the same, in the person of Geoffrey, Bishop of Langres.—Of the same subject as the preceding letter. 332

EPISTLE CLXXIII.—To Fulk himself.—He commends the cause of certain religious persons. 332

EPISTLE CLXXIV.—To the canons of Lyons, concerning the conception of Saint Mary.—The feast of the Conception is new and rests on no legitimate foundation; moreover, it should not have been instituted without consultation with the Apostolic See, to whose judgment Bernard submits his own opinion. 332

EPISTLE CLXXV.—To the Patriarch of Jerusalem.—Anticipated by his letter, he replies familiarly and commends the Knights Templar. 336

EPISTLE CLXXVI.—To Pope Innocent, in the person of Albero, Archbishop of Trier.—He declares his devotion and obedience toward Innocent and toward the Church beyond the Alps. 337

EPISTLE CLXXVII.—To the same, in the person of the same man.—He complains of the pastoral office imposed upon him; but, in carrying out the duties of his office, he is hindered by the rivalry of others, not without fault on the Pontiff’s own part. 338

EPISTLE CLXXVIII.—To Pope Innocent for Albero, Archbishop of Trier.—He complains that certain perverse and Church-destroying persons are fortified by papal authority in carrying out their wicked counsels, while meanwhile other prelates, zealous for God, are abandoned and despised. 339

EPISTLE CLXXIX.—To the same, for the same.—He pleads the cause of Albero, Archbishop of Trier, against the Abbot of Saint-Maximin and rebellious, contumacious monks. 342

EPISTLE CLXXX.—To the same, for the same.—He again commends to the Pontiff the business of the Archbishop of Trier, asking him, after a fuller examination of the case, to revoke a judgment obtained surreptitiously. 343

EPISTLE CLXXXI.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—He professes himself unequal to Haimeric’s benefits, able to be grateful only through the affection of his will. 344

EPISTLE CLXXXII.—To Henry, Archbishop of Sens.—He sharply reproves him as harsh, because he had improperly deposed an archdeacon and was difficult regarding equitable requests and counsels of peace. 344

EPISTLE CLXXXIII.—To Conrad, King of the Romans.—He commends to him reverence for the Apostolic See. 345

EPISTLE CLXXXIV.—To Pope Innocent.—The monks whom the Pontiff had requested cannot be sent. 345

EPISTLE CLXXXV.—To Eustace, occupier of the see of Valence.—He exhorts him, mindful of his age, imminent death, and divine judgment, to repent and not obey the wicked counsels of flatterers. 346

EPISTLE CLXXXVI.—To Simon, son of the Castellan of Cambrai.—He commends the monks of Vaucelles to Simon’s protection, asking him to ratify his father’s donation. 348

EPISTLE CLXXXVII.—To the bishops summoned at Sens, against Peter Abelard.—He urges the bishops vigorously to pursue the cause of religion against Abelard. 349

EPISTLE CLXXXVIII.—To the bishops and cardinals of the Curia, concerning the same.—He admonishes them to keep watch against Peter Abelard’s errors. 351

EPISTLE CLXXXIX.—To Pope Innocent, concerning the same.—He declares his distress because Abelard’s errors arose immediately after the schism, and admonishes the Pontiff to intervene against them. 354

EPISTLE CXC.—To Pope Innocent, concerning certain errors of Peter Abelard. 357

EPISTLE CXCI.—To Innocent, in the person of the Lord Archbishop of Rheims, etc.—Abelard, puffed up by vain conceit of knowledge and boasting of favor at the Roman Curia, ought promptly to be restrained by papal authority. 357

EPISTLE CXCII.—To Master Guy of Castello.—He admonishes him to love and support Abelard in such a way that he does not support Abelard’s errors. 358

EPISTLE CXCIII.—To Master Ivo, Cardinal, concerning the same.—It is unworthy that Abelard should find supporters in the Roman Curia. 359

EPISTLE CXCIV.—Reply of Pope Innocent against the heresies of Peter Abelard. 359

EPISTLE CXCV.—To the Bishop of Constance.—He admonishes him to expel Arnold of Brescia—driven from Italy and France and now hiding with the bishop—or rather to keep him confined so as to prevent greater harm. 361

EPISTLE CXCVI.—To Guy, Legate, concerning the same.—He warns him to avoid familiarity with Arnold of Brescia, lest Arnold disseminate his errors more securely under Guy’s authority. 363

EPISTLE CXCVII.—To Peter, Dean of Besançon.—He rebukes him for injuries done to the Abbot of Cherlieu. 364

EPISTLE CXCVIII.—To Pope Innocent.—He asks that Guy be defended against the force and injuries of an oppressor. Nothing so becomes the supreme prelate of the Church as zeal for justice. 365

EPISTLE CXCIX.—To the same.—On the matter above. He requests confirmation of a judgment pronounced for religious persons unjustly oppressed, and that no further audience be given to accusations. 367

EPISTLE CC.—To Master Ulger, Bishop of Angers, concerning the grave dispute between him and the abbess of Fontevraud. 367

EPISTLE CCI.—To Baldwin, Abbot of the monastery of Rieti.—He exhorts him vigorously to apply himself to his office; for this he requires the word of preaching, the example of action, and especially devotion to prayer. 369

EPISTLE CCII.—To the clergy of Sens.—The election of a new prelate must not be undertaken without deliberation or precipitately. 370

EPISTLE CCIII.—To Bishop Atto and the clergy of Troyes.—He admonishes them to recall Ansel, a cleric of Troyes, from arms and marriage. 371

EPISTLE CCIV.—To the Abbot of Saint-Alban.—He reveals his affection toward him; but their mutual sight, if the present life does not permit it, is reserved for the life to come. 372

EPISTLE CCV.—To the Bishop of Rochester.—He says that the bishop’s letter rebukes him too harshly, though with respect to a fault. 372

EPISTLE CCVI.—To the Queen of Jerusalem.—He commends a certain kinsman to her and briefly admonishes the queen to live in such a way that she may reign forever. 373

EPISTLE CCVII.—To Roger, King of Sicily.—He exhorts him to show himself kind and beneficent toward poor religious persons. 374

EPISTLE CCVIII.—To the same.—Requested by the king, he sends some of his own brethren and asks that the king receive and cherish them kindly as his very own. 375

EPISTLE CCIX.—To the same.—He praises the king’s generosity in receiving the religious persons sent by him. 375

EPISTLE CCX.—To Pope Innocent.—He commends the prelates of Rheims to the Pontiff. 376

EPISTLE CCXI.—To the same.—He commends the cause of the Archbishop of Canterbury and likewise of the Bishop of London. 376

EPISTLE CCXII.—To the same.—He urgently pleads before the Pontiff the cause of the Bishop of Salamanca, commending his notable humility. 377

EPISTLE CCXIII.—To the same.—He remonstrates with the Pontiff because the reconciliation of Peter of Pisa, effected through his own work and the Pope’s authority, is being frustrated. 378

EPISTLE CCXIV.—To the same.—He commends the Bishop of Cambrai and Abbot Godescalc. 378

EPISTLE CCXV.—To the same.—For the bishop and dean of Auxerre. 379

EPISTLE CCXVI.—To the same.—Count Ralph, who, having repudiated his wife, had taken another, finds patrons in
complains that he finds [something] at court. 379

EPISTLE CCXVII.—To the Same.—He complains that Theobald is being oppressed because of his devotion to justice and fidelity to the Apostolic See; but asks that, having been forced into unjust measures, he may be extricated with the Pope’s assistance. 380

EPISTLE CCXVIII.—To the Same: Apologetic and Final.—Observing that he has fallen from his customary favour with Innocent, he modestly removes the causes of offence arising from the affair of the will of Cardinal Ivo, his kinsman. 381

EPISTLE CCXIX.—To the Three Bishops of the Curia, Alberic of Ostia, Stephen of Palestrina, Igmar of Tusculum, and Gerard the Chancellor.—Concerning the interdict imposed upon the King’s land because of the Archbishop of Bourges. 382

EPISTLE CCXX.—To Louis, King of the French.—He rejects the King’s unjust demand in the case of Ralph, warning him not to oppress the innocent and provoke against himself the supreme King. 385

EPISTLE CCXXI.—To the Same.—On the foregoing subject.—He severely rebukes King Louis because, adhering to evil counsels, he rejects counsels of peace. Hitherto, indeed, he has been zealous for the royal name; henceforth he will be the champion of truth alone, and also a witness against the King’s evil deeds. 386

EPISTLE CCXXII.—To Joscelin, Bishop of Soissons, and Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—He complains to them, as the King’s counsellors, of his unjust schemes against Theobald, contrary to the agreement and peace that had been concluded. 387

EPISTLE CCXXIII.—To Joscelin, Bishop of Soissons.—He satisfies the bishop, whose letter bore this salutation: “Salvation in the Lord, and not the spirit of blasphemy.” Nevertheless, he demands in him a greater zeal for avenging the wrongs done to Christ and the Church. 390

EPISTLE CCXXIV.—To Stephen, Bishop of Palestrina.—He sets forth the misdeeds of King Louis and his injuries against the Church, bishops, and others. 391

EPISTLE CCXXV.—To the Lord Bishop of Soissons.—He exhorts him to pursue peace. 394

EPISTLE CCXXVI.—To Louis, King of the French.—Bernard and Hugh complain of the King’s persistence in his evil undertakings; they grieve that their labours to bring about peace are fruitless, not without the ruin of his kingdom. 394

EPISTLE CCXXVII.—To the Bishop of Soissons.—He most earnestly and urgently implores the bishop’s assistance. 396

EPISTLE CCXXVIII.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny, who complained that Bernard had not replied to him. 396

EPISTLE CCXXIX.—Peter the Venerable to Bernard the Abbot.—He answers Bernard’s letter with the greatest kindness, and at the same time explains the causes of the disagreements between the Cluniacs and Cistercians. 398

EPISTLE CCXXX.—To the Three Bishops of Ostia, Tusculum, and Palestrina.—He reminds them of their duty: to keep wolves away from Christ’s flock in the bishopric of Metz. 417

EPISTLE CCXXXI.—To the Same, on Behalf of the Abbot of Lagny.—He affirms and defends the abbot’s innocence, and refutes the charges brought against him. Finally, he asks them for zeal in the discipline of religious life. [Col. 1175] 417

EPISTLE CCXXXII.—To the Same.—Against the Abbot of Saint-Theofred. 419

EPISTLE CCXXIII.—To Abbot John of Buzay, who had left his abbey and gone into solitude.—He gently recalls him from the solitude to which he had withdrawn after abandoning the governance of his monastery. 420

EPISTLE CCXXXIV.—To Herbert, Abbot of Saint Stephen at Dijon.—He asks that John be forgiven the fault of a rash letter. 421

EPISTLE CCXXXV.—To Pope Celestine, concerning the Intruder at York.—He invokes the authority of the Apostolic See against the notorious and simoniacal usurper of the Church of York. 422

EPISTLE CCXXXVI.—To the Whole Roman Curia.—On the foregoing subject. 424

EPISTLE CCXXXVII.—To the Whole Roman Curia, when they elected the Abbot of Saint Anastasius Pope Eugenius.—He wonders that Bernard, Abbot of Saint Anastasius, should be torn from leisure and solitude and carried off to the care of the whole Church; and he fears that a man accustomed to quiet and less practised in affairs will not be equal to so great a burden. Therefore he asks that he be supported by the faithful assistance of the cardinals. 425

EPISTLE CCXXXVIII.—To Pope Eugenius, the First.—Bernard congratulates and commiserates Eugenius, newly raised to the pontificate. He encourages him courageously to discharge the apostolic office, so that he may answer the expectations which many have conceived of him. 427

EPISTLE CCXXXIX.—To the Same.—He presses the Pope for the deposition of William of York, a power which belongs to the Pope alone. 431

EPISTLE CCXL.—To the Same, concerning the Intruder at York.—He praises Eugenius’s zeal. He now wishes it shown in deposing the man of York, who fraudulently occupies that see. 432

EPISTLE CCXLI.—To Count Alfonso of Saint-Gilles, concerning the Heretic Henry.—He describes Henry, successor of the heretic Peter of Bruys, his impious doctrines, and his impure deeds; he reproaches the Count for allowing such a man to rage with impunity in his jurisdiction. 434

EPISTLE CCXLII.—To the People of Toulouse after His Return.—Heretics must be carefully avoided—indeed, expelled. Hospitality must be practised. Nor should all and sundry preachers be admitted. 436

EPISTLE CCXLIII.—To the Romans, when They Departed from Pope Eugenius.—The Romans, with the heretic Arnold inflaming the faction, endeavoured to restore the form of the ancient Republic and its liberty, leaving the Pope only the care of sacred matters. Accordingly, they claimed for themselves the revenues of the Popes, ordering the Pope to be content, as in ancient custom, to live solely on tithes and offerings. From this arose the rebellion, more violently stirred up against Eugenius. On this occasion Bernard sharply, but justly, rebukes the Romans for being so unjust toward the Pope: an injury to him redounds upon the saints and all Catholics, and will not escape God’s vengeance unless they promptly repent. 437

EPISTLE CCXLIV.—To Conrad, King of the Romans.—He exhorts the King to defend pontifical authority against the rebellious Romans. 440

EPISTLE CCXLV.—To the Pope on Behalf of the Bishop of Orléans.—He rejoices in the Pope’s zeal in the case of the Bishop of Orléans, etc. 442

EPISTLE CCXLVI.—To the Same on Behalf of the Same, when the Aforesaid Bishop of Orléans Had Been Deposed.—He commends to the Pope the Bishop of Orléans, who voluntarily renounced his bishopric, asking him to ensure that his honour is protected; this, he says, befits the bishop’s humility and the Pope’s clemency. 443

EPISTLE CCXLVII.—To the Same on Behalf of the Archbishop of Reims.—He disapproves of the hasty and overly severe sentence against Samson, Archbishop of Reims, by which the use of the pallium was withdrawn. 445

EPISTLE CCXLVIII.—To the Same.—He warns the Pope not to give a ready hearing to the Bishop of Séez, however suppliant, as he seeks to return to his bishopric. 447

EPISTLE CCXLIX.—To the Same.—He commends as worthy the Prior of La Chaise-Dieu, elected Bishop of Valence. 449

EPISTLE CCL.—To Bernard, Prior of Portes.—The religious ought not to have taken so badly the rejection of Brother Natalis, elected bishop. It was not brought about through Bernard’s agency. Perhaps the Pope feared that faults of youthful age, only now exposed, might be open to slander. 449

EPISTLE CCLI.—To Pope Eugenius.—He wishes the monks of Balmes, deservedly punished, to be restored to favour and reconciled with the people of Autun. 451

EPISTLE CCLII.—To the Same, concerning York.—He demands that the sentence long ago pronounced by Innocent against the man of York be finally carried into execution, lest his evil deeds be imputed to a Pope who overlooks them. 452

[Col. 1176]

EPISTLE CCLIII.—To the Abbot of Prémontré.—He replies calmly to the rather harsh letters of the Premonstratensians, recounting his benefits toward them. He also refutes each item of their complaints, declaring that he will remain their steadfast friend. 453

EPISTLE CCLIV.—To Guarin, Abbot of Aulps.—He praises in the aged abbot his endeavour to reform the Order. The shortness of time is no obstacle to the pursuit of perfection. In the spiritual life one must always advance and never stand still. 459

EPISTLE CCLV.—To Louis, King of the French.—He warns the King not to obstruct the council, so necessary at this time to Church and kingdom and destined to redound to the King’s own honour. 462

EPISTLE CCLVI.—To Pope Eugenius.—He urges Eugenius to bring aid to the Eastern Church; he must not lose heart at the blow received in the loss of the city of Edessa. He is astonished, however, that he himself has been chosen at Chartres as leader of the expedition. 463

EPISTLE CCLVII.—To the Same, on Behalf of Brother Philip. 465

EPISTLE CCLVIII.—To the Same, on Behalf of Brother Rualen.—He asks that Rualen, appointed at the Pope’s command abbot of Saint Anastasius, but exceedingly unwilling and resistant, be sent back to him. 466

EPISTLE CCLIX.—To the Same.—On the foregoing subject.—He wills and does not will the same things as the Pope; therefore he gladly orders his Rualen to present himself at the abbey of Saint Anastasius when the Pope commands. 467

EPISTLE CCLX.—To Rualen, Abbot.—He sympathizes with Rualen in the office of superior assigned to him, which he advises him finally to accept. 467

EPISTLE CCLXI.—To Pope Eugenius.—He asks for absolution for the Abbot of Saint-Urban, who had incurred censures for admitting a Knight Templar. 468

EPISTLE CCLXII.—To the Same, on Behalf of the Monks of Mouzon. 468

EPISTLE CCLXIII.—To the Bishop of Soissons, on Behalf of the Abbot of Caziac. 469

EPISTLE CCLXIV.—Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to Bernard the Abbot.—He declares his longing for Bernard and earnestly asks that Nicholas, dear to him, be sent as a consolation for Bernard’s absence. 469

EPISTLE CCLXV.—Bernard the Abbot’s Reply to the Same.—He declines praise as unworthy of it; nevertheless, in return he bestows praises upon his own eulogist. 470

EPISTLE CCLXVI.—To Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—He encourages him to meet death without fear. He declares his wish to see him before his death. 470

EPISTLE CCLXVII.—To the Abbot of Cluny. 472

EPISTLE CCLXVIII.—To Pope Eugenius.—He warns that the promotion of a certain unworthy person has been clandestinely procured and that the decision must therefore be revoked. 472

EPISTLE CCLXIX.—To the Same.—He deprives of force and authority letters extorted from him by deceit. 473

EPISTLE CCLXX.—To the Same.—He writes in the case of a Carthusian prior against certain transgressors. He announces the death of the Abbot of Cîteaux and commends his successor. 473

EPISTLE CCLXXI.—To Count Theobald of Champagne.—He warns that a son, on account of his very young age, ought not to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignities. 475

EPISTLE CCLXXII.—To the Bishop of Laon.—He reminds him of godly generosity. 476

Pope Eugenius’s Letter to the Chapter of Cîteaux, Prefixed to Epistle CCLXXIII.—He states that he wishes to be present at the Chapter of Cîteaux if papal business permits. He urges the promotion in the Chapter of zeal and concern for discipline and religious perfection. 476

EPISTLE CCLXXIII.—To Pope Eugenius.—He rejoices in the Pope’s letter to the Chapter, full of zeal and affection. He exhorts him to continue with that concern to cherish all, but especially the religious of Bernard’s own Order. He complains that the Abbot of Trois-Fontaines has been removed from his office. 478

EPISTLE CCLXXIV.—To Hugh, Abbot of Trois-Fontaines, when He Was at Rome.—He regrets having commended the nephew of the Bishop of Auxerre, disapproving of the provostship conferred on him. 480

EPISTLE CCLXXV.—To Pope Eugenius, concerning the Election at Auxerre.—He informs the Pope of the state of the election at Auxerre and of the fraud committed in it. 480

EPISTLE CCLXXVI.—To the Same, after the Death of the Bishop of Auxerre.—He warns the Pope concerning the irreligious will of the Bishop of Auxerre, made not without Stephen the deacon’s fraud; it ought to be annulled because of the scandal. 481

EPISTLE CCLXXVII.—To the Same, on Behalf of the Abbot of Cluny.—He asks that the Abbot of Cluny be received kindly and treated honourably. [Col. 1177] 482

EPISTLE CCLXXVIII.—To the Same, on Behalf of the Bishop of Beauvais. 484

EPISTLE CCLXXIX.—To Count Henry.—He compels the Count, because of an injury inflicted by his subjects, to make full restitution. 484

EPISTLE CCLXXX.—To Pope Eugenius concerning the Affair of Auxerre.—He complains that the apostolic judgment in the case of the election at Auxerre, which he had announced at the Pope’s command, is being disregarded. 485

EPISTLE CCLXXXI.—To Abbot Bruno of Clairvaux.—He rebukes Bruno for writing rashly and imprudently. 487

EPISTLE CCLXXXII.—To Louis the Younger, King of the French, concerning the Election at Auxerre.—He exhorts the King not to oppose the bishop elected at Auxerre. 488

EPISTLE CCLXXXIII.—To Pope Eugenius, on Behalf of the Brethren of Miroir.—Work on a certain settlement of a lawsuit has been in vain; apostolic authority is therefore needed. 489

EPISTLE CCLXXXIV.—To Pope Eugenius, on Behalf of the Archbishop of Reims and Other Persons. 490

EPISTLE CCLXXXV.—To the Same, on Behalf of Odo, Abbot of Saint-Denis.—He commends the Abbot of Saint-Denis and defends him against the suspect accusations of others, born of envy and ambition. 491

EPISTLE CCLXXXVI.—To the Same, on Behalf of the Same. 492

EPISTLE CCLXXXVII.—To His Uncle Andrew, a Knight Templar.—He laments the unhappy outcome of the holy expedition and desires his uncle’s arrival. 493

EPISTLE CCLXXXIX.—To the Queen of Jerusalem.—He instructs her how to conduct herself so as to fulfil the role of a worthy widow before God and of a queen before men. 494

EPISTLE CCXC.—To the Lord of Ostia, concerning Cardinal Jordan.—He describes the apostolic legate and the shameful traces he has left everywhere. 496

EPISTLE CCXCI.—To Pope Eugenius, on Behalf of the Church of Saint-Oyend in the Jura. 496

EPISTLE CCXCII.—To a Certain Layman.—He reproves him for having tried to draw away Peter, Bernard’s kinsman, from his purpose of religious life. 497

EPISTLE CCXCIII.—To Peter, Abbot of La Celle, on Behalf of a Monk of Caziac Who Had Transferred to Clairvaux. 498

EPISTLE CCXCIV.—To Pope Eugenius, on Behalf of the Bishop of Le Mans.—He commends the Bishop of Le Mans and others to the Pope. 499

EPISTLE CCXCV.—To Cardinal Henry, on Behalf of the Same Bishop. 499

EPISTLE CCXCVI.—To the Lord of Ostia, on Behalf of the Same. 500

EPISTLE CCXCVII.—To the Abbot of Arras.—He asks that a repentant apostate monk be received. 500

EPISTLE CCXCVIII.—To Pope Eugenius.—He exposes the frauds and impostures of Nicholas the notary. 500

EPISTLE CCXCIX.—To the Count of Angoulême, on Behalf of the Brethren of Buxia.—He complains of a heavy exaction imposed upon his brethren by the Count. 501

EPISTLE CCC.—To the Countess of Blois.—He consoles the Countess, excusing her son’s faults on account of his age and holding out hope of better conduct; therefore he advises that the boy be treated gently and mildly rather than harshly. 502

EPISTLE CCCI.—To Sancha, Sister of the Emperor of Spain.—He wishes her intervention to settle a dispute that arose between his own brethren and certain other religious over the reception of a monastery. 503

EPISTLE CCCII.—To the Apostolic Legates, on Behalf of the Archbishop of Mainz.—He commends the cause of the archbishop, who is harassed by his adversaries. 504

EPISTLE CCCIII.—To Louis the Younger, King of the French.—What the King should do in the case of a certain adulterer and excommunicate from Brittany. 505

EPISTLE CCCIV.—To the Same.—He rejoices that the King is concerned for his health; he commends Robert, the King’s brother. 506

EPISTLE CCCV.—To Pope Eugenius.—The Bishop of Beauvais has been detained from the journey to Rome for just causes. Bernard therefore entrusts his entire cause to the Pope’s judgment. 506

EPISTLE CCCVI.—To the Lord of Ostia, concerning the Election of Abbot Turold of Trois-Fontaines.—He clears himself of the slander of Hugh, Bishop of Ostia, who took ill the promotion of Turold to the abbacy of Trois-Fontaines; for he himself had nominated another, namely Nicholas. He excuses Robert’s election as abbot of a new monastery. 507

EPISTLE CCCVII.—To the Same.—He defends the Bishop of Beauvais against malicious rumours. He reports that his health is extremely afflicted, and what has happened to the Archbishop of Lyons. [Col. 1178] 510

EPISTLE CCCVIII.—To Alfonso, King of Portugal.—He replies that he has laboured at the King’s request, and foretells that the King’s brother will shortly pass from earthly to heavenly warfare. 512

EPISTLE CCCIX.—To Pope Eugenius.—He praises Abbot Suger and commends Suger’s envoys to the Pope. 513

EPISTLE CCCX.—To Arnold, Abbot of Bonneval at Chartres.—Bernard, near death, wrote this last letter to his friend. 513

Notice concerning the following letters. 513

EPISTLE CCCXI.—To Haimeric, Chancellor.—He sharply rebukes certain rivals who oppose the pious endeavours of others; he urges Haimeric, when opportunity is offered, to diligent care for the common good. 513

EPISTLE CCCXII.—To Raynald, Archbishop of Reims.—He gives thanks for the letters sent to him. 517

EPISTLE CCCXIII.—To Geoffrey, Abbot of Saint Mary’s, York.—Religious persons wishing to pass from a less strict to a stricter way of life should not be hindered; and those who, after transferring, fall back into their former life are to be regarded as apostates. 518

EPISTLE CCCXIV.—To Pope Innocent.—After the Milanese had been reconciled to the Church, Bernard went at Innocent’s command to reconcile the Lombard cities among themselves, proceeding to Pavia and Cremona. But accomplishing nothing among the Cremonese, he informs the Pope of their stubbornness and urges him to suspend for a little while the harsher sentence which he was preparing against the Archbishop of Milan. 520

EPISTLE CCCXV.—To Matilda, Queen of the English.—He asks her to grant a petition previously submitted on behalf of the monks of La Chapelle. 522

EPISTLE CCCXVI.—To Henry, Archbishop of Sens, and Haimeric, Chancellor.—He exhorts them not to oppose a certain nobleman who possesses ecclesiastical property but now wishes to yield it to certain religious. 522

EPISTLE CCCXVII.—To His Prior Godfrey.—The schism having been extinguished and peace arranged, he promises that he will return to his own people as soon as possible. 523

EPISTLE CCCXVIII.—To Pope Innocent.—He reports the dangers facing the Church of Reims and desires prompt assistance from the Pope. 523

EPISTLE CCCXIX.—To Thurstan, Archbishop of York.—He exhorts him not to abandon pastoral care; yet, if there is a just cause or the Pope’s consent, he should seek a place more observant of religious discipline. 524

EPISTLE CCCXX.—To Alexander, Prior of Fountains, and the Brethren of That Place.—He exhorts them unanimously to elect a new abbot. 525

EPISTLE CCCXXI.—To Henry of Murdach, First Abbot of Vauclair, Afterwards of Fountains, and Finally Archbishop of York.—He commands him not to refuse his election as abbot of Fountains. 526

EPISTLE CCCXXII.—To Hugh, a Novice, Later Abbot of Bonneval.—He praises his purpose of religious life, forewarns him against temptations, and urges him to steadfastness and perseverance. 527

EPISTLE CCCXXIII.—To Pope Innocent.—On behalf of the Archbishop of Trier against the Abbot of Saint-Maximin. 528

EPISTLE CCCXXIV.—To Robert, Abbot of the Dunes.—He proposes as comfort for their mutual absence the union of their minds—and indeed, someday, of their bodies. 530

EPISTLE CCCXXV.—To the Same, concerning the Novice Iderius.—Asked what should be done concerning a troublesome novice, he gives his advice. 530

EPISTLE CCCXXVI.—William the Abbot to Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, and Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.—That they should defend the cause of God and the Church against the errors of Peter Abelard, several articles of which he sets forth. 531

EPISTLE CCCXXVII.—Bernard’s Reply to Abbot William.—He praises the tract composed against Peter Abelard and promises a mutual conference after Easter. 533

EPISTLE CCCXXVIII.—To the Roman Pontiff.—Against the Bishop-Elect of Rodez. 533

EPISTLE CCCXXIX.—To the Bishop of Limoges.—Against the Same Bishop-Elect of Rodez. 534

EPISTLE CCCXXX.—To Pope Innocent.—Against Peter Abelard. 535

EPISTLE CCCXXXI.—To Stephen, Cardinal and Bishop of Palestrina.—On the same subject. 536

EPISTLE CCCXXXII.—To Cardinal G.—Likewise against Peter Abelard. 537

EPISTLE CCCXXXIII.—To Cardinal G.—Likewise on the same subject. [Col. 1179] 538

EPISTLE CCCXXXIV.—To Guido of Pisa.—Against the same Abelard. 538

EPISTLE CCCXXXV.—To a Certain Cardinal-Priest.—Likewise against Peter Abelard. 539

EPISTLE CCCXXXVI.—To a Certain Abbot.—On the same subject. 539

EPISTLE CCCXXXVII.—To Pope Innocent, in the Name of the Bishops of France.—The bishops of Gaul set before the Pope what was done in the case of Peter Abelard, who challenged Bernard to a disputation at the synod but refused to answer the articles of heresy laid against him and appealed to the Apostolic See. 540

EPISTLE CCCXXXVIII.—To Haimeric, Cardinal and Chancellor.—Peter Abelard, having been convicted of heresy, ought not to find refuge with the cardinals and the Roman curia. 542

EPISTLE CCCXXXIX.—To Pope Innocent.—He affirms the innocence of Alvisus, Bishop of Arras, against his slanderers. 544

EPISTLE CCCXL.—To Pope Innocent.—On behalf of the Bishop of Angers. 544

EPISTLE CCCXLI.—To Malachy, Archbishop of Ireland.—He gratefully receives the brethren, letters, and staff sent by Malachy. He orders that a suitable place be prepared for the religious and commends himself to Malachy’s prayers. 545

EPISTLE CCCXLII.—To Joscelin, Bishop of Soissons.—He asks that the Archbishop of Bordeaux be cleared before the King. 546

EPISTLE CCCXLIII.—Bernard, Abbot in Italy, to Innocent.—He complains that not everything in the monastery of the Saviour has occurred according to the Pope’s promises. 547

EPISTLE CCCXLIV.—The Same Bernard to Saint Bernard.—He complains of the office imposed upon him. 548

EPISTLE CCCXLV.—To the Brethren of Saint Anastasius.—He commends their zeal and observance in religious discipline. Yet he disapproves of excessive concern to preserve health by medicines. 549

EPISTLE CCCXLVI.—To Pope Innocent.—He exhorts the Pope not to favour the cause of the Archbishop of York, since it is unjust. 551

EPISTLE CCCXLVII.—To Pope Innocent.—He commends envoys journeying to Rome in the affair of the archbishopric of York. 552

EPISTLE CCCXLVIII.—To Innocent.—On behalf of Arnulf, Bishop-Elect of Lisieux. 552

EPISTLE CCCXLIX.—To the Same.—He commends a friend to the Pope. 553

EPISTLE CCCL.—To the Same.—He asks that his kinsman be fortified with the Pope’s blessing. 554

EPISTLE CCCLI.—To Innocent.—He commends certain poor persons. 554

EPISTLE CCCLII.—Privilege Granted to Saint Bernard by Pope Innocent II.—Because of Bernard’s outstanding services to the Apostolic See, Innocent grants very extensive privileges to Bernard and the Cistercian Order. 554

EPISTLE CCCLIII.—To William, Abbot of Rievaulx.—He advises him to bear with equanimity the unlawful ordination of the Archbishop of York. 556

EPISTLE CCCLIV.—To Melisende, Queen of Jerusalem, Daughter of King Baldwin and Wife of Fulk.—How she ought to conduct herself after the death of her husband Fulk. 556

EPISTLE CCCLV.—To the Same Queen of Jerusalem.—He commends Premonstratensians making pilgrimage to Jerusalem. 557

EPISTLE CCCLVI.—To Malachy, Archbishop of Ireland.—He sends back religious men, but, as he attributes to business, not yet sufficiently cultivated and instructed. 558

EPISTLE CCCLVII.—To the Same.—He asks for affection from him that continues—and indeed increases—and wishes it shown in the care and support of the brethren whom he has sent. 558

EPISTLE CCCLVIII.—To the Pope, Namely Celestine.—He asks the Pope’s aid and authority to secure peace for Count Theobald of Champagne. 560

EPISTLE CCCLIX.—The Brethren of Clairvaux to the Same Celestine.—They wish to prevent the Abbot of Morimond from making a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. 560

EPISTLE CCCLX.—To William, Abbot of Rievaulx.—Again he exhorts William to patience and equanimity. 561

EPISTLE CCCLXI.—To Theobald, Archbishop, on Behalf of John of Salisbury.—Trusting in Theobald’s friendship, he commends John to him. 562

EPISTLE CCCLXII.—To Robert Pullen, Cardinal and Chancellor.—He exhorts him, in the affairs of the Church, to give Eugenius, newly elected Pope, vigorous assistance in the discharge of his office. [Col. 1180] 565

EPISTLE CCCLXIII.—To the Clergy and People of Eastern France.—He exhorts them to take up arms against the unbelievers in defence of the Eastern Church. Moreover, against a certain turbulent preacher, he teaches that Jews are not to be persecuted, much less killed. 564

EPISTLE CCCLXIV.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.—He invites Peter to the assembly at Chartres, where aid to be given to the Eastern Church is to be discussed. 568

EPISTLE CCCLXV.—To Henry, Archbishop of Mainz.—He rebukes the monk Ralph, who was arming the faithful to kill Jews. 570

EPISTLE CCCLXVI.—To Hildegard, Abbess.—Modestly rejecting her praises, he urges her to acknowledge God’s grace in herself and asks her prayers for himself and his brethren. 572

EPISTLE CCCLXVII.—To Chancellor G.—He commends the Bishop of Metz. 572

EPISTLE CCCLXVIII.—To Cardinal-Deacon G.—He gratefully embraces the affection expressed by his letters and gifts, and calls him away from love of earthly possessions and riches. 573

EPISTLE CCCLXIX.—To Suger, Abbot.—He congratulates Suger on the happily instituted reform of the church of Saint Geneviève and urges him to persist in what he has well begun. 574

EPISTLE CCCLXX.—To the Same.—He commends to him the church of Mont. 575

EPISTLE CCCLXXI.—To the Same.—He dissuades him from a marriage between the son of the Count of Anjou and the daughter of the King of France because of the impediment of consanguinity. 575

EPISTLE CCCLXXII.—To P., Bishop of Palencia in Spain.—He praises him for humility, but above all for devotion to reading. 576

EPISTLE CCCLXXIII.—Abbot Sp. to Saint Bernard.—He laments the office imposed upon him. 578

EPISTLE CCCLXXIV.—To the Brethren in Ireland, on the Passing of Blessed Bishop Malachy.—The death of saints should be accompanied with joy rather than mourning. By a singular favour of God, Clairvaux too has been honoured by the death and burial of so great a man. 578

EPISTLE CCCLXXV.—To Ida, Countess of Nevers.—He complains that the monks of Vézelay are being harassed by the countess’s retainers. 580

EPISTLE CCCLXXVI.—To Suger, Abbot.—He exhorts and asks him to oppose certain princes’ duels. 581

EPISTLE CCCLXXVII.—To the Same.—He celebrates Suger’s zeal and concern for the common good in convening an assembly of the realm for its preservation, and exhorts him courageously to conduct the public cause. 581

EPISTLE CCCLXXVIII.—To the Same.—He asks relief in provisions for the religious of Bourges. 583

EPISTLE CCCLXXIX.—To the Same.—He asks that aid be given to a certain needy abbot. 583

EPISTLE CCCLXXX.—To the Same.—Concerning the perilous condition of the Eastern Church. 583

EPISTLE CCCLXXXI.—To the Same.—He says that he thinks rightly of Suger, yet grieves that the evils of the realm are publicly attributed to him. He exhorts him to beware lest association with those through whom these things are done should bring him into disrepute. 584

EPISTLE CCCLXXXII.—To Leonius, Abbot of Saint-Bertin.—He gratefully acknowledges his benefits toward Bernard and his brethren. Thomas of Saint-Omer, wishing to transfer to Clairvaux, ought not to be prevented. 585

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIII.—To the Same Abbot of Saint-Bertin.—He asks him to continue the humane services hitherto shown to his brethren. 586

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIV.—To the Monks of the Church of Saint-Bertin.—He gives thanks for the beneficence hitherto bestowed upon his brethren, promising them abundant recompense from God. 587

EPISTLE CCCLXXXV.—To the Same.—He congratulates them on their better observance and urges them to seek religious perfection and continual progress. 587

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVI.—John of La Maison-Dieu to Bernard the Abbot.—He consoles Bernard over the unhappy outcome of the expedition to the Holy Land. 590

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVII.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.—After declaring his sincere affection and love for Peter, he asks to be excused if he wrote anything too harshly in certain letters. 591

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVIII.—Peter the Venerable to Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.—He rejects titles and encomia, vividly shows how highly he values Bernard and his friendship, and willingly accepts Bernard’s satisfaction concerning the offence of the letters. 592

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIX.—To Peter, Abbot of Cluny.—Peter’s letters were most pleasant to him, but the weight of occupations prevented a fuller reply. 595

[Col. 1181]

EPISTLE CCCXC.—To Eskil, Archbishop of Lund, Legate of the Apostolic See in Denmark and Sweden.—He gratefully and humbly acknowledges Eskil’s love and reciprocally shows his own. 596

EPISTLE CCCXCI.—To the Abbess of Faverney.—He warns her to restore not only buildings but also morals, and to attend diligently to the hospice. 597

EPISTLE CCCXCII.—To Ralph, Patriarch of Antioch.—He especially inculcates humility in him. 599

EPISTLE CCCXCIII.—To W., Patriarch of Jerusalem.—He exhorts him to humility. 600

EPISTLE CCCXCIV.—To the Archbishop of Lyons.—On behalf of the Abbot of Athanac near Lyons. 602

EPISTLE CCCXCV.—To Alvisus, Bishop of Arras.—He says that the bishop’s request is not sufficiently equitable: Thomas of Saint-Omer, who had devoted himself to the men of Clairvaux, should not be handed over to the monks of Saint-Bertin, who wished to claim him for themselves by reason of his parents’ vow. 604

EPISTLE CCCXCVI.—To Ricuin, Bishop of Toul.—He excuses himself for having received William, Ricuin’s professed monk, without knowing this. 605

EPISTLE CCCXCVII.—To Odo, Abbot of Marmoutier near Tours.—Monks disputing with clerics over certain revenues ought to submit to the judgment of arbitrators. 606

EPISTLE CCCXCVIII.—To Guy, Abbot, and the Brethren of Arras.—Asked by the men of Arras to compose an Office for Saint Victor, their patron, he pleads his own inadequacy and the difficulty of the work. He explains what kind of compositions ought to be used publicly in divine worship, and sets forth the rules of ecclesiastical chant. 609

EPISTLE CCCXCIX.—To Lelbert, Abbot of Saint-Michael.—Having dissuaded a certain monk from an unsound plan of pilgrimage, he sends him back to his monastery. 612

EPISTLE CD.—To the Abbot of Laëties.—He wishes Brother Robert to be received and treated more kindly, and that the abbot’s decision be reported to him. 613

EPISTLE CDI.—To Baldwin, Abbot of Châtillon.—He removes his fear, arising from an imprudent remark by a certain person. 613

EPISTLE CDII.—To Baldwin, Bishop of Noyon.—He wittily commends a boy to him. 614

EPISTLE CDIII.—To Archdeacon Henry.—Whether baptism administered in this verbal form is valid: “I baptize you in the name of God, and of the holy and true cross.” 614

EPISTLE CDIV.—To Albert, an Anchorite.—He advises him to eat once daily and to admit no women whatsoever. 615

EPISTLE CDV.—To Abbot G.—A certain brother has sufficient strength to live according to the community’s rule. 616

EPISTLE CDVI.—To the Abbot of Saint Nicholas. 616

EPISTLE CDVII.—To Odo, Abbot of Belle-Lieu.—He warns that a deposit must be returned to a poor man without delay. 616

EPISTLE CDVIII.—To W., Abbot of Troyes.—He commends to the Abbot of Troyes a delicate cleric who is renouncing the world, fearing that he may be unequal to the strictness of the men of Clairvaux. 617

EPISTLE CDIX.—To Rorgon of Abbatis-Villa.—He warns that bodily presence ought not to be valued highly; he asks that some uncultivated land be assigned to religious persons. 618

EPISTLE CDX.—To Gilduin, Abbot of Saint-Victor.—He commends P. Lombard. 618

EPISTLE CDXI.—To Thomas, Provost of Beverley.—A most sweet and honeyed letter, inviting Thomas to religious life despite any sins whatever. Nothing in this world can be preferred to a good conscience. 619

EPISTLE CDXII.—To T., a Young Man Who Had Vowed Monastic Life. 620

EPISTLE CDXIII.—To Abbot Rainald.—He asks that a novice, confirmed in his resolve, be kindly received. 621

EPISTLE CDXIV.—To Alard, a Monk.—On the foregoing subject. He reproves him because, after expelling the aforesaid novice, he stubbornly opposes him as he now seeks return and amendment. 622

EPISTLE CDXV.—To a Certain Violator of His Compact.—He exhorts him, having thrown off the yoke of carnal pleasure, to perform the religious vow he had promised. 623

EPISTLE CDXVI.—To an Unknown Person.—He maintains that Count Theobald’s alms were not distributed by him. 623

EPISTLE CDXVII.—To the Abbot of Tronc-Berenger.—He asks that Brother Dodo be humanely received by him. 624

EPISTLE CDXVIII.—To Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen.—He asks the bishop to confirm a donation made to Savigny. 625

EPISTLE CDXIX.—To Peter, Abbot of La Celle.—He relinquishes an oven to the men of La Celle. 626

[Col. 1182]

EPISTLE CDXX.—To Nicholas, Bishop of Cambrai. (Fragment.) 626

NOTICE concerning the following thirty-six letters. 626

EPISTLE CDXXI.—To a Husband and His Wife.—He exhorts them to almsgiving and pious works. 629

EPISTLE CDXXII.—To a Certain Abbot.—He excuses the brevity of his letter and sends back to him a certain young man whom he could by no means admit among his own brethren. 629

EPISTLE CDXXIII.—To a Certain Bishop.—He commends to him the cause of the monastery of Saint-Martin. 630

EPISTLE CDXXIV.—To a Certain Friend.—He excuses himself because he cannot go with him to the man in bonds. 630

EPISTLE CDXXV.—To a Certain Judge.—He commends to him the cause of Fontenay Abbey. 631

EPISTLE CDXXVI.—To a Certain Friend.—He commends to him the bearer of the present letter. 631

EPISTLE CDXXVII.—To the Bishop of Troyes.—He disapproves of his having given an archdeaconry to a little boy. 631

EPISTLE CDXXVIII.—To a Certain Abbot.—He praises him and exhorts him to reform his monastery, especially its hospice. 632

EPISTLE CDXXIX.—To a Certain Friend.—He gives thanks to God for matters prosperously accomplished. 632

EPISTLE CDXXX.—To a Certain Friend.—Ecclesiastical benefices must be received not from a lay hand but from a bishop. 632

EPISTLE CDXXXI.—To Pope Innocent II.—Delegated by the Supreme Pontiff as judge to settle the dispute between two claimants to the archbishopric of Tours, he declares Philip’s election null. 633

EPISTLE CDXXXII.—To the Pope.—On behalf of the Bishop of Troyes.

635 EPISTLE CDXXXIII.—To the same person.—On behalf of the bishop of Troyes.

635 EPISTLE CDXXXIV.—To the same person.—On the same subject.

635 EPISTLE CDXXXV.—To the same person.—Commends to him the bearer of the letter.

636 EPISTLE CDXXXVI.—To the same person.—Commends to him a certain friend.

636 EPISTLE CDXXXVII.—To the same person.—On behalf of the bishop of Troyes.

636 EPISTLE CDXXXVIII.—To the same person.—On behalf of the bishop of Troyes.

636 EPISTLE CDXXXIX.—To the same person.—On behalf of the bishop of Troyes.

636 EPISTLE CDXL.—To an unnamed person.—Urges him, preferring care for his soul to concern for his body, to renounce the world.

637 EPISTLE CDXLI.—To a certain Prior.—Sends him a young man who was seeking admission to the Order.

638 EPISTLE CDXLII.—To a certain abbot of the Order of Saint Benedict.—Sends him two young men not strong enough for the Cistercian Order, but perhaps not useless to him.

638 EPISTLE CDXLIII.—To a certain friend.—Concerning a certain young man, whose depraved conduct he recounts, and who was seeking a marriage among the nobility.

638 EPISTLE CDXLIV.—To a certain abbot.—Concerning a monk who wished to transfer to another Order; he disapproves of this.

639 EPISTLE CDXLV.—To a certain abbot.—Commends to him L., a fugitive who is returning, and asks that he be received kindly.

639 EPISTLE CDXLVI.—To an unnamed person.—Writes that he has recovered from a grave illness and escaped the gates of death.

639 EPISTLE CDXLVII.—To Amadeus, abbot of Hautecombe.—Asks him to send messengers to Montpellier, which the ships of the king of Sicily were to reach, so that they may excuse him before the king for not having sent brethren to Sicily.

640 EPISTLE CDXLVIII.—To an unnamed person.—Commends to him the abbot of Farfa, cardinal of the holy Roman Church.

640 EPISTLE CDXLIX.—To the King of the Franks.—Excuses himself from accepting the dignity to which he had been elected.

641 EPISTLE CDL.—To a friend.—Writes that he is at last recovering and has been delivered from the jaws of death.

642 EPISTLE CDLI. To the brethren ***.—Urges them to give alms in a time of famine.

642 EPISTLE CDLII.—To a certain abbot.—Urges him kindly to receive a fugitive and not to relinquish the dignity of prelate.

643 EPISTLE CDLIII.—To an unnamed person.—Praises his prudence and humility.

644 EPISTLE CDLIV.—To an unnamed person.—Promises Stephen, if he perseveres, worthy fruits of repentance.

644 EPISTLE CDLV.—To the maternal aunt of the emperor of Spain.—Grants her the suffrages of the brethren, and asks that the dispute [Col. 1183] between his people and the brethren of Careda be settled through the bishops.

644 Preface to the following letter.

645 EPISTLE CDLVI.—To Raymond, lord of the Castle of Ambrus.

647 EPISTLE CDLVII.—To all the faithful.—On the expedition to the Holy Land. Appoints the feast of Saints Peter and Paul as the time for their gathering at Magdeburg.

651 EPISTLE CDLVIII.—To Wladislaus, duke, the magnates, and the people of Bohemia.—Invites all to the expedition to Jerusalem, and commends the same undertaking to the bishop of Moravia.

652 EPISTLE CDLIX.—To G. of Stopho.

652 NOTICE concerning the following letter.

653 EPISTLE CDLX.—To N.

## APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF ST BERNARD

### I. DOUBTFUL OR SPURIOUS LETTERS

**LETTER CDLXI.**—To Matthew, Bishop of Albano.—On the Gospel of Luke, chapter XVI, 1–9: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward.” 661

**LETTER CDLXII.**—To certain newly converted persons.—He exhorts them to steadfastness in their chosen religious life and not to let the sins of their former life discourage them. 662

**LETTER CDLXIII.**—To Alfonso, King of Portugal.—The king, having gained victory over the Saracens, was bound by a vow to found a monastery for Cistercians. Bernard therefore sends to Lusitania the monks requested from Clairvaux. 668

**LETTER CDLXIV.**—To John Cirita.—Having learned divinely of his zeal and desire, he sends monks from Clairvaux to establish a monastery in Lusitania. 669

**LETTER CDLXV.**—To the Abbot of Saint Benedict. 670

**LETTER CDLXVI.**—To King Louis. 671

### II. BY NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX, IN THE PERSON OF ST BERNARD

**LETTER CDLXVII.**—From Nicholas of Clairvaux to the Count and Barons of Brittany, in the person of the lord of Clairvaux, concerning the business of the Cross. 671

**LETTER CDLXVIII.**—By the same, to Manuel Comnenus, Emperor of Constantinople, in the person of the lord of Clairvaux.—That he should make the son of Count Theobald a new knight. 671

**LETTER CDLXIX.**—By the same, to the Bishop of Lucca, in the person of the lord of Clairvaux.—An exhortation to courage. 673

### III. LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO ST BERNARD AND OTHERS

**LETTER CDLXX.**—From King Alfonso to St Bernard. 675

**LETTER CDLXXI.**—From Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, to St Bernard.—He gives thanks for the consolation given him while he was at the point of death and commends himself to Bernard’s prayers. 675

**LETTER CDLXXII.**—From Everwin, Provost of Steinfeld, to St Bernard.—Concerning the heretics of his time. 676

**LETTER CDLXXIII.**—From Henry of Reims to Bernard. 680

**LETTER CDLXXIV.**—From John, Bishop of Alais, to Bernard. 680

**LETTER CDLXXV.**—From M., Bishop of Cracow, to St Bernard.—He invites him to undertake the conversion of the Ruthenians. 681

**LETTER CDLXXVI.**—From Thomas, formerly Abbot of Morigny, to St Bernard. 682

**LETTER CDLXXVII.**—From a certain matron to St Bernard. 685

**LETTER CDLXXVIII.**—From B. to St Bernard.—It concerns an undisciplined monk. 686
